## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

**Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the Apostolic Age down to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived through the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, carefully compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions completed during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indices following each individual volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject treated below; expanded by works that are doubtful or apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority and weight with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indices: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be discovered which Fathers, and in what places in their works, commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.**

**A most accurate edition, and one easily preferred to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes and its constant uniformity throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—unified, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and little works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

**FIRST SERIES**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Two Books of Questions on the Gospels by Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo

[Note: Written around the year 400 after Christ. We infer the date of these books not only from the sequence of the *Retractations*, where they occur among the smaller works published around the year 400, but also from those words of Augustine in Book 2, Question 13: “Now that the Church has been glorified and the Gentile people freed from the domination of demons, they carry out their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, those who refused to believe in Christ.” These words clearly indicate that at that time it was no longer permitted to worship idols publicly; the emperor Honorius issued laws to this effect in the year 399.]

[Note: The two books of Questions on the Gospels have been corrected against two Victorine manuscripts, the Sorbonnic, Vatican, Michaeline Cistercian, Arnulian, and Corbie manuscripts, the last of which is nearly 900 years old; against the variant readings of the Louvain editors from three or four codices; and also against the printed editions of Rat., Am., Er., and Lov.]

[Note: We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*, volume 1. M.]

(C)

## Prologue

This work was not written as though we had undertaken to expound the Gospel in its order. Rather, it was written according to the wishes and available time of the person consulting us, while the Gospel was being read with him, whenever something seemed obscure to him. Consequently, many things—and perhaps things still more obscure—have been omitted, because the person who asked about what he did not yet know already knew those matters, and did not wish his eagerness to be held back by things he had previously received in such a way that, through the continual hearing and discussion of them, he had firmly and securely committed them to memory.

Some matters also are expounded here in an order different from that in which they are narrated in the Gospel, because certain points, postponed in haste, were revisited when time became available and were written in the place that happened to be vacant in the sequence of the matters already expounded.

After I discovered this, I feared that someone who wished to read in this work an explanation of something that had moved him in the Gospel and stirred him to inquire might be offended by the weariness of the disordered arrangement. For I learned that the matters, dictated piecemeal as circumstances permitted, had been gathered together and connected into one whole. Therefore I arranged that, by means of titles and the prescribed numbering, anyone could easily locate whatever he needed.

# Book One: Questions on the Gospel According to Matthew

## Question I  
### [Matthew 11:27]

When he said, “No one knows the Son except the Father,” he did not add, “and anyone to whom the Father wishes to reveal him,” as he did when he said, “No one knows the Father except the Son,” and added, “and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him.”

This should not be understood as though the Son could be known by no one except the Father alone, whereas the Father could be known not only by the Son but also by those to whom the Son would reveal him. Rather, he spoke in this way so that we might understand that both the Father and the Son himself are revealed through the Son, because he is the light of our mind.

Thus, when he subsequently added, “and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal,” understand that this applies not only to the Father but also to the Son, for the addition belongs to the whole statement he made. For the Father is declared by his Word; but the Word declares not only what is declared through the Word, but also himself.

## Question II  
### [Matthew 12:1]

The fact that the Lord’s disciples began to pluck ears of grain and eat them—and could not do this without rubbing them—is related to the words, “Put to death what is earthly in you”: that is, no one passes into the body of Christ unless he has been stripped of his carnal garments.

Hence also the words, “Strip off the old man” (Colossians 3:5–9); and likewise, “With a circumcision not made by hand, in the stripping away of the flesh” (Colossians 2:11).

## Question III  
### [Matthew 12:20]

Concerning the smoldering flax, it should be noted that even while it gives light, it emits a smell of itself.

[Note: In the printed editions this question begins as follows: “He calls the bruised reed the Jews, because for this reason they were one and yet differed from one another.” Then follows, “Concerning the smoldering flax,” and so forth. But in all the manuscripts the first portion is absent. Accordingly, in the list of questions it is not prefaced “On the bruised reed,” but bears this title: “On the smoldering flax.”]

## Question IV  
### [Matthew 12:22]

Then a demon-possessed man, blind and mute, was brought to him: that is, one who does not believe and is subject to the devil; one who does not understand and does not confess the faith itself, concerning which it is said, “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10); or one who does not give praise to God.

## Question V  
### [Matthew 12:27–29]

What he said, “And if I cast out demons by Beelzebul,” is to be understood even in accordance with your own judgment: “Then the kingdom of God has come upon you,” because the kingdom of the devil cannot stand, since you admit that it is divided against itself.

By “the kingdom of God” he now means the kingdom by which the ungodly are condemned and separated from the faithful who are now doing penance for their sins.

He calls the devil “the strong man” because he held human beings, so that they could not by their own strength free themselves from him, but only through the grace of God. By “his vessels” he means all unbelievers.

“Unless he first binds the strong man”: by “binds” he means that he takes away from him the power of hindering the will of the faithful from following Christ and attaining the kingdom of God.

## Question VI  
### [Matthew 12:34]

He calls them a “brood of vipers” because he also calls them children of the devil. For each person is his child to the extent that he imitates him by sinning.

## Question VII  
### [Matthew 12:40]

“For just as Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights.”

Take the portion of Friday on which he was buried, together with the preceding night, as one night and day—that is, as a whole day; then take the night and day of the Sabbath; and then the Lord’s night together with the day that dawned upon it. Thus, by taking a part for the whole, you have three days and three nights.

For when a pregnant woman is said to carry for ten months, nine months are complete, but the beginning of the tenth is counted as the whole. Similarly, one evangelist says that the Lord’s manifestation on the mountain occurred “after six days” (Matthew 17:1), while another says “after eight days” (Luke 9:28). The former counts the later part of the first day on which the Lord promised that this would happen and the earlier part of the final day on which what he promised was fulfilled as whole and complete days. Thus you should understand that the one who said “after six days” counted only the middle days, which alone were completed as whole and complete days.

In Genesis, the day begins with light and ends in darkness (Genesis 1:5), signifying the fall of humanity. Now, however, it proceeds from darkness to light, as it is said, “to make light shine out of darkness” (2 Corinthians 4:6), because the human being, freed from sins, reaches the light of righteousness.

## Question VIII  
### [Matthew 12:43–45]

“When the unclean spirit has gone out from a person”: this signifies those who believe in such a way that they cannot endure the labors of self-restraint and will return to the world.

The statement that he takes with him seven other spirits is understood to mean that, when someone has fallen away from righteousness, he will also possess hypocrisy. For when the desire of the flesh has been expelled through repentance from its customary works, if it finds no pleasures in which it can rest, it returns more eagerly and again occupies the human mind—if, after it had been driven out, negligence followed, so that the word of God has not been introduced as an inhabitant into the cleansed house through sound doctrine.

And because that desire will possess not only those seven vices opposed to the seven spiritual virtues, but will also pretend through hypocrisy to possess the virtues themselves, therefore, after taking with it seven others more wicked—that is, the sevenfold hypocrisy—that desire returns, so that the final condition of the person is worse than the first.

[Note: Am., Er., and Lov. read: “when righteousness had been expelled, negligence followed.” We correct the text on the basis of eight manuscripts and the Regensburg edition.]

[Note: The Corbie manuscript and the two Victorine manuscripts read: “of the spirits of the virtues.”]

## Question IX  
### [Matthew 13:13, 23]

When he says, “One produces a hundredfold, another sixtyfold, another thirtyfold,” the hundredfold signifies martyrs, because of the fullness of life or contempt for death. [Variant: “holiness” instead of “fullness.”]

The sixtyfold signifies virgins, because of their inward leisure, since they do not struggle against the habit of the flesh. For leisure is customarily granted to those who are sixty after military service or public office.

The thirtyfold signifies married people, because this is the age of combatants. They have the sharper struggle, lest they be overcome by lust.

## Question X  
### [Matthew 13:25–30]

All impurity in the crop is called “weeds.”

The reason the weeds are said to be separated first is that, after tribulation has preceded, the ungodly will be separated from the godly. This is understood to be carried out by the good angels, because the good can perform the duties of vengeance with a good intention, as a king or a judge does; but the wicked cannot perform the duties of mercy.

[Variant: The Regensburg edition and the Cistercian manuscript read “as a king” and “as a judge”; other codices read “as law” and “as judgment.”]

## Question XI  
### [Matthew 13:31]

The mustard seed, because of the fervor of faith—or because it is said to drive out poisons—becomes greater than all vegetables, that is, than all doctrines.

Doctrines are the opinions of sects: that is, what each sect has approved.

## Question XII  
### [Matthew 13:33]

“The leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour”: by the woman he means wisdom; by the leaven, love, which makes things ferment and stirs them up.

The three measures of flour signify either the three faculties in a human being—“with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind” (Matthew 22:37); or the three fruitful measures—“a hundredfold, sixtyfold, thirtyfold” (Matthew 13:8, 23); or the three classes of human beings: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezekiel 14:14).

## Question XIII  
### [Matthew 13:44]

By the treasure hidden in the field he meant the two Testaments of the Law in the Church. When someone has grasped them even in part through understanding, he perceives that great things lie hidden there. He goes away, sells all that he has, and buys that field—that is, by despising temporal things, he acquires leisure for himself so that he may become rich in the knowledge of God.

## Question XIV  
### [Matthew 13:54]

When the Jews said, “From where does this man have such wisdom and mighty works?” they meant wisdom in the things he said and mighty works in the things he did.

For this reason, when the Apostle said that Christ is “the Power of God and the Wisdom of God” (1 Corinthians 1:24), he referred “power” to the signs, because of the Jews, and “wisdom” to the teaching, because of the Greeks—that is, the Gentiles.

## Question XV  
### [Matthew 14:26–33]

The fact that the disciples said that he was a phantom signifies what is meant by the words, “When the Son of Man comes, will he find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8), because some who have yielded to the devil will doubt Christ’s coming.

The fact that Peter implores the Lord’s help so that he may not sink signifies that, even after the final persecution, the Church must be purified through certain tribulations. Paul also signifies this when he says, “He will be saved, but only as through fire” (1 Corinthians 3:15).

The continuation—namely, that all those who were in the boat worshiped and said, “Truly you are the Son of God”—signifies that his glory will then be manifest, when those who now walk by faith will see him in appearance.

## Question XVI  
### [Matthew 15:5]

“Whatever gift is from me will benefit you”: that is, whatever gift you offer on my account will now belong to you.

These words signify that sons no longer needed their parents to make offerings on their behalf, because they had reached an age at which they could now offer on their own behalf. When they had reached this age and could say this to their parents, the Pharisees declared that they were not guilty if they failed to provide honor to their parents.

## Question XVII  
### [Matthew 15:13]

“Every planting that my heavenly Father did not plant will be uprooted”: that is, carnal desire, according to which they judged and were offended by the signs of events that had been omitted, or even by their own traditions; and they did not care about the precepts of life, which cleanse the mind from desire.

## Question XVIII  
### [Matthew 8:13; 15:28]

The fact that he saved both the centurion’s boy and the daughter of the Canaanite woman without coming to their houses signifies that the Gentiles, to whom he did not come, would nevertheless be saved through his word.

The fact that the children were healed when the persons themselves asked should be understood as representing the Church, which is both mother and children to herself. For, taken all together, those of whom the Church consists are called the mother; individually, those same people are called children.

## Question XIX  
### [Matthew 15:30]

The crowds brought mute people to the Lord: those who neither praise him nor confess the faith; blind people: those who do not understand, even if they obey those who command them; deaf people: those who do not obey, even if they understand; and lame people: those who do not fulfill the commandments.

## Question XX  
### [Matthew 16:2–3]

When the Lord said, “At evening you say, ‘It will be fair weather, for the sky is red,’” he meant that, through the blood of Christ’s passion, forgiveness of sins is granted at his first coming.

“And in the morning, ‘Today there will be a storm, for the sky is red with sadness’”: this means that at his second coming he will come with fire preceding him.

“You know how to judge the face of the sky, but you cannot recognize the signs of the times?” By “the signs of the times” he meant his coming or his passion, to which the red evening sky corresponds; and likewise the tribulation that will occur before his coming, to which the red morning sky, accompanied by sadness, corresponds.

## Question XXI  
### [Matthew 17:11]

When the Lord said, “Elijah is indeed to come, and he will restore all things,” he meant either those whom the persecution of the Antichrist will have disturbed, or that Elijah himself will restore, by dying, what he owes.

## Question XXII  
### [Matthew 17:14, 18]

When he said, “He often falls into the fire and sometimes into the water,” the fire signifies anger, because it seeks what is lofty; the water signifies the pleasures of the flesh.

Likewise, when the disciples said, “Why could we not cast him out?” they were warned, lest the performance of such miracles should lift them up into pride, to cure their earthly exaltation—which is signified by the name “mountain”—through the humility of faith, as though through a mustard seed, so that it might pass away.

## Question XXIII  
### [Matthew 17:25]

When he said, “Then the sons are free,” this should be understood of every kingdom: sons are free, that is, they are not subject to tribute.

Therefore, much more should the sons of that kingdom be free in any earthly kingdom, since all earthly kingdoms are subject to it.

## Question XXIV  
### [Matthew 18:6]

When the Lord says, “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble”—that is, one of the humble, such as he wishes his disciples to be—whether by failing to obey or even by acting against them, as the Apostle says concerning Alexander the coppersmith (2 Timothy 4:14), “it would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the depths of the sea.”

That is, a desire for temporal things, to which foolish and blind people are bound, is fittingly imposed upon him, so that, weighed down by its burden, it may lead him to destruction.

## Question XXV  
### [Matthew 18:24–31]

The fact that a debtor owing ten thousand talents was brought before the Lord, and that he ordered him, his wife, his children, and everything he possessed to be sold and the debt repaid, should be understood to mean that he was a debtor with respect to the ten commandments of the Law.

Because of his desires and works, represented as his wife and children, he ought to have paid the penalties that constituted his price. For the price of one who is sold is understood as the punishment of one condemned.

When it says that he was unwilling to forgive his fellow servant, but went away and had him put in prison, and so forth, this should be understood to mean that he retained such hostility against him that he wanted him to suffer punishment.

The fellow servants who reported to the Lord what had happened may be understood as the Church, which both releases one person and binds another.

## Question XXVI  
### [Matthew 19:23, 25]

When the Lord says that a rich man does not enter the kingdom of God, and the disciples say, “Who then can be saved?”—since the rich are few in comparison with the multitude of the poor—it should be understood that all who desire such things must recognize that they are to be counted among the rich.

## Question XXVII  
### [Matthew 20:17]

The fact that the Lord separately tells two disciples what he is going to suffer was done to establish their future testimony, because he said, “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Matthew 18:16).

In order that what he was saying might neither become widely known nor lack the firmness of human testimony, he could not tell fewer than two.

Or this may have been done to disclose the sacrament of love, for love cannot exist between fewer than two. He was going to suffer not under the necessity of a debt incurred for his own sin, but out of love, in order to pay our sins.

[Note: See Book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 12.]

## Question XXVIII  
### [Matthew 20:29–34]

The Lord leaves Jericho, already departing from this earth through the resurrection. Great crowds follow him: peoples and nations believe in him.

The two blind men sitting beside the road signify, from both peoples, certain persons who already cling through faith to the temporal dispensation according to which Christ is the way. They desire to be enlightened—that is, to understand something of the eternity of the Word—which they sought to obtain when Jesus passed by, that is, through the merit of the faith by which one believes that the Son of God was born as a human being and suffered for us.

For through this dispensation Jesus passes, because such an action is temporal. They had to cry out until they overcame the noise of the crowd resisting them: that is, they had to apply their minds in prayer and supplication with such perseverance that, through the strongest concentration, they might overcome either the habit of carnal desires—which, like a crowd, makes noise against the mind attempting to see the light of eternal truth—or the very crowd of carnal people who impede spiritual pursuits.

Therefore Jesus, hearing them—the one who said, “To the one who asks it will be given; the one who seeks will find; and to the one who knocks it will be opened” (Matthew 7:7)—touches them as they come to him, that is, as they arrive at what they desire through the very burning of their desire, and he enlightens them.

For the eternity of the Word, which remains in itself and renews all things (Wisdom 7:27), does not pass away in the manner of that temporal dispensation. Therefore, because faith in the temporal incarnation prepares us to understand eternal things, they were warned to be enlightened when Jesus passed by, and they were enlightened by him as he stood still.

Temporal things pass away; eternal things remain.

## Question XXIX  
### [Matthew 21:21]

When the Lord says to his disciples, “You will say to this mountain, ‘Take yourself up and throw yourself into the sea,’” he is speaking of pride as it belongs to worldly people.

The servant of God must say this to himself, so that he may drive pride away from himself, because it does not suit him.

Or, because the Gospel was preached through their faith and through them, the Lord himself—who is called a mountain (Isaiah 2:2)—was taken away from the Jews so that he might be cast forth among the Gentiles as into the sea.

## Question XXX  
### [Matthew 21:44]

When the Lord says, “Whoever falls upon this stone will be shattered; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him,” he is speaking of those who will fall upon him because they now despise him or inflict injuries upon him.

For this reason they do not yet perish completely, but are nevertheless shattered, so that they do not walk rightly. But upon those on whom he falls, he will come from above in judgment with the punishment of destruction.

Therefore he said, “It will crush them,” so that the ungodly may be like dust which the wind drives from the face of the earth (Psalm 1:4).

## Question XXXI  
### [Matthew 22:2–9]

When the Lord said, “The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son,” by the wedding he meant the incarnate Word, because, in the human nature he assumed, the Church has been joined to God.

When he said, “My bulls and fattened animals have been slaughtered,” by the bulls he meant the leaders of the peoples; by the fattened animals, all that has been made fat.

When the Lord said, “Go out to the ends of the roads, and invite to the wedding anyone you find,” the roads signify the doctrines of the Gentiles, because from all of them people came to the wedding—that is, they believed in Christ.

## Question XXXII  
### [Matthew 22:25]

When the Sadducees say to the Lord, “There were seven brothers among us, and the first took a wife and died, and the second, and the rest,” they signify ungodly people who were unable to bring forth the fruit of righteousness on earth throughout the seven ages of the world during which this earth endures.

Afterward the earth itself will also pass away, through which all those men passed fruitlessly, like seven husbands.

## Question XXXIII  
### [Matthew 22:40]

When the Lord says, “On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets,” by “depends” he means that the whole Law is referred to them and finds its completion there.

## Question XXXIV  
### [Matthew 23:17, 19]

When the Lord said, “Which is greater, the gold or the temple that sanctifies the gold?” and likewise, “Which is greater, the gift or the altar that sanctifies the gift?” the temple and altar should be understood as Christ himself.

The gold and the gift signify the praises and sacrifices of prayers that we offer in him and through him. For he is not sanctified by these; rather, they are sanctified through him.

## Question XXXV  
### [Matthew 23:23–24]

When the Lord said, “Straining out the gnat,” this refers to what he had said about their tithing every small thing.

“Swallowing the camel” refers to what he had said: “You have neglected the weightier matters of the Law—mercy, judgment, and faith.”

Thus the meaning is: “You observe the smallest matters but despise the greatest.”

From this perversity there also arose the action by which these words may be understood allegorically: they released Barabbas (Matthew 27:20), because he plainly did not break the Sabbath, which they observed carnally with great diligence; but they killed the Lord, who spiritually signified the Sabbath through mercy, judgment, and faith, which they chiefly despised.

Nor is it inappropriate that a seditious murderer should be represented by the name of a gnat, since this animal both disturbs by its buzzing and delights in blood. By the name of a camel, because of its great size and its humbling itself to bear burdens, the Lord is fittingly understood.

## Question XXXVI  
### [Matthew 23:37]

When the Lord said to Jerusalem, “How often I wanted to gather your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were unwilling,” this kind of animal has great affection for its young, so that, affected by their weakness, it too becomes weak. And, what you will find less readily among other animals, it fights a kite while protecting its young with its wings.

So too our mother, the Wisdom of God, having been weakened in a certain way through the assumption of flesh—for this reason the Apostle says, “The weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25)—protects our weakness and resists the devil, lest he snatch us away.

In that defense, what the hen attempts through affection against the kite, Wisdom accomplishes against the devil through power.

## Question XXXVII  
### [Matthew 24:20]

When the Lord said, “Pray that your flight may not be in winter or on the Sabbath,” he meant: do not allow yourselves to be detained by any impediment.

In winter, a person was hindered from traveling by rain or cold; on the Sabbath, travel was not permitted.

Or it may mean something else: that no one should be found on that day either in the sorrow or in the joy of temporal things.

## Question XXXVIII  
### [Matthew 24:23–27]

The Lord says, “For just as lightning comes out from the east and reaches as far as the west, so will be the coming of the Son of Man.” By the names “east” and “west” he wished to signify the whole world, throughout which the Church was destined to exist, with the Gospel beginning from Jerusalem (Luke 24:47), according to the sense in which he said, “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds” (Matthew 26:64). Appropriately, then, he has now called the Church “lightning,” since lightning especially tends to flash forth from the clouds.

[Note: [Col. 1330] Three manuscripts read, “For appropriately even now lightning, etc.” Another three read, “For indeed already now lightning, etc.”]

Once the authority of the Church had been established throughout the world, clear and manifest, he consequently admonishes the disciples, and all the faithful and those who would wish to believe in him, not to believe schismatics and heretics. For every schism and every heresy either has its own place in the world, occupying some portion of it, or deceives human curiosity in obscure and hidden gatherings. This is the point of his statement: “If anyone says to you, ‘Look, here is the Christ,’ or, ‘There,’” which signifies the regions and provinces of the earth; or, “in the inner rooms,” or “in the desert,” which signifies the obscure and hidden gatherings of heretics. When, therefore, he said that his coming would reach from east to west, this applies against those who are named according to fragments of the earth and say that Christ is with them. When he says, “As lightning,” this applies against those who gather secretly, as though in inner rooms, and a few as though in the desert. For the name “lightning” pertains to the manifestation and splendor of the Church, signifying also the night or clouds of this present age; for then the brightness of lightning appears.

### XXXIX. [Ibid. 24:32]

When the Lord said, “Learn the likeness from the fig tree,” understand the fig tree as the human race, on account of the itching of the flesh. “When its branch has already become tender”: that is, when the sons of human beings have advanced through faith in Christ toward spiritual fruits, and the honor of adoption as sons of God has become manifest in them.

### XL. [Ibid. 26:24]

When the Lord said of Judas, “It would have been better for him not to have been born,” should this be understood as referring to this life, so that he spoke in the customary manner? For nothing can be good for one who does not exist. And if anyone maintains that there was some life before this one, it is shown that not only would it not have benefited Judas to be born, but that it would have benefited no one. Does he mean that it would have been better for the devil not to be born into sin? Or was it better for him not to be born to Christ through a calling, lest he become an apostate?

### XLI. [Ibid. 26:15]

That the Lord was sold for thirty pieces of silver signifies, through Judas, the wicked Jews, who, pursuing carnal and temporal things belonging to the five bodily senses, did not wish to possess Christ. Since they did this in the sixth age of the world, it is signified that they received six times five as the price for which the Lord was sold.

[Note: [Col. 1331] The Ambrosian edition reads, “six-times-five them,” etc. [reading uncertain]. So too do most manuscripts, in which a little further below we again read, “six times five”; whereas the printed editions have “six times five impressed,” etc.]

Concerning this period the prophet taunts such people, saying, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Psalm 4:3). If there had been some excuse for pursuing vanity during the first five ages, they should at least have understood the truth in the sixth, which was preached and demonstrated through our Lord, just as on the sixth day the human being was made in the image of God (Genesis 1:26). Since they refused this, they have the image of the ruler of this age impressed six times five upon them, and they do not have Christ, through whom “the light of your countenance, O Lord,” has been stamped upon us (Psalm 4:7). And since “the word of the Lord is silver” (Psalm 12:6), while they understood even the Law itself in a carnal manner, they retained, as though impressed upon silver, the image of worldly rule after losing the Lord.

### XLII. [Ibid. 24:28]

When the Lord says, “Wherever the body is, there the eagles will gather,” this means: into heaven, where from here he lifted up with himself the body he had assumed in human form. It was also called a corpse because he was speaking these things as one who was going to die. “There the eagles will gather” was said of spiritual people who, by imitating his passion and humility, are, as it were, nourished from his body. For he assumed a body for the sake of humility and suffering on our behalf.

### XLIII. [Ibid. 26:29]

When the Lord says to the disciples at the time of his passion, “I will not drink from this fruit of the vine from now on until that day when I drink it anew with you in my Father’s kingdom,” he wishes this to be understood as old, since he calls that other wine new. Since, therefore, he had assumed a body from the stock of Adam, who is called the old human being, and was about to hand that body over to death in his passion—for this reason he also commends his blood through the sacrament of wine—what else should we understand the new wine to be except the immortality of renewed bodies? When he says, “I will drink it with you,” he also promises them the resurrection of their bodies for the putting on of immortality. “With you” should be understood as referring not to the same time, but to the same renewal. For the Apostle also says that we have risen with Christ (Colossians 2:12), so that the hope of a future reality may already bring present joy.

When he says that this new wine too comes from “this fruit of the vine,” he signifies that the same bodies that are now destined to die according to their earthly oldness will rise according to heavenly renewal. But if you understand the vine, from whose oldness he drank this cup of passion, as the Jews themselves, it is also signified that this very people will come to the body of Christ through newness of life, when, after the full number of the Gentiles has entered, “all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11:25).

### XLIV. [Ibid. 26:67]

What is said—“They spat in his face”—signified those who reject his gracious presence. Likewise, they strike him as though with blows when they place their own honors before him. They slap his face when, blinded by unbelief, they assert that he did not come, as though destroying and driving away his presence.

### XLV. [Ibid. 26:69–74]

That Peter, not yet firmly established in faith, denied God three times seems to have represented, in his threefold denial, the perverse error of heretics. For the error of heretics concerning Christ falls into three categories: they are mistaken either about his divinity, or about his humanity, or about both.

[Note: [Col. 1332] In the manuscripts, the forty-fifth question begins with the words, “The error of heretics”; the preceding words, “That Peter, not yet firmly established,” etc., are not included. In their place, some codices have “Concerning Peter’s threefold denial,” or “In Peter’s threefold denial.” Furthermore, in the printed editions of Rat., Ambros. and Erasmus, the following is added to this question:

“It should be noted that Peter denied the Lord once before the first cockcrow, signifying those who did not think Christ was God before the resurrection, having been troubled by his death. But the fact that he denied him twice before the second cockcrow signified those who now err concerning him either according to God, or according to man, or according to both, and therefore deny the truth before the resurrection of the Church. Thus the first cockcrow is understood as the resurrection of the Head, that is, of the Lord himself; the second as the resurrection of the same Head in the body of the universal Church.”

These words are absent from the other codices, except for one Cistercian manuscript.]

### XLVI. [Ibid. 26:58]

That Peter followed the Lord from a distance as he went to his passion signifies that the Church would indeed follow—that is, imitate—the Lord’s passion, but in a very different manner: the Church suffers for itself, whereas he suffered for the Church.

### XLVII. [Ibid. 26:39, 42, 44]

Just as the temptation of desire is threefold, so the temptation of fear is also threefold. Opposed to the desire that exists in curiosity is the fear of death: for just as in the former there is eagerness to know things, so in the latter there is fear of losing such knowledge. Opposed to the desire for honors or praise is the fear of disgrace and insults. Opposed to the desire for pleasure is the fear of pain. It is therefore not absurd to understand that, because of the threefold temptation of the passion, the Lord prayed three times that the cup might pass from him—but in such a way that the Father’s will would rather be fulfilled.

## BOOK TWO. Questions on the Gospel according to Luke

[Col. 1333]

### QUESTION I. [Luke, chapter 1, verses 13, 20]

When Zachariah, praying for the people, hears from the angel, “Your prayer has been heard; behold, your wife Elizabeth will conceive and bear a son, and you will call his name John,” this should first be considered: it is not plausible that, while he was offering sacrifice for the people’s sins, salvation, or redemption—since the people were indeed waiting for him to offer—an old man with an aged wife could have abandoned the public prayers and prayed to receive children. Especially since no one prays to receive what he despairs of receiving; yet Zachariah had despaired so completely of having children that he did not believe the angel who promised this to him.

Therefore, what is said to him—“Your prayer has been heard”—must be understood as referring to the people. Since the salvation, redemption, and abolition of the people’s sins were to come through Christ, Zachariah is told that a son will be born to him because he was appointed as Christ’s forerunner.

But when the same angel says to him, because he did not believe the angel, “And behold, you will be silent until these things are fulfilled in their time,” this should be understood as signifying that prophecy remained silent, as though without an intelligible sound, until John; for it was not understood until it was fulfilled in the Lord.

### II. [Ibid. 5:3–11]

That the Lord teaches the crowds from a boat signified the present time, when the Lord teaches the Gentiles from the authority of the Church. That the Lord, entering the boat belonging to Peter, asks him to put out a little way from the land signifies either that the word should be used moderately with the crowds, so that neither earthly things are commanded to them nor are they withdrawn from earthly things into the deeper mysteries in such a way that they do not understand them at all; or that the Gospel should first be preached to the Gentiles in the nearby regions. Thus what he says next to Peter, “Put out into the deep, and let down your nets for a catch,” pertains to the more distant Gentiles, to whom the Gospel was preached afterward, just as Isaiah says, “Lift up a signal among the nations, to those who are near and to those who are far away” (Isaiah 62:10; 57:19).

That the nets were breaking because of the abundance of fish, and the boats were filled so that they were sinking, signifies that such a great multitude of carnal people would arise in the Church that, even after the peace was ruptured by heresies and schisms going out from it, a great number would remain and such a great loss of faith and good morals would arise that such a Church might seem to say to Christ, “Depart from me, for I am a sinful man.” As though filled with crowds of carnal people and almost submerged by their ways, it would in a sense repel from itself the governance of spiritual people, in whom the person of Christ is especially manifest.

For people do not say this with the voice of their tongues to God’s good ministers, so as to drive them away from themselves; rather, by the voice of their ways and actions they urge them to withdraw, lest they be governed by good ministers. They do this all the more forcefully because they show them honor while nevertheless warning them by their actions to withdraw from them. Thus Peter’s falling at the Lord’s feet signified their honor, while his statement, “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man,” signified their ways.

Yet because the Lord did not do this—for he did not withdraw from them, but brought them ashore after the boats had been drawn up—it signifies that good and spiritual men ought not to have the desire to abandon their ecclesiastical office because they are disturbed by the sins of the crowds, in order to live more securely and peacefully.

That Peter, James, and John, after bringing the boats to land, left everything and followed him, can signify the end of time, when those who have clung to Christ will completely withdraw from the sea of this world.

### III. [Ibid. 5:14]

When the Lord says to the cleansed leper, “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift for your cleansing, as Moses commanded, for a testimony to them,” he seems to approve the sacrifice commanded through Moses, even though the Church has not retained it. This can be understood as having been commanded because the sacrifice of the Holy of Holies, which is his body, had not yet begun. For he had not yet offered his own holocaust in his passion. Once that sacrifice had been confirmed among believing peoples, the temple itself was destroyed, where those sacrifices used to be offered. This happened according to the prophecy of Daniel (Daniel 9:27).

For the signifying sacrifices ought not to be removed before the thing signified had been confirmed by the testimony of the Apostles preaching and by the faith of believing peoples.

### IV. [Ibid. 5:18–25]

Concerning the paralytic: the soul, dissolved in its members—that is, in good works—can be understood as seeking Christ, that is, the will of the Word of God. But it is hindered by the crowds unless it opens what is covered, that is, the things concealed in the Scriptures, so that through them it may arrive at knowledge of Christ; that is, so that through the devotion of faith it may descend to his humility. Those by whom the paralytic is lowered can signify the good teachers in the Church.

That he is lowered together with his bed signifies that Christ must be known by a human being who is still established in this flesh. Yet once healed, he is commanded to carry that bed and go to his house, so that, when the members of the soul are restored through the good hope of the remission of sins, this body may also be understood as being restored. Thus the infirmity of the soul no longer rests in carnal pleasures as on a bed; rather, it itself restrains the carnal affections and moves toward the rest of the hidden places of its heart.

### V. [Ibid. 3:23]

The question is reasonably raised: how could Joseph have had two fathers? Matthew says that he was begotten by the man called Jacob (Matthew 1:16), while Luke says that he was the son of the man called Heli. Nor can it be said here that one man had two names, as is clearly accustomed to happen not only among the Gentiles but also among the Jews. For anyone who supposes this is easily refuted by the remaining sequence of the generations.

What will he say about the grandfathers, great-grandfathers, ancestors, and the other forebears, whose different names each Evangelist weaves into his own account? Finally, what will he say about the number itself, since Luke counts forty-three generations from the Lord back to David, whereas Matthew counts twenty-eight or twenty-seven from David to the Lord? For, by a definite mystery, one person is counted twice up to the deportation and likewise from the deportation onward.

We must therefore ask how Joseph could have had two fathers. At present, three explanations occur to me, one of which the Evangelist may have followed. Either one was Joseph’s natural father and the other had adopted him; or, according to Jewish custom, when a man died without children, a relative took his wife and assigned the son he fathered to the deceased relative (Deuteronomy 25:5–6), so that, since Joseph had been begotten by one man on behalf of another, he could appropriately be said to have two fathers; or one Evangelist named the father by whom he was begotten, while the other supplied either his maternal grandfather or one of his older relatives, to whom Joseph could reasonably have been assigned as a son because of the bond of kinship, and from whom onward he therefore traced a line of generations different from Matthew’s, continuing back to David.

The explanation we placed second seems weak, because when someone among the Jews raises up offspring for a deceased brother or relative from his wife, the child born usually receives the name of the deceased.

[Note: [Col. 1335] See Retractations, book 2, chapter 12.]

Therefore, either adoption resolves this question, or the origin of the ancestors, or some other cause that does not presently occur to us. How great, then, is the folly of those who more readily rush to accuse one of the Evangelists of lying than to seek the reasons why each mentioned different names for the fathers. They rashly say that there are only two explanations by which this could properly have occurred, although finding even one explanation would be sufficient to resolve the question.

### VI. [Ibid. 3:23–38]

It may be asked what is meant by the fact that, according to the genealogies followed by Luke, seventy-seven persons are found. The Lord also mentioned this number when Peter asked him about forgiving a brother’s sins. For he said that forgiveness should be granted not merely seven times, but seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22). Hence it is rightly believed that, by mentioning this number, he commanded all sins to be forgiven, since the one through whom all sins were forgiven deigned to come humanly to human beings in the seventy-seventh generation, according to the testimony of the Evangelist mentioned.

Most appropriately, since there is another sequence of generations that Matthew sets out (ibid. 1:1–17), Luke followed the sequence in which, after the Lord had been baptized, he counts the generations upward through seventy-seven persons. For a return and, as it were, an ascent to God, with whom we are reconciled after the abolition of sins, is expressed when one ascends upward through those generations. And certainly the forgiveness of all sins takes place through Baptism, which is signified by that number.

For sins were not forgiven to the Lord himself in the Lord’s Baptism; rather, the forgiveness of all sins, which by his mercy and power was granted to human beings, was consecrated and marked there through the Lord’s Baptism and through that number of generations. Nor did the Lord come without reason or in vain in the seventy-seventh generation to abolish all sins, unless something were concealed in that number that pertained to the signification of all sins.

This should be considered in the numbers eleven and seven, which, multiplied by one another, arrive at that total: eleven times seven, or seven times eleven, makes seventy-seven. Eleven signifies a transgression of the number ten. If the perfection of blessedness is signified by ten, as is also shown by the fact that all who were hired for the vineyard received a denarius as their reward (ibid. 20:2–10), and this occurs when the sevenfold creature is joined to the Trinity of the Creator, it is clear that the transgression of ten signifies sin through the pride of one who desires to possess something more and thereby loses integrity and perfection.

This is multiplied by seven so that the transgression may be signified as having been carried out through the movement of the human being. For the incorporeal part of the human being is signified by the number three; hence we are commanded to love God with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind (Deuteronomy 6:5; Matthew 22:37). The body, however, is signified by the number four, since the nature of the body is found divided into four in many ways. Therefore, a human being composed of these joined elements is not improperly signified by the number seven.

But movement is not expressed in numbers when we say “one, two, three, four,” and so on; it is expressed when we say “once, twice, three times, four times.” Therefore, as I said, it is not seven and eleven but seven times eleven that signifies the transgression carried out through the movement of the sinning human being—that is, the transgression of the stability of his perfection through the desire to possess something more. Thus the soul was later told through the prophet, “Did you hope that, if you departed from me, you would have something more?”

From this vice of pride all sins grow wild. Yet they are forgiven when we are admonished that forgiveness must be granted seventy times seven (Matthew 18:22), so that we may understand that no sin is excluded from forgiveness when a penitent person asks pardon through the Church, whose person Peter represents.

### VII. [Ibid. 6:9]

When the Lord says to the Jews concerning the man who had a withered right hand, “I will ask you whether it is lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save a soul or to destroy it,” it is asked why, since he healed the body, he spoke in this way about saving or destroying a soul.

Perhaps it was because those miracles were performed for the sake of faith, in which the salvation of the soul consists; or because the healing of the right hand itself signified the salvation of the soul, which, ceasing from good works, seemed in a certain sense to have a withered right hand; or he used “soul” for “human being,” as is customary in speech. Thus one might say, “So many souls were there.”

### VIII. [Ibid. 6:38]

When the Lord says, “Give, and it will be given to you: a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and overflowing, they will place into your lap,” this can be understood according to the statement he makes elsewhere, “so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9). Thus the command “Give, and it will be given to you” seems to have been addressed to the people.

In accordance with this interpretation the Apostle says, “Let the one who is instructed in the word share in all good things with the one who instructs him” (Galatians 6:6). For he would not say, “They will place into your lap,” unless those who give even a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple were to merit, through the merits of those to whom they give it, the reception of a heavenly reward (Matthew 10:42).

### IX. [Ibid. 6:39]

When the Lord says, “Can a blind person lead a blind person? Will not both fall into a pit?” perhaps he added this so that they would not expect to receive from the Levites the measure of which he said, “They will place into your lap,” since they were giving tithes to the Levites. He called the Levites blind because they did not hold to the Gospel, so that the people would instead begin to hope for that recompense through the Lord’s disciples. Wishing to show that the disciples were to be their imitators, he also added, “A disciple is not above his teacher.”

### X. [Ibid. 6:47–48]

When the Lord says, “Everyone who comes to me, hears my words, and does them—I will show you whom he is like: he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid its foundation on rock,” by “digging” he meant, through Christian humility, to empty all earthly things from one’s heart, lest one worship God for the sake of anything of that kind.

To dig deeply means to dig until one reaches the rock: to follow Christ freely and worship him freely, so that one does not think God should be worshiped merely for the sake of superfluous things, or even for those things that appear necessary to this life and may be taken and possessed without guilt by any just person, but which are nevertheless temporal and earthly.

### XI. [Ibid. 7:32–35]

Concerning the children sitting in the marketplace and calling to one another, he replied to the proposals in reverse order. For when he says, “We lamented, and you did not weep,” this pertains to John, whose abstinence from food and drink signified the mourning of repentance. But when he says, “We played the flute for you, and you did not dance,” this pertains to the Lord himself, who, by eating and drinking with others, represented the joy of the kingdom.

But they wished neither to humble themselves with John nor to rejoice with Christ. They said that John had a demon, and that the Lord was a glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners. When he adds, “Wisdom is justified by all her children,” he shows that the children of wisdom understand that justice does not consist in abstaining or eating, but in equanimity when enduring want and in temperance, so as not to be corrupted by abundance, and in taking or not taking at the proper time those things whose use—not their desire—is to be blamed.

It makes no difference at all what foods you take in order to meet the body’s necessity, provided that your choice of foods is appropriate to the conditions in which you must live. Nor does the amount matter greatly, since we see that some people’s stomachs are satisfied more quickly, yet they eagerly, intolerably, and altogether shamefully crave that same small amount by which they are satisfied. Others, however, are satisfied by somewhat more but endure want more tolerably; they can even look calmly at food placed before them, without touching it, if at that time it is appropriate or necessary to do so.

What matters more, therefore, is not what kind or how much food someone takes, in accordance with human circumstances, his own condition, and the needs of his health, but with what ease and serenity of mind he can do without such things when it is appropriate or even necessary to do without them. Thus what the Apostle says may be fulfilled in the mind of a Christian:

“I know how to be in want, and I know how to abound; in every circumstance and in all things I have been instructed, both to be full and to be hungry, both to abound and to suffer want. I can do all things through him who strengthens me” (Philippians 4:12–13);

and also:

“Neither if we eat will we abound, nor if we do not eat will we lack” (1 Corinthians 8:8);

and also:

“For the kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy.”

And because people commonly rejoice greatly in carnal feasts, he added, “in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17). Wisdom, therefore, is justified by all her children, who understand that the times for using earthly things ought to be appropriate; but the readiness to do without such things, and the love of enjoying eternal things, ought not to vary with the times but to be retained perpetually.

### XII. [Ibid. 8:16]

When the Lord says, “No one who lights a lamp covers it with a vessel or places it under a bed, but puts it on a lampstand, so that those entering may see the light,” whoever hides the word of God out of fear of carnal disadvantages is certainly placing the flesh itself before the manifestation of truth and covering the word with it, as it were, by fearing to preach.

He therefore called the flesh by the names “vessel” and “bed,” beneath which he says that the one who does this places the lamp.

### XIII. [Ibid. 8:26–39]

When the Lord healed, in the region of the Gerasenes, the man in whom there was a legion of demons, the Gentiles who served many demons were signified.

That the man was without clothing means that he did not possess faith, and so forth.

That he did not live in a house means that he did not rest in his own conscience.

That he lived among the tombs means that he delighted in dead works, that is, in sins.

That he was bound with iron fetters and chains signifies the harsh and severe laws of the Gentiles, by which sins were also restrained in their commonwealth.

That, after such bonds had been broken, he was driven by the demon into the wilderness signifies that, even after transgressing those laws, he was led by desire into crimes that exceeded ordinary custom.

That the demons were permitted to enter the swine feeding on the mountains signifies unclean and proud people, whom demons rule through the worship of idols.

That they were driven headlong into the lake signifies that, once the Church had been glorified and the Gentile people had been freed from the dominion of demons, those who refused to believe in Christ practice their sacrilegious rites in hidden places, submerged in blind and profound curiosity.

[Note: [Col. 1338] This was after the laws against idols issued by Honorius in the year 399. See City of God, book 18, chapter 54.]

That the swineherds fled and reported these events signifies that certain leaders even among the impious, although they flee the Christian law, nevertheless proclaim its power among the nations with astonishment and admiration.

That the Gerasenes came out to see what had happened, found the man clothed and sitting at Jesus’ feet with a sound mind, and, recognizing what had occurred, asked Jesus to depart from them, struck with great fear, signifies the multitude that delighted in its ancient way of life. It honors the Christian law but does not wish to endure it, saying that it cannot fulfill it, while nevertheless marveling at the faithful people healed from their former lost way of life.

That the man desired already to be with Christ, but was told, “Return to your home and declare how much God has done for you,” can rightly be understood according to the Apostle’s statement: “My desire is to depart and be with Christ, which is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:23).

Thus each person should understand that, after the remission of sins, he must return to a good conscience and serve the Gospel for the salvation of others as well, so that afterward he may rest with Christ. He must not, by prematurely desiring to be with Christ, neglect the ministry of preaching, which is devoted to the redemption of his brothers and sisters.

### XIV. [Ibid. 10:1]

Concerning the seventy-two disciples: just as the whole world is traversed and illuminated by the sun in twenty-four hours, so the mystery of illuminating the world through the Gospel of the Trinity is intimated in the seventy-two disciples.

For we place twenty-four three times into seventy-two.

That he sends them two by two is a sacrament of love: either because there are two commandments of love, or because love cannot exist with fewer than two.

[Note: [Col. 1339] Rat. and the Cistercian manuscript read “ministry” rather than “mystery.”]

### XV. [Ibid. 11:35]

“If the light that is in you is darkness, how great is the darkness?” (Matthew 6:23). By “light” he means the good intention of the mind by which we act; by “darkness” he calls the actions themselves, either because others do not know with what intention we do them, or because we ourselves do not know their outcome—that is, how they will turn out and affect those for whom we perform them with a good intention.

For the most part, people are corrupted by using our benefits badly, even though we provide those benefits to them with mercy and benevolent intention.

### XVI. [Ibid. 11:39]

“Now you Pharisees cleanse what is outside the cup and the dish.” Here and thereafter, what he says against the Pharisees and teachers of the Law is the same as what he said earlier: “He set his face firmly toward Jerusalem” (Luke 9:51), so that he might openly tell them their true vices and sins.

### XVII. [Ibid. 11:20]

The Holy Spirit is therefore called the finger of God on account of the distribution of the gifts given through him, each proper to particular human beings or angels. For in none of our members is division more apparent than in the fingers.

### XVIII. [Ibid. 5:33–38]

Fasting is either in tribulation or in joy. In tribulation, it is undertaken to make God propitious on account of sins; in joy, it occurs when carnal things delight us less because spiritual nourishment is greater.

When, therefore, the Lord was asked why his disciples did not fast, he answered concerning both kinds of fasting. The kind of fasting customarily practiced in tribulation is indicated by his statement that the bridegroom’s children would fast when the bridegroom had been taken away from them. Then they would be desolate and would remain in sorrow and mourning until consoling joys were given back to them through the Holy Spirit.

Once they had received this gift, they would also most appropriately celebrate the other kind of fasting, which would be practiced through joy, since they had been renewed into spiritual life.

Before they received it, he says that they were like old garments to which a new patch is improperly sewn—that is, some portion of teaching pertaining to the moderation of the new life. If this is done, the teaching itself is somehow torn, because the portion concerning abstinence from food is handed on inappropriately, when that teaching prescribes a general fast not merely from the desire for food but from every joy in temporal pleasures.

He says that its patch—that is, the portion pertaining to food—ought not to be given to people who are still devoted to their old way of life, because a kind of tearing seems to occur there as well, and it does not suit the oldness itself.

He also says that they are like old wineskins, which, he declares, are more easily burst by new wine—that is, by spiritual commands—than able to contain it. But they were already new wineskins when, after the Lord’s ascension, they were being renewed through prayer and hope in their desire for his consolation. Then they received the Holy Spirit. Filled with him, they spoke in the languages of all who had gathered from different nations and were said to be full of new wine (Acts 2:1–13). For new wine had already come to new wineskins.

### XIX. [Ibid. 10:30–37]

“A certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho”: this man is understood as Adam in the human race.

Jerusalem, the city of that heavenly peace, is the place from whose blessedness he fell.

Jericho is interpreted as “Moon” and signifies our mortality, because it is born, grows, grows old, and dies.

The robbers are the devil and his angels, who stripped him of immortality, and, by inflicting wounds, persuaded him to sin.

[Note: [Col. 1340] Thus read eight manuscripts. But the printed editions, except Rat., read: “grows old. And he fell among robbers, the devil and his angels.”]

“They left him half-dead”: for in the part by which a human being can understand and know God, he is alive; in the part by which he wastes away and is weighed down by sins, he is dead. Therefore he is called half-dead.

The priest and Levite who saw him and passed by signify the priesthood and ministry of the Old Testament, which could not contribute to salvation.

“Samaritan” is interpreted as “Guardian,” and therefore the Lord himself is signified by this name.

The binding of the wounds is the restraint of sins.

The oil is the consolation of good hope, on account of the forgiveness granted for reconciliation to peace.

The wine is an exhortation to work with a most fervent spirit.

His beast of burden is the flesh in which he deigned to come to us.

To place him upon the beast is to believe in Christ’s incarnation itself.

The inn is the Church, where travelers returning from their pilgrimage to their eternal homeland are refreshed.

The next day is after the Lord’s resurrection.

The two denarii are either the two commandments of love, which the Apostles received through the Holy Spirit in order to preach to the others, or the promise of the present life and of the future life.

For in accordance with the two promises it was said, “He will receive in this age sevenfold,” and “in the age to come he will obtain eternal life” (Matthew 19:29).

The innkeeper, therefore, is the Apostle.

What he spends beyond this is either the counsel expressed in the statement, “Concerning virgins I have no command of the Lord, but I give counsel” (1 Corinthians 7:25), or the fact that he also worked with his own hands, so as not to burden any of the weak with the novelty of the Gospel, although he was entitled to be supported by the Gospel (2 Thessalonians 3:8–9).

[Note: [Col. 1340] The printed editions read, “He will receive a hundredfold.” But the manuscript codices, supported by Eugippius, read, “He will receive sevenfold.” Thus Augustine certainly read it in his work on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2, verse 6, and elsewhere. Perhaps the translator read for the Greek *hekatontaplasiona*—which is found in Matthew 19:29 and Mark 10:30—the form *heptaplasiona*.]

### XX. [Ibid. 10:38–42]

When Martha received him into her house, she signifies the Church as it now exists, receiving the Lord into her heart. Mary, her sister, who sat at the Lord’s feet and listened to his word, signifies this same Church in the age to come, where, ceasing from work and the ministry required by necessity, she will enjoy wisdom alone. Martha, therefore, was occupied with much service, because the Church is now engaged in such works. But when she complains that her sister does not help her, the occasion is given for the Lord’s judgment, by which he shows that this Church is anxious and troubled about many things, whereas there is one thing necessary, to which one arrives through the merits of this ministry. He says that Mary chose the better part, which will not be taken away from her. It is therefore understood to be the better part because through it one proceeds toward the other, and because it will not be taken away; the ministry, however, although good, will be taken away when the need being served has passed.

## XXI. [The same, XI, 5–8]

The friend to whom one comes at midnight to borrow three loaves is clearly presented as an image of the situation in which someone, placed in the midst of tribulation, asks God to grant him an understanding of the Trinity, by which he may be comforted in the labors of the present life. Yet the comparison is drawn from something lesser. If a human friend rises from bed and gives what is requested, compelled not by friendship but by annoyance, how much more does God give, who bestows without annoyance and with the greatest generosity what is requested—but wants himself to be asked for it so that those who ask may become capable of receiving his gifts?

In the three loaves, too, the unity of substance in the Trinity is signified. The friend whom the petitioner says has come from a journey and for whom he has nothing to set before him is understood as the human appetite, which ought to obey reason. It was serving temporal custom, which he calls a journey because of all things that pass away with time. When a person turns toward God, that appetite too is recalled from its customary ways. But if inward joy in spiritual teaching—the teaching in which the Trinity of the Creator is proclaimed—does not provide consolation, great anguish arises in the person oppressed by mortal misery: abstinence from the things that delight outwardly is imposed, while inwardly there is no refreshment from the joy of saving doctrine [Note: [Col. 1341] Two manuscripts read “spiritual.” Rat. and the Cistercian manuscript read “saviors.”]. This anguish itself is the midnight hour, when one is compelled to persist urgently in asking to receive the three loaves.

When the answer given from within is that the door has already been shut and that the children are in bed with him, this signifies a time of famine of the word, when understanding is closed, and those who, distributing evangelical wisdom as bread, preached throughout the world are now, as the householder’s children, in secret repose with the Lord. Nevertheless, by praying, the one who desires understanding is enabled to receive it from God himself, even when no human being is available through whom wisdom may be preached.

## XXII. [The same, XI, 12]

Concerning the bread, the fish, and the egg, to which he opposed their contraries, the stone, the serpent, and the scorpion. The bread is understood as charity, because it is more greatly desired and so necessary that without it the other things are nothing, just as without bread the table is empty [Note: [Col. 1342] Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read, “the table is empty.” M.]. Its contrary is hardness of heart, which he compared to a stone.

The fish, however, is understood as faith in invisible things, either because of the water of Baptism or because it is caught from invisible places. Faith, too, which is buffeted by the waves of this world but is not broken, is rightly compared to a fish. Its contrary he represented by the serpent, because of the poisons of deceit, which it also sowed in the first human being by giving evil advice.

In the egg hope is understood. An egg is not yet a fully formed offspring, but by being brooded it is awaited in hope. Its contrary he represented by the scorpion, whose venomous sting must be feared from behind. Likewise, the contrary of hope is looking backward, whereas hope extends itself toward the things that lie ahead.

## XXIII. [The same, XI, 52]

Concerning what the Lord says to the scribes, or teachers, of the Jews: “You have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and those who were entering you hindered.” They themselves neither understood nor wanted others to understand Christ’s humility in the Scripture [Note: [Col. 1342] Thus most manuscripts read. The printed editions, however, read: “what is said in Scripture concerning Christ’s humanity, which they themselves did not understand.”].

## XXIV. [The same, XII, 23]

The Lord says to his disciples: “The soul is more than food, and the body more than clothing”; and surely, if he has given you what is greater, how much more will he give what is lesser?

## XXV. [The same, XII, 35]

The Lord says: “Let your loins be girded,” because of restraint from love of worldly things; and “let your lamps be burning,” so that you may do this with a true end and right intention.

## XXVI. [The same, XII, 42]

The Lord said to Peter: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and prudent steward whom the Lord will set over his household, to give them their measure of wheat at the proper time?” He says “measure” because of the measure of each listener’s capacity.

## XXVII. [The same, XII, 54–55]

When the Lord says, “When you see a cloud rising from the west,” he signifies his flesh rising again from death. From it, the rain of evangelical preaching has been poured over all the lands. The south wind blowing before the heat signifies lighter tribulations before the judgment.

## XXVIII. [The same, XII, 26]

When the Lord says, “If you cannot do what is least,” speaking of increasing the stature of the body, this is indeed a small thing; for God, however, to fashion bodies is a small thing.

## XXIX. [The same, XII, 29]

When he was telling the disciples that they ought not to be anxious about food, he said, “And do not be lifted up on high.” At first a person seeks these things in order to satisfy necessity; but when they have become abundant, he begins also to grow proud because of them. It is as though someone wounded were to boast that he had many bandages in his house, when it would actually be good for him not to have wounds and not to need even one bandage.

## [The same, XIV, 2, 5; XIII, 11–16]

[Note: [Col. 1343] The title in the Index above, p. 1324, contains nothing concerning the remainder of this question. Nevertheless, it is also found in Eugyppius, with a fuller title in these words: “And concerning the dropsical man, or concerning the bent woman.”]

He appropriately compared the dropsical man with the animal that fell into a well, for the former suffered from fluid. Likewise, he compared the woman whom he had said had been bound for eighteen years, and whom he released from that bondage, with an animal that is untied so that it may be led to water.

We may rightly compare the dropsical man with a greedy rich person. Just as the more the former abounds in disordered fluid, the more he thirsts, so the richer the latter is in wealth that he does not use well, the more ardently he desires such things. The woman, however, so bent by illness that she could not straighten herself, signifies a soul weakened and oppressed by earthly opinions, so that it is unable to think about divine things [Note: [Col. 1343] The printed editions, contrary to the manuscripts, add here “he likened her”; what should be understood instead is “we compare her.” Shortly afterward Rat., Am., and Er. read, “by earthly opinions or works.”].

## XXX. [The same, XIV, 21, 23]

When he brings in those invited to the banquet from the city, he signifies those from the Jewish people who believed: weakened by sins and lacking the pride that passes itself off as righteousness, which falsely kept their leaders from grace. When he ordered others to be brought in from the hedges and roads, while there was still room, he signified the Gentiles, because of the various roads of sects and the thorns of sins.

## XXXI. [The same, XIV, 28–33]

The expense required to build a tower signifies the strength required to attain Christ’s discipleship. The ten thousand who are about to fight against a king who has twenty thousand signifies the simplicity of the Christian person set against the duplicity of the devil—that is, against his deceits and falsehoods—when the person has resolved to renounce everything that belongs to him [Note: [Col. 1343] Ven. and Lov. give this passage as follows: “The strength is … they show the simplicity of the Christian people … established in resolution.” Lugd. does likewise, except that the words “are,” “show,” and “people” are enclosed in brackets. M.].

For he concludes in this way: “So therefore, every one of you who does not renounce all that belongs to him cannot be my disciple.” Among all these things, temporal life itself must also be understood. One ought to possess it for a time in such a way that it does not hinder one from attaining eternal life, even if someone threatens to take it away.

Just as, concerning the unfinished tower, he deterred them by the reproachful words, “This man began to build and was not able to finish,” so, in the case of the king with whom one must fight, he criticized the peace itself when he said, “While he is still far away, sending a delegation, he asks for the terms of peace.” He also signified the threats of temptations impending from the devil: people who do not renounce everything they possess cannot withstand them, but make peace with him by consenting to commit sins.

To build the tower and fight against that king is to be Christ’s disciple. To have the expense required to complete the tower and to have ten thousand strong enough to face the king’s twenty thousand is to renounce everything that belongs to him.

## XXXII. [The same, XIV, 34–35; XV, 4–10]

Salt that has lost its savor signifies an apostate. By the lost sheep he meant all sinners who are reconciled to God through repentance. He carries the sheep on his shoulders because, by humbling himself, he raised up such people.

He said that the ninety-nine were left in the wilderness because they signify the proud, as though they carried a wilderness in their minds, since they want to appear solitary and lack the unity required for perfection. Whenever someone is torn away from true unity, he is torn away through pride: desiring to belong to himself, he does not follow the One who is God.

Therefore, both in the ninety-nine sheep and in the nine drachmas he places the signification of those who, trusting in themselves, put themselves before sinners returning to salvation. One is lacking from nine in order to make ten, and from ninety-nine in order to make one hundred. The same can be observed with the other numbers. From nine hundred ninety-nine, one is lacking to make one thousand; and from nine thousand nine hundred ninety-nine, one is lacking to make ten thousand.

The numbers can therefore vary in their smallness or greatness, while lacking one thing by which they would be completed. The one itself remains without variation and, when added, brings completion. To this one he assigns all those reconciled through repentance, which is obtained by humility.

## XXXIII. [The same, XV, 11–32]

The man who had two sons is understood as God in relation to the two peoples, as though they were two branches of the human race: one consisting of those who remained in the worship of the one God, and the other of those who abandoned God, even to the point of worshiping idols.

From the very beginning of the creation of mortal beings, the interpretation should be directed to this. The elder son therefore pertains to the worship of the one God. He says that the younger went away into a distant region. For he asked his father to give him the share of the property that fell to him, as though the soul, delighting in its own power, desired what makes it live, understand, remember, and excel through an energetic intellect. All these are divine gifts. Receiving them into his own power through free will—since the father divided his property among his children—the younger son went away into a distant region, making bad use of natural goods, precisely because he abandoned his father in his desire to enjoy creation while leaving the Creator himself.

When he says that this happened “not many days later,” when, after gathering everything together, he set out for a distant region, this is because not long after the establishment of the human race the soul decided, through free will, to carry away with it a certain power, as it were, of its own nature and to abandon the one by whom it had been created, trusting in its own strength. It consumes that strength all the more quickly the more it abandons the one from whom it received it.

Accordingly, he calls this a prodigal life: one that loves to squander itself and to roam about amid outward displays, while becoming inwardly empty, since a person follows the things that proceed from that life and abandons the one who is interior to him. The distant region, therefore, is forgetfulness of God.

The famine in that region is the lack of the word of truth. One of the citizens of that region is some aerial prince belonging to the army of the devil. His farm is the extent of his power. The pigs are the unclean spirits subject to him. The pods with which he fed the pigs are secular teachings, resounding with barren vanity.
