In various kinds of speech and song they proclaim the praises of idols and of myths concerning the gods of the Gentiles [Col. 1345], things in which demons delight. Thus, when this man desired to be filled, he wanted to find in such things something solid and upright pertaining to the blessed life, but he could not. For this is what he says: “And no one gave him anything.”

But when he came to himself—that is, when he brought his attention back from the things outside that entice and deceive in vain to the inner places of conscience—he said: “How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread!” How could he know this, when he was in such great forgetfulness of God, as all idolaters were, unless this recollection already belonged to one who was coming to his senses, at a time when the Gospel was being preached?

Such a person could now notice that many were preaching the truth, among whom were some who were not led by love of the truth itself but by the desire to obtain worldly advantages. The Apostle said of these that there were some who preached the Gospel “not sincerely” (Philippians 1:17), supposing that godliness was a means of gain (1 Timothy 6:5). They did not preach something else, as the heretics did, but what the Apostle Paul preached—yet not with the intention that moved the Apostle Paul. Hence they are rightly called hired servants: in the same house, handling the same bread of the word, but not called to an eternal inheritance; rather, hired for a temporal reward. Of such people it was said: “Truly, I tell you, they have received their reward” (Matthew 6:2).

“I am perishing here from hunger,” he says. Then he says, “I will arise,” because he was lying down; “and I will go,” because he was far away; “to my father,” because he was under the prince of pigs. The remaining words are those of someone meditating on repentance in the confession of sin, though not yet carrying it out. For he does not yet speak to his father; he promises that he will say these things when he comes.

Understand, therefore, that “coming to the father” should now be taken as being established in the Church through faith, where legitimate and fruitful confession of sins can already take place. What, then, does he say he will tell his father?

“Father, I have sinned against heaven and before you, and I am no longer worthy to be called your son; make me like one of your hired servants.”

Does “I have sinned against heaven” mean the same as “before you,” so that he has called the very summit of the Father “heaven”? Hence also the statement in the Psalm, “His going forth is from the highest heaven” (Psalm 18:7), when he wished it to be understood as proceeding from the Father himself. Or should it rather mean: “I have sinned against heaven,” before holy souls in whom God has his dwelling; “but before you,” in the innermost sanctuary of conscience itself?

And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still far away—before he understood God, although he was already seeking him devoutly—his father saw him. For the impious and proud are appropriately said not to be seen, as though they were not held before the eyes. Only those who are loved are ordinarily said to be held before one’s eyes.

And he was moved with compassion, and he ran and fell upon his neck. The Father did not abandon the only-begotten Son, in whom he ran and descended even into our distant pilgrimage, because “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19). The Lord himself also says, “The Father dwelling in me does his works” (John 14:10).

What, then, does it mean that he fell upon his neck, except that he inclined and humbled his arm in an embrace? And what is the arm of the Lord to whom it has been revealed (Isaiah 53:1), except our Lord Jesus Christ?

And he kissed him. To be comforted by the word of God’s grace toward the hope of forgiveness of sins is what it means, after long journeys, to return and receive from one’s father the kiss of charity. Once established in the Church, he now begins to confess his sins. He does not say all that he had promised he would say, but only as far as: “I am no longer worthy to be called your son.” For he wishes this to be accomplished through grace, while by his merits he confesses himself unworthy.

He does not add what he had said in his meditation: “Make me like one of your hired servants.” When he had no bread, he was willing even to be a hired servant; but after the father’s kiss, he now nobly disdains this.

The first robe is the dignity that Adam lost. The servants who bring it forth are the preachers of reconciliation. The ring on the hand is the pledge of the Holy Spirit, because of the distribution of grace [Note: [Col. 1346] Lov. reads “participation.” Other codices read “distribution,” which is better, as in question 17 above.], appropriately signified by the finger.

The shoes on the feet signify preparation for evangelizing, so as not to touch earthly things. The fattened calf is the same Lord, but according to the flesh, satiated with reproaches.

When he orders them to bring it, what else does this mean except that they should preach him and, by announcing him, make him come into the inward parts of the hungry son, exhausted by famine? For he also orders them to kill it, that is, to make known his death. Someone is killed for another when that person believes that he has been killed.

“And let us eat,” he says. This refers to joy, because of what he says next: “For this son of mine was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.” These feasting and celebrations are now held throughout the world, as the Church has been enlarged and spread abroad. For that calf is both offered to the Father in the Lord’s body and blood and feeds the entire household.

Meanwhile, the elder son—the people of Israel according to the flesh—has not gone away into a distant region, but nevertheless is not in the house. He is in the field, that is, amid the very hereditary wealth of the Law and the Prophets. There he works at earthly things, particularly in whatever Israelite interpretations there are [Note: [Col. 1346] Thus Rat. and four manuscripts read. Am. and Er. have “among Israelite interpreters”; Lov. has “in Israelite interpretations.” The Michaelinus manuscript has “among more discerning Israelites.”]. Many such people were found among them, and are often found still.

Coming from the field, he began to draw near to the house—that is, after rejecting the labor of servile work, he discerned the freedom of the Church from those same Scriptures. He heard harmony and a chorus: that is, those filled with the Spirit preaching the Gospel in harmonious voices. To them it was said: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing” (1 Corinthians 1:10). He also heard the soul and heart of those living in concord as one, praising God.

He called one of the servants and asked what these things were. He took up, as it were, one of the prophets to read, and, seeking in him an answer, asked in a certain sense why these celebrations were being held in the Church, in which he did not see himself to be present.

The servant, the father’s prophet, answered him: “Your brother has come, and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has received him safely.” Your brother had been at the ends of the earth. But from there comes the greater rejoicing of those singing a new song to the Lord, because “his praise is from the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 42:10). For the sake of him who had been absent, the man placed under affliction was killed, “a man acquainted with suffering and knowing how to bear weakness” (Isaiah 53:3); for “those to whom nothing was told about him have seen, and those who have not heard have understood” (Isaiah 52:15).

But he is now indignant as well and still refuses to enter. Therefore, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, his father will go out at the proper time, so that all Israel too may be saved. For a partial blindness has come upon it, like an absence in the field, until the fullness of the younger son—who had long remained in the idolatry of the Gentiles—returns and enters to eat the calf (Romans 11:25).

At some point there will be an open calling of the Jews to the salvation of the Gospel. He calls the manifestation of this calling the father’s going out to plead with the elder son.

Next, the elder son’s reply contains two questions: first, how that people is to be understood as never having transgressed God’s commandment; and second, who the kid is that he says he never received in order to feast with his friends.

Regarding the commandment that was not transgressed, it readily occurs to us that the statement was not made concerning every commandment, but chiefly concerning the one most necessary: the command to worship no other god besides the one Creator of all things (Exodus 20:3). Nor is this son understood as representing all Israelites, but those among them who never turned from the one God to images.

Although, like a son placed in the field, he desired earthly things, he desired these goods from the one God, even though they were goods shared with animals. Hence the words in the Psalm, spoken in the person of the Synagogue—which is interpreted as “Asaph”—are appropriately understood: “I became like an animal before you, and I am always with you” (Psalm 73:23). This is also confirmed by the testimony of his father himself when he says, “You are always with me.” He does not rebuke him as though he were lying, but approves his perseverance with him and invites him to enjoy a better and more delightful rejoicing.

Who, then, is the kid that he never received for feasting? A sinner is certainly often signified by the name “kid.” But far be it from me to understand this as the Antichrist. I find no way through this interpretation. It is very absurd that the one to whom it is said, “You are always with me,” should have desired this from his father: to believe in the Antichrist. Nor is it permissible to understand this son as referring to those Jews who will believe in the Antichrist.

How could he feast on that kid if he himself were the Antichrist and did not believe in him? Or if feasting on the slaughter of the kid means rejoicing over the destruction of the Antichrist, how does the son whom the father received say that this had not been granted to him, when all the sons of God will rejoice over the condemnation of that adversary?

Accordingly, then—though I say this concerning a very obscure matter without prejudging a more careful inquiry—he complains that the Lord himself was denied to him for feasting, because he regards him as a sinner. For when he is a kid to that people—that is, when it considers him a violator of the Sabbath and a profaner of the Law—it has not deserved to delight in his feast. Thus, when he says, “You never gave me a kid to feast with my friends,” it is as though he were saying: “You never gave me for feasting the one who seemed to me to be a kid,” refusing to grant me that very one precisely because he seemed to me to be a kid.

When he says “with my friends,” this is understood either as the rulers speaking together with the common people, or as the people of Jerusalem speaking together with the other peoples of Judea. The prostitutes with whom the younger son is accused of having squandered his property are rightly understood as superstitions: having abandoned the one legitimate marriage-bed of the word of God, he fornicated with a crowd of demons through the most shameful desire.

What, then, does it mean that, after the father had said, “You are always with me”—a statement already discussed—he added, “And all that is mine is yours”?

Here one must first take care not to understand the words “All that is mine is yours” as though they did not also belong to the brother, thereby falling into the difficulty of an earthly inheritance: how can everything belong to the elder if the younger also has his share?

The possessions of the perfected, purified, and already immortal sons are held in such a way that each thing belongs to all and all things belong to each. For just as desire holds nothing without anxiety, so charity holds nothing with anxiety.

But in what sense is everything theirs? Someone may say: “Are angels, sublime powers and authorities, and all the heavenly ministries of God also to be thought to have been subjected to such a son as his possession?”

If “possession” is understood in such a way that the possessor himself is the master, then not everything belongs to him. They will not be masters, but rather companions of the angels, concerning whom it is said: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Matthew 22:30).

But if possession is understood in the sense in which we rightly say that souls possess truth, I do not see why we cannot accept truthfully and properly all the things included in “everything.” We do not speak in such a way as to call souls the mistresses of the truth that we say is possessed by them.

Or, if the term “possession” prevents us from understanding the matter in this sense, let that term also be set aside. For the father does not say, “I will give everything to you as a possession,” or “You possess or will possess all that is mine,” but, “All that is mine is yours.”

Yet these things are not his in the same way that they are God’s. What is found in our money may be nourishment, adornment, or something of that sort for our household. And certainly, since he could rightly call the father himself his own, I do not see what of the father’s he could not rightly call his own, though in different ways.

When we have attained that blessedness, what is above us will be ours to behold; what is equal to us will be ours for companionship; and what is below us will be ours to rule. Let the utterly secure elder brother therefore rejoice, because his younger brother was dead and has come to life again; he was lost and has been found.

## XXXIV. [The same, XVI, 1–9]

In the steward whom the Lord was expelling from his stewardship, and whom he praised because he had provided for his future, we must not take everything as something to imitate. We are not permitted either to commit fraud in any matter against our Lord and then give alms from that fraud, or to understand those from whom we wish to be received into eternal dwellings as debtors of God and our Lord.

Rather, the righteous and holy are signified here as those who introduce into eternal dwellings people who have shared earthly goods with them in their necessities. Concerning such people he also says that if someone gives one of them merely a cup of cold water in the name of a disciple, he will not lose his reward (Matthew 10:42).

But these comparisons are also drawn in the opposite direction, so that we may understand that if the Lord could praise a man who was committing fraud, how much more do those please the Lord God who perform such works according to his command. He likewise drew a comparison from the unjust judge who was importuned by a widow to God the Judge, to whom the unjust judge cannot be compared in any respect (Luke 18:2–8).

As for the steward’s instruction that the debtor write fifty instead of one hundred measures of oil, and eighty instead of one hundred measures of wheat, I think it has no other purpose than that each person’s righteousness may exceed that of the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew 5:20) in what he does for Christ’s Church, as the Jews do in like manner for the Levites [Note: [Col. 1349] Thus the better manuscripts, as also Rat., Am., and Er., except that these editions read “Church” in place of “for the Church.” Lov. reads: “What each person does in Christ’s Church for the priests and Levites, as the Jews do similarly.”]. Thus, while they gave tithes, these people should give half, as Zacchaeus did—not from the produce but from his actual possessions (Luke 19:8); or at least they should double the tithe, surpassing the expenditures of the Jews by giving two tithes.

The Lord calls this money “the mammon of iniquity” because we possess it only for a time. “Mammon” is interpreted as “wealth,” and such wealth exists only for the unjust, who place in it the hope and abundance of their blessedness. When the righteous possess these things, they are indeed money, but they are not their wealth; their wealth is heavenly and spiritual. By these heavenly and spiritual riches, spiritually supplying their need and excluding the poverty of misery, they are enriched with an abundance of blessedness.

## XXXV. [The same, XVI, 12]

When he says, “If you have not been faithful in what belongs to another,” he calls earthly possessions “another’s,” because no one takes them away with him when he dies. This is what David says: “Do not be afraid when a man becomes rich and when the glory of his house is multiplied, because when he dies he will take nothing with him, nor will his glory descend with him” (Psalm 48:17–18).

## XXXVI. [The same, XVI, 13]

What he says—“Either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will cling to the one and despise the other”—must be distinguished with care. These words were not spoken casually or thoughtlessly.

No one, when asked whether he loves the devil, answers that he does, but rather that he hates him. Almost everyone proclaims that he loves God. Therefore, “he will hate the one and love the other” describes what ought to happen: he will hate the devil and love God.

But when he adds, “Or he will cling to the one and despise the other,” this means that he will cling to the devil when he pursues, as though they were the devil’s rewards, temporal rewards; but he will despise God. He did not say “hate,” but “despise,” as those commonly do who subordinate God’s threats to their desires and flatter themselves into impunity because of his goodness.

To such people Solomon says: “My son, do not add sin upon sin, and say, ‘The mercy of God is great’” (Ecclesiasticus 5:5–6).

## XXXVII. [The same, XVI, 16]

[Col. 1350]

“The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and those who use force seize it” (Matthew 11:12). This means not only that each person should despise these things, but also that he should despise the tongues of those who mock him for despising them. By this force, as though he were a violent plunderer, he somehow invades the kingdom of heaven. The Evangelist added this after saying that Jesus had been mocked by the Pharisees when he spoke about despising earthly wealth.

## XXXVIII. [The same, XVI, 19–31]

“There was a certain rich man, and he was clothed in purple and fine linen, and he feasted splendidly every day,” and so forth.

Allegorically, these things may be understood as follows. In the rich man, the proud among the Jews may be understood: those who were ignorant of God’s righteousness and wanted to establish their own (Romans 10:5). Purple and fine linen signify the dignity of kingship. “The kingdom of God,” he says, “will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing righteousness” (Matthew 21:43).

The splendid feasting signifies their boasting in the Law, in which they gloried, using it more for the display of self-exaltation than for the necessity of salvation.

The beggar named Lazarus—which is interpreted as “Helped”—signifies someone in need, such as a Gentile or a tax collector, who is helped all the more because he does not presume upon the abundance of his possessions. Such were the two men who prayed in the temple: one a tax collector and the other a Pharisee.

The rich man, therefore, as though satiated with righteousness and not numbered among those who hunger and thirst for righteousness (Matthew 5:6), says: “I thank you that I am not like this tax collector.” But the poor man, who desires to be helped, says: “Be merciful to me, a sinner” (Luke 18:10–13).

Yet he desires to be filled with the crumbs that fall from the rich man’s table, lying at his gate. He was not admitted to the rich man’s feasts, because the rich man neither used his possessions well nor gave to the needy—like the scribe who had the keys of the kingdom of heaven, but neither entered himself nor allowed others to enter (Luke 11:52).

The crumbs falling from the rich man’s table are certain words of the Law, which they tossed about as though throwing them onto the ground when they spoke proudly to the people. The sores are confessions of sins, like foul humors bursting outward from the innermost parts. The dogs that licked them are utterly wicked people who love sins and, with their broad tongues, do not cease to praise the evil works that another person, groaning and confessing, detests in himself.

Abraham’s bosom is the rest of the blessed poor, theirs being the kingdom of heaven, into which they are received after this life. The burial-place of hell is the depth of punishments that, after this life, devours the proud and merciless. Yet the Lord says in this narrative that they see from afar and perceive the rest of the blessed, though they certainly cannot cross over to it.

When he asks that his tongue be cooled, although he was burning entirely in the flame, this signifies what is written: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs 18:21). It also signifies that “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10), which he had not done because of his pride.

The tip of the finger, or the smallest work of mercy, signifies the assistance given through the Holy Spirit. When he is told, “You received good things during your life,” this refers to the fact that he loved the happiness of this age and loved no other life besides the present one, in which he swelled with pride.

He says that Lazarus received evil things because he understood the mortality, labors, pains, and troubles of this life as punishments for sin. Concerning this it is written: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3). It is written again that not even an infant whose life is a single day upon the earth is free from sin (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint), because all of us die in Adam (1 Corinthians 15:22), who became mortal through transgression.

When he says that the righteous cannot cross over, even if they wished, to the places where the impious are tormented, what else does this signify except that, after this life, when people have been received into prison so that they do not leave until they have paid the last farthing (Matthew 5:26), no assistance of mercy can be provided by the righteous, even if they wished to provide it, because of the unchangeability of the divine judgment?

By this he clearly warns people to help those whom they can during this life, lest afterward, even if they have been received in the best possible way, they be unable to assist those whom they love.

For what is written—“so that they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke 16:9)—was not written concerning the proud and merciless, such as this rich man is shown to have been, as though they might deserve to be received by the saints into those dwellings. It was written concerning those who have made friends for themselves through the most diligent works of mercy.

Even the righteous do not receive them as though by their own power, dispensing favors; rather, they receive them by the promise and permission of the one who advised them to make friends for themselves, and who, in the goodness of the Deliverer, deigned to be fed, clothed, received as a guest, and visited in each of the least of his people.

Whether this reception takes place immediately after this life, or at the end of the age, in the resurrection of the dead and the final retribution of judgment, is no small question. But whenever it occurs, Scripture certainly promises no such reception concerning people of the kind represented by that rich man.

But the five brothers whom he says he has in his father’s house signify the Jews. They are called five because they were held under the Law given through Moses, who wrote five books. By asking that Lazarus be sent to his brothers, he evidently felt himself unworthy to bear witness to the truth; and because he had not obtained even a little relief [Note: [Col. 1351] Manuscripts: “a little relief for himself.” Perhaps, “for his palate,” etc.], he believed still less that he could be released from the underworld for the preaching of the truth. When Abraham says, “If they are willing to believe, they have Moses and the Prophets,” he does not place these before the Gospel; rather, because the Gospel, as the Apostle says, has testimony from the Law and the Prophets (Rom. 3:21), he indicates that by believing them they can arrive at the Gospel. Thus the Lord himself says elsewhere, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). Finally, this is the point of what he says afterward: “If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead.” For Moses and the Prophets foretold the one who rose from the dead, including this very thing about him, that he was to rise [Col. 1352] from the dead; by not believing them, they plainly do not wish to believe Christ either. Much less, then, can they believe just anyone who rises from the dead, when they do not believe the one whose resurrection Moses and the Prophets proclaimed, though they refuse to believe them.

This narrative may also be understood in another way, so that we take Lazarus to signify the Lord, lying at the gate of that rich man because he humbled himself to the ears of the exceedingly proud Jews through the lowliness of his incarnation. He desired to be filled with the crumbs that fell from the rich man’s table, seeking from them even the smallest works of righteousness—works which, through pride, they did not claim for the use of their own table, that is, their own power. These works of mercy and humility, although minimal and performed without discipline or perseverance in a good life, they might at least do occasionally or by chance, as crumbs customarily fall from a table. The sores are the Lord’s sufferings, arising from the weakness of the flesh which he graciously undertook for us. The dogs that licked them are therefore the Gentiles, whom the Jews called sinful and unclean, yet who throughout the whole world now lick the Lord’s sufferings in the sacraments of his body and blood with the sweetest devotion.

The bosom of Abraham is now understood as the Father’s secret place, to which the Lord, rising after his passion, was taken up. I think he is said to have been carried there by angels because the angels announced to the disciples who were watching that very reception by which he withdrew into the Father’s secret place. For when they said, “Why do you stand looking into heaven?” (Acts 1:11), what else did they mean than that human eyes could in no way penetrate to that secret place where the Lord was going, when he was carried into heaven before the eyes of the disciples? The remaining details can now be understood according to the preceding interpretation, since the Father’s secret place is rightly understood as the place where, even before the resurrection, the souls of the righteous live with God. For God is truly everywhere precisely because he is contained by no place. Thus also it was said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). The Son of God never departed from there, although through the flesh he had assumed he suffered so greatly at the hands of human beings in the city of the Jews.

### XXXIX. [On XVII, 5–10]

What the disciples said to the Lord—“Increase our faith”—can indeed be understood as their request that he increase the faith by which things not seen are believed. Yet there is also a faith concerning realities themselves, when belief is directed not through words but through the realities present themselves. This will occur when God’s Wisdom itself, through which all things were made (Ps. 103:24), will offer itself to the saints for contemplation in manifest vision. Perhaps the Apostle Paul speaks of this faith in realities and of that light made present [Note: [Col. 1352] Four manuscripts read “presence.”] when he says: “For the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith” (Rom. 1:17). He says elsewhere: “But we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are transformed into the same image, from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3:18). As he says here, “from glory to glory,” so there he says, “from faith to faith”: from the glory of the Gospel, by which believers are now illumined, into the glory of that unchangeable and manifest truth [Col. 1353] in which, once transformed, they will then rejoice; thus from faith in the words by which we now believe what we do not yet see, into faith in the realities by which we shall eternally possess what we now believe. In accordance with this interpretation, John also says in his Epistle to the Parthians: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). For why are we now children of God, unless because “he gave us power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12), so that we may see “in a mirror dimly” (1 Cor. 13:12)? And why shall we then be like him, unless because, as he himself says, “we shall see him as he is”? This is also expressed in the words, “Then face to face.”

To many who do not understand it, our Lord’s answer may therefore appear unrelated to what the disciples had asked. For when they said to the Lord, “Increase our faith,” he said to them: “If you had faith like a grain of mustard seed, you would say to this mulberry tree, ‘Be uprooted and planted in the sea,’ and it would obey you.” Then he continues: “Which of you, having a servant plowing or tending sheep, who, when he returns from the field, will say to him at once, ‘Come over and recline’; and will not say to him, ‘Prepare what I may eat, gird yourself, and serve me until I have eaten and drunk, and afterward you shall eat and drink’? Does he thank that servant because he did what he had commanded? I do not think so. So you also, when you have done all that was commanded you, say: ‘We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.’”

It is difficult to see how this relates to the request, “Increase our faith,” unless we understand that he signified their being transferred from faith to faith—that is, from the faith in which God is served into the faith in which God is enjoyed. Faith will increase when belief is directed first toward the words that proclaim and afterward toward the realities that appear. But that contemplation has supreme rest, which is granted in God’s eternal kingdom; and that supreme rest is the reward of the righteous labors carried out in the ministry of the Church. Therefore, although the servant plows or tends sheep in the field—that is, conducts affairs in secular or earthly life, or serves foolish people as though they were sheep—he must return home after those labors, that is, join himself to the fellowship of the Church. He must also labor there, serving his Lord until he eats and drinks. For he too was hungry when he sought fruit on the tree (Matt. 21:18–19), and, thirsty, asked the Samaritan woman for water (John 4:7). Let him therefore eat and drink the confession and faith of the nations, while his servants—those who serve by preaching the Gospel—minister to him.

This also relates to the first answer he gave them concerning the grain of mustard seed: they must first have the faith necessary for the present life, which appears very small so long as the treasure is in earthen vessels, but which boils up and grows with immense power. Our Lord Jesus Christ, who desires to be nourished by the ministry of his servants—that is, to transfer believers into his body as though they had been slain and eaten—also nourishes them here with the word of faith and the sacrament of his passion. [Col. 1354] “For he came not to be served but to serve” (Matt. 20:28).

Let those servants therefore say through the grain of mustard seed to this mulberry tree—that is, to the very Gospel of the Lord’s cross, through its blood-red fruits, like wounds hanging upon the wood and destined to provide food for the peoples [Note: [Col. 1354] Rat. and the Cistercian manuscript read, “destined to provide wine for the peoples.”]—let them say that it should be uprooted from the unbelief of the Jews and transferred and planted in the sea of the Gentiles. By this domestic service they will minister to the hungry and thirsty Lord. Then, at last, let them seek to enjoy divine Wisdom forever in incorruptible food, when they have said: “We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we were obliged to do.” No work remains for us; we have finished the course, completed the contest; there remains for us the crown of righteousness (2 Tim. 4:7–8).

Everything may be said concerning that ineffable enjoyment of the truth—and the more so because nothing can be said about it worthily. It is the light of the illumined, the rest of those who have labored, the homeland of those returning, the food of those in need, and the crown of those who conquer. Whatever transient goods error seeks through the parts of creation, the piety of the children will find simultaneously in the Creator of all things in truer and eternal forms.

### XL. [On XVII, 12–19]

Many questions may properly arise concerning the ten lepers whom the Lord cleansed when he said, “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” Questions may be asked not only about what is meant by the number ten and by the fact that only one of them gives thanks—for such questions may freely be raised, and even if they remain unexplored they will impede the reader’s purpose little or not at all—but rather about why he sent them to the priests, so that they would be cleansed as they went. Of all those to whom he granted bodily benefits, he is found to have sent none to the priests except lepers. He had also cleansed from leprosy the man to whom he said: “Go, show yourself to the priests, and offer for your cleansing the sacrifice that Moses commanded, as a testimony to them” (Luke 5:13–14). Then there is the question of what spiritual cleansing can be understood in the case of those whom he rebuked for having proved ungrateful. In bodily terms, it is easy to see that a person may not have leprosy and yet may not possess a good disposition. But according to the significance of this miracle, the consideration troubles us: how can one who is ungrateful be called clean?

We must therefore ask what leprosy itself signifies. Those who are free from it are not called healed but cleansed, for it is a defect of color, not of health or of the integrity of the senses and limbs. Lepers may therefore reasonably be understood as those who do not possess knowledge of the true faith but profess various doctrines of error. They do not conceal their ignorance; rather, they bring it into the light as though it were supreme expertise and display it through the boastfulness [Note: [Col. 1354] All our manuscripts read “boastfulness”; a little below, instead of “with the pigments of colors,” they read “with the places of colors.”] of their speech. Moreover, there is no false doctrine that does not mix in some truths. Truths therefore mixed disorderly with falsehoods, appearing in a person’s single argument or narrative as colors in a single body, signify leprosy, as though varying and staining human bodies with the pigments of true and false [Col. 1355] colors. Such people must be avoided by the Church; if possible, they should stand at a distance and call upon Christ with a loud cry. Thus these ten stood far away and raised their voices, saying, “Jesus, Teacher, have mercy on us.” Their calling him “Teacher”—a title by which, so far as I know, no one called upon the Lord for bodily healing—adequately signifies, I think, that leprosy is false doctrine, which the good Teacher wipes away.

Almost no believer doubts that the priesthood of the Jews was a figure of the future royal priesthood that exists in the Church, through which all who belong to Christ’s body, the supreme and true chief priest, are consecrated. Now all are anointed, whereas at that time only kings and priests were anointed. And when Peter, writing to the Christian people, says, “A royal priesthood” (1 Pet. 2:9), he declares that both names belong to that people to whom the anointing pertained.

All other faults, as diseases of the soul’s members and senses, the Lord himself heals and corrects inwardly in the conscience and understanding. But teaching—whether formation through the sacraments or catechesis through spoken discourse and reading—where a certain true and sincere color is understood because it is readily apparent and most conspicuous outwardly (for these things are carried out not in hidden thoughts but in manifest actions), has been specially entrusted to the Church.

Thus Paul, although he heard the Lord’s voice—“Why are you persecuting me?” and “I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting”—was nevertheless sent to Ananias, so that through the priesthood established in the Church he might receive the sacrament of the doctrine of faith, and so that the true color of his faith might be approved (Acts 9:4–19). This is not because the Lord cannot do everything by himself—for who else performs these things even in the Church?—but so that the society of gathered believers, by approving and sharing among themselves the doctrine of the true faith in all that is spoken in words or signified in sacraments, might overlay everything with a single appearance of true color.

This is also relevant to what the same Apostle says: “Then after fourteen years I went up to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus with me. I went up according to a revelation, and I laid before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed [Note: [Col. 1355] The printed editions read, “those who seemed to be something.” Four manuscripts read “those who seem.” These codices, as well as others among the manuscripts, do not add “to be something”; this is also absent from the ancient Corbei manuscripts of the Vulgate, nor is it present in the Greek text of the Apostle except as *toîs dokoûsi*, that is, according to Augustine’s exposition in his commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, “those who were prominent in the Church.”] prominent, lest somehow I should be running, or had run, in vain.” And shortly afterward: “When they recognized,” he says, “the grace given to me, James, Cephas, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave the right hand of fellowship to me and Barnabas” (Gal. 2:1–2, 9). This very comparison displayed one form of doctrine, excluding every kind of variation. Paul also wisely admonishes the Corinthians concerning this, saying: “I appeal to you, brothers, by the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, that you all say the same thing” (1 Cor. 1:10).

Although Cornelius’s almsgiving was accepted and his prayers were heard, and an angel announced this to him, he was nevertheless commanded to send to Peter because of the unity of doctrine and the sacraments, as though it were said to him and his household: “Go, show yourselves to the priests.” For as they went, they were cleansed. Peter had already come to them, but they had not yet received the sacrament of baptism and had not yet reached the priests spiritually. Nevertheless, their cleansing was declared by the outpouring of the Holy Spirit and by the wonder of tongues (Acts 10:44).

Since these things are so, it is now easy to see that someone may acquire a complete and true doctrine within the fellowship of the Church and explain everything according to the rule of the catholic faith [Note: [Col. 1356] Three reliable manuscripts read, “explain according to the catholic rule,” omitting “of the faith.” Another reads, “explain according to the catholic rule.”], distinguishing the creature from the Creator. In this way he may be shown to have been free from the variety of falsehoods, like leprosy. Yet he may still be ungrateful to God and to his Lord and cleanser, because, lifted up by pride, he is not brought low by the pious humility of giving thanks. He becomes like those of whom the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks” (Rom. 1:21). In saying that they knew God, he shows that they had indeed been cleansed from leprosy; yet he immediately accuses them of ingratitude.

Such people will therefore remain in the number nine, as imperfect. If one is added to nine, a certain image of unity is completed; so great is the completion that the number does not proceed beyond it unless it returns again to one, and this rule is preserved through the infinity of number. Nine therefore needs one in order to be joined together into a certain form of unity and become ten; one, however, does not need them in order to preserve unity.

Accordingly, just as the nine who did not give thanks were rejected and excluded from the fellowship of unity, so the one who gave thanks was approved and praised as a sign of the one Church. Since the others were Jews, they were shown to have lost through pride the kingdom of heaven, where unity is preserved above all. But the one who was a Samaritan—whose name is interpreted as “Guardian”—gave back to the one from whom he had received what he had received, and, as it were, sang the words of the Psalm, “I will guard my strength toward you” (Ps. 58:10). By giving thanks, he became subject to the king and preserved the unity of the kingdom through humble devotion.

### XLI. [On XVII, 31]

What does the Lord mean when he says, “Whoever is on the housetop, and his vessels are in the house, let him not come down to take them”? He is on the housetop who, rising above carnal things, lives spiritually in the free air. His vessels in the house are the carnal senses, by which many, using them to investigate the truth grasped by the understanding, have gone completely astray. The vessels of this spiritual person are therefore now lying unused in the house, because, rising above the body in mind and placed, as it were, on the housetop through the sharpness of understanding, he enjoys the clarity of wisdom as though beneath a completely open sky. Let him beware, then, lest on the day of tribulation, delighted once again by carnal life—which is nourished through the bodily senses—he descend to take up such vessels.

### XLII. [On XVII, 31]

[Col. 1357]

What does the statement mean: “And whoever is in the field, likewise, let him not return backward”? Whoever works in the Church, as Paul and Apollos plant and water (1 Cor. 3:6), should not look back toward the worldly hope he has renounced.

### XLIII. [On XVII, 32]

What did Lot’s wife signify? Those who, in tribulation, look backward and turn away from the hope of the divine promise. Therefore she was made into a pillar of salt, so that, by warning people not to do this, she might, as it were, season their hearts lest they become foolish.

### XLIV. [On XVII, 34–35]

Who are the two in one bed, the two women grinding together, and the two in the field, concerning all of whom one of each pair will be taken and one left behind?

Three classes of people seem to be signified here. The first consists of those who choose leisure and quiet, occupied neither with secular business nor with ecclesiastical affairs; their rest is signified by the word “bed.” The second consists of those established among the congregations and governed by the more learned [Note: [Col. 1357] Rat. and five manuscripts read, “by teachers.”], while they carry out the affairs of this world. He signified them by the name of women because, as I have said, it is advantageous for them to be governed by the counsels of the experienced. He said that they were grinding because of the circuit and round of temporal affairs; yet he said that they were grinding together insofar as, from those very affairs and occupations, they provide things useful to the Church.

The third consists of those who work in the ministry of the Church, as in God’s field, concerning which the Apostle speaks of agriculture (1 Cor. 3:9). In each of these three classes there are again two kinds of people, distinguished according to the strength of their powers. Although all may appear to belong to the members of the Church, when the temptation of tribulation arrives, some from those who are at leisure, some from those occupied with worldly business, and some from those who serve God in the Church remain steadfast, while others fall. Those who remain are taken; those who fall are left behind.

Thus “one will be taken and one left behind” is not said as though it referred to two individual people, but to two kinds of disposition within each of the three professions. When he says “in that night,” he means “in that tribulation.”

I believe that the three classes who are taken also correspond to the three names of holy men whom the prophet Ezekiel declares alone to be delivered: Noah, Daniel, and Job (Ezek. 14:14). Noah seems to belong to those through whom the Church is governed, just as the ark was guided through the waters by him (Gen. 7:7), and the ark bore the figure of the Church. Daniel, who chose a celibate life—that is, despised earthly marriage—so that, as the Apostle says, he might live without anxiety, considering the things of God (1 Cor. 7:32, 34), signifies the class of those who are at leisure but nevertheless are exceedingly strong in temptations, so that they may be taken.

Job, because he had a wife and children and abundant stores of earthly goods (Job 1:1–3), belongs to the class to which the mill is assigned; yet they too must be exceedingly strong in temptations, as he was, for otherwise they cannot be taken. I do not think there are other classes of people of whom the Church consists besides these three, each having two divisions [Col. 1358] on account of being taken or left behind. Although within each class many differences of pursuits and desires may be found, they nevertheless converge toward harmony and unity.

### XLV. [On XVIII, 1–8]

Why did he wish to offer, as an example of praying always and not losing heart, the parable of an unjust judge who, although he did not fear God and had no regard for human beings, nevertheless yielded to a widow’s persistent appeals and avenged her, lest she weary him? For this is what he says: “Lest, by continually coming, she wear me out.”

The Lord presents parables either according to some similarity, as in the case of the servant whose master forgave what he was found to owe when the accounts were rendered, while he himself would not grant even a delay to his fellow servant (Matt. 18:23–35); and the moneylender who, when he had forgiven the debts of two debtors, was loved more by the one to whom he had forgiven more (Luke 7:41–43); and the man who had two sons, the elder near him in the field and the younger living wantonly in a distant land (Luke 15:11–32); and countless examples of this kind. From these, insofar as they are similar, an understanding is drawn of the matter to which they are applied, whether to make it known or to seek it [Note: [Col. 1358] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “of the matter to which they are applied for making known or seeking the mystery of the truth.”]

Or he proves something from the very dissimilarity, as in the statement: “If God so clothes the grass of the field, which is here today and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, how much more will he clothe you, people of little faith?” (Matt. 6:30). The parable of the servant whose master had announced that he was to be removed from his stewardship also belongs to this class. The servant defrauded his master by falsifying the accounts and remitting to his debtors whatever amount seemed advantageous to him. The Lord certainly does not exhort us to defraud him; but if someone provided for his future by fraud, he says that the man was praised by his master. How much more eagerly, then, should those provide for eternal life who are commanded to act justly with the mammon of unrighteousness (Luke 16:1)? This has been explained in its proper place (above, Question 34).

The parable of the man who was awakened, already asleep, not out of friendship but to avoid annoyance, so that he might lend his friend three loaves, also belongs to this class. If that man, compelled by irritation, gave what was requested, how much more will God, who loves his servants and urges them to ask, give good things to those who ask him (Matt. 7:7–11)? Thus the former kind of parable can be joined to the others with the words, “As that is so, so also is this”; the latter with the words, “If that is so, how much more is this?” or, “If that is not so, how much less is that?” Sometimes these comparisons are stated obscurely, sometimes plainly.

This unjust judge, then, is introduced not by similarity but by dissimilarity, so that the Lord might show how much more certain should be those who persistently beseech God, the source of justice and mercy—or, if something more excellent can be said or heard, how much more certain should they be—when the perseverance of the petitioner prevailed with an extremely unjust judge until his desire was fulfilled.

The widow herself may bear a likeness to the Church, which appears desolate until the Lord comes, although even now he cares for her in secret. If it troubles us that God’s elect are said to pray for vengeance—something also said of the martyrs in John’s Apocalypse (Rev. 6:10)—while we are most plainly instructed to pray for our enemies and persecutors (Matt. 5:44), we must understand the vengeance of the righteous to be that all wicked people perish. They perish in two ways: either by conversion to righteousness or by losing, through punishment, the power by which they now have some temporary strength against the good, for as long as this is beneficial to the good.

Thus, even if all human beings were converted to God, including the enemies for whom we are commanded to pray, the devil would nevertheless remain to be condemned at the end of the world—the one who works in the children of unbelief (Eph. 2:2). When the righteous desire that this end should come, they may therefore rightly be said to desire vengeance, even though they pray for their enemies.

### XLVI. [On XIX, 12–27]

“A certain nobleman went into a distant country to receive a kingdom for himself and return”: this is understood to be our Lord Jesus Christ. The distant country is the Church of the Gentiles, extending to the ends of the earth. Yet he says that he will return: he went away so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter, and he will return so that all Israel may be saved (Rom. 11:25).

By the ten minas he signifies the Law, because of the Decalogue. The ten servants are those placed under it, to whom grace was preached. The minas are understood to have been given to them for use when they understood that the Law itself, with its veil removed, pertained to the Gospel.

His citizens who sent an embassy after him, saying that they did not want him to reign over them, are the Jews, who even after his resurrection sent persecutors against the Apostles [Note: [Col. 1359] Rat. and two manuscripts read, “sent persecutions against the Apostles”; shortly afterward, three other manuscripts read, “and preachers of the Gospel.”] and rejected the preaching of the Gospel.

He returned after receiving the kingdom because he will come in the most manifest and exalted glory, having appeared humble to them when he said, “My kingdom is not of this world” (John 18:36). The servants who render an account of what they had received, and those who have gained profit are praised, signify that those give a good account who have used well what they received, in order to increase the Lord’s riches through those who believe in him.

Those who do not wish to do this are represented by the servant who kept his mina in a handkerchief. There are people who flatter themselves in this perverse way, saying: “It is enough for each person to give an account of himself. Why is it necessary to preach or minister to others, so that one may also be compelled to give an account of them, when even those to whom the Law was not given and who have not heard the Gospel are inexcusable before the Lord, because they could know the Creator through creation—his invisible attributes being understood and perceived through the things that have been made from the foundation of the world?” (Rom. 1:20).

This is like reaping where he did not sow: that is, holding even those guilty of impiety to whom the word of the Law or Gospel was not ministered. Seeking to avoid this apparent danger of judgment, they rest in the sluggish weakness of withdrawing from the ministry of the word. This is like tying up what they received in a handkerchief.

The table on which the money was to be placed we understand as the profession of religion, which is set forth publicly [Col. 1360], as it were, for the use necessary to salvation. The fact that one of those who used what they had received well gained ten and another five signifies that those people were gained for the flock of God by whom the Law itself was understood through grace—either because it is contained in the Decalogue or because the one through whom it was given wrote five books. The ten and five cities over which he placed them also pertain to this.

The multiplication of understanding in the very diversity that springs from each commandment or each book, when reduced to unity, makes, as it were, a city of living and eternal rational beings. For a city is not a multitude of just any living creatures but a multitude of rational beings bound together by the fellowship of one law.

The fact that what the servant who refused to use it had received is taken away and given to the one who had ten signifies that someone may lose God’s gift who, though possessing it, does not possess it—that is, does not use it—and that it may be increased in the one who possesses it by using it well.

His enemies whom he commands to be killed in his presence signify the impiety of the Jews who refused to be converted to him.

### XLVII. [On XVIII, 25–27]

What does he mean by saying, “It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God”? Here he calls rich the person who is greedy for temporal things and proud of such possessions. Opposed to these rich people are the poor in spirit, to whom the kingdom of heaven belongs (Matt. 5:3).

This makes clear that all greedy people—even if they lack the resources of this world—belong to the class of rich people being reproved. For afterward those who heard said, “Who then can be saved?” although the incomparably greater crowd consists of the poor. They evidently understood that those who do not possess such things nevertheless belong to this number if they are seized by the desire to possess them.

The meaning is that it is easier for Christ to suffer for lovers of the world than for lovers of the world to be converted to Christ. He wished himself to be understood by the name “camel,” because he humbled himself and bore burdens. What could show this more clearly than the statement, “The greater you are, the more humble yourself in all things” (Sir. 3:20)?

By the needle he signifies the pricks; by the pricks, the pains endured in the passion. The eye of the needle therefore means the constraints of the passion. When he says, “The things that are impossible with human beings are possible with God,” this must not be understood to mean that the greedy and proud, signified by the name of the rich man, will enter the kingdom of heaven with their greed and pride. Rather, it is possible for God, through his word—as we see has already happened and continues to happen daily—to convert people from the desire for temporal things to the love of eternal things, and from destructive pride to saving humility.

### XLVIII. [On XVIII, 35–43]

We could understand the phrase about those approaching Jericho to mean that they had already gone out from it but were still near the city. This is indeed less customary usage, but it might nevertheless be understood in this way, since Matthew says that two blind men who were sitting beside the road were given sight as they were leaving Jericho (Matt. 20:29–34).

There is no difficulty concerning the number if one of the Evangelists remained silent about one of them, [Col. 1361] remembering only the other. Mark also mentions one, saying that he was given sight as they were leaving Jericho; he gives both the man’s name and his father’s name (Mark 10:46–52). We should understand that this man was very well known and the other unknown, so that the well-known one could appropriately be mentioned alone.

But since what follows in the Gospel according to Luke most plainly shows that the event he narrates occurred while they were still approaching Jericho, nothing remains except to understand that this miracle happened twice: once to one blind man while he was still coming into the city, and again to two as he was leaving it. Thus Luke narrated the first event and Matthew the second, and this was not without some sacramental significance.

If we interpret Jericho as “moon,” and therefore as mortality, then, as the Lord approached death, he commanded the light of the Gospel to be preached to the Jews alone, signified by the one blind man whom Luke mentions. But when he rose from the dead and departed, he gave light both to Jews and Gentiles, whom the two blind men mentioned by Matthew appear to signify as the two peoples.

### [On XIX, 45–46]

[Note: [Col. 1361] Augustine does not list this annotation on the temple in the summary of questions prefixed to this work. In the Lovaniensis edition it begins as follows: “In the Gospel, you will understand the temple itself as God made man”; but other manuscripts add neither “God” nor “made.”]

In the Gospel, understand the temple as the human being himself, or even, with his body added, as the Church. According to what he is as the head of the Church, the saying was spoken: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). But according to what is understood as the temple together with the Church attached to it, he appears to have said: “Take these things away from here”; for it is written, “My house shall be called a house of prayer, but you have made it a house of commerce,” or “a den of robbers” (John 2:16).

He signified that there would be people in the Church who would conduct their own business there, or use it as a hiding place for concealing their crimes, rather than follow the love of Christ and, having received forgiveness through the confession of their sins, be corrected.

### XLIX. [On XX, 36]

He said, “They cannot die anymore,” because marriages exist for the sake of children, children for the sake of succession, and succession for the sake of death. Where there is no death, therefore, there are no marriages.

Just as our speech is carried out and completed through syllables that pass away and succeed one another, so human beings, whose speech it is, carry out and complete the order of this age through passing away and succeeding one another; that order is woven together by the beauty of temporal things. But in that life, since the Word of God whom we shall enjoy is not completed through any passing away and succession of syllables but always possesses simultaneously all that it has, remaining forever, those who share in him, for whom he alone will be life, will neither pass away from one another by dying nor succeed one another by being born.

### L. [On XXII, 40 and 41]

When the Lord said to the disciples, “Pray that you do not enter into temptation,” and he himself withdrew from them about a stone’s throw, it was as though he were admonishing them to direct the stone toward him—that is, to bring the intention of the Law, which had been written on stone (Exod. 31:18; 34:4, 28), all the way to him. For that stone can reach him, since “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4).

### LI. [On XXIV, 28]

What is written about the Lord, “He pretended that he was going farther,” does not pertain to lying. For not everything we pretend is a lie; rather, it is a lie when we pretend something that signifies nothing. But when our pretence refers to some meaning, it is not a lie but a certain figure of truth. Otherwise everything said figuratively by wise and holy men, or even by the Lord himself, would be judged lies, because according to the customary understanding the truth does not subsist in such statements.

For the man who had two sons, the younger of whom, having received his share of the inheritance, departed into a far country, and the other things woven into that narrative (Luke 15:11–32), is not spoken of as though there really had been some man who had either suffered or done these things with his two sons. These things, then, were invented to signify something far greater and more extensive, and incomparably different, so that through that invented man the true God might be understood.

Just as statements are invented without lying in order to signify something, so also actions are invented for the same purpose. Hence there is also that action of the same Lord in which he sought fruit on the fig tree at a time when its fruit was not yet present (Mark 11:13). It is not doubtful that this seeking was not literal, for anyone would know—if not by divine knowledge, then by the season—that the tree did not have fruit. Thus a pretence that is referred to some truth is a figure; one that is not so referred is a lie.

What, then, does it signify that the Lord pretended to go farther when he was accompanying the disciples and explaining the holy Scriptures to them, though they did not know that it was he? What else, we may suppose, than that he intimated that human beings can arrive at knowledge of him through the duty of hospitality? Although he himself has gone farther from human beings, above all the heavens, he is nevertheless so present with those who show such hospitality to his servants that, when they begin to say, “Lord, when did we see you as a stranger and bring you in?”—as though they were speaking of one who had gone far away—he may answer them, “What you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:38, 40).

Whoever, therefore, has been instructed in the word and shares all good things with the one who instructs him keeps Christ from going farther away from him, just as the Apostle says: “Let the one who is instructed in the word share all good things with the one who instructs him” [Note: [Col. 1362] Thus Erasmus, the Louvain edition, Venice, and the Lovanienses; and Augustine himself in other passages. In B., “the word.”] (Galatians 6:6). And elsewhere, after saying, “Sharing in the needs of the saints,” he immediately adds, “Pursuing hospitality” (Romans 12:13). These men too had been instructed in the word when he was explaining the Scriptures to them; and because they pursued hospitality, they recognized in the breaking of bread the one whom they had not recognized during the exposition of the Scriptures. For “it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous before God, but the doers of the law will be justified” (Romans 2:13).

[Ibid. XXIII, 11.]

[Col. 1363]

[Note: [Col. 1363] This little annotation is neither counted in the list proposed above nor found here in all the manuscripts; nevertheless, it occurs in very many, including the most ancient Corbie manuscript. [Col. 1364] It is absent from the editions of Amerbach and Erasmus. In Ratramnus, however, as well as in the Sorbonne manuscript, it belongs to the following book, *Questions on Matthew*.]

When the Jews stripped the Lord of his own clothing during the Passion and dressed him in an artificially coloured garment (Matthew 27:28), these heretics were signified who say that he did not have a true body, but an artificial one.

# SEVENTEEN QUESTIONS ON MATTHEW

[Col. 1363]

## NOTICE ON THE BOOK OF SEVENTEEN QUESTIONS ON MATTHEW

That this book of *Questions on Matthew* is presented here among Augustine’s genuine works, while nevertheless not prefaced—as is customary—with Augustine’s name, has not been done rashly or without reason. In the first place, after Erasmus, the Louvain theologians judge that its style and subject matter agree with Augustine. Moreover, Rabanus Maurus quotes certain fragments of this same book under Augustine’s name in Book 4 of his *Commentary on the Gospel of Matthew*, which he composed around A.D. 840 by gathering together expositions of earlier writers from various sources. Finally, in the catalogue of Augustine’s works by Possidius, published by Johannes Ulimmer from the Villariensis manuscript, there are listed on page 5 two books of *Questions on the Gospels*, followed immediately by one book of *Various Annotations on Matthew*.

Nevertheless, there is a consideration that properly causes concern: Augustine makes no mention of this third book in the *Retractions*. Although he acknowledges only two books of *Questions on the Gospels*, he says that he reduced to them the questions he had dictated both on Matthew and on Luke; and he later observes that, wherever passages from the Evangelists mentioned above had been expounded, his prologue indicates this by adding and numbering the same questions. The relevant retraction is found in volume 1, column 634, and above, in this volume, on page 1321, in the list of all the questions restored by us under the Prologue. Likewise, in his revision of the book *Eighty-Three Questions*, he did not hesitate to list every question in order, without omitting even one. By this diligence the holy Doctor took care that we should not accept under his name questions of some other kind, and that scribes should not attach spurious appendices to his works—as they did rather freely in this sort of writing.

Nor can it be supposed that this third book was published later than the *Retractions* and was therefore not listed in them. For the parable of the weeds is explained here in a manner quite different from Augustine’s customary interpretation, especially from the time of the Carthaginian Conference, at which the Donatists, against the protests of the Catholics, vehemently maintained what is stated in Question 11, section 1 of this book: namely, that the field itself, according to the Lord’s interpretation, should be understood not as the Church but as the world. This may be seen in the Acts of the Conference, Part 3, chapters 258, 265, and following. On this matter Augustine writes in Book 70, entitled *After the Conference, to the Donatists*, chapter 8:

“For a long time they contended, saying that the weeds which were permitted to grow together with the wheat until the harvest are not in the Church but in the world, contrary to the understanding of the martyr Cyprian, who said: ‘Although weeds appear to be in the Church, nevertheless neither our faith nor our charity ought to be hindered.’”

What is more, in Question 12, section 2, this author not only does not turn against the Donatists, in Augustine’s manner, the householder’s response forbidding the weeds to be pulled up before the harvest; he interprets it in such a way that it cannot be turned against them. For he thinks that the subject is people who are not to be removed from this life.

There is also the silence of Abbot Eugippius, who long ago—that is, at the beginning of the sixth century—when he was compiling extensive collections from Augustine’s works, copied many questions from the two preceding books: at least four from the first and eighteen from the second. Yet we find no indication that he excerpted anything from this third book.

As for the ancient manuscripts, some contain the first two books without the third; others present this third book immediately after those two under the title, “Here begin the Questions on the Gospels,” without adding Augustine’s name. One copy of this second kind exists at Corbie, written, it seems, about nine hundred years ago, in addition to a much more recent Cistercian manuscript. Although the latter does not bear the same title, it agrees with the Corbie manuscript in not attributing the aforesaid book to Augustine.

Finally, after carefully examining the catalogue of Possidius in manuscripts of the highest quality, we have nowhere found what the Ulimmer edition alone contains concerning the subsequent work.

[Col. 1365]

## SEVENTEEN QUESTIONS ON THE GOSPEL ACCORDING TO MATTHEW

[Note: [Col. 1365] The book of *Seventeen Questions on Matthew* was collated with the same manuscripts as the preceding work, *Questions on the Gospels*, except for the Michaelinus and Arnulfensis manuscripts, in which this book is not found.]

[Note: [Col. 1365] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the *Retractions*, volume 1. M.]

(C, G)*

One book.

## QUESTION I [MATTHEW, CHAPTER 2, VERSE 16]

When it is said that infants from two years old and under were killed, this signifies that the humble, possessing a twofold charity, like children of two years, are able to die for Christ.

## II. [MATTHEW 10:27]

“What I say to you in the darkness”—that is, while you are still in carnal fear, because fear is darkness—“say in the light,” that is, in confidence in the truth, having received the Holy Spirit. “And what you hear in the ear, proclaim upon the housetops”: that is, proclaim what you hear in secret after trampling down the dwelling-place of the flesh.

## III. [MATTHEW 10:34–36]

“Do not suppose that I have come to bring peace upon the earth; I have not come to bring peace but a sword. For I have come to separate a man against his father.” This is because someone renounces the devil, who was his father.

“And a daughter against her mother”: the people of God against the worldly city—that is, the destructive society of the human race, which Scripture now signifies by the name Babylon, now Egypt, now Sodom, and now by various other names.

“A daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law”: the Church against the Synagogue, which according to the flesh gave birth to Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church.

They are divided by the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians 6:17).

“And a man’s enemies will be those of his household”: those with whom previously he had been entangled through familiarity.

## IV. [MATTHEW 8:1–3]

When, after descending from the mountain, where he had given commandments to the disciples and the crowd, he immediately heals a leper by stretching out his hand, this signifies those who were doubtful about fulfilling those commandments being cleansed by his help from such wavering.

## V. [MATTHEW 8:20]

When the Lord said to the scribe who wanted to follow him, “Foxes have dens and the birds of the sky have shelters, but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head,” this is understood as follows: the scribe, stirred by the Lord’s miracles, wanted to follow him for the sake of empty boasting, which is signified by the birds; but he pretended to be a disciple’s obedient follower, and this pretence is signified by the name of foxes. By laying his head down, however, he signified his humility, which had no place in that pretender and proud man.

## VI. [MATTHEW 8:22]

“Let the dead bury their own dead.” Here he called the unbelieving dead; “their own dead” means those who, likewise without faith, would depart from the body.

## VII. [MATTHEW 10:14]

“Shake the dust from your feet”: either as a testimony against the earthly labor that they would have undertaken for them in vain [Col. 1366]; or to show that they sought nothing earthly from them to such an extent that they would not even allow the dust of their land to cling to them.

## VIII. [MATTHEW 10:16]

“Be wise, therefore, as serpents”: for avoiding evil, by guarding the head, which is Christ. For the serpent exposes its entire body to its pursuer in defense of its head; or because, contracting itself through narrow spaces and stripping off its old skin, it is renewed. Those imitate this who were told, “Enter through the narrow gate” (Matthew 7:13), when they strip off the old man.

For if he were warning them to avoid evil in such a way that they should violently resist evil people, he would not previously have said, “I am sending you like sheep among wolves.”

He wanted them to be simple as doves, so as to harm no one. For this kind of bird kills none of the animals—not only the larger ones, against which it has no strength, but also the very smallest, by which even tiny sparrows are nourished.

There is a certain fellowship among all irrational living creatures, just as there is a fellowship proper to rational beings, that is, human beings—not only among themselves but also with the angels. From the likeness of doves, then, they learn to harm absolutely no one who belongs to their fellowship through participation in reason.

## IX. [MATTHEW 11:25]

“I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth.” It should be noted that “confession” is used in the praise of God. The Lord was not confessing sins, for he had none—especially since another evangelist records that he said this while rejoicing (Luke 10:21). Indeed, the very words he uses leave no doubt that they are spoken in God’s praise.

Thus Scripture generally calls “confession” whatever is openly declared, as it is seen. For when he says, “Whoever confesses me before human beings, I also will confess him before my Father” (Matthew 10:32), or, as it says elsewhere, “before the angels of God” (Luke 12:8), the one who confesses Christ is certainly not confessing sins.

If some think that confession is called this because Christ’s name is presented as a charge during persecution, does Christ likewise confess before the Father or before the angels the person who has confessed him?

It is also written in Ecclesiasticus: “And you shall say this in confession: The works of the Lord are all very good” (Ecclesiasticus 39:20–21). In that passage, without any doubt, the praises of God are being magnified.

This has been said because of the ignorance of the brethren who, when they hear the reader pronounce this word, immediately beat their breasts, without considering the context in which it is spoken, as though confession could refer only to sins.

## X. [MATTHEW 12:1–8]

With regard to what appeared unlawful to the Jews—that the disciples had plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath—one example was given from royal authority, namely David; another from priestly authority, namely those who violate the Sabbath through their temple service. This was so that the offense of plucking ears of grain on the Sabbath might apply even less to him who is the true king and true priest, and therefore the Lord of the Sabbath.

## XI. [MATTHEW 13:25–30, 36–43]

### 1

“When the people were sleeping, his enemy came and sowed weeds among the wheat, and went away.”

When the leaders of the Church were acting negligently, or when the Apostles entered the sleep of death, the devil came and sowed those whom the Lord interprets as evil children. But it is rightly asked whether these are heretics or Catholics who live badly.

Heretics too can be called evil children, because they were generated from the same seed of the Gospel and under the name of Christ, but turned by perverse opinions toward false doctrines. Yet since he says that they were sown among the wheat, they seem to be those who belong to one communion. Nevertheless, since the Lord interpreted the field itself not as the Church but as this world, heretics are rightly understood here: they are mingled with the good in this world not through the fellowship of one Church or one faith, but through the fellowship of the Christian name alone.

Thus those who are evil while sharing the same faith should be reckoned as chaff rather than weeds, because chaff shares the very same foundation with the grain and has a common root.

In that net in which bad and good fish are enclosed (Matthew 13:47–50), bad Catholics are not unreasonably understood. For the sea is one thing, signifying this world more broadly; the net is another, appearing to indicate the communion of one faith or one Church.

The difference between heretics and bad Catholics is that heretics believe false things, whereas the latter, while believing true things, do not live as they believe.

### 2

It is also customary to ask how schismatics differ from heretics. The answer is found in this: schismatics are not made so by a different faith, but by a broken fellowship of communion.

It may be doubted whether they should be numbered among the weeds. They appear more similar to corrupted ears of grain, as it is written: “The ungodly son will be corrupted by the wind” (Wisdom 4:4)—or to the broken awns of ears of grain, or to those that have been split and torn away from the crop. For the taller they are—that is, the prouder—the more fragile and lighter they are.

Yet it does not follow that every heretic or schismatic is bodily separated from the Church. If someone believes false things about God, or concerning some part of doctrine that pertains to the building up of faith, in such a way that he is not restrained by the hesitation of one who is searching, but by the firm conviction of one who believes, and is not merely differing through ignorance, opinion, or error, then he is a heretic and is outside in spirit, even though he may appear to be inside bodily.

The Church bears many such people, because they do not defend the falsehood of their opinion in such a way as to gather a determined multitude. If they do so, then they are expelled.

Likewise, all who envy the good, so that they seek opportunities to exclude or degrade them; or who are prepared to defend their own crimes, if they are charged or exposed, in such a way that they even plan to stir up separatist gatherings or disturbances in the Church—these are already schismatics, torn away from unity in their hearts, even if, when they find no opportunity or conceal their actions, they remain joined to the Church through bodily participation in its sacramental life.

### 3

Therefore, only those bad Catholics are rightly so called who, although they believe the truths pertaining to the doctrine of faith; who, if they do not know something, consider it something to be sought and examine it in a spirit of piety, without prejudice against the truth itself; and who love and honor good people, or those whom they think good, as much as they can—nevertheless live disgracefully and criminally, contrary to what they believe one ought to live.

Even if such people are exposed or accused, and are corrected for the sake of the discipline of the Church and their own salvation, or suspended from communion, they do not in any way think that they should withdraw from Catholic communion. Wherever they are permitted, they seek an opportunity for satisfaction; and sometimes through repentance they are changed into wheat, whether they have been corrected, removed, or even frightened by the word of God without anyone accusing or rebuking them by name.
