At other times, even under the name of penitents, they live as they usually do, or not much differently—some even worse. Nevertheless, they do not withdraw from Catholic unity. If death overtakes them while they are living in this way, they are reckoned as chaff until the end.

They themselves believe this as well. For if they believe otherwise and hold that belief firmly, they must already be numbered among the heretics, thinking that God will grant forgiveness to everyone who persists until the end of life in great iniquity, merely because they have maintained the unity of the Church—not with sincere love, for then they would live well [Note: [Col. 1368] Ratramnus omits “for then they would live well,” which is found in most manuscripts. Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain edition have in its place, “unless they should live well.” The Vatican manuscript has, “so that they would live well.”]—but chiefly from fear of punishment.

These people, then, do not believe this, or do not hold the opinion firmly, although perhaps they are still seeking. Rather, they are deceived by the hope of delay, while they think they will live longer and will eventually change their corrupt habits for the better.

Against such people it is said: “Do not delay turning to God, nor put it off from day to day; for his anger will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclesiasticus 5:8–9).

Those are converted who begin to live rightly; for this is what it means to return to God. But those who persistently follow their desires have, as it were, their backs turned toward God, even though, remaining in unity, they often attempt to look back at him with their necks twisted.

Thus these too, as the Prophet says, are “flesh, and a spirit that goes away and does not return” (Psalm 77:39). Nevertheless, as has been said, because of the same faith and unity of the Church, they are numbered neither among the weeds—for those are rooted outside—nor among the chaff of the awns, which dares to rise harshly above the grain in dissension and fragile arrogance, but, although lying beneath the grain, among the chaff that is to be separated at the final winnowing.

### 4

Good Catholics, however, are those who follow both an intact faith and good morals.

With regard to the doctrine of faith, if they have something that must be sought, they seek it in such a way that dangerous contention is absent—whether for the one who is seeking, for the person with whom the matter is being sought, or for those who listen to the discussion.

If they have something to teach, they teach in such a way that customary and well-established matters are presented, as far as they can, with the utmost assurance, confidence, and gentleness. Uncustomary matters, even when they have grasped them with the clearest manifestation of truth, they present in a mode of seeking rather than commanding or affirming, because of the weakness of the hearer.

For if some truth has such weight that it exceeds the learner’s strength, it should be suspended so as to stretch the one who is growing, not imposed so as to crush the little one.

Hence the Lord’s saying: “But when the Son of Man comes, do you suppose he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

Sometimes truth must also be concealed, but with an encouraging hope, so that despair does not make people colder, but desire makes them more capable of receiving it. Hence that saying of the same Lord: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12).

As for morals, this is well and briefly stated: one must either struggle against love of temporal goods so that it does not prevail; or that love, once subdued and brought under control, must remain subject so that, whenever it begins to rise, it may easily be restrained; or it must be extinguished so completely that it is stirred in no respect whatsoever.

As a result, some people bravely undergo death for the truth, others calmly, and others willingly. These three kinds are the fruits of the fertile earth: thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold (Matthew 13:8, 23). At the time of death, anyone who rightly considers his departure from this life must be found in one of these kinds.

### 5

Not only the weeds must be tolerated until the harvest—after the devil has scattered them by sowing perverse errors and false opinions, that is, after he has imposed heresies under the name of Christ, because he felt that he could accomplish nothing against the authority of so great a name except by concealing his deceptions under that same name; thus he himself lay hidden and became utterly concealed—this is what “and went away” means—but the chaff too must be tolerated until the winnowing.

The excellence of the grain is not more strongly demonstrated than by the disturbances caused by the chaff. Anyone who cannot restrain those disturbances by defending the truth has yielded while preserving unity.

Although in this parable the Lord, as he concluded in its interpretation, is understood to have signified not some but all scandals, and those who commit iniquity, under the name of weeds.

## XII. [MATTHEW 13:26–30]

### 1

“When the grass had grown and produced fruit, then the weeds also appeared.”

For when the spiritual person begins to be one who judges all things (1 Corinthians 2:15), errors begin to appear to him.

“But the servants said to him: Do you want us to go and gather them?”

Are these the servants whom he shortly afterward calls reapers? Or, since in the explanation of the parable he said that the reapers are angels, and no one would readily dare to say that the angels did not know who had sown the weeds, or that the weeds appeared to the angels only when the grass had produced fruit, should we rather understand that the faithful themselves are signified here under the name of servants—those whom he also calls the good seed?

It is not surprising that the same people are called both good seed and the servants of the householder, just as he says of himself that he is both the door and the shepherd (John 10:7, 11). For one thing can receive many different and diverse likenesses through different meanings.

This is especially clear because, when he was speaking to the servants, he did not say, “At the time of the harvest I will say to you, Gather the weeds,” but, he says, “I will say to the reapers.” From this it is understood that the gathering of the weeds for burning is another ministry, and that no son of the Church ought to think that this office belongs to him.

### 2

When someone, therefore, begins to be spiritual, he recognizes the errors of heretics and judges and distinguishes everything he hears or reads that is contrary to the rule of truth.

But until he is perfected in these spiritual matters and, as it were, matures into the fruit produced by the grass, he may be troubled by the question of why so many falsehoods of heretics have arisen under the Christian name.

Hence the servants say: “Did you not sow good seed in your field? From where, then, does it have weeds?”

Then, once he has recognized that the devil devised this fraud—when he realized that he had no power against the authority of so great a name, and therefore sought to conceal his deceptions under that same name—the person may be moved by a desire to remove such people from human affairs, if he has any opportunity.

But he consults the justice of God as to whether God commands or permits him to do this, and whether he wants this to be a human duty. Hence the servants say: “Do you want us to go and gather them?”

Truth itself answers them that a human being has not been placed in this life in such a way that he can be certain what each person will later become, when he sees that person’s error in the present, or what benefit that error may bring to the progress of the good.

Such people are not to be removed from this life, lest, while he attempts to kill the wicked, he kill those who might become good; or lest he harm the good, to whom such people may perhaps be useful even against their will.

This is to be done at the proper time, when at the end there remains neither time for changing one’s life nor an opportunity for advancing toward truth through the occasion and comparison provided by another’s error. But then it is done not by human beings but by angels.

Hence the householder answers: “No, lest while gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat together with them. But at the time of the harvest I will say to the reapers,” and so forth.

In this way he makes them most patient and peaceful.

### 3

It may be asked why he said, “Bind them into bundles for burning,” rather than saying that one bundle or one heap of weeds should be made.

Perhaps, because of the variety of heretics, who differ not only from the wheat but also from one another, he designated by the name of bundles the separate gatherings of each heresy, in which its members are individually bound together in their own fellowship.

They already begin to be bound for burning when, separated from Catholic communion, they begin to have their own quasi-churches. Their burning is to take place at the end of the world; for now, the binding of the bundles takes place.

But if this were so, many would not later repent and return to the Catholic Church, abandoning their error. Therefore the binding of the bundles too will take place at the end, so that each person’s error may be punished not indiscriminately but according to the measure of its perversity.

### 4

“Lest while gathering the weeds you uproot the wheat together with them.”

Is this because, while they are still weak, the good need the mixture of certain evil people—either in order to be exercised by them, or so that, by comparison with them, they may receive strong encouragement to strive toward what is better? If the evil were removed, the height of charity would wither as though uprooted. For the Apostle says: “That you, rooted and grounded in charity, may be able to comprehend” (Ephesians 3:17–18).

Or is the wheat uprooted together with the weeds because many are first weeds and later become wheat? Unless they are patiently tolerated while they are evil, they do not reach a laudable change. Thus, if they are uprooted, the wheat they would have become if they had been spared is uprooted together with them.

## XIII. [MATTHEW 13:45–46]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he found one precious pearl, he went away and sold everything he had and bought it.”

The question is why he moved from the plural number to the singular, so that, when the man is seeking good pearls, he finds one precious pearl, which he buys after selling everything he has.

Either this man, seeking good people with whom he might live profitably, finds one who is without sin above all others: “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

Or, seeking commandments by which, if observed, he might live rightly with other people, he finds the love of neighbor, in which the Apostle says that everything is contained: “You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness,” and if there is any other commandment, the individual pearls are summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Romans 13:8–9).

Or a person seeks good understandings and finds that one understanding in which all are contained: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)—luminous with the brightness of truth, solid with the firmness of eternity, and everywhere like itself in the beauty of divinity—who is to be understood as God after the shell of flesh has been penetrated.

He had already arrived at the pearl itself, which had once lain hidden beneath the coverings of mortality, as though behind the obstacle of shells, in the depths of this age and among the rocky hardness of the Jews. He had already reached that pearl who said: “Even if we once knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know him in that way” (2 Corinthians 5:16).

No understanding is worthy of the name “pearl” unless it is reached after all carnal coverings have been stripped away—the coverings with which it is wrapped, whether through human words or through surrounding likenesses—so that it may be perceived by a sure reasoning as pure, solid, and nowhere discordant with itself.

Nevertheless, that one Word contains all true, firm, and perfect understandings: the Word of God through whom all things were made (John 1:3).

Whichever of these three interpretations is adopted—or if something else should occur to someone that is well signified by the name of one precious pearl—its price is us ourselves. We are not free to possess it unless, for our liberation, we despise all things that are possessed temporarily.

For when we sell our possessions, we receive no greater price for any of them than ourselves, because while entangled in such things we did not belong to ourselves. Thus we give ourselves again for that pearl, not because we are worth so much [Note: [Col. 1372] Most manuscripts: “not because it is worth so much.”], but because we cannot give more.

## XIV. [MATTHEW 13:15]

### 1

“They closed their eyes, lest at any time they should see with their eyes”: that is, they themselves were the cause of God’s closing their eyes.

For another evangelist says, “He blinded their eyes.” But was this so that they should never see? Or rather, so that they might at some time see even in this condition—displeased with their blindness, grieving over it, and thereby humbled and moved to confess their sins and seek the Lord devoutly?

For Mark says this as follows: “Lest at any time they should be converted and their sins be forgiven them” (Mark 4:12). Here they are understood to have deserved, through their sins, not to understand; yet this very thing was done to them mercifully, so that they might recognize their sins, be converted, and merit forgiveness.

But when John states this passage in the following way—“Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, and be converted, and I should heal them’” (John 12:39–40)—he appears to contradict this interpretation and to compel us entirely to understand the statement “lest they should see with their eyes” not as “lest they might at some time see even in this way,” but simply as “so that they should not see,” since he plainly says, “so that they should not see with their eyes.”

And when he says, “Therefore they could not believe,” he sufficiently shows that their blinding was not done so that, moved and distressed by their failure to understand, they might at some time be converted through repentance. For they could not do this unless they first believed, so that by believing they might be converted and by conversion be healed, and by being healed understand. Rather, they were blinded so that they would not believe. For he says this most plainly: “Therefore they could not believe.”

### 2

But if this is so, who would not rise in defense of the Jews and proclaim that they were free of blame because they did not believe? For “they could not believe because he blinded their eyes.”

Yet because God must rather be understood to be free of blame, we are compelled to admit that they deserved to be blinded because of certain other sins—and that through this blinding they could not believe.

For John’s words are these: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, ‘He has blinded their eyes.’” We therefore try in vain to understand that they were blinded so that they might be converted [Note: [Col. 1372] Amerbach, Erasmus, and the Louvain edition read “so that they might not be converted.” The negative should be removed here, since it is found neither in the manuscripts, nor in the ancient edition of Regensburg, nor in Rabanus, who transferred this passage into Book 4 of his *Commentary on Matthew*.], when they could not be converted because they did not believe, and could not believe because they had been blinded.

Or may we not say, without absurdity, that some of the Jews were capable of being healed, but were nevertheless endangered by such an inflation of pride that it was beneficial for them first not to believe? They were blinded for this purpose: so that they would not understand the Lord speaking through parables; and, not understanding them, they would not believe in him; and, not believing, they would crucify him together with the other desperate people; and then, after his resurrection, they would be converted.

By that time, humbled more deeply by the guilt of the Lord’s death, they would love more intensely the one from whom they rejoiced that so great a crime had been forgiven them. Their pride was so great that it had to be brought low by such humiliation.

Anyone may judge this to have been said inappropriately if he does not read in the Acts of the Apostles that this did indeed happen most clearly (Acts 2:37).

Therefore, what John says—“They could not believe because he blinded their eyes so that they should not see”—does not conflict with the interpretation by which we understand that they were blinded so that they might be converted. That is, the Lord’s sayings were hidden from them through the obscurity of parables so that, after his resurrection, they might recover through a more salutary repentance.

Blinded by the obscurity of the discourse, they did not understand the Lord’s words; because they did not understand them, they did not believe in him; because they did not believe, they crucified him. Then, after his resurrection, they were terrified by the miracles performed in his name, pierced and cast down by the greater guilt of their crime into repentance, and afterward, having received pardon, they were converted to obedience with the most ardent love.

5. For those whom that blindness did not benefit toward conversion—blindness produced through the language of parables—the prophet says elsewhere, as the Apostle also recalled when speaking about the obscurity of languages:

> “In other tongues and with other lips I shall speak to this people, and even then they will not hear me,” says the Lord (1 Cor. 14:21; Isa. 28:11).

For it would not be said, “Even then they will not hear me,” unless this were done so that they might hear even then—that is, so that it might benefit them toward humble confession, attentive inquiry, obedient conversion, and fervent love. There is also this analogy from bodily medicine. For many medicines first afflict in order to heal; and even those eye-salves which concern the eyes, if they must be applied internally, cannot be beneficial unless they first close and disturb the faculty of sight.

4. Nor should it trouble us that the same prophet says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint), as though this contradicted what John says: “Therefore they could not believe, because he blinded their eyes”—that is, because those parables were spoken in such a way that they could not understand them.

Someone may say: “If they had to believe in order to understand, how could they therefore be unable to believe because they did not understand—that is, because he blinded their eyes?” But what Isaiah says, “Unless you believe, you will not understand,” refers to that understanding in which one will always remain, namely, the understanding of ineffable realities. Yet when something is to be believed, unless what is said is understood, it cannot be believed. Thus the statements that can be expressed must be understood so that they may be believed; and the statements that can be expressed must be believed so that the things that cannot be expressed may be understood.

XV. [Book XIII, 34]

“And without parables he was not speaking to them.”

This does not mean that he never spoke literally, but that he scarcely explained any discourse in which he did not signify something by means of a parable, although in it he also said some things literally [Col. 1374]. Thus his entire discourse is often found to have been expressed through parables, whereas no discourse of his is found to have been spoken entirely literally.

By “explained discourses” I mean those in which, beginning from some occasion, he speaks until he has completed everything pertaining to that subject and then moves on to another. Sometimes, to be sure, one evangelist joins together material which another indicates was spoken at different times. For each arranged the narrative he had begun, not invariably according to the order of the events, but according to the capacity of his own recollection.

XVI. [Book XIII, 51, 52, 44]

“Have you understood all these things?” They said to him, “Yes.” He said to them: “Therefore every scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven is like a householder who brings forth from his treasure new things and old.” Did he intend by this conclusion to explain what he had called the treasure hidden in the field, since the holy Scriptures are understood to be contained under the name of the two Testaments, the New and the Old—just as in another Gospel writer he appears to explain the two-edged sword by a similar conclusion (Rev. 1:16)?

Or was it because he had spoken these things in parables, and, after asking them whether they had understood, they answered that they had understood? Perhaps, by this final comparison of the householder bringing forth new and old things from his treasure, he intended to show that the person should be regarded as instructed in the Church who had also understood the ancient Scriptures explained through parables, receiving their principles from these new things.

For the Lord himself also expressed these things through parables, although he himself was the fulfillment of those earlier things—that is, so that those old things might be fulfilled in him. If he himself, in whom those things are fulfilled and revealed, still speaks through parables until his passion tears the veil, so that nothing remains hidden that will not be revealed, then all the more should we recognize that the things written about him long beforehand to commend so great a salvation were covered with parables.

The Jews, however, taking them literally, refused to become instructed in the kingdom of heaven and to pass over to Christ, so that the veil placed over their hearts might be removed.

[Note: [Col. 1374] In the Ratisbon edition a question is inserted here concerning the words of Matthew, chapter 24, verse 36: “But concerning that day and hour no one knows,” etc.; yet it differs in no respect from the question which is number sixty among the Eighty-Three Questions.]

XVII. [Book XIII, 55 and 56]

1. “His brothers, James and Joseph and Simon and Judas, and his sisters—are they not all with us? Where, then, did this man get all these things?” And they were offended at him.

That among the Jews the term “brothers” was customarily used for relatives is proved to such an extent that not only persons related in a close degree of descent—such as the sons of brothers and sisters, who among us too are most commonly called brothers—but even an uncle and his sister’s son are found to have been called brothers, as Jacob and Laban were to one another (Gen. 29:15).

It is therefore not surprising that the Lord’s brothers were said to be any of his maternal relatives, since, on account of their kinship with Joseph, they could also have been called his brothers by those who thought that Joseph was the father of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 1374] Here the work ends in the printed editions of Ratisbon, Amerbach, and Erasmus, and in the Vatican, Sorbonne, and Cistercian manuscripts. We have seen the remainder only in the Louvain edition and in two Victorine manuscripts and one very ancient Corbie manuscript.]

2. No one violates general justice unless he has transgressed either through lust or against the agreement of human society, as in theft, robbery, adultery, incest, and similar offenses; or against nature, as in insult, slaughter, murder, intercourse with males or with animals; or by exceeding the proper measure in permitted things, as when someone arrogantly inflicts more blows than necessary, or eats or drinks more than necessary, or has intercourse with his own wife more often than necessary, and similar acts.

3. It is rightly understood that the Holy Spirit first gave human beings the gift of languages—languages established by human agreement and convention and learned externally through the bodily senses by the habit of hearing—in order to show them how easily he could make them wise through the wisdom of God, which is internal to them.

4. Likewise, the will of the eternal Word is always stable, because it possesses everything simultaneously. Our will, however, does not remain stable because it does not possess everything simultaneously; therefore we want this at one moment and that at another.

Likewise, all things that were made existed in that Word, and the assumption of humanity itself was foreknown by him in the same way as if a painter wished to paint an entire house and contemplated or knew the place where he too ought to paint himself. He possesses the whole thing in his art, in his preparation, and in his will, although he unfolds each part at its appointed and proper time.

Thus every creature [Col. 1376], and humanity itself—which was to bear, through a mystical and ineffable assumption, the person of that same Wisdom—was always present in Wisdom itself, as in the eternal art of God, although he brings each thing into being at its proper time. He “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly,” and, remaining in himself, “renews all things” (Wis. 8:1; 7:27).

5. Likewise, how can someone wish to wish to die? If he had reached the point of wishing to die in this way—if he already possessed a sound faith and saw where he ought to arrive—he would already be progressing toward willingly departing this life.

For seeing where one ought to arrive is also loving that destination and already desiring to be there. When this has been brought about in someone’s soul, he must necessarily wish to die.

Thus some who already hold a sound faith say without justification that they do not wish to die in order to make progress, when their very progress consists in wishing to die. If they want to speak truthfully, they should not say, “I do not wish to die in order to make progress,” but, “I do not wish to die because I have made too little progress.”

Therefore, for believers, unwillingness to die is not a plan by which they may make progress, but an indication that they have made too little progress. Consequently, what they do not want in order to be perfect, let them want—and they are perfect.

[IN ONE HUNDRED TWENTY-FOUR TREATISES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN.]

[Col. 1375]

NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING TREATISES ON JOHN

We shall not seem to have acted rashly if we assign Augustine’s Treatises on John to the year 416 after Christ, or to the immediately following period. Certainly, when he was expounding this evangelist, the struggle between Catholics and Donatists was still raging. The holy Doctor is throughout so full and vehement in refuting those factious people; moreover, their schismatic altar still stood at Hippo.

Thus, in the Treatise on the Epistle of John—the exposition of which he undertook after interrupting for a time the work on the Gospel that he had begun long before—he complains in these words: “What are two altars doing in this city?” Although this may even be referred to a period before the Conference at Carthage, which was held with the Donatists in 411, nevertheless, since throughout these very Treatises on the Gospel with which we are concerned the faith of predestination is presented as a matter beyond dispute—notably in Treatises 45, 48, 68, 83, 105, 111, and others—and since the Pelagians are also attacked without being named in Treatises 53, 67, 81, 86, and others, it could readily be understood that these Treatises were not published before the year 411 after Christ, when the Pelagian heresy first invaded Africa.

But another, much more explicit argument leads us to assign them to the year 416. In Treatise 120, Augustine proves that Nicodemus came to Christ repeatedly in order to become his disciple by listening to him, using this argument: “This,” he says, “has certainly now been made known to almost all nations in the revelation of the body of the blessed Stephen”—a revelation that took place near the end of the year 415.

Augustine delivered his Treatises or sermons on this subject on various days. For example, he indicates in Treatise 2 that he delivered the second on the day after the first, on a Sunday. Likewise, Treatise 46 was delivered on a Sunday, as is clear from Treatise 47; Treatise 45 had been delivered the day before, as is clear from Treatise 46.

Treatise 34 and the three that followed it were delivered on four consecutive days, as is evident from the opening and conclusion of each; and Treatise 37 was delivered on a Sunday, as is clear from Treatise 38. The same is true of Treatises 8, 9, and 10. Finally, the five Treatises numbered 19, 20, 21, 22, and 23 are shown to have been delivered consecutively, one on each day.

That Augustine did this so as not to omit any of the days appointed for preaching may also be understood from the fact that in Treatise 8 he excuses the omission of one such day on a particular occasion, and in Treatise 46 he postpones to the day on which he was to deliver the sermon a more careful treatment of the Gospel passage already read.

In Treatise 47, which he delivered on a Sunday, he says that he is by no means prevented, as usual, by lack of time from developing his discourse more fully. On the other hand, he sometimes testifies that he did not wish to prolong his sermon on more solemn days, because many people might have gathered more for the sake of the solemnity than from a desire to hear the sermon; this occurs at the end of Treatise 8.

From Treatise 46 and others we understand that he was accustomed to order the portion of the Gospel he intended to explain to the people to be read during the divine offices, and afterward he tried to explain what had been read. But if this had become excessively long, he postponed the remainder to another time; even then, he ordered the Gospel to be reread.

Augustine began his exposition of the Gospel of John before winter had fully ended. For in Treatise 6 he testifies that he feared the people might be deterred by the severity of the cold from attending church. In Treatise 10 he indicates that the time was approaching when the solemnity of the Lord’s passion and resurrection would be celebrated. In Treatise 11, moreover, he says that the time already required him to exhort the catechumens.

On the day before he delivered Treatise 12, he had promised the people that he would speak about the peace of the Church—either about what had already been accomplished or about what he still hoped would have to be done. But he wished first to give the customary exposition of the Gospel reading and thereby fulfill his promise. What that subject concerning the peace of the Church may have been is unknown; nor was it written down at the end of that exposition.

It seems possible to infer from the opening of Treatise 13 that the Gospel of John had been interrupted by him for not a few days. In fact, he interrupted it during the Paschal festivities, which fell on April 2 in the year 416, because on those days fixed and appointed Gospel readings had to be recited in the Church, and other readings could not be substituted for them, as he explains in the preface to his Exposition of the Epistle of John.

In the meantime he undertook to expound that very Epistle; and, having soon completed its treatment, he returned to the Gospel. In the course of its exposition he had not yet passed the festival of Lawrence the martyr when he delivered Treatise 27, whom he praises there—even though, as has already been observed, he had completed five Treatises, from 19 through 23, on five consecutive days.

Many passages excerpted from this work are found in Bede and Alcuin on John, in Florus’s Commentaries on Paul’s Epistles, published under Bede’s name, and elsewhere. Certain statements drawn from various Treatises were also cited by the ancients in defense of the Catholic faith: for example, from Treatise 2 by Cassian, *On the Incarnation*, book 7, chapter 27; and from Treatise 78 by Pope Leo in his Letter to Leo Augustus, formerly numbered 97 and now 134.

Cassiodorus Senator recalls this work in *Institutions*, chapter 7, commending John as having been illuminated by Augustine through an extensive and distinguished exposition. Possidius, in his *Index*, chapter 6, lists it in these words: “Treatises on the Gospel of John, from beginning to end, in six codices.”

Augustine himself says in the preface to the Treatises on the Epistle of John: “Your Holiness remembers that we are accustomed to expound the Gospel according to John in the order of its readings.” Again, in *On the Trinity*, book 15, chapter 27, he refers to Treatise 99 on John when he says: “On this subject we spoke in a sermon delivered to the ears of the Christian people, and we committed what we had said to writing.”

He would doubtless have said more, had he lived long enough, in the separate books of his *Retractions*. As he writes to Quodvultdeus in Letter 224, he was considering composing retractions of the popular treatises and homilies he had delivered.

In ancient manuscripts the work is entitled in some places *Treatises*, in others *Sermons*, and in still others *Homilies on John*. A somewhat longer title appears in the Audoen, Gemmetic, and Pratell manuscripts, as follows:

> “Here begin the homilies of Aurelius Augustine, Doctor and Bishop of Hippo, on the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ according to John, which he first delivered by speaking to the people and which, while he was speaking, were taken down by shorthand writers; afterward he dictated them word for word in the order in which they had been delivered.”

Finally, as for the preface placed here, you will search for it in vain either in the manuscripts or in the printed editions of Amerbach and Badius. The Louvain editors published it after Erasmus, although they themselves observe that it is neither Augustine’s nor extant in any manuscript. It is found, with a few words changed, in Bede and Alcuin on John.

[Col. 1377]

PREFACE BY AN UNCERTAIN AUTHOR

Among all the pages of divine Scripture, the Gospel excels, because what the Law and the Prophets foretold would happen, the Gospel says has been fulfilled.

Among the writers of the Gospels themselves, John stands out for the depth of the divine mysteries. From the time of the Lord’s ascension he preached the word of God for sixty-five years without the aid of writing, until the final years of Domitian’s reign.

After Domitian had been killed, and after he had returned from exile to Ephesus with Nerva’s permission, he was compelled by the bishops of Asia to write about Christ’s coeternal divinity with the Father against the heretics who had invaded his churches during his absence and denied that Christ existed before Mary.

Hence, in the figure of the four living creatures, he is rightly compared to a flying eagle, which flies higher than the other birds and looks upon the rays of the sun with unflinching eyes.

The other evangelists, who sufficiently [Col. 1378] explain Christ’s temporal birth and the temporal deeds he performed in his humanity, and who said little about his divinity, walk with the Lord on earth like creatures that move on foot. But John, explaining little about his temporal deeds and contemplating the power of his divinity from a higher vantage, flies with the Lord to heaven.

For he who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the supper drank from the fountain of the Lord’s breast a draught of heavenly wisdom more abundantly than the others.

He had indeed read the Gospels of the three other evangelists and had approved their faith and truth. In them he saw that certain elements of the history of the events were lacking, especially those things that the Lord had done at the beginning of his preaching, namely, before John the Baptist was imprisoned.

John therefore writes what they had, as it were, left aside: what Jesus did before John was imprisoned. But above all he took care to commend Christ’s divinity and the mystery of the Trinity.

The other three evangelists, pursuing at greater length the Lord’s temporal words and deeds, which are especially useful for forming the conduct of the present life [Col. 1379], devoted themselves to the active life. In that life one labors to purify the heart so as to see God.

John, however, relates few of the Lord’s deeds but records more carefully the Lord’s words that disclose the unity of the Trinity and the happiness of eternal life. Thus he directed his purpose and preaching toward commending the contemplative virtue [Col. 1379], in which one gives oneself to contemplation so that God may be seen.

This, indeed, is John, whom the Lord called away from the stormy waves of marriage and to whom he entrusted the virgin Mother to the virgin.

[Col. 1379]

OF THE HOLY AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ONE HUNDRED TWENTY-FOUR TREATISES ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

[Note: [Col. 1379] Perhaps delivered around the year 416 after Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 1379] We have collated these Treatises against the Fossat manuscript, of excellent quality, copied at the command of Abbot Ingilbert around the year 840; against two very ancient German manuscripts; and against the Corbie, Remigian, Gemmetic, Floriac, Audoen, Becheron, and Pratell manuscripts; two manuscripts from Vendôme; one belonging to the Church of Carcassonne; and one belonging to the Abbey of La Cultura. In addition, we used the variant readings of seven Belgian codices collected by the Louvain editors, as well as the older editions of Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain.]

[Note: [Col. 1379] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*. M.]

(C)

TREATISE I

On the words of John: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and so forth, up to “And the darkness did not comprehend it.” Chapter 1, verses 1–5.

1. Considering what we have just heard from the apostolic reading—that the natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God (1 Cor. 2:14)—and reflecting that in this present gathering of Your Charity there must be many who are natural, who still think according to the flesh and are not yet able to raise themselves to spiritual understanding, I am deeply uncertain how, with the Lord’s help, I can speak about or explain, according to my limited ability, what has been read from the Gospel:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

For the natural person does not perceive this.

What, then, brothers? Shall we be silent about it? Why, then, is it read if it is to be passed over in silence? Or why is it heard if it is not explained? And what is explained if it is not understood?

Since, however, I do not doubt that among you there are again some who can not only receive what is explained but also understand it before it is explained, I will not deprive those who are able to receive it merely because I fear being excessive for the ears of those who cannot receive it.

Finally, God’s mercy will be present, perhaps so that everyone may be satisfied and each person may grasp what he can, because the one who speaks also says what he can. For who can say it as it is?

I venture to say, my brothers, that perhaps not even John himself said it as it is, but he too said it as he was able, because a human being spoke about God—and indeed one inspired by God, but nevertheless a human being.

Because he was inspired, he said something; if he had not been inspired, he would have said nothing. But because he was a human being inspired by God, he did not say everything that God is; he said what a human being was able to say.

[Col. 1380]

2. This John, dearest brothers, belonged to those mountains of which it is written:

> “Let the mountains receive peace for your people, and the hills righteousness” (Ps. 71:3).

The mountains are exalted souls; the hills are little souls. But the mountains receive peace so that the hills may receive righteousness.

What is the righteousness that the hills receive? Faith, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17).

Yet the smaller souls would not receive faith unless the greater souls, who are called mountains, were illuminated by Wisdom itself, so that they could pass on to the little ones what the little ones could grasp. Thus the hills live by faith because the mountains receive peace.

It was from these mountains that the words “Peace be with you” were spoken to the Church. By announcing peace to the Church, these mountains did not separate themselves against the one from whom they had received peace (John 20:19), so that they might announce peace truthfully rather than deceptively.

3. There are also other mountains that cause shipwreck, against which anyone who drives a ship is wrecked. When those in danger see land, it is easy for them to try to make their way toward it. But sometimes land appears to be on a mountain, while rocks lie hidden beneath the mountain. When someone tries to reach the mountain, he strikes the rocks and finds there not a harbor but mourning.

There have been mountains of this kind: they appeared great among human beings and produced heresies and schisms, dividing the Church of God. But those who divided the Church of God were not the mountains of which it was said, “Let the mountains receive peace for your people.” For how could they have received peace when they divided unity?

[Col. 1381]

4. Those who received peace in order to announce it to the people contemplated Wisdom itself, insofar as it could be touched by human hearts—Wisdom “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9).

If it did not enter the human heart, how did it enter John’s heart? Was John not a human being? Or perhaps it did not enter John’s heart, but John’s heart entered into it?

For what enters the human heart comes from below to the human being; but to where the human heart enters is above the human being.

Even in this way, brothers, it can be said that if Wisdom entered John’s heart—if this can in some way be said—it entered John’s heart insofar as John himself was not a human being.

What does “he was not a human being” mean? It means that he had begun to be an angel, because all holy people are angels, that is, messengers of God.

Therefore, to those who were carnal and natural and unable to perceive the things of God, what does the Apostle say?

> “When you say, ‘I am of Paul,’ and ‘I am of Apollos,’ are you not human beings?” (1 Cor. 3:4).

What did he want them to become when he reproached them for being human beings? Do you want to know what he wanted them to become? Hear it in the Psalms:

> “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81:6).

God therefore calls us for this purpose: so that we may not remain human beings.

But then we shall be human beings in a better way if we first acknowledge that we are human beings—that is, if we rise from humility to that exalted height. Otherwise, when we think that we are something although we are nothing, we will not only fail to receive what we are not, but also lose what we are.

5. John, then, was one of these mountains, he who said:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

This mountain had received peace and contemplated the divinity of the Word. What sort of mountain was it? How lofty?

It had risen beyond all the summits of the earth, beyond all the regions of the air, beyond all the heights of the stars, beyond all the choirs and legions of angels. For unless it had risen beyond all these created things, it would not have reached the one through whom all things were made.

You cannot conceive what it rose beyond unless you see where it arrived.

Do you ask about heaven and earth? They were made. Do you ask about the things that are in heaven and earth? Certainly they too, and much more so, were made.

Do you ask about spiritual creatures—angels, archangels, thrones, dominions, virtues, principalities? They too were made.

For when the Psalm enumerated all these things, it concluded in this way:

> “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:5).

If he spoke and they were made, they were made through the Word. But if they were made through the Word, John’s heart could not have reached what he says—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”—unless it had risen beyond all the things made through the Word.

What a mountain, then! How holy, how high, among those mountains that received peace for God’s people so that the hills might receive righteousness!

6. See, then, brothers, whether John may perhaps belong to those mountains of which we sang shortly before:

> “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come.”

Therefore, my brothers, if you wish to understand, lift your eyes to this mountain [Col. 1382]; that is, raise yourselves toward the evangelist, raise yourselves toward his meaning.

But since these mountains receive peace, and since no one can be in peace who places his hope in a human being, do not raise your eyes to the mountain in such a way that you think your hope ought to be placed in a human being.

Say instead:

> “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come,”

so that you immediately add:

> “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth” (Ps. 120:1–2).

Let us therefore lift our eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to us. Yet the mountains themselves are not the place where our hope is to be placed; they receive what they minister to us. Therefore our hope must be placed where the mountains themselves receive it.

When we lift our eyes to the Scriptures, because the Scriptures were ministered through human beings, we lift our eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to us. Yet because the human beings who wrote the Scriptures were themselves human, they did not shine from themselves. Rather, he was the true light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

John the Baptist was also a mountain, and he said, “I am not the Christ” (ibid., 20), lest anyone, placing his hope in the mountain, fall away from the one who illuminates the mountains. He himself confessed and said, “For from his fullness we have all received” (ibid. 1:16).

Thus you should say:

> “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from which my help will come,”

so that you do not attribute the help that comes to you to the mountains, but follow on and say:

> “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

7. I have offered these admonitions, brothers, so that when you raised your hearts toward the Scriptures, when the Gospel resounded—

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,”

and the other things that were read—you might understand that you had lifted your eyes to the mountains.

Unless the mountains had said these things, where would you have found the means even to think about them?

Help therefore came to you from the mountains, so that you might at least hear these things. But you are not yet able to understand what you heard.

Call upon help from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. For the mountains were able to speak in such a way that they themselves could not illuminate, because they too were illuminated by hearing.

From there John received these words, brothers—that John who reclined upon the Lord’s breast (John 13:25) and drank from the Lord’s breast what he would offer us.

But you must receive understanding from the place from which he also drank who offered it to you, so that you may lift your eyes to the mountains, from which help will come to you, and receive from there, as from a cup—that is, as a word [Note: [Col. 1382] In most manuscripts, *verbo* (“by a word”).]—what has been offered.

Yet because your help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth, you must fill your breast from the place from which he filled his. Then you will say:

> “My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth.”

Let him who can fill it, then.

Brothers, this is what I have said [Note: [Col. 1382] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Therefore, brothers, let him fill what I have said.”]. Let each person raise his heart as he sees fit and receive what is said.

But perhaps you will say that I am more present to you than God is. God forbid. He is much more present. I appear to your eyes; he presides over your consciences.

Your ears are directed toward me, but your heart toward him, so that you may fill both.

Behold, you raise your eyes and these bodily senses toward us; but not toward us—for we do not belong to those mountains—but toward the Gospel itself, toward the evangelist himself. Your heart, however, must be filled toward the Lord.

Let each person raise it in such a way that he sees what he is raising and toward whom he is raising it.

What did I say: what he is raising and toward whom he is raising it? Let him consider what kind of heart he is raising, because he is raising it toward the Lord. Let him not fall before he has been lifted up, weighed down by the burden of carnal pleasure.

But does each person see that he carries the burden of the flesh? Let him strive through self-restraint to cleanse what he is raising to God.

For:

> “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

8. For what benefit is there in the words having sounded—

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?

We too spoke words when we were speaking. Was that Word with God like this? Did not the things we said sound and pass away?

Did God’s Word, then, also sound and come to an end? How were all things made through it, and without it nothing was made? How is what was created through it governed by it, if it sounded and passed away?

What kind of Word is it, then, which is both spoken and does not pass away?

Let Your Charity pay attention: this is a great matter.

Because we speak words every day, words have become cheap to us. By sounding and passing away, words have become cheap, and they seem to be nothing more than words.

There is also a word within the human being, which remains inside; the sound proceeds from the mouth. There is a word that is truly spoken spiritually: that which you understand from the sound, not the sound itself.

Behold, I say the word when I say, “God.” How brief is what I have said: four letters and two syllables! Is God, in his entirety, four letters and two syllables?

Or is what is understood in those letters as precious as the letters themselves are insignificant?

What happened in your heart when you heard “God”? What happened in my heart when I said “God”?

A great and supreme substance was conceived in thought, one that transcends every mutable creature, whether carnal or natural.

And if I ask you, “Is God mutable or immutable?” you will answer immediately: “Far be it from me either to believe or think that God is mutable; God is immutable.”

Your soul, though small and perhaps still carnal, could not answer me except that God is immutable. Yet every creature is mutable.

How, then, were you able to flash upward toward what is above every creature, so that you could answer me with certainty that God is immutable?

What, then, is that in your heart when you conceive a certain living, eternal, almighty, boundless substance, present everywhere, wholly present everywhere, confined nowhere?

When you conceive these things, that is the word concerning God in your heart.

But is this the sound consisting of four letters and two syllables?

Therefore, whatever is spoken and passes away consists of sounds, letters, and syllables. The word that sounds passes away; but what the sound signified remains both in the one who spoke it as he thinks and in the one who heard it as he understands, even while the sounds pass away.

9. Turn your attention to that word.

If you can have a word in your heart, like a plan born in your mind, so that your mind gives birth to a plan and the plan exists within it as the offspring of your mind, as the son of your heart—

First the heart generates a plan, so that you may construct some building or undertake some great work upon the earth. The plan has already been born, but the work is not yet complete.

You see what you are going to do, but another person does not marvel until you have done it and built the structure, bringing that work to its carved and finished form.

People observe the marvelous building and marvel at the builder’s plan. They are astonished by what they see and love what they do not see.

Who can see the plan?

If a human plan is praised on account of some great building, do you wish to see what kind of plan the Lord Jesus Christ, that is, the Word of God, is?

Consider the structure of this world. See what things were made through the Word, and then you will know what kind of Word it is.

Consider these two great bodies of the world, heaven and earth. Who can explain heaven’s adornment in words? Who can explain in words the earth’s fertility? Who can praise worthily the alternation of the seasons? Who can praise worthily the power of seeds?

You see what I am leaving unmentioned, lest, by recalling these things at length, I say too little about what you can contemplate [Note: [Col. 1384] One Becher manuscript reads, “and less than you can contemplate.” From this point, with sixteen other manuscripts, it omits *ex* and continues: “Having therefore observed this structure, what sort of Word…”].

From this structure, then, perceive what kind of Word it is through which it was made—and it was not the only thing made through it.

All these things are visible because they belong to bodily perception. Through that Word the angels too were made; through that Word the archangels too were made; powers, thrones, dominions, principalities—all things were made through that Word.

From this, consider what kind of Word it is.

10. Perhaps someone unknown to me now replies: “And who can conceive this Word?”

When you hear “Word,” do not therefore form for yourself something cheap and infer the words you hear every day: “He said such words; he spoke such words; you are telling me such words.” By constantly speaking the names of words, we have made words seem cheap.

When you hear, “In the beginning was the Word,” do not suppose it to be something cheap, of the kind you are accustomed to think about when you hear human words. Hear what you should conceive:

> “The Word was God.”

11. Now let some unbelieving Arian come forward and say that the Word of God was made. How can it be that the Word of God was made, when God made all things through the Word? If the very Word of God was also made, through what other Word was it made? If you say that there is a Word of the Word through which that Word was made, I say that this is the one and only Son of God. But if you do not speak of a Word of the Word, concede that the Word through which all things were made was not made. For that through which all things were made could not have made itself. Believe the Evangelist, then. He could have said, “In the beginning God made the Word,” just as Moses said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”; and he enumerates everything in this way: “God said, ‘Let it be,’ and it was made” (Gen. 1). If he said it, who said it? God, certainly. And what was made? Some creature. Between God who speaks and the creature that was made, what is there through which it was made, except the Word? For God said, “Let it be,” and it was made. This Word is unchangeable: although changeable things are made through the Word, the Word itself is unchangeable.

[Col. 1385] 12. Do not, then, believe that the one through whom all things were made was made, lest you fail to be remade through the Word through whom all things are remade. For you have already been made through the Word, but you must be remade through the Word. If your faith concerning the Word is wrong, however, you cannot be remade through the Word. And if it happened to you to be made through the Word, so that you were made through it, you are falling away through yourself. If you are falling away through yourself, let him remake you who made you. If you are becoming worse through yourself, let him recreate you who created you. But how will he recreate you through the Word if you think something wrong about the Word? The Evangelist says, “In the beginning was the Word”; and you say, “In the beginning the Word was made.” He says, “All things were made through him”; and you say that the Word itself was also made. The Evangelist could have said, “In the beginning the Word was made”; but what does he say? “In the beginning was the Word.” If he was, he was not made, so that all these things might be made through him, and without him nothing was made. If, therefore, the Word was in the beginning, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God: if you cannot conceive what this means, wait, so that you may grow. He is food; receive milk, so that you may be nourished and become strong enough to take solid food.

13. Certainly, brothers, concerning what follows—“All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”—take care not to think that “nothing” is some kind of thing. For many who understand badly are accustomed to think that “without him nothing was made” means that nothing is something. Sin, certainly, was not made through him; and it is clear that sin is nothing, and that human beings become nothing when they sin. Nor was an idol made through the Word. It does have a certain human form, but the human being himself was made through the Word; for the human form in the idol was not made through the Word. It is written, “We know that an idol is nothing” (1 Cor. 8:4).

These things, then, were not made through the Word. But whatever has been made naturally, whatever exists among created things—absolutely everything fixed in heaven, everything shining above, everything flying beneath heaven, and everything moving throughout [Note: [Col. 1385] Here, in most manuscripts, the preposition *in* is absent.] the whole order of nature—all creation, in short: let me put it more plainly, brothers, so that you may understand—from an angel all the way down to a little worm. What is more excellent than an angel among created things? What is lower than a little worm among created things? Through the one by whom the angel was made, the little worm was also made. But the angel is worthy of heaven, while the worm belongs to the earth. The one who created them also assigned their places.

If he were to put a worm in heaven, you would criticize him; if he wanted angels to be born from decaying flesh, you would criticize him. And yet God comes very close to doing this, and he is not to be criticized. For all human beings born from flesh—what are they but worms? And from worms he makes angels. If the Lord himself says, “But I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. 21:7), who would hesitate to say what is also written in Job: “How much more is man rottenness, and the son of man a worm” (Job 25:6)? First he said, “Man is rottenness,” and afterward, “The son of man is a worm”: because a worm is born from rottenness, therefore man is rottenness, and the son of man is a worm.

Behold what the one who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, wished to become for your sake. [Col. 1386] Why was this done for your sake? So that you might suckle, since you were unable to eat. Therefore, brothers, understand it in this way: “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” For the whole of creation was made through him, greater and lesser; through him the things above and the things below were made, spiritual and bodily things were made. No form, no structure, no harmony of parts, no substance of any kind that can possess weight, number, or measure exists except through that Word—and by that creative Word of whom it was said, “You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight” (Wis. 11:21).

14. Therefore, brothers, let no one deceive you when you perhaps grow weary because of flies.

[Col. 1386] The printed editions have *patimini a muscis* (“you suffer from flies”), and shortly afterward *patiebatur a muscis* (“he suffered from flies”), and later *passus est a muscis* (“he suffered from flies”). But all the manuscripts consistently have *ad muscas*, evidently a phrase used among Africans, as the Louvain editors rightly judged.

For some have been mocked by the devil and caught by flies. Bird-catchers are accustomed to place flies in a flytrap in order to deceive hungry birds; so these men too were deceived by the devil through flies. For someone—I do not know who—was growing weary of flies. The Manichaean found him distressed and, when he said that he could not endure flies and hated them intensely, immediately asked him, “Who made these?” Since the man was distressed and hated them, he did not dare say, “God made them,” although he was a Catholic. The other immediately continued: “If God did not make them, who made them?” “Clearly,” he replied, “I believe that the devil made flies.” And the other immediately said: “If the devil made the fly, as I see you confess—since you understand the matter intelligently—who made the bee, which is somewhat larger than a fly?” He did not dare say that God made the bee but not the fly, because the cases were closely related. From the bee he led him to the locust, from the locust to the lizard, from the lizard to the bird, from the bird to cattle, from there to the ox, from there to the elephant, and finally to man; and he persuaded the man that man too had not been made by God.

Thus that wretched man, when he grew weary of flies, became a fly for the devil to possess. For Beelzebub is said to be interpreted as “prince of flies,” concerning which it is written, “Dead flies destroy the sweetness of the perfume” (Eccl. 10:1).

[Col. 1386] The Louvain edition has *morientes* (“dying”), whereas other printed editions and the manuscripts have *moriturae* (“about to die”).

15. What, then, brothers? Why have I said these things? Close the ears of your hearts against the deceits of the enemy. Understand that God made all things and placed them in their proper ranks.

Why, then, do we suffer many evils from the creature God made? Because we have offended God? Do angels suffer these things? Perhaps we too would not fear those things in that life. Accuse your sin of your punishment, not the judge. For because of pride God established this smallest and most contemptible creature [Note: [Col. 1386] In most manuscripts: “established that this smallest and most contemptible creature …”] to torment us: so that when man has been proud and has vaunted himself against God; when, though mortal, he has terrified another mortal; when, though a human being, he has failed to recognize his fellow human being; when he has raised himself up, he may be subjected to fleas.

What is the reason for your swelling with human pride? A human being insulted you, and you were afraid and became angry; now resist fleas so that you may sleep. Recognize who you are.

For, brothers, so that you may know that these creatures which trouble us were created to subdue our pride, God could have humbled the proud people of Pharaoh with bears, lions, or serpents. Instead, he sent flies and frogs upon them (Exod. 8:6, 24), so that pride might be subdued by the most contemptible things.

16. Therefore, brothers, all things—absolutely all things—were made through him, and without him nothing was made. But how were all things made through him? “What was made in him was life.”

For it can also be said in this way: “What was made in him is life.” If we pronounce it thus, then everything is life. For what was not made in him? He is the Wisdom of God; and it is said in the Psalm, “You made all things in Wisdom” (Ps. 103:24). If, then, Christ is the Wisdom of God, and the Psalm says, “You made all things in Wisdom,” then, just as all things were made through him, so all things were made in him.

If, therefore, all things are in him, dearest brothers, and what was made in him is life, then the earth too is life, and the tree too is life. We do indeed call the tree life, but in the sense of the tree of the cross, from which we have received life. Then the stone too is life.

It is disgraceful to understand it in this way, lest that same most filthy sect of the Manichaeans creep back upon us and say that a stone has life, a wall has a soul, a cord has a soul, and wool and clothing have souls. In their madness they are accustomed to say this, and when they have been restrained [or: when they have been refuted] and driven back, they produce something as though from the Scriptures, saying: “Why was it said, ‘What was made in him is life’? If all things were made in him, then all things are life.”

Do not let them lead you astray. Pronounce it this way: “What was made”—pause there—and then continue, “in him was life.” What does this mean? The earth was made, but the earth itself that was made is not life. Yet in Wisdom itself there is, spiritually, a certain principle according to which the earth was made; this is life.

17. How can I put it? I shall explain it to your Charity. A craftsman makes a chest. First, he possesses the chest in his craft; for if he did not possess the chest in his craft, where would he bring it forth from when he constructed it? But the chest exists in the craft in such a way that it is not itself the chest seen by the eyes. Invisibly it exists in the craft; visibly it will exist in the work.

Behold, it has been made in the work. Has it therefore ceased to exist in the craft? The chest in the work has been made, and the chest that exists in the craft remains. For the chest in the work can decay, and another chest can again be made from the one that exists in the craft.

Consider, then, the chest in the craft and the chest in the work. The chest in the work is not life; the chest in the craft is life, because the craftsman’s soul lives, and in it all these things exist before they are brought forth.

So, dearest brothers, because the Wisdom of God, through whom all things were made, contains all things according to its craft before it makes them, the things that are made through that craft are not immediately life; but whatever has been made has life in him.

You see the earth: in the craft there is earth. You see heaven: in the craft there is heaven. You see the sun and the moon: these too are in the craft. But outside they are bodies; in the craft they are life.

See this, if you can in any way; for what has been said is a great matter. And even if it was not said by a great man, or not through me as a great man, nevertheless it was said by one who is great. These things were not spoken by me, a little one; but the one to whom I look in order to speak is not little. Let each person grasp what he can, insofar as he can; and whoever cannot, let him nourish his heart so that he may be able.

From what should he nourish it? Let him nourish it with milk, so that he may reach solid food. Let him not withdraw from Christ born in the flesh until he reaches Christ born from the one Father: the Word, God with God, through whom all things were made; for that life which is in him is the light of human beings.

[Col. 1388] Three manuscripts have: “because that life which is in him is the light of human beings.”

18. For what follows is: “And the life was the light of human beings”; and human beings are illuminated by that life itself. Animals are not illuminated, because animals do not possess rational minds capable of seeing wisdom. Human beings, however, were made in the image of God and possess a rational mind through which they can perceive wisdom.

Therefore, that life through which all things were made is itself light—and not the light of just any living creatures, but the light of human beings. Hence a little later he says, “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” John the Baptist was illuminated by that light; John the Evangelist too was illuminated by it. He was full of that light who said, “I am not the Christ”; but the one who comes after me, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie (John 1:9, 20, 27).

He who said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” was illuminated by that light. Therefore, that life is the light of human beings.

19. But perhaps foolish hearts still cannot grasp this light because they are weighed down by their sins and therefore cannot see it. Let them not think that the light is absent simply because they cannot see it: they themselves are darkness because of their sins. “And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.”

Therefore, brothers, just as a blind man placed in the sunlight has the sun present to him, while he himself is absent from the sun, so every foolish, wicked, and impious person is blind in heart. Wisdom is present, but when it is present to a blind person, it is absent from his eyes—not because it is absent from him, but because he is absent from it.

What, then, should such a person do? Let him cleanse the place by which God can be seen. If he could not see because his eyes were dirty and wounded, with dust, discharge, or smoke entering them, the physician would say to him, “Cleanse from your eye whatever is harmful, so that you may be able to see the light of your eyes.”

Dust, discharge, and smoke are sins and iniquities. Remove all these things from there, and you will see the wisdom that is present—for God himself is that wisdom. And it has been said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

TRACTATE II. On what is written, “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John,” etc., as far as “full of grace and truth.” Chapter 1, vv. 6–14.

1. It is good, brothers, that we should expound, as we are able, the text of the divine Scriptures, and especially of the holy Gospel, passing over no passage; that, according to our capacity, we may be fed and may minister to you that from which we too are fed. We remember that on the preceding Lord’s day the first chapter was treated, namely: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made. What was made in him was life; and the life was the light of human beings; and the light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” I believe that the exposition went as far as this. All who were present, remember it; and those who were not present, believe us and those who wished to be present. Since, then, we cannot always repeat everything, on account of those who wish to hear what follows and for whom the repetition of the earlier matters, at the expense of the later, is burdensome, let those who were absent kindly not demand what has passed, but now hear the present matters together with those who were present.

2. It follows: “There was a man sent from God, whose name was John.” For what was said above, dearest brothers, was said of the ineffable divinity of Christ, and almost ineffably. For who will comprehend, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God”? And lest the name Word become cheap to you through familiarity with everyday words: “and the Word was God.” This Word is that very thing of which we spoke much yesterday; and may the Lord grant that, merely by speaking, we have conveyed even so much to your hearts. “In the beginning was the Word.” It is that very thing; it is in the same way; as it is, so it is always; it cannot change: this is “is” [Note: [Col. 1389] Printed editions and manuscripts read, “this is God-is,” except for the Bech. codex, which lacks the word “God.”]. This is the name which he declared to his servant Moses: “I am who am,” and, “He who is has sent me” (Exod. 3:14).

Who, then, will comprehend this, when you see all mortal things to be changeable; when you see not only bodies altered by their qualities—being born, growing, declining, dying—but also souls themselves stretched and torn apart by the impulses of differing wills; when you see that people can receive wisdom if they bring themselves near to its light and warmth, and can lose wisdom if by an evil inclination they withdraw from it? Since, therefore, you see all these things to be changeable, what is that which is, except that which transcends all things that so are as not to be? Who, then, can comprehend this? Or who, however he may exert the strength of his mind in order to touch, as he can, that which is, can arrive at that which he has in some fashion touched with his mind?

It is as though someone sees his homeland from afar, with the sea lying between: he sees where he is going, but does not have the means by which to go. So we wish to arrive at that stability of ours where what is, is—because this alone always is as it is—but the sea of this age through which we travel lies between, although we already see where we are going; for many do not even see where they should go. Therefore, in order that there might also be a way by which we could go, he to whom we wished to go came from there. And what did he do? He established wood by which we might cross the sea. For no one can cross the sea of this age unless borne by the cross of Christ. Even one weak in eyesight sometimes embraces this cross [Note: [Col. 1389] Thus the manuscripts; printed editions read, “and a weak eye.”]; and whoever does not see far off where he is going should not withdraw from it, and it will itself bring him through.

3. Accordingly, my brothers, let me impress this upon your hearts: if you wish to live piously and Christianly, cling to Christ according to that which he was made for us, so that you may attain him according to that which he is, and according to that which he was. He came near so that he might be made this for us [Note: [Col. 1390] Thus the printed editions. The manuscripts punctuate: “And according to that which he was, he came near so that he might be made this for us”; the Bech. codex adds here: “which he was not.”], because he was made this for us, where the weak may be carried, cross the sea of the age, and reach their homeland, where there will no longer be need of a ship because no sea is crossed. It is therefore better not to see with the mind that which is, and yet not to withdraw from Christ’s cross, than to see it with the mind and despise Christ’s cross. It is good, and best of all if possible, both to see where one must go and to hold fast to that by which the traveler is borne.

This the great minds of the mountains—the mountains so called, which the light of righteousness especially illumines—were able to do: they were able, and saw that which is. For John, seeing, said, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” They saw this; and, in order to arrive at what they saw from afar, they did not withdraw from Christ’s cross and did not despise Christ’s humility. But the little ones, who cannot understand this, do not withdraw from Christ’s cross, passion, and resurrection; in that very ship they are brought to what they do not see, and in that ship also arrive those who see.

4. Yet certain philosophers of this world arose and sought the Creator through creation, because he can be found through creation, as the Apostle plainly says: “For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made; even his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse.” And it follows: “Because, although they knew God”—he did not say, “Because they did not know God,” but, “Because, although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became vain in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened.” How was it darkened? He follows and says more plainly: “For, professing themselves to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. 1:20–22).

They saw where they ought to come; but, ungrateful to him who had granted them what they saw, they wished to ascribe to themselves what they saw. Becoming proud, they lost what they saw and turned from it to idols, images, and the worship of demons, to worship the creature and despise the Creator. But these men acted thus after they had already been dashed down; yet, in order to be dashed down, they became proud, and when they became proud, they called themselves wise. Those, therefore, of whom he said, “Although they knew God,” saw what John says, namely, that all things were made through the Word of God. For these things too are found in the books of the philosophers: that God has an only-begotten Son, through whom are all things. They were able to see that which is, but saw it from afar. They did not wish to hold to Christ’s humility, in the ship of which they might safely arrive at that which they could see far off; Christ’s cross seemed contemptible to them. The sea must be crossed, and do you despise the wood? O proud wisdom! You mock Christ crucified; he is the one whom you saw from afar: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”

But why was he crucified? Because the wood of his humility was necessary for you. For you had swelled with pride and had been cast far from that homeland; the way was interrupted by the waves of this age, and there is no means of crossing to the homeland unless you are borne by wood. Ungrateful one, do you mock him who came to you so that you might return? He himself was made the way—and this through the sea: hence he walked upon the sea (Matt. 14:25), to show that there is a way in the sea. But you, since you cannot walk upon the sea as he does, be carried by a ship, be carried by wood: believe in the Crucified One, and you will be able to arrive. He was crucified for your sake in order to teach humility; and if he had come as God, he would not have been recognized. For if he had come as God, he would not have come to those who could not see God. For according to that whereby he is God, he neither comes nor departs, since he is everywhere present and is contained in no place. According to what, then, did he come? According to that wherein he appeared as a human being.

5. Therefore, because he was such a human being that God was hidden in him, a great man was sent before him, by whose testimony he might be found to be more than a human being.
