And who is this? “There was a man.” And how could this man speak truth about God? “Sent from God.” What was he called? “Whose name was John.” Why did he come? “He came as a witness, to bear witness concerning the light, that all might believe through him.” What kind of man was he, who bore witness concerning the light? This John was something great: immense merit, great grace, great eminence! Marvel—indeed, marvel—but as at a mountain. Yet a mountain is in darkness unless it is clothed with light. Therefore marvel at John only so as to hear what follows: “He was not the light,” lest, when you think the mountain to be light, you suffer shipwreck on the mountain and find no relief. But what ought you to marvel at? The mountain as a mountain. Raise yourself instead to him who illumines the mountain, which was raised up for this purpose, that it might first receive the rays and announce them to your eyes. Therefore, “he was not the light.”

6. Why, then, did he come? “But to bear witness concerning the light.” For what purpose? “That all might believe through him.” And concerning what light did he bear witness? “There was the true light.” Why was “true” added? Because an enlightened human being too is called a light; but the true light is that which enlightens. Our eyes too are called lights; yet unless a lamp is lit at night or the sun comes forth by day, these lights are open to no purpose. Thus John too was a light, but not the true light; for unless enlightened he was darkness, but by enlightenment he became light. Unless he had been enlightened, he was darkness, like all the ungodly, to whom the Apostle, now believers, said: “You were once darkness.” But now, because they had believed, what? “But now,” he says, “you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8). Unless he had added “in the Lord,” we should not understand. “You are light,” he says, “in the Lord”; you were not darkness in the Lord. “For you were once darkness”: there he did not add “in the Lord.” Therefore darkness is in yourselves, light in the Lord. So he too was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light.

7. But where is that light itself? “There was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” If every human being coming into this world, then John himself too. Therefore he was enlightening John, who wished to be pointed out by him. Let your Charity understand: for he was coming to weak minds, wounded hearts, and the bleary sight of the soul. He had come for this purpose. And by what means could the soul see that which is perfect? It is often the case that we recognize that the sun has risen by some illuminated body, though we cannot see it with our eyes. For those whose eyes are wounded are capable of seeing a wall lit and illuminated by the sun, or a mountain, a tree, or something of that sort; and in another thing that has been illumined, that rising is shown to them, for seeing which they still possess sight less capable.

Thus all those to whom Christ had come were less capable of seeing him. He caused John to shine; and through John, confessing that he had been made radiant and enlightened, not that he himself made radiant and enlightened, he who enlightens was recognized, he who illumines was recognized, he who fills was recognized. And who is he? “The one,” he says, “who enlightens every human being coming into the world.” For unless the human being had withdrawn from there, he would not need to be enlightened; but he needs to be enlightened here precisely because he withdrew from there, where he could always be enlightened.

8. What then? If he came here, where was he? “He was in the world.” He was here and came here: he was here by his divinity; he came here by his flesh. For when he was here by his divinity, he could not be seen by fools, the blind, and the wicked. Those wicked persons are the darkness of which it was said, “The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5). Behold, he is here even now; he was here and is always here; he never departs, withdraws nowhere. You need to possess that by which you may see him who never withdraws from you; you need not to withdraw from him who withdraws nowhere; you need not to forsake him, and you will not be forsaken. Do not fall, and he will not set for you. If you fall, he causes a setting for you; but if you stand, he is present to you.

But you did not stand. Remember whence you fell, whence he who first fell cast you down. For he cast you down, not by force, not by a push, but by your own will. For if you had not consented to evil, you would have stood and remained enlightened. But now, since you have already fallen and have become wounded in heart, by which that light can be seen [Note: [Col. 1392] Printed editions read “cannot be seen.” *Non* is absent from the manuscripts. Augustine’s meaning is that the light is seen not with the eye but with the heart.], he came to you such as you could see; and he presented himself as such a human being that he sought testimony from a human being. God seeks testimony from a human being, and God has a human being as witness—God has a human being as witness, but for the sake of human beings: so weak are we! Through a lamp we seek the day, because John himself was called a lamp, the Lord saying: “He was a burning and shining lamp, and you were willing to rejoice for an hour in his light; but I have testimony greater than John’s” (John 5:35–36).

9. Therefore he showed that for the sake of human beings he wished to be pointed out through a lamp to the faith of believers, so that through that lamp his enemies might be confounded. For those enemies who tested him and said, “Tell us: by what authority do you do these things?”—“I too,” he said, “will ask you one question: tell me, whence is John’s baptism? From heaven or from human beings?” They were troubled and said among themselves, “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why then did you not believe him?’” (for John had borne witness to Christ and had said, “I am not the Christ, but he is” [John 1:20, 27]). “But if we say that it is from human beings, we fear the people, lest they stone us, for they regarded John as a prophet.” Fearing stoning, but fearing still more the confession of truth, they answered falsehood to truth; and iniquity lied to itself (Ps. 26:12). For they said, “We do not know.” And because by denying that they knew what they did know they had shut themselves against him, the Lord did not open to them either, because they had not knocked. For it was said: “Knock, and it shall be opened to you” (Matt. 7:7). They not only did not knock so that it might be opened, but by denying it they barred the very door against themselves. And the Lord said to them: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. 21:23–27; Mark 11:28–33; Luke 20:2–8). And they were confounded through John, and in them was fulfilled: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (Ps. 131:17–18).

10. “He was in the world, and the world was made through him.” Do not suppose that he was in the world as the earth is in the world, heaven is in the world, the sun, moon, and stars are in the world, and trees, cattle, and human beings are in the world. He was not in the world in that way. But how was he in it? As an artisan governing what he has made. For he did not make it as a carpenter makes something. The chest he makes is outside him and is located elsewhere while it is being constructed; and although it is near, the maker himself sits elsewhere and is external to that which he makes. But God makes while poured into the world; he makes while present everywhere, and does not withdraw anywhere; he is not outside it, as though he were turning about the mass that he makes. By the presence of his majesty he makes what he makes; by his presence he governs what he has made. Thus he was in the world, as the one through whom the world was made. For the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.

11. What is meant by “the world was made through him”? Heaven, earth, sea, and everything in them are called “world.” Again, in another sense, lovers of the world are called “world.” The world was made through him, and the world did not know him. Did the heavens not know their Creator, or did the angels not know their Creator, or did the stars not know their Creator—the Creator whom demons confess? From every side all things bore witness. But who did not know him? Those who, by loving the world, were called world. For by loving we dwell in the heart; and by loving they deserved to be called that in which they dwelt. Just as we say, “That house is bad,” or “That house is good”: in the house we call bad, we do not accuse the walls, nor in the house we call good do we praise the walls; rather, by a bad house we mean bad inhabitants, and by a good house, good inhabitants. So too, the world consists of those who dwell in it by loving the world. Who are they? Those who love the world; for they dwell in the world in their hearts. Those who do not love the world, however, move about in the world in the flesh, but dwell in heaven in their hearts, as the Apostle says: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3:20). Therefore the world was made through him, and the world did not know him.

12. “He came into his own”: because all these things were made through him. “And his own did not receive him.” Who were his own? The human beings whom he made; the Jews, whom he first made to be above all nations. For the other nations worshiped idols and served demons, but that people was born from Abraham’s seed; and they were especially his own, because they were also his kinsmen through the flesh which he deigned to assume. “He came into his own, and his own did not receive him.” Did they not receive him at all? Did no one receive him? Then no one was saved? For no one will be saved unless he receives Christ when he comes.

13. But he added: “But as many as received him.” What did he grant them? Great kindness! Great mercy! He was born the Only-begotten, and did not wish to remain alone. When many people have had no children, after their time of life has passed they adopt children for themselves; by their will they do what they could not do by nature: this is what human beings do. But if someone has an only son, he rejoices in him the more because he alone will possess everything and will have no one with whom to divide the inheritance, so that he may remain poorer. God is not so. The very Only-begotten whom he had begotten, and through whom he had created all things, he sent into this world so that he would not be alone, but might have adopted brothers. For we were not born from God as that Only-begotten was, but were adopted through his grace. For the Only-begotten came to loose the sins in which we were entangled, lest, because of their impediment, he should not adopt us; those whom he wished to make his brothers, he himself loosed and made fellow heirs.

For thus the Apostle says: “But if a son, then an heir through God” (Gal. 4:7); and again, “Heirs indeed of God, but fellow heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8:17). He did not fear to have fellow heirs, because his inheritance does not become cramped if many possess it. Indeed, they themselves, while he possesses them, become his inheritance, and he in turn becomes their inheritance. Hear how they become his inheritance: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son; this day I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance’” (Ps. 2:7–8). How does he become their inheritance? He says in the Psalm: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup” (Ps. 15:5). Let us both possess him and let him possess us: let him possess us as Lord; let us possess him as salvation, let us possess him as light. What, then, did he give to those who received him? “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name”: that they might hold to the wood and cross the sea.

### 14

And how are they born of him? Since these become children of God and brothers of Christ, they are certainly born. For if they are not born, how can they be children? Human children, however, are born from flesh and blood, from the will of a man, and from the union of marriage. But how are they born of him? “Not from bloods”—as from male and female.

“Sanguina” [Note: Some manuscripts have *sanguines*, written by a second hand.] is not Latin. But because the Greek has the plural, the translator preferred to render it this way, speaking somewhat less correctly according to the grammarians, yet explaining the truth in accordance with the understanding of the less instructed. For if he had said *blood* in the singular, he would not have explained what he intended: human beings are born from the bloods of male and female. Let us therefore say it; let us not fear the grammarians’ rods, so long as we arrive at solid and more certain truth. The one who understands finds fault, ungratefully because he has understood.

“Not from bloods, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man.” He used “flesh” for “woman,” because, when she had been made from Adam’s rib, Adam said, “This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh” (Gen. 2:23); and the Apostle says, “He who loves his wife loves himself; for no one has ever hated his own flesh” (Eph. 5:28–29). Thus “flesh” is used for “wife,” just as sometimes “spirit” is used for “husband.” Why? Because the man rules and the woman is ruled: he ought to command, she to serve. For where flesh commands and spirit serves, the household is disordered. What is worse than a household in which the woman exercises authority over the man? A household is rightly ordered when the man commands and the woman obeys. So a person himself is rightly ordered when the spirit commands and the flesh serves.

### 15

These, then, were born not from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God. Yet, in order that human beings might be born of God, God was first born from human beings. For Christ is God, and Christ was born from human beings. He sought only a mother on earth, since he already had a Father in heaven: born from God, through whom we were to be made; and born from a woman, through whom we were to be remade.

Do not therefore marvel, O man, that you are made a son by grace, because you are born of God according to his Word. The Word himself first wished to be born from a human being, so that you might be born securely from God and say to yourself: “God did not wish to be born from a human being without reason, except because he considered me to be of some importance, so that he might make me immortal and be born mortally for me.”

Therefore, after saying, “They were born of God,” as though lest we marvel and recoil from so great a grace, lest it seem incredible to us that human beings are born of God, and as though making you secure, he said: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Why, then, do you marvel that human beings are born of God? Consider that God himself was born from human beings: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

### 16

Because the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, by that very birth he made an eye-salve with which the eyes of our hearts might be wiped clean, so that we might see his majesty through his humility [Note: In nearly all manuscripts, “through his humanity.”]. Therefore the Word became flesh and dwelt among us; he healed our eyes. And what follows? “And we saw his glory.”

No one could see his glory unless he were healed by the humility of the flesh. Why could we not see? Let your Charity attend, and see what I am saying. Dust had as though fallen into a man’s eye; earth had fallen in and wounded the eye, and he could not see the light. This wounded eye is anointed: it had been wounded by earth, and earth is applied to it so that it may be healed. For all eye-salves and medicines are made from earth. You were blinded by dust; by dust you are healed. Therefore the flesh had blinded you, and the flesh heals you.

For the soul had become carnal by consenting to carnal desires; from this the eye of the heart had been blinded. The Word became flesh: this physician made an eye-salve for you. And because he came in such a way as to destroy the vices of the flesh through the flesh, and through death to kill death, it was accomplished in you that, because the Word became flesh, you could say, “And we saw his glory.”

What sort of glory? How did the Son of Man appear? That was his humility, not his glory. But how far was the sight of man, healed through the flesh, brought? “We saw,” he says, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten Son from the Father, full of grace and truth.” Concerning grace and truth we shall treat more fully elsewhere in the Gospel itself, if the Lord deigns to grant it. For now let this suffice: be built up in Christ, be strengthened in faith, and be vigilant in good works. Do not withdraw from the wood by which you may cross the sea.

## TRACTATE III

From the passage written, “John bears witness concerning him,” and so forth, up to, “The only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.” Chapter 1, verses 15–18.

### 1

We have undertaken, in the name of the Lord, to distinguish the grace and truth of God, with which the only-begotten Son, our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, appeared full to the saints, from the Old Testament, since it is a reality belonging to the New Testament; and we have promised this to your Charity. Attend, then, with concentration, so that God may grant me to grasp as much as I can, and you may hear as much as you can receive.

What remains is this: if the birds do not take away the seed scattered in your hearts, if the thorns do not choke it, and if the heat does not scorch it, then, with the rain of daily exhortations added, and with your good thoughts by which what is done in the heart is like what is done in a field with rakes—so that the clod may be broken, the seed covered, and able to germinate—you may “bring forth fruit” [Note: Erasmus, Lyon edition, and Venice edition have here, “so that it may bring forth fruit.” Manuscript M has the plural, “that you may bring forth fruit.”], at which the farmer may rejoice and be glad (Matt. 13:3–23).

But if, instead of good seed and good rain, we bring forth not fruit but thorns, neither will the seed be blamed nor the rain be charged with guilt; rather, the fire owed to the thorns is being prepared.

### 2

We are human beings, something which, I think, does not need to be urged upon your Charity for long; and if we are Christians, then by that very name we belong to Christ. We bear his sign on our forehead; we are not ashamed of it if we also bear it in our heart. His sign is his humility.

The Magi recognized him by the star (Matt. 2:2); and this was a sign given by the Lord, heavenly and splendid. Yet he did not wish his star to be the sign upon the foreheads of the faithful, but his cross. From the place where he was humbled, he was glorified; from the place to which he himself descended in humility, he raised up the humble.

We therefore belong to the Gospel [Note: Most manuscripts read, “For we belong to the Gospel.”]; we belong to the New Testament. “The Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” We ask the Apostle, and he tells us that we are not under the Law but under grace (Rom. 6:14).

Therefore he sent his Son, “made of a woman, made under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4:4–5). Behold, Christ came for this purpose: to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might now be not under the Law but under grace.

Who, then, gave the Law? He gave the Law who also gave grace; but he sent the Law through a servant, whereas with grace he himself descended. And how had human beings come to be under the Law? By not fulfilling the Law. For whoever fulfills the Law is not under the Law but with the Law; whoever is under the Law is not lifted up but weighed down by the Law.

Thus the Law makes all human beings who are placed under it guilty; and for this purpose it is over their head: to display sins, not to remove them. The Law therefore commands, while the giver of the Law shows mercy in what the Law commands.

Human beings attempted by their own strength to fulfill what the Law commanded; by their own rash and headlong presumption they fell, and they became not with the Law but under the Law, guilty. And because they could not fulfill the Law by their own strength, having become guilty under the Law, they implored the help of a liberator. The guilt imposed by the Law produced sickness in the proud. The sickness of the proud became the confession of the humble. The sick now confess that they are sick; let the physician come and heal the sick.

### 3

Who is the physician? Our Lord Jesus Christ.

Who is our Lord Jesus Christ? He who was seen even by those by whom he was crucified. He who was seized, struck on the cheek, scourged, covered with spittle, crowned with thorns, suspended on the cross, killed, wounded with a spear, taken down from the cross, and placed in the tomb.

He himself is our Lord Jesus Christ; he himself, entirely and unmistakably. He is the complete physician of our wounds: the crucified one who was mocked, while he hung there and his persecutors shook their heads, saying, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matt. 27:39–40). He himself is our complete physician—entirely so.

Why, then, did he not show those who mocked him that he was the Son of God? If he allowed himself to be lifted onto the cross, at least when they said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross,” he could then have come down and shown them that he truly was the Son of God, whom they had dared to ridicule. He did not wish to.

Why did he not wish to? Was it perhaps because he could not? Certainly he could. For what is greater: to come down from the cross or to rise from the tomb? Yet he endured those who mocked him. The cross was undertaken not as a demonstration of power [Note: Some manuscripts of good quality read, “not as a demonstration of powerlessness.”], but as an example of patience.

There he healed your wounds, where he long endured his own; there he healed you from everlasting death, where he deigned to die temporarily. And did he die, or did death die in him? What sort of death is it that killed death?

### 4

Yet is this whole person our Lord Jesus Christ, who was seen, held, and crucified? Is all of him this? He is indeed himself, but not all of Christ is what the Jews saw; this is not the whole Christ.

And what is the whole Christ? “In the beginning was the Word.” In what beginning? “And the Word was with God.” And what sort of Word? “And the Word was God.”

Was this Word perhaps made by God? No. “This was in the beginning with God.” What then? Are the other things God made unlike the Word? No, “because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

How were all things made through him? Because “what was made was life in him”; and before it was made, it was life. What was made is not life, but in the art—that is, in the Wisdom of God—before it was made, it was life. What was made passed away; what is in Wisdom cannot pass away. Therefore, what was made was life in him.

And what sort of life? The soul, too, is the life of the body: our body has its own life, and when it loses that life, there is death of the body. Was that life therefore of such a kind? No; it was “the light of human beings.”

Was it the light of animals? That light belongs both to human beings and to animals. There is a certain light belonging to human beings. Let us see how human beings differ from animals, and then we shall understand what the light of human beings is.

You differ from an animal only by understanding; do not boast of anything else. Do you presume upon strength? You are defeated by beasts. Do you presume upon speed? You are defeated by flies. Do you presume upon beauty? What beauty there is in the feathers of a peacock!

How, then, are you better? By the image of God. Where is the image of God? In the mind, in the understanding. If, therefore, you are better than an animal because you have a mind by which you understand what an animal cannot understand—and if a human being is human because he is better than an animal—then the light of human beings is the light of minds.

The light of minds is above minds and surpasses all minds. This was that life through which all things were made.

### 5

Where was he? Was he here, or was he with the Father and not here? Or, what is more true, was he both with the Father and here?

If he was here, why was he not seen? Because “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.” O human beings, do not be darkness; do not be unbelieving, unjust, wicked, rapacious, greedy, lovers of the world. For these are the darkness. The light is not absent, but you are absent from the light.

A blind person has the sun present to him while he himself is absent from the sun. Do not, then, be darkness. This is perhaps the grace of which I am going to speak: that we should no longer be darkness, and that the Apostle may say to us, “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5:8).

Because the light of human beings—that is, the light of minds—was not seen, it was necessary for a human being to bear witness concerning the light: not one who was still darkness, but one who had already been illumined. Yet, because he was illumined, he was not himself the light; rather, he was to bear witness concerning the light.

For he was not the light. And what was the light? “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” And where was this light? It was in this world.

And how was it in this world? Was this light in the world in the same way as the light of the sun, moon, and lamps? No. “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him.” This is to say: the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

For the world was darkness, because the lovers of the world are the world. Did creation itself not recognize its Creator? Heaven bore witness through the star (Matt. 2:2); the sea bore witness, carrying the Lord as he walked upon it (Matt. 14:26); the winds bore witness, growing still at his command (Matt. 8:27); the earth bore witness, trembling when he was crucified (Matt. 27:51).

If all these things bore witness, how did the world not know him? Only because “the world” means the lovers of the world, who inhabit the world in their hearts. And the world is evil because its inhabitants are evil, just as a house is bad not because of its walls but because of those who inhabit it.

### 6

“He came to his own,” that is, he came among his own things, “and his own did not receive him.” What hope, then, is there, except that “to all who received him he gave power to become children of God”?

If they become children, they are born. If they are born, how are they born? “Not of flesh, not of bloods, not of the will of the flesh, not of the will of man, but of God they were born.”

Let them rejoice, then, because they were born of God; let them presume that they belong to God; let them receive proof that they were born of God: “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

If the Word was not ashamed to be born from a human being, are human beings ashamed to be born from God? By doing this he healed us; because he healed us, we see.

For this very thing—that the Word became flesh and dwelt among us—became medicine for us, so that, because we were blinded by earth [Note: Three manuscripts read, “because we were blinded from the earth.” Three others read, “because we were blinded by the earth.” One reads, “because we were blinded from dust.”], we might be healed by earth. And, once healed, what would we see? “And we saw,” he says, “his glory, glory as of the only-begotten Son from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John 1:1–14).

### 7

John bears witness concerning him and cries out, saying, “This was he of whom I said, ‘He who comes after me was made before me.’” He came after me and went before me.

What does “he was made before me” mean? He went before me. It does not mean, “He was made before I was made,” but “he was placed before me”; that is, “he was made before me.”

Why was he made before you, when he came after you? Because he was before me.

Before you, O John? What is so remarkable if he was before you? It is indeed fitting, since you bear witness concerning him. Let us hear him himself saying, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58).

But Abraham too arose within the human race; many were before him and many after him. Hear the Father’s voice to the Son: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. 109:3).

He who was begotten before the morning star himself illumines all. For a certain one who fell was called “morning star”: he was an angel and became the devil. Scripture said of him, “Morning star, which rose in the morning, has fallen” (Isa. 14:12).

Why “morning star”? Because he shone after being illumined. And why did he become dark? Because he did not stand in the truth (John 8:44).

Therefore he is before the morning star, before every illumined being; indeed, he must be before every illumined being, since all who can be illumined are illumined by him.

### 8

Therefore what follows is this: “And from his fullness we have all received.” What have you received? “And grace for grace.”

This is how the Gospel words stand when compared with the Greek copies. It does not say, “And from his fullness we have all received grace for grace,” but says, “And from his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace”—that is, we have received. It seems to me that he wished us to understand that we received something from his fullness, and, in addition, grace for grace.

For from his fullness we first received grace; and again we received grace—grace for grace. What grace did we first receive? Faith. Walking in faith, we walk in grace.

By what did we deserve this? By what preceding merits of ours? Let no one flatter himself; let him return to his conscience, seek out the hiding places of his thoughts, and return to the sequence of his deeds. Let him not consider what he is, if he is already something, but what he was in order that he might become something. He will find that he was worthy of nothing but punishment.

If, then, you were worthy of punishment, and he came not to punish sins but to forgive sins, grace was given to you, not a reward returned. Why is it called grace? Because it is given freely. You did not purchase by preceding merits what you received.

The sinner therefore received this first grace: that his sins might be forgiven. What did he deserve? Let him question justice: he finds punishment. Let him question mercy: he finds grace.

But God had also promised this through the Prophets. Therefore, when he came to give what he had promised, he gave not only grace but also truth. How was truth supplied? Because what had been promised was accomplished.

### 9

What, then, is “grace for grace”? By faith we merit God; and although we were not worthy to have our sins forgiven, because we unworthily received so great a gift, it is called grace.

What is grace? Freely given. What does “freely given” mean? Granted, not repaid. If it was owed, then a reward was repaid, not grace granted; but if it was truly owed, you were good.

But if, as is true, you were evil, yet believed in him “who justifies the ungodly” (Rom. 4:5)—what does “who justifies the ungodly” mean? He makes the ungodly godly—consider what was impending for you through the Law and what you have obtained through grace.

Having obtained this grace of faith, you will be righteous by faith; “for the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17). You will merit God by living from faith. When you have merited God by living from faith, you will receive as a reward immortality and eternal life.

And that too is grace. For by what merit do you receive eternal life? By grace. If faith is grace and eternal life is, as it were, the reward of faith, God seems to return eternal life as something owed. To whom is it owed? To the faithful, because he merited it through faith.

But because faith itself is grace, eternal life too is grace for grace.

### 10

Hear the Apostle Paul confessing grace and afterward demanding what is owed. What is Paul’s confession of grace? “I who formerly was a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man; but,” he says, “I received mercy” (1 Tim. 1:13). He declared himself unworthy to receive it; yet he received it not through his own merits but through the mercy of God.

Hear him now demanding what is owed, though he had first received unearned grace: “For I am already being poured out as a sacrifice, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought the good fight, I have finished the course, I have kept the faith. From now on the crown of righteousness is laid up for me.”

Now he demands what is owed; now he claims what is owed. For see the words that follow: “Which the Lord, the righteous judge, will repay me on that day” (2 Tim. 4:6–8).

To receive grace beforehand, he needed a merciful Father; to receive the reward of grace, a just judge. Will he who did not condemn the ungodly condemn the faithful?

And yet, if you think carefully, he himself first gave the faith by which you merited him. You did not merit anything from your own resources such that something should be owed to you. Therefore, when he later grants the reward of immortality, he crowns his own gifts, not your merits.

Thus, brothers, we have all received from his fullness: from the fullness of his mercy, from the abundance of his goodness. What have we received? Forgiveness of sins, so that we might be justified by faith. And what besides? “And grace for grace”—that is, for this grace in which we live by faith, we shall receive another. Yet what will it be except grace?

For if I say that this too is owed, I assign something to myself, as though there were someone to whom it should be owed. God crowns in us the gifts of his mercy; but this is so only if we persevere in walking in the grace that we first received.

### 11

“For the Law was given through Moses”—the Law that held people guilty. For what does the Apostle say? “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5:20).

This was useful for the proud: that transgression might abound. They thought highly of themselves and attributed much, as it were, to their own strength; yet they could not fulfill righteousness unless the one who had commanded also helped them.

Desiring to subdue their pride, God gave the Law, as though saying: “Behold, fulfill it, so that you may not think that the one who commands is lacking.” The one who commands is not lacking; but the one who fulfills is lacking.

### 12

If, then, the one who fulfills is lacking, why does he not fulfill? Because he was born with the transmission of sin and death. Born from Adam, he drew with him what had been conceived there.

The first man fell, and all who were born from him drew from him the desire of the flesh. It was necessary that another man be born who drew no desire of the flesh. Man and man: man leading to death, and man leading to life.

Thus the Apostle says: “Since by a man came death, and by a man the resurrection of the dead.” Through which man did death come, and through which man the resurrection of the dead? Do not hurry; he continues and says: “For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

Who belong to Adam? All who were born from Adam. Who belong to Christ? All who were born through Christ.

Why are all in sin? Because no one was born except from Adam. But to be born from Adam was necessary because of condemnation; to be born through Christ is a matter of will and grace. Human beings are not compelled to be born through Christ; they were born from Adam without having chosen it.

Yet all who are from Adam are sinners with sin; all who are through Christ are justified and righteous—not in themselves but in him. For if you ask what they are in themselves, they are Adam; if you ask what they are in him, they are Christ [Note: The Carcassonne manuscript reads, “they are Christ” in the singular form *Christus sunt*.].

Why? Because he, our Lord Jesus Christ, is the head and did not come with the transmission of sin; nevertheless, he came with mortal flesh.

### 13

The death of sinners was punishment [Note: Four manuscripts read, “Death in Adam was the punishment of sinners.”]; in the Lord it was a gift of mercy, not punishment for sin. For the Lord had nothing for which he might justly die.

He himself said, “Behold, the prince of this world is coming, and he found nothing in me. But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise; let us go from here” (John 14:30–31).

He had no reason to die, and he died. You have reason to die, and you disdain dying? Deign with an even spirit to endure, on account of your own merit, what he deigned to endure in order to free you from eternal death.

Man and man: but the one was only man; this one was God-man [Note: The printed editions read, “God and man.” The word *et* has been removed on the authority of the manuscripts.]. The one was a man of sin; this one of righteousness.

You died in Adam; rise again in Christ. For both are owed to you. You have already believed in Christ, yet you will still pay what you owe from Adam. But the bond of sin will not hold you forever, because the temporal death of your Lord killed your eternal death.

This is grace, my brothers; this is also truth, because it was promised and supplied.

### 14

This was not present in the Old Testament, because the Law threatened but did not help; it commanded but did not heal; it displayed sickness but did not remove it. Yet it prepared the way for the physician who was to come with grace and truth.

It was like a physician sending his servant first to someone whom he wished to heal, so that the servant might find him bound. The man was not healthy, did not wish to be healed, and, so that he would not be healed, boasted that he was healthy. The Law was sent and bound him; he discovered himself guilty and now cries out because of his bonds.

The Lord came and heals with remedies that are somewhat bitter and sharp. For he says to the sick man, “Bear it”; he says, “Endure it”; he says, “Do not love the world; have patience. Let the fire of self-restraint heal you; let the wounds of persecution endure the iron.”

Although you were bound, you were afraid. He, free and unbound, drank what he was giving you; he suffered first to console you, as though saying: “What you fear to suffer for yourself, I suffer first for you.”

This is grace, and great grace. Who can praise it worthily?

### 15

I am speaking about Christ’s humility, my brothers. Who can speak of Christ’s majesty and Christ’s divinity?

In explaining and expressing Christ’s humility, so that in some manner we might speak of it, we do not suffice; rather, we fail. We entrust the whole matter to those who contemplate it, but we cannot complete it for those who hear.

Contemplate Christ’s humility.

“But who,” you say, “can explain it to us unless you speak?” Let him speak inwardly. The one who dwells within speaks it better than the one who cries out externally. May he himself show you the grace of his humility—the one who has begun to dwell in your hearts.

But if we fail when explaining and distributing his humility, who can speak of his majesty? If “the Word became flesh” troubles us, who can explain “In the beginning was the Word”?

Hold fast, then, brothers, to this solid foundation.

### 16

“The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” Through a servant the Law was given, and it made people guilty; through the Emperor indulgence was given, and it freed the guilty.

“The Law was given through Moses.” Let the servant not attribute to himself anything more than what was accomplished through him. Chosen for a great ministry, as a faithful servant in a household, yet still a servant, he can act according to the Law; he cannot free anyone from the guilt of the Law.

Therefore, “the Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.”

### 17

And lest someone perhaps say, “Grace and truth did not come through Moses, who saw God,” he immediately added, “No one has ever seen God.”

How, then, was God made known to Moses? Because the Lord revealed himself to his servant. Which Lord? Christ himself, who sent the Law beforehand through a servant, so that he himself might come with grace and truth.

For “no one has ever seen God.” How, then, did he appear to that servant to the extent that he could receive him? “But the only-begotten Son,” he says, “who is in the bosom of the Father, he has declared him.”

What does “in the bosom of the Father” mean? In the Father’s secret place. God does not have a bosom as we have one in our garments; nor should he be imagined to sit in the manner in which we sit; nor was he perhaps girded so as to have a bosom. Rather, because our bosom is within us, the Father’s secret place is called the Father’s bosom.

In the Father’s secret place, the one who knows the Father has declared him. For “no one has ever seen God.” He therefore came and declared whatever he had seen.

What did Moses see? Moses saw a cloud; he saw an angel; he saw fire. All that is created; it bore the type of its Lord, but it did not display the presence of the Lord himself.

For you have it plainly in the Law: “And Moses spoke with the Lord face to face, as a friend with his friend.” You follow the same Scripture and find Moses saying, “If I have found grace in your sight, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you.” And it is not enough that he said this: he received the answer, “You cannot see my face” (Exod. 33:11, 13, 20).

The angel, therefore, was speaking with Moses, my brothers, bearing the type of the Lord. And all those things that were done there through the angel promised this future grace and truth.

Those who search the Law carefully know this; and when the occasion arises for us also to say something from it, we do not keep silent before your Charity, insofar as the Lord reveals it.

### 18

Know this, however: all the things that were seen bodily were not the substance of God himself. We see those things with the eyes of the flesh; but how is the substance of God seen? Ask the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

There were people [Note: Arians] who, deceived by the vanity of their hearts, said, “The Father is invisible, but the Son is visible.”

Visible in what way? If on account of the flesh, because he assumed flesh, this is clear. Those who saw Christ’s flesh—some believed, some crucified him. And those who believed stumbled when he was crucified; unless they touched him after the resurrection, their faith would not have been restored.

If, then, the Son is visible on account of the flesh, we concede this, and it is the Catholic faith. But if they say that he was visible before the flesh—that is, before he was incarnate—they are greatly delirious and greatly mistaken.

Those visible things were made bodily through a creature, in which the type might be displayed; the substance itself was certainly not thereby shown and manifested.

Let your Charity also attend to this gentle lesson [Note: Most manuscripts read, “a slight lesson”; perhaps this means “a brief lesson.”]. The Wisdom of God cannot be seen with the eyes.

Brothers, if Christ is “the Wisdom of God and the Power of God” (1 Cor. 1:24), if Christ is the Word of God, and a human word cannot be seen with the eyes, can the Word of God be seen in this way?

### 19

Therefore drive carnal thoughts from your hearts, so that you may truly be under grace and belong to the New Testament. For this reason eternal life is promised in the New Testament.

Read the Old Testament and see that the same things were indeed commanded to the people, though still carnal, as are commanded to us. We too are commanded to worship one God. “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” is also commanded to us; this is the second commandment.

“Observe the Sabbath day” is commanded even more to us, because we are commanded to observe it spiritually. For the Jews observe the Sabbath slavishly, for indulgence and drunkenness. How much better it would be for their women to make wool on that day than to dance on balconies [Note: The printed editions have *neomeniis*, “new moons,” corruptly, in place of *maenianis*, which all our manuscripts prefer. The ancients called *maeniana* balconies or roof terraces of houses.]!

Far be it from us, brothers, to say that they observe the Sabbath. A Christian observes the Sabbath spiritually by abstaining from servile work. What is servile work? Sin. And how do we prove this? Ask the Lord: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

Therefore the spiritual observance of the Sabbath is commanded to us as well.

All those other commandments are now commanded to us even more, and are to be observed: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and mother; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exod. 20:3–17).

Are not all these also commanded to us? But seek the reward, and you will find that it says there: “So that enemies may be driven from your face, and you may receive the land that God promised to your fathers” (Lev. 26:1–13).

Because they could not grasp invisible things, they were held by visible things. Why were they held by them? So that they might not perish utterly and fall into idolatry.

For they did this, my brothers, as we read: they forgot the many miracles God performed before their eyes. The sea was divided; a road was made through the midst of the waves; their pursuing enemies were covered by the same waters through which the Israelites had passed (Exod. 14:21–31).

And when Moses, the man of God, had withdrawn from their sight, they asked for an idol and said, “Make gods for us who will go before us, because that man has left us.” All their hope had been placed in a human being, not in God.

Behold, the man has died. Did the God who rescued them from the land of Egypt also die? And when they had made an image of a calf, they worshiped it and said, “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. 32:1–4).

How quickly they forgot such manifest grace [Note: The printed editions have “magnificent grace.” All manuscripts have “manifest grace.”]! By what means, then, could such a people be held except by carnal promises?

### 20

The things commanded there in the Decalogue of the Law are also commanded to us; but the things promised there are not what is promised to us.

What is promised to us? Eternal life. “And this is eternal life: that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

Knowledge of God is promised; this is grace for grace. Brothers, for now we believe; we do not see. The reward for this faith will be to see what we believe.

The Prophets knew this, but it was hidden before he came. For a certain lover, sighing in the Psalms, says: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.”

And do you ask what he seeks? Perhaps he is asking carnally for a land flowing with milk and honey, although spiritually such things should be sought and requested; or perhaps the subjection of his enemies, or the death of his foes, or the powers and resources of this age.

For he burns with love, sighs deeply, is fevered, and pants. Let us see what he seeks: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek.”

What is this that he seeks? “That I may dwell,” he says, “in the house of the Lord all the days of my life.” And suppose that you dwell in the house of the Lord: where will your joy be there? “That I may contemplate,” he says, “the delight of the Lord” (Ps. 26:4).

21. My brothers, why do you cry out, why do you exult, why do you love, unless it is because the spark of this love is there? What do you desire, I ask you? Can it be seen with the eyes? Can it be touched? Is it some beauty that delights the eyes? Were not the martyrs loved with intense affection, and, when we commemorate them, do we not burn with love? What do we love in them, brothers? Limbs torn apart by wild beasts? What could be uglier, if you ask the eyes of the flesh? What could be more beautiful, if you ask the eyes of the heart?

What does a most handsome young thief seem to you? How your eyes recoil! Do the eyes of the flesh recoil? If you ask them, there is nothing more harmonious in that body, nothing more well-proportioned [Note: The printed editions have *ornatius* (“more adorned”), but the manuscripts read *ordinatius* (“more well-proportioned”).]; the symmetry of his limbs and the pleasing color attract the eyes. Yet when you hear that he is a thief, you flee from the man in your spirit.

On the other hand, you see an old man bent over, leaning on a staff, scarcely able to move, covered everywhere with wrinkles: what do you see that delights the eyes? You hear that he is just; you love him, you embrace him.

Such rewards have been promised to us, my brothers. Love something of this kind; sigh for such a kingdom; desire such a homeland, if you wish to attain that which our Lord came with—that is, grace and truth.

But if you desire bodily rewards from God, you are still under the Law, and therefore you will not fulfill the Law itself. For when you see these temporal things abounding among those who offend God, your steps falter, and you say to yourself: “Look, I worship God; every day I run to church; my knees are worn out from prayers; and I am constantly sick. Other people commit murders and robberies; they rejoice and prosper; things go well for them.”

Were these, then, the things you were seeking from God? Certainly you belonged to grace [Note: The Germanensis manuscript reads: “You did not belong to grace.”]. If God gave you grace because he gave it freely, love him freely. Do not love God for the sake of a reward; let him himself be your reward.

Let your soul say: “One thing I asked of the Lord, this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life, that I may contemplate the delight of the Lord.”

Do not fear that you will grow weary from satiety. The delight of that beauty will be such that it will always be present to you, and you will never be sated; rather, you will always be sated and never be sated. For if I say that you will not be sated, there will be hunger; if I say that you will be sated, I fear weariness. Where there will be neither weariness nor hunger, I do not know what to say. But God possesses what he can display to those who cannot find how to express it, and what believers can receive.

# TRACTATE IV

From the passage written, “And this is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests from Jerusalem,” and so forth, up to the passage, “He is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit,” and so forth. Chapter I, verses 19–33.

[Col. 1406]

## 1

Your Holiness has very often heard—and you know it very well—that John the Baptist, the more distinguished he was among those born of women, and the more humble he was in recognizing the Lord, thereby merited being the bridegroom’s friend: zealous for the bridegroom, not for himself; seeking not his own honor but that of his judge, whom he preceded like a herald.

Thus the prophets who came before were granted the task of announcing beforehand what would happen concerning Christ; John, however, was granted the task of pointing him out with his finger. For just as Christ was unknown to those who did not believe the prophets before he came, so he was unknown to them even when he was present. He had come first in humility and hiddenness—more hidden because he was more humble. But the people, despising the humility of God through their pride, crucified their Savior and made him their condemner.

## 2

But he who first came hidden because he came humbly—will he not thereafter come openly because he is exalted? You have just heard the Psalm: “Our God will come openly, and he will not keep silence.” He kept silence in order to be judged; he will not keep silence when he begins to judge.

It would not be said, “He will come openly,” unless he had first come hidden; nor would it be said, “He will not keep silence,” unless he had first kept silence.

How did he keep silence? Ask Isaiah: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before the one who shears him [Note: The printed editions have *tondet* (“shears”), but the manuscripts read *tonderet* (“who would shear him”);] he was without a voice, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

But he will come openly and will not keep silence. How openly? “Fire will go before him, and a mighty storm will surround him” (Psalm 49:3). That storm will carry all the chaff from the threshing floor that is now being threshed, and the fire will burn what the storm has carried away.

For now he is silent: silent in judgment, but not silent in command. If Christ is silent, what are these Gospels for? What are the apostolic voices for? What are the songs of the Psalms for? What are the utterances of the prophets for? In all these Christ is not silent.

But now he is silent so as not to take vengeance; he is not silent so as not to warn. He will come in splendor for vengeance, and he will appear to everyone, including those who do not believe in him.

But because he was also present in hiddenness, he had to be despised. For unless he had been despised, he would not have been crucified; and unless he had been crucified, he would not have poured out the blood by which he redeemed us. In order to pay the price for us, he was crucified; in order to be crucified, he was despised; in order to be despised, he appeared in humility.

## 3

Nevertheless, because he appeared as if in the night, in mortal flesh, he lit a lamp for himself by which he might be seen. That lamp was John (John 5:35), about whom you have already heard much. The present Gospel reading contains John’s words, first—and this is the chief point—confessing that he himself was not the Christ.

John’s excellence was so great that he could have been believed to be the Christ. His humility was therefore proved in this: he said that he was not, although he could have been believed to be.

Thus: “This is the testimony of John, when the Jews sent priests and Levites from Jerusalem to him to question him: ‘Who are you?’”

They would not have sent them unless they had been moved by the excellence of his authority, because he had dared to baptize. “And he confessed, and did not deny. What did he confess? He confessed: ‘I am not the Christ.’”

## 4

“And they asked him, ‘What then? Are you Elijah?’” For they knew that Elijah would precede Christ. The name of Christ was certainly not unknown among the Jews. They did not suppose that this man was the Christ; they did not suppose that Christ would not come at all. While they expected him to come, they stumbled over him when he was present, as over a humble stone.

For that stone was still small, though it had already been cut from the mountain without hands, as the prophet Daniel says: he saw a stone cut from the mountain without hands. But what follows? “And that stone grew,” he says, “and became a great mountain, and filled the whole face of the earth” (Daniel 2:34–35).

Let Your Charity see what I am saying. Christ had already been cut from the mountain before the Jews. By the mountain he means the kingdom of the Jews. But the kingdom of the Jews had not filled the whole face of the earth. That stone was cut from there because the Lord was born there in the flesh.

And why “without hands”? Because the Virgin bore Christ without human action. Thus that stone had already been cut without hands and stood before the eyes of the Jews; but it was humble. Not without reason: the stone had not yet grown and filled the whole world. It displayed this in its kingdom, which is the Church, by which it filled the whole face of the earth.

Because it had not yet grown, they stumbled over it as over a stone. And what was written about them came to pass: “Whoever falls upon that stone will be shattered; and upon whomever that stone falls, it will crush him” (Luke 20:18).

At first they fell upon the humble one; the exalted one will come upon them. But in order that the exalted one might come and crush them, the humble one first shattered them. They stumbled over him and were shattered—not crushed, but shattered. He will come exalted and crush them.

Yet the Jews must be forgiven, because they stumbled over a stone that had not yet grown [Note: An old Remigian manuscript reads: “If they are not to be forgiven.”]. What of those who have stumbled over the mountain itself? You recognize whom I mean. Those who deny that the Church is spread throughout the whole world stumble not over the humble stone but over the mountain itself—the form that the stone assumed as it grew.

The blind Jews did not see the humble stone. How great, then, is the blindness of those who do not see the mountain?

## 5

They saw the humble one, therefore, but did not recognize him. He was pointed out to them by a lamp. For first, the one greater than whom no one born of women had arisen said, “I am not the Christ.”

And it was said to him, “Are you Elijah?” He answered, “I am not.”

Christ sends Elijah before him. John said, “I am not,” and this created a difficulty for us. For we must fear that those who understand less carefully may think that John said something contrary to what Christ said.

In one passage, when the Lord Jesus Christ was speaking about himself in the Gospel, the disciples answered him: “How then do the scribes—that is, the experts in the Law—say that Elijah must come first?” And the Lord said: “Elijah has already come, and they did to him whatever they wished; and, if you want to know, he is John the Baptist” (Matthew 17:10–13; 11:11–14).

The Lord Jesus Christ said, “Elijah has already come,” and that he was John the Baptist. But when John was questioned, he confessed that he was not Elijah, just as he confessed that he was not Christ.

And surely, just as he truthfully confessed that he was not Christ, so he truthfully confessed that he was not Elijah. How, then, shall we compare the herald’s words with the judge’s words? Far be it that the herald should lie; for he speaks what he hears from the judge.

Why, then, did John say, “I am not Elijah,” while the Lord said, “He is Elijah”? Because the Lord Jesus Christ wished to prefigure in him his future coming, and to say that John was in the spirit of Elijah. What John was in relation to the first coming, Elijah will be in relation to the second coming.

Just as there are two comings of the judge, so there are two heralds. There are two heralds, but not two judges. For the judge himself had to come first to be judged. He sent a first herald before him and called him Elijah, because in the second coming Elijah will be what John was in the first.

## 6

Let Your Charity attend to how true what I say is. When John was conceived—or rather, when he was born—the Holy Spirit prophesied that this would be fulfilled in that man: “He will be the forerunner of the Most High,” it says, “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17).

Therefore, not Elijah, but “in the spirit and power of Elijah.” What does “in the spirit and power of Elijah” mean? In the same Holy Spirit, in Elijah’s place.

Why in Elijah’s place? Because what Elijah will be for the second coming, John was for the first. John therefore rightly answered in the proper sense. The Lord, however, spoke figuratively: “He himself is Elijah,” meaning John. But John, as I have said, spoke properly: “I am not Elijah.”

If you consider the figure of the forerunner, John himself is Elijah: what Elijah will be for the second coming, John was for the first. If you ask about the identity of the persons, John is John and Elijah is Elijah.

Thus the Lord rightly said with reference to the prefiguration, “He himself is Elijah”; John rightly said with reference to the person, “I am not Elijah.” Neither John nor the Lord spoke falsely; neither the herald nor the Judge spoke falsely—but this is so only if you understand.

Who will understand? The one who imitates the herald’s humility and recognizes the judge’s greatness. For no one was more humble than that herald.

My brothers, John’s merit was not so great in anything as in this humility: although he could have deceived people and been thought to be Christ and accepted as Christ—for he possessed such grace and such excellence—he nevertheless openly confessed and said, “I am not the Christ.”

“Are you Elijah?” If he had answered, “I am Elijah,” then Christ would already have been coming in his second coming to judge, not still being judged in his first coming. As if saying, “Elijah will come,” he answered, “I am not Elijah.”

But observe the humble one before whom John came, lest you fail to recognize the exalted one before whom Elijah will come. The Lord himself completed the matter in this way: “He is John the Baptist who is to come.” John came in the very prefiguration in which Elijah will come in person.

Then Elijah will truly be Elijah in person; now John was Elijah by resemblance. Now John is John in person and Elijah by resemblance [Note: All the manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions instead read: “Now John was Elijah by resemblance. In person John is John; then by resemblance Elijah will be John.”].

Both heralds received their respective resemblances and retained their respective identities; but there is one Lord and judge, whether preceded by one herald or by the other.

## 7

“And they asked him: ‘What then? Are you Elijah?’ And he said: ‘No.’ And they said to him: ‘Are you the prophet?’ And he answered: ‘No.’ Therefore they said to him: ‘Who are you, so that we may give an answer to those who sent us? What do you say about yourself?’

“He said: ‘I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.’”

Isaiah said this (Isaiah 40:3), and this prophecy was fulfilled in John: “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness.”

Crying what? “Make straight the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God.”

Does it not seem characteristic of a herald to say, “Come out; make a road”? Except that a herald says, “Come out,” whereas John says, “Come.” The herald drives people away from the judge; John calls them to the judge. Rather, John calls them to the humble one, so that the judge may not yet be perceived as exalted.

“I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight the way of the Lord,” as the prophet Isaiah said.

He did not say, “I am John,” or “I am Elijah,” or “I am a prophet.” What did he say? “This is what I am called: ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: make straight the way of the Lord.’ I am the prophecy itself.”

## 8

“And those who had been sent were from the Pharisees,” that is, from the leaders of the Jews. “And they questioned him and said to him: ‘Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?’”

It seemed to be an act of audacity to baptize, as though they were asking: “In what capacity? We ask whether you are the Christ; you say that you are not. We ask whether perhaps you are his forerunner, since we know that Elijah will come before Christ; you deny that you are. We ask whether perhaps you are a herald who greatly anticipates him—that is, a prophet—and have received this authority; yet you do not say that you are a prophet.”

John was not a prophet; he was more than a prophet. The Lord gave this testimony about him:

“What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?” You should understand: “not shaken by the wind,” because John was not like that, as though he were moved by the wind. For one who is moved by the wind is blown about by every deceitful spirit.

“But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft garments?” John was dressed in rough clothing, that is, a tunic made of camel’s hair.

“Behold, those who wear soft garments are in the houses of kings. Therefore you did not go out to see a man dressed in soft garments. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet” (Matthew 11:7–9). For the prophets foretold him long beforehand; John pointed out the one who was present.

## 9

“Why then do you baptize, if you are not the Christ, nor Elijah, nor the prophet?”

John answered them and said: “I baptize in water; but one stands among you whom you do not know.”

For the humble one was not visible, and for that reason the lamp was lit. See how he gives place to the one who might otherwise have been thought to be something else.

“He is the one who comes after me, who was placed before me”—that is, who was set above me, as we have already said. “Of whom I am not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal.”

How greatly did he humble himself! And therefore he was greatly exalted, because “whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11).

Hence Your Holiness should see that if John humbled himself so much that he said, “I am not worthy to untie his strap,” how must those humble themselves who say: “We baptize; what we give is ours, and what is ours is holy”? He says, “Not I, but he”; they say, “We” [Note: The pride of the Donatists.].

John is not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal. If he had said that he was worthy, how humble would he still have been? Even if he had said, “He comes after me, who was placed before me, and I am worthy only to untie the strap of his sandal,” he would have humbled himself greatly.

But when he does not even claim to be worthy of that, he was truly full of the Holy Spirit. In this way he recognized the Lord as a servant and merited to become a friend from being a servant.

## 10

“These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing.

“The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him and said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world.’”

Let no one claim this for himself and say that he takes away the sin of the world. Now pay attention [Note: This is the reading of nearly all the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “He takes away sins. Therefore now pay attention.”], against which proud people John was pointing his finger.

The heretics had not yet been born, and already they were being pointed out. John was crying out against them then from the river, against those whom he now cries out against through the Gospel.

Jesus came. And what does John say? “Behold the Lamb of God.”

If he is an innocent lamb, then was John also a lamb? Was he not innocent too? But who is innocent? How innocent?

All come from that stock and that lineage of which David sings with a groan: “I was conceived in iniquity, and in sins my mother nourished me in the womb” (Psalm 50:7).

Therefore he alone is the Lamb who did not come in this way. He was not conceived in iniquity, because he was not conceived from mortality. Nor did his mother nourish him in sins in the womb, since a virgin conceived him and a virgin gave birth to him: she conceived by faith and received him by faith.

Therefore: “Behold the Lamb of God.” He does not derive his stock from Adam; he took only flesh from Adam, not sin. He who did not take sin from our mass is the one who takes away our sin.

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world.”

## 11

You know that certain people sometimes say: “We take away sins from human beings, because we are holy. For if the one who baptizes is not holy, how can he take away another’s sin, when he himself is a human being full of sin?”

Against such arguments, let us not offer our own words; let us read this passage: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world.”

Let there be no presumption among human beings against other human beings. Let the sparrow not flee to the mountains; let it trust in the Lord (Psalm 10:2). And if it raises its eyes to the mountains from which its help will come, let it understand that its help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth (Psalm 120:1–2).

John was of such excellence, and he was asked: “Are you the Christ?” He says, “No.” “Are you Elijah?” He says, “No.” “Are you the prophet?” He says, “No.”

“Why then do you baptize?”

“Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world. This is the one of whom I said: ‘After me comes a man who was placed before me, because he was before me.’”

He comes after me because he was born later; he was placed before me because he was set above me; he was before me because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

## 12

“And I did not know him,” he said; “but in order that he might be revealed to Israel, for this reason I came baptizing in water. And John bore witness, saying: ‘I saw the Spirit descending from heaven like a dove, and it remained upon him. And I did not know him, but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” And I saw, and I bore witness that this is the Son of God.’”

Let Your Charity pay a little attention. When did John learn who Christ was? For he was sent to baptize in water. Why, then, was he sent? “In order that he might be revealed to Israel,” he said.

What benefit did John’s baptism provide? My brothers, if it provided any benefit and remained in force even now, people would be baptized with John’s baptism and would then come to Christ’s baptism.

But what does he say? “In order that he might be revealed to Israel”—that is, in order that Christ might be revealed to Israel itself, to the people of Israel, he came baptizing in water.

John received the ministry of baptism in the water of repentance in order to prepare the way for the Lord, while not being the Lord. But once the Lord was known, the way was prepared for him in vain, because for those who know him he himself became the way. Thus John’s baptism did not last long.

But how was the Lord revealed? In humility, so that John might receive baptism for this reason: that the Lord himself might be baptized in it.

## 13

Was it necessary for the Lord to be baptized? I answer the question quickly: Was it necessary for the Lord to be born? Was it necessary for the Lord to be crucified? Was it necessary for the Lord to die? Was it necessary for the Lord to be buried?

If, then, he undertook such great humility for us, was he not going to undertake baptism? And what benefit did it provide that he received the servant’s baptism? So that you would not disdain to receive the Lord’s baptism.

Let Your Charity pay attention. There were to be in the Church catechumens of greater grace. It sometimes happens that you see a catechumen abstaining from all sexual relations, bidding farewell to the world, renouncing everything he possessed, distributing it to the poor—and he is still a catechumen, perhaps also instructed in saving doctrine beyond many of the faithful.

Such a person must beware lest he say to himself concerning holy Baptism, by which sins are forgiven: “What more will I receive? Look, I am better than this faithful person and that faithful person.” He thinks of faithful people who are married, or perhaps uneducated, or who retain and possess their property—property that he himself has already distributed to the poor—and he considers himself better than one who has already been baptized.

He might disdain to come to Baptism, saying, “I shall receive what this person and that person have,” and set before himself those whom he despises, as though it were beneath him to receive what his inferiors have received, since he already seems better to himself.

And yet all sins remain upon him. Unless he comes to saving Baptism, where sins are loosed, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven with all his excellence.

But in order to invite that excellence to his baptism, so that its sins might be forgiven, the Lord himself came to the baptism of his servant. Although he had nothing that needed to be forgiven and nothing in him that needed to be washed, he received baptism from his servant.

He thereby addressed, as it were, the son who was proud and exalting himself, who perhaps disdained to receive salvation together with the uneducated, saying:

“How highly do you stretch yourself? How greatly do you exalt yourself? How great is your excellence? How great is your grace? Can it be greater than mine? If I came to the servant, do you disdain to come to the Lord? If I received the servant’s baptism, do you disdain to be baptized by the Lord?”

## 14

For, so that you may know, my brothers, that the Lord was not coming to John because of the necessity of any bond of sin, as the other Evangelists relate, when the Lord came to him to be baptized John himself said: “You come to me? I ought to be baptized by you.”

And what did he answer him? “Let it be so for now; let all righteousness be fulfilled” (Matthew 3:14–15).

What does “let all righteousness be fulfilled” mean? “I have come to die for human beings; am I not to be baptized for human beings?” What does “let all righteousness be fulfilled” mean? Let all humility be fulfilled.

What then? Was he not going to receive baptism from a good servant, when he accepted suffering at the hands of evil servants?

Pay attention, then. If John baptized the Lord for this reason—that in John’s baptism the Lord might display humility—would no one else be baptized with John’s baptism?

Many were baptized with John’s baptism. The Lord was baptized with John’s baptism, and John’s baptism ceased. From that point John was sent to prison; thereafter no one is found being baptized with that baptism.

If John was sent to baptize for this reason, so that the Lord’s humility might be demonstrated to us, and so that, because he received baptism from a servant, we would not disdain to receive baptism from the Lord, would John baptize the Lord alone?

But if John baptized the Lord alone, there would be people who thought that John’s baptism was holier than Christ’s—as though Christ alone had merited being baptized with John’s baptism, while the human race had been baptized with Christ’s baptism.

Let Your Charity pay attention. We have been baptized with Christ’s baptism, and not only we: the whole world has been baptized, and continues to be baptized to the end.

Who among us can in any respect be compared with Christ, of whom John said that he was unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal?

If, then, Christ alone—a man who was God and of such great excellence—had been baptized with John’s baptism, what would people have said? “What kind of baptism did John have? He had a great baptism, an ineffable sacrament. See: Christ alone merited being baptized with John’s baptism.”

And thus the servant’s baptism would seem greater than the Lord’s baptism.

Others were baptized with John’s baptism so that John’s baptism would not seem better than Christ’s. But the Lord was also baptized so that, when the Lord received the servant’s baptism, other servants would not disdain to receive the Lord’s baptism.

For this reason John had been sent.

## 15

But did John know Christ, or did he not know him? If he did not know him, why did he say, when Christ came to the river: “I ought to be baptized by you”? That is: “I know who you are.”

If he already knew him, certainly he recognized him then when he saw the dove descending. It is clear that the dove did not descend upon the Lord until after he had risen from the water of baptism.

The Lord was baptized and rose from the water; the heavens were opened, and he saw the dove above him. If, then, the dove descended after the baptism, and before the Lord was baptized John said to him, “You come to me? I ought to be baptized by you,” then he already knew the one to whom he said, “You come to me? I ought to be baptized by you.”

How, then, did he say: “And I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him—he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’”?

This is no small question, my brothers. If you have seen the question, you have not seen a small matter; what remains is for the Lord himself to provide its solution.

But this I say: if you have seen the question, that is no small thing. Behold John the Baptist is set before your eyes, standing at the river. Behold the Lord comes still to be baptized, not yet baptized. Hear John’s voice: “You come to me? I ought to be baptized by you.”

Behold, he already recognizes the Lord from whom he wishes to receive baptism. The baptized Lord rises from the water; the heavens are opened; the Spirit descends. Now John recognizes him.

If he recognizes him only now, what did he mean earlier by saying, “I ought to be baptized by you”? But if he does not recognize him only now, because he already knew him, what does he mean by saying: “I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize in water said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, like a dove—he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’”?

## 16

Brothers, if this question is resolved today, it will weigh upon you—I do not doubt it—because much has already been said. But you should know that this is such a question that it alone destroys the position of Donatus.

I have mentioned this to Your Charity in order to make you attentive, as I usually do, and also so that you may pray for us and for yourselves: that the Lord may grant us to speak what is worthy, and that you may deserve to receive what is worthy.

For now, be willing to postpone the matter today. But I say this briefly in the meantime, until it is resolved: ask peacefully, without quarrels, without contention, without disputes, without hostility. Investigate it among yourselves; ask others; and say: “Our bishop proposed this question to us today, intending to solve it at some point, if the Lord grants it.”

But whether it is solved or not, think that I have proposed what troubles me. For it troubles me greatly.

John says, “I ought to be baptized by you,” as though he already recognized Christ. For if he did not know the one from whom he wished to be baptized, he would have been speaking rashly in saying, “I ought to be baptized by you.” Therefore he knew him.

If he knew him, what then does it mean when he says: “I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize in water himself said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining, like a dove—he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’”?

What shall we say? That we do not know when the dove came down? Perhaps something is hidden there [Note: The printed editions have the singular *lateat* (“perhaps something is hidden”); the manuscripts have the plural *lateant* (“perhaps things are hidden”), namely, concerning the Donatists.].
