Let the other Evangelists be read, who stated the matter more clearly, and we find most plainly that the dove descended when the Lord rose from the water.

For the heavens were opened over the baptized one, and he saw the Spirit descending (Matthew 3:16; Mark 1:10; Luke 3:21–22).

If John recognized him only after he had been baptized, how does he say to the one coming to baptism, “I ought to be baptized by you”?

For now, meditate on this with one another; discuss it with one another; work through it with one another. May our Lord God grant that, before you hear the answer from me, he may reveal it first to one of you.

Nevertheless, brothers, know this: through the solution of this question, if the position of Donatus has any sense of shame, its voice concerning the grace of Baptism—where they spread clouds before the unlearned and cast nets for flying birds—will be entirely silenced; their mouths will be completely closed.

# TRACTATE V

Again on the passage, “And I did not know him,” and so forth. What John learned about the Lord through the dove. Chapter I, verse 33.

## 1

As the Lord willed, we have reached the day of our promise. May he also grant that we may reach the fulfillment of that promise itself.

For whatever we say that is useful both to us and to you comes from him; whatever comes from a human being is falsehood, as our Lord Jesus Christ himself said: “Whoever speaks falsehood speaks from his own resources” (John 8:44).

No one has anything from his own resources except falsehood and sin. If a human being possesses any truth or righteousness, it comes from that fountain for which we must thirst in this wilderness, so that, sprinkled by it as though by drops and meanwhile comforted during this pilgrimage, we may not fail on the road but may be able to come to his rest and fullness.

If, then, the one who speaks falsehood speaks from his own resources, the one who speaks truth speaks from God.

John was truthful; Christ is truth. John was truthful, but every truthful person is truthful from the truth. If John is truthful, and a human being cannot be truthful except from the truth, from whom was he truthful if not from the one who said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6)?

Therefore truth could not speak against the truthful person, nor the truthful person against the truth. Truth sent the truthful one; and he was truthful because he had been sent by the truth.

If truth sent John, Christ sent him. But what Christ does with the Father, the Father does; and what the Father does with Christ, Christ does. The Father does nothing separately without the Son, nor does the Son do anything separately without the Father.

Love is inseparable, unity is inseparable, majesty is inseparable, power is inseparable, according to the words he himself spoke: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Who, then, sent John? If we say “the Father,” we speak the truth; if we say “the Son,” we speak the truth. More explicitly, however, let us say “the Father and the Son.”

The one whom the Father and the Son sent was sent by the one God, because the Son said, “I and the Father are one.”

How, then, did John not know the one by whom he had been sent? For he said: “I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize in water himself said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’”

I ask John: “The one who sent you to baptize in water—what did he say to you?” “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

Did the one who sent you, O John, say this to you? Clearly he did. Who, then, sent you? Perhaps the Father.

The Father is true God, and the Son is God the truth. If the Father sent you without the Son, God sent you without the truth. But if you are truthful because you speak the truth and speak from the truth, then the Father did not send you without the Son; rather, the Father and the Son sent you together.

If, then, the Son sent you with the Father, how did you not know the one by whom you were sent? The one whom you had seen in the truth sent you so that he might be recognized in the flesh, and said: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

## 2

Did John hear this so that he might come to know the one whom he did not know, or so that he might know more fully the one whom he already knew?

For if he did not know him in every respect, he would not have said to the Lord, when he came to the river to be baptized: “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” (Matthew 3:14). Therefore he knew him.

When did the dove descend? After the Lord had been baptized and had risen from the water.

But if the one who sent John said: “The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit”; and if John did not know him but recognized him when the dove descended; and if the dove descended when the Lord rose from the water; but John had recognized the Lord when the Lord was coming to the water to him—then it is revealed to us that John knew the Lord in one respect but did not yet know him in another.

Unless we understand this, John was a liar. How could he be truthful when recognizing the one of whom he said, “You come to me to be baptized, and I ought to be baptized by you”? Is he truthful when he says this? And how, again, is he truthful when he says: “I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize in water himself said to me: ‘The one upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit’”?

The Lord was made known through the dove—not to one who knew nothing of him, but to one who knew something of him and did not yet know something else.

It is therefore our task to ask what John did not yet know about him and learned through the dove.

### 3

Why was John sent baptizing? I remember having said to Your Charity as much as I was able. For if John’s baptism was necessary for our salvation, it ought still to be practiced now. For it is not the case that people are not saved now, or that more people are saved now, or that salvation was one thing then and another now. If Christ has changed, salvation too has changed; but if salvation is in Christ, and Christ himself is the same, our salvation is the same.

But why was John sent baptizing? Because Christ had to be baptized. Why did Christ have to be baptized? Why did Christ have to be born? Why did Christ have to be crucified? [Note: [Col. 1415] He responds to the question by asking questions, as above, Tractate 4, no. 13.]

For if he had come to demonstrate the way of humility, and to make himself that very way of humility, humility had to be fulfilled by him in every respect. He deigned to give authority to his baptism for this reason: so that servants might recognize with what eagerness they ought to run to the Lord’s baptism, when he himself did not disdain to receive the baptism of a servant. For John had been granted this: that his baptism should be called his own.

### 4

Let Your Charity attend to this, distinguish it, and understand it. The baptism that John received was called John’s baptism: he alone received such a gift. No righteous person before him, no righteous person after him, received a baptism that was called his baptism. [Note: [Col. 1416] Erasmus and the Lyon edition read this passage as follows: “The baptism that John received was called John’s baptism. No righteous person before him, no righteous person after him received a baptism that was called his baptism. He alone indeed received such a gift.” Venice and Louvain support this reading, though they differ among themselves: Venice has *baptisma*, while Louvain has *baptismum*. M.]

He did receive it, certainly; for he could receive nothing from himself. If someone speaks from himself, he speaks a lie from his own resources. And from whom did he receive it, unless from the Lord Jesus Christ? He received from him the power to baptize—the one whom he later baptized.

Do not be surprised. Christ did this in John as he did something in his mother. For it is said of Christ, “All things were made through him” (John 1:3). If all things were made through him, then Mary too was made through him, from whom Christ was afterward born. Let Your Charity attend: just as he created Mary and was created through Mary, so he gave baptism to John and was baptized by John.

### 5

For this reason, then, he received baptism from John: by receiving from an inferior what was inferior, he might exhort inferiors toward what was superior. But why was he not baptized by John alone, if John had been sent for this purpose—to baptize Christ and thus prepare the way for the Lord, that is, for Christ himself?

We have already said this, but we recall it because it is necessary for the present question. If our Lord Jesus Christ alone had been baptized with John’s baptism—hold fast to what we are saying; do not let the age have such power that it erases from your hearts what the Spirit of God wrote there; do not let the thorns of cares have such power that they choke the seed being sown in you—for why are we compelled to repeat the same things unless we are not confident that they remain in the memory of your hearts? If, then, the Lord alone had been baptized with John’s baptism, there would have been people who regarded it in such a way that they thought John’s baptism greater than Christ’s baptism. They would say: “That baptism must be so much greater that Christ alone was worthy to be baptized with it.”

Therefore, so that the Lord might give us an example of humility for receiving the salvation of baptism, Christ accepted what he did not need, but what was necessary for us. And again, so that what Christ received from John should not itself be preferred to Christ’s baptism, others too were permitted to be baptized by John.

But those who were baptized by John were not thereby satisfied: they were baptized with Christ’s baptism, because John’s baptism was not Christ’s baptism. Those who receive Christ’s baptism do not seek John’s baptism; those who received John’s baptism sought Christ’s baptism.

Therefore John’s baptism sufficed for Christ. How could it not suffice, when it was not necessary even for him? No baptism was necessary for him; but, to exhort us toward his own baptism, he received the baptism of a servant. And so that the servant’s baptism should not be preferred to the Lord’s baptism, others were baptized with the baptism of a fellow servant.

But those who were baptized with the baptism of a fellow servant had to be baptized with the Lord’s baptism. Those who are baptized with the Lord’s baptism, however, have no need of the baptism of a fellow servant.

### 6

Since John had received a baptism that was properly called John’s baptism, the Lord Jesus Christ did not wish to give his baptism to anyone—not so that no one would be baptized with the Lord’s baptism, but so that the Lord himself would always baptize. Thus it was arranged that the Lord would baptize through ministers: those whom the Lord’s ministers were going to baptize, the Lord would baptize, not the ministers.

For baptizing through ministry is one thing, and baptizing through authority is another. Baptism is such as the one is in whose authority it is given, not such as the one is through whose ministry it is given.

John’s baptism was such as John was: a righteous baptism, as from a righteous man, yet a human baptism. John, however, had received this grace from the Lord—and such great grace that he was worthy to go before the Judge, point him out with his finger, and fulfill the voice of his prophecy: “Prepare the way of the Lord” (Isa. 40:3).

The Lord’s baptism, however, is such as the Lord is. Therefore the Lord’s baptism is divine, because the Lord is God.

### 7

The Lord Jesus Christ could, if he wished, have given one of his servants the authority to give his baptism as his representative. He could have transferred the authority to baptize from himself, established it in one of his servants, and given a baptism transferred to that servant as much power as baptism given by the Lord himself would have had.

He did not wish this, so that the hope of those baptized would rest in the one from whom they recognized that they had received baptism. He did not wish a servant to place his hope in a servant.

For this reason the Apostle cried out when he saw people wishing to place their hope in himself: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:13).

Paul therefore baptized as a minister, not as the authority itself; the Lord baptized as the authority. Attend carefully. He could have given this authority to servants, but he did not.

For if he had given this authority to servants—that is, if what belonged to the Lord had become theirs—there would have been as many baptisms as there were servants. Just as it was called John’s baptism, so it would be called Peter’s baptism, Paul’s baptism, James’s baptism, Thomas’s baptism, Matthew’s baptism, Bartholomew’s baptism. For that baptism was called John’s baptism.

But perhaps someone resists and says: “Prove to us that it was called John’s baptism.” I will prove it by the Truth himself, when he asked the Jews: “John’s baptism, where was it from? From heaven or from human beings?” (Matt. 21:25).

Therefore, so that there should not be as many baptisms as there were servants baptizing after receiving authority from the Lord, the Lord retained the authority to baptize for himself and gave the servants the ministry.

A servant says that he baptizes; he says so rightly, as the Apostle says: “I did baptize also the household of Stephanas” (1 Cor. 1:16)—but as a minister. Therefore, even if he is evil, and happens to possess the ministry, and people do not know him although God knows him, God permits people to be baptized through him, while he himself retains the authority.

### 8

John did not yet know this about the Lord. He knew that the Lord was the Lord; he knew that he himself was to be baptized by the Lord. He confessed that the Lord was the Truth and that he himself had been sent by the Truth—this he knew.

But what did he not know about him? That the Lord would retain for himself the authority of his baptism and would not transmit or transfer it to any servant; that whether a good servant baptized in the exercise of his ministry or an evil servant baptized in the exercise of his ministry, the person being baptized would not know himself to be baptized except by the one who had retained for himself the authority to baptize.

And so that you may know, brothers, that John did not know this about him, and that he learned it through the dove: John knew the Lord, but he did not yet know that the Lord would retain for himself the authority to baptize and give it to no servant. In this respect he said, “And I did not know him.”

And so that you may know that he learned this there, attend to what follows: “But the one who sent me to baptize with water himself said to me, ‘Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one.’”

What does “he is the one” mean? The Lord. But John already knew the Lord.

Therefore imagine John saying up to this point: “I did not know him; but the one who sent me to baptize with water himself said to me”—and we ask what he said. What follows is: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one.”

I will not yet discuss what follows. For the moment, attend to this: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one.” But what does “he is the one” mean? What did the one who sent me wish to teach me through the dove? That he was the Lord?

I already knew from whom I had been sent. I already knew the one to whom I had said, “Do you come to me to be baptized? I ought rather to be baptized by you.” I knew the Lord so well that I wished to be baptized by him, not that he should be baptized by me.

And then he said to me, “Let it be so now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. 3:14–15). “I have come to suffer; have I not come to be baptized? ‘Let all righteousness be fulfilled,’ my God said to me; ‘let all righteousness be fulfilled; let me teach complete humility.’

“I know that in my future people there will be proud persons; I know that there will be people who will possess some more excellent grace. When they see certain uneducated people being baptized, they may think themselves better—whether because of continence, almsgiving, or learning—and may perhaps disdain to receive what those whom they regard as inferior have received.

“I must heal them, so that they will not disdain to come to the Lord’s baptism, because I came to the baptism of a servant.”

### 9

John therefore already knew this, and he knew the Lord. What, then, did the dove teach? What did the one who sent John wish to teach through the dove—that is, through the Spirit’s coming in this form—when he said, “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one”?

Who is “the one”? The Lord. “I know that.”

But did you already know that this Lord, possessing the authority to baptize, would give that authority to no servant, but would retain it for himself, so that everyone baptized through the ministry of a servant would attribute it not to the servant but to the Lord? Did you already know this?

“I did not know this.” What, then, did he say to me? “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

He did not say, “He is the Lord.” He did not say, “He is Christ.” He did not say, “He is God.” He did not say, “He is Jesus.” He did not say, “He is the one born from the virgin Mary, later than you yet prior to you.” He did not say this, because John already knew it.

But what did he not know? That the Lord himself would possess and retain such authority over baptism—whether present on earth or absent in body in heaven yet present in majesty—that he would retain the authority of baptism, so that Paul could not say, “My baptism,” nor Peter, “My baptism.”

For this reason observe and attend to the Apostles’ words. No Apostle said, “My baptism.” Although there is one Gospel belonging to all, you do find someone saying, “my Gospel”; you do not find anyone saying, “my baptism.”

### 10

This, then, is what John learned, my brothers. Let us also learn what John learned through the dove. For the dove did not teach John without teaching the Church, to which Church it was said, “My dove is one” (Song 6:8).

Let the dove teach the dove; let the dove know what John learned through the dove. The Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove.

But why did John learn through the dove what he was learning? It was necessary that he learn it; and perhaps it was necessary that he learn it through the dove.

What shall I say about the dove, my brothers? Or when shall I have enough ability, in heart or tongue, to say what I wish? Perhaps I do not even properly wish what ought to be said; and even if I could say it as I wished, how much less could I say it as it ought to be said? I would rather hear this from someone better than say it to you.

### 11

John learns about the one whom he knew; but he learns in him what he did not know about him. In what he knew about him, he does not learn.

And what did he know? The Lord.

What did he not know? That the authority of the Lord’s baptism would not pass from the Lord into any human being, although the ministry would certainly pass: the authority from the Lord into no one, but the ministry to both good and evil persons.

Let the dove not recoil from the ministry of evil people; let it look to the Lord’s authority. What harm does an evil minister do to you when the Lord is good? What does a malicious herald hinder in you if the judge is benevolent?

John learned this through the dove. What did he learn? Let him repeat it himself: “He himself said to me,” he says, “ ‘Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.’”

Therefore, O dove, let not deceivers mislead you when they say, “We baptize.” [Note: [Col. 1419] The Donatists.]

Dove, recognize what the dove taught: “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.” Through the dove it is learned that this is the one. And do you think that you are baptized by the authority of the one whose ministry baptizes you?

If you think this, you are not yet in the body of the dove. And if you are not in the body of the dove, it is no wonder that you do not possess simplicity. For simplicity is signified above all by the dove.

### 12

Why did John learn through the simplicity of the dove that this is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit, my brothers, unless those who disrupted the Church were not doves? They were hawks; they were kites. A dove does not tear apart.

And you see them directing their resentment against us, as though because of the persecutions they endured. They did indeed suffer bodily things resembling persecutions, when they were plainly the Lord’s scourges, administering discipline for a time so that he might not condemn them eternally, if they recognized it and corrected themselves.

Those truly persecute the Church who persecute it by deceit. Those strike the heart more grievously who strike with the sword of the tongue. Those shed blood more bitterly who, insofar as it lies in them, kill Christ in a human being.

They appear terrified, as though by the judgment of the authorities. What does authority do to you if you are good? But if you are evil, fear authority: “For he does not bear the sword in vain,” the Apostle says (Rom. 13:4).

Do not draw your sword—the sword with which you strike Christ. Christian, what are you persecuting in a Christian? What has the emperor persecuted in you? He persecuted the flesh; you persecute the spirit in a Christian.

You do not kill the flesh. And yet they do not spare even the flesh: as many as they were able, they killed by beating them; they spared neither their own nor others’. This is known to everyone.

Authority is resented because it is lawful; one who acts by right acts offensively; one who acts outside the laws does so without provoking resentment.

Let each of you attend, my brothers, to what a Christian possesses. What he is as a human being he shares with many; what he is as a Christian separates him from many. What belongs to him as a Christian is more important than what belongs to him as a human being.

For what he is as a Christian is renewed according to the image of God, in whose image the human being was made (Col. 3:10). But as a human being, he could be evil, pagan, or an idolater. [Note: [Col. 1420] Morel, *Elementa critica*, p. 241, reads *possidet* (“possesses”) three times instead of *posset* (“could be”). M.]

This is what you persecute in a Christian—the thing he possesses that is better. For this is what you wish to take away from him, that by which he lives.

He lives temporarily according to the spirit of life by which the body is animated; but he lives for eternity according to the baptism he received from the Lord. This is what you wish to take away from him, what he received from the Lord, that by which he lives.

Robbers wish to strip those whom they rob so that they themselves may possess more and the others may possess nothing. You take something away from this person, yet you will not possess more because of it; you do not become richer because you take it from him.

But truly they do what those do who take away life: they take it from another, yet they do not thereby possess two lives themselves.

### 13

What, then, do you wish to take away? Why does the person whom you wish to rebaptize displease you? You cannot give him what he already has; you make him deny what he has.

What did the pagan, the persecutor of the Church, do more cruelly? Swords were drawn against the martyrs, wild beasts were released, fires were brought near. For what purpose? So that the person suffering these things would say, “I am not a Christian.”

What are you teaching the person whom you wish to rebaptize, except that he should first say, “I am not a Christian”? What the persecutor once brought forth fire to achieve, you now bring forth your tongue to achieve. By deception you do what he did not do by killing.

And what is it that you are going to give, and to whom are you going to give it? If he tells you the truth and does not lie because you have deceived him, he will say, “I have it.”

You ask, “Do you have baptism?”

“I have it,” he says.

“As long as you say ‘I have it,’” you reply, “I will not give it.”

Then do not give it. What you wish to give cannot adhere to me, because what I received cannot be taken away from me.

But wait; let me see what you wish to teach me.

“Say first,” he says, “ ‘I do not have it.’”

“But I do have it. If I say, ‘I do not have it,’ I lie. What I have, I have.”

“You do not have it,” he says.

“Prove that I do not have it.”

“An evil person gave it to you.”

“If Christ is evil, an evil person gave it to me.”

“Not an evil Christ,” he says; “but Christ did not give it to you.”

“Who, then, gave it to me? Answer. I know that I received it from Christ.”

“He gave it to you,” he says, “but some betrayer or other—not Christ.”

“I will see who the minister was; I will see who the herald was. I do not dispute about the official; I look to the judge. And perhaps what you allege against the official is false. But I do not wish to investigate it; let the Lord of both parties examine the case of his official.

“Perhaps, if I demand that you prove it, you will not prove it; indeed, you are lying. It has been established that you have been unable to prove what you claim.” [Note: [Col. 1421] He touches upon the case of Caecilianus. Compare Letters 43, 88, 185, and others.]

“But I do not place my cause there, lest, when I begin zealously defending innocent people, you think that I have placed my hope either in them or in innocent people. Whatever sort of people they may have been, I received from Christ; I was baptized by Christ.”

“No,” he says; “that bishop baptized you, and that bishop is in communion with those others.”

“I was baptized by Christ; I know this.”

“How do you know?”

“The dove whom John saw taught me.”

“O wicked kite, do not tear me away from the dove’s inward parts. I am counted among the dove’s members, because I know what the dove taught.

“You tell me, ‘That man baptized you,’ or ‘This man baptized you.’ Through the dove it is said to you and to me: ‘This is the one who baptizes.’ Whom should I believe, O kite, you or the dove?”

### 14

Certainly, tell me this, so that you may be confounded by that lamp by which your predecessors, your fellow Pharisees, were also confounded. When they asked the Lord by what authority he did these things, he said: “I too will ask you this question. Tell me: John’s baptism, where was it from? From heaven or from human beings?”

And they, who were preparing to cast their snares, became entangled in the question. They began turning it over among themselves and saying: “If we say, ‘From heaven,’ he will say to us, ‘Why, then, did you not believe him?’” For John had said of the Lord, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29).

“What, then, are you asking—in what authority I act? O wolves, I act by the authority of the Lamb. But so that you might know the Lamb, why did you not believe John, who said, ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world’?”

Knowing, therefore, what John had said about the Lord, they said among themselves: “If we say that John’s baptism is from heaven, he will say to us, ‘Why, then, did you not believe him?’ If we say that it is from human beings, we will be stoned by the people, because they regard John as a prophet.”

They feared human beings in one direction and were ashamed to confess the truth in the other. Darkness answered darkness, but they were overcome by the light.

What did they answer? “We do not know.” They said what they knew: “We do not know.” And the Lord said, “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matt. 21:23–27).

And the first enemies were confounded. By what? By the lamp.

Who was the lamp? John.

Do we prove that he was a lamp? We do. For the Lord says: “He was the burning and shining lamp” (John 5:35).

Do we prove that the enemies were also confounded by him? Hear the Psalm: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with confusion” (Ps. 131:17–18).

### 15

Still walking by the lamp of faith amid the darkness of this life, let us also hold fast to John the lamp and thereby confound the enemies of Christ—or rather, let Christ himself confound his enemies through his lamp.

Let us also ask what the Lord asked the Jews, and let us ask: “John’s baptism, where was it from? From heaven or from human beings?”

Consider what they will say, if they too are not confounded by the lamp like enemies. What will they say?

If they say, “From human beings,” their own people will stone them. But if they say, “From heaven,” let us say to them: “Why, then, did you not believe him?”

Perhaps they say, “We do believe him.”

“Then how do you say that you baptize, when John says, ‘This is the one who baptizes’?”

“The ministers,” they say, “of so great a judge ought to be righteous, since baptism is administered through them.”

And I say, and we all say, that the ministers of so great a judge ought to be righteous. Let them be righteous ministers, if they wish. But if those who sit on Moses’ seat do not wish to be righteous, my teacher has made me secure—the one of whom his Spirit said, “This is the one who baptizes.”

How has he made me secure? He says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore do whatever they tell you, but do not do what they do; for they say things and do not do them” (Matt. 23:2–3). [Note: [Col. 1422] Louvain, with five manuscripts, reads *qui cathedram Moysi sedent*; according to Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice, the reading should be *in cathedra Moysi sedent*, “sit on Moses’ seat.” M.]

If the minister is righteous, I count him with Paul; I count him with Peter. I count righteous ministers with these men, because truly righteous ministers do not seek their own glory. They are ministers; they do not wish to be regarded as judges; they shudder at having hope placed in them. Therefore I count a righteous minister with Paul.

For what does Paul say? “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:6–7).

But if the minister is proud, he is counted with the devil. [Note: [Col. 1422] In several manuscripts, instead of *zabuli* (“of the devil”), the word *diaboli* (“of the devil”) is found throughout.]

Yet Christ’s gift is not defiled: what flows pure through him and passes through him clear reaches the fertile soil. Suppose that he himself is stony ground, unable to produce fruit from the water. Water still passes through the stone channel and reaches the garden beds. Nothing grows in the stone channel, yet it brings abundant fruit to the gardens. [Note: [Col. 1422] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read: “through the stone channel the water passes to the garden beds.” M.] [Note: [Col. 1422] All manuscripts read *hortus* (“garden”).]

The spiritual power of the sacrament is like light: it is received pure by those who are illuminated, and if it passes through the unclean, it is not polluted.

Let the ministers indeed be righteous and seek not their own glory but the glory of the one whose ministers they are. Let them not say, “It is my baptism,” because it is not theirs.

Let them attend to John himself. Behold, John was full of the Holy Spirit, and he had baptism from heaven, not from human beings. But to what extent did he have it? He himself said, “Prepare the way of the Lord” (John 1:23).

When the Lord became known, he himself became the way. John’s baptism, by which the way was to be prepared for the Lord, was no longer necessary.

### 16

Yet what do they usually say to us? “Behold, people were baptized after John. Are people not baptized after heretics?”

Before this question was properly treated in the Catholic Church, many people—great and good men—went astray in it. [Note: [Col. 1422] He chiefly has Cyprian in mind, and with him the Council of Carthage, concerning which see Books 6 and 7 of *On Baptism against the Donatists*.]

But because they belonged to the members of the dove, they did not cut themselves off. And what the Apostle said took place in them: “If you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3:15).

Therefore those who separated themselves became incapable of learning.

What, then, do they usually say? “Behold, people were baptized after John. Are people not baptized after heretics?”

Because certain people who had John’s baptism were ordered by Paul to be baptized (Acts 19:3–5): they did not have Christ’s baptism.

Why, then, do you exaggerate John’s merit and, as though in contrast, cast away the wretchedness of the heretics? I grant you that the heretics are wicked. But the heretics gave Christ’s baptism—a baptism John did not give.

### 17

I return to John and say: “This is the one who baptizes.”

John is better than a heretic in the same way that John is better than a drunkard, and in the same way that John is better than a murderer.

If we ought to baptize after an inferior because the Apostles baptized after a superior, then whoever among them has been baptized by a drunkard—not to mention by a murderer, not to mention by an accomplice of some criminal, not to mention by one who seizes another’s possessions, not to mention by one who oppresses orphans, not to mention by one who separates husbands and wives—I say nothing of any of these. [Note: [Col. 1423] He refers to Optatus, bishop of Thamugadi, who was called an accomplice of Gildo. Compare Letter 87, to Emeritus.]

I mention what is customary; I mention what is daily; I mention the behavior in which everyone is invited to participate. In this city, when people say to them, “Let us feast; may it go well with us,” and on such a feast day of the January celebrations, “You must not fast”—I mention these light, everyday matters. [Note: [Col. 1423] Bad. and Am. read *alongemur*; Louvain, *alogiemur*; several good manuscripts, *alogiemus*. The word is derived from *alogia*, which, as Augustine explains in Letter 36 to Casulanus, no. 2, means indulgence in feasting such that one strays from the path of reason.]

When someone is baptized by a drunkard, who is better, John or the drunkard? Answer, if you can, that your drunkard is better than John. You will never dare say this.

Therefore, since you are sober, baptize after your drunkard. For if the Apostles baptized after John, how much more ought a sober man to baptize after a drunkard?

Or do you say, “The drunkard is in communion with me”? Then was John, the friend of the Bridegroom, not in communion with the Bridegroom?

### 18

But I say to you yourself, whoever you are: Are you better, or John? You will not dare say, “I am better than John.”

Then let your followers baptize after you, if they are better than you. If people were baptized after John, be ashamed that people are not baptized after you.

You will say: “But I have Christ’s baptism, and I teach.”

Then recognize the judge at last, and do not be a proud herald. You give Christ’s baptism; that is why no one is baptized again after you. People were baptized after John because he did not give Christ’s baptism but his own, since he had received it in such a way that it belonged to him.

You are not therefore better than John; the baptism given through you is better than John’s. For the former is Christ’s, while the latter is John’s.

What was given by Paul, and what was given by Peter, belongs to Christ; and if it was given by Judas, it belonged to Christ. Judas gave baptism, and people were not baptized again after Judas. John gave baptism, and people were baptized again after John.

For if the baptism was given by Judas, it was Christ’s; but what was given by John was John’s.

We do not rightly prefer Judas to John. Rather, we prefer Christ’s baptism, given even through Judas’s hands, to John’s baptism, given even through John’s hands.

For it was said of the Lord, before he suffered, that he was baptizing more people than John; and then it was added: “Although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples” (John 4:1–2).

He himself, and not himself: himself in authority, they in ministry. They supplied the service of baptizing; the authority to baptize remained in Christ.

Therefore his disciples were baptizing, and Judas was still among his disciples. Those whom Judas baptized were not baptized again, while those whom John baptized were baptized again?

Certainly they were baptized again, but not with a repeated baptism. For those whom John baptized, John baptized; but those whom Judas baptized, Christ baptized.

Thus, those whom a drunkard baptized, those whom a murderer baptized, those whom an adulterer baptized—if it was Christ’s baptism, Christ baptized them.

I do not fear an adulterer, a drunkard, or a murderer, because I look to the dove, through which it is said to me: “This is the one who baptizes.”

### 19

In any case, my brothers, it is madness to say that anyone—not Judas, but any human being—had greater merit than the one of whom it was said: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11).

Therefore no servant is preferred to John; rather, the Lord’s baptism, even when given through an evil servant, is preferred to the baptism even of the Lord’s servant-friend.

Hear what the Apostle Paul says about certain false brothers who preached the word of God out of envy, and what he says about them: “In this I rejoice, and I will rejoice. For they proclaim Christ, indeed out of envy, but nevertheless Christ” (Phil. 1:15–18).

Do not look at the reason but at the one who is preached. Is Christ preached to you out of envy? Look to Christ; avoid envy. Do not imitate the bad preacher, but imitate the good one who is preached to you. [Note: [Col. 1424] The printed editions read *quod* (“which”); the manuscripts read *qui* (“who”), correctly, since it refers to Christ.]

Christ, then, was preached by certain people out of envy. And what is envy? A terrible evil. The devil was cast down by that very evil; that greatly malignant plague cast him down. [Note: [Col. 1424] In several manuscripts: “by that evil he cast down many; it is a malignant plague.”]

Certain preachers of Christ possessed that evil, yet the Apostle permits them to preach. Why? Because they preached Christ.

But the one who envies hates; and what is said of the one who hates? Hear the Apostle John: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15).

Behold, people were baptized after John; they were not baptized after a murderer, because John gave his own baptism, while the murderer gave Christ’s baptism.

The sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer.

### 20

I do not reject John; rather, I believe John. What do I believe John about? What he learned through the dove.

What did he learn through the dove? “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

Therefore, brothers, hold fast to this and impress it upon your hearts. For if I wished to explain fully today why it was through the dove, the time would not be sufficient.

I have explained to Your Holiness, as far as I think appropriate, the matter that was indicated to John for learning through the dove: something John did not know about Christ, although he already knew Christ.

But why this very matter had to be demonstrated through the dove—if it could be said briefly, I would say it. But since it requires a lengthy explanation, and I do not wish to burden you, the reason why John, in learning about the Lord that he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit and did not transfer the authority to baptize to any of his servants, had to learn this through the dove will also become clear to you, with the help of your prayers—just as I was helped to fulfill what I promised—and with the continued assistance of your devout attention and good intentions.

---

## TRACTATE VI

### On the Same Passage of the Gospel: Why God Wished to Show the Holy Spirit through the Form of a Dove

### Chapter I, verses 32–33

### 1

I confess to Your Holiness that I had feared this cold weather might make you cold toward gathering here. But since, by your celebration and your large attendance, you show that you are fervent in spirit, I do not doubt that you have also prayed for me, so that I might discharge what I owe you.

For I had promised, in Christ’s name, to explain today—when the pressure of time had then prevented us from fully treating it—why God wished to show the Holy Spirit through the form of a dove.

The present day has dawned for the explanation of this matter, and I perceive that you have gathered in greater numbers because of your eagerness to hear and your devout dedication.

May God fulfill your expectation through our mouth.

You loved coming here; but what did you love? If you loved us, that too is good, for we wish to be loved by you—but not in ourselves. Since we love you in Christ, love us again in Christ, and let our mutual love groan toward God. For this is the dove’s groaning.

### 2

If, then, the groaning of the dove is something we all know—and doves groan out of love—listen to what the Apostle says, and do not be surprised that he wished the Holy Spirit to be manifested in the form of a dove: “For we do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8:26).

What, then, my brothers, are we going to say? Does the Spirit groan, when he possesses perfect and eternal blessedness with the Father and the Son? For the Holy Spirit is God, just as the Son of God is God, and the Father is God. I have said “God” three times, but I have not said “three gods”: rather, “God” three times than “gods” three times, because the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God. You know this very well.

The Holy Spirit, then, does not groan within himself, by himself, in that Trinity, in that blessedness, in that eternity of substance; rather, he groans within us, because he makes us groan. Nor is it a small matter that the Holy Spirit teaches us to groan: he makes us understand that we are strangers and pilgrims, and teaches us to long for our homeland; and through that very longing we groan.

Whoever is well off in this world—or rather, whoever thinks that he is well off, exulting in the joy of carnal things, the abundance of temporal goods, and empty happiness—has the voice of a raven. For the raven’s voice is loud and raucous, not a voice of groaning. But whoever knows that he is under the pressure of this mortality and is a stranger from the Lord (2 Cor. 5:6), who does not yet possess that everlasting blessedness promised to us, but holds it in hope and will possess it in reality when the Lord comes in glorious manifestation—he who formerly came hidden in humility—whoever knows this groans. And as long as he groans for this reason, he groans well: the Spirit has taught him to groan; he has learned to groan from the dove.

Many people groan amid earthly misery: shaken by losses, weighed down by bodily illness, shut up in prisons, bound in chains, tossed about by the waves of the sea, or surrounded by some ambushes of their enemies. But they do not groan with the groaning of the dove; they do not groan out of love for God; they do not groan in the Spirit. Therefore, when such people have been freed from those very pressures, they exult in loud cries. Then it becomes clear that they are ravens, not doves.

Rightly, the raven was sent out from the ark and did not return; the dove was sent out and returned. Noah sent out those two birds (Gen. 8:6–9). He had a raven there, and he also had a dove; that ark contained both kinds. And if the ark represented the Church, you surely see that, amid this flood of the world, the Church must contain both kinds: the raven and the dove.

Who are the ravens? Those who seek what is their own. Who are the doves? Those who seek the things that belong to Christ (Phil. 2:21).

### 3

For this reason, when he sent the Holy Spirit, he manifested him visibly in two ways: through a dove and through fire—through a dove upon the Lord after he had been baptized, and through fire upon the disciples gathered together.

When the Lord had ascended into heaven after his resurrection, having spent forty days with his disciples, and when the day of Pentecost had been fulfilled, he sent them the Holy Spirit, as he had promised. When the Spirit came, he filled that place; and, after the first sound came from heaven, like the rushing of a mighty wind, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “There appeared to them divided tongues as of fire, which also rested upon each of them; and they began to speak in tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance” (Acts 2:1–4).

Here we saw the dove upon the Lord; there, the divided tongues upon the disciples gathered together. In the one case simplicity is shown; in the other, fervor. For there are people who are called simple but are sluggish; they are called simple, but they are idle.

Stephen was not such a person, for he was full of the Holy Spirit. He was simple because he harmed no one; he was fervent because he rebuked the impious. He did not keep silent before the Jews. These are his flaming words: “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears, you always resist the Holy Spirit.”[Note: [Col. 1426] It should be read this way according to the manuscripts; [cujus] in the printed editions.]

What force! Yet the dove rages without gall. To show that he raged without gall, those who were ravens, as soon as they heard these words, ran to the stones against the dove; and Stephen began to be stoned. The man who shortly before, roaring and burning in spirit, had made an assault upon them as upon enemies, and had attacked them with fiery words so aflame that, as you heard, “You stiff-necked people, uncircumcised in heart and ears,” that anyone hearing these words might have thought that Stephen, if he had been able, wanted them to be consumed immediately—when the stones came upon him from their hands, he knelt and said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:51, 59).[Note: [Col. 1426] In Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain: “he said with bent knee.” The manuscript reading is “he said, having bent his knee.”]

He had clung to the unity of the dove. For the Master, upon whom the dove descended, had done this first. Hanging on the cross, he said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

Thus, to prevent those sanctified by the Spirit from having deceit, the Spirit was shown in the dove; and, to prevent simplicity from remaining cold, he was shown in fire.

Nor should it trouble you that the tongues were divided. Tongues differ from one another; therefore he appeared in divided tongues. “There appeared,” it says, “divided tongues as of fire, which also rested upon each of them.” The tongues differ from one another, but the difference of tongues is not schism. In the divided tongues, do not fear dispersion; recognize unity in the dove.

### 4

Thus, then—thus it was necessary for the Holy Spirit coming upon the Lord to be manifested, so that each person may understand that, if he has the Holy Spirit, he ought to be simple like a dove and to have true peace with his brothers, which the kisses of doves signify.

Ravens also have kisses, but among ravens peace is false, while among doves peace is true. Therefore not everyone who says, “Peace be with you,” is to be heard as a dove. How, then, are the kisses of ravens distinguished from the kisses of doves?

Ravens kiss, but they tear apart; the nature of doves is innocent of tearing. Wherever there is tearing, there is no true peace in the kisses. Those have true peace who have not torn the Church apart. For ravens feed on death; the dove does not do this. It lives on the fruits of the earth; its food is innocent. This, truly, brothers, is remarkable in the dove.

There are very small birds, and they kill flies; the dove does none of this, for it does not feed on death. Those who have torn the Church apart feed on the deaths of others.

God is powerful; let us pray that those who are devoured by them and do not perceive it may come back to life. Many recognize this and come back to life; for every day we rejoice at their arrival in the name of Christ.

Be only so simple that you are also fervent.[Note: [Col. 1427] The printed editions read: “so that you may be prudent and fervent.” The words “and prudent” are absent from the manuscripts.] Let your fervor be expressed in your tongues. Do not remain silent. Speaking with tongues that are burning, set the cold ablaze.

### 5

What, then, my brothers? Who does not see what they do not see? It is no wonder, for they do not wish to return from there, like the raven that was sent out from the ark.[Note: [Col. 1427] Erasmus and Louvain read: “It is no wonder, for they do not wish to return from there, like the raven that was sent out from the ark.”]

Who, then, does not see what they do not see? They themselves are ungrateful also toward the Holy Spirit.

Behold, the dove descends upon the Lord—and upon the Lord after he has been baptized—and there the holy and true Trinity appears, which is one God for us. For the Lord came up from the water, as we read in the Gospel: “And behold, the heavens were opened to him, and he saw the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him; and immediately a voice followed: ‘You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’” (Matt. 3:16–17).

The Trinity appears most clearly: the Father in the voice, the Son in the human being, and the Spirit in the dove.

Let us see, in this Trinity into whose name the Apostles were sent, what we see and what is astonishing that they do not see. For they do not truly fail to see; rather, they close their eyes to what strikes their faces.

Into whose name were the disciples sent? “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” by him of whom it was said, “This is the one who baptizes.” For it was said to the ministers by the one who kept this authority for himself.

### 6

This is what John saw in him and came to know, which he had not known—not that he did not know him to be the Son of God, or did not know him as Lord, or did not know him as Christ, or indeed did not know even this, that he himself would baptize in water and the Holy Spirit; for he knew this also.

Rather, what he learned in the dove was that Christ would retain that very authority for himself and would transfer it to none of his ministers. This authority Christ alone kept for himself and passed on to none of his ministers, although he was pleased to baptize through his ministers. Through this authority the unity of the Church stands firm, signified in the dove, concerning which it was said: “My dove is one; she is one to her mother” (Song 6:8).

For if, as I have already said, brothers, authority were transferred from the Lord to a minister, there would be as many baptisms as there were ministers, and the unity of Baptism would no longer stand.

### 7

Pay attention, brothers. Before our Lord Jesus Christ came to baptism—for after the baptism the dove descended, and in it John recognized something distinctive, when it was said to him, “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit”—John knew that Christ himself baptized in the Holy Spirit.

But he learned there, through that distinctive feature, that the authority did not pass from Christ to another, although the ministers baptized by Christ’s grant.

And how do we prove that John already knew that the Lord would baptize in the Holy Spirit, so that it may be understood that what he learned in the dove was that the Lord would baptize in the Holy Spirit in such a way that this authority would not pass to any other human being? How do we prove it?

The dove descended after the Lord had been baptized. But before the Lord came to be baptized by John in the Jordan, we said that John knew him, in those words where he said: “Do you come to me to be baptized? I ought to be baptized by you.” But clearly he knew the Lord; he knew the Son of God.

How do we prove that he already knew that the Lord would baptize in the Holy Spirit? Before he came to the river, when many were flocking to John to be baptized, he said to them: “I indeed baptize you in water; but the one who comes after me is greater than I, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to loosen; he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matt. 3:11, 14).

He already knew this also.

What, then, did he learn through the dove, lest he later be found to be a liar—which God forbid us to suppose—unless it was that a certain distinctive feature would belong to Christ: although many ministers, whether just or unjust, would baptize, the holiness of Baptism would be attributed only to the one upon whom the dove descended, of whom it was said, “This is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit”?

Peter may baptize: this is the one who baptizes. Paul may baptize: this is the one who baptizes. Judas may baptize: this is the one who baptizes.

### 8

For if Baptism is holy because of differences in merit, since merits differ, baptisms will differ; and each person will be thought to receive something better in proportion as he appears to have received it from someone better.

The saints themselves—understand this, brothers—good people belonging to the dove, belonging to the share of that city, Jerusalem, good people in the Church concerning whom the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19)—possess different gifts of grace. They do not all have equal merits. Some are holier than others; some are better than others.

Why, then, if one person is baptized, for example, by a just and holy man, and another by someone of lesser merit before God, of lower rank, lesser continence, and lesser virtue of life, is what they received nevertheless one, alike, and equal—unless it is because “this is the one who baptizes”?

Therefore, when a good and a better minister baptize, why does one person not receive something good and the other something better? Although the ministers are good and better, what they received is one and equal; it is not better in one person and inferior in the other. So also when an evil person baptizes, whether through some ignorance of the Church or through toleration—for evil people are either unknown or tolerated, and the chaff is tolerated until the threshing floor is winnowed at the end—what is given is one and not unequal because the ministers are unequal, but alike and equal because of the words, “This is the one who baptizes.”

### 9

Therefore, beloved, let us see what they do not wish to see—not that they do not see it, but that they are distressed to see it, as though it had been shut up against them.

Into whose name were the disciples sent, as ministers, to baptize? Into whose name were they sent?

“Go,” he said, “baptize the nations.” You have heard, brothers, how that inheritance came: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Ps. 2:8).

You have heard how the law went forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem (Isa. 2:3). There the disciples heard: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

We became attentive when we heard, “Go, baptize the nations.” In whose name? In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.

This is one God, because it does not say “in the names of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit,” but “in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” Wherever you hear one name, there is one God.

So, concerning the offspring of Abraham, it was said—and the Apostle Paul explains it—“In your offspring all the nations will be blessed.” He did not say “in offspring,” as though in many, but as though in one: “And in your offspring, which is Christ” (Gen. 22:18; Gal. 3:16).

Therefore, just as the Apostle wished to teach you that Christ is one because Scripture does not say “in offspring,” but “in your offspring,” so also here, when it says “in the name,” not “in the names”—just as there it says “in the offspring,” not “in the offsprings”—the one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, is proved.

### 10

But, they say, the disciples say to the Lord: “Behold, we have heard in whose name we should baptize. You have made us ministers and said to us, ‘Go, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.’ Where shall we go?”

Where? Have you not heard? To my inheritance.

“You ask, ‘Where shall we go?’ To that which I purchased with my blood.”

“Where, then?”

“To the nations,” he says.

I thought he said, “Go, baptize the Africans in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

Thanks be to God: the Lord has resolved the question; the dove has taught us. Thanks be to God: the Apostles were sent to the nations; if to the nations, then to all languages.

This the Holy Spirit signified, divided among the tongues and united in the dove. Through the tongues there is division; through the dove, union.[Note: [Col. 1429] In four manuscripts, “they divide.”]

The languages of the nations were brought into agreement, while one language of Africa was divided? What could be clearer, my brothers? In the dove there is unity; in the languages of the nations there is fellowship.

At one time, too, languages were divided through pride, and then many languages were made from one. For after the flood certain proud people, as though trying to fortify themselves against God—as though anything were lofty enough for God, or anything secure enough for pride—raised a tower,[Note: [Col. 1430] This is the manuscript reading. The printed editions read: “or anything secure, pride raised a tower.”] as though to prevent themselves from being destroyed by a flood should one occur again.

For they had heard and remembered that every iniquity had been destroyed by the flood; they did not wish to abstain from iniquity, and they sought the height of a tower against the flood. They built a lofty tower.

God saw their pride and caused this error to be imposed upon them, so that they could not understand one another’s speech; and different languages were made through pride (Gen. 11:1–9).[Note: [Col. 1430] Nearly all the manuscripts read: “languages were divided because of pride.”]

If pride made the diversity of languages, the humility of Christ gathered the diversity of languages. What that tower had separated, the Church gathers together.

From one language many were made: do not be surprised—pride did this. From many languages one is made: do not be surprised—love did this.

For although the sounds of the languages are different, one God is invoked in the heart and one peace is preserved.

Where, then, beloved, ought the Holy Spirit to have been manifested, as signifying a certain unity, except through the dove, so that it might be said to the Church at peace: “My dove is one”?

Where ought humility to have been shown except through a simple and groaning bird, not through a proud bird lifting itself up like a raven?

### 11

And perhaps they will say: “Since it is a dove, and one dove, there can be no Baptism apart from the one dove. Therefore, if the dove is with you—or if you are the dove—when I come to you, give me what I do not have.”

You know that this is their argument. In a moment it will become clear to you that it does not come from the voice of the dove, but from the cry of the raven.

Let your Charity pay close attention, and beware of snares. Rather, guard yourselves and reject the words of those who contradict, words that should be spat out, not swallowed and delivered into the entrails.

Do what the Lord did when they offered him a bitter drink: he tasted it and rejected it (Matt. 27:34). So also you: listen, and cast it away.

What do they say? Let us see.

“Behold,” he says, “you are the dove, O Catholic Church. It was said to you, ‘My dove is one, the only one of her mother.’ Surely it was said to you.”

“Wait; do not question me. If it was said to me, prove it first. If it was said to me, I am eager to hear it quickly.”

“It was said to you,” he says.

I answer with the voice of the Catholic Church: “To me.”

But this, brothers, which sounded only from my mouth sounded, I think, also from your hearts, and together we all said: “It was said to the Catholic Church, ‘My dove is one, the only one of her mother.’”

“Apart from that dove,” he says, “there is no Baptism. I was baptized apart from that dove; therefore I do not have Baptism. If I do not have Baptism, why do you not give it to me when I come to you?”

### 12

And I ask in return: for the moment let us set aside to whom it was said, “My dove is one, the only one of her mother.” We are still investigating. Either it was said to me or it was said to you; let us set aside to whom it was said.

This, then, is what I ask: if the dove is simple, innocent, without gall, peaceful in its kisses, and not savage in its claws, do the greedy, robbers, deceivers, drunkards, and criminals belong among the members of this dove? Are they members of this dove?

“Certainly not,” he says.[Col. 1431]

And indeed, brothers, who would say such a thing? To say nothing else, if I mention robbers alone, they may be members of a hawk, but not members of a dove. Kites rob, hawks rob, ravens rob; doves do not rob or tear apart. Therefore robbers are not members of the dove.

Was there not even one robber among you? Why, then, does the Baptism given by a hawk remain, and not by a dove? Why do you not baptize again among yourselves after robbers, adulterers, and drunkards, after the greedy among you? Are all these people members of the dove? You dishonor your dove so much that you make her members vulturine.

What, then, brothers, what are we to say? There are evil and good people in the Catholic Church; among them, however, there are only evil people.

But perhaps I say this with hostile intent; let this also be examined later. Certainly, they too say that they have good and evil people. For if they were to say that they have only good people, let their own people believe them, and I will agree.

“Among us,” let them say, “there are only saints, just people, chaste people, sober people; no adulterers, no usurers, no deceivers, no perjurers, no drunkards.”

Let them say it. For I am not attending to their tongues; I am touching their hearts. Since they are known to us, to you, and to their own people—as you too are known both to yourselves in the Catholic Church and to them—neither should we reproach them, nor should they flatter themselves.

We confess that there are both good and evil people in the Church, but as grain and chaff. Sometimes the person baptized by the grain is chaff, and the person baptized by the chaff is grain.

Otherwise, if the person baptized by the grain is effective, while the person baptized by the chaff is not effective, then the statement “This is the one who baptizes” is false.

But if “This is the one who baptizes” is true, then what is given by him is effective, and he baptizes as the dove does. For that evil man is not the dove, nor does he belong to the members of the dove. Nor can this be said of the Catholic Church, nor among them, if they say that their church is the dove.

What, then, do we understand, brothers? Since it is manifest and known to all—and even if they are unwilling, they are convicted by it—when evil people give Baptism there, people are not baptized again after them; and when evil people give Baptism here, people are not baptized again after them.

The dove does not baptize after the raven. Why, then, does the raven wish to baptize after the dove?

### 13

Let your Charity pay attention. Why was something signified through the dove—so that, after the Lord had been baptized, the dove would come, that is, the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove, and remain upon him—when, at the coming of the dove, John recognized in the Lord a certain distinctive authority for baptizing?

Because, as I said, through this distinctive authority the peace of the Church was established firmly.

It can happen that someone possesses Baptism apart from the dove; but that Baptism cannot benefit him apart from the dove.

Let your Charity pay attention and understand what I am saying. For by this very deception they often mislead our brothers who are sluggish and cold. Let us be more simple and more fervent.

“Behold,” they say, “I received it. Did I not receive it?”

I answer: “You received it.”

“If, then, I received it, there is nothing you can give me. I am secure, even by your testimony. For I say that I received it, and you admit that I received it. The tongue of each of us makes me secure. What, then, do you promise me? Why do you want to make me Catholic, when you are not going to give me anything more and you admit that I have already received what you say you possess?”

But when I say, “Come to me,” I mean that you do not possess what you admit that I possess. Why, then, do you say, “Come to me”?

### 14

The dove teaches us. For she answers on behalf of the Lord, the head, and says: “You have Baptism, but you do not have the love over which I groan.”

“What is this?” he says. “I have Baptism, but I do not have love?”

“Do you possess the sacraments and not love?”[Note: [Col. 1432] The printed editions have “the sacrament”; the manuscripts have “the sacraments.”]

“Do not shout. Show me how someone who divides unity can have love.”

“I have Baptism,” he says.

“You have it. But that Baptism without love benefits you nothing, because without love you are nothing. For that Baptism, even in one who is nothing, is not nothing. Baptism is something—indeed, something great—because of the one of whom it was said, ‘This is the one who baptizes.’

“But lest you think that what is great can benefit you if you are not in unity, the dove descended upon the baptized one, as though saying: ‘If you have Baptism, be in the dove, so that what you have may not fail to benefit you.’

“Come, then, to the dove,” we say—not so that you may begin to have what you did not have, but so that what you had may begin to benefit you. For outside you had Baptism to your destruction; inside, if you possess it, it begins to benefit you for salvation.”

### 15

For it was not merely that Baptism did not benefit you; it also harmed you. Holy things can harm. In good people, holy things are present for salvation; in evil people, for judgment.

Certainly, brothers, we know what we receive, and surely what we receive is holy; no one says that it is not holy. What does the Apostle say? “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

He does not say that the thing itself is evil, but that the person is evil and, by receiving it evilly, receives the good thing he receives for judgment.

Was the morsel that the Lord handed to Judas evil (John 13:26)? Certainly not. The physician would not give poison; the physician gave health. But by receiving it unworthily, the one who received it without peace received it to his destruction.

So also with the person who is baptized.

“I have it,” he says, “for myself.”

“I admit that you have it. Guard what you have. By the very thing you have, you will be condemned.”

“Why?”

“Because you have the thing belonging to the dove apart from the dove. If you have the thing belonging to the dove within the dove, you have it securely.

“Suppose that you are a soldier. If you bear within you the mark of your emperor, you serve securely. If you bear it outside, that mark not only does not benefit you in military service; you will also be punished as a deserter.”

Come, then—come—and do not say, “I already have it; it is already enough for me.” Come. The dove calls you; she calls you with groaning.

My brothers, I speak to you: call them with groaning, not with quarrelling. Call them by praying, call them by inviting, call them by fasting; let them understand from your love[Note: [Col. 1432] The printed editions have “call them by fasting in love.” The manuscripts have “from love” and omit “call them by fasting,” except for a few manuscripts.] that you grieve over them.

I do not doubt, my brothers, that if they see your grief, they will be ashamed and come back to life.

Come, then—come. Do not be afraid; be afraid if you do not come. Indeed, do not be afraid, but weep.

Come, and you will rejoice if you come. You will indeed groan amid the tribulations of your pilgrimage, but you will rejoice in hope.

Come to where the dove is, to whom it was said, “My dove is one, the only one of her mother.”

You see one dove above the head of Christ; do you not see tongues throughout the whole world? The same Spirit is present through the dove, and the same Spirit through the tongues. If the same Spirit is present through the dove and through the tongues, the Holy Spirit has been given to the whole world,[Note: [Col. 1433] The printed editions have “the Holy Spirit has been given throughout the world”; the manuscripts have “the Holy Spirit has been given to the whole world.”] from which you have cut yourself off, so that you cry out with the raven instead of groaning with the dove.

Come, then.

### 16

But perhaps you are troubled and say: “I was baptized outside; I am afraid that I am guilty because I received it outside.”

You have already begun to recognize what ought to be lamented. You are speaking the truth: you are guilty—not because you received it, but because you received it outside.

Therefore, keep what you received; correct the fact that you received it outside. You hear two things: “You received it,” and “You received it apart from the dove.”

What you received, I approve; because you received it outside, I disapprove.

Keep, then, what you received. It is not changed, but recognized. It is the mark of my King; I will not commit sacrilege. I correct the deserter; I do not alter the mark.

### 17

Do not boast about Baptism because I say that it is the same. Behold, I say that it is the same; the entire Catholic Church says that it is the same.

The dove notices it, recognizes it, and groans because you possess it outside. She sees there what she recognizes, and she sees also what she must correct.

“It is the same; come.”

You boast because it is the same, and you do not wish to come? What, then, of the evil people who do not belong to the dove?

The dove says to you: “The evil people among whom I groan, who do not belong to my members and among whom I must groan—do they not have what you boast that you possess? Do not many drunkards possess Baptism? Do not many greedy people? Do not many idolaters—and, what is worse, secretly? Did not pagans go, or once go, openly to idols? Now Christians secretly seek out diviners and consult astrologers.

“These people too possess Baptism, but the dove groans among the ravens.

“Why, then, do you rejoice because you possess it? You possess what the evil person also possesses. Possess humility, love, and peace. Possess the good that you do not yet possess, so that the good you possess may benefit you.”

### 18

For what you possess was also possessed by Simon Magus. The Acts of the Apostles bears witness to this—that canonical book which is read every year in the Church.

At the annual solemnity after the Lord’s Passion, you know that this book is read, where it is written how the Apostle was converted and became a preacher instead of a persecutor (Acts 9:1–30). It is also where, on the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit was sent in divided tongues as of fire (Acts 2:1–4).

There we read that many in Samaria believed through the preaching of Philip. It is understood that he was either one of the Apostles or one of the deacons, since we read that seven deacons were ordained there, among whom Philip’s name is also found (Acts 6:3–6).

Through Philip’s preaching, then, the Samaritans believed; Samaria began to abound in believers. Simon Magus was there. Through his magical practices he had driven the people mad, so that they thought him to be the power of God.

Yet, moved by the signs that Philip performed, he himself also believed. But what sort of belief his was, the events that follow later demonstrate. Simon was baptized as well.

The Apostles who were in Jerusalem heard this, and Peter and John were sent to them. They found many who had been baptized. Since none of them had yet received the Holy Spirit as he was then descending, to display the sign of the Gentiles who would believe—for those upon whom the Holy Spirit descended spoke in tongues—they laid hands on them, praying for them, and they received the Holy Spirit.

That Simon, who was not in the Church as a dove but as a raven, because he sought what was his own and not what belonged to Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21), and who therefore had loved power among Christians more than righteousness, saw that the Holy Spirit was given through the laying on of the Apostles’ hands—not because they themselves gave him, but because he was given while they prayed—and he said to the Apostles:

“What do you want from me in exchange for money, so that the Holy Spirit may also be given through the laying on of my hands?”

Peter said to him: “May your money perish with you, because you thought that the gift of God could be purchased with money.”

To whom does he say, “May your money perish with you”? Surely to one who had been baptized. He already possessed Baptism, but he did not cling to the inner life of the dove.

Listen, and you will see that he did not cling to it. Consider the very words of the Apostle Peter, for what follows says: “You have neither part nor share in this faith, for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness” (Acts 8:5–23).

The dove has no gall; Simon had it. Therefore he was separated from the inner life of the dove.

What good did Baptism do him? Do not boast about Baptism, as though salvation were sufficient for you through it alone. Do not be angry; put away your gall; come to the dove. Here what you possess will benefit you—what outside not only did not benefit you, but even harmed you.

### 19

Nor should you say: “I will not come because I was baptized outside.”

Begin to have love; begin to have fruit. Let fruit be found in you, and the dove will send you inside.[Note: [Col. 1434] The printed editions have “may she send you”; the manuscripts have “she will send you.”]

We find this in Scripture.

The ark had been constructed from incorruptible wood (Gen. 6:14). The incorruptible wood represents the saints, the faithful who belong to Christ. Just as the living stones from which the temple is built are called faithful human beings, so the incorruptible wood signifies people who persevere in faith.

Thus, within the ark there was incorruptible wood; for the ark is the Church. There the dove baptizes, for that ark was carried upon the water. The incorruptible wood within was baptized.

We find certain wood baptized outside: all the trees that were in the world. Yet the water was the same; it was not another water. All the water had come from heaven and from the abysses of the springs. It was the same water in which the incorruptible wood in the ark was baptized and in which the wood outside was baptized.

The dove was sent out, and at first she found no resting place for her feet. She returned to the ark, for the waters still covered everything; and she preferred to return rather than be baptized again.

But that raven was sent out before the water had dried.[Note: [Col. 1434] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have “before the water was dried.”] Having been baptized again, it did not wish to return; it perished in those waters.

May God avert from us the death of that raven. For why did it not return, unless it was because it was seized by the waters?

But the dove, finding no resting place for her feet, while the water cried out to her from every side, “Come, come, be immersed here”—just as these heretics cry, “Come, come, you have it here”—finding no resting place for her feet, returned to the ark.

Noah sent her out again, just as the ark sends you out, so that you may speak to them. And what did the dove do afterward?

Because there was wood baptized outside, she brought back to the ark a branch from an olive tree. That branch had leaves and fruit (Gen. 8:6–11).

Let there not be words alone in you; let there not be leaves alone in you. Let there be fruit, and you will return to the ark—not by yourself; the dove calls you back.

Groan outside, so that you may call them back inside.

### 20

Indeed, if this fruit of the olive is examined, you will discover what it signified.

The fruit of the olive signifies love. How do we prove this? Just as oil is not pressed down by any liquid but, when everything else is displaced, springs forth and rises above it, so love cannot be pressed down into the depths; it must rise to what is above.[Note: [Col. 1435] In nearly all the manuscripts, “shine forth.”]

For this reason the Apostle says of it: “I show you a still more excellent way.”

Since we have spoken of oil, because it rises above, lest perhaps the Apostle’s words, “I show you a still more excellent way,” should not refer to love, let us hear what follows: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels but do not have love, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (1 Cor. 12:31; 13:1).

Go now, Donatus, and cry out, “I am eloquent.” Go now, and cry out, “I am learned.”

How eloquent are you? How learned? Have you perhaps spoken in the tongues of angels? And yet, even if you spoke in the tongues of angels, without love I would hear sounding bronze and clanging cymbals.

I am looking for something solid. Let me find fruit among the leaves. Let there not be words alone. Let them have the olive; let them return to the ark.

### 21

“But,” you will say, “I have the sacrament.”

You are speaking the truth. The sacrament is divine; you have Baptism, and I acknowledge it.

But what does the same Apostle say? “If I know all the sacraments and have prophecy and all faith, so that I could move mountains”—perhaps you would say this too: “I believed; it is enough for me.”

But what does James say? “Even the demons believe—and tremble” (James 2:19).

Faith is great, but it is of no benefit if it does not have love. The demons also confessed Christ. Therefore, believing but not loving, they said: “What have we to do with you?” (Mark 1:24).

They had faith, but they did not have love. That is why they were demons.
