Do not boast of faith; you must still be compared with demons. Do not say to Christ, “What is there between me and you?”[Note: [Col. 1435] This is the reading of the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Do not say to the Christian, ‘What is there between me and you?’”]

For the unity of Christ speaks to you. Come; recognize peace; return to the inner life of the dove.

You were baptized outside. Have fruit, and you will return to the ark.

### 22

And you say: “Why do you seek us, if we are evil?” So that you may be good. That is why we seek you: because you are evil. For if you were not evil, we would have found you; we would not be seeking you. Whoever is good has already been found; whoever is evil is still being sought. That is why we seek you: return to the ark.

“But I already have Baptism.” If I should know all the sacraments and have prophecy and all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. Let me see the fruit there; let me see the olive there—and may you be brought back to the ark.

### 23

“But look,” you say, “we suffer many evils.” [Col. 1436] If you suffered these things for Christ, you would not suffer them for your honors. Hear what follows: for they sometimes boast that they give many alms and give to the poor, and that they endure hardships—but for Donatus, not for Christ.

See how you suffer. For if you suffer for Donatus, you suffer for a proud man. You are not in the dove if you suffer for Donatus. He was not the friend of the Bridegroom. For if he were the friend of the Bridegroom, he would seek the Bridegroom’s glory, not his own (John 3:29). See the friend of the Bridegroom saying, “This is he who baptizes.” The one for whom you suffer was not the friend of the Bridegroom.

You do not have the wedding garment; and if you came to the banquet, you must be thrown out (Matthew 22:11–13). Indeed, because you have been thrown out, you are wretched. Return at last, and do not boast.

Hear what the Apostle says: “If I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love”—there is what you do not have. “If,” he says, “I hand over my body so that I may be burned”—and certainly for the name of Christ—“but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2–3). Since there are many who do this boastfully and without love, he therefore says: “If I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing.”

Those martyrs who suffered during the time of persecution acted out of love; they acted out of love. But these act out of swelling pride. For when there is no persecutor, they throw themselves to destruction.

Come, then, so that you may have love.

“But we have martyrs.”

Which martyrs? They are not doves; therefore they tried to fly and fell from the rock.

### 24

You see, then, my brothers, that all the divine pages cry out against them: all prophecy, the entire Gospel, all the apostolic letters, and every groan of the dove. And still they do not awaken; still they do not rouse themselves.

But if we are the dove, let us groan, endure, and hope. The mercy of God will be present, so that the fire of the Holy Spirit may burn fervently in your simplicity; and they will come. We must not despair. Pray, preach, love; the Lord is altogether powerful.

They have already begun to recognize their own face. Many have recognized it; many have been ashamed. Christ will be present so that the rest may recognize it as well.

And certainly, my brothers, let even the chaff alone remain there, while all the grains are gathered. Whatever has borne fruit there, let it return to the ark through the dove.

### 25

Now, failing everywhere and finding nothing to say, what do they put before us? “They have taken our estates; they have taken our lands.” They produce human wills. “Look, Gaius Seius gave an estate to the Church over which Faustinus presided.”

Of what Church was Faustinus the bishop?

“Of the Church,” he says, “over which Faustinus presided.”

But Faustinus did not preside over the Church; he presided over a party. The Church, however, is the dove.

Why do you cry out? We have not swallowed up the estates. Let the dove have them. Let it be determined which is the dove, and let the dove itself have them.

For you know, my brothers, that these estates do not belong to Augustine. And if you do not know this, and think that I rejoice in possessing the estates, God knows—he himself knows—what I think about those estates, or what I endure there. He knows my groans, if he has deigned to grant me any share in the dove.

Here are the estates. By what right do you defend them—divine or human?

Let them answer: “We have divine right in the Scriptures, and human right in the laws of kings.”

By what right, then, does each person possess what he possesses? Is it not by human right? For by divine right, “The earth is the Lord’s and its fullness” (Psalm 23:1). God made the poor and the rich from one lump of earth, and one earth supports both poor and rich.

Yet by human right one says, “This estate is mine; this house is mine; this slave is mine.” Therefore, by human right—by the right of emperors.

Why? Because God distributed these human laws to the human race through emperors and kings of this world.

Do you want us to read the laws of the emperors and conduct the matter of the estates according to them? If you want to possess them by human right, let us recite the laws of the emperors. Let us see whether they wanted anything to be possessed by heretics.

“But what have I to do with the emperor?”

According to his law, you possess the land. Or remove the laws of the emperors, and who dares say, “That estate is mine,” or “That slave is mine,” or “This house is mine”?

But if these human beings received the laws of kings so that such things might be held, do you want us to recite the laws, so that you may rejoice that you possess even one garden, and attribute it only to the gentleness of the dove that you are even permitted to remain there?

For clear laws are read in which the emperors ordered that those who, outside the communion of the Catholic Church, usurp the name Christian for themselves, and do not wish to worship the author of peace in peace, should dare to possess nothing in the name of the Church. [Col. 1437]

### 26

“But what have we to do with the emperor?”

But I have already said: the matter concerns human law. And yet the Apostle wanted kings to be served; he wanted kings to be honored, and said, “Revere the king” (1 Peter 2:17).

Do not say, “What have I to do with the king?” What, then, have you to do with property? Possessions are held by the laws of kings. You said, “What have I to do with the king?” Do not claim your possessions, because you have renounced the very human laws by which possessions are held.

“But I am speaking of divine law,” he says.

Then let us recite the Gospel. Let us see how far the Catholic Church of Christ extends—Christ upon whom the dove came, teaching, “This is he who baptizes.” How, then, can one who says, “I baptize,” possess anything by divine right, when the dove says, “This is he who baptizes,” and Scripture says, “My dove is one, one belonging to her mother”?

Why have you torn the dove apart? Rather, you have torn apart your own inward parts. For you tear yourselves apart; the dove remains whole.

Therefore, my brothers, if everywhere they have nothing to say, I say what they should do: let them come to the Catholic Church. With us they will have not only the earth, but also the one who made heaven and earth.

## TRACTATE VII

From the passage written, “And I saw, and bore witness that this is the Son of God,” up to, “Truly I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and angels ascending and descending upon the Son of Man.” Chapter 1, verses 34–51.

### 1

We rejoice together with you in your attendance, because you have gathered so eagerly, beyond what we could have hoped. This is what gladdens us and consoles us amid all the labors and dangers of this life: your love for God, your devoted zeal, your firm hope, and the fervor of your spirit.

You heard, when the Psalm was read, that “the needy and poor man cries out to God in this world” (Psalm 73:21). For it is, as you have often heard and ought to remember, [Col. 1438] the voice not of one man and yet of one man: not of one, because there are many faithful people—many grains groaning among the chaff, scattered throughout the whole world—but of one, because all are members of Christ and therefore one body.

This needy and poor people does not know how to rejoice in the world. Its sorrow is within, and its joy is within, where no one sees except the one who hears the groaning person and crowns the one who hopes.

The world’s joy is vanity. It is awaited with great anticipation, that it may come, but when it comes it cannot be held. For this day, which is joyful today to those who are lost in this city, will certainly not exist tomorrow; nor will these same people tomorrow be what they are today. Everything passes away, everything flies away, and everything vanishes like smoke. Woe to those who love such things!

For every soul follows what it loves. “All flesh is grass, and all the honor of flesh is like the flower of grass; the grass withers, the flower falls, but the word of the Lord remains forever” (Isaiah 40:6–8). See what you should love, if you wish to remain forever.

But you might say: “From where can I grasp the word of God?” “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

### 2

Therefore, dearest brothers and sisters, let it belong to our neediness and poverty that we grieve for those who seem to themselves to have abundance. Their joy is like that of madmen. Just as a madman often rejoices in his madness and laughs, and pities the person who is sane, so we too, dearest brothers and sisters, if we have received the medicine that comes from heaven—for we too were all mad—now that we have been saved, because we no longer love the things we used to love, should groan before God for those who are still insane. For he is powerful enough to save them as well.

And it is necessary that they look at themselves and become displeased with themselves.

They want to be looked at [Note: [Col. 1438] The manuscripts read: “they want to be looked at” (*spectari volunt*)], but they do not know how to look at themselves. For if they turn their eyes toward themselves even slightly, they see their own disgrace.

Until this happens, let our pursuits be different; let the diversions of our souls be different. Our sorrow is worth more than their joy.

As for the number of brothers, it is difficult that any man has been carried away by that celebration. But as for the number of sisters, it saddens us—and this is more grievous because those women whom public shame ought to have recalled, if not fear, to the Church do not run to the Church instead. Let the one who sees this see to it, and may his mercy be present to heal everyone.

But let us who have gathered feed upon God’s banquets, and let his word be our joy. For he has invited us to his Gospel, and he himself is our food, sweeter than anything—if someone has a healthy palate in his heart.

### 3

I think that Your Charity will rightly remember that this Gospel is being recited in order, in readings appropriate to it. And I think you have not forgotten what has already been discussed, especially the more recent matters concerning John and the dove.

Concerning John, what new thing did he learn about the Lord through the dove, since he already knew the Lord? This was discovered under the inspiration of the Spirit of God: John already knew the Lord, but through the dove he learned that the Lord himself would baptize in such a way that he would transfer the power of baptizing [Col. 1439] from himself to no one. For it had been said, “Upon whomever you see the Spirit descending like a dove and remaining upon him, this is he who baptizes in the Holy Spirit” (John 1:33).

What does “this is he” mean? Not another, even if through another.

Why through a dove? Many things have been said, and I cannot, nor need I, repeat them all. Above all, however, it was because of peace. For the dove also brought to the ark the pieces of wood that had been baptized outside, because it found fruit on them—as you remember, the dove was sent out by Noah from the ark, which floated upon the flood and was washed by baptism, not submerged.

When it had been sent out, it brought back an olive branch; but it had not only leaves—it also had fruit (Genesis 8:8–11). Therefore this is what we should desire for our brothers who are baptized outside: that they may have fruit. The dove will not leave them outside unless it brings them back to the ark.

The fruit is entirely love, without which a human being is nothing, whatever else he may possess. We recalled and reviewed this very fully as spoken by the Apostle. For he says:

“If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal; and if I have all knowledge, and know all the mysteries, and have all prophecy, and have all faith”—how did he say “all faith”?—“so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:1–3).

In no way can those who divide unity say that they have love. These things have been said; let us examine what follows.

### 4

John bore witness because he had seen. What testimony did he bear? That he is the Son of God.

It was therefore necessary that the one who is the only Son of God, not an adopted son, should baptize. Adopted sons are ministers of the Only-Begotten; the Only-Begotten has the authority, while the adopted have the ministry.

Even if a minister who does not belong to the number of the sons baptizes because he lives and acts badly, what consoles us? “This is he who baptizes.”

### 5

On the next day John was standing again, with two of his disciples. Looking upon Jesus as he walked by, he said, “Behold, the Lamb of God.”

Certainly this Lamb is singular. For the disciples too were called lambs: “Behold, I send you as lambs into the midst of wolves” (Matthew 10:16). They too were called light: “You are the light of the world” (ibid. 5:14). But he is different, of whom it was said, “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

So also with the Lamb: he is singular, alone without stain, without sin—not one whose stains have been wiped away, but one whose stain has never existed.

What, then? Because John was saying of the Lord, “Behold, the Lamb of God,” was John himself not a lamb? Was he not a holy man? Was he not the friend of the Bridegroom?

Therefore he is singular: “This is the Lamb of God,” because it was by the blood of this Lamb alone that human beings could be redeemed.

### 6

My brothers, if we recognize our price—that it is the blood of the Lamb—who are those who today celebrate the festival of the blood of some woman, I do not know whom? [Col. 1440] And how ungrateful they are!

They say that gold was snatched from the woman’s ear, that blood flowed, and that the gold was placed on a balance or scale, and that much of the blood outweighed it.

If the blood of a woman had weight enough to incline the gold, what weight does the blood of the Lamb have to incline the world—the blood through which the world was made?

And indeed, some spirit, I do not know which, was appeased by blood so that it might press down the weight. The unclean spirits knew that Jesus Christ was going to come. They had heard it from the angels; they had heard it from the prophets; and they hoped that he would come.

For if they had not hoped, why did they cry out, “What have we to do with you? Have you come before the time to destroy us? We know who you are, the Holy One of God” (Mark 1:24)? They knew that he would come, but they did not know the time.

But what did you hear in the Psalm about Jerusalem? “For your servants have taken pleasure in its stones, and they will pity its dust. You will arise,” he says, “and have mercy on Zion, because the time has come to have mercy on her” (Psalm 102:15, 14).

When the time came for God to have mercy, the Lamb came.

What kind of Lamb is this, whom wolves fear? What kind of Lamb is this, who, when killed, killed the lion? For the devil is called a lion, prowling around and roaring, seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8). The lion was conquered by the blood of the Lamb.

Behold the spectacles of Christians! And, what is more, they see vanity with the eyes of the flesh, while we see truth with the eyes of the heart.

Do not think, brothers, that our Lord God has left us without spectacles. For if there are no spectacles, why have you gathered today? Behold, you have seen what we said, and you cried out; you would not have cried out unless you had seen.

And it is a great thing to behold throughout the whole world the lion conquered by the blood of the Lamb, and the members of Christ drawn from the lions’ teeth and joined to the body of Christ.

Therefore some spirit imitated something similar, wishing its image to be purchased with blood, because it knew that the human race would one day be redeemed with precious blood.

For evil spirits fashion certain shadows of honor for themselves, so that they may deceive those who follow Christ. Indeed, my brothers, those very people who seduce through amulets, incantations, and the devices of the enemy mix the name of Christ into their incantations. Since they can no longer deceive Christians by giving them poison, they add something of honey, so that what is bitter may be concealed by what is sweet and may be drunk to destruction.

Indeed, I know that at one time a priest of that Pilleatus used to say, “Pilleatus himself is also a Christian.”

Why is this, brothers, except that otherwise they cannot deceive Christians?

### 7

Therefore, do not seek Christ elsewhere than where Christ wanted himself to be preached to you. And in the manner in which he wished to be preached to you, hold fast to him; write him in your heart in that manner. He is a wall against every attack and every ambush of the enemy.

Do not be afraid. He does not tempt unless he has been permitted to do so. It is certain that he does nothing unless he has been permitted or sent.

He is sent like an evil angel by the ruling power; he is permitted when he asks for something. And this, brothers, happens only so that the righteous may be tested and the unjust punished.

Why, then, are you afraid? Walk in the Lord your God; be confident. What he [Col. 1441] does not wish you to suffer, you will not suffer. What he permits you to suffer is the scourge of one correcting, not the punishment of one condemning.

We are being instructed for an everlasting inheritance, and yet we disdain being scourged!

My brothers, if a child refused to be struck by blows or whips from his father, how would he be called—proud, hopeless, ungrateful for his father’s discipline? And why does a human father educate his human son? So that the son may not lose temporal things that the father acquired or gathered for him, things he does not want him to lose, although the one who leaves them was himself unable to hold them forever.

He does not teach his son so that he may possess them together with him, but so that he may possess them after him.

My brothers, if a father teaches his son to be his successor, and teaches one who himself will likewise pass through all those things through which the one giving the instruction must pass, how do you want our Father to educate us—our Father whose successors we will not be, but to whom we will approach, and with whom we will remain forever in an inheritance that does not wither, die, or know hail?

And he himself is both the inheritance and the Father. Shall we possess him and not be willing to be instructed?

Let us therefore endure the Father’s instruction.

When our head hurts, let us not run to incantations, diviners, and remedies of vanity. [Note: [Col. 1441] In most manuscripts, “incantations.”]

My brothers, should I not mourn for you? Every day I encounter these things. And what should I do? Have I not yet persuaded Christians that hope must be placed in Christ?

Suppose someone has had such a remedy applied to him; let him die. For how many have died with remedies, and how many have lived without remedies! With what face did his soul go forth to God? He lost the sign of Christ and received the sign of the devil.

Or perhaps he says, “I did not lose the sign of Christ.”

Then you had the sign of Christ together with the sign of the devil. Christ does not want partnership; he wants alone to possess what he purchased. He purchased it at such a price that he alone might possess it. You make the devil a partner for him, although you had sold yourself to the devil through sin.

“Woe to the double-hearted” (Sirach 2:14), who make one portion for God in their heart and one portion for the devil. God is angered because a portion is made there for the devil; he departs, and the devil will possess the whole.

Therefore the Apostle does not say without reason, “Nor give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:27).

Let us therefore recognize the Lamb, brothers; let us recognize our price.

### 8

John was standing, and two of his disciples were with him. Behold two of John’s disciples. John was such a friend of the Bridegroom that he did not seek his own glory but bore witness to the truth. Did he want his disciples to remain with him and not follow the Lord? Rather, he himself showed his disciples whom they should follow.

They regarded him as a lamb, but he said to them, “Why do you look to me? I am not the Lamb. Behold the Lamb of God.” He had also said above, “Behold the Lamb of God.”

And what does the Lamb of God profit us? “Behold,” he says, “the one who takes away the sin of the world.”

After hearing this, the two who had been with John followed him.

### 9

Let us see what follows. “Behold the Lamb of God”: this was John’s statement.

“And the two disciples heard him speaking, and they followed Jesus. But Jesus turned, and seeing them following him, said to them, ‘What are you seeking?’ They said to him, ‘Rabbi’”—which is translated, “Teacher”—“where are you staying?”

They were not following him as though they were already going to remain attached to him. For it is clear when they became attached to him: he called them from the boat.

One of these two was Andrew, as you have just heard. Andrew was Peter’s brother. And we know from the Gospel that the Lord called Peter and Andrew from the boat, saying, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matthew 4:19). From that moment they became attached to him, so as not to withdraw.

Thus, when these two now follow him, they are not following as though they would not later depart. Rather, they wanted to see where he lived and to do what is written: “Let your foot wear out the threshold of his doors; rise continually to go to him and be instructed by his commandments” (Sirach 6:36–37).

He showed them where he was staying. They came and remained with him. How blessed a day they spent; how blessed a night! Who can tell us what they heard from the Lord?

Let us build ourselves up in our own hearts, and make a house for him to enter and teach us, to speak with us.

### 10

“What are you seeking?” They said to him, “Rabbi”—which is translated, “Teacher”—“where are you staying?” He said to them, “Come and see.” And they came and saw where he was staying, and remained with him that day. It was about the tenth hour.

Do we think that it was irrelevant for the Evangelist to tell us what hour it was? Could it be that he intended us to notice nothing there and seek nothing? It was the tenth hour.

This number signifies the Law, because the Law was given in ten commandments. But the time had come for the Law to be fulfilled through love, because it could not be fulfilled by the Jews through fear. Hence the Lord says, “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5:17).

Rightly, then, at the tenth hour these two followed him as witnesses of the Bridegroom’s friend; and at the tenth hour they heard, “Rabbi,” which is translated “Teacher.”

If the Lord was called Rabbi at the tenth hour, and the number ten pertains to the Law, the teacher of the Law is no one other than the giver of the Law. Let no one say that one person gave the Law and another teaches the Law. He himself teaches it who gave it; he himself is the teacher of his own Law, and he teaches it.

And there is mercy on his tongue. Therefore he teaches the Law mercifully, as it is said of Wisdom: “She carries the Law and mercy on her tongue” (Proverbs 31:26).

Do not fear that you cannot fulfill the Law. Flee to mercy. If fulfilling the Law is too much for you, use that covenant; use the bond; use the prayers that the heavenly jurist has established and composed for you.

### 11

For those who have a case and wish to petition the emperor seek some learned jurist, from whom their petitions may be composed, lest, if they ask in some way other than they ought, they not only fail to obtain what they seek but also receive punishment instead of a benefit. [Note: [Col. 1442] Most manuscripts: “deserve.”]

When the Apostles wished to petition and did not know how to approach God the emperor, they said to Christ, “Lord, teach us to pray.” That is: “Our jurist, our assessor—indeed, one who sits with God—compose petitions for us.”

And the Lord taught them from the book of heavenly law; he taught them how to pray. In what he taught, he inserted a certain condition: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Luke 11:1–4). [Col. 1443]

If you do not ask according to the law, you will be guilty. Do you tremble because you have become guilty before the emperor? Offer the sacrifice of humility; offer the sacrifice of mercy. Say in your prayers, “Forgive me, because I also forgive.”

But if you say this, do it. What will you do, where will you go, if you have lied in your prayers? It is not as it is said in court, “You will lose the benefit of the rescript”; rather, you will not obtain the rescript at all.

For it is a rule of forensic law that, when someone has lied in a petition, what he has obtained does not benefit him. But this is among human beings, because a human being can be deceived. The emperor could have been deceived when you sent the petition: you said what you wished, and the one to whom you said it does not know whether it is true. He sent you to be convicted by your adversary, so that, if you were convicted before the judge of having lied—because he could only grant the request, not knowing whether you had lied—you would there lose the very benefit of the rescript by which you had obtained it.

But God, who knows whether you are lying or speaking the truth, does not merely ensure that it does not benefit you in judgment; he does not even permit you to obtain it, because you dared to lie to the truth.

### 12

What, then, will you do? Tell me. To fulfill the Law in every respect, so that you offend in nothing, is difficult. Your guilt, therefore, is certain. Do you not wish to use a remedy?

Behold, my brothers, what remedy the Lord has established against the illnesses of the soul.

What remedy? When your head hurts, we praise you if you place the Gospel on your head and do not run to an amulet. Human weakness has been brought to such a state, and those who run to amulets must be so greatly pitied, that we rejoice when we see a person lying in his bed, tossed by fevers and pains, who has placed his hope nowhere except in putting the Gospel on his head—not because the Gospel was made for this purpose, but because he preferred the Gospel to amulets.

If, then, the Gospel is placed on the head so that the pain of the head may cease, should it not be placed on the heart so that it may be healed of sins?

Let it be done, then.

What should be done? Let it be placed on the heart; let the heart be healed.

It is good—good indeed—not to be concerned for the health of the body except to ask God for it. If he knows that it benefits you, he will give it. If he does not give it to you, it would not have benefited you to have it.

How many innocent people are sick in bed, and, if they become healthy, go out to commit crimes? How many are harmed by health? How much better would it have been for the thief who goes out to cut a man’s throat to be sick? How much better for the man who rises at night to dig through another’s wall to be tossed by fevers? He would be sick innocently; healthy, he is criminal.

God therefore knows what is good for us. Let us do only this: let our heart be healthy from sins. And when we are perhaps scourged in the body, let us entreat him.

The Apostle Paul asked him to remove the thorn of the flesh, and he did not remove it. Was he disturbed? Did he grieve and say that he had been abandoned? Rather, he said that he had not been abandoned, because what he wanted removed had not been removed, so that that weakness might be healed.

For he found this in the voice of the physician: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Corinthians 12:8–9).

How, then, do you know that God does not wish to heal you? It is still beneficial for you to be scourged.

How do you know how rotten is the thing the physician is cutting, driving his instrument through the decayed parts? Does he not know the proper measure—what he should do and how far he should go? Does the cry of the one being cut cause the hand of the skillful physician [Col. 1444] to withdraw?

The patient cries; the physician cuts. Is he cruel because he does not heed the one crying, or rather merciful because he pursues the wound in order to heal the sick person?

I have said these things, my brothers, so that no one may seek anything beyond God’s help when we happen to be under some correction from the Lord.

Take care lest you perish; take care lest you withdraw from the Lamb and be devoured by the lion.

### 13

We have therefore said why it was the tenth hour. Let us see what follows.

“Andrew, Simon Peter’s brother, was one of the two who had heard from John and followed him. He found his brother Simon and said to him, ‘We have found the Messiah’”—which is translated “Christ.”

Messiah in Hebrew, Christ in Greek, is Unctus in Latin, “Anointed.” He is called Christ from anointing. Χρῖσμα (*chrisma*) is “anointing” in Greek; therefore Christ means “anointed.”

He is singularly anointed, especially anointed. Hence all Christians are anointed, but he is especially so. Hear how the Psalm says: “Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Psalm 45:8).

All the saints are his companions, but he alone is singularly the Holy of Holies, singularly anointed, singularly Christ.

### 14

And he led him to Jesus. When Jesus looked at him, he said, “You are Simon, the son of John; you shall be called Cephas,” which is translated “Peter.”

It is not a great thing that the Lord said whose son this man was. What is difficult for the Lord? He knew all the names of his saints, whom he predestined before the foundation of the world. Are you surprised that he said to one man, “You are the son of this person, and you will be called that”?

What is great is that he changed his name and made Peter out of Simon.

Peter comes from *petra*, “rock,” and the rock is the Church. Therefore the Church was represented in Peter’s name.

And who is secure except the one who builds upon the rock?

What does the Lord himself say?

“Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man building upon rock”—he does not yield to temptations—“the rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and struck that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon rock.

“But everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them”—now let each one of us fear and beware—“I will compare him to a foolish man who built his house upon sand. The rain descended, the rivers came, the winds blew, and struck that house, and it fell; and its fall was great” (Matthew 7:24–27).

What does it profit the person who enters the Church if he wishes to build upon sand? By hearing and not doing, he does build—but upon sand.

For if he hears nothing, he builds nothing. But if he hears, he builds. Yet we ask: where?

If he hears and does, he builds upon rock. If he hears and does not do, he builds upon sand.

There are two kinds of builders: either upon rock or upon sand.

What, then, of those who do not hear? Are they secure? Does he call them secure because they build nothing? They are naked under the rain, before the winds, before the rivers. When these things come, they carry them away before they can throw down their houses.

Therefore there is one security: both to build and to build upon the rock.

If you wish to hear and not do, you build—but you build a ruin. When temptation comes, it throws down the house, and in throwing down your house it carries you away with it.

But if you do not hear, you are naked, and you yourself are dragged away by those temptations.

Hear, therefore, [Col. 1445] and do. This is the one remedy.

How many people today, perhaps, by hearing and not doing, have been swept away by the flood of this celebration? By hearing and not doing, the flood itself—the annual celebration—comes; the torrent is filled, but it will pass and dry up. Yet woe to the one whom it carries away!

Let Your Charity know this: unless someone both hears and does, he does not build upon the rock, and he does not belong to the great name that the Lord commended in this way.

For he made you attentive. If Peter had been called this before, you would not have seen the mystery of the rock so clearly, and you might have thought that he had been called this by chance, not by God’s providence. Therefore he first wished him to be called something else, so that through the change of the name itself the vitality of the sacrament might be commended.

### 15

“On the following day he wished to depart for Galilee, and he found Philip. He said to him, ‘Follow me.’ Now he was from the city of Andrew and Peter. Philip found Nathanael, who had already been called by the Lord Philip. And he said to him, ‘We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, whom Moses wrote about in the Law, and the Prophets.’”

He was called his son because Joseph was betrothed to his mother. For all Christians know well from the Gospel that she conceived and gave birth while remaining untouched.

Philip said this to Nathanael and added the place: “from Nazareth.”

And Nathanael said to him, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

What should we understand, brothers? Not as some pronounce it, for it is also commonly pronounced this way: “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” For Philip’s reply follows: “Come and see.”

But this statement can follow either pronunciation—whether you pronounce it as an affirmation, “Something good can come from Nazareth,” followed by “Come and see,” or as a doubt and a complete question, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” followed by “Come and see.”

Since the subsequent words fit either pronunciation and contradict neither, it is our task to inquire what we should understand more appropriately in these words.

### 16

What sort of man Nathanael was, we prove from what follows. Hear what sort of man he was: the Lord himself bears witness to him.

The great Lord was known through John’s testimony; blessed Nathanael was known through the testimony of Truth.

For even if the Lord were not commended by John’s testimony, he himself bore witness to himself, because truth is sufficient for its own testimony. But because human beings could not grasp the truth, they sought the truth through a lamp. Therefore John was sent, through whom the Lord might be revealed.

Hear the Lord bearing testimony to Nathanael:

“And Nathanael said to him, ‘Can anything good come from Nazareth?’ Philip said to him, ‘Come and see.’ Jesus saw Nathanael coming toward him and said of him, ‘Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.’”

A great testimony! This was said neither of Andrew, nor of Peter, nor of Philip, but of Nathanael: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”

17. What, then, are we to do, brothers? Should this man have been the first among the Apostles? Not only is Nathanael not found among the Apostles as the first, but not even as the middle or the last of the Twelve—he to whom the Son of God bore such testimony, saying, “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit” [Col. 1446]. The reason is sought; insofar as the Lord intimates it, we find it with reasonable probability. We should understand that Nathanael himself was learned and well versed in the Law. For this reason the Lord did not wish to place him among the disciples, because he chose uneducated men, through whom he might confound the world. Hear the Apostle saying this: “For consider your calling, brothers: not many are powerful, not many noble; but God chose the weak things of the world, in order to confound the strong; and God chose the lowly things of the world and the despised, and the things that are not, as though they were, in order to bring to nothing the things that are” (1 Cor. 1:26–28). If a learned man had been chosen, perhaps he would have said that he had been chosen because his learning had made him worthy of election. Our Lord Jesus Christ, wishing to break the necks of the proud, did not seek an orator through a fisherman; rather, through a fisherman he won an emperor. The great Cyprian was an orator, but Peter was a fisherman before him, and through Peter not only an orator but also an emperor would later believe. No nobleman was chosen first, no learned man; for God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong.

This man, then, was great and without deceit. For this one reason he was not chosen, lest anyone should think that the Lord had chosen learned men. And it was from this very knowledge of the Law that his response arose when he heard about Nazareth. He had searched the Scriptures and knew that the Savior was to be expected from there—something that the other scribes and Pharisees did not easily know. Thus this man, most learned in the Law, when he heard Philip say, “We have found Jesus, whom Moses wrote about in the Law, and the Prophets: Jesus, son of Joseph, from Nazareth,”—he who knew the Scriptures so well, on hearing the name Nazareth, was lifted up into hope and said, “Can anything good come from Nazareth?”

18. Let us now consider the rest concerning him: “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” What does “in whom there is no deceit” mean? Perhaps he had no sin? Perhaps he was not sick? Perhaps he did not need a physician? Far from it. No one here was born in such a way that he did not need that physician. What, then, does “in whom there is no deceit” mean? Let us inquire somewhat more attentively; it will become clear presently in the name of the Lord.

The Lord speaks of deceit; and everyone who understands Latin words knows that deceit is present when one thing is done and another is pretended. Let Your Charity pay attention. *Dolus* does not mean *dolor* (“pain”); I say this because many brothers who are less skilled in Latin speak in such a way that they say, “Dolus torments him,” when they mean “pain.” *Dolus* is fraud, pretense. When someone conceals one thing in his heart and speaks another, there is deceit, and he has, as it were, two hearts: one recess of the heart in which he sees the truth, and another recess in which he conceives falsehood.

And so that you may know that this is deceit, it is said in the Psalms, “Deceitful lips.” What does “deceitful lips” mean? What follows explains it: “They spoke evil with heart and heart” (Ps. 11:3). What does “with heart and heart” mean, unless “with a double heart”? If, then, there was no deceit in this man, the physician judged him curable, not healthy. For one thing is healthy, another curable, and another incurable. Someone who is sick with hope is called curable; someone who is sick in despair is incurable; but one who is already healthy does not need a physician. The physician, therefore, who had come to heal saw that this man was curable, because there was no deceit in him [Col. 1447].

How was there no deceit in him? If he is a sinner, he confesses himself to be a sinner. For if he is a sinner and calls himself righteous, there is deceit in his mouth. Therefore, in Nathanael the Lord praised the confession of sin; he did not judge him to be without sin.

19. For this reason, when the Pharisees—who seemed righteous in their own eyes—rebuked the Lord because the physician mingled with the sick, saying, “Behold the company he keeps: with tax collectors and sinners,” the physician answered those delirious men: “Those who are healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick; I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:11–13). This means: “Because you call yourselves righteous when you are sinners, you judge yourselves healthy while you languish; you reject the medicine and do not retain health.” [Note: [Col. 1447] The manuscripts read *praedicatis* (“proclaim yourselves”).]

Hence that Pharisee who had invited the Lord to dinner seemed healthy to himself. But that sick woman burst into the house where she had not been invited; made shameless by her desire for salvation, she approached not the Lord’s head, not his hands, but his feet. She washed them with her tears, wiped them with her hair, kissed them, anointed them with ointment; the sinful woman made peace with the Lord’s footsteps.

That Pharisee who reclined there, as though he were healthy, rebuked the physician and said to himself, “If this man were a prophet, he would know what sort of woman has touched his feet.” He suspected that the Lord did not know because he had not driven her away, as though he feared being touched by unclean hands. But the Lord knew; he allowed himself to be touched so that the touch itself might heal her.

Seeing the Pharisee’s heart, the Lord proposed a parable: “Two debtors owed money to a certain moneylender. One owed him fifty denarii, the other five hundred. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Which of them loved him more?” And he replied, “I suppose, Lord, the one to whom he forgave more.” And turning to the woman, he said to Simon: “Do you see this woman? I entered your house; you did not give me water for my feet, but she washed my feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair. You gave me no kiss, but she has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not give me oil, but she anointed my feet with ointment. Therefore I tell you: her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much; but the one to whom little is forgiven loves little” (Luke 7:36–47).

This is to say: “You are more seriously ill, but you think yourself healthy; you think little is forgiven you, although you are the greater debtor.” This woman, because there was no deceit in her, rightly obtained medicine. What does “there was no deceit in her” mean? She confessed her sins. This is also what he praises in Nathanael: that there was no deceit in him. For many Pharisees, who abounded in sins, called themselves righteous and brought deceit with them, by which they could not be healed.

20. The Lord, then, had already seen this man in whom there was no deceit, and said, “Behold, truly an Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.” Nathanael said to him, “How do you know me?” Jesus answered and said, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you”—that is, under the fig tree.

Nathanael answered him and said, “Rabbi, you are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” Nathanael may have understood something great in the words, “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you,” before Philip called him [Col. 1448]. For he uttered, “You are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel,” just as Peter did much later, when the Lord said to him, “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:17). There too he named the rock and praised the Church’s foundation in this faith. Here he already says, “You are the Son of God; you are the King of Israel.” Why? Because it had been said to him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.”

21. We must ask whether this fig tree signifies something. Listen, then, my brothers. We find a fig tree cursed because it had leaves alone and no fruit (Matt. 21:19). At the origin of the human race, when Adam and Eve had sinned, they made themselves coverings from fig leaves (Gen. 3:7). The fig leaves, therefore, are understood as sins.

Nathanael was under the fig tree, as though under the shadow of death. The Lord saw him, of whom it was said, “For those who sat under the shadow of death, light has arisen” (Isa. 9:2).

What, then, was said to Nathanael? You say to me, O Nathanael, “How do you know me?” Now you are speaking with me because Philip called you. The one whom he called through the apostle, the Lord already saw as belonging to his Church.

O Church, O Israel in whom there is no deceit: if you are the people of Israel in whom there is no deceit, you have now come to know Christ through the Apostles, just as Nathanael came to know Christ through Philip. Yet in his mercy he saw you before you knew him [Note: [Col. 1448] All our manuscripts omit “before you knew him”], when you were lying under sin.

For did we first seek Christ, and did he not seek us? Did we, being sick, come to the physician, and did the physician not come to the sick? Had that sheep not gone astray, and did the shepherd not leave the ninety-nine, seek it, and find it, carrying it back joyfully on his shoulders? Had that drachma not been lost, and did the woman not light a lamp and search throughout her entire house until she found it? And when she had found it, she said to her neighbors, “Rejoice with me, because I have found the drachma that I had lost” (Luke 15:4–10).

So we too had gone astray like a sheep and had been lost like a drachma. Our shepherd found the sheep, but he sought the sheep; the woman found the drachma, but she sought the drachma. Who is the woman? The flesh of Christ. What is the lamp? “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Ps. 131:17).

Therefore we were sought so that we might be found; having been found, we speak. Let us not be proud, because before we were found, we had perished if we had not been sought.

Let those whom we love and whom we wish to win to the peace of the Catholic Church not say to us, “Why do you want us? Why do you seek us, if we are sinners?” We seek you for this reason: so that you may not perish. We seek you because we have been sought; we wish to find you because we have been found.

22. Accordingly, when Nathanael had said, “How do you know me?” the Lord said to him, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you.” O Israel without deceit, whoever you are; O people living by faith: before I called you through my Apostles, when you were under the shadow of death and did not see me, I saw you.

The Lord then says to him: “Because I said to you, ‘I saw you under the fig tree,’ you believe; you will see greater things than these.” What does “you will see greater things than these” mean? And he says to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, you will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending over the Son of Man.”

Brothers, I do not know what could be greater than the statement, “I saw you under the fig tree.” For it is greater that the Lord justified us after calling us than that he saw us lying under the shadow of death. What benefit would it have been to us if we had remained where he saw us? Would we not still be lying there? What, then, is this greater thing? When have we seen the angels ascending and descending over the Son of Man?

23. I have already spoken at some length about these ascending and descending angels. But so that you will not have forgotten, I shall speak briefly, as one recalling what was said. I would say more if I were not recalling it; but now I am merely introducing it again.

Jacob saw a ladder in a dream, and on that ladder he saw angels ascending and descending; and he anointed the stone that he had placed beneath his head (Gen. 28:12–18). You have heard that Christ is the Messiah; you have heard that Christ is the Anointed One. He did not anoint the stone in order to come and worship it; otherwise it would have been idolatry, not a sign of Christ. The sign, then, was made for as long as it was necessary for the sign to be made, and Christ was signified.

An anointed stone, but not as an idol. An anointed stone—why a stone? “Behold, I place in Zion a chosen, precious stone, and whoever believes in him will not be put to shame” (Isa. 28:16; 1 Pet. 2:6). Why anointed? Because *Christus* comes from *chrisma*, “anointing.”

What, then, did he see on the ladder at that time? Angels ascending and descending. So it is also with the Church, brothers: the angels of God, good preachers, preaching Christ, ascend and descend over the Son of Man.

How do they ascend, and how do they descend? We have an example in one man. Hear the Apostle Paul; what we find in him, let us believe concerning the other preachers of the truth.

See Paul ascending: “I know a man in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know; God knows—was caught up to the third heaven, and heard ineffable words that it is not permitted for a human being to speak” (2 Cor. 12:2–4).

You have heard him ascending; hear him descending: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Cor. 3:1–2). Behold, he descends who had ascended. Ask where he had ascended: to the third heaven. Ask where he descended: to the point of giving milk to infants.

Hear that he descended: “I became,” he says, “a little child among you, as a nurse cherishes her own children” (1 Thess. 2:7). We see nurses and mothers descending to little children. Even if they know how to speak Latin words, they shorten them and somehow shake their tongues so that eloquent speech may become childish endearments. For if they spoke in that eloquent manner, the infant would not listen, nor would the infant make progress.

And if some eloquent father were so great an orator that the courts echoed with his voice and the tribunals trembled; if he had a small son, when he returned home he would set aside the forensic eloquence to which he had ascended and descend to the child with childish speech.

Hear the same Apostle ascending and descending in one place, in a single sentence: “Whether,” he says, “we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you” (2 Cor. 5:13).

What does “we are beside ourselves” mean? So that we may see those things “which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.” What does “we are sober, it is for you” mean? “Did I judge myself to know anything among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified?” (1 Cor. 2:2).

If the Lord himself ascended and descended, it is clear that his preachers also ascend by imitation and descend by preaching.

24. And if we have kept you a little longer, it was with the intention that the unsuitable hour might pass. We suppose that they have now completed their frivolity [Note: [Col. 1450] Manuscripts of better quality read *illas* (“those women”); perhaps this celebration was directed especially toward women. See above, nos. 2 and 6.]

But let us, brothers, now that we have been nourished by saving banquets, do what remains, so that we may solemnly complete the Lord’s day in spiritual joys, and compare the joys of truth with the joys of vanity. If we shudder, let us grieve; if we grieve, let us pray; if we pray, let us be heard; if we are heard, let us also win them.

# TREATISE VIII

From the Gospel passage, “And on the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee,” up to, “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” Chapter 2:1–4.

1. The miracle of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which he made wine from water, is not astonishing to those who know that it was God who made it. For the one who made wine on that day at the wedding in those six water jars, which he commanded to be filled with water (John 2:6–11), makes the same thing every year in the vines.

Just as what the servants poured into the jars was changed into wine by the Lord’s work, so also what the clouds pour forth is changed into wine by the work of that same Lord. We are not astonished at the latter because it happens every year; through constant repetition it has lost its power to amaze.

Indeed, it deserves greater consideration than what was done in the jars of water. Who is there who considers the works of God by which this entire world is governed and administered and is not struck dumb and overwhelmed by miracles? If one considers the power of a single grain, of any seed whatsoever, it is something immense, and it inspires awe in the one who considers it.

But because human beings, intent upon other things, have lost their consideration of God’s works—the consideration by which they might daily give praise to the Creator—God seems to have reserved certain unusual deeds for himself, so that, as though waking sleeping people, he might arouse them more remarkably to worship him.

A dead man rose again, and people were astonished; every day so many are born, and no one is astonished. If we consider the matter more wisely, it is a greater miracle for something that did not exist to come into being than for something that existed to come back to life.

Yet the same God, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, does all these things through his Word, and he governs what he created. He performed the earlier miracles through his Word, God who was with him; he performed the later miracles through that same Word incarnate and made human for our sake.

Just as we marvel at what was done through the man Jesus, let us marvel at what was done through God Jesus. Through God Jesus heaven and earth were made, the sea and all the adornment of heaven, the abundance of the earth, and the fecundity of the sea. All these things that lie before our eyes were made through Jesus God.

We see these things, and if his Spirit is in us, they please us in such a way that the craftsman is praised. We must not be turned away from the craftsman toward his works, placing our face, so to speak, toward what he made and our back toward the one who made it [Col. 1451].

2. We see these things, and they lie before our eyes. What of those things that we do not see—such as angels, virtues, powers, dominions, and the entire population of this supercelestial structure, which does not lie before our eyes? Yet angels too often showed themselves to human beings when it was necessary.

Did God not make all these things through his Word, that is, through his only Son, our Lord Jesus Christ? What of the human soul itself, which is not seen, yet through the works it displays in the flesh provides great cause for admiration to those who consider well? From whom was it made, unless from God? And through whom was it made, unless through the Son of God?

I do not yet speak of the human soul. Consider the soul of any animal: how it governs its bodily mass, extends all its senses, gives eyes for seeing, ears for hearing, nostrils for perceiving odors, the judgment of the mouth for distinguishing tastes, and finally the limbs themselves for carrying out their functions. Is it the body, and not the soul—that is, the inhabitant of the body—that does these things? Yet the soul is not seen by the eyes, and from the things it does it arouses admiration.

Now let your consideration also turn to the human soul, to which God has granted understanding so that it may know its Creator and recognize and distinguish between good and evil—that is, between what is just and unjust. How much it accomplishes through the body!

Consider the whole ordered world in the human commonwealth: its administrations, its hierarchies of powers, the conditions of its cities, its laws, customs, and arts. All this is carried on through the soul, yet this power of the soul is not seen.

When the soul is withdrawn from the body, a corpse lies there. When it is present in the body, it first somehow restrains putrefaction. For all flesh is corruptible and flows away into decay unless it is held together by some seasoning of the soul.

But this is something it shares with the soul of an animal. More remarkable are the things I mentioned that pertain to mind and understanding, where the soul is also renewed according to the image of its Creator, in whose image the human being was made (Col. 3:10).

What will this power of the soul be when this body also puts on incorruption and this mortal body puts on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53–54)? If it can do so much through corruptible flesh, what will it be able to do through a spiritual body after the resurrection of the dead?

This soul, then, as I said, a thing admirable in nature and substance, is invisible and intelligible. Yet it too was made through Jesus God, because he is the Word of God. “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

3. Since, then, we see so many things made through God Jesus, why are we astonished that water was changed into wine through the man Jesus? For he did not become man in such a way as to lose what he was as God. Humanity was added to him; God was not lost.

The one who did all those things did this also. Let us not, therefore, marvel because God did it; rather, let us love him because he did it among us and did it for our restoration.

For he also hints at something to us in the very things he did. I think he did not come to the wedding without a reason. Apart from the miracle, some mystery and sacrament lies hidden in the deed itself. Let us knock so that he may open and intoxicate us with invisible wine. For we too were water, and he made us wine; he made us wise. For we savor his faith, whereas before we were foolish.

Perhaps it belongs to wisdom itself—together with the honor of God, the praise of his majesty, and love for his most powerful mercy—to understand what was accomplished in this miracle.

4. The Lord, invited to the wedding, came. Is it surprising that he came to that house for a wedding, when he came into this world for a wedding? For if he did not come for a wedding, he does not have a bride here.

And what does the Apostle mean when he says, “I betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ”? What does he fear when he says that the virginity of Christ’s bride may be corrupted through the devil’s cunning? “I fear,” he says, “that just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that are in Christ” (2 Cor. 11:2–3).

He has a bride here whom he redeemed with his blood and to whom he gave the Holy Spirit as a pledge (ibid. 1:22). He rescued her from the slavery of the devil: he died for her offenses and rose again for her justification (Rom. 4:25).

Who would offer so much to his bride? Let human beings offer whatever earthly ornaments they wish—gold, silver, precious stones, horses, slaves, estates, and properties. Would anyone offer his own blood? For if he gave his blood to his bride, there would be no one left to marry her.

But the Lord, dying securely, gave his blood for her whom he would possess when he rose again, whom he had already joined to himself in the Virgin’s womb. For the Word is the bridegroom, and human flesh is the bride; and both are one Son of God and the same Son of Man.

There he became the head of the Church. The womb of the Virgin Mary was his bridal chamber; from there he came forth like a bridegroom from his chamber, as Scripture foretold: “And he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course” (Ps. 18:6). He came forth from the chamber like a bridegroom, and, invited, came to the wedding.

5. For the sake of a certain sacramental meaning, he seems not to recognize the mother from whom the bridegroom came forth, saying to her, “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

What does this mean? Did he come to the wedding in order to teach that mothers should be despised? Surely the one whose wedding he attended was taking a wife in order to produce children, and naturally wished to be honored by those whom he desired to produce. Did he, then, come to the wedding in order to dishonor his mother, when weddings are celebrated and wives are taken for the sake of having children, to whom God commands that parents be honored?

Without doubt, brothers, something lies hidden there. For the matter is so significant that certain people—those whom the Apostle warned us to avoid, as we recalled above when he said, “I fear that just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the simplicity and purity that are in Christ”—attempted to draw from this an argument for their error, saying, “How could she be his mother, when he said to her, ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’”

We must answer them and explain why the Lord said this, lest, in their madness, they seem to have found something against sound faith by which the chastity of the virgin bride—that is, the faith of the Church—might be corrupted.

Indeed, brothers, the faith of those who place falsehood before truth is corrupted. For those who seem to honor Christ in such a way as to deny that he had flesh proclaim nothing else about him than that he was a liar.

Those, then, who build falsehood among human beings—what do they drive out except the truth? They admit the devil and exclude Christ; they admit the adulterer and exclude the bridegroom. They are, indeed, the serpent’s attendants—or rather, the serpent’s procurers. They speak for this purpose: so that the serpent may take possession and Christ may be excluded.

How does the serpent take possession? When falsehood takes possession. When falsity takes possession, the serpent possesses; when truth takes possession, Christ possesses. For he himself said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Of the other he said, “He did not stand in the truth, because there is no truth in him” (ibid. 8:44).

Christ is truth in such a way that you must accept everything true in Christ: the true Word, God equal to the Father; a true soul; true flesh; true man; true God; a true birth; a true passion; a true death; a true resurrection.

If you say that any one of these is false, corruption enters. Worms of falsehood are born from the serpent’s poison, and nothing will remain whole.

6. “What, then,” he says, “does it mean that the Lord said, ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’” Perhaps the Lord shows us why he said this in what follows: “My hour,” he says, “has not yet come.” For he says, “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” We must inquire why this was said.

First, then, let us resist the heretics on this point. What does the ancient serpent say, the serpent that hisses and breathes out poisons, the ancient deceiver? What does it say? “Jesus did not have a human mother.” How do you prove this? “Because,” it says, “he said, ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’”

Who reported this, so that we may believe that he said it? Who reported it? The evangelist John, of course. But this same evangelist John said, “The mother of Jesus was there.” For he reported it in this way: “On the third day a wedding took place at Cana in Galilee, and the mother of Jesus was there.” He had been invited to the wedding there with his disciples.

We have two statements uttered by the Evangelist. “The mother of Jesus was there,” the Evangelist said; and what Jesus said to his mother, the same Evangelist said.

And how did he report Jesus answering his mother? First he says, “His mother said to him.” Look, brothers, so that you may have a heart’s virginity fortified against the serpent’s tongue.

There in the Gospel itself, narrated by that very Evangelist, it is said, “The mother of Jesus was there,” and, “His mother said to him.” Who reported this? The evangelist John.

And what did Jesus answer his mother? “What is there between me and you, woman?” Who reports this? That same evangelist John.

O most faithful and most truthful Evangelist, you report to me that Jesus said, “What is there between me and you, woman.” Why did you add that she was his mother, whom he does not recognize? For you said that the mother of Jesus was there and that his mother said to him. Why did you not rather say, “Mary was there,” and, “Mary said to him”?

You report both: “His mother said to him,” and, “Jesus answered her, ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’” Why is this, unless both are true?

But these people want to believe the Evangelist when he reports that Jesus said to his mother, “What is there between me and you, woman,” yet do not want to believe the Evangelist when he says, “The mother of Jesus was there,” and, “His mother said to him.”

Who, then, resists the serpent and holds to the truth, whose heart’s virginity is not corrupted by the devil’s cunning? The one who believes both: that the mother of Jesus was there and that Jesus gave that answer to his mother.

But if he does not yet understand how Jesus said, “What is there between me and you, woman,” let him meanwhile believe that he said it and that he said it to his mother. Let piety come first in the believer, and understanding will bear fruit.

7. I ask you, faithful Christians: “Was the mother of Jesus there?” Answer: “She was.” How do you know? Answer: “The Gospel says so.” What did Jesus answer his mother? Answer: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.” And how do you know this? Answer: “The Gospel says so.”

Let no one corrupt this faith in you, if you wish to preserve a chaste virginity for the bridegroom. But if you are asked why he gave this answer to his mother, let the one who understands explain it. The one who does not yet understand must nevertheless firmly believe that Jesus gave this answer and that he gave it to his mother.

Through this piety he will also deserve to understand why he answered in this way, if he knocks by praying and approaches the door of truth without quarrelling.

Let him take care lest, while he thinks he knows—or is ashamed not to know—why Jesus answered in this way, he is forced to believe either that the Evangelist lied when he said, “The mother of Jesus was there,” or that Christ himself suffered a false death for our offenses and displayed false wounds for our justification; and that he falsely said, “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32).

For if the mother was false, the flesh false, the death false, the wounds of the passion false, and the scars of the resurrection false, then it will not be truth but rather falsehood that sets free those who believe in him.

No indeed: let falsehood yield to truth, and let all those be confounded who wish to seem truthful for this reason—that they attempt to prove Christ deceitful. They do not want to be told, “We do not believe you, because you lie,” even though they say that the truth itself lied.

Yet if we ask them, “How do you know that Christ said, ‘What is there between me and you, woman?’” they answer that they have believed the Gospel. Why do they not believe the Gospel when it says, “The mother of Jesus was there,” and, “His mother said to him”?

Or if the Gospel lies in this, how can they believe it when it reports that Jesus said, “What is there between me and you, woman”? Why do these wretched people not rather believe faithfully that the Lord gave this answer not to a stranger but to his mother, and piously inquire why he answered in this way?

There is a great difference between one who says, “I want to know why Christ gave this answer to his mother,” and one who says, “I know that Christ did not give this answer to his mother.”

It is one thing to want to understand what is closed; it is another to refuse to believe what is open. The one who says, “I want to know why Christ answered his mother in this way,” wants the Gospel, in which he believes, to be opened to him. But the one who says, “I know that Christ did not give this answer to his mother,” accuses the very Gospel of falsehood at the point where he believed that Christ gave this answer.

[Col. 1455]

8. Now, then, if it pleases you, brothers, having dismissed those people—who always wander in their blindness unless they are humbly healed—let us inquire why our Lord answered his mother in this way.

He was uniquely born from the Father without a mother and from a mother without a father: without a mother as God, without a father as man; without a mother before the ages, without a father at the end of the ages.

What he answered, he answered to his mother, because “the mother of Jesus was there,” and, “His mother said to him.” The whole Gospel says this.

There we know that the mother of Jesus was there, in the same place where we know that he said to her, “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come.”

Let us believe everything, and let us seek what we do not yet understand.

And first observe this: just as the Manichaeans found an occasion for their faithlessness because the Lord said, “What is there between me and you, woman?” so perhaps the astrologers may find an occasion for their deceit because he said, “My hour has not yet come.”

If he said this according to the astrologers, then we committed sacrilege by burning their books. But if we acted rightly, as was done in the time of the Apostles (Acts 19:19), then the Lord did not say, “My hour has not yet come,” according to them.

For those empty talkers and deceived deceivers say, “You see that Christ was under fate, since he says, ‘My hour has not yet come.’”

Whom, then, must we answer first: the heretics or the astrologers? Both come from that serpent, wishing to corrupt the virginity of the Church’s heart, which she possesses in an uncorrupted faith.

First, if it pleases you, let us address those whom we had proposed to answer and to whom we have already responded in large part. But lest they think that we have nothing to say about these words that the Lord answered his mother, we are instructing you more fully against them. For I think that what has already been said is sufficient to refute them.

### 9

Why, then, did the Son say to his mother, “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come”? Our Lord Jesus Christ was both God and man. Insofar as he was God, he had no mother; insofar as he was man, he had one. His mother, therefore, was the mother of his flesh, the mother of his humanity, the mother of the weakness he assumed for our sake.

The miracle he was about to perform, however, he would perform according to his divinity, not according to his weakness; according to the fact that he was God, not according to the fact that he had been born in weakness. Yet “the weakness of God is stronger than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25).

His mother, therefore, was asking for a miracle; but he, as though not recognizing human maternal bonds, was about to perform divine deeds—as though saying: “That in me which performs the miracle was not begotten by you; you did not beget my divinity. But because you gave birth to my weakness, I shall recognize you when that very weakness hangs upon the cross.” For this is what “My hour has not yet come” means.

Then he recognized her—although, of course, he had always known her. Before he was born from her, he knew her as his mother in predestination; and before God himself created the one from whom he, as man, would be created, he knew her as his mother. Yet, in the mystery, he does not recognize her until a certain hour; and at another hour, which had not yet come, he again recognizes her in the mystery.

For he recognized her when what she had borne was dying. What had made Mary did not die; what had been made from Mary died. [Col. 1456] The eternity of his divinity did not die; the weakness of his flesh died.

His answer, therefore, distinguished in the faith of believers who he was and in what manner he had come. He came through a woman, his mother, as God and Lord of heaven and earth. Insofar as he is Lord of the world, Lord of heaven and earth, he is also Lord of Mary; insofar as he is creator of heaven and earth, he is also creator of Mary. But insofar as it is said that he was “made from a woman, made under the Law” (Gal. 4:4), he is the son of Mary.

The very Lord of Mary is the son of Mary; the very creator of Mary is the one created from Mary. Do not be surprised that he is both son and Lord. For just as he was called the son of Mary, so also he was called the son of David; and he was the son of David because he was the son of Mary.

Hear the Apostle speaking plainly: “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3). Hear him also as Lord of David. Let David himself say this: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand” (Ps. 109:1). Jesus himself also proposed this to the Jews and convicted them by it (Matt. 22:45).

How, then, was he both David’s son and David’s Lord? He was David’s son according to the flesh, and David’s Lord according to his divinity. In the same way, he was Mary’s son according to the flesh, and Mary’s Lord according to his majesty.

Therefore, since she was not the mother of his divinity, and since the miracle she requested was to be accomplished through his divinity, he answered her, “What is there between me and you, woman?” But so that you would not think that he was denying her as his mother, he added, “My hour has not yet come.” He would recognize her there, when the weakness of which she was the mother began to hang upon the cross.

Let us see whether this is true. When the Lord suffered, the same Evangelist who knew the Lord’s mother and who had also introduced the Lord’s mother to us at this wedding tells the story:

“There stood,” he says, “near the cross of Jesus his mother, and Jesus said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold your son’; and to the disciple, ‘Behold your mother’” (John 19:25–27).

He entrusts his mother to the disciple. He entrusts his mother—the man who was about to die before his mother and rise again before his mother’s death. He entrusts a human being to a human being. This is what Mary had borne. That hour had now come, the hour of which he had then said, “My hour has not yet come.”

### 10

I think, brothers, that the heretics have now been answered. Let us answer the astrologers as well. From what do they try to prove that Jesus was subject to fate? “Because,” they say, “he himself said, ‘My hour has not yet come.’”

So we believe him; and if he had said, “I have no hour,” he would have silenced the astrologers. “But look,” they say, “he himself said, ‘My hour has not yet come.’ If he had said, ‘I have no hour,’ he would have silenced the astrologers, and they would have had no basis for their accusations. But now, because he said, ‘My hour has not yet come,’ what can we say against his own words?”

It is astonishing that the astrologers, by believing Christ’s words, try to prove to Christians that Christ lived under a fatal hour. Let them therefore believe Christ when he says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10:18).

Is this power, then, subject to fate? Let them show us a human being who has power over when he will die and how long he will live. They certainly will not show one.

Let them therefore believe God when he says, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again,” and let them ask why he said, “My hour has not yet come.” Let them not for that reason place the maker of heaven, the creator and governor of the stars, [Col. 1457] under fate.

For if fate arose from the stars, the creator of the stars could not be subject to the necessity imposed by the stars. Moreover, Christ not only did not have what you call fate; neither did you, nor I, nor that man, nor any human being.

### 11

Nevertheless, the deceived deceive others and set their falsehoods before people. They stretch out traps to catch human beings—and they do so in the public squares. Those who set traps for wild animals do this in forests and wildernesses; how wretchedly foolish are the people for whom traps are set in the marketplace!

They receive money when they sell themselves as slaves to other human beings; these people pay money so that they may sell themselves into slavery to vanities. They enter an astrologer’s establishment in order to purchase masters for themselves—whatever masters the astrologer chooses to give them: Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, or some other name belonging to sacrilege.

A free man enters, so that after paying money he may leave as a slave. Indeed, he would not enter if he were free; but the master of error and the mistress of desire dragged him in. Hence Truth also says: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

### 12

Why, then, did he say, “My hour has not yet come”? Rather, it was because he had power over when he would die, but did not yet see that it was appropriate to use that power.

For example, brothers, how do we speak when we say, “The appointed hour has now come for us to go out and celebrate the sacraments”? If we went out before it was necessary, would we not be acting perversely and prematurely?

Because we do something only when it is appropriate, do we therefore consider fate in such actions when we speak in this way?

What, then, does “My hour has not yet come” mean? “When I know that it is appropriate for me to suffer, when my suffering will be beneficial, that hour itself has not yet come. Then I shall suffer willingly.” Thus both statements are preserved: [Note: In some manuscripts, “and both are true.”] “My hour has not yet come,” and “I have power to lay down my life and to take it up again.”

He therefore came with power over when he would die. But if he had died before choosing his disciples, that would certainly have been premature. If he were an ordinary human being who did not have power over his own hour, he could have died before choosing his disciples; and if he happened to die after they had been chosen and instructed, that would have happened to him rather than being something he himself accomplished.

But he came with power in his hand over when he would depart, when he would return, how far he would go, and to whom the underworld would be opened—not only when he died, but also when he rose again. He wished to show us the hope of immortality belonging to his Church; and in the head he showed what the members ought to expect. He who rose in the head will also rise in the other members.

The hour, therefore, had not yet come; the appropriate time had not yet arrived.
