The disciples had to be called, the kingdom of heaven had to be announced, mighty works had to be performed, the Lord’s divinity had to be commended through miracles, and the Lord’s humanity had to be commended in the very compassion of mortality.

For the one who was hungry because he was human fed so many thousands with five loaves because he was God; and the one who slept because he was human commanded the winds and the waves because he was God.

All these things had first to be commended, so that the Evangelists would have something to write and the Church something to preach. But when he had done as much as he judged sufficient, the hour came—not an hour of necessity but of will, [Col. 1458] not of constraint but of power.

### 13

What, then, brothers? Since we have answered those people and these, shall we say nothing about what the water jars mean, what the water changed into wine means, what the master of the feast means, what the bridegroom means, what the mother of Jesus means in the mystery, and what the wedding itself means?

Everything must be explained, but you must not be burdened. Indeed, yesterday, in the name of Christ, on the day when I usually owe a sermon to Your Charity, I wanted to do this with you, but I was not permitted to do so because certain necessities intervened.

If it pleases Your Holiness, then, let us postpone until tomorrow what concerns the mystery of this event, and let us not burden either your weakness or ours. Perhaps many people have gathered today because of the solemnity of the day, not in order to hear a sermon. Let those who come tomorrow come in order to listen, so that we neither disappoint the eager nor burden the disinterested.

## TREATISE IX

On the same Gospel reading: What mystery is contained in the miracle performed at the wedding in Cana of Galilee. Chapter 2, verses 1–11.

### 1

May the Lord our God be present and grant us the ability to deliver what we promised. Yesterday, if Your Holiness remembers, because we were prevented by the pressure of time from completing the sermon we had begun, we postponed it until today, so that, with his help, the things mystically contained in the sacramental meaning of this event in the Gospel reading might be opened up.

There is therefore no need to linger any longer in praising God’s miracle. He is the God who performs daily miracles throughout the whole creation—miracles that have become cheap in human estimation, not because they are easy but because they are constant. The rare miracles performed by the same Lord—that is, by the Word made flesh for our sake—have brought greater astonishment to human beings, not because they were greater than those he performs daily in creation, but because the things that happen daily seem to occur according to a natural course, whereas those things appear to human eyes as displays of the efficacy of power present before them.

As you remember, we said that one dead man rose, and people were astonished; yet no one is astonished that those who did not exist are born every day. In the same way, who would not be astonished that water was changed into wine, when God does this every year in the vines?

But because everything the Lord Jesus did not only serves to awaken our hearts through miracles, but also to build us up in the doctrine of faith, we ought to investigate what all those things mean—that is, what they signify. For, as you remember, we postponed until today the meanings of all these things.

### 2

That the Lord, when invited, came to the wedding—even apart from its mystical significance—he wished to confirm that he himself had made marriage.  
[Note: Some manuscripts do not add “marriage” here.]

For there would be people who, as the Apostle says, would forbid marrying (1 Tim. 4:3), and would say that marriage was evil and that the devil had made it. Yet the same Lord, when asked in the Gospel whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife for any reason, says that it is not lawful except on account of fornication.

In that reply, if you remember, he said: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate” (Matt. 19:3–6).  
[Col. 1459]

Those who are well instructed in the Catholic faith know that God made marriage, and that just as union comes from God, so divorce comes from the devil.

But divorce is permitted in the case of fornication because the woman herself first refused to be a wife when she did not preserve marital fidelity toward her husband.

Nor are those women who vow virginity to God without marriage, although they hold a higher degree of honor and holiness in the Church. For they too belong to the marriage with the whole Church, in which marriage Christ is the bridegroom.

Therefore the Lord was invited and came to the wedding so that marital chastity might be strengthened and the sacrament of marriage displayed. For the bridegroom of that wedding also represented the person of the Lord, to whom it was said, “You have kept the good wine until now.”

Christ kept the good wine until now—that is, his Gospel.

### 3

Let us now begin to uncover the hidden things of the sacraments, insofar as he grants this, in whose name we made our promise to you.

There was prophecy in ancient times, and no age was ever without the dispensation of prophecy. But that prophecy, when Christ was not understood in it, was water. For in water, in a certain way, wine lies hidden.

The Apostle tells us what we should understand by this water:

“Until this present day,” he says, “whenever Moses is read, the same veil lies over their heart; it is not revealed, because it is abolished in Christ. But when you pass over to the Lord,” he says, “the veil will be taken away” (2 Cor. 3:14–16).

[Note: Lov., “now it is revealed.” But the other printed editions and the manuscripts have “it is not revealed”; in the Apostle, the Vulgate reads, “it remains unrevealed.”]

[Note: The Vulgate has “when he has turned.” But Augustine writes *transieris* not only here but also in *Against Faustus*, book 12, chapter 4, and elsewhere. Perhaps the translator took the Greek *epistrepsē* from a middle verb in the second person.]

By “veil” he means the covering of prophecy, so that it was not understood. The veil is removed when you pass over to the Lord. In the same way, foolishness is removed when you pass over to the Lord, and what was water becomes wine for you.

Read all the prophetic books. Without understanding Christ, what will you find that is so tasteless and foolish? Understand Christ there: then what you read not only has flavor but also intoxicates, changing the mind from bodily things, so that, forgetting what lies behind, you may reach forward to what lies ahead (Phil. 3:13).

### 4

Therefore prophecy, from ancient times—from the moment the order of human generation began to run its course—did not keep silent about Christ. But he was hidden there; for it was still water.

How do we prove that throughout all the earlier ages, until the age when the Lord came, prophecy concerning him never ceased? By the Lord’s own words.

When he had risen from the dead, he found his disciples doubting the one whom they had followed. They had seen him dead and had not hoped that he would rise; their entire hope had collapsed.

Why did that praised criminal deserve to be in paradise on that very day? Because, fixed to the cross, he confessed Christ at the very time when the disciples doubted him (Luke 23:40–43).

Thus the Lord found them wavering and, in a certain sense, reproaching themselves for having hoped for redemption in him. Nevertheless, they grieved that he had been killed without guilt, because they knew him to be innocent.

They themselves said this after the resurrection, [Col. 1460] when he had found some of them sorrowful on the road:

“You alone are a stranger in Jerusalem, and have not known the things that have happened there in these days?” But he said to them, “What things?” They said to him, “Concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a man, a prophet, mighty in deed and word before God and all the people—how our priests and rulers handed him over to the sentence of death and crucified him. But we were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel. And now today is the third day since these things happened.”  
[Note: Several manuscripts have, “Today is the third day”; compare the Greek *tritēn tautēn hēmeran agei sēmeron*.]

After one of the two whom he found traveling toward a nearby village had said these and other things, he answered them:

“O foolish men and slow of heart to believe in all that the Prophets have spoken! Was it not necessary for Christ to suffer all these things and to enter into his glory?”

And beginning with Moses and all the Prophets, he interpreted to them in all the Scriptures the things concerning himself.

Likewise, in another passage, when he also wished to be touched by the hands of his disciples so that they would believe that he had risen bodily, he said:

“These are the words that I spoke to you while I was still with you, that everything written about me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled.”

Then he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures, and he said to them:

“Thus it is written: that Christ should suffer”  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer.” The words “and thus it was necessary” are absent from the manuscripts, as the Louvain edition observes.]

“and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and the forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

### 5

Once these things from the Gospel, which are certainly clear, have been understood, all the mysteries hidden in this miracle of the Lord will become evident.

Observe what he says: it was necessary that in Christ the things written about him should be fulfilled. Where were they written? “In the Law,” he says, “and the Prophets and the Psalms.”

He omitted nothing from the ancient Scriptures. That was water. And for this reason the Lord called them foolish: because the water still tasted like water to them, not wine.

But how did he make wine from water? When he opened their understanding and explained the Scriptures to them, beginning with Moses and proceeding through all the Prophets.

Hence, once they had become intoxicated, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us on the road, when he opened the Scriptures to us?” (Luke 24:13–47).

They understood Christ in the books in which they had not known him. Thus our Lord Jesus Christ changed water into wine, and what had not tasted now has flavor; what had not intoxicated now intoxicates.

If he had ordered the water to be poured out and then himself supplied wine from the hidden recesses of creation, from which he also made bread when he fed so many thousands—for the five loaves did not themselves possess enough to satisfy five thousand people, or at least to fill twelve baskets (Matt. 14:17–21), but the Lord’s omnipotence was, as it were, a fountain of bread—he could likewise have poured wine into the emptied water.

But if he had done this, he would have seemed to reject the ancient Scriptures. By changing the water itself into wine, he showed us that the Old Scripture also comes from him. For at his command the water jars were filled.

That Scripture too comes from the Lord; but it has no flavor if [Col. 1461] Christ is not understood there.

### 6

Consider what he himself says: “The things written in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms concerning me.”

We know the periods about which the Law narrates: it begins from the origin of the world—“In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1).

From there until the present time, the age in which we now live is the sixth age, as you have often heard and know. The first age is counted from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; and, as Matthew the Evangelist follows and distinguishes the succession, the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth from the deportation to Babylon to John the Baptist (Matt. 1:17); and the sixth from that point to the end of the world.

For this reason God also made the human being in his image on the sixth day (Gen. 1:27): because in this sixth age the reformation of our mind is manifested through the Gospel, according to the image of the one who created us (Col. 3:10). Water is changed into wine so that, now that Christ has been revealed, we may taste him in the Law and the Prophets.

That is why there were six water jars there, which he commanded to be filled with water. Those six water jars therefore signify the six ages in which prophecy was never absent.

Those six periods, divided and distinguished as if by their joints, would be like empty vessels unless they were filled by Christ. What am I saying? The periods would run emptily unless the Lord Jesus were preached in them.

The prophecies have been fulfilled; the jars are full. But for the water to be changed into wine, Christ must be understood throughout the whole of prophecy.

### 7

What, then, does “They held two or three measures” mean?

This expression especially commends a mystery to us. By “measures” he means certain measures, as if he had said “urns,” “amphorae,” or something of that kind.

*Metreta* is the name of a measure, and the measure took its name from measurement. The Greeks call a measure *metron* (*μέτρον*); hence these are called *metretae*.

“They held two or three measures.” What shall we say, brothers? If he had said only “three,” our mind would immediately turn to the mystery of the Trinity.

But perhaps even now we should not quickly turn our understanding away from that mystery, because he said “two or three.” For once the Father and the Son have been named, the Holy Spirit must consequently also be understood.

The Holy Spirit is not only the Spirit of the Father or only the Spirit of the Son; he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son. For it is written: “If anyone loves the world, the Spirit of the Father is not in him” (1 John 2:15). It is also written: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9).

[Note: All the manuscripts read “Spirit”; the Vulgate has “love,” in agreement with the Greek.]

The Spirit of the Father and the Son is one and the same Spirit. When the Father and the Son are named, the Holy Spirit is understood, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son.

When the Father and the Son are named, they are, as it were, two measures. When the Holy Spirit is understood there, there are three measures.

For this reason it is not said that some of the six jars held two measures and others three. Rather, the six jars themselves held two or three measures—as though he were saying: “When I say ‘two,’ I also want the Spirit of the Father and the Son to be understood with them; and when I say ‘three,’ I proclaim the Trinity more explicitly.”

### 8

[Col. 1462]

Whoever, therefore, names the Father and the Son ought to understand there, as it were, the love between the Father and the Son, which is the Holy Spirit.

Perhaps a careful examination of the Scriptures indicates this—not that I am saying it in such a way that I could teach it fully today, or as though nothing else could be found—but perhaps the Scriptures, when searched, indicate that the Holy Spirit is love.

And do not think that love is something trivial. How can it be trivial when all things that are said not to be trivial are called “dear” (*cara*)? If things that are not trivial are dear, what is dearer than love itself?

The Apostle commends love in such a way that he says:

“I show you a still more excellent way. If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal. And if I know all mysteries and all knowledge, and have prophecy and all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing. And if I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and hand over my body so that I may be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 12:31; 13:1–3).

How great, then, is love, without which all other things are possessed in vain, but with which everything is rightly possessed? [Note: “Rightly” is omitted in the manuscripts.] Yet while the Apostle Paul praises love most abundantly and richly, he said less about it than the Apostle John, whose Gospel this is, said briefly. For he did not hesitate to say, “God is love” (1 John 4:16).

It is also written: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Who, then, names the Father and the Son without understanding there the love of the Father and the Son? When a person begins to possess that love, he will possess the Holy Spirit; if he does not possess it, he will be without the Holy Spirit.

And just as your body, if it is without the spirit—that is, your soul—is dead, so your soul, if it is without the Holy Spirit—that is, without love—will be reckoned dead.

The jars therefore held two measures, because in the prophecy of all the ages the Father and the Son are preached. But the Holy Spirit is also there; hence “or three” has been added.

“I and the Father are one,” he says (John 10:30). But far be it from us to suppose that the Holy Spirit is absent where we hear, “I and the Father are one.”

Nevertheless, because he named the Father and the Son, let the jars hold two measures; but hear also, “or three”: “Go, baptize the nations in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28:19).

Thus, when two are spoken of, the third is not expressed but understood; when three are spoken of, the Trinity is also expressed.

### 9

There is another interpretation that must not be omitted, and I shall present it as well. Let each person choose what he prefers; we do not withhold what is suggested to us.

The Lord’s table is before us, and the minister ought not to defraud the guests, especially when they are so hungry that your eagerness is evident.  
[Note: Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain have “so that your eagerness appears.”]

The prophecy administered from ancient times pertains to the salvation of all nations.

Moses was indeed sent only to the people of Israel, and the Law was given through him only to that people. The Prophets also came from that people, [Col. 1463] and the division of the ages was distinguished according to that same people. Hence the jars are also said to correspond to the purification of the Jews.

Nevertheless, it is clear that this prophecy was also announced to the other nations, since Christ was hidden in that prophecy through whom all nations are blessed, as was promised to Abraham when the Lord said, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. 22:18).

But he was not yet understood, because the water had not yet been changed into wine. Thus prophecy was administered for all nations.

To make this more pleasingly evident, let us recall, according to the occasion, something from each age, as though from each of the water jars.

### 10

In the very beginning, Adam and Eve were the parents of all nations, not only of the Jews. Whatever was prefigured in Adam concerning Christ certainly pertained to all nations, for whom salvation is in Christ.

What, then, should I say most importantly about the water of the first jar, except what the Apostle says about Adam and Eve? No one can accuse me of misunderstanding when I present not my own interpretation but that of the Apostle.

Consider how great a mystery concerning Christ is contained in the one thing the Apostle recalls when he says: “The two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery” (Eph. 5:31–32).

And lest anyone understand this greatness of the mystery as applying to individual men who have wives, he says: “But I am speaking of Christ and the Church.”

What is this great mystery, “The two shall be one flesh”? When the Book of Genesis was speaking about Adam and Eve, it came to these words: “Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Gen. 2:24).

If Christ clung to the Church so that the two might be one flesh, how did he leave his Father? How did he leave his mother?

He left his Father because, although he was in the form of God, he did not consider equality with God something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7).

This is what it means that he left his Father—not that he abandoned or departed from the Father, but that he did not appear to human beings in the form in which he is equal to the Father.

How did he leave his mother? By leaving the synagogue of the Jews, from which he was born according to the flesh, and cleaving to the Church, which he gathered from all nations.

Thus the first jar also contained prophecy concerning Christ. But when the things I am describing were not yet preached among the peoples, it was still water; it had not yet been changed into wine.

And because the Lord enlightened us through the Apostle to show us what we should seek in that single statement—“The two shall be one flesh: a great mystery in Christ and the Church”—we may now seek Christ everywhere and drink wine from all the jars.

Adam sleeps so that Eve may be made; Christ dies so that the Church may be made. Eve is made from Adam’s side while he sleeps (Gen. 2:21); after Christ’s death, his side is pierced by a lance (John 19:34), so that the sacraments may flow forth by which the Church would be formed.

Who would fail to see that future things were prefigured in those events, since the Apostle says that Adam himself was a type of the one to come? “He is,” he says, “a type of the one who was to come” (Rom. 5:14).

Everything was prefigured mystically. [Col. 1464] Surely God could have taken a rib from a man who was awake and formed a woman. Or was it perhaps necessary for him to sleep so that his side would not hurt when the rib was removed? Who sleeps so deeply that his bones can be torn from him without his waking?

Or did the man not feel because God was removing the rib? The one who could remove it from a sleeping man without pain could also have removed it from a man who was awake.

But without doubt the first jar was being filled: the prophecy of that time was administering a prophecy concerning this future time.

### 11

Christ was also prefigured in Noah and in that ark, which represented the world. Why were all the animals enclosed in the ark (Gen. 7:7–9), unless they signified all nations?

It was not beyond God to create every kind of animal again. When none of them existed, did he not say, “Let the earth bring forth,” and the earth brought them forth (Gen. 1:24)?

Why, then, did he create them then from the same source from which he could restore them now? He made them by the word, and by the word he could restore them—unless he was commending a mystery and filling the second jar of the prophetic dispensation, so that through wood the figure of the world might be delivered, because on wood the life of the world was to be fixed.

### 12

In the third jar, as I have already mentioned, it was said to Abraham himself: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.”

Who does not see whom his only son prefigured—the son who carried the wood for the sacrifice on which he himself was being led to be offered?

For the Lord carried his own cross, as the Gospel says (John 19:17). This reference to the third jar will suffice.

### 13

What shall I say about David, whose prophecy pertained to all nations, when we have just heard a Psalm, and it is difficult to name a Psalm in which this does not resound?

Certainly, as I said, we have just sung:

“Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit all the nations” (Ps. 81:8).

Therefore the Donatists are like people cast out from the wedding. Like the man who did not have a wedding garment, they were invited and came, but were cast out from the number of the invited because they did not have a garment for the bridegroom’s glory.

Whoever seeks his own glory rather than Christ’s does not have a wedding garment. For they do not wish to agree with the voice of the one who was the bridegroom’s friend and said, “This is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33).

Not without reason was this reproach brought against the man who did not have a wedding garment: “Friend, how did you come in here?” And just as he was silenced (Matt. 22:11–13), so are they.

What benefit is there in the clamor of the mouth when the heart is mute? Within themselves they know that they have nothing to say. Within they are silent; outwardly they make a noise.

Whether they wish it or not, they hear even among themselves the song, “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit all the nations.” And by refusing communion with all nations, what else do they acknowledge but that they themselves have been disinherited?

### 14

What I was saying, brothers, is that prophecy pertains to all nations. I wish to show another meaning in the words, “They held two or three measures.”

Prophecy pertains to all nations. We have just recalled that this was demonstrated in [Col. 1465] Adam, who is a type of the one to come.

Who does not know that all nations arose from him? And in his name, through four letters, the four parts of the world are indicated by their Greek names.

For if East, West, North, and South are said in Greek—as Holy Scripture mentions them in many places—then, in the initial letters of the words, you find *Adam*. The four parts of the world are called in Greek:

- ἀνατολή (*anatolē*), East;
- δύσις (*dysis*), West;
- ἄρκτος (*arktos*), North;
- μεσημβρία (*mesēmbria*), South.

If these four names are written one beneath another like four lines of verse, *Adam* is read in their initial letters.

This was prefigured in Noah, because of the ark in which all the animals were found, signifying all nations. It was prefigured in Abraham, to whom it was said more plainly, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed.” It was prefigured in David, from whose Psalms—to omit other examples—we have just sung: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit all the nations.”

To what God is it said, “Arise,” except the one who slept? “Arise, O God, judge the earth”—as though it were said: “You slept, judged by the earth; arise, so that you may judge the earth.”

And to what does that prophecy pertain: “For you shall inherit all the nations”?

### 15

Now, in the fifth age, as in the fifth jar, Daniel saw a stone cut from a mountain without hands. It shattered all the kingdoms of the earth; then the stone grew and became a great mountain, so that it filled the whole face of the earth (Dan. 2:34–35).

What could be clearer, my brothers? A stone is cut from a mountain. It is the stone that the builders rejected, and it became the cornerstone (Ps. 117:22).

From what mountain is it cut except from the kingdom of the Jews, from which our Lord Jesus Christ was born according to the flesh? It is cut without hands, without human action, because he arose from a virgin without marital embrace.

That mountain from which it was cut had not filled the whole face of the earth; the kingdom of the Jews had not held all nations. But the kingdom of Christ, as we see, occupies the whole world.

### 16

Now the sixth age belongs to John the Baptist, than whom no greater man has arisen among those born of women; of him it was said, “Greater than a prophet” (Matt. 11:11, 9). How did he too show that Christ was sent to all nations? When the Jews came to him to be baptized, and so that they might not pride themselves on the name of Abraham, he said: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruit worthy of repentance”—that is, “Be humble”; for he was speaking to the proud. But on what were they proud? On their carnal descent, not on the fruit of imitating their father Abraham. What did he say to them? “Do not say, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (ibid. 3:7–9).

By “stones” he meant all the nations—not because of their firmness, as the stone is called the one rejected by the builders, but because of the stupidity and hardness of their foolishness, since they had become like those whom they worshiped: they worshiped senseless images and were themselves equally senseless. Why senseless? Because it is said in the Psalm: “Let those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 113:8).

Therefore, when people begin to worship God [Col. 1466], what do they hear? “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and sends rain upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:45). Accordingly, if a person becomes like the one he worships, what does “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” mean? Let us ask ourselves, and we see that it has happened. For we have come from the nations; but we would not have come from the nations unless God had raised up children for Abraham from stones. We have become children of Abraham by imitating his faith, not by being born according to the flesh. Just as they were disinherited by degenerating, so we have been adopted by imitating.

Therefore, brothers, this prophecy of the sixth water jar also pertained to all nations; and for this reason it was said of them all: “Containing two or three measures.”

### 17

But how do we show that all nations pertain to the two or three measures? It was, in a way, a matter of reckoning that he called the same measures both two and three, in order to commend the mystery. How are there two measures? Circumcision and uncircumcision. Scripture mentions these two peoples and omits no human race when it says, “Circumcision and uncircumcision” (Col. 3:11). In these two names you have all nations: they are the two measures.

For these two walls, coming from different directions to be made one in peace, Christ became the cornerstone (Eph. 2:14–20). Let us also show the three measures in these same nations altogether. There were three sons of Noah (Gen. 5:31), through whom the human race was restored. Hence the Lord says: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until it was all leavened” (Luke 13:21). Who is this woman except the Lord’s flesh? What is the leaven except the Gospel? What are the three measures except all nations, on account of Noah’s three sons?

Therefore the six water jars, containing two or three measures, are the six ages of the world, containing a prophecy that pertains to all nations—whether in the two classes of human beings, that is, Jews and Greeks, as the Apostle often mentions (Rom. 2:9; 1 Cor. 1:24, etc.), or in the three classes signified on account of Noah’s three sons. For the prophecy was figuratively represented as extending to all nations. Indeed, because it extends to them, it was called a measure, as the Apostle says: “We have received a measure extending as far as you” (2 Cor. 10:13). In evangelizing the nations, he says this: a measure extending as far as you.

## TREATISE X

From the passage of the Gospel, “After this he went down to Capernaum, he and his mother,” and so forth, up to the passage, “But he was speaking of the temple of his body.” Chapter II, verses 12–21.

### 1

In the Psalm you heard the groaning of the poor man, whose members suffer tribulations throughout the whole earth until the end of the age. Take great care, my brothers, to be among these members and to belong to these members, for the whole tribulation will pass away. “Woe to those who rejoice” (Luke 6:25)! The Truth says: “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted” (Matt. 5:5).

God became man: what will man become, for whom God became man? Let this hope [Col. 1467] comfort us in every tribulation and temptation of this life. The enemy does not cease to persecute; and if he does not rage openly, he acts by ambush. For what does he do [Note: [Col. 1467] The majority of manuscripts read: “For what does he say? And in addition to their anger.”]? “And in addition to their anger they acted deceitfully” (Ps. 34:20).

For this reason he is called both a lion and a dragon. But what is said to Christ? “You shall tread upon the lion and the dragon” (Ps. 90:13). A lion because of open rage, a dragon because of hidden ambushes. The dragon drove Adam from paradise; that same lion persecuted the Church, as Peter says: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls about, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

Do not suppose that the devil has lost his ferocity: when he flatters, then he must be feared all the more. But amid all these ambushes and his temptations, what shall we do except what we heard there: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting”?

There is one who hears; do not hesitate to pray. He who hears remains within. Do not direct your eyes toward some mountain; do not raise your face to the stars, or to the sun, or to the moon. Do not imagine that you will be heard when you pray above the sea; rather, detest such prayers. Only cleanse the chamber of your heart. Wherever you are, wherever you pray, the one who hears is within, within in the secret place, which he calls his bosom when he says: “And my prayer shall return into my bosom” (Ps. 34:13).

He who hears you is not outside you. Do not go far away, and do not exalt yourself as though you might reach him with your hands. If you exalt yourself, you will fall; if you humble yourself, he himself will draw near. Here is the Lord our God: the Word of God, the Word made flesh, the Son of the Father, the Son of God, the Son of man—exalted in order to raise us up, humble in order to restore us, walking among human beings, enduring human things, concealing divine things.

### 2

“He went down,” as the Evangelist says, “to Capernaum, he and his mother and his brothers and his disciples, and there they remained not many days.” Behold, he has a mother, he has brothers, and he has disciples: brothers from the same source as his mother. For our Scripture is accustomed to call brothers not only those who are born of the same man and woman, or of the same womb, or of the same father though by different mothers, or certainly those related in the same degree, such as paternal or maternal cousins. Our Scripture knows how to call not only these people brothers.

It must be understood according to the way it speaks. It has its own language. Whoever does not know this language is troubled and says: “Where did the Lord get brothers? Did Mary give birth again?” Certainly not. From her began the dignity of virgins. That woman could be a mother; she could not be a married woman. She was called “woman” according to the female sex, not according to the corruption of virgin integrity—and this is clear from the language of Scripture itself.

For Eve too, immediately after she had been made from the side of her husband, before she had been touched by her husband, was called “woman”: “And he formed her into a woman” (Gen. 2:22).

Where, then, did the brothers come from? Mary’s relatives were the Lord’s brothers, relatives in whatever degree. How do we prove this? From Scripture itself. Lot was called Abraham’s brother (ibid. 13:8; 14:14), although he was his brother’s son. Read on, and you will find that Abraham was Lot’s uncle (ibid. 11:27, 31), and they were called brothers [Col. 1468]. Why, except because they were relatives?

Likewise, Jacob had Laban the Syrian as his maternal uncle; for Laban was the brother of Jacob’s mother, that is, of Rebekah, Isaac’s wife (ibid. 28:2). Read Scripture, and you will find that an uncle and his sister’s son are called brothers (ibid. 29:12–15). Once this rule is understood, you will find that all Mary’s blood relatives are Christ’s brothers.

### 3

But those disciples were more truly brothers, because those relatives would not have been brothers if they had not been disciples; and they would have been brothers without purpose if they had not recognized the Master as their brother.

In one place, when his mother and brothers were reported to him as standing outside while he was speaking with his disciples, he said: “Who is my mother, or who are my brothers?” And stretching out his hand over his disciples, he said: “These are my brothers”; and, “Whoever does the will of my Father, he is my mother and brother and sister” (Matt. 12:46–50).

Therefore Mary too, because she did the will of the Father. The Lord magnified this in her: that she did the will of the Father, not that flesh gave birth to flesh. Let Your Charity pay attention. For this reason, when the Lord appeared wonderful amid the crowd, performing signs and wonders and showing what was hidden in the flesh, certain admiring souls said: “Blessed is the womb that bore you.” And he replied: “Rather, blessed are those who hear the word of God and keep it” (Luke 11:27–28).

This is what he meant: “My mother, whom you have called blessed, is blessed for this reason, that she keeps the word of God—not because the Word became flesh in her and dwelt among us” (John 1:14), but because she keeps that very Word of God through which she was made and which became flesh in her.

Let people not rejoice in temporal offspring; let them exult if they are joined to God in spirit. We have said this because the Evangelist says that he lived in Capernaum for a few days with his mother, his brothers, and his disciples.

### 4

What follows from there? “And the Passover of the Jews was near, and he went up to Jerusalem.” He relates another event, as the memory of the narrator preserved it:

“And he found in the temple those selling oxen and sheep and doves, and money-changers sitting there. And when he had made something like a whip from cords, he drove them all out of the temple, the sheep and the oxen as well; and he poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables. To those who sold doves he said, ‘Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of commerce.’”

What have we heard, brothers? Behold, that temple was still a figure, and the Lord drives out from it all who were seeking their own interests, who had come to conduct business. And what were they selling there? Things that people needed for the sacrifices of that time.

Your Charity knows that such sacrifices were given to that people on account of their carnality and their still-stony heart, so that they might be restrained from falling into idolatry. They offered sacrifices there—oxen, sheep, and doves. You know this, because you have read it.

It was therefore not a great sin if they sold in the temple what was bought in order to be offered in the temple; and yet he drove them out. What would the Lord have done if he had found drunkards there? If he expelled those selling things that are lawful and not contrary to justice—for what is honestly bought is not illicitly sold—and did not permit a house of prayer to become a house of commerce, if a house of commerce must not become the house of God, may it become a house of drinking?

But when we say these things, they gnash their teeth against us. The Psalm you heard comforts us: “They gnashed their teeth against me.” We too know where to listen so that we may be healed, even if the whips are redoubled against Christ, because his word is being scourged: “Scourges were gathered against me, and they did not know” [Note: [Col. 1469] The printed editions read, “they did not know” (*nesciebant*); the manuscripts, “they did not know” (*nescierunt*). The Vulgate has, “I did not know.”].

He was scourged with the scourges of the Jews; he is scourged by the blasphemies of false Christians. They multiply the whips against their Lord, and they do not know. Let us do what he helps us to do: “But when they troubled me, I clothed myself in sackcloth and humbled my soul with fasting” (Ps. 34:13–16).

### 5

Nevertheless, brothers, we say—and he himself did not spare them, for he who was to be scourged by them scourged them first—that he showed us a certain sign by making a whip from cords and using it to scourge the undisciplined people who were making the temple of God a place of commerce.

For each person weaves a cord for himself out of his sins. The Prophet says: “Woe to those who drag sins like a long cord!” (Isa. 5:18, according to the Septuagint). Who makes a long cord? The one who adds sin to sin.

How are sins added to sins? When sins that have been committed are covered over by other sins. He committed a theft; to prevent anyone from discovering that he committed it, he consults an astrologer. It would have been enough to commit the theft; why do you want to add sin to sin? Behold, there are two sins.

When you are forbidden to go to the astrologer, you blaspheme the bishop. Behold, three sins. When you hear, “Send him outside the Church,” you say, “I am joining the party of Donatus.” Behold, you add a fourth. The cord grows. Fear the cord.

It is good for you to be scourged here and corrected, so that at the end it may not be said: “Bind his feet and hands and throw him into the outer darkness” (Matt. 22:13). For each person is bound by the cords of his own sins (Prov. 5:22). The Lord says this; another Scripture says this—but both are spoken by the Lord. People are bound by their sins and sent into the outer darkness.

### 6

Who, then, are those who sell oxen, if we seek the mystery of the event in its figurative meaning? Who are those who sell sheep and doves? They are those who seek their own interests in the Church, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21).

They have everything for sale, those who do not wish to be redeemed [Note: [Col. 1469] The manuscripts read: “because they do not wish to be redeemed.”]: they do not wish to buy, and they wish to sell. It is good for them to be redeemed by the blood of Christ, so that they may attain the peace of Christ.

For what does it profit to acquire in this world some temporal and passing thing—whether money, or the pleasure of the belly and throat, or honor in human praise? Are not all things smoke and wind? Do not all things pass away and hurry onward? And woe to those who cling to passing things, because they pass away together with them. Is not everything a rushing river flowing into the sea? And woe to the one who falls into it, because he will be dragged into the sea.

Therefore we must keep all our affections away from such desires. My brothers, those who seek such things are sellers. That Simon too wanted to buy the Holy Spirit because he wanted to sell the Holy Spirit (Acts 8:[Col. 1470] 18–19); and he thought the Apostles were merchants like those whom the Lord drove from the temple with a whip. For he himself was such a man, and he wanted to buy what he intended to sell. He belonged to those who sell doves.

For the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove (Matt. 3:16). Therefore, brothers, who are those who sell doves except those who say, “We give the Holy Spirit”? Why do they say this, and at what price do they sell him? At the price of their own honor. They receive the price of temporal chairs, so that they themselves may appear to sell doves. Let them beware of the whip made from cords.

The dove is not for sale. It is given freely, because it is called grace. Therefore, my brothers, just as you see sellers, as peddlers, each praising what he sells [Note: [Col. 1470] Three manuscripts read *popularios*. But the reading *propolarios* is better in the others—that is, *propolas*, a word which some think to be of Greek origin, derived from the verb *pōlein*, “to sell.” Augustine, however, indicates here that it is entirely Latin and arose from the fact that every seller praises the goods he displays for sale.]. How many separate claims have they made? Primianus has one claim at Carthage; Maximianus another; Rogatus another in Mauretania; and those men have yet another in Numidia—men whom we can no longer even name [Note: [Col. 1470] These names indicate the leaders of several factions into which the Donatists were themselves divided, to such an extent that each faction boasted that the true and valid Baptism was found only among them. On this matter Augustine writes in *On Baptism against the Donatists*, Book 1, chapter 6: “The same party of Donatus,” he says, “has been torn into many tiny fragments. All these small factions criticize the much larger one in which Primianus is found because of the Baptism received from the Maximianists, and each tries to assert that true Baptism has remained only with itself.” On Primianus and Maximianus, consult *Exposition 2 on Psalm 36*, sermon 2, §§18–23; on Rogatus, Letter 93, to Vincentius.].

Thus someone comes seeking to buy a dove, and each person praises what he sells for his own display. Let his heart turn away from every seller and come where the gift is received freely.

Nor are they ashamed, brothers, because through their bitter and malicious dissensions, attributing to themselves what they are not and exalting themselves while thinking they are something though they are nothing (Gal. 6:3), they have made so many factions out of themselves. But what has been fulfilled in them, since they refuse to be corrected, except what you heard in the Psalm: “They were divided, and they were not pierced with remorse”?

### 7

Who, then, are those who sell oxen? The oxen are understood as those who have dispensed the Holy Scriptures to us. The Apostles were oxen; the Prophets were oxen. Hence the Apostle says:

“‘You shall not muzzle an ox while it is threshing.’ Is God concerned about oxen? Or does he say this for our sake? Indeed, for our sake he says it, because the one who plows ought to plow in hope, and the one who threshes in hope of sharing” (1 Cor. 9:9–10).

Therefore those oxen left us the memory of the Scriptures. They did not dispense from their own resources, because they sought the glory of the Lord. For what did you hear in that very Psalm? “And let them always say, ‘May the Lord be magnified, those who desire the peace of his servant’” (Ps. 34:16, 27).

The servant of God, the people of God, is the Church of God. Those who desire the peace of his Church should magnify the Lord, not the servant, and should always say, “May the Lord be magnified.”

Who should say this? Those who desire the peace of his servant. It is the clear voice of his people, of his servant, which you heard in the Psalm’s lamentations and which moved you when you heard it, because you belong to that people. What was sung by one voice resounded from every heart. Blessed are those who recognized themselves in those voices as in a mirror [Col. 1471].

Those who desire the peace of his servant, the peace of his people, the peace of the one whom he calls “the only one” and whom he wishes to be snatched from the lion—“Deliver my only one from the hand of the dog” (Ps. 21:21–22)—are those who always say, “May the Lord be magnified.”

Therefore those oxen magnified the Lord, not themselves. See the ox magnifying its Lord, because “the ox knows its owner” (Isa. 1:3). Observe the ox fearing lest the owner of the ox be abandoned and confidence be placed in the ox. See how it recoils from those who wish to place their hope in it: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. 1:13).

“What I gave, I did not give from myself. You received freely; the dove descended from heaven.” “I planted,” he says, “Apollo watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (ibid. 3:6–7). “And let them always say, ‘May the Lord be magnified, those who desire the peace of his servant.’”

### 8

These people deceive the crowds by means of the Scriptures themselves, so that they may receive honors and praise from them and so that people may not turn toward the truth. Since they deceive the crowds by the very Scriptures from which they seek honors, they sell oxen; they sell sheep as well—that is, the congregations themselves. And to whom do they sell them except to the devil?

For, my brothers, if Christ’s Church is one and is unique, whatever is cut off from it—who takes it away except that roaring lion who prowls about seeking someone to devour (1 Pet. 5:8)? Woe to those who are cut off! For that Church which is whole will remain. “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19).

Nevertheless, insofar as they are able, they sell oxen and sheep; they sell doves as well. Let them beware of the whip of their sins. Certainly, when they suffer something on account of these iniquities of theirs, let them recognize that the Lord made a whip from cords and admonishes them for this purpose: that they may change and cease to be merchants. For if they do not change, at the end they will hear: “Bind their hands and feet and throw them into the outer darkness.”

### 9

Then the disciples remembered that it had been written, “Zeal for your house has consumed me,” because the Lord had driven these people from the temple out of zeal for God’s house.

Brothers, let every Christian who is among the members of Christ be consumed by zeal for God’s house. Who is consumed by zeal for God’s house? The one who, whenever he sees something there that is perhaps perverse, earnestly seeks its correction and desires its amendment [Note: [Col. 1471] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “earnestly seeks to amend it and desires to correct it.”], and does not rest. If he cannot correct it, he tolerates it and groans.

The grain is not shaken out of the threshing floor; it endures the chaff so that it may enter the granary when the chaff has been separated. You, if you are grain, do not allow yourself to be shaken out of the threshing floor before the granary, lest you be gathered first by the birds before you are brought into the granary. The birds of heaven, the aerial powers, wait to snatch something from the threshing floor, and they snatch only what has been shaken out of it.

Therefore let zeal for God’s house consume you. Let zeal for God’s house consume every Christian, since he is a member of that house. For your own house is not more truly your house than the house where you have eternal salvation. You enter your own house for temporal rest; you enter God’s house for eternal rest.

If, then, you take care that nothing perverse happens in your own house, in God’s house—where salvation and rest [Col. 1472] without end have been set before you—should you not endure, insofar as you are able, if you happen to see something perverse?

For example, do you see a brother running to the theater? Forbid him, warn him, rebuke him, if zeal for God’s house consumes you. Do you see others running about and wishing to become drunk, wishing to do so in holy places, where it is appropriate nowhere? Forbid those whom you can; restrain those whom you can; frighten those whom you can; show kindness to those to whom you can. Nevertheless, do not rest.

Is he a friend? Let him be gently admonished. Is she a wife? Let her be restrained with the utmost severity. Is she a maidservant? Let her even be checked with blows. Do everything you can, according to the person entrusted to your care, and you fulfill the saying, “Zeal for your house has consumed me.”

But if you are cold, sluggish, concerned only with yourself, and as though sufficient for yourself, saying in your heart, “Why should I care about the sins of others? My soul is enough for me; let me preserve it whole for God,” then surely you do not remember that servant who hid the talent and refused to put it out at interest? Was he accused because he lost it, and not because he preserved it without profit (Matt. 25:25–30)?

Listen, then, my brothers, in such a way that you do not rest. I am about to give you advice; let the one within give it, because even if he gives it through me, he is the one who gives it.

You know what each of you does in your own house with your friend, your tenant, your client, your superior, and your inferior. As God gives an opportunity and opens a door through his word, do not cease to win people for Christ, because you have been won by Christ.

### 10

“The Jews said to him: ‘What sign do you show us, since you do these things?’ And the Lord replied: ‘Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.’ Then the Jews said: ‘This temple was built in forty-six years, and you say, “In three days I will raise it up”?’”

They were carnal and understood carnal things; he, however, was speaking spiritually. Who could understand what temple he meant? But we do not have to search far: through the Evangelist he made it clear to us, saying of what temple he was speaking: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

“This temple was built in forty-six years, and you will raise it up in three days?” But he was speaking, the Evangelist says, about the temple of his body.

It is clear that after three days the Lord rose from the dead. This is known to all of us. If it was closed to the Jews because they stand outside, it is nevertheless open to us because we know in whom we believe.

We are about to celebrate the destruction and rebuilding of that temple in the annual solemnity. We exhort you to prepare yourselves for it, if any of you are catechumens, so that you may receive grace. The time is now; let what is then to be born now be gestated. Therefore we know this much.

### 11

But perhaps we are being asked whether the temple built in forty-six years has some sacramental significance. There are indeed many things that could be said about this, but for the moment we shall say what can be said briefly and easily understood.

Brothers, unless I am mistaken, we said yesterday that Adam was one man and that he himself is the whole human race. For this is what we said, if you remember (in the preceding Treatise). He was, as it were, broken and scattered, and is gathered together; as it were, he is fused into one through spiritual fellowship and concord [Note: [Col. 1472–1473] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “into one spiritual fellowship and concord.”].

And now that one poor man—Adam himself—groans [Col. 1473], but he is renewed in Christ, because Adam came without sin in order to undo Adam’s sin in his own flesh and to restore Adam to the image of God [Note: [Col. 1473] The Fossatensis manuscript reads: “into the image.”].

Therefore Christ’s flesh is from Adam; therefore the temple that the Jews destroyed and the Lord raised after three days was from Adam. For he raised his own flesh. See that he was God, equal to the Father.

My brothers, the Apostle says, “He who raised him from the dead.” Of whom is he speaking? Of the Father: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also raised him from the dead [Note: [Col. 1473] Three manuscripts read: “exalted him from the dead.”] and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:8–9).

The Lord was raised and exalted. Who raised him? The Father, to whom he said in the Psalms: “Raise me up, and I shall repay them” (Ps. 40:11). Therefore the Father raised him.

Did he not raise himself? But what does the Father do without the Word? What does the Father do without his Only-Begotten? Listen, for he too was God: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” Did he say, “Destroy the temple, which the Father will raise after three days”? But just as when the Father raises, the Son also raises, so when the Son raises, the Father also raises, because the Son said: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

### 12

What, then, does the number forty-six signify? For the moment, Adam—because he is spread throughout the whole world—has already been discussed by you yesterday in four Greek letters and four Greek words.

If you write these four words one beneath another, namely, the names of the four parts of the world—East, West, North, and South, which constitute the whole world—from which the Lord says that he will gather his elect from the four winds when he comes for judgment (Mark 13:27), then, if you write these four Greek names—ἀνατολή, which means East; δύσις, which means West; ἄρκτος, which means North; μεσημβρία, which means South—you have *anatolē*, *dysis*, *arctos*, *mesēmbria*. The beginnings of these words contain *Adam*.

How, then, do we find the number forty-six there as well? Because Christ’s flesh was from Adam. The Greeks calculate numbers by letters. What we make the letter A, they write in their language as alpha, α, and alpha is called one. When they write beta, β, which is their B, it is called two in their numerical system. When they write gamma, γ, it is called three in their numerical system. When they write delta, δ, it is called four. And so they have numerical values for all their letters.

The letter M, which we call M and which they call mu, μ, signifies forty. For they say μ τεσσαράκοντα, “mu, forty.” Now observe what number these letters have, and there you will find the temple built in forty-six years.

*Adam* contains alpha, α, which is one; it contains delta, δ, which is four—making five. It contains alpha again, α, which is one—making six. It also contains mu, μ, which is forty—making forty-six.

These things, my brothers, were also said by our earlier predecessors, and this number, forty-six, was found in the letters [Note: See the book *On Mounts Sinai and Zion against the Jews*, among the works of Cyprian].

And because our Lord Jesus [Col. 1474] Christ received his body from Adam, though he did not derive sin from Adam, he took from him the bodily temple, not the iniquity that had to be driven from the temple. The flesh that he took from Adam—for Mary was from Adam, and the Lord’s flesh was from Mary—the Jews crucified. He was going to raise that very flesh after three days, the flesh that they were going to kill on the cross. They destroyed the temple built in forty-six years, and he raised it again in three days.

### 13

Let us bless the Lord our God, who has gathered us together for spiritual joy. Let us always be humble in heart, and let our joy rest with him. Let us not become inflated by any prosperity of this world, but let us know that our happiness exists only when these things have passed away.

For now, my brothers, let our joy be in hope. Let no one rejoice as though the hoped-for thing were already present, lest he become attached to the road. Let all our joy be in future hope; let our whole desire be for eternal life. Let all our sighs breathe toward Christ.

Let that one supremely beautiful one be desired, who loved even the ugly in order to make them beautiful. Let us run toward him alone; let us groan toward him; and let us always say, “May the Lord be magnified, those who desire the peace of his servant.”

## TREATISE XI

From the passage written, “When he was in Jerusalem at the Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name,” up to the passage, “Unless someone is born of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” Chapter II, verses 23–25, and chapter III, verses 1–5.

### 1

The Lord has fittingly arranged for us the order of today’s reading. Since we undertook to consider and expound the Gospel according to John in sequence, I believe that Your Charity has noticed this. It was therefore fitting that today you should hear from the Gospel: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not see the kingdom of God.”

It is time for us to exhort you who are still catechumens—who have believed in Christ in such a way that you still carry your sins. No one burdened with sins will see the kingdom of heaven, because unless someone’s sins have been forgiven, he will not reign with Christ. They cannot be forgiven except for one who has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit.

But let us attend to how all the words are arranged, so that those who are sluggish may discover here with what urgency they must hasten to lay down their burden. If they were carrying some heavy load—of stone, or wood, or even some profitable commodity; if they were carrying grain, wine, or money—they would run in order to put down their burdens. They carry the burden of sins, and they are sluggish about running.

We must run so that this burden may be put down. It weighs us down and sinks us.

### 2

You have heard that, when the Lord Jesus Christ was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name, seeing the signs that he performed. “Many believed in his name”: and what follows? “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them.” What, then, does this mean: “They believed in his name,” and “Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them”? Perhaps they had not believed in him, but pretended that they had, and for that reason Jesus did not entrust himself to them. But the Evangelist would not have said, “Many believed in his name,” unless he were bearing true testimony concerning them.

This, then, is a great and wondrous thing: human beings believe in Christ, yet Christ does not entrust himself to human beings. Especially since he is the Son of God: certainly he suffered willingly; and if he had not wished to suffer, he would never have suffered. If he had not wished to be born, he would not even have been born. If he had wished only to be born and not to die, he could have done whatever he wished, because the omnipotent Son of the omnipotent Father is himself omnipotent.

Let us prove this from the events themselves. When they wanted to seize him, he departed from them. The Gospel says: “And when they wanted to throw him headlong from the brow of the mountain, he departed from them unharmed” (Luke 4:29–30). And when they came to arrest him, after he had already been betrayed by Judas the traitor—who thought that he had it in his power to hand over his Master and Lord—there also the Lord showed that he suffered by his will, not by necessity.

For when the Jews wanted to arrest him, he said to them, “Whom are you seeking?” They answered, “Jesus the Nazarean.” And he said, “I am he.” When they heard this voice, they drew back and fell to the ground (John 18:4–6). In the fact that, by his answer, he struck them down, he showed his power; in the fact that he was arrested by them, he showed his will. Therefore, what he suffered was an act of mercy. “For he was handed over because of our offenses, and he rose again for our justification” (Romans 4:25).

Hear his own words: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of myself, so that I may take it up again” (John 10:18). Since, then, he possessed such great power, proclaiming it in words and demonstrating it by his deeds, what does it mean that “Jesus did not entrust himself to them,” as though they could harm him or accomplish anything against his will—especially since they had already believed in his name? The Evangelist says of these very people, “They believed in his name,” and of them he says, “But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them.”

Why? Because “he knew all people, and because he had no need for anyone to testify concerning a human being; for he himself knew what was in a human being.” The craftsman knew more about what was in his work than the work itself knew about what was in itself. The Creator of humanity knew what was in humanity, whereas the human being, himself created, did not know.

Do we not prove this in the case of Peter? He did not know what was in himself when he said, “I will remain with you even unto death.” Hear that the Lord knew what was in the human being: “‘You will remain with me unto death?’ Truly, truly, I say to you, before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:33–34; Luke 22:33–34). The human being, then, did not know what was in himself; but the Creator of humanity knew what was in humanity.

Many nevertheless believed in his name, yet Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them. What shall we say, brothers? Perhaps what follows will show us the meaning of the mystery contained in these words. That people believed in him is clear and true: no one doubts it; the Gospel speaks, and the truthful Evangelist bears witness. Likewise, that Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them is also clear, and no Christian doubts it, because the Gospel speaks of this as well, and the same truthful Evangelist bears witness.

Why, then, did they believe in his name, while Jesus did not entrust himself to them? Let us examine what follows.

### 3

“There was a man of the Pharisees, named Nicodemus, a ruler of the Jews. He came to him by night and said to him, ‘Rabbi.’” You already know that *Rabbi* means “teacher.” “We know that you have come from God as a teacher, for no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

This Nicodemus, then, was among those who had believed in his name, seeing the signs and wonders that he performed. Earlier the Evangelist had said: “When he was in Jerusalem at Passover, on the feast day, many believed in his name.” Why did they believe? The text continues and says, “Seeing the signs that he performed.” And what does it say about Nicodemus? “There was a ruler of the Jews, named Nicodemus. He came to him by night and said to him, ‘Rabbi, we know that you have come from God as a teacher.’” He too, then, had believed in his name. And on what basis had he believed? The text continues: “For no one can perform these signs that you perform unless God is with him.”

If Nicodemus, then, was among the many who had believed in his name, let us now consider in this Nicodemus why Jesus did not entrust himself to them. “Jesus answered and said to him: ‘Truly, truly, I say to you, unless someone is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.’”

Jesus entrusts himself to those who have been born again. There they are: they had believed in him, but Jesus did not entrust himself to them. Such are all catechumens: they already believe in the name of Christ, but Jesus does not entrust himself to them. Let your Charity attend and understand.

If we say to a catechumen, “Do you believe in Christ?” he answers, “I believe,” and makes the sign of the cross. He already bears Christ’s cross on his forehead [Note: Most manuscripts, along with the editions of Badius and Amelote, have this reading. Erasmus and Lovaniensis, however, have: “he makes the sign of himself with Christ’s cross, he bears it,” etc. Some manuscripts have “bearing it.”], and he is not ashamed of the cross of his Lord. Behold, he has believed in his name. Let us ask him, “Do you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink the blood of the Son of Man?” He does not know what we are saying, because Jesus has not entrusted himself to him.

### 4

Since Nicodemus, then, was among that number, he came to the Lord. But he came by night—and perhaps this is significant. He came to the Lord, and he came by night; he came to the light, and he came in darkness.

But what do those who have been born again through water and the Spirit hear from the Apostle? “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord; walk as children of light” (Ephesians 5:8). And again: “But since we belong to the day, let us be sober” (1 Thessalonians 5:8).

Those, then, who have been born again belonged to the night, but now belong to the day; they were darkness, but now they are light. Jesus already entrusts himself to them, and they do not come to Jesus by night, as Nicodemus did; they do not seek the day in darkness.

For such people now also make their profession. Jesus has come to them and brought salvation to them, because he himself said: “Unless someone has eaten my flesh and drunk my blood, he will not have life in himself” (John 6:54).

And although the catechumens bear the sign of the cross on their foreheads, they already belong to the great household. But let them become sons from slaves. For those who already belong to the great household are not nothing.

When did the people of Israel eat manna? After they had crossed the Red Sea. But hear from the Apostle what the Red Sea signifies: “I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud and all passed through the sea.” Why did they pass through the sea? As though you were asking him, he continues: “And all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:1–2).

If, then, the figure of the sea possessed such power, how much power will the reality of Baptism possess? If what took place in a figure led the people, once they had crossed over, to manna, what will Christ provide in the reality of his Baptism for his people, whom he has led across?

Through his Baptism Jesus leads believers across, with all their sins—like pursuing enemies—put to death, just as all the Egyptians perished in that sea. Where does he lead them, my brothers? Where does Jesus lead them through Baptism—the Jesus whose figure Moses then represented, when he led the people through the sea? Where does he lead them?

To manna.

What is manna? “I am,” he says, “the living bread that came down from heaven” (John 6:51). The faithful receive manna, having already crossed through the Red Sea.

Why the Red Sea? It is already the sea—but why also “red”? That Red Sea signified the Baptism of Christ. How does Christ’s Baptism become red except by being consecrated through Christ’s blood?

Where, then, does he lead believers and the baptized? To manna. I speak of manna: it is known what the Jews, that people of Israel, received; it is known what God rained down upon them from heaven. Yet the catechumens do not know what Christians receive. Let them therefore be ashamed that they do not know; let them cross through the Red Sea and eat manna, so that just as they believed in the name of Jesus, Jesus may likewise entrust himself to them.

### 5

Therefore, my brothers, pay attention to what this man who came by night says to Jesus. Although he came to Jesus, nevertheless, because he came by night, he still speaks from the darkness of his flesh. He does not understand what he hears from the Lord; he does not understand what he hears from the light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1:9).

The Lord has already said to him, “Unless someone is born again, he will not see the kingdom of God.” Nicodemus says to him, “How can a human being be born when he is old?”

The Spirit speaks to him [Note: Four manuscripts read, “Christ speaks to him.”], but he understands in a carnal way. He understands his own flesh, because he does not yet understand Christ’s flesh.

When the Lord Jesus had said, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself,” some who followed him were scandalized and said among themselves, “This is a hard saying; who can listen to it?” They thought that Jesus meant that they could cut him up like a lamb, cook him, and eat him. Horrified by his words, they withdrew and no longer followed him.

The Evangelist says: “And the Lord himself remained with the Twelve.” They said to him, “Lord, behold, they have left you.” And he said, “Do you also wish to depart?” [Note: Manuscripts here and below read, “Do you wish to go?”] He wished to show that he was necessary to them, not that they were necessary to Christ.

Let no one frighten Christ when he is told to become a Christian, as though Christ would be happier if you became a Christian. It is good for you to be a Christian; for if you are not, Christ will suffer no harm.

Hear the voice of the Psalm: “I have said to the Lord, ‘You are my God, for you have no need of my goods’” (Psalm 15:2). “You are my God,” therefore, “because you have no need of my goods.” If you are without God, you will be lesser; if you are with God, God will not become greater. He does not become greater through you; rather, without him you are lesser.

Grow, then, in him; do not withdraw from him, as though he might fail. You will be restored if you approach; you will fail if you withdraw. He remains whole when you approach, and he remains whole when you fall.

When he had therefore said to the disciples, “Do you also wish to depart?” Peter—that rock—answered on behalf of them all: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life.” The flesh of the Lord was rightly understood in his mouth.

The Lord, however, explained this to them and said: “It is the Spirit who gives life.” Having said, “Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself,” he added, lest they understand this carnally: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing. The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life” (John 6:54–69).

### 6

This Spirit and this life were not understood by Nicodemus, who had come to Jesus by night. Jesus said to him, “Unless someone is born again, he will not see the kingdom of God.”

But Nicodemus, understanding in a fleshly manner—and with Christ’s flesh not yet understood in his mouth—said, “How can a human being, being old, be born again? Can he enter his mother’s womb a second time and be born?”

He knew only one birth, from Adam and Eve; he did not yet know birth from God and the Church. He knew only parents who generate for death; he did not yet know parents who generate for life. He knew only parents who generate successors; he did not yet know those who, themselves always living, generate those who will remain forever.

Since there are two births, he understood only one. One is from earth, the other from heaven; one is from flesh, the other from Spirit; one is from mortality, the other from eternity; one is from male and female, the other from God and the Church.

Yet each of these two births occurs only once; neither can be repeated. Nicodemus rightly understood birth according to the flesh. So you too should understand birth according to the Spirit, just as Nicodemus understood birth according to the flesh.

What did Nicodemus understand? “Can a human being enter his mother’s womb again and be born?” So, whoever tells you that you must be born again spiritually, answer what Nicodemus said: “Can a human being enter his mother’s womb again and be born?” I have already been born from Adam; Adam cannot generate me again. I have already been born from Christ; Christ cannot generate me again.

Just as the womb cannot be repeated, neither can Baptism.

### 7

Whoever is born from the Catholic Church, as from Sarah [Note: In the manuscripts, here and elsewhere consistently *Sarra*, with double *r*], is born from a free woman; whoever is born from heresy, as from a slave woman, is born from a slave woman, but from the seed of Abraham.

Let your Charity attend to how great a mystery this is. God testifies and says, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Were there no other patriarchs? Was there not, before these men, the holy Noah, who alone in the whole human race, together with his entire household, deserved to be delivered from the flood, and in whom and in his sons the Church was prefigured? They escaped the flood by means of wood bearing them (Genesis 7:7).

Afterward there were other great men whom we know and whom Holy Scripture commends: Moses, “faithful in all his house” (Numbers 12:7). Yet these three alone are named, as though they alone had pleased him: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. This is my name forever” (Exodus 3:6, 15).

A great mystery! The Lord is powerful both to open our mouths and your hearts, so that we may say what he has deigned to reveal, and so that you may understand it as is expedient for you.

### 8

These three patriarchs, then, are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. You already know that Jacob’s sons were twelve, and that from them came the people of Israel: Jacob himself was Israel, and the people of Israel consisted of twelve tribes belonging to the twelve sons of Israel.

Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob: three fathers and one people [Note: In the manuscripts, after the word “Jacob,” the phrase “three fathers” is not added here, nor is “one” added after “and people.”].

Three fathers, as it were, at the beginning of the people; three fathers in whom the people were prefigured; and the people itself, the former people and the present people. For in the Jewish people the Christian people was prefigured. There was the figure; here is the truth. There was the shadow; here is the body. The Apostle says: “These things happened to them as a figure.” And again the Apostle says: “They were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Corinthians 10:11).

Let your minds now return to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. In these three we find free women giving birth, and slave women giving birth; there we find the offspring of free women, and there also the offspring of slave women.

The slave woman signifies nothing good: “Cast out the slave woman,” he says, “and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman.” The Apostle recalls this, and says that in the two sons of Abraham there was a figure of the two Testaments, the Old and the New.

Those who love temporal things, those who love the world, belong to the Old Testament; those who love eternal life belong to the New Testament. Therefore that Jerusalem on earth was a shadow of the heavenly Jerusalem, the mother of us all, which is in heaven. These are also the words of the Apostle (Genesis 21:10; Galatians 4:22–30).

You know much, and have already heard much, about that city from which we are pilgrims.

In these births—in these offspring, in these generations of free women and slave women—we find a remarkable thing: namely, four kinds of human beings. In these four kinds the figure of the future Christian people is completed. Therefore it is not surprising that it was said of those three, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.”

For among all Christians, brothers, pay attention: either the good are born through the bad, or the bad through the good, or the good through the good, or the bad through the bad. You cannot find more than these four kinds.

I shall repeat them; pay attention and remember them. Examine your hearts; do not be sluggish. Understand, so that you may not be trapped: these are the four kinds of all Christians. Either the good are born through the good, or the bad through the bad, or the bad through the good, or the good through the bad.

I think this is clear.

Good through good: when those who baptize are good, and those who are baptized believe rightly and are rightly numbered among the members of Christ.

Bad through bad: when those who baptize are bad, and those who are baptized approach God with a double heart and do not maintain the conduct they hear taught in the Church, so that they are not chaff there but grain. Your Charity knows how many such people there are.

Good through bad: sometimes an adulterer baptizes, and the one who is baptized is justified.

Bad through good: sometimes those who baptize are holy, while those who are baptized do not wish to hold to the way of God.

### 9

I think, brothers, that these things are known in the Church and made evident by daily examples. But let us consider them in our earlier fathers, for they too possessed these four kinds.

Good through good: Ananias baptized Paul (Acts 9:18).
