What is bad through bad? The Apostle speaks of certain preachers of the Gospel who, he says, were accustomed to proclaim the Gospel insincerely. He tolerates them within the Christian fellowship and says, “What then? In every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed, and in this I rejoice” (Philippians 1:18).

Was he malicious, rejoicing in another’s evil? No. Rather, because the truth was proclaimed even through the bad, and Christ was proclaimed through the mouths of the bad, if such men baptized people like themselves, the bad baptized the bad.

If they baptized people of the sort whom the Lord warns about when he says, “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 23:3), the bad baptized the good.

The good baptized the bad, as the holy Philip baptized Simon Magus (Acts 8:13).

These four kinds, then, are known, my brothers. Behold, I repeat them again: hold them, count them, pay attention to them. Avoid what is bad; hold to what is good.

Good are born through the good when holy people baptize holy people.

Bad through bad when both those who baptize and those who are baptized live wickedly and impiously.

Good through bad when those who baptize are bad, but those who are baptized are good.

Bad through good when those who baptize are good, but those who are baptized are bad.

### 10

How do we find these things in the three names, “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”?

We understand the slave women as representing the bad and the free women as representing the good. The free women give birth to the good: Sarah gave birth to Isaac (Genesis 21:3). The slave women give birth to the bad: Hagar gave birth to Ishmael (Genesis 16:15).

In one Abraham we have both the kind in which the good are born through the good and the kind in which the bad are born through the bad.

Where are the bad through the good prefigured? Rebecca, the wife of Isaac, was free. Read the account: she gave birth to twins, one good and the other bad.

You have Scripture plainly saying in God’s voice, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Malachi 1:2–3; Romans 9:13). Rebecca gave birth to these two, Jacob and Esau: one is chosen from them, the other rejected [Note: The manuscripts read “disapproved”]; one succeeds to the inheritance, the other is disinherited.

God does not make his people from Esau, but from Jacob. One seed, yet those conceived are different; one womb, yet those born are different.

Did not the free woman give birth to Jacob, just as the free woman gave birth to Esau? They struggled in their mother’s womb, and when they struggled there, it was said to Rebecca, “Two peoples are in your womb” (Genesis 25:22–24).

Two human beings, two peoples: a good people and a bad people. Yet they struggle in one womb.

How many bad people there are in the Church, and one womb carries them until they are distinguished at the end! The good cry out against the bad, and the bad protest against the good, and both struggle within one set of innards.

Will they always remain together? At the end, they will emerge into the light; the birth that is here represented in the sacrament will be revealed. Then it will become clear: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”

### 11

We have therefore found, brothers, the good from the good: Isaac from the free woman; the bad from the bad: Ishmael from the slave woman; and the bad from the good: Esau from Rebecca.

Where shall we find the good from the bad? Jacob remains, so that in the three patriarchs the completion of these four kinds may be brought to its conclusion.

Jacob had free wives, and he also had slave women. Both the free women and the slave women gave birth, and the twelve sons of Israel were born from them (Genesis 29, 30, 35).

If you count all from whom they were born, they were not all from free women, nor all from slave women; yet they were all from one seed.

What, then, my brothers? Did those who were born from slave women not possess the promised land together with their brothers?

There we find good sons of Jacob born from slave women, and good sons of Jacob born from free women. Their birth from the wombs of slave women did them no harm, because in their father they recognized their seed, and consequently they held the kingdom together with their brothers.

Just as, among Jacob’s sons, birth from slave women did not prevent those born from them from holding the kingdom and receiving the promised land equally with their brothers—birth from slave women did not harm them, but the paternal seed prevailed—so also whoever is baptized through the bad appears to have been born from slave women. Yet because he is from the seed of the word of God, which is represented in Jacob, he should not be distressed: he will possess the inheritance together with his brothers.

Let the one who is born from good seed therefore be secure; only let him not imitate the slave woman if he is born from a slave woman. Do not imitate the wicked, proud slave woman.

Why did Jacob’s sons who were born from slave women possess the promised land together with their brothers, while Ishmael, born from a slave woman, was expelled from the inheritance? Why, unless because he was proud, while they were humble? He raised his neck and wanted to lead his brother astray, mocking him as he played with him.

### 12

There is a great mystery here. Ishmael and Isaac were playing together. Sarah saw them playing and said to Abraham, “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

When Abraham was distressed, the Lord confirmed his wife’s words to him. Here the mystery is already clear, because that event was giving birth to I know not what future reality.

She saw them playing and said, “Cast out the slave woman and her son.” What does this mean, brothers? What evil had Ishmael done to the boy Isaac by playing with him?

But that play was mockery; that play signified deception. Let your Charity attend to the great mystery.

The Apostle calls that persecution. He calls the very play, the very game, persecution. For he says: “But just as at that time the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one who was born according to the Spirit, so it is now”—that is, those who are born according to the flesh persecute those who are born according to the Spirit.

Who are those born according to the flesh? Lovers of the world, lovers of this age.

Who are those born according to the Spirit? Lovers of the kingdom of heaven, lovers of Christ, desiring eternal life, worshiping God freely.

They play, and the Apostle calls it persecution. For after the Apostle had said, “Just as at that time the one who was born according to the flesh persecuted the one who was born according to the Spirit, so it is now,” he continued and showed what persecution he meant: “But what does Scripture say? ‘Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac’” (Genesis 21:9–12; Galatians 4:29–30).

We ask where Scripture says this, so that we may see whether some persecution of Ishmael against Isaac preceded it. We find that it was said by Sarah when she saw the boys playing together.

The play that Scripture says Sarah saw, the Apostle calls persecution.

Those who mock you and deceive you therefore persecute you more: “Come, come; be baptized here; here you have the true Baptism.” Do not play. There is only one true Baptism; that other play is a game. You are being deceived [Note: Three manuscripts read, “the game is deceiving.” One has “of the deceiver.”], and this persecution will be grievous for you.

It would have been better for you to win Ishmael himself for the kingdom, but Ishmael does not wish this, because he wants to play.

Hold fast to your father’s inheritance, and hear: “Cast out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac.”

### 13

These people also dare to say that they customarily suffer persecution from Catholic kings or Catholic rulers. What persecution do they endure? Bodily affliction—if indeed they have ever suffered it, or however they suffered it, let them know and examine their consciences. Nevertheless, they have suffered bodily affliction; the persecution they inflict is more grievous.

Take care when Ishmael wants to play with Isaac, when he flatters you, when he offers you another Baptism. Answer: “I already have Baptism.” For if the Baptism that he wishes to give you is true, he wants to mock you.

Beware the persecutor of your soul. If the party of Donatus has ever suffered something from Catholic rulers, it suffered bodily affliction, not the persecution of spiritual deception.

Hear and see in the very events of ancient times all the signs and indications of future realities. Sarah is found to have afflicted her slave woman Hagar. Sarah was free. After the slave woman began to grow proud, Sarah complained to Abraham, saying, “She has raised her neck against me.”

As though the matter had been caused by Abraham, the woman complained to Abraham. But Abraham was not held by lust to abuse the slave woman; he was concerned with the duty of generating offspring, since Sarah had given her to him for that purpose. He therefore said to her, “Behold, your slave woman; use her as you wish.”

Sarah afflicted her severely, and Hagar fled from her presence.

There you have it: the free woman afflicted the slave woman, yet the Apostle does not call this persecution. The slave plays with the master, and he calls that persecution. This affliction is not called persecution, while that play is called persecution.

What do you think, brothers? Do you not understand what was signified?

Thus, when God wishes to stir up the authorities against heretics, against schismatics, against those who tear the Church apart, against those who spit upon Christ, against those who blaspheme Baptism, let them not be surprised. God stirs them up so that Hagar may be beaten by Sarah.

Let Hagar recognize herself and lower her neck. For when she had departed from her mistress in humiliation, an angel met her and said, “What is this, Hagar, Sarah’s slave woman?” When she had complained about her mistress, what did she hear from the angel? “Return to your mistress” (Genesis 16:5–9).

She is afflicted, then, for this purpose: that she may return. And would that she return! For her offspring, like the sons of Jacob, will possess the inheritance together with their brothers.

### 14

They are astonished that Christian authorities are moved against those detestable destroyers of the Church. Should they not be moved? And how would they render an account to God for their rule?

Let your Charity attend to what I say, for it concerns the Christian kings of this world: in their own times they should desire that their mother, the Church from whom they were spiritually born, should be at peace.

We read Daniel’s visions and prophetic deeds. Three young men praised the Lord in the fire. King Nebuchadnezzar was astonished to see the boys praising God, and the fire around them harmless [Note: The printed editions read “not harmful”; the manuscripts read “harmless.”].

And when he was astonished, what did King Nebuchadnezzar say—he who was neither a Jew nor circumcised, he who had erected his own statue and compelled everyone to worship it? Yet, moved by the praises of the three young men, when he saw the majesty of God present in the fire, what did he say?

“And I will issue a decree to all tribes and languages throughout the whole land.”

What decree?

“Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be put to death, and his house shall be destroyed” (Daniel 3).

Behold how a foreign king rages lest the God of Israel be blasphemed, because he was able to deliver three young men from the fire. Yet people do not want Christian kings to rage because Christ is spat upon—Christ by whom not three young men, but the whole world together with those kings, is delivered from the fire of Gehenna.

For those three young men, my brothers, were delivered from temporal fire. Is he not the same God of the Maccabees as of the three young men? He delivered the three young men from fire; the Maccabees perished bodily in fiery torments, but remained steadfast in spirit in the lawful commandments. The former were openly delivered; the latter were secretly crowned (2 Maccabees 7).

It is a greater thing to be delivered from the flames of Gehenna than from the furnace of human power.

If, then, King Nebuchadnezzar praised, proclaimed, and glorified God because he had delivered three young men from the fire, and gave him such great glory that he sent throughout his kingdom the decree, “Whoever speaks blasphemy against the God of Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego shall be put to death, and his house shall be destroyed,” how could these kings not be moved when they see not three young men delivered from the flames, but themselves delivered from Gehenna—when they see Christ, by whom they were delivered, spat upon among Christians, and hear it said to a Christian, “Say that you are not a Christian”?

They want to do such things, and at least they do not want to suffer such things.

### 15

For consider what they do and what they suffer. They kill souls and are afflicted in body; they inflict eternal deaths and complain that they themselves endure temporal ones.

And yet what do they suffer? They produce for us certain people as their martyrs in the persecution. Behold, Marculus was thrown down from a rock; behold, Donatus of Bagai was thrown into a well.

When did the Roman authorities decree such punishments, that people should be thrown down? What, then, do our people reply? I do not know what happened; nevertheless, what do our people report? That these men threw themselves down and brought disgrace upon the authorities.

Let us recall the customary conduct of the Roman authorities and see whom we should believe. Our people say that they threw themselves down. Unless they are disciples of those who now throw themselves from rocks without anyone pursuing them, let us not believe it. What is surprising if they did what they are accustomed to do?

For the Roman authorities have never used such punishments. Could they not have killed them openly? But those who wanted themselves to be honored as dead found no more notorious death.

In the end, whatever it was, I do not know.

And if you have suffered bodily affliction from the Catholic Church, O party of Donatus, you have suffered it from Sarah, as Hagar did. Return to your mistress.

The demands of the occasion have held us here somewhat longer, so that we have been quite unable to explain the whole text of the Gospel reading. Brothers, let what has been said suffice your Charity for the present, lest, by saying other things, we drive these matters from your hearts.

Hold fast to these things; speak such things; proceed there aflame; kindle those who are cold.

## TREATISE XII

From the passage of the Gospel, “What is born of the flesh is flesh,” and so forth, up to, “But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.” Chapter 3, verses 6–21.

### 1

From the attention with which we engaged your Charity yesterday, we understand that you have gathered with greater eagerness and in greater numbers. But for the present, if it pleases you, let us give the Gospel reading its due exposition in the proper order. Afterward your Charity will hear about the peace of the Church—what we have done, or what we still hope should be done.

Now, then, let the whole attention of your heart be directed toward the Gospel; let no one think about anything else. If even the person who is wholly present scarcely comprehends, will not the one who divides himself among various thoughts also lose what he had grasped?

Your Charity remembers how, last Sunday, the Lord deigned to help us speak about spiritual regeneration (in the preceding treatise). We had the reading read to you again, so that what was not said then might, in Christ’s name and with the assistance of your prayers, be completed.

### 2

There is one spiritual regeneration, just as there is one bodily generation. What Nicodemus said to the Lord was true: a human being, being old, cannot return again to his mother’s womb and be born.

He said, indeed, that a person who is old cannot do this—as though one who was an infant could. In fact, no one can do it, whether newly born from the womb or already advanced in years: no one can return again to the maternal womb and be born.

But just as the woman’s womb is suited to bodily birth for giving birth once, so the womb of the Church is suited to spiritual birth, so that each person may be baptized once.

Therefore, lest someone perhaps say, “But this person was born in heresy, and that person was born in schism,” everything is resolved—if you remember what was discussed with you concerning our three fathers. God wished to be called their God, not because they alone existed, but because in them alone the integrity of signifying the future people was completed.

For we find one born from a slave woman and disinherited, and another born from a free woman and made heir. Again, we find one born from a free woman and disinherited, and those born from slave women made heirs.

Ishmael was born from a slave woman and disinherited (Genesis 21:10); Isaac was born from a free woman and made heir (Genesis 25:5). Esau was born from a free woman and disinherited (Genesis 27:35); Jacob’s sons, born from slave women, were made heirs (Genesis 49).

In those three fathers, therefore, the entire figure of the future people was disclosed. And not without reason does God say, “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. This is my name forever” (Exodus 3:6, 15).

Let us remember more carefully what was promised to Abraham himself, for this was promised to Isaac, and this was also promised to Jacob: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Genesis 22:18).

At that time one man believed what he did not yet see; now people see, and are blinded. What was promised to one has been fulfilled among the nations; yet those who refuse to see what has been fulfilled separate themselves from fellowship with the nations.

But what does it profit them that they refuse to see? They see, whether they wish it or not. The truth, openly revealed, strikes even closed eyes.

3. It was answered to Nicodemus, who was one of those who had believed in Jesus—and Jesus himself did not trust them. For he did not trust certain people, although they had already believed in him. Thus you have it written: “Many believed in his name when they saw the signs that he was doing. But Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them, because he had no need for anyone to testify about a man; for he himself knew what was in man” (John 2:23–25). Behold, they already believed in Jesus, and Jesus himself did not entrust himself to them. Why? Because they had not yet been born again of water and the Spirit. Hence we have exhorted, and continue to exhort, our brothers who are catechumens. For if you ask them, they have already believed in Jesus; but because they do not yet receive his flesh and blood, Jesus has not yet entrusted himself to them. What must they do so that Jesus may entrust himself to them? Let them be born again of water and the Spirit; let the Church bring forth those whom she bears. They have been conceived; let them be brought into the light. She has breasts with which they may be nourished. Let them not fear that, once born, they may be suffocated; let them not withdraw from their mother’s breasts.

4. No human being can return into his mother’s womb and be born again. But was someone born of a slave woman? Did those who were born of slave women then return into the wombs of free women in order to be born again? Abraham’s seed was also in Ishmael; and, so that Abraham might have a son by a slave woman, his wife was the author of the arrangement. He was born from the man’s seed, not from the womb but solely by the wife’s decision (Genesis 16:2–4). Was he disinherited because he was born of a slave woman? If for that reason he was disinherited—because he was born of a slave woman—no sons of slave women would be admitted to an inheritance. Jacob’s sons were admitted to the inheritance. Ishmael, however, was not disinherited because he was born of a slave woman, but because he was arrogant toward his mother and toward his mother’s son; for his mother was Sarah rather than Hagar. Sarah’s womb was made available, and Sarah’s will was added; Abraham would not have done what Sarah did not wish. Therefore he was more truly Sarah’s son.

But because he was arrogant toward his brother, and arrogant in his play—because he was mocking—what does Sarah say? “Cast out the slave woman and her son; for the son of the slave woman shall not be heir with my son Isaac” (Genesis 21:9–10). It was not, then, the slave woman’s womb that cast him out, but a servile neck. And if a free man is arrogant, he is a slave—and what is worse, he is the slave of an evil mistress: his own arrogance.

Therefore, my brothers, answer the man that a human being cannot be born again; answer confidently that a human being cannot be born again. Whatever happens again is an illusion; whatever happens again is a game. Ishmael is playing; let him be sent outside. For Scripture observes that Sarah saw them playing and said to Abraham, “Cast out the slave woman and her son.” Sarah was displeased by the children’s play; she saw the children playing something new. Do not women who have children wish to see their own children playing? She saw it and disapproved. I do not know what she saw in the play: she saw deception in that play; she noticed the slave’s arrogance, and it displeased her, so she cast him out.

Wicked children born of slave women are sent outside [Note: [Col. 1486] Three manuscripts: “The sons of Jacob, born of slave women, are admitted to the inheritance, and the one born of a free woman,” etc.]. And one born of a free woman—Esau—is sent outside. Therefore let no one presume because he is born of good people; let no one presume because he is baptized by holy people. Whoever is baptized by holy people must still beware lest he be not Jacob but Esau.

So, brothers, let me say this: it is better to be baptized by people seeking their own interests and loving the world—for this is what the name “slave woman” signifies—and to seek Christ’s spiritual inheritance, so as to be like Jacob, the son of a slave woman, than to be baptized by holy people and grow proud, becoming Esau, who must be sent outside, although born of a free woman.

Hold fast to these things, brothers. We are not flattering you; let there be no hope for you in us. We neither flatter ourselves nor you; each person carries his own burden. Our task is to speak, lest we be judged badly; yours is to hear—and to hear with the heart—lest what we give be required of us; or rather, when it is required, let gain be found, not loss.

5. The Lord speaks to Nicodemus and explains to him: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of God.” “You,” he says, “understand carnal generation when you say, ‘Can a man return into his mother’s womb?’ He must be born of water and the Spirit for the sake of the kingdom of God. If he is born for the inheritance of a human father, which is temporal, let him be born from the womb of a carnal mother; if for the eternal inheritance of God the Father, let him be born from the womb of the Church.”

A mortal father generates a son through his wife, one who will succeed him; God generates through the Church sons who will not succeed him, but will remain with him. And it follows: “What is born of the flesh is flesh, and what is born of the Spirit is spirit.” We are therefore born spiritually, and in the Spirit we are born through the word and the sacrament. The Spirit is present so that we may be born; the Spirit is invisibly present from whom you are born, because you too are born invisibly.

For he continues and says: “Do not marvel that I said to you, ‘You must be born again.’ The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.” No one sees the Spirit; how, then, do we hear the Spirit’s voice? The Psalm sounds: it is the voice of the Spirit. The Gospel sounds: it is the voice of the Spirit. The divine word sounds: it is the voice of the Spirit. “You hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from and where it goes.” But if you too are born of the Spirit, you will be such that one who has not yet been born of the Spirit does not know where you come from or where you are going. For after this he says: “So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

6. Nicodemus answered and said to him: “How can these things happen?” And indeed, because he understood carnally, he did not understand. In him what the Lord had said was taking place: he was hearing the voice of the Spirit, but he did not know where it had come from or where it was going.

Jesus answered and said to him: “You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not understand these things?” O brothers, do we suppose that the Lord wished to insult this teacher of the Jews? The Lord knew what he was doing; he wanted Nicodemus to be born of the Spirit. No one is born of the Spirit unless he is humble, because humility itself makes us born of the Spirit; for “the Lord is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 33:19).

Nicodemus was inflated by his teaching office and seemed to himself to be a person of some importance because he was a teacher of the Jews. The Lord removes his pride so that he may be able to be born of the Spirit. He reproaches him as though he were ignorant—not because the Lord wishes to appear superior. What is remarkable about God in relation to a human being, or truth in relation to falsehood? Christ ought to be called greater than Nicodemus—he may be called so, and it must be thought so. If it were said that Christ is greater than the angels, that would be laughable, since he is incomparably greater than every creature, through whom every creature was made.

But he stirs up the man’s pride: “You are a teacher in Israel, and you do not understand these things?” It is as though he were saying: “Behold, you know nothing, proud leader; be born of the Spirit. For if you are born of the Spirit, you will hold fast to God’s ways, so as to follow Christ’s humility.”

For he is exalted above all the angels because, “although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a slave, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a man. He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death”—and lest some particular kind of death please you—“even death on a cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

He was hanging there, and people were insulting him. He could have come down from the cross, but he postponed it so that he might rise from the tomb. The Lord endured proud slaves; the physician endured the sick. If this was true of him, what of those who must be born of the Spirit? What of him, the true teacher in heaven—not only of human beings, but also of angels? For if the angels are taught, they are taught by the Word of God. If they are taught by the Word of God, seek where they were taught, and you will find: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

The human neck is brought low—though rough and hard—so that the neck may become gentle for bearing Christ’s yoke, of which it is said: “My yoke is gentle, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:30).

7. And it follows: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” What earthly things did he tell them, brothers? “Unless someone is born again”—is that earthly? “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes”—is that earthly?

For if he were speaking about this wind, as some have understood, when they were asked what earthly thing the Lord had said by declaring, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”, then, when certain people were asked what earthly thing the Lord had said, they were driven into difficulty and replied: “When he said, ‘The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes,’ he was speaking about this wind.”

What earthly thing did he name? He was speaking about spiritual generation; afterward he said: “So it is with everyone who is born of the Spirit.” Besides, brothers, who among us does not see, for example, the south wind going from south to north, or another wind coming from east to west? How, then, do we not know where it comes from and where it goes?

What earthly thing, then, did he say that people did not believe? Was it what he had said about raising the temple? For he had received his body from the earth, and he was preparing to raise that very earth, taken from an earthly body. They did not believe him when he was going to raise the earthly body.

“If I have told you earthly things,” he says, “and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” That is: If you do not believe that I can raise up the temple thrown down by you, how will you believe that human beings can be regenerated through the Spirit?

8. And it follows: “And no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” Behold, he was here, and he was in heaven: here in the flesh, in heaven in his divinity—or rather, in his divinity everywhere. Born of his mother, yet not departing from the Father.

Two births of Christ are understood: one divine, the other human; one by which we were made, the other by which we were remade. Both are wondrous: the former without a mother, the latter without a father.

But because he had received a body from Adam—for Mary was from Adam—and was going to raise that body, he had said something earthly: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John 2:19). But he said something heavenly: “Unless someone is born again of water and the Spirit, he will not see the kingdom of God” (John 3:5).

Come, brothers: God willed to be the Son of Man, and he willed human beings to be sons of God. He descended for our sake; let us ascend for his sake. For the one who said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven,” is the only one who descended and ascended.

Will those whom he makes sons of God not ascend into heaven? Certainly they will ascend. This is the promise made to us: “They will be equal to the angels of God” (Matthew 22:30). How, then, does no one ascend except the one who descended? Because one descended and one ascended. What of the others? What is to be understood except that they will be his members, so that one may ascend?

For this reason it follows: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven.” Do you marvel that he was both here and in heaven? He made his disciples such. Hear the apostle Paul saying: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3:20). If Paul the apostle, a human being, walked in the flesh on earth and lived as a citizen of heaven, could the God of heaven and earth not be both in heaven and on earth?

9. If, then, no one but he descended and ascended, what hope is there for the others? There is this hope for the others: he descended for the very purpose that in him and with him they might be one—those who would ascend through him. The Apostle does not say, “And to seeds,” as though referring to many, “but as though referring to one: ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ.” And he says to the faithful: “You are Christ’s; and if you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s seed” (Galatians 3:16, 29).

By saying “one,” he said that all of us are one. Therefore in the Psalms several sometimes sing, to show that one is made from many; sometimes one sings, to show what is made from many. For this reason one man was healed in that pool (John 5:4), while no other who descended was healed. Therefore this one commends the unity of the Church.

Woe to those who hate unity and make divisions among human beings for themselves! Let them hear the one who wished to make them one, in one, toward one. Let them hear him saying: “Do not make yourselves many: I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

They were saying: “I am of Paul, I of Apollos, I of Cephas.” And he says: “Is Christ divided?” (1 Corinthians 1:12–13). Be in one; be one; be the one: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven.”

“We wish to belong to you,” they were saying to Paul. And he replied: “I do not want you to belong to Paul; belong to the one to whom Paul, together with you, belongs.”

10. For he descended and died, and by that very death he freed us from death. He was killed by death, and he killed death. And you know, brothers, that this death entered the world through the devil’s envy.

“God did not make death,” Scripture says; “nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the living, for he created all things that they might exist” (Wisdom 1:13–14). But what does it say there? “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wisdom 2:24).

Man would not have come to the death offered by the devil under compulsion, for the devil did not possess the power to force him, but the cunning to persuade him. If you had not consented, the devil would have brought nothing upon you. Your consent, O man, brought you to death.

Mortals were born from a mortal; from immortals they became mortal. From Adam all human beings are mortal. But Jesus, the Son of God, the Word of God through whom all things were made, the only-begotten one equal to the Father, became mortal, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:13–14).

11. Therefore he assumed death and suspended death upon the cross; and by that very death mortals are delivered. The Lord recalls what was done in symbolic form among the ancients: “And just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

A great sacrament—and those who have read know it. Let those who have not read, or who perhaps have forgotten what they read or heard, listen. In the wilderness the people of Israel were being struck down by the bites of serpents, and a great slaughter of many deaths was taking place.

[Note: In the manuscripts: “a slaughter of many dead.”]

For it was God’s wound, correcting and scourging them in order to instruct them. There a great sacrament of a future reality was displayed. The Lord himself bears witness to it in this reading, so that no one can interpret it as anything other than what the truth itself reveals concerning him.

For the Lord commanded Moses to make a bronze serpent and lift it up on wood in the wilderness, and to warn the people of Israel that if anyone were bitten by a serpent, he should look upon that serpent lifted up on the wood. It was done: people were bitten, they looked, and they were healed (Numbers 21:6–9).

What are the serpents that bite? Sins arising from the mortality of the flesh. Who is the serpent lifted up? The Lord’s death on the cross. Because death came through the serpent, it was represented through the serpent’s likeness. The serpent’s bite was deadly; the Lord’s death is life-giving. The serpent is looked upon so that the serpent may have no power. What does this mean? Death is looked upon so that death may have no power.

But whose death? The death of life—or, if it may be said, the death of life. Indeed, because it may be said, it is said wondrously. But surely what had to be done must also be said. Should I hesitate to say what the Lord deigned to do for me? Is Christ not life? And yet Christ was on the cross. Is Christ not life? And yet Christ died.

But in Christ’s death, death itself died, because life when dead killed death; the fullness of life swallowed up death. Death was absorbed in Christ’s body. Thus we too shall say at the resurrection, when we sing in triumph: “Where, O death, is your contest? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Corinthians 15:54–55).

For now, brothers, so that we may be healed from sin, let us look upon Christ crucified. For “just as Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but have eternal life.”

Just as those who looked upon that serpent did not perish from the serpents’ bites, so those who look with faith upon Christ’s death are healed from the bites of sins. But they were healed from death into temporal life; here, however, he says that they may have eternal life.

This is the difference between the symbolic image and the reality itself: the symbol bestowed temporal life; the reality of which that symbol was a figure bestows eternal life.

12. For God did not send his Son into the world to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him. Therefore, insofar as it depends on the physician, he came to heal the sick. The one who refuses to observe the physician’s prescriptions kills himself.

The Savior came into the world. Why is he called the world’s Savior, unless to save the world, not to judge the world? You do not wish to be saved by him; you will be judged by yourself. And what shall I say—“you will be judged”? See what he says: “Whoever believes in him is not judged; but whoever does not believe”—what do you expect him to say, except “is judged”? “He has already been judged,” he says.

The judgment has not yet appeared, but judgment has already taken place. For the Lord knows who are his; he knows who will remain for the crown and who will remain for the fire. He knows the wheat on his threshing floor; he knows the chaff. He knows the grain; he knows the weeds.

“He has already been judged,” whoever does not believe. Why has he been judged? Because he did not believe [Note: The ancient Corbie Bibles also read this way, in accordance with the Greek *pepisteuken* (“has believed”). The Vulgate now has *credit* (“believes”).] in the name of the only-begotten Son of God.

13. “And this is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil.”

My brothers, whose works did the Lord find good? No one’s. He found everyone’s works evil. How, then, did some do the truth and come to the light? For it follows: “But whoever does the truth comes to the light, so that his works may be revealed, because they have been done in God.”

How did some perform a good work so as to come to the light—that is, to Christ? And how did some love darkness? If he found all people sinners, and heals all from sin, and that serpent in which the Lord’s death was represented heals those who had been bitten—and the serpent was raised because of the serpent’s bite, that is, the Lord’s death was raised because of mortal human beings whom he found unrighteous—how is it understood that “this is the judgment: that the light has come into the world, and people loved darkness more than light, for their works were evil”?

What does this mean? Whose works were good? Did you not come to justify the ungodly? But he says, “They loved darkness more than light.” There he placed the emphasis. Many have loved their sins; many have confessed their sins. For whoever confesses his sins and accuses his sins is already acting together with God.

God accuses your sins; if you also accuse them, you are joined to God. There seem to be two things: the human being and the sinner. What you hear called “human being,” God made; what you hear called “sinner,” that same human being made. Erase what you made, so that God may save what he made.

You must hate in yourself what you have made, and love in yourself what God has made. When what you have done begins to displease you, your good works begin there, because you accuse your evil works. The beginning of good works is confession of evil works.

You do the truth and come to the light. What does “you do the truth” mean? You do not flatter yourself, you do not indulge yourself, you do not court your own favor; you do not say, “I am righteous,” when you are unrighteous—and you begin to do the truth.

You come to the light so that your works may be revealed, because they have been done in God. For even the fact that your sin displeased you would not displease you unless God were shining upon you and his truth were showing it to you.

But whoever, even after being admonished, loves his sins hates the light that admonishes him and flees it, so that his evil works—which he loves—may not be exposed. But whoever does the truth accuses his evils in himself; he does not spare himself or forgive himself, so that God may forgive him. For what he wishes God to forgive, he himself acknowledges, and he comes to the light, giving thanks to it because it has shown him what he should hate in himself.

He says to God, “Turn your face away from my sins.” And with what face does he say this unless he also says, “For I acknowledge my crime, and my sin is always before me” (Psalm 50:11, 5)? Let what you do not want to be before God be before you. But if you put your sin behind you, God turns it back before your eyes—and he turns it back when there will no longer be any fruit of repentance.

14. “Run, lest the darkness overtake you” (John 12:35), my brothers. Wake up for your salvation; wake up while there is time. Let no one be held back from the temple of God; let no one be held back from the work of the Lord; let no one be diverted from continual prayer; let no one be deprived of his customary devotion.

Wake up, then, while it is day. The day shines; Christ is the day. He is ready to forgive those who acknowledge their sins, but he is ready to punish those who defend themselves, boast that they are righteous, and think they are something when they are nothing.

Whoever walks in his love and mercy, even after being delivered from those deadly and grave sins—such as crimes, murders, thefts, and adulteries—yet, because of those sins that seem small, of the tongue or of thoughts or of excess in permitted things, does the truth of confession and comes to the light in good works, does so because many small sins, if neglected, kill.

The drops are small that fill rivers; grains of sand are small. But if much sand is placed upon someone, it weighs down and overwhelms him. A neglected bilge does what an overwhelming wave does: water enters gradually through the bilge, but by entering for a long time and not being pumped out, it sinks the ship.

What does it mean to pump it out except to act through good works so that sins do not overwhelm us—by groaning, fasting, giving, and forgiving?

The journey of this age is difficult and full of temptations: in prosperity, lest it exalt us; in adversity, lest it break us. The one who gave you the happiness of this age gave it for your consolation, not for your corruption. Again, the one who scourges you in this age does so for correction, not for condemnation. Endure the father who instructs you, lest you experience the judge who punishes you.

We say these things to you every day, and they must often be said, because they are good and salutary.

# TREATISE XIII

From the Gospel passage beginning, “After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea,” etc., up to, “But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice.” Chapter 3, verses 22–29.

1. The order of the Gospel reading according to John, as you who are concerned for your progress may remember, proceeds in such a way that what has just been read is proposed for our treatment today. You remember that what was said from the very beginning up to today’s reading has already been treated. And even if you have perhaps forgotten much of it, surely at least our ministry remains in your memory.

What you have heard up to this point about John’s baptism—even if you do not retain everything, I nevertheless believe that you retain having heard it—was also said: why the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, and how that very difficult question was resolved, namely, that John learned from the Lord, through the dove, something he had not known, although he already knew him when, as the Lord came to be baptized, John said, “I need to be baptized by you, and you come to me?” The Lord answered him, “Let it be so for now, so that all righteousness may be fulfilled” (Matthew 3:14–15).

2. Now, therefore, the order of the reading compels us to return to that same John. He is the one who was prophesied through Isaiah: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness, ‘Prepare the way for the Lord; make his paths straight’” (Isaiah 40:3).

He gave such testimony to his Lord—and, because the Lord deigned to do so, to his friend. The Lord himself, both his Lord and his friend, also bore witness to John. For he said of John: “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist.”

But because he placed himself above John, he was God in that wherein he was greater than John. “Yet the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven is greater than he” (Matthew 11:11). He was less in birth, greater in power, greater in divinity, majesty, and glory: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

In the earlier readings John had borne witness to the Lord in such a way that he called him the Son of God, but did not call him God, though he did not deny it. He had been silent about his being God; he had not denied that he was God, but he had not remained entirely silent about it. Perhaps we find this in today’s reading.

He had called him the Son of God—but human beings too are called sons of God. He had said that he possessed such great excellence that John himself was not worthy to untie the strap of his sandal (John 1:1, 34, 27).

This greatness gives us much to understand: the one whose sandal strap he was unworthy to untie was the one greater than whom no one had arisen among those born of women. For he was greater than all human beings and angels.

We find, for example, that an angel forbade a human being to fall at his feet. When an angel showed certain things in the Apocalypse to John, who wrote this Gospel, John was terrified by the greatness of the vision and fell at the angel’s feet. The angel said to him: “Rise; see that you do not do this. Worship God” [Note: Most manuscripts have “Worship him,” that is, God], “for I am your fellow servant and the fellow servant of your brothers” (Revelation 22:8–9).

The angel therefore forbade a human being to fall at his feet. Is it not clear that the one to whom such a man—greater than whom no one has arisen among those born of women—says that he is unworthy to untie the strap of his sandal is above all the angels?

3. Yet let John say something more plainly: that our Lord Jesus Christ is God. Let us find this in the present reading, for perhaps we also sang about him: “God reigns over all the earth.” Against this the deaf are opposed, those who think that he reigns in Africa alone.

For it was certainly said of Christ when it was said, “God reigns over all the earth.” Who else is our king except our Lord Jesus Christ? He is our king.

And what did you hear in that same Psalm, in the verse just sung? “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our king, sing praises. Sing praises intelligently.” The one whom he called God, he called our king: “Sing praises to our God, sing praises; sing praises to our king, sing praises intelligently.”

Do not wish to understand only in one part whom you are praising: “For God is the king of all the earth” (Psalm 46:3, 7–8).

How is he king of all the earth, when he was seen in one part of the earth—in Jerusalem, in Judea—walking among human beings, being born, suckling, growing, eating, drinking, keeping watch, sleeping, sitting tired beside a well, being seized, scourged, smeared with spittle, crowned with thorns, hung upon wood, struck with a spear, dying, and being buried?

How, then, is he king of all the earth? What was visible in a particular place was flesh; flesh appeared to fleshly eyes. Immortal majesty was hidden in mortal flesh. And with what eyes can immortal majesty be seen through the structure of flesh? There is another eye, an inner eye.

For Tobias too was not without eyes when, blind in his bodily eyes, he gave his son instructions for life (Tobit 4). His son held his father’s hand so that he could walk with his feet; the father gave his son counsel so that he might keep to the way of righteousness.

With these eyes I see, and with these eyes I understand. The eyes of the one who gives counsel for life are better than the eyes of the one who holds a hand.

Jesus sought such eyes when he said to Philip: “Have I been with you for so long, and you have not known me?” He sought such eyes when he said, “Philip, whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9). These eyes are in understanding; these eyes are in the mind.

Therefore, after the Psalm had said, “For God is the king of all the earth,” it immediately added, “Sing praises intelligently.” For when I say, “Sing praises to our God, sing praises,” I call God our king.

But you saw our king among human beings as a human being; you saw him suffering, crucified, dead. Something was hidden in that flesh which you were able to see with fleshly eyes [Note: The manuscripts have this reading. The printed editions have: “which you were not able to see with fleshly eyes.”]

What was hidden there? “Sing praises intelligently.” Do not seek with your eyes what is perceived with the mind. Praise with the tongue, because he was flesh among you; but because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” give sound to the flesh, and give the gaze of the mind to God. “Sing praises intelligently,” and you will see that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

4. Let John also bear witness: “After these things Jesus and his disciples came into the land of Judea, and there he stayed with them and baptized.” The baptized one was baptizing. He was not baptizing with the baptism by which he himself was baptized.

The Lord, baptized by a servant, gives baptism, showing the way of humility and leading to the Lord’s baptism—that is, his own baptism—by providing an example of humility, because he himself did not reject the servant’s baptism.

And in the servant’s baptism a way was prepared for the Lord; and, having been baptized, the Lord made himself the way for those who come [Note: Four manuscripts have: “he made the way to himself for those who come.” Three others have: “he made himself the way to himself for those who come.”]

Let us hear him himself: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6). If you seek the truth, hold to the way; for the way itself is the truth. It is the destination to which you go; it is the way by which you go. You do not go through one thing to another, nor do you come to Christ through something else: through Christ you come to Christ.

How do you come through Christ to Christ? Through Christ the man to Christ God; through the Word made flesh to the Word who in the beginning was God with God; from what the human being ate to what the angels eat every day.

For it is written: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Psalm 77:24–25). What is the bread of angels? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

How did man eat the bread of angels? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

5. But because we said that angels eat, brothers, do not suppose that this happens by biting. For if you understand it this way, it would be as though God, whom the angels eat, were torn apart. Who tears apart righteousness?

But someone says to me again: Who eats righteousness? How, then, does it say, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew 5:6)?

The food that you eat through the flesh, so that you may be restored, diminishes; it is consumed in order to restore you. Eat righteousness, and you are restored while righteousness remains whole.

Consider how, by seeing this bodily light, our eyes are restored, and the thing seen by bodily eyes is corporeal. For many people, after remaining for a long time in darkness, have their sight weakened, as though by a fast from light. Deprived of their food—for they are nourished by light—the eyes grow weary through fasting and are weakened, so that they cannot see the very light by which they are restored. If it remains absent for a longer time, they go blind, and the faculty of light itself seems to die in them.

What, then? Because so many eyes are nourished every day by this light, does it become less? The eyes are restored, and the light itself remains whole.

If God was able to provide this with bodily light for bodily eyes, does he not provide for pure hearts that light which does not grow weary, which remains whole and does not diminish in any part?

What light? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.” Let us see whether it is light: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10).

On earth, the fountain is one thing and the light another. When you are thirsty, you seek a fountain; and to reach the fountain, you seek light. If it is not day, you light a lamp so that you may reach the fountain.

That fountain is itself light. To the thirsty it is a fountain; to the blind it is light. Let the eyes be opened so that they may see the light; let the mouth of the heart be opened so that it may drink the fountain. What you drink, you see; what you drink, you hear.

God becomes everything to you, because he is everything to you in whatever you love. If you attend to visible things, God is neither bread, nor water, nor this light, nor clothing, nor a house. For all these things are visible, and each is distinct: what is bread is not water; what is clothing is not a house; and what these things are, God is not. They are visible things.

God is everything to you. If you hunger, he is bread to you; if you thirst, he is water to you; if you are in darkness, he is light to you, because he remains incorruptible; if you are naked, he is the garment of immortality to you, when this corruptible puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality (1 Corinthians 15:53–54).

Everything can be said of God, and nothing can be said worthily of God. Nothing is broader than this poverty. You seek a fitting name and do not find one; you seek some way to speak, and you find everything.

What resemblance is there between a lamb and a lion? Both have been said of Christ: “Behold, the Lamb of God” (John 1:29). How is he a lion? “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Revelation 5:5).

6. Let us listen to John: “Jesus was baptizing.” We have said that Jesus was baptizing. How Jesus? How the Lord? How the Son of God? How the Word? “But the Word became flesh.” Now John also was baptizing at Aenon near Salim. Aenon was a certain lake [Note: [Col. 1495] In several manuscripts: “Salim, a certain place; Aenon, a lake.”]. How is it understood that it was a lake? Because there were many waters there, and people came and were baptized. For John had not yet been sent into prison.

If you remember—for I say it again—I explained why John was baptizing: because it was necessary for the Lord to be baptized. And why was it necessary for the Lord to be baptized? Because many would despise Baptism, since they appeared already to possess a greater grace than they saw other believers possessing. For example, a catechumen already living continently might despise a married man and say that he was better than that believer. That catechumen might say in his heart: “Why do I need to receive Baptism, in order to have what this man has, when I am already better than he is?”

Therefore, so that this neck—of those excessively puffed up by their merits of righteousness—might not bring some crashing down, the Lord wished to be baptized by a servant, as though addressing proud sons: “Why do you exalt yourselves? Why do you hold yourselves erect because one of you possesses prudence, another learning, another chastity, another strength of endurance? Can you possess as much as I, who gave these things? And yet I was baptized by a servant, while you disdain being baptized by the Lord.” This was “in order to fulfill all righteousness” (Matt. III, 15).

[Col. 1496] 7. But someone may say: “Then it was enough for John to baptize the Lord; why was it necessary for others to be baptized by John?” We have also explained this: if the Lord alone had been baptized by John, people would not have lacked the thought that John possessed a better baptism than the Lord. They would say: “The baptism John received was so great that Christ alone was worthy to be baptized with it.”

Therefore, to show that the baptism the Lord was going to give was better, and that John was to be understood as a servant and Christ as Lord, the Lord was baptized, so that he might offer an example of humility. But he was not the only one baptized by John, lest John’s baptism appear better than the Lord’s baptism.

For this purpose our Lord Jesus Christ opened the way, as you have heard, brothers, so that no one, arrogating to himself an abundance of some grace, might disdain being baptized with the Lord’s baptism. However far a catechumen may progress, he still carries the burden of his iniquity; it is not removed from him until he comes to Baptism. Just as the people of Israel were not freed from the people of the Egyptians until they had come to the Red Sea (Exod. XIV), so no one is free from the oppression of sins until he has come to the font of Baptism.

8. A dispute therefore arose between John’s disciples and the Jews concerning purification. John was baptizing, and Christ was baptizing. John’s disciples were disturbed: people were flocking to Christ, and people were coming to John [Note: [Col. 1496] Two manuscripts: “people were coming from John.”]. Those who came to John he sent to Jesus to be baptized; those who were baptized by Christ were not sent to John.

John’s disciples were troubled and began, as is customary, to discuss the matter with the Jews. Understand that the Jews were saying that Christ was greater and that people ought to flock to his baptism. Still not understanding this, they defended John’s baptism.

They came to John himself, so that he might resolve the dispute. Let your Charity understand. Here too the very usefulness of humility is recognized, and it is shown whether, when people were erring in this dispute, John wished to glory in himself. For perhaps he might have said: “You speak truly; your contention is correct; my baptism is better. For, so that you may know that my baptism is better, I myself baptized Christ.”

John could have said this after Christ had been baptized. If he had wished to stretch himself out, how much room he had in which to stretch! But he knew better before whom he should humble himself. He knew that he himself preceded Christ in birth, and he wished, by his confession, to yield to him. He understood that his salvation was in Christ.

Earlier he had said, “We have all received from his fullness” (John I, 16); and to confess this is to confess God. For how do all human beings receive from his fullness unless he is God? If he is man in such a way that he is not God, then he too receives from God’s fullness, and so he is not God. But if all human beings receive from his fullness, he is the fountain and they are those who drink. Those who drink from a fountain can both thirst and drink; the fountain never thirsts, and the fountain has no need of itself. Human beings need the fountain. With dried-up innards and parched throats they run to the fountain to be refreshed; the fountain flows in order to refresh them. Thus the Lord Jesus—

[Col. 1497] 9. Let us see, then, what John replied. They came to John and said to him: “Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness—look, he is baptizing, and everyone is coming to him.” That is: “What do you say? Should they not be prevented, so that they may come to you instead?”

He answered and said: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.”

Of whom do you think John said this? Of himself: “As a human being,” he says, “I received from heaven.” Let your Charity attend. “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven. You yourselves bear witness to me that I said, ‘I am not the Christ.’”

As though he were saying: “Why do you deceive yourselves? How did you yourselves frame this question to me? What did you say to me? ‘Rabbi, the one who was with you across the Jordan, to whom you bore witness.’ You know, then, what testimony I bore to him. Am I now going to say that he is not the one I said he was? Therefore, because I received something from heaven so that I might be something, do you want me to become nothing by speaking against the truth? ‘A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.’ You yourselves bear witness to me that I said, ‘I am not the Christ.’”

“You are not the Christ; but what if you are greater than he, because you baptized him?”

“I was sent. I am the herald; he is the judge.”

10. And hear a testimony much more forceful, much more explicit. See what is happening among us; see what we ought to love; see that to love some human being in place of Christ is adultery.

Why do I say this? Let us attend to John’s voice. People could have gone astray concerning him; he could himself have been thought to be someone he was not. He rejected false honor from himself, so that he might hold fast to solid truth. See what he says of Christ and what he says of himself: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.”

Be chaste; love the bridegroom.

“But who are you, who tell us, ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom’?”

“But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

May the Lord our God be present for the movement of my heart. For it is filled with great anguish to say what grieves me. But I beseech you by Christ himself: whatever I may be unable to say, think through yourselves. I know that my grief cannot be expressed with sufficient dignity.

For I see many adulterers who wish to possess the bride purchased at so great a price, loved and made beautiful from being foul by the one who purchased her, liberated her, and adorned her; and by their words they work to have themselves loved in place of the bridegroom.

Of Christ it was said, “This is the one who baptizes” (John I, 33). Who comes here and says, “I baptize”? Who comes here and says, “What I give is holy”? Who comes forward and says, “It is good for you to be born from me”?

Let us listen to the friend of the bridegroom, not to the bridegroom’s adulterers. Let us listen to one who is zealous, but not for himself.

11. Brothers, return in your hearts to your own homes. I am speaking carnally; I am speaking earthly things; I am speaking as a human being, because of the weakness of your flesh (Rom. VI, 19). Many of you have wives; many wish to have them; many, even if you do not wish to, have had them; and many who absolutely do not wish to have wives were born from the wives of your fathers. There is no heart untouched by this feeling. No one in human affairs is so remote from the human race [Col. 1498] that he does not understand what I am saying.

Imagine someone who has gone abroad and entrusted his bride to a friend: “Please look after her. You are dear to me; make sure that, while I am away, no one is loved in my place.”

How, then, does that man appear to the whole human race if, while guarding his friend’s bride or wife and indeed taking care that no one else be loved, he should wish to be loved in place of his friend and should wish to make use of the woman entrusted to him? How detestable would he appear!

Suppose he sees her looking somewhat flirtatiously through the window or joking with someone. He forbids it, as though out of jealousy. I see that he is jealous, but for whom? For his absent friend, or for himself, who is present?

Imagine that our Lord Jesus Christ did this. He entrusted his bride to his friend and went abroad to receive a kingdom, as he himself says in the Gospel (Luke XIX, 12), and yet he is present in majesty.

Let the friend who has gone across the sea be deceived; but if he is deceived, woe to the one who deceives him! Why do they attempt to deceive God, who observes the hearts of all and searches out all their secrets?

A heretic appears and says: “I give; I sanctify; I justify; I do not want you to go to that sect.” He is indeed rightly jealous—but see for whom. “Do not go to idols”: he is rightly jealous. “Do not go to diviners”: he is rightly jealous. Let us see for whom he is jealous: “What I give is holy because I give it. The one whom I baptize is baptized; the one whom I do not baptize is not baptized.”

Listen to the friend of the bridegroom; learn to be jealous for your friend. Listen to his voice: “This is the one who baptizes.”

Why do you wish to arrogate to yourself what is not yours? Is the one who left his bride here so completely absent? Do you not know that the one who rose from the dead sits at the right hand of the Father? If the Jews despised him hanging on the tree, do you despise him seated in heaven?

Let your Charity know that I suffer great anguish over this matter. But, as I said, I leave the rest to your thoughts. For I could not say enough even if I spoke all day; nor could I say enough if I wept all day. I do not mean merely if I possessed—as the prophet says—a fountain of tears (Jer. IX, 1); but even if I were turned into tears, and became a tear [Note: [Col. 1498] Almost all manuscripts omit “turned into tears, and became a tear.”], and into tongues, and became tongues, it would be too little.

12. Let us return and see what this man says: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom”; the bride is not mine.

“And do you not rejoice at the wedding?”

“Indeed I rejoice,” he says. “But the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

“I do not,” he says, “rejoice because of my own voice; I rejoice because of the bridegroom’s voice. I am in the position of hearing, he in that of speaking; for I am to be enlightened, he is the light; I am in the ear, he is the Word.”

Therefore, the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him.

Why does he stand? Because he does not fall.

Why does he not fall? Because he is humble.

See him standing on solid ground: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John I, 27). You humble yourself well; rightly you do not fall; rightly you stand; rightly you hear him and rejoice greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice.

So too the Apostle, the friend of the bridegroom, is zealous—not for himself, but for the bridegroom. Hear the voice of the one who is zealous: “I am jealous for you with the jealousy of God,” he says—not with my own jealousy, not for myself, but with the jealousy of God.

“For whom? In what way? Whom do you make the object of your jealousy, or for whom are you jealous?”

“For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.”

“What, then, do you fear? Why are you jealous?”

“I fear,” he says, “that just as the serpent deceived Eve by its cunning, so your minds may be corrupted from the purity that is in Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2, 3).

The whole Church is called a virgin. You see that the members of the Church are diverse, endowed with and rejoicing in diverse gifts. Some are married men, some married women; some widowers no longer seek wives, some widows no longer seek husbands; some preserve their integrity from an early age, some have vowed their virginity to God. The gifts are diverse, but all these together are one virgin.

Where is this virginity? It is not in the body [Note: [Col. 1499] Thus several manuscripts. The printed editions have: “For it is not in the body. In the body it belongs to a few women.” Later, instead of “holy integrity,” they have “holiness, integrity.”]. In the Church, bodily virginity belongs to a few women; and, if virginity can be spoken of in men, the holy integrity of the bodies of a few men is also present in the Church, and is a more honorable member. The other members, however, preserve their virginity not in the body but entirely in the mind.

What is virginity of mind? An undivided faith, a firm hope, a sincere love. It was this virginity that the one who was zealous for the bridegroom feared might be corrupted by the serpent.

For just as a bodily member is violated in some particular place, so the heart’s virginity is violated by the seduction of the tongue. Let that which does not wish to preserve bodily virginity without cause not be corrupted in the mind.

13. What, then, shall I say, brothers? Heretics too have virgins, and there are many virgins among heretics. Let us see whether they love the bridegroom, so that this virginity may be preserved. For whom is it preserved?

“For Christ,” they say.

Let us see whether it is for Christ, and not for Donatus. Let us see for whom this virginity is kept; you will quickly be able to prove it.

Behold, I show you the bridegroom, because he has shown himself. John bears witness to him: “This is the one who baptizes.”

O virgin, if you preserve your virginity for this bridegroom, why do you run to the one who says, “I baptize,” when the friend of your bridegroom says, “This is the one who baptizes”?

Furthermore, your bridegroom possesses the whole world. Why are you corrupted in a part?

Who is the bridegroom? “For God is the king of all the earth” (Ps. XLVI, 8). Your bridegroom himself possesses the whole, because he purchased the whole.

Consider at what price he purchased it, so that you may understand what he bought. What price did he pay? He gave blood. Where did he give and shed his blood? In his Passion.

Do you not sing to your bridegroom—or pretend to sing—when the whole world was purchased:

“They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones. They themselves looked and gazed upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots”?

You are the bride; recognize your bridegroom’s garment. Over what garment was the lot cast? Ask the Gospel; see to whom you have been betrothed; see from whom you receive the pledge.

Ask the Gospel; see what it tells you in the Lord’s Passion. There was a tunic there; let us see what kind it was: woven from the top.

What does the tunic woven from the top signify, if not love? What does the tunic woven from the top signify, if not unity?

Attend to this tunic, which not even Christ’s persecutors divided. For it says: “They said to one another, ‘Let us not divide it, but let us cast lots over it’” (John XIX, 23, 24).

Behold the source of the Psalm you heard. The persecutors did not tear the garment apart; Christians divide the Church.

[Col. 1500] 14. But what shall I say, brothers? Let us look openly at what he purchased. For he purchased it there where he paid the price [Note: [Col. 1500] Erasmus: ibi (“there”). Mss.].

For how much did he pay? If he paid for Africa, let us be Donatists—and let us not be called Donatists, but Christians—because Christ purchased Africa alone. Although even here the Donatists are not alone.

But he did not conceal in his contract what he purchased. He drew up the deed. Thanks be to God, he did not deceive us. The bride must hear it and understand there to whom she has vowed her virginity.

There, in the very Psalm where it says, “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones,” where the Lord’s Passion is declared most openly—a Psalm that is read every year during the final week, with the whole congregation attentive as Christ’s Passion approaches, and that is read both among us and among them—attend, brothers, to what he purchased there.

Let the commercial deed be read. Hear what he purchased there:

“All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship before him; for the kingdom is his, and he shall rule the nations” (Ps. XXI, 17–29).

Behold what he purchased. Behold that your bridegroom is God, the king of all the earth.

Why, then, do you wish to reduce such a rich man to rags? Recognize him: he purchased the whole, and you say, “You possess a part here.”

O, if you pleased the bridegroom! O, if you did not speak while corrupted—and, worse, corrupted in heart, not in body! You love a human being in place of Christ; you love the one who says, “I baptize.” You do not listen to the friend of the bridegroom saying, “This is the one who baptizes”; you do not listen to him saying, “He who has the bride is the bridegroom.”

“I do not have the bride,” he said. “But what am I? The friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice” (I Cor. XIII, 1).

15. Clearly, then, my brothers, it is of no benefit to these people to preserve virginity, practice continence, or give alms. All those things that are praised in the Church benefit them nothing, because they tear apart unity—that is, that garment of love.

What do they do? Many among them are eloquent, men of great speech, rivers of words. Do they speak in the language of angels?

Let them listen to the friend of the bridegroom, jealous for the bridegroom and not for himself: “If I speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels, but do not have love, I have become like resounding bronze or a clanging cymbal” (I Cor. XIII, 1).

16. But what do they say?

“We have Baptism.”

“You have it, but it is not yours. It is one thing to possess something, another to exercise mastery over it. You have Baptism because you received it in order to be baptized; you received it as one enlightened—provided that you have not been darkened by yourself. And when you give it, you give it as a minister, not as an owner; you cry out as a herald, not as a judge. The judge speaks through the herald, and yet in the records it is not written, ‘The herald said,’ but ‘The judge said.’

“Therefore, see whether what you give is yours by authority. But if you received it, confess with the friend of the bridegroom: ‘A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.’ Confess with the friend of the bridegroom: ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him.’

“But O, if you would stand and hear him, and not fall in order to hear yourself! By hearing him, you would stand and hear. For you speak and inflate your own head.

“‘I,’ says the Church, ‘if I am the bride, if I have received the pledge, if I have been redeemed by the price of his blood, hear the bridegroom’s voice. And I hear the voice of the bridegroom’s friend only when he gives glory to my bridegroom, not to himself.’

“Let the friend say, ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice.’”

“Behold, you have the sacraments.”

“And I grant you that you have them. You have the form, but you are a branch cut off from the vine. You display the form; I seek the root. Fruit does not come from the form except where there is a root; and where is the root except in love?

“And hear the form of the branches. Let Paul speak: ‘If I know all the sacraments and possess all prophecy and all faith’—and what faith!—‘so that I move mountains, but do not have love, I am nothing’” (I Cor. XIII, 1, 2).

17. Therefore, let no one sell you fables: “Pontius also performed a miracle”; “Donatus prayed, and God answered him from heaven.”

First, either they are deceived or they deceive. Finally, let him move mountains: “But if I do not have love,” he says, “I am nothing.”

Let us see whether he had love. I would believe it if he had not divided unity.

For God made me cautious also against these wonder-workers, so to speak, when he said: “In the last times false prophets will arise, performing signs and wonders, in order to lead astray, if possible, even the elect. Behold, I have foretold it to you” (Mark XIII, 22, 23).

Therefore the bridegroom made us cautious, because we must not be deceived even by miracles. Sometimes a deserter also frightens a provincial; but the person who does not wish to be frightened or led astray considers whether he is in the camp and whether that mark by which he has been sealed is of any benefit to him.

Let us therefore hold fast to unity, my brothers. Outside unity, even the one who performs miracles is nothing.

The people of Israel were in unity, and they did not perform miracles. Outside unity were Pharaoh’s magicians, and they performed things like those Moses performed (Exod. VII, 12, 22; VIII, 7). The people of Israel, as I said, did not perform them. Which were safe before God: those who performed them, or those who did not?

The Apostle Peter raised a dead man (Acts IX, 40); Simon Magus performed many things (ibid. VIII, 10). There were some Christians there who could perform neither what Peter performed nor what Simon performed. But what did they rejoice in? That their names were written in heaven.

When the disciples returned, our Lord Jesus Christ said this concerning the faith of the nations. For the disciples themselves returned exulting and said: “Lord, even the demons are subject to us in your name.”

They confessed well; they paid honor to Christ’s name. Yet what did he say to them?

“Do not rejoice in this, that the demons are subject to you; but rejoice because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 17–20).

Peter cast out demons. Some old widow—who knows who, some ordinary layman—possessing love and holding fast to the integrity of faith, does not do this. Peter is an eye in the body; that person is a finger in the body. Yet he is in the same body in which Peter is. And although a finger is less powerful than an eye, it is not cut off from the body.

It is better to be a finger and be in the body than to be an eye and be torn from the body.

18. Therefore, my brothers, let no one deceive you; let no one lead you astray. Love the peace of Christ, who was crucified for you, although he was God.

Paul says: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 7).

And does any one of us say that he is something? If we say that we are something and do not give glory to him, we are adulterers. We want to be loved, not the bridegroom.

Love Christ, and love us in him, in whom you too are loved by us. Let the members love one another, but let them all live under the head.
