In grief, my brothers, I have been compelled to say many things, and I have said only a little. I could not finish the reading [Note: [Col. 1502] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “and I said only a few things; yet I could not finish the reading.”]. The Lord will be present so that it may be finished at the proper time.

For I did not wish to burden your hearts further. I want them to be free for groans and for prayers on behalf of those who are still deaf and do not understand.

# TREATISE XIV

From the Gospel passage, “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled,” and so forth, up to, “But whoever is unbelieving toward the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.” Chapter III, verses 29–36.

1. This reading from the holy Gospel teaches us the excellence of the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ and the humility of the human being who deserved to be called the friend of the bridegroom, so that we may distinguish what difference there is between a human being and a human being who is God.

For our Lord Jesus Christ is a human being who is God: God before all ages, and a human being in our age; God from the Father, a human being from the Virgin; yet one and the same Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ, Son of God, God and human being.

John, however, was sent before him with outstanding grace, enlightened by the one who is light. For it was said of John: “He was not the light, but he came to bear witness to the light” (John I, 8).

He can indeed be called light, and he is rightly called light, but light that has been enlightened, not light that enlightens. For one kind of light is what illuminates, and another kind of light is what is illuminated. Our eyes too are called lights, yet they are open in darkness and do not see.

The light that illuminates is light from itself and light for itself. It does not need another light in order to shine; rather, other things need it in order to shine.

2. Therefore John confessed, as you have heard, that when Jesus was making many disciples and this was reported to him—as though to provoke him—“Behold,” they said, “he is making more disciples than you.” He confessed what he was, and thereby deserved to belong to Christ, because he did not dare to say that he was what Christ was.

This, then, is what John said: “A person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven.” Therefore Christ gives, and a human being receives.

“You yourselves bear witness to me that I said, ‘I am not the Christ,’ but that I was sent before him. ‘He who has the bride is the bridegroom; but the friend of the bridegroom, who stands and hears him, rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice’” (ibid. III, 26–29).

He did not make joy for himself from himself. For the one who wishes to rejoice in himself will be sad; but the one who wishes to rejoice in God will always rejoice, because God is eternal.

Do you wish to possess eternal joy? Cling to the one who is eternal.

John described himself in this way. “The friend of the bridegroom rejoices because of the bridegroom’s voice,” he says, not because of his own voice; “and he stands and hears him.”

If, then, he falls, he does not [Col. 1503] hear him. For it was said of one who fell, “He did not stand in the truth” (John VIII, 44); this was said of the devil.

Therefore the friend of the bridegroom ought to stand and hear.

What does “stand” mean? To remain in the grace he has received. And he hears the voice in which he may rejoice.

Such was John. He knew the source of his joy; he did not arrogate to himself what he was not. He knew that he had been enlightened, not that he was the enlightener.

“But it was the true light,” says the Evangelist, “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (ibid. I, 9).

If every human being, then John himself, because he too was among human beings. For although “no one has arisen greater than John among those born of women” (Matt. XI, 11), he too was nevertheless one of those born of women.

Can he be compared with the one who, because he wished to, was born—and therefore by a new birth, because he was newly born? Both of the Lord’s generations are extraordinary, the divine and the human: the divine has no mother; the human has no father.

John, then, was one of the rest, yet he possessed greater grace, so that among those born of women no one arose greater than he. He gave such a great testimony to our Lord Jesus Christ that he called Christ the bridegroom and himself the friend of the bridegroom, though not worthy to loosen his sandal strap.

Your Charity has already heard much about this. Let us see what follows, for it is somewhat dense to understand. But since John himself says that a person cannot receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven, whatever we do not understand, let us ask of the one who gives from heaven. For we are human beings and cannot receive anything unless the one who is not a human being gives it.

3. This, then, follows, and John says: “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.”

What is his joy? That he may rejoice at the bridegroom’s voice.

“It has been fulfilled in me. I have my grace; I do not claim more for myself, lest I lose even what I have received.”

What is this joy? “He rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom’s voice.”

Therefore let the human being understand that he ought not to rejoice in his own wisdom, but in the wisdom he has received from God. Let him seek nothing more, and he will not lose what he has found.

For many have become foolish because they said that they were wise. The Apostle rebukes them and says of them: “What can be known of God,” he says, “is manifest among them, for God has manifested it to them.”

Hear what he says concerning certain ungrateful and impious people: “For God has manifested it to them. For his invisible things, from the creation of the world, are understood and perceived through the things that have been made; likewise his eternal power and divinity, so that they are without excuse.”

Why “without excuse”? “Because although they knew God”—he did not say, “because they did not know”—“although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; instead, they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. Claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I, 19–22).

For if they had known God, they would also have known that God alone had made them wise. Therefore they should not have attributed to themselves what they did not possess from themselves, but to the one from whom they had received it.

By failing to give thanks, however, they became foolish. Thus God took away from the ungrateful what he had freely given.

John did not wish to be like this. He wished to be grateful. He confessed that he had received, and he said that he rejoiced because of the bridegroom’s voice, and he said: “Therefore this joy of mine has been fulfilled.”

[Col. 1504] 4. “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

What does this mean? “He must be exalted, but I must be humbled.”

How does Jesus increase? How does God increase? The perfect does not increase. God neither increases nor decreases. For if he increases, he is not perfect; if he decreases, he is not God.

How, then, does Jesus, who is God, increase? If it is in age, because he graciously consented to be human and was a child; and although he is the Word of God, he lay as an infant in a manger; and although he himself created his mother, he suckled infancy’s milk from his mother—if Jesus therefore grew in the age of his flesh, perhaps this is why it was said, “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

But why this as well? John and Jesus were of the same age with respect to the flesh: they were six months apart (Luke I, 36) and grew together. And if our Lord Jesus Christ had wished to remain here longer before his death, and had wished John himself to remain here with him, just as they had grown together, so they could have grown old together. Why, then, “He must increase, but I must decrease”?

First, because the Lord was already thirty years old (ibid. III, 23). Does a young man still grow if he is already thirty years old? From that age human beings already begin to decline and move toward a more serious age, and from there toward old age.

But even if both had been children, he would not have said, “He must increase, but I must decrease”; he would have said, “We must both grow together.”

Now, however, one was thirty years old, and the other thirty as well. The six months between them do not constitute a distinction in age. The reading has discovered this more readily than observation.

5. What, then, is “He must increase, but I must decrease”? It is a great mystery. Let your Charity understand.

Before the Lord Jesus came, human beings gloried in themselves. He came so that human glory might decrease and God’s glory increase.

For he came without sin and found everyone with sin. If he came in order to forgive sins, let God bestow freely and let the human being confess. For the confession of the human being is the humility of the human being; the mercy of God is the exaltation of God.

If, then, he came to forgive human beings their sins, let the human being acknowledge his humility, and let God perform his mercy.

“He must increase, but I must decrease.” That is: he must give, but I must receive; he must be glorified, but I must confess.

Let the human being understand his rank, confess to God, and hear the Apostle speaking to the proud and uplifted human being who wishes to exalt himself: “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

Let the human being understand, then, that he has received, since he wished to call his own what is not his; and let him decrease. For it is good for him that God be glorified in him. Let him decrease in himself, so that he may increase in God.

Christ and John also signified these testimonies and this truth by their sufferings. John was diminished by the cutting off of his head; Christ was exalted on the cross, so that there too it might appear what “He must increase, but I must decrease” means.

Furthermore, Christ was born when the days were already beginning to increase; John was born when the days began to decrease. [Col. 1505] Creation itself and the sufferings themselves bore witness to the words of John: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

Therefore let God’s glory increase in us, and let our glory decrease, so that our glory too may increase in God. For this is what the Apostle says; this is what holy Scripture says: “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord” (I Cor. I, 31; and Jer. IX, 23, 24).

Do you wish to boast in yourself? You wish to increase—but you increase badly, to your own harm. For the one who increases wrongly is rightly diminished.

Therefore let God increase—God who is always perfect—and let him increase in you. For the more you understand God, and the more you grasp, the more God appears to increase in you. In himself, however, he does not increase, but is always perfect.

Yesterday you understood a little; today you understand more; tomorrow you will understand much more. God’s light itself increases in you. Thus God appears to increase, although he always remains perfect.

It is as though someone’s eyes were being healed from their former blindness and he began to see a little light; on another day he saw more, and on the third day still more. The light would seem to increase for him; yet the light itself is perfect, whether he sees or does not see.

So it is with the inner human being. He does indeed progress in God [Note: [Col. 1505] The Vindocinensis manuscript has “toward God.”], and God appears to increase in him. Yet he himself decreases, so that he may fall away from his own glory and rise into the glory of God.

6. What we have just heard now appears distinctly and clearly. “The one who comes from above is above all.”

See what he says about Christ. What does he say about himself? “The one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth.”

“The one who comes from above is above all”: this is Christ.

“But the one who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth”: this is John.

Is this all? John is from the earth and speaks from the earth? Does the whole testimony he bears concerning Christ speak from the earth? Are no words of God heard from John when he bears witness to Christ?

How, then, does he speak from the earth?

He was speaking with respect to the human being himself. Insofar as he concerns the human being himself, he is from the earth and speaks from the earth. But if he speaks any divine things, he has been enlightened by God.

For if he had not been enlightened, earth would be speaking of earth.

Thus God’s grace is one thing, and human nature another. Ask human nature now: it is born and grows; it learns the customary things of human beings. What does it know except earth from earth? It speaks human things, knows human things, thinks human things; being carnal, it judges carnally and suspects carnally. Behold, this is the whole human being.

Let God’s grace come; let it enlighten his darkness, as it says: “You will light my lamp, O Lord; my God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII, 29). Let it take up the human mind and turn it [Note: [Col. 1505] The printed editions have “be turned.” The manuscripts have the better reading, “turn it,” namely, grace.] toward its own light.

Then he begins to say what the Apostle says: “Not I, but the grace of God with me” (I Cor. XV, 10); and, “I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II, 20).

This is: “He must increase, but I must decrease.”

Therefore John, insofar as he is John, is from the earth and speaks from the earth. If you have heard anything divine from John, it belongs to the one who enlightens, not to the one who receives.

### 7

“He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies; and no one accepts his testimony.” He comes from heaven; he is above all: our Lord Jesus Christ. Of him it was said above: “No one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). He is above all, and he speaks what he has seen and heard.

For the Son himself also has a Father; he has a Father, and he hears from the Father. And what is it that he hears from the Father? Who can explain this? When could my tongue, when could my heart, be sufficient—my heart to understand, or my tongue to express—what it is that the Son has heard from the Father? Perhaps the Son heard the Father’s Word? Rather, the Son is the Father’s Word.

You see how every human effort is exhausted here; you see how every conjecture of our breast fails here, and every effort of our darkened mind. I hear Scripture saying that the Son speaks what he hears from the Father; and again I hear Scripture saying that the Son himself is the Father’s Word: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

We speak words that fly away and pass. As soon as your word has sounded from your mouth, it passes; it completes its noise and passes into silence. Can you follow your sound and hold it so that it remains? Yet your thought remains, and from that abiding thought you speak many passing words.

What shall we say, brothers? When God spoke, did he employ a voice, sounds, and syllables? If he employed these, in what language did he speak—Hebrew, Greek, or Latin? Languages are necessary where there is a distinction of nations. But there no one can say that God spoke in this language or that language.

Attend to your own heart. When you conceive the word that you are going to speak—for I shall say, if I can, what we may observe in ourselves, not how we may comprehend it—when, then, you conceive the word that you are to utter, you wish to say something, and the conception of that thing is already a word in your heart. It has not yet proceeded forth, but it has already been born in the heart and remains there, waiting to proceed. You consider to whom it is to proceed, with whom you are speaking. If he is Latin-speaking, you seek a Latin sound; if he is Greek, you formulate Greek words; if he is Punic, you consider whether you know the Punic language. According to the diversity of your hearers, you employ different languages in order to express the word conceived. But what you had conceived in your heart was held by no language.

When God, therefore, was speaking and did not need to seek a language or assume any mode of expression [Note: [Col. 1506] All manuscripts read “elocutionis” (“of expression”).], how was he heard by the Son, when God himself spoke the Son? For just as you possess in your heart the word you speak, and it is with you, and its conception is spiritual—for just as your soul is spirit, so also the word you have conceived is spirit; it has not yet received sound so as to be divided into syllables, but remains in the conception of the heart and in the mirror of the mind [Note: [Col. 1506] Most manuscripts read “in the spectacle of the mind.”]—so God brought forth the Word, that is, begot the Son.

You, indeed, beget a word in your heart in time; God, without time, begot the Son, through whom he created all times. Since the Word was the Son of God, and the Son spoke to us—not his own word, but the Father’s Word—he wished to speak himself to us as the one who was speaking the Father’s Word. How this was fitting and necessary, John said. We have explained it as we were able.

Whoever has not yet received in his heart an understanding worthy of so great a matter has somewhere to turn, someone to whom he may knock, someone of whom he may ask, someone from whom he may seek, and someone from whom he may receive.

### 8

“He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies; and no one accepts his testimony.” If no one does, why did he come? It means, therefore, that no one among a certain group does. There is a people prepared for the wrath of God, to be condemned with the devil: none of these accepts Christ’s testimony.

For if absolutely no one did—if there were no human being at all—what is the meaning of what follows: “But he who accepts his testimony has certified that God is truthful”? Clearly, then, “no one” does not mean absolutely no one, since you yourself say, “He who accepts his testimony has certified that God is truthful.”

Perhaps John, if questioned, would answer and say: “I know what I said: ‘No one.’” There is indeed a people born for wrath and foreknown for this destiny. God knows who will believe and who will not believe; he knows who will persevere in what they have believed and who will fall away. All who are destined for eternal life are already numbered before God, and he already knows that distinct people. If he himself knows it, and gave the prophets knowledge of it through his Spirit, he also gave it to John.

John, therefore, was looking not with his own eye—for as far as John himself is concerned, he is earthly and speaks from the earth—but in that grace of the Spirit which he had received from God. He saw a certain impious and unbelieving people, and, observing them in their unbelief, he said: “No one accepts the testimony of him who came from heaven.”

Whom does “no one” mean? Those who will be on the left; those to whom it will be said: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels.” Who, then, accept it? Those who will be on the right; those to whom it will be said: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:41, 34).

Thus, in the spirit, John observed the division, while in the human race he observed the mingling. What has not yet been separated in place, he separated in understanding and in the vision of his heart. He saw two peoples, the faithful and the unfaithful. He looked upon the unfaithful and said: “He who comes from heaven is above all; and what he has seen and heard, this he testifies” [Note: [Col. 1507] The manuscripts read “speaks”; and afterward, where the printed edition has “transferred,” they read “removed.”]; “and no one accepts his testimony.”

Then he turned from the left and looked toward the right, and continued: “He who accepts his testimony has certified that God is truthful.”

What does “has certified that God is truthful” mean, except that the human being is a liar and God is truthful? No human being can speak what is true unless he is enlightened by the one who cannot lie. God, therefore, is truthful; and Christ is God. Do you wish to prove it? Accept his testimony, and you will find it: “He who accepts his testimony has certified that God is truthful.” Who is this? The one who came from heaven and is above all—he is the truthful God.

But if you do not yet understand him as God, you have not yet accepted his testimony. Accept it, and you certify it: boldly you understand, decisively you acknowledge, that God is truthful.

### 9

“For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God.” He is the truthful God, and God sent him: God sent God. Join the two: one God, the truthful God sent by God. Ask about each individually: God. Ask about both together: God. Not each individually a god and both together gods, but each individually God and both together God [Note: [Col. 1508] Thus all the manuscripts read. The printed editions have: “Not each individually gods and both together gods.”]

For so great is the love of the Holy Spirit there, so great the peace of unity, that when you ask about each individually, the answer given to you is “God”; and when you ask about the Trinity, the answer given to you is “God.”

If the human spirit, when it cleaves to God, is one spirit, as the Apostle plainly says, “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Corinthians 6:17), how much more is the Son, equal to the Father and cleaving to him, one God together with him?

Hear another testimony. You know how many believed when they sold everything they possessed and placed it at the apostles’ feet, so that it might be distributed to each according to need. And what does Scripture say about that assembly of holy people? “They had one soul and one heart in the Lord” (Acts 4:32).

If love made one soul out of so many souls and one heart out of so many hearts, how great is the love between the Father and the Son? Surely it can be greater than that which existed among those people who had one heart. If, then, the hearts of many brothers are one because of love, and the souls of many brothers are one because of love, will you say that God the Father and God the Son are two?

If there are two gods, there is not supreme love there. For if love here is so great that it makes your soul and your friend’s soul one soul, how could the Father and the Son not be one God there? May an unfeigned faith never think this.

Understand from this how greatly that love surpasses all others. There are many souls belonging to many human beings, and if they love one another, there is one soul; but they may still be called many souls, and may exist as such among human beings, because their union is not so complete. There, however, you may say “one God”; you may not say “two gods” or “three gods.” From this you are taught the supremacy and highest excellence of that love, so great that it cannot be greater.

### 10

“For he whom God has sent speaks the words of God.” He was speaking this about Christ, in order to distinguish himself from him. What then? Did God not also send John himself? Did he not say, “I have been sent before him” (John 3:28), and, “He who sent me to baptize in water” (John 1:33)? And was it not said of him: “Behold, I send my messenger before you, and he will prepare your way”? Did he not also speak the words of God, although it was even said of him that he was more than a prophet (Malachi 3:1; Matthew 11:10, 9)?

If God sent John himself, then, and he speaks the words of God, how are we to understand that John said this about Christ as a distinction: “He whom God has sent speaks the words of God”?

But consider what he adds: “For God does not give the Spirit by measure.” What does this mean: “God does not give the Spirit by measure”? We find that God does give the Spirit by measure. Hear the Apostle saying: “According to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4:7).

He gives to human beings by measure; to his only Son he does not give by measure. How does he give to human beings by measure? “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another faith in the same Spirit; to another prophecy; to another the discernment of spirits; to another kinds of tongues; to another gifts of healing” (1 Corinthians 12:8, 9, 10, 29, 30).

Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Are all powers? Do all possess gifts of healing? Do all speak in tongues? Do all interpret? One has one gift, another another; what one possesses, another does not possess. It is a measure, a certain division of gifts.

Thus gifts are given to human beings by measure, and there concord makes one body. Just as the hand receives one function in order to work, the eye another in order to see, the ear another in order to hear, and the foot another in order to walk, while the soul is nevertheless one and performs everything—in the hand, so that it may work; in the foot, so that it may walk; in the ear, so that it may hear; in the eye, so that it may see—so also are the various gifts of the faithful distributed according to their proper measure, as to members.

But Christ, who gives, does not receive by measure.

### 11

Hear still what follows, since he had said of the Son, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure”: “The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.”

He added, “He has given all things into his hand,” so that you might understand with what distinction “The Father loves the Son” was said here [Note: [Col. 1509] A manuscript from Remiremont reads, “because it was said as a distinction.”]

Why? Does the Father not love John? Yet he did not give all things into his hand. Does the Father not love Paul? Yet he did not give all things into his hand.

“The Father loves the Son”—but as a Father loves the Son, not as a master loves a servant; as he loves the Only-Begotten, not as he loves an adopted son. Therefore, “he has given all things into his hand.”

What does “all things” mean? It means that the Son is as great as the Father. For he begot him equal to himself, “for whom it was not robbery to be equal with God in the form of God” (Philippians 2:6).

“The Father loves the Son, and has given all things into his hand.” Therefore, when he deigned to send the Son to us, let us not think that something less than the Father was sent to us. In sending the Son, the Father sent another self.

### 12

For the disciples still thought that the Father was something greater than the Son. Seeing the flesh and not understanding the divinity, they said to him: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

It was as though they were saying: “We already know you, and we bless you because we know you. We give you thanks because you have shown yourself to us. But we do not yet know the Father. Therefore our heart burns and yearns with a certain holy desire to see your Father, who sent you. Show him to us, and we shall desire nothing more from you. For it is enough for us once he has been revealed, than whom no one can be greater.”

A good desire, a good longing—but a small understanding. The Lord Jesus, observing that they were small people seeking great things, and that he himself was great among the small and small among the small, said to Philip, one of the disciples who had spoken these words: “Have I been with you for so long a time, and you have not known me, Philip?”

Philip could have replied: “We have known you; but did we ever say to you, ‘Show us yourself’? We know you, but we are seeking the Father.”

He immediately added: “He who has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:8–9).

Since, then, the one equal to the Father was sent, let us not judge him by the weakness of the flesh, but let us consider the majesty clothed with flesh, not crushed by flesh. Remaining God with the Father, he became human among human beings, so that through the one who became human for you, you might become such as can receive God.

A human being could not receive God. A human being could see a human being, but could not receive God. Why could he not receive God? Because he did not possess the eye of the heart with which to receive him.

Something within, therefore, was wounded, while something outward was sound. He had sound eyes in his body, but wounded eyes in his heart. He became human for the bodily eye, so that, believing in him who could be seen bodily, you might be healed for seeing the very one whom you could not see spiritually [Note: [Col. 1510] The printed editions read “so that you might run.” The manuscripts agree in reading “so that you might be healed,” except for two manuscripts, which also read “so that you might be healed.”]

“Have I been with you for so long a time, and you have not known me, Philip? He who has seen me has seen the Father.”

Why did they not see the Father? Behold, they saw him, but they did not see the Father: they saw the flesh, but the majesty was hidden. What the disciples who loved him saw, the Jews who crucified him also saw. The whole of him, therefore, was within, and he was so within the flesh that he remained with the Father. For he did not abandon the Father when he came into the flesh.

### 13

Carnal thought does not comprehend what I am saying. Let it postpone understanding and begin from faith. Let it hear what follows: “He who believes in the Son has eternal life; but he who is disobedient to the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him.”

He did not say, “The wrath of God has come upon him,” but “The wrath of God remains upon him.”

All who are born mortal have the wrath of God with them. What wrath of God? The wrath received by the first Adam. For if the first human being sinned and heard, “You shall surely die” (Genesis 2:17), he became mortal, and we began to be born mortal. We were born under the wrath of God.

Then the Son came without sin and clothed himself with flesh; he clothed himself with mortality. If he shared the wrath of God with us, are we sluggish about sharing the grace of God with him?

Therefore, whoever does not wish to believe in the Son, the wrath of God remains upon him. What wrath of God? The wrath of which the Apostle says: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3). All, therefore, are children of wrath, because they come from the curse of death.

Believe in Christ, who became mortal for you, so that you may receive him as immortal. For when you have received his immortality, you too will not be mortal. He was living; you were dying. He died so that you might live.

He brought the grace of God and took away the wrath of God. God conquered death, so that death would not conquer humanity [Note: [Col. 1510] Thus several manuscripts of excellent quality read. The printed editions have: “He drank death, so that death would not drink humanity.”]

## TRACTATUS XV

From the Gospel passage beginning, “When Jesus therefore knew that the Pharisees had heard that Jesus was making and baptizing more disciples than John,” and continuing up to, “And we know that this is indeed the Savior of the world.” Chapter 4, verses 1–42.

### 1

Your Charity is not unfamiliar with the Evangelist John flying higher, like an eagle, rising above the earth’s darkness and gazing upon the light of truth with stronger eyes. For many passages from his Gospel have already been treated through our ministry, with the Lord’s help. In due order, then, there follows this reading which has been recited today. Many of you will hear what I am about to say, by the Lord’s gift, in such a way that you recognize it more than learn it. Nevertheless, your attention should not therefore be sluggish, because this is not knowledge but recognition.

This has been read, and we have in our hands this reading to be treated: what the Lord Jesus was saying to the Samaritan woman at Jacob’s well. Great mysteries were spoken there, and images of great realities—feeding the hungry soul and refreshing the weary one.

### 2

The Lord, “when he had heard that the Pharisees had learned that he was making more disciples and baptizing more than John (although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples), left the land of Judaea and departed again into Galilee.”

There is no need to dispute this at greater length, lest by lingering over what is clear we suffer a shortage of time for examining and opening what is obscure. Certainly, if the Lord had known that the Pharisees had learned of him in such a way that making more disciples and baptizing more would benefit them for salvation—so that they too might become disciples and might wish to be baptized by him—he would rather not have left the land of Judaea but would have remained there for their sake. But because he knew that their knowledge was accompanied by envy—for they had not learned this in order to follow him, but in order to persecute him—he departed from there.

He could indeed have remained present without being seized by them, if he had not wished it; he could have avoided being killed, if he had not wished it; for he could also have avoided being born, if he had not wished it. But because in everything he did as a human being he offered an example to human beings who would believe in him—for a servant of God does not sin if he withdraws to another place when he sees, perhaps, the fury of those persecuting him or seeking his life for evil purposes; yet the servant of God might seem to himself to sin in doing this unless the Lord had gone before him in doing it—the good teacher did this in order to teach, not because he was afraid.

### 3

Perhaps this also causes difficulty: why was it said, “Jesus was baptizing more than John,” and after it had been said, “he was baptizing,” there was added, “although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples”? What then? Was the statement false and corrected when it was added, “although Jesus himself did not baptize, but his disciples”? Or are both true, because Jesus both baptized and did not baptize?

He baptized, because he himself cleansed; he did not baptize, because he himself did not immerse. The disciples supplied the ministry of the body; he supplied the assistance of his majesty. For when would he cease baptizing, so long as he does not cease cleansing? Of him the same John said, speaking through the person of John the Baptist: “This is he who baptizes” (John 1:33). Therefore Jesus still baptizes; and for as long as we are being baptized, Jesus baptizes. Let a human being approach the lesser minister without fear, for he has a higher teacher.

### 4

But perhaps someone says: “Christ baptizes in the Spirit, not in the body.” As though anyone were imbued with the sacrament of bodily and visible Baptism by the gift of anyone other than him.

Do you wish to know that he himself baptizes not only in the Spirit but also in water? Hear the Apostle: “As Christ,” he says, “loved the Church and gave himself for her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word, so that he might present the glorious Church to himself, not having spot or wrinkle or anything of this kind” (Ephesians 5:25–27).

“Cleansing her.” By what means? “By the washing of water in the word.” What is Christ’s baptism? The washing of water in the word. Take away the water: it is not baptism. Take away the word: it is not baptism.

### 5

Now, having laid down these preliminary matters by which he came to converse with that woman, let us see what remains, full of mysteries and pregnant with sacraments.

“He had to pass through Samaria. So he came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the estate which Jacob gave to his son Joseph. Now Jacob’s well was there.”

It was a well; but every well is a spring, though not every spring is a well. For where water flows from the earth and is made available for those drawing it, it is called a spring. But if it is readily accessible and lies on the surface, it is called only a spring; if it is high up or deep below, it is called a well, without losing the name of spring.

### 6

Jesus, therefore, wearied from the journey, was sitting thus beside the spring. It was about the sixth hour.

Now the mysteries begin. For Jesus is not wearied without reason; the Power of God is not wearied without reason; he through whom the weary are refreshed is not wearied without reason; he whose departure makes us weary and whose presence strengthens us is not wearied without reason.

Yet Jesus is weary; he is weary from the journey, and he sits; he sits beside the well, and, wearied at the sixth hour, he sits. All these things suggest something; they wish to indicate something. They make us attentive and urge us to knock. May he himself, therefore, open both to us and to you, who deigned to urge us in this way by saying, “Knock, and it will be opened to you” (Matthew 7:7).

For your sake Jesus was wearied from the journey. We find Jesus as Power [Note: [Col. 1512] Four manuscripts read “the strong one.”], and we find Jesus as weakness; Jesus strong and weak. Strong, because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.” Do you wish to see how strong this Son of God is? “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made”; and they were made without labor. What, then, is stronger than the one through whom all things were made without labor?

Do you wish to know him as weak? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 3, 14). Christ’s strength created you; Christ’s weakness restored you. Christ’s strength brought it about that what did not exist should exist; Christ’s weakness brought it about that what existed should not perish. By his strength he created us; by his weakness he sought us.

### 7

Thus, in his weakness, he nourishes the weak, like a hen her chicks; for he made himself like this. “How often,” he says to Jerusalem, “I wished to gather your children under my wings, like a hen her chicks, and you were unwilling” (Matthew 23:37).

You see, brothers, how a hen becomes weak with her chicks. No other bird is recognized as being a mother. We see sparrows of every kind nesting before our eyes; every day we see swallows, storks, and doves nesting. Unless we see them in their nests, we do not recognize them as parents. But a hen becomes so weak with her chicks that even if the chicks themselves do not follow, though you do not see the children, you still recognize the mother.

She becomes like this, with wings drooping, feathers ruffled, voice hoarse, all her limbs lowered and cast down, so that, as I said, even if you do not see the children, you nevertheless recognize the mother.

Thus Jesus is weak, wearied from the journey. His journey is the flesh assumed for our sake. For how can one who is everywhere and absent nowhere have a journey? Where does he go, or from where does he come, unless it is because he would not come to us without assuming the form of visible flesh? Since he deigned to come to us in this manner, appearing in the assumed flesh of a servant, that assumption of flesh itself is his journey.

Therefore, what else does “wearied from the journey” mean than wearied in the flesh? Jesus is weak in the flesh; but do not you become weak. In his weakness be strong, because “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (1 Corinthians 1:25).

### 8

In this image of things, Adam, who “was a type of the one to come” (Romans 5:14), gave us a great indication of the mystery—indeed, God gave it through him. For while Adam slept, he merited receiving a wife, and a wife was made for him from his rib (Genesis 2:21), because the Church was destined to come from Christ while he slept on the cross, from his side—from the side, that is, of the one who slept. For from the side of the one hanging on the cross, struck by a lance (John 19:34), the sacraments of the Church flowed forth.

But why did I wish to say this, brothers? Because Christ’s weakness makes us strong. A great image preceded us there. God could have taken flesh from the man from which to make the woman, and this might seem more fitting. The weaker sex was being made, and weakness ought rather to have been made from flesh than from bone, for bones are stronger than flesh.

He did not take flesh from which to make the woman; rather, he took a bone, and when the bone had been removed, the woman was formed, while flesh was filled in its place. He could have restored bone for bone; he could have taken flesh rather than a rib to make the woman.

What, then, did he signify? The woman was made from the rib as though strong; Adam was made from flesh as though weak. Christ and the Church are one: his weakness is our strength.

### 9

Why, then, the sixth hour? Because it is the sixth age of the world. Count in the Gospel as one hour, one age, from Adam to Noah; the second from Noah to Abraham; the third from Abraham to David; the fourth from David to the deportation to Babylon; the fifth from the deportation to Babylon to the baptism of John. From there the sixth age is being enacted.

Why are you surprised? Jesus came, and in humbling himself he came to the well. He came wearied, because he bore weak flesh. The sixth hour, because it was the sixth age of the world. To the well, because he came to the depth of this dwelling of ours. Hence it is said in the Psalms: “From the depths I have cried to you, Lord” (Psalm 129:1).

He sat, as I said, because he was humbled [Note: [Col. 1513] Thus the manuscripts, together with the editions of Badius and Amerbach. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “he came humble.”]

### 10

And a woman came. She was a figure of the Church, not yet justified but already destined to be justified; for this is what the discourse is doing. She came ignorant, found him, and he dealt with her.

Let us see what happened, and why: “A woman came from Samaria to draw water.” The Samaritans did not belong to the Jewish nation; they were foreigners, although they inhabited neighboring lands. It would take too long to trace the origin of the Samaritans, lest much detain us and we fail to say what is necessary. It is enough, therefore, to count the Samaritans among foreigners.

And lest you think that I have said this more boldly than truthfully, hear the Lord Jesus himself, what he said about that Samaritan, one of the ten lepers whom he had cleansed, who alone returned to give thanks: “Were not ten cleansed? And where are the nine? Was no one else found to give glory to God except this foreigner?” (Luke 17:17–18).

It belongs to the image of the reality that this woman, who bore the type of the Church, came from foreigners. For the Church was destined to come from the Gentiles, foreign to the Jewish race.

Let us therefore hear ourselves in her, recognize ourselves in her, and give thanks to God for ourselves in her. For she was a figure, not the reality, since she too preceded the figure, and the reality came to be. For she believed in him who was displaying that figure to us through her.

She came, then, to draw water. She had simply come to draw water, as men or women customarily do.

### 11

“Jesus says to her: ‘Give me a drink.’ For his disciples had gone into the city to buy food. Therefore that Samaritan woman says to him: ‘How is it that you, though you are a Jew, ask a drink from me, who am a Samaritan woman?’ For Jews do not use vessels with Samaritans.”

You see that they were foreigners: Jews did not use their vessels at all. And because the woman was carrying a vessel with which she could draw water, she was surprised that a Jew asked her for a drink, something Jews were not accustomed to do.

But he who was asking for a drink was thirsting for the faith of that woman.

### 12

Finally, hear who it is that asks for a drink.

“Jesus answered and said to her: ‘If you knew the gift of God, and who it is that says to you, “Give me a drink,” you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.’”

He asks for a drink, and promises a drink. He is in need, as though he were about to receive; and he overflows, as though he were about to satisfy.

“If you knew,” he says, “the gift of God.” The gift of God is the Holy Spirit. But he still speaks secretly to the woman, and gradually enters her heart. Perhaps he is already teaching her. For what is sweeter and kinder than this exhortation?

“If you knew the gift of God, and knew who it is that says to you, ‘Give me a drink,’ you perhaps would ask, and he would give you living water.” Up to this point he suspends her expectation.

In ordinary usage, water that comes forth from a spring is called living water. Water collected from rain in pools or cisterns is not called living water. And if water has flowed from a spring and has collected in some place and stood there, no longer receiving the source from which it flowed, but its course having been interrupted [Note: [Col. 1514] The manuscripts read “inrupto,” that is, “irrupto.”], so that it has been separated from the channel of the spring, it is not called living water. Rather, that water is called living which is received while flowing.

Such water was in that spring. What, then, was he promising that he was asking for?

### 13

Nevertheless, the woman, still perplexed, says: “Lord, you have nothing with which to draw, and the well is deep.”

See how she understood “living water”: water, namely, that was in the spring. “You wish to give me living water, while I have what to draw with, and you have nothing. This living water is here; how will you give it to me?”

Understanding something else and thinking in a carnal way, she knocks, in a sense, so that the teacher may open what is closed. Her ignorance was knocking, not her eagerness; she was still to be pitied, not yet ready to be instructed.

### 14

The Lord says something more evident about that living water. The woman had said: “Can you be greater than our father Jacob, who gave us the well, and himself drank from it, and his sons and his livestock? You cannot give me this living water, because you have no vessel for drawing. Perhaps you promise another spring? Can you be better than our father, who dug this well and himself used it with his household?”

Let the Lord, then, say what he meant by living water.

“Jesus answered and said to her: ‘Everyone who drinks from this water will thirst again; but whoever drinks from the water that I shall give him will never thirst forever. Rather, the water that I shall give him will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life.’”

The Lord spoke more plainly: “It will become in him a spring of water leaping up into eternal life. Whoever drinks from this water will never thirst forever.”

What could be clearer—that he was promising not visible but invisible water? What could be clearer—that he was speaking not carnally but spiritually?

### 15

Yet the woman still thinks carnally. She was pleased at the prospect of not being thirsty, and thought that the Lord had promised this to her according to the flesh. Indeed, this will happen, but in the resurrection of the dead. That is what she wanted already.

For God had once granted his servant Elijah that for forty days he should neither hunger nor thirst (1 Kings 19:8). If he could grant this for forty days, could he not grant it forever?

She was nevertheless longing not to be in need, not to labor. She was compelled to come continually to that spring, to be burdened with the weight of the vessel, in order to supply her need; and when what she had drawn was exhausted, she was forced to return again. This labor was daily for her, because that need was refreshed, not extinguished.

Delighted, therefore, by such a gift, she asks him to give her the living water.

### 16

Nevertheless, let us not pass over the fact that the Lord was promising something spiritual. What does “Whoever drinks from this water will thirst again” mean?

It is true with respect to this water, and it is true with respect to what that water signified. For the water in the well is the pleasure of the world in a dark depth. From there people draw it with the jar of desire. They lower their desire downward, as it were, so that they may reach the pleasure drawn from the depth; and they enjoy the pleasure, with desire preceding and preparing the way.

For whoever has not first sent desire ahead cannot reach pleasure. Therefore, take the vessel as desire, and the water from the depth as pleasure. When someone reaches the pleasure of this world, it is food, drink, bathing, spectacle, sexual intercourse. Will he not thirst again?

Therefore, “Whoever drinks from this water,” he says, “will thirst again.” But if he receives water from me, he will not thirst forever. “We shall be satisfied,” he says, “with the good things of your house” (Psalm 64:5).

From what water, then, is he going to give, except that of which it is said, “With you is the fountain of life”? For how will those thirst who “shall be inebriated with the abundance of your house” (Psalm 35:10, 9)?

### 17

He was therefore promising a kind of richness and satiety of the Holy Spirit. She did not yet understand this; and, not understanding, what did she answer?

The woman says to him: “Lord, give me this water, so that I may not thirst, nor come here to draw.”

Need compelled her to labor, and weakness shrank from the labor. If only she had heard: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I shall refresh you” (Matthew 11:28). Jesus was saying this to her, so that she would no longer labor, but she did not yet understand.

### 18

Finally, wishing her to understand, Jesus says to her: “Go, call your husband and come here.”

What does “Call your husband” mean? Did he wish to give her that water through her husband? Or, because she did not understand, did he wish to teach her through her husband?

Perhaps it was in the manner of what the Apostle says about women: “If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home.” But it says, “Let them ask their husbands at home,” where Jesus is not present to teach. Hence it is said to the women whom the Apostle forbade to speak in the Church (1 Corinthians 14:35, 34).

But when the Lord himself was present and was speaking face to face, what need was there for him to speak to her through her husband? Did he speak through her husband to Mary, who sat at his feet and received his word, when Martha, occupied with much serving, was even complaining about her sister’s blessedness? (Luke 10:39–40).

Therefore, my brothers, let us hear and understand what the Lord said to the woman: “Call your husband.” Perhaps he also says this to our soul: “Call your husband.”

Let us inquire about the soul’s husband. Why is Jesus himself no longer the true husband of the soul? Let understanding be present, since what we are about to say can scarcely be grasped except by those who are attentive. Let understanding, then, be present so that it may be grasped; and that very understanding will perhaps be the husband of the soul.

19. Seeing, then, that the woman did not understand, and wishing her to understand, Jesus said, “Call your husband.” For this is why you do not know what I am saying: your understanding is not present. I speak according to the spirit; you hear according to the flesh. What I am saying pertains neither to the pleasure of the ears, nor to the eyes, nor to the sense of smell, nor to taste, nor to touch; it is grasped by the mind alone and received by the understanding alone. That understanding is not present in you; how, then, do you grasp what I am saying? “Call your husband”: bring forward your understanding.

What does it mean for you to have a soul? It is not a great thing, for even an animal has one. In what respect are you superior? Because you have understanding, which an animal does not have. What, then, does “Call your husband” mean? You do not grasp me; you do not understand me. I am speaking to you about God’s gift, but you are thinking of the flesh. You do not wish to thirst according to the flesh; I am addressing the spirit. Your understanding is absent: “Call your husband.”

Do not be like a horse or a mule, which have no understanding (Ps. 31:9). Therefore, my brothers, to have a soul and not to have understanding—that is, not to apply it and not to live according to it—is a beastlike life. There is indeed within us something beastlike, by which we live in the flesh; but it must be governed by the understanding. For the movements of a soul that moves according to the flesh and longs to overflow immoderately into carnal pleasures are governed from above by the understanding.

Who ought to be called the husband: the one who governs, or the one who is governed? Without doubt, when life is ordered, the understanding governs the soul, belonging as it does to that very soul. For the understanding is not something other than the soul, but something belonging to the soul—just as the eye is not something other than flesh, but something belonging to the flesh.

[Col. 1517] Although the eye is something belonging to the flesh, it alone enjoys the light. The other bodily members may be flooded with light, but they cannot perceive it; only the eye is both flooded with light and enjoys it. So, in our soul there is something called the understanding. This very part of the soul, which is called understanding and mind, is illuminated by a higher light. Now that higher light by which the human mind is illuminated is God: “For he was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

Christ was such a light; such a light was speaking with the woman. But her understanding was not present to be illuminated by that light—not merely flooded by it, but also to enjoy it. Thus the Lord was, as it were, saying: “I wish to illuminate, but there is no one here whom I may illuminate.” He said, “Call your husband”: apply the understanding by which you may be taught and by which you may be governed.

Therefore, regard the soul, apart from the understanding, as a woman; and having understanding as having a husband. But this husband does not govern his woman rightly unless he himself is governed by one higher. “The husband is the head of the woman, and Christ is the head of the husband” (1 Cor. 11:3). The head of the husband was speaking with the woman, but the husband was not present. It was as though the Lord were saying: “Apply your head, so that he may receive his head.” Therefore, “Call your husband and come here”—that is, be present, be at hand. You are as though absent while you do not understand the voice of the Truth who is present. Be present, but do not be present alone: be present with your husband.

20. Yet she still does not understand, even though that husband has not yet been called; she still thinks according to the flesh. The husband is absent. “I have no husband,” she says. And the Lord continues and speaks mysteries.

Understand that this woman truly did not then have a husband; but she was living with some man, I know not what, who was not a lawful husband—an adulterer rather than a husband. And the Lord says to her, “You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband.’” Why, then, did you tell her, “Call your husband”? And hear how well the Lord knew that she had no husband: he says to her, and so forth.

Lest the woman suppose that the Lord said, “You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband,’” because he had learned this from the woman rather than because he had known it by his divinity, hear something that you did not say: “For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband; this you have truly said.”

21. Again, we are compelled to investigate these five husbands with greater subtlety. Many have understood—certainly not absurdly or altogether improbably—the five husbands of this woman as the five books of Moses. [Note: [Col. 1517] Ambrose understood it in this way in *In Luc.*, chapters 14 and 20. Origen, together with Augustine, thought that the bodily senses were signified.] The Samaritans used these books, and they were under the same Law; indeed, circumcision also came to them from it.

But since what follows causes us difficulty—“And the one whom you now have is not your husband”—it seems to me that we can more easily take the five former husbands to be the five bodily senses of the soul. For whenever a person is born, before he is able to use his mind and reason, he is governed only by the senses of the flesh. In a small child, the soul desires or avoids whatever is heard, seen, smelled, tasted, or perceived by touch. It desires whatever delights these five senses and avoids whatever offends them. Pleasure delights these five senses; pain offends them.

According to these five senses, as though according to five husbands, [Col. 1518] the soul lives at first, because it is governed by them. Why, however, are they called husbands? Because they are legitimate. They were made by God and given by God to the soul.

The soul that is still governed by these five senses and acts under these five husbands is weak. But when it reaches the age at which reason can be exercised, if it receives sound discipline and instruction in wisdom, another husband does not succeed those five in governing it unless he is a true and legitimate husband, better than they, one who governs better and governs toward eternity, cultivating and instructing it for eternity.

For the five senses do not govern us toward eternity, but toward temporal things, whether to be desired or avoided. When, however, the understanding, imbued with wisdom, begins to govern the soul, it knows no longer merely how to avoid the pit and walk on level ground, as the eyes show the weak soul; nor merely how to hear melodious sounds pleasantly and reject discordant ones; nor how to delight in pleasant odors and reject foul ones; nor how to be captivated by sweetness and offended by bitterness; nor how to be soothed by what is smooth and hurt by what is rough. All these things are necessary for the weak soul.

What kind of governance, then, is supplied by that understanding? It will not distinguish white from black, but just from unjust, good from evil, useful from useless; chastity from unchastity, so that it may love the one and avoid the other; charity from hatred, so that it may abide in the one and not abide in the other.

22. This husband had not succeeded those five husbands in this woman. For where he does not succeed, error dominates. When the soul becomes capable of reason, it is governed either by a wise mind or by error. But error does not govern; it destroys.

Thus, after those five senses, that woman was still wandering, and error was tossing her about. That error was not a legitimate husband but an adulterer. Therefore the Lord said to her, “You have spoken well in saying, ‘I have no husband.’ For you have had five husbands: the five senses of the flesh governed you first. You came to the age at which reason is to be used, but you did not attain wisdom; instead, you fell into error. Therefore, after those five husbands, the one whom you now have is not your husband.”

And what was he, if he was not a husband, except an adulterer? Therefore call not the adulterer but your husband, so that you may grasp me through understanding and not form some false notion about me through error. The woman was still in error, thinking of that water, while the Lord was already speaking about the Holy Spirit. Why was she in error, unless because she had an adulterer rather than a husband? Therefore remove from here this adulterer who corrupts you, and go, call your husband. Call him and come, so that you may understand me.

23. The woman said to him, “Lord, I see that you are a prophet.” The husband had begun to come, but had not yet come fully. She thought the Lord was a prophet. Indeed, he was also a prophet, for he said of himself, “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Luke 4:24). It was likewise said of him to Moses, “I will raise up for them a prophet from among their brothers, like you” (Deut. 18:18)—like him, that is, in the form of the flesh, not in the eminence of majesty.

Thus we find the Lord Jesus called a prophet. Accordingly, this woman is no longer greatly in error. “I see,” she says, “that you are a prophet.” She begins to call her husband and exclude the adulterer: “I see that you are a prophet.” And she begins to ask about what usually troubled her.

There had been contention between the Samaritans and the Jews, because the Jews worshiped God in the temple built by Solomon, [Col. 1519] while the Samaritans, living far away, did not worship there. For this reason the Jews boasted that they were superior, because they worshiped God in the temple.

The Jews did not associate with the Samaritans. They said to them: “How can you boast and claim that you are better than we are because you have a temple that we do not have? Did our fathers, who pleased God, worship in that temple? Did they not worship on this mountain, where we are? We therefore pray to God better on this mountain, where our fathers prayed.”

Both sides contended in ignorance, because they had no husband: the Jews were puffed up on behalf of the temple, the Samaritans on behalf of the mountain, and they opposed one another.

24. What, then, does the Lord now teach the woman, as though her husband had begun to be present? The woman says to him, “Lord, I see that you are a prophet. Our fathers worshiped on this mountain, and you say that Jerusalem is the place where one ought to worship.” [Note: [Col. 1519] In the manuscripts, *est locus ubi* is omitted.]

Jesus says to her, “Woman, believe me.” For the Church will come, as it is said in the *Song of Songs*: “She will come and pass over from the beginning of faith” (Song 4:8, according to the Septuagint). She will come in order to pass over, and she cannot pass over except from the beginning of faith.

Appropriately, now that her husband is present, she hears, “Woman, believe me.” For there is already within you one who can believe, because your husband is present. You began to be present in understanding when you called me a prophet. “Woman, believe me,” because “unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore, “Woman, believe me, because the hour is coming when you will worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem. You worship what you do not know; we worship what we know, because salvation is from the Jews.”

“But the hour is coming”—when? “And now it is.” What hour is this? When true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth—not on this mountain, not in the temple, but in spirit and truth. For the Father also seeks such people to worship him.

Why does the Father seek such people to worship him—not on the mountain, not in the temple, but in spirit and truth? “God is spirit.” If God were a body, he ought to be worshiped on a mountain, because a mountain is corporeal; he ought to be worshiped in a temple, because a temple is corporeal. God is spirit, and those who worship him ought to worship in spirit and truth.

25. We have heard it, and it is clear: we had gone outside, and we have been sent inside. “If only,” you were saying, “I could find some high and solitary mountain! For I believe that God is in a high place and that from a height he will hear me more readily.”

Because you are on a mountain, do you think that you are near God and will quickly be heard, as though you were shouting from nearby? He dwells in high places, but he regards the lowly. “The Lord is near.” To whom? Perhaps to the lofty? No: to those who have crushed their heart (Ps. 34:18).

It is a marvelous thing: he both dwells in high places and draws near to the humble; he regards the lowly, but “the lofty he knows from afar” (Ps. 138:6). He sees the proud from afar, and is less near to them the higher they seem to themselves.

You were seeking a mountain; descend in order to reach it. But you wish to ascend? Ascend—do not seek a mountain. “The ascents,” the Psalm says, “are in his heart, in the valley of weeping” (Ps. 84:5–6). A valley signifies humility.

Therefore do everything inwardly. And if perhaps you are seeking some high place, [Col. 1520] some holy place, present yourself inwardly as a temple to God. “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). Do you wish to pray in the temple? Pray within yourself. But first be God’s temple, because he will hear the one who prays in his temple.

26. “The hour is coming, and now is, when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth. We worship what we know; you worship what you do not know, because salvation is from the Jews.”

He gave much to the Jews; but do not understand this as referring to the rejected Jews. Understand it as referring to that wall to which another wall has been joined, so that, pacified in the cornerstone—which is Christ—they may be united. One wall is from the Jews and one from the Gentiles. These walls are far from one another until they are joined at the corner.

The Gentiles were “strangers and foreigners to the covenants of God” (Eph. 2:12–22). In this sense, then, it was said, “We worship what we know.” It was said in the person of the Jews, but not of all Jews—not of the rejected Jews. It was said of those from whom the Apostles came, of those from whom the Prophets came, of all those holy people who sold all they possessed and placed the proceeds of their possessions at the feet of the Apostles (Acts 4:34–35). For “God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:2).

27. This woman heard this and added something. A little earlier she had called him a prophet. She saw him saying things that went beyond what a prophet would say [Note: [Col. 1520] In six manuscripts, “went beyond a prophet” (*plus esset a propheta*).], and observe what she answered:

The woman said to him, “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will declare all things to us.”

What does this mean? “At present,” she says, “the Jews contend about the temple and we contend about the mountain. When he comes, he will despise the mountain and overturn the temple; he will teach us all things, so that we may know how to worship in spirit and truth.”

She knew who could teach her, but she did not yet recognize the one who was already teaching her. She was now worthy, therefore, to have him revealed to her.

“Messiah” means “anointed”; in Greek, *Christos*; in Hebrew, *Messias*. Hence in Punic also *Messe* means “anoint.” These languages are related and neighboring languages: Hebrew, Punic, and Syriac.

28. Therefore the woman says to him, “I know that the Messiah is coming, who is called Christ; when he comes, he will announce all things to us.”

Jesus says to her, “I am he, the one speaking with you.”

She called her husband; he became the head of the woman, and Christ became the head of the husband (1 Cor. 11:3). The woman is now being ordered in faith and is being well governed so that she may live rightly.

After she heard, “I am he, the one speaking with you,” what more could she say—when Christ the Lord wished to reveal himself to the woman to whom he had said, “Believe me”?

29. And immediately his disciples came, and they marveled that he was speaking with a woman. They marveled because he had come to seek what had perished and was seeking the lost. They marveled at something good; they did not suspect anything evil. Nevertheless, no one said, “What are you seeking, or why are you speaking with her?”

30. The woman therefore left her water jar. After hearing, “I am he, the one speaking with you,” and receiving Christ the Lord into her heart, what could she do except leave her jar and run to evangelize? She cast away her desire and hurried [Col. 1521] to announce the truth.

Let those who wish to evangelize learn to cast away the jar at the well. Recall what I said earlier about the jar: it was a vessel from which water was drawn; in Greek it is called *hydria*, because in Greek ὕδωρ means “water”—as though it were called an “aquarium.”

She therefore cast away the jar, which was no longer useful but had become a burden. For she had eagerly desired to be satisfied with that water. To announce Christ, she cast off the burden, ran to the city, and said to the men there: “Come, and see a man who told me everything I have done.” She proceeded cautiously, lest they become angry, indignant, and persecute her: “Come, and see a man who told me everything I have done. Can he possibly be the Christ?”

They went out from the city and were coming to him.

31. Meanwhile his disciples were asking him, saying, “Rabbi, eat.” They had gone to buy food and had returned. But he said to them, “I have food to eat of which you do not know.”

The disciples therefore said to one another, “Has someone brought him something to eat?”

What wonder if that woman did not understand the water? Behold, the disciples still do not understand the food.

But he heard their thoughts and now teaches them as a teacher—not indirectly, as he had taught the woman who still had to seek her husband, but openly: “My food,” he says, “is to do the will of him who sent me.”

Therefore that woman herself was also the drink, so that he might do the will of the one who had sent him. For this reason he said, “I thirst; give me to drink”—namely, so that he might work faith in her, drink her faith, and transfer her into his body; for his body is the Church.

“Therefore,” he says, “my food is to do the will of him who sent me.”

32. “Do you not say that there are still four months, and then the harvest comes?” He was ardently engaged in the work and preparing to send workers.

“You count four months until the harvest; I show you another harvest, white and ready. Behold, I tell you: lift up your eyes and see that the fields are already white for harvest.”

Therefore he is about to send reapers. “For in this the saying is true: one is he who sows, another he who reaps, so that the one who sows may rejoice together with the one who reaps. I sent you to reap what you did not labor for; others have labored, and you have entered into their labor.”

What does this mean? Did he send reapers, not sowers? Where did he send the reapers? Where others had already labored. For where the labor had already been done, certainly the sowing had already taken place; and what had been sown had already ripened and required the sickle and threshing floor.

Where, then, were the reapers to be sent? Where the Prophets had preached—for they were the sowers. If they were not sowers, how had the woman come to say, “I know that the Messiah is coming”? This woman was already ripe fruit; the harvests were white and were seeking the sickle.

“I sent you, therefore, to reap.” Where? “To reap what you did not sow; others have sown, and you have entered into their labors.”

Who labored? Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob themselves. Read their labors: in all their labors there was a prophecy of Christ; therefore they were sowers. Moses and the other Patriarchs and all the Prophets—how much they endured in that cold season when they were sowing!

Therefore the harvest in Judea [Col. 1522] was already prepared. It was rightly like a ripe crop when many thousands of people brought the proceeds of their possessions, placed them at the feet of the Apostles, and, with their shoulders freed from worldly burdens, followed Christ the Lord: truly a ripe harvest.

What happened from that harvest? A few grains were taken from it and sowed throughout the world, and another harvest arose, to be reaped at the end of the age. Of this harvest it is said, “Those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 126:5).

For this harvest, then, not Apostles but angels will be sent. “The reapers,” he says, “are angels” (Matt. 13:39). This harvest grows among the weeds and awaits cleansing at the end. But that harvest was already ripe—the one to which the disciples were first sent, where the Prophets had labored.

Nevertheless, brothers, observe what was said: “Let the one who sows and the one who reaps rejoice together.” They had labors belonging to different times [Note: [Col. 1522] In three manuscripts, *disparis* (“of unequal [times]”).], but they will enjoy the same joy and receive their reward together: eternal life.

33. Many Samaritans from that city believed in him because of the word of the woman, who testified, “He told me everything I have done.”

When the Samaritans came to him, they asked him to remain with them, and he stayed there two days. Many more believed because of his word. And they said to the woman, “We no longer believe because of what you said; for we ourselves have heard him, and we know that this is truly the Savior of the world.”

This deserves a little attention, because the reading has come to an end. The woman first announced him, and at the woman’s testimony the Samaritans believed. They asked him to remain with them, and he stayed there two days; many more believed. And when they had believed, they said to the woman, “We no longer believe because of your word; we ourselves have come to know, and we know that he truly is the Savior of the world.” First through report, afterward through his presence. [Note: [Col. 1522] Lovaniensis reads *per feminam* (“through the woman”); the other printed editions and the manuscripts differ.]

This is what happens today with those who are outside and are not yet Christians. Christ is announced through Christian friends. As they came to Christ through the woman—that is, through the announcing Church—so they come through this report and believe. He remains with them for two days—that is, he gives them the two commandments of love—and many more believe in him, and believe more firmly, because he truly is the Savior of the world.

# TREATISE XVI

From the Gospel passage, “After the two days he departed from there and went into Galilee,” to “He himself believed, and his whole household.” Chapter 4, verses 43–53.

1. Today’s Gospel reading follows yesterday’s reading, which is presented to us for discussion. Its meanings are not difficult to investigate, but they are worthy of proclamation, admiration, and praise. Therefore let us recall this passage of the Gospel with commendation rather than treat it as a difficulty.

Jesus went into Galilee, where he had been brought up, after the two days he had spent in Samaria. The Evangelist then says: “For Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country” [Col. 1523] (John 4:43–44).

Jesus did not leave Samaria after the two days because he had no honor in Samaria; Samaria was not his country, but Galilee. Since, then, he left Samaria so quickly and came to Galilee, where he had been brought up, how does the Evangelist testify that a prophet has no honor in his own country? It would seem that he could have testified more appropriately that a prophet has no honor in his own country if Jesus had refused to go to Galilee and had remained in Samaria.

2. Therefore let your Charity attend to the not insignificant mystery that has been disclosed to us, with the Lord suggesting and granting what I am to say. You know the question that has been proposed; seek its solution. But let us repeat the proposition, so that we may make the solution desirable.

What troubles us is why the Evangelist said, “Jesus himself testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country.” Moved by this, we retraced the preceding words, so that we might discover why the Evangelist wished to say this. We find that his preceding words recount that Jesus departed from Samaria for Galilee after two days.

“For this reason, then, Evangelist, you said that Jesus testified that a prophet has no honor in his own country: because after two days he left Samaria and hurried to come to Galilee?”

On the contrary, it seems to me that I understand more appropriately that if Jesus had no honor in his own country, he would not have hurried there after leaving Samaria. But if I am not mistaken—or rather, because this is true, I am not mistaken—the Evangelist understood what he was saying better than I do. He saw the truth better than I, since he drank it from the Lord’s breast.

For he is John the Evangelist, who reclined upon the Lord’s breast among all the disciples, and whom the Lord, although owing love to all, loved more than the others (John 13:25; 21:20). Could he then have been mistaken, while I understood correctly? On the contrary, if I think piously, I will obediently listen to what he said, so that I may deserve to understand what he understood.

3. Receive, then, dearest brothers, what I think here, without prejudice, if you have understood something better. We all have one Teacher, and we are fellow disciples in one school. This is what I think; see whether what I think is not true or at least close to the truth.

He spent two days in Samaria, and the Samaritans believed in him. He spent so many days in Galilee, and the Galileans did not believe in him.

Retrace or recall yesterday’s reading and sermon. He came to Samaria, where that woman had first preached him—the woman with whom he had spoken at Jacob’s well about great mysteries. When the Samaritans saw and heard him, they believed in him because of the woman’s word; they believed more firmly because of his word, and many more believed. So it is written.

After spending two days there—the number of days mystically commending the number of the two commandments, on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matt. 22:37–40), as you remember our having commended yesterday—he proceeded into Galilee and came to the Galilean city of Cana, where he had made water into wine.

When he converted water into wine, as John himself records, his disciples believed in him (John 2:1–11) [Col. 1524]. The house, of course, was filled with crowds of guests at the feast. So great a miracle was performed, and no one believed in him except his disciples.

Now he returned to this Galilean city. And behold, a certain royal official, whose son was ill, came to him and began to ask him to go down to that city or house and heal his son, for he was beginning to die.

Did the man who asked believe? What do you expect me to tell you? Ask the Lord what he thought about him. When asked, he answered: “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.”

He rebuked the man as lukewarm or cold in faith, or altogether without faith: a man who wished to test, through the health of his son, what kind of person Christ was, who he was, and how much power he possessed. We heard the words of the man making the request, but we do not see the heart of the one who doubted. Yet the one who heard the words and examined the heart declared the truth.

Finally, the Evangelist himself shows through the testimony of his narrative that the man who wanted the Lord to come to his house to heal his son had not yet believed.
