For after it was announced to him that his son was well, and he discovered that he had been healed at the very hour when the Lord had said, “Go, your son lives,” the Evangelist says, “He himself believed, and his whole household.”

If, then, he himself and his whole household believed because his son was reported well, and because he compared the hour of the report with the hour foretold by the Lord, then when he was making his request he did not yet believe.

The Samaritans had not awaited any sign; they had believed his word alone. But his fellow citizens deserved to hear, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” And yet, after so great a miracle had been performed there, only he and his household believed.

Many Samaritans believed at the mere word; only that household believed at the miracle that took place there.

What, then, brothers, what does the Lord commend to us? At that time Galilee was the Lord’s country according to the flesh, because he had been brought up there. But now, because that event signified something—for signs are not called signs without reason, unless they signify something—let us understand the matter as pointing to something.

A miracle is called a *prodigium*, as though it were a *porrodicium*, something that speaks or signifies what lies ahead and foretells that something will occur. [Note: [Col. 1524] In most manuscripts, *prodicium*.] Since, therefore, all those things pointed to something and foretold something, let us now make the Jewish people the country of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh. For he had no country on earth except according to the flesh that he received on earth.

Let us therefore make the Jewish people the Lord’s country. Behold, in his own country he has no honor.

Now observe the Jewish crowds; observe that nation already dispersed throughout the whole world and torn up by the roots; observe the branches broken, cut off, scattered, and dried up, into which the wild olive was deemed worthy to be grafted (Rom. 11:17).

Look at the Jewish crowd. What does it say now? “The one whom you worship and adore was our brother.”

And let us answer: “A prophet has no honor in his own country.”

They saw the Lord Jesus walking on earth and working miracles: illuminating the blind, opening the ears of the deaf, loosening the mouths of the mute, strengthening the limbs of the paralyzed, walking upon the sea, commanding the winds and the waves, raising the dead. They saw him performing so many signs, and scarcely [Col. 1525] a few of them believed.

I am speaking to the people of God: we have believed, though we are so many—what signs did we see? Therefore what happened then foreshadowed what is happening now.

The Jews were—or are—like the Galileans; we are like those Samaritans. We heard the Gospel, assented to the Gospel, and through the Gospel believed in Christ. We saw no signs and demanded none.

4. Although he was one of the twelve chosen and holy men, Thomas was nevertheless an Israelite, belonging to the Lord’s people—the Thomas who wished to put his fingers into the places of the wounds. The Lord rebuked him as he had rebuked the royal official.

To the royal official he said, “Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.” To Thomas he said, “Because you have seen me, you have believed.”

Why, unless because “a prophet has no honor in his own country”? But because this prophet has honor among foreigners, what follows? “Blessed are those who have not seen and yet have believed” [Note: [Col. 1525] The manuscripts read, “who do not see and believe.”] (John 20:25–29). We were foretold by this saying, and what the Lord previously praised he has deigned to fulfill in us.

Those who crucified him saw him and touched him, and only a few believed. We have not seen him or touched him; we heard and believed. May the blessedness that he promised be made real and perfected in us—both here, because we have been placed above his country, and in the age to come, because we have been grafted in place of the broken branches.

5. He showed that he would break off those branches and graft in this wild olive when, moved by the faith of the centurion, who said to him, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof; but only say the word, and my child will be healed. For I too am a man set under authority, having soldiers under me; and I say to this one, ‘Go,’ and he goes; and to another, ‘Come,’ and he comes; and to my servant, ‘Do this,’ and he does it,” he turned to those who followed him and said, “Amen I say to you, I have not found such faith in Israel.”

Why did he not find such faith in Israel? Because “a prophet has no honor in his own country.”

Could the Lord not also have said to that centurion what he said to this royal official: “Go, your child lives”? Observe the distinction.

This royal official wanted the Lord to go down to his house; the centurion said that he was unworthy. To the one it was said, “I will come [Note: [Col. 1525] Lovaniensis reads, “I will come” (*Ego veniam*); the other books read, “I come” (*Ego venio*).] and heal him”; to the other it was said, “Go, your child lives.” To the one he promised his presence; the other he healed by his word.

This man nevertheless extorted his presence; the other declared himself unworthy of his presence. Here, pride was yielded to; there, humility was granted.

It was as though the Lord were saying to this man: “Go, your child lives; do not trouble me. ‘Unless you see signs and wonders, you do not believe.’ You want my presence in your house; I can also command by my word. [Col. 1526] Do not believe because of signs. The foreigner believed that I could accomplish it by my word, and he believed before I acted; you do not believe unless you see signs and wonders.”

Therefore, if this is so, let the proud branches be broken off, and let the humble wild olive be grafted in. Nevertheless, let the root remain, with those branches cut away and these received.

Where does the root remain? In the Patriarchs. For Israel is Christ’s country, because he came from them according to the flesh. But the root of this tree is Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the holy Patriarchs.

And where are they? In rest with God, in great honor. Thus, after his departure from the body, that poor man was helped and lifted into Abraham’s bosom, and from far away was seen in Abraham’s bosom by the proud rich man (Luke 16:22–23). [Note: The editions of Amerbach, Badus, and Erasmus read *justus* (“the righteous man”). The manuscript of Vindocinensis reads *ad justos* (“to the righteous”). Other manuscripts, together with Lovaniensis, read *adjutus* (“helped”); this word itself is the interpretation of Lazarus’s name.]

The root remains; the root is praised. But the proud branches deserved both to be cut off and to wither, while the humble wild olive found room through their cutting off.

6. Hear, then, how the natural branches are cut off and how the wild olive is grafted in, from the very centurion whom I thought ought to be mentioned for comparison with this royal official.

“Amen,” he says, “I tell you, I have not found such faith in Israel. Therefore I tell you that many will come from the east and the west.”

How widely the wild olive had spread across the earth! This world was a bitter forest. But because of humility—because he said, “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof”—“many will come from the east and the west.”

And suppose that they will come: what will happen to them? If they will come, they have already been cut off from the forest. Where will they be grafted, so that they may not wither?

“They will recline,” he says, “with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.”

At what banquet? Perhaps you do not invite them to live forever, but to drink a great deal? “They will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” Where? “In the kingdom of heaven,” he says.

And what will happen to those who came from Abraham’s stock? What will happen to the branches with which the tree was full? What, except that they will be cut off so that these may be grafted in?

Prove that they will be cut off: “But the sons of the kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (Matt. 8:5–12).

7. Let the Prophet therefore have honor among us, because he did not have honor in his own country. He did not have honor in the country in which he was created; let him have honor in the country he founded. For in that country the Creator of all was created, created there according to the form of a servant. Indeed, he himself founded the very city in which he was formed, that very Zion, that very nation of the Jews, that very Jerusalem, when he was with the Father as the Word of God: “For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.” Of that man, therefore, whom we heard of today, “the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5), the Psalm also foretold, saying, “A man shall say, Mother Zion.” A certain man, the mediator between God and human beings, the man, says, “Mother Zion.” Why does he say, “Mother Zion”? Because from there he received flesh; from there came the Virgin Mary, from whose womb the form of a servant was assumed, in which he deigned to appear in the deepest humility. “A man shall say, Mother Zion,” and this man who says, “Mother Zion,” was made in her, was made a man in her. For he was God before her, and he was made man in her. He who was made man in her, “the Most High himself founded her” (Ps. 86:5), not the one who was most humble. He was made man in her in humility, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us”; “the Most High himself founded her,” because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; “all things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3, 14). Since he founded this country, therefore, let him have honor here. His own country, in which he was born, rejected him; let the country he regenerated receive him.

## TRACTATE XVII

From the passage written, “After this there was a feast of the Jews, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem,” to the passage, “The Jews were seeking to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.” Chapter 5, verses 1–18.

### 1

There should be nothing astonishing about a miracle performed by God; it would be astonishing if a human being had performed it. We ought to rejoice more than marvel [Note: [Col. 1527] Thus the printed editions and manuscripts read. Perhaps through a scribal error, *quam mirari* was substituted for *et admirari*, or, as they formerly wrote, *et ammirari*.], because our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ became human, than because God, while among human beings, performed something divine. For what he became for our salvation is greater than what he did among human beings; and what he did to heal the diseases of souls is greater than what he did to heal the illnesses of mortal bodies. But because the soul itself did not yet know the one by whom it was to be healed, and had eyes in the flesh with which it could see bodily things, but did not yet have a sound heart with which to recognize the hidden God, he did what it could see, so that it might be healed in the part through which it could not see.

He entered a place where a great multitude of sick people, blind, lame, and withered, were lying. Although he was the physician of souls and bodies, and had come to heal all the souls of those who would believe, he chose one of those sick people to heal, in order to signify unity. If we consider the one performing the deed with a mediocre understanding, as it were with human perception and intelligence, then, as far as power was concerned, he accomplished nothing remarkable, and as far as kindness was concerned, he did little [Note: [Col. 1527] In the manuscripts, *parvum* (“a small thing”).]. So many were lying there, yet only one was healed, although he could have raised them all with a single word. What, then, are we to understand except that that power and kindness were concerned more with what souls were to understand from his deeds for eternal salvation than with what bodies deserved for temporal salvation?

For the bodily salvation that is truly awaited from the Lord will come at the end, in the resurrection of the dead. Then what lives will not die; what is healed will not become sick; what is satisfied will not hunger or thirst; what is renewed will not grow old. But now, in those deeds of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the eyes of the blind that were opened were closed by death; the limbs of the paralytics that had been strengthened were dissolved by death; and whatever was healed temporarily in mortal limbs eventually failed. But the soul that believed passed over into eternal life.

Thus, for the believing soul whose sins he had come to forgive, and for whose illnesses he had humbled himself, he gave a great sign through the healing of this sick man. I shall speak, as I am able, of the profound mystery of this matter and sign, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant it, while you attend and assist our weakness by your prayers. Whatever I cannot do, he himself, with whose help I do what I can, will supply in you.

### 2

I remember having often discussed that pool which was surrounded by five porticoes, in which a great multitude of sick people lay; and I am about to speak of something that many of you will recognize with me rather than learn. Yet there is nothing inappropriate in repeating even what is familiar, so that those who did not know it may be instructed and those who did know it may be strengthened. Accordingly, what is familiar should be touched on briefly, not repeated at tedious length.

That pool and that water seem to me to have signified the Jewish people. That peoples are signified by the name “waters” is plainly indicated to us by the Apocalypse of John, where, when many waters were shown to him and he asked what they were, he received the answer that they were peoples (Rev. 17:15). That water, then—that people—was enclosed by the five books of Moses, as if by five porticoes. But those books exposed the sick; they did not heal them. For the Law convicted sinners; it did not absolve them. Thus the letter without grace made guilty those whom grace liberated when they confessed.

For the Apostle says this: “If a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the Law.” Why, then, was the Law given? He continues and says: “But Scripture imprisoned all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ” (Gal. 3:21–22). What could be clearer? Did these words not explain to us both the five porticoes and the multitude of sick people? The five porticoes are the Law. Why did the five porticoes not heal the sick? Because “if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would truly have come from the Law.” Why, then, did they contain those whom they did not heal? Because “Scripture imprisoned all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ.”

### 3

What, then, happened so that those who could not be healed in the porticoes might be healed in that troubled water? The water would suddenly appear troubled, but by whom it was troubled could not be seen. You may believe that this ordinarily happened through angelic power, yet not without some sacramental sign.

After the water had been troubled, one person who was able would enter it, and he alone would be healed; whoever entered after him would act in vain. What, then, does this mean except that the one Christ came to the Jewish people? By doing great things and teaching what was useful, he troubled sinners; by his presence he troubled the water and stirred it toward his Passion. Yet he troubled it while remaining hidden. “For if they had understood, they would not have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

To descend into the troubled water, then, is to believe humbly in the Lord’s Passion. There one person was healed, signifying unity; afterward, whoever came was not healed, because whoever is outside unity cannot be healed.

### 4

Let us therefore see what he wished to signify in that one man whom he himself, preserving the mystery of unity, as I said beforehand, deigned to heal from among so many sick people. He found in the man’s years a certain number signifying illness: he had been ill for thirty-eight years. How this number pertains more to illness than to health must be explained somewhat more carefully.

I want you to be attentive. The Lord will be present, so that I may speak appropriately and you may hear sufficiently. The number forty is commended to us as sacred in a certain perfection. I suppose it is well known to Your Charity; the divine Scriptures attest it very frequently. Fasting has been consecrated by this number; you know this well. Moses fasted for forty days (Exod. 34:28), and Elijah for the same number (1 Kings 19:8), and our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself completed this period of fasting (Matt. 4:2).

Moses signifies the Law, Elijah signifies the Prophets, and the Lord signifies the Gospel. Therefore these three appeared on that mountain where he showed himself to the disciples in the glory of his face and clothing. He appeared in the middle between Moses and Elijah (ibid. 17:1–3), as though the Gospel had testimony from the Law and the Prophets (Rom. 3:21).

Thus, whether in the Law, the Prophets, or the Gospel, the number forty is commended to us in fasting. The great and universal fast is abstaining from the iniquities and unlawful pleasures of the world: this is the perfect fast, so that, renouncing ungodliness and worldly desires, we may live temperately, justly, and piously in this age. What reward does the Apostle add to this fast? He continues and says: “Awaiting the blessed hope and the manifestation of the glory of the blessed God and our Savior Jesus Christ” (Titus 2:12–13).

In this age, then, we celebrate something like a Lent of abstinence when we live well and abstain from iniquities and unlawful pleasures. But because this abstinence will not be without reward, we await that blessed hope and the revelation of the glory of the great God and our Savior Jesus Christ. In that hope, when what is hoped for has become reality, we shall receive the reward of the denarius. For according to the Gospel, that is the reward given to the laborers working in the vineyard (Matt. 20:9–10), which I believe you remember; not everything needs to be recalled as though you were untrained and inexperienced.

The denarius, therefore, which receives its name from the number ten, is given, and when joined to forty it becomes fifty. Hence we celebrate Lent with labor before Easter, but the Fifty Days after Easter with joy, as though we had received our reward. For to this labor of good works, which pertains to the number forty, the ten of rest and happiness is added, so that it becomes fifty.

### 5

The Lord Jesus himself signified this much more plainly when, after his resurrection, he remained on earth with his disciples for forty days (Acts 1:3); and on the fortieth day, when he had ascended into heaven, after ten further days he sent the reward of the Holy Spirit (ibid. 2:1–4). These things were signified, and the realities themselves were anticipated through certain signs. We are nourished by signs so that we may persevere and reach the realities themselves.

For we are laborers, and we are still working in the vineyard. When the day and the work are finished, the reward will be restored. But what laborer perseveres to receive his reward unless he is nourished while he works? You will not give your laborer only his wages; will you not also bring him something by which he may restore his strength during his work? Surely you feed the one to whom you are going to give his wages. In the same way, the Lord feeds us as we labor in these scriptural signs.

For if the joy of understanding these mysteries is taken away from us, we fail in our labor, and no one will reach the reward.

### 6

How, then, is the work perfected by the number forty? Perhaps because the Law was given in ten commandments and was to be preached throughout the whole world. The whole world is represented by its four parts—East and West, South and North—so that ten multiplied by four reaches forty.

Or perhaps because the Law is fulfilled through the Gospel, which has four books, since the Gospel says, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). Whether this is the reason, or that one, or some other more plausible reason unknown to us but not unknown to the learned, it is nevertheless certain that the number forty signifies a certain perfection in good works. These good works are especially exercised in a certain abstinence from the unlawful desires [Note: [Col. 1530] The manuscripts read *voluptatibus* (“pleasures”).] of the world—that is, in the universal fast.

Hear the Apostle also saying, “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. 13:10). Love—from where does it come? Through the grace of God, through the Holy Spirit. We would not have it from ourselves, as though we had made it for ourselves. It is God’s gift, and a great gift: “God’s love,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid. 5:5).

Love, then, fulfills the Law, and it is most truly said, “Love is the fullness of the Law.” Let us seek this love and see how it is commended by the Lord. Remember what I proposed: I want to explain why the number thirty-eight years in that sick man signifies illness rather than health.

As I was saying, love fulfills the Law. The number forty pertains to the fullness of the Law in all works; but in love two commandments are commended to us. Attend, I beg you, and fix what I say in your memory. Do not be contemptuous of the word, lest your soul become a road where the seeds scattered do not sprout: “Then the birds of the air came and gathered them up” (Mark 4:4). Receive these words and store them in your hearts.

Two commandments of love have been commended by the Lord: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40).

It was fitting, too, that the widow put all her means—two small coins—into the gifts of God (Luke 21:2–4). It was fitting that, for the wounded man attacked by robbers, the innkeeper received two coins with which he might be healed (Luke 10:35). It was fitting that Jesus remained two days among the Samaritans in order to strengthen them in love (John 4:40).

Whenever something good is signified by this number two, therefore, the love divided into two parts is especially commended. If, then, the number forty possesses the perfection of the Law, and the Law is fulfilled only in the twofold commandment of love, why are you surprised that the man was ill who lacked two in relation to forty?

### 7

Let us therefore see by what mystery this sick man is healed by the Lord. The Lord himself came, the teacher of love, full of love, shortening, as was foretold of him, “the word upon the earth” (Isa. 10:23; 28:22; Rom. 9:28). He showed that the Law and the Prophets hang upon the two commandments of love. From this, then, Moses hung with his forty; from this, Elijah with his; and the Lord brought this number in his testimony.

This sick man is healed by the Lord who is present. But what does he say to him first? “Do you want to become well?” The man replied that he had no one to put him into the pool. Truly, a man was necessary for his healing—but the man who is also God. “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

The necessary man came; why should healing be delayed? “Rise,” he says, “take up your mat, and walk.” He said three things: “Rise, take up your mat, and walk.” But “Rise” was not a command concerning a work; it was the operation of healing. To the healed man he gave two commands: “Take up your mat, and walk.”

I ask you, why would “Walk” not have been sufficient? Or, certainly, why would “Rise” not have been sufficient? For if he had risen healthy, he would not have remained in that place. Would he not have risen for the purpose of going away? I am therefore moved also by the fact that he gave two commands, since he found the man lying there short by two—as though, by commanding two things, he completed what was lacking.

### 8

How, then, shall we find in these two commands of the Lord those two commandments of love signified? “Take up,” he says, “your mat, and walk.” What are those two commandments, brothers? Recall them with me. They ought to be very well known, and they should not merely come to mind when we mention them; they must never be erased from your hearts.

Always and altogether consider that God and neighbor must be loved: God with all the heart, with all the soul, and with all the mind; and one’s neighbor as oneself. These things must always be thought about, meditated upon, retained, practiced, and fulfilled.

The love of God is prior in the order of command; the love of neighbor is prior in the order of practice. For the one who commanded you this love in two commandments would not first have commended your neighbor and afterward God, but first God and afterward your neighbor.

But because you do not yet see God, by loving your neighbor you earn the right to see him. By loving your neighbor you cleanse your eye for seeing God, as John clearly says: “If you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see?” (1 John 4:20).

Behold, you are told, “Love God.” If you say to me, “Show me whom I should love,” what shall I answer except what John himself says: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1:18)? And lest you think yourself altogether alien from seeing God: “God is love, and whoever remains in love remains in God” (1 John 4:16).

Love your neighbor, therefore, and look within yourself to see from where you love your neighbor; there you will see God, insofar as you can. Begin, then, to love your neighbor. “Break your bread for the hungry, and bring the homeless poor into your house; if you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise those of your own lineage.” What will you gain by doing these things? “Then your light shall break forth like the dawn” (Isa. 58:7–8).

Your light is your God, dawn for you because he will come to you after the night of this world. For he neither rises nor sets, because he always remains. He will be like dawn for you when you return to him who had become your setting when you were perishing.

Thus, “Take up your mat,” seems to me to mean: “Love your neighbor.”

### 9

But the matter is still obscure and, as I think, requires explanation: why is love of neighbor commended through taking up the mat? Unless, perhaps, what troubles us is that the neighbor is commended through a foolish and senseless object, the mat. Let the neighbor not be angry if he is commended to us through something without soul or sense.

Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself is called the cornerstone, “that he might create the two in himself” (Eph. 2:14–20). He is also called the rock from which water flowed: “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). What wonder, then, if Christ is the rock and the neighbor is wood? Yet not just any wood—just as it was not just any rock, but the one from which water flowed for the thirsty; nor just any stone, but the cornerstone, which joined together in itself two walls coming from opposite directions.

In the same way, do not take the neighbor as just any kind of wood, but as a mat. What, I ask you, is in the mat? Is it not that the sick man was carried on a mat? But once healed, he carries the mat. What does the Apostle say? “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. 6:2).

The law of Christ, then, is love, and love is not fulfilled unless we bear one another’s burdens. “Bearing with one another in love, striving to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4:2–3).

When you were sick, your neighbor carried you; now that you have been healed, carry your neighbor: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ.” In this way, human being, you will fulfill what was lacking in you. “Take up your mat,” then.

But when you have taken it up, do not remain where you are; walk. By loving your neighbor and caring for your neighbor, you are making your journey. Where are you journeying, except to the Lord God, the one whom we ought to love with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind? We have not yet reached the Lord, but we have our neighbor with us. Carry, then, the one with whom you walk, so that you may reach the one with whom you desire to remain. “Take up your mat, and walk.”

### 10

The man did this, and the Jews were scandalized. They saw a man carrying his mat on the Sabbath, but they did not accuse the Lord of having healed him on the Sabbath, so that he could answer them that if anyone’s animal had fallen into a pit, he would certainly pull it out on the Sabbath and save his animal (Luke 14:5). Thus they no longer objected that the man had been healed on the Sabbath, but that he was carrying his mat.

If healing was not to be postponed, was the work itself also necessary to command? “It is not lawful for you,” they said, “to do what you are doing, to take up your mat.” But he set the author of his healing before his accusers: “The one who made me well,” he said, “himself told me, ‘Take up your mat, and walk.’” Would I not accept a command from the one from whom I had received healing? And they said: “Who is the man who told you, ‘Take up your mat, and walk’?”

### 11

But the man who had been healed did not know who it was from whom he had heard this. Jesus, however, after doing this and giving the command, had withdrawn from him into the crowd.

See how this too is fulfilled. We carry our neighbor and walk toward God, but we do not yet see the one toward whom we walk; therefore that man also did not yet know Jesus. This mystery has been commended to us because we believe in the one whom we do not yet see; and, so that he might not be seen, he withdraws into the crowd.

It is difficult to see Christ in a crowd. A certain solitude is necessary for our mind; God is seen through a certain solitude of attention. A crowd makes noise; this vision demands seclusion.

Take up your mat, carry the neighbor by whom you were carried, and walk, so that you may reach him. Do not seek Jesus in the crowd; he is not like one of the crowd. He precedes the whole crowd. That great fish first ascended from the sea, and sits in heaven interceding for us. Like a great high priest, he alone entered within the veil; the crowd remains outside.

You, who carry your neighbor, walk, if you have learned to carry the one who used to carry you. Finally, at this point you do not yet know Jesus; you do not yet see Jesus. What follows? Because the man did not stop taking up his mat and walking, “Jesus afterward saw him in the temple.”

He did not see him in the crowd; he saw him in the temple. The Lord Jesus, of course, saw him both in the crowd and in the temple. But the sick man did not recognize Jesus in the crowd; he recognized him in the temple. He therefore reached the Lord and saw him in the temple, in a consecrated place, in a holy place. And what did he hear from him? “Behold, you have become well; do not sin, so that nothing worse may happen to you.”

### 12

Then, after he had seen Jesus and recognized Jesus as the author of his healing, he was not slow to proclaim the one he had seen: “He went away and announced to the Jews that it was Jesus who had made him well.” He was proclaiming, while they were raging; he was proclaiming his salvation, while they were not seeking their own salvation.

### 13

The Jews persecuted the Lord Jesus because he did these things on the Sabbath. What, then, did the Lord answer the Jews at this point? Let us hear.

Regarding people healed on the Sabbath, I have said what he usually answers: they did not disregard their animals on the Sabbath, whether by rescuing them or feeding them. What did he answer concerning the carried mat? A plainly physical deed had been performed before the eyes of the Jews: not the healing of the body, but a bodily action, which did not appear as necessary as the healing.

Therefore let the Lord openly declare the mystery of the Sabbath, and that the sign of observing one day was given to the Jews for a time, but that the fulfillment of the mystery itself had come in him. “My Father,” he says, “is working until now, and I am working.”

He caused a great disturbance among them. At the Lord’s coming the water is troubled, but the one who troubles it remains hidden. Nevertheless, one great sick man must be healed in the troubled water: the whole world, with the Lord having suffered.

### 14

Let us therefore examine the answer of the Truth: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.” Did Scripture then speak falsely in saying that “God rested from all his works on the seventh day” (Gen. 2:2)? And does the Lord Jesus speak against this Scripture, administered through Moses, when he himself says to the Jews, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46)?

See, then, whether Moses wished to signify something by saying that God rested on the seventh day. God had not grown weary in creating his work and needed rest as a human being does. How could the one who made everything by his word have grown weary?

Yet this is also true: God rested from his works on the seventh day. And what Jesus says is also true: “My Father is working until now.” But who can explain in words—one human being to human beings, a weak man to the weak, an unlearned man to those eager to learn, and perhaps, if he has any understanding, unable to bring it forth and explain it to people who may find it difficult to grasp, even if what is grasped could be explained—who, I say, my brothers, can explain in words how God both rests while working and works while resting?

I beg you to defer this until you are making progress. This vision seeks the temple of God; it seeks a holy place. Carry your neighbor and walk; there you will see him, where you will not seek human words.

### 15

Perhaps we can say more aptly that, in the fact that God rested on the seventh day, he signified through a great mystery our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ himself, who was speaking these words: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

For the Lord Jesus is certainly God. He is the Word of God, and you heard that “in the beginning was the Word.” It was not just any word, but “the Word was God,” and “all things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3). Perhaps he was signified as the one who would rest from all his works on the seventh day.

Read the Gospel and see how many things Jesus did. He accomplished our salvation on the cross, so that everything foretold by the Prophets might be fulfilled in him. He was crowned with thorns; he was hung on the wood; he said, “I thirst”; he received vinegar on a sponge, so that what had been said might be fulfilled: “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 69:22).

But when all his works had been fulfilled, on the sixth day, with his head bowed, he gave up his spirit; and in the tomb, on the Sabbath, he rested from all his works (John 19).

Thus, as though he were saying to the Jews: “Why do you expect me not to work on the Sabbath? The day of the Sabbath was prescribed for you as a sign of me. You consider the works of God; I was there when they were made, and all things were made through me—I know them. My Father is working until now.

“The Father made the light, but he spoke so that light might be made” (Gen. 1:3). If he spoke, he worked through the Word. I was his Word; I am his Word. Through me the world was made in those works; through me the world is governed in these works. My Father worked then when he made the world, and he works until now when he governs the world. Therefore, through me he made it when he made it, and through me he governs it when he governs it.”

He said these things—but to whom? To the deaf, the blind, the lame, the sick, who did not recognize the physician and, as though their minds had been lost in madness, wanted to kill him.

### 16

What, then, did the Evangelist say next? “For this reason the Jews were seeking all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God.”

Not in just any manner—but how? “Making himself equal to God.” For we all say to God, “Our Father who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9). We also read that the Jews said, “You are our father” (Isa. 63:16; 64:8).

Therefore they were not angry because he called God his Father, but because he did so in a manner altogether different from that of human beings. Behold, the Jews understood what the Arians do not understand. The Arians say that the Son is unequal to the Father, and for this reason the heresy was driven from the Church [Note: [Col. 1535] So reads the old manuscript of Carcassonne, and more correctly. For below, Tractate 23, section 6, where he speaks of the Apollinarists, he says: “There were certain heretics, and they were driven from the Church”; and he frequently uses this manner of expression. [“and for this reason the heresy drives the Church.”]].

Behold, those very blind men, those very killers of Christ, nevertheless understood Christ’s words. They did not understand that he was the Christ, nor did they understand that he was the Son of God; yet they did understand from those words that the Son of God was being presented as one who was equal to God. They did not know who he was, but they recognized that such a one was being proclaimed, because he called God his Father, making himself equal to God.

Was he, then, not equal to God? He did not make himself equal; rather, the one who begot him made him equal. If he made himself equal to God, he would have fallen through robbery. For whoever wished to make himself equal to God when he was not equal fell (Isa. 14:14–15), and from being an angel became the devil; and he offered this pride to human beings, from the place where he himself had been cast down.

For he said this to the human being whom he, fallen himself, envied while the human being stood: “Taste, and you will be like gods” (Gen. 3:5). That is: seize by usurpation what you were not made to be, because I too was cast down by seizing. He did not reveal this openly, but he urged it.

Christ, however, was born equal to the Father, not made equal: born from the substance of the Father. Thus the Apostle commends him: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as robbery.” What does “he did not regard it as robbery” mean? He did not usurp equality with God; he was in that equality in which he was born.

And how could we reach equality with God? “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7). He did not empty himself by losing what he was, but by taking what he was not.

The Jews, despising this form of a servant, could not understand that the Lord Christ was equal to the Father, although they had no doubt that he was saying this about himself, and therefore they raged. Yet even then he bore with them and sought the healing of those who were raging.

## TRACTATE XVIII

On the Gospel passage: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing; for whatever he does, the Son likewise does.” Chapter 5, verse 19.

### 1

The evangelist John received from the Lord, among his fellow evangelists and partners, this special and distinctive gift—he who reclined upon the Lord’s breast at the meal (John 13:25), thereby signifying that he drank deeper secrets from the intimacy of the Lord’s heart—so that he might say concerning the Son of God things capable perhaps of stirring the attentive minds of little ones, though they are not yet able to contain them. But to minds somewhat more mature, which have inwardly reached a certain spiritual manhood, he gives through these words something by which they may both be exercised and nourished.

You heard the passage when it was read, and you remember where this sermon came from. For yesterday it was read that the Jews wanted to kill Jesus because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God (John 5:18). What displeased the Jews pleased the Father himself. Without doubt it also pleases those who honor the Son as they honor the Father; for if it does not please them, they will themselves be displeasing. God will not be greater because he pleases you; rather, you will be less if he displeases you.

Against this accusation of theirs, arising either from ignorance or from malice, the Lord speaks—not in a way they can wholly grasp, but in a way by which they may be shaken and disturbed, and perhaps, once disturbed, seek the physician. He said these things so that they might be written and later read by us.

Let us therefore consider what happened in the hearts of the Jews when they heard these things; and let us think still more about what happens in us when we hear them. For heresies and certain doctrines of perversity, which entangle souls and plunge them into the depths, arise only when good Scriptures are not understood correctly, and what is not correctly understood is asserted rashly and boldly.

Therefore, beloved, we must hear these things with great caution, since we are little ones in regard to grasping them; and with a devout heart and trembling, holding to this rule of soundness: whatever we are able to understand according to the faith with which we have been instructed, let us rejoice in as food; but whatever we are not yet able to understand according to the sound rule of faith, let us remove doubt and postpone understanding. That is, even if we do not know what something is, we must not doubt that it is good and true.

And I, brothers, who have undertaken to speak to you, must be considered by you in terms of who I am and what I have undertaken. I have undertaken to discuss divine things as a human being, spiritual things as one who is carnal, eternal things as one who is mortal.

Let vain presumption be far from me, beloved, if I wish to conduct myself soundly in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God, “the pillar and foundation of the truth” (1 Tim. 3:15). According to my measure, I grasp what I set before you. Where it is opened, I am nourished with you; where it is closed, I knock together with you.

### 2

The Jews, then, were disturbed and indignant—rightly so, because a human being dared to make himself equal to God; but wrongly, because they did not understand God in the human being. They saw the flesh but did not know God; they saw the dwelling but did not recognize the inhabitant. That flesh was a temple; God dwelt within.

Jesus was not therefore making the flesh equal to the Father, nor comparing the form of a servant with the Lord; he was not comparing what was made for our sake, but what he was when he made us.

For who Christ is, I am speaking to Catholics—you know, because you have believed rightly: he is not the Word alone, nor flesh alone, but the Word became flesh so that he might dwell among us.

I recall concerning the Word what you know: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Here there is equality with the Father. But “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1–14). In respect of this flesh, the Father is greater.

Thus the Father is both equal and greater: equal to the Word, greater than the flesh; equal to the one through whom he made us, greater than the one who was made for our sake.

According to this sound Catholic rule, which you ought especially to know and which you who know it must hold fast—your faith must not slip away from it, and no human arguments should wrest it from your heart—let us direct what we understand; and what perhaps we do not understand, let us defer directing to this rule until we become capable.

We know, then, that the Son of God is equal to the Father, because we know that in the beginning the Word was God. Why, then, did the Jews want to kill him? Because he not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God: they saw the flesh but did not see the Word.

Let the Word, then, speak against them through the flesh; let the inner inhabitant sound forth through his dwelling, so that whoever can may know who dwells within.

### 3

What, then, does he say to them? “Jesus therefore answered and said to them,” since they were stirred up because he made himself equal to God: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” What the Jews replied to this is not written, and perhaps they were silent. Yet some who wish to be regarded as Christians do not remain silent; in a certain way they derive from these words certain arguments against us. These must not be disregarded, both for their sake and for ours.

For the Arians—heretics who say that the Son himself who assumed flesh is less than the Father, not according to the flesh but before the flesh and is not of the same substance as the Father—take from these words an opportunity for slander and answer us: “You see that when the Lord Jesus noticed that the Jews were troubled because he made himself equal to God the Father, he added such words as to show that he was not equal. The Jews,” they say, “were stirred against Christ because he made himself equal to God; and Christ, wishing to correct them concerning this disturbance and to show them that the Son is not equal to the Father, that is, equal to God, said—as though he were saying: ‘Why are you angry? Why are you indignant? I am not equal, because the Son can do nothing of himself except what he has seen the Father doing.’ For he who cannot do anything of himself except what he has seen the Father doing is clearly less, not equal.”

### 4

In accordance with this distorted and crooked rule of his heart, let the heretic hear us—not yet rebuking him, but still, as it were, questioning him—and let him explain to us what he thinks. For I suppose, whoever you are—for let us imagine that he is present with us—you hold with us that “in the beginning was the Word.”

“I hold it,” he says.

“And that the Word was with God?”

“I hold that too,” he says.

“Then go on, and hold this even more firmly: ‘The Word was God.’”

“I hold that too,” he says, “[but] that God is greater and that God is lesser.”

Now I no longer know what paganism this resembles; I had thought I was speaking with a Christian. If there is a greater God and a lesser God, we worship two gods, not one God.

“Why?” he asks. “Do you not say that two gods are equal to one another?”

“I do not say that. For I understand this equality in such a way that I also understand indivisible love in it; and, with indivisible love, perfect unity. For if the love that God has sent to human beings makes one heart from the many hearts of human beings, and makes one soul from the many souls of human beings—as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles concerning those who believed and loved one another, ‘They had one soul and one heart toward God’ (Acts 4:32)—if, then, my soul and your soul become one soul when we have the same understanding and love one another, how much more are God the Father and God the Son one God in the fountain of love?”

[Note: [Col. 1538] Twelve manuscripts read: “and thus indivisible love.”]

### 5

But attend to these words by which your heart has been troubled, and recall with me what we were seeking concerning the Word. We already hold this: “The Word was God.” I add something else: after he had said, “This was in the beginning with God,” the Evangelist immediately added, “All things were made through him.”

Now I challenge you by questioning you; now I stir you against yourself and interrogate you against yourself. Hold in your memory only these things concerning the Word: that the Word was God, and that all things were made through him. Now hear the words by which you were troubled, so that you said the Son was lesser—namely, because he said, “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he has seen the Father doing.”

“That is so,” he says.

“Explain this to me a little. As I understand you, you think that the Father does certain things, while the Son observes how the Father does them, so that he too may do what he has seen the Father doing. You have set up two craftsmen, the Father and the Son, as teacher and pupil—just as artisan fathers commonly teach their sons their craft.

“Behold, I descend to your carnal understanding; for the moment I think as you do. Let us see whether this thought of ours finds an outcome consistent with what we have already spoken and agreed upon together: that the Word is God, and that all things were made through him.

“Suppose, then, that the Father is like a craftsman making certain works, while the Son is like an apprentice who can do nothing except what he has seen the Father doing. He somehow fixes his attention on the Father’s hands, so that, having seen how the Father makes something, he too may make something of that kind in his own works. But this Father makes all those things that he makes, and wants the Son to observe him and to make such things himself—through whom does he make them?”

Now it is time for you to stand by your earlier opinion, which you reviewed and held together with me: that in the beginning was the Word, that the Word was with God, that the Word was God, and that all things were made through him.

When you have held with me that all things were made through the Word, you again, with carnal taste and childish agitation, imagine in your mind God making something and the Word observing, so that, when God has made it, the Word may make it too.

For what does God make apart from the Word? If he does make something apart from the Word, then “all things were made through the Word” is false, and you have lost what you were holding. But if “all things were made through the Word” is true, correct what you were wrongly understanding.

The Father made, and he made nothing except through the Word. How, then, does the Word observe, so as to see the Father making something without the Word, which the Word might likewise make? Whatever the Father made, he made through the Word; otherwise “all things were made through him” is false.

But it is true: “All things were made through him.” Perhaps that seemed too little to you? “Without him nothing was made.”

[Note: [Col. 1538] Lov. has this passage as follows: “But this Father makes all those things that he makes, and wants the Son to observe him and to make such things himself, through whom he makes them.” M.]

[Col. 1539]

### 6

Withdraw, then, from this wisdom of the flesh, and let us seek how it was said: “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” Let us seek, if we are worthy to grasp it.

For I confess that it is a great and altogether difficult matter: to see the Father making through the Son—not the Father and the Son each making separate works, but the Father making every work through the Son, so that no works are done either by the Father without the Son or by the Son without the Father; for “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

When these things have been established most firmly in the foundation of faith, what does it mean to see that “the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing”? You want, I suppose, to know the Son making; first seek to know the Son seeing.

For what does he say? “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing.” Pay attention to what he said: “except what he sees the Father doing.” Seeing comes first, and doing follows; he sees in order to do.

Why, then, do you already seek to know how he does, when you do not yet know how he sees? Why do you hurry toward what comes later, leaving aside what comes first? He said “seeing and doing,” not “doing and seeing,” because he can do nothing of himself except what he has seen the Father doing.

Do you want me to explain to you how he does? You explain to me how he sees. If you cannot explain this, neither can I explain that. If you are not yet capable of grasping this, neither am I capable of grasping that. Let both of us therefore seek; let both of us knock, so that both of us may deserve to receive.

Why do you, as though learned, accuse one who is unlearned? I am unlearned concerning doing, you concerning seeing; let both of us, unlearned, seek from the teacher, rather than quarrel childishly in his school.

Nevertheless, we have already learned together that all things were made through him. Therefore it is clear that the Father does not perform one set of works which the Son sees, so that the Son may perform similar works; rather, the Father performs the same works through the Son, because all things were made through the Word.

Who now knows how God makes? I do not mean how he made the world, but how he made your eye, while you cling carnally to that eye and compare visible things with invisible things. You think about God in terms of the things you are accustomed to seeing with these eyes.

But if God could be seen with these eyes, he would not say, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). You have the eye of the body with which to see a craftsman, but you do not yet have the eye of the heart with which to see God. Therefore you want to transfer to God what you ordinarily see in a craftsman.

Put earthly things on earth; raise your heart upward.

### 7

What, then, beloved? Are we going to explain what we have asked: how the Word sees, how the Father is seen by the Word, and what it means for the Word to see?

I am not so bold or reckless as to promise that I can explain this either to myself or to you. I have some sense of your measure, but I know my own.

If it pleases you, let us not linger any longer. Let us run through the reading and see the carnal hearts troubled by the Lord’s words—troubled so that they do not remain in what they have grasped. Let something be wrested from them, as from children, some toy with which they distract themselves to their harm, so that more useful things may be inserted into minds capable of greater matters, and so that those who were crawling on the ground may make progress.

Rise up; seek; sigh; pant with desire; knock at what is closed. But if we do not yet desire, if we do not yet hunger, if we do not yet sigh, we shall either cast pearls before just anyone or find pearls of whatever sort for ourselves.

Let me therefore stir up desire in your hearts, beloved. Conduct leads to understanding; one kind of life leads to another kind of life. There is one earthly life and another heavenly life; one life belongs to animals and another to human beings; another belongs to angels.

The life of animals seethes with earthly pleasures, seeks only earthly things, and is bent and cast down toward them. The life of angels is purely heavenly. Human life lies between the life of angels and that of animals.

If a human being lives according to the flesh, he is compared with animals; if he lives according to the spirit, he is joined to the angels. When you live according to the spirit, seek also, within that angelic life, to discover whether you are small or mature.

For if you are still small, the angels say to you: “Grow. We eat solid bread; you must be nourished with milk—the milk of faith—so that you may reach the food of direct vision.”

But if you still hunger for filthy pleasures, if deceit is still being devised, if lies are not avoided, if lies are piled up with perjuries, does such an impure heart dare to say, “Explain to me how the Word sees”—even if I could explain it, even if I already saw myself?

But suppose that I am not of such character and yet remain far from that vision. How much farther away is the one who is not yet carried away by this heavenly desire but is weighed down by earthly desires?

There is a great difference between one who turns away and one who desires; and again there is a great difference between one who desires and one who enjoys. You live like the animals: you turn away. The angels enjoy.

But if you do not live like the animals, you no longer turn away; you desire something but do not grasp it. Through that very desire you have begun the life of angels. May it grow in you and be brought to perfection in you, and may you receive this not from me but from him who made both me and you.

### 8

Yet the Lord did not leave us without guidance. He wished us to understand that when he said, “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing,” the Father does not perform one set of works which the Son sees, while the Son performs another set after seeing the Father doing them. Rather, the Father and the Son perform the same works.

For he continued: “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does.” He did not say, “When the Father has done something, the Son likewise does something else”; rather, “Whatever the Father has done, the Son likewise does.”

If the Son does what the Father has done, the Father does it through the Son. If the Father does through the Son what the Father does, the Father does not perform one set of works and the Son another; the works of the Father and the Son are the same.

And how does the Son perform the same works? Both the same and likewise. Lest you perhaps think that they are the same but not performed in the same manner, he says, “The same and likewise.”

And how could the same things be performed otherwise than likewise? Receive an example which, I think, is not too difficult for you. When we write letters, our heart first makes them, and then our hand. Surely this is why you all cried out together: because you recognized the point. What I have said is certain and plain to all of us.

Letters are made first by our heart and then by our body. The hand serves the commanding heart; both heart and hand make the same letters. Does the heart make some letters and the hand others? The hand certainly makes the same letters, but not in the same manner: our heart makes them intelligibly, while the hand makes them visibly.

See how the same things are made differently. Therefore it was not enough for the Lord to say, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does,” unless he added, “and likewise.”

For what if you understood it in the following way: whatever the heart makes, the hand makes too, but not in the same manner? Here, however, he added, “The Son likewise does these things.” If he does these things and does them likewise, wake up; let the Jew be constrained, let the Christian believe, let the heretic be convicted: the Son is equal to the Father.

### 9

“For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does” (John 5:20). There it is: “shows.” Shows—as to whom? Clearly, as to one who sees. We return to what we cannot explain: how the Word sees.

Behold, the human being was made through the Word. Yet the human being has eyes, ears, hands, and different bodily members. Through the eyes he can see, through the ears he can hear, and through the hands he can work: different members, different functions of the members.

The member that can perform one function cannot perform the other. Yet, because of the unity of the body, the eye sees both for itself and for the ear, and the ear hears both for itself and for the eye.

Should we suppose that something of this kind exists in the Word, since all things were made through him? Scripture says in the Psalm: “Understand, you senseless among the people; and you fools, become wise at last. He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, shall he not see?” (Ps. 93:8–9).

If, then, the Word formed the eye, since all things were made through the Word; if the Word planted the ear, since all things were made through the Word, we cannot say, “The Word does not hear; the Word does not see,” lest the Psalm rebuke us and say, “Fools, become wise at last.”

Therefore, if the Word hears and the Word sees, the Son hears and the Son sees. But are we nevertheless going to look for eyes and ears in him in different places? Does he hear in one place and see in another? And can his ear not do what his eye can, while his eye cannot do what his ear can?

Or is he wholly sight and wholly hearing? Perhaps so—indeed, not perhaps, but truly so—provided that his seeing and his hearing are understood as being entirely different from ours.

In the Word, seeing and hearing occur simultaneously. It is not one thing there to hear and another to see; rather, hearing is sight, and sight is hearing.

### 10

And we, who hear in one way and see in another, how do we know this? Perhaps we return to ourselves, if we are not transgressors, to whom it was said, “Return, you transgressors, to your heart” (Isa. 46:8).

Return to your heart. Why do you go away from yourselves and perish through yourselves? Why do you travel the roads of desolation? You wander by straying; return.

Where? To the Lord. It is close at hand: first return to your own heart.

[Note: [Col. 1541] Lov. reads, “Return quickly to the Lord,” omitting “is,” which the other manuscripts contain.] As an exile from yourself, you wander outside; you do not know yourself, and you seek the one by whom you were made. Return, return to your heart. Take yourself away from the body.

Your body is your dwelling place; your heart also perceives through your body. But your body is not what your heart is. Leave even your body; return to your heart.

In your body you found eyes in one place and ears in another. Do you find this in your heart? Do you not have ears in your heart? What, then, did the Lord mean when he said, “He who has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8)?

Do you not have eyes in your heart? This is why the Apostle says, “The eyes of your heart having been enlightened” (Eph. 1:18).

Return to your heart. See there what you may perhaps perceive concerning God, because there the image of God is found. “Christ dwells in the inner person” (ibid. 3:16–17); in the inner person you are renewed according to the image of God. In his image, recognize its author.

See how all the senses of the body report inwardly to the heart what they have sensed outwardly. See how many ministers the one inner ruler has, and what the heart does within itself even without these ministers.

The eyes report white and black to the heart; the ears report harmonious and discordant sounds to the same heart; the nostrils report fragrant and foul odors to the same heart; taste reports bitter and sweet to the same heart; touch reports smooth and rough to the same heart. The heart also reports to itself what is just and unjust.

Your heart both sees and hears, and judges the other objects of sense; and it distinguishes just from unjust, evil from good—things toward which the bodily senses do not aspire.

Show me the eyes, ears, and nostrils of your heart. Different things are reported to your heart, but no different members are found there. In your flesh you hear in one place and see in another; in your heart you hear where you see.

If this is true of the image, how much more powerful is the one whose image it is? Therefore the Son hears, and the Son sees; and the Son himself is both seeing and hearing. For him, hearing is the same as being, and seeing is the same as being.

For you, seeing is not the same as being: even if you lose your sight, you can still exist; and if you lose your hearing, you can still exist.

### 11

Do we think that we have knocked? Has something been raised up in us by which we may at least faintly discern from where the light comes to us?

I think, brothers, that when we speak and meditate on these things, we are exercising ourselves. And when we exercise ourselves in them, only to be thrown back by our own weight toward our accustomed ways, we are like people with sore eyes who are brought out to see the light.

Suppose that previously they had no sight at all and are beginning, through the physicians’ care, somehow to regain it. When the physician wishes to test how much health has returned to them, he tries to show them what they desired to see but could not see when they were blind.

As the sharpness of their vision begins to return, they are brought out into the light. When they have seen it, they are somehow struck back by the brightness itself, and they reply to the physician who is showing it to them: “Now, now I have seen—but I cannot see.”

What, then, does the physician do? He brings them back to familiar things and applies more salve, so that they may nourish their desire for what they have seen but could not see, and may be more fully healed through that desire. If any painful remedies are applied for the restoration of health, they endure them bravely, so that, kindled by love of that light, they may say to themselves: “When will I be able with sound eyes to see what I could not see with eyes wounded and weak?”

They press the physician and ask him to heal them.

Therefore, brothers, if something of this kind has happened in your hearts—if you have somehow raised your heart to see the Word, and, struck by the light itself, have fallen back into your accustomed ways—ask the physician to apply painful eye-salves: the commandments of righteousness.

There is something for you to see, but you do not yet have the means by which to see it. Previously you did not believe me when I said that there is something to see; you have been led by a certain argument. You drew near, focused your attention, trembled, and recoiled.

You certainly know that there is something to see, but you are not fit to see it. Therefore, be healed.

What are the eye-salves? Do not lie; do not swear falsely; do not commit adultery; do not steal; do not defraud.

“But I am accustomed to these things,” you say, “and I am recalled from my habit with some pain.”

That is what stings, but it heals. For I speak to you more freely, out of fear both for myself and for you: if you stop seeking to be healed and neglect the health of your eyes, so as to become fit to enjoy this light, you will love the darkness. By loving the darkness, you will remain in darkness; and by remaining in darkness, you will also be cast into the outer darkness. There will be weeping and gnashing of teeth there (Matt. 22:13).

If love of the light accomplishes nothing in you, let fear of pain accomplish something.

### 12

I think I have spoken sufficiently, yet I have not finished the Gospel reading. If I discuss what remains, I shall burden you, and I fear that even what has already been taken in may be poured out. Let these things suffice for your Charity.

We are debtors—not merely now, but always, for as long as we live, because we live for you. Nevertheless, comfort our weak, laborious, and dangerous life in this world by living well. Do not grieve us and wear us down by your evil conduct.

For when your bad life offends us, if we withdraw from you, separate ourselves from you, and do not come near you, will you not complain and say: “If we were languishing, you should have healed us; if we were weak, you should have visited us”?

Behold, we heal; behold, we visit. But let what you heard from the Apostle not happen to us: “I fear that I have labored over you in vain” [Gal. 4:11].

[Note: [Col. 1543] Lov. reads, “in you.” Other printed editions and manuscripts read, “over you,” in accordance with the Greek.]

## TREATISE XIX

From the passage written, “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing,” up to the passage, “I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” Chapter 5, verses 19–30.

### 1

In the preceding discourse, insofar as our feeling and our poverty of understanding moved us, we spoke, prompted by the Gospel words where it is written, “The Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing,” about what it means for the Son to see—that is, for the Word to see, since the Son is the Word—and how it can be understood that the Son first sees the Father doing something and then himself does what he has seen, when the Father has done nothing except through the Son.

“For all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

We did not, however, explain anything; rather, we did not understand anything that was explained. Sometimes speech fails where understanding makes progress; how much more does speech suffer failure when understanding has not reached perfection?

Now, therefore, insofar as the Lord grants it, let us briefly run through the reading and perhaps fulfill today’s appointed task. If some time or strength should remain, we shall return, if we can—as far as this can be done by us and among you—to the question of what it means for the Word to see and what is shown to the Word.

Everything here has been said in such a way that, if it is understood according to human, carnal perception, the soul full of phantasms constructs nothing but certain images, as though of two human beings: the Father showing, and the Son seeing; the one speaking, and the other hearing.

All these are idols of the heart. If they have already been thrown down from their temples, how much more must they be thrown down from Christian hearts?

### 2

“The Son,” he says, “can do nothing of himself except what he has seen the Father doing.”

This is true; hold firmly to it. But do not lose what you held at the beginning of the Gospel itself: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and especially this: “All things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3).

Join what you have now heard to what you heard before, and let both agree in your hearts.

Thus the Son can do nothing of himself except what he sees the Father doing, while nevertheless the Father does not do the things he does except through the Son, because the Son is his Word.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and “all things were made through him.”

“Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does”—not other things, but these; not differently, but likewise.

### 3

“For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does.”

The words spoken above, “except what he sees the Father doing,” seem to be connected with this statement also: “He shows him everything that he himself does.”

But if the Father shows what he does, and the Son can do nothing unless the Father has shown it, while the Father cannot show it unless he has done it, it will follow that the Father does not do everything through the Son.

Yet if we hold firmly and unshakably that the Father does everything through the Son, then before he does it he shows it to the Son.

For if the Father shows it to the Son after he has done it, so that the Son may do what has been shown—things that have already been shown as done—the Father clearly does something without the Son.

But the Father does not do anything without the Son, because the Son is the Word of God, and all things were made through him.

It remains, then, perhaps, that the Father shows what he is going to do as things to be done, so that they may be done through the Son. For if the Son does what the Father shows as already done, then what the Father shows as already done he certainly did not do through the Son.

It could not be shown to the Son unless it had been done; and the Son could not do it unless it had been shown. Therefore it was done without the Son.

But it is true that “all things were made through him.” Therefore, before they were made, they were shown.

We said, however, that this question should be deferred, so that after running through the reading we might return to it, if, as we said, some time or strength remained, and reconsider the matters we have postponed.

### 4

Hear something further and more difficult: “He will show him works greater than these, so that you may marvel.”

“Greater than these”—greater than what? It is easy to understand this as referring to the cures of bodily illnesses that you have just heard about.

For the whole occasion of this discourse arose from the case of the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years and was healed by Christ’s word. For this reason the Lord could say, “He will show him works greater than these, so that you may marvel.”

There are works greater than these, and the Father will show them to the Son. He did not say “he showed,” as though speaking of the past, but “he will show,” that is, “he is going to show.”

Again a difficult question arises. Is there something with the Father that has not yet been shown to the Son? Was there something with the Father that remained hidden from the Son when the Son spoke these words?

For if he “will show,” that is, is going to show, then he has not yet shown it; and he is going to show it to the Son at the same time as to these people, for it follows: “so that you may marvel.”

It is difficult to see how the eternal Father, who is coeternal with the Son, shows something to the Son in a temporal manner, when the Son knows everything that is with the Father.

### 5

What, nevertheless, are those greater works? This may perhaps be easy to understand.

“For just as the Father,” he says, “raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.”

The greater works, then, are raising the dead, rather than healing the sick. But just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.

Does the Father give life to some and the Son to others? But all things were made through him. Therefore the Son gives life to the very ones to whom the Father does—not other things and not differently, but the same things and likewise.

This must be understood and held firmly. But remember that the Son gives life to whomever he wills.

Hold firmly here, then, not merely the Son’s power but also his will. The Son gives life to whomever he wills, and the Father gives life to whomever he wills; and the Son gives life to the very ones to whom the Father does. Consequently, the Father and the Son have the same power and the same will.

What, then, follows? “For neither does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.” He added this as though giving the reason for the preceding statement.

This is very perplexing; pay close attention. The Son gives life to whomever he wills; the Father gives life to whomever he wills. The Son raises the dead, just as the Father raises the dead.

“For neither does the Father judge anyone.” If the dead are to be raised in judgment, how does the Father raise the dead if he judges no one? For “he has given all judgment to the Son.”

In that judgment the dead are raised, and some rise to life, others to punishment. If the Son does all this, while the Father does not do it because the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, this will seem contrary to what was said: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.”

Therefore they raise them together. If they raise them together, they give them life together. Therefore they judge together. How, then, is it true that “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”?

For the moment, let the questions that have been proposed stir us; the Lord will grant that their solutions delight us. So it is, brothers: unless a question, once proposed, makes a person attentive, its exposition will not delight him.

Let the Lord himself, then, continue, lest perhaps in what he adds he may reveal himself to us somewhat. He places his light beneath a cloud; and it is difficult, like an eagle, to fly above all the mist with which the whole earth is covered (Ecclus. 24:6) and to see the purest light in the Lord’s words.

Perhaps, then, he may disperse our darkness by the warmth of his rays and deign to reveal himself somewhat in what follows. Let us set these matters aside and examine what comes next.

### 6

“He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.”

This is true and plain. For he has given all judgment to the Son, as he said above, “so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

What if there are people who honor the Father but do not honor the Son?

“It cannot happen,” he says. “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.”

Therefore no one can say, “I honored the Father because I did not know the Son.” If you did not yet honor the Son, neither did you honor the Father.

For what does it mean to honor the Father except to acknowledge that he has a Son? It is one thing when God is commended to you because he is God, and another when God is commended to you because he is Father.

When he is commended to you as God, the Creator is commended to you; the Almighty is commended to you; a certain supreme, eternal, invisible, immutable Spirit is commended to you.

But when he is commended to you as Father, nothing other than the Son is commended to you, because he cannot be called Father if he does not have a Son, just as the Son cannot be called Son if he does not have a Father.

But perhaps you honor the Father as greater and the Son as lesser, so that you say to me: “I honor the Father. I know that he has a Son, and I do not err concerning the name ‘Father,’ for I do not understand the Father without the Son. Nevertheless, I honor the Son as lesser.”

The Son himself corrects you and recalls you, saying that all should honor the Son—not less, but “just as they honor the Father.”

Therefore, he who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.

“I wish,” you say, “to give greater honor to the Father and lesser honor to the Son.”

You remove honor from the Father precisely where you give less to the Son. For what else does your view imply except that the Father either did not wish or was unable to beget a Son equal to himself? If he did not wish to, he was envious; if he was unable to, he failed.

Do you not see that by thinking this way, precisely where you wish to give greater honor to the Father, you insult the Father?

Therefore honor the Son as you honor the Father, if you wish to honor both Father and Son.

### 7

“Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed—not now is passing, but has already passed—from death into life.”

Pay attention also to this: “Whoever hears my word.” He did not say, “believes me,” but “believes him who sent me.”

Let him hear the Son’s word, so that he may believe the Father.

Why does he hear your word and believe another? When we hear someone’s word, do we not believe the one who speaks the word, entrusting our faith to the one speaking to us?

What, then, did he wish to say by, “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me,” except that his word is in me?
