And what does “hears my word” mean except “hears me”? But he believes him who sent me because, when he believes the Father, he believes his word; and when he believes his word, he believes me, because I am the Word of the Father.

There is therefore peace in the Scriptures, and everything is arranged so that nothing fights against anything else. Cast away the quarrel in your heart; understand the harmony of the Scriptures.

Would the truth speak contradictions to itself?

### 8

“Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and does not come into judgment, but has passed from death into life.”

You remember that earlier we had established that just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.

He now begins to reveal himself and to speak of the resurrection of the dead—and behold, the dead are already rising.

“For whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life and will not come into judgment.”

Prove that he has risen. “He has passed,” he says, “from death into life.”

The one who has passed from death into life has unquestionably risen. For he would not pass from death into life unless he had first been in death and not in life. But when he has passed over, he will be in life and will no longer be in death.

Therefore he was dead and has come to life; he was lost and has been found (Luke 15:32).

Thus a certain resurrection is already taking place, and people pass from one kind of death to one kind of life: from the death of unbelief to the life of faith; from the death of falsehood to the life of truth; from the death of iniquity to the life of righteousness.

There is, then, also a certain resurrection of the dead.

### 9.

“May he open it more fully, and may it grow clear for us, as it has begun to do.” “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is.” We were expecting the resurrection of the dead at the end, for so we have believed; indeed, we were not merely expecting it, but plainly ought to expect it. For we do not falsely believe that at the end the dead will rise.

Therefore, when the Lord Jesus wished to disclose to us a certain resurrection of the dead before the resurrection of the dead—not like that of Lazarus (John 11:43–44), or of the son of the widow (Luke 7:14–15), or of the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Mark 5:41–42), who rose again only to die—for in their case, too, a certain resurrection of the dead occurred before the resurrection of the dead—but as he says here: “He has,” he says, “eternal life; and he does not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.” To what life? To eternal life. Therefore it is not like the body of Lazarus: for he too passed from the death of the tomb to the life of human beings, but not to eternal life, since he was destined to die again. The dead who will rise at the end of the age, however, will pass into eternal life.

Therefore, when our Lord Jesus Christ, the heavenly Teacher, the Word of the Father and the Truth, wished to show us a certain resurrection of the dead into eternal life before the resurrection of the dead into eternal life, he said: “The hour is coming.” You, undoubtedly instructed in faith in the resurrection of the flesh, were expecting that hour at the end of the age, the day of judgment. But so that you would not expect it in this passage, he added, “and now is.” Thus, when he says, “The hour is coming,” he is not speaking of that final hour when, “at the command and at the voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, the Lord himself will descend from heaven, and the dead in Christ will rise first; then we who are alive, who remain, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thessalonians 4:15–16). That hour will come, but it is not now.

Consider, then, what this present hour is: “The hour is coming, and now is.” What happens in it? What, except the resurrection of the dead? And what kind of resurrection? So that those who rise may live forever. This will also happen in the final hour.

### 10.

What, then? How do we understand these two resurrections? Perhaps those who rise now will not rise then, so that now one group rises and then another? It is not so. For by this resurrection, if we have believed rightly, we have risen; and we ourselves who have already risen await another resurrection at the end. [Col. 1548] But even now we have risen into eternal life, if we remain steadfast in that faith; and then we will rise into eternal life when we become equal to the angels (Luke 20:36).

Let him himself distinguish and open what we have dared to say: how a resurrection occurs before the resurrection—not of different people, but of the same people—and not one like Lazarus’s, but into eternal life. He will certainly open it. Listen to the Teacher as he grows bright, and to our Sun entering our hearts—not the sun desired by the eyes of the flesh, but the one to whom the eyes of the heart burn to be opened.

Let us therefore listen to him himself: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is, when the dead”—observe that the resurrection is being expressed—“when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” Why did he add, “Those who hear will live”? Could they hear unless they were alive? It would therefore have been enough to say, “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God.” We would already understand that they were alive, since, unless they were alive, they could not hear.

“No,” he says; “they do not hear because they live, but by hearing they return to life: they will hear, and those who hear will live.” What, then, is “they will hear,” except “they will obey”? As far as the hearing of the ears is concerned, not everyone who hears will live. For many hear and do not believe; by hearing and not believing, they do not obey; by not obeying, they do not live. Thus here “those who hear” means nothing other than “those who obey.” Therefore those who obey will live: let them be certain, let them be secure—they will live.

Christ is preached as the Word of God, the Son of God, through whom all things were made; certainly [Note: [Col. 1548] Or “certain.”], by the grace of the dispensation, he assumed flesh and was born of a Virgin: an infant in the flesh, a young man in the flesh, suffering in the flesh, dying in the flesh, rising in the flesh, ascending in the flesh, promising resurrection to the flesh, promising resurrection to the mind—the mind before the flesh, the flesh after the mind.

Whoever hears and obeys will live; whoever hears and does not obey—that is, hears and despises, hears and does not believe—will not live. Why will he not live? Because he does not hear. What does “he does not hear” mean? He does not obey. Therefore those who hear will live.

### 11.

Now attend to what we had said should be postponed, so that it may, if possible, be opened now. He immediately added concerning this same resurrection: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself.”

What does “the Father has life in himself” mean? He does not have life elsewhere, but in himself. His living is in him; it is not from another and is not something foreign. He does not borrow life, nor does he become a participant in a life that is not what he himself is. Rather, he has life in himself, so that he himself is that life.

If I can still say something slight about this, I shall be able, with the Lord’s help and with the pious attentiveness of your minds, to shape your understanding by the examples I have set before you. God lives, and the soul also lives; but God’s life is unchangeable, whereas the soul’s life is changeable. God neither advances nor declines, but is always himself in himself; he is as he is—not one way now, another way later, or another way earlier.

The soul’s life, however, is very different at different times: it was foolish, and it becomes wise; it was unjust, and it becomes just. Now it remembers, now it forgets; now it learns, now it cannot learn; now it loses what it had learned, now it grasps [Col. 1549] what it had lost. The soul’s life is changeable.

And when the soul lives in iniquity, that is its death. But when it becomes just, it becomes a participant in another life, which is not what it itself is. For by raising itself toward God and cleaving to God, it is justified by him. It is written: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). By declining from him it becomes unjust; by advancing toward him it becomes just.

Does it not seem to you that something cold, brought near to fire, grows hot, and when removed from the fire grows numb? Does it not seem to you that something dark, brought near to the light, grows bright, and when removed from the light grows black? The soul is something like this; God is not.

A human being can also say that he now has light in his eyes. Let your eyes, if they can, speak as though with a voice of their own: “We have light in ourselves.” The answer is: “You do not properly say that you have light in yourselves. You have light, but in the heavens; you have light, if it happens to be night, but in the moon and in lamps, not in yourselves. For when your eyes are closed, you lose what you perceive when they are open.”

You do not have light in yourselves. When the sun sets, retain the light, if you can. It is night, and you enjoy nocturnal illumination; once the lamp has been taken away, retain the light. But when the lamp has been removed and you remain in darkness, you do not have light in yourselves.

This, then, is what it means to have light in oneself: not to need light from another. Here, if anyone understands, he shows the Son to be equal to the Father, where he says: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself.” The sole distinction between the Father and the Son is that the Father has life in himself, given to him by no one, while the Son has life in himself, given by the Father.

### 12.

But here, too, a cloud arises that must be dispersed. Let us not falter; let us remain attentive. These are the pastures of the mind; let us not grow weary of them, so that we may live.

“Behold,” you say, “you yourself confess that the Father granted life to the Son, so that he might have it in himself, just as the Father has life in himself. If the Father does not need another, neither does the Son; so that the Father may be life and the Son also life, and both together one life, not two, because there is one God, not two gods; and that this very thing may be to be life. How, then, did the Father give life to the Son?”

Not as though the Son had previously been without life and received life from the Father in order to live. For if that were so, he would not have life in himself.

I was speaking about the soul. There is a soul: even if it is not wise, even if it is not just, it is a soul; even if it is not pious, it is a soul. Therefore, for it, being a soul is one thing, and being wise, just, or pious is another.

There is, then, something by which it is not yet wise, not yet just, not yet pious; nevertheless it is not nothing, nor is it devoid of all life. For by certain of its works it shows itself to be life [Note: [Col. 1549] Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read vivam, “alive,” for vitam, “life.” M.], even though it does not show itself to be wise, pious, or just. Unless it were alive, it would not move the body; it would not direct the feet in walking, the hands in work, the eyes in seeing, or the ears in hearing; it would not open the mouth for speech, nor move the tongue to distinguish sounds.

By these works, therefore, it shows itself to be alive and to be something better than the body. But does it show itself by these works to be wise, pious, or just? [Col. 1550] Do not foolish, impious, and unjust people also walk, work, see, hear, and speak?

But when the soul raises itself toward something that it is not, something above itself, and from which it itself comes, it perceives wisdom, justice, and piety. Without these, while it was without them, it was dead; it did not possess the life by which it itself lived, but only the life by which it gave life to the body.

For one thing in the soul gives life to the body, and another gives life to the soul. The soul is better than the body, but God is better than the soul itself.

The soul, therefore, even when foolish, unjust, and impious, is the life of the body. But because God is its life, just as, when the soul is in the body, it supplies the body with vigor, beauty, movement, and the functions of its members, so, when God its life is in the soul, he supplies it with wisdom, piety, justice, and love.

Thus one thing is supplied to the body by the soul, and another is supplied to the soul by God: the soul gives life and receives life; though dead, it gives life if it itself is not given life.

When, therefore, the Word comes and is poured into those who hear, and they become not merely hearers but also obedient, the soul rises from its own death to its own life—that is, from iniquity, foolishness, and impiety to its God, who is its wisdom, justice, and brightness.

Let it rise to him; let it be illuminated by him. “Draw near to him,” he says, “and be enlightened” (Psalm 33:5). If, then, by drawing near you are enlightened and by withdrawing you are darkened, your light was not in yourselves but in your God.

Draw near, so that you may rise; if you withdraw, you will die. If, then, by drawing near you live and by withdrawing you die, your life was not in yourselves. For your life is the same as your light: “For with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:10).

### 13.

Therefore, just as the soul is something different before it is illuminated and becomes better when it is illuminated by participation in something better, so the Word of God, the Son of God, was not something different before he received life, so as to have life by participating in it. Rather, he has life in himself, and therefore he himself is life.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “He granted the Son to have life in himself”? I shall put it briefly: he begot the Son.

For he was not without life and then received life; rather, by being born he is life. The Father is life without being born; the Son is life by being born. The Father is from no father; the Son is from God the Father. The Father, as what he is, is from no one; but the Father is Father because of the Son. The Son, both as Son and as what he is, is because of the Father; and what he is, he is from the Father.

This, then, is what he said: “He gave life to the Son, so that he might have it in himself,” as though he were saying, “The Father, who is life in himself, begot the Son, who would be life in himself.” For “begot” he wished to be understood by “gave.”

It is as if we said to someone, “God gave you being.” To whom did he give it? If he gave being to someone who already existed, he did not give him being, because he existed before being given it and could receive it. When, therefore, you hear, “He gave you being,” you understand that you did not exist as one who could receive it, and that by coming into existence you received being.

A builder gave this house its existence. But what did he give it? That it should be a house. To whom did he give it? To this house. What did he give it? That it should be a house. How could he give the house the quality of being a house? For if it was already a house, to whom would he give it so that it might be a house, when it was already a house?

What, then, does [Col. 1551] “He gave it to be a house” mean? He made it a house.

What, then, did he give the Son? He gave him to be Son; he begot him to be life. That is, he gave him to have life in himself, so that he would be life, not needing life, and so that he would not be understood to have life by participation.

For if he had life by participation, he could also become without life by losing it. Do not understand this of the Son; do not think it; do not believe it.

The Father, therefore, remains life, and the Son also remains life: the Father is life in himself, not from the Son; the Son is life in himself, but from the Father. He was begotten by the Father to be life in himself; the Father, however, is unbegotten life in himself.

Nor did he beget a lesser Son who would become equal by growing. He was not assisted by time toward his perfection, through whom the times themselves were perfectly created. He is coeternal with the Father before all times. For the Father was never without the Son; but the Father is eternal, therefore the Son is coeternal.

What of you, soul? You were dead; you had lost life. Hear the Father through the Son. Rise; receive life, so that in him you may receive the life that you do not have in yourself, while he has life in himself.

The Father and the Son therefore give you life. The first resurrection takes place when you rise to participate in a life that you are not, and by participating become alive.

Rise from your death into your life, which is your God, and pass from death into eternal life. For the Father has eternal life in himself; and unless he had begotten such a Son as would have life in himself, the Son would not give life to whom he willed, just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life.

### 14.

What, then, of that resurrection of the body? For these who hear and live—whence do they live, except by hearing? “The friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29), not because of his own voice. They hear and live by participation, not by being what they hear; and all who hear live, because all who obey live.

Say something, Lord, also about the resurrection of the flesh. For there were people who denied it and said that this alone is the resurrection that takes place through faith. The Lord has just made mention of this resurrection and inflamed us, because certain [Note: [Col. 1551] In four manuscripts, quidem, “indeed.”] dead will hear the voice of the Son of God and live. It is not that some of those who hear will die and others will live; all who hear will live, because all who obey will live.

Behold, we see the resurrection of the mind. Therefore let us not lose faith in the resurrection of the flesh [Note: The manuscripts, with great agreement, read: “Therefore let us not lose the resurrection of the flesh from our faith.”].

And unless you, Lord Jesus, speak of it, what shall we set against those who contradict it? For all sects that have presumed to introduce some religion among human beings have not denied this resurrection of minds. Otherwise one could say to them: “If the soul does not rise again, why do you speak to me? What do you wish to do in me? If you do not make what is worse better, why do you speak? If you do not make the unjust just, why do you speak? But if you make the unjust just, the impious pious, and the foolish wise, you confess that my soul rises again if I obey you and believe you.”

[Col. 1552] Therefore, all who established a sect of any—even false—religion, wishing people to believe them, could not deny this resurrection of minds; all agreed about it. But many denied the resurrection of the flesh and said that the resurrection had already taken place in faith.

The Apostle resists such people, saying: “Among them are Hymenaeus and Philetus, who have strayed from the truth, saying that the resurrection has already taken place, and they overthrow the faith of some” (2 Timothy 2:17–18).

They said that the resurrection had already taken place, but in such a way that no other resurrection was hoped for. They reproached people who hoped for the resurrection of the flesh, as though the resurrection that had been promised were fulfilled in the mind by believing.

The Apostle reproved them. Why did he reprove them? Were they not saying what the Lord was saying here: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live”?

But Jesus still says to you: “I am speaking about the life of minds; I am not yet speaking about the life of bodies. I am speaking about the life of the bodies’ life—that is, about the souls in which the bodies have life. For I know that there are bodies lying in tombs; I know also that your bodies will be in tombs. I am not yet speaking about that resurrection; I am speaking about this one. Rise in this resurrection, so that you may not rise in that one for punishment.”

But so that you may know that I am speaking of that resurrection, what do I add? “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself.”

This life—which the Father is and which the Son is—to what does it pertain? To the soul or to the body? The body does not perceive that life of wisdom; the rational mind does. For not every soul can perceive wisdom. An animal also has a soul, but the soul of an animal cannot perceive wisdom.

The human soul, therefore, can perceive this life that the Father has in himself and granted the Son to have in himself, because he is the true light that illuminates not every soul, but every human being coming into this world.

When, therefore, I speak to the mind itself, let it hear—that is, obey—and live.

### 15.

Therefore, Lord, do not remain silent about the resurrection of the flesh, lest people fail to believe it and we remain arguers rather than preachers.

“Therefore, just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself.” Let those who hear understand; let them believe so that they may understand; let them obey so that they may live.

Let them hear something further, lest they think that the resurrection ends here: “And he gave him authority to execute judgment.” Who gave it? The Father. To whom did he give it? To the Son. For to the one to whom he gave the power to have life in himself, he also gave authority to execute judgment.

“Because he is the Son of Man.” This Christ is both the Son of God and the Son of Man.

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God; he was in the beginning with God.” This shows how he gave him to have life in himself. But because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:9, 1, 2, 14), becoming human from the Virgin Mary, he is the Son of Man.

Therefore, because he is the Son of Man, what did he receive? Authority and judgment to execute. What judgment? At the end of the age. There will be the resurrection of the dead there—but of bodies.

God therefore raises souls through Christ, the Son of God; God raises [Col. 1553] bodies through that same Christ, the Son of Man. “He gave him authority.” He would not have this authority unless he received it, and he would be a human being without authority. But he himself is the Son of Man who is also the Son of God.

By being joined in the unity of person, the Son of Man to the Son of God became one person, the same person who is both Son of God and Son of Man.

What belongs to each, and for what reason, must be distinguished. The Son of Man has a soul and a body. The Son of God, who is the Word of God, has humanity as a soul has a body. Just as a soul possessing a body does not make two persons but one human being, so the Word possessing humanity does not make two persons but one Christ.

What is a human being? A rational soul possessing a body. What is Christ? The Word of God possessing humanity.

I see what matters I am discussing, who is speaking, and to whom I am speaking.

### 16.

Now hear about the resurrection of bodies—not me, but the Lord speaking—on behalf of those who have risen by rising from death and clinging to life. To what life? To the life that does not know death.

Why does it not know death? Because it does not know change. Why does it not know change? Because it has life in itself.

“And he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.” What judgment? What kind of judgment?

Do not be astonished at this, because I said, “He gave him authority to execute judgment.” “Because the hour is coming.” He did not add, “and now is”; therefore he wishes to indicate an hour at the end of the age.

The hour is now for the dead to rise; the hour will be at the end of the age for the dead to rise. But let them rise now in mind, then in the flesh: let them rise now in mind through the Word of God, the Son of God; then let them rise in the flesh through the Word of God made flesh, the Son of Man.

For the Father himself will not come to judge the living and the dead; yet the Father does not withdraw from the Son. How, then, will he himself not come? Because he himself will not be seen in the judgment. “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37).

That form will be the judge which stood under judgment; that form will judge which was judged. It was judged unjustly; it will judge justly.

The form of a servant will therefore come, and it will itself appear. For how could the form of God appear to the just and the unjust? If judgment were to occur only among the just, the form of God could appear to the just. But since judgment will be of the just and the unjust, and the unjust are not permitted to see God—“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8)—the judge will appear in such a form as can be seen both by those whom he will crown and by those whom he will condemn.

The form of a servant, therefore, will be seen; the form of God will remain hidden. The Son of God will be hidden in the servant, and the Son of Man will appear, because “he gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

And because he alone will appear in the form of a servant, while the Father will not appear because he was not clothed in the form of a servant, he therefore said above, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

It was therefore fittingly postponed that he himself should be the expositor who had been the one presenting the statement. Above, the matter was hidden; now, as I think, it is already clear: he gave him authority to execute judgment because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” Judgment will take place through that form [Col. 1554] which the Father does not have.

And what judgment? “Do not be astonished at this, because the hour is coming”—not the hour that now is, when souls rise, but the hour that is to come, when bodies rise.

### 17.

Let him say this more explicitly, so that the heretical denier of the resurrection of the body may find no opening for calumny, although the meaning is already becoming clear.

When it had previously been said, “The hour is coming,” he added, “and now is.” But now he says, “The hour is coming,” and does not add, “and now is.” Nevertheless, by open truth let him shatter all the handles, all the little hinges of slander, and all the knots of their snares.

“Do not be astonished at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs”—what could be clearer? What more explicit? Bodies are in the tombs; souls are not in the tombs, neither those of the just nor those of the unjust. The soul of the just man was in Abraham’s bosom; the soul of the unjust man was being tormented in hell (Luke 16:22–25). Neither soul is in the tomb.

Above, when he said, “The hour is coming, and now is,” I beg you, pay attention. You know, brothers, that one reaches bread for the stomach with labor; how much more, then, bread for the mind? You stand and listen with labor; but we stand and speak with greater labor. If we labor on your behalf, ought you not to labor together with us on behalf of those same selves of yours?

When he said above, “The hour is coming,” and added, “and now is,” what did he add? “When the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” He did not say, “All the dead will hear, and those who hear will live.” He wanted the unjust dead to be understood.

And do all the unjust obey the Gospel? The Apostle plainly says: “But not all obey the Gospel” (Romans 10:16). Yet those who hear will live, because all who obey the Gospel will pass through faith into eternal life. Nevertheless, not all obey—and this is the meaning of “now is.”

But at the end, all who are in the tombs—that is, the just and the unjust—will hear his voice and come forth. Why did he not wish to say, “and they will live”? All will come forth, but not all will live.

For when above he said, “Those who hear will live,” he wished eternal and blessed life to be understood in that obedience, a life that not all who come forth from the tombs will possess.

Thus, both by mentioning the tombs and by explicitly describing the coming forth from the tombs, we clearly understand the resurrection of bodies.

### 18.

“All will hear his voice and come forth.” And where is the judgment, if all will hear and all will come forth? Everything seems confused; I see nothing distinguished.

Certainly you have received authority to judge because you are the Son of Man. Behold, you will be present in the judgment, and the bodies will rise. Say something about the judgment itself—that is, about the distinction between the evil and the good.

Hear this also: “Those who have done good will come forth in the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, in the resurrection of judgment.”

Earlier, when he was speaking about the resurrection of minds and souls, did he make any distinction? All who hear will live, because they will live by obeying.

But when they rise and come forth from the tombs, not all will go to eternal life, but those who have done good; those who have done evil will go to judgment. Here he has used “judgment” for punishment.

There will be a separation, and it will not be like the separation that exists now. For even now we are separated—not by places, but by conduct, affections, desires, faith, hope, and love. We live together with the unjust, but not everyone has the same life. We are divided secretly, separated secretly [Col. 1555]—not like grain on the threshing floor, but like grain in the granary.

Grain is separated on the threshing floor and mixed together. It is separated when it is stripped from the chaff; it is mixed because it has not yet been winnowed.

Then the separation will be open, of life as well as conduct, of bodies as well as wisdom. Those who have done good will go to live with the angels of God; those who have done evil will go to be tormented with the devil and his angels.

And the form of a servant will pass away. For he had presented himself for this purpose, to execute judgment. After the judgment, he will go from here, take with him the body of which he is the head, and offer the kingdom to God (1 Corinthians 15:24).

Then that form of God will plainly be seen, which could not be seen by the unjust, for whose sight the form of a servant had to be displayed.

He says elsewhere: “These will go into eternal burning” (speaking of certain people on the left), “but the just into eternal life” (Matthew 25:46). Of this life he says in another place: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

Then he will appear who, “though he was in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized” (Philippians 2:6). Then he will show himself as he promised to show himself to those who love him.

“For the one who loves me,” he says, “keeps my commandments; and the one who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him.” He was present to those to whom he was speaking, but they saw the form of a servant; they did not see the form of God.

By means of the beast of burden they were being led to the stable for healing; once healed, they will see him, because he says, “I will show myself to him.”

How is he shown to be equal to the Father? When he says to Philip, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:21, 9).

### 19.

“I can do nothing from myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just.”

For we were going to say to him: “You will judge, and the Father will not judge, because he has given all judgment to the Son. Therefore you will not judge according to the Father.” He added: “I can do nothing from myself; as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just, because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

Certainly, the Son gives life to those whom he wishes. He does not seek his own will, but the will of him who sent him. Not my will, not a will of my own; not my will, not the will of the Son of Man; not my will that resists God.

For people do their own will and not God’s when they do what they wish rather than what God commands. But when they do what they wish in such a way that they nevertheless follow God’s will, they do not do their own will, although they do what they wish.

Do willingly what you are commanded; thus you will both do what you wish and not do your own will, but the will of the one who commands.

### 20.

What, then? “As I hear, so I judge.” The Son hears, the Father shows him, and the Son sees the Father acting.

We had postponed treating these matters somewhat more carefully, as far as our abilities allowed, if, after completing the reading, time and strength remained for us. If I say that I can continue speaking, perhaps you can no longer listen. Perhaps, from eagerness to hear, you say, “We can.”

It is better, then, for me to confess my weakness: being tired, I cannot continue speaking, rather than, when you are already well satisfied, continue [Col. 1556] pouring into you something that you cannot properly digest.

Therefore, with the Lord’s help, keep me as your debtor for tomorrow concerning this promise, which I had postponed until today if time remained.

## TREATISE XX

Again on the passage: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing from himself unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.” Chapter 5, verse 19.

### 1.

The words of our Lord Jesus Christ, especially those recalled by John the Evangelist, who did not recline upon the Lord’s breast without reason (John 13:23), unless it was so that he might drink in the secrets of his deeper wisdom and, having drunk what he had received through love, belch it forth by evangelizing, are so secret and profound for understanding [Note: [Col. 1556] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read “of profound understanding.” M.] that they trouble all who are perverse in heart and exercise all who are upright in heart.

Therefore let Your Charity attend to the few words that have been read. Let us see whether, with him who wished his words to be recited to us—words once heard and written down so that they might now be read—granting and assisting us, we can in some way understand what he means by what you have just heard him say:

“Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son can do nothing from himself unless he sees the Father doing it; for whatever the Father does, the Son does likewise.”

### 2.

You must be reminded where this speech arose, in view of the preceding part of the reading, where the Lord had healed a certain man among those who lay in the five porticoes of that pool of Solomon. He had said to him, “Take up your pallet and go to your home.” He had done this on the Sabbath; hence the Jews, disturbed, slandered him as though he were an overturner and transgressor of the Law.

Then he had said to them: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John 5:8, 17).

For they understood the observance of the Sabbath carnally and thought that God, after the labor of making the world, was, as it were, sleeping until that day, and that he had therefore sanctified the day on which he began, so to speak, to rest from his labors.

But the Sabbath is a sacrament commanded to our ancient fathers (Exodus 20:8–11), which we Christians observe spiritually, so that we may abstain from every servile work—that is, from every sin, since the Lord says, “Everyone who commits sin is the slave of sin” (John 8:34)—and have rest in our heart, that is, spiritual tranquility.

And although we strive for this in the present age, we shall not attain that perfect rest until we have departed from this life.

But Scripture said that God rested because, after all things had been perfected, he was no longer creating any creature. Scripture called it “rest” in order to admonish us that we shall rest after good works.

For we have this written in Genesis: “And God made all things very good, and God rested on the seventh day” (Genesis 1:31; 2:2). Thus, when you observe that God himself rested after good works, do not hope for rest except when you have done good works.

And just as God, after he made the human being according to his image and likeness on the sixth day and completed in him all [Col. 1557] his very good works, rested on the seventh day, so you too should not hope for rest unless you have returned to the likeness in which you were made, which you lost by sinning.

For God cannot be said to have labored, since he spoke and they were made. Who, after such ease of work, would wish to rest as though after labor? If he commanded and someone resisted him, if he commanded and it was not done, and he labored in order that it might be done, then he could rightly be said to have rested after labor.

But since even in the book of Genesis we read, “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light; God said, ‘Let there be a firmament,’ and there was a firmament” (Genesis 1:3, 6–7), and the rest came into being immediately at his word—and the Psalm also bears witness, saying, “He spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalms 32:9; 148:5)—how could he, who had never labored in commanding, require rest after the world had been made, as though he were going to cease?

Those things, therefore, are mystical, and they were set forth in this way so that we might hope for rest after this life, but only if we have done good works.

Therefore, refuting the Jews’ shamelessness and error and showing that they did not think rightly about God, the Lord said to them, when they were scandalized [Note: The manuscripts read “scandalizing”; likewise consistently below, instead of “scandalized”], because he worked the healing of a human being on the Sabbath: “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

Do not therefore think that my Father rested on the Sabbath in such a way that from then on he no longer works; rather, just as he himself now works, so I also work.

But just as the Father works without labor, so does the Son. God spoke, and they were made; Christ said to the sick man, “Take up your pallet and go to your home,” and it was done.

### 3

The catholic faith, however, holds that the works of the Father and the Son are not separable. This is what I wish, if I can, to say to Your Charity—but in accordance with the Lord’s words, “Let him who is able to grasp it, grasp it” (Matt. 19:12). Whoever cannot grasp it should not attribute this to me, but to his own slowness; let him turn to the One who opens the heart, so that He may pour into it what He gives. Finally, if anyone does not understand for the reason that I have not expressed it as it ought to have been expressed, let him forgive human weakness and entreat divine goodness.

For we have Christ the teacher within us. Whatever you have been unable to grasp through your ears and my mouth, turn in your heart to Him who both teaches me what I say and distributes to you as He deigns. He knows what to give and to whom to give it; He will be present to the one who asks and will open to the one who knocks. And if perhaps He does not give, let no one say that he has been abandoned. Perhaps He delays giving something, but He leaves no one who hungers without nourishment. For if He does not give it at once, He exercises the one who seeks; He does not despise the one who asks.

See, then, and attend to what I wish to say, even if perhaps I cannot say it. The catholic faith holds this—established by the Spirit of God in His holy ones, against every heretical perversity—that the works of the Father and the Son are inseparable. What is the meaning of what I have said? Just as the Father and the Son themselves are inseparable, so the works of the Father and the Son are inseparable.

How are the Father and the Son inseparable? Because He Himself said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Because the Father and the Son are not two gods but one God; [Col. 1558] the Word and the One whose Word He is, one and Only-begotten; one God, the Father and the Son embraced by love, and the one Spirit of their love, so that the Trinity may be the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, not only the works of the Father and the Son, but also those of the Holy Spirit, just as the persons are equal and inseparable, are likewise inseparable. I shall make still clearer what it means that the works are inseparable. The catholic faith does not say that God the Father did one thing and the Son did something else; rather, what the Father did, the Son also did, and the Holy Spirit also did. For all things were made through the Word. When He spoke and they were made, they were made through the Word; they were made through Christ. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”; “all things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3). If all things were made through Him, then when God said, “Let there be light,” and light was made, He made it in the Word and through the Word.

### 4

Behold, then, we have now heard the Gospel: it tells how He answered the Jews who were angry because He not only was breaking the sabbath but also called God His own Father, making Himself equal with God (ibid. 5:18). For so it is written in the preceding passage. When, therefore, the Son of God and the Truth was answering their misguided indignation, He said, “Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.”

It is as though He had said: “Why are you scandalized because I called God my Father and because I make myself equal with God? I am equal in such a way that He begot me; I am equal in such a way that He is not from me, but I am from Him.” This is understood in the words, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” That is: whatever the Son has in order to do, He has from the Father in order to do it.

Why does He have it from the Father in order to do it? Because He has from the Father that He is the Son. Why does He have from the Father that He is the Son? Because He has from the Father that He is able, because He has from the Father that He exists. For in the Son, being is the same as being able.

This is not so with a human being. By comparison with human weakness, which lies far below, raise your hearts as best you can. And lest perhaps one of us should reach the secret place and, startled as though by the flash of a great light, grasp something—lest he remain foolish—let him nevertheless not think that he understands everything, lest he become proud and lose what he has understood.

With a human being, what he is is one thing and what he can do is another. Sometimes a person exists but cannot do what he wishes; sometimes, however, he exists in such a way that he can do what he wishes. Thus his being is one thing and his ability another.

For if his being were the same as his ability, then whenever he wished, he would be able. But God has neither one substance by which He exists and another power by which He can act; whatever belongs to Him is consubstantial with Him, and whatever He is, He is because He is God. [Note: [Col. 1558] Eight manuscripts read: “but whatever belongs to Him is consubstantial with Him, and whatever belongs to Him is that which is, because He is God.” Remigianus, however, adds “is” at this point: “and whatever belongs to Him is, is that which is, because He is God”; and this is no less correct.] He does not exist in one way and have power in another; rather, He possesses being and power simultaneously, because He possesses willing and doing simultaneously.

Therefore, because the Son’s power is from the Father, the Son’s substance too is from the Father; and because the Son’s substance is from the Father, the Son’s power too is from the Father. There is not one power in the Son and another substance, but the power is itself the substance: substance, by which He is; power, by which He is able.

Therefore, because the Son is from the Father, [Col. 1559] He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” Because the Son is not from Himself, He cannot act from Himself.

### 5

For He seems, as it were, to have made Himself lesser when He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” Here heretical presumption raises its neck—namely, that of those who say that the Son is lesser than the Father, lesser in power, majesty, and capability, because they do not understand the mystery of Christ’s words.

But let Your Charity attend, and see how, in their carnal understanding, they are now disturbed by Christ’s very words. I said a little earlier that this disturbs every perverse heart, just as the Word of God exercises devout hearts—especially what is said through the evangelist John. For through him profound things are said, not ordinary things, not things easily understood.

Behold, if a heretic happens to hear these words, he raises himself up and says to us: “Behold, the Son is lesser than the Father. Listen to the words of the Son, who says, ‘The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.’”

Wait. Consider how it is written: “Be gentle in listening to the word, so that you may understand” (Eccli. 5:13). Suppose that I have been disturbed by these words, since I say that the power and majesty of the Father and the Son are equal, yet I have heard, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” Disturbed by these words, I ask you, who now think that you have understood: We know from the Gospel that the Son walked upon the sea (Matt. 14:25). Where did He see the Father walking upon the sea?

Now he is disturbed. So set aside what you thought you had understood, and let us inquire together. What, then, shall we do? We have heard the Lord’s words: “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” He Himself walked upon the sea; the Father never walked upon the sea. Certainly the Son does nothing except what He has seen the Father doing.

### 6

Return with me, then, to what I was saying, lest perhaps it should be understood in such a way that we may both emerge from the question. For, according to the catholic faith, I see how I may emerge without offense or scandal; but you, enclosed on every side, are asking how you may get out. Look at how you entered. Perhaps you did not understand even this that I said, “Look at how you entered.” Hear Him Himself saying, “I am the door” (John 10:7).

It is not without reason, then, that you seek a way out and do not find one: you did not enter through the door, but fell through the wall. Therefore, as best you can, gather yourself up from your ruin and enter through the door, so that you may enter without offense and leave without error.

Come through Christ, and do not bring forth from your own heart what you are to say; speak what He shows. Behold how the catholic faith emerges from this proposition. The Son walked upon the sea, placing the feet of His flesh upon the waves; the flesh was walking, and the divinity was guiding. When, then, the flesh was walking and the divinity guiding, was the Father absent?

If He was absent, how does the Son Himself say, “The Father, who remains in me, himself does his works” (ibid. 14:10)? If, therefore, the Father, remaining in the Son, Himself does His works, that walking of the flesh upon the sea was done by the Father and was done through the Son. Therefore that walking is a work inseparable between the Father and the Son.

I see both of Them working there. [Col. 1560] Neither did the Father abandon the Son, nor did the Son depart from the Father. Thus whatever the Son does, He does not do without the Father, because whatever the Father does, He does not do without the Son.

### 7

We have emerged from this. See that we rightly say that the works of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are inseparable. For how do you understand this? Behold: God made light, and, according to your carnal understanding, the Son saw the Father making light—since you wish to understand Him as lesser because He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” God the Father made light. What other light did the Son make?

God the Father made the firmament, the heaven between the waters and the waters. According to your dull and gross understanding, the Son saw Him making the firmament, and said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing.” Give me another firmament. Or have you lost the foundation?

Those who are built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus Himself as the chief cornerstone, are at peace in Christ (Eph. 2:14–20); they do not contend and go astray in heresy.

We understand, then, that the light was made by God the Father, but through the Son; that the firmament was made by God the Father, but through the Son. For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

Shake off your understanding—or rather, it should not be called understanding, but plainly folly. God the Father made the world. What other world did the Son make? Give me the Son’s world. This world in which we are—whose is it? Tell us by whom it was made.

If you say, “By the Son,” and not by the Father, you have strayed from the Father. If you say, “By the Father,” and not by the Son, the Gospel answers you: “The world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1:3, 10). Recognize, then, Him through whom the world was made, and do not be among those who did not know Him who made the world.

### 8

The works of the Father and the Son are therefore inseparable. But this statement—“The Son can do nothing of himself”—would be equivalent to saying, “The Son is not from himself.” For if He is the Son, He was born; if He was born, He is from Him of whom He was born.

Yet He begot One equal to Himself. Nothing was lacking in the One who begot; nor did He who begot the coeternal Son wait for time in order to beget; nor did He who brought forth the Word from Himself seek a mother in order to beget; nor had the begetting Father preceded the Son in age, so as to beget a lesser Son.

Perhaps someone says that after many ages, in His old age, God received a Son. Just as the Father is without old age, so the Son is without growth. Neither did the Father grow old nor did the Son grow; rather, the equal begot the equal, the eternal the eternal.

“How,” someone asks, “does the eternal beget the eternal?” In the way that a temporal flame generates temporal light. The flame that generates is coeval with the light it generates; the generating flame does not precede the generated light in time. From the moment the flame begins, the light begins.

Give me a flame without light, and I will give you God the Father without the Son.

This, then, is the meaning of “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing”: the Son’s seeing is His being born from the Father. His vision is not one thing and His substance another; nor is His power one thing and His substance another. Everything that He is, He is from the Father; everything that He can do, He can do from the Father, because what He can do and what He is are one, and all of it is from the Father.

### 9

[Col. 1561] He continues in His own words and disturbs those who misunderstand, in order to recall the erring to a correct understanding. After saying, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing,” lest a carnal understanding creep in, turn the mind aside, and make a person imagine two craftsmen in the simple divinity—one a master and the other a pupil attending to the master, for example, as he makes a chest, so that just as the master made one chest, the pupil might make another according to the vision he observed in the master at work—He continued, so that carnal understanding would not duplicate anything of this kind for itself in that simple divinity: “For whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does these same things.”

The Father does not do one set of similar things and the Son another; He does the same things in the same way. For He did not say, “Whatever the Father does, the Son does other similar things,” but, “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does these same things.”

What the Father does, the Son does; the Father made the world, the Son made the world, the Holy Spirit made the world. If there are three gods, there are three worlds; if there is one God, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one world was made by the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.

The Son therefore does the things that the Father does, and He does them not dissimilarly. He does these things, and He does them similarly.

### 10

He had already said, “He does these things.” Why did He add, “similarly”? So that another perverse understanding or error might not arise in the mind.

You see a human being’s work. There is a mind in the human being and a body. The mind commands the body, but there is a great difference between body and mind: the body is visible, the mind invisible. There is also a great difference between the power and strength of the mind and those of any—even heavenly—body.

Nevertheless, the mind commands its own body and makes the body act. What the mind appears to do, the body also does. Thus the body appears to do this same thing as the mind, but not similarly.

How does it do the same thing, but not similarly? The mind forms a word within itself, commands the tongue, and the tongue brings forth the word formed by the mind. The mind has done it, and the tongue has done it; the master of the body has done it, and the servant has done it. But for the servant to do it, he received from the master what he was to do, and he did it at the master’s command.

The same thing was done by both—but was it done similarly?

“How not similarly?” someone asks. Behold: the word formed by my mind remains in me; the word formed by my tongue, striking the air, passes away and is no more. When you have spoken a word in your mind and it has sounded through your tongue, return to your mind and see that the word you formed is there. Did it remain on your tongue as it remained in your mind?

What sounded through your tongue was made by the sounding tongue; it was made by the thinking mind. But what sounded through the tongue passed away; what the mind thought remains.

The body therefore did what the mind did, but not similarly. The mind made something that the mind could retain; the tongue made something that sounds and strikes the ear through the air. Do you follow the syllables and make them remain?

The Father and the Son are not like this. Rather, the Son does these same things and does them similarly. If God made the heaven, which remains, the Son made that same heaven, which remains. If God the Father made the human being who dies, the Son made that same human being who dies.

Whatever the Father made enduring, the Son also made enduring, because He made it similarly. Whatever the [Col. 1562] Father made temporal, the Son likewise made temporal, because He not only made the same things but also made them similarly. For the Father made all things through the Son, because the Father made all things through the Word.

### 11

Seek separation between the Father and the Son, and you will not find it—but only if you have risen above; only if you have touched something beyond your mind will you fail to find it.

For if you remain among the things that an erring mind constructs for itself, you are speaking with your own images, not with the Word of God. Your images deceive you.

Go beyond the body and learn to savor the mind; go beyond the mind and learn to savor God. You do not touch God unless you have also passed beyond the mind. How much less do you touch Him if you have remained in the flesh?

Those, then, who savor the flesh—how far are they from savoring what God is? For they would not be there even if they savored the mind. A person departs far from God when he thinks carnally, and there is a great difference between flesh and mind; yet there is a still greater difference between mind and God.

If you are in the mind, you are in the middle. If you attend below, there is the body; if you attend above, there is God. Raise yourself from the body; pass beyond yourself as well.

Consider what the Psalm said, and you will be instructed how God is to be savored: “My tears have become my bread day and night, while it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’” (Ps. 41:4–5). It is as though the pagans were saying: “Behold our gods; where is your God?” They point out what is visible; we worship what is invisible.

And to whom should we display Him? To a person who has no means by which to see? For if they see their gods with their eyes, we too have other eyes by which we may see our God. Those very eyes must be cleansed by our God, so that we may see our God: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

When, therefore, he had said that he was troubled because it was said to him daily, “Where is your God?”, he continues: “These things I remembered, since it is said to me daily, ‘Where is your God?’ And, as though wishing to grasp his God, he says, “These things I remembered, and I poured out my soul upon myself” (Ps. 41:4–5).

Thus, in order to reach my God, of whom it was said to me, “Where is your God?”, I did not pour out my soul upon my flesh, but upon myself. I passed beyond myself in order to touch Him. For He is above me who made me; no one touches Him except the one who has passed beyond himself.

### 12

Consider the body: it is mortal, earthly, fragile, corruptible. Cast it aside. But perhaps the flesh is merely temporal. Consider other bodies; consider the heavenly bodies. They are greater, better, and splendid. Attend to them also: they revolve from east to west; they do not remain still. They are visible to the eyes, not only to human beings but even to animals. Pass beyond them also.

“And how,” you will say, “do I pass beyond the heavenly bodies while I walk upon the earth?” You pass beyond them not with the flesh but with the mind. Cast them aside as well. Although they shine, they are bodies; although they gleam from heaven, they are bodies.

Come, then, since perhaps you do not think you have anywhere to go when you consider all these things. “Beyond the heavenly bodies,” you say, “where shall I go, and what shall I pass beyond with my mind?”

You have considered all these things?

“I have,” you say.

From where did you consider them? Let the one who considers them appear. For the one who considers, distinguishes, separates, and, as it were, weighs all these things on the scales of wisdom is the [Col. 1563] mind.

Without doubt, the mind by which you considered all these things is better than all the things you considered. This mind, then, is spirit, not body. Pass beyond it also.

First compare the mind itself, so that you may see what you are to pass beyond; compare it with the flesh. Far be it from you to think it worthy of comparison. Compare it with the radiance of the sun, moon, and stars: the mind’s radiance is greater.

First observe the mind’s swiftness. See whether the spark of a thinking mind is not more powerful than the splendor of the shining sun. You see the rising sun with your mind. How slow is its movement in relation to your mind? You could quickly think what the sun is going to do. It will come from east to west; tomorrow it will already rise on the other side. While your thought has accomplished this, the sun is still slow, and you have traversed everything.

Great, then, is the mind. But why do I say that it is? Pass beyond it also, because the mind too is changeable, although it is better than every body. Now it knows, now it does not know; now it forgets, now it remembers; now it wills, now it does not will; now it sins, now it is just.

Pass beyond, then, every changeability—not only everything that is seen, but also everything that changes. You passed beyond the flesh, which is seen; you passed beyond heaven, the sun, the moon, and the stars, which are seen. Pass beyond everything that changes.

After passing beyond these things, you had come to your mind; but there too you found the changeability of your mind. Is God changeable? Pass beyond your mind also. Pour out your soul upon yourself, so that you may touch God, of whom it is said to you, “Where is your God?”

### 13

Do not think that you will do something impossible for a human being. John the evangelist himself did this. He passed beyond the flesh; he passed beyond the earth upon which he trod; he passed beyond the seas that he saw; he passed beyond the air where birds fly; he passed beyond the sun; he passed beyond the moon; he passed beyond the stars; he passed beyond all spirits that are not seen; he passed beyond his own mind by the very reason of his mind. [Note: [Col. 1563] One manuscript reads, “reason itself.” Another reads, “and reason itself.”]

Passing beyond all these things and pouring out his soul above himself, where did he arrive? What did he see? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.”

If, then, you do not see separation in the light, why do you seek separation in the work? See God; see His Word adhering to the Word that speaks [Note: So the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “see His word: adhere to the word that speaks.”], because He who speaks does not speak in syllables; rather, to shine with the splendor of wisdom is to speak.

What has been said about His Wisdom? “She is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26). Consider the radiance of the sun. It is in the heavens, and it spreads its brightness throughout all the lands and all the seas; and certainly it is bodily light. If you separate the sun’s radiance from the sun, separate the Word from the Father.

I speak of the sun. A small flame in a lamp, which could be extinguished by a single breath, spreads its light over everything beneath it. You see the light spread forth, generated by the flame; you see an emission, but you do not see a separation.

Understand, therefore, dearly beloved brothers, that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit adhere inseparably to one another; that this Trinity is one God; and that all the works of the one God are the works of the Father, the works of the Son, and the works of the [Col. 1564] Holy Spirit.

The remaining matters that follow, which concern the discourse of our Lord Jesus Christ in the Gospel—since a sermon is also owed to you tomorrow—be present to hear them.

# TREATISE XXI

From the passage written, “For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does,” up to, “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” Chapter 5, verses 20–23.

### 1

Yesterday, insofar as the Lord deigned to grant it, we discussed with whatever ability we possessed, and understood with whatever capacity we possessed, how the works of the Father and the Son are inseparable: the Father does not do one set of things and the Son another, but the Father does all things through the Son, as through His Word, of whom it is written, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

Today let us examine the words that follow, and let us both implore and hope for mercy from the same Lord, so that, first, if He Himself judges us worthy, we may understand what is true; but if we are unable to do this, we may not turn toward what is false. For it is better not to know than to err; yet it is better to know than not to know.

Therefore, before all else, we must strive to know. If we are able, thanks be to God; but if meanwhile we cannot reach the truth, let us not turn to falsehood.

For we must consider what we are and what we are discussing. We are human beings bearing flesh and walking in this life. And although we have already been reborn from the seed of the Word of God, we have been so renewed in Christ that we have not yet been completely stripped of Adam.

For what is mortal and corruptible in us “weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15); it is plainly evident and manifest that this comes from Adam. But what is spiritual in us lifts up the soul; it comes from God’s gift and His mercy—He who sent His Only-begotten to share our death with us and lead us to His immortality.

We have Him as our teacher, so that we may not sin; as our defender, if we have sinned, confessed, and turned back; as our intercessor for us, if we desire any good from the Lord; and as giver together with the Father, because the Father and the Son are one God.

But He, the hidden God, was speaking as a human being to human beings, the manifest human being, so that He might make manifest human beings into gods; and the Son of God, made the son of man, so that He might make the sons of men sons of God.

By what art of His wisdom He accomplishes this, we recognize in His words. He speaks as a little one to little ones, but He Himself is so little that He is also great; we, however, are little, but in Him we are great. He therefore speaks as one cherishing and nourishing infants, and causing them to grow through love.

### 2

He had said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing” (John 5:19). We understood that the Father does not separately do something which the Son, after seeing it, might also do by observing His Father’s work; rather, He said, “The Son can do nothing of himself, except what he sees the Father doing,” because the whole Son is from the Father, and His whole substance and power are from Him who begot Him.

But now, after saying that He does similarly the things that the Father does—so that we may not understand the Father to do one thing and the Son another, but that the Son, with similar power, does the very things that the [Col. 1565] Father does, since the Father does them through the Son—He continued with what we heard read today: “For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does.”

Again mortal thought is disturbed. “The Father shows the Son what He Himself does,” someone says. “Therefore the Father acts separately, so that the Son may see what He does.”

Once again two craftsmen present themselves to human thought, as though a craftsman were teaching his son his craft and showing him whatever he does, so that the son too might be able to do it. “He shows him,” it says, “everything that he himself does.”

When, therefore, the Father acts, does the Son not act, so that the Son may see what the Father does? Certainly “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

We see how the Father shows the Son what He does, when the Father does nothing except what He does through the Son. What did the Father make? The world. Did He show the Son the world after it had been made, so that He too might make something of that kind?

Let the world made by the Son be given to us. Yet “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made,” and “the world was made through him” (John 1:3, 10). If the world was made through Him, if all things were made through Him, and the Father does nothing that He does not do through the Son, where does the Father show the Son what He does, except in the very Son through whom He does it?

For where is there a place in which the Father’s work might be shown to the Son, as though He acted outside and sat outside, while the Son watched the Father’s hand to see how He acted? Where is that inseparable Trinity? Where is the Word of whom it was said that He is “the Power and Wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24)? Where is what Scripture says about that Wisdom: “For she is the brightness of eternal light” (Wis. 7:26)? Where is what is said of her again: “She reaches from end to end mightily and orders all things sweetly” (ibid. 8:1)?

If the Father does anything, He does it through the Son; if He does it through His Wisdom and His Power, He does it through them. He does not show Him externally something for Him to see; rather, He shows Him within Himself what He does.

### 3

What does the Father see—or rather, what does the Son see in the Father, so that He too may act? I might perhaps be able to say; but let Him give someone who can grasp it. Or perhaps I might be able to think it but not say it; or perhaps I cannot even think it.

For that divinity surpasses us as God surpasses human beings, as the immortal surpasses mortals, as the eternal surpasses the temporal. May He breathe upon us and grant us something from that fountain of life; may He deign now to sprinkle and drip something into our thirst, lest we wither in this wilderness.

Let us say to Him what we have learned to say: “Lord,” and “Father.” We dare to do this because He Himself willed us to dare—provided that we live in such a way that He does not say to us, “If I am a Father, where is my honor? If I am a Lord, where is my fear?” (Mal. 1:6).

Let us say to Him, then, “Our Father.” To whom do we say, “Our Father”? To the Father of Christ. Therefore, whoever says to the Father of Christ, “Our Father,” what does he say to Christ except “Our brother”?

Yet the Father of Christ is not our Father in the same way. Christ never joined us to Himself in such a way as to make no distinction between us and Him. He is the Son equal to the Father; He is eternal with the Father and coeternal with the Father. We, however, were made through the Son and adopted through the Only-begotten.

Accordingly, it has never been heard from the mouth of our Lord Jesus Christ, when He spoke to His disciples, that He called the supreme [Col. 1566] God His Father “our Father.” He either said “my Father” or “your Father.” He did not say “our Father”—to such an extent that in one passage He placed these two together: “I am going,” He said, “to my God and your God.” Why did He not say, “our God”? He said “my Father” and “your Father” (John 20:17); He did not say, “our Father.”

He joins in such a way as to distinguish; He distinguishes in such a way as not to separate. He wishes us to be one in Him, but the Father and Him to be one.

### 4

However much we may understand and however much we may see—even when we have been made equal to the angels—we shall not see as the Son sees.

For even when we do not see, we are something. What else are we when we do not see except non-seeing? Yet we exist even when we do not see. And in order to see, we turn ourselves toward the One whom we are to see, and a vision comes to be in us that was not there, even though we already existed.

A human being exists without seeing, and that same person, when he has seen, is called a seeing human being. Therefore, seeing is not the same thing for him as being human; for if seeing were the same for him as being human, he would never be human unless he were seeing.

But when a person is not seeing and seeks to see what he does not see, there is one who seeks and one who turns himself so as to see. When he has turned himself well and seen, the human being who was previously not seeing becomes a seeing human being.

Seeing, then, comes to him and departs from him. It comes to him when he turns himself; it departs from him when he turns away.

Is the Son like this? Far be it from us. The Son was never not seeing and afterward became seeing. Rather, seeing the Father is for Him the same as being the Son.

We, by turning away toward sin, lose illumination; by turning ourselves toward God, we receive illumination. The light by which we are illuminated is one thing, and we who are illuminated are another. But the light itself by which we are illuminated neither turns away from itself nor loses its radiance, because it is light.

Thus the Father shows the Son the thing He does in such a way that the Son sees all things in the Father, and the Son is all things in the Father. He was born by seeing, and by being born He sees.

But it is not that He was once not born and afterward was born, just as it is not that He was once not seeing and afterward saw. Rather, in what it is for Him to see lies what it is for Him to be; in what it is for Him to be lies what it is for Him to have been born; in what it is for Him to have been born lies what it is for Him to remain; in what it is for Him to remain lies what it is for Him not to change; and in what it is for Him not to change lies what it is for Him to persist without beginning and without end.

Let us not, then, understand this carnally, as though the Father sits, performs a work, and shows it to the Son; and as though the Son sees the work that the Father does and performs it in another place or from another material. For “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”

The Son is the Father’s Word. God said nothing that He did not say in the Son. By saying in the Son what He was going to make through the Son, He begot the Son Himself, through whom He would make all things.

### 5

“And he will show him greater works than these, so that you may marvel.” Again this causes disturbance. And who is capable of examining so great a mystery worthily?

But since He has deigned to speak to us, He Himself opens it. For He would not wish to say what He did not wish to be understood. Since He has deigned to speak, He surely aroused the attention of His hearers. Would He arouse someone to listen and then abandon the one He had aroused?

We said, as best we could, that the Son does not know temporally; that the Son’s knowledge is not one thing and the Son Himself another; that the Son’s vision is not one thing and the Son Himself another; rather, that the vision itself is the Son, and that the very knowledge or wisdom of the Father is the Son. We said that this wisdom and this vision are eternal from eternity and coeternal with Him from whom He is [Note: The manuscripts read, “eternal from eternity and also coeternal with Him to whom He is coeternal.”]; that there nothing changes with time; [Col. 1567] nothing comes into being that was not there; nothing that was there perishes.

We said this as best we could. What, then, is time doing here, when He says, “He will show him greater works”? That is, “He is going to show” or “He will show.” “He showed” is one thing; “He will show” is another. “He showed” is said of the past; “He will show” is said of the future.

What, then, are we to do here, brothers? Behold, we had said that He is coeternal with the Father, that nothing in Him changes with time, that nothing moves through intervals either of moments or of places, that He remains always with the Father, seeing the Father and existing by seeing Him. Yet again, He names times for us, saying, “He will show him greater works than these.”

Is He therefore still going to show the Son something that the Son does not know? What shall we do? How shall we understand this?

Behold, our Lord Jesus Christ was above and is below. When was He above? When He said, “Whatever the Father does, the Son likewise does these same things.” How is He now below? “He will show him greater works than these.”

O Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, Word of God through whom all things were made, what is the Father going to show You that You do not yet know? What is hidden from You that is in the Father, whom nothing is hidden from? What works is He going to show You that are greater? Or greater than what are the works that He is going to show?

For when He said, “greater than these,” we must first understand what things they are greater than.

### 6

Let us recall where this discourse began. When the man who had been ill for thirty-eight years was healed, and [the Lord] commanded him, now restored to health, to pick up his pallet and go to his house. From this arose the disturbance of the Jews with whom he was speaking: he was speaking in words, but was silent in understanding; in a certain way he was hinting to those who understood and concealing [his meaning] from those who were angry. Since the Jews were therefore disturbed because the Lord had done this on the Sabbath, they gave occasion for this discourse.

Let us not, then, hear these words as though we had forgotten what was said above, but let us look back to that sick man of thirty-eight years, suddenly made well, while the Jews marveled and were angry. They were seeking darkness concerning the Sabbath more than light concerning the miracle. Speaking, then, to those who were indignant, he said, “The Father will show him works greater than these.” Greater than these—which works? What you saw: a man made well, whose sickness had lasted until he was thirty-eight years old. The Father will show the Son works greater than these.

What are these greater works? He continues and says: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.” Clearly, these are greater. It is much more for a dead man to rise than for a sick man to recover; these are greater works.

But when will the Father show them to the Son? Does the Son not know them? Did the one who was speaking not know how to raise the dead? Did he still have to learn to raise the dead, through whom all things were made? He who made us live when we did not exist—did he still have to learn how we should be raised? What, then, does he mean?

### 7

For he descended to us, and the one who shortly before was speaking as God began to speak as man. Yet he himself is both man and God, because God became man: he became what he was not, without losing what he was. Thus man was added to God, so that he who was God might be man—not so that he would now be man and cease to be God.

Let us therefore hear him as brother, whom we heard as creator: as creator, because he was the Word in the beginning; as brother, because he was born of the Virgin Mary. [Note: At Col. 1568, two manuscripts read “whom” (quem).] He was creator before Abraham, before Adam, before the earth, before heaven, before all corporeal and spiritual things; but he was brother from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Judah, from the Israelite Virgin.

If, then, we know that the one speaking to us is both God and man, let us understand the words of God and of man. At one time he says things that pertain to majesty; at another, things that pertain to humility. He is himself exalted, who became humble in order to make us humble people exalted. [Note: Col. 1568: this is the reading of Bad., Am., Er., and seven manuscripts; Lov. reads, “who makes humble people exalted.”]
