What, then, does he say? “The Father will show me works greater than these, so that you may marvel.” Therefore, he will show them to us, not to him. [Col. 1568] Since the Father is going to show them to us, he said, “so that you may marvel.” He explained what he meant by “The Father will show me.”

Why did he not say, “The Father will show you,” but “will show the Son”? Because we too are members of the Son; and, since we are members, in a certain way he himself learns what we learn in his members.

How does he learn in us? As he suffers in us. How do we prove that he suffers in us? From that voice from heaven: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

Is he not the one who will sit as judge at the end of the age, placing the righteous at his right hand and the wicked at his left, and will say, “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom, for I was hungry and you gave me food”? And when they answer him, “Lord, when did we see you hungry?” he will say to them, “When you gave to one of the least of mine, you gave to me” (Matt. 25:31–40).

Therefore, let us now question the one who said, “When you gave to one of the least of mine, you gave to me,” and say to him: “Lord, when will you be learning, when you teach all things?” He immediately answers us in our faith: “When one of the least of mine learns, I learn.”

### 8

Let us therefore rejoice and give thanks—not merely that we have become Christians, but that we have become Christ. Do you understand, brothers, the grace of God upon us as the Head? Marvel, rejoice: we have become Christ. [Note: Col. 1568: Lov. reads “are hungry” (esuris), and below, “Do you understand, brothers, the grace of God upon us as the Head? Marvel,” etc.; both passages are corrected from earlier editions and manuscripts.] For if he is the head and we are the members, the whole man is he and we.

This is what the apostle Paul says: “So that we may no longer be children, tossed and carried about by every wind of doctrine.” Earlier he had said: “Until we all attain to the unity of faith and to the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4:14, 13).

The fullness of Christ, therefore, is the head and the members. What is the head and the members? Christ and the Church. We would arrogantly claim this for ourselves [Col. 1569] if he himself did not deign to promise it, when through the same apostle he says: “Now you are the body of Christ and individually members of it” (1 Cor. 12:27).

### 9

When, therefore, the Father shows something to the members of Christ, he shows it to Christ. A great miracle occurs, yet it is true: Christ is shown what Christ already knew, and Christ is shown it through Christ.

It is a remarkable and great thing, but this is how Scripture speaks. Shall we contradict the divine utterances instead of understanding them and giving thanks, from the gift of the one who gave it? What did I mean by saying that Christ is shown something through Christ? It is shown to the members through the head.

Look at an example within yourself. Suppose that, with your eyes closed, you wanted to pick something up. The hand would not know where to go—and certainly your hand is your member, for it is not separated from your body. Open your eyes: now the hand sees where it should go. The member follows when the head shows it the way.

If, then, something of this kind could be found in you, so that your body showed something to your body, and something was demonstrated to your body through your body, do not be surprised that it is said that Christ is shown something through Christ. The head shows so that the members may see, and the head teaches so that the members may learn; yet the head and the members are one man.

He did not wish to separate himself from us, but deigned to be joined to us. He was far from us—very far. For what is as far apart as creature and Creator? What is as far apart as God and man? What is as far apart as righteousness and wickedness? What is as far apart as eternity and mortality?

Behold how far away the Word was: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,” through whom all things were made. How, then, did he draw near, so that he might be what we are, and we might be in him? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

### 10

This, then, is what he will show us. He showed this to his disciples, who saw him in the flesh. What is it? “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.”

Does the Father raise some and the Son others? Certainly all things were made through him. What are we to say, my brothers? Christ raised Lazarus. Did the Father raise the dead man so that Christ might see how to raise Lazarus? Or, when Christ raised Lazarus, did he not raise him with the Father, and did the Son act alone without the Father?

Read the passage itself and see that he invokes the Father there so that Lazarus may rise (John 11:41–44). As man, he invokes the Father; as God, he acts with the Father.

Therefore Lazarus, who rose again, was raised by both the Father and the Son, through the gift and grace of the Holy Spirit; and the Trinity performed that wonderful work.

Let us not, then, understand “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills” as though some were raised and given life by the Father and others by the Son. Rather, those whom the Father raises and gives life, the Son also raises and gives life, because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.

And to show that, although he had received this power from the Father, he nevertheless possessed equal power, he therefore said, “So also the Son [Col. 1570] gives life to whomever he wills,” thereby showing that his own will is present. [Note: Col. 1569: four manuscripts read “received”; most others, with the Louvain edition, omit it and read, “yet power with the Father”; Am., Bad., and Er. read, “the Father’s power, received nevertheless.”] Otherwise someone might say: “The Father raises the dead through the Son, but the Father acts as the powerful one, as the one possessing authority, while the Son acts as though from another’s authority, like an angel acting as a minister.” He indicated his authority when he said, “So also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.”

For the Father does not will anything different from the Son; but just as they have one substance, so also they have one will.

### 11

Who, then, are these dead whom the Father and the Son give life? Are they those of whom we spoke—Lazarus, or the son of the widow (Luke 7:14–15), or the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue (Luke 8:54–55)? We know that these were raised by Christ the Lord.

He wishes to suggest something else to us: namely, the resurrection of the dead, which we all await—not the resurrection experienced by certain people so that the rest might believe. Lazarus rose again only to die; we shall rise again to live forever.

Does the Father bring about such a resurrection, or the Son? Rather, the Father in the Son. Therefore, the Son, and the Father in the Son.

How do we prove that he is speaking of this resurrection? After saying, “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills,” lest we understand the resurrection of the dead that he performs as a miracle rather than for eternal life, he immediately added, “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

What does this mean? He was speaking of the resurrection of the dead when he said, “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whomever he wills.” Hence he immediately added, as though supplying the reason, something about judgment: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” This can only mean that he had spoken of that resurrection of the dead which will take place in judgment.

### 12

“For the Father,” he says, “judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

Shortly before, we thought that the Father did something the Son did not do, when he said, “For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does.” It was as though the Father acted and the Son watched. Such was the carnal understanding creeping into our minds: as though the Father did what the Son did not do, while the Son watched the Father showing him what the Father was doing.

Now, however, we see the Son doing something the Father does not do. How he turns us about and works upon our minds! He leads us here and there, not allowing us to remain in one carnal position, so that by turning us he may exercise us, by exercising us cleanse us, by cleansing us make us capable, and, having made us capable, fill us.

What do these words do to us? What was he saying? What is he saying? Shortly before he said that the Father shows the Son whatever he does. I saw, as it were, the Father acting and the Son waiting. Now again I see the Son acting and the Father remaining inactive: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

When, then, the Son is going to judge, will the Father be inactive and not judge? What is this? What am I to understand? Lord, what are you saying? You are the Word, God; I am a man. You say that the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.

Elsewhere I read you saying, “I judge no one; there is one who seeks and judges” (John 8:15, 50). Of whom do you say, “There is one who seeks and judges,” [Col. 1571] if not of the Father? He seeks redress for your injuries; he judges concerning your injuries.

How, then, is it said here that the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son?

Let us question Peter also and hear him speaking in his Epistle: “Christ suffered for us,” he says, “leaving us an example, so that we should follow his footsteps. He committed no sin, neither was deceit found in his mouth. When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but entrusted himself to the one who judges justly” (1 Pet. 2:21–23).

How is it true that the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son?

Here we are troubled; troubled, let us labor; laboring, let us be cleansed. Let us attempt, with his help, to penetrate somehow the profound secrets of these words. Perhaps we act rashly in wishing to examine and scrutinize the words of God. And why were they spoken, unless they were to be known? Why did they sound forth, unless they were to be heard? Why were they heard, unless they were to be understood?

Let him therefore strengthen us and grant us something insofar as he deigns to do so. And if we have not yet reached the source, let us drink from the stream. Behold, John himself has flowed forth for us like a stream; he has brought the Word to us from the heights, humbled him, and in a certain sense laid him low, so that we would not dread what is high, but approach the humble one.

### 13

There is certainly a true and powerful understanding, if only we can hold on to it in some way: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” This was said because, in the judgment, the Son alone will appear to human beings. The Father will remain hidden; the Son will be manifest.

In what form will the Son be manifest? In the form in which he ascended. For in the form of God he is hidden with the Father; in the form of a servant he is manifest to human beings.

Therefore, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son”—that is, to the Son who is manifest. In this manifest judgment the Son will judge, because he himself will appear to those who are to be judged.

Scripture shows us more clearly that he himself will appear. On the fortieth day after his resurrection he ascended into heaven, while his disciples watched. An angelic voice said to them: “Men of Galilee, why do you stand looking into heaven? This Jesus, who has been taken up from you into heaven, will come in the same way as you saw him go into heaven” (Acts 1:3, 9–11).

How did they see him go? In the flesh that they touched and handled, whose scars they also tested by touching; in that body in which he entered and left with them for forty days, revealing himself to them in reality, not in some false appearance—not a phantom, not a shadow, not a spirit—but as he himself said, without deceiving them: “Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39).

That body is now worthy of heavenly habitation; it is no longer subject to death and does not change through the stages of life. For just as it had grown from infancy to that age, so it will not decline from the age that was youth into old age. It remains as it ascended, and will come to those to whom, before he comes, he has willed that his word be preached.

Thus he will come in human form. The wicked will see this form, and those placed at the right will see it, and those separated to the left will see it, as it is written: “They will look on him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12:10; John 19:37).

If they will look on him whom they pierced, they will see the very body that they struck with the spear. [Col. 1572] The Word cannot be struck by a spear. Thus the wicked will be able to see what they were also able to wound.

They will not see the hidden God in the body; after the judgment, he will be seen by those who will be at the right hand. This, then, is what he means: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” because the Son will come manifest for judgment, appearing to human beings in a human body.

He will say to those at the right: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom.” To those at the left he will say: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:34, 41).

### 14

Behold, the form of a man will be seen by the godly and the ungodly, by the just and the unjust, by the faithful and the unbelieving, by those who rejoice and those who mourn, by those who are confident and those who are put to shame. Behold, it will be seen.

When that form has been seen in the judgment, and the judgment has been completed—when it has been said that the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, because the Son will appear in the judgment in the form he received from us—what will happen afterward?

When will the form of God be seen, which all the faithful long for? When will that which was “the Word in the beginning, God with God, through whom all things were made” be seen? When will that form of God be seen of which the apostle says, “Though he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped” (Phil. 2:6)?

Great indeed is that form in which the equality of the Father and the Son is still recognized—ineffable, incomprehensible, especially to little ones. When will it be seen?

Behold, the righteous are at the right and the unrighteous at the left. All alike see the man; they see the Son of Man; they see the one who was pierced; they see the crucified one; they see the humbled one; they see the one born of the Virgin; they see the Lamb from the tribe of Judah. When will they see the Word, God with God?

He will be there then also, but the form of a servant will appear. The form of a servant will be shown to servants; the form of God will be reserved for sons.

Let servants therefore become sons; let those at the right Let them go into the eternal inheritance promised long ago, which the martyrs believed without seeing and for whose promise they shed their blood without hesitation. Let them go there and see.

When will they go there? Let the Lord himself say: “So these will go away into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. 25:46).

### 15

Behold, he has named eternal life. Did he thereby tell us that there we shall see and know the Father and the Son? What if we shall live forever but shall not see that Father and Son?

Hear elsewhere where he named eternal life and made clear what eternal life is. Do not be afraid; I am not deceiving you. I did not promise this without cause to those who love me, saying: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them, that is the one who loves me; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

Let us answer the Lord and say: “What is so great, Lord our God? What is so great? You will manifest yourself to us? Did you not also manifest yourself to the Jews? Did not those who crucified you see you?”

“But you will manifest yourself in the judgment, when we stand at your right hand.” Will those who stand at the left not also see you? What does it mean that you will manifest yourself to us? Do we not see you now, when you speak?

He answers: [Col. 1573] “I will manifest myself in the form of God; for now you see the form of a servant.” I will not defraud you, faithful man: believe, and you will see.

You love, yet you do not see. Will love itself not lead you to see? Love; persevere in loving. “I will not defraud,” he says, “your love, I who cleansed your heart.” For why did I cleanse your heart, unless so that God might be seen by you? “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

But, says the servant, as though arguing with the Lord, “You did not make this explicit when you said, ‘The righteous will go into eternal life.’ You did not say, ‘They will go so that they may see me in the form of God and see the Father, to whom I am equal.’”

Consider what he said elsewhere: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

### 16

And now [Note: Col. 1573: most manuscripts read, “And how, then, afterward?”; others read, “And how? Therefore also afterward.”], after the judgment has been mentioned—the judgment which the Father, judging no one, has given entirely to the Son—what will happen? What follows? “That all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”

The Jews now honor the Father, while the Son is despised. [Note: Col. 1573: the text should be read thus according to Er., Lugd., and Ven.; the printed text has, “The Father is honored by the Jews.”] For the Son appeared as a servant, while the Father was honored as God. The Son will also appear equal to the Father, so that all may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.

For now, then, we possess this in faith. Let no Jew say, “I honor the Father; what have I to do with the Son?” Let him answer: “Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father.” You are altogether lying: you blaspheme the Son and do an injury to the Father. For the Father sent the Son, and you despise the one he sent. How do you honor the sender when you blaspheme the one sent?

### 17

“Behold,” someone says, “the Son was sent; and the Father is greater, because he sent him.”

Turn away from the flesh. The old man suggests oldness to you; in the new man, recognize newness. May the one who is new to you, yet ancient before the world, perpetual and eternal, call you back to this understanding. [Note: Col. 1573: three manuscripts read “by oldness” (vetustate); others, with the editions, “for oldness” (vetustati). The editions later read “new to you, ancient to the world,” without the preposition “before” (a), which is nevertheless found in all manuscripts; Lov. below reads “call you back from this understanding,” against the other editions and manuscripts.]

Is the Son lesser because he is called sent? I hear mission, not separation.

“But,” he says, “we see this in human affairs: the one who sends is greater than the one who is sent.”

Human affairs deceive human beings; divine affairs cleanse them. Do not attend to human affairs, where the sender seems greater and the one sent lesser. Even human affairs themselves bear witness against you.

For example, if someone wished to seek a wife but could not do so himself, he might send a more important friend to make the request for him. There are many situations in which the one selected to be sent is himself the greater, while the sender is lesser.

Why, then, do you now wish to make an accusation because one sent and the other was sent?

The sun sends forth its ray without separating from it; the moon sends forth its brightness without separating from it; a lamp pours out its light without separating from it. I see mission there, but I see no separation. [Note: Col. 1573: the manuscripts read “emanation” (emissionem).]

If you seek examples from human affairs, O heretical vanity—although, as I said shortly before, human affairs themselves, in certain examples, refute and convict you—consider how different human affairs are from the divine matters to which you wish to transfer these examples.

A man who sends remains where he is, while the one who is sent goes on. [Col. 1574] Does the man go with the one whom he sends? But the Father who sent the Son did not withdraw from the Son.

Hear the Lord himself saying: “Behold, the hour is coming when each of you will be scattered to his own place, and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32).

How did he send the one with whom he came? How did he send the one from whom he did not withdraw? Elsewhere he said: “But the Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14:10). Behold, he is in him; behold, he is at work. The sender did not withdraw from the one sent, because the one sent and the sender are one.

---

## Treatise XXII

From the passage: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life,” to the passage: “I do not seek my own will but the will of him who sent me.” Chapter 5, verses 24–30.

### 1

The Gospel reading of today follows the sermons delivered to you the day before yesterday and yesterday. [Col. 1575] Let us discuss it in order—not according to its worth, but according to our strength—for you too receive it not according to the abundance of the overflowing spring, but according to your own capacity.

We do not speak into your ears as much as the spring itself flows, but only as much as we can grasp and convey into your understanding, while he himself works more abundantly in your hearts than we do in your ears.

A great matter is being handled, but not by great men—indeed, by very little ones. Yet he gives us hope and confidence: he who became small for our sake is great. For if he did not encourage us and invite us to understand him, but abandoned us as contemptible; if he had not himself taken on our mortality and come to us to speak the Gospel to us, because we cannot grasp his divinity; if he had not wished to share with us what is lowly and least in us, we would think that he did not wish to give us what is great in him, since he assumed what is little in us.

I have said this so that no one may either criticize us for discussing these matters, as though we were excessively bold, or despair of himself, thinking that he cannot grasp by God’s gift what the Son of God has deigned to speak to him.

Therefore, what he has deigned to speak to us we ought to believe, because he wished us to understand it. But if we cannot, he grants understanding when asked—the one who granted the word without being asked.

### 2

Pay attention to what these words conceal. “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life.”

Certainly we are all striving toward eternal life. And he says, “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life.” Did he wish us to hear his word but not to understand it? For if life eternal is found in hearing and believing, much more is it found in understanding.

Faith is the step of devotion; understanding is the fruit of faith. Thus we may reach eternal life, where the Gospel will not be read to us, but the one who now dispenses the Gospel to us will appear to all his attendants whose hearts have been purified. All the pages of reading, the reader’s voice, and the interpreter’s exposition will have been removed. He will appear to those already living in an immortal body and never again to die, cleansing and illuminating them as they live and see “what was in the beginning: the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1).

Now, therefore, let us consider who we are and whom we are hearing. Christ is God, and he speaks with human beings. He wishes to be grasped: let him make them capable. He wishes to be seen: let him open their eyes. Yet he does not speak to us without cause, since what he promises us is true.

### 3

“Whoever hears my words,” he says, “and believes him who sent me, has eternal life, and will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life.”

Where and when do we pass from death to life, so that we may not come into judgment? In this life one passes from death to life; in this life, which is not yet life, one passes from death to life.

What is this passage? “Whoever hears my words,” he said, “and believes him who sent me.” By holding to these things, you believe, and you pass over.

Can someone pass over while remaining standing? Certainly. He stands in body but passes over in mind.

Where was he, from which he passed, and where does he pass? He passes from death to life.

Look at one person standing, in whom this whole process described is taking place. He stands and hears. Perhaps he did not believe; by hearing, he believes. A short while before he did not believe; now he believes. As though he had passed from the region of unbelief to the region of faith, his heart has been moved, not his body; moved toward what is better. [Note: Col. 1575: editions read, “He made the transition by a movement of the heart, not of the body, a movement toward what is better”; the manuscripts read, “his heart having been moved, not his body, moved toward what is better.”] For those who abandon the faith are moved toward what is worse.

Behold, in this life—which, as I said, is not yet life—one passes from death to life, so that one may not come into judgment.

Why did I say that this is not yet life? If it were life, the Lord would not say to someone, “If you wish to enter life, keep the commandments” (Matt. 19:17). He did not say, “If you wish to enter eternal life”; he did not add “eternal,” but simply said, “life.”

Therefore this should not even be called life, because it is not true life. What is true life except eternal life?

Hear the apostle speaking to Timothy: “Command those who are rich in this present age not to be proud, nor to set their hopes on the uncertainty of riches, but on the living God, who richly provides us with everything for enjoyment. Let them do good, be rich in good works, generous and ready to share.”

Why this? Hear what follows: “Thus they will store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of the true life” (1 Tim. 6:17–19).

If they must store up for themselves a good foundation for the future, so that they may take hold of true life, then surely the life in which they were living is a false life. For why would you wish to take hold of true life if you already possessed true life?

Is true life to be taken hold of? Then one must depart from the false. And where must one depart? Where must one go? Hear and believe: you make the passage from death to life, and you do not come into judgment.

### 4

What does this mean: “You will not come into judgment”? And who will be better than the apostle Paul, who says: “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5:10)?

Paul says, “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ,” and you dare promise yourself that you will not come into judgment?

“Far be it from me,” you say, “to dare promise myself this. But I believe the one who promises.”

The Savior speaks; Truth makes the promise. He himself said to me: “Whoever hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and passes from death to life, and will not come into judgment.”

I therefore heard the words of my Lord and believed. Whereas I was an unbeliever, I became a believer. As he instructed me, I passed from death to life; I do not come into judgment—not through my own presumption, but through his promise.

But Paul speaks against Christ: a servant against his Lord, a disciple against his teacher, a man against God. The Lord says that whoever hears and believes passes from death to life and will not come into judgment; the apostle says, “We must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.”

Or, if the one who appears before the judgment seat does not come into judgment, I do not know how I am to understand it.

### 5

Our Lord God therefore reveals and teaches us through his Scriptures how the word “judgment” is to be understood when it is used.

I urge you to pay attention. Sometimes “judgment” means punishment; sometimes “judgment” means separation or discrimination.

In the sense in which judgment means separation, “we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each may receive what he has done through the body, whether good or evil.” This is separation: good things are assigned to the good, and bad things to the bad.

For if judgment always meant something evil, the Psalm would not say, “Judge me, O God.” Someone may hear a person saying, “Judge me, O God,” and wonder. A person usually says, “May God forgive me; spare me, O God.” Who says, “Judge me, O God”?

Sometimes this very verse is placed in the psalm at the diapsalma, to be supplied by the reader and answered by the people. Perhaps someone’s heart is struck, and he is afraid to sing to God and say, “Judge me, O God.” Yet the believing people sing it and do not think that they are wishing for something evil when they have learned it from divine Scripture. If they understand little, they believe that what they sing is something good.

Yet that Psalm itself did not leave the person without understanding. For it continues and shows by its subsequent words what kind of judgment it meant: not condemnation, but discrimination. It says, “Judge me, O God.” What does “Judge me, O God” mean? “And distinguish my cause from an unholy nation.”

According to this judgment of discrimination, therefore, we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ.

According to the judgment of condemnation, however, he says, “Whoever hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life, and passes from death to life, and will not come into judgment.”

What does “will not come into judgment” mean? He will not come into condemnation.

Let us prove from the Scriptures that “judgment” is used where punishment is understood. Indeed, later in this very reading you will hear the word “judgment” used only in the sense of condemnation and punishment (below, §13).

The apostle says in one passage, writing to believers who were treating the Body, as you know, improperly, and for this reason were being chastised with the Lord’s scourge: “That is why many among you are weak and ill, and many sleep” (1 Cor. 11:30–32). [Note: Cols. 1576–77: all manuscripts have “sufficiently” (sufficienter), although the Apostle has not hikanōs, “sufficiently,” but hikanoi, “many” or “sufficient.”]

Many were therefore also dying. He continues: “For if we judged ourselves, we would not be judged by the Lord.” That is, if we corrected ourselves, we would not be corrected by the Lord. “But when we are judged, we are chastened by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.”

There are therefore some who are judged here according to punishment, so that they may be spared there. There are others who are spared here, so that they may be tormented more severely there. There are also those on whom the punishments themselves are inflicted without a chastising scourge, if they have not been corrected by God’s scourge. When here they have despised the father who strikes, there they will feel the judge who punishes.

There is therefore a judgment into which God—that is, the Son of God—will send the devil and his angels, and all unbelievers and ungodly people with him, at the end. The one who now believes and passes from death to life will not come into this judgment.

### 6

For you might think that by believing you would not die according to the flesh, and, understanding the words carnally, say to yourself: “My Lord told me, ‘Whoever hears my words and believes him who sent me has passed from death to life.’ Therefore I have believed; I will not die.”

Know that you must pay the death which you owe as punishment from Adam. For he received the sentence in whom we all were at that time: “You shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17). The divine sentence cannot be annulled.

But when you have paid the death of the old man, you will be received into the eternal life of the new man, and you will pass from death to life.

Meanwhile, make the passage of life now. What is your life? Faith: “The righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2:4; Rom. 1:17).

What of unbelievers? They are dead. Among such dead was the man who was dead in body, of whom the Lord says: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Matt. 8:22).

Therefore, even in this life there are dead and living, and all seemingly live. Who are the dead? Those who have not believed. Who are the living? Those who have believed.

What is said to the dead by the apostle? “Awake, O sleeper.” But, he says, he spoke of sleep, not death. Hear what follows: “Awake, O sleeper, and arise from the dead.”

And as though he were saying, “Where shall I go?”—“Christ will shine on you” (Eph. 5:14).

Now, when Christ has illuminated you as a believer, you pass from death to life. Remain in that into which you have passed, and you will not come into judgment.

### 7

He himself now explains that, and continues: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” Since he had said, “He has passed from death to life,” perhaps we might understand this as referring to the future resurrection; wishing to show how the one who believes passes over—and that passing consists in passing from unbelief to faith, from injustice to justice, from pride to humility, from hatred to love—he now says: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the hour is coming, and now is.”

[Note: [Col. 1577] In this wording of verse 25, you will scarcely find a single manuscript that agrees consistently even with itself: printed editions and manuscripts have, in some places, *will come* (*veniet*), and in others, *is coming* (*venit*). Later, likewise, in verse 28 of the same fifth chapter of John, they interchange this word inconsistently.]

What could be clearer? He has plainly disclosed what he meant: it is happening now, in the way Christ urges us. “The hour is coming.” What hour? “And now is,” when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.

We have already spoken about these dead. What do we think, my brothers? In this crowd listening to me, are there no dead people? Those who believe and [Col. 1578] act according to the true faith live and are not dead; but those who either do not believe, or believe like the demons—trembling, as they do [James 2:19]—and live wickedly, confessing the Son of God but not possessing love, are rather to be counted among the dead.

And yet this hour is still in progress. For the hour of which the Lord spoke will not be one hour among the twelve hours of a single day. From the time he spoke until now, and until the end of the age, that one hour is in progress, of which John says in his Epistle: “Little children, it is the last hour” [1 John 2:18]. Therefore, “now is.” Whoever lives, let him live; whoever was dead, let him live. Let him who lay dead hear the voice of the Son of God, rise, and live.

The Lord cried out to Lazarus’s tomb, and the man who had been dead four days rose again. He who was giving off an odor came forth into the air; he had been buried, a stone had been placed over him, and the Savior’s voice broke through the hardness of the stone. Yet your heart is so hard that the divine voice still does not break through to you! Rise in your heart; come forth from your tomb. You were indeed lying dead in your heart as in a tomb, and you were weighed down as though by a stone, by the burden of evil habit. Rise and come forth.

What does “Rise and come forth” mean? Believe and confess. Whoever has believed has risen; whoever confesses has come forth. Why have we said that the one who confesses has come forth? Because before confessing he was hidden; but when he confesses, he comes forth from darkness into light.

And when he has confessed, what is said to the ministers? What was said at Lazarus’s funeral: “Unbind him, and let him go” [John 11:38–44]. How? He said to the apostolic ministers: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” [Matthew 18:18].

### 8

“The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” From where will they live? From life. From what life? From Christ. How do we prove that they live from Christ, who is life? “I am,” he says, “the way, the truth, and the life” [John 14:6]. Do you wish to walk? “I am the way.” Do you not wish to be deceived? “I am the truth.” Do you not wish to die? “I am the life.”

Your Savior says this to you: There is nowhere for you to go except to me; there is no way for you to go except through me.

Now, therefore, this hour is in progress. This is precisely what is happening, and it never ceases. People who had been dead rise, pass over into life, and live at the voice of the Son of God, living from him and persevering in his faith. For the Son possesses life from which believers may live.

### 9

And how does he possess it? As the Father possesses it. Hear him saying: “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has also granted the Son to have life in himself.”

Brothers, I shall explain this as I am able. These are the words that disturb a limited understanding. Why did he add “in himself”? It would have been sufficient to say, “Just as the Father has life, so he granted the Son to have life.” He added “in himself”: the Father has life in himself, and the Son likewise has life in himself.

He wished us to understand something in what he said, “in himself.” And here a mystery has been enclosed in this word: let it be knocked upon, so that it may be opened.

O Lord, what is it that you have said? “In himself”—why did you add this? For did not the Apostle Paul, whom you caused to live, possess life? “He did,” you say. When human beings were dead, so that they might revive and pass over by believing into your word, once they have passed over, will they not have life in you? [Col. 1579] They will; for I myself said a little earlier: “Whoever hears my words and believes him who sent me has eternal life.”

Therefore those who believe in you have life, and you did not say “in themselves.” But when you were speaking of the Father, you said, “As the Father has life in himself”; and again, when speaking of yourself, you said, “So he granted the Son also to have life in himself.” “As he has, so he granted him to have.” Where does he have it? “In himself.” Where did he grant him to have it? “In himself.”

Where does Paul have life? Not in himself, but in Christ. Where do you, as a believer, have it? Not in yourself, but in Christ. Let us see whether the Apostle says this: “Yet I live—no longer I, but Christ lives in me” [Galatians 2:20].

Our life, considered as our own—that is, arising from our own will—will be nothing but evil, sinful, and wicked. True life, however, comes from God in us, not from us; it is given to us by God, not produced by us.

Christ, however, has life in himself, as the Father does, because he is the Word of God. He does not live badly at one time and well at another; a human being, however, lives badly at one time and well at another. The one who was living badly was in his own life; the one who lives well has passed over into the life of Christ.

Having become a participant in life, you were not what you received, though you were one who could receive it. The Son of God, however, was not at first without life and then received life. For if he had received it in that way, he would not have had it in himself.

What, then, does “in himself” mean? It means that he himself was that life.

### 10

Perhaps I can say something still clearer. Someone lights a lamp.

[Note: [Col. 1579] He indicates somewhat obscurely that he delivered this sermon by lamplight, although he delivered it in summer, as may be inferred from Treatise XXVII, preached on the feast of the martyr Lawrence.]

For example, in relation to the little flame that burns there, that fire possesses light in itself. Your eyes, however, which, when the lamp was absent, lay in darkness and saw nothing, now possess light themselves—but not in themselves.

Accordingly, if they turn away from the lamp, they become dark; if they turn toward it, they are illumined. But that fire shines for as long as it exists. If you wish to take its light away, you extinguish the fire itself at the same time; for without light it cannot remain.

Christ, however, is light unquenchable and coeternal with the Father: always glowing, always shining, always burning. For if he did not burn, would it be said in the Psalm, “There is none who can hide himself from his heat” [Psalm 18:7]?

But you were cold in your sin; you turn toward him so that you may grow warm. If you withdraw, you grow cold. In your sin you were in darkness; you turn toward him so that you may be illumined. If you turn away, you will be darkened.

Accordingly, because you were darkness in yourself, when you are illumined you will not be light, although you are in the light. For the Apostle says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” [Ephesians 5:8]. After saying, “Now you are light,” he added, “in the Lord.” In yourself, therefore, you are darkness; in the Lord, light.

Why are you light? Because by participating in that light you are light. But if you withdraw from the light by which you are illumined, you return to your darkness.

Christ is not so; the Word of God is not so. How, then? “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he granted the Son to have life in himself”—so that he might not live by participation, but live unchangeably, and altogether be life itself.

“So he granted the Son to have life.” “As he has, so he granted.” What is the difference? The Father granted; the Son received. Was the Son already existing when he received? Do we understand Christ ever to have been [Col. 1580] without light, when he is himself the Wisdom of the Father, of which it is said: “She is the radiance of eternal light” [Wisdom 7:26]?

Therefore, when it is said that he “granted it to the Son,” this is equivalent to saying that he begot the Son; for in begetting him, he granted it to him. Just as he granted him existence, so he granted him to be life; and just as he granted him to be life, so he granted him to have life in himself.

What does it mean that he should have life in himself? It means that he would not need life from elsewhere, but would himself be the fullness of life from which other believers would live while they lived.

Therefore he granted him to have life in himself. To whom did he grant it? To his Word, to him who in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.

### 11

Then, because he became human, what did he grant him? “And he granted him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

Insofar as he is the Son of God, “just as the Father has life in himself, so he granted the Son to have life in himself.” But insofar as he is the Son of Man, he granted him authority to execute judgment.

This is what I explained to Your Charity yesterday: in the judgment, the human being will be seen, but God will not be seen. After the judgment, however, God will be seen by those who have conquered in the judgment; by the wicked, God will not be seen [in the preceding discourse].

Since, therefore, he will be seen in the judgment in that form in which he will come as he ascended, he had earlier said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” [John 5:22]. He repeats this here also when he says: “And he granted him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man.”

Suppose you were to say: “He granted him authority to execute judgment”—why? When did he not possess this authority to execute judgment? When “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” when “all things were made through him” [John 1:1, 3], did he not possess authority to execute judgment?

But I say that he granted him authority to execute judgment because he is the Son of Man; in this respect he received authority to judge, because he is the Son of Man. For insofar as he is the Son of God, he always possessed this authority.

He who was crucified received it. He who was in death is in life. The Word of God was never in death, but always in life.

### 12

Perhaps someone among us was now saying concerning the resurrection: “Look, we have risen. Whoever hears Christ, whoever believes, passes from death to life and will not come into judgment. ‘The hour is coming, and now is,’ so that whoever hears the voice of the Son of God may live. He was dead; he heard; look, he is rising. What, then, is meant by the resurrection that is said to come afterward?”

Spare yourself; do not rush to judgment, lest you proceed beyond it.

There is indeed a resurrection taking place now: unbelievers were dead, the wicked were dead; the righteous live, passing from the death of unbelief to the life of faith. But do not consequently believe that there will be no bodily resurrection afterward. Believe that there will also be a bodily resurrection.

Hear what follows after this resurrection accomplished through faith has been commended, lest anyone should think that this is the only resurrection and fall into the despair and error of those who were perverting the minds of others, saying that the resurrection had already taken place. Of them the Apostle says: “They overthrow the faith of some” [2 Timothy 2:18].

For I think they were saying things such as this to them: “Look, the Lord [Col. 1581] says, ‘Whoever believes in me has passed from death to life.’ The resurrection has already taken place in believers who had been unbelievers. How, then, is another resurrection spoken of?”

Thanks be to our Lord God: he supports those who waver, directs those who hesitate, and strengthens those who doubt. Hear what follows, for you have no grounds on which to create for yourself the darkness of death. If you have believed, believe the whole.

“What whole?” you ask. “What am I to believe?” Hear what he says: “Do not marvel at this, because he has granted the Son authority to execute judgment.” He is speaking of the end.

How does he speak of the end? “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming.” Here he did not say, “and now is.”

What did he say concerning the resurrection of faith? “The hour is coming, and now is.” But concerning this resurrection, which he declares will come for dead bodies, he said, “The hour is coming”; he did not say, “and now is,” because it will come at the end of the age.

### 13

“And from where,” you ask, “do you prove to me that he spoke of this resurrection?”

If you listen patiently, you yourself will now prove it to yourself. Let us therefore continue: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs”—what could be clearer concerning this resurrection?

A little earlier he had not said, “Those who are in the tombs,” but “The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” He did not say, “Some will live and others will be condemned,” because all who believe will live.

But what does he say concerning the tombs? “All who are in the tombs will hear his voice and will come forth.” He did not say, “They will hear and live.” For if they lived badly and lay in the tombs, they will rise to death, not to life.

Let us therefore see who will come forth. Although a little earlier the dead came to life by hearing and believing, no distinction was made there. It was not said, “The dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and when they hear, some will live and others will be condemned”; rather, “All who hear will live,” because those who believe will live, those who have love will live, and no one will die.

But concerning the tombs, he says: “They will hear the voice and will come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment.”

This is the judgment: that punishment of which he had said a little earlier, “Whoever believes in me has passed from death to life and will not come into judgment.”

### 14

“I can do nothing from myself. As I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just.”

If you judge as you hear, from whom do you hear? From the Father? Certainly, “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

When you are, in a sense, the Father’s herald, do you say what you hear?

[Note: [Col. 1581] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition have several minor differences here; they read: “Since you are, in a sense, the Father’s herald, so that you may say what you hear.” M.]

“What I hear, I say,” because what the Father is, I am. For speaking is my own nature, because I am the Father’s Word.

This is what Christ says to you. From this, consider what belongs to you. What does “As I hear, I judge” mean except “As I am, I judge”? For how does Christ hear?

Brothers, let us ask—I beseech you. Does Christ hear from the Father? How does the Father speak to him? Certainly, if he speaks to him, he addresses words to him; for everyone who says something to someone says it by means of a word.

How does the Father speak to the Son when the Son is the Father’s Word? Whatever the Father says to us, he says through his Word. The Son is the Father’s Word; through what other word, then, does he speak to that Word? God is one, and he has one Word; in that one Word he contains all things.

What, then, does “As I hear, I judge” mean? “As I am from the Father, so I judge.”

Therefore, [Col. 1582] “my judgment is just.” For if you do nothing from yourself, O Lord Jesus, as carnal people understand it, if you do nothing from yourself, how did you say shortly before, “So also the Son gives life to whomever he wishes”?

Now you say, “I do nothing from myself.” But what does the Son commend except that he is from the Father? Whoever is from the Father is not from himself. He is from the Father. If the Son were from himself, he would not be the Son; he is from the Father.

The Father is not from the Son in order to be the Father; the Son is from the Father in order to be the Son. He is equal to the Father; nevertheless, the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son.

### 15

“Because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

The only-begotten Son says, “I do not seek my own will,” while human beings want to do their own will! He who is equal to the Father humbles himself so greatly; and he who lies in the lowest place exalts himself so greatly, though he cannot rise unless a hand is extended to him!

Let us therefore do the will of the Father, the will of the Son, [Note: [Col. 1582] In all manuscripts, “the will of Christ.”] and the will of the Holy Spirit, because this Trinity has one will, one power, and one majesty.

Nevertheless, the Son says, “I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me,” because Christ is not from himself, but is from his Father. As for what he possessed so that he might appear as a human being, he assumed it from the creature that he himself formed.

---

## TREATISE XXIII

On the Gospel reading, “If I bear witness concerning myself,” and so forth, up to “And you are unwilling to come to me, so that you may have life.” The preceding readings already treated are also repeated, namely, from the words, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the Son cannot do anything from himself,” and so forth. Chapter 5, verses 19–40.

### 1

At one point in the Gospel the Lord says that a prudent hearer of his word ought to be like a man who wishes to build, digs deeper and deeper until he reaches the foundation of the rock’s stability, and there securely establishes what he is building against the force of the river, so that when the river comes, it is rather checked by the building’s solidity than causes that house to collapse by its own force [Matthew 7:24–25].

Let us think of God’s Scripture as a field where we wish to build something. Let us not be lazy or content with the surface. Let us dig deeper, until we reach the rock. “The rock, however, was Christ” [1 Corinthians 10:4].

### 2

Today’s reading has spoken to us about the Lord’s testimony: that he does not need testimony from human beings, but possesses testimony greater than human beings are. He said what that testimony is: “The works that I do bear witness concerning me.” Then he added: “And the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.”

He also says that the very works he performs he received from the Father. The works, therefore, bear witness; the Father bears witness.

Did John bear no witness? Certainly he did, but as a lamp—not to satisfy friends, but to confound enemies.

[Note: [Col. 1582] In B., “not to satisfy friends, but to confound enemies.” We have restored this passage from Erasmus and Lovaniensis, whose reading appears more polished. M.]

For it had already been foretold in the person of the Father: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ; I will clothe his enemies with confusion, but upon him my sanctification will flourish” [Psalm 131:17–18].

Suppose you were placed in the night [Col. 1583]. You paid attention to a lamp, admired the lamp, and rejoiced in the lamp’s light. But that lamp says that there is a sun in which you ought to rejoice; and although it burns in the night, it orders you to await the day.

It is not, then, because that man’s testimony was unnecessary. For why would he have been sent if he were unnecessary? But lest a person remain with the lamp and think the lamp’s light sufficient for him, the Lord neither says that the lamp was superfluous nor says that you ought to remain with the lamp.

The Scripture of God gives another testimony. There, certainly, God bore witness to his Son, and in that Scripture the Jews had placed their hope—in God’s Law, namely, which had been administered to them through Moses, God’s servant.

“Search the Scriptures,” he says, “in which you think you have eternal life; they bear witness concerning me. And you are unwilling to come to me, so that you may have life.”

Why do you think that you have eternal life in the Scriptures? Ask the one to whom they bear witness, and understand what eternal life is.

And because they wanted to reject Christ on account of Moses, as though Christ were opposed to Moses’ institutions and commands, he again refutes them as though by means of another lamp.

### 3

For all human beings are lamps, since they can both be lit and extinguished. Lamps indeed shine when they possess understanding and burn in spirit; for even if they were burning and have been extinguished, they too may become putrid.

They remained good servants of God as lamps through the oil of his mercy, not through their own strength. For God’s freely given grace is the oil of the lamps.

“One who has labored more than all of them,” says one lamp; and lest he seem to burn by his own strength, he added: “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” [1 Corinthians 15:10].

All prophecy, therefore, before the Lord’s coming, is a lamp. Concerning it the Apostle Peter says: “We possess the prophetic word, made more certain, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts” [2 Peter 1:19].

The Prophets, then, are lamps, and all prophecy is one great lamp. What of the Apostles? Are they not also lamps? Certainly they are lamps. For he alone is not a lamp. He is not lit and extinguished, because, “just as the Father has life in himself, so he granted the Son to have life in himself.”

The Apostles, therefore, are lamps, and they give thanks because they have been kindled by the light of Truth, burn with the Spirit of love, and possess an abundant supply of the oil of God’s grace.

If they were not lamps, the Lord would not say to them, “You are the light of the world.” After saying, “You are the light of the world,” he showed that they should not think their light to be of the kind of which it is said, “He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.”

This was said of the Lord when he was distinguished from John. For concerning John the Baptist it had been said: “He was not that light, but came to bear witness concerning the light” [John 1:9, 8].

And lest you say, “How was he not light, when Christ says that he was a lamp?”—in comparison with the other light, he was not the light. For there was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into this world.

Therefore, when he also said to the disciples, “You are the light of the world,” lest they think something had been attributed to them that should be understood of Christ alone, and thus the lamps should be [Col. 1584] extinguished by the wind of pride, after saying, “You are the light of the world,” he immediately added: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and put it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for all who are in the house.”

But what if he did not call the Apostles a lamp, but those who lighted the lamp that they were to place upon the lampstand? Hear that he called them the lamp itself: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify—not you, but your Father who is in heaven” [Matthew 5:14–16].

### 4

Moses, therefore, bore witness to Christ; John bore witness to Christ; and the other Prophets and Apostles bore witness to Christ.

He places the testimony of his own works above all these testimonies, because through them all it was God alone who bore witness to his Son.

But God bears witness to his Son in another way: through the Son himself, God reveals the Son; through the Son, he reveals himself. If a human being can reach him, that person will need no lamps; and by digging deeper, he will truly bring his building to the rock.

### 5

Today’s reading is therefore easy, brothers. But because of yesterday’s debt—for I know what I postponed, not removed, and the Lord has deigned to grant me to speak to you today as well—remember what you ought to demand, if perhaps, while preserving devotion and salutary humility, we stretch ourselves not against God but toward God, and lift our soul to him, pouring it out over ourselves, as did the one to whom it was said, “Where is your God?”

“I meditated on these things,” he says, “and poured out my soul over myself” [Psalm 41:4–5].

Let us therefore lift our soul to God, not against God, for it is also said: “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul” [Psalm 24:1]. And let us lift it with his help, for it is heavy.

Why is it heavy? “Because the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” [Wisdom 9:15].

Perhaps, then, we may be able to gather our mind from many things into one, and raise it, torn away from many things, toward one—which, as I have said, we shall not be able to do unless he helps who wishes our souls to be raised toward himself—and may touch, in some measure, how the Word of God, the only-begotten, coeternal, and equal Son of the Father, does nothing except what he sees the Father doing, although the Father himself does nothing except through the Son who sees.

It seems to me that the Lord Jesus, wishing in this passage to insinuate something great to attentive minds and pour it into receptive minds, while stirring the unreceptive to study so that by living well they may become receptive, has revealed to us that the human soul and rational mind—which is present in human beings but not in beasts—is neither enlivened, blessed, nor illumined except by the very substance of God.

He has also revealed that this soul does something through the body and from the body, possesses the body as its subject, and that bodily senses can be soothed or offended by bodily things. For this reason—that is, because of a certain partnership and union of soul and body in this life—the soul is delighted by the body’s pleasures or saddened by offenses to the bodily senses.

Yet the blessedness by which the soul itself becomes blessed is produced only by participation in that ever-living, unchangeable, and [Col. 1585] eternal substance which is God.

Thus, just as the soul, which is lower than God, causes what is lower than itself—that is, the body—to live, so that same soul is caused to live blessedly only by what is higher than the soul itself. The soul is higher than the body, and God is higher than the soul. The lower receives a benefit from it, and the higher grants a benefit to it.

Let it serve its Lord, lest it be trampled by its servant.

This, my brothers, is the Christian religion preached throughout the world: while its enemies shudder; where they are defeated, they grumble; where they prevail, they rage.

This is the Christian religion: that one God, not many gods, should be worshiped, because only one God makes the soul blessed. It becomes blessed by participation in God.

A weak soul does not become blessed by participating in a holy soul; a holy soul does not become blessed by participating in an angel. If a weak soul seeks to be blessed, let it seek the source of the holy soul’s blessedness. You do not become blessed through an angel; rather, you and the angel become blessed from the same source.

### 6

With these points stated beforehand and established most firmly—that the rational soul is made blessed only by God, that the body is enlivened only through the soul, and that the soul is a kind of intermediary between God and the body—pay attention and recall with me not today’s reading, about which we have spoken sufficiently, but yesterday’s reading, which we have now been turning over and discussing for three days, digging into it as best we can until we reach the rock.

Christ is the Word; Christ the Word of God is with God; Christ is the Word, and God is the Word; Christ, God, and the Word are one God.

Proceed there, O soul, disregarding everything else, or even rising beyond it; proceed there. There is nothing more powerful than this creature called the rational mind, nothing more sublime than this creature. Whatever is above it is already the Creator.

I was saying that Christ is the Word, Christ is the Word of God, and Christ is God the Word. But Christ is not only the Word, because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” [John 1:14]. Therefore Christ is both Word and flesh.

When he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized. And what of us below, who in our weakness crawled upon the ground and could not reach God? Were we to be abandoned? Certainly not.

“He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” [Philippians 2:6–7]. He did not therefore lose the form of God. He who was God became human by taking what he was not, without losing what he was; thus God became human.

There you have something for the sake of your weakness; there you have something else for the sake of your perfection. Let Christ raise you through what he is as a human being; let him lead you through what he is as God-human; let him bring you to what he is as God.

And the whole preaching and dispensation through Christ is this, brothers, and nothing else: that souls may rise and bodies may rise as well. Both had died: the body through weakness, the soul through iniquity. Because both had died, let both rise. What two? Soul and body.

Through what, then, does the soul rise, if not through God Christ? Through what does the body rise, if not through the human being Christ?

For in Christ there was also a human soul—an entire soul: not merely the irrational part of the soul, but also the rational part, which is called the mind.

There were certain heretics, and they were expelled from the Church, who thought that Christ’s body did not possess a rational mind, but something like a beast’s soul.

[Note: [Col. 1586] The Apollinarists.]

For when the rational mind is excluded, what remains is animal life. But because they were expelled, and were expelled by the truth, receive the whole Christ: the Word, the rational mind, and the flesh. All this is Christ.

Let your soul rise from iniquity through what he is as God; let your body rise from corruption through what he is as human being.

Therefore, beloved, hear the great depth of this reading, as it seems to me, and see how Christ speaks here of nothing other than why Christ came: so that souls might rise from iniquity and bodies from corruption.

I have already said through what souls rise: through the very substance of God; and through what bodies rise: through the human dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

### 7

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the Son cannot do anything from himself, except what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son likewise does.”

Heaven, earth, and sea; the things in heaven, on earth, and in the sea; visible and invisible things; animals on the land; plants in the fields; creatures swimming in the waters; those flying in the air; those shining in the heavens; and, beyond all these, Angels, Powers, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, and Authorities: “all things were made through him” [John 1:3].

Did God make all these things and display them as made to the Son, so that the Son might also make another world filled with all these things? Certainly not.

What, then? “Whatever things he does, these”—not other things, but these—“the Son likewise does,” not differently, but likewise.

For the Father loves the Son and shows him everything that he himself does. The Father shows the Son that souls are to be raised, because souls are raised through the Father and the Son; and souls cannot live unless God is their life.

Therefore, if souls cannot live unless God is their life, just as they themselves are the life of bodies, what the Father shows the Son—that is, what he does—he does through the Son.

For he does not show the Son by doing; rather, by showing, he does through the Son. The Son sees the Father showing before anything comes to be, and from the Father’s showing and the Son’s seeing, that which is done by the Father through the Son comes to be.

Thus souls are raised, if they can see this union of unity: the Father showing, the Son seeing, and the creature coming to be through the Father’s showing and the Son’s seeing. What comes to be through the Father’s showing and the Son’s seeing is neither the Father nor the Son, but whatever is made by the Father through the Son, beneath the Father and the Son.

Who sees this?

### 8

Look, once again we turn to carnal perceptions; look, once again we humble ourselves and descend to you—if indeed we have ever risen above you at all.

You wish to show something to your son so that he may do what you do. You are going to do it, and in this way you will show it.

What you are going to do in order to show it to your son, you certainly do not do through your son. You alone do what you want him to see done, so that he may do another thing of the same kind.

That is not how it is there. Why do you proceed to your own likeness and erase the likeness of God in yourself? It is entirely different there.

Find some way to show your son what you are doing before you do it, so that after you have shown it, you may [Col. 1587] do through your son what you are doing.

Perhaps the following has occurred to you: “Look,” you say, “I am thinking of building a house, and I want it to be built through my son. Before I build it myself, I show my son what I want to build; he builds it, and I build it through him, to whom I have shown my intention.”

You have moved away from the earlier likeness, but you still remain in a great unlikeness.

For before you build the house, you inform your son and show him what you wish to build, so that, after you have shown it to him before doing it, he may do what you have shown, and you may do it through him. But you are going to speak words to your son; words will pass between you and him. Between the one showing and the one seeing, or the one speaking and the one hearing, an articulated sound flies—something that is neither you nor he.

That sound which comes out of your mouth, strikes your son’s ear after beating against the air, and conveys your thought to his heart once his power of hearing has been filled: that sound is not you yourself, nor is it your son himself.

A sign has been given from your mind to your son’s mind, a sign that is neither your mind nor your son’s mind, but something else.

Are we therefore to think that the Father spoke with the Son? Were there words between God and the Word? How can this be?

Or, if the Father wished to say anything to the Son by means of a word, is the Son himself the Father’s Word?

[Note: [Col. 1587] The editions contain several variant readings here, arising chiefly from differences in punctuation. Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read: “Were there words between God and the Word? How can this be? Or, if the Father wished to say anything to the Son? If . . . . . the Father’s Word.” The Lovaniensis reads: “Or, if the Father wished to say anything to the Son? If he wished to speak words, he himself is the Father’s Word. Is it so?” M.]

Would he speak to the Word through a word? Or, because the Son is a great Word, were lesser words to pass between the Father and the Son? Was some sound, some temporal and fleeting creature, going to come forth from the Father’s mouth and strike the Son’s ear?

Does God possess a body, so that something might proceed, as it were, from his lips? Does the Word possess bodily ears into which a sound might enter?

Remove all bodily things; see simplicity, if you are simple. How will you be simple? If you do not entangle yourself in the world, but disentangle yourself from the world. For by disentangling yourself, you will be simple.

And see whether you can understand what I am saying—or, if you cannot, believe what you do not see.

You speak to your son by means of a word; the word that sounds is neither you nor your son.

9. “I have,” you say, “another way by which I can demonstrate this: my son is so well instructed that he does not even listen when I speak, but by a gesture I show him what he should do.” Very well: make the gesture by which you wish to show something. Certainly your mind wishes to show what it has within itself. From where do you make the gesture? From the body, obviously—from the lips, face, eyebrows, eyes, hands. None of these is what your mind is; these too are intermediaries. Something is understood through these signs, which are neither what your mind is nor what your son’s mind is. Yet all that you do with the body is below your mind and below your son’s mind; and your son cannot know your mind unless you give him bodily signs.

What, then, am I to do? That is not the case here: here there is simplicity. The Father shows the Son what he does, and by showing he begets the Son. I see what I have said; but because I also see to whom I have said it, may this understanding eventually come to be in you [Col. 1588].

If now you cannot comprehend what God is, at least comprehend what God is not. You will have made great progress if you do not think of God as anything other than he is. You cannot yet reach what he is; reach what he is not. God is not a body, not earth, not heaven, not the moon, not the sun, not the stars, none of these bodily things. For if he is not any of the heavenly things, how much less any of the earthly? Remove every body.

Listen to something else: God is not a changeable spirit. For I confess—and it must be confessed, since the Gospel says it—that “God is spirit.” But pass beyond every changeable spirit; pass beyond the spirit that at one moment knows and at another does not know, at one moment remembers and then forgets; that wills what it did not will, and does not will what it did will; whether it already undergoes these changes or is capable of undergoing them. Pass beyond all these things.

You will find nothing changeable in God, nothing that is now one way and a little earlier was another way. For wherever you find “one way and another,” a kind of death has occurred there; for death is not being what one was. The soul is called immortal. It is indeed immortal, because the soul always lives, and there is in it a certain enduring life—but a changeable life. In accordance with the changeability of this life, it can also be called mortal: if it lived wisely and then becomes foolish, it has died for the worse; if it lived foolishly and then becomes wise, it has died for the better.

Scripture teaches us that there is a death for the worse and a death for the better. Those of whom it is said, “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Matthew 8:22), had certainly died for the worse; and likewise: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Ephesians 5:14). Concerning this reading also: “When the dead will hear, and those who hear will live.” They had died for the worse, and therefore they come back to life.

By coming back to life they die for the better, because in coming back to life they will no longer be what they were; and not being what one was is death. But perhaps, if it is for the better, it is not called death? The Apostle called it death: “But if you have died with Christ to the elements of this world, why, as though you were living in the world, do you submit to regulations?” (Colossians 2:20). And again: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (ibid. 3:3). He wants us to die so that we may live, because we lived in order to die.

Whatever therefore dies either from better to worse or from worse to better is not God, because supreme goodness cannot go to something better, nor can true eternity go to something worse. True eternity is where there is nothing of time. Was this so a moment ago, and now it is something else? Then time has already been admitted; it is not eternal.

To let you know that God is not like the soul: certainly the soul is immortal. What then does the Apostle say of God—“who alone possesses immortality” (1 Timothy 6:16)—unless he has plainly said by this, “He alone possesses unchangeableness,” because he alone possesses true eternity? Therefore there is no change there.

10. Recognize in yourself something that I wish to speak about—within you, within you; not in you as though in your body, although even in that sense something can be said to be in you. Health is in you, and every age you possess is in you, but according to the body; your hand and your foot are in you. Yet one thing is within you, and another is in you as though in your garment.

But leave outside both your garment and your flesh; descend into yourself, enter your inner chamber, your mind, and there see what I wish to say, if you can. For if you yourself are far from yourself, how can you draw near to God? I was speaking about God, and you supposed that you would understand; now I speak about the soul, about yourself. Understand, and there I shall test you.

I do not go very far for examples when I wish to offer some likeness to your God from your mind, since humanity was made in the image of God—not in the body, but in the mind itself. Let us seek God in his likeness; let us recognize the Creator in his image. There within, if we can, let us find what we are saying: how the Father demonstrates to the Son, and the Son sees what the Father demonstrates, before anything is made by the Father through the Son.

But when I have said this and you have understood it, do not for that reason suppose that the matter is already such that you can preserve there the reverence which I wish you to preserve and which I especially urge upon you: namely, that if you cannot comprehend what God is, you should not consider it a small thing to know what he is not.

11. Look: in your mind I see two things—your memory and your thought, that is, something like a certain edge and gaze of your soul. You see something through your eyes, perceive it, and entrust it to your memory. There within is what you entrusted to memory, stored away in hiding, as in a granary, as in a treasury, as in some inner chamber and innermost sanctuary.

You think about something else; your attention is elsewhere. What you saw is in your memory, but it is not seen by you, because your thought is directed toward something else. Now I shall prove this; I am speaking to those who know. I name Carthage, and all of you who know it have just seen Carthage inwardly. Are there as many Carthages as there are souls among you? All of you have seen it through this name. Through these four familiar syllables, issuing from my mouth, your ears were touched; the sense of the soul was touched through the body, and the mind was turned back from another concern toward what was already there, and it saw Carthage.

Was Carthage then made there? It was already there, but it was hidden. Why was it hidden? Because your mind was attending to something else. But when your thought was turned back toward what was in your memory, it was formed from there, and a kind of vision of the mind came into being. Before that there was no vision, but there was memory. When thought was turned back toward memory, vision was made.

Your memory therefore demonstrated Carthage to your thought, and what was in the memory before you directed your attention to it, it showed to your thought when its attention had turned toward itself. Behold: a demonstration was made by memory, and a vision was made in thought. No words ran between them; no bodily sign was given. You neither gestured nor wrote nor uttered a sound, and yet thought saw what memory demonstrated.

That which demonstrated and that to which it demonstrated are of the same substance. But for your memory to possess Carthage, this image was absorbed through the eyes; you saw what you were to store in memory. Thus you saw the tree you remember, the mountain, the river, the face of your friend, of your enemy, of your father, mother, brother, sister, son, and neighbor; the letters written in a book, the book itself, and this basilica. You saw all these things, and because they had already been seen, you entrusted them to memory; and you placed them there, as it were, so that you might see them by thinking whenever you wished, even when they were absent from these bodily eyes.

You saw Carthage when you were in Carthage; your soul received its form through the eyes. This form was stored in your memory, and while you were located at Carthage you preserved something within yourself that you could see within yourself even when you were not there.

You received all these things from outside.
