What the Father demonstrates to the Son, however, he does not receive from outside: everything takes place within, because nothing of the creatures would exist outside unless the Father had made it through the Son. Every creature was made by God; before it was made, it did not exist.

It was not therefore first made visible and then retained in memory, so that the Father might show it to the Son as memory shows something to thought. Rather, the Father demonstrated that it was to be made, the Son saw that it was to be made, and the Father made it by demonstrating it, because he made it through the Son who saw it.

Therefore it should not trouble us that it was said, “unless he sees the Father doing something”; it was not said, “demonstrating it.” For by this it was signified that, for the Father, doing is the same as demonstrating, so that it may be understood that he does all things through the Son who sees.

Neither that demonstration nor that vision is temporal. Since all times are made through the Son, they could not be demonstrated to him as things to be made at some particular time. The Father’s demonstration thus begets the Son’s vision, just as the Father begets the Son. For demonstration generates vision, not vision demonstration.

If we could contemplate this more purely and perfectly, perhaps we would discover that the Father is not one thing and his demonstration another, nor the Son one thing and his vision another. But if we have scarcely grasped this and have scarcely been able to explain how memory shows thought what it has received from outside, how much less shall we be able to grasp or explain how God the Father demonstrates to the Son what he has from nowhere else, or what is not other than he himself?

We are little ones. I am telling you what God is not; I am not showing what he is. Therefore, in order that we may grasp what he is, what shall we do? Will you be able to do so from me, or through me? I shall say this to little ones—to you and to me: there is one through whom we can.

Just now we sang and heard: “Cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you” (Psalm 54:23). You cannot do this, O human being, because you are little. If you are little, you must be nourished. Once nourished, you will become mature, and what you could not see as a little one, you will see as a mature person. But in order to be nourished, “cast your care upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you.”

12. Let us now briefly run through what remains, and see here what I have commended: how the Lord makes it known. “The Father loves the Son, and shows him everything that he himself does.” He himself raises souls, but through the Son, so that the souls raised may enjoy the substance of God—that is, of the Father and the Son.

“And he will show him works greater than these.” Greater than what? Than the healings of bodies. We have already dealt with this earlier (Treatise 19, nos. 4–5, and Treatise 21, nos. 5–10), and we should not linger over it. For the resurrection of the body to eternity is greater than that bodily healing which took place temporarily in the sick man.

“And he will show him works greater than these, so that you may marvel.” He will show them, as though temporally; therefore, as though to one who was made in time. For the Word is God and was not made in time; through him all times were made. But Christ was made human in time.

It is evident under which consul, on what day, the virgin Mary conceived by the Holy Spirit and gave birth to Christ. Therefore he was made human in time, through whom times were made by God. Thus, as though in time, he will show him works greater than these—that is, the resurrection of bodies—so that you may marvel at the resurrection of bodies accomplished through the Son.

13. Then he returns to that resurrection of souls: “For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills,” but according to the spirit. The Father gives life; the Son gives life. The Father wills certain ones; the Son wills certain ones; but the Father wills the very ones whom the Son wills, because all things were made through him.

“For just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.” This was said concerning the resurrection of souls. What about the resurrection of bodies? He returns to it and says: “For neither does the Father judge anyone, but he has given all judgment to the Son.”

The resurrection of souls takes place through the eternal and unchangeable substance of the Father and the Son. The resurrection of bodies, however, takes place through the temporal dispensation of the Son’s humanity, which is not coeternal with the Father. Therefore, when he mentioned the judgment where the resurrection of bodies would take place, he said: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

Concerning the resurrection of souls he said: “Just as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills.” The former, therefore, is performed simultaneously by the Father and the Son; but concerning the resurrection of bodies he says: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

“So that all may honor the Son as they honor the Father.” This was applied to the resurrection of souls: “So that all may honor the Son.” How? “As they honor the Father.” For the Son accomplishes the resurrection of souls as the Father does; the Son gives life as the Father does. Therefore, in the resurrection of souls, all should honor the Son as they honor the Father.

What does he say about honor in relation to the resurrection of the body? “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” He did not say “as”; he said “honors” and “honors.” Christ the human being is honored, but not as God the Father is honored. Why? Because in this respect he said, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

When, then, is the Son honored as the Father is honored? When “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God,” and “all things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3). Therefore, in this second honor he says: “He who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him.” The Son was sent only because he was made human.

14. “Amen, amen, I say to you.” He returns again to the resurrection of souls, so that we may grasp him who speaks repeatedly—for we could not follow the discourse as it seemed to fly past us. Behold, the Word of God lingers with us; behold, it dwells, as it were, with our weaknesses. He returns once more to commending the resurrection of souls.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life”—but as coming from the Father. For he who hears my word and believes him who sent me has eternal life from the Father, by believing in him who sent me [Col. 1592].

“And he will not come into judgment, but has passed from death to life”—but he is given life by the Father, in whom he believes. What then? Do you not give life? See that the Son also gives life to whom he wills.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: the hour is coming when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” Here he did not say, “They will believe him who sent me, and therefore they will live”; rather, by hearing the voice of the Son of God, those who hear—that is, those who obey the Son of God—will live.

Therefore they will live from the Father when they believe the Father, and they will live from the Son when they hear the voice of the Son of God. Why will they live both from the Father and from the Son? “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself.”

15. He has completed his discussion of the resurrection of souls. It remains to speak more clearly about the resurrection of bodies. “And he gave him authority also to execute judgment”: not only to raise souls through faith and wisdom, but also to execute judgment.

Why this? “Because he is the Son of man.” The Father therefore does something through the Son of man which he does not do from his substance, to which the Son is equal—such things as his being born, his being crucified, his dying, and his rising again. None of these things happened to the Father. So too with the resurrection of bodies.

For the Father accomplishes the resurrection of souls from his own substance through the substance of the Son, by which the Son is equal to him [Note: In eleven manuscripts: “from his substance the Father, from your substance the Son, by which he is equal to him,” with the verb facit (“accomplishes”) omitted.]. Souls, after all, become participants in that unchangeable light; bodies do not. But the Father accomplishes the resurrection of bodies through the Son of man.

“For he gave him authority also to execute judgment, because he is the Son of man”—in accordance with what he said above: “For neither does the Father judge anyone.” And to show that he said this concerning the resurrection of bodies: “Do not marvel at this, because the hour is coming.” It is not now, but the hour is coming when “all who are in the tombs”—you heard this very fully yesterday as well [In the preceding Treatise, no. 13]—“will hear his voice and will come forth.”

And where will they go? “Into judgment.” “Those who have done good, into the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, into the resurrection of judgment.”

And do you do this alone, because the Father has given all judgment to the Son and judges no one? “I do it,” he says. But how do you do it? “I can do nothing from myself: as I hear, I judge, and my judgment is just.”

When he was speaking about the resurrection of souls, he did not say, “I hear,” but “I see.” “I hear,” as though referring to the command of the Father who gives orders. Now therefore, as a human being, as one for whom the Father is greater, now in the form of a servant and not in the form of God, “as I hear, I judge”; and “my judgment is just.”

From where does a human being have just judgment? My brothers, pay attention: “Because I do not seek my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

# TREATISE XXIV

From the passage written, “After this Jesus went across the Sea of Galilee, which is the Sea of Tiberias,” up to, “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.” Chapter 6, verses 1–14.

1. The miracles performed by our Lord Jesus Christ are indeed divine works, and from visible things they admonish the human mind to understand God. Because he is not a substance that can be seen with the eyes, and because his miracles—by which he governs the whole world and administers the entire creation—have become commonplace through their continual occurrence, so that scarcely anyone deigns to pay attention to the wondrous and astonishing works of God in any grain of seed, in accordance with his own mercy he reserved certain acts to perform at an opportune time beyond the customary course and order of nature. Thus, by seeing things not greater but unusual, those whose daily experiences had become commonplace might be astonished.

For the governance of the whole world is a greater miracle than the feeding of five thousand people with five loaves; yet no one marvels at the former. People marvel at the latter, not because it is greater, but because it is rare. For who even now feeds the whole world except the one who creates harvests from a few grains? He therefore acted as God acts. From the source by which he multiplies harvests from a few grains, he multiplied the five loaves in his hands. For power was in Christ’s hands; those five loaves were like seeds—not indeed cast into the earth, but multiplied by him who made the earth.

This was therefore brought before the senses so that the mind might be raised up, and presented to the eyes so that understanding might be exercised. Thus we might marvel at the invisible God through visible works, and, raised up toward faith and purified through faith, might desire also to see invisibly the one whom, through visible things, we had come to know as invisible.

2. Yet it is not enough to contemplate these things in Christ’s miracles. Let us question the miracles themselves about what they tell us concerning Christ; for, if they are understood, they have their own language. Since Christ himself is the Word of God, even the deed of the Word is a word for us.

Let us therefore seek, just as we have heard how great this miracle is, how profound it is also. Let us not delight merely in its surface, but search out its depth. For it has something within, this thing that we marvel at outwardly.

We saw and observed something great, something splendid, something altogether divine, which could not be done except by God; and from the deed we praised its doer. But just as, if we were looking somewhere at beautiful letters, it would not be enough for us to praise the writer’s hand because he had made them alike, even, and beautiful unless we also read what he had indicated to us through them, so the person who merely observes this deed is captivated by the beauty of the deed and marvels at the craftsman; but the person who understands is like one who reads.

A painting is seen in one way, letters in another. When you see a painting, seeing and praising it is the whole of what you do. When you see letters, that is not the whole, because you are urged to read. Indeed, when you see letters, if perhaps you do not know how to read them, you say, “What do we suppose is written here?” You ask what it means, although you already see something. Someone else is going to demonstrate to you what you have seen, and you ask him to recognize it. He has one kind of eyes, and you another. Do you not both see the same characters in the same way? Yet you do not recognize the signs in the same way.

You therefore see and praise; he sees, praises, reads, and understands. Since we have seen and praised, let us also read and understand.

3. The Lord is on the mountain. Let us understand all the more that the Lord on the mountain is the Word on high [Col. 1594]. Therefore, what took place on the mountain does not lie there in a lowly way, as it were; nor should it be passed over casually, but it should be looked up to.

He saw the crowds, recognized that they were hungry, and mercifully fed them—not only through goodness, but also through power. For what good would goodness alone have done where there was no bread with which the hungry crowd could be fed? Unless power accompanied goodness, that fasting and hungry crowd would have remained so.

Moreover, the disciples who were with the Lord, themselves hungry, wanted to feed the crowds so that they would not remain empty-handed, but they had nothing with which to feed them. The Lord asked where bread could be bought to feed the crowds. Scripture says, “But he said this to test him”—namely, the disciple Philip, whom he had questioned. For he himself knew what he was going to do.

For what purpose, then, did he test him, except to reveal the disciple’s ignorance? Perhaps in revealing the disciple’s ignorance he signified something. This will become clear when the mystery of the five loaves itself begins to speak to us and indicate what it signifies. There we shall see why the Lord wished, by asking about something he knew, to reveal the disciple’s ignorance in this event.

Sometimes we ask about what we do not know because we wish to hear the answer and learn; sometimes we ask about what we know because we wish to discover whether the person we question also knows it. The Lord knew both things: he knew what he was asking, for he himself knew what he was going to do, and he likewise knew that Philip did not know it. Why, then, did he ask, unless to demonstrate Philip’s ignorance? Why he did this, as I said, we shall understand later.

4. Andrew said: “There is a boy here who has five loaves and two fish; but what are these among so many?” After Philip, when questioned, had said that two hundred denarii worth of bread would not be enough to refresh so great a crowd, there was a boy carrying five barley loaves and two fish.

And Jesus said, “Make the people recline.” There was much grass in the place, and about five thousand men reclined. Then the Lord Jesus took the loaves, gave thanks, and commanded; the loaves were broken and placed before those reclining. They were no longer merely five loaves, but what the one who had created them had increased. And there was as much of the fish as was sufficient.

It is little to say that the crowd was satisfied: fragments also remained. He commanded that these too be gathered up, lest they perish, and they filled twelve baskets with fragments.

5. To proceed briefly: the five loaves are understood as the five books of Moses. Appropriately, they were not wheat loaves but barley loaves, because they belong to the Old Testament.

You know that barley is so formed that one scarcely reaches its kernel. The kernel is covered with a husk of chaff, and the chaff itself is tough and clinging, so that it is stripped away only with difficulty. Such is the letter of the Old Testament, clothed in the coverings of carnal sacraments. But if one reaches its kernel, it feeds and satisfies.

A certain boy therefore carried five loaves and two fish. If we ask who this boy was, perhaps he was the people of Israel: with a child’s understanding he carried them, but did not eat. For the things he carried burdened him while closed, but fed him when opened [Col. 1595].

The two fish, it seems to us, signify those two eminent persons in the Old Testament who were anointed to sanctify and govern the people: the priest and the king. And he himself, in the mystery, came at a certain time—the one signified through them. He came who was shown through the kernel of the barley, while he was concealed through the chaff of the barley.

He came as one person bearing both roles in himself, that of priest and king: priest, because he offered himself to God as a sacrifice for us; king, because we are ruled by him. And the things carried while closed are opened. Thanks be to him: he fulfilled in himself what was promised through the Old Testament.

And he commanded the loaves to be broken. By being broken, they were multiplied. Nothing is more truthful. For those five books of Moses, how many books have they produced when they are expounded—as though by being broken, that is, by being discussed?

But because in that barley the ignorance of the first people was concealed—of that first people it was said, “As long as Moses is read, a veil lies over their hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:15)—the veil had not yet been removed, because Christ had not yet come; the veil of the temple had not yet been torn while he hung on the cross.

Because, therefore, the ignorance of the people was in the Law, that is why the Lord’s testing demonstrated the disciple’s ignorance.

6. Nothing, then, is without significance; everything gives a sign, but it requires someone who understands. The number of the people who were fed also signified the people placed under the Law. Why were there five thousand, unless because they were under the Law, which is set forth in the five books of Moses?

For this reason, too, the sick were displayed in the five porticoes—not healed there. But the one who healed the sick man there (John 5:2–9) is the one who here fed the crowds with five loaves.

They also reclined on the grass: therefore they had a carnal understanding and rested in carnal things. “All flesh is grass” (Isaiah 40:6).

What are those fragments, then, except what the people could not eat? They are understood as certain more hidden matters of understanding, which the multitude cannot grasp. What remains, then, except that those more hidden matters of understanding, which the multitude cannot grasp, should be entrusted to those who are capable of teaching others, as the Apostles were? Hence twelve baskets were filled.

This was done both miraculously, because it was a great deed, and beneficially, because it was a spiritual deed. Those who saw it then marveled; we do not marvel when we hear it. It happened so that they might see it; it was written so that we might hear it. What their eyes were able to do, faith does in us. We see with the mind what we could not see with our eyes, and we have been placed above them because it was said of us: “Blessed are those who do not see and yet believe” (John 20:29).

I add that perhaps we have also understood what that crowd did not understand. And truly we have been fed, since we have been able to reach the kernel of the barley.

7. Finally, what did those people who saw this think? “Those people,” he says, “when they had seen the sign that he had performed, said, ‘This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world.’”

Perhaps they still thought Christ was a prophet for this reason: they had reclined on grass. Yet he was the Lord of the Prophets, the fulfiller of the Prophets, the sanctifier of the Prophets, and also a prophet. For it was said to Moses, “I will raise up for them a prophet like you.” Like you according to the flesh, not according to majesty.

That the Lord’s promise is to be understood of Christ is openly explained and read in the Acts of the Apostles (Deuteronomy 18:18; Acts 7:37). The Lord himself also said of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (John 4:44).

The Lord is a prophet, and the Lord is the Word of God, and no prophet prophesies without the Word of God. With the Prophets there was the Word of God, and the prophet was the Word of God. Earlier ages deserved prophets inspired and filled with the Word of God; we have deserved the prophet who is himself the Word of God.

Christ is therefore a prophet, as he is the Lord of the Prophets; just as Christ is an angel, he is the Lord of the Angels. For he himself is also called “the Angel of great counsel” (Isaiah 9:6, according to the Septuagint).

Yet what does the prophet say elsewhere? “It was not an ambassador or an angel, but he himself who came and saved them” (Isaiah 35:4): that is, to save them he would not send an ambassador or an angel, but would come himself.

Who will come? That same angel. Certainly not through an angel—unless this one is an angel in such a way that he is also the Lord of the Angels. For angels are called nuntii, “messengers,” in Latin.

If Christ announced nothing, he would not be called an angel; if Christ prophesied nothing, he would not be called a prophet. He exhorted us to faith and to take hold of eternal life. He announced something present and foretold something future. In what he announced as present, he was an angel; in what he foretold as future, he was a prophet. In that the Word of God became flesh, he was the Lord both of Angels and of Prophets.

# TREATISE XXV

From the passage written, “When Jesus therefore knew that they were about to come and seize him,” up to, “And I will raise him up on the last day.” Chapter 6, verses 15–44.

1. Today’s reading from the Gospel is the continuation of yesterday’s, and therefore today’s sermon is owed to it. After that miracle, in which Jesus fed five thousand people with five loaves, when the crowds marveled and called him the great Prophet who has come into the world, this follows:

“Jesus therefore, when he knew that they were about to come and seize him and make him king, fled again into the mountain by himself alone.”

We are therefore given to understand that, when the Lord was sitting on the mountain with his disciples and saw the crowds coming toward him, he had descended from the mountain and fed the crowds in the lower places. For how could he flee there again unless he had first descended from the mountain? This signifies something: the Lord descended from on high in order to feed the crowds. He fed them, and he ascended.

2. Why did he ascend when he knew that they wished to seize him and make him king? What then? Was he not a king, since he feared being made king? He certainly was—but not the kind of king who is made by human beings; rather, the kind who gives a kingdom to human beings.

Perhaps Jesus, whose deeds are words, signifies something to us here as well. In the fact that they wished to seize him and make him king, and that for this reason he fled alone into the mountain, is this event silent in him, saying nothing and signifying nothing? Or perhaps their desire to seize him meant that they wished to anticipate the time of his kingdom?

For he had come at that time, not yet to reign in the manner meant by the words, “Your kingdom come” (Matthew 6:10). Certainly he always reigns with the Father insofar as he is the Son of God, the Word of God, the Word through whom all things were made.

The Prophets foretold his kingdom also according to the fact that Christ was made human and made his faithful ones Christians. There will therefore be a kingdom of Christians, which is now being gathered, now being prepared, now being purchased with Christ’s blood. His kingdom will at some time become manifest, when the glory of his saints is revealed after the judgment carried out by him—of that judgment he himself said above that the Son of man would carry it out (John 5:22).

Concerning this kingdom the Apostle also said: “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Corinthians 15:24). Hence he himself also said: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34).

The disciples and the believing crowds thought that he had come in such a way that he would already reign. This is what it means to wish to seize him and make him king: they wanted to anticipate his appointed time, which he was keeping hidden within himself so that he might reveal it at the proper time and disclose it at the end of the age.

3. To let you know that, when they wanted to make him king—that is, to anticipate him—and already have Christ’s kingdom made manifest, although he first had to be judged and then judge: when he was crucified, and those who had hoped in him had lost hope in his resurrection, after rising from the dead he found two of them speaking together in despair and discussing with groaning what had happened.

Appearing to them as though he were unknown, while their eyes were held so that they would not recognize him, he joined their conversation. As they recounted to him what they were discussing, they said that the great prophet, mighty in deed and word, had been killed by the chief priests.

“And we,” they said, “were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24:13–21).

You were right to hope; your hope was true. In him is the redemption of Israel. But why are you in such haste? You wish to seize him.

This same interpretation is also indicated to us by the fact that, when the disciples asked him about the end, they said: “Will you at this time present yourself, and when will the kingdom of Israel come?” [Note: The printed editions have: “If at this time you will present [it].” But it should be read as in the manuscripts: “Will you present yourself at this time?” The same wording occurs below in Treatise 10 on the First Epistle of John, no. 9. Hence in Treatise 101 on the Gospel of John, no. 4: “when he was asked when he would present himself” [“if at this time you will present [it]”].]

For they already wanted it to exist; they already desired it. This is what it means to wish to seize him and make him king. But he said to the disciples—because he was still about to ascend alone: “It is not for you to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own authority” [Note: Two manuscripts read: “to know the times which the Father has placed,” omitting, as they often do, “or moments”], “but you will receive power from on high, when the Holy Spirit comes upon you” [Note: Two manuscripts: “when the Holy Spirit has come upon you”], “and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:6–8) [Col. 1598].

You want me to reveal the kingdom now; first I will gather what I am to reveal. You love the heights, and you will attain the heights; but follow me through humility.

Thus it was also foretold of him: “The congregation of peoples will surround you, and for their sake return on high” (Psalm 7:8)—that is, so that the congregation of peoples may surround you and so that you may gather many, return on high. He did this: he fed them, and he ascended.

4. But why is it said that he fled? Surely, if he did not wish to be held, he could not be held; if he did not wish to be seized, he could not be seized; and if he did not wish it, he could not even be recognized.

To let you know that this was done mystically, not from necessity but according to a meaningful arrangement, you will now see it in what follows. He appeared to the same crowds who were seeking him, and while speaking with them he said many things, discussing at length the heavenly bread.

Was he not speaking with the very people from whom he had fled so as not to be held? Could he not then have acted so that they would not seize him, just as he did later when he spoke with them?

His flight therefore signified something. What does “he fled” mean? His greatness could not be understood. Whatever you do not understand, you say, “It has escaped me.” Therefore “he fled again into the mountain by himself alone”: “the firstborn from the dead” (Colossians 1:18), ascending above all the heavens and interceding for us (Romans 8:34).

### 5

Meanwhile, with him alone placed above as the great priest—he who entered into the inner part of the veil while the people remained outside—for that priest in the Old Law signified this, since he did this once a year [Heb. IX, 12]—with him, then, placed above, what were the disciples suffering in the boat? For, with him established in the heights, that boat prefigured the Church. If we do not understand first in the Church what that boat was suffering, those things were not significant but merely passing events. But if we see the reality of those meanings expressed in the Church, it is clear that Christ’s deeds are forms of speech.

“But when it had become evening,” he says, “his disciples went down to the sea; and having boarded a boat, they came across the sea to Capernaum.” He quickly stated what happened afterward: “They came across the sea to Capernaum.” Then he returns to explain how they came, because they crossed while sailing over the lake. And while they were sailing toward the place to which he has already said they came, he explains by recapitulation what happened: “It was already dark, and Jesus had not come to them.” Rightly was it dark, because the light had not come: “It was already dark, and Jesus had not come to them.”

The nearer the end of the world approaches, the more errors grow, terrors multiply, iniquity increases, and unbelief increases. Finally, the light—which in that same evangelist John is shown clearly enough to be love, so that he said, “He who hates his brother is in darkness” (1 John II, 11)—is very frequently extinguished. These darknesses of fraternal hatred are growing; every day they grow, and Jesus has not yet come.

How does it become apparent that they are growing? Because “iniquity will abound, the love of many will grow cold.” Darkness grows, and Jesus has not yet come. As darkness grows, love grows cold, and iniquity abounds; these are the waves disturbing the boat. Storms and winds are the cries of those who curse [Col. 1599]. Thus love grows cold, thus the waves increase, and the boat is thrown into confusion.

### 6

When a great wind was blowing, the sea rose up. Darkness was increasing, understanding was diminishing, and iniquity was growing. “When they had rowed, therefore, about twenty-five or thirty stadia.” Meanwhile they were moving forward; they made progress. Those winds, storms, waves, and darkness did not bring it about either that the boat failed to advance or that, having been loosened, it sank. Rather, amid all those evils it continued on.

For although iniquity has abounded and the love of many has grown cold, although the waves increase, the darkness grows, and the wind rages, nevertheless the boat continues. “For he who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. XXIV, 12–13).

Nor should the number of stadia itself be dismissed. It could not really be the case that nothing was signified by the statement: “When they had rowed twenty-five stadia, or thirty, then Jesus came to them.” Twenty-five would have been sufficient; thirty would have been sufficient—especially since this was an estimate, not an assertion. Would the truth be endangered by an estimate if he said “about thirty stadia,” or “about twenty-five stadia”? Yet from twenty-five he made thirty.

Let us seek the number twenty-five. From where does it come, and how is it formed? From five. That number five pertains to the Law. There are the five books of Moses; there are the five porticoes containing the sick; there are the five loaves feeding five thousand people. Therefore the number twenty-five signifies the Law, since five times five—that is, five multiplied by five—makes twenty-five, the square of five.

But this Law lacked perfection before the Gospel came. Perfection, however, is comprehended in the number six. For this reason God completed the world in six days (Gen. I), and the five is multiplied by six, so that the Law may be fulfilled through the Gospel, making six times five equal thirty.

To those, therefore, who fulfill the Law Jesus comes. And how does he come? Treading upon the waves, holding beneath his feet all the world’s swelling pride and pressing down all the heights of this age. This takes place as time is added and as the age of the world advances. Tribulations increase in this world, evils increase, afflictions increase; all these things are magnified. Jesus passes on, treading upon the waves.

### 7

And yet the tribulations are so great that even those who have believed in Jesus and are trying to persevere to the end become afraid that they may fail. While Christ treads upon the waves and crushes the ambitions and heights of this age, the Christian is afraid.

Were these things not foretold to him? Rightly, even while Jesus was walking upon the waves, they were afraid. Thus Christians, although they have hope in the age to come, are often disturbed when they see the height of this present age being brought low, because of the ruin of human affairs.

They open the Gospel; they open the Scriptures; and there they find all these things foretold, because this is what the Lord is doing. He brings down the heights of this age, so that he may be glorified by the lowly. Concerning those heights it was foretold: “You will destroy the strongest cities”; and, “The enemies’ swords have failed utterly, and you have destroyed their cities” (Ps. IX, 7).

What, then, are you afraid of, Christians? Christ speaks: “It is I; do not be afraid.” Why are you terrified by these things? Why are you afraid? “I foretold these things; I am bringing them about; it is necessary that they happen. It is I; do not be afraid.”

They therefore wanted to take him into the boat, recognizing him and rejoicing, having become secure. And immediately the boat was at the land to which they were going. An end was made at the land: from the watery element to solid ground, from turmoil to stability, from the journey to its end.

### 8

On the following day the crowd that stood across the sea, from which they had come, saw that there was no boat there except one, and that Jesus had not entered the boat with his disciples, but that his disciples alone had gone away. Other boats, however, had arrived from Tiberias, near the place where they had eaten the bread, giving thanks to the Lord.

When the crowd therefore saw that Jesus was not there, nor his disciples, they got into the boats and came to Capernaum, seeking Jesus. Yet so great a miracle had been suggested to them. For they had seen that the disciples alone had boarded the boat, and that there was no other boat there.

But boats had come from that place and arrived near the spot where they had eaten the bread, in which the crowd had followed him. He had not boarded with the disciples, and no other boat had been there. How, then, did Jesus suddenly appear across the sea, unless he had walked upon the sea in order to display a miracle?

### 9

“And when the crowd had found him.” Behold [Note: [Col. 1600] According to Er., Lugd., and Ven.: “may he present” (repraesentet). M.], he presents himself to the crowds from whom he had feared being seized and had fled into the mountain. He completely confirms and makes known to us that all those things were spoken mysteriously and that they were done within a great sacrament, so that they might signify something.

Behold, he is the one who had fled from the crowd into the mountain. Is he not speaking with that same crowd? Let them now seize him; let them now make him king. “And when they had found him across the sea, they said to him: Rabbi, when did you come here?”

### 10

After the sacramental meaning of the miracle, he introduces a discourse, so that, if possible, those who had been fed might themselves be fed, and that the minds of those whose stomachs he had filled with bread might also be satisfied with his words—if they are able to grasp them. And if they do not grasp them, let what they do not grasp be taken up [Note: [Col. 1600] Most manuscripts: “And if they do not grasp, let them take what they do grasp.” But perhaps the other three are better: “And if they do not grasp, let those who grasp take it.”], lest the fragments perish.

Let him speak, then, and let us listen.

“Jesus answered and said: Truly, truly, I say to you, you seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves.” You seek me for the sake of the flesh, not for the sake of the spirit.

How many do not seek Jesus except that he may do them some temporal good? One has a business matter and seeks the intercession of clerics; another is oppressed by someone more powerful and flees to the church; another wants someone to intervene for him with a person before whom he has little influence. One does this, another that; every day the church is filled with such people. Jesus is scarcely sought for Jesus’ own sake.

“You seek me, not because you saw signs, but because you ate from my loaves. Work not for food that perishes, but for food that endures to eternal life.” You seek me for the sake of something else; seek me for my own sake.

For he is indicating himself as this food, as becomes clear in what follows: “Which the Son of Man will give you.” You were expecting, I suppose, to eat bread again, to recline at table again, to be filled again. But he had said: food “not which perishes, but which endures to eternal life.” It was as he had said to that Samaritan woman: “If you knew who it is that asks you to drink, you perhaps would have asked him, and he would have given you living water.” When she said, “From where do you have it, since you have no vessel, and the well is deep?” he answered the Samaritan woman: “If you knew who asks you to drink, you would have asked him, and he would have given you water, so that whoever drinks it will never thirst again.” For whoever drinks from this water will thirst again.

She rejoiced and wanted to receive it, as though she would no longer suffer bodily thirst, she who was wearied by the labor of drawing water. Thus, amid such exchanges, he brought her to spiritual drink (John IV, 5–26). It is entirely the same here.

### 11

“This food, then, not which perishes but which endures to eternal life, which the Son of Man will give you—for God the Father has sealed him.”

Do not understand this Son of Man as though he were one of the other sons of men, concerning whom it is said: “The sons of men will hope under the protection of your wings” (Ps. XXXV, 8). This Son of Man, set apart by a certain grace of the Spirit and, according to the flesh, a son of man, set apart from the number of human beings—this Son of Man is also Son of God. This man is also God.

In another place, questioning his disciples, he said: “Who do people say that the Son of Man is?” And they replied: “Some say John, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” And he said: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI, 13–16).

He called himself the Son of Man, and Peter called him the Son of the living God. The one most fittingly recalled what he had mercifully displayed; the other recalled what remained in glory. The Word of God commends his humility; man recognizes the glory of his Lord.

And indeed, brothers, I think this is right: he humbled himself for us; let us glorify him. For he is not Son of Man for his own sake, but for ours. Thus he was Son of Man in that manner when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 14).

For this reason God the Father sealed him. What does “to seal” mean except to mark something as distinctive? To seal is to place something upon it that will not be confused with other things. To seal is to place the mark of the thing. When you place a mark upon something, you place it there so that, once distinguished from other things, it may be recognized by you.

The Father, therefore, sealed him. What does “he sealed him” mean? He gave him something distinctive, so that he would not be compared with other human beings. For this reason it was said of him: “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. XLIV, 8).

What, then, does “to seal” mean? To hold as set apart: “above your companions.” Therefore, he says, do not despise me because I am the Son of Man; and seek from me food not which perishes but which endures to eternal life.

For I am Son of Man in such a way that I am not one of you; I am Son of Man in such a way that the Father God sealed me. What does “sealed me” mean? He gave me something distinctive, by which I would not be confused with the human race, but through which the human race would be freed.

### 12

Therefore they said to him: “What shall we do, so that we may work the works of God?” For he had said to them: “Work for food not which perishes but which endures to eternal life.” “What shall we do?” they ask. “By observing what commandment shall we be able to fulfill this?”

Jesus answered and said to them: “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.”

This, then, is to eat food not which perishes but which endures to eternal life. Why do you prepare your teeth and your stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.

Faith is indeed distinguished from works, as the Apostle says: “A person is justified by faith apart from works of the Law” (Rom. III, 28). There are works that appear good without the faith of Christ, but they are not good, because they are not directed toward that end from which they are good: “For Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (ibid. X, 4).

Therefore he did not wish to distinguish faith from work, but said that faith itself is the work. For it is faith “which works through love” (Gal. V, 6). Nor did he say, “This is your work,” but, “This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent”—so that “he who boasts may boast in the Lord” (1 Cor. I, 31).

Since, then, he was inviting them to faith, they were still seeking signs by which they might believe. See whether the Jews do not ask for signs. Therefore they said to him: “What sign, then, do you perform, so that we may see and believe you? What do you work?”

Was it not enough that they had been fed from five loaves? They knew this, certainly, but they preferred manna from heaven to that food. The Lord Jesus, however, was presenting himself as one greater than Moses. Moses did not dare to say of himself that he would give food not which perishes but which endures to eternal life. This man was promising something greater than Moses.

Through Moses, after all, a kingdom was promised, and a land flowing with milk and honey, temporal peace, an abundance of children, bodily health, and all the other things that were temporal, though spiritual in figure, because they were promised to the old person in the Old Testament.

They were therefore considering the promises made through Moses, and they were considering the promises made through Christ. Moses promised a full belly in the land, but with food that perishes; this man promised food not which perishes but which endures forever.

They considered that he was promising more, and as though they had not yet seen him do greater things, they considered what Moses had done and still wanted greater things to be done by the one who made such great promises.

“What do you do,” they ask, “so that we may believe you?” And so that you may know that they were comparing those miracles with this miracle, and therefore judging the things Jesus was doing as though they were lesser, they say: “Our fathers ate manna in the wilderness.”

But what is manna? Perhaps you despise it. As it is written: “He gave them manna to eat.” Through Moses our fathers received bread from heaven, and Moses did not say to them, “Work for food not which perishes.” You promise food not which perishes but which endures to eternal life, and you do not perform works such as Moses performed. He did not give barley loaves; he gave manna from heaven.

### 13

Therefore Jesus said to them: “Truly, truly, I say to you, Moses did not give you bread from heaven, but my Father gives you bread from heaven. For the true bread is the one that comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”

The true bread, then, is the one that gives life to the world; and it is the very food about which I spoke a little earlier: “Work for food not which perishes but which endures to eternal life.”

Thus that manna also signified this, and all those things were my signs. You loved my signs; do you despise the one who was signified? Therefore Moses did not give the bread from heaven; God gives the bread.

But what bread? Perhaps manna? No, but the bread that the manna signified—namely, the Lord Jesus himself. “My Father gives you the true bread. For the bread of God is the one who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.”

Therefore they said to him: “Lord, give us this bread always.” It was like that Samaritan woman, to whom it was said: “Whoever drinks from this water will never thirst.” Immediately, taking the words according to the body but nevertheless wishing to be free from want, she said: “Lord, give me this water.” So these people also say: “Lord, give us this bread, which may refresh us and not fail.”

### 14

Jesus then said to them: “I am the bread of life. Whoever comes to me will not hunger, and whoever believes in me will never thirst.”

“Whoever comes to me”—this is what he means by “whoever believes in me.” And when he said, “will not hunger,” this is to be understood together with “will never thirst.” By both expressions he signifies eternal fullness, where there is no deprivation.

You desire bread from heaven; you have it before you, and you do not eat. But I told you that you have both seen me and have not believed.

Yet I have not therefore destroyed the people. For has your unbelief nullified the faithfulness of God? (Rom. III, 3.) See what follows: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me, and whoever comes to me I will not cast out.”

What kind of interior is that from which no one is cast out? A great inner chamber, and a sweet secret place! O secret place without weariness, without the bitterness of evil thoughts, without the interruption of temptations and sorrows! Is it not that secret place into which the Lord will have him enter to whom he will say, as to a servant who has served well: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. XXV, 23)?

### 15

“And whoever comes to me I will not cast out.” Because “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.”

Is this, then, why you will not cast out the one who comes to you: because you came down from heaven not to do your own will but the will of him who sent you? A great mystery!

I beg you, let us knock together, so that something may come forth to us that may nourish us, according to what has delighted us. That great and sweet secret: “Whoever comes to me.” Pay attention, pay attention, and weigh the words: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out.”

Therefore, he says, whoever comes, I will not cast out. Why? “Because I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.”

Is that, then, the reason why you do not cast out the one who comes to you—that you came down from heaven not to do your own will but the will of him who sent you? It is. Why do we ask whether it is? It is; he himself speaks. We are not permitted to suppose anything other than what he says: “Whoever comes to me I will not cast out.”

And as though you were asking, “Why?” he answers: “Because I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.”

I fear that the soul went out from God for this reason: because it was proud. Indeed, I do not doubt it. For it is written: “The beginning of every sin is pride”; and, “The beginning of human pride is apostasy from God.” It is written; it is firm; it is true.

Then what does Scripture say about the proud mortal, girded with the rags of flesh, weighed down by the burden of corruptible body, yet exalting himself and forgetting with what skin he is clothed? “Why is earth and ashes proud?” Why is it proud? Let it say why it is proud: “Because in its life it cast away its inner parts” (Ecclus. X, 15, 14, 9–10).

What does “it cast away” mean except “it threw outward”? This is to go out. To enter within is to seek the inner parts; to cast away the inner parts is to go outside. The proud person casts away the inner parts; the humble person seeks the inner parts. If we are cast out by pride, we return by humility.

### 16

Pride is the head of all diseases, because pride is the head of all sins. When a physician examines an illness, if he treats what has occurred through some cause but does not treat the cause itself by which it occurred, he seems to heal for a time; while the cause remains, the disease returns.

For example, I shall express this more clearly: a humor in the body produces scabies or ulcers; a great fever and no small pain arise in the body. Certain medicines are administered to suppress the scabies and calm the heat of the ulcer. They are applied and they are effective. You see a person who had been ulcerous and covered with scabies become well. But because that humor was not expelled, the ulcer returns.

Recognizing this, the physician cleanses the humor and removes the cause, and there will be no ulcers. Why does iniquity abound? Through pride. Cure pride, and there will be no iniquity.

Therefore, in order to cure the cause of all diseases—that is, pride—the Son of God descended and became humble. Why are you proud, human being? God became humble for your sake. Perhaps you would be ashamed to imitate a humble human being; at least imitate a humble God.

The Son of God came in a human being and became humble. You are commanded to be humble; you are not commanded to become a beast from a human being. He, God, became human; you, human being, recognize that you are human. Your entire humility consists in recognizing yourself.

Therefore, because God teaches humility, he said: “I did not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.” This is a commendation of humility. Pride does its own will; humility does the will of God.

Therefore the one who comes to me will not be cast out. Why? “Because I did not come to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.”

I came humbly; I came to teach humility; I came as the teacher of humility. Whoever comes to me is incorporated into me; whoever comes to me becomes humble; whoever clings to me will be humble, because he does not do his own will but God’s. And therefore he will not be cast out, because when he was proud, he was cast out.

### 17

See how those inner things are commended in the Psalm: “The sons of men will hope under the protection of your wings.” See what it means to go within; see what it means to flee for refuge to his protection; see what it means even to run beneath a father’s blows. For he scourges every son whom he receives.

“The sons of men will hope beneath the covering of your wings.” And what is within? “They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house.” When you send them inside, entering into the joy of their Lord, “they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight. For with you is the fountain of life.”

Not outside, beyond you, but within, with you, is the fountain of life. “And in your light we shall see light.” Extend your mercy to those who know you, and your righteousness to those who are upright in heart.

Those who follow the will of their Lord, seeking not their own interests but those of the Lord Jesus Christ, are upright in heart; their feet are not shaken. “For God is good to Israel, to those who are upright in heart.”

“But as for me,” he says, “my feet had almost slipped.” Why? “Because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the prosperity of sinners” (Ps. LXXII, 1–3).

To whom, then, is God good except to those who are upright in heart? For God displeased me when my heart was crooked. Why did he displease me? Because he gave happiness to the wicked. And so my feet faltered, as though I had served God without cause.

Therefore my feet had almost slipped because I was not upright in heart. What, then, is being upright in heart? Following the will of God.

One person is happy; another labors. One lives wickedly and is happy; another lives justly and labors. Let the one who lives justly and labors not be indignant. He has within what that happy person does not have. Therefore let him not grieve, torment himself, or fail.

That happy person has gold in his chest; this one has God in his conscience. Now compare gold with God, and a chest with a conscience. The former has what perishes, and in that very place he has what can perish; the latter has God, who cannot perish, and in that very place he has what cannot be taken away—provided that he is upright in heart. For then he enters and does not go out.

Therefore what did that man say? “For with you is the fountain of life”—not with us. We must therefore enter in order to live, not pretend that we are sufficient to ourselves and thereby perish, nor pretend that we can be satisfied from our own resources and thereby wither. We must place our mouth at that fountain, where the water does not fail.

Adam wished to live by his own counsel, and he fell through the one who had first fallen through pride and who offered him the cup of his own pride to drink.

Since, then, “with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light,” let us drink within; let us see within. Why did one go out from there? Listen to why: “Let not the foot of pride come to me.” Therefore the one to whom the foot of pride came went out.

Show that he went out for this reason: “And let not the hand of sinners move me,” because of the foot of pride. Why do you say this? “There all those who work iniquity fell.” Where did they fall? In pride itself. “They were driven out and could not stand” (Ps. XXXV, 8–13).

If, then, pride expelled those who could not stand, humility brings in those who are able to stand forever. For the one who said, “The humbled bones will rejoice,” had earlier declared: “You will give gladness and joy to my hearing” (Ps. L, 10).

What does “to my hearing” mean? In hearing you I am happy; from your voice I am happy; drinking within, I am happy. Therefore I do not fall. Therefore “the humbled bones will rejoice.” Therefore the friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him (John III, 29); he stands because he hears. He drinks from the inner fountain; therefore he stands.

Those who did not wish to drink from within fell there. They were expelled and could not stand.

### 18

The teacher of humility, then, came not to do his own will but the will of him who sent him. Let us come to him; let us enter into him; let us be incorporated into him, so that we too may do not our own will but the will of God. He will not cast us out, because we are his members, because he wished to be our head by teaching humility.

Finally, hear him preaching himself: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened; take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart. And when you have learned this, you will find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI, 28–29)—a place from which you will not be cast out.

For “I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will but the will of him who sent me.” I teach humility; no one can come to me unless he is humble. Pride alone sends one outside. How can one who preserves humility and does not fall away from the truth go outside?

Much has been said, brothers, about the hidden meaning. For the meaning is sufficiently concealed here, and I do not know whether I have drawn it out and carved it forth in suitable words: namely, why he does not cast out the one who comes to him—because he did not come to do his own will but the will of him who sent him.

### 19

“This is the will of him who sent me, the Father,” he says: “that I should lose nothing of everything that he has given me.”

The one who preserves humility has been given to him; he receives this person. Whoever does not preserve humility is far from the teacher of humility.

“That I should lose nothing of everything that he has given me.” Thus it is not the will of your Father that one of these little ones should perish. The swollen may perish; none of the little ones perishes: “Unless you become like this little one, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. XVIII, 14, 4).

“Everything that the Father has given me I will not lose, but I will raise it up on the last day.”

See how here too he outlines that twofold resurrection. Whoever comes to me now rises by becoming humble among my members; but “I will also raise him up on the last day,” according to the flesh.

“For this is the will of my Father who sent me: that everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life; and I will raise him up on the last day.”

Above he said: “Whoever hears my word and believes him who sent me.” Now, however: “Whoever sees the Son and believes in him.” He did not say, “sees the Son and believes in the Father,” for believing in the Son is the same as believing in the Father. “For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John V, 24, 26).

“Everyone who sees the Son and believes in him should have eternal life”: by believing and passing over into life, as through that first resurrection. And because this resurrection is not the only one, “I will raise him up,” he says, “on the last day.”

## TRACTATE XXVI

From the passage written, “The Jews therefore murmured about him because he had said, ‘I am the bread that came down from heaven,’” up to, “Whoever eats this bread will live forever.” Chapter VI, verses 41–59.

### 1

When our Lord Jesus Christ, as we heard when the Gospel was read, had said that he was the bread that came down from heaven, the Jews murmured and said: “Is this not Jesus, the son of Joseph, whose father and mother we know? How, then, does he say, ‘I came down from heaven’?”

They were far from the bread of heaven and did not know how to hunger for it. They had languid throats of the heart; with their ears open, they were deaf; they saw, yet stood blind.

For this bread seeks the hunger of the inner person. Hence, in another place, he says: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be satisfied” [Col. 1607] (Matt. V, 6). The Apostle Paul says that Christ is our righteousness (1 Cor. I, 30).

Accordingly, whoever hungers for this bread should hunger for righteousness—but for the righteousness that comes down from heaven, the righteousness that God gives, not the righteousness that a human being makes for himself.

For if a human being did not make any righteousness for himself, the same Apostle would not say concerning the Jews: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X, 3).

These people belonged among those who did not understand the bread descending from heaven because, being satisfied with their own righteousness, they did not hunger for the righteousness of God.

What is this distinction between the righteousness of God and the righteousness of a human being? Here “the righteousness of God” does not mean the righteousness by which God is righteous, but the righteousness that God gives to a person so that the person may be righteous through God.

And what was their righteousness? It was the righteousness by which they presumed upon their own strength and claimed that they themselves, by their own virtue, were fulfillers of the Law.

But no one fulfills the Law unless grace helps him—that is, the bread that comes down from heaven. For the fullness of the Law, as the Apostle says in brief, is love (ibid. XIII, 10): not love of money, but love of God; not love of earth or heaven, but love of the one who made heaven and earth.

Where does this love come to a human being? Let us hear him himself: “The love of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (ibid. V, 5).

Therefore, since the Lord was going to give the Holy Spirit, he said that he was the bread that came down from heaven, urging us to believe in him. To believe in him is to eat the living bread. Whoever believes eats; he is invisibly nourished, because he is invisibly reborn. The infant is within; the new person is within. Where he is renewed, there he is satisfied.

### 2

What, then, did Jesus answer such people while they were murmuring? “Do not murmur among yourselves.” It was as though he were saying: “I know why you do not hunger and why you neither understand nor seek this bread.”

“Do not murmur among yourselves. No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

A great commendation of grace! No one comes unless drawn. Whom he draws and whom he does not draw, why he draws one and does not draw another—do not wish to judge, if you do not wish to err. Accept this once and understand it: are you not yet being drawn [Note: [Col. 1607] Printed editions: “you are not being drawn.” Manuscripts: “you are not yet being drawn.”]? Pray that you may be drawn.

What are we saying here, brothers? If we are drawn to Christ, then we believe unwillingly; then force is applied, and the will is not stirred. Someone can enter a church unwillingly; he can approach the altar unwillingly; he can receive the Sacrament unwillingly. He cannot believe unless he wills to do so.

If belief took place in the body, it would occur in unwilling people; but belief does not take place in the body. Hear the Apostle: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness.” And what follows? “With the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (ibid. X, 10).

This confession rises from the root of the heart. Sometimes you hear someone confessing and do not know whether he believes [Note: [Col. 1607] Am. Bad. and Er. add: “you call him one who confesses, and you do not know whether he believes.”]. But neither should you call someone a confessor whom you judge not to believe.

For to confess means to say what you have in your heart. If you have one thing in your heart and say another, you are speaking, but you are not confessing.

Since, then, one believes in Christ with the heart—which certainly no one does unwillingly—while the one who is drawn appears to be compelled as though unwilling, how do we resolve this question: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him”?

### 3

“If he is drawn,” someone says, “he comes unwillingly.” If he comes unwillingly, he does not believe; if he does not believe, he does not come.

For we do not run to Christ by walking, but by believing; we do not approach by bodily movement but by the will of the heart. For this reason the woman who touched the fringe of his garment touched more than the crowd that pressed against him. Therefore the Lord said: “Who touched me?” (Luke VIII, 44–46).

And the disciples, wondering, said: “The crowds are pressing around you, and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” But he repeated: “Someone touched me.”

She touches; the crowd presses. What does “touched” mean except “believed”?

Therefore after the resurrection he also said to that woman who wished to throw herself at his feet: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John XX, 17).

You think that I am only what you see; do not touch me. What does this mean? You think that I am only what appears to you; do not believe in me in that way. This is what “Do not touch me; for I have not yet ascended to the Father” means.

I have not ascended to the Father for you, for I have never departed from there. While he stood on earth she did not touch him; how could she touch him as he ascended to the Father? Yet in this way, in this way, he wished to be touched: in this way he is touched by those who touch him rightly—as he ascends to the Father, remains with the Father, and is equal to the Father.

4. Hence here too, if you pay attention, “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him.” Do not imagine that he is drawn unwillingly [Note: [Col. 1608] Several manuscripts read: “Do not imagine that he is drawn unwillingly unwillingly.”]: the mind is drawn by love. Nor should we fear that we may perhaps be reproached for this evangelical saying of the holy Scriptures by people who weigh words but are far removed from understanding divine realities, and that they may say to us, “How can I believe voluntarily if I am drawn?” I reply: it is not merely by the will that you are drawn; you are drawn also by delight. What does it mean to be drawn by delight? “Delight in the Lord, and he will grant you the desires of your heart” (Ps. 36:4). There is a certain delight of the heart, for which that heavenly bread is sweet.

Moreover, if poets have been permitted to say, “Each is drawn by his own pleasure” (Virgil, *Eclogue* 2)—not by necessity, but by pleasure; not by obligation, but by enjoyment—how much more strongly should we say that a person is drawn to Christ when he delights in truth, delights in blessedness, delights in justice, delights in eternal life—which altogether is Christ? Do the bodily senses indeed have their pleasures, while the mind is abandoned by its own pleasures? If the mind has no pleasures of its own, why is it said, “The sons of men will hope under the shelter of your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Ps. 35:8–10)?

Give me someone who loves, and he understands what I am saying. Give me someone who desires, someone who hungers [Note: [Col. 1608] Most manuscripts read, “someone who burns with fervor.” Shortly afterward, all omit *nescit* and read as follows: “But if I speak to someone who is cold, what am I saying?”], someone who is journeying in this wilderness and thirsting, sighing for the fountain of his eternal homeland: give me such a person, and he knows what I am saying. But if I speak to someone who is cold, he does not know what I am saying. Such were those who were murmuring among themselves. “The one,” he says, “whom the Father draws comes to me.”

5. But what does “the one whom the Father draws” mean, when Christ himself draws? Why did he wish to say, “the one whom the Father draws”? [Col. 1609] If we are to be drawn, let us be drawn by the one to whom the beloved says, “After the fragrance of your ointments we will run” (Song 1:3). But let us consider, brothers, what he wished to be understood, and grasp it as far as we can.

The Father draws to the Son those who therefore believe in the Son because they think that he has God as Father. For God the Father begot a Son equal to himself. Thus, whoever thinks, feels in his faith, and meditates that the one in whom he has believed is equal to the Father—the Father himself draws that person to the Son.

Arius believed him to be a creature; the Father did not draw him, because he does not consider the Father when he does not believe the Son to be equal. What do you say, Arius? What do you say, heretic? What is Christ? “He is not,” you say, “the true God, but one whom the true God made.” The Father did not draw you, for you did not understand the Father, whose Son you deny. You imagine something else; it is not the Son himself. You are drawn neither by the Father nor to the Son, for the Son is one thing, and what you say is another.

Photinus said, “Christ is merely a human being; he is not also God.” Whoever believes this has not been drawn by the Father. The one whom the Father drew says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” Not as a prophet, not as John, not as some great righteous man, but as the only one, as the equal one: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” See that he has been drawn, and drawn by the Father.

“Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 16:16–17). That revelation is itself the drawing. You show a green branch to a sheep, and you draw it. Nuts are shown to a child, and he is drawn; and wherever he runs, he is drawn [Note: [Col. 1609] Several manuscripts read, “And that which runs.”]. He is drawn by loving; he is drawn without bodily injury; he is drawn by the bond of the heart.

If, then, these things that are revealed to lovers amid earthly delights and pleasures draw them—for it is true that “Each is drawn by his own pleasure”—does Christ, revealed by the Father, not draw? What does the soul desire more strongly than truth? Where should it have such eager appetite, and from where should it desire the palate within to be sound for judging truly, except that it may eat and drink wisdom, justice, truth, and eternity?

6. But where is this? There it is better; there it is truer; there it is fuller. Here we can more easily hunger—and even this only if we have good hope—than be satisfied: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matt. 5:6), but here; “for they shall be satisfied,” but there.

Therefore, after he had said, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” what did he add? “And I will raise him up on the last day.” I return to him what he loves; I return what he hopes for. He will see what, because he does not yet see it, he has believed; he will eat what he hungers for; he will be filled with what he thirsts for. Where? In the resurrection of the dead, because “I will raise him up on the last day.”

7. For it is written in the Prophets, “And they shall all be taught by God.” Why did I say this, O Jews? The Father has not taught you; how can you recognize me? All the people of that kingdom will be taught by God; they will not hear from human beings. And if they do hear from human beings, nevertheless what they understand is given within, flashes within, and is revealed within.

What do human beings do when they announce outwardly? What am I doing now as I speak? I thrust the noise of words into your ears. Unless, therefore, the one who is within reveals it, what am I saying, or what am I speaking? The external cultivator of the tree is the Creator within. The one who plants and the one who waters work outwardly; this is what we do. “Neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the growth” (1 Cor. 3:7). This is what is meant by, “They shall all be taught by God.”

Who are they all? “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.” See how the Father draws: by teaching he delights, not by imposing necessity. See how he draws. “They shall all be taught by God”: this is God’s drawing. “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me”: this is God’s drawing.

8. What then, brothers? If everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to Christ, did Christ teach nothing here? What of the fact that human beings did not see the Father as teacher, but saw the Son? The Son was speaking, but the Father was teaching.

I, although I am a human being, whom do I teach? Whom, brothers, except the one who hears my word? If I, although I am a human being, teach the one who hears my word, then the Father also teaches the one who hears his Word. If the Father teaches the one who hears his Word, ask what Christ is, and you will find that he is his Word: “In the beginning was the Word.”

It does not say, “In the beginning God made the Word,” as it says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). Behold, then, that the Word is not a creature. Learn to be drawn to the Son by the Father; let the Father teach you; hear his Word.

“What Word of his,” you ask, “do I hear?” “In the beginning was the Word.” He was not made, but was. “And the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” How could people established in the flesh hear such a Word? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

9. He himself explains this and shows us what he meant by, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me.” He immediately added what we might have wondered about: “Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.”

What does he mean? “I have seen the Father; you have not seen the Father; and yet you do not come to me unless you are drawn by the Father.” But what is it for you to be drawn by the Father except to learn from the Father? What is it to learn from the Father except to hear from the Father? What is it to hear from the Father except to hear the Father’s Word—that is, me?

Therefore, lest perhaps when I say to you, “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned,” you say among yourselves, “But we have never seen the Father; how could we have learned from the Father?” hear from me: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, but the one who is from God has seen the Father.”

I know the Father; I am from him—but as a word is from the one whose word it is: not as a sound that is uttered and passes away, but as one that remains with the speaker and draws the hearer.

10. Let what follows admonish us: “Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever believes in me has eternal life.” He wished to reveal what he was, for he could have said briefly, “Whoever believes in me has me.” Christ himself is true God and eternal life.

“Whoever therefore believes in me,” he says, “goes into me; and whoever goes into me has me” [Note: [Col. 1610] The Vindobonensis manuscript reads, “lives in me, and whoever lives in me.” But the editions of Amerbach, Badanus, and Erasmus lack the sentence: “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “goes into me; and whoever goes into me has me,” although it is found in the other manuscripts.]. But what does it mean to have me? To have eternal life.

Eternal life assumed death; eternal life wished to die, but from what was yours, not from what was its own. It received from you that in which it might die for you. For it assumed flesh from human beings, but not in the manner of human beings. Having the Father in heaven, it chose a mother on earth: there it was born without a mother, and here without a father.

Life therefore assumed death, so that Life might kill death. “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “has eternal life”—not what is apparent, but what is hidden. For eternal life is the Word: “In the beginning he was with God, and the Word was God,” and “life was the light of human beings” (John 1:2, 4). He himself, eternal life, also gave eternal life to the flesh he assumed. He came to die, but rose again on the third day. Between the Word assuming flesh and the flesh rising again, death was destroyed.

11. “I am,” he says, “the bread of life.” And what was the source of their pride? “Your fathers,” he says, “ate manna in the wilderness, and they died.” What is it that you boast of? They ate manna, and they died.

Why did they eat, and die? Because they believed what they saw; what they did not see, they did not understand. Therefore, “your fathers,” because you are like them [Note: [Col. 1611] In ten manuscripts there is added here, “and unbelieving fathers of unbelieving children.”].

As far as this visible and bodily death is concerned, brothers, do we not also die, who eat the bread that came down from heaven? They died just as we shall die, insofar as—as I have said—it concerns the visible and bodily death of this flesh.

But as far as that death is concerned of which the Lord warns us, and by which the fathers of these people died: Moses ate manna, Aaron ate manna, Phinehas ate manna, and many there who pleased the Lord ate it—and they did not die. Why? Because they understood the visible food spiritually, hungered for it spiritually, and tasted it spiritually, so that they might be satisfied spiritually.

We too today receive visible food; but the Sacrament is one thing, and the power of the Sacrament another. How many receive something from the altar and die—and die by receiving it? Hence the Apostle says, “He eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

For the Lord’s morsel was not poison to Judas [Note: [Col. 1611] So read Badanus, Amerbach, and all the manuscripts. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “Was not the Lord’s morsel poison to Judas?” See above, *Tractatus* 6.15.]. Yet he received it, and when he received it, the enemy entered into him—not because he received something evil, but because, being evil, he received something good in an evil manner.

See, then, brothers: eat the heavenly bread spiritually; bring innocence to the altar. Even if your sins are daily, at least let them not be deadly. Before you approach the altar, consider what you say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6:12). You forgive, and you will be forgiven; approach without fear: it is bread, not poison.

But see whether you forgive. For if you do not forgive, you are lying, and you are lying to the one whom you do not deceive. You can lie to God; you cannot deceive God. He knows what he does [Note: [Col. 1611] Erasmus and Lovaniensis read, “what you do,” against the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]. Within, he sees you; within, he examines you; within, he looks into you; within, he judges you; within, he either condemns or crowns you.

But the fathers of these people [Col. 1612] [Note: [Col. 1612] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and Lovaniensis read *ergo* (“therefore”) instead of *autem* (“but”).]—that is, evil fathers of evil people, unbelieving fathers of unbelievers, murmuring fathers of murmurers—for that people is said to have offended the Lord over no matter more than by murmuring against God.
