Therefore, wishing to show them to be children of such fathers, the Lord began here by saying to them: “Why are you murmuring among yourselves, murmurers, children of murmurers? Your fathers ate manna, and they died”—not because the manna was evil, but because they ate it evilly.

12. “This is the bread that came down from heaven.” The manna signified this bread; the altar of God signified this bread [Note: [Col. 1612] Most manuscripts read, “The altar of God signifies this bread.”]. Those were Sacraments: they differ in their signs, but in the reality signified they are equal.

Hear the Apostle: “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses” [Note: [Col. 1612] The printed editions read, “through Moses.” Several manuscripts read, “into Moses.” Most of the others read, “into Moses,” according to the Greek *eis ton Mōusēn*. The Greek interpretation is explained by Chrysostom as *tharrēsantes tō Mōusei*—that is, “the Israelites, trusting in Moses, entered upon their journey under the cloud and through the sea, with him leading the way”—and thus prefigured us, who are baptized as believers in Christ.] “in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food.”

The same spiritual food, certainly; for the bodily food was different, since they had manna and we have something else. But the spiritual food was the same as ours. Yet they were our fathers, not the fathers of those people: they are the ones to whom we are similar, not the ones to whom those people were similar.

And he adds: “And all drank the same spiritual drink.” One thing was theirs, another is ours, in visible form; nevertheless, it signified the same thing through spiritual power [Note: [Col. 1612] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read, “but in visible form, nevertheless signifying the same thing through spiritual power.”].

How did they drink the same drink? “They drank,” he says, “from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:1–4). From there came the bread; from there came the drink. Christ was the rock in the sign; the true Christ was in the Word and in the flesh.

And how did they drink? “The rock was struck twice with the rod” (Num. 20:11): the double striking signifies the two pieces of wood of the cross.

This, then, is the bread that comes down from heaven, so that if anyone eats of it, he will not die. But this concerns the power of the Sacrament, not the visible Sacrament: the one who eats inwardly, not outwardly; the one who eats in the heart, not the one who presses with his teeth.

13. “I am the living bread that came down from heaven.” Living, therefore, because I came down from heaven. Manna also came down from heaven, but manna was a shadow; this is the truth.

“If anyone eats of this bread, he will live forever; and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world.”

When could flesh understand what he called bread—flesh? It is called flesh, though flesh cannot comprehend it; and for that very reason flesh comprehends it even less, because it is called flesh. This is what they recoiled from; this they said was too much for them; this they thought could not happen.

“My flesh,” he says, “is for the life of the world.” The faithful know the body of Christ, if they do not neglect to be the body of Christ. Let them become the body of Christ, if they wish to live by the Spirit of Christ. No one lives by the Spirit of Christ unless he is the body of Christ [Note: [Col. 1612] All manuscripts read, “He will not live by the Spirit of Christ unless he is the body of Christ.”].

Understand, my brothers, what I have said. You are a human being, and you have a spirit and a body. By “spirit” I mean what is called the soul, by which you are a human being; for you consist of soul and body. You therefore have an invisible spirit and a visible body.

Tell me what lives from what: does your spirit live from your body, or your body from your spirit? Everyone who is alive answers; whoever cannot answer this, I do not know whether he is alive. What does everyone who is alive answer? Surely, “My body lives from my spirit.”

Do you therefore wish also to live from the Spirit of Christ? Be in the body of Christ. Does my body live from your spirit? Mine lives from my spirit, and yours from yours. The body of Christ cannot live except from the Spirit of Christ.

This is why the Apostle Paul, explaining this bread to us, says, “Because there is one bread, we who are many are one body” (1 Cor. 10:17).

O Sacrament of piety! O sign of unity! O bond of charity! Whoever wishes to live has where he may live and has from what he may live. Let him approach, let him believe [Note: [Col. 1613] Ten manuscripts add, “let him believe, live in God, from God; let him be incorporated,” and so forth.]; let him be incorporated, so that he may be given life.

Let him not recoil from the structure of the members; let him not be a diseased member deserving to be cut away; let him not be a twisted member of which one is ashamed. Let him be beautiful, fitting, healthy; let him cling to the body; let him live for God from God. Now let him labor on earth, so that afterward he may reign in heaven.

14. The Jews therefore quarreled among themselves, saying, “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” They certainly quarreled among themselves because they did not understand the bread of concord, nor did they wish to receive it. For those who eat such bread do not quarrel among themselves, because “we who are many are one body, one bread.” And through this God causes people of one mind to dwell in a house (Ps. 67:7).

15. As for what they ask while quarreling among themselves—how the Lord can give his flesh to eat—they do not immediately hear the answer. Instead, they are still told: “Amen, amen, I say to you, unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.”

You do not know how it is eaten, or what the manner of eating this bread is; nevertheless, “unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” He was not speaking these words to corpses, but to living people.

Therefore, lest they understand this life and quarrel about it, he continued and added: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life.” Whoever does not eat this bread and drink this blood does not have this life. People can have temporal life without him; eternal life they absolutely cannot have.

Whoever therefore does not eat his flesh or drink his blood does not have life in himself; whoever eats his flesh and drinks his blood has life. What he said in response to both is the word “eternal.”

It is not so with this food, which we take to sustain this temporal life. Whoever does not take it will not live; yet whoever takes it will not necessarily live. For it can happen that very many who have taken it die from old age, illness, or some other circumstance.

But with this food and drink—that is, with the body and blood of the Lord—it is not so. Whoever does not receive it does not have life; whoever receives it has life, and that life is certainly eternal.

He wishes this food and drink to be understood as fellowship in his body and members, which is the holy Church consisting of his predestined, called, justified, glorified, and faithful saints.

Of these realities, the first has already occurred, namely predestination. The second and third have occurred, are occurring, and will occur: calling and justification. The fourth is presently held in hope but will be realized in the future: glorification.

The Sacrament of this reality—that is, of the unity of Christ’s body and blood—is prepared daily in some places and at appointed intervals of days in others on the Lord’s table, and is received from the Lord’s table: for some unto life, for others unto destruction. But the reality itself, of which it is the Sacrament, is life for every person who participates in it, and destruction for no one.

16. But lest they suppose that eternal life is promised in this food and drink in such a way that those who receive it would no longer die bodily, he graciously anticipated this thought. For after he had said, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life,” he immediately added, “And I will raise him up on the last day.”

Thus, meanwhile, he has eternal life according to the spirit, in the rest that receives the spirits of the saints; but as regards the body, he is not deprived of eternal life either, but receives it in the resurrection of the dead on the last day.

17. “For my flesh,” he says, “is truly food, and my blood is truly drink.” Since people desire food and drink so that they may not hunger or thirst, this is truly provided only by this food and drink, which makes those who receive it immortal and incorruptible—that is, by the fellowship itself of the saints, where there will be peace and complete and perfect unity.

For this reason, as men of God before us also understood, our Lord Jesus Christ commended his body and blood in things that are brought together into one from many. One thing is made into one from many grains; another flows together into one from many grapes [Note: [Col. 1614] So Cyprian, *To Caecilius*, Letter 63, and *To Magnus*, Letter 76.].

18. Finally, he now explains how what he is saying happens, and what it means to eat his body and drink his blood: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him.”

To eat that food and drink that drink, then, is to remain in Christ and to have him remain in oneself. Accordingly, whoever does not remain in Christ, and in whom Christ does not remain, undoubtedly neither eats [spiritually] his flesh nor drinks his blood [although bodily and visibly he presses the Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood with his teeth]; rather, he eats and drinks the Sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment, because, being unclean, he presumes to approach Christ’s Sacraments, which no one receives worthily except one who is clean.

Of these it is said, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8) [Note: [Col. 1615] Some printed editions read this way; all our manuscripts, however, have the following: “He neither eats his flesh nor drinks his blood, even if he eats and drinks the Sacrament of so great a reality to his own judgment.” They also lack the words enclosed here in brackets: “Although bodily and visibly he presses the Sacrament of Christ’s body and blood with his teeth.” The Lovanienses attest that these words are contained in none of their manuscripts; they are found in the commentaries on John by Bede and Alcuin.].

19. “As the living Father sent me,” he says, “and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.”

He does not say, “As I eat the Father and live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.” The Son does not become better through participation in the Father, for he was born equal; whereas through participation in the Son, by the unity of his body and blood—which that eating and drinking signifies—we become better [Note: [Col. 1615] Nearly all manuscripts read, “he makes us better.”].

We therefore live because of him, eating him—that is, receiving from him the eternal life that we did not possess from ourselves. But he lives because of the Father, having been sent by him, because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8).

If we understand “I live because of the Father” according to what he says elsewhere, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28), just as we live because of him who is greater than we are, this came about because he was sent. For his sending is his emptying of himself and his taking the form of a servant. This is rightly understood while preserving the equality of the Son’s nature with the Father.

The Father is greater than the human son, but he has God the Son as his equal. The same person is both God and human being, the Son of God and the son of a human being, one Christ Jesus.

If these words are correctly understood in this sense, he said: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so whoever eats me will live because of me.” It is as though he had said: “That I live because of the Father—that is, that I refer my life to him as the greater one—was accomplished by my emptying, in which he sent me. But that someone may live because of me is accomplished by the participation through which he eats me.”

Thus I, having been humbled, live because of the Father; he, having been exalted, lives because of me. But if “I live because of the Father” was said because he is from the Father, and not the Father from him, it was said without diminishing equality.

Nevertheless, by saying, “Whoever eats me will live because of me,” he did not signify the equality of himself and us; rather, he displayed the grace of the Mediator.

20. “This is the bread that came down from heaven,” so that by eating it we may live, since we cannot possess eternal life from ourselves.

“Not as your fathers ate,” he says, “and died: whoever eats this bread will live forever.” By saying that they died, he wishes it to be understood that they do not live forever. For temporally, those who eat Christ will certainly also die; but they live forever because Christ is eternal life.

## TREATISE XXVII

From the passage written, “He said these things in the synagogue while teaching in Capernaum on the Sabbath,” up to, “For he knew who would betray him, since he was one of the twelve.” Chapter 6, verses 60–72.

1. We have heard the words of the Lord from the Gospel, which follow upon the preceding sermon. A sermon is therefore owed to your ears and minds, and it is not inappropriate to this day. For it concerns the body of the Lord, which he said he would give to be eaten for eternal life.

He explained the manner of this gift and of his giving: how he would give his flesh to be eaten, saying, “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57). The sign that someone has eaten and drunk is this: that he remains and is remained in, that he dwells and is indwelt, that he clings so as not to be abandoned [Note: [Col. 1616] Erasmus reads, “and will not be abandoned.”].

This, then, he taught and admonished us through mystical words: that we should be in his body under the one head, as his members, eating his flesh and not abandoning his unity.

But many of those who were present were scandalized because they did not understand. When they heard these things, they thought only of flesh—which they themselves were. Yet the Apostle speaks truly when he says, “To set the mind on the flesh is death” (Rom. 8:6).

The Lord gives us his flesh to eat, and to set the mind on the flesh is death, although he says of his flesh that eternal life is there. Therefore we must not set our minds on the flesh according to the flesh, just as in these words:

2. Accordingly, when many heard him—not from his enemies, but from his disciples—said, “This is a hard saying; who can hear it?” If the disciples regarded this saying as hard, what did the enemies think? Yet it was necessary that what would not be understood by everyone should be said. God’s secret ought to make people attentive, not hostile.

But these people quickly failed while the Lord Jesus was speaking such things. They did not believe that he was saying something great and concealing some grace within those words. Instead, they understood them as they wished, and, in the human manner, thought that Jesus either could or intended to cut up the flesh with which the Word had been clothed and distribute it to those who believed in him.

“This is a hard saying,” they said; “who can hear it?”

3. But Jesus, knowing within himself that his disciples were murmuring about this, replied—for they said these things among themselves in such a way that they were not heard by him, but he, who knew them within themselves, heard them within himself—and said, “Does this scandalize you?”

That is, “Does this scandalize you because I said, ‘I give you my flesh to eat and my blood to drink’?” What, then, if you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?

What does this mean? Does he resolve here what had disturbed them? Does he disclose here the source of their scandal? Certainly—if they understood. For they thought that he would distribute his body; but he said that he would ascend into heaven, certainly whole and entire.

“When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before,” then surely you will see that he does not distribute his body in the way you suppose; surely then you will understand that his grace is not consumed by bites.

4. And he said, “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing.”

Before we explain this, as the Lord grants us, we must not pass over carelessly what he said: “If then you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before?”

For Christ is the Son of Man, from the virgin Mary. Thus the Son of Man began here on earth, where he assumed flesh from the earth. Hence it had been prophetically said, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Ps. 84:12).

What, then, does he mean by saying, “When you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before”? There would be no question if he had said, “When you see the Son of God ascending where he was before.” But when he says that the Son of Man is ascending where he was before, was the Son of Man previously in heaven, when he began to be on earth?

Here he said “where he was before,” as though he were not there at the time he was speaking. But elsewhere he says, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13). He did not say “was,” but, “the Son of Man,” he says, “who is in heaven.”

He was speaking on earth and said that he was in heaven. And he did not say, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of God who is in heaven.”

What does this imply except that we should understand what I also commended to your Charity in the preceding sermon: Christ God and human being is one person, not two, lest our faith be not a Trinity but a quaternity?

Christ therefore is one: the Word, soul, and flesh are one Christ; the Son of God and the son of a human being are one Christ. He is always the Son of God, and the son of a human being in time; nevertheless, he is one Christ according to the unity of person.

He was in heaven when he was speaking on earth. The Son of Man was in heaven in the same way that the Son of God was on earth: the Son of God on earth in the flesh he assumed, and the Son of Man in heaven in the unity of person.

5. What, then, does he add: “It is the Spirit who gives life; the flesh profits nothing”?

Let us say to him—for he permits us to speak, not in contradiction but in the desire to understand—“O Lord, good teacher, how does the flesh profit nothing, when you have said, ‘Unless someone eats my flesh and drinks my blood, he will not have life in himself’? Or does life profit nothing? And for what reason are we what we are, except that we may have the eternal life which you promise through your flesh? What, then, does ‘the flesh profits nothing’ mean?”

It profits nothing—but only in the way they understood it. They understood flesh as it is torn apart in a corpse or sold in a butcher’s shop, not as it is enlivened by the Spirit.

Thus it was said, “The flesh profits nothing,” in the same way that it is said, “Knowledge puffs up.” Must we therefore hate knowledge? Certainly not. What does “knowledge puffs up” mean? Knowledge alone, without charity. Therefore he added, “But charity builds up” (1 Cor. 8:1).

Add charity, then, to knowledge, and knowledge will be useful—not through itself, but through charity. So also here: “The flesh profits nothing,” but flesh alone. Let the Spirit be added to the flesh, just as charity is added to knowledge, and it will profit greatly.

For if the flesh profited nothing, the Word would not have become flesh in order to dwell among us. If Christ profited us greatly through the flesh, how does the flesh profit nothing? Through the flesh, the Spirit accomplished something for our salvation.

The flesh was a vessel; consider what it contained, not what it was. The apostles were sent: did their flesh profit us nothing? If the flesh of the apostles profited us, could the flesh of the Lord profit nothing? From where does the sound of the word come to us except through the voice of flesh? From where do the stylus and the writing come? All these are works of flesh, but with the Spirit moving it as his instrument [Col. 1618].

Therefore, “It is the Spirit who gives life, but the flesh profits nothing”: I do not give my flesh to be eaten in the way they understood flesh.

6. Therefore he says, “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.”

We have said, brothers, that in the eating of his flesh and drinking of his blood the Lord commended this: that we should remain in him, and he in us. We remain in him when we are his members; he remains in us when we are his temple.

But in order that we may be his members, unity joins us together. And what produces unity except charity? And from where does the charity of God come? Ask the Apostle: “The charity of God,” he says, “has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life; for the Spirit makes the members alive. Nor does the Spirit make members alive unless he finds them in the body that he himself animates.

For the spirit that is in you, O human being, by which you exist as a human being—does it give life to a member that it finds separated from your flesh? I mean your spirit, your soul: your soul gives life only to the members that are in your flesh. If you remove one, it is no longer given life by your soul, because it is not joined to the unity of your body.

These things are said so that we may love unity and fear separation. For nothing should a Christian fear so much as being separated from the body of Christ.

If he is separated from the body of Christ, he is not his member. If he is not his member, he is not given life by his Spirit. “Whoever,” the Apostle says, “does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9).

Therefore it is the Spirit who gives life, but the flesh profits nothing. “The words that I have spoken to you are spirit and life.” What does “they are spirit and life” mean? They are to be understood spiritually.

Have you understood spiritually? They are spirit and life. Have you understood carnally? Even so, they are spirit and life—but they are not so for you.

### 7

“But there are some among you,” he says, “who do not believe.” He did not say, “There are some among you who do not understand,” but he stated the reason why they do not understand: “There are some among you who do not believe”; and therefore they do not understand, because they do not believe. For the Prophet said, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint). Through faith we are joined; through understanding we are given life. Let us first cling through faith, so that there may be something to be given life through understanding. For whoever does not cling resists; whoever resists does not believe. And whoever resists—how can he be given life? He is an adversary to the ray of light by which he must be penetrated: he does not turn away his gaze, but closes his mind.

There are therefore some who do not believe. Let them believe and open themselves; let them open themselves and they will be enlightened. For Jesus knew from the beginning who would believe, and who would betray him. Judas was there also. Some had been scandalized; but he remained, not in order to understand, but in order to lie in wait. And because he had remained for that reason, the Lord did not remain silent about him. He did not identify him, but neither was he silent about him, so that all might fear, although only one would perish.

But after he had spoken of and distinguished believers from unbelievers, he stated the reason why they did not believe: “For this reason I told you,” he says, “that no one can come to me unless it has been granted him by my Father.” Therefore even believing is granted to us; for believing is not nothing. But if it is something great, rejoice that you have believed, yet do not become arrogant: “For what do you have that you did not receive?” (1 Cor. 4:7).

### 8

“From that time many of his disciples went back and no longer walked with him.” They went back, but after Satan, not after Christ. For on one occasion the Lord Christ called Peter “Satan,” chiefly because he wanted to go before his Lord and give him counsel not to die—although he had come in order to die, so that we might not die eternally. And he said to him: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men” (Matt. 16:23).

He did not drive him away to go back after Satan, though he called him Satan; rather, he made him go behind him, so that by walking after the Lord he would not be Satan. These others, however, went back in the manner of those women about whom the Apostle says: “For some have turned back after Satan” (1 Tim. 5:15). They no longer walked with him. Behold, cut off from the body, they lost life, because perhaps they had never truly been in the body. They must be counted among the unbelievers, although they were called disciples.

They went back—not a few, but many. This perhaps happened for our consolation, since it sometimes occurs that a person speaks the truth, but what he says is not understood, and those who hear him are scandalized and depart. The person then regrets having said what was true: he says to himself, “I should not have spoken in that way; I should not have said that.” Behold, this happened to the Lord: he spoke and lost many; he remained with a few. Yet he was not disturbed, because from the beginning he knew both who would believe and who would not believe. When this happens to us, we are troubled. Let us find consolation in the Lord, and nevertheless speak our words carefully.

### 9

Then he turned to the few who had remained. “Jesus therefore said to the Twelve”—that is, to those Twelve who had remained—“Do you also want to go away?” Judas did not depart either. But why he remained was already apparent to the Lord; it was manifested to us only afterward.

Peter answered on behalf of all: one on behalf of many, unity on behalf of the whole: “Simon Peter therefore answered him, ‘Lord, to whom shall we go?’” You drive us away from yourself; give us another yourself. “To whom shall we go?” If we depart from you, to whom shall we go? “You have the words of eternal life.”

See how Peter, by God’s gift and through the restoring action of the Holy Spirit, understood. How could it be except because he believed? “You have the words of eternal life.” For you have eternal life in the ministry of your body and blood. “And we have believed, and we have come to know.” He did not say, “We have come to know, and we have believed,” but “We have believed, and we have come to know.” We believed in order to come to know; for if we had wished first to know and afterward to believe, we would have been able neither to know nor to believe.

What did we believe, and what did we come to know? “That you are the Christ, the Son of God”—that is, that you yourself are eternal life, and that in your flesh and blood you give nothing other than what you are.

### 10

The Lord Jesus therefore said: “Did I not choose you Twelve, and one of you is a devil?” Therefore, should he have said, “I chose eleven”? Or is the devil also chosen, and is the devil among the chosen?

The chosen are usually called so in praise. Or was this man chosen because, without willing or knowing it, something of great benefit would come about through him? This is characteristic of God; it is contrary to the wicked. For just as the wicked make evil use of God’s good works, so God, in contrast, makes good use of the evil works of wicked people.

How good is it that the members of the body are such that they can be arranged only by God the Craftsman! Yet how badly wantonness makes use of the eyes! How badly deceit makes use of the tongue! Does not a false witness first slaughter his own soul with his tongue, and then, having destroyed himself, attempt to injure another? He makes evil use of his tongue, but the tongue is not therefore evil. The tongue is God’s work, but that wickedness makes evil use of God’s good work.

How do those who run toward crimes make use of their feet? How do murderers make use of their hands? And how badly do evil people make use of those good creatures of God that are externally available to them? With gold they corrupt judgments and oppress the innocent. The wicked make evil use of this light: by living wickedly, they even seize the light by which they see for the service of their crimes. For when a wicked person wants to do something evil, he wants there to be light for him, lest he stumble—he who has already stumbled and fallen inwardly. What he fears in the body he has already suffered in the heart.

To avoid going through each case individually, then, the wicked person makes evil use of all God’s good things. In contrast, the good person makes good use of the evils of wicked people. And what is as good as the one God? Indeed, the Lord himself said, “No one is good except one, God” (Mark 10:18). Therefore, the better he is, the better use he makes even of our evils.

What was worse than Judas? Among all those who clung to the Teacher, among the Twelve, the money purse had been entrusted to him, and the distribution to the poor had been assigned to him. Ungrateful for so great a benefit and so great an honor, he received money and lost justice; he handed over Life while dead, pursuing as an enemy the one whom he had followed as a disciple.

All this was Judas’s evil; but the Lord made good use of his evil. He endured being handed over in order to redeem us. Behold, Judas’s evil was turned into good.

How many martyrs did Satan persecute? If Satan had ceased persecuting, we would not today be celebrating the glorious crown of Saint Lawrence. If, therefore, God makes good use of the devil’s evil works, what the wicked person does by making evil use of them harms himself; it does not contradict God’s goodness. The Craftsman makes use of him—and he is a great Craftsman: if he did not know how to make use of him, he would not even permit him to exist.

“Therefore one of you is a devil,” he says, “although I chose you Twelve.” What he said, “I chose twelve,” can also be understood in this way, because the number is sacred. The honor of that number was not removed because one of them perished; for another was appointed in the place of the one who perished (Acts 1:26). The consecrated number remained—the number twelve—because throughout the whole world, that is, through the four quarters of the world, they were going to proclaim the Trinity. Hence three times four.

[Note: [Col. 1620] Earlier editions read, “Therefore also four,” but here the reading has been corrected in accordance with the manuscripts.]

Judas therefore destroyed himself; he did not violate the number twelve. He abandoned his Teacher, while God appointed a successor to him.

### 11

All that the Lord spoke concerning his flesh and blood; his promise of eternal life to us through the grace of their distribution; his intention that we should understand by this that those who eat and drink his flesh and blood remain in him and he in them; the fact that those who did not believe failed to understand; the fact that they were scandalized because they understood spiritual things in a carnal way; and the fact that, when they had been scandalized and were perishing, the Lord was present as a consolation to the disciples who remained [Note: [Col. 1621] Thus the manuscripts; the printed editions read, “the consolation of the Lord was present.”]—to whom, in order to test them, he asked, “Do you also want to go away?” so that their answer, revealing that they would remain, might become known to us, although he already knew that they would remain—all this, beloved, should serve this purpose for us: that we should not merely eat the flesh of Christ and drink the blood of Christ in the sacrament, as many wicked people also do, but that we should eat and drink unto participation in the Spirit, so that we may remain in the Lord’s body as members, be given life by his Spirit, and not be scandalized even if many now eat and drink the sacraments with us temporarily, although at the end they will have eternal punishments.

For now the body of Christ is mixed together like grain on a threshing floor; “but the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2:19). If you know what you are threshing, because a hidden mass is there, and threshing does not consume what winnowing will purify, we are certain, brothers, that all of us who are in the Lord’s body and remain in him, so that he too may remain in us, must in this age live among the wicked until the end.

I do not mean among those wicked people who blaspheme Christ. Few are now found who blaspheme with the tongue, but many who blaspheme by their lives. It is therefore necessary that we live among them until the end.

### 12

But what does he mean when he says, “Whoever remains in me, and I in him” (John 6:57; 15:5)? What else does this mean than what the martyrs heard: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 24:13)?

How did Saint Lawrence remain in him, whose feast we celebrate today? He remained through temptation; he remained through the tyrant’s interrogation; he remained through the fiercest threats; he remained through death. It is little to say that he remained through death: he remained through monstrous torture. For he was not killed quickly, but tortured in the fire. He was permitted to live for a long time—or rather, he was not permitted to live long, but was compelled to die slowly.

In that prolonged death, amid those tortures, because he had eaten well and drunk well, as though fattened by that food and drunk from that cup, he did not feel the torments. For the one who said, “It is the Spirit who gives life,” was there. His flesh was burning, but the Spirit was giving life to his soul. He did not yield, and he entered into the kingdom.

The holy martyr Sixtus—whose day we celebrated three days ago—had said to him: “Do not grieve, son.” He was a bishop; this man was a deacon. “Do not grieve,” he said; “you will follow me after three days.” By “three days” he meant the interval between the day of Saint Sixtus’s passion and the day of Saint Lawrence’s passion today. The three days were the intervening period.

What consolation! He did not say, “Do not grieve, son; the persecution will cease, and you will be safe.” Rather: “Do not grieve. Where I go before you, you will follow; your following will not be delayed. There will be three intervening days, and you will be with me.” He received the prophecy, conquered the devil, and attained the triumph.

# TRACTATE XXVIII

From the Gospel passage, “After this Jesus went about in Galilee,” to, “Yet no one spoke openly about him, because of fear of the Jews.” Chapter 7, verses 1–13.

[Col. 1622]

### 1

In this chapter of the Gospel, brothers, our Lord Jesus Christ, according to his humanity, commended himself greatly to our faith. For he always brings this about by his words and deeds: that he should be believed both God and man—God, who made us; man, who sought us; God, always with the Father; man, with us in time.

For he would not seek the one whom he had made unless he himself became what he had made. But remember this, and do not let it depart from your hearts: Christ became man in such a way that he did not cease to be God. Remaining God, he assumed humanity—the one who made humanity.

Therefore, when he hid himself as a man, we must not think that he had lost his power; rather, he was offering an example to our weakness. For he was arrested when he wished, and killed when he wished.

But because his members were going to exist—his faithful, that is, who would not possess the power that our God himself possessed—what he concealed, what he hid himself as though to prevent his being killed, indicated what his members would do, since he himself was present in those members. For Christ is not merely in the head and not merely in the body; rather, Christ is wholly in the head and in the body.

Therefore, what his members are, he is; but what he is, is not immediately his members. For if his members were not himself, he would not say, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). Saul was not persecuting him personally, but his members—his faithful—on earth. Yet he did not wish to say, “My saints,” or “My servants,” or, finally, in the more honorable expression, “My brothers,” but “Me”—that is, my members, of whom I am the head.

### 2

Having said this, I think we will not have to labor over this chapter that has just been read. For what was going to happen in the body was often signified in the head.

“After this,” he says, “Jesus went about in Galilee; for he did not want to go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him.” This is what I said: he was offering an example to our weakness. He had not lost his power, but was consoling our frailty.

For, as I said, it was going to happen that one of his faithful would hide himself so as not to be found by persecutors. And lest hiding be held against him as a crime, he went before, in the head, what was to be confirmed in the member.

Thus it is said, “He did not want to go about in Judea, because the Jews were seeking to kill him,” as though Christ could not both walk among the Jews and not be killed by the Jews. He demonstrated this power when he wished. For when they already wanted to seize him for his impending passion, he said to them, “Whom do you seek?” They answered, “Jesus.” And he said to them, “I am he”—not hiding himself, but revealing himself. Yet at that revelation they did not stand their ground; instead, they stepped backward and fell (John 18:4–6).

Nevertheless, because he had come to suffer, they rose, seized him, brought him before the judge, and killed him. But what did they do? As a certain Scripture says, “The earth has been handed over into the hands of the wicked” (Job 9:24): the flesh was given into the power of the Jews. And this happened so that, as it were, the purse might be torn open from which our price would flow.

### 3

Now the Jewish feast of Booths was near. Those who have read the Scriptures know what the feast of Booths is. On the feast they made booths in imitation of the tabernacles in which they had lived when, after being led out of Egypt, they traveled as pilgrims in the wilderness.

This was a feast, a great solemnity. The Jews celebrated it as though remembering the Lord’s benefits, although they were going to kill the Lord.

On this feast—for there were several feast days, and among the Jews a feast was called a feast not because it lasted only one day, but because it lasted several days—his brothers spoke to the Lord Christ.

Understand “his brothers” in the way you know; what you are hearing is not new. The blood relatives of the Virgin Mary were called the Lord’s brothers. It was customary in the Scriptures to call any blood relatives and close relations “brothers,” in a way outside our ordinary usage, not in the manner in which we speak.

For who would call an uncle and his sister’s son brothers? Yet Scripture calls even such relations brothers. Thus Abraham and Lot are called brothers, although Abraham was Lot’s paternal uncle (Gen. 11:27, 31; 13:8; 14:14); and Laban and Jacob are called brothers, although Laban was Jacob’s maternal uncle (Gen. 28:2; 29:10, 15).

Therefore, when you hear “the Lord’s brothers,” think of Mary’s blood relationship, not of any further offspring from her. For just as in the tomb where the Lord’s body was placed no dead person lay either before or afterward, so Mary’s womb conceived nothing mortal either before or afterward.

### 4

We have said who the brothers were; let us hear what they said.

“Go away from here and depart into Judea, so that your disciples also may see the works that you do.” The Lord’s works were not hidden from his disciples, but they were hidden from these men. These brothers—that is, blood relatives—were able to have Christ as their kinsman, but because of that very relationship they disdained to believe in him.

It is said in the Gospel; we do not dare to conjecture this ourselves—you have just heard it. They add and urge him: “For no one does anything in secret while he himself seeks to be known publicly. If you do these things, reveal yourself to the world.” And immediately: “For not even his brothers believed in him.”

Why did they not believe in him? Because they were seeking human glory. Even in what they appear to advise him, they are concerned for his glory: “You do marvelous things; make yourself known”—that is, “Appear to everyone, so that everyone may praise you.”

Flesh was speaking to flesh—but flesh without God to flesh united with God. For the wisdom of the flesh was speaking to the Word who became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1:14).

### 5

What does the Lord say in response? “Jesus therefore said to them: ‘My time has not yet come, but your time is always ready.’”

What does this mean? Had Christ’s time not yet come? Why, then, had Christ come, if his time had not yet come? Have we not heard the Apostle say, “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4)? If he was sent in the fullness of time, then he was sent when he ought to have been sent; he came when it was fitting. What, then, does “My time has not yet come” mean?

Understand, brothers, with what disposition those men spoke who appeared to be advising their brother. They were giving him advice about attaining glory, admonishing him in a worldly and earthly spirit not to remain obscure and hidden.

Therefore, when the Lord says, “My time has not yet come,” he answers those who were advising him about glory: “The time of my glory has not yet come.”

See how profound this is. They were urging him toward glory, but he wished to precede exaltation with humility and to pave the way to that very height through humility.

Those disciples, too, were certainly seeking glory when they wanted one to sit at his right hand and another at his left. They were looking to where they would come, but they did not see by what way. The Lord recalled them to the way, so that they might come to their homeland in proper order.

For the homeland is lofty, but the way is humble. The homeland is Christ’s life; the way is Christ’s death. The homeland is Christ’s dwelling; the way is Christ’s passion. Whoever refuses the way—what homeland does he seek?

Accordingly, he answered those who were seeking height: “Can you drink the cup that I am going to drink?” (Matt. 20:21–22). Behold the way by which one comes to the height you desire. For he was referring to the cup of humility and passion.

### 6

Therefore here too, “My time has not yet come; but your time”—that is, the glory of the world—“is always ready.”

This is the time about which Christ speaks in prophecy—that is, Christ’s body: “When I receive the time, I will judge uprightly” (Ps. 74:3).

[Note: [Col. 1624] Most manuscripts read: “of which Christ speaks in the prophet.”] For now is not the time of judging, but of tolerating the wicked. Let Christ’s body therefore bear with them now and tolerate the wickedness of those who live badly.

Let it nevertheless possess justice now, before it possesses judgment; for through justice it will arrive at judgment. While the members tolerate the wickedness of this age, what does Holy Scripture say in the Psalm? “The Lord will not reject his people.” His people labor among the unworthy, among the wicked, among blasphemers, among murmurers, slanderers, persecutors, and, if they are able, killers. They labor, indeed; “but the Lord will not reject his people, nor abandon his inheritance, until justice is turned into judgment” (Ps. 93:14–15).

[Note: [Col. 1624] The manuscripts, here and a little below, read “to judgment” (*ad judicium*).]

Until the justice that now exists in his saints is turned into judgment—when what was said to them is fulfilled: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

The Apostle possessed justice, but not yet that judgment of which he says, “Do you not know that we will judge angels?” (1 Cor. 6:3). Let there therefore now be a time for living justly; afterward there will be a time for judging those who have lived badly. “Until justice,” he says, “is turned into judgment.”

This will be the time of judgment about which the Lord now said, “My time has not yet come.” For there will be a time of glory, so that he who came in humility may come in exaltation. He who came to be judged will come to judge; he who came to be killed by the dead will come to judge the living and the dead.

“God,” the Psalm says, “will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. 49:3). What does “he will come openly” mean? It means that he came secretly. Then he will not be silent. For when he came secretly, he was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he did not open his mouth (Isa. 53:7). He will come and will not be silent. “I have kept silent,” he says; “shall I always keep silent?” (Isa. 42:14, according to the Septuagint).

### 7

But what is necessary now for those who possess justice? What is read in that very Psalm: “Until justice is turned into judgment”—and for those who possess it, “all who are upright in heart.”

Perhaps you ask who the upright in heart are. In Scripture we find that those are upright in heart who endure the evils of the world and do not accuse God.

See, brothers: what I am saying is a rare bird.

[Note: [Col. 1625] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition have this passage as follows: “This is a rare case of what I am saying.” M.]

For somehow, whenever something bad happens to a person, he rushes to accuse God, although he ought to accuse himself. When you do something good, you praise yourself; when you suffer something bad, you accuse God. This is a crooked heart, not an upright one.

If you are corrected from this distortion and perversity, what you were doing will be turned into its opposite. Previously, what were you doing? You praised yourself for God’s good gifts and accused God for your evils. With your heart turned and made straight, you will praise God for his good gifts and accuse yourself for your evils. These are the upright in heart.

Finally, the man whose heart was not yet upright—because he was displeased by the prosperity of the wicked and the suffering of the good—said after being corrected: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart! But as for me, when I was not upright in heart, my feet almost slipped; my steps nearly gave way. Why? Because I was jealous of sinners, seeing the peace of sinners” (Ps. 72:1–3).

“I saw,” he says, “wicked people happy, and God displeased me.” For this was what I wanted: that God would not allow the wicked to be happy.

Let a person understand: God never allows this. The wicked person is considered happy because what happiness is remains unknown. Let us therefore be upright in heart. The time of our glory has not yet come.

Let it be said to the lovers of this age, such as the Lord’s brothers were: “Your time is always ready; our time has not yet come.” Let us dare to say this ourselves. Since we are the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, since we are his members, since we gladly acknowledge our head, let us say it plainly, because for our sake he himself deigned to say this.

When the lovers of this age insult us, let us say to them: “Your time is always ready; our time has not yet come.” For the Apostle said to us: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” When will our time come? “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

### 8

What does he add next? “The world cannot hate you.”

What does this mean except, “The world cannot hate those who love it, false witnesses”? For you call evil things good, and good things evil. “But it hates me, because I testify about it that its works are evil.”

“You go up to this feast.” What does “this” mean? The feast at which you seek human glory. What does “this” mean? The feast at which you want to extend carnal joys, rather than think about eternal ones.

“I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.”

At this feast you seek human glory; but my time—that is, the time of my glory—has not yet come.

[Note: [Col. 1626] [This note appears at the foot of column 1626, but its callout number has not been printed in the text.] Erasmus reads, “It is in that one.” M.]

[Col. 1626]

That will be my feast—not one that comes before and passes with these days, but one that remains forever. It will be festivity itself: joy without end, eternity without stain, serenity without cloud.

After saying this, he himself remained in Galilee. But when his brothers had gone up, then he too went up to the feast—not openly, but as though secretly.

For this reason he did not go up to “this feast”: because he did not wish to glory temporarily, but to teach something salutary, correct people, remind them of the eternal feast, turn their love away from this age, and direct it toward God.

What does it mean that he went up to the feast as though secretly? This too is not without significance on the Lord’s part.

[Note: [Col. 1626] Erasmus and the Lyon edition read: “This too is not without significance for understanding. It seems …” M.]

It seems to me, brothers, that by going up as though secretly he wished to signify something here as well. For what follows will show that he went up midway through the feast—that is, after some of those days had passed—in order also to teach openly. But he said “as though secretly,” so that he would not reveal himself to people.

It is not without significance that Christ went secretly to the feast, because he himself was hidden in that feast. Even what I have said is still hidden. Let the veil be revealed, then; let it be lifted, and let what was secret appear.

### 9

Everything that was said to the ancient people of Israel in the various writings of the holy Law—what they were to do in sacrifices, priesthoods, feast days, and altogether in whatever matters by which they worshiped God—whatever was said and commanded to them was a shadow of things to come.

Of what things to come? Of those fulfilled in Christ. Hence the Apostle says, “Whatever the promises of God are, in him also” (2 Cor. 1:20)—that is, in him they have been fulfilled.

Then he says elsewhere: “All these things happened to them as a figure; but they were written for our sake, upon whom the end of the ages has come” (1 Cor. 10:11). He also says elsewhere: “For Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4). And again elsewhere: “Let no one judge you in food or drink, or in respect of a feast, or a new moon, or sabbaths, which are a shadow of things to come” (Col. 2:16–17).

If all those things were shadows of things to come, then the feast of Booths was also a shadow of things to come. Let us therefore ask of what future reality this feast was a shadow.

I have explained what the feast of Booths was: it was a celebration of tabernacles, because the people, having been freed from Egypt and journeying through the wilderness toward the promised land, lived in tabernacles.

Let us take notice of what this means, and we too shall be that people—those of us who are members of Christ, if indeed we are.

[Note: [Col. 1626] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read: “who are members of Christ, if we are. But if we are in him …” M.]

If we are members of Christ, we are so because he deigns it, not because we have earned it.

Let us therefore pay attention to ourselves, brothers. We have been led out of Egypt, where we were serving the devil as Pharaoh, where we were doing works of clay in earthly desires and laboring greatly in them. For Christ cried out to us as though we were making bricks: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matt. 11:28).

From there we were led out through Baptism as through the Red Sea—called red because it was consecrated by Christ’s blood. After all our enemies who were pursuing us had died—that is, after all our sins had been blotted out—we were brought across.

Now, before we come to the promised homeland, that is, the eternal kingdom, we are in the wilderness, in tabernacles. Those who recognize these things are in tabernacles; for it was going to happen that certain people would recognize this.

The one who understands that he is a pilgrim in the world is in tabernacles. He understands himself to be on pilgrimage when he sees himself longing for his homeland. When Christ’s body is in tabernacles, Christ is in tabernacles. But at that time he was not evident, but hidden.

For the shadow still obscured the light. When the light came, the shadow was removed. Christ was hidden; Christ was in the feast of Booths, but Christ was hidden.

Now, since these things have been revealed, we recognize that we are traveling through the wilderness. If we recognize this, we are in the wilderness.

What is “in the wilderness”? In the desert. Why in the desert? Because we are in this world, where one thirsts on a waterless road. But let us thirst, so that we may be satisfied. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for justice, for they will be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6).

And our thirst is filled from the rock in the wilderness. “For the rock was Christ,” and the rock was struck with the rod so that water might flow. In order that it might flow, it was struck twice (1 Cor. 10:4; Num. 20:11), because the cross has two pieces of wood.

All these things, therefore, which took place in figure are revealed in us. Nor is it without significance that it was said of the Lord, “He went up to the feast, not openly, but as though secretly.” The feast itself was represented in secret, because Christ was hidden in that feast; for that feast signified Christ’s members who would make their pilgrimage.

### 10

The Jews therefore were seeking him at the feast, before he went up. His brothers went up first, and he did not go up at the time they thought and wanted him to go up. Thus even this was fulfilled: “Not to this”—that is, not on the first or second day to which you want him to go.

He went up afterward, as the Gospel says, midway through the feast—that is, when as many days of the feast had already passed as remained. For, as we must understand, they celebrated the feast itself over several days.

### 11

They were saying, therefore, “Where is he?” And there was much murmuring about him among the crowd.

Why the murmuring? Because of disagreement. What was the disagreement? Some were saying, “He is good”; others, “No, but he deceives the crowds.”

This must be understood of all his servants; it is said in this way today. Whoever excels in some spiritual grace, some will certainly say, “He is good,” while others say, “No, but he deceives the crowds.”

[Note: [Col. 1627] According to Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition, the reading should be: “in some spiritual grace and progress, others say.” M.]

Why does this happen? Because “our life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3).

For this reason, during winter one may say of a tree—say, a fig tree, a pear tree, or some similar fruit tree—“This tree is dead”; it looks like a dry tree and, as long as it is winter, its condition does not appear. Summer proves it; judgment proves it.

Our summer is the revelation of Christ: “God will come openly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Ps. 49:3). Fire will go before him; this fire will burn his enemies (Ps. 96:3). The fire will seize the dry trees.

For then they will appear dry, when it is said to them, “I was hungry, and you did not give me anything to eat.” On the other side, that is, on the right, the fruitfulness of the fruits and the dignity of the leaves will appear. Their greenness will be eternity.

To those who are like dry trees it will therefore be said, “Go into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25:41–42). For, behold, “the axe has been laid at the root of the trees. Every tree, therefore, that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire” (Matt. 3:10).

Let people say of you, if you are making progress in Christ, “He deceives the crowds.” This is said of Christ himself, of the whole body of Christ. Consider Christ’s body still in the world; consider Christ’s body still on the threshing floor. See how it is blasphemed by the chaff.

They are threshed together, but the chaff is crushed and the grain is purified. What was said of the Lord therefore serves as consolation concerning any Christian of whom this is said.

### 12

“Yet no one spoke openly about him, because of fear of the Jews.”

But who were those who did not speak about him because of fear of the Jews? Clearly, those who were saying, “He is good,” not those who were saying, “He deceives the crowds.”

Those who said, “He deceives the crowds,” made their sound heard like the rustling of dry leaves. “He deceives the crowds” sounded more loudly; “He is good” they whispered more quietly.

But now, brothers, although that glory of Christ has not yet come which will make us eternal, his Church nevertheless grows in such a way, and he has deigned to spread it throughout the whole world so fully, that it is already whispered, “He deceives the crowds,” while “He is good” resounds more loudly.

# TRACTATE XXIX

On the Gospel passage, “Now, about the middle of the feast, Jesus went up into the temple,” to, “The one who sent him is true, and there is no injustice in him.” Chapter 7, verses 14–18.

[Col. 1629]

### 1

Let us accordingly examine what follows in the Gospel, which was also read today, and say what the Lord grants us to say.

Yesterday the reading extended this far: although they had not seen the Lord Jesus in the temple during the feast, they were nevertheless speaking about him. “Some were saying, ‘He is good’; others, ‘No, but he deceives the crowds’” (John 7:12).

This was said for the consolation of those who would later preach the word of God and be regarded as both deceivers and truthful (2 Cor. 6:8).

If “to deceive” means to mislead, then neither Christ nor his Apostles was a deceiver, and no Christian ought to be a deceiver. But if “to deceive” means to lead someone from one thing to another by persuasion, then we must ask from what and toward what. If from evil toward good, the deceiver is good; if from good toward evil, the deceiver is evil.

In this sense, then, in which people are led from evil toward good, would that we might all be called deceivers and actually be so!

### 2

The Lord therefore went up afterward to the feast, midway through the feast, and taught. The Jews were amazed, saying, “How does this man know letters, since he has not been educated?”

The one who had been hiding was teaching; he was speaking openly, and he was not being seized. His hiding had been an example; this was an exercise of power.

But when he taught, the Jews were amazed. All of them, I suppose, were amazed, but not all were converted. Why were they amazed? Many knew where he had been born and how he had been raised. They had never seen him learning letters, yet they heard him disputing about the Law and producing testimonies from the Law—things no one could produce unless he had read them, and no one could read unless he had learned letters. For this reason they were amazed.

Their amazement, however, became for the Teacher an occasion for introducing a deeper truth. From their amazement and their words, the Lord spoke something profound, worthy of being examined and investigated more carefully.

For this reason I call your Charity to attentive listening—not only so that you may listen for your own sake, but also so that you may pray for us.

### 3

What, then, did the Lord answer those who wondered how he knew letters that he had not learned? “My teaching,” he said, “is not mine, but his who sent me.” Here is the first profundity: for he seems to have spoken, in a few words, almost contrary to himself. He did not say, “This teaching is not mine,” but, “My teaching is not mine.” If it is not yours, how is it yours? If it is yours, how is it not yours? You yourself say both: “my teaching” and “not mine.” For if he had said, “This teaching is not mine,” there would be no question. Now, brothers, first attend to the question, and then await the solution in due order. For whoever does not see the question being posed, how can he understand what is explained?

The question, then, is this: he says “mine—not mine.” This seems contradictory: how is it mine, and how is it not mine? If, therefore, we carefully consider what the holy Evangelist says at the beginning—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)—the solution to this question hangs upon it.

What, then, is the Father’s teaching except the Father’s Word? Therefore Christ himself is the Father’s teaching, if he is the Father’s Word. But because the Word cannot be no one’s, but must belong to someone, he both called his teaching his own—meaning himself—and not his own, because he is the Father’s Word. For what is as much yours as you yourself? And what is as much not yours as you yourself, if what you are belongs to someone?

### 4

The Word, then, is also God, and the Word is the stable Word of the teaching—not a sound uttered in syllables and passing away, but one abiding with the Father. To this abiding Word we are to turn, admonished by passing sounds [Note: [Col. 1629] Lovaniensis reads “to whom,” against the other printed editions and the manuscripts.]

For that which passes does not admonish us in such a way as to summon us to passing things. We are admonished to love God. Everything I have just said consisted of syllables: they struck and beat the air so that they might reach the sense of your ears [Note: [Col. 1629] The manuscripts read “sound”]; by being sounded, they passed away. Yet what I admonished you about ought not to pass away, because he whom I admonished you to love does not pass away. And when, admonished by passing syllables, you have turned toward him, neither will you pass away, but you will remain with him who remains.

This, then, is the great, profound, and eternal thing in the teaching: that which remains, and to which all things that pass away in time call us when they signify rightly and are not uttered falsely [Note: [Col. 1629] Thus the manuscripts. The Amiens, Basel, and Erasmus editions read, “which they call”; Lovaniensis, “to which they are called.”].

For all the signs that we express through sounds signify something that is not sound. It is not the case that two short syllables are God, that we worship two short syllables, [Col. 1630] adore two short syllables, and desire to reach two short syllables—which almost cease to sound before they have begun, and in which there is no place for the second unless the first has passed away.

Something great, then, remains which is called God, although the sound does not remain when the word “God” is spoken. Attend in this way to Christ’s teaching, and you will reach the Word of God. When you have reached the Word of God, attend to the words “the Word was God,” and you will see that it was rightly said, “my teaching.” Attend also to whose Word he is, and you will see that it was rightly said, “it is not mine.”

### 5

In brief, I say to your Charity: it seems to me that the Lord Jesus Christ meant this when he said, “My teaching is not mine,” as if he were saying, “I am not from myself.”

Although we say and believe that the Son is equal to the Father, that there is no difference of nature or substance between them, and that no interval of time intervened between the one who begets and the one begotten, nevertheless, while preserving and safeguarding these truths, we say this: the one is Father, and the other is Son.

The Father is not Father unless he has a Son, and the Son is not Son unless he has a Father. Yet the Son is God from the Father, whereas the Father is God, but not God from the Son. The Father is the Son’s Father, but not God from the Son; the Son is the Father’s Son and God from the Father.

For the Lord Christ is called “Light from Light.” Thus there is Light not from Light, and equal Light from Light: together, one Light, not two lights.

### 6

If we have understood, thanks be to God. But if someone has understood little, the human worker has done what he could; let him see from where he should hope for the rest. Externally, as workers, we can plant and water, but it is God who gives the growth (1 Corinthians 3:6).

“My teaching,” he says, “is not mine, but his who sent me.” Let the person who says, “I have not yet understood,” hear the counsel. For when this great and profound matter had been spoken, the Lord Christ himself surely saw that not everyone would understand so profound a statement, and in what followed he gave counsel.

Do you wish to understand? Believe. For God said through the prophet, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

To this belongs what the Lord also added immediately afterward: “If anyone wills to do his will, he will know concerning the teaching whether it is from God, or whether I speak from myself.”

What does this mean: “If anyone wills to do his will”? But I had said, “If anyone believes,” and I had given this counsel: “If you have not understood, believe.” Understanding is the reward of faith. Therefore do not seek to understand in order to believe; believe in order to understand, since, “unless you believe, you will not understand.”

Since, then, in order to make understanding possible, I have counseled obedience in believing, and have said that the Lord Jesus Christ added this very point in the sentence that follows, we find that he said, “If anyone wills to do his will, he will know concerning the teaching.”

What does “he will know” mean? It means “he will understand.” But “if anyone wills to do his will” means “to believe.”

Everyone understands that “he will know” means “he will understand.” But because the statement “if anyone wills to do his will” refers to believing, so that this may be understood more carefully, we need our Lord himself as interpreter, to show us whether doing his Father’s will truly refers to believing.

Who does not know [Col. 1631] that doing God’s will means carrying out his work—that is, doing what pleases him? Yet the Lord himself plainly says elsewhere: “This is the work of God, that you believe in him whom he sent” (John 6:29).

He says, “that you believe in him,” not merely “that you believe him.” But if you believe in him, you believe him; nevertheless, one who believes him does not immediately believe in him. For the demons believed him, but they did not believe in him.

Again, concerning his Apostles we can say, “We believe Paul,” but not, “We believe in Paul”; “We believe Peter,” but not, “We believe in Peter.”

“To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is reckoned as righteousness” (Romans 4:5). What, then, does it mean to believe in him? It means to love by believing, to cherish by believing, to go toward him by believing, and to be incorporated into his members by believing.

This, then, is the faith that God requires from us; and he does not find anything to require unless he has granted what he is to find. What faith is this except the faith that the Apostle defined most fully elsewhere, saying: “Neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but faith that works through love” (Galatians 5:6)?

It is not just any faith, but faith that works through love. Let this faith be in you, and you will understand the teaching. What will you understand? That “this teaching is not mine, but his who sent me”—that is, you will understand that Christ, the Son of God, who is the Father’s teaching, is not from himself, but is the Father’s Son.

### 7

This statement dissolves the Sabellian heresy. For the Sabellians dared to say that the one who is Son is himself also Father: that there are two names but one reality.

If there were two names and one reality, it would not be said, “My teaching is not mine.” Certainly, if your teaching is not yours, Lord, whose is it unless there is another to whom it belongs?

The Sabellians do not understand what you have said. They did not see the Trinity, but followed the error of their own hearts. We, who worship the Trinity and the unity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and one God, should understand concerning Christ’s teaching that it is not his own [Note: In accordance with Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions, and Lovaniensis: “how it is not his own.” M.].

Therefore he said that he did not speak from himself, because Christ is the Father’s Son, the Father is Christ’s Father, and the Son is God from God the Father. The Father, however, is God, but is not God from the Son, who is God.

### 8

The one who speaks from himself seeks his own glory. This will be the one called Antichrist, exalting himself, as the Apostle says, “above everything that is called God or is worshiped” (2 Thessalonians 2:4).

The Lord, announcing that he would seek his own glory and not the glory of the Father, said to the Jews: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43).

He indicated that they would receive Antichrist, who will seek the glory of his own name—puffed up, not substantial, and therefore not stable but destined to ruin.

Our Lord Jesus Christ, however, gave us a great example of humility. He is certainly equal to the Father; certainly “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Certainly he himself said, and said most truly, “I have been with you for so long, and you have not known me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9). Certainly he himself said, and said most truly, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

If, then, he is one with the Father, equal to the Father, God from [Col. 1632] God, God with God, coeternal, immortal, equally unchangeable, equally beyond time, equally Creator and disposer of times—yet because he came in time, took the form of a servant, and was found in appearance as a man (Philippians 2:7), he seeks the Father’s glory, not his own.

What, then, ought you, a human being, to do? When you do something good, you seek your own glory; but when you do something evil, you devise accusations against God.

Pay attention to yourself. You are a creature: acknowledge the Creator. You are a servant: do not despise the Lord. You have been adopted, but not through your own merits. Seek the glory of him from whom you have received this grace, adopted human being—the glory sought by the one who was uniquely born from him.

But the one who seeks the glory of him who sent him is truthful, and there is no injustice in him. In Antichrist, however, there is injustice, and he is not truthful, because he will seek his own glory, not that of the one by whom he was sent. For he was not sent; he was permitted to come.

Therefore, all who belong to Christ’s body, lest we be led into the snares of Antichrist, should not seek our own glory. But if he sought the glory of the one who sent him, how much more should we seek the glory of the one who made us?

# TRACTATE XXX

From the passage, “Did not Moses give you the Law, and none of you keeps the Law?” up to, “Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.” Chapter 7, verses 19–24.

### 1

The reading from the holy Gospel that has just been read follows today upon the one about which we spoke to your Charity some time ago.

The disciples and the Jews heard the Lord speaking; truthful people and liars heard truth speaking; friends and enemies heard love speaking; good people and evil people heard goodness speaking.

They heard, but he discerned. He saw and foresaw to whom the word would be useful and would prove useful. In those who were present then he saw; in us, who were yet to be, he foresaw.

Let us therefore hear the Gospel as though the Lord were present, and let us not say, “How happy were those who were able to see him!” For many among those who saw him killed him; many among us who did not see him have believed.

What sounded precious from the Lord’s mouth was written for our sake, preserved for us, recited for our sake [Note: [Col. 1632] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read, “is recited”], and will also be recited for the sake of our descendants, until the age comes to an end.

The Lord is above; but the Lord who is truth is also here. The Lord’s body in which he rose can be in one place [Note: Some manuscripts omit “the Lord’s”; but later, in the words “can be in one place,” all the printed editions and manuscripts available to us agree, although Ivo in the *Decretum*, part 2, chapter 8; Gratian, *De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter *Prima quidem*; the Master, *Sentences* IV, distinction 10, chapter 1; and, after them, Thomas Aquinas, *Summa*, part 3, question 75, article 1, report this statement as “must be in one place.”]; his truth is spread everywhere.

Let us therefore hear the Lord, and let us say what he himself grants us from his words.

### 2

“Did not Moses,” he says, “give you the Law, and none of you keeps the Law? Why do you seek to kill me?”

For this reason you seek to kill me: because none of you keeps the Law. For if you kept the Law, you would recognize Christ in the very Scriptures and would not kill him while he is present.

And they answered [Note: In Erasmus, the Lyons, and Venetian editions, the words “and they do not have” are omitted, and the text continues immediately, “For the crowd answered.” Lovaniensis differs from this reading only in having “the crowd answered him” instead of “for the crowd answered.” M.]: “The crowd answered him.”

It answered as a crowd—not belonging to order, but to confusion. Finally, see what the confused crowd answered: “You have a demon; who is seeking to kill you?”

As though it were not worse to say, “You have a demon,” than to kill him. For this was said to the one who drove out demons: that he had a demon.

What else could a turbulent crowd say? What else could stirred-up mud smell like? The crowd was disturbed. By what? By the truth.

The brightness of light disturbed the crowd’s diseased eyes. For eyes lacking health cannot endure the brightness of light.

### 3

The Lord, however, was not really disturbed, but tranquil in his truth. He did not repay evil with evil or insult with insult (1 Peter 3:9).

If he had said to them, “You have a demon,” he would certainly have spoken the truth. For they would not have said such things to the truth unless the devil’s falsehood had provoked them.

What, then, did he answer? Let us hear tranquilly and drink in what is tranquil:

“I performed one work, and you all wonder.”

It was as if he were saying, “What would you do if you saw all my works?” For the works they saw in the world were his, but they did not see the one who made everything.

He performed one deed, and they were disturbed because he made a man well on the Sabbath. As if, if some sick person were made sound on the Sabbath, someone other than the one who scandalized them by saving one man on the Sabbath had made him well [Note: In three manuscripts: “if he made a sick person sound on the Sabbath”; in the others: “if a sick person became sound on the Sabbath,” that is, became well through himself, without the intervention of a physician’s work. Erasmus has “if a sick person were healed,” while the Lyons and Venetian editions read “if he healed a sick person.” M.].

For who else has saved others except salvation itself—the one who gives the salvation he gave this man also to animals? It was bodily salvation. Bodily health is restored and it dies; when it is restored, death is postponed, not removed.

Yet, brothers, even this health comes from the Lord, regardless of through whom it is given. However it may be imparted through one who heals and ministers, it is given by him from whom all salvation comes, to whom it is said in the Psalm:

“You will save humans and animals, Lord; as you have multiplied your mercy, O God.”

Because you are God, your multiplied mercy reaches even the health of human flesh and even the health of mute animals. But you who give humans and animals a common bodily health—is there no salvation that you reserve for human beings?

Certainly there is another kind, one that is not merely shared by humans and animals, but is not even shared by good and evil human beings alike.

When the Psalm had spoken there of the health that cattle and humans receive in common, for the sake of the salvation that human beings—but good human beings—ought to hope for, it continued:

“But the children of human beings will hope under the shelter of your wings; they will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight; for with you is the fountain of life, and in your light we shall see light” (Psalm 35:7–10).

[Col. 1634] This is the salvation that belongs to the good, whom he called “children of human beings,” after saying above, “You will save humans and animals, Lord.”

What, then? Were those humans not children of human beings, so that after saying “humans” he might go on to say “children of human beings,” as though humans were one thing and children of human beings another?

Nevertheless, I do not think that the Holy Spirit said this without some meaningful distinction. “Humans” refers to the first Adam; “children of human beings” refers to Christ. Perhaps “humans” belong to the first human being, while “children of human beings” belong to the Son of Man.

### 4

“I performed one work, and you all wonder.” And immediately he adds:

“For this reason Moses gave you circumcision.”

It was rightly done that you received circumcision from Moses—not because it is from Moses, but because it is from the Fathers. Abraham was the first to receive circumcision from the Lord (Genesis 17:10).

“And you circumcise on the Sabbath.”

Moses convicted you. In the Law you received the command to circumcise on the eighth day (Leviticus 12:3); in the Law you received the command to rest on the seventh day (Exodus 20:10).

If the eighth day of the one who has been born falls on the seventh day of the Sabbath, what will you do? Will you rest, in order to keep the Sabbath, or will you circumcise, in order to fulfill the sacrament of the eighth day?

“But I know,” he says, “what you do: you circumcise a man.”

Why? Because circumcision belongs to a certain sign of salvation, and people ought not to rest from salvation on the Sabbath.

“Therefore do not be angry with me because I made the whole man well on the Sabbath.
