If,” he says, “a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses may not be broken”—for something salutary was established through Moses in that ordinance of circumcision—“why are you angry with me for working salvation on the Sabbath?”

### 5

Perhaps that circumcision signified the Lord himself, at whom these people were indignant when he healed and restored.

Circumcision was commanded to be performed on the eighth day. And what is circumcision except the stripping away of flesh?

This circumcision therefore signifies the stripping away from the heart of carnal desires. It was not given without reason, nor was it commanded to be performed on that particular member, since through that member the mortal race is generated.

“And through one man came death, just as through one man came the resurrection of the dead” (1 Corinthians 15:21); and “through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death” (Romans 5:12).

Therefore everyone is born with a foreskin, because every human being is born with the defect inherited through descent. God cleanses us either from the defect with which we are born or from the defects we add by living badly only through the stone knife, the Lord Christ.

“For the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10:4). They circumcised with stone knives, and by the name of the rock they symbolized Christ; yet they did not recognize him when present, and even desired to kill him.

Why, however, on the eighth day, unless because after the seventh day of the Sabbath the Lord rose on the Lord’s day? Therefore Christ’s resurrection—which took place on the third day after his passion, but on the eighth day in the cycle of the week—circumcises us.

Hear the Apostle admonishing those circumcised by the true rock:

“If, then, you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; [Col. 1635] set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are on earth” (Colossians 3:1–2).

He speaks to the circumcised: Christ has risen; he has taken away your carnal desires, taken away evil lusts, taken away the excess with which you were born, and, much worse, what you had added by living badly.

You have been circumcised by the rock; why do you still set your minds on earth?

Finally, because Moses gave the Law and you circumcise a man on the Sabbath, understand that this signifies the good work I performed in making the whole man well on the Sabbath: he was healed so that he might be sound in body, and he believed so that he might be sound in soul.

### 6

“Do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment.”

What does this mean? You who circumcise on the Sabbath according to the Law of Moses are not angry with Moses; but because I made a man well on the Sabbath, you are angry with me.

You judge according to appearance; attend to the truth.

“I do not place myself above Moses,” says the Lord, who was also Moses’ Lord. Consider how you regard the two of us as human beings, as though we were both merely human. Judge between us, but judge with true judgment. Do not honor me by condemning him; honor me by understanding him.

For elsewhere he said to them: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). But here he did not wish to say this, as though he had placed himself and Moses before them.

For the sake of Moses’ Law you circumcise even when the Sabbath occurs; and do you not wish me to show the benefit of performing healings on the Sabbath?

The Lord of circumcision and the Lord of the Sabbath is the author of salvation. You have been forbidden to perform servile works on the Sabbath. If you truly understand what servile works are, you do not sin.

“For everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

Is it a servile work to heal a man on the Sabbath? You eat and drink—as I may say by recalling something from the admonition and words of our Lord Jesus Christ. Why, then, do you eat and drink on the Sabbath, unless what you do pertains to salvation?

By this you show that works of salvation must in no way be omitted on the Sabbath.

Therefore do not judge according to appearance, but judge with righteous judgment. Consider me as a human being; consider Moses as a human being. If you judge according to the truth, you will condemn neither Moses nor me. Once you have recognized the truth, you will recognize me, because I am the truth (John 14:6).

### 7

This vice that the Lord noted here—judging according to appearance rather than retaining righteous judgment—is very difficult to escape in this age.

The Lord admonished the Jews, but he also admonished us. He convicted them, but instructed us; he rebuked them, but sharpened our understanding.

Let us not suppose that this was not said to us because we were not there at that time. It was written; it is read; when it was recited, we heard it. But we heard it as though it had been said to the Jews.

Let us not place ourselves behind them and, as if looking at enemies being reproved, make ourselves into what the truth itself may reprove in us.

The Jews did judge according to appearance. But for that reason they do not belong to the New Testament; for that reason they do not possess the kingdom of heaven in Christ; for that reason they are not joined to the fellowship of the holy angels.

They sought earthly things from the Lord: the land of promise, victory over enemies, fertility [Col. 1636] in childbirth, increase of children, abundance of crops. All these things, although promised to them by the true and good God, were promised to them as carnal people. All these things constituted the Old Testament for them.

What is the Old Testament? It is like an inheritance belonging to the old human being.

We have been renewed; we have become a new human being, because that new human being also came. What is as new as being born from a virgin?

Since there was nothing [Note: [Col. 1636] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Lovaniensis read “that”] in him that needed renewal, because he had no sin, a new birth was given. In him there was a new birth; in us there is a new human being.

What is the new human being? One renewed from oldness.

For what purpose is he renewed? To desire heavenly things; to long for eternal things; to desire the homeland that is above and fears no enemy—where we do not lose a friend or fear an enemy; where we live with good affection, without any defect; where no one is born, because no one dies; where no one now progresses and no one declines; where there is no hunger and no thirst, but fullness is immortality and food is truth.

Since we have these promises, belong to the New Testament, have become heirs of a new inheritance, and are coheirs of the Lord himself, we have a very different hope: let us not judge according to appearance, but retain righteous judgment.

### 8

Who is the one who does not judge according to appearance? The one who loves equally.

Equal love prevents the acceptance of persons. It is not when we honor people differently according to their rank that we need fear accepting persons.

But when we judge between two people—and sometimes between those close to us—judgment may arise between a father and a son. A father complains about a bad son, or a son complains about a harsh father.

We preserve the honor due to the father from the son. We do not make the son equal to the father in honor; but if the son has the better case, we place him first. We make the son equal to the father in truth, and thus assign the honor that is due without allowing equity to lose its merit.

In this way we advance through the Lord’s words, and, so that we may advance, we are helped by his grace.

# TRACTATE XXXI

From the passage, “Some of those from Jerusalem were saying, ‘Is this not the man whom they were seeking to kill?’” up to, “You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” Chapter 7, verses 25–36.

### 1

Your Charity remembers that in earlier sermons it was both read in the Gospel and discussed by us as best we could that the Lord Jesus went up to the feast as though secretly, not because he feared being seized—since he had the power to prevent himself from being seized—but in order to signify that even on the very feast celebrated by the Jews he was hidden, and that the mystery was his.

In today’s reading, therefore, the power that had been thought to be timidity became apparent. For he was speaking openly in the midst of the feast, so that the crowds wondered and said what we heard when the reading was recited:

“Is this not the man whom they were seeking to kill? And behold, he speaks openly, and they say nothing to him. Have the rulers really recognized that this is the Christ?”

Those who knew with what savagery he was being sought wondered at the power by which he was not seized [Col. 1637].

Then, not fully understanding his power, they supposed that the rulers’ knowledge consisted in their having recognized that he was indeed the Christ. For this reason they spared the one whom they had sought so eagerly to kill.

### 2

Then those same people who had said among themselves, “Have the rulers recognized that this is the Christ?” raised for themselves the question by which it seemed to them that he was not the Christ.

For they added: “But we know where this man is from; when the Christ comes, no one will know where he is from.”

Where did this opinion arise among the Jews—that when the Christ comes no one will know where he is from? It did not arise without reason.

If we consider the Scriptures, we find, brothers, that the holy Scriptures said of Christ that he would be called a Nazaraean (Matthew 2:23). Thus they foretold where he would be from.

Again, if we seek the place of his birth, as though he were from the place where he was born, this too was not hidden from the Jews, because the Scriptures had foretold it.

When the Magi, having seen the star, sought him in order to worship him, they came to Herod and stated what they were seeking and what they wanted. He summoned those who knew the Law and asked them where the Christ would be born. They answered, “In Bethlehem of Judea,” and they also brought forward prophetic testimony (Matthew 2:1–6).

If, then, the Prophets had foretold both the place from which his fleshly origin would come and the place where his mother would give birth to him, how did this opinion arise among the Jews, which we have just heard: “When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from”?

The Scriptures had both predicted and announced both things. According to his humanity, the Scriptures had foretold where he would be from; according to his divinity, he was hidden from the impious and sought by the godly.

For this reason they also said, “When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from,” because this opinion had been generated in them by what was said through Isaiah: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53:8).

Finally, the Lord himself answered both points: that they knew where he was from and that they did not know. In this way he bore witness to the holy prophecy previously spoken about him, both according to the weakness of his humanity and according to the majesty of his divinity.

### 3

Hear, then, the Word of the Lord, brothers, and see how he confirmed both what they had said—“We know where this man is from”—and what they had said—“When the Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.”

Jesus therefore cried out while teaching in the temple:

“You know me, and you know where I am from; yet I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know.”

This means: “You know me, and you do not know me”; this means: “You know where I am from, and you do not know where I am from.”

You know where I am from: Jesus of Nazareth, whose parents you also know. For in this matter only the virgin’s childbirth was hidden, although her husband was its witness. He alone could faithfully disclose this, since he could, as a husband, become jealous [Note: [Col. 1637] Thus the manuscripts, together with the Amiens and Basel editions. Erasmus and Lovaniensis read: “who could, as a husband, conceal it.”].

Except for the virgin’s childbirth, they knew everything in Jesus that pertained to the human being: his face was known, his homeland was known, his ancestry was known, and where he was born was known.

He therefore rightly said, “You know me, and you know where I am from,” according to the flesh and the human appearance he bore. But according to his divinity: [Col. 1638] “I have not come from myself, but he who sent me is true, whom you do not know.”

But in order that you may know him, believe in the one whom he sent, and you will know him. For “no one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 1:18). And, “No one knows the Father except the Son, and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matthew 11:27).

### 4

Finally, after saying, “But he who sent me is true, whom you do not know,” in order to show them how they could know what they did not know, he added:

“I know him.”

Therefore ask me, so that you may know him.

Why do I know him? “Because I am from him, and he sent me.”

Magnificently he displayed both points. “I am from him,” he says, because the Son is from the Father, and whatever the Son is, he is from the one whose Son he is.

Therefore we call the Lord Jesus “God from God.” We do not call the Father “God from God,” but simply “God.” We call the Lord Jesus “Light from Light”; we do not call the Father “Light from Light,” but simply “Light.”

This, then, is what belongs to the statement, “I am from him.”

But when you see me in the flesh, “he sent me.” When you hear “he sent me,” do not understand a dissimilarity of nature, but the authority of the one who begets.

### 5

They therefore sought to seize him, and no one laid hands on him, because his hour had not yet come—that is, because he did not wish it.

What does “his hour had not yet come” mean? The Lord was not born under fate. You should not believe this even about yourself, much less about him through whom you were made [Note: Erasmus, the Lyons and Venetian editions, and Lovaniensis read: “how much less about him.” M.].

If your hour is his will, what is his hour except his own will? He therefore did not mean the hour at which he would be compelled to die, but the hour at which he would deign to be killed.

He was awaiting the time at which he would die, just as he had awaited the time at which he would be born.

Speaking of this time, the Apostle says: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Galatians 4:4).

For this reason many ask, “Why did Christ not come earlier?” They should be answered: because the fullness of time had not yet come, as he ordered it through whom the times were made. For he knew when he ought to come.

First, through a long succession of times and years, he had to be proclaimed. For one who was coming was not insignificant: he had to be proclaimed for a long time and held always in mind.

The greater the Judge who was coming, the longer the succession of heralds that preceded him.

Finally, when the fullness of time came, the one who would free us from time also came. For, freed from time, we shall come to that eternity where there is no time. There it is not said, “When will the hour come?” For the day there is everlasting: it is preceded by no yesterday and excluded by no tomorrow.

In this age, however, days revolve; some pass away and others come; none remains. The moments in which we speak drive one another away, and the first syllable does not stand still so that the second may sound.

Since we began speaking, we have aged somewhat; and without any doubt I am older now than I was in the morning. Thus nothing stands still, nothing remains fixed in time.

We ought therefore to love him through whom the times were made, so that we may be freed from time and fixed in eternity, where there is now no mutability of times.

Great, then, is the mercy of our Lord Jesus Christ: that the one through whom the times were made was made for our sake in time; that the one through whom all things were made was made among all things [Col. 1639]; that the one who made became what he had made.

For he became what he had made: the one who had made humanity became human, lest what he had made should perish.

According to this dispensation, the hour of his birth had already come, and he had been born; but the hour of his passion had not yet come, and therefore he had not yet suffered [Note: The printed editions read: “therefore he was not destined to suffer.” The manuscripts read: “therefore he had not suffered.”].

### 6

Finally, so that you may know that it was not necessity but the power of the one who was dying [Note: [Col. 1639] Compare Tractate 37, §§8–10.], I say this for the sake of certain people who, when they hear, “His hour has not yet come,” are built up in their belief in fate, and their hearts become foolish: so that you may know the power of the one who was dying, recall the passion itself and look upon the crucified one. While hanging on the wood, he said, “I thirst.” When they heard this, they offered him vinegar on a sponge placed on a reed at the cross. He received it and said, “It is finished”; and, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.

You see the power of the one who was dying, because he waited for this until everything had been fulfilled that had been foretold as destined to happen to him before his death. For the prophet had said: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Ps. 68:22). He was waiting for all these things to be fulfilled; after they had been fulfilled, he said, “It is finished,” and departed by his power, because he had not come by necessity.

For this reason some were more astonished at this power of the one who was dying than at the power of the one performing miracles. The time came for the bodies to be taken down from the wood, because the Sabbath was dawning, and the thieves were found still alive. The punishment of the cross was harsher because it tormented for a longer time, and all those crucified were killed by a prolonged death. But, so that they would not remain on the wood, the thieves were compelled to die after their legs had been broken, so that they could be taken down.

The Lord, however, was found dead (John 19:28–33), and people were astonished. Those who had despised him while he was alive were so astonished at him when dead that some of them said, “Truly this is the Son of God” (Matt. 27:54). This is also the meaning of that other episode, brothers, where, when those who sought him asked who he was, he said, “I am he”; and when they all drew back, they fell to the ground (John 18:6). There was therefore supreme power in him.

He was not compelled to die at that hour; rather, he was waiting for the hour at which his will would appropriately be accomplished, not for the hour at which necessity would be fulfilled against his will.

### 7

Many from the crowd, however, believed in him. The Lord was saving the humble and the poor. The rulers were raging; and therefore they not only failed to recognize the physician, but even wanted to kill him. There was a certain crowd that quickly saw its own sickness and recognized his healing without delay.

See what the crowd itself, stirred by the miracles, said: “When the Christ comes, will he perform more signs than this man?” Surely, if there are no two Christs, this is he. Therefore they believed in him, saying these things.

### 8

But when those rulers heard of the crowd’s faith and of the acclaim by which Christ was being glorified, they sent officers to arrest him. Whom were they going to arrest? Someone who still did not wish to be arrested? Since, then, they could not arrest one who did not wish to be arrested, they were sent to hear him teaching.

What did he teach? Jesus said: “I am with you for a little while longer. What you now wish to do, you will do—but not now, because now I do not wish it.” Why do I not wish it yet? “Because I am with you for a little while longer; and then I am going to him who sent me.” I must fulfill my dispensation and thus arrive at my passion.

### 9

“You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come.” Here he foretold his resurrection. They had refused to recognize him while he was present, and afterward they sought him when they saw that the crowd had already come to believe in him.

Great signs were performed even when the Lord rose and ascended into heaven. At that time great things were done through the disciples; but he did them through those disciples who also performed them through themselves—for he himself had said to them, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

When that lame man who sat at the gate rose at Peter’s voice and walked on his own feet, so that people were astonished, Peter addressed them in this way, because he had not done these things by his own power but by the power of the one whom they had killed (Acts 3:2–16). Many were cut to the heart and said, “What shall we do?” (Acts 2:37). For they saw themselves bound by the enormous crime of impiety when they had killed the one whom they ought to have revered and worshiped; and they thought this was unforgivable.

It was indeed a great crime, the consideration of which might make them despair. Yet they should not have despaired, for the Lord, hanging on the cross, had deigned to pray for those for whom he was dying. For he had said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). He saw some of his own people among many who were alien to him; he was already asking pardon for those from whom he was still receiving injury.

He was not considering that he was dying at their hands, but that he was dying for their sake. Great indeed is what was granted to them, and granted by them and for them, so that no one might despair of the forgiveness of his sin, since those who killed Christ were deemed worthy of pardon.

Christ died for us—but surely not by us? Yet they saw Christ dying through their own crime, and believed in Christ forgiving their crimes. Until they drank the blood they had shed, they despaired of their salvation.

Thus he said, “You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come,” because, after the resurrection, they were going to seek him once they had been cut to the heart. He did not say, “where I will be,” but “where I am.” For Christ was always there to whom he was going to return; he came in such a way that he did not depart from there.

Accordingly, elsewhere he says, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man, who is in heaven” (John 3:13). He did not say, “who was in heaven.” He was speaking on earth and said that he was in heaven. He came in such a way that he did not depart from there; he returned in such a way that he did not abandon us.

Why are you astonished? God does this. A human being, according to the body, is in a place and moves away from a place; and when he has come to another place, he will not be in the place from which he came. God, however, fills all things and is wholly everywhere; he is not confined to places according to spatial dimensions.

The Lord Christ was nevertheless, according to visible flesh, on earth, and according to invisible majesty, in heaven and on earth. Therefore he says, “Where I am, you cannot come.” He did not say, “you will not be able to come,” but “you cannot come,” for at that time they were such as could not come.

But so that you may know that this was not said to produce despair, he said something similar to his disciples: “Where I am going, you cannot come” (John 13:33), although, when praying for them, he had said, “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24).

Finally, he explained this to Peter, saying to him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but afterward you will follow” (John 13:36).

### 10

The Jews therefore said—not to him, but among themselves: “Where is this man going, that we will not find him? Surely he is not going to the Dispersion among the Gentiles, to teach the Gentiles?”

They did not know what they were saying; but because he willed it, they prophesied. The Lord was indeed going to the Gentiles—not by the presence of his body, but nevertheless by his feet.

What were his feet? Those whom Saul wished to trample by persecuting them, when the head cried out to him: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). “What is this statement that he made: ‘You will seek me and will not find me; and where I am, you cannot come?’”

They did not know why the Lord said this, yet, without knowing it, they foretold something that was going to happen. The Lord said this because they did not know the place—if it may properly be called a place—that is, the bosom of the Father, from which the Only-begotten Son never departs. Nor were they capable of considering where Christ was: where Christ had not departed, to which Christ was going to return, where Christ remained.

How could the human heart conceive this, much less explain it with the tongue [Note: [Col. 1641] Erasmus: “with the tongue.” According to the Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions, “of the tongue.” M.]?

They therefore understood this in no way; yet on this occasion they foretold our salvation, namely, that the Lord would go to the Dispersion of the Gentiles and fulfill what they read but did not understand: “The people whom I did not know served me; at the hearing of the ear they obeyed me” (Ps. 18:45). Those who saw him with their eyes did not listen; those in whose ears his voice sounded did listen.

### 11

The woman who suffered from a flow of blood was a figure of that future Church from the Gentiles: she touched him, and was not seen; she was not known, and was healed. It was indeed a figure when the Lord asked, “Who touched me?” As though unaware, he healed the woman whose touch was unknown (Luke 8:43–48). So he also acted toward the Gentiles.

We did not come to know him in the flesh, yet we were found worthy to eat his flesh and to be members in his flesh. Why? Because he sent to us.

Whom did he send? His heralds, his disciples, his servants, his redeemed—those whom he created, but whom he also redeemed as his brothers. I have said too little: he sent his members, himself; for he sent his members to us and made us his members.

Nevertheless, according to the bodily appearance that the Jews saw and despised, Christ was not among us. For this too had been said of him, as the Apostle says: “For I say that Christ became a servant of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.” He had to come to those whose fathers he came from and to whose fathers he had been promised. Therefore he himself also says, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

But what does the Apostle say next? “The Gentiles, however, glorify God for his mercy” (Rom. 15:8–9). And what does the Lord himself say? “I have other sheep that are not of this fold” (John 10:16).

The one who had said, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel”—how does he have other sheep to whom he was not sent? It is because he indicated that, in bodily presence, he presented himself as sent only to the Jews, who saw him and killed him.

Yet many of them believed, both before and afterward. The first harvest was winnowed from the cross, so that it might be the seed from which another harvest would arise.

Now, when his faithful are stirred by the fame of the Gospel and its good fragrance and believe throughout all the nations, there will be an expectation of the nations: for the one who has already come will come (Gen. 49:10); the one whom some did not see and others did see will be seen by all; the one who came to be judged will come to judge; and the one who came so as not to be distinguished will come to distinguish.

For Christ was not distinguished from the impious, but was judged with the impious. Of him it was said, “He was reckoned among the wicked” (Isa. 53:12). The thief escaped; Christ was condemned (Mark 15:15; John 18:40). The criminal received pardon; the one who released the crimes of all who confess them was condemned.

Yet the cross itself, if you pay attention, was also a tribunal. With the judge set in the middle, one thief who believed was liberated (Luke 23:43), while the other, who insulted him, was condemned. He was already signifying what he would do with the living and the dead: he would place some at the right and others at the left; that thief was like those who would be at the left, while the other was like those who would be at the right. He was being judged, yet he threatened judgment.

## TRACTATE XXXII

From the passage, “On the last day of the festival Jesus stood and cried out, saying, ‘If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,’” up to, “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” Chapter 7, verses 37–39.

### 1

Amid the disagreements and doubts of the Jews concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, and amid the other things he said—by which some would be confounded and others instructed—on the last day of that festival, which is called the Feast of Booths, that is, the construction of tents, a festival about which Your Charity has already heard us speak at length, the Lord Jesus Christ calls out, and not merely speaking but crying out, so that the one who thirsts may come to him.

If we thirst, let us come; not with our feet, but with our affections; not by changing our location, but by loving. Nevertheless, according to the inner person, the one who loves also moves. There is one kind of movement in the body and another in the heart. A person moves in the body who changes place through bodily motion; a person moves in the heart who changes affection through movement of the heart. If you love one thing now and loved another before, you are not where you were.

The Lord therefore cries out to us. For he stood and cried: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, as Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” What this means, the Evangelist himself explained, and we need not linger over it. For after the Lord had said, “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink,” and, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly,” the Evangelist accordingly explained, saying: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

There is therefore an inner thirst and an inner belly, because there is an inner person. The inner person is invisible, while the outer person is visible; but the inner person is better than the outer. And what is not seen is loved more: for it is clear that a person loves the inner person more than the outer.

How is this clear? Let each person test it in himself. Although those who live wickedly devote their minds to the body, they nevertheless want to live—and life belongs only to the mind—and they reveal themselves more clearly as the ones who rule than those things which are ruled. For minds rule, while bodies are ruled.

A person rejoices in pleasure and takes pleasure from the body. But remove the mind, and nothing remains in the body that can rejoice; and if he rejoices in the body, it is the mind that rejoices. If he rejoices in his house, should he not rejoice in himself? And if the mind has something outside itself by which it may be delighted, does it remain without delights within?

It is entirely clear that a person loves his soul more than his body. But in another person too, a person loves the soul more than the body. What is loved in a friend, where love is more sincere and chaste? What is loved in a friend—the soul or the body?

If faithfulness is loved, the soul is loved. If goodwill is loved, the soul is the seat of goodwill. If you love something in another because that person also loves you, you love the soul, because it is not the flesh but the soul that loves. You love because he loves you; ask where he loves you from, and see what you love. What is pious, then, is loved, though it is not seen.

### 3

I also wish to say something by which it may become still clearer to Your Love how greatly the soul is loved and how it is preferred to the body. Those very wanton lovers who delight in bodily beauty and are inflamed by the form of the limbs love more intensely when they are loved. For if a lover loves and realizes that he is hated, he is more angry than loving. Why is he more angry than loving? Because what he gives is not returned to him.

If, then, even lovers of bodies want to be loved in return, and are more delighted if they are loved, what sort of lovers are lovers of souls? And if lovers of souls are great lovers, what sort are lovers of God, who makes souls beautiful? For as the soul gives beauty to the body, so God gives beauty to the soul. Nothing makes the body lovable except the soul: when it has departed, you shudder at the corpse, and however much you loved those beautiful limbs, you hurry to bury them. Therefore the soul is the beauty of the body; God is the beauty of the soul.

### 4

The Lord cries out to us to come and drink if we thirst inwardly, and he says that when we have drunk, rivers of living water will flow from our belly. The belly of the inner person is the conscience of the heart. Drink, then, this fluid, and the purified conscience will come to life; and as it draws in, it will have a spring—and will itself become a spring.

What is the spring, and what is the river that flows from the belly of the inner person? Goodwill, by which one wishes to benefit one’s neighbor. For if someone thinks that what he has drunk ought to be sufficient for himself alone, living water does not flow from his belly. But if he hastens to benefit his neighbor, it does not dry up, because it flows.

We shall now see what those who believe in the Lord are drinking. For certainly we are Christians, and if we believe, we drink. Each person ought to recognize in himself whether he drinks and whether he lives from what he drinks. For the spring does not abandon us if we do not abandon the spring.

### 5

The Evangelist explained, as I said, why the Lord cried out, what drink he invited them to receive, and what he offered to those who drank, saying: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive. For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

What Spirit does he mean except the Holy Spirit? Every human being has a spirit of his own, the spirit of which I was speaking when I commended the mind. The mind of each person is his own spirit. Concerning this the Apostle Paul says: “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the human spirit that is in him?” Then he added: “So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11).

No one knows what is ours except our spirit. For I do not know what you are thinking, nor do you know what I am thinking. These thoughts that we think inwardly are our own; and the spirit of each person is witness to that person’s thoughts.

So also no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God. We know what is ours with our spirit; God knows what is his with his. Yet God, with his Spirit, also knows what is happening in us, whereas without his Spirit we cannot know what is happening in God. God knows in us even what we ourselves do not know in us.

Peter did not know his own weakness when he heard from the Lord that he would deny him three times (Matt. 26:33–35); he was unaware of his illness, while the physician knew the sick man. There are therefore certain things that God knows in us while we do not know them.

Nevertheless, as far as human beings are concerned, no one knows a person as that person knows himself. Another does not know what is happening within him, but his spirit does.

After receiving the Spirit of God, we also learn what is happening in God—not everything, because we have not received everything. We know many things from the pledge, for we have received a pledge, and the fullness of this pledge will be given later.

Meanwhile, in this pilgrimage, let the pledge console us, because the one who has deigned to give us himself as a pledge is very ready to give much more. If the pledge is such, what must the thing be of which it is the pledge?

### 6

But what does he mean when he says, “For the Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified”? The meaning is evident. It is not that the Spirit of God, who was with God, did not exist; rather, he had not yet been in those who believed in Jesus.

For the Lord Jesus arranged not to give them this Spirit of whom we are speaking until after his resurrection, and not without reason. Perhaps, if we ask, he will grant that we find; and if we knock, he will open so that we may enter. Piety knocks, not the hand—although the hand also knocks if it does not cease from works of mercy.

What, then, is the reason why the Lord Jesus Christ decided to give the Holy Spirit only once he had been glorified? Before we say what we can about this, we must first ask, lest someone be troubled by the question of how the Spirit was not yet in holy people when the Gospel records that, concerning the Lord who had just been born, Simeon recognized him in the Holy Spirit, and Anna, the widow and prophetess, also recognized him (Luke 2:25–38); that John himself, who baptized him, recognized him (John 1:26–34); and that Zechariah, filled with the Holy Spirit, said many things (Luke 1:67–79). Mary herself received the Holy Spirit so that she might conceive the Lord (Luke 1:35).

We therefore have many indications of the Holy Spirit preceding the Lord’s glorification through the resurrection of his flesh. The prophets who foretold that Christ would come did not have some other spirit.

But a certain mode of giving this Spirit was yet to come, a mode that had not appeared at all before; it is of this that he is speaking here. For nowhere do we previously read that people gathered together, having received the Holy Spirit, spoke in the languages of all nations.

After his resurrection, however, when he first appeared to his disciples, he said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” It is therefore of this that it was said, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified.”

“And he breathed into their faces” (John 20:22)—he who by breathing first gave life to the human being and formed him from the clay, by whose breath he gave a soul to the limbs (Gen. 2:7). He signified that he was the one who had breathed into their faces, so that they might rise from the mud and renounce works of clay.

Then, for the first time after his resurrection—which the Evangelist calls his glorification—the Lord gave his disciples the Holy Spirit. Afterward, having remained with them for forty days, as the book of the Acts of the Apostles demonstrates, he ascended into heaven before their eyes, while they followed his ascent with their sight (Acts 1:3, 9).

After ten days had passed there, on the day of Pentecost, he sent the Holy Spirit from above. When those who had been gathered in one place received him and were filled, they spoke in the languages of all nations, as I have said (Acts 2:1–6).

### 7

What then, brothers? Since now someone who is baptized in Christ and believes in Christ does not speak in the languages of all nations, should we not believe that he has received the Holy Spirit? Far be it that such unbelief should tempt our hearts.

We are certain that every person receives him, but he fills each person according to the measure of the vessel of faith that he has brought to the fountain.

Since the Spirit is also received now, someone may ask: Why does no one speak in the languages of all nations? Because now the Church itself speaks in the languages of all nations. Formerly the Church existed in one nation, where it spoke in the languages of all nations. By speaking in the languages of all nations, he signified that, as the Church grew among the nations, it would speak in the languages of all.

The person who is not in this Church does not now receive the Holy Spirit either. Cut off and separated from the unity of the members, which unity speaks in the languages of all, let him renounce himself; he does not have him [Note: [Col. 1645] In most manuscripts: “let him renounce himself if he does not have him.”].

For if he has him, let him give the sign that was then given. What does it mean, “let him give the sign that was then given”? Let him speak in all languages.

He answers me: “What? Do you speak in all languages?” I certainly do, because every language is mine—that is, it belongs to the body whose member I am. The Church, spread throughout the nations, speaks in all languages. The Church is the body of Christ, and you are a member of this body. Since you are therefore a member of the body that speaks in all languages, believe that you speak in all languages.

The unity of the members is joined together by love, and this unity speaks in the same way that one person then spoke.

### 8

We too therefore receive the Holy Spirit if we love the Church, if we are joined together by love, and if we rejoice in the Catholic name and faith. Let us believe, brothers: the more each person loves the Church of Christ, the more he has the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit was given, as the Apostle says, “for manifestation.” What manifestation? As he himself says: “To one is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge according to the same Spirit; to another, faith in the same Spirit; to another, gifts of healings in the one Spirit; to another, the working of powers in the same Spirit.”

Many things are given for manifestation, but perhaps you possess none of all the things I have mentioned. If you love, you do not possess nothing. For if you love unity, whatever anyone possesses in it belongs also to you.

Remove envy, and what I have is yours. I will remove envy, and what you have is mine. Envy separates; health joins together.

Only the eye sees in the body. But does the eye see only for itself? It sees for the hand, the foot, and the other members as well. If some blow falls upon the foot, the eye does not turn away from it so as not to take precautions.

Again, only the hand works in the body. But does it work only for itself? It also works for the eye. If a blow comes—not to the hand but merely to the face—does the hand say, “I will not move, because it is not directed at me”?

So the foot, by walking, serves all the members. The other members are silent, while the tongue speaks for all.

We therefore have the Holy Spirit if we love the Church; and we love it if we remain in its structure and love. For after the Apostle had said that different gifts are given to different people, like the functions of the various members, he said, “I will show you a still more excellent way,” and began to speak about love.

He placed love above the languages of human beings and angels; above miracles of faith; above knowledge and prophecy; and even above that great work of mercy by which a person distributes his possessions to the poor. Finally, he placed love even above the suffering of the body. Above all these great things he placed love (1 Cor. 12:7–13:3).

Have love itself, and you will have everything; for without it, whatever you may be able to possess will profit nothing. Since the love of which we are speaking belongs to the Holy Spirit—for the Gospel passage now concerns the Holy Spirit—listen to the Apostle saying: “The love of God has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

### 9

Why, then, did the Lord wish to give the Spirit, whose greatest benefits are in us because through him the love of God has been poured into our hearts, only after his resurrection? What did he signify?

He signified that, at our resurrection, our love should burn and separate us from love of the world, so that it might run wholly toward God. Here we are born and die; let us not love this place. Let us move by love; by love let us dwell above, through that love by which we love God.

Let us meditate on nothing else during the pilgrimage of this life except that we will not always be here, and that by living well we are preparing a place for ourselves there from which we will never move.

For after our Lord Jesus Christ rose, he no longer dies; “death,” as the Apostle says, “will no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9). Behold what we should love.

If we live and believe in the one who rose, he will give us—not what people who do not love God love here, or what they love more because they love him less. They love such things less to the extent that they love him more.

Let us see what he promised us: not earthly and temporary riches; not honors and powers in this world—for you see all these things given even to wicked people, so that good people may not value them too highly.

Finally, he did not promise bodily health—not because he does not give it, but because, as you see, he gives it even to animals. Nor did he promise a long life. For what is long if it eventually ends? He did not promise us believers great longevity or a decrepit old age, which everyone desires before it comes, and about which everyone complains when it arrives.

Nor did he promise bodily beauty, which either bodily illness or the old age that is desired destroys. A person wants to be beautiful and wants to be old; these two desires cannot agree with one another. If you become old, you will not be beautiful. When old age comes, beauty will flee; the vigor of beauty and the groans of old age cannot dwell together in one person.

He therefore did not promise us any of these things when he said, “Whoever believes in me, let him come and drink; and rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

He promised eternal life, where we fear nothing; where we are not troubled; from which we do not move; where we do not die; where no predecessor is mourned and no successor is awaited.

Because what he promised is of this kind for those who love and burn with the love of the Holy Spirit, he did not wish to give the Spirit until he had been glorified, so that in his own body he might display the life that we do not yet possess but hope for in the resurrection.

## TRACTATE XXXIII

From the passage of the Gospel, “When the crowd heard these words of his,” and so forth, up to, “Neither will I condemn you; go, and from now on do not sin.” Chapter 7, verses 40–53, and chapter 8, verses 1–11.

### 1

Your Charity remembers that in our previous sermon, taking the Gospel reading as our occasion, we spoke to you about the Holy Spirit. When the Lord had invited believers in him to drink this Spirit, speaking among those who were planning to seize him and wanted to kill him but could not because he did not wish it, disagreement about him arose in the crowd after he had said these things.

Some thought that he was the Christ; others said that the Christ would not arise from Galilee. But those who had been sent to seize him returned free from guilt and full of amazement. They even bore witness to his divine teaching when they said to those who had sent them, “Why did you not bring him?” For they answered that they had never heard anyone speak in this way: “No one has ever spoken as this man speaks.”

He spoke in this way because he was God and human being. Yet the Pharisees rejected their testimony and said to them: “Have you also been led astray? We see that you have been delighted by his words. Has any one of the rulers believed in him, or any of the Pharisees? But this crowd, which does not know the Law, is accursed.”

Those who did not know the Law were themselves believing in the one who had given the Law; and those who taught the Law were despising the one who had given it. Thus what the Lord himself had said was fulfilled: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).

The Pharisees, who were teachers, became blind; the people who did not know the Law were enlightened and believed in the author of the Law.

### 2

Nicodemus, however, one of the Pharisees, who had come to the Lord by night, was not unbelieving, but timid. For he had come by night to the light because he wished to be enlightened, yet feared being recognized.

He answered the Jews: “Does our Law judge a person unless it first hears him and learns what he does?” They wanted perversely to become condemners before becoming investigators.

Nicodemus knew—or rather believed—that if they merely wished to listen to him patiently, they might perhaps become like those who had been sent to seize him and had preferred to believe.

They answered him from the prejudice of their hearts, as they had answered the others: “Are you also a Galilean?” That is, “Have you too been deceived by a Galilean?”

The Lord was called a Galilean because his parents were from the city of Nazareth. I said “parents” with reference to Mary, not to a male seed; for the one who already had a Father above sought on earth only a mother. Both of his births were miraculous: divine birth without a mother, human birth without a father.

What, then, did they say to Nicodemus, as though they were teachers of the Law? “Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet arises from Galilee.”

Yet the Lord of the prophets arose from there. “They returned,” the Evangelist says, “each to his own home.”

### 3

From there Jesus went to the mountain—the Mount of Olives, the fruitful mountain, the mountain of ointment, the mountain of chrism. For where was it fitting that Christ should teach, if not on the Mount of Olives?

The name “Christ” comes from chrism. For χρίσμα (chrísma) is Greek for “anointing,” called unctio in Latin. He anointed us so that he might make us wrestlers against the devil.

“And at dawn he came again into the temple, and all the people came to him; and sitting down, he taught them.” He was not seized, because he had not yet deigned to suffer.

### 4

Now pay attention to where the Lord’s gentleness was tested by his enemies.

“They brought to him a woman caught in adultery and set her in the midst. And they said to him: ‘Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. In the Law, Moses commanded us to stone such women. What, then, do you say?’ But they said this to test him, so that they might be able to accuse him.”

Of what would they accuse him? Had they caught him committing any crime? Or was it said that the woman belonged to him in some way? What, then, does it mean that they tested him so that they might be able to accuse him?

We understand, brothers, that an extraordinary gentleness prevailed in the Lord. They had noticed that he was exceedingly mild and exceedingly gentle. For this had previously been foretold concerning him: “Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most powerful one; in your appearance and your beauty advance, prosper, and reign, for the sake of truth and gentleness and righteousness” (Ps. 45:4–5).

Thus he brought truth as teacher, gentleness as liberator, and righteousness as judge. The prophet had foretold that he would reign because of these things in the Holy Spirit (Isa. 11).

When he spoke, truth was recognized; when he was not moved against his enemies, gentleness was praised. Since, then, his enemies were tormented by jealousy and envy on account of these two qualities—his truth and his gentleness—they set a trap concerning the third, namely righteousness.

Why? Because the Law had commanded that adulterers be stoned, and certainly the Law could not command what was unjust. If anyone said something other than what the Law commanded, he would be exposed as unjust.

They therefore said among themselves: “He is considered truthful; he appears gentle. We must seek a charge against him concerning righteousness. Let us bring him a woman caught in adultery and tell him what the Law prescribes concerning her. If he orders her to be stoned, he will not have gentleness; if he judges that she should be released, he will not uphold righteousness.

“But,” they said, “so that he does not lose the gentleness by which he has already become beloved by the people, he will certainly say that she ought to be released. Here we have an opportunity to accuse him, and we will make him guilty as a transgressor of the Law, saying to him: ‘You are an enemy of the Law; you answer against Moses—or rather, against the one who gave the Law through Moses. You are guilty of death, and both she and you must be stoned.’”

With these words and arguments, envy could be inflamed, accusation could burn, and condemnation could be demanded. But against whom? Perversity against uprightness, falsehood against truth, a corrupt heart against a righteous heart, folly against wisdom.

When they were preparing snares for him, into which would they not first thrust their own heads? Behold, in his answer the Lord will preserve righteousness and will not depart from gentleness. He was not caught by the trap laid for him; rather, those who laid it were caught, because they did not believe in the one who could free them from their snares.

### 5

What, then, did the Lord Jesus answer? What did Truth answer? What did Wisdom answer? What did that very Justice answer, against which the accusation had been contrived? He did not say, “Let her not be stoned,” lest he seem to speak against the Law. But far be it from him to say, “Let her be stoned”: for he came not to destroy what he had found, but to seek what had perished (Luke 19:10).

What, then, did he answer? See how full it is of justice, full of gentleness and truth! “Let the one among you who is without sin,” he said, “be the first to throw a stone at her.” O answer of Wisdom! How he brought them inside themselves! For outwardly they were accusing, but inwardly they were not examining themselves: they saw the adulteress, but they did not see themselves. Transgressors of the Law wanted the Law fulfilled, and wanted this through accusation—not truly, as condemning adulteries by chastity.

You have heard, Jews; you have heard, Pharisees; you have heard, teachers of the Law, the guardian of the Law—but you have not yet understood the Lawgiver. What else does he signify to you when he writes on the ground with his finger? For the Law was written by the finger of God; but, because of hard hearts, it was written on stone (Exodus 31:18). Now the Lord was writing on the ground because he was seeking fruit.

You have heard, then: “Let the Law be fulfilled; let the adulteress be stoned.” But is the Law to be fulfilled in punishing her by those who themselves deserve punishment? Let each one of you consider himself, enter into himself, ascend the tribunal of his own mind, place himself before his conscience, and compel himself to confess. For he knows who he is [Col. 1650; Note: In Erasmus, “who he is.”]—“because no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him” (1 Corinthians 2:11).

Each person, turning his attention inward, finds himself a sinner. Precisely so. Therefore either release this woman, or together with her undergo the punishment of the Law. If he had said, “Let the adulteress not be stoned,” he would have been convicted of injustice; if he had said, “Let her be stoned,” he would not have appeared gentle. Let him say what he ought to say, both gentle and just: “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

This is the voice of justice: “Let the sinner be punished, but not by sinners; let the Law be fulfilled, but not by transgressors of the Law.” This is altogether the voice of justice. Struck by it as though by a spear of great force, they looked at themselves, found themselves guilty, and all withdrew one by one.

Two were left: the wretched woman and Mercy. When the Lord had struck them with that weapon of justice, he did not even deign to attend to them as they fell; turning his gaze away from them, he again wrote on the ground with his finger.

### 6

When that woman alone had been left, and everyone had gone away, he raised his eyes toward her. We have heard the voice of justice; let us also hear the voice of gentleness. I believe that the woman was more terrified when she heard the Lord say, “Let the one among you who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her.”

They, therefore, turning their attention to themselves, and confessing their own condition by their very departure, had left the woman with her great sin to the one who was without sin. And because she had heard, “Let the one who is without sin be the first to throw a stone at her,” she expected to be punished by him in whom no sin could be found.

But he who had driven away her adversaries with the tongue of justice, raising toward her the eyes of gentleness, questioned her: “Has no one condemned you?” She answered, “No one, Lord.” And he said, “Neither will I condemn you”—the one by whom you perhaps feared to be condemned, because you found no sin in me. “Neither will I condemn you.”

What is this, Lord? Do you therefore favor sins? Certainly not. Observe what follows: “Go, and from now on do not sin.”

Thus the Lord also condemned—but the sin, not the person. For if he were a favorer of sins, he would have said, “Neither will I condemn you; go, live as you wish. Be confident of my deliverance: however greatly you sin, I will free you from every punishment, even from the tortures of Gehenna and hell.” He did not say this.

### 7

Therefore let those who love gentleness in the Lord pay attention, and let them fear the truth. For “the Lord is sweet and upright” (Psalm 24:8). Love what is sweet; fear what is upright. As the gentle one he said, “I was silent”; but as the just one, “Shall I always be silent?” (Isaiah 42:14, according to the Septuagint).

“The Lord is merciful and compassionate.” Precisely so. Add further: long-suffering; add further: “and very merciful.” But fear what comes at the end: “and truthful” (Psalm 85:15). For those whom he now endures while they sin, he will judge when they despise him.

“Do you despise the riches of his patience and gentleness, not knowing that God’s patience leads you to repentance? But according to your hardness and impenitent heart, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God, who will repay each according to his works” (Romans 2:4–6).

The gentle Lord, the long-suffering Lord, [Col. 1651] the merciful Lord—but also the just Lord and the truthful Lord. He grants you time for correction, but you love delay more than amendment. Were you evil yesterday? Be good today. And if you have spent today in wickedness, change tomorrow.

You are always waiting, and you make great promises to yourself on the basis of God’s mercy—as though the one who promised you forgiveness through repentance [Note: Thus the Carcassonne manuscript; the other books read, “through patience.”] had also promised you a longer life. How do you know what tomorrow will bring?

You rightly say in your heart: “When I reform, God will forgive me all my sins.” We cannot deny that God has promised forgiveness to those who reform and turn back. For in the prophet, wherever you read that God promised forgiveness to the one who reforms, you do not thereby read that God promised you a long life.

### 8

Human beings are endangered by both things—by hoping and by despairing, through contrary circumstances and contrary dispositions.

Who is deceived by hope? [Note: In B: “He who is deceived by hoping is he who is deceived, who says.” Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain are followed.] The one who says: “God is good; God is merciful. I will do what pleases me, what I desire. I will loosen the reins on my passions; I will fulfill the desires of my soul.” Why? “Because God is merciful, God is good, God is gentle.” Such people are endangered by hope.

But who is endangered by despair? Those who have fallen into serious sins, thinking that they can no longer be forgiven if they repent, and concluding that they are certainly destined for condemnation. They say to themselves: “We are already to be condemned” [Note: In two manuscripts: “we are already condemned.”], “so why should we not do what we want?”—like gladiators assigned to the sword. Therefore the despairing are troublesome: they no longer have anything to fear, and so they are greatly to be feared.

Despair kills these people; hope kills the others. The mind fluctuates between hope and despair. One must fear lest hope kill you, and, while you hope greatly in mercy, you fall under judgment. Again, one must fear lest despair kill you, and, when you think that the grave sins you have committed can no longer be forgiven, you fail to do penance and fall under the judgment of Wisdom, which says, “I too will laugh at your destruction” (Proverbs 1:26).

What, then, does the Lord do for those endangered by either disease? To those endangered by hope he says: “Do not delay to turn to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day; for his wrath will come suddenly, and at the time of vengeance he will destroy you” (Ecclesiasticus 5:8–9).

What does he say to those endangered by despair? “On whatever day the wicked person turns back, I will forget all his iniquities” (Ezekiel 18:21–22, 27).

For those endangered by despair, therefore, he has set forth a harbor of forgiveness; for those endangered by hope and deceived by delays, he has made the day of death uncertain. You do not know when the last day will come. Are you ungrateful because you have today, in which you may reform?

Thus he says also to this woman: “Neither will I condemn you”; but, made secure concerning the past, beware of the future. “Neither will I condemn you”: I have blotted out what you committed; observe what I have commanded, so that you may find what I have promised.

## TREATISE XXXIV

**On the words, “I am the light of the world: whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.” Chapter 8, verse 12.**

[Col. 1652]

### 1

What we have just heard and received attentively when the holy Gospel was read—I do not doubt that we all also tried to understand. Each of us, according to his capacity, grasped what he could from the great matter that was read; and when the bread of the word was set before us, no one can complain that he tasted nothing.

But I also do not doubt that hardly anyone has understood the whole. Yet even if there is someone who sufficiently understands all the words of our Lord Jesus Christ just recited from the Gospel, let him tolerate our ministry until, with the Lord’s help, we may, by discussing them, bring it about that all—or at least many—understand what the few rejoice that they have understood.

### 2

When the Lord said, “I am the light of the world,” I think this is clear to those who have eyes by which they may become participants in this light. But those who have eyes only in the flesh are astonished that the Lord Jesus Christ said, “I am the light of the world.”

Perhaps someone says to himself: “Could the Lord Christ perhaps be this sun, which completes the day by its rising and setting?” For there have indeed been heretics who thought this. The Manichaeans believed that this sun, visible and publicly exposed to the eyes of the flesh—not only for human beings but also for animals to see—was the Lord Christ.

But the right faith of the Catholic Church rejects such an invention and recognizes it as a diabolical doctrine. It recognizes this not only by believing it, but also, insofar as it can, by refuting it in argument.

Let us therefore reject this kind of error, which the holy Church anathematized from the beginning. Let us not suppose that the Lord Jesus Christ is this sun whom we see rising in the east and setting in the west; whose course is followed by night; whose rays are obscured by a cloud; who moves by a fixed motion from place to place. The Lord Christ is not this.

The Lord Christ is not the sun that was made, but the one through whom the sun was made. “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3).

### 3

There is therefore a light that made this light. Let us love it, let us desire to understand it, let us thirst for it, so that one day, led by that very light, we may come to it and live in it in such a way that we may never die at all.

This is the light of which an ancient prophecy, previously given, sang in the Psalm: “You will save human beings and animals, Lord; as your mercy has been multiplied, O God.”

These are the words of the holy Psalm. Pay attention to what the ancient discourse of the holy men of God said beforehand about such a light. “You will save human beings and animals, Lord; as your mercy has been multiplied, O God.”

Because you are God and possess manifold mercy, the multiplicity of your mercy reaches not only human beings, whom you created in your image, but also the animals whom you subjected to human beings. From him from whom comes the salvation of human beings comes also the salvation of animals.

Do not be ashamed to think this about the Lord your God; rather, presume upon it, trust it, and beware of thinking otherwise. The one who saves you [Col. 1653] saves your horse; he saves your sheep; to come to the very smallest things, he saves your hen. “Salvation belongs to the Lord” (Psalm 3:9), and God saves these creatures.

This moves you, and you ask questions; I am amazed that you doubt. Will the one who deigned to create refuse to save? Salvation belongs to the Lord of angels, of human beings, and of animals; salvation belongs to the Lord.

Just as no one exists from himself, so no one is saved from himself. Therefore the Psalm says most truly and most excellently: “You will save human beings and animals, Lord.” Why? “As your mercy has been multiplied, O God.” You are God; you created; you save. You gave being; you give soundness of being.

### 4

If, then, because God’s mercy has been multiplied, human beings and animals are saved by him, do human beings not possess something else that God the Creator grants to them but does not grant to animals? Is there no distinction between an animal made in the image of God and an animal subjected to the image of God?

There certainly is. In addition to this common salvation that we share with mute creatures, there is something that God grants to us but does not grant to them. What is it? Continue in the same Psalm:

“But the children of human beings will hope under the shelter of your wings.”

While possessing this common salvation with their animals, “the children of human beings will hope under the shelter of your wings.” They have one kind of salvation in reality and another in hope. This salvation, which exists in the present, is common to human beings and animals; but there is another salvation that human beings hope for. Those who hope receive it; those who despair do not.

“For the children of human beings,” he says, “will hope under the shelter of your wings.” Those who persevere in hope are protected by you, so that they may not be cast down from hope by the devil: “under the shelter of your wings they will hope.”

If they will hope, what will they hope for except what animals will not possess? “They will be intoxicated by the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight.”

What kind of wine is this, from which it is praiseworthy to become intoxicated? What kind of wine does not disturb but directs the mind? What kind of wine makes one perpetually sound, rather than making one insane through intoxication?

“They will be intoxicated.” From what? “From the abundance of your house, and you will give them drink from the torrent of your delight.” From what? “For with you is the fountain of life.”

The fountain of life itself walked on earth; it itself said, “Let the one who thirsts come to me” (John 7:37). Behold the fountain.

But we had begun to speak about light, and we were discussing the question proposed from the Gospel concerning light. We had heard the Lord say, “I am the light of the world.” From this arose the question, lest someone thinking carnally should suppose that the sun was meant. We came from there to the Psalm, and, considering it, found meanwhile that the Lord is the fountain of life.

Drink and live. “With you,” he says, “is the fountain of life.” Therefore the children of human beings hope beneath the shelter of your wings, seeking to become intoxicated from this fountain.

But we were speaking about light. Continue, then. For when the Prophet had said, “With you is the fountain of life,” he followed by adding, “In your light we will see light” (Psalm 35:8, 10)—God from God, light from light.

Through this light the light of the sun was made; and the light that made the sun, under which it also made us, was made under the sun for our sake. The light that made the sun was made, I say, under the sun for our sake.

Do not despise [Col. 1654] the cloud of flesh: it is covered by a cloud not so that it may be obscured, but so that it may be tempered.

### 5

Speaking, therefore, through the cloud of flesh, the unfailing light, the light of wisdom, said to human beings: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

How he removed you from the eyes of the flesh and recalled you to the eyes of the heart! For it is not enough to say, “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have light”; he added “of life,” just as it was said there, “For with you is the fountain of life.”

See, therefore, my brothers, how the Lord’s words agree with the truth of that Psalm. There, light was placed together with the fountain of life, and by the Lord the light of life was mentioned.

In bodily matters, however, light is one thing and a fountain another. The throat seeks a fountain; the eyes seek light. When we are thirsty, we seek a fountain; when we are in darkness, we seek light. And if we happen to be thirsty at night, we light a lamp so that we may come to the fountain.

It is not so with God. What is light is also fountain; the one who shines upon you so that you may see is himself the one who flows for you to drink.

### 6

You see, therefore, my brothers—you see, if you see inwardly—what kind of light this is of which the Lord says, “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness.”

Follow this sun; let us see whether you will not walk in darkness. Behold, by rising it comes forth for you; by its course it proceeds toward the west. Perhaps your journey is toward the east. Unless you proceed in the opposite direction from that toward which it is going, by following it you will certainly go astray, and instead of east you will take hold of west.

If you follow it on land, you will go astray; if a sailor follows it at sea, he will go astray. Finally, it seems to you that you ought to follow the sun, and you yourself also move toward the west, where it is moving. Let us see, when it has set, whether you will not walk in darkness.

See how, even if you do not wish to abandon it, it will abandon you, completing its day by the necessity of its service.

But meanwhile our Lord Jesus Christ, even when he did not appear to everyone through the cloud of flesh, held all things through the power of wisdom. Your God is wholly everywhere. If you do not fall away from him, he will never set from you.

### 7

“Whoever follows me,” he says, “will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

What he promised he expressed with a verb of future time. He did not say, “has,” but “will have the light of life.” Yet he did not say, “Whoever will follow me,” but “whoever follows me.”

In what we ought to do, he used the present tense; but what he promised to those who do it, he signified with a verb of future time: “Whoever follows will have.”

Now he follows; afterward he will have. Now he follows through faith; afterward he will have through sight. “As long as we are in the body,” the Apostle says, “we are away from the Lord; for we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:6–7).

When will it be by sight? When we have the light of life; when we have come to that vision; when this night has passed.

For concerning that day which will dawn it is said, “In the morning I will stand before you, and I will contemplate” (Psalm 5:5).

What is “in the morning”? After the night of this world has passed; after the terrors of temptation have passed; after that lion has been overcome which prowls about at night, roaring and seeking whom it may devour (1 Peter 5:8). “In the morning I will stand [Col. 1655] before you, and I will contemplate.”

But now, my brothers, what do we think suits this present time except what is again said in the Psalm: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6:7)? “Every night,” he says, “I will weep; I will burn with desire for the light.”

The Lord sees my desire, since another Psalm says to him: “All my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you” (Psalm 37:10).

Do you desire gold? You can be seen; for when you seek gold, you will be visible to human beings. Do you desire grain? You ask who has it; and, wishing to obtain what you desire, you make your desire known.

Do you desire God? Who sees this except God? From whom do you ask for God, as you ask for bread, water, gold, silver, or grain? From whom do you ask for God except from God? He himself is requested from himself, the one who promises himself.

Let the soul extend its desire, and with a more capacious breast seek to embrace what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the heart of man” (1 Corinthians 2:9). It can be desired, longed for, and sighed after; it cannot be worthily conceived or expressed in words.

### 8

Therefore, my brothers, since the Lord briefly said, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life,” one thing is what he commanded and another what he promised.

Let us do what he commanded, lest with shameless boldness we desire what he promised; lest he say to us in his judgment: “You did what I commanded—so that you might seek what I promised?”

What, then, did you command, Lord our God? He tells you: “That you should follow me.” You asked for the counsel of life. Whose life, if not the life of which it was said, “With you is the fountain of life”?

A certain man heard, “Go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me.” He went away sorrowful; he did not follow. He had sought a good teacher, had addressed a master, and had despised the teacher’s instruction.

He went away sorrowful, bound by his desires; he went away sorrowful, carrying a great burden of greed upon his shoulders (Matthew 19:16–22). He was laboring and sweating; and the one who wished to have him lay down his burden was not thought worthy to be followed, but to be abandoned.

Later, when the Lord proclaimed through the Gospel, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you; take my yoke upon you and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart” (Matthew 11:28–29), how many did, on hearing the Gospel, what that rich man had not done when he heard it from his own mouth?

Therefore let us act now; let us follow the Lord; let us loose the fetters by which we are hindered from following. And who is capable of loosening such knots unless he helps to whom it was said, “You have broken my bonds” (Psalm 115:16)? Of him another Psalm says, “The Lord releases those in chains; the Lord raises up those who have been cast down” (Psalm 145:8).

### 9

And what do those who have been released and raised up follow except the light from which they hear, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness”? For the Lord gives light to the blind.

Therefore we are now being enlightened, brothers, possessing the eye-salve of faith. His saliva, mixed with earth, went before—the means by which the one born blind was anointed (John 9:6).

We too were born blind from Adam, and we need [Col. 1656] him to give us light. He mixed saliva with earth: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14). He mixed saliva with earth; therefore it was foretold, “Truth has sprung up from the earth” (Psalm 84:12).

He himself said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

We will enjoy the truth when we see face to face, because this too is promised to us. For who would dare hope for what God had not deigned either to promise or to give?

“We will see face to face.” The Apostle says: “Now I know in part; now through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Corinthians 13:12). And the Apostle John says in his Epistle: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

This is the great promise. If you love, follow.

“I love,” you say, “but by what route do I follow?” If the Lord your God had said to you, “I am the truth and the life,” and, desiring truth and longing for life, you sought the way by which you could reach these things, you would certainly seek it and say to yourself: “Truth is a great thing; life is a great thing. If only there were some way by which my soul could reach them!”

You ask by what way? Hear him first saying, “I am the way.” The way to where? “And the truth and the life.”

First he said by what route you should come; afterward he said where you should come: “I am the way, I am the truth, I am the life.”

Remaining with the Father, he is truth and life; clothing himself with flesh, he became the way.

You are not told, “Labor in seeking the way so that you may reach truth and life.” You are not told this. Lazy one, arise! The way itself has come to you and awakened you from sleep—if indeed it has awakened you. Arise and walk.

Perhaps you try to walk and cannot, because your feet hurt. Why do your feet hurt? Did they run over rough paths at the command of greed? But the Word of God healed the lame.

“Behold,” you say, “I have sound feet, but I do not see the way itself.” He also gave light to the blind.

### 10

All this occurs through faith, as long as we are away from the Lord, remaining in the body. But when we have traveled the whole way and come to our homeland, what will be more joyful for us? What will be more blessed? For nothing will be more peaceful; nothing will rebel against the human being.

Now, however, brothers, it is difficult for us to be without conflict. We have indeed been called to harmony, and we are commanded to have peace among ourselves. We must strive for this with all our strength, so that one day we may come to perfect peace.

For now, however, we often quarrel with those whom we wish to help. Someone is in error, and you want to lead him to the way; he resists you, and you quarrel. A pagan resists; you argue against the errors of idols and demons. A heretic resists; you argue against other doctrines of demons.
