An evil Catholic does not want to live well; you rebuke even your own brother within. He remains in the same household with you and seeks destructive paths; you are distressed over how to correct him, so that you may give the Lord a good account concerning both of you.

How many necessities of quarrels arise on every side! Often a person, wearied by it, says to himself: “Why must I endure those who contradict me, those who return evil for good? I want to help; they want to perish. I consume my life in quarrelling; I have no peace. Moreover, I make enemies of those whom I ought to have as friends, if only they would pay attention to the goodwill [Col. 1657] of the one who advises them. Why must I endure this perpetually? Let me return to myself; I will be with myself; I will call upon my God.”

Return to yourself, and there you find conflict. If you have begun to follow God, there you find conflict.

“What conflict,” you ask, “do I find?” “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Galatians 5:17).

Behold, you yourself are there; behold, you are alone; behold, you are with yourself; behold, you suffer no other human being. But you see another law in your members, resisting the law of your mind and taking you captive in the law of sin that is in your members.

Cry out, then, and from this inner conflict cry out to God, that he may make peace within you: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord” (Romans 7:23–25).

For “whoever follows me,” he says, “will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

When all conflict has ended, immortality will follow, because the last enemy, death, will be destroyed. And what peace there will be! “This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality” (1 Corinthians 15:26, 53).

In order that we may come to this—which will then exist in reality—let us now follow in hope the one who said, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

## TREATISE XXXV

**From the passage, “Then the Pharisees said, ‘You bear witness concerning yourself,’ etc.”, to the passage, “Your testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.” Chapter 8, verses 13–14.**

### 1

Yesterday, those of you who were present remember that there was a lengthy discussion of the words of our Lord Jesus Christ in which he said, “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12).

And if we still wish to discuss that light, we can speak for a long time, for we cannot explain it briefly. Therefore, my brothers, let us follow Christ, the light of the world, so that we may not walk in darkness.

The darknesses to be feared are those of conduct, not of the eyes; and if they concern the eyes, they are not the external eyes but the inward ones, by which not white and black but just and unjust are discerned.

### 2

When our Lord Jesus Christ had said this, the Jews answered: “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.”

Before our Lord Jesus Christ came, he kindled and sent before him many prophetic lamps. Among these was John the Baptist, to whom the great Light itself, the Lord Christ, bore testimony such as he bore to no other human being. For he said, “Among those born of women no one has arisen greater than John the Baptist” (Matthew 11:11).

Yet this man, than whom no one born of women was greater, says concerning the Lord Jesus Christ: “I indeed baptize you with water; but the one who comes is mightier than I, whose sandal I am not worthy to untie” (John 1:26–27).

See how the lamp submits itself to the day.

The Lord himself testifies that John was a lamp: “He was,” he says, “a burning and shining lamp; and you were willing for a while to rejoice in his light” (John 5:35).

When the Jews said to the Lord, “Tell us, by what authority do you do these things?” the Lord knew that they held John the Baptist in great esteem, and that the very one whom they held in great esteem had borne witness concerning the Lord. [Col. 1658]

He answered them: “I too will ask you one question. Tell me: John’s baptism—where was it from, from heaven or from human beings?”

They were troubled among themselves. If they said, “From human beings,” they could be stoned by the crowd, which believed John to be a prophet. If they said, “From heaven,” he would answer them: “The one whom you acknowledge to have received prophecy from heaven bore witness concerning me, and from him you heard by what authority I do these things.”

They saw, therefore, that whichever answer they gave, they would fall into a snare. And they said, “We do not know.”

And the Lord said to them: “Neither do I tell you by what authority I do these things” (Matthew 21:23–27).

“I do not tell you what I know, because you are unwilling to acknowledge what you know.” Justly repelled, they withdrew in confusion. And what God the Father says through the Prophet in the Psalm was fulfilled: “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ”—that is, John himself—“I will clothe his enemies with shame” (Psalm 131:17–18).

### 3

The Lord Jesus Christ therefore had the testimony of the Prophets who had been sent before him, heralds who preceded the Judge; he had testimony from John. But he himself was the greater testimony that he bore concerning himself [Note: Lov. has “the greater testimony itself.” Am., Bad., and Er. have “he himself.” The manuscripts likewise mostly have *magis*—“more”—instead of *majus*—“greater.”].

They sought lamps because their weak eyes could not bear the day. For that same John the Apostle whose Gospel we hold in our hands says at the beginning of his Gospel concerning John:

“There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. He came for testimony, to bear witness concerning the light, so that all might believe through him. He was not the light, but came to bear witness concerning the light. He was the true light, which enlightens every human being coming into the world.”

If it enlightens every human being, then it also enlightens John. Hence John himself says: “We have all received from his fullness” (John 1:6–9, 16).

Distinguish these things, then, so that your mind may advance in the faith of Christ. Do not remain always infants seeking breasts and recoiling from solid food. You ought to be nourished and weaned in the holy mother, the Church of Christ, and to approach more solid nourishment—not with the belly, but with the mind.

Distinguish this, then: one thing is the light that illuminates, another is what is illuminated. For our eyes too are called lights. Each person swears in this way, touching his eyes: “By my lights, may my lights live”—this is a customary oath.

If these lights really are lights, let the light be absent from your closed room, and let them be open and shining for you. They cannot do so. Thus these things that we have in the face, which we call lights, even when they are sound and open, need the help of external light. When that light is removed or not supplied, they are sound and open, yet they do not see.

So it is with our mind, which is the eye of the soul. Unless it is irradiated by the light of truth and wonderfully illumined by the one who illuminates but is not himself illuminated, it will be able to attain neither wisdom nor justice. For our way is to live justly. But how can one not stumble on a road when no light shines for him? Therefore, on such a road, it is necessary to see; on such a road, seeing is a great thing.

Tobit, for instance, had his eyes closed in his face, and his son gave his hand [Col. 1659] to his father; the father showed the way to his son by giving directions (Tobit 2:11; 4).

### 4

Then the Jews answered, “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.”

Let us see what they hear; let us also hear—but not as they did. They heard while despising; let us hear while believing. They wanted to kill Christ; we desire to live through Christ. Meanwhile, let this difference distinguish our ears and minds, and let us hear what the Lord answered the Jews.

Jesus answered and said to them: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.”

Light demonstrates other things and also demonstrates itself. You light a lamp, for example, so that you may look for a tunic, and the burning lamp enables you to find the tunic. But do you light the lamp in order to see the burning lamp?

A burning lamp is capable both of uncovering other things that were hidden by darkness and of displaying itself to your eyes. So too the Lord Christ distinguished between his faithful and the hostile Jews, as between light and darkness; as between those whom he drenched with the ray of faith and those whose closed eyes he surrounded.

For even this sun illuminates both the face of the seeing person and that of the blind. Both stand equally beneath it, and both have their faces turned toward the sun; both are illuminated in the flesh, but both are not illuminated in their sight. One sees; the other does not see. The sun is present to both, but one is absent from the sun that is present.

So too the Wisdom of God, the Word of God, the Lord Jesus Christ, is present everywhere, because truth is everywhere and wisdom is everywhere.

One person understands justice in the east; another understands justice in the west. Is the justice understood by one different from that understood by the other? They are separated in body, but their minds have their sight in one thing.

The justice that I see while established here—if it is justice—is seen by the just person who is separated from me by who knows how many residences in the flesh, yet joined to me in the light of that justice.

Therefore light bears witness to itself: it opens healthy eyes, and is itself its own witness, so that light may be recognized.

But what are we to do about unbelievers? Is it not present to them? It is present to them also, but they do not have the eyes of the heart by which they may see it.

Hear the judgment pronounced concerning them from the Gospel itself: “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5).

Therefore the Lord says—and rightly says: “Even if I bear witness concerning myself, my testimony is true, because I know where I came from and where I am going.”

He wanted the Father to be understood; the Son gave glory to the Father. The equal glorifies the one by whom he was sent. How much, then, ought a human being to glorify the one by whom he was created?

### 5

“I know where I came from and where I am going.”

This one who is now speaking to you has what he did not abandon, and yet he came. By coming, he did not depart from there; by returning, he did not leave us.

Why are you amazed? He is God.

This cannot be done by a human being; it cannot be done even by the sun itself. When the sun proceeds toward the west, it abandons the east; until it rises again and returns to the east, it is not in the east.

But our Lord Jesus Christ both came and is there; he returns and is here.

Hear the Evangelist himself saying elsewhere—and if you can, grasp it; if you cannot, believe it: “No one has ever seen God except the only-begotten [Col. 1660] Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known” (John 1:18).

He did not say, “He was in the bosom of the Father,” as though by coming he had abandoned the bosom of the Father.

He was speaking here and saying that he was there. And when he was about to depart from here, what did he say? “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

6. Therefore the testimony of the light is true, whether it reveals itself or something else; for without light you cannot see light, and without light you cannot see anything else that is not light. If light is sufficient to display things that are not lights, does it fail in itself? Does it not reveal itself, without which other things cannot be made manifest? The Prophet spoke truth; but from where would he have it, unless he drew it from the fountain of truth? John spoke truth; but ask him from where he spoke: “We have all received from his fullness,” he says. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ is competent to bear witness to himself.

But plainly, my brothers, let us listen attentively in the night of this age also to prophecy. For our Lord has now wished to come humbly into our frailty and the innermost nocturnal darkness of our hearts. He came as one to be despised and honored, denied and confessed: despised and denied by the Jews, honored and confessed by us; to be judged and to judge—judged unjustly, and to judge justly. He therefore came in such a way that a lamp had to bear witness to him.

For what need would there have been for John, like a lamp, to bear witness to the day, if the day itself could be seen by our weakness? But we could not. He became weak for the weak; through weakness he healed weakness. Through mortal flesh he removed the death of the flesh; from his own body he made an ointment for our eyes. Therefore, since the Lord has come and we are still in the night of the age, we must also listen to the prophecies.

7. For by prophecy we refute the opposing pagans. “Who is Christ?” the pagan asks. We answer him: “The one whom the Prophets foretold.” And he asks: “Which Prophets?” We recite Isaiah, Daniel, Jeremiah, and the other holy Prophets; we say how long before him they came and how long before his coming they preceded it.

This, then, is our answer: “The Prophets preceded him and foretold that he would come.” One of them replies: “Which Prophets?” We recite those who are recited to us every day. He asks: “Who are these Prophets?” We answer: “Those who also foretold the things that we see taking place.” He says: “You yourselves fabricated these things. You saw them happen and, as though they had been foretold as future events, wrote them down in whatever books you wished.”

Here another testimony from enemies comes to our aid against our pagan enemies. We produce books belonging to the Jews and answer: “Surely both you and they are enemies of our faith. Therefore they have been scattered among the nations, so that we may refute some enemies by means of others.”

Let the Book of Isaiah be produced by the Jews. Let us see whether I do not read there:

> “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer he was without a voice; so he did not open his mouth. In his humiliation his judgment was taken away; by his bruise we were healed. We all went astray like sheep, and he himself was handed over for our sins.”  
> *(Isaiah 53:5–8.)*

[Col. 1661] Behold one lamp. Let another be produced; let the Psalm be opened, and from it too let the foretold passion of Christ be recited:

> “They pierced my hands and my feet; they counted all my bones. But they themselves observed and looked upon me; they divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots. With you is my praise; in the great assembly I will confess you. All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the nations’ peoples shall worship in his presence; for the kingdom is the Lord’s, and he himself shall rule the nations.”  
> *(Psalm 21:17–29.)*

Let one enemy blush, because another enemy supplies me with the book. But behold: from the books produced by one enemy I have defeated the other. Nor should the one who produced the book for me be left untouched; from him let something be produced by which he himself may be defeated.

I read another Prophet and find the Lord speaking to the Jews:

> “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, and I will not accept sacrifice [Note: [Col. 1661] The manuscripts, in great agreement, read *sacrificia*, “sacrifices.”] from your hands; for from the rising of the sun to its setting a pure sacrifice is offered to my name.”  
> *(Malachi 1:10–11.)*

You do not come, Jew, to the pure sacrifice; I prove that you are impure.

8. Behold, the lamps also bear witness to the day because of our weakness, since we cannot endure or see the day’s brightness. Indeed, we Christians ourselves are already light in comparison with unbelievers; hence the Apostle says:

> “For you were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.”  
> *(Ephesians 5:8.)*

And elsewhere he says:

> “The night has advanced, and the day has drawn near. Therefore let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day.”  
> *(Romans 13:12–13.)*

Yet because, in comparison with that light to which we are going, the day in which we now live is still night, listen to the apostle Peter. He says that a voice was brought to the Lord Christ from the majestic glory:

> “You are my beloved Son, in whom I was well pleased.”

“We heard this voice,” he says, “brought from heaven when we were with him on the holy mountain.” But because we were not there and did not hear that voice brought from heaven at that time, Peter himself says to us:

> “And we have the prophetic word made more certain.”

You did not hear the voice brought from heaven, but you have a more certain prophetic word. For the Lord Jesus Christ, foreseeing that certain impious people would arise who would slander his miracles by attributing them to magical arts, sent the Prophets beforehand.

For if he was a magician and by magical arts caused himself to be worshiped even after his death, was he a magician before he was born? Hear the Prophets, you dead man; hear the Prophets, you slanderer who are wasting away. Hear those who came before the Lord.

“We have,” the apostle Peter says, “the prophetic word made more certain, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts.”  
*(2 Peter 1:17–19.)*

9. Therefore, when our Lord Jesus Christ comes and, as the apostle Paul also says, “brings to light the hidden things of darkness and reveals the counsels of the heart, so that each one’s praise may come from God” *(1 Corinthians 4:5)*, then, when such a day is present, lamps will not be necessary. The Prophet will not be read to us; the Apostle’s book will not be opened; we will not seek John’s testimony; we will not need the Gospel itself.

Therefore all the Scriptures that were kindled for us like lamps in the night of this age, lest we remain in darkness, will be removed from our midst. When all these things have been taken away, so that they no longer shine for us in our need, and when the very men of God through whom these things were supplied are seeing that true and brilliant light with us, what will we see once these aids have been taken away? From what will our mind be nourished? At what will that vision rejoice? Where will there be that joy “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart”? *(1 Corinthians 2:9.)*

What will we see? I beg you, love with me; run with me by believing. Let us desire our heavenly homeland; let us sigh for our heavenly homeland; let us recognize that here we are strangers.

What will we see then? Let the Gospel speak now:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”  
> *(John 1:1.)*

From the place where the dew has been sprinkled upon you, you will come to the fountain. From the place where a ray has been sent to your darkened heart through indirect and winding paths, you will see the light itself naked—the light for whose sight and endurance you are being cleansed.

Beloved, as I also recalled yesterday, John himself says:

> “We are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”  
> *(1 John 3:2.)*

I feel your affections rising with me toward heavenly things. But “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks of many things” *(Wisdom 9:15)*.

I too am about to lay down this book, and each of you will depart to your own affairs. We have been well together in the common light; we have rejoiced well and exulted well. But when we depart from one another, let us not depart from him.

# TREATISE XXXVI

From the passage written, “You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one,” up to, “I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.” Chapter 8, verses 15–18.

1. In the four Gospels—or rather, in the four books of one Gospel—the holy apostle John, not without reason compared to an eagle in his spiritual understanding, raised his preaching higher and much more sublimely than the other three, and by its elevation wished also to raise our hearts.

For the other three evangelists, as though walking on earth with the Lord in his humanity, said little about his divinity. But this evangelist, as though he had been unwilling to walk on earth, thundered at the very beginning of his discourse and raised himself not merely above the earth and the whole circuit of air and heaven, but also above the entire army of angels and every order of invisible powers. He reached the one through whom all things were made, saying:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made.”  
> *(John 1:1–3.)*

To so lofty a beginning he added the other things appropriate to it, and he spoke of the Lord’s divinity as no one else did. He belched forth what he had drunk. For it is not without reason that this same Gospel tells us that at the supper he reclined upon the Lord’s breast *(John 13:23)*.

He was secretly drinking from that breast; but what he drank in secret he belched forth openly, so that all nations might learn not only of the Son of God’s incarnation, passion, and resurrection, but also what he was before the incarnation: the Only-Begotten of the Father, the Father’s Word, coeternal with the one who begot him, equal to the one by whom he was sent, yet made lesser in the very act of being sent, so that the Father might be greater.

2. Whatever you have heard stated humbly about the Lord Jesus Christ, understand it as referring to the dispensation of the flesh he assumed. Consider what he became for us, not what he was in order to make us. Whatever you hear or read stated about him in the Gospel in a sublime manner, exalted above all creatures, divine, equal and coeternal with the Father—know that you are reading what pertains to the form of God, not what pertains to the form of a servant.

If you hold to this rule—which those who can comprehend may hold, though not everyone can comprehend, while everyone must believe—you will fight securely against the slanders of heretical darkness, walking as though in the light.

There have been people who, by reading only those evangelical testimonies that speak of Christ’s humility, followed them and were deaf to the testimonies that speak of his divinity—deaf for this reason, that they might be perversely talkative. Others, attending only to what was said about the Lord’s exaltation, even if they read of his mercy by which he became human for our sake, did not believe it and thought that it had been introduced by human beings and was false. They insisted that our Lord Christ was God alone and not also human.

Some went one way, others another; both were in error. The catholic faith, however, holding as true what it holds from both sides, preaching what it believes, understood Christ as God and believed him to be human. Both are written, and both are true.

If you say that Christ is God alone, you deny the medicine by which you were healed. If you say that Christ is human alone, you deny the power by which you were created. Hold both, therefore, faithful soul and catholic heart; hold both, believe both, and faithfully confess both. Christ is both God and human.

What kind of God is Christ? Equal to the Father, one with the Father. What kind of human is Christ? Born of a virgin, receiving mortality from humanity but not receiving iniquity.

3. These Jews therefore saw the human being but neither understood nor believed that he was God. Among the other things, you have already heard how they said to him:

> “You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true.”  
> *(John 8:13.)*

You also heard what he answered when this was read yesterday and discussed according to our ability. Today these words of his were read:

> “You judge according to the flesh.”

“Therefore,” he says, “you say to me, ‘You bear witness concerning yourself; your testimony is not true,’ because you judge according to the flesh. You do not understand God; you see a human being, and by persecuting the human being you offend the God who is hidden. Therefore you judge according to the flesh.”

“For this reason I seem arrogant to you, because I bear witness concerning myself. Every human being, when he wishes to offer praiseworthy testimony about himself, appears arrogant and proud. Hence it is written: ‘Let your own mouth not praise you, but let the mouth of your neighbor praise you’” *(Proverbs 27:2)*.

But this was said to a human being. We are weak, and we speak among the weak. We can speak the truth, and we can lie. Although we ought to speak the truth, we can nevertheless lie whenever we wish.

The light cannot lie. Far be it from the splendor of divine light that the darkness of falsehood should be found in it. He spoke as the light; he spoke as the truth. But “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it”; therefore they judged according to the flesh.

“You,” he says, “judge according to the flesh.”

4. “I judge no one.” Does the Lord Jesus Christ, then, judge no one? Is he not the one whom we confess to have risen on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sat at the right hand of the Father, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead? Is this not our faith, of which the Apostle says, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” *(Romans 10:10)*?

When we confess these things, are we speaking against the Lord? We say that he will come as judge of the living and the dead, while he says, “I judge no one.”

This question can be resolved in two ways. We may understand “I judge no one” to mean “now,” as he says elsewhere, “I did not come to judge the world but to save the world” *(John 12:47)*—not denying his judgment, but postponing it.

Or, because he had said, “You judge according to the flesh,” he added, “I judge no one,” with “according to the flesh” understood. Let no doubt, therefore, remain in our hearts against the faith that we hold and proclaim concerning Christ the judge.

Christ came first to save and afterward to judge: judging for punishment those who were unwilling to be saved, and bringing to life those who, by believing, did not reject salvation.

The first dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ is therefore medicinal, not judicial. For if he had first come to judge, he would have found no one to whom he could give the rewards of justice. Since he saw that all were sinners and that absolutely no one was free from the death of sin, his mercy had to be brought forward first, and afterward judgment had to be exercised.

For the Psalm had sung of him:

> “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord.”  
> *(Psalm 100:1.)*

It does not say “judgment and mercy.” If judgment came first, there would be no mercy; rather, mercy comes first, and afterward judgment.

What is this mercy that comes first? The Creator of humanity deigned to become human. He became what he had made, so that what he had made would not perish. What could be added to this mercy? Yet he added more.

It was not enough for him to become human; he was also [Note: [Col. 1664] Lugd., Ven., and Lov. read, “but he also willed.” In B the margin notes, “supply ADDED.” M.] rejected by human beings. It was not enough to be rejected; he was dishonored. It was not enough to be dishonored; he was killed. But even this was not enough: it was death on a cross.

When the Apostle commended his obedience unto death, it was not enough for him to say, “He became obedient unto death.” He did not mean just any death; he added, “even death on a cross” *(Philippians 2:8)*.

Among all kinds of death, nothing was worse than that. Hence, wherever the most severe pains rage, the suffering is called *cruciatus*, “torment,” a name derived from the cross. Those hanging on the wood were crucified, their feet and hands fastened to the wood with nails, and they were killed by a prolonged death.

To be crucified was not simply to be killed. One remained alive on the cross for a long time—not because a longer life was chosen, but because death itself was prolonged, so that the pain would not end quickly.

He wished to die for us. We say too little: he deigned to be crucified and became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. He chose the most extreme and worst kind of death—the one who was going to remove all death. By the worst death he killed every death.

It was worst in the eyes of the Jews who did not understand; but it had been chosen by the Lord. He was to have that very cross as his sign; he was to place that cross, like a trophy over the defeated devil, upon the foreheads of the faithful, so that the Apostle might say:

> “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”  
> *(Galatians 6:14.)*

At that time nothing in the flesh was more intolerable; now nothing on the forehead is more glorious. What does he reserve for his faithful one who has given such honor to his punishment?

Indeed, it is no longer found among the punishments of criminals among the Romans. Once the Lord’s cross had been honored, it was thought that a criminal too would be honored if he were crucified.

He therefore came for this reason and judged no one; he endured evil men and suffered an unjust judgment in order to carry out a just one. But in enduring the unjust judgment there was mercy.

He became so humble as to come even to the cross. He delayed his power, but made his mercy public. How did he delay his power? Because he who could rise from the tomb did not wish to descend from the cross. How did he make his mercy public? Because, hanging on the cross, he said:

> “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”  
> *(Luke 23:34.)*

Therefore, either because he had not come to judge the world but to save the world, he said, “I judge no one”; or, as I have recalled, because he had said, “You judge according to the flesh,” he added, “I judge no one,” so that we might understand that Christ does not judge according to the flesh, as he himself was judged by human beings.

5. But so that you may now recognize Christ as judge also, hear what follows:

> “And if I judge, my judgment is true.”

Behold, you have the judge as well; but recognize the Savior, so that you may not fear the judge.

Why did he say that his judgment was true?

> “Because,” he says, “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

I have told you, brothers, that this evangelist John flies very high; it is scarcely possible to grasp him with the mind. Yet I must recall to your Charity the mystery of the one who flies so high.

Both in the prophet Ezekiel and in the Apocalypse of John himself, whose Gospel this is, a fourfold living creature is mentioned, having four forms: that of a human being, a calf, a lion, and an eagle *(Ezekiel 1:5–10; Revelation 4:6–7)*.

Most of those who before us interpreted the mysteries of the Holy Scriptures understood in this living creature—or rather, in these four living creatures—the four evangelists.

The lion represents the king, since the lion appears in some way to be king of the beasts, because of its power and terrifying strength. This form was assigned to Matthew, because in the genealogies of the Lord he traced the royal line, showing how the Lord came through the royal stock from the seed of King David.

Luke, because he began with the priesthood of the priest Zechariah, mentioning the father of John the Baptist, was assigned the calf, since the calf was a great sacrificial victim in the offerings of priests.

To Mark, Christ as human was rightly assigned, because he said nothing about royal power and did not begin from the priesthood, but began simply from the human Christ.

All these evangelists remained, so to speak, close to earthly things—that is, to the things our Lord Jesus Christ did on earth. They spoke very little about his divinity, as though walking with him on earth.

The eagle remains. It is John, the preacher of sublime things and the contemplator, with fixed eyes, of the inner and eternal light.

For it is said that even the young of eagles are tested in this way by their parents: the father suspends them by his talon and exposes them to the rays of the sun. Whoever gazes steadily is recognized as a son; if he flutters his eyes, he is released from the talon as illegitimate.

See, then, how sublime he had to speak who is compared to an eagle. Yet even we, crawling on the ground, weak and scarcely of any account among human beings, dare to discuss and explain these things. We think either that we can grasp them while we reflect on them, or that they can be grasped while we speak of them.

6. Why have I said this? Perhaps after these words someone might rightly say to me: “Then put down the book. Why do you take into your hands what exceeds your measure? Why entrust your tongue to it?”

I answer as follows: There are many heretics, and God has permitted them to abound for this purpose, so that we may not always be nourished on milk and remain in childish stupidity.

Because they did not understand how Christ’s divinity was commended, they formed opinions as they wished. By failing to think rightly, however, they brought exceedingly troublesome questions upon the catholic faithful, and the hearts of the faithful began to be shaken and tossed about.

Then necessity arose for spiritual men who had not only read something in the Gospel concerning the divinity of our Lord Jesus Christ but had also understood it, so that they might bring forth Christ’s weapons against the weapons of the devil and fight openly, with all the strength they could, against false and deceptive teachers concerning Christ’s divinity—lest, while they themselves remained silent, others should perish.

All who have believed that our Lord Jesus Christ is of a substance different from the Father’s, or that Christ is only one person in such a way that he himself is the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit; all who have wished to believe that he was merely human and not God made human, or that he was God in such a way as to be changeable in his divinity, or God in such a way as not also to be human—all have suffered shipwreck in the faith and have been cast out of the harbor of the Church, lest in their disturbance they break the ships moored alongside them.

This compelled even us, the least of all and, so far as we are concerned, wholly unworthy, yet, through his mercy, appointed to some place among his stewards, not to keep silent before you. We speak so that you may either understand and rejoice with me, or, if you are not yet able to understand, remain safely in the harbor by believing.

7. I shall speak, then. Let whoever can comprehend do so; let whoever cannot comprehend believe. Nevertheless, I shall say what the Lord said:

> “You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one”—either now or according to the flesh. “But if I judge, my judgment is true.”

Why is your judgment true?

> “Because,” he says, “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

What then, Lord Jesus? If you were alone, would your judgment be false, and do you judge truly because you are not alone, but are accompanied by the Father who sent you?

What shall I answer? Let him answer for himself:

> “My judgment is true,” he says. “Why? Because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

If he is with you, how did he send you? Did he send you and remain with you? Did you come to us and remain there? How can this be believed? How can it be grasped?

To these two questions I answer: “How can it be grasped?”—you are right to say that. “How can it be believed?”—you are not right to say that. Indeed, it is believed precisely because it is not quickly grasped. For if it were quickly grasped, there would be no need for it to be believed; it would be seen.

You believe because you do not grasp it; but by believing you become capable of grasping it. For if you do not believe, you will never grasp it, because you will remain less capable.

Let faith cleanse you, so that understanding may fill you.

> “My judgment is true,” he says, “because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

Therefore, Lord our God Jesus Christ, your being sent is your incarnation. This is how I see it; this is how I understand it; finally, this is how I believe it, lest it be arrogance for me to say, “This is how I understand it.”

The Lord our Jesus Christ is here also—or rather, here he was according to the flesh; now he is here according to his divinity. He was with the Father and had not departed from the Father.

Therefore, when he is said to have come to us as one sent, his incarnation is being commended, because the Father was not incarnate.

8. For certain heretics were called Sabellians; they are also called Patripassians, because they say that the Father himself suffered.

Do not be one of them, catholic Christian. If you become a Patripassian, you will not be sound.

Understand, then, that the mission of the Son is called the incarnation of the Son. Do not believe that the Father was incarnate, but do not believe that the Father departed from the incarnate Son. The Son carried the flesh; the Father was with the Son.

If the Father was in heaven and the Son on earth, how was the Father with the Son? Because both the Father and the Son were everywhere. God is not in heaven in such a way as not to be on earth.

Hear the one who wished to flee from God’s judgment and could find no place to go:

> “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend into heaven, you are there.”

The question concerned the earth; hear what follows:

> “If I descend to the underworld, you are present.”  
> *(Psalm 139:7–8.)*

If he is said to be present even in the underworld, what place remains where he is not? For God says through the Prophet:

> “I fill heaven and earth.”  
> *(Jeremiah 23:24.)*

He is everywhere, therefore, because no place confines him. Do not turn away from him, and he is with you. If you wish to reach him, do not be slow to love; you run not with your feet but with your affections. Though lame in one respect, you come to him if you believe and love.

He is everywhere. If he is everywhere, how is he not with the Son? Is he not with the Son who, if you believe, is also with you?

9. From where, then, is his judgment true, unless he is the true Son? This is what he said:

> “And if I judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

It is as though he were saying: “My judgment is true because I am the Son of God.”

How do you prove that you are the Son of God?

> “Because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

Blush, Sabellian! You hear the Son; you hear the Father. The Father is Father; the Son is Son.

He did not say, “I am the Father, and I myself am the Son,” but, “I am not alone,” he says.

Why are you not alone?

> “Because the Father is with me. I am, and the Father who sent me is”—[the text is corrupt here].

I am, and the one who sent me. Do not destroy the distinction of persons; distinguish the persons. Distinguish them with understanding, but do not separate them through unbelief, lest, fleeing from Charybdis, you fall again into Scylla.

The whirlpool of Sabellian impiety was swallowing you, so that you said that the one who is the Father is himself the Son. Now you have learned: “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.”

You recognize that the Father is Father and the Son is Son. You recognize this well; but do not say, “The Father is greater and the Son lesser.” Do not say, “The Father is gold and the Son is silver.”

There is one substance, one divinity, one coeternity, perfect equality, and no dissimilarity.

For if you believe only that Christ is one person, and nevertheless suppose that he who is not the Father is different in nature in some respect, you have escaped Charybdis but suffered shipwreck upon the rocks of Scylla. Sail between them and avoid both dangerous sides.

The Father is Father; the Son is Son. Now you say, “The Father is Father; the Son is Son.” You have rightly escaped the danger of the engulfing whirlpool. Why do you wish to go to the other side and say, “The Father is one thing, the Son another”?

“He is another,” you say correctly; “another thing,” you do not say correctly. The Son is another person because he is not the Father himself, and the Father is another person because he is not the Son himself. Yet he is not another thing; the Father and the Son are the same thing.

What does “the same thing” mean? There is one God.

You have heard, “Because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me.” Hear how you should believe concerning the Father and the Son; hear the Son himself:

> “I and the Father are one.”  
> *(John 10:30.)*

He did not say, “I am the Father,” or, “I and the Father is one,” but he says, “I and the Father are one.” [Note: [Col. 1668] The editions read *unum est* (“is one”), and a little below, *unum non diceret de diversis* (“he would not say ‘one’ of things that are different”). But all the manuscripts have *unus est*, and afterward *de diverso*; these codices are supported by what is read in Treatise 37, no. 6: “Therefore, not different because one; not one [person], because ‘we are.’”]

Hear both: “one” and “are.” You will be freed both from Charybdis and from Scylla. In these two words, “one” frees you from Arius; “are” frees you from Sabellius.

If “one,” then they are not different. If “are,” then there are both Father and Son. For he would not say “are” of one person, nor would he say “one” of different things.

Therefore, he says, my judgment is true—in brief, so that you may hear it—because I am the Son of God. But I persuade you that I am the Son of God in such a way that you understand that the Father is with me.

I am not the Son in such a way that I have abandoned him. I am not here in such a way that I am not also with him. He is not there in such a way that he is not with me.

I have taken the form of a servant *(Philippians 2:7)*, but I have not lost the form of God.

> “I am not alone,” he says, “but I and the Father who sent me.”

10. He had spoken about judgment; now he wishes to speak about testimony.

> “In your Law,” he says, “it is written that the testimony of two human beings is true. I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me.”

He also explained the Law to them, if they were not ungrateful. For there is a great question here, my brothers, and it seems to me that the matter has been established in a mystery, where God said:

> “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand.”  
> *(Deuteronomy 19:15; Matthew 18:16.)*

Is truth sought through two witnesses? Certainly; this is how human custom operates. Yet it can happen that two people also lie. The chaste Susanna was pressed by two false witnesses. Were they not false witnesses simply because there were two?

Are we speaking of two or three? The whole people [the transmitted text reads *me titus*, evidently corrupt] was assembled against Christ *(Luke 23:1)*. If a people consisting of a great multitude of human beings was found to be a false witness, how should we understand, “At the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand,” unless the Trinity is commended here through a mystery—the Trinity in which there is the perpetual stability of truth?

Do you wish to have a good case? Have two or three witnesses: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

Finally, when the chaste woman Susanna, a faithful wife, was pressed by two false witnesses, the Trinity supported her in her conscience and in secret. That Trinity brought Daniel forth from concealment as a single witness, and through him convicted the two *(Daniel 13:36–62)*.

Therefore, because it is written in your Law that the testimony of two human beings is true, accept our testimony, lest you experience judgment.

> “For I,” he says, “judge no one, but I bear witness concerning myself. I postpone judgment; I do not postpone testimony.”

11. Let us choose for ourselves, against the tongues of human beings and the weak suspicions of the human race, God as judge and God as witness.

He does not disdain to be a witness who is judge, nor is he promoted when he becomes judge, since the one who is witness will himself be judge.

Why is he himself the witness? Because he does not seek another from whom to learn who you are.

Why is he himself the judge? Because he himself has the power to kill and give life, to condemn and absolve, to cast into hell and raise into heaven, to join one to the devil and crown another with the angels.

Since he possesses this power, he is judge. But because he does not seek another witness in order to know you, the one who will judge you then sees you now. There will be no way to deceive him when he begins to judge.

You will not bring forward false witnesses who could circumvent that judge when he begins to judge you.

God says this to you: “When you despised me, I saw it; and when you did not believe, I did not annul my sentence. I postponed it; I did not remove it. You did not wish to hear what I commanded; you will experience what I foretold. But if you listen to what I commanded, you will not experience the evil things I foretold; you will receive the good things I promised.”

12. Let no one be troubled by what he says:

> “My judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me,”

when elsewhere he says:

> “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”  
> *(John 5:22.)*

We discussed this in the same words of the Gospel before, and now we remind you that this was not said because the Father will not be with the Son when he judges. Rather, it was said because, at the judgment, the Son alone will appear to the good and the evil—in the form in which he suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven.

For while the disciples were looking upon him as he ascended, an angelic voice sounded:

> “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven.”  
> *(Acts 1:11.)*

That is, he will judge in the human form in which he was judged, so that the prophetic word may also be fulfilled:

> “They will look upon the one whom they pierced.”  
> *(Zechariah 12:10; John 19:37.)*

But when the righteous go into eternal life, we shall see him as he is. That will not be the judgment of the living and the dead, but only the reward of the living.

13. Likewise, let no one be troubled by what he says:

> “In your Law it is written that the testimony of two human beings is true,”

and therefore suppose that the Law was not God’s Law because he did not say, “In God’s Law.”

Let him understand that he said, “In your Law,” as though he were saying, “In the Law that was given to you”—and by whom, unless by God? It is like our saying, “Give us this day our daily bread” *(Matthew 6:11)*, while nevertheless we say, “Our daily bread.”

# TREATISE XXXVII

From the passage written, “They therefore said, ‘Where is your father?’” up to, “And no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.” Chapter 8, verses 19–20.

1. What is said briefly in the holy Gospel ought not to be explained briefly, so that what is heard may be understood. For the Lord’s words are few, but great: they are to be measured not by number but by weight. Nor are they to be despised because they are few; rather, they are to be sought because they are great.

Those of you who were present yesterday heard us, insofar as we were able, discuss what the Lord said: “You judge according to the flesh; I judge no one. Yet even if I do judge, my judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me. In your law it is written that the testimony of two people is true. I am the one who bears witness concerning myself, and the Father who sent me bears witness concerning me” (John 8:15–18).

As I said, these words were yesterday brought to your ears and minds. When the Lord had said this, those who heard him—“You judge according to the flesh”—showed what they had heard. For they answered the Lord, who was speaking of God his Father, and said, “Where is your father?”

They understood Christ’s Father carnally, because they judged Christ’s words according to the flesh. The one who was speaking was flesh openly, but the Word secretly: a manifest man, a hidden God. They saw the garment and despised the one clothed in it. They despised him because they did not know; they did not know because they did not see; they did not see because they were blind; they were blind because they did not believe.

2. Let us therefore see what the Lord answered them concerning this. “Where is your father?” they said. For we have heard you say, “I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me”: we see only you, and we do not see your father with you. How then do you say that you are not alone, but are with your father? Or show us that your father [Col. 1671] is with you.

And the Lord said: “Do you see me, so that I may show you the Father?” This is what follows; this is what he himself answered in his own words, whose explanation we have already given above. For observe what he said: “You know neither me nor my Father. If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.”

You say, then, “Where is your Father?” as though you already knew me—as though I were wholly what you see. Since you do not know me, therefore I do not show you my Father. You think that I am a human being; therefore you seek my Father as a human being, because you judge according to the flesh. But since, according to what you see, I am one thing, and according to what you do not see, another, and since I speak of my Father—hidden, of the hidden—first you must know me; then you will know my Father also.

3. “For if you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.” He who knows all things, when he says “perhaps,” does not doubt but rebukes. Consider how the very word “perhaps,” which seems to be a word of doubt, is spoken as a rebuke.

It is a word of doubt when spoken by a human being, who doubts because he does not know. But when a word of doubt is spoken by God, since nothing is hidden from God, that doubt accuses unbelief; it does not express uncertainty in the Godhead.

Human beings sometimes, concerning matters of which they are certain, use doubt as a rebuke—that is, they employ a word of doubt while not doubting in their hearts. For example, if you are angry with your servant and say, “You despise me; consider that perhaps I am your master.” Likewise the Apostle, speaking to certain people who despised him, says: “I think that I too have the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 7:40). Whoever says “I think” appears to doubt; but he was rebuking, not doubting.

The Lord Christ himself, elsewhere rebuking the future unbelief of the human race, says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18:8).

4. By now, I suppose, you understand how “perhaps” is being used. This is so that no one who weighs words and examines syllables, as though he knew how to speak Latin, should criticize the word spoken by the Word of God; and, by criticizing the Word of God, remain not eloquent but mute.

For who speaks as the Word who was in the beginning with God speaks? Do not consider these words and try to measure by these familiar words the Word who is God. You hear “Word” and despise it; hear “God” and fear: “In the beginning was the Word.”

You reduce it to the usage of your own speech and say to yourself, “What is a word? What greatness is there in a word? It sounds and passes away; striking the air, it hits the ear, and afterward it no longer exists.”

Hear further: “The Word was with God.” It remained; it did not pass away by sounding. Perhaps you still despise it: “The Word was God” (John 1:1).

When a word is in your heart, O human being, it is something other than sound. Yet the word that is with you, in order to pass from you to me, seeks sound as a kind of vehicle. It assumes sound, places itself, so to speak, in a vehicle, travels through the air, and comes to me, while it does not depart from you.

But when the sound came to me, it departed from you and did not remain with me. Did the word that was in your heart therefore pass away when the sound passed? You said what you were thinking; and, so that what was hidden with you might reach me, you uttered syllables. The sound of the syllables brought your thought to my ear; through my ear your thought descended into my heart, while the intervening sound flew away.

[Col. 1672] But the word that took on the sound was with you before you sounded it; because you sounded it, it is with me, and it did not depart from you. Consider this, whoever you are who examines sounds. You despise the Word of God, though you do not comprehend the word of a human being!

5. He through whom all things were made therefore knows all things, and yet rebukes by using a question: “If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also.” He rebukes unbelievers.

For he spoke a similar saying to the disciples, but there is no word of doubt there, because there was no reason to rebuke unbelief. What he has just said to the Jews—“If you knew me, perhaps you would know my Father also”—he also said to the disciples when Philip questioned him, or rather requested him, saying: “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

It was as though he said: We already know you; you have appeared to us, we have seen you. You have deigned to choose us; we have followed you. We have seen your miracles and heard words of salvation; we have received your commandments and hope for your promises. You yourself have deigned to grant us much by your presence. Yet, although we know you, we do not yet know the Father, and we burn with the desire to see the one whom we do not yet know. Since we know you but are not satisfied until we also know the Father, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.

And the Lord, so that they might know that they did not know what they thought they already knew, said: “Have I been with you for so long, and you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (John 14:8–9).

Does this saying contain a word of doubt? Did he say, “Whoever has seen me has perhaps seen the Father also”? Why not? Because a believer was listening, not a persecutor of the faith. Therefore the Lord was not rebuking but teaching.

“Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also”; and here, “If you knew me, you would know my Father also.” Let us remove the word by which the unbelief of the hearers was marked, and the statement itself remains.

6. Yesterday we commended to your Charity, and said that the sayings of John the Evangelist, in which he reports to us what he learned from the Lord, would not need to be examined if it were possible, unless the inventions of heretics compelled us to do so.

Briefly, then, yesterday we made known to your Charity that there are heretics called Patripassians, or, after their founder, Sabellians. They say that the one who is Father is himself the Son: the names are different, but the person is one. “When he wishes,” they say, “he is Father; when he wishes, Son; nevertheless he is one.”

There are also other heretics called Arians. They confess indeed that our Lord Jesus Christ is the only Son of the Father: the Father is the Father of the Son, and this one is the Son of the Father. They confess that the one who is Father is not Son, and that the one who is Son is not Father. They confess generation, but deny equality.

We—that is, the catholic faith, coming from the teaching of the Apostles, planted in us, received through the succession of transmission, and to be handed on soundly to those who come after—have held the truth between both errors.

In the error [Col. 1673] of the Sabellians there is only one: the one who is Father is himself Son. In the error of the Arians, the Father is indeed one and the Son another; but the Son is not only another person, he is also another thing or substance.

What, then, do you say in the middle? You have excluded the Sabellian; exclude the Arian as well. The Father is Father; the Son is Son: another person, not another thing, because he says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), as I also commended yesterday as far as I could.

When he hears “we are,” let the confused Sabellian depart; when he hears “one,” let the confused Arian depart. Let the catholic guide the vessel of his faith between the two, since shipwreck must be avoided on both sides.

Say, then, what the Gospel says: “I and the Father are one.” Therefore they are not different, because they are one; they are not one person, because he says, “we are.”

7. A little earlier he said, “My judgment is true, because I am not alone, but I and the Father who sent me”—as though he were saying: My judgment is true because I am the Son of God, because I speak the truth, because I myself am the truth.

Those people, understanding carnally, said, “Where is your father?” Now listen, Arian: “You know neither me nor my Father, because if you knew me, you would know my Father also.”

What does “If you knew me and my Father, you would know my Father also” mean, except “I and the Father are one”?

When you see one person resembling another—and let your Charity attend, for this is ordinary daily speech; do not find difficult what you recognize as customary—when you see someone resembling someone else, and you know whom he resembles, you say in astonishment, “How like that man this man is!” You would not say this unless there were two.

Someone who does not know the person to whom you say this man is similar asks, “Is he really similar?” And you say to him, “What? Do you not know that man?” He replies, “I do not.”

Then, so that you may make known to him the person he does not know through the one present whom he sees, you answer: “You have seen this man; you have seen that man.” In saying this, you have certainly not asserted that they are one and denied that there are two. Rather, because of their similarity, you have given this answer: You know this man and you know that man; he is exceedingly similar, and there is absolutely no difference.

So also the Lord says: “If you knew me, you would know my Father also”—not because the Father is the Son, but because the Son is like the Father.

Let the Arian blush. Thanks be to the Lord, for the Arian himself has departed from the Sabellian error and is not a Patripassian. He does not say that the Father himself, clothed in flesh, came to human beings, that he himself suffered, that he himself rose again, and that he somehow ascended to himself. He does not say this. With me he acknowledges that the Father is Father and the Son is Son.

But, brother, you have escaped that shipwreck; why are you heading toward another? The Father is Father; the Son is Son. Why do you say that they are unlike? Why different? Why of another substance?

If he were unlike the Father, would he have said to his disciples, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also”? Would he have said to the Jews, “If you knew me, you would know my Father also”? How could this be true unless that too were true: “I and the Father are one”?

8. Jesus spoke these words in the treasury, teaching in the temple: with great confidence, without fear. For he would not suffer what he did not wish to suffer; nor would he have been born if he had not wished to be born.

What follows, finally? “And no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come.”

When some people hear this, they believe that the Lord Christ was subject to fate [Col. 1674], and say: “Look, Christ had a fate.”

If only your heart were not foolish, you would not believe in fate! If “fate,” as some have understood it, is derived from *fari*, “to speak,” how can the Word of God have a fate, when in the Word itself are all things that have been created?

God did not determine something that he previously did not know. In his Word was what was made. The world was made; it was made, and it was there. How was it both made and there?

Because the house that a builder constructs first existed in his art; and there it existed better, without age and without ruin. Yet, to display his art, he builds the house, and the house somehow proceeded from the house. If the house collapses, the art remains.

So, in the Word of God were all things that were created, because “God made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103:24), and made everything known. He did not learn because he made; he made because he knew.

Things are known to us because they have been made. If they had not been known to him, they would not have been made. The Word therefore preceded them.

And what was before the Word of God? Absolutely nothing. For if something existed before it, it would not have been said, “In the beginning was the Word,” but “In the beginning the Word was made.”

Finally, what does Moses say about the world? “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1). He made what did not exist. If he made what did not exist, what existed beforehand? “In the beginning was the Word.” And from where came heaven and earth? “All things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3).

Do you therefore place Christ under fate? Where are the fates? “In heaven,” you say, “in the order and revolutions of the stars.”

How, then, can the one through whom heaven and the stars were made have a fate, when your own will, if you think rightly, transcends even the stars? Or because you know that Christ’s flesh was beneath heaven, do you therefore think that Christ’s power was subject to heaven?

9. Listen, fool: “His hour had not yet come”—not the hour when he would be compelled to die, but the hour when he would deign to be killed.

He himself knew when he ought to die. He attended to everything that had been foretold about him and waited for all that had been foretold as destined to occur before his passion to be completed, so that when they had been fulfilled, his passion would then come—in the order of a plan, not by fatal necessity.

Finally, listen, so that you may prove this. Among the other things prophesied about him, it was also written: “They gave me gall for food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68:22).

How these things happened, we know from the Gospel. First they gave him gall; he received it, tasted it, and spat it out. Later, hanging on the cross, so that all the predictions might be fulfilled, he said, “I thirst.” They took a sponge full of vinegar, tied it to a reed, and brought it to him as he hung there. He received it and said, “It is finished.”

What does “It is finished” mean? Everything that had been prophesied before my passion has been fulfilled. Why, then, am I still here?

After he said, “It is finished,” he bowed his head and gave up his spirit (John 19:28–30).

Did the thieves who were crucified beside him breathe their last when they wished? They were held by the bonds of the flesh, because they were not creators of flesh. Nailed to the cross, they suffered for a long time because they did not rule over their weakness.

But the Lord, when he wished, took flesh in the Virgin’s womb; when he wished, he came forth among human beings; as long as he wished, he lived among human beings; when he wished, he departed from the flesh. This is power, not necessity.

He was therefore awaiting this hour [Col. 1675]—not a fated hour, but an opportune and voluntary one—so that everything that needed to be fulfilled before his passion might first be completed.

For how could he have been placed under the necessity of fate who said elsewhere: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again. No one takes it from me, but I lay it down of my own accord, and I take it up again” (John 10:18)?

He displayed this power when the Jews were seeking him. “Whom do you seek?” he asked. They answered, “Jesus.” And he said, “I am he.” When they heard this voice, they drew back and fell to the ground (John 18:4–6).

10. Someone may say: If he possessed this power, why, when the Jews insulted him as he hung there and said, “If he is the Son of God, let him come down from the cross” (Matthew 27:40), did he not come down, so that by coming down he might show them his power?

Because he was teaching patience, he deferred the display of power. If he had come down as though provoked by their words, he might have been thought to have been overcome by the pain of their insults.

He did not come down at all; he remained fixed there, though he would depart whenever he wished. For what great thing would it have been for him to come down from the cross, when he was able to rise from the tomb?

Let us therefore understand—for this has been ministered to us—the hidden power of our Lord Jesus Christ at that time, which will be manifest in the judgment. Of that judgment it is said: “God will come manifestly, our God, and he will not be silent” (Psalm 49:3).

What does “he will come manifestly” mean? He came hidden; he will come manifestly as our God—that is, Christ.

And “he will not be silent”: what does this mean? It means that at first he was silent.

When was he silent? When he was judged, so that this too might be fulfilled, which the prophet had foretold: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and like a lamb before its shearer is silent, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7).

If he had not wished to suffer, he would not have suffered. If he had not suffered, that blood would not have been poured out. If that blood had not been poured out, the world would not have been redeemed.

Let us therefore give thanks both for the power of his divinity and for the compassion of his weakness: for the hidden power that the Jews did not know, concerning which it was just now said to them, “You know neither me nor my Father”; and for the flesh he assumed, which the Jews did know, whose homeland they knew, concerning which he said to them elsewhere, “You know me, and you know where I am from” (John 7:28).

Let us recognize both in Christ: the manner in which he is equal to the Father, and the manner in which the Father is greater than he. The one is Word; the one is flesh. The one is God; the one is human. Yet Christ is one, God and human.

## TREATISE XXXVIII

From the passage written, “Then Jesus said to them: I am going away, and you will seek me,” up to the passage, “Jesus said to them: The Beginning, because I also speak to you.” Chapter 8, verses 21–25.

1. The reading from the holy Gospel that preceded today’s reading had concluded in this way: the Lord spoke in the treasury, teaching in the temple whatever he wished and whatever you heard, “and no one seized him, because his hour had not yet come” (John 8:20).

On Sunday we discussed this, as he himself deigned to grant. We explained to your Charity why it was said, “His hour [Col. 1676] had not yet come,” lest any impiety should rashly suppose that Christ had been placed under some fatal necessity.

For the hour had not yet come when, in accordance with its proper order and with what had been foretold about him, he would not be compelled to die unwillingly but would be killed when ready.

2. Now he spoke to the Jews about that very passion of his, which lay not in necessity but in his power, saying: “I am going away.”

For death was a departure for Christ the Lord to the place from which he had come and from which he had never departed. “I am going away,” he says, “and you will seek me”—not from desire but from hatred.

After he had withdrawn from human sight, both those who hated him and those who loved him sought him: the former by persecuting him, the latter because they desired to possess him.

The Lord himself says through the prophet in the Psalms: “Flight has perished from me, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Psalm 141:5). Again, elsewhere in a psalm he says: “Let those who seek my soul be confounded and put to shame” (Psalm 39:15).

He blamed those who did not seek him and condemned those who did seek him. For it is evil not to seek Christ’s soul—but one should seek it in the manner in which the disciples sought it; and it is evil to seek Christ’s soul in the manner in which the Jews sought it. The former sought him in order to possess him; the latter in order to destroy him.

Therefore, because they were seeking him in this evil way, with a perverse heart, what did he add? “You will seek me, and”—lest you think that you will seek me rightly—“you will die in your sin.”

This is to seek Christ wrongly: to die in one’s sin. This is to hate the one through whom alone one could be saved.

Although people whose hope is in God ought not to return evil, or even evil for evil [Note: [Col. 1676] “nor” is absent from all manuscripts.], these people were returning evil for good. The Lord therefore foretold to them and, in his foreknowledge, pronounced the sentence that they would die in their sin.

Then he adds: “Where I am going, you cannot come.”

He said this elsewhere also to the disciples; yet he did not say to them, “You will die in your sin.” What did he say? The same thing he said to these people: “Where I am going, you cannot come” (John 13:33).

He did not take away their hope but foretold a delay. When the Lord spoke this to the disciples, they could not then come where he was going, but they were going to come later. These others, however, would never come, to whom he said in his foreknowledge, “You will die in your sin.”

3. When they heard these words, those who habitually thought carnally, judged according to the flesh, and heard and understood everything carnally, said: “Will he kill himself, because he said, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?”

Foolish words, utterly full of stupidity. What do you mean? Could they not go where he would have gone if he had killed himself? Were they not themselves going to die?

What, then, does “Will he kill himself, because he said, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come’?” mean?

If he were speaking of human death, what human being does not die? Therefore, when he said, “Where I am going,” he was not speaking of the place to which one goes at death [Note: [Col. 1676] Several manuscripts read “not to which” (*non quo*)], but of the place to which he himself was going after death.

Not understanding this, they gave that answer.

4. And what did the Lord say to those who savored earthly things?

He said to them: “You are from below.” That is why you savor earthly things: because, like serpents, you eat earth.

What [Col. 1677] does “you eat earth” mean? You feed on earthly things, delight in earthly things, gape after earthly things; you do not have your heart above.

“You are from below; I am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world.”

How could he be of this world, through whom the world was made? All human beings are from the world after the world, because the world existed first and then the human being came from the world. But Christ existed first, and then the world, because Christ was before the world, and before Christ there was nothing: “In the beginning was the Word; all things were made through him” (John 1:1, 3).

Thus he was from above. From what things above? From the air? Certainly not: birds fly there too. From the heaven that we see? Certainly not that either: the stars, sun, and moon move there. From the angels? Do not understand it in that way either: through him the angels were made, through whom all things were made.

From what heights, then, is Christ? From the Father himself. Nothing is higher than that God who begot the Word equal to himself, coeternal with himself, only-begotten, without time, through whom he created times.

Understand Christ as being from above in such a way that, by your thought, you surpass everything that has been made: the whole of creation, absolutely everything; every body, every created spirit, everything in any way subject to change. Surpass it all, just as John surpassed it, so that he might reach this: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

5. “I therefore,” he says, “am from above. You are of this world; I am not of this world. Therefore I told you that you will die in your sins.”

He has explained to us, brothers, what he intended us to understand by “You are of this world.” He said, “You are of this world” because they were sinners, because they were unjust, because they were unbelievers, because they savored earthly things.

What do you think, then, about the holy Apostles? How great was the difference between the Jews and the Apostles? How great the difference between darkness and light, faith and unbelief, piety and impiety, hope and despair, love and desire? The difference was great.

What then? Since there was so great a difference, were the Apostles not of this world? If you consider how they were born and from where they came—for they all came from Adam—they were of this world.

But what did the Lord himself say to them? “I chose you out of the world” [Note: Manuscripts read, “I chose you out of this world.”] (John 15:19).

Those who were of the world were therefore made not of the world and began to belong to the one through whom the world was made. These others, however, remained of the world, to whom it was said, “You will die in your sins.”

6. Let no one therefore say, brothers, “I am not of this world.” Whoever you are, as a human being you are of this world. But the one who made the world came to you and freed you from this world.

If the world delights you, you always wish to remain unclean. But if this world no longer delights you, you are already clean.

Nevertheless, if through some weakness the world still delights you, let the one who cleanses dwell in you, and you will be clean.

But if you are clean, you will not remain in the world, nor will you hear what the Jews heard: “You will die in your sins.”

For we were all born with sin; by living, we have all added to what we were born with [Col. 1678], and have become more of the world than we were when we were born from our parents.

And where would we be if the one who had absolutely no sin [Note: Manuscripts read, “who had no sin,” omitting “absolutely.”] had not come to release us from every sin? Because the Jews did not believe in him, they rightly heard, “You will die in your sins.”

For you could not possibly be without sin, since you were born in sin; but if you believe in me, he says, although you were born with sin, you will not die in your sin.

The Jews’ entire misery, then, consisted not in having sin, but in dying in their sins. This is what every Christian ought to flee.

This is why people hasten to Baptism. This is why those endangered by illness or by some other circumstance desire assistance. This is why even a nursing infant is carried from its mother to the Church in pious hands, lest it depart this life without Baptism and die in the sin in which it was born.

Most miserable is the condition, wretched the lot, of those who heard from the truthful mouth: “You will die in your sins.”

7. He explains, however, how this will happen to them: “For if you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.”

I believe that among the multitude listening to the Lord there were also those who were going to believe. Yet that extremely severe sentence—“You will die in your sin”—seemed to have fallen upon everyone; thus hope had also been taken away from those who were going to believe. Some were raging; others were afraid—or rather, they were not afraid but had already despaired.

He called them back to hope. For he added: “If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.” Therefore, if you believe that I am, you will not die in your sins.

Hope was restored to those who had despaired; those who were asleep were awakened; their hearts became alert. From that point many believed, as the subsequent narrative of the Gospel itself bears witness.

For there were there members of Christ who had not yet adhered to the body of Christ. And among that people by whom he was crucified, by whom he was hung upon the wood, by whom he was mocked as he hung, by whom he was wounded with a spear, by whom he was given gall and vinegar to drink, there were members of Christ, for whom he said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

What is not forgiven to one who turns, if the blood poured out by Christ is forgiven? What murderer should despair, if the one who even killed Christ has been restored to hope?

Many of them believed. Christ’s blood was given to them, so that they might drink it and be freed by it rather than be held guilty of having poured it out. Who should despair?

And if the thief was saved on the cross—shortly before a murderer, shortly afterward accused, convicted, condemned, and hung, yet set free—do not be surprised. Where he was convicted, there he was condemned; but where he was changed, there he was set free (Luke 23:34–43).

Among this people to whom the Lord was speaking, then, there were those who were going to die in their sin. There were also those who were going to believe in the one who was speaking and be freed from every sin.

8. Yet attend to what the Lord Christ says: “If you do not believe that I am, you will die in your sins.”

What does “If you do not believe that I am” mean? “I am” what? He added nothing; and because he added nothing, he commended something immense.

[Col. 1679] For it was expected that he would say what he was, yet he did not say it. What was expected? Perhaps: “Unless you believe that I am the Christ; unless you believe that I am the Son of God; unless you believe that I am the Word of the Father; unless you believe that I am the creator of the world; unless you believe that I am the maker and restorer of humanity, the creator and re-creator, the maker and remaker—unless you believe this, that I am, you will die in your sins.”

Great indeed is what he said in the words “I am” [Note: [Col. 1679] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain read: “Great is what he said himself, ‘I am.’” M.], because God had also said this to Moses: “I am who I am.”

Who can worthily express what “I am” means?

God was sending his servant Moses through his angel, to free his people from Egypt. You have read and heard this and know it, but I recall it nevertheless. He was sending Moses, who trembled, made excuses, yet obeyed.

When Moses was making excuses, he said to God, whom he understood to be speaking through the angel: “If the people say to me, ‘What is the name of the God who sent you?’ what shall I say to them?”
