And the Lord said to him: “I am who I am.” And he repeated: “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

Even there he did not say, “I am God,” or “I am the maker of the world,” or “I am the creator of all things,” or “I am the one who brought forth this very people who are to be freed.” He said only, “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you.’”

He did not add, “He who is your God,” or, “He who is the God of your fathers,” but simply said, “He who is has sent me to you.”

Perhaps this was too great even for Moses himself to grasp, just as it is great for us, and much more so for us, to understand what was said: “I am who I am,” and, “He who is has sent me to you.”

And even if Moses could grasp it, when would those to whom he was sent grasp it? The Lord therefore postponed what the human being could not grasp and added what he could grasp. For he continued: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exodus 3:13–15).

You can grasp this. But “I am who I am”—what mind can grasp that?

9. What, then, shall we do? Shall we dare to say something from what was said, “I am who I am,” or rather from what you heard the Lord say, “Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins”?

With my very small and almost nonexistent powers, shall I dare to discuss what the Lord Christ meant by “Unless you believe that I am”?

I shall dare to question the Lord himself. Listen to me questioning rather than arguing, seeking rather than presuming, learning rather than teaching. And certainly, through me or within me, question along with me.

The Lord himself is present, he who is everywhere. May he hear the desire to question and grant the result of understanding.

For by what words can I bring to your hearts whatever I may perhaps grasp? What sound would be sufficient? What eloquence is available? What powers of understanding? What ability to express it?

10. I shall therefore speak to our Lord Jesus Christ; I shall speak, and may he hear me [Note: Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read, “and he will hear me.” M.].

I believe that he is present; I have no doubt at all. For he himself said, “Behold, I am with you until the completion of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

O Lord [Col. 1680] our God, what is it that you said: “Unless you believe that I am”?

For what is not among the things you have made? Is heaven not there? Is earth not there? Are the things in heaven and on earth not there? Is the human being to whom you speak not there? Is the angel whom you send not there?

If all these things exist because they were made through you, what is it that you have kept as uniquely your own—“to be”—which you did not give to other things, so that you alone might be?

For how do I hear, “I am who I am,” as though other things were not? And how do I hear, “Unless you believe that I am”? Were those who heard him not existing? And if they were sinners, they were human beings.

What shall I do? Let the meaning of “to be” itself speak to the heart; let it speak within, let it speak inwardly. Let the inner human being hear; let the mind truly grasp “to be”: it is always to be in the same manner.

For any thing whatsoever—let me begin to argue and then cease from seeking; perhaps I wish to speak what I have heard, so that what I heard may give joy to my hearing and, as I speak, to yours—for any thing whatsoever, however excellent it may be, if it is changeable, does not truly exist.

There is no true being where there is also non-being. Whatever can be changed, once changed, is no longer what it was. If it is no longer what it was, a kind of death has occurred there: something that was has been destroyed there and is no longer.

The blackness has died from the head of a white-haired old man; beauty has died from the body of a tired and stooping old man; strength has died from the body of one who is ill; standing has died from the body of one who is walking; walking has died from the body of one who is standing; both walking and standing have died from the body of one who is lying down; speech has died from the tongue of one who is silent.

Whatever changes and becomes what it was not: I see there a kind of life in what now is, and death in what was.

Finally, when someone speaks of a dead person and asks, “Where is that man?” the answer is, “He was.”

O truth, which truly are!

For in all our actions and movements, and in every movement of creation altogether, I find two times: past and future. I seek the present, but nothing stands still.

What I have said is no longer; what I am going to say is not yet. What I have done is no longer; what I am going to do is not yet. What I have lived is no longer; what I am going to live is not yet.

In every movement of things I find past and future. In the truth that remains, I find neither past nor future, but only the present—and this incorruptibly, something that does not exist in creation.

Examine the changes of things: you will find “He was” and “He will be.” Think of God: you will find “He is,” where “He was” and “He will be” cannot exist.

Therefore, that you too may be, transcend time. But who can transcend it by his own powers? May the one who said to the Father, “I desire that where I am, they too may be with me,” raise you to that place.

In promising this, so that we may not die in our sins, the Lord Jesus Christ seems to me to have said nothing other than this in the words, “Unless you believe that I am”: “Unless you believe that I am God, you will die in your sins.”

Thanks be to God, because he said, “Unless you believe”; he did not say, “Unless you grasp.” For who could grasp this?

Or, because I have dared to say it, and you seem to have understood, have you grasped something of so great an ineffability [Col. 1681]? [Note: Louvain reads, “and unless”; the other printed editions and the manuscripts read, “you seem.”]

If you do not grasp it, faith frees you. Therefore the Lord did not say, “Unless you grasp that I am,” but said what they could do: “Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins.”

### 11.

And those people, always setting their minds on earthly things and always hearing and answering according to the flesh—what did they say to him? “Who are you?” For when you said, “Unless you believe that I am,” you did not add what you were. “Who are you, that we should believe?” And he replied, “The Beginning.” Behold what it means to be. The Beginning cannot be changed: the Beginning remains in itself and renews all things; it is the Beginning to whom it was said, “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Psalm 101:28).

“The Beginning,” he says, “because I also speak to you.” [Note: The printed editions read *qui* (“who”), but most manuscripts read *quia* (“because”), in accordance with the Greek, *hoti*.] Believe me to be the Beginning, lest you die in your sins. For, as though in saying “Who are you?” they had said nothing other than, “What are we to believe you to be?” he replied, “The Beginning”—that is, “Believe me to be the Beginning.”

For in the Greek expression the distinction is discernible which cannot be made in Latin. Among the Greeks, *archē* (“beginning”) is feminine, just as among us *lex* (“law”) is feminine, whereas among them it is masculine; likewise, *sapientia* (“wisdom”) is feminine both among us and among them. The customary usage of speech therefore varies the genders of words across different languages, because in the things themselves one does not find biological sex. Wisdom is not truly female, since Christ is the Wisdom of God (1 Corinthians 1:24), while Christ is called by a masculine noun and wisdom by a feminine one.

When the Jews therefore said, “Who are you?” he who knew that some people there would believe, and that they had said “Who are you?” in order to learn what they ought to believe about him, replied, “The Beginning”—not as though he were saying, “I am the Beginning,” but as though he were saying, “Believe me to be the Beginning.” [Note: In Greek it is *tēn archēn*; to some this has here the force of an adverb, like the Latin *principio* and *primum* (“in the beginning,” “first”); this is certainly how it sounded to Chrysostom. Ambrose, Bernard, and others, however, support Augustine’s interpretation.]

It is as though he wished to say that he was the Truth, and, when they said, “Who are you?” he answered, “The Truth,” although in response to the words “Who are you?” he might seem to have needed to say, “Truth”—that is, “I am Truth.” But he answered more profoundly, since he saw that they had said “Who are you?” as if they were saying: “Since we have heard from you, ‘Unless you believe that I am,’ what are we to believe you to be?” To this he replied, “The Beginning,” as though he were saying, “Believe me to be the Beginning.”

And he added, “Because I also speak to you”—that is, because I have become humble for your sake and descended to these words. For if the Beginning had remained with the Father as it is, without taking the form of a servant and speaking as a human being to human beings, how would they have believed in him, when weak hearts could not hear the intelligible Word without perceptible speech?

“Therefore,” he says, “believe me to be the Beginning; because, so that you may believe, I not only am, but also speak to you.” But it would take too long now to speak to you about this matter. Let it therefore please Your Charity that, with his help, we preserve what remains and return tomorrow.

# TRACTATE XXXIX

From the passage written, “I have many things to say about you and to judge,” up to, “And they did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father.” Chapter 8, verses 26–27.

### 1.

The words of our Lord Jesus Christ which he spoke with the Jews—moderating his speech in such a way that the blind would not see, while the faithful would open their eyes—are those which have been read today from the holy Gospel:

“Then the Jews said, ‘Who are you?’” For above the Lord had said, “Unless you believe that I am, you will die in your sins” (John 8:24–25). They therefore said to him, “Who are you?” as though seeking to know in whom they ought to believe, lest they die in their sin.

He replied to those who said, “Who are you?” and said, “The Beginning, because I also speak to you.”

If the Lord said that he was the Beginning, it may be asked whether the Father too is the Beginning. For if the Son is the Beginning, since he has a Father, how much more readily should God the Father be understood to be the Beginning, since he has a Son to whom he is Father, but does not have anyone from whom he is?

The Son is the Father’s Son, and the Father is certainly the Son’s Father. But the Son is called God from God, light from light. The Father is called light, but not light from light; the Father is called God, but not God from God.

If, therefore, God from God and light from light is the Beginning, how much more readily is the Beginning understood to be the light from whom comes light, and the God from whom comes God? It therefore seems absurd, beloved, that we should call the Son the Beginning and not call the Father the Beginning.

### 2.

But what shall we do? Will there then be two Beginnings? We must be careful not to say this. What, then? If the Father is the Beginning and the Son is the Beginning, how are there not two Beginnings?

How do we call the Father God and the Son God, yet do not call them two gods? For it is impious to say “two gods,” impious to say “three gods.” Yet he who is Father is not Son, and he who is Son is not Father. The Holy Spirit, however, is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, and is neither Father nor Son.

Although, then, Catholic ears have been instructed in the bosom of Mother Church that he who is Father is not Son, he who is Son is not Father, and the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son is neither Son nor Father, we nevertheless do not say that there are three gods. Yet if each one individually is asked about, we must confess that whichever one we are asked about is God.

### 3.

These things seem absurd to people accustomed to applying ordinary categories to extraordinary things, visible things to invisible things, and comparing the creature with the Creator. For unbelievers sometimes ask us:

“Do you call the Father whom you speak of God?”

We answer: “God.”

“Do you call the Son whom you speak of God?”

We answer: “God.”

“Do you call the Holy Spirit whom you speak of God?”

We answer: “God.”

“Then,” they say, “the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three gods?”

We answer: “No.”

They are disturbed because they are not enlightened. They have a closed heart because they do not possess the key of faith.

Let us therefore, brothers, with faith preceding us—for faith heals the eye of our heart—grasp without obscurity what we understand, and believe without hesitation what we do not understand. Let us not depart from the foundation of faith, so that we may come to the summit of perfection.

The Father is God, the Son is God, the Holy Spirit is God; and yet the Father is not the one who is the Son, nor the Son the one who is the Father, nor is the Holy Spirit of the Father and the Son either Father or Son.

The Trinity is one God; the Trinity is one eternity, one power, one majesty: three—but not gods. [Note: The printed editions read “three persons.” All the manuscripts lack the word “persons,” and the Louvain editors had ordered that it be removed in the *Castigations* to volume nine.]

Let no malicious critic answer me, “What, then, are three?” For if there are three, he says, you ought to say what three are.

I answer: “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.”

“Behold,” he says, “you have named three; but state what three are.”

Rather, you count them; for I complete the three when I say, “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.” What the Father is in relation to himself is God; what he is in relation to the Son is Father. What the Son is in relation to himself is God; what he is in relation to the Father is Son.

### 4.

You can recognize these things I am saying from everyday comparisons. One human being and another human being: if one is a father and the other a son, what each is as a human being is in relation to himself; what one is as father is in relation to the son; and what the son is as a human being is in relation to himself, while what he is as son is in relation to the father.

“Father” is a name said in relation to something, and “son” likewise in relation to something; yet these two are human beings.

But the Father who is God is Father in relation to something, namely, the Son; and the Son who is God is Son in relation to something, namely, the Father. Yet they are not two gods in the way those two are two human beings.

Why is it not so there? Because one thing is this and another thing that; because there it is divinity. There is something ineffable which cannot be explained in words, so that there is number and yet there is no number.

For see whether number does not seem to appear in “Father, Son, and Holy Spirit”—the Trinity. If there are three, what are the three? Number fails. Thus God neither departs from number nor is contained by number.

Because there are three, it is as though there were number; but if you ask what the three are, there is no number. Hence it is said, “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and of his wisdom there is no number” (Psalm 147:5).

When you begin to think, you begin to count; when you have counted, you cannot answer what you have counted.

The Father is Father; the Son is Son; the Holy Spirit is the Holy Spirit. What are these three—the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit? Are they three gods? No. Are they three omnipotent beings? No. Are they three creators of the world? No.

Is the Father therefore omnipotent? Certainly. Is the Son therefore not omnipotent? Certainly the Son too is omnipotent. Is the Holy Spirit therefore not omnipotent? He too is omnipotent.

Are there therefore three omnipotent beings? No, but one omnipotent being.

They suggest number only in what they are in relation to one another, not in what they are in relation to themselves. Because God the Father is God in relation to himself, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, there are not three gods. Because he is omnipotent in relation to himself, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, there are not three omnipotent beings.

But because the Father is not Father in relation to himself, but to the Son; nor is the Son Son in relation to himself, but to the Father; nor is the Spirit in relation to himself insofar as he is called the Spirit of the Father and the Son, there is nothing I can call “three” except the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—one God, one omnipotent being.

Therefore there is one Beginning.

### 5.

Receive something from the holy Scriptures by which you may somehow grasp what is being said.

After our Lord Jesus Christ had risen and, when he wished, ascended into heaven, when ten days had been completed there, he sent the Holy Spirit from heaven. Those who were present, filled with him in one room, began to speak in the languages of all nations.

The Lord’s slayers were terrified by the miracle; pierced with remorse, they grieved; grieving, they were changed; changed, they believed. Three thousand people joined the body of the Lord—that is, the number of the faithful.

Then, after another miracle, another five thousand joined them. A single, considerable people came into being. All of them, having received the Holy Spirit, by whom spiritual love was kindled, were brought into one through that very charity and the fervor of the spirit. They began, in the unity of their fellowship, to sell everything they possessed and place the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, so that they might be distributed to each person according to his need.

Scripture says of them that “they had one soul and one heart directed toward God” (Acts 2–4).

Attend, then, brothers, and recognize here the mystery of the Trinity: how we say, “The Father is, the Son is, and the Holy Spirit is,” and yet there is one God.

Behold, there were so many thousands, and there was one heart. Behold, there were so many thousands, and there was one soul. But where? In God. How much more, then, is God himself one?

Am I wrong when I say “two human beings, two souls,” or “three human beings, three souls,” or “many human beings, many souls”? Certainly I am speaking correctly.

Let them draw near to God, and there is one soul of all. If, by drawing near to God, many souls become one soul through charity, and many hearts become one heart, what does that very fountain of charity accomplish in the Father and the Son? Is the Trinity not even more truly one God there?

For charity comes to us from him, from the Holy Spirit himself, as the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

If, then, the love of God poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit given to us makes many souls one soul and many hearts one heart, how much more are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit one God, one light, and one Beginning?

### 6.

Let us therefore hear the Beginning speaking to us.

“I have many things,” he says, “to say about you and to judge.”

You remember that he said, “I judge no one” (John 8:15). Yet now he says, “I have many things to say about you and to judge.”

But “I do not judge” is one thing, and “I have to judge” another. “I do not judge,” he said with reference to the present. For he had come to save the world, not to judge the world (John 12:47).

But when he says, “I have many things to say about you and to judge,” he speaks of the future judgment. For this reason he ascended, so that he might come to judge the living and the dead. No one will judge more justly than the one who was unjustly judged.

“I have many things,” he says, “to say about you and to judge; but the one who sent me is truthful.”

See how the Son, being equal to the Father, gives glory to the Father. He provides an example for us and, as it were, speaks within our hearts:

“O faithful human being, if you hear my Gospel, your Lord God says to you: ‘I, the Word who was in the beginning, God with God, equal to the Father and co-eternal with the one who begot me, give glory to him whose Son I am. How then are you proud against the one whose servant you are?’”

### 7.

“I have many things,” he says, “to say about you and to judge; but the one who sent me is truthful”—as though he were saying, “I judge truly because I am the Truth, the Son of the truthful one.”

The Father is truthful; the Son is Truth. What are we to think is greater? Let us consider, if we can, what is greater: one who is truthful or Truth.

Let us ask about certain examples. Is a pious person greater, or piety? Piety itself is greater. A person is pious from piety; piety is not pious from a person. Piety can exist even if the one who was pious has become impious. He has lost piety; he has taken nothing away from piety.

Again, what of a beautiful person and beauty? Beauty is greater than the beautiful person. Beauty makes something beautiful; the beautiful does not make beauty.

What of the chaste person and chastity? Certainly chastity is greater than the chaste person. If chastity did not exist, from where would this person be chaste? He would not possess it. But if he does not wish to remain chaste, chastity remains intact.

If, then, piety is greater than a pious person, beauty greater than a beautiful person, and chastity greater than a chaste person, shall we say that Truth is greater than the one who is truthful?

If we say this, we will begin to say that the Son is greater than the Father. For the Lord himself says most plainly: “I am the way, and the Truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Therefore, if the Son is Truth, what is the Father except what Truth itself says: “The one who sent me is truthful”?

The Son is Truth; the Father is truthful. I ask which is greater, but I find equality. For the truthful Father is not truthful from some part of the Truth which he has received, but from the Truth which he has begotten in its entirety.

### 8.

I see that this must be explained more clearly. And certainly, so that I do not keep you here too long, let the discussion continue only this far today. When I have finished what I wish to say, with God’s help the sermon will be concluded.

I have said this in order to make you attentive.

Every soul, because it is a changeable thing, and although a great creature, nevertheless a creature; although better than the body, nevertheless made—every soul, therefore, because it is changeable, is sometimes believing and sometimes not believing; sometimes willing and sometimes unwilling; sometimes adulterous and sometimes chaste; sometimes good and sometimes evil. It is changeable.

But God is what he is; therefore he has retained for himself the proper name, “I am who I am” (Exodus 3:14).

This is what the Son means when he says, “Unless you believe that I am.” The same applies to the question, “Who are you?”—“The Beginning” (John 8:24–25).

God, therefore, is unchangeable; the soul is changeable.

When the soul receives from God the source of its goodness, it becomes good by participation, just as your eye sees by participation. When the light is removed, it does not see; it sees because it has become a participant in the light.

Because the soul becomes good by participation, if it changes and begins to be evil, the goodness of which it had been a good participant remains. It became a participant in a certain goodness when it was good; when it changes for the worse, that goodness remains intact.

If the soul departs and becomes evil, goodness is not diminished. If it returns and becomes good, goodness is not increased.

Your eye has become a participant in this light, and you see. Is it closed? You have not diminished this light. Is it open? You have not increased this light.

With this comparison given, brothers, understand that if the soul is pious, piety exists with God, in which the soul participates; if the soul is chaste, chastity exists with God, in which the soul participates; if the soul is good, goodness exists with God, in which the soul participates; if the soul is truthful, Truth exists with God, in which the soul participates.

If the soul does not participate in it, “every human being is a liar” (Psalm 115:11). If every human being is a liar, no human being is truthful from himself.

But the Father is truthful from himself, because he has begotten Truth.

It is one thing to say, “This human being is truthful,” because he has already received a share in Truth; it is another to say, “God is truthful,” because he has begotten Truth.

Behold how God is truthful—not by participating, but by begetting Truth.

I see that you have understood, and I rejoice. Let this be enough for you today. Whatever remains, when it pleases the Lord, we shall explain as he grants it.

# TRACTATE XL

From the passage, “Then Jesus said to them: When you have lifted up the Son of Man,” up to, “And you will know the Truth, and the Truth will set you free.” Chapter 8, verses 28–32.

### 1.

Your Charity has already heard much from the holy Gospel according to John, which you see us carrying in our hands. By God’s gift, we have discussed it as best we could, commending to you above all this evangelist’s choice to speak about the Lord’s divinity, according to which the only-begotten Son of God is equal to the Father, and for that reason his comparison to an eagle—for no bird is said to fly higher.

Therefore listen with the greatest attention to what follows in sequence, as the Lord grants us to discuss it.

### 2.

In the preceding reading we spoke to you, explaining how the Father is to be understood as truthful and the Son as Truth.

When the Lord Jesus had said, “The one who sent me is truthful” (John 8:26), the Jews did not understand that he was speaking to them about the Father.

And he said to them what you have just heard when it was read:

“When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am, and that I do nothing from myself, but speak these things as the Father taught me.”

What does this mean? He seems to have said nothing other than that they would come to know who he was after his Passion.

Without a doubt, then, he saw there some people whom he himself knew, whom he himself, together with all his saints, had chosen in foreknowledge before the foundation of the world, and who would believe after his Passion.

These are the people whom we continually commend and set before you for imitation with great exhortation.

After the Holy Spirit had been sent from above, following the Lord’s Passion, resurrection, and ascension, miracles were performed in the name of the one whom the Jews had despised as they persecuted him as though he were dead. They were pierced in heart; those who had killed him in their fury were changed and believed; and the blood which they had shed in their fury they drank by believing.

These were the three thousand and the five thousand Jews (Acts 2:37, 41; 4:4) whom he saw there when he said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.”

It was as though he were saying, “I defer your knowledge in order to complete my Passion. In due course [or: according to your own order] you will know who I am.” [Note: The printed editions read *verso*; the manuscripts read *vestro*.]

Not all those who were listening would then believe—that is, after the Lord’s Passion. For shortly afterward he says, “As he was saying these things, many believed in him,” and the Son of Man had not yet been lifted up.

By “lifting up” he means the lifting up of the Passion, not glorification; of the cross, not heaven. For he too was lifted up there when he hung upon the wood.

But that lifting up was a humiliation. For then he became obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8).

This had to be fulfilled through the hands of those who would later believe, to whom he says, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.”

Why this, unless so that no one might despair, no matter what crime he was conscious of in himself, when he saw that the murderers of Christ were forgiven?

### 3.

Recognizing these people in that crowd, the Lord said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am.”

You already know what “I am” means, and it need not be repeated constantly, lest so great a matter produce weariness. Recall, “I am who I am,” and “He who is has sent me” (Exodus 3:14), and you will understand what was said: “Then you will know that I am.”

But the Father is, and the Holy Spirit is. The whole Trinity pertains to being.

Because the Lord was speaking as the Son, however, lest the error of the Sabellians—also called Patripassians—should enter into what he said, “Then you will know that I am,” an error which I have commended to you not to hold but to avoid, namely, the error of those who said, “He himself is the Father; he himself is the Son. There are two names, but one reality”—because of this error, then, which had to be avoided, when the Lord had said, “Then you will know that I am,” he immediately added, “And I do nothing from myself, but speak these things as the Father taught me.”

The Sabellian had begun to rejoice, having found an opportunity for his error. But as soon as he raised himself up, as it were, in the darkness, he was confounded by the light of the following sentence.

You thought he was the Father because he said, “I am.” Hear that he is the Son: “I do nothing from myself.”

What does “I do nothing from myself” mean? “I am not from myself.”

The Son is God from the Father; the Father, however, is not God from the Son. The Son is God from God; the Father is God, but not from God. The Son is light from light; the Father is light, but not from light. The Son is, but he is from the one from whom he is; the Father is, but he is not from one from whom he is.

### 4.

When he added, “As the Father taught me, so I speak,” let no carnal thought creep into the mind of any of you, my brothers.

Human weakness cannot think except of what it is accustomed to do or hear. Do not therefore place before your eyes, as it were, two human beings, one a father and the other a son, with the father speaking to the son—as you do when you say certain words to your son, admonishing and instructing him how to speak, so that whatever he has heard from you he may commit to memory, and, after committing it to memory, bring it forth with his tongue, distinguish it by sounds, and convey to other ears what he has received in his own.

Do not think in this way, lest you construct idols in your heart.

Do not imagine in that Trinity a human form, the human outlines of limbs, the shape of human flesh, these perceptible senses, bodily stature and movement, the function of the tongue, or distinctions of sound—except insofar as these belong to the form of a servant which the only-begotten Son assumed when the Word became flesh in order to dwell among us (John 1:14).

There I do not forbid you, human weakness, to think what you know; indeed, I even compel you to do so. If true faith is in you, think of Christ in this way. But think of him as such from the virgin Mary, not from God the Father.

He was an infant; he grew as a human being; he walked as a human being; he hungered and thirsted as a human being; he slept as a human being; finally, he suffered as a human being, was hung upon the wood, killed, and buried as a human being.

In the same form he rose again; in the same form he ascended into heaven before the eyes of the disciples; in the same form he will come to judgment.

For the voice of the angels is expressed in the Gospel: “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11).

When, therefore, you think of the form of a servant in Christ, think of a human likeness, if faith is in you. But when you think, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1), let every human image vanish from your heart.

Let whatever is bounded by bodily limits, whatever is contained by spatial extension, or whatever is spread out by however great a mass be driven from your thoughts. Let such an image perish from your heart.

Think, if you can, of the beauty of wisdom; let the beauty of justice come before you. Is it a form? Is it a stature? Is it a color? None of these, and yet it exists.

For if it did not exist, it would neither be loved nor rightly praised, nor, being loved and praised, would it be held in heart and conduct. Yet human beings become wise. From where would they become wise unless wisdom existed?

Moreover, human being, if you cannot see your wisdom with the eyes of the flesh, nor think of it through an image of the kind by which bodily things are thought, do you dare to impose the form of a human body upon the Wisdom of God?

### 5.

What, then, shall we say, brothers? How did the Father speak to the Son, since the Son says, “As the Father taught me, so I speak”?

Did he speak to him? When the Father taught the Son, did he form words as you do when you teach your son? How does he form words for the Word? What multiplicity of words could be made for the one Word?

Did the Father’s Word have ears at the Father’s mouth? These are carnal thoughts; let them perish from your hearts.

For consider what I am saying. If you have understood what I said, I certainly spoke, and my words sounded; through their sounds they struck your ears, and through your sense of hearing they conveyed a meaning to your heart—if you have understood.

Suppose someone heard a Latin-speaking person, merely heard him, but did not understand what he said. As far as the noise issuing from my mouth is concerned, the one who did not understand became a participant in it just as you did. He heard the sound; the same syllables struck his ears; but they produced nothing in his heart. Why? Because he did not understand.

But if you understood, how did you understand? I made a sound at your ear. Did I kindle a light in your heart? Without a doubt, if what I said is true, and if you not only heard this truth but also understood it, two things occurred there. Distinguish them: hearing and understanding.

Hearing was produced through me; understanding, through whom?

I spoke to your ear so that you might hear. Who spoke to your heart so that you might understand?

Without doubt, someone also spoke something to your heart, so that not only this noise of words might strike your ear, but some truth might also descend into your heart. Someone spoke to your heart as well, but you do not see him.

If you understood, brothers, something was spoken to your heart too. Understanding is God’s gift.

Who spoke this in your heart, if you understood? To whom the Psalm says, “Give me understanding, that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm 119:73).

For example, a bishop has spoken. Someone asks, “What did he say?” You answer what he said and add, “He spoke the truth.”

Then another, who did not understand, says, “What did he say, or what is it that you praise?”

Both heard me; I spoke to both. But God spoke to one of them.

If it is permitted to compare small things with great, since what are we in relation to him? Nevertheless, God does something in us in an incorporeal and spiritual way which is neither a sound striking the ear, nor a color distinguished by the eyes, nor a scent perceived by the nostrils, nor a taste judged by the throat, nor something hard or soft sensed by touch.

Yet it is something which is easy to feel and impossible to explain.

If, then, as I began to say, God speaks in our hearts without sound, how does he speak to his Son?

Think in this way, brothers; think in this way, as far as you can, as I have said, if it is in any way permissible to compare small things with great.

The Father spoke incorporeally to the Son because the Father begot the Son incorporeally.

He did not teach him as though he had begotten him ignorant. Rather, “to teach him” means to beget him knowing; and “the Father taught me” means “the Father begot me knowing.”

For if, as few understand, the nature of Truth is simple, then for the Son to be is the same as for him to know.

Therefore he receives from the one from whom he receives his being that he knows. It is not that he first existed from him and afterward came to know from him. Rather, just as by begetting the Father gave him being, so by begetting he gave him knowledge.

For in a simple nature, as has been said, being and knowing are not two different things, but the very same thing.

### 6.

He said these things to the Jews and added, “And the one who sent me is with me.”

He had already said this before, but he repeatedly recalls a great truth: “He sent me, and he is with me.”

If he is with you, Lord, then it was not one sent by the other, but both came. Yet although both are together, one was sent and the other sent him, because sending is incarnation, and the incarnation belongs only to the Son, not to the Father.

The Father therefore sent the Son, but did not depart from the Son. For the Father was not absent from the place to which he sent the Son.

Where is the one who made all things not present? Where is the one who said, “Do I not fill heaven and earth?” (Jeremiah 23:24)

But perhaps the Father is everywhere while the Son is not everywhere? Hear the evangelist: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him” (John 1:10).

Therefore, he says, “The one who sent me”—by whose, as it were, paternal authority I was made incarnate—“is with me; he has not left me.”

Why has he not left me? “He has not left me alone,” he says, “because I always do the things that please him.”

This is the equality which exists always—not from some beginning and thereafter, but without beginning and without end. For God’s generation has no beginning in time, because time itself was made through the one who was begotten.

### 7.

As he was saying these things, many believed in him.

Would that, while I am speaking, many who had held another opinion might understand and believe in him.

Perhaps there are some Arians in this crowd. I do not dare suspect that there are Sabellians, who say that the Father himself is the Son, for that heresy is very ancient and has gradually been disemboweled.

The Arians, however, still seem to have some movements, like a rotting corpse—or, at most, like a person in the process of dying. The rest must be freed from it, as many have already been freed.

Indeed, this city did not have them; but after many foreigners arrived, some of them came as well.

Behold: while the Lord was speaking, many Jews believed in him. Let the Arians also believe while I am speaking—not in me, but together with me.

### 8.

Then the Lord said to the Jews who had believed in him, “If you remain in my word.”

He says “remain” because you have been initiated, because you have also begun to be there. If you remain—that is, in the faith which began to exist in you who believe—where will you arrive?

See what kind of beginning it is and where it leads. You have loved the foundation; look toward the summit, and from this humility seek another height.

Faith possesses humility. Knowledge, immortality, and eternity do not possess humility, but height: elevation, no falling away, eternal stability, no conquest by the enemy, and no fear of failing.

It is a great thing that begins from faith, but it is despised. Even in a building, the foundation is usually despised by the inexperienced. A great trench is made; stones are thrown in here and there in whatever fashion; no refinement or beauty appears there.

The same is true of the root of a tree: no beauty appears there. Yet everything that delights you in the tree rose from the root.

You see the root and are not delighted; you see the tree and marvel. Fool, what you marvel at arose from what does not delight you.

The faith of believers seems small to you because you do not have a scale with which to weigh it. Hear, then, where it leads, and see how great it is, just as the Lord himself says elsewhere: “If you have faith like a mustard seed” (Matthew 17:20).

What is more humble? What is more powerful? What is smaller? What is more fervent?

“Therefore,” he says, “if you remain in my word, in which you have believed, where will you be led? You will truly be my disciples.”

“And what benefit is that to us?”

“And you will know the Truth.”

### 9.

What does he promise believers, brothers? “And you will know the Truth.”

What then? Had they not known the Truth when the Lord was speaking? If they had not known it, how did they believe?

They did not believe because they had known; rather, they believed so that they might know. For we believe in order to know; we do not know in order to believe.

What we are going to know is what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (Isaiah 64:4; 1 Corinthians 2:9).

For what is faith except believing what you do not see? Faith, then, is believing what you do not see; Truth is seeing what you have believed, as he himself says in another passage.

For this reason the Lord first walked upon the earth in order to establish faith. He was human; he had become humble. He was seen by everyone, but was not recognized by everyone. He was rejected by many; he was killed by the crowd; a few grieved for him. Yet even by those who grieved for him he was not yet recognized as he truly was.

All this is, as it were, the beginning of the outlines of faith and the structure of what was to come.

The Lord himself, considering this, says in another passage: “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments; and whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and show myself to him” (John 14:21).

Those who heard him were already seeing him, yet he promised that they would see him if they loved him.

So here too: “You will know the Truth.”

What then? Is what you said not the Truth? It is Truth, but it is still believed; it is not yet seen. If one remains in what is believed, one arrives at what is to be seen.

For this reason the holy evangelist John himself says in his Epistle:

“Beloved, we are children of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We already are, and we shall be something. What more shall we be than we are?”

Listen: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him. Why? Because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

A great promise—but it is the reward of faith. Do you seek the reward? Let the work precede it. If you believe, demand the reward of faith; but if you do not believe, with what face do you seek faith’s reward?

“If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples,” so that you may contemplate Truth itself as it is—not through sounding words, but through shining light, when what is read in the Psalm has satisfied us: “The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, O Lord” (Psalm 4:7). [Note: All the manuscripts read *cum satiaverit nos* (“when it has satisfied us”); the printed editions read *cum signaverit nos* (“when it has marked/sealed us”).]

We are God’s coin; we wandered away from the treasury. What had been impressed upon us has been worn away by our wandering. The one who formed us has come to restore us, because he himself had formed us. He too seeks his own coin, just as Caesar seeks his own coin.

Therefore he says, “Give back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar, and to God what belongs to God” (Matthew 22:21): coins to Caesar, yourselves to God.

Then, therefore, Truth will be stamped upon us.

### 10

What shall I say to Your Charity? Oh, if only our heart were somehow sighing for that ineffable glory! If only we sensed our pilgrimage amid groaning, did not love the world, and continually knocked with devout mind at him who called us! Desire is the bosom of the heart; we shall receive, if we extend our desire as far as we can. The divine Scripture works this in us, the gathering of peoples works this, the celebration of the sacraments works this, holy baptism works this, the hymns of praise to God work this, and this very discourse of ours works this: that this desire may not merely be sown and germinate, but also be enlarged to the measure of such capacity that it may be fit to receive what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor entered into the human heart.

But love with me. He who loves God does not love money much. And I have felt our weakness; I did not dare to say, “He does not love money,” but “He does not love money much”—as though money ought to be loved, but not much. Oh, if only we loved God worthily, we would not love money at all! Money will be an instrument of your pilgrimage, not a stimulus to greed; something you use for necessity, not something you enjoy for pleasure.

Love God, if what you hear and praise has accomplished anything in you. Use the world, but do not let the world possess you. You have entered [Note: [Col. 1691] Two manuscripts read, “the world which you entered.” As many others read, “the place into which you entered.”]; you are making a journey, and you came to depart, not to remain. You are making a journey; this life is an inn. Use money as a traveler at an inn uses the table, cup, pitcher, and little bed: you will leave them, not remain with them.

If you are such people, lift up your heart, you who can, and listen to me. If you are such people, you will come to his promises. For this is not difficult for you, because great is the hand of him who called you. He called; let him be invoked. Say to him: “You called us; we invoke you. Behold, we have heard you calling; hear us invoking you. Lead us to what you promised; complete what you began. Do not abandon your gifts; do not abandon your field. [Col. 1692] May your shoots enter the granary.” Temptations abound in the world [Note: [Col. 1692] The printed editions read, “storms abound in the world.” But the manuscripts read, “temptations abound.”]; but greater is he who made the world. Temptations abound; but the one who places his hope in him in whom there is no failing does not fail.

### 11

For this reason I have encouraged you with these words, brothers: the freedom of which our Lord Jesus Christ speaks does not belong to this present time. See what he added: “You will truly be my disciples, and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free.” What does “it will set you free” mean? It will make you free. Finally, the carnal Jews, judging according to the flesh—not those who had believed, but those in that crowd who did not believe—thought that an insult had been directed against them because he said to them, “The truth will set you free.” They were indignant that he had implied they were slaves. And indeed they were slaves. He explains to them what slavery is and what the future freedom is that he himself promises. But it would be too long to discuss this freedom and that slavery today.

## TRACTATE XLI

Again on the passage, “Jesus was saying to those Jews who had believed in him,” up to, “If therefore the Son sets you free, you will truly be free.” John 8:31–36.

### 1

What follows from the previous reading and was read to us today from the holy Gospel I postponed saying, because I had already said much, and the freedom to which the grace of the Savior calls us deserved to be discussed neither cursorily nor negligently. Therefore, with the Lord’s help, we have decided to speak to you about it today.

Those to whom the Lord Jesus Christ was speaking were Jews: for the most part enemies, but in part already becoming friends—and destined to become so. For among them he saw certain people who, as we have already said, would believe after his Passion. Looking at them, he had said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28).

There were also people there who immediately believed when he spoke these words. To them he spoke what we heard today: “Jesus was therefore saying to the Jews who had believed him: If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” By remaining, you will become so; for because you are now believers, by remaining you will become seeing believers.

Therefore it follows: “And you will know the truth.” The truth is unchangeable. The truth is bread: it refreshes minds and does not fail; it changes the one who eats, but is not itself changed into the one who eats. This truth is the Word of God, God with God, the only-begotten Son.

This Truth clothed itself in flesh for our sake, so that it might be born of the Virgin Mary and the prophecy might be fulfilled: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). When this Truth was therefore speaking with the Jews, it was hidden in flesh—not hidden so that it might be denied, but so that it might be deferred: deferred so that it might suffer in the flesh; and it suffered in the flesh so that sinful flesh might be redeemed.

Thus our Lord Jesus Christ, standing visibly according to the weakness of the flesh but hidden according to the majesty of his divinity, said to those who had believed him while he was saying these things: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples.” “The one who perseveres [Col. 1693] to the end will be saved” (Matthew 10:22). “And you will know the truth,” which now lies hidden from you and is speaking to you. “And the truth will set you free.”

The Lord used this expression, “will set you free,” with reference to freedom. For “to set free” properly means nothing other than “to make free.” To save means nothing other than “to make safe”; to heal means nothing other than “to make healthy”; to enrich means nothing other than “to make rich”; so to set free means nothing other than “to make free.”

This is clearer in the Greek word [Note: [Col. 1693] Greek: *eleutherōsei*, “he will set free”]. For in Latin usage we often say that a person is “set free” when this has nothing to do with freedom but only with deliverance—for example, someone is said to be “set free” from an illness. This is customary speech, but not strictly precise. The Lord used the expression in this way when he said, “The truth will set you free,” so that in the Greek language no one could doubt that he was speaking of freedom.

### 2

Finally, the Jews understood it in this way also, and answered him—not those who had already believed, but those who were in the crowd and did not yet believe. They answered him: “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

Yet the Lord had not said, “You will be free,” but, “The truth will set you free.” Nevertheless, because in that expression—as I said—the reference to freedom is plain in Greek, they understood only freedom; and they exalted themselves because they were Abraham’s offspring. They said, “We are Abraham’s offspring, and we have never been slaves to anyone. How can you say, ‘You will be free’?”

O inflated skin! This is not greatness, but swelling. And even according to the freedom of this present time, how could you truthfully say, “We have never been slaves to anyone”? Was Joseph not sold into slavery (Genesis 37:28)? Were the holy prophets not led into captivity (2 Kings 24)? Moreover, was it not that very people who made bricks in Egypt and served harsh kings—not merely in gold and silver, but in clay (Exodus 1:14)?

If you have never served anyone, ungrateful people, what is the meaning of God’s constant reminder that he freed you from the house of slavery (Exodus 13:3; Deuteronomy 5:6, and elsewhere)? Perhaps your fathers served, but you who are speaking have never served anyone?

How, then, were you already paying tribute to the Romans? This was also the occasion on which you set a snare, as though for the purpose of entrapment, for Truth itself, so that you might say, “Is it lawful to pay tribute to Caesar?” If he said, “It is lawful,” you would seize him as though he had wished evil upon the freedom of Abraham’s offspring. But if he said, “It is not lawful,” you would slander him before the kings of the earth, claiming that he prohibited the payment of tribute to kings.

When the coin was produced, you were rightly defeated, and you yourselves were compelled to answer your own trap. For there you were told, “Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s,” when you yourselves had answered that the coin bore Caesar’s image (Matthew 22:15–21). For just as Caesar seeks his own image on the coin, so God seeks his own image in the human being.

This, then, was his answer to the Jews. I am moved, brothers, by the vain pride of human beings, since even about the very freedom they understood carnally they lied, saying, “We have never been slaves to anyone.”

### 3

But let us listen more carefully and attentively to what the Lord answered, lest we ourselves be found to be slaves.

[Col. 1694] Jesus answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

He is a slave—would that he were a slave of a human being and not of sin! Who would not tremble at these words? May our Lord God grant this to us—that is, to me and to you—that I may speak according to the truth about seeking this freedom and avoiding that slavery.

“Amen, amen, I say to you.” Truth speaks. And what does it mean for our Lord God to say, “Amen, amen, I say to you”? He greatly commends what he declares in this way. In a certain sense, if one may speak so, it is his oath: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” For *amen* is interpreted as “truly.” Yet it has not been translated, although it could have been said, “Truly I say to you.”

Neither the Greek translator nor the Latin one dared to do this. For the word *amen* is neither Greek nor Latin, but Hebrew. It remained untranslated so that it might possess the honor of a veil of secrecy—not so that it would be denied, but so that, once stripped bare, it would not become cheap. Nor was the Lord’s word said only once, but twice: “Amen, amen, I say to you.” Learn from the very repetition how greatly this was being emphasized.

### 4

What, then, was being emphasized? “Truly, truly, I say to you,” says Truth. Even if it did not say, “I speak truly,” it could not possibly lie. Nevertheless, it emphasizes and presses the point; it awakens those who are, as it were, asleep, makes them attentive, and does not wish to be despised.

What does it say? “Amen, amen, I say to you: everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin.”

O miserable slavery! Often, when people suffer under wicked masters, they ask to be sold—not seeking to have no master, but at least to change masters. What can the slave of sin do? Whom can he appeal to? Before whom can he appeal? From whom can he ask to be sold?

Furthermore, a human slave, at times exhausted by his master’s harsh commands, finds rest by fleeing. Where does the slave of sin flee? Wherever he flees, he drags himself along with him. An evil conscience does not flee from itself. There is nowhere for it to go; it follows itself—indeed, it does not depart from itself, for the sin he commits is within.

He committed sin in order to obtain some bodily pleasure. The pleasure passes; the sin remains. What delighted him has gone by; what pricks him remains. Evil slavery!

Sometimes people flee to the Church, and we often have to endure them as undisciplined: they want to be rid of their masters [Note: [Col. 1694] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition have this passage as follows: “Although undisciplined, unwilling to be rid of divine things.” Manuscript M.]. They do not want to be rid of their sins.

At other times, people subject to an unlawful and wicked yoke flee to the Church because, though free by birth, they are being held in slavery, and the bishop is appealed to. Unless he takes care to prevent their freedom from being oppressed, he is considered merciless.

Let us all flee to Christ; let us appeal to God our liberator against sin. Let us ask to be sold, so that we may be redeemed by his blood. For the Lord says, “You were sold without payment, and you shall be redeemed without silver” (Isaiah 52:3). Without payment—though not without a payment: not with yours, because with mine. The Lord says this; for he gave the price—not silver, but his own blood. For we had remained both slaves and needy.

### 5

Therefore the Lord alone frees from this slavery: [Col. 1695] He who did not have it himself frees from it; for he alone came in this flesh without sin.

For the little ones whom you see being carried in their mothers’ arms do not yet walk, and already they are fettered. They have drawn from Adam what is to be loosed by Christ. This grace that the Lord promises pertains even to them when they are baptized, because only he can free from sin who came without sin and became a sacrifice for sin.

For you heard when the Apostle was being read: “We are ambassadors for Christ,” he says, “as though God were exhorting through us; we beseech you on behalf of Christ”—that is, as though Christ himself were beseeching you. What does he beseech? “Be reconciled to God.”

If the Apostle exhorts and beseeches us to be reconciled to God, we were enemies of God. For no one is reconciled except after enmity. Sin, not nature, made us enemies. From the same source from which we became his enemies, we became slaves of sin.

God has no free people who are enemies; they must be slaves. And they will remain slaves unless they are freed by the one whom, through sinning, they chose to make their enemy.

“Therefore,” he says, “we beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God.” But how are we reconciled unless what separates us from him is removed? For the prophet says: “His ear is not too heavy to hear, but your sins separate you from God” (Isaiah 59:1–2).

Since, therefore, we are not reconciled unless what lies between us is removed and what ought to stand between us is put in its place, there is a separating mediator and a reconciling mediator. The separating middle is sin; the reconciling mediator is the Lord Jesus Christ: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy 2:5).

Therefore, to remove the dividing wall—which is sin—that mediator came and himself became both priest and sacrifice. Since he became a sacrifice for sin, offering himself as a burnt offering on the cross of his Passion, the Apostle continues. After saying, “We beseech you on behalf of Christ: be reconciled to God,” it is as though we asked, “How can we be reconciled?”

He says: “Him”—that is, Christ himself—“who knew no sin, he made to be sin for us, so that we might become the righteousness of God in him” (2 Corinthians 5:20–21).

He says, “Christ himself, God, who knew no sin.” He came in the flesh—that is, in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3)—but not in sinful flesh, since he had absolutely no sin. Therefore he became a true sacrifice for sin, because he himself had no sin.

### 6

But perhaps I have spoken from my own understanding in saying that sin is a sacrifice for sin. Let those who have read recognize it; let those who have not read not be lazy. Let them, I say, not be lazy about reading, so that they may be truthful in judging.

When God commanded sacrifices to be offered for sin, those sacrifices did not contain the expiation of sins but were a shadow of future things. The Law itself calls the very same sacrifices, offerings, victims, and animals brought to be slaughtered for sins—whose blood prefigured that Blood—“sins.” In certain passages it is even written that the priests, when they were about to sacrifice, placed their hands upon the head of “sin,” that is, upon the head of the victim to be sacrificed for sin.

[Col. 1696] Thus our Lord Jesus Christ became such “sin”—that is, a sacrifice for sin—he who knew no sin.

### 7

It is rightly he who frees from this slavery of sin who says in the Psalms, “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Psalm 87:5–6). For he alone is free, because he had no sin.

He himself says in the Gospel: “Behold, the ruler of this world is coming,” signifying that the devil would come through the persecuting Jews. “Behold,” he says, “he is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John 14:30–31). Unlike in those whom he kills, including the righteous, in whom he finds some kind of sin, he will find nothing in me.

And as though someone had said to him, “If he will find nothing in you, why will he kill you?” he added: “But so that all may know that I do the will of my Father, rise, let us go from here.”

He does not pay the debt of my death out of the necessity of my sin, he says. Rather, in the fact that I die, I do my Father’s will. In this I do more than I suffer, because if I did not wish it, I would not have suffered.

You have him saying elsewhere, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). Behold, he is truly free among the dead.

### 8

Since, then, everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin, hear what our hope of freedom is.

“A slave,” he says, “does not remain in the house forever.” The Church is the house; the sinful person is the slave. Many sinners enter the Church. He did not therefore say, “A slave is not in the house,” but, “A slave does not remain in the house forever.”

If no slave will be there, who will be there? For when the just king sits upon the throne, as Scripture says, “Who can boast that he has a pure heart? Or who can boast that he is clean from sin?” (Proverbs 20:8–9).

He greatly frightened us, my brothers, by saying, “A slave does not remain in the house forever.” But he adds and says, “The Son remains forever.”

Will Christ alone, then, be in his house? Will no people belong to him? Whose head will he be if there is no body? Or perhaps all this is the Son—head and body?

For it was not without reason that he both frightened us and gave us hope. He frightened us so that we would not love sin; he gave us hope so that we would not despair of the remission of sin.

“Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin is a slave of sin. A slave does not remain in the house forever.” What hope, then, is there for us, who are not without sin? Hear your hope: “The Son remains forever.” “If therefore the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

This is our hope, brothers: that we may be freed by the Free One, and that by freeing us he may make us slaves. For we were slaves of desire; once freed, we become slaves of charity.

The Apostle says this too: “You were called to freedom, brothers; only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through charity serve one another” (Galatians 5:13).

Let no Christian therefore say, “I am free; I have been called to freedom. I was a slave, but I have been redeemed, and by that redemption I have been made free. I will do what I wish; let no one prevent me from doing what I wish, since I am free.”

But if you commit sin by that very will, you are a slave of sin. Do not therefore abuse freedom as an opportunity to sin freely, but use it not to sin. Your will will be free if it is devout.

You will be free if you are a slave: free from sin, a slave of righteousness. [Col. 1697] The Apostle says, “When you were slaves of sin, you were free from righteousness. But now, having been freed from sin and made slaves of God, you have your fruit leading to sanctification, and its end is eternal life” (Romans 6:20, 22).

Let us strive for this; let us pursue it.

### 9

The first freedom is freedom from crimes. Pay attention, my brothers, pay attention, lest I perhaps be able to bring before your understanding both what this freedom is now and what it will be in the future.

Examine anyone who is exceedingly righteous in this life. Although he may already be worthy of the name “righteous,” he is nevertheless not without sin. Hear holy John himself, whose Gospel this also is, saying in his Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

Only the one who was free among the dead could say this; it could be said only of him who knew no sin. Of him alone it could be said: “He was tested in every respect according to likeness, without sin” (Hebrews 4:15). He alone could say, “Behold, the ruler of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me.”

You may examine anyone else, however righteous, and he is not entirely without sin. Nor was Job such a person, to whom the Lord bore such testimony that the devil envied him and requested that he be tested—and, while testing him, was overcome, so that Job might be proved (Job 1–2).

He was proved not because God was unaware that he would be crowned, but so that he might become known to human beings as one to imitate.

What does Job himself say? “For who is clean? Not even an infant, whose life upon the earth is but one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint).

Yet many righteous people are called “without complaint,” which is understood as “without crime.” For no just complaint can be made about those human affairs in which people have no crime.

A crime, however, is a grave sin, most deserving of accusation and condemnation. God does not therefore condemn some sins while justifying and praising others. He praises none; he hates them all.

Just as a physician hates the sick person’s illness and works through treatment to drive out the illness and relieve the sick person, so God by his grace works this in us: that sin may be consumed and the human being freed.

“But when is it consumed?” you ask. If it is diminished, why is it not consumed? It is diminished in the life of those who are making progress, and consumed in the life of those who are perfect.

### 10

The first freedom, then, is freedom from crimes. Therefore, when the Apostle Paul chose people to be ordained as presbyters or deacons—and anyone who is to be ordained to leadership in the Church—he did not say, “If anyone is without sin.” For if he had said this, every human being would be rejected and no one would be ordained. Rather, he said, “If anyone is without crime” (1 Timothy 3:10; Titus 1:6), such as murder, adultery, some impurity of fornication, theft, fraud, sacrilege, and other things of this kind.

When a person begins not to have these things—and every Christian ought not to have them—he begins to raise his head toward freedom. But this freedom is begun, not perfected.

“Why,” someone asks, “is it not perfect freedom?” Because, “I see another law in my members, fighting against the law of my mind. For I do not do what I wish,” he says, “but I do what I hate” (Galatians 5:17). “The flesh,” he says, “desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do the things you wish.”

Freedom in part, [Col. 1698] slavery in part: not yet complete, not yet pure, not yet full freedom, because not yet eternity. We have weakness in part, and in part we have received freedom.

Whatever sin was ours was previously erased in baptism. But because all iniquity has been erased, has no weakness remained? If none had remained, we would live here without sin. Who would dare to say this except a proud person, one unworthy of the mercy of the liberator, one who wishes to deceive himself, and in whom the truth is not?

Therefore, because some weakness has remained, I dare to say that in the part by which we serve God we are free; in the part by which we serve the law of sin, we are still slaves.

Hence the Apostle says what we had begun to quote: “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” There is the source of our freedom; there is the source of our delight in the law of God, for freedom itself delights.

As long as you do what is just out of fear, God does not delight you [Note: [Col. 1698] One manuscript omits “God.” Perhaps the text should read, “you do not yet delight in it.” Immediately afterward, the old codices of Fossatensis and Carcassonensis continue as follows: “As long as it does not delight you, you still act as a slave.”].

As long as you still act as a slave, it does not delight you. Let it delight you, and you are free. Do not fear punishment, but love righteousness. You cannot yet love righteousness? At least fear punishment, so that you may arrive at loving righteousness.

### 11

Thus the one who was speaking already felt himself free in the higher part, from which he said, “I delight in the law of God according to the inner person.” The law delights me; what the law commands delights me; righteousness itself delights me.

“But I see another law in my members.” This is the weakness that remained: “fighting against the law of my mind and making me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.”

In this part he feels captivity, where righteousness has not been fulfilled. For where he delights in the law of God, he is not captive but a friend of the law; and therefore free, because he is its friend.

What, then, follows from what remains? What but that we look to the one who said, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free”?

Finally, the one who was speaking also looked to him: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me,” he says, “from this body of death? The grace of God, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Therefore, if the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free.”

Finally, he concluded in this way: “Therefore it is I myself who with my mind serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin” (Romans 7:19–25).

“It is I myself,” he says. We are not two people opposed to each other and coming from different principles. Rather, it is I myself who with my mind serve the law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin, as long as illness struggles against salvation.

### 12

But if with your flesh you serve the law of sin, do what the Apostle himself says: “Therefore, do not let sin reign in your mortal body so as to obey its desires, nor present your members as weapons of iniquity to sin” (Romans 6:12–13).

He does not say, “Let sin not exist,” but, “Let it not reign.” As long as sin must exist in your members, at least let its reign be taken away; do not do what it commands.

Anger arises? Do not give your tongue to anger for cursing; do not give your hand or foot to anger for striking. This irrational anger would not arise unless sin were in your members. But take away its reign. Let it have no weapons with which to fight against you. It will even learn not to rise when it begins to find no weapons.

“Do not present your members [Col. 1699] as weapons of iniquity to sin.” Otherwise you will be entirely captive, and it will not be possible to say, “With my mind I serve the law of God.” For if the mind holds the weapons, the members are not moved into the service of raging sin.

Let the inner commander hold the citadel, since he stands in need of help under the greater commander. Let him restrain anger; let him curb desire. Yet there is something to be restrained, something to be curbed, something to be held in check.

What did that righteous man, serving the law of God with his mind, wish for except that there might be nothing at all to restrain? Everyone who strives toward perfection ought to work for this also: that the desire to which the members are not given for obedience may daily be diminished in the person who is making progress.

“To will,” he says, “is present to me, but to accomplish the good is not” (Romans 7:18). Did he say, “To do good is not present to me”? If he had said this, there would be no hope. He did not say, “To do is not present to me,” but, “To accomplish is not present to me.”

For what is the perfection of the good except the consumption and end of evil? And what is the consumption of evil except what the Law says, “You shall not covet” (Exodus 20:17)? Not to covet at all is the perfection of the good, because it is the consumption of evil.

That man was saying, “To accomplish the good is not present to me,” because he could not make himself cease to covet. He only managed to restrain his desire, not to consent to it, and not to offer his members to desire as its attendants.

“To accomplish the good,” therefore, he says, “is not present to me.” I cannot fulfill what was said, “You shall not covet.”

What, then, is necessary? That you fulfill, “Do not go after your desires” (Sirach 18:30). Do this for the time being, as long as illicit desires are present in your flesh: “Do not go after your desires.”

Remain in the slavery of God, in the freedom of Christ. With your mind serve the law of your God. Do not surrender yourself to your desires. By following them, you add strength to them. How will you overcome them by giving them strength, when you nourish your enemies against yourself with your own strength?

### 13

What, then, is the full and perfect freedom in that Lord Jesus who said, “If the Son sets you free, then you will truly be free”? When will freedom be full and perfect?

When there are no enemies; when “the last enemy, death, will be destroyed.” For “this corruptible body must put on incorruption, and this mortal body must put on immortality. But when this mortal body has put on immortality, then the saying that is written will come to pass: ‘Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your contention?’” (1 Corinthians 15:26, 53–55).

What does “Where, O death, is your contention?” mean? The flesh desired against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh—but this was when the flesh of sin was strong.

“Where, O death, is your contention?” We shall already live; we shall no longer die, in him who died and rose again for us, so that, as he says, “those who live may no longer live for themselves, but for him who died and rose again for them” (2 Corinthians 5:15).

Let us, wounded as we are, pray to the physician; let us be carried to the inn for healing. For he is the one who promises health, who had mercy on the half-dead man abandoned by robbers on the road [Note: [Col. 1699] The manuscripts read, “had mercy, on the road, on the half-dead man abandoned by robbers.”]. He poured in oil and wine, treated the wounds, lifted him onto his animal, brought him to the inn, and entrusted him to the innkeeper.

To which innkeeper? Perhaps to the one who said, “We are ambassadors for Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:20). [Col. 1700]

He also gave two coins to be spent on caring for the wounded man (Luke 10:30–35). Perhaps these are the two commandments on which the whole Law and the Prophets depend (Matthew 22:37–40).

Therefore, brothers, even the Church in this present time, in which the wounded man is healed, is the inn of the traveler. But above the Church itself is the inheritance of the possessor.

## TRACTATE XLII

From the passage written, “I know that you are Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me,” up to, “Therefore you do not hear, because you are not of God.” John 8:37–47.

### 1

Our Lord, even in the form of a servant, was not a slave, but in the form of a servant he was Lord. For that was the servant-like form of flesh; yet although it was the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3), it was not sinful flesh.

He promised freedom to those who believed in him. But the Jews, as though proud of their own freedom, disdained to be made free, although they were slaves of sin. They said they were free because they were Abraham’s offspring.

What the Lord answered them, when today’s reading was recited, we have heard: “I know,” he says, “that you are Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you.”

“I recognize you,” he says. “You are Abraham’s children, but you seek to kill me. I recognize the origin of your flesh, not the faith of your heart. You are Abraham’s children, but according to the flesh.”

“Therefore,” he says, “you seek to kill me, because my word finds no place in you.” If my word were received, it would catch you; if you were caught, you would be enclosed within the nets of faith like fish.

What does “it finds no place in you” mean? It does not find a place in your heart, because it is not received by your heart. For the word of God is—and ought to be for the faithful—like a hook for a fish: it catches when it is itself caught. No injury is done to those who are caught; they are caught for salvation, not destruction.

Hence the Lord said to his disciples, “Come after me, and I will make you fishers of human beings” (Matthew 4:19).

These people were not such. And yet they were Abraham’s children: children of a man of God, but wicked human beings. They drew their descent from his flesh, but had become degenerate because they did not imitate the faith of the one whose children they were.

### 2

You certainly heard the Lord saying, “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” Hear what he says afterward: “I speak what I have seen with my Father, and you do what you have seen with your father.”

He had already said, “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” But what do they do? They do what he told them: “You seek to kill me.” They never saw this in Abraham.

When the Lord says, “What I have seen with my Father,” he wants God the Father to be understood. I saw the truth; I speak the truth, because I am Truth.

For if the Lord speaks the truth that he saw with the Father, he saw himself and speaks himself, because he himself is the Father’s Truth, which he saw with the Father. For he is the Word, and “the Word was with God.”

Where, then, did these people see the evil that they do—the evil that the Lord rebukes and reproves? With their father. When we hear more clearly in what follows who their father is, then we shall understand what they saw with such a father. For he has not yet named their father.

A little earlier he mentioned Abraham, but in reference to their origin according to the flesh, not to a likeness of life. He is going to identify another father of theirs, who neither [Col. 1701] begot them nor created them as human beings; yet they were his children insofar as they were evil, not insofar as they were human beings—children by imitation, not by creation.

### 3

They answered and said to him, “Our father is Abraham,” as though to say, “What will you say against Abraham? Or, if you are capable of anything, dare to criticize Abraham.”

Not that the Lord did not dare to criticize Abraham. Rather, Abraham was such a person that the Lord would not criticize him but instead praise him. Yet these people seemed to be provoking him to say something evil about Abraham, so that they might have an opportunity to do what they were planning.

“Our father is Abraham.”

### 4

Let us hear how the Lord answered them, praising Abraham while condemning them:

Jesus says to them, “If you are Abraham’s children, do the works of Abraham. But now you seek to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth that I heard from God. Abraham did not do this.”

There he is praised; they are condemned. Abraham was not a murderer.

“I do not say,” he says, “that I am the Lord of Abraham”—though if I said this, I would speak the truth. For elsewhere he said, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). Then they wanted to stone him; he did not say that now.

For the moment, what you see, what you behold, what you think I alone am—I am a human being. Why do you want to kill a human being telling you what he heard from God, unless you are not Abraham’s children?

And yet earlier he said, “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” He does not deny their origin, but condemns their deeds. Their flesh was from him, but their life was not.
