5. But as for us, beloved, surely we do not come from Abraham’s lineage, nor was Abraham in any way our father according to the flesh? The Jewish people derive their bodily origin from his flesh, not Christians: we have come from other nations; and yet, by imitating him, we have become Abraham’s children. Hear the Apostle: “The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring.” He does not say, “And to offsprings,” as though referring to many, but as referring to one: “And to your offspring,” which is Christ. “And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s offspring, heirs according to the promise” (Gal. 3:16, 29).

We, then, have become Abraham’s offspring by God’s grace. God did not make them Abraham’s co-heirs from Abraham’s flesh. He disinherited those people and adopted these; and from that olive tree whose root is in the Patriarchs he cut off the proud natural branches and grafted in the lowly wild olive (Rom. 11:17). Therefore, when the Jews came to John to be baptized, he broke out against them and said, “Brood of vipers!” For they especially prided themselves on the nobility of their ancestry; but he called them a brood of vipers—not merely of human beings, but of vipers. He saw the form of human beings, but recognized the poison. Yet they had come to be changed [Note: [Col. 1701] Thus in all the manuscripts. But in the printed editions, “to be cleansed.”], since they had certainly come to be baptized; and he said to them, “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath? Therefore produce fruits worthy of repentance. And do not say among yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father’; for God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matt. 3:7–9).

If you do not produce fruits worthy of repentance, do not flatter yourselves about that stock: God is able both to condemn you and not to deprive Abraham of children. For he has the means by which to raise up children for Abraham; children will become those who imitate his faith: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.” We are those children. In our ancestors we were stones, when we worshiped stones in place of God; from such stones God formed a family for Abraham.

6. Why, then, does empty and vain boasting lift itself up? Let the children of Abraham cease boasting now: they have heard what they ought to have heard: “If you are Abraham’s children, prove it by your deeds, not by your words.” “You are seeking to kill me, a man who has spoken to you the truth”—for the moment I do not say “the Son of God,” I do not say “God,” I do not say “the Word,” since the Word does not die; I say what you see, because you can kill what you see, and offend the one whom you do not see. “Abraham did not do this. You are doing the works of your father.” And still he does not say who this father of theirs is.

7. What did they reply at that point? They began, in some measure, to understand that the Lord was not speaking about physical descent, but about the conduct of one’s life. And because it is the custom of the Scriptures they read to call spiritual fornication the subjection of the soul, as though prostituted, to many and false gods, they answered accordingly: “They said to him, ‘We were not born of fornication; we have one father, God.’”

Abraham had now been cast aside. They had been rebuffed as they ought to have been rebuffed by a truthful mouth, because Abraham was the sort of man whose deeds they did not imitate, although they boasted of descending from him. And they changed their reply; I suppose they said to themselves: “Whenever we mention Abraham, he will say to us, ‘Why do you not imitate the one whose lineage you boast of?’ We cannot imitate such a holy, just, innocent, and outstanding man. Let us call God our father; let us see what he will say to us.”

8. Falsehood surely found something to say, and truth would not find something to answer? Let us hear what they say; let us hear what they hear: “We have one father, God,” they say. Jesus therefore said to them, “If God were your father, you would certainly love me, for I proceeded from God and came. For I did not come of my own accord, but he sent me.”

You call God your father; acknowledge me at least as your brother. Yet he raised the hearts of those capable of understanding and touched upon what he usually says: “I did not come of my own accord; he sent me. I proceeded from God and came.” Remember what we customarily say: “He came from him”; and from whom he came, he came together with him.

Christ’s being sent, then, is his incarnation. But the Word’s proceeding from God is an eternal procession: it is timeless, through whom time itself was made. Let no one say in his heart, “Before the Word existed, how was God?” Never say, “Before the Word of God existed.” God was never without the Word, because the Word remains rather than passes away; he is God, not a sound; through him heaven and earth were made, not something that passed away along with the things made upon the earth.

Therefore he proceeded from him as God, as equal, as the only Son, as the Father’s Word; and he came to us, because “the Word became flesh, so that he might dwell among us” (John 1:14). His coming is his humanity; his dwelling is his divinity. His divinity is the destination toward which we go; his humanity is the way by which we go. Unless he became for us the way by which we might go, we would never reach him who remains.

9. “Why,” he says, “do you not understand my speech? Because you cannot hear my word.” They could not understand because they could not hear. But from where did they lack the ability to hear, unless because they were unwilling to be corrected by believing? And how had this come about? “You are of your father the devil.” How long will you keep mentioning fathers? How long will you keep changing fathers—now Abraham, now God? Hear from the Son of God whose children you are: “You are of your father the devil.”

10. Here we must guard against the heresy of the Manichaeans, which says that there is a certain nature of evil and a certain nation of darkness with its rulers, which dared to fight against God; and that the true God, so that this hostile nation would not overthrow his kingdom, sent against it, as though they were his own entrails, rulers from his own light. They say that this nation was defeated, and that the devil derives his origin from it.

They say that our flesh derives its origin from this source; and accordingly they think the Lord meant, “You are of your father the devil,” because they were, as it were, by nature evil, deriving their origin from the hostile nation of darkness. Thus they err, thus they are blinded, thus they make themselves a nation of darkness by believing what is false against the one by whom they were created.

Every nature is good; but human nature has been corrupted through an evil will. What God made cannot be evil, unless the human being himself is evil to himself. Yet plainly, the Creator is the Creator, and the creature is the creature; the creature cannot be made equal to the Creator. Distinguish the one who made from what he made. A bench cannot be equated with a carpenter, nor a column with a builder; and yet, if the carpenter made the bench, he did not himself create the wood.

But because the Lord our God is omnipotent, and made what he made by the Word, he had no material from which to make all the things he made, and yet he made them. They came to be because he willed it; they came to be because he spoke. But things made cannot be compared with their maker. If you seek something to compare, acknowledge the only Son.

From where, then, are the Jews children of the devil? By imitation, not by birth. Hear the custom of Holy Scripture. The Prophet says to those same Jews: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite” (Ezek. 16:3). The Amorites were a particular nation from which the Jews did not derive their origin; the Hittites likewise had their own nation, wholly foreign to the lineage of the Jews. But because the Amorites and Hittites were impious, and the Jews imitated their impieties, they found parents for themselves—not parents from whom they would be born, but parents whose ways they followed and whose condemnation they thereby shared.

Perhaps you ask where the devil himself came from. From the same place, certainly, as the other angels. But the other angels remained in their obedience; he fell through disobedience and pride: he was an angel, and became the devil.

11. But now hear what the Lord says: “You are of your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires.” There is the reason they are his children: because you desire such things, not because you were born from him. What are his desires? “He was a murderer from the beginning.” There is what it means for you to wish to do your father’s desires: “You are seeking to kill me, a man who tells you the truth.” He envied the human being and killed the human being.

For when the devil envied the human being, he spoke to the woman disguised as a serpent, and through the woman he poisoned the man as well. They died by listening to the devil (Gen. 3:1), whom they would not have listened to if they had wished to listen to the Lord. For the human being had been placed between the one who created him and the one who had fallen; he ought to obey the Creator, not the deceiver.

Therefore, “he was a murderer from the beginning.” Consider the kind of murder, brothers. The devil is called a murderer, although he was not armed with a sword or girded with iron. He came to the human being, sowed an evil word, and killed him. Do not therefore suppose that you are not a murderer when you persuade your brother to do evil: if you persuade your brother to do evil, you kill him. And so that you may know that you kill, hear the Psalm: “The children of men—their teeth are weapons and arrows, and their tongue a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5).

“You therefore wish to do the desires of your father”: this is why you rage against the flesh, because you cannot rage against the mind. “He was a murderer from the beginning”—certainly in the first human being. He was a murderer from the point at which murder could occur; murder could occur from the point at which the human being was made. For the human being could not be killed unless the human being had first been made.

He was therefore a murderer from the beginning. And from where was he a murderer? “And he did not stand in the truth.” Therefore he was in the truth, but he fell by failing to stand. And why did he not stand in the truth? “Because the truth is not in him.” Not as in Christ is the truth in him, so that Christ himself is the truth. If this one had stood in the truth, he would have stood in Christ; but he did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him.

12. “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own,” because “he is a liar and its father.” What does this mean? You have heard the words of the Gospel; you received them attentively. See, I repeat them so that you may recognize what you are asking. The Lord was speaking about the devil what ought to be said by the Lord about the devil: “He was a murderer from the beginning”—this is true, for he killed the first human being—“and he did not stand in the truth,” because he fell away from the truth. “When he speaks a lie”—the devil himself, of course—“he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father.”

From these words some have thought that the devil has a father, and they have asked who the devil’s father was. Here the detestable error of the Manichaeans found yet another means of deceiving the inexperienced. They commonly say: “Suppose the devil was an angel and fell. Sin began from him, as you say. Who was his father?”

We answer them: “Who among us ever said that the devil had a father?” They reply: “The Lord says it; the Gospel speaks. Speaking about the devil, it says: ‘He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father.’”

13. Listen and understand; I am not sending you far away. Understand in the very words themselves. The Lord called the devil the father of falsehood. What does that mean? Listen to what it means; repeat the words themselves now and understand. For not everyone who lies is the father of his lie.

If you received a lie from someone else and repeated it, you certainly lied by uttering the lie; but you are not the father of that lie, because you received it from another. The devil, however, was a liar from himself; he generated his own lie and heard it from no one. Just as God the Father generated the Son, who is truth, so the fallen devil generated falsehood as though it were his son.

Having heard this, now repeat and recall the Lord’s words. Catholic understanding, pay attention to what you have heard; attend to what he says. “He”—who? “The devil”—“was a murderer from the beginning.” We recognize this: he killed Adam. “And he did not stand in the truth.” We recognize this, because he fell away from the truth. “Because the truth is not in him.” It is true: by departing from the truth [Note: [Col. 1705] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read, “because by departing from the truth.” The Louvain editions place the word “because” in brackets. M.] he does not possess truth.

“When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own.” He does not receive elsewhere what he speaks. “When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar and its father.” He is both a liar and the father of falsehood. You, perhaps, are a liar because you speak a lie; but you are not its father. If you received what you say from the devil and believed the devil, you are a liar, but not the father of the lie. But because the devil did not receive his lie from elsewhere—the lie by which, like poison, he killed the human being through the serpent—he is the father of falsehood, just as God the Father is the Father of truth.

Depart from the father of falsehood; run to the Father of truth. Embrace truth, so that you may receive freedom.

14. Those Jews, then, saw in their father what they were saying—which was what, if not a lie? But the Lord saw in his Father what he would say—which was what, if not himself? What, if not the Father’s Word? What, if not the Father’s eternal and co-eternal truth?

“He was therefore a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because the truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own, because he is a liar.” And he is not only a liar, but also its father—that is, he is the father of the very lie he speaks, because he himself generated his lie.

“But because I speak the truth, you do not believe me. Which of you convicts me of sin?” In the same way that I convict you and your father, “if I speak the truth, why do you not believe me?” Unless it is because you are children of the devil?

15. “Whoever is of God hears the words of God. The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God.” Again, do not consider nature, but corruption. Thus these people are of God and are not of God: by nature they are of God; through corruption they are not of God.

I beg you, pay attention. In the Gospel you have the means by which you may be healed against the poisonous and wicked errors of heretics. For the Manichaeans also customarily say concerning these words: “See, there are two natures, one good and the other evil.” The Lord says—what does the Lord say? “The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God.”

The Lord says this. “What, then,” he asks, “do you say to this?” Hear what I say. They are both of God and not of God: by nature they are of God; through corruption they are not of God. The good nature that is from God sinned by its will, believing what the devil persuaded it to believe, and was corrupted; therefore it seeks a physician, because it is not healthy.

That is what I say. But it seems impossible to you that they are of God and are not of God. Hear that it is not impossible. They are of God and are not of God in the same way that they are Abraham’s children and are not Abraham’s children. Here you have the answer; there is nothing for you to say.

Hear the Lord himself. He said to them, “I know that you are Abraham’s children.” Would the Lord lie? Certainly not. Therefore what the Lord said is true? It is true. Therefore it is true that they were Abraham’s children. It is true. Hear him denying it. The one who said, “You are Abraham’s children,” himself denied that they were Abraham’s children: “If you are Abraham’s children, do the deeds of Abraham. But now you are seeking to kill me, a man who has told you the truth that I heard from God; Abraham did not do this. You are doing the works of your father,” that is, of the devil.

How, then, were they both Abraham’s children and not Abraham’s children? He showed both realities in them: they were Abraham’s children because of the origin of their flesh; and they were not Abraham’s children because of the corruption produced by the devil’s persuasion.

So also understand our Lord and God: they were from him, and they were not from him. How were they from him? Because he himself created the human being from whom they were born. How were they from him? Because he is the creator of nature; he is the creator of flesh and soul. How, then, were they not from him? Because they had made themselves corrupt. They were not from him because, by imitating the devil, they had become children of the devil.

16. The Lord God therefore came to the sinful human being. You heard two designations: “human being” and “sinner.” The fact that he is a human being is from God; the fact that he is a sinner is not from God. Let corruption be separated from nature. Let nature be acknowledged, so that the Creator may be praised; let corruption be acknowledged, because of which the physician must be called upon.

When the Lord therefore says, “Whoever is of God hears the words of God; the reason you do not hear is that you are not of God,” he was not distinguishing the merits of natures, nor did he discover in human beings, besides their soul and flesh, some nature that had not been corrupted by sin. Rather, because he had foreknown those who would believe, he called them “of God,” since through the adoption of regeneration they would be born again from God.

To these applies the saying, “Whoever is of God hears the words of God.” But what follows—“The reason you do not hear is that you are not of God”—was said to those who were not merely corrupted by sin—for this evil was common to all—but were also foreknown as not going to believe with the faith by which alone they could be freed from the bondage of sins.

Therefore he foreknew that those to whom he spoke such words would remain in the condition of being from the devil: that is, they would die in their sins and impiety, in which they resembled him, and would not come to the regeneration in which they would be children of God—that is, born from God, by whom they had been created as human beings.

The Lord spoke according to this predestination—not because he had found any human being who, according to regeneration, was already from God, or who, according to nature, was already not from God.

**TRACTATE XLIII**

From the passage that says, “Then the Jews answered and said to him,” up to the passage, “Then the Jews took up stones to throw at him; but Jesus hid himself and went out of the temple.” Chapter 8, verses 48–59.

1. In this reading from the holy Gospel, which was recited today, we learn patience from power. For what are we, servants in relation to the Lord, sinners in relation to the just one, creatures in relation to the Creator? Yet just as, if we are in any way evil, we are evil from ourselves, so whatever good we are, we are from him and through him.

Nothing does a human being seek so much as power. The Lord Christ possesses great power; but first let him imitate his patience, so that he may reach power. Who among us would patiently hear it said to someone, “You have a demon”—said to the one who not only saved human beings but also commanded demons?

2. When the Jews had said, “Are we not right in saying that you are a Samaritan and have a demon?” he denied one of the two charges brought against him and did not deny the other. He answered, “I do not have a demon.” He did not say, “I am not a Samaritan.” There had, of course, been two charges. Although he did not return insult for insult, although he did not refute abuse with abuse, it nevertheless pertained to him to deny one matter and not deny the other.

This was not without reason, brothers. “Samaritan” is interpreted as “Guardian.” He knew that he was our guardian. For “he who guards Israel neither slumbers nor sleeps” (Ps. 120:4); and, “Unless the Lord guards the city, those who guard it keep watch in vain” (Ps. 127:1). He is therefore our guardian, who is our Creator. For did it pertain to him that we should be redeemed, but not that we should be preserved?

Finally, so that you may understand more fully the mystery of why he ought not to deny that he was a Samaritan, consider that very well-known parable in which a certain man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers. They severely wounded him and left him half-dead on the road. A priest passed by and ignored him; a Levite passed by and likewise went on; a certain Samaritan passed by—he is our guardian. He approached the wounded man, showed him mercy, and made himself his neighbor, not regarding him as a stranger (Luke 10:30–37).

He therefore replied only that he did not have a demon, but did not deny that he was a Samaritan.

3. Then, after such an insult, he said only this concerning his glory: “But I honor my Father, and you have dishonored me.” That is: “I do not honor myself, lest I seem arrogant to you; I have one whom I should honor. But if you recognized me, then just as I honor the Father, so you too would honor me. I do what I ought to do; you do not do what you ought to do.”

4. “But I,” he says, “do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.” Whom does he wish to be understood except the Father?

How, then, does he say elsewhere, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22), while here he says, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges”? If the Father judges, how does he not judge anyone, but has given all judgment to the Son?

5. To resolve this question, pay attention: it can be resolved by a similar expression. You have it written, “God tempts no one” (James 1:13); and again you have it written, “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3). Certainly there is a question here—you see it. How does God tempt no one, and how does the Lord your God test you, to know whether you love him?

Likewise, it is written, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear” (1 John 4:18); and elsewhere it is written, “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. 19:9). Here too there is a question. How does perfect love drive out fear, if the pure fear of the Lord endures forever and ever?

[Col. 1708] 6. We understand, then, that there are two kinds of testing: one that deceives and another that proves. According to the testing that deceives, God tests no one; according to the testing that proves, “the Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him.”

But here another question arises: how does he test in order to know, when nothing can be hidden from him before he tests? God does not therefore lack knowledge; rather, “to know” means “to cause you to know.”

Expressions of this kind occur both in our ordinary speech and in authors of eloquence. I shall say something from our own speech. A blind ditch is called blind not because it has lost its eyes, but because, by being hidden, it makes people unable to see. I shall also say something from those authors. Someone calls lupines “sad” (Virgil, *Georgics* 1.75), that is, bitter—not because they themselves are sad, but because, when tasted, they make people sad.

Expressions of this kind therefore also occur in Scripture. Those who labor to understand such questions do not labor when it comes to resolving them.

“The Lord your God is testing you, to know.” What does “to know” mean? “To cause you to know whether you love him.” Job was hidden from himself, but not from God. He permitted the tempter and made him the one who revealed Job’s character.

7. What shall we say about the two kinds of fear? There is servile fear, and there is chaste fear. There is fear lest you suffer punishment, and there is another fear lest you lose righteousness.

The fear lest you suffer punishment is servile. What great thing is it to fear punishment? The most wicked slave does this; the most savage robber does this. It is not a great thing to fear punishment, but it is a great thing to love righteousness.

Does the one who loves righteousness therefore fear nothing? Certainly he fears—not lest he fall into punishment, but lest he lose righteousness.

My brothers, believe me, and infer what I say from what you love. Some of you love money. Do you think I can find anyone who does not love it? Yet from the very fact that he loves money, let him understand what I am saying. He fears loss. Why does he fear loss? Because he loves money. As much as he loves money, so much does he fear losing money.

Therefore one can be found who loves righteousness and fears loss in his heart more deeply—who fears being stripped of righteousness more than you fear being stripped of money. That is chaste fear; it endures forever and ever. Love does not remove it or drive it out, but embraces it more fully, keeps it as a companion, and possesses it together with itself.

For we are coming to the Lord in order to see him face to face. There chaste fear preserves us; that fear does not disturb but strengthens. An adulterous woman fears that her husband will come; a chaste woman fears that her husband will depart.

8. Therefore, just as according to one kind of testing God tests no one, but according to another kind the Lord your God tests you; and just as according to one kind of fear there is no fear in love, but perfect love drives out fear, while according to another kind the pure fear of the Lord endures forever and ever; so here too, according to one kind of judgment, the Father judges no one but has given all judgment to the Son, while according to another kind of judgment he says, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

9. Let this question also be resolved by the word itself. In the Gospel you have judgment mentioned as punishment: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18). And elsewhere: “The hour is coming when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John 5:28–29).

See how he used “judgment” for condemnation and punishment. Yet if “judgment” were always understood as condemnation, would we hear the Psalm say, “Judge me, O God”? There judgment is used with reference to affliction; here, with reference to distinction.

How does it refer to distinction? How does the one who says, “Judge me, O God,” explain it? Read on and see what follows: “What does ‘Judge me, O God’ mean?” He says, “And distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 43:1).

Thus, when it says, “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation,” the Lord Christ says here in accordance with this meaning, “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

How is there one who seeks it and judges? There is a Father who distinguishes and separates my glory from your glory. You glory according to this world; I do not glory according to this world. I say to the Father, “Father, glorify me with the glory that I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:5).

What is “that glory”? Glory distinguished from human vainglory. According to this, the Father judges. What does “judges” mean? He distinguishes. What does he distinguish? The glory of his Son from the glory of human beings, because it was said, “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 45:7).

For simply because he became human, he is not thereby to be compared with us. We human beings are with sin; he is without sin. We human beings draw both death and transgression from Adam; he received mortal flesh from the Virgin, but no iniquity.

Finally, we were not born because we wished to be born; we do not live as long as we wish; nor do we die in the manner we wish. He, before he was born, chose from whom he would be born. Once born, he caused the Magi to worship him. He grew as an infant, and by his miracles showed himself to be God, while by his weakness he demonstrated himself to be human.

Finally, he also chose the kind of death he would undergo—that is, to hang upon a cross—and he set that very cross upon the foreheads of the faithful, so that the Christian might say, “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14).

Upon that cross, when he wished, he gave up his body and departed. In the tomb, as long as he wished, he lay; when he wished, he rose as though from a bed.

Therefore, brothers, according to that very form of a servant—for who could worthily speak of the other form: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God”?—according to that form of a servant, I say, there is a great difference between Christ’s glory and the glory of all other human beings.

It was of this glory that he spoke when he heard the charge that he had a demon: “I do not seek my own glory; there is one who seeks it and judges.”

10. But what do you say about yourself, Lord? “Amen, amen, I say to you: if anyone keeps my word, he will never see death.”

“You,” he says, “say, ‘You have a demon’; I call you to life. Keep my word, and you will not die.”

They heard, “He who keeps my word will never see death,” and they were angry, because they were already dead with the death that ought to have been avoided.

The Jews therefore said, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the Prophets, and you say, ‘If anyone keeps my word, he will never taste death forever.’”

Observe the scriptural expression: “He will not see death,” that is, “he will taste death.” “He will see death”; “he will taste death.” Who sees? Who tastes? What eyes does a human being have to see when he dies? When death comes, it closes those very eyes so that they see nothing. How, then, is it said, “He will not see death”? Likewise, with what palate or throat is death tasted, so that one can determine what it tastes like? When it takes away every sense, what remains on the palate?

But “he will see” and “he will taste” are said in place of “he will experience.”

11. The Lord was speaking these words—if I say “to those who were going to die,” it is not enough; he was speaking as one who was going to die to those who were going to die, since “the ways out of death belong to the Lord” (Ps. 68:20), as the Psalm says.

Since he was speaking both to those who were going to die and as one who was going to die, what does he mean when he says, “Whoever keeps my word will never see death forever,” except that the Lord saw another death, from which he had come to free us: the second death, eternal death, the death of Gehenna, the death of condemnation with the devil and his angels?

That is the true death; the present one is a departure. What is this present death? The abandonment of the body, the laying down of a heavy burden—unless another burden is carried by which the human being is cast into Gehenna.

It was therefore concerning that death that the Lord said, “Whoever keeps my word will never see death forever.”

12. Let us not fear this death; let us fear that other one. But what is worse, many, by perversely fearing this death, have fallen into that one.

It was said to some people, “Worship idols”; and if they did not, they would be killed. Or, as Nebuchadnezzar said, “If you do not do this, you will be thrown into a furnace of burning fire.” Many were afraid and worshiped. Unwilling to die, they died. By fearing the death that cannot be escaped, they fell into the death from which they could have escaped happily, if they had not unhappily feared the death that cannot be escaped.

You were born a human being; you will die. Where will you go so that you may not die? What will you do so that you may not die? To console you, who were destined by necessity to die, your Lord deigned to die by his own will. When you see Christ dead, do you disdain to die?

Therefore you will die; you have no means of escaping this. It may be today; it may be tomorrow; it is destined to happen, and the debt must be paid.

What, then, does a person do who fears, flees, and hides so as not to be found by the enemy? Is he thereby acting so that he will not die? No, only so that he will die a little later. He does not receive security from the debt; he asks for a postponement. However long the postponement, what has been postponed will come.

Let us fear the death feared by the three men when they said to the king, “God is able to free us even from this flame—but even if he does not” (Dan. 3:15, 17–18). There was the fear of that death [Note: [Col. 1710] According to the Erfurt, Lyons, and Venice editions, it should read: “deliver us, and if there was not there fear of that death” [the reading is uncertain]. M.], the death that the Lord now threatens, when they said: “But even if he does not openly wish to free us, he can crown us secretly.”

Therefore the Lord himself, when he was about to make martyrs and was to be the head of martyrs, said: “Do not fear those who kill the body, and afterward have nothing more that they can do.”

What does it mean, “they have nothing more that they can do”? What if, after they have killed the body, they throw it to the beasts to be torn apart and to birds to be devoured? It seems that their cruelty still has something it can do. But to whom do they do it? To one who has departed. The body remains, but there is no sensation; the dwelling lies there, but the inhabitant has departed.

Therefore afterward they have nothing more that they can do: they do nothing to one who does not feel.

“But fear the one who has power to destroy both body and soul in the fire of Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28; Luke 12:4–5).

See what death he was speaking about when he said, “Whoever keeps my word will never see death forever.”

Let us therefore keep his word, brothers, in faith, so that we may come to the vision when we have received complete freedom.

13. But those people, dead in their indignation and predestined for eternal death, answered insultingly and said, “Now we know that you have a demon. Abraham died, and the Prophets.”

But with the death that the Lord wished to be understood, neither Abraham nor the Prophets died. They died, and they live; these people were living, and they were dead.

When the Sadducees raised a question concerning the resurrection, the Lord himself answered at one point: “Concerning the resurrection of the dead, have you not read how the Lord spoke from the bush to Moses: ‘I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob’? He is not the God of the dead, but of the living” (Matt. 22:31–32; Exod. 3:6).

If they live, then let us labor to live in such a way that, when we have died, we may be able to live with them [Note: [Col. 1711] Am., Bad., Er., and most manuscripts read, “and live with them,” omitting “we may be able.”].

“Who are you making yourself out to be,” they say, “that you say, ‘He who keeps my word will never see death forever,’ when you know that Abraham and the Prophets died?”

14. Jesus answered, “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing; it is my Father who glorifies me.”

He said this because of what they had said: “Who are you making yourself out to be?” He refers his glory to the Father, from whom he has what he is as God.

At times the Arians also slander our faith on the basis of this saying, and they say: “See, the Father is greater, since he certainly glorifies the Son.”

Heretic, have you not read the Son himself saying that he glorifies his Father (John 17:4)? If the Father glorifies the Son, and the Son glorifies the Father, abandon your obstinacy, acknowledge their equality, and correct your perversity.

15. “It is my Father,” he says, “who glorifies me, whom you call your God, and yet you have not known him.” See, my brothers, how he shows that the very one who was proclaimed to the Jews is the Father of Christ. I say this because certain heretics again maintain that the God proclaimed in the Old Testament is not the Father of Christ, but some ruler of the evil angels. The Manichaeans say this; the Marcionites say this. There are perhaps other heretics whom it is either unnecessary to mention or whom I cannot presently recall by name; nevertheless, there have been those who said this. Therefore pay attention, so that you may have something to say against them also. The Lord Christ calls his Father the one whom they called their God, “and yet have not known him”: for if they had known him, they would have received his Son.

“But I know him,” he says. To those judging according to the flesh, he might even for this reason have seemed arrogant, because he said, “I know him.” But see what follows: “If I should say that I do not know him, I would be like you, a liar.” Therefore arrogance must not be avoided in such a way that truth is abandoned. “But I know him, and I keep his word.” As Son, he was speaking the Father’s word; and he himself was the Father’s Word, which was speaking to human beings.

16. “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad.” He bears great witness to Abraham—the offspring of Abraham, the creator of Abraham: “Abraham rejoiced,” he says, “that he might see my day.” He did not fear, but rejoiced that he might see it. For there was in him that love which casts out fear (1 John 4:18). He did not say, “He rejoiced because he saw,” but “He rejoiced that he might see.” Believing, he rejoiced in hope, so that he might see through understanding. “And he saw.” What more could the Lord Jesus Christ have said, or what more ought he to have said? “And he saw,” he says, “and was glad.”

Who can explain this joy, my brothers? If those for whom the Lord opened the eyes of the flesh rejoiced, what kind of joy was that of the one who saw with the eyes of his heart [Note: [Col. 1712] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have, “of those seeing with the eyes of the heart.” Although the word “eyes” is absent from Bad. and from some manuscripts.] the ineffable light, the abiding Word, the splendor shining upon devout minds, unfailing wisdom abiding with the Father as God, and destined one day to come in the flesh without departing from the Father’s bosom? Abraham saw all this.

For when he says “my day,” it may be uncertain what he meant: whether the temporal day of the Lord, when he was to come in the flesh, or the day of the Lord that knows neither rising nor setting. But I have no doubt that the father Abraham knew the whole. And where shall I find this? Should the testimony of our Lord Jesus Christ not be sufficient for us? Let us suppose that we cannot find it, because perhaps it is difficult to show how it is manifest that Abraham rejoiced that he might see the day of Christ, and saw it and was glad. And if we do not find it, could Truth lie? Let us believe the Truth, and have no doubt at all about Abraham’s merits.

Nevertheless, hear one passage that occurs to me for the moment. When Father Abraham sent his servant to seek a wife for his son Isaac, he bound him by this oath so that he would faithfully fulfill what he was commanded and would himself know what he was doing. For a great matter was being undertaken when a marriage was being sought for Abraham’s offspring. But so that the servant might understand what Abraham knew—that he did not desire descendants in a merely carnal way, nor think carnally about anything arising from his lineage—he said to the servant whom he was sending: “Put your hand under my thigh, and swear by the God of heaven” (Genesis 24:2–4).

What does the God of heaven have to do with Abraham’s thigh? You already understand the sacrament: by “thigh,” lineage. What, then, was the meaning of that oath, except that it signified that the God of heaven would come in the flesh from Abraham’s lineage? Fools criticize Abraham because he said, “Put your hand under my thigh.” Those who criticize the flesh of Christ criticize what Abraham did. But we, brothers, if we acknowledge that Christ’s flesh is to be venerated, should not despise that thigh; rather, we should accept it as spoken prophetically. For Abraham was a prophet. Whose prophet? Of his own offspring and of his Lord. He signified his offspring when he said, “Put your hand under my thigh”; he signified his Lord when he added, “and swear by the God of heaven.”

17. The Jews, angered, replied: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” And the Lord said: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am.”

Weigh the words and recognize the mystery. “Before Abraham came to be.” Understand that “came to be” pertains to human making, while “I am” pertains to the divine substance. “Came to be,” because Abraham is a creature. He did not say, “Before Abraham existed, I was,” but “Before Abraham came to be”—he who could not come to be except through me—“I am.” Nor did he say, “Before Abraham came to be, I came to be.” For “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Genesis 1:1), while “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” Recognize the Creator; distinguish the creature. He who was speaking had become Abraham’s offspring; and in order that Abraham might come to be, he himself existed before Abraham.

18. At this point they were stirred to greater anger, as though by an utterly blatant insult against Abraham. For the Lord Christ seemed to them to have blasphemed, since he said, “Before Abraham came to be, I am.” So they took up stones to throw at him. What direction could such hardness take except toward those who were like them?

But Jesus—as man, as one in the form of a servant, as humble, as destined to suffer, as destined to die, as destined to redeem us by his blood—not as the one who is, not as the Word in the beginning and the Word with God. For when they took up stones to throw at him, what great thing would it have been if the earth had immediately split open and swallowed them, so that instead of stones they found the underworld? It would not have been difficult for God; but patience had to be commended more than power displayed. Therefore he hid himself from them, lest he be stoned. As man, he fled from stones; but woe to those from whose stony hearts God flees!

# TREATISE XLIV

From the passage written, “And as he passed by, he saw a man blind from birth,” to the passage, “But now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains.” Chapter 9.

1. A lengthy reading was recited concerning the man whom the Lord Jesus illuminated, who had been born blind. If we attempted to treat the whole of it, considering each point as fully as we are able, its importance would not allow the day to suffice. Therefore I ask and admonish Your Charity not to look for our exposition where the meaning is already clear, since it would take too long to linger over every detail.

Briefly, then, I commend the mystery of this blind man’s illumination. The things our Lord Jesus Christ did, things astonishing and wondrous, are both works and words: works, because they were done; words, because they are signs. If, therefore, we consider what this event signifies, this blind man is the human race. For this blindness occurred in the first man through sin, from whom we all derive our origin—not only of death, but also of iniquity.

If blindness is unbelief and illumination is faith, whom did Christ find faithful when he came? The Apostle, born among the people of the Prophets, says: “We too were once by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Ephesians 2:3). If children of wrath, children of vengeance, children of punishment, children of Gehenna—how by nature, unless, when the first man sinned, vice grew in place of nature? If vice grew in place of nature, then according to the mind every human being is born blind. For if he sees, he does not need a guide; if he needs a guide and illuminator, then he is blind from birth.

2. The Lord came. What did he do? He commended a great mystery. He spat on the ground and made clay from his saliva, because “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14). And he anointed the blind man’s eyes. He had been anointed, but still did not see. He sent him to the pool called Siloam. It was important for the Evangelist to make the name of this pool known to us, and he said, “which is interpreted ‘Sent.’”

You already recognize who was sent: unless he had been sent, none of us would have been released from iniquity. He therefore washed his eyes in the pool called “Sent”; he was baptized in Christ. If, then, when he baptized him in himself, so to speak, he illuminated him, when he anointed him he perhaps made him a catechumen.

The depth of so great a sacrament can certainly be explained and treated in different ways [Note: [Col. 1714] In most manuscripts: “the rationale of so great a sacrament can be explained in different ways, and its depth treated.”] But let this suffice for Your Charity; you have heard a great mystery.

Ask the man, “Are you a Christian?” If he is a pagan or a Jew, he answers you, “I am not.” But if he says, “I am,” you ask him further, “A catechumen or a believer?” If he answers, “A catechumen,” he has been anointed but not yet washed. But from where has he been anointed? Ask, and he answers. Ask him in whom he believes; by the very fact that he is a catechumen, he says, “In Christ.”

Behold, I am speaking now both to the believers and to the catechumens. What did I say about the spittle and the clay? That the Word became flesh. The catechumens hear this too, but it is not enough for them for the purpose for which they have been anointed. Let them hurry to the washing if they seek the light.

3. Because of certain questions in this same reading, let us now run through the words of the Lord and of the entire reading rather than expound them. “As he went out, he saw a blind man”—not blind in some ordinary way, but “from birth.”

“And his disciples asked him: Rabbi”—you know that “Rabbi” means “teacher.” They called him Teacher because they desired to learn. They proposed a question to the Lord as to a teacher: “Who sinned, this man or his parents, that he should be born blind?”

Jesus answered: “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents, that he should be born blind.” What does this mean? If no human being is without sin, were the parents of this blind man without sin? Was he himself born without original sin, or had he added nothing by living? Or, because he had his eyes closed, did the desires not keep watch? [Note: [Col. 1714] Thus nearly all the manuscripts. The printed editions have “kept watch,” singular.]

How many evils do blind people commit! From what evil does an evil mind abstain, even with its eyes closed? He could not see, but he knew how to think, and perhaps to desire something that, though blind, he could not carry out, yet which could be judged in his heart by the searcher of hearts.

If, then, both his parents had sin and he had sin, why did the Lord say, “Neither did this man sin, nor his parents”—unless this referred to the matter about which he had been asked, namely, that he should be born blind? His parents did have sin, but it was not through that sin that he was born blind.

If, then, it was not through his parents’ sin that he was born blind, why was he born blind? Hear the teacher teaching: he questions one who believes, so as to make him understand. He himself gives the reason why that man was born blind: “Neither did this man sin,” he says, “nor his parents, but that the works of God might be manifested in him.”

4. Then what follows? “I must work the works of him who sent me.” Behold the one who was sent, in whom the blind man washed his face. And see what he said: “I must work the works of him who sent me, while it is day.”

Remember how he gives all the glory to the one from whom he is, because that one has a Son who is from him, whereas he himself has no one from whom he is. But why did you say, Lord, “while it is day”? Hear why: “Night comes, when no one can work.” [Note: [Col. 1715] Most manuscripts read, “Night will come.”]

Not even you, Lord? Will that night be so powerful that you cannot work in it, whose work night itself is? I think, Lord Jesus—indeed, I do not merely think, but believe and affirm—that you were there when God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light (Genesis 1:3). For if he made it through the Word, he made it through you. Therefore it is said, “All things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). God divided the light from the darkness; he called the light “day” and the darkness “night” (Genesis 1:4–5).

5. What is that night which, when it comes, no one will be able to work? Hear what the day is, and then you will understand what the night is. From whom shall we hear what this day is? Let him say it himself: “As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world.” Behold, he himself is the day. Let the blind man wash his eyes in the day, so that he may see the day. “As long as I am in the world,” he says, “I am the light of the world.”

Therefore, I do not know what night there will be when Christ is not there; that is why no one will be able to work. It remains for us to inquire, my brothers. Receive me patiently as I inquire; I seek together with you, and together with you I will find from the one of whom I seek.

It is clear, explicit, and definite that in this passage the Lord referred to himself as the day, that is, the light of the world: “As long as I am in the world,” he says, “I am the light of the world.” Therefore he himself works.

But how long is he in this world? Do we suppose, brothers, that he was here then and is not here now? If we suppose this, then this fearful night has already come after the Lord’s ascension, in which no one can work. If this night came after the Lord’s ascension, how did the Apostles accomplish so much?

Was it night when the Holy Spirit came, filled all who were in one place, and gave them the ability to speak in the languages of all nations (Acts 2:1–6)? Was it night when that lame man was saved at Peter’s word—or rather, at the word of the Lord dwelling in Peter (Acts 3:6–8)? Was it night when, as the disciples passed by, the sick were placed on beds so that at least the shadow of those passing might touch them (Acts 5:15)?

When the Lord himself was here, however, his passing shadow saved no one. But he himself had said to the disciples, “You will do greater things than these” (John 14:12). The Lord had indeed said, “You will do greater things than these”; but let not flesh and blood exalt itself. Let it hear him saying, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

6. What, then? What shall we say about this night? When will it be, when no one can work?

This night will be the night of the impious. This night will belong to those to whom it will be said at the end: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels.” But it is called night, not flame, not fire. Hear that it is also night. Of a certain servant he says: “Bind him hand and foot and cast him into the outer darkness” (Matthew 22:13).

Let a person therefore work while he lives, lest he be overtaken by that night in which no one can work. Now is the time for faith to work through love; and if we work now, this is the day, this is Christ.

Hear him promising, and do not suppose that he is absent. He himself said, “Behold, I am with you.” How long? Let us who are living have no anxiety. If it were possible, we would make even those who will come after us utterly secure through this word. “Behold,” he says, “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20).

This day, which is completed by the circuit of the sun, has only a few hours; the day of Christ’s presence extends until the consummation of the age. But after the resurrection of the living and the dead, when he says to those placed at his right hand, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom,” and to those placed at his left, “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41), there will be the night in which no one can work, but can only receive what he has done.

The time of working is one thing; the time of receiving is another. For the Lord will repay each according to his works (Matthew 16:27). While you live, act, if you are going to act; for then there will be a powerful night that will envelop the impious.

But even now every unbeliever, when he dies, is received by that night; he cannot work anything there. In that night the rich man was burning and asking for a drop of water from the poor man’s finger. He suffered, was tormented, confessed, and received no help; yet he tried to do good. For he said to Abraham: “Father Abraham, send Lazarus to my brothers, so that he may tell them what is happening here, lest they too come to this place of torment” (Luke 16:24–28).

O unhappy man! When you were alive, then was the time to work; now you are already in the night in which no one can work.

7. “When he had said these things, he spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, and spread the clay over his eyes, and said to him: ‘Go and wash in the pool of Siloam’” (which is interpreted “Sent”). “He therefore went and washed, and came back seeing.”

Since these things are clear, let us pass on.

8. “Therefore the neighbors and those who had previously seen him, because he was a beggar, said: ‘Is this not the one who used to sit and beg?’ Others said, ‘It is he’; others, ‘No, but he resembles him.’” His opened eyes had changed his appearance.

“He was saying, ‘It is I.’” A welcome voice, lest it be condemned as ungrateful.

“Therefore they said to him: ‘How were your eyes opened?’ He answered: ‘That man who is called Jesus made clay and anointed my eyes, and said to me, “Go to the pool of Siloam and wash.” I went, and I washed, and I saw.’”

Behold, he has become a herald of grace; behold, he evangelizes, he confesses while seeing. That blind man was confessing, and the hearts of the impious were being shattered [Note: [Col. 1716] In two manuscripts, “were being constricted.”], because they did not have in their hearts what he already had in his face.

They said to him: “Where is the one who opened your eyes?” He said: “I do not know.” In these words his mind was still like that of one who had been anointed [Col. 1717] but did not yet see. Let us suppose, brothers, that he had that anointing in his mind. He proclaims, and does not know whom he proclaims.

9. “They bring to the Pharisees the man who had been blind. Now it was the sabbath when Jesus made the clay and opened his eyes. Again, therefore, the Pharisees asked him how he had seen. But he said to them: ‘He put clay on my eyes, and I washed, and I see.’ Therefore some of the Pharisees said”—not all, but some; for some were already being anointed.

What, then, did those who neither saw nor had been anointed say? “This man is not from God, because he does not keep the sabbath.” Rather, he did keep it, because he was without sin. For this is the spiritual sabbath [Note: [Col. 1717] In some manuscripts, “spiritually.”]: not to have sin.

Finally, brothers, this is what God teaches when he commends the sabbath: “You shall do no servile work” (Leviticus 23:8). These are the words of God commending the sabbath: “You shall do no servile work.” Ask the earlier readings what servile work is (Treatise 20, §2), and hear the Lord: “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8:34).

But these people, neither seeing, as I said, nor anointed, observed the sabbath carnally and violated it spiritually. Others said: “How can a sinful man perform such signs?” Behold, these had been anointed. And there was a division among them. That day had divided the light from the darkness.

Therefore they say to the blind man again: “What do you say about him who opened your eyes?” What do you think of him? What do you suppose? What judgment do you give? They were seeking a way to accuse the man, so that he might be expelled from the synagogue but found by Christ.

But he firmly expressed what he thought. For he said: “He is a prophet.” Still anointed in heart, he does not yet confess the Son of God, but he does not lie. For the Lord himself said of himself: “A prophet is not without honor except in his own country” (Matthew 13:57).

10. “Therefore the Jews did not believe about him that he had been blind and had seen, until they called his parents, who had seen”—that is, who had been blind and had seen.

“And they questioned them, saying: ‘Is this your son, whom you say was born blind? How then does he now see?’ His parents answered them and said: ‘We know that this is our son and that he was born blind; but how he now sees we do not know, or who opened his eyes, we do not know. Ask him; he is of age; let him speak for himself.’”

He is indeed our son, but we would rightly be compelled to speak for an infant, because he could not speak for himself. He has long been able to speak; now he sees. We know that he was blind from birth; we know that he has long been able to speak; now we see that he sees. Ask him, so that you may be informed. Why do you accuse us?

His parents said these things because they feared the Jews. For the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed him to be the Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue. By then it was no longer an evil to be expelled from the synagogue. They expelled him, but Christ received him. Therefore his parents said, “He is of age; ask him.”

11. Therefore they called again the man who had been blind and said to him: “Give glory to God.” What does “Give glory to God” mean? Deny what you have received. This plainly is not to give glory to God, but rather to blaspheme God.

“Give glory to God,” they say. “We know that this man is a sinner.”

He then said: “Whether he is a sinner, I do not know. One thing I know: that though I was blind, now I see.”

Therefore they said to him: “What did he do to you? How did he open your eyes?” And he, now becoming angry at the Jews’ hardness and seeing though he had been blind, unable to endure the blind, answered them: “I have already told you, and you heard. Why do you want to hear it again? Do you also want to become his disciples?”

What does “Do you also” mean except “I already am”? “Do you also want to?” I see now, but I do not begrudge you.

12. They cursed him and said: “You be his disciple.” May such a curse fall upon us and upon our children. For it is a curse if you examine the heart, not if you weigh the words.

“But we are disciples of Moses. We know that God spoke to Moses; but as for this man, we do not know where he is from.”

Would that you knew that God spoke to Moses! You would know that God was proclaimed through Moses. For you have the Lord saying: “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46).

Are you really following the servant and turning your back on the Lord? But you are not even following the servant, for through him you would be led to the Lord.

13. The man answered and said to them: “This is astonishing: you do not know where he is from, and yet he opened my eyes. We know that God does not hear sinners; but if anyone is a worshiper of God and does his will, he hears him.”

He is still speaking as one who has been anointed. For God does hear sinners. If God did not hear sinners, that tax collector would have prayed in vain, lowering his eyes to the ground and striking his breast: “Lord, be merciful to me, a sinner.” This confession earned justification, just as the blind man received illumination.

“From the beginning of the world it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of a man born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing.”

Freely, firmly, truthfully. For the things that were done by the Lord—by whom could they have been done except by God? Or when could such things have been done by the disciples except that the Lord dwelled in them?

14. They answered and said to him: “You were born entirely in sins.” What does “entirely” mean? With your eyes closed. But the one who opened your eyes also saves the whole person. The one who gave illumination to the face will give resurrection at the right hand [Note: [Col. 1718] All the manuscripts have, “gave illumination to the face.”].

“You were born entirely in sins, and you teach us?” And they cast him out. They themselves made him a teacher; they themselves questioned him so many times in order to learn, and, ungrateful toward the one teaching them, they cast him out.

15. But what I said a little earlier, brothers, has happened: they expel him, but the Lord receives him. Indeed, because he was expelled, he became a Christian all the more.

Jesus heard that they had cast him out, and when he had found him, he said to him: “Do you believe in the Son of God?” Now he washes the face of his heart.

He answered and said, as though still anointed: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?”

And Jesus said to him: “You have both seen him, and the one speaking with you is he.” He was the one sent; this man was washing his face in Siloam, which is interpreted “Sent.”

Finally, with the face of his heart now washed and his conscience cleansed, recognizing him not merely as the son of man—which he had previously believed—but now as the Son of God who had assumed flesh, he said: “I believe, Lord.” “I believe” is not enough; do you wish to see what kind of faith he had? “Falling down, he worshiped him.”

16. And Jesus said to him: Now that day is present, distinguishing between light and darkness. “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind.”

What is this, Lord? You have brought a great question before those who are weary. But raise our strength, so that we may understand what you have said.

You came so that those who do not see may see: rightly, because you are light; rightly, because you are day; rightly, because you free from darkness. Every soul accepts and understands this. What does the following mean: “And those who see may become blind”? Since you have come, will those who saw become blind? Hear what follows, and perhaps you will understand.

17. Therefore some of the Pharisees were stirred by these words and said to him: “Are we also blind?”

Hear now what was troubling them: “Those who see may become blind.”

Jesus said to them: “If you were blind, you would not have sin.” Yet blindness itself is sin. “If you were blind”—that is, if you recognized yourselves as blind, if you called yourselves blind and ran to the physician—if you were blind in this way, you would not have sin, because I came to take away sin.

“But now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains.” Why? Because by saying, “We see,” you do not seek the physician; you remain in your blindness.

This, then, is what we had not understood shortly before when he said, “I came so that those who do not see may see.” What does “those who do not see may see” mean? Those who confess that they do not see and seek the physician in order to see.

And “those who see may become blind”: what does this mean? Those who think they see and do not seek the physician should remain in their blindness.

Therefore he called this distinction “judgment” when he said, “For judgment I came into this world”—the judgment by which he distinguishes the case of believers and confessors from that of the proud, who think they see and are therefore blinded more gravely—as though the sinner who confesses and seeks the physician had said to him: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my case from that of an unholy nation” (Psalm 42:1), namely, from those who say, “We see,” and whose sin remains.

But he did not yet bring that judgment upon the world by which he will judge the living and the dead at the end of the age. For in this sense he had said, “I judge no one” (John 8:15), because he came first not to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him (John 3:17).

# TREATISE XLV

From the passage written, “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber,” to the passage, “I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.” Chapter 10, verses 1–10.

1. The Lord’s discourse to the Jews arose from the account of the one who had been born blind and illuminated. Your Charity should know and be reminded that today’s reading is connected with that one.

When the Lord had said, “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind”—which we explained as best we could when it was read—some of the Pharisees said: “Are we also blind?” He answered them: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say, ‘We see’; your sin remains” (John 9:39–41). After these words he added what we heard today when it was read.

2. “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber.”

They had said that they were not blind. But they could see only if they were Christ’s sheep. From where did they claim light for themselves, when they were stealing against the day?

Because of their vain, proud, and incurable arrogance, the Lord Jesus joined these words to the preceding ones. In them he gave us a salutary warning, if we pay attention.

There are many who, according to a certain pattern of life in this world, are called good people—good men, good women, innocent, as though observing the commandments prescribed in the law: honoring their parents, not committing adultery, not committing murder, not stealing, not bearing false witness against anyone, and observing the other things commanded by the law. Yet they are not Christians. Often they boast in the same way as these people: “Are we also blind?”

But because they do not know toward what end to direct all these things they do, they do them in vain. Therefore in today’s reading the Lord put forward a likeness concerning his flock and the door through which one enters the sheepfold.

Let the pagans say, “We live well.” If they do not enter through the door, what benefit is there in what they boast of? Living well ought to benefit each person for this purpose: that he may be granted everlasting life. For if he is not granted everlasting life, what benefit is there in living well?

Nor should those be called people who live well who, through blindness, do not know the end of good living, or who, through pride, despise it. No one has true and certain hope of living forever unless he recognizes Life, which is Christ, and enters the sheepfold through the door.

3. Such people often seek to persuade others to live well without being Christians. They wish to climb in by another way, to rob and kill—not, like the shepherd, to preserve and save.

There were certain philosophers who treated many matters concerning virtues and vices with subtlety, dividing and defining them, drawing conclusions through the sharpest reasoning, filling books, and displaying their wisdom with puffed-out cheeks. They even dared to say to people: “Follow us; hold to our school if you wish to live happily.”

But they had not entered through the door. They wanted to destroy, slaughter, and kill.

4. What shall I say about these people? Behold, the Pharisees themselves read, and in what they read they proclaimed Christ and hoped for his coming, yet they did not recognize him when he was present. They too boasted of being among those who saw—that is, among the wise—while denying Christ and not entering through the door.

Therefore, if they should happen to lead anyone astray, they would lead them to be slaughtered and killed, not liberated. Let us leave them aside and see whether those who glory in the name of Christ himself perhaps enter through the door.

5. For there are innumerable people who not only boast that they see, but want to appear to have been illuminated by Christ. Yet they are heretics. Did they perhaps enter through the door? Certainly not.

Sabellius says: “The one who is Son is himself the Father.” But if he is Son, he is not Father. He does not enter through the door who calls the Son the Father.

Arius says: “The Father is one thing, the Son another.” He would speak correctly if he said, “one person is another,” not “one thing is another.” For when he says “another thing,” he contradicts the one from whom he hears: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Therefore he too does not enter through the door, for he proclaims Christ as he imagines him, not as Truth declares him.

You possess the name, but not the reality. Christ is the name of some reality; hold to the reality itself if you wish the name to benefit you.

Someone else—I do not know from where, like Photinus—says: “Christ is a man; he is not God.” He too does not enter through the door, because Christ is both man and God.

What need is there to go through many things and enumerate the many empty heresies? Hold to this: the Catholic Church is Christ’s sheepfold. Whoever wishes to enter the sheepfold should enter through the door and proclaim the true Christ.

Let him not merely proclaim the true Christ, but seek Christ’s glory, not his own; for many, by seeking their own glory, have scattered Christ’s sheep rather than gathered them.

For Christ the Lord is a humble door. Whoever enters through this door must humble himself, so that he may enter with a sound head. But whoever does not humble himself and instead exalts himself wants to climb over the wall. Whoever climbs over the wall is lifted up in order to fall.

6. Yet the Lord Jesus is still speaking figuratively; he is not yet understood. He names the door, he names the sheepfold, he names the sheep; he commends all these things, but does not yet explain them.

Let us therefore continue reading, because he will come to those words in which he deigns to explain certain things he has said to us. From his explanation, perhaps he will also enable us to understand what he has not explained. For he feeds us with what is clear and exercises us through what is obscure.

“Whoever does not enter through the door into the sheepfold, but climbs in by another way.” Woe to the wretched man, for he is going to fall! Let him therefore be humble and enter through the door; let him come with steady feet, and he will not stumble.

“He,” he says, “is a thief and a robber.” He means that he calls other people’s sheep his own: his own in the sense that they have been stolen—not in order to save them, but to kill them. Therefore he is a thief because he calls what belongs to another his own; a robber because he kills what he has stolen.

“But whoever enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep. To him the doorkeeper opens.”

We shall ask about this doorkeeper when we have heard from the Lord himself what the door is and who the shepherd is.

“And the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name.” He has their names written in the book of life. He calls his own sheep by name. Hence the Apostle says: “The Lord knows those who are his” (2 Timothy 2:19).

“And he leads them out. And when he has brought out his own sheep, he goes before them; and the sheep follow him because they know his voice. But they do not follow a stranger; rather, they flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.”

These words are veiled, full of questions, pregnant with mysteries. Let us therefore follow and listen to the teacher opening something from these obscurities; and through what he opens, perhaps making us enter as well.

### 7

Jesus spoke this proverb to them, but they did not understand what he was saying to them. Perhaps neither do we. What, then, is the difference between them and us, before we too come to recognize these words? We knock so that it may be opened to us [Col. 1722]; they, however, by denying Christ, did not wish to enter in order to be saved, but preferred to remain outside and be lost. The fact, then, that we hear these words devoutly, and that before we understand them we believe them to be true and divine, marks a great difference between us and them.

For when two people hear the words of the Gospel—one impious, the other devout—and perhaps neither understands them, one says, “He said nothing,” while the other says, “He spoke the truth, and what he said is good, but we do not understand it”: the latter, because he believes, is already knocking and is worthy that the door be opened to him, provided he persists in knocking; the former is still hearing, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isa. VII, 9, according to the Septuagint).

Why do I emphasize this? Because even when I have explained these obscure words as best I can—either because they are very hidden, or because I have not grasped their meaning, or because I lack the ability to explain what I understand, or because someone is so slow that he cannot follow even an explanation—he must not despair of himself. Let him remain in the faith, let him walk in the way, and let him hear the Apostle saying, “And if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you; nevertheless, let us walk according to that to which we have attained” (Philipp. III, 15).

### 8

Let us therefore begin to hear the one explaining whom we heard making the statement. Jesus said to them again:

> “Amen, amen, I say to you: I am the door of the sheep.”

Behold, he has opened the very door that he had presented as closed. He himself is the door. We have recognized it; let us enter—or let us rejoice that we have entered.

> “All who came are thieves and robbers.”

What does this mean, Lord: “All who came”? What then? Did you not come? But understand: I said, “All who came,” meaning, of course, apart from me.

Let us recall what came before. Before his coming, the Prophets came. Were they thieves and robbers? Certainly not. They did not come apart from him, because they came with him. He was sending heralds of his coming, but he possessed the hearts of those whom he sent. Do you wish to know that they came with him, who is always the same? He assumed flesh in time. What, then, does “always” mean? “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1). They came with him, therefore, who came with the Word of God.

“I am,” he says, “the way, and the truth, and the life” (ibid. XIX, 6). If he is the truth, those who were truthful came with him. All, therefore, who came apart from him are thieves and robbers—that is, they came to steal and to kill.

### 9

“But the sheep did not listen to them.” This is the greater difficulty: “The sheep did not listen to them.”

Before the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, who came humbly in the flesh, righteous people went before us, believing in him as one who would come, just as we believe in him who has come. The times have changed, not the faith. The words themselves also change according to time, when they are inflected differently: “He is going to come” has one sound; “He has come” has another. The sound has changed—“he is going to come” and “he has come”—but the same faith joins together both those who believed that he would come and those who believed that he had come.

Although we live in different times, we see both groups entering through one door of faith, that is, through Christ. We believe that the Lord Jesus Christ was born of a Virgin, came in the flesh, suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven. We believe all this already to have been accomplished, just as you hear the words expressed in the past tense.

In fellowship with our faith are those fathers who believed that he would be born of a Virgin, suffer, rise again, and ascend into heaven. The Apostle points to them when he says:

> “But having the same spirit of faith, as it is written: ‘I believed, therefore I spoke’; we also believe, and therefore we speak” (II Cor. IV, 13).

The Prophet said, “I believed, therefore I spoke” (Ps. CXV, 10); the Apostle says, “We also believe, and therefore we speak.” To show you that the faith is one, hear him say, “Having the same spirit of faith … we also believe.”

Thus, in another passage:

> “For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that our fathers were all under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (I Cor. X, 1–4).

The Red Sea signifies Baptism; Moses, the leader through the Red Sea, signifies Christ; the people crossing signify the faithful; the death of the Egyptians signifies the abolition of sins. In different signs there is the same faith—just as in different words—because words change their sounds according to the times, and words are, in any case, nothing other than signs. Words are signs by signifying: remove the signification from a word, and it is empty noise.

Everything, therefore, was signified. Did those through whom these signs were administered, through whom the same things we believe were prophetically foretold, not believe the same things? They certainly did believe them. But they believed that these things were going to happen, whereas we believe that they have happened.

Thus he also says, “They drank the same spiritual drink”—the same spiritual drink, not the same bodily drink. What did they drink? “They drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 1–4).

See, then: while the faith remains, the signs have changed. There the rock was Christ; for us Christ is what is placed upon the altar of God. They drank, as a great sacrament of this same Christ, water flowing from the rock; the faithful know what we drink. If you attend to the visible appearance, it is something else; if to the intelligible signification, “they drank the same spiritual drink.”

All, therefore, who at that time believed Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, or the other Patriarchs and Prophets who foretold Christ, were sheep, and they heard Christ. They heard not the voice of a stranger, but his own voice. The Judge was present in the herald. For when a judge speaks through a herald, the shorthand writer does not record, “The herald said,” but, “The judge said.”

Those, therefore, whom the sheep did not hear are people in whom the voice of Christ was absent: people who wandered, spoke falsely, chattered empty things, invented vanities, and led the miserable astray.

### 10

What, then, did I mean when I said that this is the greater difficulty? What is obscure and difficult to understand here? Listen, I ask you.
