Behold, the Lord Jesus Christ himself came and preached. Surely, then, his voice was much more plainly the shepherd’s voice, coming from the shepherd’s own mouth. If the shepherd’s voice was heard through the Prophets, how much more did the shepherd’s own tongue utter the shepherd’s voice?

Not everyone listened. But what are we to think? Were those who listened sheep? Judas listened, and he was a wolf. He followed, but, covered with sheep’s clothing, he lay in wait for the shepherd.

Some, however, of those who crucified Christ did not listen, and they were sheep. He saw them in the crowd when he said:

> “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John VIII, 28).

How is this difficulty resolved? Those who are not sheep listen, and sheep do not listen. Some wolves follow the shepherd’s voice, while certain sheep oppose him. Finally, sheep kill the shepherd.

The difficulty is resolved in this way: someone may answer, “When they did not listen, they were not yet sheep; at that time they were wolves. The voice they heard changed them and made sheep out of wolves. Once they became sheep, they listened, found the shepherd, and followed him; they hoped for the shepherd’s promises because they obeyed his commands.”

### 11

This difficulty has been resolved somehow, and perhaps this answer is sufficient for someone. But it still troubles me, and I am sharing with you what troubles me, so that, as it were, by seeking together with you, I may deserve to find together with you, with him revealing the answer.

Listen, then, to what troubles me. Through the prophet Ezekiel the Lord rebukes the shepherds and says, among other things, about the sheep:

> “You did not bring back the wandering sheep” (Ezek. XXXIV, 4).

He calls it wandering, and he calls it a sheep. If, when it was wandering, it was a sheep, whose voice had it heard so that it wandered? Certainly it would not have wandered if it had heard the shepherd’s voice. But it wandered precisely because it heard the voice of a stranger; it heard the voice of a thief and robber.

Certainly the sheep do not hear the voice of robbers:

> “All who came,” he says—and we understand him to mean, “apart from me”—“all who came apart from me are thieves and robbers, and the sheep did not listen to them.”

Lord, if the sheep did not listen to them, how do sheep wander? If the sheep hear no one but you—and you are the truth—then whoever hears the truth certainly does not wander. Yet they wander, and they are called sheep. For if they were not called sheep while in their error, it would not be said through Ezekiel, “You did not bring back the wandering sheep.”

How can it both wander and be a sheep? Did it hear the voice of a stranger? Certainly, “the sheep did not listen to them.”

Moreover, many are now gathered into Christ’s fold and, from being heretics, become Catholics. They are taken away from thieves and restored to the shepherd. Sometimes they complain and grow weary of the one bringing them back, and fail to perceive the one cutting their throats. Nevertheless, even when they come as resistant sheep, they recognize the shepherd’s voice, rejoice that they have come, and are ashamed that they wandered.

When, therefore, they gloried in that error as though it were the truth—and certainly they were not hearing the shepherd’s voice, and for that reason were following a stranger—were they sheep or were they not? If they were sheep, how is it that sheep do not hear strangers? If they were not sheep, why are those rebuked to whom it is said, “You did not bring back the wandering sheep”?

Even among Christians who have already become Catholics, faithful people of good hope, bad things sometimes happen. They are led astray into error and afterward brought back. When they have been led into error and rebaptized, or when, after belonging to the Lord’s fold, they have again fallen back into their former error, were they sheep or were they not? Certainly they were Catholics. If they were faithful Catholics, they were sheep. If they were sheep, how could they have heard the voice of a stranger, when the Lord says that the sheep did not listen to them?

### 12

You have heard, brothers, the depth of the difficulty. I therefore say: “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19). He knows those foreknown; he knows those predestined. For it is said of him:

> “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers. And those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified. If God is for us, who is against us? Add this as well: He who did not spare his own Son, but handed him over for us all, how will he not also, with him, grant us all things?”

But to which “us” does this refer? To the foreknown, the predestined, the justified, and the glorified. Of them it continues:

> “Who will bring an accusation against God’s elect?” (Rom. VIII, 29–33).

The Lord therefore knows those who are his; they are the sheep. Sometimes they do not know themselves, but the shepherd knows them according to this predestination, according to this foreknowledge of God, according to the election of the sheep before the foundation of the world. For the Apostle also says:

> “As he chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Eph. I, 4).

According to this foreknowledge and predestination of God, how many sheep are outside, and how many wolves inside; and how many sheep inside, and how many wolves outside!

What did I mean by saying, “How many sheep are outside”? How many now live in luxury but will become chaste; how many blaspheme Christ but will believe in Christ; how many get drunk but will become sober; how many seize the property of others but will give away their own! Yet at present they hear the voice of a stranger and follow strangers.

Likewise, how many now praise inside but will later blaspheme; are chaste but will fornicate; are sober but will later bury themselves in wine; stand but will fall! They are not sheep. We are speaking of the predestined, of those whom the Lord knows to be his.

And yet, as long as these people think rightly, they hear Christ’s voice. Behold, these hear it, while those do not—and yet, according to predestination, these are not sheep, while those are.

### 13

The difficulty still remains, but for the moment it seems to me that it can be resolved in this way. There is a certain voice—I mean, there is a certain voice of the shepherd—in which sheep do not hear strangers, and in which those who are not sheep do not hear Christ.

What voice is this?

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. X, 22).

One who belongs to him does not disregard this voice; a stranger does not hear it. For the stranger also preaches to him that he should persevere with him to the end, but by not persevering with him he does not hear this voice.

He comes to Christ and hears various words—all true, all sound. Among all these words is also this one:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

Whoever hears this is a sheep.

But some person was hearing it, then became foolish, grew cold, and heard a stranger. If he is predestined, he wandered for a time but was not lost forever. He returns to hear what he neglected and to do what he heard.

For if he belongs to those who are predestined, God foresaw both his error and his future conversion. If he has strayed, he returns to hear the shepherd’s voice and follows the one saying:

> “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

A good voice, brothers—a true, pastoral voice. It is the voice of salvation in the tents of the righteous (Ps. CXVII, 15).

It is easy to hear Christ; it is easy to praise the Gospel; it is easy to applaud the preacher. To persevere to the end: this belongs to the sheep who hear the shepherd’s voice.

Temptation comes: persevere to the end, because temptation does not persevere to the end.

[Note: [Col. 1726] This sentence, “because temptation does not persevere to the end,” is absent from most manuscripts.]

To what end will you persevere? Until you finish the journey. As long as you do not hear Christ, your adversary is on this journey—that is, in this mortal life. But what does he say?

> “Come to an agreement with your adversary quickly, while you are with him on the way” (Matt. V, 25).

You heard, believed, and came to an agreement. If you were opposed, come to an agreement. If it has been granted to you to come to an agreement, do not continue to quarrel. You do not know when the journey will end, but he knows.

If you are a sheep, and if you persevere to the end, you will be saved. Thus those who belong to him do not despise this voice, while strangers do not hear it.

As I was able, as he himself granted, I have either explained to you or discussed with you this very deep difficulty. If some have understood less, let devotion remain, and the truth will be revealed. Those who have understood should not exalt themselves as though they were swifter than the slower, lest, by exalting themselves, they go astray, while the slower arrive more easily.

May he lead us all, to whom we say:

> “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I will walk in your truth” (Ps. LXXXV, 11).

### 14

Because the Lord has explained that he himself is the door, let us enter into those matters that he proposed but did not explain.

Who the shepherd is, although he did not say so in the reading recited today, he states most clearly in what follows:

> “I am the good shepherd.”

Even if he had not said this, whom else should we understand apart from him in the words:

> “The one who enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep. The doorkeeper opens for him; and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name, and leads them out. And when he has brought out his own sheep, he goes before them; and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice”?

Who else calls his own sheep by name and leads them from here to eternal life, except the one who knows the names of the predestined? Hence he says to his disciples:

> “Rejoice, because your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20).

For this reason he calls them by name.

And who else brings them out, except the one who forgives their sins, so that, freed from harsh bonds, they can follow him?

And who has gone before them so that they may follow him, except the one who, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him (Rom. VI, 9)? When he was visible here in the flesh, he said:

> “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John XVII, 24).

Hence comes what he says:

> “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved; and he will enter and go out, and will find pasture.”

Here he clearly shows that not only the shepherd but also the sheep enter through the door.

### 15

But what does “he will enter, and go out, and find pasture” mean?

To enter the Church through Christ, the door, is certainly very good. To go out of the Church, however, is not good, as this same John the Evangelist says in his Epistle:

> “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (John II, 19).

Such an exit, therefore, could not be praised by the good shepherd, so that he would say, “He will enter, and go out, and find pasture.”

There is, then, not only a good entrance but also a good exit through the good door, which is Christ. But what is this praiseworthy and blessed exit?

I could say that we enter when we think something inwardly, and go out when we do something outwardly. Since, as the Apostle says, Christ dwells in our hearts through faith (Eph. III, 17), to enter through Christ means to think according to that faith; to go out through Christ means also to act outwardly, that is, before human beings, according to that faith.

Hence we read in the Psalm:

> “A person goes out to his work” (Ps. CIII, 23);

and the Lord himself says:

> “Let your works shine before human beings” (Matt. V, 16).

But I am more pleased by the fact that the truth itself, like a good shepherd—and therefore a good teacher—has in a certain way instructed us how we should understand the words, “He will enter, and go out, and find pasture,” when it immediately adds:

> “The thief comes only to steal, slaughter, and destroy; I came so that they may have life, and have it more abundantly.”

It seems to me that he meant: “So that they may have life when entering, and have it more abundantly when going out.”

No one can go out through the door—that is, through Christ—to eternal life, which will be in vision, unless through that same door, Christ, he has entered his Church, which is his fold, into temporal life, which exists in faith.

Therefore he says:

> “I came so that they may have life”—

that is, faith, which works through love (Gal. V, 6). Through this faith they enter the fold so that they may live, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Rom. I, 17).

“And that they may have it more abundantly”: those who persevere to the end go out through that door, that is, through faith in Christ, because true believers die; and they will have life more abundantly when they come to where that shepherd has gone before them, where they will never again die.

Although even here, in the fold itself, there is no lack of pasture—for we can understand “he will find pasture” in relation to both entrance and exit—nevertheless they will then find true pasture, where those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled (Matt. V, 6). Such was the pasture found by the one to whom it was said:

> “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII, 43).

But how he himself is the door and himself the shepherd, so that in some way he himself is also understood to enter and go out through himself, and who the doorkeeper is—it would take too long to inquire into this today and to explain it as he himself may grant.

# TRACTATE XLVI

From the passage written, “I am the good shepherd,” etc., up to, “But the hired servant flees, because he is a hired servant and has no concern for the sheep.” Chapter X, verses 11–13.

### 1

The Lord Jesus was speaking to his sheep, both those present and those who would be in the future, who were then already present—because there were already sheep who were his, and there were those who would become his sheep. To both the present and the future, to them and to us, and to however many of his sheep there may be after us, he showed who had been sent to them.

All, therefore, hear the voice of their shepherd saying:

> “I am the good shepherd.”

He would not add “good” unless there were bad shepherds. But the bad shepherds are the thieves and robbers—or, at most, the hired servants.

We must inquire into, distinguish, and recognize all the persons whom he has introduced. The Lord has already opened two matters that he had presented as closed, in a certain sense: we now know that he himself is the door; we know that he himself is the shepherd.

Who the thieves and robbers are was revealed in yesterday’s reading. Today we heard about the hired servant, and we also heard about the wolf; yesterday the doorkeeper was named as well.

Among the good, therefore, are the door, the doorkeeper, the shepherd, and the sheep. Among the bad are thieves and robbers, hired servants, and the wolf.

### 2

We understand the Lord Christ to be the door, and the shepherd himself. Who, then, is the doorkeeper? For he explained these two matters himself and left the doorkeeper for us to seek.

And what does he say about the doorkeeper?

> “The doorkeeper opens for him.”

For whom does he open? For the shepherd. What does he open for the shepherd? The door. And what is the door itself? The shepherd himself.

If the Lord Christ had not explained it, and had not himself said, “I am the shepherd,” and, “I am the door” (John X, 3, 9), would any of us dare to say that Christ himself is both shepherd and door?

If he had said, “I am the shepherd,” but had not said, “I am the door,” we would have sought what the door was and, perhaps supposing it to be something else, remained outside the door.

By his grace and mercy he explained the shepherd to us and said that it was himself; he explained the door and said that it was himself; he left the doorkeeper for us to seek.

Whom shall we call the doorkeeper? Whoever we find, we must take care not to consider him greater than the door itself. For among human houses the doorkeeper is greater than the door. The doorkeeper is placed before the door, not the door before the doorkeeper, because the doorkeeper guards the door, not the door the doorkeeper.

I do not dare to say that anyone is greater than the door. For I have already heard what the door is. I am not left to my own conjecture; human speculation has not been granted free rein. God has spoken; the truth has spoken; what the immutable one has spoken cannot be changed.

### 3

In the depth of this difficulty, therefore, I shall say what seems to me to be the case. Let each person choose what seems right, but let him think devoutly, as it is written:

> “Think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart” (Wis. I, 1).

Perhaps we ought to understand the Lord himself as the doorkeeper. The difference between a shepherd and a door in human affairs is much greater than that between a doorkeeper and a door, and yet the Lord called himself both shepherd and door.

Why, then, should we not understand him also as the doorkeeper?

If we consider the properties of things, the Lord Christ is not a shepherd in the way shepherds are ordinarily known and seen; nor is he a door, for a carpenter did not make him. But if we understand him according to some likeness, he is both door and shepherd. I dare say that he is also a sheep: a sheep is under a shepherd, yet he is both shepherd and sheep.

Where is the shepherd? Behold, you have it here; read the Gospel:

> “I am the good shepherd.”

Where is the sheep? Ask the prophet:

> “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isa. LIII, 7).

Ask the friend of the bridegroom:

> “Behold the Lamb of God; behold the one who takes away the sin of the world” (John I, 29).

I shall say something still more marvelous according to these likenesses. A lamb, a sheep, and a shepherd are friendly with one another; against lions, however, sheep are customarily guarded by shepherds. Yet of Christ, although he is both sheep and shepherd, we read:

> “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered” (Rev. V, 5).

[Col. 1729]

Receive all these statements, brothers, according to likenesses, not according to the proper nature of the things.

We are accustomed to see shepherds sitting upon a rock and guarding from there the animals entrusted to them. Certainly the shepherd is better than the rock upon which the shepherd sits; yet Christ is both shepherd and rock.

All this is according to likeness.

But if you ask me about his proper nature:

> “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

If you ask me about his proper nature: the only-begotten Son, eternally and from eternity begotten of the Father, equal to the one who begets him; through whom all things were made; immutable with the Father; and, having assumed the form of a human being, not changed; through the incarnation, a human being, the Son of Man and the Son of God.

All that I have said is not likeness but reality.

### 4

Let us not therefore hesitate, brothers, to understand him according to certain likenesses as both the door and the doorkeeper.

For what is a door? That through which we enter. Who is a doorkeeper? The one who opens. Who, then, opens himself, except the one who explains himself?

Behold, the Lord had called himself the door, but we had not understood. When we did not understand, it was closed. The one who opened it is himself the doorkeeper.

There is therefore no necessity to seek anything else—no necessity. But perhaps there is a desire to do so. If there is such a desire, do not go astray; do not depart from the Trinity.

If you seek another person as the doorkeeper, let the Holy Spirit come before you. For the Holy Spirit will not disdain to be the doorkeeper, since the Son deigned to be the door himself.

Consider, perhaps, the Holy Spirit as the doorkeeper. The Lord himself says of the Holy Spirit to his disciples:

> “He himself will teach you all truth” (ibid. XVI, 13).

What is the door? Christ. What is Christ? The truth. Who opens the door except the one who teaches all truth?

### 5

What shall we say about the hired servant? He is not mentioned among the good.

> “The good shepherd,” he says, “lays down his life for the sheep. The hired servant, who is not the shepherd and whose own the sheep are not, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep.”

The hired servant does not play a good role here, and yet he is useful in some respect. Nor would he be called a hired servant unless he received wages from the one who hired him.

Who, then, is this hired servant, both blameworthy and necessary?

Here, brothers, may the Lord himself enlighten us, so that we may understand hired servants and not be hired servants ourselves.

Who, then, is the hired servant? There are certain leaders in the Church of whom the Apostle Paul says:

> “Seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.”

What does “seeking their own interests” mean? It means not loving Christ freely, not seeking God for God’s sake, pursuing temporal advantages, gaping after profits, and desiring honors from human beings.

When such things are loved by a leader, and God is served for their sake, whoever is like this is a hired servant. Let him not count himself among the children.

For of such people the Lord also says:

> “Amen, I say to you, they have received their reward” (Matt. VI, 5).

Hear what the Apostle Paul says about the holy Timothy:

> “I hope in the Lord Jesus to send Timothy to you soon, so that I too may be encouraged when I learn how things are with you. For I have no one of like mind who will genuinely be concerned for you. For all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ” (Philipp. II, 19–21).

Among the hired servants the shepherd groaned. He sought someone who would sincerely love Christ’s flock, and among those who were with him at that time he found no one else.

It was not that there was no one in Christ’s Church at that time, apart from the Apostle Paul and Timothy, who was genuinely concerned for the flock. Rather, when Paul sent Timothy, it happened that he had no other son with him; only hired servants were with him, seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.

And yet, because Timothy was genuinely concerned for the flock, Paul preferred to send his son and remain among the hired servants.

We also find hired servants, and only the Lord can distinguish them. The one who looks into the heart is the one who distinguishes them. Yet sometimes they can be recognized by us as well. For the Lord himself did not say without reason, even concerning wolves:

> “You will know them by their fruits” (Matt. VII, 16).

Many are tested by temptations, and then their thoughts become apparent; many, however, remain hidden.

Let the Lord’s fold have leaders who are both children and hired servants.

The leaders who are children are shepherds. If they are shepherds, how is there one shepherd? Because all of them are members of the one shepherd, whose own the sheep are. For they too are members of that one sheep, because:

> “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter.”

### 6

Hear also that hired servants are necessary. Many in the Church pursue earthly advantages, yet still preach Christ, and through them Christ’s voice is heard. The sheep follow not the hired servant but the shepherd’s voice through the hired servant.

Hear the hired servants identified by the Lord himself:

> “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat. Therefore do and observe whatever they tell you, but do not do according to their works” (ibid. XXIII, 2).

What else did he say except, “Through hired servants hear the shepherd’s voice”?

By sitting on Moses’ seat they teach God’s law; therefore God teaches through them. But if they wish to teach their own interests, do not hear them; do not do what they do.

Certainly such people seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. Yet no hired servant dares to say to Christ’s people, “Seek your own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.” What he does badly, he does not preach from Christ’s seat. He harms from the place where he does evil, not from the place where he speaks good.

Pluck the grape; beware the thorn.

Good—you have understood. But for the slower ones I shall say the same thing more plainly.

How did I say, “Pluck the grape; beware the thorn,” when the Lord says:

> “Do people gather grapes from thorns, or figs from thistles?” (ibid. VII, 16)

It is altogether true, and yet what I said is also true: “Pluck the grape; beware the thorn.”

For sometimes a cluster of grapes, springing from the root of a vine, hangs in a hedge; the vine-shoot grows, is intertwined with thorns, and bears fruit that does not belong to the thorn. The vine did not produce the thorn; rather, the vine-shoot rested among the thorns.

Do not question anything except the roots. Seek the root of the thorn, and you will find it outside the vine. Seek the origin of the grape, and the vine produced it from its root.

Moses’ seat, therefore, was a vine; the conduct of the Pharisees was a thorn. True doctrine passed through the wicked, like a vine-shoot in a hedge, a cluster among thorns.

Read carefully.

[Note: [Col. 1730] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have: “Carefully read the cluster among the thorns.”]

Do not tear your hand while seeking the fruit. When you hear someone saying good things, do not imitate the one doing evil.

> “Do whatever they tell you”: gather the grapes.
>
> “But do not do what they do”: beware the thorns.

Even through hired servants hear the shepherd’s voice, but do not be hired servants, since you are members of the shepherd.

The holy Apostle Paul himself said:

> “I have no one who will genuinely be concerned for you; for all seek their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ.”

Elsewhere, distinguishing between hired servants and children, see what he says:

> “Some indeed preach Christ from envy and contention, but others from good will. Some do so out of love, knowing that I have been appointed for the defense of the Gospel; others proclaim Christ out of defiance, not sincerely, thinking to stir up affliction for my bonds.”

These were hired servants; they envied the Apostle Paul. Why did they envy him, except because they were seeking temporal things?

But pay attention to what he adds:

> “What then? Only that in every way, whether in pretense or in truth, Christ is proclaimed; and in this I rejoice, and I will also rejoice” (Philipp. I, 15–18).

Christ is the truth. Let the truth be proclaimed by hired servants in pretense; let the truth be proclaimed by children in truth. Children patiently await the Father’s eternal inheritance; hired servants eagerly desire the temporal reward of the one who hired them.

May human glory—which I see the hired servants envying me—be diminished for me; and yet, through both the tongues of hired servants and those of children, may the divine glory of Christ be spread abroad, whether Christ is proclaimed in pretense or in truth.

### 7

We have also seen who the hired servant is. Who is the wolf except the devil?

And what is said about the hired servant?

> “When he sees the wolf coming, he flees, because the sheep are not his own and he has no concern for the sheep.”

Was the Apostle Paul such a man? Certainly not. Was Peter? Certainly not. Were the other Apostles such men, except Judas, the son of perdition? Certainly not.

They were shepherds, then? Clearly they were shepherds.

And how is there one shepherd? I have already said: they are shepherds because they are members of the shepherd. They rejoiced in that head, agreed under that head, and lived by one Spirit in the structure of one body. Thus they all belonged to one shepherd.

If they were shepherds and not hired servants, why did they flee when they suffered persecution? Explain this to us, Lord.

I saw Paul fleeing in the Epistle: he was lowered in a basket through a wall to escape the hands of his persecutor (II Cor. XI, 33). Was he therefore unconcerned for the sheep whom he abandoned when the wolf came?

He was certainly concerned for them, but he commended them in prayer to the shepherd seated in heaven. By fleeing, he preserved himself for their benefit, as he says in one place:

> “To remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (Philipp. I, 24).

For they had all heard from that shepherd himself:

> “If they persecute you in one city, flee to another” (Matt. X, 23).

May the Lord deign to explain this difficulty to us.

Lord, you said to those whom you certainly wished to be faithful shepherds, whom you were forming to be your members, “If they persecute you, flee.” You therefore do them an injury when you rebuke the hired servants who see the wolf coming and flee.

We ask you to show us what depth this difficulty contains. Let us knock; the one who opens—the doorkeeper of the door, who is himself—will be present.

[Col. 1732] 8. Who is the hireling who sees the wolf coming and flees? The one who seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ; who does not dare freely rebuke the sinner (I Tim. 5:20). Look: someone has sinned—he has sinned grievously; he must be rebuked, he must be excommunicated. But once excommunicated, he will become an enemy, will lie in wait, and will do harm whenever he can. Now the one who seeks his own interests, not those of Jesus Christ, lest he lose what he pursues—the advantage of human friendship—and incur the trouble of human enmities, remains silent and does not rebuke. Look: the wolf has seized the sheep by the throat; the devil has persuaded a believer to commit adultery; you are silent, you do not rebuke. O hireling, you saw the coming wolf and fled.

Perhaps he answers and says: “Look, I am here; I have not fled.” You fled because you were silent; you were silent because you were afraid. The flight of the mind is fear. You stood bodily, but in spirit you fled—the very thing that he did not do who said, “Although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit” (Col. 2:5). How could he flee in spirit who, though absent in body, rebuked fornicators in his letters?

Our affections are movements of the soul. Joy is the soul’s expansion; sorrow, the soul’s contraction; desire, the soul’s advance; fear is the soul’s flight. You are expanded in soul when you take delight; contracted in soul when you are troubled; you advance in soul when you desire; you flee in soul when you are afraid. This, then, is why the hireling is said to flee when he sees the wolf. Why? Because he has no concern for the sheep. Why has he no concern for the sheep? Because he is a hireling. What does “he is a hireling” mean? He is seeking a temporal reward, and “he will not remain in the house forever” [Note: [Col. 1732] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Louvain editions read: “he seeks, and he will not remain in the house forever.” M.]. There are still matters to be sought and discussed with you, but it is not advisable to burden you. We distribute the Lord’s provisions to our fellow servants; in the Lord’s pastures we feed the sheep, and at the same time we ourselves are fed. Just as what is necessary must not be withheld, so a weak heart must not be overburdened by an excess of nourishment. Therefore let it not trouble Your Charity that I do not discuss today everything that I think still needs to be examined here; rather, the same reading will be recited to us again on another day appointed for our discourse [Note: [Col. 1732] Manuscripts: “to you.”], and, with his help, will be treated more carefully in the Lord’s name.

TRACTATE XLVII. From the passage, “I am the good shepherd, and I know my sheep,” etc., up to the passage, “Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” Chapter 10, verses 14–21.

1. You who listen to the word of our God not only willingly but attentively surely remember our promise. For the Gospel reading itself was read today that had been read on the preceding Sunday; because, being detained by certain necessities, we were unable to discuss everything that we owed to your understanding. Accordingly, we are not seeking today those things that have already been said and treated, lest, by repeating the same matters again, I should be prevented from reaching what has not yet been said.

You already know, in the Lord’s name, who the good shepherd is, and how the good shepherds are his members, and therefore there is one shepherd; [Col. 1733] you know which hireling must be endured; who the wolf is, and which thieves and robbers must be avoided; what the sheep are; what the door is through which both the sheep enter and the shepherd; and how the doorkeeper is to be understood. You also know that whoever does not enter through the door is a thief and a robber, and comes only to steal, kill, and destroy. All these matters, so far as I judge, have been sufficiently treated.

Today we must say, insofar as the Lord assists—for Jesus Christ himself our Savior both declared himself to be the shepherd and the door, and said that the good shepherd enters through the door—in what manner he himself enters through himself. For if no one is a good shepherd except the one who enters through the door, and he himself is especially the good shepherd, and he himself is the door, I cannot understand this except as meaning that he himself also enters through himself to his sheep and gives them his voice so that they may follow him, and that, entering and going out, they may find pasture, which is eternal life.

2. I shall speak briefly. As I seek to enter among you—that is, into your hearts—I preach Christ. If I preach anything else, I shall be trying to climb up by another route. Christ, then, is the door for me to you; through Christ I enter, not to your walls but to your hearts. Through Christ I enter; you gladly heard Christ in me. Why did you gladly hear Christ in me? Because you are Christ’s sheep; you were acquired by Christ’s blood. You recognize your price: it is not given by me, but preached through me. He purchased you, who poured out precious blood; precious is the blood of one without sin.

Yet he himself also made the blood of his own precious, for whom he paid the price of blood. For if he had not made the blood of his own precious, it would not be said, “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115:15). Therefore, even when he says, “The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep,” he alone did not do this; and yet, if those who did it are his members, that one same person did it. For he was able to do it without them; but how could they do it without him, when he himself said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)?

We show, however, that others also did this because the apostle John himself, who preached the Gospel you have heard, said in his Epistle: “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (I John 3:16). “We ought,” he said; the one who first demonstrated it made us debtors. Therefore it is written in one place: “If you sit down to dine at the table of a ruler, understand wisely what is set before you; and put your hand to it, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Prov. 23:1–2, according to the Septuagint). You know what the table of the ruler is: there are the body and blood of Christ. Whoever approaches such a table should prepare such things.

And what does “prepare such things” mean? Just as he laid down his life for us, so we also ought, “for building up the people and defending the faith” [Note: [Col. 1733] Most manuscripts do not contain the words “for building up the people and defending the faith.”], to lay down our lives for the brethren. Therefore to Peter, whom he wished to make a good shepherd, he said—not in Peter himself, but in his own body: “Peter, do you love me? Feed my sheep.” This once, this a second time, this a third time, even to his sorrow. And when the Lord had asked him as much as he judged ought to be asked, so that the one who had denied him three times might confess him three times, and had entrusted his sheep to him to feed a third time, he said to him: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” And the Evangelist explained what the Lord had said: “This,” he says, “he said, signifying by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:15–19). “Feed my sheep,” then, means that you should lay down your life for my sheep.

3. As for what he says, “As the Father knows me, and I know the Father,” who does not know it? He knows the Father through himself; we know the Father through him. That he knows through himself, we know; that we also know through him, we know as well, because we know even this through him. For he himself said: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father; he has declared him” (ibid. 1:18). Therefore we too know through him, since he has declared him to us. Elsewhere also he says: “No one knows the Son except the Father; nor does anyone know the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

Therefore, just as he himself knows the Father through himself, while we know the Father through him, so he enters the sheepfold through himself, and we through him. We said that through Christ we have the door to you; why? Because we preach Christ. We preach Christ, and therefore we enter through the door. But Christ preaches Christ, because he preaches himself; and therefore the shepherd enters through himself.

When light displays other things that are seen in the light, does it need something else in order to be displayed? Light therefore demonstrates both other things and itself. Whatever we understand, we understand by understanding; and understanding itself—by what else do we understand it, if not by understanding? Is it the same with the bodily eye, by which you see both other things and the eye itself? Although people see with their eyes, they do not see their own eyes. The bodily eye sees other things but cannot see itself; the intellect, however, understands both other things and itself. Just as the intellect sees itself, so Christ preaches himself. If he preaches himself, and by preaching enters into you, he enters into you through himself.

He himself is also the door to the Father, because there is no way by which one comes to the Father except through him. “For there is one God and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (I Tim. 2:5).

Many things are said by means of a word: these very things I have said, I certainly said by means of a word. If I wished to say the word itself by which I speak, by what would I say it except by a word? Thus by means of the word other things are said, things that are not the word; and the word itself cannot be said except by means of a word.

With the Lord’s help, we have drawn abundantly on examples. Understand, then, how the Lord Jesus Christ is both the door and the shepherd: the door by opening himself, the shepherd by entering through himself. Indeed, brothers, he also gave what it means to be a shepherd to his members: Peter is a shepherd, Paul is a shepherd, the other Apostles are shepherds, and good bishops are shepherds. But none of us calls himself the door; he reserved this as his own prerogative, the way by which the sheep enter.

Accordingly, the apostle Paul was fulfilling the office of a good shepherd when he preached Christ, because he was entering through the door. But when undisciplined sheep began to create schisms and to set up other doors for themselves—not doors by which they might enter in order to be gathered, but by which they might wander in order to be divided—saying, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Cephas,” “I to Apollos,” “I to Christ,” he was alarmed at those who said, “I belong to Paul,” as though crying out to the sheep, “Wretched ones, where are you going? I am not the door.” “Was Paul,” he says, “crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (I Cor. 1:12–13). But those who said, “I belong to Christ,” had found the door.

4. Concerning one sheepfold and one shepherd, you regularly hear us speak already; for we have strongly commended the one sheepfold, preaching unity, so that all the sheep might enter through Christ and no one might follow Donatus. Nevertheless, from what the Lord specifically said this is sufficiently clear.

He was speaking among the Jews, and had been sent to the Jews—not on account of certain people in that nation who persisted in savage hatred and continued in darkness, but on account of certain others within that very people whom he calls his sheep. Of them he says, “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 15:24).

He knew them also amid the raging crowd, and foresaw them among believers at peace. What, then, does “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” mean, except that he did not display his bodily presence except to the people of Israel? He himself did not go to the Gentiles, but sent others; whereas to the people of Israel he both sent others and came himself, so that those who despised him might receive a greater judgment, because his presence also had been offered to them.

The Lord himself was there; there he chose his mother; there he wished to be conceived, there to be born, there to pour out his blood. There are [Note: [Col. 1735] The Louvain editors note that “there are” is omitted in two of their manuscripts; it is found in all ours. The marks of Christ’s feet impressed in the ground on the Mount of Olives are also mentioned in the book On Hebrew Places among Jerome’s works, and in Bede’s work On the Names of Places in the Acts of the Apostles. They are likewise mentioned in Sulpicius Severus, Sacred History, book 2.] his footprints, now venerated where he last stood, from which he ascended into heaven. But to the Gentiles he sent others.

5. Perhaps someone thinks that, since he himself did not come to us but sent others to us, we did not hear his voice but the voice of those whom he sent. Away with it; let that thought be driven from your hearts. He himself was in those whom he sent. Hear Paul himself, whom he sent—for he sent the apostle Paul chiefly to the Gentiles. Paul himself says, warning us that it is not he but Christ who speaks through him: “Do you wish to receive proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (II Cor. 13:3).

Hear the Lord himself also: “I have other sheep,” that is, among the Gentiles, “which are not of this fold,” that is, of the people of Israel; “I must bring them also.” Therefore it is not another who brings them through his own servants. Hear further: “They will hear my voice.” Look: he himself speaks through his servants, and his voice is heard through those whom he sends, “so that there may be one sheepfold and one shepherd.”

For these two flocks, as though they were two walls, he became the cornerstone (Eph. 2:11–22). Therefore he is both the door and the cornerstone: all these things are by way of analogy, none of them in the proper sense.

6. I have already said this and strongly commended it; those who grasp it understand—or rather, those who understand grasp it. And those who do not yet understand it intellectually should hold by faith what they are not yet able to understand.

By way of analogy Christ is many things that he is not in the proper sense. By analogy Christ is a rock, Christ is a door, [Col. 1736] Christ is a cornerstone, Christ is a shepherd, Christ is a lamb, Christ is a lion. How many things there are by analogy, besides others whose enumeration would be lengthy!

But if you examine the proper characteristics of the things you are accustomed to see, he is not a rock, because he is not hard and without sensation; he is not a door, because a craftsman did not make him; he is not a cornerstone, because a builder did not assemble him; he is not a shepherd, because he is not the keeper of four-footed sheep; he is not a lion, because he is not a wild animal; he is not a lamb, because he is not livestock.

All these things, then, are by analogy. What, then, is he in the proper sense? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” What of the human being who appeared? “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

7. Hear what follows also. “Therefore the Father loves me,” he says, “because I lay down my life, so that I may take it up again.” What does he say? “Therefore the Father loves me”: because I die so that I may rise again [Note: [Col. 1736] Perhaps something is either added or missing here.].

For it is said with great emphasis: “I.” “Because I lay down,” he says; “I lay it down.” What does “I lay it down” mean? I lay it down myself. Let the Jews not boast: they were able to rage, but they were not able to exercise power. Let them rage as much as they can; if I do not wish to lay down my life, what will they accomplish by raging?

They were overthrown by a single answer. When they were asked, “Whom are you seeking?” they said, “Jesus.” And he said to them, “I am.” They drew back and fell (ibid. 18:4–6). Those who fell at one utterance of Christ, destined to die, what will they do under the voice of one who judges?

“I—I say—lay down my life, so that I may take it up again.” Let the Jews not boast as though they had prevailed; he himself laid down his life. “I slept,” he says. You know the Psalm: “I slept and took my sleep; and I arose, because the Lord will sustain me” (Ps. 3:6). The Psalm itself has just been read; we have just heard: “I slept and took my sleep; and I arose, because the Lord will sustain me.”

What does “I slept” mean? Because I wished to, I slept. What does “I slept” mean? I died. Did he not sleep who, when he wished, rose from the tomb as from a bed?

But he loves to give glory to the Father, so that he may teach us to give glory to the Creator. For when he added, “I arose, because the Lord will sustain me,” do you suppose that his power failed here, so that he was able to die by his own power but was unable to rise again by his own power? For words not understood attentively seem to sound this way: “I slept”—that is, because I wished to, I slept—“and I arose”; why? “Because the Lord will sustain me.”

What then? Would you not be able to rise by yourself? If you were not able, you would not say, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again.” Hear elsewhere in the Gospel that not only did the Father raise the Son, but the Son also raised himself. “Destroy this temple,” he says, “and in three days I will raise it up.” And the Evangelist says: “But he was speaking about the temple of his body” (John 2:19, 21). For what was raised was what had died. The Word did not die; that soul did not die. If yours does not die, would the Lord’s have died?

8. “How do I know,” you ask, “whether mine does not die?” Do not kill it yourself, and it will not die. “How,” you ask, “can I kill my soul?” To leave other sins aside for the moment, “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1:11).

“How,” you ask, “can I be sure that it does not die?” Hear the Lord himself giving security to his servant: “Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do.” But what does he clearly say? “Fear the one who has power to kill both body and soul in Gehenna” (Matt. 10:28; Luke 12:4–5).

Look: it dies; look: it does not die. What is the death of the soul? What is the death of your flesh? The death of your flesh is the loss of its life; the death of your soul is the loss of its life. The life of your flesh is your soul; the life of your soul is your God. Just as the flesh dies when it loses the soul, which is its life, so the soul dies when it loses God, who is its life.

Certainly, then, the soul is immortal. Entirely immortal, because it lives even while dead. What the Apostle said about the pleasure-loving widow can also be said of the soul if it has lost its God: “She is dead while she lives” (I Tim. 5:6).

9. How, then, does the Lord lay down his life? Brothers, let us examine this somewhat more attentively. The hour that usually constrains us on Sunday does not constrain us now [Note: [Col. 1737] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice add here “Christ”; in Louvain the word “Christ” is enclosed in brackets. M.]. We have time; let those who come even today to the word of God gain this benefit.

“I lay down,” he says, “my life.” Who lays it down? What does he lay down [Note: [Col. 1737] The punctuation has been arranged in this way: not as in the earlier editions, “The hour that usually constrains us, on Sunday we have time.” The immediately following words—“let those who come even today to the word of God gain this benefit”—make it sufficiently clear that the sermon was delivered on a day other than Sunday.]?

What is Christ? The Word and a human being. Not a human being in such a way that he is flesh alone; rather, because he is human, he consists of flesh and soul, and the whole human being is in Christ. For he would not have assumed the inferior part and abandoned the superior part; the superior part of a human being is the soul rather than the body.

Since, then, the whole human being is in Christ, what is Christ? The Word, I say, and a human being. What are the Word and the human being? The Word, soul, and flesh.

Hold fast to this, because there have been heretics even on this point, driven long ago from Catholic truth; nevertheless, like thieves and robbers who do not enter through the door, they do not cease to lie in wait for the sheepfold. They are called the heretics Apollinarists, who dared to teach that Christ is nothing but Word and flesh; they maintain that he did not assume a human soul.

Some of them could not deny that there was a soul in Christ. See the absurdity and intolerable madness. When they wished him to have an irrational soul, they denied that he had a rational one: they gave him the soul of an animal and removed the soul of a human being. They took reason away from Christ by failing to hold to reason.

Let this be far from us, who have been nourished and established in the Catholic faith. Taking this occasion, then, I would remind Your Charity that, just as in earlier readings we sufficiently instructed you against the Sabellians and Arians—the Sabellians who say, “The one who is Father is himself the Son”; the Arians who say, “The Father is one thing, the Son another,” as though the Father and the Son were not of the same substance—we have also instructed you, as you remember and ought to remember, against the Photinian heretics, who said that Christ was merely a human being without God [Note: [Col. 1738] All manuscripts read: “who said that Christ was a human being”; they do not contain “without God.”]; and against the Manichaeans, who say that there is only God without a human being.

On this occasion let us instruct you concerning the soul also, against the Apollinarists, who say that our Lord Jesus Christ did not have a human soul—that is, a rational soul, an intelligent soul, a soul, I say, by which we differ from animals, since we are human beings.

10. How, then, did the Lord say here, “I have power to lay down my life”? Who lays down the soul, and takes it up again? Does Christ, insofar as he is the Word, lay down the soul and take it up again? Or, insofar as he is a human soul, does the soul itself lay itself down and take itself up again? Or, insofar as he is flesh, does the flesh lay down the soul and take it up again?

I have proposed three possibilities; let us treat them all, and choose what accords with the rule of truth. For if we say that the Word of God laid down his soul and took it up again, we must fear that a perverse thought may enter and someone say to us: “Then at some point that soul was separated from the Word, and at some point the Word, from the time it assumed that soul, existed without a soul.”

I see that the Word existed without a human soul when “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” But from the time “the Word became flesh, so that it might dwell among us” (John 1:1, 14), and the human being was assumed by the Word—that is, the whole human being, soul and flesh—what did suffering accomplish, what did death accomplish, except to separate the body from the soul? It did not separate the soul from the Word.

For if the Lord died—indeed, because the Lord died, for he died for us on the cross—without doubt his flesh breathed out its soul. For a short time the soul departed from the flesh, but it would return so that the flesh might rise again. I do not say that the soul was separated from the Word.

He said to the soul of the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43). He did not abandon the faithful thief’s soul, while abandoning his own, did he? Far be it from us. As Lord, he guarded the thief’s soul, while he possessed his own inseparably.

But if we say that the soul itself laid itself down and took itself up again, this is a most absurd interpretation. For what was not separated from the Word could not be separated from itself.

11. Let us therefore say both what is true and what can easily be understood. Here is any human being—not consisting of Word, soul, and flesh, but of soul and flesh. Let us ask of this human being how any human being lays down his soul.

Or perhaps no human being can lay down his soul? You might say to me: “No human being has the power to lay down his soul and take it up again.” If a human being could not lay down his soul, the apostle John would not say, “As Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brethren” (I John 3:16).

Therefore it is also permitted for us—if we are filled with his power, since without him we can do nothing—to lay down our lives for the brethren. When any holy martyr laid down his life for the brethren, who laid it down, and what did he lay down? If we understand this, there we shall see how Christ’s statement, “I have power to lay down my life,” is to be understood.

“O human being, are you ready to die for Christ?” “I am ready,” he says. I shall say this in other words: “Are you ready to lay down your life for Christ?” To these words he answers me, “I am ready,” just as he answered me when I said, “Are you ready to die?”

To lay down one’s life, then, is to die. But for whom is the contest there? All human beings, when they die, lay down their lives; but not all lay them down for Christ. And no one has the power to take up again what he has laid down. Christ, however, laid down his life for us and, when he wished, laid it down; and, when he wished, took it up again.

To lay down one’s life, then, is to die. Thus the apostle Peter also said to the Lord, “I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37)—that is, “I will die for you.” Attribute this to the flesh: the flesh lays down its soul and the flesh takes it up again—not, however, by the power of the flesh itself, but by the power of the one who dwells in the flesh. The flesh therefore lays down its soul by breathing it out.

See the Lord himself on the cross. He said, “I thirst.” Those standing nearby soaked a sponge in vinegar, fastened it to a reed, and applied it to his mouth. When he had received it, he said, “It is finished.” What does “It is finished” mean? Everything that had been prophesied beforehand as destined to happen before my death has been fulfilled.

And because he had the power to lay down his life when he wished, after he had said, “It is finished,” what does the Evangelist say? “And he bowed his head and gave up his spirit” (ibid. 19:28–30). This is to lay down one’s life.

Let Your Charity attend here. “He bowed his head and gave up his spirit.” Who gave it up? What did he give up? He gave up his spirit; the flesh gave it up. What does “the flesh gave it up” mean? The flesh emitted it; the flesh breathed it out. That is why it is called exspirare, “to breathe out”: to become outside the spirit. Just as exsulare means “to be outside one’s soil,” and exorbitare means “to be outside the track,” so exspirare means “to be outside the spirit,” and the spirit is the soul.

When, then, the soul departs from the flesh and the flesh remains without the soul, the human being is said to lay down his life. When did Christ lay down his life? When the Word willed it. Sovereignty was in the Word; there was the power to determine when the flesh should lay down the soul and when it should take it up.

12. If, then, the flesh laid down the soul, how did Christ lay down his soul? Is Christ not flesh? Certainly he is: Christ is flesh, Christ is soul, and Christ is Word. Yet these three are not three Christs, but one Christ.

Ask about a human being, and from yourself take a step toward the things above you—things that, if you cannot yet understand, you should at least believe. Just as one human being is soul and body, so one Christ is Word and human being.

See what I have said, and understand. Soul and body are two things, but one human being; Word and human being are two things, but one Christ.

Ask, then, about a human being. Where is the apostle Paul now? If someone answers, “At rest with Christ,” he speaks truly. If someone else answers, “In Rome, in the tomb,” he too speaks truly. The first answer concerns his soul; the second, his flesh.

Yet we do not therefore say that there are two apostles Paul: one resting in Christ and another placed in the tomb. Although we say that the apostle Paul lives in Christ, we also say that the same apostle Paul lies dead in the tomb.

Someone dies, and we say, “He was a good man, a faithful man; he is at peace with the Lord.” And immediately afterward: “Let us go to his funeral and bury him.” You are about to bury the one whom you had just said was at peace with God. One thing is the soul, which remains alive immortally; another is the body, which lies corruptibly.

But once the union of flesh and soul had received the name “human being,” each of them individually and separately retained the name “human being,” whichever of the two it might be.

13. Let no one, then, hesitate when he hears the Lord say, “I lay down my life, and I take it up again.” The flesh lays it down, but by the power of the Word; the flesh takes it up, but by the power of the Word.

The Lord Christ himself is also called flesh alone. “How,” you ask, “do you prove this?” I dare to say that Christ was called Christ even as flesh alone.

Certainly we believe not only in God the Father, but also in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord. I have just stated the whole: “in Jesus Christ, his only Son, our Lord.” Understand the whole there: the Word, the soul, and the flesh.

But surely you also confess what the same faith contains: that you believe in that Christ who was crucified and buried. Therefore you do not deny that Christ was buried; and yet only his flesh was buried. For if his soul was there, he was not dead; but if it was a true death, so that his resurrection might also be true, he was in the tomb without his soul. Yet Christ was buried.

Therefore Christ was also flesh without a soul, because only flesh was buried. Learn this also from the apostolic words: “Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” Who is meant here, insofar as he is the Word, except Christ Jesus, God with God?

See what follows: “But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant; being made in the likeness of human beings, and found in appearance as a human being.” And who is meant here except that same Christ Jesus?

But here everything is present: the Word in the form of God, which took the form of a servant; and soul and flesh in the form of a servant, which was taken by the form of God. “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death” (Phil. 2:6–8).

In death, then, only the flesh was killed by the Jews. For if he said to his disciples, “Do not fear those who kill the body but cannot kill the soul” (Matt. 10:28), could they in his case have killed more than the body? And yet, when the flesh was killed, Christ was killed.

Thus, when the flesh laid down the soul, Christ laid down the soul; and when the flesh took up the soul in order to rise again, Christ took up the soul. Yet this did not happen by the power of the flesh, but by the power of the one who assumed both soul and flesh, in which these things were to be fulfilled.

14. “This commandment,” he says, “I received from my Father.” The Word did not receive a commandment from a word; rather, every commandment is in the Father’s only-begotten Word [Note: [Col. 1740] The printed editions read, “not from the word”; the manuscripts lack the preposition “from.”].

But when the Son is said to receive from the Father what he possesses substantially, how is it said, “As the Father has life in himself, so he has given to the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26), when the Son himself is life? His power is not diminished; rather, his generation is revealed.

For the Father did not add something to a son born to him as though the son were imperfect; he gave everything by begetting him whom he begot perfect. Thus he gave him his equality, whom he did not beget unequal.

While the Lord was saying these things, however, because the light was shining in the darkness and the darkness did not comprehend it (John 1:5), “a dissension arose again among the Jews because of these words.”

Many of them were saying, “He has a demon and is insane; why do you listen to him?” Such was the densest darkness. Others were saying, “These are not the words of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” The eyes of these people had already begun to be opened.

TRACTATE XLVIII. From the passage, “The Feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem,” up to the passage, “But everything that John said about this man was true, and many believed in him.” Chapter 10, verses 22–42.

1. You ought firmly to remember what I have already commended to Your Love: the holy Evangelist John does not wish us always to be nourished with milk, but to eat solid food. Whoever is still less capable of taking solid food, however, should be nourished with the milk of faith and should not hesitate to believe the word that he cannot understand. Faith is the merit; understanding is the reward.

Through the very labor of our effort, the edge of our mind sweats, so that it may remove the little clouds of human mist and be cleared for the Word of God. Let labor not therefore be refused if love is present; for you know that the one who loves does not labor. Every labor is burdensome to those who do not love. If desire carries so many labors along with the avaricious, will charity not carry them along with us?

2. Attend to the Gospel: “The Feast of the Dedication took place in Jerusalem.” Encaenia was the festival of the dedication of the temple. In Greek, καινόν (kainon) means “new”; whenever something new has been dedicated, it is called Encaenia [Note: [Col. 1741] The manuscripts read: “Encoenia is called.”]. The word has also entered common usage: if someone puts on a new tunic, he is said to “encaenize” it.

The Jews solemnly celebrated the day on which the temple was dedicated. It was this feast day when the Lord spoke the words that have been read.

3. It was winter. “And Jesus was walking in the temple, in Solomon’s colonnade. Therefore the Jews surrounded him and were saying to him: ‘How long will you keep our soul in suspense? If you are the Christ, tell us openly.’”

They did not desire the truth, but were preparing an accusation. It was winter, and they were cold: they were reluctant to approach that divine fire. But to approach is to believe. Whoever believes approaches; whoever denies withdraws. The soul is not moved by feet but by affections.

They had grown cold from the charity of love, and were burning with the desire to do harm. They were far away and yet were there: they did not approach by believing, but pressed upon him by persecuting.

They sought to hear the Lord say, “I am the Christ,” and perhaps they understood Christ only according to his humanity. The Prophets preached Christ; but neither heretics nor the Jews understand Christ’s divinity, whether in the Prophets or in the Gospel itself, as long as a veil lies over their heart (II Cor. 3:15).

Accordingly, in one place the Lord Jesus, knowing that they conceived of Christ according to his humanity and not according to his divinity—according to what he was as a human being, not according to what he remained as God even after assuming humanity—said to them: “What do you think about the Christ? Whose son is he?”

They answered according to their opinion: “David’s.” For they had read this and held on to this alone; they read about his divinity but did not understand it.

The Lord, however, to raise them toward seeking the divinity of the one whose weakness they despised, answered them: “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand, until I place your enemies beneath your feet’? If David, then, in the Spirit, calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matt. 22:42–45).

He did not deny it; he asked a question. Let no one, on hearing this, think that the Lord Jesus denied that he was David’s son. If the Lord Christ had denied being David’s son, he would not have illuminated the blind who called upon him in this way.

On one occasion he was passing by, and two blind men sitting beside the road cried out: “Have mercy on us, Son of David.” When he heard this cry, he had mercy, stood still, healed them, and gave them light (ibid. 20:30–34), because he acknowledged the name.

The apostle Paul also says, “who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. 1:3); and to Timothy: “Remember Jesus Christ, risen from the dead, from the seed of David, according to my Gospel” (II Tim. 2:8). Since the Virgin Mary derived her origin from the seed of David, the Lord likewise came from the seed of David.

### 4.

This was what the Jews were asking Christ as a great matter: if he said, “I am the Christ,” then, since they understood only that he was descended from David, they could accuse him of arrogating royal power to himself. What he answered them was greater: they wanted to bring an accusation against him as the son of David, but he replied that he was the Son of God. And how did he do so? Listen:

Jesus answered them: “I speak to you, and you do not believe; the works that I do in my Father’s name, these bear witness about me. But you do not believe, because you are not of my sheep.” You have already learned above (in Treatise 45) what the sheep are: be sheep. They are sheep by believing; they are sheep by following the shepherd; they are sheep by not despising the redeemer; they are sheep by entering through the door; they are sheep by going out and finding pasture; they are sheep by enjoying eternal life. How, then, did he say to these people, “You are not of my sheep”? Because he saw that they had been predestined for everlasting destruction, not acquired for eternal life at the price of his blood.

### 5.

“My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life.” Here, then, is the pasture. If you remember, he had said above: “He will enter and go out and find pasture.” We have entered by believing; we go out by dying. But just as we entered through the door of faith, so let us, as believers, go out from the body: for we go out through that same door so that we may be able to find pasture.

Good pasture is called eternal life. There no grass withers; everything is green, everything flourishes. A certain plant is accustomed to be called “ever-living” [*semper viva*] [Note: [Col. 1742] In the manuscripts, *semper vivit* (“it always lives”); in Greek it is called *aeizôn* or *aeizôon*.]: there alone true life is found.

“I will give them eternal life,” he says, to my sheep. You seek accusations for this reason: you are thinking about the present life.

### 6. [Col. 1743]

“And they will never perish”: you should understand this as though he had said to them, “You will perish forever, because you are not of my sheep.” “No one will snatch them from my hand.”

Understand this more attentively: “What my Father has given me is greater than all.” What can the wolf do? What can the thief and robber do? They destroy only those predestined for destruction. But as for those sheep of whom the Apostle says, “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II, 19), and, “Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined; and those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified; and those whom he justified, he also glorified” (Rom. VIII, 29–30): of these sheep neither the wolf snatches nor the thief takes nor the robber kills.

He is secure concerning their number, because he knows what he has given for them. This is what he says: “No one will snatch them from my hand”; and again: “What my Father has given me is greater than all.”

What did the Father give the Son that is greater than all? That he himself should be his only-begotten Son. What, then, does “gave” mean? Was there already someone to whom he could give, or did he give by begetting? For if there was someone to whom he could give the status of Son, then at some time he existed and the Son did not exist. Far be it from us to say that the Lord Christ ever existed without being the Son.

This can be said of us: at one time we were sons of human beings, but we were not sons of God. Grace made us sons of God; nature made him so, because he was born in this way. Nor can you say, “He did not exist before he was born”: for he who was coeternal with the Father was never unborn.

Let whoever understands grasp it; whoever does not understand, let him believe [Note: [Col. 1743] All the manuscripts read: “Whoever does not understand, let him believe.”], be nourished, and he will understand. The Word of God was always with the Father, and was always the Word; and because he is the Word, therefore he is the Son. Thus he was always the Son, and always equal. He is not equal by growing, but by being born: he who was always born from the Father is the Son from God, God from God, coeternal from the eternal.

The Father, however, is not God from the Son; the Son is God from the Father. Therefore, by begetting him, the Father gave him to be God; by begetting him, he gave him to be coeternal with himself; by begetting him, he gave him to be equal. This is what is greater than all.

How is the Son life, and how does the Son have life? What he has, he is. You are one thing, and what you have is another. For example, you have wisdom: surely you are not wisdom itself? Indeed, because you are not identical with what you have, if you lose what you have, you return to being without it [Note: [Col. 1743] Thus the manuscripts. The printed editions have *reddis* (“you return”), rather than *redis*.]; and sometimes you recover it, sometimes you lose it.

Our eye does not possess light inseparably in itself: it opens and receives it; it closes and loses it. The Son of God is not like this, nor is the Word of the Father; nor is the Word one that passes away by being uttered, but one that remains by being born. He possesses wisdom in such a way that he himself is wisdom and makes others wise; he possesses life in such a way that he himself is life and makes others live.

This is what is greater than all. The evangelist John himself surveyed heaven and earth, intending to speak about the Son of God; he surveyed them and transcended them. He considered the thousands of angelic armies above heaven, considered them and transcended the whole creation—as an eagle transcends the clouds—by his mind. He transcended all great things, reached what is greater than all, and said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John I, 1).

But since the one whose Word it is is not from the Word, whereas the Word is from the one whose Word it is, he therefore says: “What the Father gave me”—that is, that I should be his Word, that I should be his only-begotten Son, that I should be the radiance of his light—is greater than all.

Therefore he says, “No one snatches my sheep away from my hand. No one can snatch them from the hand of my Father.”

### 7.

“From my hand, and from the hand of my Father”: what does this mean—“No one snatches them from my hand,” and “No one snatches them from the hand of my Father”? Is the hand of the Father and the Son one hand? Or perhaps the Son himself is the hand of his Father?

If we understand “hand” as power, the power of the Father and the Son is one, because their divinity is one. But if we understand “hand” as it is said through the prophet, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” (Isa. LIII, 1), then the Son himself is the hand of the Father.

This is not said as though God had a human form and bodily members, but because all things were made through him. Human beings, too, are accustomed to call other people their hands when they accomplish through them what they wish. Sometimes the work itself that a person performs is called his hand, because it is done through his hand; thus someone is said to recognize his own hand when he recognizes what he has written.

Since, then, even in the case of a human being—who properly has a hand among the members of his body—the term “hand” is used in many ways, how much more should “the hand of God” be understood in more than one way, since he has no bodily form? Accordingly, in this passage we should better understand the hand of the Father and the Son as the power of the Father and the Son. Otherwise, if we take the Son himself to be called the hand of the Father, carnal thought may begin to seek a Son of that Son as well, whom it might similarly believe to be Christ’s hand.

Thus: “No one snatches them from the hand of my Father”—that is, no one snatches them from me.

### 8.

But lest you still hesitate, hear what follows: “I and the Father are one.”

Up to this point the Jews were able to endure it. They heard, “I and the Father are one,” and they could bear it no longer; hard-hearted as usual, they ran for stones. They picked up stones in order to stone him. Since the Lord did not suffer what he did not wish to suffer, and suffered only what he wished to suffer, he addressed them while they were still eager to stone him:

“The Jews picked up stones to stone him. Jesus answered them: ‘I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me?’ They answered him: ‘We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because you, though you are a man, make yourself God.’”

They gave this answer to what he had said: “I and the Father are one.” Behold, the Jews understood what the Arians do not understand. They were angry because they perceived that “I and the Father are one” could not be said except where there is equality between the Father and the Son.

### 9.

But observe what the Lord answered those who were slow to understand. He saw that they could not endure the splendor of the truth, and he tempered it in his words.

“Is it not written in your Law”—that is, the Law given to you—“‘I said, You are gods’?”

God says through the Prophet in the Psalm to human beings: “I said, You are gods” (Ps. LXXXI, 6). The Lord called all those Scriptures “the Law” in a general sense, although elsewhere he specifically calls the Law “the Law,” distinguishing it from the Prophets, as in: “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke XVI, 16), and: “On these two commandments hang all the Law and the Prophets” [Col. 1745] (Matt. XXII, 40).

At times, however, he divides those same Scriptures into three parts, when he says: “Everything written about me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms had to be fulfilled” (Luke XXIV, 44). Here, then, he has also called the Psalms by the name of the Law, where it is written: “I said, You are gods.”

“If he called those people gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be annulled—do you say of the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?

“If the word of God came to human beings so that they might be called gods, how is the Word of God, who is with God, not God? If human beings become gods through the word of God, if they become gods by participating in him, then is not God the one from whom they receive their participation? If illuminated lights are gods, is the light that illuminates them not God? If those who are warmed, as it were, by a saving fire become gods, is the one from whom they are warmed not God?

“You approach the light and are illuminated, and you are counted among the children of God; if you withdraw from the light, you become darkened and are counted among the darkness. Yet that light does not approach itself, because it does not withdraw from itself.

“If, then, the word of God makes you gods, how is the Word of God not God?

“The Father, therefore, sanctified his Son and sent him into the world.” Perhaps someone may say: “If the Father sanctified him, was he therefore at some time not holy?” He sanctified him in the same way as he begot him. To make him holy, he gave this to him by begetting him, because he begot him holy.

For if what is sanctified was previously not holy, how do we say to God the Father, “Hallowed be your name” (Matt. VI, 9)?

### 10.

“If I do not perform the works of my Father, do not believe me; but if I do them, even if you do not wish to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I am in the Father.”

The Son does not say, “The Father is in me and I am in the Father,” in the same way that human beings can say it. For if we think rightly, we are in God; and if we live rightly, God is in us. As believers participating in his grace and illuminated by him, we are in him, and he is in us.

But the only-begotten Son is not so. He is in the Father, and the Father is in him, as an equal in the one to whom he is equal.

Indeed, we can sometimes say, “We are in God, and God is in us.” But can we say, “I and God are one”? You are in God because God contains you; God is in you because you have been made a temple of God. But because you are in God and God is in you, can you say, “Whoever sees me sees God”? How, then, did the Only-Begotten say, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John XIV, 9), and, “I and the Father are one”?

Recognize what belongs properly to the Lord and what is the servant’s gift. The Lord’s proper possession is equality with the Father; the servant’s gift is participation in the Savior.

### 11.

They therefore sought to seize him. Would that they had seized him by believing and understanding, not by raging and killing.
