For now, my brothers, when I speak of such things—weak as I am speaking of strong things, small as I speak of great things, fragile as I speak of solid things—and you, as though made from the same mass from which I too am made, and I myself, the one speaking to you, all of us together wish to seize Christ [Note: [Col. 1745] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and Venice edition have *et ego* only once; M.].

What does “to seize” mean? You have understood: you have seized him. But not so the Jews. You seized him in order to possess him; they wanted to seize him in order not to possess him [Col. 1746]. And because they wanted to seize him in that way, what did he do to them? He went out of their hands.

They did not seize him because they did not have the hands of faith. “The Word became flesh”; but it was not difficult for the Word to cast his flesh out of the hands of flesh. To seize the Word with the mind: this is to seize Christ rightly.

### 12.

“And he went again across the Jordan, to the place where John had first been baptizing, and he remained there. Many came to him and said: ‘John performed no sign at all.’”

You remember that you were told about John: he was a lamp, and he bore witness to the day (John V, 35, 33).

What, then, did these people mean when they said among themselves, “John performed no sign”? “He showed no miracle,” they said. “John did not cast out demons, did not drive away a fever, did not give sight to the blind, did not raise the dead, did not feed so many thousands of people with five or seven loaves, did not walk upon the sea, did not command the winds and waves. John did none of these things.” Yet everything John said bore witness to this man.

Let us come to the day through the lamp. John performed no sign. But everything John said about this man was true.

Behold those who seized him—not in the way the Jews did. The Jews wanted to seize him as he was departing; these people seized him as he remained. What follows, then? “And many believed in him.”

## TREATISE XLIX

From the passage that reads, “Now there was a certain sick man, Lazarus,” up to, “He went into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and there he remained with his disciples.” Chapter XI, verses 1–54.

### 1.

Among all the miracles that our Lord Jesus Christ performed, the resurrection of Lazarus is especially proclaimed. But if we consider who performed it, we ought to rejoice rather than wonder. He raised a human being who made the human being; for he himself is the Father’s Only-Begotten, through whom, as you know, all things were made.

If, then, all things were made through him, what is so astonishing if one person was raised through him, since so many are born every day through him? It is greater to create human beings than to raise them. Yet he deigned both to create and to raise: to create all, to raise some.

For although the Lord Jesus did many things, not all were written down. The holy evangelist John himself bears witness that the Lord Christ both said and did many things that were not written down (John XX, 30). But those things were chosen for writing that seemed sufficient for the salvation of believers.

You have heard that the Lord Jesus raised a dead man. It is enough for you to know that, if he wished, he could raise all the dead. He has reserved this for the end of the world. For he whom you heard raised from the tomb as a four-day corpse through a great miracle—there will come an hour, as he himself says, when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth.

He raised one who had begun to decay, but even in that decaying corpse the form of the limbs was still present. On the last day, by a single command, he will restore ashes to flesh. But it was necessary for him now to perform certain deeds by which, once these signs of his power had been given, we might believe in him and prepare ourselves for that resurrection [Col. 1747] which will be to life, not to judgment.

For he says: “The hour will come when all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come forth: those who have done good, to the resurrection of life; those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” (John V, 28–29).

### 2.

Nevertheless, we read in the Gospel that three dead people were raised by the Lord, and perhaps not without reason. The Lord’s deeds are not merely deeds, but signs. If they are signs, then, beyond the fact that they are marvelous, they surely signify something. To discover the meaning of these deeds is somewhat more laborious than merely reading or hearing them.

When the Gospel was read, we listened in wonder, as though a spectacle of a great miracle had been set before our eyes, hearing how Lazarus came back to life. If we attend to the more wondrous works of Christ, everyone who believes rises again [Note: [Col. 1747] Perhaps it should be read this way: “By the more wondrous work of Christ everyone who believes rises again.” And below: “By the more detestable death everyone who sins dies.”]. If we attend to them all and understand the more detestable deaths, everyone who sins dies.

But every human being fears the death of the flesh; few fear the death of the soul. Everyone takes care to prevent the death of the flesh, which will certainly come at some time, from coming; this is why they labor. A person who is bound to die labors not to die, but does not labor not to sin, though he is destined to live forever.

And when he labors not to die, he labors in vain; for what he achieves is merely that death may be delayed for a long time, not that it may be escaped. But if he does not wish to sin, he will not labor and will live forever.

If only we could awaken human beings, and be awakened together with them, so that we might become lovers of enduring life like those who are lovers of the life that is passing away!

What does a person not do when placed in danger of death? With a sword hanging over their necks, people have betrayed everything they had reserved for themselves as the means of staying alive. Who did not immediately betray it in order not to be struck? And perhaps, even after the betrayal, he was struck.

Who, in order to live, did not immediately wish to lose the means by which he lived, choosing a beggar’s life rather than a swift death? Who, when told, “Sail, lest you die,” delayed? Who, when told, “Work, lest you die,” was lazy?

God commands easy things so that we may live forever, and we neglect to obey. God does not say to you, “Give up everything you possess so that you may live for a short time, anxious amid labor”; rather: “Give to the poor from what you possess, so that you may live forever, secure and free from labor.”

The lovers of temporal life accuse us—a life which they neither possess whenever they wish nor possess for as long as they wish. Yet we do not accuse one another, though we are so lazy and lukewarm in pursuing eternal life, which we will have if we wish, and which, once we have it, we will not lose. But this death which we fear we will have even if we do not wish it.

### 3.

If, then, the Lord, through his great grace and great mercy, raises souls so that we may not die forever, we rightly understand that those three dead whom he raised in their bodies signify and prefigure something concerning the resurrections of souls that take place through faith.

He raised the daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, still lying in the house (Mark V, 41–42). He raised the young son of a widow, carried outside the gates of the city (Luke VII, [Col. 1748] 14–15). He raised Lazarus, buried and four days dead.

Let each person look at his own soul. If it sins, it dies; sin is the death of the soul. But sometimes a person sins only in thought. What is evil pleased you, you consented, you sinned; that consent killed you. Yet the death is inward, because the evil thought has not yet emerged into action.

To signify that he raises such a soul, the Lord raised the little girl who had not yet been carried outside, but lay dead in the house, as though the sin were hidden.

But if you not only consented to an evil pleasure but also committed the evil itself, you have carried the dead person outside the gate, as it were. You are already outside, and you have been carried out dead.

Yet the Lord also raised this person and restored him to his widowed mother. If you have sinned, repent; and the Lord raises you and restores you to your mother, the Church.

The third dead person is Lazarus. There is a terrible kind of death called an evil habit. For it is one thing to sin, another to establish a habit of sinning. Whoever sins and immediately corrects himself quickly comes back to life, because he has not yet become entangled in habit; he has not been buried.

But whoever has become accustomed to sinning has been buried, and it is rightly said of him that he stinks. He begins to have a very bad reputation, like an exceedingly foul odor.

Such are all who are accustomed to crimes, ruined in their morals. You say to such a person, “Do not do it.” When will he listen to you, whom the earth presses down so heavily, who is corrupted by decay and weighed down by the mass of habit?

Yet Christ’s power was not diminished in raising him. We have known, we have seen, and every day we see people who, after abandoning the worst habits, live better than those who used to criticize them.

You detested that woman. Behold, Lazarus’s own sister—if indeed she is the same woman who anointed the Lord’s feet with ointment and wiped them with her hair, which she had washed with tears—was raised to a better life than her brother: she was freed from the great mass of an evil habit.

For she had been a notorious sinner, and it was said of her: “Her many sins are forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII, 37–47).

We see many such people; we know many. Let no one despair; let no one presume upon himself. To despair is evil, and to presume upon oneself is evil. Do not despair in such a way that you fail to choose the one in whom you ought to place your confidence.

### 4.

Thus the Lord also raised Lazarus. You have heard what sort of person he was—that is, what the resurrection of Lazarus signifies. Let us now read the passage; and since many things in this reading are clear, let us not seek an explanation for every single detail, but discuss what is necessary.

“Now there was a certain sick man, Lazarus, from Bethany, the village of Mary and Martha his sisters” [Note: [Col. 1748] In all the manuscripts, “his sisters” is omitted.].

In the preceding reading you remember that the Lord went out of the hands of those who wanted to stone him and departed across the Jordan, where John was baptizing (John X, 39–40). While the Lord was there, Lazarus fell ill in Bethany, a village near Jerusalem.

### 5.

“Now Mary was the one who anointed the Lord with ointment and wiped his feet with her hair; her brother Lazarus was ill. His sisters therefore sent to him, saying…”

We already understand where they sent—to the place where the Lord was, since he was absent, namely, across the Jordan [Note: [Col. 1748] Compare Book I, On the Sermon on the Mount, no. 35.] [Col. 1749]. They sent to the Lord to announce that their brother was ill, so that, if he deigned to come, he might free him from his illness.

He delayed healing him so that he might raise him. What, then, did his sisters announce?

“Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill.”

They did not say, “Come,” for it was enough merely to inform the one who loved him. They did not dare say, “Come and heal him”; they did not dare say, “Command from there, and it will happen here.”

Why did they not do so, if the faith of the centurion is praised for precisely this? For he said: “I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word, and my servant will be healed” (Matt. VIII, 8, 10).

These women said none of this, but only: “Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill.” It is enough that you know; for you do not love and then abandon.

Someone may say: How could Lazarus signify a sinner and nevertheless be loved by the Lord in this way? Let him hear the Lord saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX, 13). For if God did not love sinners, he would not have descended from heaven to earth.

### 6.

“When Jesus heard this, he said to them: ‘This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it.’”

Such glorification did not increase him; it benefited us. Thus he says that it is not unto death, because the death itself was not unto death, but rather unto a miracle through which people would believe in Christ and avoid true death.

Observe carefully how, as though indirectly, the Lord called himself God, for the sake of certain people who deny that the Son is God. There are heretics who deny that the Son of God is God.

Let them hear: “This illness,” he says, “is not unto death, but for the glory of God.” Whose glory? Of which God? Hear what follows: “So that the Son of God may be glorified.”

Therefore, he says, this illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it. Through what? Through that illness.

### 7.

“Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister Mary, and Lazarus.”

He was ill, they were grieving, and all were beloved. Yet he loved them as the savior of the sick, indeed as the raiser even of the dead and the consoler of the grieving.

When he heard that Lazarus was ill, he remained in the same place for two days. They had announced it to him, and he remained there; he allowed the time to pass until the four days were completed. This was not without reason, since perhaps—indeed, certainly—the number of days itself conveys some mystery.

After this he again says to his disciples: “Let us go into Judea,” where he had nearly been stoned and from which he had therefore seemed to depart lest he be stoned. He departed as a human being; but in returning, as though he had forgotten his weakness, he displayed his power. “Let us go,” he says, “into Judea.”

### 8.

After he had said this, observe how frightened the disciples became.

The disciples say to him: “Rabbi, just now the Jews were seeking to stone you, and you are going there again?”

Jesus answered: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight?”

What does this answer mean? They had said, “Just now the Jews wanted to stone you, and you are going there again so that they may stone you?” And the Lord replied: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight?”

“If anyone walks during the day, he does not stumble, because he sees the light of this world; but if anyone walks during the night, he stumbles, because the light is not in him.”

He was speaking of the day, but in our understanding it is still as though night. Let us invoke the day, so that it may drive away the night and illuminate the heart with light.

What did the Lord wish to say? As far as I can see, as far as the height and depth of the saying shine through, he wished to rebuke their hesitation and unbelief. For they wanted to give the Lord advice so that he would not die, although he had come to die so that they themselves would not die.

Likewise, in another passage, the holy Peter, loving the Lord but not yet fully understanding why he had come, feared that he might die and displeased Life—that is, the Lord himself. For when he told the disciples what he would suffer at the hands of the Jews in Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 1750] In six manuscripts: “what he was going to suffer.”], Peter replied among the others and said: “Far be it from you, Lord; may God be favorable to you; this shall not happen.”

Immediately the Lord said: “Get behind me, Satan; for you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings.”

A little earlier, when he confessed the Son of God, he had deserved praise. For he had heard: “Blessed are you, Simon son of Jonah, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matt. XVI, 16–23).

To the one to whom he had said, “Blessed are you,” he says, “Get behind me, Satan.” The reason is that he was not blessed from himself. From where, then? “Because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” This is the cause of your blessedness: not from what is yours, but from what is mine.

Not because I am the Father, but because everything that the Father has is mine (John XVI, 15). If he was blessed from what belonged to the Lord himself, from whom was he Satan? There he gives the reason for his blessedness, saying: “Flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” This is the cause of your blessedness.

But as for what I said, “Get behind me, Satan,” hear also the reason for that: “For you do not understand the things of God, but those of human beings.”

Let no one flatter himself. From what is his own, he is Satan; from what is God’s, he is blessed. What does “from what is his own” mean except “from his own sin”? Remove sin, which is yours. “Righteousness,” he says, “is from me” [Note: [Col. 1750] This is Erasmus’s punctuation at this passage: “Remove sin, which is yours; righteousness, he says, is from me.” The Lovanienses place a colon after *tuum*.].

“For what do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV, 7).

When, therefore, human beings wanted to give advice to God—the disciples to the teacher, servants to the Lord, the sick to the physician—he rebuked them and said: “Are there not twelve hours of daylight? If anyone walks during the day, he does not stumble.”

Follow me if you do not wish to stumble. Do not give advice to me, when you ought to receive advice from me.

What, then, does “Are there not twelve hours of daylight?” refer to? It refers to this: to show that he himself was the day, he chose twelve disciples.

“If I am the day,” he says, “and you are the hours, do the hours give advice to the day? The hours follow the day, not the day the hours.”

If they are the hours, then, what about Judas? Was he himself also among the twelve hours? If he was an hour, he was shining; if he was shining, how was he handing the day over to death?

But in this saying the Lord was not foreseeing Judas himself, but his successor. When Judas fell, Matthias succeeded him, and the number twelve remained (Acts I, 26).

The Lord therefore did not choose twelve disciples without reason, except because he himself is the spiritual day. Let the hours follow the day, proclaim the day, be illuminated by the day, be enlightened by the day, and through the preaching of the hours let the world believe in the day.

Thus he said, in brief: “Follow me if you do not wish to stumble.”

### 9.

“After this he says to them: ‘Our friend Lazarus is sleeping, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.’”

He spoke truly. He was dead to his sisters, but he was sleeping to the Lord. He was dead to human beings, who could not raise him; for the Lord awakened him from the tomb with as much ease as you awaken a sleeping person from bed.

Thus he called him sleeping according to his own power, because other dead people are also frequently called “sleeping” in Scripture, as the Apostle says: “But concerning those who are sleeping, brothers, I do not want you to be ignorant, so that you may not grieve like the rest who have no hope” (I Thess. IV, 12).

For this reason he also called them sleeping: because he foretold that they would rise again. Every dead person therefore sleeps, both good and wicked.

But just as among those who sleep and rise each day there is a difference according to what each person sees in dreams—some experience joyful dreams, others tormenting dreams, so that on waking a person fears to sleep lest he return to the same dreams—so each human being sleeps with his own cause and rises with his own cause.

And it makes a difference under what sort of custody each person is received, since he is later to be brought before the judge. For people are assigned to custodial conditions according to the merits of their cases. Some are ordered to be guarded by lictors, an office that is humane, gentle, and civic; others are handed over to *optiones* [Note: [Col. 1751] In the manuscripts it is written with *b*, *obtionibus*, incorrectly. Varro, Isidore, and others think that *optiones* derives from *optare* (“to choose”), since they were men chosen as assistants and aides of the decurions in military affairs. They were also assigned various additional duties; hence there were *optiones fabricae* and *optiones officii* or of the prison. It is in this last sense that they are mentioned here, as also in the Commentary on Ephesians, chapter 4, among the works of Ambrose, in these words: “Nor did Paul and Silas delay the time at which they would baptize the prison *optio*.”]; others are sent to prison.

And even in prison not all are treated alike; according to the seriousness of their cases, some are thrust into the lowest depths of the prison.

Thus, just as there are different custodial conditions for those carrying out official duties, so there are different custodial conditions for the dead, and different merits among those who will rise.

The poor man was received, and the rich man was received; but the one into Abraham’s bosom, the other where he was thirsty and could not find even a drop [Luke XVI, 22–24].

### 10.

All souls, then, have—so that I may instruct your Charity through this occasion—after they have departed from the world, their various places of reception. The good have joy; the evil have torments.

But when the resurrection has taken place, the joy of the good will be greater, and the torments of the evil more severe, when they are tormented together with their bodies.

The holy Patriarchs, Prophets, Apostles, Martyrs, and faithful believers have been received in peace. Yet all will still receive at the end what God has promised. For the resurrection of the flesh has also been promised, as well as the destruction of death and eternal life with the angels.

We will all receive these things together. For the rest that is given immediately after death, each person receives it at death, if he is worthy of it.

The Patriarchs received it first. Consider how long they have been resting. The Prophets came later, the Apostles more recently, the holy Martyrs much more recently, and good believers every day.

Some have already been in this rest for a long time [Note: [Col. 1751] So several manuscripts read. The printed editions have *tamdiu sunt* (“have been there so long”); and shortly below, [Col. 1752], “others in recent time,” omitting *nec* (“not even”). For *nec*, some manuscripts have *in*.]; others not so long; others for fewer years; and others not even for a recent period.

But when they awaken from this sleep [Col. 1752], all will receive together what has been promised.

### 11.

“Our friend Lazarus is sleeping, but I am going to awaken him from sleep.”

The disciples therefore said—as they understood it, so they answered:

“Lord, if he is sleeping, he will be safe.”

Sleep is ordinarily a sign of recovery in the sick. But Jesus had spoken of his death, while they thought he was speaking about ordinary sleep.

Then Jesus said to them plainly. For he had said somewhat obscurely, “He is sleeping.” He therefore said plainly: “Lazarus has died; and I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there.”

He knew that Lazarus had died, and yet he had not been there; for he had been announced as sick, not dead. But what could be hidden from the one who had created him, and to whose hands the soul of the dying man had departed?

This is what he says: “I rejoice for your sake, so that you may believe, because I was not there.” They were now beginning to wonder that the Lord could declare someone dead whom he had neither seen nor heard about.

Here we should remember that even the faith of those disciples who had already believed in him was still being strengthened by miracles—not so that something that did not exist might begin to exist, but so that what had already begun to exist might grow. Nevertheless, he used an expression as though they were then beginning to believe.

For he did not say, “I rejoice for your sake, so that your faith may increase or be strengthened,” but said, “so that you may believe.” This should be understood as meaning: so that you may believe more fully and more firmly.

### 12

But let us go to him. Then Thomas, who is called Didymus, said to his fellow disciples: “Let us also go, and let us die with him.”

And so Jesus came and found that he had already been four days in the tomb. Much can indeed be said about these four days, just as is the case with the obscure passages of Scripture, which, according to the diversity of those who understand them, produce many meanings. Let us also say what it seems to us that a dead man of four days signifies.

For just as in that blind man we understand, in a certain sense, the human race, so perhaps in this dead man too we shall understand many things; for one and the same reality can be signified in different ways.

When a human being is born, he is already born with death, because he derives sin from Adam. Hence the Apostle says: “Through one man sin entered the world, and through sin, death; and so it passed into all human beings, in whom all sinned” (Romans 5:12). Behold, you have one day of death, which a human being draws from the propagation of death.

Then he grows and begins to approach the rational years, so that he may recognize the natural law, which everyone has fixed in his heart: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” Is this learned from books [Note: [Col. 1752] According to Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition: “Is this said by the pagans?” M.], and is it not, in some manner, read in nature itself?

Do you wish to suffer theft? Certainly not. Behold the law in your heart: “What you do not wish to suffer, do not do.” And human beings transgress this law: behold another day of death.

The Law was then also given divinely through God’s servant Moses. There it was said: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness; honor your father and your mother; you shall not covet your neighbor’s property; you shall not covet your neighbor’s wife” (Exodus 20:12–17). Behold, the Law is written [Col. 1753], and it too is despised: behold the third day of death.

What remains? The Gospel also comes; the kingdom of heaven is preached; Christ is proclaimed everywhere; he threatens Gehenna and promises eternal life—and this too is despised. Human beings transgress the Gospel: behold the fourth day of death. With good reason, then, he already stinks.

But is mercy to be denied even to such people? Far from it: the Lord does not disdain to approach even such people in order to raise them up.

### 13

Many of the Jews had come to Martha and Mary to console them concerning their brother. When Martha therefore heard that Jesus had come, she went out to meet him; but Mary was sitting at home.

Then Martha said to Jesus: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died; but even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

She did not say, “But even now I ask you to raise my brother.” For how did she know whether it would be useful for her brother to rise? She said only this: “I know that you can do it, if you wish; whether you do it, however, is a matter of your judgment, not of my presumption.” “But even now I know that whatever you ask of God, God will give you.”

### 14

Jesus said to her: “Your brother will rise.”

This was ambiguous. He did not say, “Now I will raise your brother,” but “Your brother will rise.”

Martha said to him: “I know that he will rise in the resurrection, on the last day.” I am certain about that resurrection; about this one I am uncertain.

Jesus said to her: “I am the resurrection.”

You say, “My brother will rise on the last day”: that is true. But through whom will he rise then? He can also rise now, because, he says, “I am the resurrection and the life.”

Listen, brothers; listen to what he says. Certainly the entire expectation of those standing around was that Lazarus, one who had been dead for four days, would come back to life. Let us listen—and rise.

How many there are in this people whom the weight of habit presses down! Perhaps some are listening to me who are told, “Do not become drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery” (Ephesians 5:18). They say, “We cannot.”

Perhaps some impure people are listening to me, stained by lusts and crimes, to whom it is said, “Do not do this, lest you perish.” And they answer, “We cannot be freed from our habit.”

O Lord, raise these people up. “I am,” he says, “the resurrection and the life.” He is the resurrection because he is life.

### 15

“Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, will live; and everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.”

What does this mean? Whoever believes in me, even if he has died, as Lazarus died, will live, because God is not the God of the dead but of the living.

Concerning the fathers who had long since died—that is, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—he gave the Jews this answer: “I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. He is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live” (Matthew 22:32; Luke 20:37–38).

Believe, then; and if you have died, you will live. But if you do not believe, even while you live, you are dead.

Let us prove this also: if you do not believe, even though you live, you are dead. To a certain man who delayed following him and said, “Let me first go and bury my father,” the Lord said: “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, come and follow me” (Matthew 8:21–22).

There was a dead man there to be buried, and there were also dead men there to bury the dead man: he was dead in the flesh, they in the soul.

What is the source of death in the soul? The absence of faith. What is the source of death in the body? The absence of the soul [Col. 1754]. Therefore faith is the life of your soul.

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “even if he has died in the flesh, will live in the soul, until the flesh also rises and afterward never dies.” This means: “Whoever believes in me, even though he dies, will live.”

“And everyone who lives in the flesh and believes in me, even if he dies for a time because of the death of the flesh, will not die forever because of the life of the spirit and the immortality of the resurrection.” This is what he says: “Everyone who lives and believes in me will never die.”

“Do you believe this?” She said to him: “Certainly, Lord. I have believed that you are the Christ, the Son of God, who has come into the world. When I believed this, I believed that you are the resurrection; I believed that you are life; I believed that whoever believes in you, even if he dies, will live; and that whoever lives and believes in you will never die.”

### 16

And when she had said this, she went away and quietly called her sister Mary, saying: “The Teacher is here and is calling you.”

We should note how she called “silence” a suppressed voice. For how was she silent when she said, “The Teacher is here and is calling you”? We should also note how the Evangelist did not say where, when, or how the Lord called Mary, so that this might rather be understood from Martha’s words, while the brevity of the narrative was preserved.

### 17

When she heard this, she rose quickly and went to him. Jesus had not yet come into the village but was still in the place where Martha had met him.

Therefore the Jews who were with her in the house and were consoling her, when they saw Mary, because she rose quickly and went out, followed her, saying that she was going to the tomb to weep there.

Why did it matter to the Evangelist to report this? So that we may see what occasion caused a larger number of people to be there when Lazarus was raised. For the Jews, thinking that she was hurrying for this reason—to seek consolation for her grief through tears—followed her, so that the great miracle of the resurrection of a man dead four days might find many witnesses.

### 18

But when Mary came to where Jesus was and saw him, she fell at his feet and said to him: “Lord, if you had been here, my brother would not have died.”

When Jesus therefore saw her weeping, and the Jews who had come with her also weeping, he groaned in spirit and troubled himself, and said: “Where have you laid him?”

I do not know what he indicated to us by groaning in spirit and troubling himself. For who could trouble him, unless he himself did so?

Therefore, my brothers, first consider his power, and then inquire into the meaning. You are troubled unwillingly; Christ was troubled because he wished to be.

Jesus grew hungry, that is true, but because he wished to. Jesus slept, that is true, but because he wished to. Jesus was sorrowful, that is true, but because he wished to. Jesus died, that is true, but because he wished to. It was within his power to be affected in one way or another, or not to be affected.

For the Word assumed a soul and flesh, joining to himself the nature of the whole human being in the unity of his person. The Apostle’s soul, too, was illumined by the Word; Peter’s soul was illumined by the Word; Paul’s soul and the souls of the other Apostles and of the holy Prophets were illumined by the Word. But of none of them was it said, “The Word became flesh” (John 1:14); of none was it said, “I and the Father are one” (ibid. 10:30).

The soul and flesh of Christ, together with the Word of God, are one person [Col. 1755]; there is one Christ. And therefore, where supreme power exists, weakness is governed according to the inclination of the will [Note: [Col. 1755] In one manuscript and in Alcuin: “weakness is troubled.”]. This is what is meant by “he troubled himself.”

### 19

I have spoken of power; now consider the meaning.

The man whom the four days of death and that burial signify is a great offender. What, then, does Christ’s troubling himself mean, except that he signifies to you how you ought to be troubled when you are weighed down and oppressed by such a great mass of sin?

For you have examined yourself; you have seen yourself as guilty; you have reckoned with yourself: “I did that, and God spared me; I committed that, and he postponed punishment; I heard the Gospel and despised it; I was baptized and returned again to the same things. What shall I do? Where shall I go? From where shall I escape?”

When you say these things, Christ is already groaning, because faith is groaning. In the voice of the one who groans, the hope of the one who rises appears.

If faith itself is within, Christ is there, groaning. If faith is in us, Christ is in us. For what else does the Apostle say? “That Christ may dwell through faith in your hearts” (Ephesians 3:17). Therefore your faith concerning Christ is Christ in your heart.

This is what happened when he was sleeping in the boat. When the disciples were in danger, with shipwreck already threatening, they came to him and woke him. Christ arose, commanded the winds and the waves, and a great calm came about (Matthew 8:24–26).

So it is with you. Winds enter your heart—certainly, where you are sailing, where you are crossing this life as a stormy and perilous sea. Winds enter, stir up the waves, and disturb the boat.

What are the winds? You heard an insult and became angry. The insult is the wind; anger is the wave. You are in danger; you intend to answer; you intend to return insult for insult. The boat is already approaching shipwreck. Awaken Christ who is sleeping.

For this is why you are tossed about and prepare to return evil for evil: Christ is sleeping in the boat. The sleep of Christ in your heart is the forgetting of faith.

But if you awaken Christ—that is, recall your faith—what does Christ, as though awake in your heart, say to you? “I heard, ‘You have a demon’” (John 7:20), “and I prayed for them.” The Lord hears and endures; the servant hears and becomes indignant!

But you wish to avenge yourself. What of it? Have I already been avenged? When your faith speaks these things to you, it is as though the winds and waves are commanded, and a great calm comes about.

Therefore, just as awakening Christ in the boat means awakening faith, so in the heart of a person whom the great weight and habit of sin oppress—in the heart of a transgressor even against the holy Gospel, a despiser of eternal punishments—let Christ groan, and let the person rebuke himself.

Listen further: Christ wept; let the human being weep for himself. Why did Christ weep, except to teach the human being to weep? Why did he groan and trouble himself, except because the faith of a person who rightly displeases himself ought, in a certain way, to groan in accusation of evil deeds, so that the habit of sinning may yield to the force of repentance?

### 20

And he said: “Where have you laid him?”

You knew that he had died, and you did not know where he had been buried? This too is a signification, because God acts as though he does not know the human being who has been lost.

I do not dare to say, “He does not know.” For what does he not know? But he acts as though he does not know.

How do we prove this? Hear the Lord saying [Col. 1756] in judgment: “I do not know you; depart from me” (Matthew 7:23).

What does “I do not know you” mean? “I do not see you in my light; I do not see you in that righteousness which I know.”

So here also, as though he did not know such a sinner, he said: “Where have you laid him?”

Such is the voice of God in paradise after the human being had sinned: “Adam, where are you?” (Genesis 3:9).

They say to him: “Lord, come and see.”

What does “see” mean? Have mercy. For the Lord sees when he has mercy. Hence it is said to him: “See my humiliation and my labor, and forgive all my sins” (Psalm 24:18).

### 21

Jesus wept.

Then the Jews said: “See how he loved him.”

What does “he loved him” mean? “I did not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance” (Matthew 9:13).

But some of them said: “Could not this man, who opened the eyes of the blind man, have made it so that this man also would not die?”

He who did not wish to make him not die is about to do something greater: raise him after death.

### 22

Jesus therefore, groaning again within himself, came to the tomb.

Let him groan in you too, if you intend to come back to life. To every person who is oppressed by a most evil habit it is said: “He came to the tomb.”

It was a cave, and a stone had been placed over it. The dead man was beneath the stone; the guilty person was beneath the Law.

For you know that the Law given to the Jews was written on stone (Exodus 31:18). All the guilty are under the Law; those who live rightly are with the Law. “The law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Timothy 1:9).

What, then, does “Remove the stone” mean? Preach grace.

For the Apostle Paul says that he is a minister of the New Testament, “not of the letter but of the spirit” [Note: [Col. 1756] The printed editions have “not of the letter but of the spirit.” The manuscripts, however, have “not of the letter but of the spirit,” with the genitives, in accordance with the Greek, οὐ γράμματος, ἀλλὰ πνεύματος (“not of letter, but of spirit”).]. For “the letter kills,” he says, “but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3:6).

The killing letter is like a stone pressing down. “Remove,” he says, “the stone.” Remove the burden of the Law; preach grace.

For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would certainly have come through the Law. But Scripture imprisoned everything under sin, so that the promise might be given to those who believe through faith in Jesus Christ (Galatians 3:21–22). Therefore remove the stone.

### 23

Martha, the sister of the one who had died, said to him: “Lord, he already stinks, for he has been dead four days.”

Jesus said to her: “Did I not tell you that if you believed, you would see the glory of God?”

What does “you would see the glory of God” mean? It means that he raises even one who stinks and has been dead four days.

For “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Romans 3:23), and “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (ibid. 5:20).

### 24

Therefore they removed the stone.

But Jesus, lifting his eyes upward, said: “Father, I thank you that you have heard me. I knew, however, that you always hear me; but because of the crowd standing around I said this, so that they may believe that you sent me.”

When he had said this, he cried out with a loud voice.

He groaned, he wept, he cried out with a loud voice. How difficult it is for one whom the weight of evil habit presses down to rise! Yet he rises. By hidden grace he is inwardly given life; he rises after the loud voice.

What happened? “He cried out with a loud voice: Lazarus, come out.”

And immediately the one who had been dead came out, his hands and feet bound with strips of cloth [Note: [Col. 1756] “With strips of cloth” is absent from the manuscripts.]; and his face was bound with a cloth.

You marvel that he came out with his feet bound [Col. 1757], and do not marvel that he rose after four days? In both cases the Lord’s power was at work, not the dead man’s strength.

He came out, and he was still bound; still wrapped, yet already he had come out.

What does this signify? When you despise, you lie dead; and if you despise as much as I have said, you lie buried. When you confess, you come out.

For what does “to come out” mean except to become manifest by emerging, as it were, from hidden things?

But so that you may confess, God acts by crying out with a loud voice—that is, by calling with great grace.

Therefore, when the dead man had come out still bound—confessing and still guilty—the Lord said this to the ministers, so that his sins might be loosed: “Unbind him and let him go.”

What does “Unbind him and let him go” mean? “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16:19).

### 25

Many of the Jews who had come to Mary and had seen what Jesus did believed in him. But some of them went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done.

Not all the Jews who had gathered around Mary believed, but many did. Some of them, whether from among the Jews who had gathered or from among those who had believed, went to the Pharisees and told them what Jesus had done—either announcing it so that they too might believe, or rather betraying him so that they might rage.

However it happened, and whoever they were, these things were reported to the Pharisees.

### 26

The chief priests and the Pharisees convened a council and said: “What are we to do?”

Yet they did not say, “Let us believe.” For these lost men were more concerned with how they might harm him and destroy him than with how they might take care of themselves so as not to perish. Nevertheless, they were afraid and seemed to be deliberating.

They said: “What are we to do? For this man is performing many signs. If we let him go on in this way, everyone will believe in him, and the Romans will come and take away our place and our nation.”

They feared losing temporal things and did not consider eternal life; and thus they lost both.

For after the Lord’s passion and glorification, the Romans did take away both their place and their nation, by conquering them and transferring them elsewhere. And that saying also came upon them which is spoken elsewhere: “The sons of this kingdom will go into the outer darkness” (ibid. 8:12).

They feared that, if everyone believed in Christ, no one would remain to defend the city and temple of God against the Romans, because they perceived Christ’s teaching as opposed to that very temple and to their ancestral laws.

### 27

But one of them, Caiaphas, who was high priest that year, said to them: “You know nothing at all, nor do you consider that it is advantageous for us that one man should die for the people and that the whole nation should not perish” [Note: [Col. 1757] The printed editions have “for you.” The manuscripts, however, have “for us,” supported by the Greek, ἡμῖν (“for us”).].

He did not say this on his own, but, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied.

Here we are also taught that, through wicked people, the Spirit of prophecy foretells future events. Yet the Evangelist attributed this to a divine sacrament because he was high priest—that is, the chief priest.

It may, however, be questioned how he is called “high priest that year,” since God established one high priest, and when he died another was to succeed him.

But it must be understood that afterward, through ambitions and disputes among the Jews, it was arranged that there should be several, serving in rotation from year to year.

The same is said [Col. 1758] of Zechariah: “It happened that, while he was serving as priest in the order of his division before God, according to the custom of the priesthood, he was chosen by lot to enter the temple of the Lord and burn incense” (Luke 1:8–9).

From this it is clear that there were several of them and that they had their assigned turns. For only the high priest was permitted to offer incense (Exodus 30:7). Perhaps, too, several served during one year, while in another year others succeeded them, and from among them one was chosen by lot to offer the incense.

What, then, did Caiaphas prophesy? That Jesus was about to die for the nation—and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the children of God who were scattered.

The Evangelist added this. Caiaphas prophesied only concerning the Jewish nation, in which were the sheep of whom the Lord himself said: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24).

But the Evangelist knew that there were other sheep that were not of this fold, which had to be brought in, so that there might be one flock and one shepherd (John 10:16).

These things were spoken according to predestination. For they were not yet his sheep, nor were they yet children of God, since they had not yet believed.

### 28

From that day, therefore, they planned to kill him.

Jesus therefore no longer walked openly among the Jews, but went away into the region near the wilderness, to a city called Ephraim, and remained there with his disciples.

This was not because his power had failed, for if he had wished, he could certainly have continued to move about openly among the Jews, and they could have done nothing to him. Rather, in human frailty he was demonstrating to his disciples an example of how to live. Thus it became clear that there is no sin if his faithful, who are his members, withdraw from the eyes of their persecutors and avoid the fury of wicked people by hiding, rather than inflaming it further by offering themselves openly.

## TREATISE L

From the passage “The Passover of the Jews was near” up to “Many, because of him, were going away and believing in Jesus.” Chapter 11, verses 55–56, and chapter 12, verses 1–11.

### 1

Yesterday’s reading from the holy Gospel, about which we spoke what the Lord granted, is followed today by another reading, about which we shall speak what the Lord grants.

Some things in Scripture are so clear that they require an auditor rather than an expositor. We ought not to linger over them, so that sufficient time may remain for the necessary matters over which we must linger.

### 2

The Passover of the Jews was therefore near.

The Jews wished to make that feast a bloody one through the Lord’s blood. On that feast the Lamb was slain, the one who consecrated that same feast for us through his blood.

There was a plot among the Jews to kill Jesus. He who had come from heaven in order to suffer wished to draw near to the place of his passion, because the hour of his passion was approaching.

Many therefore went up to Jerusalem from the region before the Passover, in order to sanctify themselves.

The Jews did this according to the Lord’s command given through holy Moses in the Law: on the feast that was the Passover, everyone was to gather from everywhere and be sanctified by the celebration of that day.

But that celebration was a shadow of what was to come [Col. 1759]. What is “a shadow of what was to come”? The prophecy of Christ who was to come, the prophecy of the one who was to suffer for us on that day: so that the shadow might pass away and the light come; so that the signification might pass away and the truth be held fast.

The Jews therefore had the Passover in shadow; we have it in the light.

For what need was there for the Lord to command them, through the feast itself, to kill a sheep, unless it was because that sheep was the one of whom it was prophesied: “Like a sheep he was led to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7)?

The doorposts of the Jews were marked with the blood of the slaughtered animal; our foreheads are marked with the blood of Christ.

And that marking, because it was a signification, was said to keep the destroyer away from the marked houses (Exodus 12:22–23). The sign of Christ drives the destroyer away from us if our heart receives the Savior.

Why have I said this? Because many have marked doorposts, but no inhabitant remains within. They readily have the sign of Christ on their forehead, but they do not receive Christ’s word in their heart.

Therefore I said, brothers—and I repeat it—the sign of Christ drives the destroyer away from us if our heart has Christ as its inhabitant.

I have said this lest anyone perhaps wonder what those Jewish feasts meant. The Lord therefore came as to a victim, so that we might have the true Passover when we celebrate his passion as the sacrifice of a sheep.

### 3

They were therefore seeking Jesus—but wrongly.

Blessed are those who seek Jesus, but rightly. They were seeking Jesus so that neither they nor we might have him; but when he withdrew from them, we received him.

Those who seek are reproved; those who seek are praised. For the mind of the one who seeks finds either praise or condemnation.

You have this also in the Psalms: “Let them be confounded and put to shame who seek my soul” (Psalm 39:15). These are the ones who were seeking wrongly.

But elsewhere he says: “My escape has perished, and there is no one who seeks my soul” (Psalm 141:5). Those who sought are blamed; those who did not seek are blamed.

Therefore let us seek Christ in order to have him; let us seek him in order to hold him fast, but not in order to kill him. For they too were seeking him in order to seize him, but so that they would soon no longer have him.

They were therefore seeking him and saying among themselves: “What do you think? Surely he will not come to the feast?”

### 4

The chief priests and the Pharisees had issued an order that, if anyone knew where he was, he should report it, so that they might arrest him.

Let us now tell the Jews where Christ is. If only those who are of the lineage of the people who issued the order that Christ’s whereabouts be reported would be willing to hear and seize him!

Let them come to the Church; let them hear where Christ is, and seize him. Let them hear it from us; let them hear it from the Gospel.

He was killed by their ancestors, buried, recognized by his disciples, and before their eyes ascended into heaven. There he sits at the right hand of the Father. He who was judged will come as judge. Let them hear and hold him fast.

They reply: “How shall I hold one who is absent?” [Note: [Col. 1759] The printed editions have: “Whom shall I hold, who is absent?” Several manuscripts have: “How shall I hold him?”] “How shall I stretch my hand into heaven so as to hold him who sits there?”

Send faith, and you have held him. Your ancestors held him in the flesh; you hold him in your heart, because Christ, though absent, is also present.

If he were not present, he could not be held by us [Col. 1760]. But since what he said is true—“Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)—he went away, and yet he is here; he returned, and yet he does not abandon us.

For he carried his body into heaven; he did not remove his majesty from the world.

### 5

Jesus therefore came to Bethany six days before the Passover, where Lazarus had been dead, whom Jesus raised.

They made him a supper there, and Martha served; Lazarus was one of those reclining at table.

Lest people think that a phantom had appeared because a dead man had risen, he was one of those reclining at table: he was alive, he spoke, he ate. The truth was displayed, and the Jews’ unbelief was confounded.

The Lord therefore reclined with Lazarus and the others; Martha, one of Lazarus’s sisters, served.

### 6

Mary, the other sister of Lazarus, took a pound of costly perfume of genuine nard, anointed Jesus’ feet, wiped his feet with her hair, and the house was filled with the fragrance of the perfume.

We have heard what happened; let us seek its mystery.

Whatever faithful soul you wish to be, anoint the Lord’s feet with costly perfume along with Mary. That perfume was righteousness; therefore it was a pound. It was, moreover, perfume of costly genuine nard.

By saying “genuine” [pistic], we should perhaps understand that the perfume came from some place from which such costly perfume was obtained. Yet the word is not without significance and agrees very well with the sacrament.

In Greek, πίστις (*pistis*) means “faith.” You were seeking to practice righteousness: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17).

Anoint Jesus’ feet: by living well, follow the Lord’s footsteps.

Wipe them with your hair: if you have surplus possessions, give them to the poor, and you have wiped the Lord’s feet. For hair seems to be a bodily surplus.

You have something to do with your surplus possessions. They are surplus for you, but necessary for the Lord’s feet. Perhaps the Lord’s feet on earth are in need.

For of whom other than his members will he say at the end: “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matthew 25:40)?

You spent your surplus possessions, but you ministered to my feet.

### 7

The house was filled with the fragrance; the world was filled with a good reputation. For a good fragrance is a good reputation.

Those who live badly while being called Christians insult Christ. Concerning such people it was said that through them the name of the Lord is blasphemed (Romans 2:24).

If the name of God is blasphemed through such people, through good people the name of the Lord is praised.

Hear the Apostle: “We are the good fragrance of Christ,” he says, “in every place.”

It is also said in the Song of Songs: “Your name is perfume poured out” (Song of Songs 1:2).

Return your attention to the Apostle: “We are,” he says, “the good fragrance of Christ in every place, both among those who are being saved and among those who are perishing; to some we are the fragrance of life unto life, to others the fragrance of death unto death. And who is sufficient for these things?” (2 Corinthians 2:14–16).

The present reading from the holy Gospel gives us an occasion to speak about this fragrance, so that we may say enough and you may listen attentively, since the Apostle himself says, “And who is sufficient for these things?”

Therefore, as we attempt to speak about it, are we sufficient, or are you sufficient to hear these things?

We are not sufficient; but he is sufficient who deigns to say through us what it is beneficial for you to hear [Note: [Col. 1760] In four manuscripts: “deigns,” rather than “deigns to.”].

Behold, the Apostle [Col. 1761] is a good fragrance, as he himself says. But this good fragrance is for some the fragrance of life unto life, and for others the fragrance of death unto death. Yet it is a good fragrance.

For does he say, “To some we are a good fragrance unto life, and to others a bad fragrance unto death”? He called himself a good fragrance, not a bad one; and he said that the same good fragrance is for some unto life and for others unto death.

Happy are those who live by a good fragrance. But what is more wretched than those who die by a good fragrance?

### 8

“And who,” someone says, “is killed by a good fragrance?”

This is what the Apostle says: “And who is sufficient for these things?”

How God accomplishes in wondrous ways that good people live by a good fragrance and evil people die by it—how this happens, insofar as the Lord deigns to inspire [Note: [Col. 1761] The printed editions add “I shall show,” which is absent from the manuscripts]—for perhaps a higher understanding lies hidden here, which I cannot penetrate [Note: [Col. 1761] “Lies hidden,” according to the Lyon, Venetian, and Louvain editions, and M.]; nevertheless, what I have been able to penetrate ought not to be withheld from you.

Paul the Apostle, acting well, living well, preaching righteousness in word and demonstrating it in deed, a remarkable teacher and faithful steward, was widely celebrated in reputation. Some loved him; some envied him.

For he himself says in one place concerning certain people that they were proclaiming Christ not chastely but out of envy, “thinking,” he says, “to stir up affliction for my bonds.”

But what does he say? “Whether in pretense or in truth Christ is proclaimed” (Philippians 1:17–18).

Those who love me proclaim him; those who envy me proclaim him. The former live by a good fragrance, and the latter die by a good fragrance. Yet through both groups’ preaching, the name of Christ is proclaimed and the world is filled with the finest fragrance.

You loved the person acting well; you lived by a good fragrance. You envied the person acting well; you died by a good fragrance. Did you make that fragrance bad merely because you wished to die?

Do not envy, and the good fragrance will not kill you.

### 9

Finally, hear here also, through this perfume, how for some it was a good fragrance unto life and for others a good fragrance unto death.

After the devout Mary had done this in service to the Lord, immediately one of his disciples, Judas Iscariot, who was about to betray him, said: “Why was this perfume not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?”

Woe to you, wretched man! The good fragrance killed you.

Why he said this, the holy Evangelist revealed. If the Gospel had not exposed his mind to us, we might have thought that he could have said it out of concern for the poor.

It was not so. But what was the truth? Hear the truthful witness: “He said this not because he cared about the poor, but because he was a thief, and, having the money box, he used to carry away what was put into it.”

Did he carry it, or carry it away? He carried it in the service of the ministry; he carried it away by theft [Note: [Col. 1761] Epistle 108, chapter 3, section 8.].

### 10

Behold, hear that this Judas did not become wicked only then, when, bribed by the Jews, he betrayed the Lord.

Many who are careless about the Gospel suppose that Judas perished at the time when he accepted money from the Jews to betray the Lord. He did not perish then. He was already a thief and, having been lost, was following the Lord, because he followed him not in heart but in body.

He completed the number twelve [Col. 1762] among the Apostles, but did not possess apostolic blessedness. He had been the twelfth in image. When he departed and another succeeded him, apostolic fullness was restored and the integrity of the number remained (Acts 1:26).

What, then, did our Lord Jesus Christ wish to admonish his Church when he wished to have one lost man among the twelve, except that we should tolerate the wicked and not divide the body of Christ?

Behold, Judas is among the holy ones; behold, Judas is a thief. And lest you dismiss the matter, he was a thief and a sacrilegious person—not an ordinary thief: a thief of money boxes, but the Lord’s money boxes; of money boxes, but sacred ones.

If crimes are distinguished in the courts—between ordinary theft and embezzlement, for embezzlement is theft from public property, and theft from private property is not judged in the same way as theft from public property—how much more severely must a sacrilegious thief be judged, one who has dared to take not from just anywhere but from the Church?

Whoever steals something from the Church is compared with the lost Judas.

Such was this Judas, and yet he entered and went out with the eleven holy disciples. He came with them to the Lord’s supper. He was able to associate with them; he was not able to defile them.

Peter and Judas both received from the one bread. Yet what share is there between the faithful and the unfaithful? Peter received it unto life; Judas unto death.

As the fragrance was good, so the food was good. Just as a good fragrance gives life to the good and kills the wicked, so also good food gives life to the good and kills the wicked.

“For whoever eats unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Corinthians 11:29)—judgment upon himself, not upon you.

If judgment is upon himself, not upon you, tolerate the wicked, being good, so that you may come to the rewards of the good and not be sent into the punishment of the wicked.

### 11

Take the example of the Lord as he lived among human beings on earth.

Why did the one whom angels served have a money box, unless it was because his Church would have its own money boxes? Why did he admit a thief, unless it was so that his Church might patiently tolerate thieves?

But the man accustomed to take money from the money box did not hesitate, once he had received money, to sell the Lord himself.

Let us see what the Lord responds to these things.

Look, brothers: he did not say to him, “You say this because of your thefts.” He knew that he was a thief but did not expose him. Rather, he tolerated him and offered us an example of patience for enduring the wicked in the Church.

Then Jesus said to him: “Leave her alone, so that she may keep it for the day of my burial.”

He announced that he was going to die.

12. But what does what follows mean? “For you will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.” We certainly understand “You will always have the poor with you”: what he said is true. When has the Church been without the poor? But what does “You will not always have me” mean? How are we to understand “You will not always have me”? Do not be frightened: it was said to Judas. Why, then, did he not say, “You will have,” but “You will have” in the plural? Because Judas is not alone. One evil man signifies the body of evil people, just as Peter signifies the body of the good—indeed, the body of the Church, but among the good [Note: [Col. 1762] Five manuscripts of good quality read: “the body of the good, the body of the Church, indeed the body the Church, but among the good.” Two others agree, reading: “the body of the Church, indeed the body the Church, but,” etc. Bad. and Am. read: “the body of the Church, indeed the body of the Church, but among the good.”].

For if the sacrament of the Church had not been represented in Peter, the Lord would not have said to him: “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). If this was said only to Peter, the Church does not do this. But if it is also done in the Church, so that what is bound on earth is bound in heaven, and what is loosed on earth is loosed in heaven—for when the Church excommunicates someone, the excommunicated person is bound in heaven, and when the Church reconciles someone, the reconciled person is loosed in heaven—if, then, this is done in the Church, Peter, when he received the keys, signified the holy Church.

If the good in the Church were represented in the person of Peter, the evil in the Church were represented in the person of Judas; to these latter it was said, “You will not always have me.” What does “not always” mean? And what does “always” mean? If you are good, if you belong to the body represented by Peter, you have Christ both in the present and in the future: in the present through faith, in the present through the sign, in the present through the sacrament of Baptism, in the present through the food and drink of the altar. You have Christ in the present, but you will have him always, because when you depart from here, you will come to him who said to the thief, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43).

But if you live wickedly, you seem to have Christ in the present, because you enter the Church, mark yourself with the sign of Christ, are baptized with Christ’s baptism, mingle yourself with Christ’s members, and approach Christ’s altar: in the present you have Christ, but by living wickedly you will not always have him.

13. It can also be understood in this way: “You will always have the poor with you, but you will not always have me.” Let the good also accept this, but let them not be troubled: for he was speaking of the presence of his body. In respect of his majesty, his providence, and his ineffable and invisible grace, what he said is fulfilled: “Behold, I am with you always, to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). But in respect of the flesh which the Word assumed, in respect of that which was born from the Virgin, that which was seized by the Jews, fastened to the wood, taken down from the cross, wrapped in linen cloths, placed in the tomb, and manifested in the resurrection, you will not always have him with you. Why? Because he lived with his disciples in the bodily presence for forty days, and while they escorted him by seeing him rather than following him, he ascended into heaven (Acts 1:3, 9, 10), and he is not here. For he is there, seated at the right hand of the Father; and he is here, because the presence of his majesty has not departed.

Alternatively: in respect of the presence of his majesty, we always have Christ; in respect of the presence of his flesh, it was rightly said to the disciples, “You will not always have me.” The Church had him in the presence of the flesh for a few days; now it holds him by faith but does not see him with its eyes. Therefore, whether “You will not always have me” was said in this way or in that, the question, as I think, is no longer difficult, since it has been resolved in two ways.

14. Let us hear the few things that remain: “The great crowd of the Jews therefore learned that he was there, and they came, not only because of Jesus, but also to see Lazarus, whom Jesus had raised from the dead.” Curiosity, not love, brought them; they came and saw. Listen to the astonishing plan of vanity. When they saw Lazarus raised, because so great a miracle of the Lord had been spread abroad with such compelling evidence and declared with such manifest clarity that they could neither conceal what had happened nor deny it, observe what they devised. “But the chief priests resolved to kill Lazarus also, because many of the Jews were going away on his account and believing in Jesus.”

O foolish plan and blind savagery! The Lord Christ, who was able to raise a dead man, could he not raise one who had been killed? When you inflicted death on Lazarus, did you take away the Lord’s power? If you think there is a difference between someone being dead and someone being killed, behold, the Lord did both: he raised Lazarus, who was dead, and raised himself, who had been killed.

## TRACTATE LI

From the passage written, “On the next day the great crowd that had come to the feast,” and so forth, up to, “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” Chapter 12, verses 12–26.

1. After the Lord had raised the four-day-old corpse, while some Jews, astonished, believed when they saw, and others perished through envy—because of the good fragrance which is life to some and death to others (II Cor. 2:15)—after he had reclined in the house with Lazarus, who had been dead and raised, after the ointment had been poured over his feet, by which the house was filled with its fragrance, and after the Jews, with hearts corrupted, had conceived even the empty savagery and most foolish and senseless crime of killing Lazarus—concerning all these matters we have spoken in the preceding sermons as the Lord granted us to do—now let Your Charity attend to how great a fruit of his preaching appeared before the Lord’s Passion, and how great a flock of sheep from those lost sheep of the house of Israel heard the shepherd’s voice.

For the Gospel speaks in this way, as you heard when it was read just now: “On the next day the great crowd that had come to the feast, when they heard that Jesus was coming to Jerusalem, took branches of palm trees and went out to meet him, and cried out, ‘Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.’”

The branches of palm trees are praises signifying victory, because the Lord was going to overcome death by dying and triumph over the devil, the prince of death, by the trophy of the cross. The cry “Hosanna” is that of one pleading, as some who know the Hebrew language say; it indicates an emotion more than it signifies any particular thing. Such expressions exist in the Latin language as well, which are called interjections—for example, when we say “Alas!” in grief, or “Ha!” in delight, or, when we are amazed, “O great thing!” For then “O” signifies nothing except the feeling of one who is amazed. This should be believed to be the case because neither Greek nor Latin has been able to translate it, just as with the expression, “Whoever says to his brother, ‘Raca’” (Matt. 5:22). For this too is said to be an interjection, showing the feeling of one who is indignant.

3. “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel,” should rather be understood as meaning “in the name of the Lord,” that is, in the name of God the Father. Yet it can also be understood as “in his own name,” since he himself is also Lord. Hence it is written elsewhere, “The Lord rained from the Lord” (Gen. 19:24). But his own words guide our understanding better, for he said: “I have come in my Father’s name, and you did not receive me; another will come in his own name, and him you will receive” (John 5:43).

Christ is the teacher of humility, who “humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2:8). He does not therefore lose his divinity when he teaches us humility: in the one he is equal to the Father, in the other he is like us. By that in which he is equal to the Father, he created us so that we might exist; by that in which he is like us, he redeemed us lest we perish.

4. The crowd was praising him in these words: “Hosanna! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel.” What cross of mental anguish could the envy of the Jewish leaders endure when such a great multitude was proclaiming Christ as its king? But what was it for the Lord to be the King of Israel? What great thing was it for the King of the ages to become king of human beings? For Christ was not King of Israel in order to exact tribute, arm an army with iron, or visibly defeat enemies; he was King of Israel in order to rule minds, provide for them eternally, and lead believers, those who hope and love, into the kingdom of heaven.

Therefore, for the Son of God, equal to the Father, the Word through whom all things were made, to will to be King of Israel is condescension, not advancement; a sign of mercy, not an increase of power [Note: [Col. 1765] Lov. reads “argument.” Other printed editions and manuscripts read “increase.”]. For he who was called King of the Jews on earth is Lord of the angels in heaven.

5. “And Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it.” This is stated briefly here; how it happened is read in full in the other evangelists (Matt. 21:1–16; Mark 11:1–11; and Luke 19:29–48). A prophetic testimony is added to this event, so that it might become clear that the wicked leaders of the Jews did not understand the one in whom what they were reading was being fulfilled.

“Jesus found a young donkey and sat upon it,” as it is written: “Do not fear, daughter of Zion; behold, your king is coming, seated upon a donkey’s colt.” In that people, therefore, there was a daughter of Zion; she is Jerusalem, which is Zion. In that people, I say, a rejected and blind people, there nevertheless was a daughter of Zion, to whom it would be said, “Do not fear: behold, your king is coming, seated upon a donkey’s colt.”

This daughter of Zion, to whom these things are divinely spoken, was among those sheep who heard the shepherd’s voice; she was among that multitude which praised the Lord who was coming with such devotion and escorted him in so great a throng. To her it was said, “Do not fear”: recognize the one whom you praise, and do not tremble when he suffers, because that blood is being poured out through which your offense may be blotted out and life restored.

But by the colt of the donkey on which no one had sat—for this is found in the other evangelists—we understand the people of the Gentiles, who had not received the Law of the Lord. By the she-donkey, however—since both animals were brought to the Lord—we understand his people that was coming from the people of Israel, not wholly unbroken, but one that recognized the Lord’s manger.

[Col. 1766] 6. His disciples did not understand these things at first. But when Jesus had been glorified—that is, when he had displayed the power of his resurrection—then they remembered that these things had been written about him, and that they had done these things for him: that is, they had not done other things for him than those that had been written about him. For, recalling according to Scripture the things that had been fulfilled before the Lord’s Passion or during the Lord’s Passion, they found there also that, in accordance with the sayings of the prophets, he had sat upon a donkey’s colt.

7. “The crowd that had been with him when he called Lazarus from the tomb and raised him from the dead therefore bore witness.” For this reason the crowd also came to meet him, because they had heard that he had performed this sign.

The Pharisees therefore said among themselves: “You see that we are accomplishing nothing? Behold, the whole world has gone after him.” A crowd disturbed a crowd. Why are you envious, blind crowd, because the world is going after him through whom the world was made?

8. “Now there were some Gentiles among those who had gone up to worship at the feast. These therefore approached Philip, who was from Bethsaida of Galilee, and asked him, saying, ‘Lord, we wish to see Jesus.’ Philip came and told Andrew; Andrew and Philip in turn told Jesus.”

Let us hear what the Lord answered them. Behold, the Jews wish to kill him, while the Gentiles wish to see him; but those who were crying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, the King of Israel,” were also from the Jews. Behold, some from the circumcision and others from the uncircumcision, like two walls coming from different directions and meeting in the one faith of Christ through the kiss of peace. Let us therefore hear the voice of the cornerstone.

“Jesus,” he says, “answered them, saying: ‘The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.’” Someone might perhaps think that he said this because the Gentiles wished to see him. It is not so. Rather, he saw that these Gentiles would believe in him after his Passion and resurrection among all the nations, because, as the Apostle says, “A hardening in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter” (Rom. 11:25).

Taking occasion, therefore, from these Gentiles who desired to see him, he announces the future fullness of the Gentiles and declares that the hour of his glorification was already at hand, by which, once accomplished in heaven, the Gentiles would believe. Hence it was foretold: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory over all the earth” (Ps. 107:6). This is the fullness of the Gentiles of which the Apostle says, “A hardening in part has happened to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.”

9. But the exaltation of glorification had to be preceded by the humility of suffering. Therefore he continued: “Amen, amen, I say to you: unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” He was speaking of himself. He was the grain that had to be put to death and multiplied: put to death through the unbelief of the Jews, multiplied through the faith of the peoples.

10. Then, exhorting them to follow in the footsteps of his Passion, he said: “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” This can be understood in two ways: “Whoever loves will lose”—that is, if you love, lose; if you desire to preserve life in Christ, do not fear death for Christ.

It can also be understood in another way: “Whoever loves his life will lose it.” Do not love it, lest you lose it; do not love it in this life, lest you lose it in eternal life. What I said subsequently seems more consistent with the evangelical meaning, for it follows: “And whoever hates his life in this world will preserve it for eternal life.” Therefore, in what was said above, “Whoever loves,” we should understand “in this world”: he himself will lose it. But whoever hates it—certainly in this world—will himself preserve it for eternal life.

Great and astonishing is the meaning: how can love of one’s life cause a person to perish, while hatred prevents perishing? If you love wrongly, then you have hated; if you hate rightly, then you have loved. Blessed are those who hate in order to preserve, lest they lose by loving.

But take care lest the thought creep upon you that you should kill yourself, by understanding that you must hate your life in this world. For some wicked and perverse people, murderers more cruel and criminal toward themselves, have therefore given themselves to flames, suffocated themselves in water, thrown themselves from heights, and perished. Christ did not teach this. Indeed, when the devil suggested a leap from the height, he replied: “Get behind me, Satan; it is written, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’” (Matt. 4:7).

But he said to Peter, signifying by what death he would glorify God: “When you were younger, you girded yourself and went where you wished; but when you grow old, another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish” (John 21:18–19). There he sufficiently indicated that the one who follows Christ’s footsteps must be killed not by himself but by another.

Therefore, when the decisive moment comes, so that this condition is proposed—either that one must act against God’s command or depart from this life—and a person is forced to choose one of the two, with the persecutor threatening death, let him choose to die for the God he loves rather than live having offended him. There let him hate his life in this world, so that he may preserve it for eternal life.

11. “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” What does “let him follow me” mean except “let him imitate me”? For the apostle Peter says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps” (I Pet. 2:21). Behold what was said: “If anyone serves me, let him follow me.” With what fruit? With what payment? With what reward? “And where I am,” he says, “there also will my servant be.” Let him be loved freely, so that for the work by which he serves him, the reward may be to be with him. For where can it be well without him, or when can it be ill with him?
