Listen more clearly: “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him.” With what honor, except that he may be with his Son? For what he said above, “Where I am, there also will my servant be,” he explained when he said, “My Father will honor him.” For what greater honor can one who has been adopted receive than to be where the Only-Begotten is—not made equal to the divinity, but joined to eternity?

12. But what it means to serve Christ, for which such a great reward is proposed, we ought rather to investigate. For if we should think that serving Christ means preparing the things necessary for the body, or cooking and setting food before him while he dines, or giving him a cup and mixing his drink, those who were able to have Christ present in the body did this, such as Martha and Mary, when Lazarus was one of those reclining at table.

But in this way even the lost Judas served Christ, for he himself kept the money box; and although he wickedly stole from what was put into it, nevertheless through him the necessities were also prepared (John 12:2, 6). This is the reason why, when the Lord said to him, “What you are doing, do quickly,” some thought that he had ordered him to prepare what was necessary for the feast day or to give something to the needy (John 13:27, 29).

The Lord would in no way say of such servants, “Where I am, there my servant will also be,” and, “If anyone serves me, my Father will honor him,” since we see Judas, serving in such ways, rejected rather than honored.

Why, then, do we seek elsewhere what it means to serve Christ, instead of recognizing it in these very words? When he said, “If anyone serves me, let him follow me,” he meant this, as though he had said: “If anyone does not follow me, he does not serve me.” Therefore they serve Jesus Christ who seek not their own interests but those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2:21).

For “let him follow me” means: let him walk in my ways, not his own. As it is written elsewhere: “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (I John 2:6). If he offers bread to the hungry, he ought also to do so out of mercy, not ostentation; he should seek nothing there except the good work, with his left hand not knowing what his right hand is doing (Matt. 6:3)—that is, so that the intention of greed may be removed from the work of charity.

Whoever serves in this way serves Christ, and rightly it will be said to him, “When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me” (Matt. 25:40). And not only when doing things pertaining to bodily mercy, but when doing every good work for Christ’s sake—for then they will be good, since “Christ is the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. 10:4)—he is Christ’s servant, even unto that great work of charity which consists in laying down his life for his brothers. For this too is to lay it down for Christ.

He will say this on account of his members: “When you did it for these, you did it for me.” Concerning such a work he also deigned to make and call himself a servant, when he said: “The Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to lay down his life for many” (Matt. 20:28). From this, therefore, each person is Christ’s servant, from which Christ himself is also a servant. The Father will honor one who serves Christ in this way with that great honor: that he may be with his Son, and that his happiness may never fail.

13. Therefore, when you hear, brothers, the Lord saying, “Where I am, there also will my servant be,” do not think only of good bishops and clergy. You too, according to your ability, serve Christ by living well, giving alms, and proclaiming his name and teaching to those to whom you can, so that every head of a household may recognize in this name that he owes a fatherly concern to his family.

For Christ’s sake and for eternal life, let him admonish, teach, exhort, and correct all those under his care; let him show goodwill and exercise discipline. In this way, in his own house, he will fulfill an ecclesiastical and, in a certain sense, episcopal office, serving Christ so that he may be with him forever.

For many among your number have also served in that supreme ministry of suffering: many who were neither bishops nor clergy—young men and virgins, older people with younger people, many married men and married women, many fathers and mothers of families—serving Christ, they also laid down their lives in his martyrdom, and when the Father honored them, they received most glorious crowns.

## TRACTATE LII

From the passage written, “Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say?” up to, “Jesus said these things, and he departed and hid himself from them.” Chapter 12, verses 27–36.

1. After the Lord Jesus Christ had exhorted his servants in yesterday’s reading to follow him, having foretold his Passion in this way—that unless a grain of wheat falling into the earth died, it would remain alone, but if it died, it would bear much fruit—after he had stirred up those who wished to follow him to the kingdom of heaven, so that they might hate their life in this world if they intended to preserve it for eternal life, he once again adapted his expression to our weakness and said what today’s reading began with: “Now my soul is troubled.”

Why is your soul troubled, Lord? A little earlier you said, “Whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life.” Is your soul therefore loved in this world, and for that reason troubled as the hour approaches when it must depart from this world? Who would dare to affirm this about the Lord’s soul?

But he transferred us into himself; he received us into himself, our head received the feeling of his members. Therefore he was not troubled by anyone; rather, as it is said of him when he raised Lazarus, “He troubled himself” (John 11:33). For it was necessary that the one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, should, just as he raised us to the heights, also suffer with us in the depths [Note: [Col. 1769] Nearly all manuscripts read: “and should suffer the weak things with us.”].

2. I hear him saying above, “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified”: if the grain is put to death, it bears much fruit. I hear, “Whoever hates his life in this world preserves it for eternal life.” I am not merely permitted to marvel; I am commanded to imitate. Then, in the words that follow, “If anyone serves me, let him follow me; and where I am, there also will my servant be,” I am kindled to despise the world, and in my sight the whole of this life, however long it may be, is nothing but vapor. Because of my love for eternal things, all temporal things become worthless to me.

And again I hear my Lord himself, who by those words snatched me from my weakness into his strength, saying, “Now my soul is troubled.” What is this? How do you command my soul to follow you if I see your soul troubled? How can I bear what such great strength feels as burdensome? What foundation shall I seek if the rock gives way?

But I seem to hear the Lord answering me in my thoughts, and in a certain manner saying: “You will follow more closely because I place myself between you and what you must endure. You have heard the voice of my strength directed toward you; hear in me the voice of your weakness. I supply strength so that you may run, and I do not restrain what you hasten toward; but I transfer into myself what makes you tremble, and I lay myself beneath the path on which you pass.”

O Lord our mediator, God above us, human being for our sake, I recognize your mercy! For in your greatness, by the will of your love, you are troubled, and thus you console many in your body who are troubled by the necessity of their weakness, lest they perish through despair.

3. Finally, let the person who wishes to follow hear how he should follow. Perhaps a terrible hour has come: the choice is proposed either of committing iniquity or undergoing suffering. The weak soul is troubled, and for its sake the invincible soul was voluntarily troubled. Set God’s will before your own will.

For attend to what your Creator and Teacher next adds—he who made you and, in order to teach you, himself became what he had made. For the one who made the human being became human; but he remained the unchangeable God and changed the human being for the better.

Hear, then, what he adds after saying, “Now my soul is troubled”: “And what shall I say?” he says. “Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour. Father, glorify your name.”

He taught you what to think, taught you what to say, whom to call upon, in whom to hope, and whose certain and divine will you should set before your own weak human will. Therefore do not think that he has failed from the heights because he wishes you to advance from the depths.

For he also deigned to be tempted by the devil; and if he had not wished to be tempted, he certainly would not have been tempted, just as, if he had not wished to suffer, he would not have suffered. He gave the devil the answers that you ought to give in temptations (Matt. 4:1–10). He was tempted, but he was not placed in danger, so that he might teach you, when endangered in temptation, to answer the tempter, not to follow the tempter, and to escape from the danger of temptation.

As he said here, “Now my soul is troubled,” so also where he says, “My soul is sorrowful even unto death,” and, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me,” he took upon himself human weakness [Note: [Col. 1770] So read the manuscripts. But the printed editions read: “he displayed the weakness of the humanity he had assumed.”], in order to teach one who is thus sorrowful and troubled to say what follows: “Nevertheless, not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matt. 26:38–39).

For in this way the human being is directed from human things to divine things, when the divine will is placed before the human will. But what is, “Glorify your name,” except: in his Passion and resurrection? What else, then, does it mean except that the Father glorifies the Son, who also glorifies his name in the similar sufferings of his servants?

Hence it is written concerning Peter that he said, “Another will gird you and carry you where you do not wish,” because he wished to signify by what death Peter would glorify God (John 21:18–19). Therefore God also glorified his name in Peter, because he thus glorifies Christ even in his members.

4. Then a voice came from heaven: “I have glorified it, and I will glorify it again.” “I have glorified it” before I made the world; “and I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead and ascends into heaven.

It can also be understood in another way. “I have glorified it” when he was born from the Virgin, when he performed mighty works, when he was worshiped by the Magi, with heaven bearing witness through the star, when he was recognized by holy men filled with the Holy Spirit, when he was declared by the Spirit descending in the form of a dove, when he was revealed by the voice sounding from heaven, when he was transfigured on the mountain, when he performed many miracles, when he healed and cleansed many, when he fed such a multitude with very few loaves, when he commanded the winds and waves, when he raised the dead.

“And I will glorify it again” when he rises from the dead, when death will no longer rule over him, when God is exalted above the heavens and his glory is over all the earth.

5. The crowd standing there, which had heard this, said that thunder had occurred. Others said, “An angel has spoken to him.” Jesus answered and said: “This voice did not come for my sake, but for yours.”

Here he showed that the voice did not announce to him something he already knew, but to those to whom it was necessary that it be announced. And just as that voice was produced by divine power not for his sake but for the sake of others, so his soul was troubled by his will not for his sake but for the sake of others.

6. Attend to what follows. “Now,” he says, “is the judgment of the world.” What, then, is to be expected at the end of the age? At the end, the judgment that is expected will be the judgment of the living and the dead; it will be the judgment of eternal rewards and punishments.

What kind of judgment, then, is taking place now? In the earlier readings, as far as I could, I reminded Your Charity that “judgment” can also mean not condemnation but discernment. Hence it is written, “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1).

There are many judgments of God. Hence it is said in the Psalm, “Your judgments are a great abyss” (Ps. 36:7). The Apostle also says, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments!” (Rom. 11:33).

Among these judgments is also what the Lord says here: “Now is the judgment of the world,” while the judgment at the end is reserved for the time when the living and the dead will finally be judged.

The devil therefore possessed the human race and held the guilty under the document of their sins; he ruled in the hearts of unbelievers and, with the Creator abandoned, dragged the deceived and enslaved into the worship of the creature. But through faith in Christ, which was confirmed by his death and resurrection, and through his blood, which was poured out for the remission of sins, thousands of believers are freed from the devil’s dominion, joined to Christ’s body, and, under so great a head, his faithful members are given life by one Spirit.

This he called judgment: this discernment, this expulsion of the devil from those whom he had redeemed.

7. Finally, attend to what he says. As though we were asking what he meant by saying, “Now is the judgment of the world,” he explained it immediately. For he said: “Now the prince of this world will be cast out.”

We have heard what kind of judgment he said it was. It is not, therefore, the judgment that will come at the end, when the living and the dead are to be judged, some separated to the right and others to the left; it is the judgment by which the prince of this world will be cast out.

How, then, was he inside, and where did he say that he would be cast out? Was he in the world and sent outside the world? If he were speaking of the judgment that will come at the end, someone might suppose that he meant the eternal fire into which the devil will be sent with his angels and with all who belong to his side—not by nature but by vice; not because he created or begot them, but because he persuaded and held them. Someone might therefore suppose that this eternal fire is outside the world, and that this is what “he will be cast out” means.

But since he says, “Now is the judgment of the world,” and, explaining what he means by “now,” says, “Now the prince of this world will be cast out,” we must understand this as something happening now, not something that will happen much later on the last day.

The Lord therefore foretold what he knew: after his Passion and glorification, many peoples throughout the world would believe, and the devil, who was inside their hearts, would be cast out when they renounced him through faith.

8. But someone may say: Was he not cast out from the hearts of the patriarchs, prophets, and ancient righteous people? He certainly was cast out. How, then, was it said, “Now he will be cast out”? How should we understand it except that what had then happened among very few people was now foretold as about to happen very soon among many great peoples?

The same question and a similar solution can apply to what was said: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). For the prophets did not announce future things without the Holy Spirit. Nor did the elder Simeon and the widow Anna recognize the infant Lord in the Holy Spirit (Luke 2:25–38)? Nor did Zechariah and Elizabeth, through the Holy Spirit, make such great prophecies concerning him who had not yet been born but had already been conceived (Luke 1:41–45, 67–79)?

But “the Spirit had not yet been given” means: that abundance of spiritual grace had not yet been given by which those gathered together would speak in the languages of all peoples (Acts 2:4–6), and thus the future Church would be announced in the languages of all nations; by which grace of the Spirit peoples would be gathered, sins would be forgiven far and wide, and thousands upon thousands would be reconciled to God.

9. “What, then,” someone may say, “since the devil will be cast out from the hearts of believers, does he now tempt no faithful person?” On the contrary, he does not cease tempting them. But it is one thing to reign within and another to attack from without. An enemy sometimes attacks a most strongly fortified city without conquering it.

And if some of his arrows reach their mark, the Apostle teaches where they do not wound: he recalls the breastplate and shield of faith (I Thess. 5:8). And if he sometimes wounds, the one who heals is present.

For just as those who are fighting are told, “I write these things to you so that you may not sin,” so those who are wounded hear what follows: “And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; he himself is the propitiation for our sins” (I John 2:1–2).

What do we pray for when we say, “Forgive us our debts,” except that our wounds may be healed? And what else do we ask when we say, “Do not bring us into temptation” (Matt. 6:12–13), except that the one who lies in ambush or struggles against us from outside may not break in from any direction, and may not overcome us by any deceit or force?

However many engines of war he raises against us, when he does not possess the place of the heart where faith dwells, he has been cast out. But “unless the Lord guards the city, the one who guards it watches in vain” (Ps. 127:1). Therefore do not presume upon yourselves, if you do not wish to call the devil, once cast out, back inside again.

10. But far be it from us to think that the devil is called “the prince of the world” in such a way that we believe he can rule heaven and earth. Rather, “world” is the name given to wicked human beings who are spread throughout the entire earth, just as “house” is the name given to those by whom it is inhabited. Accordingly, we say, “It is a good house” or “It is a bad house,” not when we praise or blame the building of walls and roofs, but when we refer to the conduct either of good people or of bad people.

Thus, then, it was said, “the prince of this world”—that is, the prince of all the wicked who dwell in the world.

“World” is also used of the good, who likewise are spread throughout the entire earth. Hence the Apostle says, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (II Cor. 5:19). These are the people from whose hearts the prince of this world is cast out.

11. When, therefore, he had said, “Now the prince of this world will be cast out,” he added, “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all things after me.” What are “all things” except those from among which he is cast out? He did not say “all people,” but “all things”: for faith does not belong to everyone (II Thess. 3:2). He therefore did not refer this to the totality of human beings, but to the wholeness of the creature—that is, spirit, soul, and body; that by which we understand, that by which we live, and that by which we are visible and tangible. For he who said, “Not a hair of your head will perish” (Luke 21:18), draws all things after himself.

Or, if “all things” is to be understood as the human beings themselves, we may say that all those predestined to salvation are meant: of all of them he said that nothing would perish, when above he was speaking about his sheep (John 10:28). Or certainly “all things” means every class of human beings—whether in all languages, all ages, all ranks of honor, all varieties of intellect, all professions of lawful and useful arts, and whatever else can be named according to the innumerable differences by which human beings differ from one another apart from sins alone—from the highest to the lowest, from king to beggar. “I will draw all things,” he says, “after me,” so that he may be their head and they his members.

“But if I am lifted up,” he says, that is, “when I am lifted up”; for he does not doubt that what he came to fulfill will happen. This refers to what he said earlier: “But if the grain dies, it produces much fruit.” For what else did he call his exaltation than his passion on the cross? The Evangelist himself did not leave this unstated: he immediately added, “But he said this to signify by what death he was going to die.”

12. The crowd answered him: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever; and how can you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? And who is this Son of Man?” They remembered well that the Lord constantly said that he was the Son of Man. For here he did not say, “If the Son of Man is lifted up from the earth”; but above he had said what was read and expounded yesterday, when the Gentiles who wished to see him were announced to him: “The hour has come for the Son of Man to be glorified” [Col. 1774] (John 12:23).

Keeping this in mind, and understanding his present words—“When I am lifted up from the earth”—as referring to the death of the cross, they asked him and said: “We have heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever; and how can you say, ‘The Son of Man must be lifted up’? For who is this Son of Man?” “If he is the Christ,” they said, “he remains forever; and if he remains forever, how will he be lifted up from the earth—that is, how will he die through the passion of the cross?” They understood that he had said this, which they were planning to do. Thus it was not wisdom poured into them that disclosed the obscurity of these words, but a conscience goaded by guilt.

13. Jesus therefore said to them: “You still have a little light among you. This is why you understand that the Christ remains forever. Walk, therefore, while you have the light, so that darkness may not overtake you.” Walk; draw near; understand everything: both that Christ would die and that he would live forever; that he would pour out his blood to redeem, and that he would ascend on high to lead you there. Darkness will overtake you if you believe in Christ’s eternity in such a way that you deny in him the humility of death.

“And whoever walks in darkness does not know where he is going.” Thus he can stumble against the stone of stumbling and rock of offense, which the Lord became for the blind Jews; whereas for believers the stone which the builders rejected became the cornerstone (I Peter 2:6–8). For this reason they disdained believing in Christ: their impiety despised the dead man and mocked the one who had been killed. Yet this was precisely the death of the grain destined to multiply, and the exaltation of the one who draws all things after himself.

“While you have the light,” he says, “believe in the light, so that you may be sons of light.” When you have heard something true, believe in the truth, so that you may be reborn in the truth.

14. Jesus said these things, and he went away and hid himself from them. Not from those who had begun to believe and love, nor from those who had come to meet him with palm branches and praises, but from those who saw and envied—for they did not truly see, but stumbled in blindness against that stone. When Jesus hid himself from those who wished to kill him—a point you have often been reminded of because of forgetfulness—he provided for our weakness; he did not detract from his own power.

### TREATISE LIII

From the passage beginning, “Though he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him,” to, “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.” Chapter 12, verses 37–43.

1. The Lord Christ had foretold his passion and his fruitful death in the exaltation of the cross, where he said that he would draw all things after himself. When the Jews understood that he was speaking of his own death and put to him the question how he could say that he was going to die, since they had heard from the Law that the Christ remains forever, he urged them, while they still had a little light within them by which they had learned that Christ is eternal, to walk so that they might learn everything and not be overtaken by darkness. After saying these things, he hid himself from them. You learned this in the preceding Sunday readings and sermons.

[Col. 1775] 2. Then the Evangelist introduced the passage from which today’s reading is taken, saying: “Though he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him,” so that the word of the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled, where he said, “Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

Here he sufficiently showed that the arm of the Lord is called the Son of God—not because God the Father is defined by the shape of human flesh, with the Son clinging to him like a bodily limb, but because all things were made through him; therefore he is called the arm of the Lord. Just as your arm is the means by which you work, so God’s Word is called his arm, because he worked the world through the Word.

Why does a human being extend an arm in order to accomplish something, except because what he has said does not come about immediately? But if he possessed such power that whatever he said came to be without any movement of his body, his word would be his arm [Note: [Col. 1775] Erasmus and Louvain add here, “because a word is something conceivable or utterable”; this entire phrase is absent from the manuscripts, except for a few which, along with Am and Bad, read, “because a word is not something conceivable or utterable.”].

But the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God the Father, just as he is not a member of the Father’s body, so also is he not a conceivable, utterable, transitory word; for, since all things were made through him, he was the Word of God.

3. Therefore, when we hear that the Son of God is the arm of God the Father, let no bodily habit of thought obstruct us. As far as we can by his gift, let us contemplate the Power and Wisdom of God through which all things were made. Such an arm is neither extended when it is stretched out nor contracted when it is drawn back. He is not the same person as the Father, but he and the Father are one; and he is wholly equal to the Father everywhere, just as the Father is wholly himself.

This leaves no opening for the detestable error of those who say that the Father alone exists, but that, according to the diversity of circumstances, he himself is called Son and he himself is called the Holy Spirit. In these words they dare [Note: [Col. 1775] Thus in the manuscripts. But the editions read, “they dare.”] to say: “You see that the Father alone exists, if the Son is his arm; for a human being and his arm are not two persons, but one.”

They neither understand nor attend to the way in which words are transferred from one set of things to another because of some resemblance, even in ordinary speech about visible and familiar things—how much more, then, must words be transferred when we attempt, however inadequately, to speak of things ineffable, which cannot be described as they truly are?

A human being also calls another person, through whom he ordinarily accomplishes whatever he does, his arm. If that person is taken away from him, he says in grief, “I have lost my arm”; and to the one who took him away he says, “You have taken my arm from me.” Let them therefore understand how the Son is called the Father’s arm, through whom the Father worked all things, lest, by failing to understand this and remaining in the darkness of their error, they become like those very Jews of whom it was said, “And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?”

4. Here another question arises. To discuss it adequately, and to examine and sift all its most obscure recesses as they deserve, is, I believe, beyond my powers, beyond the limits of the available time, and beyond your capacity. Yet because your expectation does not allow us to pass on to other matters [Col. 1776] without saying something about it, accept what we can offer; and where we do not satisfy your expectation, ask for increase from him who appointed us to plant and water. For, as the Apostle says, “Neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Corinthians 3:7).

Some people mutter among themselves, and whenever they can they loudly proclaim and argue with turbulent disputation: “What did the Jews do, or what was their fault, if it was necessary that the word of the prophet Isaiah be fulfilled, where he said, ‘Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’”

We answer them that the Lord, foreknowing the future, foretold through the Prophet the unbelief of the Jews; he foretold it, however, rather than causing it. For God does not compel anyone to sin merely because he already knows the future sins of human beings. He foreknew their sins—not his own, not someone else’s, but theirs. Therefore, if what he foreknew as theirs is not theirs, then he did not truly foreknow it. But because his foreknowledge cannot be mistaken, without doubt it is not someone else but they themselves who sin, whom God foreknew as going to sin.

The Jews therefore committed the sin which the one who does not delight in sin did not compel them to commit, but foretold that they would commit, since nothing is hidden from him. And so, if they had wished to do good rather than evil, they would not have been prevented; and they would have been foreseen as going to do this by him who knows what each person will do and what he will receive in return for his deed.

5. But the Gospel’s following words press the matter further and make the question more profound. It adds: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again: ‘He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I should heal them.’”

We are asked: “If they could not believe, what sin is it for a person not to do what he cannot do? But if they sinned by not believing, then they could believe and did not do so. If they could, how does the Gospel say, ‘Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again, “He has blinded their eyes and hardened their heart”’—so that, what is more serious, the cause of their unbelief is referred to God, since he himself blinded their eyes and hardened their heart?”

This is not even said of the devil, but of God, as the prophetic Scripture itself testifies. For if we suppose that this was said of the devil—that he blinded their eyes and hardened their heart—we must labor to show how their guilt can be established, since they are said not to have been able to believe. Moreover, what shall we answer concerning another testimony of the same prophet, which the Apostle Paul quoted, saying: “What Israel was seeking, it did not obtain; but the elect obtained it. The rest were hardened, as it is written: ‘God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear, to this very day’” (Romans 11:7; Isaiah 6:10)?

6. You have heard the question, brothers, and you see how profound it is; but we answer as we can. “They could not believe because the prophet Isaiah foretold this.” The Prophet foretold it because God foreknew that it would happen.

But if I am asked why they could not [Col. 1777], I answer quickly: because they were unwilling. God foresaw their evil will, and the one from whom future things cannot be hidden announced it beforehand through the Prophet.

“But,” you say, “the Prophet gives another cause, one that does not depend on their will.” What cause does the Prophet give? “Because God gave them a spirit of compunction, eyes so that they should not see, and ears so that they should not hear; and he blinded their eyes and hardened their heart.”

I answer that this too was deserved by their will. For God blinds and hardens in this way: by abandoning and not helping. What he can do by a hidden judgment, he cannot do unjustly. Piety in religious people must preserve this conviction unshaken and inviolate. Thus the Apostle, when treating this very difficult question, says: “What shall we say, then? Is there injustice with God? By no means!” (Romans 9:14).

If, then, there is no injustice with God, whether he helps, he acts mercifully, or whether he does not help, he acts justly: he does everything not arbitrarily but by judgment. And if the judgments of holy human beings are just, how much more just are those of God, who sanctifies and justifies?

His judgments are therefore just, but hidden. Thus, when questions of this kind arise—why one person is this way and another that way; why one is blinded when God abandons him, while another is illuminated when God helps him—let us not arrogate to ourselves judgment concerning the judgment of so great a Judge. Rather, trembling, let us exclaim with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How inscrutable are his judgments and unsearchable his ways!” (Romans 11:33). Hence it is said in the Psalm: “Your judgments are like a great abyss” (Psalm 35:7).

7. Therefore, brothers, do not let your loving expectation press me to penetrate this height, investigate this abyss, and search out what is inscrutable. I recognize my measure, and I seem also to perceive yours. This matter is higher than my growth and stronger than my powers; I think it is also higher and stronger than yours.

Let us therefore listen together to Scripture admonishing us and saying: “Do not seek what is too high for you, and do not search out what is too strong for you” (Ecclesiasticus 3:22). This does not mean that these things have been denied to us, since God our teacher says, “Nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10:26). But if we walk in what we have attained, as the Apostle says, God will reveal to us not only what we do not know and ought to know, but also, if we think differently in anything, that too (Philippians 3:15–16).

We have reached the way of faith; let us hold to it with the greatest perseverance. It will lead us to the king’s chamber, where all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2:3). The Lord Jesus was not begrudging those great and especially chosen disciples of his when he said, “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). We must walk, advance, and grow, so that our hearts may become capable of those things which we cannot now contain. And if the final day finds us making progress, there we shall learn what we could not learn here.

8. If anyone knows and is confident that he can explain this question more clearly and more adequately, let me be ready to learn rather than to teach. Only let no one dare [Col. 1778] to defend free will in such a way as to try to take away from us the prayer in which we say, “Do not lead us into temptation.” And, conversely, let no one deny the freedom of the will and dare to excuse sin.

Let us listen to the Lord, both commanding and helping: commanding what we ought to do and helping us to fulfill it. For excessive confidence in their own will has lifted some into pride, while excessive distrust of their own will has cast others down into negligence.

The former say: “Why do we ask God not to be overcome by temptation, if this lies within our power?” The latter say: “Why do we strive to live well, if this lies within God’s power?”

O Lord, O Father who are in heaven, do not lead us into any of these temptations, but deliver us from evil (Matthew 6:13)!

Let us listen to the Lord saying, “I prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail” (Luke 22:32), so that we do not suppose that our faith lies in free will in such a way that it needs no divine help. Let us also listen to the Evangelist saying, “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12), so that we do not suppose altogether that what we believe is not within our power. Nevertheless, in both matters let us acknowledge his benefits.

We must give thanks because power has been given; and we must pray that weakness may not succumb (Galatians 5:6). This is the faith which works through love, according to the measure that the Lord has apportioned to each person (Romans 12:3), so that “whoever boasts may boast not in himself but in the Lord” (I Corinthians 1:31).

9. It is therefore no wonder that those whose will was so proud that, in ignorance of God’s righteousness, they wished to establish their own, could not believe. As the Apostle says of them, “They were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:3). Because they swelled up as though by works rather than by faith, blinded by their own swelling pride, they stumbled against the stone of stumbling.

The word “could not” is used here in a sense in which “were unwilling” is to be understood, just as it is said of the Lord our God: “If we do not believe, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself” (II Timothy 2:13). “Cannot” is said of the Almighty. Therefore, just as the fact that the Lord cannot deny himself is praise of the divine will, so the fact that they could not believe is blame of the human will.

10. I say this as well: those who think so proudly that they attribute so much to the powers of their own will that they deny the necessity of divine help for living well cannot believe in Christ. The syllables of Christ’s name and the sacraments of Christ are of no benefit where faith in Christ is resisted.

The faith of Christ is to believe in the one who justifies the ungodly (Romans 4:5); to believe in the Mediator, without whom we are not reconciled to God; to believe in the Savior who came to seek and save what was lost (Luke 19:10); to believe in the one who said, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Because such a person, ignorant of God’s righteousness by which the ungodly is justified, wishes to establish his own righteousness by which the proud are convicted, he cannot believe in Christ. This is why they too could not believe—not because human beings cannot be changed for the better, but because, as long as they hold such opinions, they cannot believe.

This is why they are blinded and hardened: because, by denying divine [Col. 1779] help, they are not helped. God foreknew this concerning the Jews who were blinded and hardened, and the Prophet foretold it in God’s Spirit.

11. As for what he added, “and let them turn, and I will heal them,” should “not” be understood here—that is, “let them not turn”—in accordance with the sentence connected with what precedes, where it was said, “so that they should not see with their eyes and understand with their heart”? For here too, should it be understood as saying, “so that they should not understand”? [Note: [Col. 1779] Perhaps one should read, “it was not said,” unless the sense is that the negation prefixed to “see” is to be mentally joined to “understand.” The printed Vulgate version of the Gospel indeed has, “and they do not understand with their heart”; but the ancient Corbie Bibles, agreeing with the Greek, do not repeat the negation at this point.] The turning itself, after all, is also from the grace of the one to whom it is said, “O God of hosts, restore us” (Psalm 79:8).

Or should this also be understood as having been brought about by the mercy of heavenly healing? Since they were proud and perverse in will and wanted to establish their own righteousness, were they abandoned for this purpose, so that they might be blinded; blinded for this purpose, so that they might stumble against the stone of stumbling and their faces might be filled with disgrace; and then, having been humbled, might seek the name of the Lord—not their own righteousness, by which the proud person is puffed up, but God’s righteousness, by which the ungodly is justified?

For this benefited many of them for good: pierced by compunction over their crime, they afterward believed in Christ. For them he himself had prayed, saying, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Concerning this ignorance of theirs the Apostle also says: “I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” He then adds: “For, being ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, they were not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans 10:2–3).

12. “Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory, and he spoke about him.” What Isaiah saw, and how this relates to the Lord Christ, must be read and understood in Isaiah’s book. For he did not see him as he is, but in a certain signifying manner, as the prophet’s vision was to be formed.

Moses also saw him, and yet he said to the one he saw, “If I have found favor before you, show yourself to me openly, so that I may see you” (Exodus 33:13), because he did not see him as he is.

When this will happen to us, the same holy evangelist John says in his Epistle: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John 3:2).

He could have said, “We shall see him,” without adding “as he is.” But because he knew that certain fathers and prophets had seen him, though not as he is, after saying “we shall see him,” he added “as he is.”

Let no one deceive you, brothers, among those who say that the Father is invisible but the Son visible. Those who assert this think that he is a creature; they do not understand in what sense it was said, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

Certainly, in the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, the Son too is invisible. But in order to be seen by human beings, he took the form of a servant and was made in the likeness of human beings (Philippians 2:7), and thus became visible. Therefore, even before he [Col. 1780] assumed flesh, he showed himself to human eyes as he willed, in a creature subject to him—not as he is.

Let us cleanse our hearts through faith, so that we may be prepared for that ineffable and, so to speak, invisible vision. For “blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

13. Nevertheless, even among the rulers many believed in him; but because of the Pharisees they did not confess him, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue. For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God.

See how the Evangelist marked and censured certain people whom he nevertheless said had believed in him. If they advanced in this beginning of faith, then, as they progressed, they would also overcome the love of human glory—a love which the Apostle had overcome when he said, “But far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6:14).

For this reason the Lord himself also fixed his cross—where the madness of proud impiety mocked him—on the foreheads of those who believe in him, where the seat of shame is, in a sense, located, so that faith would not be ashamed of his name but would love the glory of God more than that of human beings.

### TREATISE LIV

From the passage where Jesus says, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me,” to, “The things that I speak, just as the Father said to me, so I speak.” Chapter 12, verses 44–50.

1. While our Lord Jesus Christ was speaking among the Jews and performing so many miraculous signs, some believed, predestined to eternal life, whom he also called his sheep. Others, however, did not believe and could not believe, because by the hidden yet not unjust judgment of God they had been blinded and hardened, as he abandoned them who resists the proud but gives grace to the humble (James 4:6).

Among those who believed, some confessed him so openly that, taking palm branches, they went out to meet him, rejoicing in that same confession of praise. Others, however, among the rulers did not dare to confess him, so that they would not be expelled from the synagogue. The Evangelist censured them, saying that they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God (John 12:43).

Among those who did not believe, some would later believe; he foresaw them when he said, “When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will know that I am he” (John 8:28). Others, however, would remain in the same unbelief. The Jewish people of the present day imitate these latter: later conquered, they were dispersed throughout almost the whole world as a testimony to the prophecy written concerning Christ.

2. With these things as they were, and his passion now approaching, Jesus cried out and said what today’s reading began with: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me; and whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.”

In another place he had already said, “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me” (John 7:16). There we understood him to have called his teaching the Word of the Father, which is himself. By saying, “My teaching is not mine but his who sent me,” he signified that he was not from himself but had the one from whom he was.

God from God, the Son from the Father; but the Father is not [Col. 1781] God from God, but God the Father of the Son.

Now, when he says, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me,” how are we to understand this except that he appeared as a human being to human beings while God remained hidden? And lest they think that he was only what they saw, he wished them to believe him to be such and so great as the Father is: “Whoever believes in me,” he says, “does not believe in me”—that is, in what he sees—but “in the one who sent me”—that is, in the Father.

But whoever believes in the Father must necessarily believe that he is the Father; and whoever believes that he is the Father must necessarily believe that he has a Son. Therefore whoever believes in the Father must necessarily believe in the Son.

But lest anyone suppose this about the only-begotten Son which is true of those who are called sons of God by grace rather than by nature, as the Evangelist says, “He gave them power to become sons of God” (John 1:12)—and as the Lord himself recalled that it was said in the Law, “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High” (John 10:34)—for this reason he said, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me,” lest everything believed concerning Christ be believed only according to his humanity.

Therefore, he says, the person believes in me who does not believe in me according to what he sees in me, but believes in the one who sent me. Thus, when he believes in the Father, he believes that the Father has a Son equal to himself, and then he truly believes in me.

For if he thinks that the Father has only sons according to grace—who are, of course, his creatures, made through the Word, not the Word himself—and does not believe that he has a Son equal and coeternal with him, eternally begotten, equally unchangeable, in no respect unlike or unequal to him, he does not believe in the Father who sent Christ, because this is not the Father who sent him.

3. Therefore, after saying, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me,” lest anyone think that the Father was to be understood as the Father of many sons regenerated by grace, rather than as the Father of the one Word equal to himself, he immediately added: “And whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.”

Did he say, “Whoever sees me does not see me but the one who sent me,” as he had said, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me”? He said the former so that he would not be believed to be merely the Son of Man, as he appeared. He said the latter so that he would be believed equal to the Father.

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “does not believe in what he sees in me, but believes in the one who sent me.” Or, when he believes in the Father who begot me equal to himself, let him believe in me not as he sees me, but as he believes in the one who sent me. For there is so little difference between him and me that whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.

The Lord Christ certainly sent his Apostles, as their name itself indicates. Just as in Greek angels are called *angeloi* and in Latin *nuntii* (“messengers”), so in Greek Apostles are called *apostoloi* and in Latin *missi* (“those who have been sent”).

Yet none of the Apostles would ever dare to say, “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me.” Indeed, he would not say, “Whoever believes in me” at all. We believe an apostle, but we do not believe in an apostle; for an apostle does not justify the ungodly. But the faith of the person who believes in the one who justifies the ungodly is reckoned as righteousness (Romans 4:5).

An apostle could say, “Whoever receives me receives the one who sent me,” or, “Whoever hears me hears the one who sent me.” For the Lord himself [Col. 1782] said to them, “Whoever receives you receives me, and whoever receives me receives the one who sent me” (Matthew 10:40). The lord is honored in the servant, and the father in the son—but the father as in a son, and the lord as in a servant.

The only-begotten Son, however, could rightly say, “Believe in God, and believe in me” (John 14:1), and what he says here: “Whoever believes in me does not believe in me but in the one who sent me.”

He did not withdraw faith in himself from the believer, but he did not wish the believer to remain in the form of a servant. For when someone believes in the Father who sent Christ, he certainly believes in the Son, without whom he recognizes that the Father does not exist; and he believes in such a way as to believe him equal, since it follows: “And whoever sees me sees the one who sent me.”

4. Attend to what follows: “I have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness.”

In one place he said to his disciples, “You are the light of the world. A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden, nor do they light a lamp and place it under a bushel, but on a lampstand, so that it may shine for everyone in the house. Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:14–16).

Yet he did not say to them, “You have come as light into the world, so that everyone who believes in you may not remain in darkness.” I affirm that this cannot be read anywhere.

All the saints, therefore, are lights; but by believing they are illuminated by him, and if anyone withdraws from him, that person becomes darkened. The light by which they are illuminated cannot withdraw from itself, because it is wholly unchangeable.

We believe the illuminated light—as we believe the prophets and the Apostle—but we believe them for this reason: not to believe in the illuminated one himself, but, together with him, to believe in the light by which he is illuminated, so that we too may be illuminated—not by him, but together with him, by the one who illuminates him.

When he says, “So that everyone who believes in me may not remain in darkness,” he plainly shows that he found everyone in darkness. But so that they may not remain in the darkness in which they were found, they ought to believe in the light that came into the world, because through it the world was made.

5. “And if anyone hears my words,” he says, “and does not keep them, I do not judge him.”

Remember what I know you heard in the preceding readings; and those of you who may have forgotten, recall it; and those who were not present before but are present now, hear how the Son says, “I do not judge him,” while elsewhere he says, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22).

This must be understood as, “I do not judge him now.” Why does he not judge now? Attend to what follows: “For I did not come,” he says, “to judge the world, but to save the world”—that is, to make the world safe. Now, therefore, is the time of mercy; afterward will be the time of judgment, because it is said, “I will sing of mercy and judgment to you, O Lord” (Psalm 100:1).

6. But concerning that final judgment still to come, see what he says: “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him: the word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day.”

He does not say, “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words, I do not judge him on the last day.” If he had said this, I do not see how it could fail to contradict the statement [Col. 1783] where he says, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.”

But when he says, “Whoever despises me and does not receive my words has one who judges him,” and those waiting to know who that judge might be hear him add, “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day,” he clearly shows that he himself will judge on the last day.

For he spoke himself; he announced himself; he established himself as the door through which he himself, as shepherd, would enter to the sheep. Those who did not hear will therefore be judged differently from those who heard and despised.

“For all who have sinned without the Law,” the Apostle says, “will also perish without the Law; and all who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Romans 2:12).

### 7

“For I,” he says, “have not spoken from myself.” He says that he did not speak from himself because he is not from himself. We have already said this many times; as something thoroughly familiar, we should now not teach it but recall it. “But the Father who sent me himself gave me a commandment—what I should say and what I should speak.”

We would not be laboring if we knew that we were speaking with those with whom we had spoken earlier—and even then, not with all of them, but with those who retain in memory what they heard. But now, because perhaps some are present who did not hear, and are like those who have forgotten what they heard, let those who remember what they heard bear patiently with our delays on their account.

How does the Father give a commandment to the only-begotten Son? By what word does he speak to the Word, when the Son himself is the only-begotten Word? Through an angel, perhaps, when the angels were created through him? Through a cloud, perhaps—which, when it sounded to the Son, did not sound for his sake, as he himself says elsewhere, but for the sake of others who needed to hear in that way? Through a sound emitted by the lips, perhaps—a sound which has no body, and from which the Son is not separated from the Father by any interval of space, so that air might lie between them, be struck, and produce a voice that would enter the ear? Far be it from us to imagine such things concerning that incorporeal and ineffable substance.

The only Son is the Word of the Father and the Wisdom of the Father; in him are all the Father’s commandments. For the Son did not at some point fail to know the Father’s commandment, so that he would have needed, at a particular time, to acquire what he had not possessed before. He received from the Father what he has in such a way that he received it by being born, and gave it to him by begetting him. For he is also life, and he received life by being born—not by previously existing without life. The Father too has life, and what he has, he is; yet he did not receive it, because he is not from another. The Son, however, received life from the Father, from whom he is; and he too is what he has. He has life, and he is life.

Hear him speaking: “Just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life in himself” (John 5:26). Did he give it to one who existed but did not have it? Rather, he gave it by begetting him—he who begot life, and begot life as life. And because he begot life equal, not unequal, it is therefore said: “Just as he himself has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself.” He gave life; for by begetting life, what did he give except to be life? And because that birth is eternal, the Son who is life was never not present; the Son was never without life. And just as his birth is eternal, so the one who was born is eternal life.

Thus the Father [Col. 1784] did not give the Son a commandment that the Son did not possess. Rather, as I said, in the Wisdom of the Father, which is the Word of the Father, all the Father’s commandments are present. It is said that a commandment was given because the one to whom it is said to be given is not from himself. And this is what it means to give to the Son, without whom the Son never existed: it is to beget the Son, who never did not exist.

### 8

Then he continues: “And I know that his commandment is eternal life.” If, therefore, the Son himself is eternal life, and the Father’s commandment is eternal life, what else is meant than: “I am the Father’s commandment”?

Accordingly, when he adds, “What I speak, I speak just as the Father told me,” we must not understand “he told me” as though the Father spoke words to the only Word, or as though God’s Word needed words from God. The Father spoke to the Son in the same way as he gave life to the Son—not something the Son did not know or possess, but something that the Son himself was.

What, then, is “Just as he told me, so I speak,” except “I speak truth”? He spoke as the truthful one; the Son speaks as the truth. The truthful one begot truth. What, then, would he say to the truth? The truth was not imperfect, so that something true might be added to it. He spoke to the truth because he begot the truth.

The truth itself, moreover, speaks just as it was told to speak—but to those who understand, whom it teaches as it was born. Yet, so that people might believe what they are not yet able to understand, words sounded from the mouth of flesh and passed away. The sounds resounded, flying across the brief intervals of their appointed times; but the realities signified by those sounds were, in a certain way, transferred into the memory of those who heard them, and through letters—which are visible signs—they have reached even us.

Truth does not speak in this way. It speaks inwardly to minds capable of understanding; without sound it instructs, and floods them with intelligible light. Whoever is able to see in it the eternity of its birth hears it speaking in the way the Father told it to speak.

He has awakened us to a great desire for its inward sweetness. But we grasp it by growing; we grow by walking; we walk by advancing, so that we may be able to arrive.

[Note: [Col. 1784] Two manuscripts have this reading; the others, as in the printed editions, read *verbum loquor* (“I speak the word”).]

[Note: [Col. 1784] So the manuscripts. Lovaniensis has *audire* (“to hear”); other printed editions have *credere* (“to believe”).]

[Note: [Col. 1784] The printed editions have *sed credendo capimus* (“but we grasp by believing”). The manuscripts have *sed crescendo* (“but by growing”); five of them have the optative form: *capiamus … crescamus … ambulemus* (“let us grasp … let us grow … let us walk”).]

# TREATISE 55

From the passage, “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come,” to the passage, “And he began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.” Chapter 13:1–5.

### 1

With the Lord’s help, the Lord’s supper according to John must be explained in appropriate treatises, and expounded insofar as he grants us the ability.

“Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end.”

Brothers, Passover is not, as some think, a Greek name, but a Hebrew one. Nevertheless, a very fitting correspondence between the two languages occurs in this name. Since “to suffer” is said in Greek as *paschein* (πάσχειν), Passover has therefore been taken to mean suffering, as though the name were derived from suffering. But in its own language—that is, in Hebrew—[Col. 1785] Passover means “passing over.” For this reason the people of God first celebrated Passover when, fleeing from Egypt, they crossed the Red Sea (Exodus 14:29).

Now that prophetic figure has been fulfilled in reality, when Christ is led like a sheep to be sacrificed (Isaiah 53:7). When our doorposts have been smeared with his blood—that is, when our foreheads have been marked with the sign of the cross—we are freed from the destruction of this age as from Egyptian captivity or slaughter (Exodus 12:23). We make a most saving passage when we pass from the devil to Christ, and from this unstable age to his firmly established kingdom.

For this reason we pass over to the God who endures, so that we may not pass away with the world that passes away. Praising God for this grace granted to us, the Apostle says: “He has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1:13).

This name, then—Passover—which in Latin, as I have said, is called “passing over,” is as though the blessed Evangelist were interpreting it for us when he says: “Before the feast of Passover, Jesus, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father.” Behold Passover; behold the passage. From where, and to where? From this world, certainly, to the Father.

Hope was given to the members in the head: as he passed over, they would undoubtedly follow him. What, then, of unbelievers, who are alienated from this head and from his body? Do they not also pass over, since they do not remain? They certainly pass over too. But it is one thing to pass from the world, and another to pass away with the world; one thing to pass to the Father, and another to pass to the enemy. The Egyptians also passed over; yet they did not pass through the sea to a kingdom, but in the sea to destruction.

### 2

“Jesus, therefore, knowing that his hour had come to pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them to the end.” This was so that they too might pass from this world, in which they were, to their head, who had passed from here, through his love.

What does “to the end” mean except “to Christ”? For “Christ is the end of the Law,” the Apostle says, “for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:4). He is the end that perfects, not the end that destroys; the end toward which we go, not the end at which we perish.

This must certainly be understood in the saying: “Christ, our Passover, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). He is our end; our passage is to him.

I see, however, that these Gospel words can also be understood in a human way, as though Christ loved his own until death, so that “he loved them to the end” would seem to mean this. This is a human interpretation, not a divine one. For he who loves us always and without end did not love us only up to this point. Far be it from us to suppose that he ended his love by dying, when he was not ended by death.

That proud and wicked rich man loved his five brothers even after his death (Luke 16:27–28); are we then to think that Christ loved us only until death? Far be it from us, beloved. He would not have come to death by loving us if he had ended his love by death.

Unless perhaps “he loved them to the end” is to be understood in this way: he loved them so greatly that he died for them. For he testified to this when he said: “No one has greater love than this, that someone should lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). In this sense, certainly, we do not prohibit understanding “he loved them to the end”: that is, love itself [Col. 1786] led him as far as death.

### 3

“And when supper had taken place,” he says, “when the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him—Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God, rose from supper, laid aside his garments; and, taking a towel, girded himself. Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.”

[Note: [Col. 1786] The manuscripts consistently read: “Judas, the son of Simon Scariot.”]

We must not understand “when supper had taken place” as though supper had already been completed and finished.

[Note: [Col. 1786] Thirteen manuscripts read: “already consumed and finished.”]

They were still dining when the Lord rose and washed his disciples’ feet. For afterward he reclined again and later gave the morsel to his betrayer—obviously while supper was not yet finished, that is, while bread was still on the table. Thus “when supper had taken place” means that it had been prepared and brought to the table and made available for the diners’ use.

### 4

As for the statement, “When the devil had already put it into the heart of Judas Iscariot, the son of Simon, to betray him,” if you ask what was put into Judas’s heart, it was certainly this: that he should betray him.

This putting is a spiritual suggestion. It does not occur through the ear but through thought; therefore it occurs not bodily but spiritually. Yet what is called spiritual is not always to be understood as praise. The Apostle knows of “spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places,” against which he testifies that we struggle (Ephesians 6:12). There would not be evil spiritual forces if there were not evil spirits. Spiritual things are named from the spirit.

But how these things happen—how demonic suggestions are introduced and mingled with human thoughts, so that a person regards them as his own—how does a person know? Nor should we doubt that good suggestions are likewise made secretly and spiritually by a good spirit. The question is which of them the human mind consents to, either abandoned by divine help because of its merits or assisted by grace.

Thus it had already happened in Judas’s heart, through a demonic intrusion, that the disciple would betray his teacher—though he had not learned that he was God. Such was the man who had come to the banquet: the Shepherd’s spy, the Savior’s ambusher, the Redeemer’s seller. Such he had come, and he was seen, tolerated, and imagined himself unknown, because he was deceived by the one whom he wished to deceive. But Christ, looking inwardly into that very heart, knowingly made use of him without his knowledge.

### 5

“Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands”—therefore, the betrayer also. For if he did not have him in his hands, he certainly could not use him as he wished.

Accordingly, the betrayer had already been handed over to the one whom he desired to betray. He was committing evil by betraying him, while from the one who was betrayed there would come a good of which he was unaware.

The Lord knew what he would do for his friends, since he patiently made use of his enemies. Thus the Father had given all things into his hands: both for the use of evil and for the accomplishment of good.

He also knew that he had come from God and was going to God—not abandoning God when he came from him, nor abandoning us when he returned.

### 6

Knowing these things, he rose from supper, laid aside his garments; and, taking a towel, girded himself. [Col. 1787] Then he poured water into a basin and began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded.

Beloved, we must carefully attend to the Evangelist’s meaning. Since he was about to speak of such great humility on the Lord’s part, he first wished to commend his greatness. This is the point of his saying: “Knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come from God and was going to God.”

When, therefore, the Father had given all things into his hands, he washed not the hands but the feet of his disciples. Although he knew that he had come from God and was going to God, he performed not the office of God and Lord but of a human servant.

This is also why he wished to mention beforehand the betrayer himself, who had already come in such a state, and who was not unknown to him: so that this too might contribute to the greatest accumulation of humility—that he did not disdain to wash even the feet of the man whose hands he already foresaw engaged in crime.

### 7

What wonder is it that he rose from supper and laid aside his garments, when, though he existed in the form of God, he emptied himself? What wonder is it that he girded himself with a towel, when, taking the form of a servant, he was found in appearance as a human being (Philippians 2:6–7)?

What wonder is it that he poured water into a basin to wash the disciples’ feet, when he poured out his blood upon the earth to cleanse the uncleanness of sinners? What wonder is it that with the towel with which he was girded he wiped the feet he had washed, when by the flesh with which he was clothed he confirmed the footsteps of the Evangelists?

To gird himself with the towel, he laid aside the garments he possessed. But when he took the form of a servant, emptying himself, he did not lay aside what he had; he took on what he did not have.

Certainly, when he was to be crucified, he was stripped of his garments; and when dead, he was wrapped in linen cloths. His entire passion is our cleansing.

About to undergo such sufferings, therefore, he first performed acts of service—not only for those for whom he was about to die, but also for the one who was going to betray him to death. Such is the usefulness of human humility that divine sublimity itself commended it by its example. For the proud human being would have perished forever unless the humble God had sought him out.

The Son of Man came “to seek and to save what was lost” (Luke 19:10). The human being had been lost by following the pride of the deceiver; having been found, let him therefore follow the humility of the Redeemer.

# TREATISE 56

From the passage, “Then he came to Simon Peter,” and so forth, to the passage, “The one who has been washed does not need anything except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.” Chapter 13:6–10.

### 1

As the Lord was washing the disciples’ feet, “he came to Simon Peter; and Peter said to him: Lord, are you washing my feet?” Who would not be terrified at having his feet washed by the Son of God?

Although it would have been a great act of boldness to contradict a servant’s Lord and a human being’s God, Peter preferred to do this rather than endure having his feet washed by the Lord and God.

We must not think that Peter alone among the others feared and refused this, since the others had willingly or calmly allowed it to be done to them before him. The Gospel’s words are more easily [Col. 1788] understood in this way: after it had been said, “He began to wash the disciples’ feet and to wipe them with the towel with which he was girded,” it is then added, “He came therefore to Simon Peter,” as though he had already washed some and had come afterward to the first.

For who does not know that blessed Peter was the first of the Apostles? Yet this should not be understood to mean that he came to Peter after some others, but that he began with him. When he began to wash the disciples’ feet, he came to the one with whom he began—that is, to Peter. Then Peter was terrified, as any of them would have been, and said: “Lord, are you washing my feet?”

What does “you” mean? What does “my” mean? These things ought rather to be contemplated than spoken, lest perhaps what the soul conceives as somehow worthy from these words the tongue should fail to express.

### 2

“But Jesus answered and said to him: What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand.”

Yet Peter, terrified by the greatness of the Lord’s action, does not allow what he does not know the reason for to be done. He still does not wish to see Christ humble himself even to his feet; he cannot bear it.

“You shall never wash my feet,” he says. What does “never” mean? I will never endure this, never suffer it, never permit it. For what never happens does not happen “forever.”

Then the Savior, frightening the sick man who resisted by warning him of the danger to his very salvation, said: “If I do not wash you, you have no share with me.”

He said, “If I do not wash you,” although only the feet were in question, just as one commonly says, “You are treading on me,” when only the sole is being trodden upon.

But Peter, disturbed by love and fear, and fearing Christ’s refusal more than Christ’s humbling himself to his feet, said: “Lord, not only my feet, but also my hands and my head.” Since you threaten me in this way, that my limbs must be washed, I not only do not withhold the lowest parts, but also offer the highest. Only do not deny me a share with you; I deny you no part of my body to wash.

### 3

“Jesus said to him: The one who has been washed does not need anything except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean.”

Here someone may perhaps be troubled and say: If he is entirely clean, what need does he have even to wash his feet? But the Lord knew what he was saying, even if our weakness does not penetrate his mysteries.

Nevertheless, insofar as he deigns to instruct us and teach us from his law, I too, according to my capacity and limited ability, will answer something about the depth of this question, with his help. First, I will very easily show that the wording itself is not contradictory.

Who could not speak entirely correctly by saying: “He is entirely clean, except for his feet”? It is more elegantly expressed if one says: “He is entirely clean, unless it be his feet”—which has the same meaning.

[Note: [Col. 1788] One manuscript reads: “whom he has only to wash.”]

This, then, is what the Lord says: “He does not need anything except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean”—entirely, that is, except for his feet, or unless it be his feet, which he needs to wash.

### 4

But what does this mean? What is its significance? Why is it necessary for us to investigate this?

[Note: [Col. 1788] The editions Erfurt, Lyons, Venice, Louvain, and M. read *quid hic* (“why is this necessary here?”).]

The Lord speaks; the truth speaks: even the one who has been washed needs to wash his feet. What do you think, my brothers? Why, except that in holy Baptism a human being is washed entirely—not excepting the feet, but wholly and altogether? Yet [Col. 1789] afterward, while living amid human affairs, he necessarily treads upon the earth. Yet afterward, while living amid human affairs, he necessarily treads upon the earth.

The human affections themselves, without which one cannot live in this mortality, are therefore like feet: they are where we are affected by human things. And we are affected in such a way that, if we say we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us (1 John 1:8).

Therefore he washes our feet daily—he who intercedes for us (Romans 8:34). And that we need to wash our feet daily, that is, to direct the paths of our spiritual steps, we confess in the Lord’s Prayer itself when we say: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

For if we confess our sins, as it is written, then surely the one who washed the feet of his disciples is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness (1 John 1:9)—that is, even to the feet with which we walk upon the earth.

### 5

Accordingly, the Church whom Christ cleanses “with the washing of water in the word” is without stain or wrinkle (Ephesians 5:26–27) not only in those who, after the washing of regeneration, are immediately taken away from the contagion of this life and do not tread upon the earth so as to need their feet washed. She is also without stain in those to whom the Lord, granting this mercy, has enabled them to depart from this world with even their feet washed.

But those who remain here, even if they are clean because they live justly, still need to wash their feet, because they are certainly not without sin.

For this reason she says in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song of Songs 5:3). She says this when she is compelled to come to Christ and, in coming, to tread upon the earth.

Another question arises. Is Christ not above? Did he not ascend into heaven and sit at the right hand of the Father? Does not the Apostle cry out and say: “If, therefore, you have been raised with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2)?

How, then, are we compelled to tread upon the earth in order to go to Christ, when our heart ought rather to be above with the Lord, so that we may be able to be with him?

You see, brothers, how the constraints of the present time press this question. Even if you perhaps see it less clearly, I perceive to some extent how much discussion it requires. Therefore I ask you to allow it to be postponed rather than treated either too carelessly or too narrowly—not with the expectation defrauded, but with its fulfillment deferred.

For the Lord will be present, the one who makes us debtors so that he may also make us repay what we owe.

# TREATISE 57

How the Church fears defiling her feet while she goes to Christ.

### 1

I have not forgotten my debt; I recognize that the time has come to repay it. May he grant me what I may repay, who granted that I should be in debt.

He granted love, concerning which it is said: “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (Romans 13:8). May he also grant the word, which I see that I owe to those whom I love.

I had postponed your expectation for this purpose: [Col. 1790] to explain, as I could, how one also comes to Christ through the earth, when we are rather commanded to seek the things that are above, not the things that are upon the earth (Colossians 3:1–2).

Christ is above, seated at the right hand of the Father; but he is certainly also here. For this reason he says to Saul, who was raging on earth: “Why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4).

To undertake this inquiry, we were considering the fact that the Lord washed the disciples’ feet when the disciples had already been washed and needed nothing except to wash their feet. It seemed that this should be understood as follows: in Baptism a human being is washed entirely; but while afterward living in this world, treading upon the earth with human affections as though with feet, he contracts something for which he says: “Forgive us our debts” (Matthew 6:12).

Thus he is also cleansed by the one who washed the feet of his disciples (John 13:5), and who does not cease to intercede for us (Romans 8:34).

At this point the words of the Church arose from the Song of Songs, where she says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” She wished to go and open to him who had come to her, knocked, and asked that it be opened to him—the one “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44:3).
