From this arose the question which we did not wish to confine within the narrow limits of time, and which we therefore postponed: how does the Church fear defiling the feet she had washed in Christ’s Baptism while she goes to Christ?

### 2

For she says:

> “I sleep, but my heart is awake; the voice of my beloved knocks at the door.”

Then he himself also says:

> “Open to me, my sister, my neighbor, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of night.”

And she answers:

> “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Song of Songs 5:2–3)

O wondrous sacrament! O great mystery! Does she, then, fear defiling her feet by coming to him who washed the feet of his disciples?

Certainly she fears, because she comes to him through the earth—he who is also on earth, since he does not abandon his own who are established here. Did he not himself say: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28:20)? Did he not himself say: “You will see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending to the Son of Man” (John 1:51)?

If they ascend to him because he is above, how do they descend to him unless he is also here?

The Church therefore says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” She says this in those who, cleansed from every impurity, are able to say: “I desire to depart and be with Christ, but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:23–24).

She says this in those who preach Christ and open the door to him, so that he may dwell through faith in human hearts (Ephesians 3:17). She says it in those who deliberate whether to accept such a ministry, considering themselves less capable of fulfilling it without fault, lest perhaps, while preaching to others, they themselves should become disqualified (1 Corinthians 9:27).

Truth is heard more safely than it is preached, because when it is heard, humility is preserved; but when it is preached, however little vainglory can scarcely fail to creep into any human being—and in that vainglory the feet are certainly defiled.

[Col. 1791]

### 3

Therefore, as the Apostle James says: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak” (James 1:19). Another man of God also says: “You will grant joy and gladness to my hearing, and the bones that have been humbled will rejoice” (Psalm 50:10).

This is what I said: when truth is heard, humility is preserved.

Another says: “The friend of the bridegroom stands and hears him, and rejoices with joy because of the bridegroom’s voice” (John 3:29).

Let us enjoy hearing, while truth speaks to us inwardly without noise. Yet even when it resounds outwardly through one who reads, announces, preaches, argues, instructs, consoles, exhorts, or even sings and chants, those who perform these actions should fear defiling their feet when, through an encroaching love of human praise, they seek to please people.

But the one who hears them willingly and devoutly has no opportunity to boast in another’s labors. His bones are not puffed up; rather, humbled, he rejoices with joy because of the voice of the Lord’s truth.

Accordingly, in those who know how to listen willingly and humbly, and who lead a quiet life in sweet and health-giving studies, let the holy Church delight and say: “I sleep, but my heart is awake.”

What does “I sleep, but my heart is awake” mean except: I rest in such a way that I hear? My leisure is not spent nourishing laziness but receiving wisdom.

“I sleep, but my heart is awake”: I am at leisure, and I see that you are the Lord (Psalm 45:1), because “the wisdom of the scribe comes in a time of leisure, and whoever is less occupied with activity will acquire it” (Ecclesiasticus 38:25).

“I sleep, but my heart is awake”: I rest from busy actions, and my mind directs itself toward divine affections.

[Note: [Col. 1791] Three manuscripts have *affatibus* (“utterances”) instead.]

### 4

But while the Church rests in this way, sweetly and humbly, and delights in leisure, behold, the one who says, “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matthew 10:27), knocks.

His voice therefore knocks at the door and says:

> “Open to me, my sister, my neighbor, my dove, my perfect one; for my head is filled with dew, and my locks with the drops of night.”

It is as though he were saying: You are at leisure, but the door is closed against me.

[Note: [Col. 1791] The manuscripts read: “and against me it is closed,” omitting the word “door.”]

You devote yourself to the leisure of a few, while, because iniquity abounds, the love of many grows cold (Matthew 24:12). Night is iniquity; its dew and drops are those who grow cold and fall, and cause Christ’s head—that is, God—not to be loved. For “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

But they are carried in the hair—that is, they are tolerated in visible sacraments; they do not at all reach the inner faculties of understanding.

He therefore knocks in order to shake the repose of the holy who are at leisure, and cries: “Open to me”—my sister, from my blood; my neighbor, from my coming near; my dove, from my Spirit; my perfect one, from my word, which you have learned more fully through leisure. Open to me; preach me.

For how shall I enter those who have closed themselves against me without someone opening? “How will they hear without someone preaching?” (Romans 10:14).

### 5

Thus it happens that even those who love the leisure of good studies and do not wish to endure the difficulties of laborious actions—because they feel themselves less capable of administering these things and carrying them out without blame—would, if it were possible, prefer that the holy Apostles and the ancient preachers of truth be raised up against the abundance of iniquity by which the fervor of love has grown cold.

But concerning those who have already departed from the body and have been stripped of the garment of flesh—though they have not been separated from it—the Church answers: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?”

That tunic will indeed be received again, and in those who have already been stripped of it, the Church will once more be clothed with flesh. But this will not happen now, when those who are cold must be made fervent; it will happen then, when the dead are to rise.

Having therefore suffered difficulty because of the scarcity of preachers, and recalling those members of hers who were sound in speech and holy in conduct but already stripped of their bodies, the holy Church groans and says: “I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on?”

Those members of mine who were able, with exceptional excellence, to open me to Christ by evangelizing—how can they now return to the bodies from which they have been stripped?

[Col. 1792]

### 6

Then, looking toward those who are able in some measure to preach, acquire and govern peoples, and thereby open to Christ, but who fear sinning amid the difficulties of these actions, she says: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?”

For whoever does not offend in speech is a perfect person. And who is perfect? Who does not offend amid such an abundance of iniquity and such a coldness of love?

“I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” For I read and hear: “Do not become many teachers, my brothers, since you will receive a stricter judgment; for we all offend in many things” (James 3:1–2).

“I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” Yet behold, I rise and open.

Christ, wash them. “Forgive us our debts,” because our love has not been extinguished; for we too forgive our debtors (Matthew 6:12).

When we hear you, the humbled bones rejoice with you in the heavenly places (Psalm 50:10). But when we preach you, we tread upon the earth in order to open to you. Therefore, if we are criticized, we are disturbed; if we are praised, we are inflamed.

Wash our feet, previously cleansed, but defiled as we go through the earth to open to you.

Beloved, let this suffice for you today. If perhaps, in saying something otherwise than we ought, we have offended, or if we have been lifted up by your praises more than was fitting, obtain cleansing for our feet through your prayers that please God.

# TREATISE 58

From the passage where the Lord says, “And you are clean, but not all,” to the passage, “I have given you an example, so that just as I have done for you, you also should do.” Chapter 13:10–15.

### 1

We have expounded to your Love, as the Lord has deigned to grant us, those words of the Gospel in which the Lord, washing the feet of his disciples, says: “The one who has been washed once has no need except to wash his feet, but is entirely clean” (John 13:10).

Now let us consider what follows: “And you are clean, but not all.” The Evangelist himself made clear what this means, adding: “For he knew who it was that would betray him; therefore I said, ‘You are not all clean.’”

What could be clearer? Let us therefore proceed to what follows.

### 2

“After he had washed their feet and taken his garments, when he had reclined again, he said to them: Do you know what I have done to you?”

Now it is time for that promise to blessed Peter to be fulfilled. It had been postponed when, terrified, he said, “You shall never wash my feet,” and received the answer: “What I am doing you do not know now, but afterward you will understand” (John 13:8, 7).

Behold that “afterward”; now it is time for what was postponed a little earlier to be stated.

The Lord remembered that he had long ago promised knowledge of his action—so unexpected, so extraordinary, and so terrifying that, unless he himself had strongly frightened Peter, Peter would in no way have allowed the teacher not only of the disciples but also of the angels, and the Lord not only of the disciples but of all things, to wash the feet of his disciples and servants.

Since, then, he had promised knowledge of this great action by saying, “You will understand afterward,” he now begins to teach what he did.

### 3

“‘You call me Teacher and Lord,’ he says, ‘and you speak rightly, for so I am.’ You speak rightly because you speak the truth; for I am what you say. Human beings have been commanded: ‘Let not your own mouth praise you, but let the mouth of your neighbor praise you’ (Prov. 27:2). For it is dangerous to please oneself when one must beware of becoming proud. But he who is above all things, however much he praises himself, does not exalt himself improperly in his loftiness; nor can God rightly be called arrogant. For it benefits us to know him, not him; and no one knows him unless he himself, who knows, makes himself known. If, then, by refusing to praise himself he wished to avoid the appearance of arrogance, he would deny us wisdom.

“No one would reproach him for saying that he is a teacher, even one who believed him to be nothing other than a human being, since he professes what human beings themselves profess without arrogance in every kind of art, so much so that they are called professors. But that he also calls himself the Lord of his disciples, although they are also freeborn according to worldly status—who could tolerate that in a human being? Yet God is speaking. Here there is no arrogance in such lofty eminence, no falsehood in the truth. It is useful for us to be subject to his eminence; it is useful for us to serve the truth. His saying that he is Lord is not a fault in him but a benefit to us.

“The words of a certain secular author are praised because he said, ‘Although every arrogance is hateful, that of talent and eloquence is by far the most offensive’ (Cicero, *Against Quintus Caecilius*); and yet the same man, when speaking of his own eloquence, said, ‘I would call it perfect if I judged it to be so; nor would I fear the charge of arrogance in speaking the truth’ (the same, *The Orator*). If, then, that most eloquent man did not fear arrogance in speaking the truth, how does the truth itself fear arrogance? Let him who is Lord say that he is Lord; let him who is truth speak the truth, lest I fail to learn what is useful while he keeps silent about what he is.

“The most blessed Paul—certainly not the only-begotten Son of God, but the servant and apostle of the only-begotten Son of God; not truth, but a participant in the truth—says freely and confidently, ‘And if I should wish to boast, I shall not be foolish; for I speak the truth’ (2 Cor. 12:6). For he would boast not in himself, but humbly and truthfully in the truth itself, which is above him [Col. 1794], since he himself also commanded that ‘whoever boasts should boast in the Lord’ (1 Cor. 1:31). Would a lover of wisdom not fear foolishness if he wished to boast, and would wisdom itself fear foolishness in its own praise? He who said, ‘In the Lord my soul shall be praised’ (Ps. 33:3), did not fear arrogance; and would the Lord’s power—in which the soul of his servant is praised—fear arrogance in its own praise?

“‘You call me Teacher and Lord,’ he says, ‘and you speak rightly, for so I am.’ You speak rightly because I am; for if I were not what you say, you would speak wrongly, even if you were praising me. How, then, could the truth deny what the disciples of truth say? How could the truth itself deny what those who have learned say? How could the fountain deny what the drinker proclaims? How could the light conceal what the one who sees indicates?”

### 4

“‘If, then,’ he says, ‘I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do.’”

This is what you did not know, blessed Peter, when you would not allow it to be done. This is what he promised you would know later, when your Teacher and Lord, washing your feet, terrified you into allowing it.

We have learned humility from the Exalted One, brothers; let us make ourselves humble toward one another, doing humbly what the Exalted One did. Great is this commendation of humility. Brothers do this to one another even in the visible action itself, when they receive one another as guests; for among many peoples there is a custom of this humility, expressed even in an act that can be seen. Hence, when the Apostle was commending a widow who had lived well, he said, “If she has received guests, if she has washed the feet of the saints” (1 Tim. 5:10).

And wherever this custom is not practiced among the saints, what they do not perform with their hands they do in their hearts, if they belong to the number of those addressed in the hymn of the three blessed young men: “Bless the Lord, saints and humble in heart” (Dan. 3:87). Yet it is much better, and without dispute truer, that it should also be done with the hands; nor should a Christian disdain to do what Christ did. For when the body is bent down to the feet of a brother, the affection of humility is either aroused in the heart itself or, if it was already present, strengthened.

### 5

But apart from this moral interpretation, we remember having commended the profundity of this deed of the Lord in this way: by washing the feet of disciples who had already been washed and cleansed, the Lord signified that, because of the human affections amid which we live on earth, no matter how far we may have advanced in grasping righteousness, we should know that we are not without sin. He subsequently washes this away by interceding for us when we pray to the Father who is in heaven that he forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors (Matt. 6:12).

How, then, can this interpretation apply to what he himself taught later, when he explained the reason for his action, saying: “If, then, I, the Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do”? Can we say that a brother can cleanse his brother from the contagion of sin? Rather, let us understand that in the profundity of this deed of the Lord we too have been admonished to confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, just as Christ intercedes for us (Rom. 8:34).

Let us hear the Apostle James most clearly commanding this very thing and saying, “Confess your sins to one another, and pray for one another” (James 5:16). For the Lord also gave us an example for this. If he who neither has, nor had, nor will have any sin prays for our sins, how much more ought we to pray for one another’s sins? And if he to whom we have nothing to forgive forgives us, how much more ought we to forgive one another, since we cannot live here without sin?

For what does the Lord seem to signify in this profundity of the sacrament when he says, “For I have given you an example, so that just as I have done to you, you also should do,” except what the Apostle says most openly: “Forgiving one another, if anyone has a complaint against another; just as the Lord forgave you, so you also should” (Col. 3:13)?

Let us therefore forgive one another’s sins and pray for one another’s sins, and thus in a certain manner wash one another’s feet. It is our task, by his gift, to offer the ministry of charity and humility; it is his task to hear us and to cleanse us from every contamination of sins through Christ and in Christ, so that what we forgive others—that is, what we loose on earth—may be loosed in heaven.

## TREATISE LIX

From the passage where the Lord says, “Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his lord,” to the passage, “But whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” Chapter 13, verses 16–20.

### 1

We heard the Lord speaking in the holy Gospel and saying: “Amen, amen, I say to you: a servant is not greater than his lord, nor an apostle greater than the one who sent him. If you know these things, blessed are you if you do them.” He said this because he had washed the disciples’ feet, the teacher of humility both in word and in example. With his help, however, we shall be able to discuss more fully what requires extended discussion, provided that we do not linger over what is clear.

When the Lord had prefaced these things, he added: “I do not speak of all of you: I know whom I have chosen. But let the Scripture be fulfilled: ‘He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me.’” What else does this mean except, “He will trample me”? It is known of whom he is speaking: that traitor Judas is being indicated. Therefore he had not chosen him among those whom he chose; by this statement he separates him from them.

What I say, then—“Blessed are you if you do these things”—I do not say of all of you: there is one among you who will not be blessed and will not do them. “I know whom I have chosen.” Whom, except those who will be blessed by doing what he commanded and showed should be done, he who is able to make them blessed? Judas the traitor, he says, was not chosen.

What, then, is the meaning of his saying elsewhere, “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil” (John 6:71)? Was he also chosen for some purpose, one for which he was certainly necessary, but not for the blessedness of which he now says, “You will be blessed if you do these things”? He does not say this of all of them, for he knows whom he has chosen for fellowship in this blessedness [Col. 1796]. This man is not among those who ate his bread in such a way as to lift up his heel against him. They ate the Lord’s bread; he ate the bread of the Lord against the Lord. They ate life; he ate punishment. “For whoever eats unworthily,” the Apostle says, “eats judgment for himself” (1 Cor. 11:29).

“From now on,” he says, “I tell you before it happens, so that when it happens you may believe that I am”—that is, that I am the one concerning whom that Scripture went before, where it was said, “He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me.”

### 2

Then he continues and says: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

Did he intend it to be understood that the distinction between the one whom he sends and himself is as great as that between himself and God the Father? If we accept this in that manner, we shall construct—God forbid—certain gradations in the manner of the Arians. For when they hear or read these Gospel words, they immediately run to those gradations of their doctrine, by which they do not ascend to life but are hurled headlong into death.

They immediately say: Just as the apostle of the Son differs from the Son, although he said, “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me,” so the Son differs from the Father, although he said, “Whoever receives me receives him who sent me.”

But if you say this, heretic, you have forgotten your own gradations. If, because of these words of the Lord, you distinguish the Son from the Father by as great an interval as you distinguish the apostle from the Son, where will you place the Holy Spirit? Have you forgotten that you usually place him after the Son? He will therefore stand between the apostle and the Son, and the Son will be separated from the apostle by a much greater interval than the Father is from the Son.

Or perhaps, so that this distinction may remain at equal intervals between the Son and the apostle and between the Father and the Son, the Holy Spirit will be equal to the Son? But you do not want this either. Where, then, will you place him, if you subordinate the apostle to the Son by a distinction as great as that between the Son and the Father?

Restrain, then, the audacity of your presumption, and do not seek in these words a distance between Father and Son as great as that between Son and apostle. Rather, hear the Son himself saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Here the truth has left you no suspicion of distance between the Begetter and the Only-Begotten; here Christ has shattered your gradations, and the Rock has broken your ladders.

### 3

But once the calumny of the heretics has been refuted, how are we to receive these words of the Lord: “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me”?

If we wish to understand the statement “Whoever receives me receives him who sent me” as meaning that the Father and the Son are of one nature, it will seem to follow, by the same rule of the words in which it was said, “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me,” that the Son and the apostle are of one nature.

This too could indeed be understood without impropriety, since he is the twofold-natured giant who rejoiced to run his course (Ps. 18:6). For “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14), that is, God became man. Accordingly, he could seem to have said: “Whoever receives anyone whom I send receives me according to my humanity; but whoever receives me according to my divinity [Col. 1797] receives him who sent me.”

Yet when he said these things, it was not the unity of nature that he was commending, but the authority of the one who sends in the one who is sent. Thus each person should receive the one who has been sent in such a way that in him he attends to the one who sent him.

If, then, you attend to Christ in Peter, you will find the Teacher of the disciple; but if you attend to the Father in the Son, you will find the Begetter of the Only-Begotten. Thus, in the one who has been sent, you receive the one who sends without any error.

The things that follow in the Gospel must not be compressed by the shortness of time. And therefore, dearest brothers, let this discourse be received beneficially as food for holy sheep: if it is sufficient, let it be taken as nourishment; if it is scant, let it be ruminated upon with desire.

## TREATISE LX

On the passage, “When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit.” Chapter 13, verse 21.

### 1

A question of no small importance is presented to us, brothers, from the Gospel of blessed John, where he says: “When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit, and testified and said: ‘Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.’”

Was Jesus troubled for this reason—not in the flesh but in spirit—because he was about to say, “One of you will betray me”? Did this thought come to him for the first time then, or was it only then suddenly revealed to him, so that the sudden novelty of so great an evil troubled him? Had he not shortly before been speaking of this very thing, saying, “He who eats bread with me will lift up his heel against me”? Had he not also said earlier, “And you are clean, but not all”? There the Evangelist added, “For he knew who would betray him” (John 13:18, 10–11). Had he not already indicated him by saying, “Did I not choose you twelve, and one of you is a devil” (John 6:71)?

What, then, is the meaning of his now being troubled in spirit when he testified and said, “Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me”? Was he troubled because he was now about to identify him explicitly, so that he would no longer remain hidden among the others but would be distinguished from them? Or because the traitor was now about to leave, in order to bring the Jews—to whom the Lord would be handed over by him—and thus the approaching Passion, the imminent danger, and the traitor’s impending hand, whose intention he had foreknown, troubled him?

For this is like the statement, “Jesus was troubled in spirit,” as is also that which he said: “Now my soul is troubled; and what shall I say? Father, save me from this hour. But for this reason I came to this hour” (John 12:27). Just as his soul was then troubled as the hour of the Passion approached, so now, when Judas was about to depart, and the great crime of the traitor was approaching, he was troubled in spirit.

### 2

Jesus was therefore troubled, although he had power to lay down his life and power to take it up again (John 10:18). Such immense power is troubled; the firmness of the Rock is troubled. Or rather, is it not our weakness that is troubled in him? Indeed it is. Let servants believe nothing unworthy of their Lord, but recognize themselves as members in their Head.

The one who died for us was himself troubled for us. Therefore, the one who died by his power was troubled by his power. He who transformed the body of our humiliation to conform to the body of his glory (Phil. 3:21) also transformed in himself the feeling of our weakness, sympathizing with us through the feeling of his soul.

Therefore, when the great, strong, steadfast, invincible one is troubled, let us not fear as though he were failing. He does not perish; he seeks us. Us, I say—he seeks us altogether in this way. Let us see ourselves in his disturbance, so that when we are troubled we may not perish in despair. When he is troubled who would not be troubled unless he willed it, he consoles the one who is troubled unwillingly.

### 3

Let the arguments of the philosophers perish—those who deny that disturbances of the soul can befall the wise. “God has made foolish the wisdom of this world” (1 Cor. 1:20), and “the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are futile” (Ps. 94:11).

Let the Christian soul indeed be troubled—not by misery but by mercy. Let it fear that human beings may perish apart from Christ; let it grieve when someone perishes apart from Christ; let it desire that human beings be gained for Christ; let it rejoice when human beings are gained for Christ. Let it fear for itself, lest it perish apart from Christ; let it grieve that it is a stranger to Christ; let it desire to reign with Christ; let it rejoice while it hopes that it will reign with Christ.

These are certainly the four disturbances that they call by those names: fear and sadness, love and joy. Let Christian souls possess them for just reasons, and let us not assent to the error of the Stoic philosophers or of any similar people. They regard vanity as truth, and thus regard insensibility as health, ignorant that the soul of a human being, like a bodily limb, is more dangerously ill when it has also lost the sensation of pain.

### 4

But someone may say: Should the Christian soul also be troubled when death is imminent? For where is the Apostle’s statement that he desires to depart and be with Christ (Phil. 1:23), if what he desires can trouble him when it comes?

It is easy for those who call joy itself a disturbance to answer these questions. What if he is troubled by the imminence of death precisely because he rejoices in the imminence of death? But they say that this should be called gladness, not joy. What is this except to experience the same realities while wishing to change their names?

But let us attune our hearing to the sacred Scriptures, and with the Lord’s help resolve this question according to them. Since it is written, “When Jesus had said these things, he was troubled in spirit,” let us not say that he was troubled with joy, lest he himself convict us by his words when he says, “My soul is sorrowful even to death” (Matt. 26:38).

Something of this sort must also be understood here, when Jesus was troubled in spirit because his betrayer was then about to depart alone and shortly return with his companions.

### 5

There are indeed very steadfast Christians, if there are any, who are not at all troubled when death is imminent. But are they more steadfast than Christ? Who would say such a thing except the utterly insane?

What, then, is the meaning of his being troubled, except that he consoled the weak in his body—that is, in his Church—by the voluntary likeness of his own weakness? Thus, if any of his people are still troubled in spirit when death is imminent [Col. 1799], they may look to him, lest, thinking themselves rejected for this very reason, they be swallowed up by the worse death of despair.

How great a good, then, ought we to expect and hope for from participation in his divinity, whose disturbance tranquillizes us and whose weakness strengthens us?

Whether, therefore, he was troubled in pity for Judas as he perished, or troubled because his own death was approaching, there is nevertheless no doubt that he was troubled not by weakness of soul but by power, lest despair of salvation arise in us when we are troubled not by power but by weakness.

He bore the weakness of the flesh, and that weakness was consumed by the resurrection. But because he was not only human but also God, he surpassed the whole human race by an ineffable distance in strength of soul. He was not therefore troubled because something compelled him, but he troubled himself. This was clearly shown when he raised Lazarus, for it is written there that he troubled himself (John 11:33). Thus this should also be understood where it is not written, although he is read to have been troubled.

For when he judged it appropriate, he stirred human feeling in himself by his power—he who by his power took up the whole human being.

## TREATISE LXI

From the passage where the Lord says, “Amen, amen, I say to you: one of you will betray me,” to the passage, “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped morsel.” Chapter 13, verses 21–26.

### 1

This passage of the Gospel has been set before us for exposition in this reading, brothers, so that we must now also say something about the Lord’s betrayer, who is clearly identified by the dipped morsel that was given to him.

I discussed him in the preceding discourse, when Jesus was troubled in spirit because he was about to identify him. But perhaps the Lord was also graciously signifying to us by his disturbance what I did not say there: namely, that false brothers, the weeds of the Lord’s field, must necessarily be tolerated among the wheat until the time of the harvest (Matt. 13:29–30), in such a way that whenever an urgent cause compels some of them to be separated even before the harvest, it cannot happen without disturbance to the Church.

Foretelling in a certain manner the disturbance that would come upon his saints through schismatics and heretics, the Lord prefigured it in himself. When Judas, an evil man, was about to depart, leaving behind in a completely open separation the mingling with the wheat in which he had long been tolerated, the Lord was troubled not in the flesh but in spirit. For his spiritual people are troubled by such scandals not through perversity but through charity, lest in the separation of some weeds some wheat also be uprooted.

### 2

Jesus was therefore troubled in spirit, and testified and said: “Amen, amen, I say to you, one of you will betray me.”

“One of you”—in number, not in merit; in appearance, not in virtue; by bodily association, not by spiritual bond; by attachment of flesh, not by unity of heart. Therefore, not one who is truly from you, but one who is going to depart from you.

For how would what the Lord testified and said be true—“One of you”—if what he himself says in his Epistle, whose author is also the author of this Gospel, is true [Col. 1800]: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us” (1 John 2:19)?

Judas was therefore not truly of them; for he would have remained with them if he had been of them. What, then, does “One of you will betray me” mean except, “One who will depart from you will betray me”? For the one who said, “If they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us,” had already said, “They went out from us.”

Thus both statements are true: he was from them and he was not from them—according to one aspect, from them; according to another, not from them. He was from them according to communion in the sacraments; he was not from them according to the distinct character of his crimes.

### 3

The disciples therefore looked at one another, uncertain about whom he was speaking. Such pious love toward their Teacher existed among them, yet human weakness stirred each one against the others. Each person’s conscience was known to himself, but because the conscience of his neighbor was unknown, each was certain about himself while all were uncertain about the others, and the others uncertain about each individual.

### 4

“One of his disciples was reclining at the breast of Jesus, whom Jesus loved.”

What he meant by “at his breast” he says shortly afterward, when he says “upon the breast of Jesus.” This was John, whose Gospel this is, as he later makes clear (John 21:20–24).

It was the custom of those who supplied the sacred Scriptures to us that, whenever one of them was narrating divine history and came to himself, he would speak as though of another person and insert himself into the order of his narrative as a writer of events, not as a promoter of himself.

The blessed Matthew did this as well. When he came to himself in the text of his narrative, he said: “He saw a certain tax collector sitting at the tax booth, named Matthew, and he said to him, ‘Follow me’” (Matt. 9:9). He did not say, “He saw me and said to me.”

Blessed Moses did the same: he narrated everything about himself as though about another person and said, “The Lord spoke to Moses” (Exod. 6:1). The Apostle Paul did this in a more unusual way—not in history, where the narrative of events is to be unfolded, but in an Epistle. For he says of himself: “I know a man in Christ fourteen years ago—whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows—such a one was caught up to the third heaven” (2 Cor. 12:2).

Accordingly, when the blessed Evangelist here also does not say, “I was reclining at the breast of Jesus,” but says, “One of the disciples was reclining,” let us recognize rather than wonder at the custom of our authors. For what is lost to the truth when the fact itself is stated while boasting is avoided by a certain manner of speaking? He was narrating what contributed greatly to his praise.

### 5

But what does “whom Jesus loved” mean? As though he did not love the others, concerning whom this same John said earlier, “He loved them to the end” (John 13:1). And the Lord himself said, “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

Who could enumerate all the testimonies of the divine books by which the Lord Jesus is shown to be the lover not only of that man or of those who existed at that time, but also of the members who would come afterward [Col. 1801] and of his whole Church?

But surely something is hidden here, and it concerns the breast at which the one who said these things was reclining. For what else is signified by the breast than a secret? But another place will be more suitable, where the Lord may grant us to say something about this secret, as much as is sufficient.

### 6

“Simon Peter therefore motioned to him and said to him.”

This expression should be noted: something is said not by speaking aloud but merely by making a sign. “He motioned,” it says, “and said”—that is, he spoke by making a sign. If something can be said by thinking, as Scripture says, “They said among themselves” (Wisdom 2:1), how much more can it be said by making a sign, when what had been conceived in the heart is already expressed outwardly by whatever signs?

What, then, did he say by making a sign? Nothing other than what follows: “Who is it about whom he speaks?” Peter indicated these words because he spoke not by the sound of his voice but by a movement of his body.

“Therefore, when he had reclined upon the breast of Jesus”—this is certainly the breast’s secret place, the hidden wisdom. He says to him, “Lord, who is it?”

Jesus answered: “It is the one to whom I shall give the dipped morsel.” And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot. And after the morsel, Satan entered into him.

The betrayer was identified; the hiding places of darkness were exposed. What he received was good, but he received it to his own harm, because the evil man received the good evilly.

But concerning this dipped morsel that was given to the pretended friend, and concerning the things that follow, much remains to be said. They require more time than we now have at the end of this discourse.

## TREATISE LXII

From the passage written, “And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas,” to the passage, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” Chapter 13, verses 26–31.

### 1

I know, dearest brothers, that some may be troubled by this—pious people in seeking an explanation, or impious people in finding fault—that after the Lord gave the dipped bread to his betrayer, Satan entered into him.

For it is written: “And when he had dipped the bread, he gave it to Judas, son of Simon Iscariot; and after the morsel Satan entered into him.” They say: Did the bread of Christ, handed from the table of Christ, deserve this—that after it Satan should enter his disciple?

We answer that by this we are taught rather how greatly we must beware of receiving a good thing wrongly. For it matters greatly not what someone receives but who receives it; and not what sort of thing is given but what sort of person the recipient is. Good things harm, and bad things benefit, according to those to whom they are given.

“Sin,” says the Apostle, “so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good” (Rom. 7:13). Behold: through a good thing evil was produced, when the good was received wrongly.

He also says: “So that I might not become exalted because of the abundance of revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan to buffet me. For this I pleaded with the Lord three times, that he might take it away from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (2 Cor. 12:7–9). Behold: through an evil thing good was produced, when the evil was received rightly.

Why, then, are you surprised if the bread of Christ was given to Judas, through which he would be handed over to the devil, when you see, conversely, that an angel of the devil was given to Paul, through whom he would be perfected in Christ? Thus the good harmed the evil man, and the evil benefited the good man.

Remember where it is written: “Whoever eats the bread or drinks the cup of the Lord unworthily will be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. 11:27). The Apostle was speaking about those people when he said this: they were indiscriminately and carelessly taking the Lord’s body as though it were any other food.

If, then, the person who does not judge—that is, does not distinguish the Lord’s body from other foods—is reproved, how is [Note: [Col. 1802] Thus all the manuscripts. But the printed editions read, “how is not condemned.”] the one who approaches his table as an enemy while pretending to be a friend not condemned? If the negligence of a diner is touched by reproach, with what punishment is the seller of the one who invites struck?

What else was the bread given to the betrayer except a demonstration of the grace toward which he had been ungrateful?

### 2

After this bread, then, Satan entered the Lord’s betrayer, so that he might possess more fully the one who had now been handed over to him—he who had earlier entered him in order to deceive him.

For Satan was certainly already in him when he went to the Jews and agreed upon the price for handing over the Lord, as the Evangelist Luke openly testifies when he says: “Satan entered into Judas, who was called Iscariot, one of the twelve; and he went away and spoke with the chief priests” (Luke 22:3–4).

There it is shown that Satan had already entered Judas. He had entered earlier by putting into his heart the thought of betraying Christ; for such was the man who had already come to dine. But now, after the bread, he entered him not in order to tempt one who was still alien, but in order to possess one who was his own.

### 3

Some careless readers think that Judas then received Christ’s body. But it must be understood that the Lord had already distributed the sacrament of his body and blood to all of them, and Judas was among them, as blessed Luke most clearly narrates (ibid., 19–21).

Then the narrative reached the point where, according to John’s account, the Lord most openly identifies his betrayer by the dipped and offered morsel, perhaps signifying by the dipping of the bread his deceitfulness.

For not everything that is dipped is washed; some things are dipped so that they may be stained.

[Note: [Col. 1802] Most manuscripts read *factionem* (“faction”); this is less suitable, as is clear from Treatise 61, section 6.]

But if the dipping signifies something good here, the condemnation that followed was not undeserved for one ungrateful toward that good.

### 4

Although Judas was now possessed—not by the Lord but by the devil—when the bread entered the ungrateful man’s stomach and the enemy entered his mind, the outcome of so great an evil still remained to be carried out. The condemned intention had already preceded it.

Therefore, when the Lord, the living bread, had handed bread to the dead man, and by handing over the bread had identified the betrayer of the bread, he said: “What you are doing, do quickly.”

He did not command the crime; he foretold Judas’s evil and our good. For what was worse for Judas, and what was better for us, than Christ being handed over—by him, against him, and for us, apart from him?

“What you are doing, do quickly.” O word of one more ready than angry! O word expressing not so much the punishment of the betrayer [Col. 1803] as the reward of the Redeemer!

For he said, “What you are doing, do quickly,” not so much by raging against the destruction of the faithless man as by hastening the salvation of the faithful, because Christ “was handed over for our offenses” (Rom. 4:25), and “loved the Church and handed himself over for it” (Eph. 5:25). Hence the Apostle also says of himself: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20).

Unless Christ handed himself over, no one would hand over Christ. What does Judas have except sin? For in handing over Christ he did not consider our salvation, for the sake of which Christ was handed over; he considered the profit of money and found the loss of his soul.

He received the payment he wanted, but against his will he was given the payment he deserved. Judas handed over Christ; Christ handed himself over. The one was conducting the business of his own sale; the other, that of our redemption.

“What you are doing, do quickly”—not because you have the power, but because the one who has power over all wills this.

### 5

None of those reclining at table knew why he had said this to him. Some thought that, because Judas kept the money box, Jesus was telling him, “Buy what we need for the feast,” or to give something to the poor.

The Lord therefore also had a money box, preserving what had been offered by the faithful and distributing it both for the needs of his own people and to other needy persons. Thus the first form of ecclesiastical funds was established. We understand from this that the command not to think about tomorrow (Matt. 6:34) was not given so that the saints should keep no money, but so that they should not serve God for the sake of money or abandon righteousness through fear of poverty.

For the Apostle too, making provision for the future, says: “If any believer has widows, let him provide sufficiently for them, so that the Church may not be burdened and may be able to provide sufficiently for those who are truly widows” (1 Tim. 5:16).

### 6

When he had received the morsel, he went out immediately. And it was night. The one who went out was himself night.

When the night had gone out, Jesus said: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.”

Day therefore poured forth speech for day—that is, Christ for his faithful disciples, so that they might hear him and love him by following him. And night announced knowledge to night (Ps. 18:3)—that is, Judas to the unfaithful Jews, so that they might come to him and seize him in persecution.

But from this point the listener is summoned to greater attention for the Lord’s discourse, which he delivered to the devout before he was seized by the impious. Therefore the speaker must not rush ahead, but should rather defer the discussion.

## TREATISE LXIII

On the passage where the Lord says, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” to the passage, “And immediately he will glorify him.” Chapter 13, verses 31–32.

1. Let us direct the gaze of our mind and, with the Lord’s help, seek God. The voice of the divine song says, “Seek God, and your soul shall live” (Ps. 68:33). Let us seek him in order to find him; let us seek him once found. In order that he may be sought, he is hidden; in order that, once found, he may still be sought, he is boundless. Hence elsewhere it is said, “Seek his face always” (Ps. 104:4). For he satisfies the seeker insofar as the seeker can receive, and makes the finder more capacious so that he may again seek to be filled [Note: [Col. 1803] Thus several manuscripts. But the printed editions have implere, “to fill.”], once he has begun to receive more [Col. 1804]. Therefore the words “Seek his face always” were not spoken in the same sense as the words concerning certain people: “Always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth” (2 Tim. 3:7). Rather, they were spoken as that man says: “When a person has finished, then he begins” (Ecclus. 18:6). Let us continue until we come to that life where we shall be so filled that we cannot become more capacious, because we shall be so perfect that we shall no longer progress. Then what is sufficient for us will be shown to us.

Here, however, let us always seek, and let the fruit of discovery not be the end of the search. For we shall not be seeking always merely because we seek only here; rather, we say that here we must always seek, lest we ever suppose that here the search should cease. For those of whom it is said, “Always learning and never arriving at a knowledge of the truth,” are indeed always learning here; but when they have departed this life, they will no longer be learning, but receiving the reward of their error. For it is as though it had been said: “Always walking and never arriving at the way.” Let us, however, always walk in the way until we come to where the way leads. Let us nowhere remain in it until it brings us to the place where we shall remain. Thus, by seeking we press forward; by finding we arrive at something; and by seeking and finding we pass on to what remains, until the search itself comes to an end where no desire for further progress remains in perfection.

May this introduction, dearly beloved, have made Your Charity attentive to this discourse of the Lord, which he delivered to his disciples before his passion. For it is profound, and wherever the speaker will labor greatly, the listener ought not to be inattentive.

2. What, then, did the Lord say after Judas went out, so that he might more quickly do what he was going to do—that is, betray the Lord? What did the day say when the night had gone out? What did the Redeemer say when the seller had gone out? “Now,” he said, “the Son of Man has been glorified.”

Why now? Was it because the betrayer had gone out, because those who would seize and kill him were close at hand? Is he now glorified because he is about to be humbled still further—because he is soon to be bound, judged, condemned, mocked, crucified, and killed? Is this glorification, or rather humiliation? Yet did not this same John say of him, when he was performing miracles, “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39)? He was not yet glorified, then, when he raised the dead; and now he is glorified when he approaches the dead? He was not yet glorified while doing divine works, and he is glorified when he is about to suffer human things? It would be strange if that divine Teacher meant and taught this by these words.

The saying of the Most High must be examined more deeply. He reveals himself somewhat so that we may find him, and again conceals himself so that we may search for him; and from what we have found, he gives us something like steps by which to lean toward what remains to be found. Here I see something that foreshadows a great reality. Judas went out, and Jesus was glorified; the son of perdition went out, and the Son of Man was glorified.

For he had gone out concerning whom it had been said to them, “And you are clean, but not all” (John 13:10). When the unclean man had gone out, therefore, all who remained were clean, and they remained with their purifier [Col. 1805]. Something similar will occur when this world, conquered by Christ, has passed away, and no one among Christ’s people will remain unclean; when the weeds have been separated from the wheat, “the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

Foreseeing what was to happen, and testifying that it was now signified, the Lord—when Judas departed like weeds separated from the wheat, while the holy apostles remained like wheat—said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” It was as though he said: “Behold what will occur in that glorification of mine, where no evil person will remain and no good person will perish.”

It was not said, “The glorification of the Son of Man has now been signified,” but, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified.” Likewise, it was not said, “The rock signified Christ,” but, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4). Nor was it said, “The good seed signified the sons of the kingdom,” or, “The weeds signified the sons of the evil one,” but, “The good seed—these are the sons of the kingdom; the weeds are the sons of the evil one” (Matt. 13:38). Thus, as Scripture customarily speaks, calling the things that signify by the names of the things signified, the Lord said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified”: after the most wicked man had been separated from them, while the holy remained with him, his glorification was signified—the time when, after the wicked have been separated, he will remain with the holy in eternity.

3. When he had said, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified,” he added, “And God has been glorified in him.” For this is the glorification of the Son of Man: that God may be glorified in him. If it is not he himself who is glorified in himself, but God who is glorified in him, then God glorifies him in himself.

Finally, explaining this, he adds and says: “If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself.” That is: If God has been glorified in him because he did not come to do his own will, but the will of the one who sent him, “God will also glorify him in himself,” so that the human nature in which he is the Son of Man, which was assumed by the eternal Word, may also be granted immortal eternity.

“And immediately,” he says, “he will glorify him.” By this testimony he foretold his resurrection, which was to occur immediately—not like ours at the end of the world. This is the glorification of which the Evangelist had already spoken, as I mentioned shortly before: the Spirit had not yet been given to them in that new manner in which he was to be given to those who would believe after the resurrection, because Jesus had not yet been glorified. That is, mortality had not yet been clothed with immortality, and temporal weakness had not yet been changed into eternal strength [Note: [Col. 1805] Most manuscripts omit “and temporal weakness had been changed into eternal strength.”].

The words “Now the Son of Man has been glorified” may also be understood as referring to this glorification, so that the “now” is believed to refer not to the imminent passion but to the resurrection that was near at hand—as though what was so soon to happen had already happened.

Today these things will be sufficient for Your Love. When the Lord grants it, we shall discuss what follows.

TRACTATE LXIV. On the passage in which the Lord says, “Little children, I am with you only a little longer; you will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you.” Chapter 13, verses 33.

[Col. 1805]

[Col. 1806] 1. Beloved, we must observe the ordered connection of the Lord’s words. For after he had said above, once Judas had gone out and had been separated even from the bodily fellowship of the saints, “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him”—whether he said this signifying the future kingdom, when the wicked will be separated from the good, or because his resurrection was then to occur, that is, was not to be postponed as ours is postponed until the end of the world—and after he had added, “If God has been glorified in him, God will also glorify him in himself, and he will glorify him immediately,” testifying without any ambiguity that his resurrection was to occur immediately, he added and said, “Little children, I am with you only a little longer.”

He did not want them to suppose that God would glorify him in such a way that he would no longer be joined to them in the fellowship by which he is on earth. “I am with you only a little longer,” he said—as though he were saying: “I shall indeed be glorified immediately by the resurrection; nevertheless, I shall not immediately ascend into heaven, but I am with you only a little longer.”

For, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, after his resurrection he spent forty days with them, coming and going, eating and drinking (Acts 1:3). He did not have the need to hunger or thirst, but by these actions he continued to establish the reality of his flesh, which no longer had the necessity of eating and drinking, but did have the power to do so.

Did he signify these forty days when he said, “I am with you only a little longer,” or something else? The words can also be understood in this way: “I am with you only a little longer; I too am still, like you, in this weakness of the flesh”—that is, until he should die and rise again. For after he had risen, he was indeed with them for the forty days mentioned, by the manifestation of bodily presence; but he was no longer with them in the fellowship of human weakness.

2. There is also another divine presence unknown to mortal senses, concerning which he likewise says, “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20). Certainly this is not what is meant by “I am with you only a little longer,” for the period until the consummation of the age is not short.

Or, if this too is short—for time flies, and in God’s sight a thousand years are like one day, or like a watch in the night (Ps. 89:4)—nevertheless we should not think that he wished to signify this here, since he immediately adds, “You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come.’”

Certainly, after this short time during which I am with you, “you will seek me, and where I am going, you cannot come.” Will they be unable to come after the consummation of the age to where he is going? And what of the statement he will make somewhat later in this same discourse: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:24)?

Therefore, when he says, “I am with you only a little longer,” he is not speaking of that presence of his with his own by which he is with them until the consummation of the age. He is speaking either of the mortal weakness by which he was with them until his passion, or of the bodily presence by which [Col. 1807] he was to be with them until his ascension. Whichever of these one chooses, one does not contend against the faith.

3. So that no one may think this interpretation contrary to the truth—namely, that by saying, “I am with you only a little longer,” the Lord could have signified his sharing of mortal flesh, in which he was with the disciples until his passion—let him consider his words in another Evangelist after the resurrection, where he says, “These are my words that I spoke to you while I was still with you” (Luke 24:44). He was surely then present with them as they stood before him, saw him, touched him, and spoke with him.

What, then, does “while I was still with you” mean, unless “while I was still in mortal flesh, in which you also are”? At that time he had indeed been raised in the same flesh; but he was no longer with them in the same mortality.

Therefore, just as there he truly said, though already clothed in the immortality of the flesh, “while I was still with you,” where we can understand nothing other than “while I was still with you in the mortality of the flesh,” so here he can reasonably be understood to have said, “I am with you only a little longer,” as though he were saying: “For only a little longer I am mortal, as you are.” Let us therefore examine what follows.

4. “You will seek me, and as I said to the Jews, ‘Where I am going, you cannot come,’ so now I say to you.” That is, “You cannot come now.” When he said this to the Jews, he did not add “now.” They therefore could not then come where he was going, but they could afterward; for shortly afterward he said this most clearly to the apostle Peter.

When Peter had said, “Lord, where are you going?” he answered him, “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now; but you will follow afterward” (John 13:36).

This must not be passed over carelessly. Where could the disciples not follow the Lord then, but could afterward? If we say, “To death,” there is no time in the life of a human being when he is unfit to die, since such is the condition of human beings in corruptible bodies that life is not easier within it than death.

They were not, therefore, less fit to follow the Lord to death; rather, they were less fit to follow the Lord to the life that does not have death. The Lord was going where, having risen from the dead, he would die no more, and death would no longer rule over him (Rom. 6:9).

How could they then have followed the Lord who was to die for righteousness, when they were not yet mature for martyrdom? Or how could they have followed the Lord who was going to the immortality of the flesh, when they were destined to die at some time and to rise only at the end of the age? Or how could they have followed the Lord who was going to the bosom of the Father without leaving them—just as he did not leave it when he came to them—when no one can be in that blessedness unless perfected in love?

Therefore, teaching how they could become fit to go where he was preceding them, he said, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34). These are the steps by which Christ must be followed. But a fuller discourse on these matters must be postponed to another time.

TRACTATE LXV. On the passage in which the Lord says, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another; just as I have loved you, you also should love one another. By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” Chapter 13, verses 34–35.

[Col. 1807]

[Col. 1808] 1. The Lord Jesus testifies that he gives his disciples a new commandment, that they should love one another: “I give you,” he says, “a new commandment, that you love one another.”

Was this commandment not already present in the ancient law of God, where it is written, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19:18)? Why, then, is what is demonstrably so ancient called new by the Lord? Is it a new commandment because, having stripped off the old person, he clothes us with the new person?

For it renews the one who hears—or rather, the one who obeys—not every kind of love, but the love that the Lord, in order to distinguish it from carnal love, qualified by adding, “Just as I have loved you.” Husbands and wives love one another, parents and children love one another, and every other human relationship by which people are bound together loves one another. Let us say nothing of the culpable and damnable love by which adulterers and adulteresses, fornicators and prostitutes, and all those whom not human relationship but the shameful depravity of human life joins together love one another.

Christ therefore gave us a new commandment: that we love one another as he also loved us. This love renews us, so that we may be new people, heirs of the New Testament, singers of the new song. This love renewed the righteous of old—the patriarchs and prophets—as it afterward renewed the blessed apostles. It also now renews the nations, and from the whole human race spread throughout the world it makes and gathers a new people, the body of the new bride, the bride of the only-begotten Son of God. Concerning her it is said in the Song of Songs, “Who is this that comes up, made white?” (Song 8:5, according to the Septuagint)—made white, certainly, because renewed; and renewed by what, unless by the new commandment?

For this reason the members of this body are concerned for one another: “If one member suffers, all the members suffer together; if one member is honored, all the members rejoice together” (1 Cor. 12:25–26). They hear and keep the commandment: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” They are not to love one another as those love one another who corrupt one another, nor as human beings love one another merely because they are human beings, but as those who love one another because they are gods and all sons of the Most High, so that they may be brothers to his only Son, loving one another with the love by which he loved them and by which he will lead them to that end which is sufficient for them, where their desire will be satisfied with good things (Ps. 102:5).

Then desire will lack nothing, when God is all in all (1 Cor. 15:28). Such an end has no end. No one dies there; no one reaches it unless he dies to this age—not by the death common to all, by which the body is abandoned by the soul, but by the death of the elect, by which, even while one remains in mortal flesh, the heart is set above.

The Apostle spoke of such a death: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3:3). Perhaps this is why it is said, “Love is strong as death” (Song 8:6). By this love it comes about that, while we are still established in this corruptible body, we die to this age and our life is hidden with Christ in God. Indeed, love itself is our death to the age and our life with God.

If death occurs when the soul leaves the body, how can it not also be death when our love leaves the world? Love, therefore, is strong as death. What is stronger than it, by which the world is conquered?

2. Therefore, my brothers, do not suppose that when the Lord says, “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another,” the greater commandment has been omitted—the commandment that orders us to love the Lord our God with all our heart, with all our soul, and with all our mind.

For it seems to have been said, as though that commandment had been omitted, “that you love one another,” as though this did not belong to the other commandment in which it is said, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments,” he says, “hang all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40).

But for those who understand rightly, both commandments are found in each one. For the person who loves God cannot despise him when he commands love of one’s neighbor; and the person who loves his neighbor in a holy and spiritual way loves in him none other than God.

This is the love distinguished from every worldly love, which the Lord distinguished by adding, “Just as I have loved you.” For what did he love in us except God? He loved not what we possessed, but so that we might possess him, leading us—as I said shortly before—to where God will be all in all.

Thus a physician is rightly said to love the sick. What does he love in them except health, which he certainly desires to restore—not the disease, which he came to drive away?

So let us also love one another, so that, insofar as we can, we may draw one another by the care of love toward possessing God within us. He himself grants us this love, who says, “Just as I have loved you, you also should love one another.”

He loved us for this purpose: that we too should love one another. By loving us he bestows this upon us, that we may be bound together by mutual love and, joined together by so sweet a bond, may be the body of so great a head.

3. “By this,” he says, “all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” It is as though he were saying: “Others who are not mine share with you my other gifts—not only nature, life, sensation, reason, and the salvation common to human beings and animals, but also tongues, sacraments, prophecy, knowledge, faith, the distribution of their possessions to the poor, and the handing over of their bodies so that they may burn. But because they do not have love, they sound like clanging cymbals; they are nothing, and none of these things benefits them” (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

Therefore, it is not by those gifts of mine, however good, which even those who are not my disciples may possess, but by this that all will know that you are my disciples: if you have love for one another.

O beautiful bride of Christ among women! O you who come up made white and lean upon your kinsman! For you are illumined by his light so that you may shine, and supported by his help so that you may not fall. How well it is sung to you in that Song of Songs, as though in your wedding song: “Love is in your delights” (Song 7:6, according to the Septuagint)!

Love does not destroy your soul with the impious; it distinguishes your cause; and, like death, it is strong and is in your delights. What a wondrous kind of death is this, to which it was not enough merely not to be in punishments unless it was also in delights!

But let this discourse now be brought to a close [Col. 1810]. What follows must be treated from another beginning.

TRACTATE LXVI. On the passage in which the Lord says, “Simon Peter said to him, ‘Lord, where are you going?’” up to, “Amen, amen, I say to you, the rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.” Chapter 13, verses 36–38.

1. When the Lord Jesus was commending to his disciples the holy love by which they were to love one another, “Simon Peter said to him, ‘Lord, where are you going?’” The disciple spoke thus to the Teacher, and the servant to the Lord, as though ready to follow.

Therefore the Lord, who saw why he had asked this question, answered him: “Where I am going, you cannot follow me now.” It was as though he were saying: “With regard to what you are asking, you cannot do so now.”

He did not say, “You cannot,” but, “You cannot now.” He introduced a delay, but did not take away hope. Indeed, he confirmed the same hope that he had not taken away but rather granted, by adding in the next sentence, “But you will follow afterward.”

Why are you in haste, Peter? The rock has not yet strengthened you by his Spirit. Do not be lifted up by presumption: you cannot now. Do not be cast down by despair: you will follow afterward.

But what does he say next? “Why can I not follow you now? I will lay down my life for you.”

He saw what desire existed in Peter’s heart, but Peter did not see what strength he possessed. The weak man boasted of his will, but the physician examined his condition. One promised; the other foresaw. The one who did not know dared; the one who foresaw taught.

How much Peter assumed for himself by looking at what he wished while not knowing what he could do! How much he assumed when, as the Lord was coming to lay down his life for his friends—and therefore also for Peter—he presumed to offer this to the Lord, and before Christ had laid down his life for him, promised that he would lay down his own life for Christ!

Jesus therefore answered, “Will you lay down your life for me?” Will you do for me what I have not yet done for you? “Will you lay down your life for me?” Can you go ahead when you cannot follow? Why presume so greatly? What do you think of yourself? What do you believe yourself to be?

Hear what you are: “Amen, amen, I say to you, the rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times.”

Behold how quickly you will appear to yourself, you who speak great things and do not know how small you are. You promise me your death; three times you will deny your life. You who now think that you can die for me, first live for yourself. For by fearing the death of your flesh, you will bring death upon your soul. For just as great as life is in confessing Christ, so great is death in denying Christ.

2. Did the apostle Peter, as some try to excuse him through misguided partiality (Ambrose, on Luke 22), not deny Christ because, when questioned by a maidservant, he answered that he did not know the man, as the other Evangelists testify more explicitly?

As though a person who denies Christ as man did not deny Christ, and as though he denied in him what he became for our sake, so that what he had made might not perish.

Therefore, whoever confesses Christ as God in such a way as to deny him as man has not died for him, because Christ died according to his humanity. Whoever denies Christ as man is not reconciled to God through the mediator. “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5).

Whoever denies Christ as man is not justified, because “just as by the disobedience of one human being the many were made sinners, so by the obedience of one human being the many will be made righteous” (Rom. 5:19).

Whoever denies Christ as man will not rise in the resurrection of life, because “through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead; for as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22).

And through what is he the head of the Church, unless through his humanity, by which the Word became flesh? That is, the only-begotten God of God the Father became a human being.

How, then, is the person who denies Christ as man in the body of Christ? For if he denies the head, how is he a member?

But why linger over many arguments, when the Lord himself has removed every evasion of human reasoning? He did not say, “The rooster will not crow until you deny the man,” or, as he customarily speaks in a more familiar manner of condescension to human beings, “The rooster will not crow until you deny the Son of Man three times.” Rather, he said, “Until you deny me three times.”

What does “me” mean except what he was? And what was he except Christ? Whatever part of him Peter denied, he denied him himself; he denied Christ; he denied the Lord his God.

For his fellow disciple Thomas, when he cried out, “My Lord and my God,” touched not the Word but the flesh; with inquisitive hands he handled not the incorporeal nature of God but the human body (John 20:27–28). He touched a human being and nevertheless recognized God.

If, therefore, Peter denied what Thomas touched, then Peter offended against what Thomas proclaimed. “The rooster will not crow until you deny me three times.”

You may say, “I do not know the man”; you may say, “Man, I do not know what you are saying”; you may say, “I am not one of his disciples” (Matt. 26:34, 69–74; Luke 22:55–60): “You will deny me.”

If—what it is impious to doubt—Christ said this and truly foretold it, then Peter undoubtedly denied Christ. Let us not accuse Christ while defending Peter. Let weakness acknowledge its sin, for truth has no lie.

Peter’s weakness acknowledged its sin—entirely acknowledged it—and by weeping he showed how great an evil he had committed by denying Christ. He himself refuted his defenders and brought forth his tears as witnesses by which to convict them.

Nor, when we say these things, do we take pleasure in accusing the first of the Apostles. Rather, by looking at him we ought to be warned that no human being should trust in human strength.

For what else was appropriate to our Teacher and Savior except to demonstrate, in the example of the first of the Apostles himself, that no one should presume upon himself?

Thus what had been offered in Peter’s body occurred in his soul. He did not go ahead of the Lord, as he rashly presumed, but went ahead in a way different from what he imagined. Before the Lord’s death and resurrection, he died by denying and came back to life by weeping. He died because he presumptuously relied on himself; but he came back to life because the Lord mercifully looked upon him.

TRACTATE LXVII. On the passage in which the Lord says, “Let not your heart be troubled,” up to, “I will come again and take you to myself.” Chapter 14, verses 1–3.

[Col. 1812]

1. Brothers, we must raise our attention more fully toward God, so that we may in some measure grasp in our minds the words of the holy Gospel that have just sounded in our ears.

For the Lord Jesus says: “Let not your heart be troubled. Believe in God, and believe in me.” [Note: [Col. 1812] A smaller number of manuscripts read “You believe,” following the Vulgate; moreover, the Greek verb occurring twice in this verse, pisteuete, is ambiguous, meaning either “you believe” or “believe.”] So that they would not fear death as human beings and consequently be troubled, he comforts them while also testifying that he is God. “Believe,” he says, “in God, and believe in me.”

It follows that if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me. This would not follow if Christ were not God.

Believe in God, and believe in the one whose nature—not by robbery—is to be equal with God: “For he emptied himself,” not by losing the form of God, but by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:6–7). You fear death in this form of a servant; let not your heart be troubled: the form of God will raise it up.

2. But what does the following mean: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places,” unless they were also afraid for themselves? Hence they needed to hear, “Let not your heart be troubled.”

For which of them would not have been afraid, when Peter, more confident and ready than the others, had been told, “The rooster will not crow until you have denied me three times” (John 13:38)?

Since they seemed destined to perish away from him, they were rightly troubled. But when they heard, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, would I have told you that I go to prepare a place for you?” they were restored from their disturbance, certain and confident that after the dangers of temptation they would remain with God and with Christ.

For even if one is stronger than another, one wiser than another, one more righteous than another, and one holier than another, “in my Father’s house are many dwelling places.” None of them will be excluded from that house, where each will receive a dwelling according to his merit.

The denarius, however, is equal for all. The householder commands that it be given equally to all who worked in the vineyard, making no distinction between those who labored less and those who labored more (Matt. 20:9). By that denarius eternal life is signified, where no one lives more than another, because the measure of living is not different in eternity.

But the many dwelling places signify the different dignities of merit within the one eternal life. “There is one glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars; for star differs from star in glory. So also is the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15:41–42).

Like stars, the saints receive different dwelling places of different brightness [Note: [Col. 1812] Thus the manuscripts. But the printed editions have “different brightnesses.”], as though in heaven, within the kingdom. Yet because of the one denarius, no one is separated from the kingdom.

Thus “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28), because, since “God is love” (1 John 4:8), love causes what each possesses to be common to all. Each person also possesses what belongs to another when he loves in another what he himself does not possess.

There will therefore be no envy on account of unequal brightness, because the unity of love will reign in all.

3. Therefore those must be rejected from the Christian heart [Col. 1813] who think that “there are many dwelling places” was said because there will be something outside the kingdom of heaven where blessed innocent people may remain—those who departed this life without baptism, since without it they cannot enter the kingdom of heaven.

This belief is not faith, because it is not true and catholic faith.

So, foolish people, blinded by carnal thoughts, if you would be condemned for separating from the kingdom of heaven not the dwelling place of Peter and Paul or any of the Apostles, but the dwelling place of any baptized child, do you not think you should be condemned for separating the house of God the Father from it?

For the Lord did not say, “In the whole world,” or “In every creature,” or “In everlasting life or blessedness there are many dwelling places,” but, “In the house,” he says, “of my Father are many dwelling places.”

Is this not the house in which “we have a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens” (2 Cor. 5:1)? Is this not the house concerning which we sing to the Lord, “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; forever and ever they will praise you” (Ps. 83:5)?

Will you therefore dare to separate from the kingdom of heaven not the house of some baptized brother, but the house of God the Father himself, to whom all brothers say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9)?
