Or will you dare to divide it in such a way that some of its dwelling places are in the kingdom of heaven and others outside the kingdom of heaven?

Far be it—far be it—from those who wish to dwell in the kingdom of heaven that they should wish to dwell with you in this folly. Far be it, I say, that since the entire house of the reigning children exists nowhere except in the kingdom, some part of the royal house itself should not be in the kingdom.

4. “And if I go,” he says, “and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be. And you know where I am going, and you know the way.”

O Lord Jesus, how do you go to prepare a place if there are already many dwelling places in your Father’s house, where your people will dwell with you? Or if you take them to yourself, how do you come again when you do not depart?

Beloved, if we try to explain these matters briefly, insofar as seems sufficient for today’s discourse, they will certainly not become clear when compressed, and the brevity itself will become another obscurity. Therefore let us postpone this debt, so that our Father and Master may repay it to you at a more suitable time.

TRACTATE LXVIII. On the same reading.

1. Dearly beloved brothers, we recognize that what we postponed is owed to you and must now be repaid: how can these two statements of the Lord be understood as not contradictory?

He said, “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places; if it were not so, I would have told you that I go to prepare a place for you,” thereby sufficiently showing that he said this because there are already many dwelling places there and no need exists to prepare one.

Yet again he says: “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.”

How does he go and prepare a place if there are already many dwelling places? If they did not exist, he would have said, “I go to prepare them.” Or if they still had to be prepared, why would he not rightly have said, “I go to prepare them”?

Are these dwelling places both already present and still to be prepared? If they did not exist, he would have said, “I go to prepare them.” Yet because they exist in such a way that they must be prepared, he does not go to prepare them as they already are. Rather, if he goes and prepares them as they are to be, then, coming again, he will take his own to himself, so that where he is, they too may be.

How, then, are the dwelling places in the Father’s house not different ones, but the very same ones, and without doubt already present insofar as they do not need to be prepared, yet not already present insofar as they still need to be prepared?

How are we to understand this except in the way the prophet also proclaims God, saying that he “made the things that are to be”? For he does not say, “He who will make the things that are to be,” but, “He who made the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, according to the Septuagint).

Therefore he both made them and will make them. For they are not made unless he himself made them; nor are they future unless he will make them.

He made them, therefore, by predestining them; he will make them by carrying them out.

The Gospel sufficiently indicates when he chose the disciples—namely, when he called them (Luke 6:13). Yet the Apostle says, “He chose us before the foundation of the world” (Eph. 1:4)—by predestining, certainly, not by calling.

“Those whom he predestined, he also called” (Rom. 8:30). He chose them by predestining before the foundation of the world; he chose them by calling before the consummation of the world.

So also he prepared and prepares the dwelling places—not different ones, but those which he prepared he prepares, he who made the things that are to be. Those which he prepared by predestining, he prepares by carrying them out.

They therefore already exist in predestination. If that were not so, he would have said, “I will go and prepare”—that is, “I will predestine.” But because they do not yet exist in their actual realization, he says, “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself.”

2. Yet he prepares the dwelling places in a certain manner by preparing inhabitants for the dwelling places. For when he said, “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places,” what are we to understand God’s house to be except God’s temple? But let the Apostle be asked what this is, and let him answer: “For God’s temple is holy, and that is what you are” (1 Cor. 3:17). This is also the kingdom of God, which the Son will hand over to the Father. Hence the same Apostle says: “Christ the firstfruits; afterward those who belong to Christ at his coming; then the end, when he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (ibid. 15:23–24)—that is, he will hand over to his Father those whom he redeemed by his blood, also through contemplation.

This is the kingdom of heaven of which it is said: “The kingdom of heaven is like a man sowing good seed in his field.” The good seed, however, is “the children of the kingdom.” Although they now have weeds mixed among them, at the end the King himself will send his angels, and they will gather out of his kingdom all scandals. “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:24, 38–43). The kingdom will shine in the kingdom when the kingdom comes into the kingdom for which we now pray and say, “Your kingdom come” (ibid. 6:10).

Now, therefore, it is already called a kingdom, but it is still being gathered into one. For if it were not called a kingdom, it would not be said, “They will gather out of his kingdom all scandals.” Yet this kingdom does not still reign. Accordingly, it is already a kingdom in such a way that, when all scandals have been gathered out of it, it will then arrive at the kingdom, so that it may possess not merely the name of a kingdom but also the power of reigning. To this kingdom, standing at the right hand, it will be said at the end: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (Matt. 25:34)—that is, “You who were a kingdom but did not reign, come, reign,” so that you may be in reality what you had been in hope.

This, then, the house of God; this, the temple of God; this, the kingdom of God and the kingdom of heaven—is still being built, still being fashioned [Note: [Col. 1815] “Still being fashioned” is absent from most manuscripts.], still being prepared, still being gathered together. In it there will be dwelling places, just as the Lord is still preparing them; in it they already exist, just as the Lord has already predestined them.

3. But what does it mean that he went away in order to prepare them, when plainly he was preparing us ourselves [Note: [Col. 1815] “He prepares,” according to Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice manuscripts.]—something he will not do if he leaves us? I recognize, Lord, as far as I can, what you mean: surely you signify that, in order for these dwelling places to be prepared, “the righteous must live by faith” (Rom. 1:17). For whoever is away from the Lord needs to live by faith, because through faith he is prepared for the contemplation of the vision (2 Cor. 5:6–8).

“For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); and, “He purified their hearts by faith” (Acts 15:9). The former is read in the Gospel, the latter in the Acts of the Apostles. The faith by which the hearts of those who are to see God are purified while they are away from him believes what it does not see; for if you see, it is not faith. Merit is gathered for the believer; the reward is given to the one who sees.

Let the Lord therefore go away and prepare the place; let him go away so that he may not be seen, let him remain hidden so that he may be believed. The place is prepared when one lives by faith. Let him who is believed be desired, so that he who is desired may be possessed; the desire of love is the preparation of the dwelling place.

Thus, Lord, prepare what you are preparing: you are preparing us for yourself, and you are preparing yourself for us, since you are preparing a place both for yourself in us and for us in you. For you said, “Remain in me, and I in you” (John 15:4). In proportion as each person participates in you—one less, another more—so will be the diversity of rewards according to the diversity of merits. Such will be the multitude of dwelling places according to the diversity of the inhabitants; yet all will live in eternity and be blessed without end.

What does it mean that you go away? What does it mean that you come? If I understand you correctly, you neither depart from where you go nor from where you come. You go away by hiding; you come by appearing. But unless you remain to guide us, so that we may progress by living well, how will the place be prepared where we can remain by enjoying you?

Let this suffice concerning the Gospel words that have been read, up to the point where the Lord says, “Again I am coming, and I will take you to myself.” But what follows—“so that where I am, you also may be”—and the words, “And you know where I am going, and you know the way,” we shall hear and discuss more suitably after the question that follows, asked by one of the disciples, as though through him we too were asking.

# TREATISE LXIX

On the words of the Lord, “And you know where I am going, and you know the way,” up to the words, “No one comes to the Father except through me.” Chapter 14:4–6.

1. Now, dearly beloved, it is time for us, as far as we are able, to understand the earlier words of the Lord through the later ones, and the preceding words through what follows, in the answer given to the Apostle Thomas when he asked a question.

Earlier, when speaking about the dwelling places—which he said both exist in his Father’s house and which he was going to prepare—the Lord had said that he was going away to prepare them. We understood that the dwelling places already exist in predestination and that they are prepared when the hearts of those who will remain there are purified through faith, since they themselves are God’s house. For what else is it to remain in God’s house than to be in God’s people, when those same people are in God and God is in them?

To prepare this, the Lord went away: so that, by believing in the one who is not seen, the dwelling place might now be prepared through faith for that vision which will always be future in its fullness. For this reason he had said, “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be. And you know where I am going, and you know the way.”

To this Thomas says to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going; and how can we know the way?” The Lord had said that they knew both things; this man says that they know neither—the place to which he is going nor the way by which he is going.

But he does not know how to lie. Therefore they did know, and did not know that they knew. Let him now prove that they know what they think they still do not know.

Jesus says to him: “I am the way, and the truth, and the life.” What does this mean, brothers? We have heard the disciple asking a question; we have heard the teacher instructing; and yet, even after the voice has sounded, we still do not grasp the meaning hidden within it.

But what are we unable to grasp? Could his Apostles, to whom he was speaking, say to him, “We do not know you”? Therefore, if they knew him, and he himself is the way, they knew the way. If they knew him, and he himself is the truth, they knew the truth. If they knew him, and he himself is the life, they knew the life. They are shown to know what they did not know themselves to know.

2. What, then, have we not grasped in this discourse? What do you think, my brothers, except that he said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way”? And now we have recognized that they knew the way because they knew him who is the way. But the way is what one travels by; is it also the destination to which one travels? Yet he had said that they knew both: where he was going and the way.

It was therefore necessary for him to say, “I am the way,” in order to show that those who knew him knew the way which they had thought they did not know. But why was it necessary for him to say, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life,” when, once the way by which he was going was known, it remained to know where he was going—unless it was because he was going to the truth, he was going to the life?

He was therefore going to himself, through himself. And where do we go except to him? And by what way do we go except through him? He therefore goes to himself through himself; we go to him through him—or rather, both he and we go to the Father. For elsewhere he says of himself, “I am going to the Father” (John 16:10); and in this passage, on our account, he says, “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

Thus he himself goes through himself both to himself and to the Father, while we go through him both to him and to the Father. Who grasps these things except one who understands spiritually? And how much does even one who understands spiritually grasp here?

Brothers, what do you want me to explain to you? Consider how exalted these things are. You see what I am; I see what you are. In all of us, “the body that is corrupted weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling burdens the mind occupied with many thoughts” (Wis. 9:15).

Can we perhaps say, “To you I have lifted up my soul, you who dwell in heaven” (Ps. 122:1)? But under so great a weight, where we groan while burdened, how shall I lift up my soul, unless the one who laid down his soul for me lifts it together with me?

I shall therefore say what I can; let whoever can grasp it grasp it. By his gift I speak; by his gift the one who grasps it grasps; and by his gift the one who does not yet grasp it believes. “Unless you believe,” says the prophet, “you will not understand” (Isa. 7:9, according to the Septuagint).

3. Tell me, my Lord, what I should say to your servants, my fellow servants. The Apostle Thomas had you before him when he questioned you; yet he would not understand you unless he had you within him. I question you because I know that you are above me; but I question you insofar as I can pour out my soul over myself, where I may hear you—not sounding, yet teaching.

Tell me, I beg you: how do you go to yourself? Surely, when you came to us, you had not left yourself—especially since you did not come from yourself, but the Father sent you? I know indeed that you emptied yourself; but because you took the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), not because you either laid aside the form of God in order to return to it or lost it in order to receive it again.

And yet you came, not only as far as the eyes of flesh, but even as far as the hands of human beings. How, except in the flesh? Through it you came while remaining where you were; through it you returned without leaving the place from which you had come.

If, therefore, through it you came and returned, then through it, undoubtedly, you were not only the way for us by which we might come to you, but also for you by which you might come and return. And when you went to the life—which you yourself are—you surely led that same flesh of yours from death to life.

For the Word of God is one thing, and the human being another; but “the Word became flesh,” that is, became human. There is not one person of the Word and another of the human being, since both are one person, Christ. Accordingly, just as when the flesh died, Christ died, and when the flesh was buried, Christ was buried—for thus we believe with the heart unto righteousness, and thus we confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10:10)—so, when the flesh came from death to life, Christ came to life.

And because Christ is the Word of God, Christ is life. Thus, in a wondrous and ineffable manner, the one who never set aside or lost himself came to himself.

As has been said, God came through the flesh to human beings; truth came to liars. “For God is truthful, and every human being is a liar” (ibid. 3:4). When he took his flesh away from human beings and lifted it to that place where no one lies, he himself—because the Word became flesh—returned through himself, that is, through the flesh, to the truth, which he himself is.

He preserved that truth even among liars and in death. For Christ was dead at one time, but he was never false.

4. Receive an example that is different and very unequal, yet in some way useful for understanding God, drawn from things more closely subject to God.

Behold, I myself, as far as my soul is concerned, since I am what you are also: if I am silent, I am with myself. But if I speak to you what you may understand, I proceed, in a certain manner, toward you; I do not leave myself, but I also approach you and do not withdraw from where I proceed.

When I have become silent, I return, in a certain manner, to myself; and I remain, in a certain manner, with you if you retain what you heard in the discourse I deliver.

If the image made by God can do this, what can God—the Image of God, not made by God but begotten from God—do? His body, through which he went forth to us and through which he returned from us, did not pass away like my voice; rather, it remains there where it no longer dies, and “death shall no longer rule over it” (Rom. 6:9).

Much more could perhaps—and perhaps should—be said about these Gospel words. But your hearts should not be burdened with spiritual foods, however sweet, especially since “the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matt. 26:41).

# TREATISE LXX

On the words of the Lord, “If you had known me, you would certainly have known my Father also,” up to the words, “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” Chapter 14:7–10.

1. The words of the holy Gospel, brothers, are rightly understood when they are found to agree with what precedes; for when truth speaks, the preceding words must harmonize with what follows.

Earlier the Lord had said: “And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, so that where I am, you also may be.” Then he had added: “And you know where I am going, and you know the way.” He showed that this meant nothing other than that they knew him.

What, then, does it mean to go to himself through himself—a privilege he also grants the disciples, so that they may go to him through him? We have already discussed this as well as we could in the previous discourse.

When he says, “So that where I am, you also may be,” where were they going to be except in him? Thus he is also in himself, and they are there where he is—that is, in him.

He is therefore the eternal life in which we shall be when he has received us to himself. And that eternal life, which he himself is, is in him, so that where he is, we also may be—that is, in him.

For just as the Father has life in himself, and surely the life he has is nothing other than what he himself is who has it, so he gave the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26), since he himself is the same life that he has in himself.

But shall we become the life that he is when we begin to be in that life—that is, in him? Certainly not. He, by existing, has life, and he is what he has; and what is life in him, he himself is in himself. We, however, are not that life itself, but participants in that life. Thus we shall be there in such a way that, within ourselves, we cannot be what he is; rather, we ourselves, who are not life, shall have him as life—him who possesses himself as life because he is life.

Finally, he is both immutably in himself and inseparably in the Father. But when we wished to be in ourselves, we were thrown into turmoil within ourselves. Hence the saying, “My soul is troubled within me” (Ps. 42:7). Changed for the worse, we could neither remain what we had been nor continue to be what we were.

But when through him we come to the Father, as he says, “No one comes to the Father except through me,” while we remain in him, no one will be able to separate us either from the Father or from him.

2. Connecting what follows with what precedes, he says: “If you have known me [Note: [Col. 1818] Here the manuscripts read, “If you have known me”; elsewhere in this verse, “you will certainly know.” But now more manuscripts, by a second hand, have “you would have known” in both places.], you have certainly known my Father.” [Col. 1819] This is what he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

Then he adds: “And from now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” But Philip, one of the Apostles, not understanding what he had heard, says: “Lord, show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

The Lord says to him: “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

See how he rebukes him for having been with them for so long a time and yet not being known. Had he not himself said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way”? And when they said that they did not know, had he not proved that they knew this by adding and saying, “I am the way, the truth, and the life”?

How then does he now say, “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not known me,” when they plainly knew both where he was going and the way, for no other reason than that they certainly knew him?

The question is easily resolved if we say that some of them knew him and some did not, and that Philip was among those who did not know him. Thus, when he said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way,” he is understood to have spoken to those who knew, not to Philip, to whom he said, “For so long a time I have been with you, and you have not known me, Philip?”

To those, therefore, who already knew the Son, the words concerning the Father were also spoken: “From now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” This was said on account of the complete likeness that he has with the Father, so that they might now be said to know the Father because they knew the Son who was like him.

Therefore they already knew the Son—if not all of them, at least some of those to whom he said, “You know where I am going, and you know the way.” For he is the way. But they did not know the Father; therefore they hear: “If you have known me, you have certainly known my Father also”—through me, certainly, they will know him.

I am one, and he is another. But lest they think him unlike the Father, he says: “From now on you will know him, and you have seen him.” For they had seen the Son, utterly like the Father, but they needed to be reminded that the Father whom they did not yet see was such as the Son whom they saw.

This is also the force of what is later said to Philip: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.” This does not mean that the Father and the Son are the same person—a belief condemned by the Catholic faith in the Sabellians, who are also called Patripassians—but that the Father and the Son are so alike that whoever knows one knows both.

We customarily speak in this way of two people who are very much alike. To someone who sees one of them and wishes to know what the other is like, we say, “You have seen this one; you have seen the other.” Thus it is said, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also”—not that the Son is himself the Father, but that the Son differs in absolutely nothing from the likeness of the Father.

For unless the Father and the Son were two, it would not have been said, “If you have known me, you have certainly known my Father.” Since, then, he says, “No one comes to the Father except through me,” it follows: “If you have known me, you will have known my Father also,” because I, through whom one comes to the Father, will lead you to him so that you may also know him.

But because I am altogether like him, from now on you will know him when you know me; and you have seen him if you have seen me with the eyes of the heart.

3. What, then, is the meaning of what you say, Philip: “Show us the Father, and that is enough for us”? “For so long a time,” he says, “I have been with you, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also.”

If this seeing is too much for you, at least believe what you do not see. For how do you say, “Show us the Father”? If you have seen me, who am altogether like him, you have seen him to whom I am like.

And if you cannot see this, do you at least not believe that “I am in the Father and the Father is in me”? Philip could perhaps say here: “I do see you, and I believe that you are very much like the Father. But should someone who sees one who is like another be blamed and rebuked for wanting also to see the one to whom he is like? I know the likeness, but I still know the one without the other; it is not enough for me unless I also know the one whose likeness this man is. Therefore show us the Father, and that is enough for us.”

But the teacher rebuked the disciple because he saw what the petitioner’s heart desired. Philip wanted to know the Father as though the Father were better than the Son; and for that reason he did not know the Son either, since he believed that something could be better than him.

To correct this understanding, he said: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.” “How can you say, ‘Show us the Father’?” I see what you mean by saying this: you are not asking to see another who is like me; you think that the other is better.

“Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” Why do you desire to see a difference between those who are alike? Why do you wish to know separately those who are inseparable?

He then speaks not to Philip alone but to the disciples in the plural. His words should not be compressed into narrow limits, but, with his help, should be explained more carefully.

# TREATISE LXXI

On the words of the Lord, “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself,” up to the words, “If you ask the Father for anything in my name, I will do it.” Chapter 14:10–14.

1. Hear with your ears and receive with your minds, dearly beloved—not indeed while we speak, but while he himself teaches, for he does not withdraw from us.

The Lord says what you have just heard when it was read: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works.”

Are words therefore also works? Clearly they are. For certainly one who builds up his neighbor by speaking performs a good work.

But what does “I do not speak from myself” mean except “I am not from myself, I who speak”? He attributes what he does to the one from whom he himself is.

For God the Father is not from anyone, whereas the Son is indeed God, equal to the Father, but is from God the Father. Therefore the Father is God, but not from God; light, but not from light. The Son, however, is God from God, light from light.

2. In these two statements—one, “I do not speak from myself,” and the other, “The Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works”—various heretics take hold of one statement each and oppose us. They stray from the way of truth, not by striving from the same side but in opposite directions.

The Arians say: “Behold, the Son is unequal to the Father; he does not speak from himself.” The Sabellians, on the contrary—that is, the Patripassians—say: “Behold, the one who is the Father is himself the Son. For what is ‘The Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works’ except ‘I, who do the works, remain in myself’?”

You speak contrary things, but not in the way that what is false is contrary to what is true; rather, you speak two false things contrary to one another. In wandering in different directions, you have left the way that lies between you [Note: [Col. 1820] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read this passage as follows: “You go in different directions; the way you leave is in the middle.”].

You are farther separated from one another than you are from the way itself, whose deserters you are. You, from this side; you, from that side—come here. Do not cross over from one to the other, but come from both sides to us and meet one another.

Sabellians, acknowledge the one whom you omit. Arians, make equal the one whom you subordinate. Then you will walk with us on the true way.

Each side must be reminded by the other of something that both ought to recognize. Hear, Sabellian: the Son is so far from being the Father himself, but is another, that the Arian asserts him to be unequal to the Father. Hear, Arian: the Son is so far equal to the Father that the Sabellian says he is the same as the Father.

Add what you remove; make complete what you diminish; and both of you will stand with us. For when neither of you removes nor diminishes the one who is both other than the Father, so as to refute the Sabellian, and equal to the Father, so as to refute the Arian, you will stand with us.

To both sides he cries: “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30). Let the Arians hear “one”; let the Sabellians hear “are.” Neither should be foolish by denying that he is equal to the Father, nor by denying that he is another.

If, then, because he said, “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself,” he is thought to have such unequal power that he does not do what he himself wills, let this be heard: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wills” (ibid. 5:21).

Again, if, because he said, “The Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works,” he is thought not to be another from the Father, let this be heard: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (ibid. 5:19). Let it be understood that there are not two instances of one person, but two who are one.

Yet because each is equal to the other while one is nevertheless from the other, the Son does not speak from himself because he is not from himself. And therefore the Father, dwelling in him, himself does the works, because the one through whom and with whom the Father acts is from the Father alone.

Finally, he adds and says: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me? Otherwise, believe on account of the works themselves.”

Earlier Philip alone was rebuked; now it is shown that he was not the only one there who deserved rebuke. “Believe,” he says, “on account of the works themselves, that I am in the Father and the Father is in me.” For if we were separated, there would be no way for us to work inseparably.

3. But what is the meaning of what follows?

“Amen, amen, I say to you, whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these, because I am going to the Father. And whatever you ask in my name, I will do it, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son. If you ask anything in my name, I will do it.”

He therefore promised that he himself would also do those greater works. Let not the servant exalt himself above the Lord, nor the disciple above the teacher (ibid. 13:16). He says that they will do greater works than he does, but with him doing them in or through them—not with them doing them as though from themselves.

For it is to him that the song is sung: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. 18:2).

But what, finally, are these greater works? Perhaps it was that, as the disciples passed by, even their shadow healed the sick (Acts 5:15). For it is greater that a shadow should heal than a fringe (Matt. 14:36). The former he did through himself, the latter through them; yet he himself did both.

Nevertheless, when he said these things, he was commending the works of his words. For he had said: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works.”

What works was he then speaking of except the words he was uttering? They heard and believed, and the fruit of those same words was their faith. Yet when the disciples preached, not merely as few as the disciples themselves believed, but the nations also believed. These are unquestionably the greater works.

He did not, however, say, “You will do greater works than these,” so that we would think that only the Apostles would do them. Rather, he says: “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these.”

Does everyone who believes in Christ therefore do the works Christ does, or even greater works than Christ? These matters must not be passed over casually or hurriedly brought to a conclusion. But since this discourse must now be brought to an end, it compels us to defer them.

# TREATISE LXXII

On the same reading.

1. What the Lord meant, and how we should understand his words, “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do,” is not easy to grasp. And since this is exceedingly difficult to understand, he added something still more difficult: “And he will do greater works than these.”

What does this mean? We could not find anyone who did the works Christ did; shall we find someone who will do greater works? In the previous discourse we had said that what the disciples did—healing the sick as they passed by and their shadow touched them (Acts 5:15)—was greater than what the Lord himself did when the sick were healed by touching his fringe (Matt. 14:36).

We had also said that more people believed through the Apostles than through the Lord himself preaching with his own mouth. Thus these things seemed to be the greater works that should be understood—not because the disciple was greater than the teacher, the servant greater than the Lord, the adopted son greater than the Only-Begotten, or the human being greater than God, but because he himself graciously did these greater works through them, who says to them elsewhere, “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

He himself, to leave aside countless other things, made them without them; he made this world without them. And because he himself graciously became human, he made himself without them as well.

But what could they do without him except sin? Finally, here too he quickly removed whatever might disturb us about this matter. For when he had said, “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these,” he immediately continued: “Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, I will do it.”

He first said, “He will do,” and afterward said, “I will do,” as though he were saying: “Let this not seem impossible to you. The one who believes in me will not be able to be greater than I; rather, I will do these things, and then greater things than now—greater through the one who believes in me than, apart from him, through me. Yet I myself do them apart from him, and I myself do them through him. But when I do them apart from him, he does not do them; when I do them through him, although not through himself, he too does them.”

To do greater things through him than apart from him is not a falling short but a condescension. “What shall servants render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to them?” (Ps. 116:12). Among the other good things, he graciously granted them this also: that he should do greater works through them than apart from them.

Did the rich and sorrowful man not go away from his presence when he asked for advice about eternal life (Matt. 19:16–22)? He heard and rejected it. Yet afterward, what one man did not do after hearing it from him, many did when the good teacher spoke through the disciples. It was contemptible to the rich man whom he instructed directly, but beloved by those whom he made poor from the rich through the poor.

Behold, when preached by believers, he did greater works than when he spoke to those who heard him.

2. Yet this still causes difficulty: he did these greater works through the Apostles. But he did not mean only the Apostles when he said, “The works that I do, you will do, and you will do greater works than these.” Rather, wishing all who belonged to his household to be understood, he said: “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do, and he will do greater works than these.”

If, then, the one who believes will do them, the one who does not do them certainly does not believe. This is like the saying, “Whoever loves me keeps my commandments” (John 14:21); therefore the one who does not keep them does not love.

Again, elsewhere he says: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them I will compare to a wise man who builds his house upon rock” (Matt. 7:24). Therefore whoever is not like this wise man certainly either hears these words and does not do them, or does not hear them at all.

“Whoever believes in me,” he says, “even if he dies, will live” (John 11:25). Therefore the one who will not live certainly does not believe.

The same applies here: “Whoever believes in me will do them.” The one who does not do them certainly does not believe.

What does this mean, brothers? Is someone who does not do works greater than Christ to be counted among those who believe in Christ? It is harsh; it is absurd; it cannot be accepted. It is tolerated only if it is understood.

Let us therefore hear the Apostle: “To the one who believes in him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness” (Rom. 4:5).

In this work let us do the works of Christ, because even believing in Christ is the work of Christ. He works this in us, certainly not without us. Hear, then, and understand: “Whoever believes in me will himself do the works that I do.” First I do them, and afterward he too will do them, because I make it possible for him to do them.

What works are these except that the ungodly may become righteous?

3. “And he will do greater works than these.” Greater than which, I ask? Does the person who works out his own salvation with fear and trembling (Phil. 2:12) do works greater than all Christ’s works? Christ certainly works this in him, but not without him.

I would say plainly that this is greater than heaven and earth and all that is seen in heaven and on earth. For “heaven and earth will pass away” (Matt. 24:35), but the salvation and justification of the predestined—that is, of those whom he foreknows—will remain.

In the former there are only the works of God; in the latter there is also the image of God. Yet in the heavens as well, Thrones, Dominions, Principalities, Powers, Archangels, and Angels are works of Christ. Does the person in whom Christ works, cooperating in his own eternal salvation and justification, do works greater even than these?

I do not dare to rush to a judgment here. Let whoever can understand; let whoever can judge whether it is greater to create the righteous than to justify the ungodly. Certainly, if the power required for both is equal, the latter is the greater act of mercy.

This is the great mystery of piety: “he was manifested in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, appeared to angels, was preached among the nations, was believed in the world, was taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3:16).

But no necessity compels us to understand all the works of Christ when he says, “He will do greater works than these.” For perhaps he said “these” of the works he was doing at that hour. At that time he was speaking words of faith, and he had already spoken of these works when he said: “The words that I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father, dwelling in me, himself does the works.”

At that time, therefore, his words were his works. And certainly preaching words of righteousness—which he did without us—is less than justifying the ungodly, which he does in us in such a way that we also do it.

It remains to inquire how we should understand: “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do it.” For, because of the many things his faithful ask for and do not receive, a considerable question arises from this. But since this discourse must now be concluded, let us grant at least a brief delay for considering and treating it.

# TREATISE LXXIII

Also on the same reading.

1. The Lord promised great hope to those of his people who hoped [Note: [Col. 1824] Three manuscripts read, “to those who prayed.”], saying: “Because I am going to the Father, and whatever you ask in my name, I will do it.”

He therefore went to the Father in such a way that he did not leave those in need, but answered those who asked. But what does “whatever you ask” mean, when we often see his faithful ask and not receive? Is it perhaps because they ask wrongly?

For the Apostle James reproved this, saying: “You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, so that you may spend it on your passions” (James 4:3). When someone would use what he wishes to receive wrongly, God, in his mercy, does not grant it. Therefore, if someone asks God for something by which he would be harmed, and God hears him, it is more to be feared that God, in anger, may give what he could have withheld in mercy.

Do we not see that the Israelites obtained, to their own harm, what they asked for in culpable desire? For they had desired to eat meat (Num. 11:32), although manna was being rained down for them from heaven. They were disgusted with what they had and shamelessly asked for what they did not have—as though they should not rather have asked that, not by an improper desire, the food they lacked be supplied, but that the food they already had might be consumed once their disgust had been healed.

When evils delight us and goods do not delight us, we should ask God rather to make the good pleasing to us than to grant the evil. This is not because it is evil to eat meat, since the Apostle says concerning this matter, “Every creature of God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4:4). But, as he also says, “It is evil for a person to eat through giving offense” (Rom. 14:20); and if it is offensive to a human being, how much more to God?

The Israelites gave considerable offense to God by rejecting what wisdom gave and asking for what desire craved—although they did not even ask, but complained because it was lacking.

Yet to show us that the blame lay not in God’s creature but in stubborn disobedience and disordered desire, the first human being found death not because of a pig but because of an apple (Gen. 3:6), and Esau lost his birthright not because of a hen but because of lentils (ibid. 25:34).

### 2

How, then, are we to understand the statement, “Whatever you ask, I will do,” if God, even in consulting for faithful petitioners, does not do some things they ask? Or should we perhaps understand it as having been said only to the Apostles? Certainly not. For when he came to this point, he had said above, “Whoever believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater works than these”; we dealt with this subject in the preceding discourse. And lest anyone attribute to himself the ability to perform even those greater works, he added and said: “Because I am going to the Father; and whatever you ask in my name, I will do.”

Did only the Apostles believe in him? He was therefore speaking to them when he said, “Whoever believes in me”—and by his gift we too are among those who believe—yet we certainly do not receive whatever we ask. Even if we consider those most blessed Apostles themselves, we find that the one who labored more than all the others—not he himself, but “the grace of God with him” (1 Cor. 15:10)—asked the Lord three times that the angel of Satan might depart from him, and yet did not receive what he had asked (2 Cor. 12:8).

What shall we say, beloved? [Note: At Col. 1825, B reads, “What do we say, beloved?” We follow Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. M.] Shall we suppose that this promise, in which he says, “Whatever you ask, I will do,” was not fulfilled even for the Apostles? And to whom, finally, will he fulfill what he promises, if he defrauded his own Apostles of his promise?

### 3

Wake up, therefore, faithful one, and listen attentively to what is written there: “in my name.” For he does not say simply, “Whatever you ask,” but, “Whatever you ask in my name.” What, then, is the name of the one who promised so great a benefit? Surely, Christ Jesus. “Christ” signifies “king,” and “Jesus” signifies “Savior.” It is not just any king who will save us, but the King who is Savior. Therefore, whatever we ask against the welfare of salvation, we do not ask in the name of the Savior.

And yet he is the Savior not only when he does what we ask, but also when he does not do it; for when he sees that something is being requested against our salvation, by not doing it he shows himself the Savior. A physician knows what the sick person requests for his health and what he requests against his health; therefore he does not do the will of one who asks for harmful things, so that he may bring about health.

Whenever, therefore, we want him to do whatever we ask, let us ask not in some arbitrary way, but in his name—that is, let us ask in the name of the Savior. Let us not ask for what is against our salvation. If he were to do so, he would not be acting as the Savior, which is the name he bears for his faithful. For the ungodly he is also Judge and Condemner, while he deigns to be Savior for the faithful.

Whoever, then, believes in him: whatever that person asks in the name that he bears for those who believe in him, he does, because he does it as Savior. But if someone who believes in him asks, through ignorance, for something against his own salvation, he is not asking in the name of the Savior; for the Savior will not be his Savior if he does what hinders his salvation. It is therefore more beneficial at that time that, by not doing what he is invoked to do, he should do what his name signifies.

For this reason, in order to do whatever we ask, he taught us what we should ask in the prayer that he gave us—not only as Savior but also as the good Teacher. Thus we may understand that when we ask for something contrary to the rule of his teaching, we are not asking in the Teacher’s name.

### 4

[Col. 1826] Certainly, there are some things that, although we ask for them in his name—that is, according to the Savior and according to the Teacher—he does not do when we ask, yet he does do them. For merely because we ask that the kingdom of God come, does it follow that he does not do what we ask because we do not immediately reign with him in eternity? What we ask is delayed, not denied.

Nevertheless, let us not grow weary in praying, like those who sow; “for in due season we shall reap” (Gal. 6:9). And when we ask rightly, let us also ask that he not do what we ask wrongly; for this too is included in what we say in the same Lord’s Prayer: “Do not lead us into temptation” (Matt. 6:9–13). It is no small temptation if your petition works against your own cause.

Nor should we listen carelessly to what the Lord said. Lest anyone think that he had promised to do what those who ask him request independently of the Father, after saying, “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do,” he immediately added: “So that the Father may be glorified in the Son; if you ask anything in my name, I will do it.” The Son therefore does this in no way without the Father, since he does it precisely so that the Father may be glorified in him.

The Father therefore acts in the Son, so that the Son may be glorified in the Father; and the Son acts in the Father, so that the Father may be glorified in the Son, because the Father and the Son are one.

# TRACTATE LXXIV

On the statement, “If you love me, keep my commandments,” up to the statement, “He will remain with you, and he will be in you.” Chapter 14, verses 15–17.

### 1

We heard, brothers, when the Gospel was read, the Lord saying: “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees him nor knows him. But you will know him, because he will remain with you, and he will be in you.”

Many things demand investigation in these few words of the Lord; but it would be too much for us either to inquire into everything that might be sought here or to discover everything we seek. Nevertheless, insofar as the Lord deigns to grant us understanding according to our capacity and yours, let us attend to what we ought to say and what you ought to hear. Receive through us what we can offer, beloved, and ask from him for what we cannot offer.

Christ promised the Spirit, the Paraclete, to the Apostles. Let us consider how he made the promise. “If you love me,” he says, “keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, to remain with you forever, the Spirit of truth.”

This is certainly the Holy Spirit within the Trinity, whom the catholic faith confesses to be consubstantial and coeternal with the Father and the Son. He is the one of whom the Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

How, then, does the Lord say, “If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” when he is speaking of the Holy Spirit, without whom we can neither love God nor keep his commandments? How do we love in order to receive him whom, unless we have him, we cannot love? [Col. 1827] Or how do we keep the commandments in order to receive him whom, unless we have him, we cannot keep the commandments?

Or perhaps love precedes in us—the love by which we love Christ—so that, by loving Christ and doing his commandments, we may deserve to receive the Holy Spirit, so that it is not the love of Christ, which had already preceded, but the love of God the Father that is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us?

That opinion is perverse. For whoever believes that he loves the Son but does not love the Father certainly does not love the Son either, but some fiction that he has invented for himself. Moreover, the apostolic word says: “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3). And who says “Jesus is Lord” except one who loves him, if he says it in the sense in which the Apostle intended it to be understood?

Many say it with their voice, but deny it in heart and deeds, as it is said of such people: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Tit. 1:16). If he is denied by deeds, then undoubtedly he is also confessed by deeds. No one, therefore—mind, word, deed, heart, mouth, action—says “Jesus is Lord” except in the Holy Spirit; and no one says it in this way except one who loves him.

The Apostles were already saying, “Jesus is Lord.” And if they said it in such a way that they were not speaking falsely—confessing with their mouths while denying him in heart and deeds—then, if they said it truthfully, they undoubtedly loved him. How, then, did they love him, except in the Holy Spirit? Yet they are first commanded to love him and to keep his commandments, so that they may receive the Holy Spirit; for unless they had him, they could certainly neither love nor keep the commandments.

### 2

It remains, therefore, for us to understand that whoever loves possesses the Holy Spirit, and that by possessing him deserves to possess more, and by possessing more loves more.

The disciples already had the Spirit whom the Lord promised, without whom they would not have called him Lord; yet they did not have him in the manner in which the Lord promised him. They both had him and did not have him: they did not yet have as much of him as they were destined to have. They had less; more was to be given them. They had him secretly and were going to receive him openly, since this too belonged to the greater gift of the Holy Spirit: that what they possessed should become known to them.

Speaking of this gift, the Apostle says: “We have received not the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God” (1 Cor. 2:12).

For the Lord himself brought about the manifest bestowal of the Holy Spirit not once but twice. Immediately after he rose from the dead, he breathed on them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). Does it follow that, because he gave him then, he did not also send afterward the one whom he had promised? Or is the Holy Spirit not the same one who was then breathed forth by him and afterward sent by him from heaven (Acts 2:4)?

Why this manifest gift of the Spirit was made twice is another question. Perhaps it was because of the two commandments of love, namely, love of neighbor and love of God, so that it might be shown that love belongs to the Holy Spirit; thus his gift was manifested in a twofold manner. If another explanation is sought, this discourse should not now be diverted into a longer inquiry than is appropriate.

[Col. 1828] Let it nevertheless remain certain that without the Holy Spirit we cannot love Christ or keep his commandments; and that the less we receive of him, the less we are able to do and accomplish these things, while the more we receive of him, the more we are able.

Therefore the promise is made not only to one who does not have him, but also to one who has him—not in vain: to the one who does not have him, so that he may have him; to the one who has him, so that he may have more of him. For unless one possessed less and another more, the holy Elisha would not have said to the holy Elijah: “Let the spirit that is in you be doubled in me.”

[Note: The printed editions have, “Let it be doubled in me.” The manuscripts have, “Let it be twice as much in me.”]

### 3

When John the Baptist says, “For God does not give the Spirit by measure” (John 3:34), he was speaking of the Son of God himself, to whom the Spirit was not given by measure, because “the whole fullness of divinity dwells in him” (Col. 2:9).

For the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Tim. 2:5), is not without the grace of the Holy Spirit. He himself says that the prophetic statement was fulfilled in him: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me and sent me to evangelize the poor” (Luke 4:18–21).

The fact that the Only-Begotten is equal to the Father belongs not to grace but to nature. But the fact that a human being was assumed into the unity of the person of the Only-Begotten belongs to grace, not to nature. The Gospel acknowledges this when it says: “The child grew and became strong, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was in him” (Luke 2:40).

To all others the Spirit is given by measure, and what is given is increased until the proper measure allotted to each person according to the degree of his perfection is completed. Hence the Apostle also exhorts us: “Do not be wiser than it is necessary to be wise, but be wise with sobriety, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned” (Rom. 12:3).

For the Spirit himself is not divided, but gifts are distributed through the Spirit: “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:4).

### 4

By saying, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” he shows that he himself is also the Paraclete. For *Paraclete* is rendered in Latin as *advocate*; and it is said of Christ: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous” (1 John 2:1).

He said that the world cannot receive the Holy Spirit in the same sense in which it is said, “The mind of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the law of God, nor indeed can it be” (Rom. 8:7)—as if we were to say, “Injustice cannot be just.”

By “the world” here he means the lovers of the world, since this love is not from the Father (1 John 2:16). Therefore the love of God, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us, is opposed to this love of the world, which we are diligently striving to diminish and consume within us. [Note: Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., and M. read *satagimus* (“we strive earnestly”) for *satis agimus*.]

The world therefore cannot receive him, because it does not see him and does not know him. Worldly love does not possess the invisible eyes through which the Holy Spirit can be seen—unless he is seen invisibly.

### 5

“But you,” he says, “will know him, because he will remain with you, and he will be in you.” He will be in them in order that he may remain, not remain in order that he may be there; for being somewhere comes before remaining.

But lest they suppose that “he will remain with you” was said in the manner in which [Col. 1829] a guest ordinarily remains visibly with another person, he explained what he meant by “he will remain with you” when he added, “and he will be in you.”

He is therefore seen invisibly. Nor, unless he is in us, can knowledge of him be in us. In this way he is seen by us in ourselves, just as our consciousness is seen by us. We see another person’s face, but cannot see our own; we see our own consciousness, but not another’s. Consciousness exists only in us. The Holy Spirit, however, can exist even without us; for he is given so that he may be both present and in us.

But he cannot be seen and known by us in the manner in which he ought to be seen and known unless he is in us.

# TRACTATE LXXV

On the statement of Jesus, “I will not leave you orphans,” up to the statement, “And I will love him and manifest myself to him.” Chapter 14, verses 18–21.

### 1

After the promise of the Holy Spirit, lest anyone think that the Lord would give him in such a way that the Lord himself would not also remain with them, he added and said: “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.”

Orphans are the fatherless. The Greek word is the name for the same thing, while this is the Latin term. Thus, in the psalm where we read, “You will be the helper of the fatherless” (Ps. 9:14), the Greek text has *orphan*.

Although the Son of God has adopted us as children for his Father and has willed that we should have as Father by grace the one who is his Father by nature, he nevertheless also shows toward us, in a certain way, a fatherly affection when he says, “I will not leave you orphans; I will come to you.”

This is also why he calls us the children of the bridegroom when he says: “The hour will come when the bridegroom is taken away from them, and then the children of the bridegroom will fast” (Matt. 9:15). And who is the bridegroom except the Lord Christ?

### 2

Then he continues and says: “A little while, and the world will no longer see me.” What does this mean? Did the world see him then, since by “the world” he wishes to mean those of whom he spoke above when he said of the Holy Spirit: “The world cannot receive him, because it does not see him or know him”?

The world certainly saw him with bodily eyes, visible in the flesh; but it did not see the Word hidden in the flesh. It saw a human being, but did not see God; it saw the garment, but did not see the one clothed in it.

But since, after the resurrection, he did not wish to display even his flesh—which he showed to his own not only to be seen but also to be touched—to those who were not his, perhaps this is to be understood as the meaning of the words: “A little while, and the world will no longer see me; but you will see me, because I live, and you will live.”

### 3

What does “because I live, and you will live” mean? Why did he say that he lives in the present, but that they would live in the future, unless it is because he promised them the life of the flesh as well—the life of the resurrected flesh, such as was already present in him and was destined to follow in them?

Since his resurrection was soon to occur, he used a verb in the present tense to signify its rapid arrival. But because their resurrection is postponed until the end of the age, he did not say, “You live,” but, “You will live.”

Thus, in two words—one in the present tense and one in the future—he elegantly and briefly promised two resurrections: his own, which was soon to occur, and [Col. 1830] ours, which would come at the end of the age.

“Because I live,” he says, “you will live also.” Because he lives, we too will live. For “through a human being came death, and through a human being the resurrection of the dead. For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Cor. 15:21–22). No one comes to death except through him, and no one comes to life except through Christ.

Because we have not lived, we are dead; because he lives, we will live. [Note: Printed editions read, “Because for us”; most manuscripts, “Because we.”] We died to him when we lived for ourselves; but because he died for us, he lives both for himself and for us. Because he lives, we too will live. For although through ourselves we were able to possess death, we cannot likewise possess life through ourselves.

### 4

“In that day,” he says, “you will know that I am in my Father, and you are in me, and I am in you.” What day is this, except the day of which he said, “You will live”? For then we will be able to see what we believe.

Even now he is in us, and we are in him; but now we believe this, whereas then we will also know it. Although even now, by believing, we know it in some sense, then we will know it by contemplating it.

As long as we are in the body as it now is—that is, corruptible and weighing down the soul—we are away from the Lord; for “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5:6). Then we will walk by sight, because we will see him “as he is” (1 John 3:2).

For if Christ were not even now in us, the Apostle would not say: “If Christ is in you, although the body is dead because of sin, the Spirit is life because of righteousness” (Rom. 8:10).

That we too are even now in him he clearly shows where he says: “I am the vine, you are the branches” (John 15:5).

In that day, therefore, when we live by the life in which death will be swallowed up, we will know that he is in the Father, and we are in him, and he is in us; because then what has already been begun through him will be brought to completion, so that he may be in us and we in him.

### 5

“Whoever has my commandments,” he says, “and keeps them—that person is the one who loves me.” Whoever has them in memory and keeps them in life; whoever has them in words and keeps them in conduct; whoever has them by hearing and keeps them by doing; or whoever has them by doing and keeps them by persevering—that person, he says, is the one who loves me.

Love must be demonstrated by action, lest the name be an unfruitful designation.

“And whoever loves me,” he says, “will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him.”

What does “I will love” mean? Is it as though he will love him then and does not love him now? Certainly not. How could the Father love us without the Son, or the Son without the Father? Since they work inseparably, how could they love separately?

He said, “I will love him” with reference to what follows: “and I will manifest myself to him.” “I will love, and I will manifest”—that is, I will love for the purpose of manifesting myself.

For now he loved us so that we might believe and hold fast to the commandment of faith; then he will love us so that we may see and receive the vision itself as the reward of faith. [Note: Thus the manuscripts. Printed editions read, “by that vision itself”; and below, “believing what we do not see.”] Even now we love by believing what we will see; then we will love by seeing what we believe.

# TRACTATE LXXVI

On what follows, “Judas says to him—not the Iscariot,” and so forth, up to the statement, “The word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s, who sent me.” Chapter 14, verses 22–24.

[Col. 1831]

### 1

When the disciples asked questions and Jesus the Teacher answered them, we too learn as though we were learning with them whenever we read or hear the holy Gospel.

Since the Lord had said, “A little while, and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me,” Judas asked him about this very matter—not his betrayer, who was called Iscariot, but the Judas whose Epistle is read among the canonical Scriptures:

“Lord, what has happened, that you are going to manifest yourself to us and not to the world?”

Let us be with them as questioning disciples and listen also to the common Teacher. The holy Judas—not the unclean one, nor a persecutor of the Lord, but his follower—asked why Jesus would manifest himself to his own and not to the world; why, after a little while, the world would not see him, while they themselves would see him.

### 2

Jesus answered and said to him: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our dwelling with him. Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”

Here the reason is set forth why he will manifest himself to his own and not to strangers, whom he calls by the name “the world”; and it is also the reason why these love while those do not love.

This is the reason of which the sacred Psalm resounds: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause from an unholy nation” (Ps. 42:1).

Those who love are chosen because they love. [Note: Ten manuscripts read, “Those who are loved.”] But those who do not love—even if they speak in the tongues of human beings and of angels—become “a sounding bronze and a clanging cymbal”; and even if they have prophecy, know all mysteries and all knowledge, and possess all faith so as to move mountains, they are nothing; and even if they distribute all their possessions and hand over their body to be burned, it profits them nothing (1 Cor. 13:1–3).

Love distinguishes the saints from the world; love makes them “dwell together in unity” (Ps. 68:7). In this dwelling the Father and the Son make their habitation—the same ones who give love itself to those to whom, at the end, they also grant their own manifestation. This is what the disciple asked the Teacher, so that not only those who were then listening through his mouth, but we also, through his Gospel, might know it.

He had asked about Christ’s manifestation, and he heard about love and dwelling. There is therefore a certain inward manifestation of God, entirely unknown to the ungodly, for whom there is no manifestation of God the Father or of the Holy Spirit.

The manifestation of the Son, however, could be theirs—but in the flesh. Yet that manifestation is neither of the same kind as the inward manifestation nor, whatever its nature, can it remain with them always; it lasts only for a brief time, and that for judgment, not joy; for punishment, not reward.

### 3

Now, then, let us understand, insofar as he himself deigns to disclose it, how the statement is to be understood: “A little while, and the world will no longer see me, but you will see me.”

It is indeed true that shortly afterward he was going to remove from their eyes his body itself, in which even the ungodly could see him; for after the resurrection none of them saw him.

[Col. 1832] But since it was said with the testimony of the angels, “He will come in the same way as you saw him going into heaven” (Acts 1:11), and since we believe nothing other than that he will come in the same body for the judgment of the living and the dead, undoubtedly the world will then see him—the world by which those alienated from his kingdom are signified.

It is therefore far better understood that he wished to signify the time at the end of the age when he said, “A little while, and the world will no longer see me”: at that time he will be taken from the eyes of the condemned, so that thereafter those who love him, among whom the Father and he make their dwelling, may see him.

He said “a little while” because what seems prolonged to human beings is exceedingly brief before the eyes of God. The same John the Evangelist speaks of this brief period when he says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2:18).

### 4

Furthermore, lest anyone think that only the Father and the Son, without the Holy Spirit, make their dwelling with those who love them, let him recall what was said above concerning the Holy Spirit: “The world cannot receive him, because it does not see him or know him; but you will know him, because he will remain with you, and he will be in you” (John 14:17).

Behold, the Holy Spirit too makes his dwelling in the saints together with the Father and the Son—within them, certainly, as God in his temple.

God the Trinity—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—comes to us as we come to them. They come by assisting; we come by obeying. They come by enlightening; we come by contemplating. They come by filling; we come by receiving. Thus their vision in us is not external but inward, and their dwelling in us is not temporary but eternal.

The Son does not manifest himself in this way to the world. For “the world” here refers to those of whom he immediately added: “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.”

These are the ones who never see the Father or the Holy Spirit. They see the Son for a little while, not in order to be blessed but in order to be judged; nor do they see him in the form of God, where he is equally invisible with the Father and the Holy Spirit, but in the form of a human being, in which he willed to be contemptible to the world through suffering and terrifying through judgment.

### 5

As for what he added, “And the word that you hear is not mine but the Father’s, who sent me,” let us neither wonder nor be afraid. He is not less than the Father, but he is from the Father alone; he is not unequal to the Father, but he is not from himself.

For he did not lie when he said, “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words.” Behold, he called the words his own. Is he contradicting himself when he again says, “The word that you hear is not mine”?

Perhaps, because of a certain distinction, when he called them his own he used the plural—“words”; but when he spoke of “the word,” that is, the Word, he said that it was not his but the Father’s, wishing himself to be understood.

“For in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). The Word is not his in such a way as to be separate from the Father, but belongs to the Father. In the same way, the image is not his but the Father’s; nor is the Son himself his own, but the Father’s.

It is therefore right that the equal one should attribute to the author whatever he does, since he receives from him the very fact that he is equally and without distinction equal to him.

# TRACTATE LXXVII

On what follows, “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you,” up to the statement, “I give you my peace; not as the world gives do I give you.” Chapter 14, verses 25–27.

[Col. 1833]

### 1

In the preceding reading from the holy Gospel, which is followed by the one just recited, the Lord Jesus had said that he and the Father would come to those who love him and make their dwelling with them.

Earlier he had also said concerning the Holy Spirit: “You will know him, because he will remain with you, and he will be in you” (John 14:17). From this we understood that God the Trinity dwells together in the saints as in his temple.

Now, however, he says: “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you.” That dwelling, therefore, is one dwelling—the dwelling that he promised would be future—while this is another, the dwelling that he testifies is present.

The former is spiritual and is established inwardly in the mind; the latter is bodily and is displayed outwardly to the eyes and ears. The former blesses the liberated eternally; the latter visits those who are to be liberated in time.

According to the former, the Lord does not depart from those who love him; according to the latter, he goes away and departs.

[Note: Lov. has “returns.” The other manuscripts have “departs.”]

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you while remaining with you”—that is, in his bodily presence, by which he spoke visibly with them.

### 2

“But the Paraclete,” he says, “the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and remind you of everything that I have said to you.”

Does the Son speak and the Holy Spirit teach, so that we receive the words when the Son speaks but understand those same words when the Holy Spirit teaches? As though the Son spoke without the Holy Spirit, or the Holy Spirit taught without the Son! Or, rather, do not both the Son teach and the Holy Spirit speak, and when God speaks and teaches something, does not the Trinity itself speak and teach?

But since the Trinity exists, it was necessary to indicate its individual persons and for us to hear them distinctly while understanding them inseparably.

Hear the Father speaking where you read: “The Lord said to me, ‘You are my Son’” (Ps. 2:7). Hear him also teaching where you read: “Everyone who has heard from the Father and learned comes to me” (John 6:45).

You have just heard the Son speaking; for he says of himself: “Whatever I have said to you.” If you wish to know him also as teacher, recall the Teacher: “One is your Teacher,” he says, “Christ” (Matt. 23:10).

As for the Holy Spirit, whom you have just heard teaching in the statement, “He will teach you all things,” hear him also speaking where you read in the Acts of the Apostles that the Holy Spirit said to blessed Peter: “Go with them, because I have sent them” (Acts 10:20).

The whole Trinity therefore both speaks and teaches. But unless it were also commended individually, human weakness could in no way grasp it. Since the Trinity is wholly inseparable, it would never be known to be a Trinity if it were always spoken of inseparably.

For even when we say “the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit,” we surely do not say them simultaneously, although they cannot fail to exist simultaneously.

As for the addition “he will remind you,” we should understand that the command not to forget the most salutary admonitions also belongs to grace, which the Spirit brings to our remembrance.

[Col. 1834]

### 3

“I leave you peace,” he says; “I give you my peace.” This is what we read in the prophet: “Peace upon peace.” He leaves us peace as he departs; he will give us his peace when he comes at the end.

He leaves us peace in this age; he will give us his peace in the age to come. He leaves us his peace, in which we remain while conquering the enemy; he will give us his peace when we reign without an enemy.

He leaves us peace so that even here we may love one another; he will give us his peace where we can never disagree. He leaves us peace so that, while we are in this world, we may not judge one another concerning what is hidden within us; he will give us his peace when he reveals the thoughts of the heart, and then each person will receive praise from God (1 Cor. 4:5).

Yet our peace is in him and from him, whether it is the peace he leaves us as he departs to the Father or the peace he will give us when he leads us to the Father.

What does he leave us as he ascends from us except himself, while not departing from us? For he is our peace, “who has made both one” (Eph. 2:14).

He himself is therefore our peace, both when we believe that he exists and when we see him as he is (1 John 3:2). If, as long as we are in the corruptible body that weighs down the soul, we walk by faith and not by sight, he does not abandon us while we are pilgrims away from him (2 Cor. 5:6–7); how much more, then, when we come to sight itself, will he fill us from himself?

### 4

But what does it mean that when he says, “I leave you peace,” he does not add “my,” whereas when he says, “I give you,” he says “my”? Should “my” be understood even where it is not stated, since what is stated once may be referred to both expressions?

Or perhaps something is hidden here that must be requested and sought, something that is to be opened to those who knock. What if he wished his peace to be understood as the peace he himself possesses?

The peace that he leaves us in this age should rather be called our peace than his. Nothing contends within him, since he has no sin at all; but we now possess a peace in which we still say, “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6:12).

There is therefore some peace for us, since we delight in the law of God according to the inward person; but it is not complete, because we see another law in our members, warring against the law of our mind (Rom. 7:22–23).

Likewise, among ourselves we have peace because we trust one another to love one another; but this peace too is not complete, because we do not see one another’s thoughts, and we form opinions about one another—either for better or for worse—that do not correspond to what is actually within us.

Thus, even if this peace has been left to us by him, it is our peace. Unless it came from him, we would not possess even such peace; but he does not possess this kind of peace himself.

If we hold to the peace we have received until the end, we will possess the peace that he has, where nothing within us will oppose us and nothing in our hearts will be hidden from one another.

Nor am I unaware that the Lord’s words may also be understood as a repetition of the same statement: “I leave you peace; I give you my peace.” What he said once—“peace”—he repeated by saying “my peace,” and what he said once—“I leave you”—he repeated by saying “I give you.”

[Col. 1835] Let each person understand it as he wishes. But I am pleased—and I believe you are too, my beloved brothers—to hold fast to this understanding of peace: here we conquer the adversary in concord, and therefore we desire the peace in which we will have no adversary.

### 5

As for what the Lord added and said, “Not as the world gives do I give you,” what else does this mean except: I do not give to you as human beings who love the world give?

They give themselves peace so that, without the trouble of disputes and wars, they may enjoy not God but their friend, the world. And when they give peace to the righteous so that they will not persecute them, that peace cannot be true where there is no true concord, because their hearts are divided.

For just as one is called a partner who joins his lot with another’s, so one should be called *concordant* who joins hearts.

Let us therefore, beloved, to whom Christ leaves peace and gives his peace—not as the world gives, but as the one through whom the world was made gives it—join our hearts to one another and have one heart raised upward, lest it be corrupted on earth.

# TRACTATE LXXVIII

On the statement of the Lord, “Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid,” and so forth. Chapter 14, verses 27–28.

1. We have heard, brothers, the words of the Lord saying to his disciples: “Let not your heart be troubled, nor let it be afraid. You have heard that I said to you, ‘I am going away, and I am coming to you.’ If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I.”

Their hearts could therefore be troubled and afraid because he was going away from them, although he was to come to them—lest perhaps the wolf should attack the flock during this interval, in the shepherd’s absence. But from those whom the man was leaving, God was not abandoning them—for he himself was both Christ the man and Christ God.
