Thus he was going away in respect of what he was as man, and remaining in respect of what he was as God; he was going away in respect of what was confined to one place, and remaining in respect of what was everywhere. Why, then, should the heart be troubled and afraid when he was withdrawing from their eyes in such a way as not to withdraw from their hearts?

Indeed, even God, who is contained by no place, departs from the hearts of those who abandon him in their conduct, not with their feet; and he comes to those who turn toward him, not with their face but with faith, and draw near to him in mind, not in the flesh. But so that they might understand that he had said, “I am going away, and I am coming to you,” in respect of what he was as man, he added and said: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I.”

In that respect, therefore, in which the Son is not equal to the Father, he was going to the Father, from whom he will come to judge the living and the dead. But in that respect in which the Only-Begotten is equal to the one who begot him, he never departs from the Father; rather, with him he is wholly everywhere, in an equal divinity that no place contains.

“For when he was in the form of God,” as the Apostle says, “he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized.” For how could that be regarded as seizure which was not usurped but born by nature? “But he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II, 6–7)—not, therefore, by losing that form, but by taking this one. He emptied himself in such a way that here he appeared less than he remained with the Father. The form of a servant was added; the form of God did not depart. The former was assumed, not the latter destroyed.

On account of the former he says, “The Father is greater than I”; on account of the latter, “I and the Father are one” (John X, 30).

2. Let the Arian attend to this, and let him be sound through attention, lest through contentiousness he be vain—or, what is worse, insane. For this is the form of a servant, in which the Son of God is less not only than the Father but also than the Holy Spirit—and not merely that, but also less than himself, because in the form of God he is greater than himself.

For Christ the man is indeed called the Son of God, since even his flesh alone merited to be called so in the tomb. For what else do we confess when we say that we believe in the only-begotten Son of God, who was crucified and buried under Pontius Pilate? And what of him was buried except his flesh, without the soul? Accordingly, when we believe in the Son of God who was buried, we certainly call even the flesh that alone was buried the Son of God.

That same Christ, therefore, the Son of God, equal to the Father in the form of God, because he emptied himself—not by losing the form of God, but by taking the form of a servant—is greater even than himself, because the form of God, which was not lost, is greater than the form of a servant, which was assumed.

What, then, is surprising or unworthy if, speaking according to this form of a servant, the Son of God says, “The Father is greater than I,” while, speaking according to the form of God, that same Son of God says, “I and the Father are one”? They are one according to what he was as God, the Word; the Father is greater according to what “the Word became flesh” (John I, 1, 14).

I shall also say something which the Arians and Eunomians cannot deny: according to this form of a servant, the child Christ was also less than his parents when, being little, he was subject to his elders, as it is written (Luke II, 51).

What then, heretic? Although Christ is God and man, he speaks as man, and do you slander God? He commends human nature in himself; do you dare to disfigure the divine nature in him? Unbelieving and ungrateful, do you diminish the one who made you because he says what he became for your sake? The Son through whom man was made is equal to the Father; in order to be less than the Father, he became man. If this had not happened, what would man be?

3. Let our Lord and Teacher plainly say: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I.” Let us hear the teacher’s words with the disciples, and not follow the cunning of the deceiver with outsiders.

Let us acknowledge the twofold substance of Christ: the divine, in which he is equal to the Father, and the human, in which the Father is greater. Yet both together are not two but one Christ, lest God be a quaternity rather than a Trinity. For just as one man consists of a rational soul and flesh, so one Christ is God and man; and therefore Christ is God, a rational soul, and flesh.

We confess Christ in all these parts, and Christ in each one of them. Who is he through whom the world was made? Christ Jesus, but in the form of God. Who was crucified under Pontius Pilate? Christ Jesus, but in the form of a servant.

Likewise, concerning the individual components of which man consists: Who was not abandoned in hell? Christ Jesus, but in the soul alone. Who lay in the tomb for three days, awaiting resurrection? Christ Jesus, but in the flesh alone.

Thus Christ is spoken of in each of these individual parts. Yet all these together are not two or three, but one Christ.

Therefore he said, “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father.” Human nature ought to rejoice because it was so taken up by the only-begotten Word that it was established as immortal in heaven, and earth was so exalted that incorruptible dust should sit at the right hand of the Father.

This, then, is the way in which he said he would go to the Father. For clearly he was going to the one who was with him. But to go to him and withdraw from us meant to transform and make immortal what he had assumed from us as mortal, and to lift into heaven that by which he had been on earth for us.

Who would not rejoice at this, if he loves Christ in such a way that he rejoices that his own nature is already immortal in Christ and hopes that through Christ he himself will become so?

## TREATISE LXXIX

On the words, “And now I have told you before it happens,” etc., up to “Rise, let us go from here.” Chapter XIV, verses 29–31.

1. Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ had said to his disciples: “If you loved me, you would surely rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I.” Faith, fixed in religious minds rather than fabricated by slanderous and deranged minds, knows that he said this according to the form of a servant, not according to the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father.

Then he added: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened, you may believe.”

Why is this so, when a person ought rather to believe before what is to be believed happens? This is indeed the praise of faith: that what is believed is not seen. For what great thing is it if one believes what one sees, in accordance with that saying of the same Lord when he rebuked the disciple, saying, “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who have not seen and have believed” (John XX, 29)?

And I do not know whether someone should be said to believe what he sees; for faith itself is defined in the Epistle written to the Hebrews in this way: “Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things not seen” (Hebrews XI, 1).

[Note: [Col. 1837] Three manuscripts read “of things to be hoped for” (*sperandorum*); Am. and Bad., “of things to be hoped for” (*sperandarum*); Er., Lov., and most manuscripts, “of those hoping” (*sperantium*). Thus they vary again below, Treatise 95.]

Therefore, if faith concerns things that are believed, and that same faith concerns things that are not seen, what does the Lord’s saying mean: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened, you may believe”? Should he not rather have said: “And now I have told you before it happens, so that you may believe what you will see when it has happened”?

For the one to whom it was said, “Because you have seen me, you have believed,” did not believe what he saw; he saw one thing and believed another. He saw a man and believed God. He was seeing and touching living flesh, which he had seen dying, and he believed that God was hidden in that very flesh. He therefore believed with his mind what he did not see, through what appeared to the bodily senses.

But even if things that are seen are said to be believed—as each person says that he has believed his own eyes—this is not the faith that is built up in us. Rather, from things that are seen, we are moved to believe things that are not seen.

Accordingly, beloved, the point at issue in the Lord’s saying, “And now I have told you before it happens, so that when it has happened, you may believe,” is this: when it had happened, they would see him alive after his death and ascending to the Father. When they had seen this, they would believe that he was the Christ, the Son of the living God, who had been able to do this because he had foretold it before doing it.

They would believe this not with a new faith but with a strengthened one—or, more precisely, a faith that had almost failed when he died would be restored when he rose again. For they had believed even before that he was the Son of God; but when what he had foretold beforehand had happened in him, the faith that had been small when he spoke to them, and almost nothing when he died, revived and grew.

2. What does he say next? “I will no longer speak much with you, for the prince of this world is coming.” Who is this, except the devil? “And he has nothing in me”—that is, absolutely no sin.

Thus he shows that the devil is not the prince of creatures but of sinners, whom he now calls “this world.” Whenever the name “world” is used in an evil sense, it signifies only the lovers of this world, concerning whom it is written elsewhere: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world makes himself an enemy of God” (James IV, 4).

Let it therefore be far from us to understand the devil as the prince of the world as though he held dominion over the whole world—that is, over heaven and earth and all that is in them. It is of this world that it was said, when the Word Christ was being discussed: “The world was made through him” (John I, 10).

The whole world, therefore, from the highest heavens to the lowest earth, is subject to its creator, not to its deserter; to its redeemer, not to its destroyer; to its liberator, not to its captor; to its teacher, not to its deceiver.

But the Apostle Paul made clearer how the devil is to be understood as the prince of the world. After saying, “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood”—that is, against human beings—he added: “but against principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world” (Ephesians VI, 12).

In the following word he explained what he meant by “world,” when he added, “of this darkness,” so that no one would understand by “world” the entire creation, whose rulers the apostate angels certainly are not.

“Of this darkness,” he says—that is, of the lovers of this world. Yet from among these lovers some were chosen, not through their own merit but through the grace of God, to whom he says: “For you were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (ibid. V, 8).

For all were once under the rulers of this darkness—that is, under impious human beings—as darkness under darkness. But thanks be to God, who, as the same Apostle says, “has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians I, 12–13).

The prince of this world, that is, of this darkness, had nothing in Christ, because God had neither come with sin nor had the Virgin given birth to his flesh from the propagation of sin.

And as though someone were saying to him, “Why, then, do you die, if you have no sin deserving the punishment of death?” he immediately added: “But so that the world may know that I love the Father, and that I do just as the Father commanded me: rise, let us go from here.”

While reclining, he was speaking to those reclining with him. “Let us go,” he said—but where, except to the place from which he was to be handed over to death, although he had no merit deserving death?

Yet he had the Father’s command that he should die, like the one of whom it had been foretold: “What I did not steal, then I restored” (Psalm LXVIII, 5)—about to pay a death he did not owe and redeeming us from the death we did owe.

Adam, however, had stolen sin when, deceived by presumption, he stretched out his hand toward the tree, seeking to seize the incommunicable name of an unauthorized divinity—a divinity that nature, not theft, had bestowed upon the Son of God.

## TREATISE LXXX

On the words, “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer,” up to “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” Chapter XV, verses 1–3.

1. This Gospel passage, brothers, in which the Lord says that he is the vine and his disciples are the branches, is spoken according to the fact that he is the head of the Church and we are his members, “the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (I Timothy II, 5).

The vine and the branches are of one nature. For this reason, although he was God, whose nature we do not share, he became man, so that in him there might be a human nature that was the vine, of which we human beings could also be branches.

What, then, does “I am the true vine” mean? Did he add “true” in reference to that vine from which this likeness has been transferred? For he is called a vine by likeness, not by proper identity, just as he is called a sheep, a lamb, a lion, a rock, a cornerstone, and other things of this kind. Those things are more truly what they are in themselves, and these likenesses are drawn from them rather than being their proper identities.

But when he says, “I am the true vine,” he clearly distinguishes himself from the one of whom it is said: “How have you turned into bitterness, a foreign vine?” (Jeremiah II, 21). For how is that a true vine which was expected to produce grapes but produced thorns instead (Isaiah V, 4)?

2. “I am,” he says, “the true vine, and my Father is the farmer. Every branch in me that does not bear fruit, he will take away; and every one that bears fruit, he will cleanse, so that it may bear more fruit.”

Are the farmer and the vine, then, one and the same? Accordingly, Christ is the vine in the respect of which he says, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV, 28). But in the respect of which he says, “I and the Father are one” (ibid. X, 30), he himself is also the farmer.

He is not like those who perform their ministry by working externally; rather, he is such that he also gives growth internally. “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.”

Certainly Christ is God, because “the Word was God”; hence he and the Father are one. And if “the Word became flesh” (ibid. I, 1, 14)—something that it was not—it remains what it was.

Finally, after saying concerning the Father as farmer that he removes the fruitless branches but cleanses the fruitful ones so that they may bear more fruit, he immediately also showed himself to be the cleanser of the branches, which is the farmer’s work, not the vine’s. “Now you are clean,” he says, “because of the word that I have spoken to you.”

Behold, he too is the cleanser of the branches, and he has made his workers into branches. Although they do not give the growth, they do provide some assistance—but not from themselves: “For without me,” he says, “you can do nothing.”

Hear the workers themselves confessing this: “What, then, is Apollos? And what is Paul? Ministers through whom (δι’ ὧν) you believed, and each as the Lord gave. I planted, Apollos watered” (I Corinthians III, 5–7).

And this too was “as the Lord gave to each”; therefore it was not from themselves. But what follows, “God gave the growth,” he accomplishes not through them but through himself. This surpasses human humility and angelic sublimity, and belongs altogether to the farming Trinity.

“Now you are clean”—clean, that is, and still to be cleansed. For unless they were clean, they could not bear fruit; and yet every one who bears fruit the farmer cleanses, so that he may bear more fruit.

Who in this life is so clean that he does not need to be cleansed more and more? For “if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us; but if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity” (I John I, 8–9). He cleanses the clean—that is, the fruitful—so that they may be more fruitful the cleaner they become.

3. “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.” Why did he not say, “You are clean because of the Baptism with which you were washed,” but instead say, “because of the word that I have spoken to you”? Is it not because the word also cleanses in the water?

Take away the word, and what is water except water? The word is added to the element, and it becomes a sacrament, itself also as a kind of visible word.

He had certainly said this when he washed the disciples’ feet: “The one who has been washed has no need except to wash his feet, but is wholly clean” (John XIII, 10).

Whence does water have such great power that it touches the body and cleanses the heart, unless this is accomplished by the word—not because it is spoken, but because it is believed? For even in the word itself, one thing is the passing sound, and another the enduring power.

“This is the word of faith that we preach,” says the Apostle, “that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans X, 8–10).

Hence it is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Cleansing their hearts by faith” (Acts XV, 9). And blessed Peter says in his Epistle: “So also Baptism now saves you—not the removal of dirt from the flesh, but the appeal of a good conscience” (I Peter III, 21).

This is the word of faith that we preach, by which Baptism is undoubtedly consecrated so that it can cleanse.

Christ, the vine with us, and the farmer with the Father, loved the Church and gave himself for her. Read the Apostle and see what he adds: “That he might sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing of water in the word” (Ephesians V, 25–26).

Cleansing, therefore, would by no means be attributed to the flowing and transitory element unless “in the word” were added.

This word of faith has such power in the Church of God that through the believer who offers it, blesses it, and baptizes with it, it cleanses even a tiny infant, although the infant is not yet able to believe with the heart unto righteousness or confess with the mouth unto salvation.

All this is accomplished through the word of which the Lord says: “Now you are clean because of the word that I have spoken to you.”

[Note: [Col. 1840] Lov., “through her believing.” Other printed editions, “through him believing”; the manuscripts agree, lacking the word “offering.”]

## TREATISE LXXXI

On the words, “Remain in me, and I in you,” up to “Whatever you wish, ask, and it will be done for you.” Chapter XV, verses 4–7.

[Col. 1841]

1. Jesus said that he was the vine, his disciples the branches, and the Father the farmer; this was discussed earlier as well as we were able. In this reading, while he was still speaking about himself, who is the vine, and his branches, that is, his disciples, he says: “Remain in me, and I in you.”

They are not in him in the same way that he is in them. Yet both are beneficial not to him but to them. The branches are in the vine in such a way that they contribute nothing to the vine but receive from it the source of their life. The vine, however, is in the branches in such a way that it supplies them with vital nourishment rather than receiving it from them.

Therefore, both having Christ remain in them and remaining in Christ benefit the disciples, not Christ. For when one branch is cut off, another can sprout from the living root; but the branch that has been cut off cannot live without the root.

2. Finally he adds and says: “Just as the branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine, so neither can you, unless you remain in me.”

Great is the commendation of grace, my brothers: it instructs the hearts of the humble and closes the mouths of the proud. Let those who, “ignorant of God’s righteousness and wishing to establish their own, are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Romans X, 3), answer this, if they dare.

Let those who are pleased with themselves and do not think God necessary for doing good works answer this. Do not people of corrupt mind, “reprobate concerning the faith” (II Timothy III, 8), resist this truth—people who speak and utter iniquity, saying, “From God we have the fact that we are human beings, but from ourselves we have the fact that we are righteous”?

What are you saying, you who deceive yourselves—not defenders but destroyers of free choice—falling from the height of arrogance through the emptiness of presumption into the depths of submersion?

Indeed, your voice says that a person makes righteousness from himself. This is the height of your arrogance. But the truth contradicts you and says: “The branch cannot bear fruit by itself unless it remains in the vine.”

Go now over the precipices, and, having nowhere to take hold, boast yourselves in your windy speech. These are the emptinesses of your presumption.

But see what follows you, and if you have any understanding, shudder. For whoever thinks that he bears fruit from himself is not in the vine; whoever is not in the vine is not in Christ; whoever is not in Christ is not a Christian. These are the depths of your submersion.

3. Consider again and again what the truth further adds and says: “I am the vine,” he says, “you are the branches. Whoever remains in me, and I in him, bears much fruit, because without me you can do nothing.”

Lest anyone should think that a branch could bear at least some small fruit by itself, when he had said, “He bears much fruit,” he did not say, “because without me you can do little,” but “you can do nothing.”

Whether little or much, it cannot be done without the one without whom nothing can be done. For even if a branch has produced little, the farmer cleanses it so that it may produce more. Yet unless it remains in the vine and lives from the root, it cannot bear any amount of fruit by itself.

Although Christ would not be the vine unless he were man, he would not provide this grace to the branches unless he were also God.

But because one cannot live without this grace, while death nevertheless remains within the power of free choice, he says: “If anyone does not remain in me, he will be cast out like a branch, and will wither; and they will gather him and throw him into the fire, and he will burn.”

The wood of the vine is therefore all the more contemptible if it does not remain in the vine, and all the more glorious if it does remain. Finally, as the Lord also says concerning these things through the prophet Ezekiel, once cut off they are useful for none of the farmer’s purposes and are fit for no craftsman’s work (Ezekiel XV, 5).

One of two things awaits the branch: either the vine or the fire. If it is not in the vine, it will be in the fire. Therefore, so that it may not be in the fire, let it be in the vine.

4. “If you remain in me,” he says, “and my words remain in you, whatever you wish, ask, and it will be done for you.”

By remaining in Christ, what can they wish for except what accords with Christ? By remaining in the Savior, what can they wish for except what is not foreign to salvation?

We wish for one thing because we are in Christ, and another because we are still in this world. From our dwelling in this world something sometimes steals upon us, so that we ask for what, unknowingly, is not good for us.

But if we remain in Christ, far be it from us that this should be done for us, since when we ask, he does only what is beneficial to us.

Therefore, when we remain in him and his words remain in us, whatever we wish, we will ask, and it will be done for us. For if we ask and it is not done, we are not asking for what has a place in remaining in him, nor for what his words have that remain in us. We are asking instead from the desire and weakness of the flesh, which are not in him and in which his words do not remain.

The prayer that he taught certainly belongs to his words, in which we say: “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matthew VI, 9). Let us not depart in our petitions from the words and meaning of this prayer, and whatever we ask will be done for us.

His words are said to remain in us when we do what he commanded and love what he promised. But when his words remain in our memory and are not found in our life, the branch is not counted as being in the vine, because it does not draw life from the root.

The distinction is expressed in what is written: “To those who remember his commandments, so as to do them” (Psalm CII, 18). For many remember them in order to despise, mock, or even attack them.

Christ’s words do not remain in such people. They touch them in a certain way but do not cling to them; and therefore they will not be for their benefit but for their testimony. Since his words are in them in such a way that they do not remain in them, they are held by them for the purpose of being judged by them.

## TREATISE LXXXII

On the words, “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit,” up to “And I remain in his love.” Chapter XV, verses 8–10.

1. The Savior commends more and more to his disciples, by speaking to them, the grace by which we are saved: “In this,” he says, “my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit and become my disciples.”

Whether one says “glorified” or “made glorious,” both are translated from one Greek word, δοξάζειν (*doxazein*). For the Greek word δόξα (*doxa*) is *gloria* in Latin.

I thought this should be mentioned because the Apostle says: “If Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Romans IV, 2).

This is the glory before God by which God, not man, is glorified: when a person is justified not by works but by faith, so that what he also does well comes from God. For, as I have already said above, a branch cannot bear fruit by itself (Treatise 81, no. 2).

If God the Father is glorified in this—that we bear much fruit and become Christ’s disciples—let us not attribute this to our own glory, as though we possessed it from ourselves. This grace belongs to him, and therefore in this it is not our glory but his.

Hence elsewhere, after saying, “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works,” lest they think their good works came from themselves, he immediately added: “And let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew V, 16).

In this the Father is glorified: that we bear much fruit and become Christ’s disciples. By whom are we made so, except by him whose mercy precedes us? “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works” (Ephesians II, 10).

2. “As the Father loved me,” he says, “so I loved you. Remain in my love.”

Behold, from where our good works come. From where would they come to us except because “faith works through love” (Galatians V, 6)? And how would we love unless we were first loved?

The same evangelist said this most clearly in his Epistle: “Let us love God, because he first loved us” (I John IV, 19).

When he says, “As the Father loved me, and I loved you,” he is not showing an equality of our nature with his, as there is an equality between the Father and him, but the grace by which the man Christ Jesus is the mediator between God and human beings (I Timothy II, 5).

He shows himself to be the mediator when he says, “The Father loved me, and I loved you.” For the Father certainly loves us also, but in him, because in this the Father is glorified: that we bear fruit in the vine—that is, in the Son—and become his disciples.

3. “Remain,” he says, “in my love.” How shall we remain? Hear what follows: “If you keep my commandments,” he says, “you will remain in my love.”

Does love cause the commandments to be kept, or does keeping the commandments cause love? But who could doubt that love comes first? For one who does not love cannot keep the commandments.

When he says, therefore, “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love,” he shows not where love is generated but where it is demonstrated. It is as though he were saying: “Do not think that you remain in my love if you do not keep my commandments. If you keep them, you will remain.”

That is, it will be evident that you remain in my love if you keep my commandments. Let no one deceive himself by saying that he loves him if he does not keep his commandments. We love him precisely to the extent that we keep his commandments; to the extent that we keep them less, we love him less.

Although when he says, “Remain in my love,” it is not clear whether he means the love with which we love him or the love with which he loves us, the preceding words make the meaning clear. For he had said, “And I loved you,” and immediately added, “Remain in my love.” He therefore means the love with which he loved us.

What, then, does “Remain in my love” mean except “Remain in my grace”? And what does “If you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love” mean except this: “You will know by this that you remain in my love, with which I love you, if you keep my commandments”?

We do not therefore keep his commandments first so that he may love us; rather, unless he loves us, we cannot keep his commandments. This is the grace that is open to the humble and hidden from the proud.

4. But what is the meaning of what he adds: “As I have kept my Father’s commandments and remain in his love”?

Here too he surely wished this to be understood as the love with which the Father loves him. He had said, “As the Father loved me, and I loved you,” and then immediately added, “Remain in my love”—clearly, the love with which I loved you.

Therefore, when he also says of the Father, “I remain in his love,” we must understand this as the love with which the Father loved him.

But is grace also to be understood here as the means by which the Father loves the Son, just as grace is the means by which the Son loves us, since we are sons by grace, not by nature, whereas the Only-Begotten is Son by nature, not by grace?

Or must this also be referred in the Son himself to his humanity? Certainly so. For by saying, “As the Father loved me, and I loved you,” he shows the grace of the mediator.

The mediator between God and human beings is Christ Jesus not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is man. Indeed, according to what he is as man, it is written of him: “And Jesus advanced in wisdom and age and grace with God and human beings” (Luke II, 52).

Accordingly, we may rightly say that although human nature does not belong to the nature of God, human nature nevertheless belongs by grace to the person of the only-begotten Son of God—and with such grace that none is greater and none is equal to it.

For no merits preceded that assumption of humanity; rather, all his merits began from that assumption.

The Son therefore remains in the love with which the Father loved him, and for that reason he kept his commandments. For what is that man, indeed, except one whose protector is God (Psalm III, 4)? For God was the Word, the Only-Begotten coeternal with the one who begot him. But so that he might be given to us as mediator, through ineffable grace “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 1, 14).

## TREATISE LXXXIII

On the words, “I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be fulfilled. This is my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.” Chapter XV, verses 11–12.

1. You have heard, beloved, the Lord saying to his disciples: “I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be fulfilled.”

What is Christ’s joy in us except that he deigns to rejoice over us? And what is the joy of ours that he says is to be fulfilled except having fellowship with him? For this reason he had said to blessed Peter: “If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me” (ibid. XIII, 8).

His joy, therefore, in us is the grace that he has bestowed upon us; this same grace is also our joy.

[Note: [Col. 1845] Printed editions read “he is” (*ipse est*); the manuscripts read “it is” (*ipsa est*).]

Yet he rejoiced in it from all eternity, when he chose us before the foundation of the world (Ephesians I, 4). We cannot rightly say that his joy was not full. For God never rejoiced imperfectly.

But that joy of his was not in us, because we did not yet exist in whom it could be; nor, when we began to exist, did we begin to exist with him. Yet it was always in him, who rejoiced in us as those who would be his, with the absolute certainty of his foreknowledge.

Indeed, he already had perfect joy concerning us when he rejoiced in foreknowing and predestining us. For there could be no fear in that joy of his, lest what he knew he would do should perhaps not come to pass.

Nor, when he began to do what he had foreknown he would do, did his joy—the joy by which he is blessed—increase; otherwise he would have become more blessed because he made us. Far be this from us, brothers. God’s blessedness, which was not less without us, does not become greater because of us.

His joy, therefore, concerning our salvation, which was always in him when he foreknew and predestined us, began to be in us when he called us. And we rightly call this our joy, by which we too will be blessed.

But this joy of ours grows and advances, and through perseverance moves toward its perfection. It begins in the faith of those being reborn and will be fulfilled in the reward of those rising again.

This, I think, is the meaning of the words: “I have spoken these things to you so that my joy may be in you and your joy may be fulfilled.” Let my joy be in you; let your joy be fulfilled.

For my joy was always full, even before you were called, when you were foreknown by me as those who would be called. But it comes to be in you when you are made what I foreknew you would be.

Let your joy be fulfilled, because you will be blessed—something you are not yet—just as you were created, although you did not previously exist.

2. “This is,” he says, “my commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you.”

Whether one says “commandment” or “mandate,” both are translated from one Greek word, ἐντολή (*entolē*).

He had already spoken this saying earlier, and you should remember that I discussed it with you as best I could (above, Treatise 65). For there he said: “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another as I have loved you, so that you also may love one another” (John XIII, 34).

The repetition of this commandment is therefore a commendation of it. The difference is that there he says, “I give you a new commandment,” while here he says, “This is my commandment.” There, it is as though such a commandment had not existed before; here, as though he had no other commandment.

But there it was called “new” so that we should not remain in our old condition; here it is called “my” so that we should not think it may be disregarded.

### 3

But since he said here, “This is my commandment,” as though there were no other, what are we to think, my brothers? Is his only commandment the one concerning that love by which we love one another? Is there not also another, greater commandment—that we love God? Or did God command us only to love, so that we need seek nothing else? Certainly the Apostle commends three things when he says: “But faith, hope, and love remain—these three; but the greatest of these is love” (1 Cor. 13:13). And although those two commandments are included in love—that is, in charity—love is nevertheless said to be the greatest, not the only one.

How many commandments, then, have been given to us concerning faith, and how many concerning hope? Who can gather them all, or suffice to enumerate them? But let us consider what the same Apostle says: “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. 13:10). Where love is, what can be lacking? But where it is not, what can be of benefit? The demon believes (Jas. 2:19), but does not love; no one loves who does not believe. Someone who does not love may indeed hope for forgiveness—but in vain; whereas no one who loves can despair.

Therefore, wherever love is, faith and hope are necessarily present; and wherever there is love of neighbor, there is necessarily also love of God. For how can one who does not love God love his neighbor as himself, since he does not even love himself? He is impious and unrighteous; but whoever loves unrighteousness plainly does not love, but “hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6).

Let us therefore hold fast to this commandment of the Lord, that we love one another; and whatever else he has commanded, we will do [Note: Lovaniensis reads *faciamus* (“let us do”); other printed editions and most manuscripts read *faciemus* (“we will do”)], since whatever else there is, we have it here. For this love is distinguished from that love by which people love one another merely as human beings. To make the distinction, he added: “as I have loved you.” For why does Christ love us except so that we may be able to reign with Christ? Therefore let us also love one another for this purpose, so that our love may be distinguished from that of others, who do not love one another for this purpose—indeed, who do not truly love at all.

Those who love themselves for the sake of possessing God truly love themselves; therefore, in order to love themselves, they love God. This love is not found in all people: only a few love one another for the sake of this, “that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

## TRACTATE LXXXIV

### On the words, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” Chapter 15, verse 13

### 1

The Lord, dearly beloved brothers, defined the fullness of the love with which we ought to love one another when he said: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” Since, therefore, he had said above, “This is my commandment, that you love one another, as I have loved you,” he added the words you have now heard: “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” From this it follows that the same evangelist John says in his Letter: “Just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16)—loving one another, that is, as he loved us, who laid down his life for us.

Clearly this is what we read in the Proverbs of Solomon: “If you sit down to dine at the table of a powerful man, consider carefully and understand what is set before you; and so put out your hand, knowing that you must prepare such things” (Prov. 23:1–2). For what is the table of the powerful man except the place from which the body and blood of the one who laid down his life for us are received? And what is it to sit at that table except to approach humbly? What is it to consider and understand what is set before you except to reflect worthily upon so great a grace? And what is it to put out your hand in such a way that you know you must prepare such things, except what I have already said: that, just as Christ laid down his life for us, so we too ought to lay down our lives for the brothers?

As the Apostle Peter also says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). This is what it means to prepare such things. The blessed martyrs did this with ardent love. If we celebrate their memorials without emptiness or futility, and if we approach the Lord’s table at the feast by which they too were filled, then we ought, like them, to prepare such things.

For this reason we commemorate them at that very table not in the same way as we commemorate others who rest in peace, so that we may pray for them; rather, we commemorate them so that they may pray for us, and so that we may cling to their footsteps. They fulfilled the love concerning which the Lord said that there can be no greater. For they displayed to their brothers the very things they had received together from the Lord’s table.

### 2

Let this not be understood as though we could thereby become equal to the Lord Christ if we endured martyrdom for him even unto blood. He had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again (John 10:18); we, however, do not live as long as we wish, and we die even when we do not wish to die. When he died, he immediately killed death in himself; by his death we are delivered from death. His flesh did not see corruption (Acts 2:31); ours, after corruption, will at the end of the age be clothed by him with incorruption [Note: *Incorruptione* (“with incorruption”), according to Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition]. He did not need us in order to save us; without him we can do nothing. He offered himself to us as the vine to its branches; apart from him we cannot possess life.

Finally, even if brothers die for brothers, no martyr’s blood is poured out for the remission of the sins of his brothers, as his blood was poured out for us. In this matter he did not give us something to imitate, but something for which to give thanks. Thus, insofar as the martyrs shed their blood for their brothers, they displayed such things as they had received from the Lord’s table [Note: Six manuscripts add here: “Someone could imitate the one who was dying, but no one could imitate the one who was redeeming.” Three other manuscripts place this immediately before the words “if anyone should…”].

In the other matters I have mentioned—although I was unable to mention them all—the martyr of Christ is far unequal to Christ. If anyone were to compare himself not with Christ’s power, but with Christ’s innocence—if he were to claim not that he could heal someone else, but merely that he himself had no sin—even then he would be more presumptuous than the reason of salvation allows. He is far from him; he is not capable of so much.

It is well that this saying from Proverbs gives warning, for it immediately continues: “If you are too eager, do not desire his foods; for it is better that you take nothing from them than that you take more than you ought.” For these things, it says, possess a deceptive life—that is, hypocrisy. By saying that he is without sin, a person cannot make himself righteous; he can only pretend to be righteous. Therefore it is said: “For these things possess a deceptive life.”

There is only one who could both possess human flesh and be without sin. It is fitting, then, that what follows is commanded to us, and that human weakness is reproved by such a saying and proverb [Col. 1848]: “Do not exalt yourself, though you are poor, against the rich.” For Christ is rich: he was never subject either to inherited debt or to any debt of his own; he is himself righteous and justifies others.

Do not exalt yourself against him, poor as you are—so poor that you appear daily in prayer as a beggar for the remission of sins. “By your own counsel,” it says, “restrain yourself.” From what, if not from deceptive presumption? For because he is not merely human but also God, he is therefore never guilty.

“If you direct your eye toward him, it will nowhere appear” (Prov. 23:3–5). Your eye, that is, the human eye by which you perceive human things: if you direct it toward him, it will nowhere appear, because he cannot be seen in the way that you are able to see. “For he will prepare wings for himself like an eagle and will go to the house of his governor” (Prov. 23:5). From there he came to us, and he did not find us as he himself was.

Let us therefore love one another, as Christ also loved us and “gave himself for us” (Gal. 2:20). “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.” Let us imitate him through devout obedience, but let us never presume with any audacity to compare ourselves with him.

## TRACTATE LXXXV

### On the words, “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing.” Chapter 15, verses 14–15

### 1

When the Lord Jesus had commended the love he showed us by dying for us, and had said, “Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends,” he continued: “You are my friends if you do what I command you.”

What great condescension! A good servant cannot be one unless he has done the commands of his master; yet from the very thing by which good servants can be proved, the Lord wished his servants to be understood as his friends. But, as I have said, this is a condescension: the master knows them to be his servants, yet deigns to call them his friends.

To show that doing the commands of one’s master belongs to the duty of servants, the Lord rebukes servants elsewhere, saying: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46). When you say “Lord,” he says, show what you mean by carrying out his commands. Will he not say to an obedient servant: “Well done, good servant! Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. 25:21)? A person who is a good servant can therefore be both servant and friend.

### 2

But let us attend to what follows: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing.” How, then, are we to understand that a good servant is both servant and friend, when he says, “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing”?

He establishes the name “friends” in such a way as to remove the name “servants”—not so that both remain in one person, but so that one succeeds the other when the other departs. What does this mean? When we have done the Lord’s commands, will we not be servants? Will we not then be servants, when we have become good servants?

Who can contradict the truth that says, “I no longer call you servants”? And he explains why he said this: “Because a servant,” he says, “does not know what his master is doing.” Does a master not also entrust his secrets to a good and approved servant? What, then, does he mean by saying, “A servant does not know what his master is doing”? Very well: suppose he does not know what his master is doing. Does he not at least know what his master commands? For if he does not know even this, how does he serve? Or how is he a servant who does not serve?

Yet the Lord says: “You are my friends if you do what I command you. I no longer call you servants.” What a remarkable thing! Since we cannot serve unless we do the Lord’s commands, how will we not be servants by doing those commands? If I will not be a servant by doing the commands, and if I cannot serve unless I do the commands, then by serving I will not be a servant.

### 3

Let us understand, brothers; let us understand—and may the Lord make us understand this in ourselves, and also make us do what we have understood. If we know this, we certainly know what the Lord does, because the Lord alone makes us such people; and through this we belong to his friendship.

For just as there are two kinds of fear, which produce two kinds of people who fear, so there are two kinds of servitude, which produce two kinds of servants. There is a fear that perfect love casts out (1 John 4:18), and there is another fear, a holy fear, that endures forever and ever (Ps. 18:10).

The Apostle had in view the fear that is not in love when he said: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear” (Rom. 8:15). But he had the holy fear in view when he said: “Do not be arrogant, but fear” (Rom. 11:20). In the fear that love casts out, there is also a servitude that must be cast out together with that fear. For the Apostle joined the two—servitude and fear—when he said: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear.”

The Lord was considering the servant belonging to this servitude when he said: “I no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his master is doing.” It is not the servant belonging to holy fear, the one to whom it is said, “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your Lord,” but the servant belonging to the fear that must be cast out by love—the one of whom he says elsewhere: “A servant does not remain in the house forever; the son remains forever” (John 8:35).

Since, therefore, he has given us the power to become children of God (John 1:12), let us be children, not servants, so that, in a wondrous and ineffable yet nevertheless true manner, we may be servants who are not servants: servants, namely, through holy fear, to which belongs the servant who enters into his lord’s joy; but not servants through the fear that must be cast out, to which belongs the servant who does not remain in the house forever.

Let us recognize that the Lord makes us such servants who are not servants [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition think that the reading should be *Dominum facere scimus* (“we know that the Lord does this”). The manuscript reading is *Dominum facere sciamus* (“let us recognize that the Lord does this”)]. But that servant does not know this—the servant who does not know what his master is doing [Note: Most manuscripts do not contain the words “the servant who does not know”]. When he does something good, he is lifted up as though he himself were doing it, not his master; and he glories in himself rather than in his master, deceiving himself because he glories as though he had not received what he has (1 Cor. 4:7).

But we, dearly beloved, if we are to be able to be the Lord’s friends, must know what our Lord does [Col. 1850]. He makes us not merely human beings, but righteous human beings; and we do not make ourselves righteous. And who makes us know this, except he himself? For we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things given to us by God (1 Cor. 2:12).

Whatever good there is is given by him. Therefore, since this too is a good, it is given by him: namely, that we may know from whom every good is given, so that in every good thing the one who boasts may boast in the Lord (1 Cor. 1:31).

But what follows—“You, however, I have called friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you”—is so profound that it must not be confined within this discourse, but deferred to another.

## TRACTATE LXXXVI

### On the words, “But you I have called friends,” up to “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.” Chapter 15, verses 15–16

### 1

It is rightly asked how we should understand what the Lord said: “But you I have called friends, because everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you.” Who would dare affirm or believe that any human being knows everything that the only-begotten Son heard from the Father, when no one can even grasp how he hears any word from the Father, since he himself is the Father’s one Word?

Moreover, a little later, in this same discourse, which he delivered to the disciples after supper and before his passion, he says: “I have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). How, then, are we to understand that he made known to the disciples everything he heard from the Father, when he refrains from saying many things because he knows that they cannot yet bear them?

Without doubt, he says that he has done what he will do—he who made the things that are still to come. For through the prophet he says: “They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. 22:16), not “They will pierce,” speaking as though of past events while nevertheless proclaiming future ones. So here too he says that he has made known to the disciples everything that he knows he will make known in that fullness of knowledge of which the Apostle says: “When the perfect comes, the partial will pass away.” There he also says: “Now I know in part; then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known. Now we see through a mirror in a riddle; then face to face” (1 Cor. 13:10, 12).

The Apostle himself also says that we have been saved through the washing of regeneration (Titus 3:5); yet elsewhere he says: “In hope we have been saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience” (Rom. 8:24–25).

Hence his fellow Apostle Peter likewise says: “Though you do not now see him, you believe in him; and when you see him, you will rejoice with inexpressible and glorious joy, obtaining the reward of your faith, the salvation of your souls” (1 Pet. 1:8–9).

If, then, the present is the time of faith, while the salvation of souls is the reward of faith, who would doubt that the day must be completed in faith, which works through love (Gal. 5:6), and that at the end of the day the reward must be received—not only the redemption of our bodies, of which the Apostle Paul speaks (Rom. 8:23), but also the salvation of our souls, of which the Apostle Peter speaks?

The blessedness of both realities is therefore held in this present time and in this mortality more in hope than in possession. Yet there is this difference: our outward person, that is, our body, is still being corrupted, while the inward person, that is, the soul, is already being renewed day by day (2 Cor. 4:16).

Thus, just as we await the future immortality of the flesh and the salvation of our souls, although we are said already to have been saved by receiving a pledge of them, so we must hope for the future knowledge of everything that the only-begotten Son heard from the Father, although Christ has said that he has already accomplished this.

### 2

“You did not choose me,” he says, “but I chose you.” This is that ineffable grace. What were we when we had not yet chosen Christ, and therefore did not love him? For how can one who has not chosen him love him?

Was what is sung in the Psalm already in us: “I chose to be rejected in the house of the Lord rather than to dwell in the tents of sinners” (Ps. 84:10)? Certainly not. What, then, were we except unrighteous and lost?

We had not yet believed in him so that he might choose us. For if he chose us when we were already believers, then the one who was chosen chose [Note: All books read *electos elegit* (“he chose the chosen”), except one Remigius manuscript, which reads *electus elegit* (“the chosen one chose”). The Lovanienses had arrived at this latter reading by conjecture].

Why, then, would he say, “You did not choose me,” except because his mercy preceded us (Ps. 59:10)? Here the vain reasoning of those who defend God’s foreknowledge against God’s grace has no place. They say that we were chosen before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4) because God foreknew that we would become good, rather than because he himself would make us good.

This is not what the one who says, “You did not choose me,” says. For if he chose us because he foreknew that we would become good, he would also have foreknown that we would not first choose him. We could not otherwise become good—unless, perhaps, someone who does not choose the good is to be called good.

What, then, did he choose in those who were not good? They were not chosen because they were good, for they would not have been good unless they had been chosen. Otherwise grace is no longer grace, if we insist that merits came first.

This is the election of grace about which the Apostle says: “So too at the present time there is a remnant, chosen by grace.” And he immediately adds: “But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. 11:5–6).

Listen, ungrateful person, listen: “You did not choose me, but I chose you.” You cannot say, “I was chosen because I already believed.” For if you believed in him, you had already chosen him. But listen: “You did not choose me.”

You cannot say, “Before I believed, I was already doing good works; therefore I was chosen.” For what good work exists before faith, when the Apostle says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23)?

What, then, are we to say when we hear, “You did not choose me,” except that we were evil and were chosen so that, through the grace of the one choosing us, we might become good? It is not grace if merits came first; but grace does exist. Therefore grace did not find merits; it produced them.

### 3

And observe, dearly beloved, how he does not choose the good, but makes good those whom he has chosen. “I chose you,” he says, “and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.”

Is this not the fruit of which he had already said: “Apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5)? He therefore chose us and appointed us to go and bear fruit. We had no fruit from which he could choose us. “That you may go,” he says, “and bear fruit.” We go in order to bear fruit, and he himself is the way by which we go—the way in which he appointed us to go.

Thus, in everything, his mercy precedes us. “And that your fruit,” he says, “should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.”

Let love, then, remain; for love itself is our fruit. At present this love exists in desire, not yet in satisfaction, and even according to this desire the Father gives us whatever we ask in the name of his only-begotten Son.

But whatever is not expedient for those who are to be saved, let us not think that we ask in the name of the Savior. We ask in the name of the Savior for what belongs to the order of salvation.

## TRACTATE LXXXVII

### On the words of Jesus, “These things I command you, that you love one another,” up to “But I chose you out of the world; therefore the world hates you.” Chapter 15, verses 17–19

### 1

In the Gospel reading that preceded this one, the Lord had said: “You did not choose me, but I chose you and appointed you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain, so that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you.” You remember that we discussed these words as the Lord granted us to do.

But here, in the following reading, which you have just heard as it was read, he says: “These things I command you, that you love one another.” Accordingly, we must understand that this is our fruit, of which he said: “I chose you to go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain.”

And when he added, “So that whatever you ask the Father in my name, he may give you,” he will certainly give it to us if we love one another—provided that he himself has given us this very love, he who chose us when we had no fruit, because we had not chosen him; and appointed us to bear fruit, that is, to love one another.

We cannot have this fruit without him, just as branches can do nothing without the vine. Love, then, is our fruit, which the Apostle defines as proceeding “from a pure heart and a good conscience and sincere faith” (1 Tim. 1:5).

By this love we love one another; by this love we love God. For we would not love one another with true love unless we loved God. Each person loves his neighbor as himself if he loves God; for if he does not love God, he does not love himself.

“On these two commandments of love depend all the Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:40). This is our fruit. Therefore, commanding us concerning the fruit, he says: “These things I command you, that you love one another.”

Hence the Apostle Paul, when he wished to commend the fruit of the Spirit over against the works of the flesh, placed love at the beginning: “The fruit,” he says, “of the Spirit is love.” Then he connected the remaining qualities as though they had arisen from and been bound together with this head: joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control (Gal. 5:22–23).

Who rejoices well if he does not love the good from which he rejoices? Who can have true peace except with the one whom he truly loves? Who is patient in persevering steadfastly in the good unless he is fervent in love? Who is kind unless he loves the person whom he helps? Who is good unless he is made good through loving? Who is healthily faithful except with that faith which works through love? Who is usefully gentle if love does not govern him? Who restrains himself from what disgraces him unless he loves what ennobles him?

Rightly, then, the good teacher so often commends love as though it alone were to be commanded, since without it the other good qualities cannot profit, and since it cannot be possessed without the other good qualities by which a person becomes good.

### 2

For the sake of this love we must also patiently endure the world’s hatred. It is necessary that the world hate us when it sees that we do not desire what it loves.

But the Lord greatly consoles us by his own example. After saying, “These things I command you, that you love one another,” he added: “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before you.”

Why, then, does a member exalt itself above the head? You refuse to be in the body if you do not wish to endure the world’s hatred together with the head.

“If you were of the world,” he says, “the world would love what was its own.” He certainly says this to the whole Church, which he often also calls “the world,” as in the passage: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5:19). Likewise: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17).

And in his Letter John says: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2).

Thus the whole world is the Church, and the whole world hates the Church. The world hates the world: the enemy hates the reconciled, the condemned hates the saved, the polluted hates the cleansed.

### 3

But this world, which God reconciles to himself in Christ, which is saved through Christ, and to which every sin is forgiven through Christ, has been chosen out of the world that is hostile, condemned, and defiled.

From that mass which entirely perished in Adam are made vessels of mercy, in which there is the world belonging to reconciliation. This world is hated by the world belonging to the vessels of wrath, which are prepared for destruction (Rom. 9:21–23).

Finally, after saying, “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own,” he immediately added: “But because you are not of the world, and I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.”

They too, then, were from that place—from which they were chosen so that they might no longer be of it. They were chosen not because of their own merits, since no good works had preceded them; nor because of their nature, which had been wholly corrupted at its root through free choice; but by a free gift—that is, by true grace.

For the one who chose the world out of the world made what he chose; he did not find it already made. “A remnant,” he says, “has been saved by the election of grace. But if it is by grace, it is no longer by works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace” (Rom. 11:5–6).

### 4

But if it is asked how the world of destruction loves itself, since it hates the world of redemption, the answer is that it loves itself with a false love, not a true one. It therefore falsely loves itself [Col. 1854] and truly hates itself.

For “whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Ps. 10:6). He is said to love himself because he loves the iniquity by which he is unrighteous; and he is again said to hate himself because he loves what harms him.

Thus he hates nature in himself and loves vice; he hates what he was made to be through God’s goodness and loves what was made in him through free will.

Accordingly, we are both forbidden and commanded to love that world, if we understand rightly. We are forbidden when it is said to us: “Do not love the world” (1 John 2:15); but we are commanded when it is said: “Love your enemies” (Luke 6:27).

These are the very people who constitute the world that hates us. Therefore we are forbidden to love in them what they themselves love in themselves, and commanded to love in them what they themselves hate in themselves—namely, God’s workmanship and the various consolations of his goodness.

We are forbidden to love vice in them and commanded to love their nature, since they love vice in themselves and hate their nature. Thus we are to love and hate them rightly, while they love and hate themselves perversely.

## TRACTATE LXXXVIII

### On the words of Jesus, “Remember the word that I said,” and so forth, up to “But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.” Chapter 15, verses 20–21

### 1

As the Lord exhorted his servants to endure the world’s hatred patiently, he set before them no greater or better example than his own. For, as the Apostle Peter says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21).

If we do this, we do it with his help—he who said, “Apart from me you can do nothing.” To those to whom he had already said, “If the world hates you, know that it has hated me before you,” he now says, in the passage you heard when the Gospel was read:

“Remember the word that I said to you: ‘A servant is not greater than his master.’ If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours.”

By saying, “A servant is not greater than his master,” does he not clearly show how we ought to understand what he said above: “I no longer call you servants” (John 15:5; 18:15)? For here he plainly calls them servants.

What else does “A servant is not greater than his master; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” mean? It is therefore clear that the servant who does not remain in the house forever (John 8:35)—the servant belonging to the fear that love casts out (1 John 4:18)—is to be understood where it was said, “I no longer call you servants.”

But here, where it is said, “A servant is not greater than his master; if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you,” the servant belonging to the holy fear that endures forever and ever is signified (Ps. 18:10). This is the servant who will hear: “Well done, good servant; enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25:21).

### 2

“But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.”

What “all these things” will they do, except the things he mentioned—namely, hate them, persecute them, and despise their word? For if they did not keep their word but nevertheless did not hate them or persecute them—or even if they hated them but did not persecute them—they would not do all these things.

“They will do all these things to you on account of my name” means nothing other than this: they will hate me in you, persecute me in you, and will not keep your word because it is mine. For “they will do all these things to you on account of my name”—not your name, but mine.

Thus those who do such things on account of this name are all the more miserable, while those who suffer such things on account of this name are all the more blessed, as he says elsewhere: “Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness’ sake” (Matt. 5:10).

For this is what it means to suffer for me, or for my name: as the Apostle teaches, Christ “became for us wisdom from God, and righteousness and sanctification and redemption, so that, as it is written, ‘Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord’” (1 Cor. 1:30–31).

The wicked do these things to the wicked, but not for the sake of righteousness; and therefore both are miserable, both those who do them and those who suffer them. The good also do such things to the wicked; and although the good do them for the sake of righteousness, the wicked do not suffer them for the sake of righteousness.

### 3

Someone may say: If the wicked, when they persecute the good on account of Christ’s name, cause the good to suffer for the sake of righteousness, then surely the wicked do these things to them for the sake of righteousness. If this is so, then when the good persecute the wicked for the sake of righteousness, the wicked too suffer for the sake of righteousness.

For if the wicked can persecute the good on account of Christ’s name, why can the wicked not suffer persecution from the good on account of Christ’s name—and what would this be except suffering for righteousness?

If the wicked do not suffer for the same reason for which the good act—if the good act for the sake of righteousness, while the wicked suffer for the sake of unrighteousness—then the wicked cannot act for the same reason for which the good suffer. The wicked act because of unrighteousness, while the good suffer because of righteousness.

How, then, can it be true that “they will do all these things to you on account of my name,” when they do not act on account of Christ’s name—that is, not on account of righteousness, but on account of their own unrighteousness?

The question is resolved if we understand the words “They will do all these things to you on account of my name” as referring entirely to the righteous, as though it had been said: “You will suffer all these things from them on account of my name.” Thus “they will do to you” means “you will suffer from them.”

But if “on account of my name” is understood as though he were saying, “on account of my name, which they hate in you,” it can also be understood as “on account of the righteousness that they hate in you” [Note: Most manuscripts omit the words, “It can also be understood as ‘on account of the righteousness that they hate in you.’”].

Accordingly, when the good persecute the wicked, they can rightly be said to act both for the sake of righteousness, which they pursue by loving it, and because of the unrighteousness that they hate in the wicked. So too the wicked can be said to suffer both because of the unrighteousness that is punished in them and because of the righteousness exercised in their punishment.

### 4

A further question may be asked. If the wicked also persecute the wicked—as when impious kings and judges, while persecutors of the godly, punished murderers, adulterers, and every kind of criminal whom they found to have acted contrary to the public laws—how are we to understand the Lord’s saying: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own” (John 15:19)?

For the world does not love those whom it punishes, although we see it often punishing the kinds of crimes just mentioned. The answer is that the world exists among those by whom such crimes are punished, and the world exists among those by whom such crimes are loved.

The world, therefore, which is understood to exist among the wicked and impious, hates what is its own insofar as it harms the criminal; and it loves what is its own insofar as it favors those very criminals who share in the same crimes.

Thus, “They will do all these things to you on account of my name” either means “because of what you suffer,” or “because of what they themselves do,” since, in persecuting you, they hate this very thing in you.

And he added: “Because they do not know him who sent me.” This must be understood according to the kind of knowledge of which it is written elsewhere: “To know you is complete understanding” (Wis. 6:16).

Those who know the Father from whom Christ was sent by this knowledge can in no way persecute those whom Christ gathers, because they themselves are gathered together with them by Christ.

## TRACTATE LXXXIX

### On the words of the Lord, “If I had not come and spoken to them,” up to “Whoever hates me hates my Father also.” Chapter 15, verses 22–23
### 1

Above, the Lord had said to his disciples: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.” If we ask of whom he was speaking, we find that he came to these words from what he had said: “If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you.” But now, when he added, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” he indicated the Jews more explicitly. Thus he was speaking of them in those earlier statements as well; the very sequence of the words shows this.

For he says of them, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” of those concerning whom he had said: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you; if they kept my word, they will also keep yours. But they will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know him who sent me.” To these words he adds this also: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.”

The Jews, therefore, persecuted Christ, as the Gospel most clearly indicates. Christ spoke to the Jews, not to the other nations. In them, therefore, he intended the world to be understood—the world that hates Christ and his disciples; indeed, he showed that not they alone, but also these disciples, belong to that same world.

What, then, does he mean by: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin”? Were the Jews without sin before Christ came to them in the flesh? Who, even if utterly foolish, would say that? Rather, he wishes a certain great sin—not every sin—to be understood under the general designation. This is the sin that holds all sins together, and if anyone does not have it, all his sins are forgiven. It is this: that they did not believe in Christ, who came precisely so that people might believe in him. If he had not come, they would certainly not have had this sin.

His coming became as salutary for believers as it became destructive for unbelievers—as though he himself, the head and prince of the Apostles, had become for some what they themselves said of him: “For some we are an aroma from life to life, and for others an aroma from death to death” (II Cor. 2:16).

### 2

But what he added—“Now, however, they have no excuse for their sin”—may trouble those who ask whether those to whom Christ did not come and to whom he did not speak have an excuse for their sin. If they do not have one, why is it said here that these people do not have one because he came and spoke to them? If they do have one, is it so that they may be exempted from punishment, or so that they may be punished more mildly?

In response to these questions, as far as I understand them, with the Lord’s help I answer that they do have an excuse—not for all their sin, but for the sin by which they did not believe in Christ, who did not come to them and did not speak to them.

Those, however, to whom he came in the disciples, and to whom he spoke through the disciples—which he still does—are not included among them. For through his Church he came to the Gentiles, and through the Church he speaks to the Gentiles. To this belongs what he said: “Whoever receives you receives me” (Matt. 10:40), and: “Whoever despises you despises me” (Luke 10:16). Or do you wish, the apostle Paul says, “to receive proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ” (II Cor. 13:3)?

### 3

It remains to ask whether those who were overtaken by the end of this life—whether before Christ came to the Gentiles in the Church and before they heard his Gospel, or before those events reached them—can have this excuse.

They certainly can, but for that reason they cannot escape condemnation. “For all who have sinned without the Law will also perish without the Law, and all who have sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Rom. 2:12).

Since the Apostle’s words—“they will perish”—sound more terrifying than “they will be judged,” they seem not only to offer no support for this excuse, but even to make the burden heavier. Those who excuse themselves because they did not hear will perish without the Law.

### 4

But it is rightly asked whether those who, when they heard, despised or even resisted—opposing not merely by contradiction but also by persecuting with hatred those from whom they heard—are to be counted among those concerning whom the statement “they will be judged by the Law” seems to signify something less severe.

If perishing without the Law is one thing and being judged by the Law another, and if the former is more severe while the latter is milder, then these people certainly must not be placed under the milder punishment. For they did not sin under the Law; rather, they altogether refused to receive Christ’s Law and, so far as they were concerned, wanted it to be entirely null.

Those sin under the Law who are under the Law—that is, those who accept it and confess it to be holy, and the commandment to be holy, just, and good (Rom. 7:12), but who through weakness do not fulfill what they cannot doubt is most rightly commanded by it.

These people perhaps can in some way be distinguished from the perdition of those who are without the Law—provided that the Apostle’s statement, “they will be judged by the Law,” is to be understood as though he had said, “they will not perish.” It would be strange if that were so.

For he was not speaking of unbelievers and believers when he said this, but of Gentiles and Jews. Certainly, unless both are saved in that Savior who came “to seek what was lost” (Luke 19:10), they will without doubt belong to perdition. It may, however, be said that some will perish more severely and others more mildly—that is, that some will suffer heavier and others lighter punishments in their perdition.

For whoever is separated by punishment from that blessedness which God gives to his saints is said to perish for God. The punishments are as varied as the sins; how these matters are ordered, divine wisdom judges more deeply than human conjecture can investigate or declare.

Certainly, those to whom Christ came and to whom he spoke do not have, regarding the great sin of unbelief, the excuse by which they could say, “We did not see; we did not hear”—whether that excuse would not be accepted by him whose judgments are inscrutable, or whether it would be accepted, not so that they might be freed from all condemnation, but certainly so that they might be condemned somewhat more lightly.

### 5

“Whoever hates me,” he says, “hates my Father.”

Perhaps someone will say to us here: Who can hate someone whom he does not know? And certainly, before saying, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin,” he had said to his disciples: “They will do these things to you because they do not know him who sent me.” How, then, can they both not know and hate him?

For if they form an opinion not of what he actually is but of something else about him, then they are not found to hate him himself, but that which they invent—or rather suppose in error.
