Yet unless human beings could hate what they do not know, the Truth would not have said both that they do not know and that they hate his Father.

How this can happen may be demonstrated through us with the Lord’s help; but since this discussion must now be brought to a close, it cannot be done here.

## TREATISE XC

### On the words, “Whoever hates me hates my Father.” Chapter 15, verse 23

### 1

You have heard the Lord saying: “Whoever hates me hates my Father.” Earlier he had said: “They will do these things to you because they do not know him who sent me.” Thus a question necessarily arises that must not be concealed: How can they hate someone whom they do not know?

If they suspect or believe God to be not what he is but something else, and hate that, then they do not hate him himself, but what they conceive through their false suspicion or empty belief. If, however, they think of him as he is, how are they said not to know him?

With human beings, it can happen that we love people whom we have never seen; consequently, by the converse reasoning, it is not impossible that we hate people whom we have never seen. For a report about someone, whether speaking well or ill, can reasonably cause us to love or hate someone unknown.

But if the report is true, how can the person about whom we have learned the truth be called unknown? Is it because we have not seen his face? Yet he himself does not see his own face, and nevertheless no one can be more known to him than he is to himself. Knowledge of someone, therefore, is not communicated to us through his bodily face. Rather, he becomes open to our knowledge when his character and life are not hidden.

Otherwise, no one could know himself, since no one can see his own face. Yet he certainly knows himself more surely than he is known by others, insofar as he can more surely see, by his inward vision, what he understands, what he desires, and what he lives. When these things are also disclosed to us, then he truly becomes known to us.

Since such matters are often conveyed to us about absent people, or even the dead, either by report or by letters, it happens that we frequently hate or love people whose bodily faces we have never seen—though not people whom we entirely fail to know.

### 2

Yet our belief about such people is often deceived, because both history and, even more, rumor sometimes lie. It is important for us not to be deceived by a destructive opinion. Since we cannot investigate the conscience of human beings, we should form a true and certain judgment about the things themselves [Note: [Col. 1859] Eight manuscripts read “knowledge.”].

That is, if we do not know whether this or that person is unchaste or chaste, we should nevertheless hate unchastity and love chastity. If we do not know whether this or that person is unjust or just, we should nevertheless love justice and detest injustice—not those qualities that we ourselves invent in error, but those that we faithfully discern in God’s truth as to be sought or avoided.

Thus, when we desire what ought to be desired in the things themselves and avoid what ought to be avoided, we are forgiven for sometimes—or rather, continually—forming false opinions about the hidden things of human beings.

For I think this belongs to the human temptation without which this life cannot be lived, so that the Apostle says: “No temptation has overtaken you except what is human” (I Cor. 10:13). What is more human than being unable to look into the human heart, and therefore not to search out its hidden places, but often to suspect that something other than what is happening there is taking place?

Nevertheless, even amid these darknesses of human affairs—that is, of other people’s thoughts—even if, because we are human beings, we cannot understand our suspicions, we must still maintain judgments, that is, definite and firm conclusions. We must judge nothing before the proper time, until the Lord comes, “who will bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the intentions of hearts; and then each one will receive praise from God” (I Cor. 4:5).

Therefore, when we do not err concerning things, so that our rejection of vices and approval of virtues are right, then, even if we err concerning people, the human temptation is pardonable.

### 3

Through this darkness of human hearts, something greatly astonishing and greatly grievous occurs: sometimes we think someone unjust, although he is just, and, while unknowingly loving the justice in him, we avoid and shun him, prevent him from approaching us, and refuse to share life and livelihood with him. If the necessity of imposing discipline compels us—either to prevent him from harming others or to make him more corrigible—we may even pursue him with salutary severity. Thus, without knowing it, we afflict a good person as though he were evil, even though we love him.

This happens, for example, if someone is chaste but is believed by us to be unchaste. For if I love the chaste person, then the person I love is precisely what he is. Therefore I also love him himself, though I do not know it. And if I hate the unchaste person, then I do not hate him himself, because he is not what I hate. Yet, unknowingly, I wrong my beloved, with whom my soul always dwells in the charity of chastity—not by erring in distinguishing virtues and vices, but amid the darkness of human hearts.

Accordingly, just as it can happen that a good person unknowingly hates a good person—or rather, unknowingly loves him, since he loves the person himself when he loves what is good, because he loves in the other what that person is—but unknowingly hates not the person himself, but what he thinks the person is, so it can happen that an unjust person hates a just person.

While he thinks he loves an unjust person like himself, he unknowingly loves the just person; yet, while believing him to be unjust, he loves not the person himself but what he thinks the person is.

The same applies to God as to a human being. Finally, if the Jews were asked whether they loved God, what else would they answer but that they did love him—not lying deliberately, but rather forming that opinion in error? For how could they love the Father of truth when they hated the truth?

They do not want their deeds to be condemned, while it belongs to truth to condemn such deeds. Thus they hate the truth as much as they hate the punishments that truth inflicts upon such deeds. But they do not know that the truth is what condemns people such as themselves. Therefore they hate what they do not know; and when they hate it, they certainly cannot help hating him from whom it was born.

Since they do not know that the truth by which they are condemned in judgment was born from God the Father, they both do not know him and hate him.

O wretched people! They want to be evil, yet do not want the truth by which the evil are condemned to exist. They do not want truth to be what it is, when they ought instead not to want to be what they are, so that, while truth remains what it is, they might be changed and not be condemned when truth judges.

## TREATISE XCI

### On the words, “If I had not done among them works that no one else did,” up to, “Because they hated me without cause.” Chapter 15, verses 24–25

### 1

The Lord had said: “Whoever hates me hates my Father.” For whoever hates the truth must necessarily hate him from whom the truth was born; we have spoken about this as far as was granted to us.

Then he added the words about which we must now speak: “If I had not done among them works that no one else did, they would not have sin.” This refers, of course, to that great sin about which he had also said above: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” It is the sin by which they did not believe in him who spoke and acted among them.

They certainly did have other sins before he spoke and acted among them. But this sin—their failure to believe in him—is mentioned in this way because all the others are held together by it. If they did not have this sin and believed in him, the others would also be forgiven.

### 2

But what does it mean that, after saying, “If I had not done works among them,” he immediately added, “that no one else did”?

Among Christ’s works, none seem greater than the raising of the dead. Yet we know that the ancient prophets also did this. Elijah did so (III Kings 17:21–22); Elisha did so both while he was living in the flesh (IV Kings 4:35) and while he lay buried in his tomb. For some people carrying a dead man, having taken refuge there when enemies attacked, laid him down in the tomb, and he immediately came back to life (ibid. 13:21).

Nevertheless, Christ did certain things that no one else did: he fed five thousand people with five loaves and four thousand with seven loaves (Matt. 14:15–21; 15:32–38); he walked upon the waters and enabled Peter to do the same (ibid. 14:25, 29); he changed water into wine (John 2:9); he opened the eyes of a man born blind (ibid. 9:7); and there are many other examples that would take too long to recount.

But we are answered that others did works that Christ himself did not do, while some works were done that no one else did. For who but Moses struck the Egyptians with so many and such great plagues (Exod. 7–12), led the people through the divided sea (ibid. 14:21–29), obtained manna from heaven for the hungry (ibid. 16), and poured water from the rock for the thirsty (ibid. 17:6)?

Who but Joshua son of Nun divided the waters of the Jordan for the people to cross (Josh. 3), and, through prayer addressed to God, restrained and fixed the moving sun (ibid. 10:12–14)?

Who but Samson, because of his thirst, was refreshed by the overflowing jawbone of a dead ass (Judg. 15:19)? Who but Elijah was carried aloft in a fiery chariot (IV Kings 2:11)? Who but Elisha, as I mentioned shortly before, gave life to another corpse through his own buried body? Who but Daniel lived unharmed among the mouths of hungry lions shut up with him (Dan. 6:22)? Who but the three men—Ananias, Azariah, and Mishael—walked unharmed amid blazing flames that did not burn them (ibid. 3:93)?

### 3

I pass over the remaining examples, since I think these are sufficient to show that certain holy people also performed wondrous works that no one else did.

But no one among the ancients is recorded to have healed so many diseases, infirmities, and afflictions of mortals with such power. To say nothing of those whom he saved individually by commanding them, as they came before him, the evangelist Mark says in one place:

“When evening came, after the sun had set, they brought to him all who were sick and those possessed by demons. And the whole city was gathered at the door. He healed many who were afflicted with various diseases, and he cast out many demons” (Mark 1:32–34).

When Matthew recalled this, he also added prophetic testimony, saying: “So that what was spoken through the prophet Isaiah might be fulfilled: ‘He himself took our infirmities and bore our diseases’” (Matt. 8:17).

In another place Mark says: “Wherever he entered, into villages or towns or cities, they laid the sick in the marketplaces and begged him that they might touch even the fringe of his garment; and all who touched him were healed” (Mark 6:56).

No one else did these things among them. For “among them” must be understood not as “among” or “before” them, but precisely “in them,” because he healed them.

He intended these works to be understood as works that not only inspired wonder but also plainly conferred salvation. For such benefits they ought to have returned love, not hatred.

All the miracles of the others are indeed surpassed by the fact that he was born of a virgin, and that alone he was able neither to violate his mother’s integrity by being conceived nor by being born. But this did not take place before them or in them. The Apostles reached knowledge of the truth of this miracle not through a common sight shared with them, but through discipleship distinct from them.

The fact that, on the third day, he restored himself alive from the tomb in the flesh in which he had been killed, and then ascended with that flesh into heaven, never again to die, surpasses everything he did. But this too did not take place in the Jews or before them; and he had not yet done it when he said: “If I had not done among them works that no one else did.”

Clearly, therefore, he means the works by which he displayed such great miracles of healing in their infirmities as no one had previously bestowed upon them. They saw these works, and, reproaching them for this, he adds and says:

“Now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father. But this is so that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘Because they hated me without cause.’”

He calls it “their Law,” not because they invented it, but because it was given to them—just as we say, “our daily bread,” although we ask it from God when we add, “Give it to us” (Matt. 6:11).

A person hates without cause when he seeks no advantage from his hatred or avoids no disadvantage. Thus the ungodly hated the Lord; thus the righteous love him—that is, without cause—so that they expect no other good besides him, since he himself will be all things in all.

Whoever considers more deeply what Christ says—“If I had not done among them works that no one else did”—will find that he himself performed such works whenever a human being belonging to God performed anything of the kind. Even if the Father or the Holy Spirit performed these works, no one else performed them, because the whole Trinity has one substance.

He will find that Christ himself performed them. For he can do all things in himself and through himself, while no one can do anything without him. Christ, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, is not three gods but one God, of whom it is written: “Blessed is the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wondrous things” (Ps. 71:18).

No one else, therefore, performed whatever works he performed among them, because whenever another human being performed any of them, he performed it through Christ, who was acting. But Christ performed these works himself, without their performing them.

## TREATISE XCII

### On the words, “When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth,” and so forth. Chapter 15, verses 26–27

### 1

The Lord Jesus, in the discourse he delivered to his disciples after supper, when his passion was near and he was about to go away and leave them in bodily presence, but was to remain with all his own in spiritual presence until the end of the age, encouraged them to endure the persecutions of the ungodly, whom he called by the name “the world.”

Yet he also said that he had chosen the disciples themselves from this world, so that they might know that they are what they are by God’s grace, whereas by their own vices they had been what they once were.

Then he clearly identified the persecutors of both himself and his disciples as Jews, so that it might be entirely evident that even these people were included under the designation of the condemnable world—the world that persecutes the saints [Note: [Col. 1862] Five manuscripts read, “who persecute the saints.”].

When he said that they did not know the one by whom he had been sent and nevertheless hated both the Son and the Father—that is, both the one who was sent and the one by whom he was sent—we have already discussed these matters in other sermons. He came to the point where he said: “So that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘Because they hated me without cause.’”

Then, as though this naturally followed, he added the passage about which we have now begun to speak:

“When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me; and you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

How does this relate to what he had said: “Now they have both seen and hated both me and my Father. But this is so that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘Because they hated me without cause’”?

Is it because, when the Paraclete—the Spirit of truth—came, he convicted those who had seen and hated with a more manifest testimony? Indeed, he also converted some of those who had seen and still hated to the faith that works through love (Gal. 5:6), by revealing himself to them.

To understand this in that way, let us recall how it happened. On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit came upon one hundred and twenty people gathered together, among whom were all the Apostles. When they had been filled with the Spirit and spoke in the languages of all nations, many of those who hated him [Note: [Col. 1863] The manuscripts read, “were present.”], astonished by so great a miracle—for they saw, while Peter spoke, such a great and divine testimony being borne about Christ that the one whom they had killed and counted among the dead was proved to have risen and to be alive—were cut to the heart and converted.

They received forgiveness for having shed such an immense amount of blood so impiously and savagely, being themselves redeemed by the very blood they had shed (Acts 2:2).

For Christ’s blood was poured out for the forgiveness of all sins in such a way that it could even blot out the very sin by which it was poured out.

With this in view, the Lord said: “They hated me without cause. But when the Paraclete has come, he will bear witness about me”—as though he were saying: “They hated me and killed me while they saw me; but the Paraclete will bear such testimony about me that he will make them believe in me without seeing me.”

### 2

“And you,” he says, “will also bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.”

The Holy Spirit will bear witness, and you will also bear witness. Since you have been with me from the beginning, you can proclaim what you know. The reason you do not do so now is that the fullness of that Spirit is not yet present in you.

He, therefore, will bear witness about me, and you will bear witness. For God’s love, poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who will be given to you, will give you confidence to bear witness (Rom. 5:5).

This confidence was still lacking in Peter when, terrified by the questioning of a servant girl, he could not bear true witness, but, compelled by great fear, denied the Lord three times, contrary to his promise (Matt. 26:69–74).

But this fear is not in love; rather, perfect love casts out fear (I John 4:18).

Finally, before the Lord’s passion, his servile fear was questioned by a female servant; after the Lord’s resurrection, his free love was questioned by the Prince of freedom himself (John 21:15). Therefore, in the first situation he was troubled, but in the second he was calm; there he denied the one he had loved, while here he loved the one he had denied.

Yet even at that time his love was still weak and narrow, until the Holy Spirit strengthened and expanded it. After the abundance of a more generous grace had been poured into him, the Spirit kindled his formerly cold heart to bear witness to Christ and opened those previously trembling lips that had suppressed the truth.

Thus, when all those upon whom the Holy Spirit had come were speaking in the languages of all nations, while the crowds of Jews stood around, Peter alone emerged more boldly than the rest to bear witness to Christ and confound his killers with the testimony of his resurrection.

If anyone delights in contemplating such a holy spectacle, so pleasing to the taste [Note: [Col. 1864] Three manuscripts read, “so agreeable”], let him read the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2–5). There he will marvel at the blessed Peter preaching, whom he had grieved when he denied the Lord. There let him see that tongue transferred from distrust to confidence and from servitude to freedom, converting so many tongues of enemies to confession of Christ—tongues one of which he had been unable to endure and therefore had turned to denial.

Why say more? Such a great radiance of grace and such fullness of the Holy Spirit appeared in him; such precious treasures of truth proceeded from the preacher’s mouth; that he made a vast multitude of Jewish adversaries, the killers of Christ, ready to die for him, though Peter had feared being killed with him by those very people.

This is what the Holy Spirit did when he was sent, having been promised beforehand.

The Lord foresaw these great and wondrous benefits when he said:

“They have both seen and hated both me and my Father, so that the word written in their Law might be fulfilled: ‘Because they hated me without cause.’ When the Paraclete has come, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me; and you will also bear witness.”

By bearing witness and making the witnesses exceedingly courageous, he took fear away from Christ’s friends and transformed the hatred of his enemies into love.

## TREATISE XCIII

### On the words, “I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized,” up to, “But I have spoken these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.” Chapter 16, verses 1–4

### 1

In the passages preceding this chapter of the Gospel, the Lord strengthened his disciples to endure the hatred of their enemies and also prepared them by his own example, so that by imitating him they might become stronger.

He added and promised them that the Holy Spirit would come, who would bear witness about him, and he added that they too would become his witnesses, with the Holy Spirit himself working this in them. For he said:

“He will bear witness about me, and you will also bear witness.”

Since he will bear witness, you too will bear witness: he in your hearts, you in your voices; he by inspiring, you by sounding forth. Thus the statement might be fulfilled: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18:5).

It would have been too little to encourage them by his example unless he also filled them with his Spirit.

Finally, when the apostle Peter had already heard the Lord’s words—“A servant is not greater than his master: if they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15:20)—and saw this fulfilled in himself, he ought, if example alone had been sufficient, to have imitated the patience of his Lord. Yet he succumbed and denied him, not enduring what he saw the Lord endure.

But when he truly received the gift of the Holy Spirit, he preached the one he had denied, and he was not afraid to confess the one whom he had feared to acknowledge.

Previously, he had indeed been instructed by the example, so that he knew what ought to be done; but he had not yet been strengthened by power to do what he knew. He had been taught to stand, but had not been made firm so as not to fall.

After this had been accomplished through the Holy Spirit, he proclaimed unto death the one whom, fearing death, he had denied.

Therefore, in this succeeding chapter, about which we must now speak, the Lord says: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized.”

For it is sung in the Psalm: “Great peace have those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them” (Ps. 118:165).

Accordingly, after promising the Holy Spirit, through whose work in them they would become his witnesses, he rightly added: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may not be scandalized.”

For when God’s love is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5:5), there is great peace for those who love God’s Law, so that there is no scandal for them.

### 2

Then, describing what they would suffer, he says: “They will put you out of the synagogues.”

But what harm was it for the Apostles to be expelled from the Jewish synagogues, as though they would not have separated themselves from them even if no one expelled them?

Clearly, he wished to announce that the Jews would not receive Christ, whereas these disciples would not depart from Christ. Therefore it would happen that they would be cast outside with him by those who did not wish to be in him—those who could not exist without him.

For plainly, since there was no other people of God than that seed of Abraham, if they had recognized and received Christ, they would have remained as natural branches in the olive tree (Rom. 11:17). There would not have been one Church of Christ and another synagogue of the Jews; they would have been the same, if they had wished to remain in the same one.

Because they did not wish this, what remained except that, while remaining outside Christ, they should put outside the synagogues those who did not abandon Christ?

After receiving the Holy Spirit and becoming his witnesses, they would certainly not be like those of whom it is said: “Many of the rulers of the Jews believed in him, but because of fear of the Jews they did not confess him, lest they be expelled from the synagogues. For they loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God” (John 12:42–43).

They believed in him, therefore, but not in the manner in which he wanted them to believe—the one who said: “How can you believe, when you receive glory from one another and do not seek the glory that comes from God alone?” (ibid. 5:44).

To disciples who believed in him in such a way that, filled with the Holy Spirit—that is, with the gift of God’s grace—they were not among those who, “being ignorant of God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, were not subject to God’s righteousness” (Rom. 10:3), nor among those of whom it was said, “They loved the glory of human beings more than the glory of God,” belongs the prophecy that is found fulfilled in them:

“Lord, they will walk in the light of your countenance, and they will exult in your name all day long, and in your righteousness they will be exalted; for you are the glory of their strength” (Ps. 88:16–18).

It is rightly said to them: “They will put you out of the synagogues”—those, namely, who have zeal for God but not according to knowledge. Because they are ignorant of God’s righteousness and seek to establish their own (Rom. 10:2–3), they expel those who are exalted not in their own righteousness but in God’s righteousness.

Those who are expelled by human beings are not ashamed, because God himself is the glory of their strength.

### 3

Finally, after saying this to them, he added: “But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that by doing so he is offering service to God. And they will do these things to you because they have not known the Father or me.” That is, they have not known God or his Son, in whose service they imagine themselves to be when they kill you. The Lord appended these words as though by them he were consoling his own, who were to be expelled from the Jewish synagogues. For, foretelling the evils they would suffer for his testimony, he says: “They will make you outcasts from the synagogues.” He does not say, “And the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that by doing so he is offering service to God.” What, then, does he say? “But the hour is coming”—as though he were predicting something good after those evils.

What, then, does “They will make you outcasts from the synagogues; but the hour is coming” mean? It is as though he were going to say: “They will indeed separate you, but I shall gather you”; or, “They will indeed separate you, but the hour of your joy is coming.” What, then, does this word “but the hour is coming” accomplish, as though he were promising them consolation after tribulation, when he seems rather to have had to say in the indicative mood, “And the hour is coming”? Yet he does not say “And it is coming,” because he was predicting that tribulation upon tribulation, not consolation after tribulation, would come upon them.

Or perhaps that separation from the synagogues would disturb them so greatly that they would prefer to die rather than remain in this life without the congregations of the Jews? Far be it that those who sought the glory of God, not of human beings, should be disturbed in such a way. What, then, is meant by “They will make you outcasts from the synagogues; but the hour is coming,” when he seems rather to have had to say, “And the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that by doing so he is offering service to God”? For it is not even said, “But the hour is coming when they will kill you,” as though death were to come upon them as a consolation for that separation [Note: [Col. 1866] Manuscripts read *accederet* (“would come upon”), rather than *accideret* (“would happen”).]; rather, he says: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that by doing so he is offering service to God.”

I certainly do not think that he wished to signify anything else than that they should understand and rejoice that they would win so many people for Christ when they were expelled from the Jewish congregations—so many that it would not be enough for their persecutors merely to expel them; they would not allow them to live, lest by their preaching they convert everyone to the name of Christ and turn them away from the observance of Judaism as though it were divine truth.

We must understand this as spoken about the Jews, of whom he had said, “They will make you outcasts from the synagogues.” For although witnesses—that is, martyrs—of Christ were also killed by the Gentiles, those Gentiles did not think that in doing this they were offering service to God, but to their false gods. Among the Jews, however, everyone who killed Christ’s preachers thought that he was offering service to God [Col. 1867], believing that all who turned to Christ were abandoning the God of Israel.

For they were moved by this reasoning even to kill Christ himself. Their words concerning this matter have also been written down: “You see that the whole world has gone after him” (John XII, 19); “If we let him live, the Romans will come and take away from us both our place and our nation.” And there is also what Caiaphas said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people, and that the whole nation should not perish” (John XI, 48, 50). In this discourse, therefore, he also strengthened his disciples by his own example. He had said to them: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John XV, 20). Thus, just as by killing him they thought that they had offered service to God, so also they would think this when killing them.

### 4

This, then, is the meaning contained in these words: “They will make you outcasts from the synagogues; but do not fear solitude. For, separated from their assembly, you will gather so many in my name that they, fearing that the temple which was among them and all the sacred observances of the former Law might be abandoned, will kill you—thus shedding your blood while imagining that they are offering service to God.”

Here is what the Apostle said about them: “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge” (Romans X, 2). They think that they are offering service to God by killing God’s servants. O dreadful error! Is it in order to please God that you strike down one who pleases God? And is the living temple of God thrown down when you strike it, so that the stone temple of God may not be abandoned? O accursed blindness!

But this has happened to Israel in part, so that the fullness of the Gentiles might enter; in part, I say, not entirely. For not all, but some of the branches were broken off, so that the wild olive might be grafted in (Romans XI, 25, 17). When the disciples of Christ were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke in the languages of all nations, when divine miracles were performed abundantly through them and divine utterances were spread abroad, Christ, even after being killed, was loved in such a way that his disciples, expelled from the assemblies of the Jews, gathered a great multitude even from among the Jews themselves and feared no solitude (Acts II–IV).

At this the remaining reprobate and blind were inflamed—those who had zeal for God, but not according to knowledge—and, believing that they were offering service to God, they killed them. But the one who was killed for them was gathering them: he had instructed them beforehand about these future events, before he was killed, so that unexpected and unforeseen evils, although quickly passing, would not disturb minds that were ignorant and unprepared, but that, foreknown and patiently endured, they would lead them to eternal blessings.

He himself also showed that this was the reason why he foretold these things to them, adding: “But I have said these things to you so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you.” Their hour was a dark hour, a nocturnal hour. Yet “by day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Psalm XLI, 9): when the night of the Jews did not, by any confusion, darken the day of the Christians that had been separated from it; and when it was able to kill the flesh, it was not able to darken the faith.

## TREATISE XCIV

### On the words of Jesus, “But these things I did not tell you from the beginning, because I was with you,” up to “But if I go, I will send him to you”

Chapter XVI, verses 5–7.

[Col. 1868]

### 1

When the Lord Jesus had foretold to his disciples the persecutions they would suffer after his departure, he added and said: “But these things I did not tell you from the beginning, because I was with you; but now I am going to him who sent me.”

The first matter to be considered is whether he had not foretold the future persecutions before his Passion. The other three evangelists clearly show that he did foretell these things before they came to the supper (Matthew XXIV, 9; Mark XIII, 9–13; and Luke XXI, 12–17). According to John, however, he spoke these words after the supper, when he said: “But these things I did not tell you from the beginning, because I was with you.”

Or perhaps the question is resolved by the fact that the other evangelists also report him as being close to his Passion when he said these things? Therefore he did not say this “from the beginning,” when he was with them, because by then he was about to depart and proceed to the Father. Thus, even according to those evangelists, what is said here is true: “But these things I did not tell you from the beginning.”

But what are we to do with the testimony of the Gospel according to Matthew, who records that these things were announced to them by the Lord not only when Passover was already near and he was about to dine with the disciples before his Passion, but also from the beginning, when the Apostles are first named individually and sent out to perform divine works (Matthew X, 17)?

What, then, does he mean here by saying, “But these things I did not tell you from the beginning, because I was with you,” except that he did not tell them from the beginning those things he now says about the Holy Spirit: that he would come to them and bear witness when they were to suffer those evils? He did not tell them these things from the beginning because he was with them.

### 2

That Comforter, or Advocate—for both meanings are conveyed by the Greek word *paracletus*—was therefore necessary when Christ departed. For this reason he had not spoken of him from the beginning, when he was with them, because they were being comforted by Christ’s presence. But as he was about to depart, it was necessary for him to say that the Spirit would come, through whom, once love had been poured into their hearts, they would preach the word of God with confidence; and while he bore inner witness among them concerning Christ, they too would bear witness.

They would not be scandalized when their Jewish enemies made them outcasts from the synagogues and killed them, imagining that they were offering service to God, because “love endures all things” (1 Corinthians XIII, 7)—the love that was to be poured into their hearts through the gift of the Holy Spirit (Romans V, 5).

The whole meaning, then, is that he was going to make them his martyrs, that is, his witnesses, through the Holy Spirit, so that, while the Spirit worked in them, they would endure whatever hardships persecution brought and would not grow cold in the love of preaching, being kindled by that divine fire.

“Therefore,” he says, “I have told you these things so that, when their hour comes, you may remember that I told you” (John XVI, 4). I have told you these things not only because you will suffer them, but because, when that Paraclete comes, he will bear witness concerning me, so that you will not remain silent through fear of these things; and thus you too will bear witness.

“But these things I did not tell you from the beginning, because I was with you,” and I myself comforted you by my bodily presence, presented to your human senses, which, being little ones, you were able to receive [Col. 1869].

### 3

“But now I am going to him who sent me.” And no one among you, he says, asks me, “Where are you going?” He signifies that he will go in such a way that none of them will ask, because they will see with the sight of the body that it is happening openly. Earlier they had asked him where he was going, and he had answered that he was going where they could not then come (John XIII, 36). Now, however, he promises that he will go in such a way that none of them asks where he is going.

For a cloud received him when he ascended from them; and as he went into heaven, they did not inquire with words but accompanied him with their eyes (Acts I, 9–11).

### 4

“But because I have said these things to you,” he says, “sorrow has filled your heart.” Certainly he saw what those words of his were doing in their hearts. They did not yet possess inwardly the spiritual consolation they were to have through the Holy Spirit, and they feared losing what they saw outwardly in Christ. Since they could not doubt that he was truly announcing that they would lose him [Note: [Col. 1869] Eleven manuscripts read *illo vera denuntiante* (“while he truly announced it”).], human feeling was saddened because the bodily sight was being left desolate.

But he knew what was more beneficial for them, because the inward vision, by which the Holy Spirit was going to console them, is certainly better. The Spirit was not going to thrust a human body before the bodily eyes of those who saw, but was going to pour himself into the breasts of believers.

Finally, he adds: “But I tell you the truth: it is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.” It was as though he were saying:

“It is expedient for you that this form of a servant be taken away from you. The Word made flesh dwells among you, but I do not wish you still to love me carnally and, content with this milk, to desire always to remain infants. It is expedient for you that I go away. For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.

“If I do not withdraw the tender nourishment with which I have fed you, you will not hunger for solid food. If you cling to the flesh in a carnal way, you will not be capable of the Spirit.”

For what is meant by “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you”? Could he not send him while he was present here? Who could say that? For the one did not depart from where the other was; and he had come from the Father in such a way that he did not remain in the Father.

Finally, how could he not send the one whom we know came upon him and remained upon him when he was baptized (John I, 32)? Indeed, we know that the one was never separable from him.

What, then, is meant by “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you,” except: You cannot receive the Spirit as long as you persist in knowing Christ according to the flesh? Hence the one who had already received the Spirit says: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him thus no longer” (2 Corinthians V, 16).

Indeed, even Christ’s flesh is not known according to the flesh by one who spiritually knows the Word made flesh. This is precisely what the good Teacher wished to signify when he said: “For if I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go, I will send him to you.”

### 5

When Christ departed bodily, not only the Holy Spirit but also the Father and the Son were spiritually present with them. For if Christ departed from them in such a way that the Holy Spirit was in them in his place, rather than with him, where is his promise: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew XXVIII, 20); and, “We shall come to him—I and the Father—and we shall make our dwelling with him” (John XIV, 23)? For he also promised that he would send the Holy Spirit in such a way that the Spirit would be with them forever.

Accordingly, when they were going to become spiritual instead of carnal or merely soulish, they were certainly going to possess the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit more fully. The Father must not be believed to exist anywhere without the Son and the Holy Spirit, nor the Father and the Son without the Holy Spirit, nor the Son without the Father and the Holy Spirit, nor the Holy Spirit without the Father and the Son, nor the Father and the Holy Spirit without the Son. Rather, wherever any one of them is, there is the Trinity, the one God.

It was necessary, however, that the Trinity be disclosed in such a way that, although there is no diversity of substances, the distinction of persons would nevertheless be commended individually. To those who understand rightly, there can never appear here a separation of natures.

### 6

What follows—“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment: concerning sin, indeed, because they do not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me; concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged” (John XVI, 8–11)—is exceedingly obscure if it is taken as though the only sin were not believing in Christ, as though righteousness itself were simply not seeing Christ, and as though the judgment itself were simply that the ruler of this world, that is, the devil, has been judged.

It should not be confined within this discourse, lest brevity make it more obscure. Rather, it should be explained elsewhere, insofar as the Lord grants assistance.

## TREATISE XCV

### On these words from the preceding reading: “When he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness,” etc.

Chapter XVI, verses 8–11.

### 1

The Lord, promising that he would send the Holy Spirit, says: “When he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment.”

What does this mean? Did the Lord Christ not convict the world concerning sin when he said: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin”? But lest someone perhaps say that this applies specifically to the Jews and not to the world, does he not say elsewhere: “If you were of the world, the world would love what is its own” (John XV, 22, 19)?

Did he not convict the world concerning righteousness when he said: “Righteous Father, the world has not known you” (John XVII, 25)? Did he not convict it concerning judgment when he says that he will say to those on the left: “Go into the eternal fire, which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew XXV, 41)?

Many other passages are found in the holy Gospel where Christ convicts the world concerning these things. What, then, does it mean that he seems to attribute this specifically to the Holy Spirit?

Or perhaps, because Christ spoke only among the Jewish nation, he is not thought to have convicted the world, so that the one who is understood to be convicted is the one who hears the one convicting? But the Holy Spirit, in Christ’s disciples spread throughout the whole world, is understood to have convicted not one nation but the world.

For, as he was about to ascend into heaven, he said to them: “It is not for you to know times or seasons that the Father has placed in his own authority; but you will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts I, 7–8). This is what it means to convict the world.

But who would dare say that the Holy Spirit convicts the world through Christ’s disciples and that Christ himself does not convict it, when the Apostle cries out: “Do you wish to receive proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” (2 Corinthians XIII, 3). Therefore, those whom the Holy Spirit convicts, Christ also convicts.

But, as it seems to me, because love was to be poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit (Romans V, 5)—love that casts out fear (1 John IV, 18), by which they might have been prevented from daring to convict the world that raged with persecutions—he therefore said, “He will convict the world,” as though he were saying: “He will pour love into your hearts; for when fear has been driven away, you will have freedom to convict.”

We have often said that the works of the Trinity are inseparable (above, Treatise 20), but that the persons had to be commended individually, so that both unity and Trinity might be understood—not only without separation, but also without confusion.

### 2

He then explains what he meant concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment.

“Concerning sin,” he says, “because they did not believe in me.” He placed this sin, as though it were the only one, before the others, because while it remains the others are retained, and when it departs the others are forgiven.

“Concerning righteousness,” he says, “because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

Here it must first be considered whether, if someone is rightly convicted concerning sin, he can also rightly be convicted concerning righteousness. For if a sinner is to be convicted because he is a sinner, will anyone think that a righteous person should also be convicted because he is righteous? Far be it.

Indeed, if a righteous person is sometimes convicted, he is rightly convicted because, as it is written, “There is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin.” Therefore, even when a righteous person is convicted, he is convicted concerning sin, not concerning righteousness.

Likewise, in what we read as divinely spoken—“Do not become excessively righteous” (Ecclesiastes VII, 21, 17)—it is not the righteousness of the wise person that is censured, but the pride of one who presumes. Whoever becomes excessively righteous becomes unrighteous through that very excess.

For a person makes himself excessively righteous when he says that he has no sin, or when he thinks that he becomes righteous not by the grace of God but by the sufficiency of his own will. He is not righteous by living rightly, but rather puffed up by thinking himself to be what he is not.

How, then, is the world to be convicted concerning righteousness, except concerning the righteousness of believers? It is therefore convicted concerning sin because it does not believe in Christ, and it is convicted concerning the righteousness of those who believe. For the comparison with the faithful itself is a reproach of the unfaithful.

The explanation itself makes this sufficiently clear. Wishing to disclose what he meant, he says: “Concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.” He does not say, “And they will no longer see me,” speaking of those of whom he had said, “because they did not believe in me.” When explaining what he called sin, he spoke of them, saying, “because they did not believe in me.” But when explaining what righteousness he meant—the righteousness concerning which the world is convicted—he turned to those to whom he was speaking and said: “Because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

Therefore, the world is convicted concerning its own sin, but concerning another’s righteousness [Col. 1872], just as darkness is convicted by light. For the Apostle says: “Everything that is convicted is manifested by the light” (Ephesians V, 13).

How great an evil it is not to believe can appear not only from the unbelievers themselves, but also from the good found in those who believe. And because unbelievers are accustomed to say, “How can we believe what we do not see?”, the righteousness of believers had to be defined in this way: “Because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me.”

For blessed are those who do not see and yet believe (John XX, 29). Even when those who saw Christ believed in him, their faith was not praised because they believed what they saw—that is, the Son of Man—but because they believed what they did not see—that is, the Son of God.

But when even the form of a servant had been removed from their sight, then the saying was fulfilled in every respect: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans I, 17; Habakkuk II, 4; Hebrews XI, 1). For faith is defined in the Epistle to the Hebrews as “the substance of things hoped for, the conviction of things that are not seen.”

### 3

But what does “You will no longer see me” mean? He does not say, “I am going to the Father, and you will not see me,” so that the interval of time during which he would not be seen might be understood—whether short or long, but in any case limited. Rather, by saying, “You will no longer see me,” the Truth seems to foretell that they will never afterward see Christ.

Is this righteousness—to never see Christ and yet believe in him—when faith, by which the righteous person lives, is praised precisely because he believes that he will one day see the Christ whom he does not now see?

Finally, according to this righteousness, are we to say that the Apostle Paul was not righteous, when he confessed that he saw Christ after his ascension into heaven (1 Corinthians XV, 8), although Christ had already said of that time, “You will no longer see me”? According to this righteousness, was the most glorious Stephen not righteous, who, while he was being stoned, said: “Behold, I see the heavens opened and the Son of Man standing at the right hand of God” (Acts VII, 55)?

What, then, is meant by “I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me,” except: You will no longer see me as I am while I am with you?

At that time he was still mortal, in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans VIII, 3); he could hunger and thirst, grow weary, and sleep. When this Christ—that is, Christ in such a condition—had passed from this world to the Father, they would no longer see him. And this is the righteousness of faith of which the Apostle says: “Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, we know him thus no longer” (2 Corinthians V, 16).

“Therefore,” he says, “your righteousness, concerning which the world will be convicted, will be this: that I am going to the Father and you will no longer see me. For you will believe in me, whom you will not see. And when you see me, as I shall then be, you will not see me as I am with you now. You will not see me humble, but exalted; you will not see me mortal, but everlasting; you will not see me being judged, but judging” [Note: [Col. 1872] Manuscripts read *judicatorem* (“judge”) rather than *judicaturum* (“about to judge”).]. Concerning this faith of yours—that is, your righteousness—the Holy Spirit will convict the unbelieving world.”

### 4

He will also convict it concerning judgment, “because the ruler of this world has been judged.” Who is this, except the one of whom he says elsewhere: “Behold, the ruler of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me” (John XIV, 30)—that is, nothing belonging to his jurisdiction, nothing pertaining to him, absolutely no sin?

For this is how the devil is the ruler of the world. He is not the ruler of heaven and earth and of all that is in them, in the sense in which “world” is understood when it is said, “And the world was made through him.” Rather, the devil is the ruler of the world of which the same passage immediately goes on to say: “And the world did not know him” (John I, 10)—that is, of unbelieving human beings, with whom the world is filled throughout the earth.

Among them the faithful world groans, the world that he chose out of the world, through whom the world was made. Concerning this world he himself says: “The Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John III, 17).

The world is condemned when he judges; the world is saved when he comes to its aid. For just as a tree is full of leaves and fruits, and a threshing floor is full of chaff and grain, so the world is full of unbelievers and believers.

The ruler, therefore, of this world—that is, the ruler of these darknesses, meaning of unbelievers, from whom the world is delivered, to whom it is said, “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians V, 8)—the ruler of this world, of whom he says elsewhere, “Now the ruler of this world has been cast out” (John XII, 31), has certainly been judged, because he has been irrevocably assigned by judgment to the fire of eternity.

Concerning this judgment, by which the ruler of the world has been judged, the Holy Spirit also convicts the world, because it is judged along with its ruler, whom the proud and impious person imitates [Note: [Col. 1873] Lovaniensis reads *superbum atque impium imitatur* (“imitates the proud and impious one”). Here we follow the other printed editions and the manuscripts.].

For if God, as the Apostle Peter says, “did not spare angels when they sinned, but thrust them into the prisons of darkness and delivered them to be kept for punishment in judgment” (2 Peter II, 4), how is the world not convicted by the Holy Spirit concerning this judgment, when the Apostle speaks these things in the Holy Spirit?

Let people therefore believe in Christ, so that they may not be convicted concerning the sin of their unbelief, by which all sins are retained. Let them pass into the number of the faithful, so that they may not be convicted concerning the righteousness of those whom they do not imitate, though they have been justified. Let them beware of the future judgment, so that they may not be judged with the ruler of the world, whom they imitate although he has been judged.

For, lest the hardened pride of mortals imagine that it will be spared, it must be terrified by the punishment of the proud angels.

## TREATISE XCVI

### On these words: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now; but when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth”

Chapter XVI, verses 12–13.

### 1

In this chapter of the holy Gospel, where the Lord says to his disciples, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” the first question that presents itself is how he could earlier have said, “All things that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV, 15), and here say, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

But how he said that he had done what he had not yet done—as though he had already done it—just as the prophet testifies that God has done future things when he says, “Who has made the things that are to come” (Isaiah XLV, 11, according to the Septuagint), we explained as best we could when we were treating those very words.

Now, then, perhaps you wish to know what these things were that the Apostles could not bear at that time. But who among us would dare to say that he is already capable of receiving what they were unable to receive? Accordingly, you should not expect me to say things that I might perhaps be unable to receive if they were told to me by someone else; nor would you be able to bear them even if I were so great that you could hear from me things higher than yourselves.

It is possible, of course, that some among you are already capable of receiving what others are not yet able to receive; and, if not all the things concerning which that divine Teacher said, “I still have many things to say to you,” perhaps some of them. But it is rash to presume and say what those things are that he himself did not say.

At that time the Apostles were not even capable of dying for Christ, though he said to them, “You cannot follow me now.” Hence their foremost member, Peter, who had presumed that he could already do this, experienced something other than what he had thought (John XIII, 36–38).

Yet afterward men and women, boys and girls, young men and virgins, old people together with the young, were crowned in countless numbers by martyrdom. Sheep were found capable of doing what the shepherds could not yet bear when the Lord was speaking these words.

Should it therefore have been said to those sheep, at that moment of trial when it was necessary to contend even unto death and to shed blood for the truth and for the name or teaching of Christ—should it, I say, have been said to them: “Who among you dares to think himself capable of martyrdom, when Peter was not yet capable of it”? This would be despite the fact that the Lord himself was instructing Peter face to face.

In the same way, someone might say that Christian peoples who desire to hear what the Lord meant when he said, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” should not be told: “If the Apostles could not bear them, much less can you.” For perhaps many can hear what Peter then could not, just as many can be crowned with martyrdom, though Peter then could not.

This is especially so now that the Holy Spirit has been sent—the Spirit who had not yet been sent at that time—about whom he immediately continued and said: “But when that Spirit of truth comes, he will teach you all truth.” By this he clearly showed that they could not bear the things he had to say because the Holy Spirit had not yet come to them.

### 2

Let us grant that it is so: that, once the Holy Spirit has been sent, many are now able to bear what the disciples could not bear when the Spirit had not yet been sent. Do we therefore know what the things were that he did not wish to say—things that we would know if we read or heard them spoken by him?

It is one thing to know whether those things can be borne by us or by you; it is another to know what they are, whether they can be borne or not. Since he himself kept silent about them, who among us can say, “These or those are the things”? And if someone dares to say so, where does he prove it?

For who is so empty or rash that, even if he says things that are true to whomever he wishes, he would affirm without any divine testimony that these are the things the Lord then did not wish to say? Who among us would do this without incurring the greatest guilt of rashness, when he possesses neither prophetic nor apostolic authority of distinction?

Certainly, if we had read some of these things in books confirmed by canonical authority that were written after the Lord’s ascension, it would not have been enough merely to have read them, unless we also read there that they were among the things the Lord then did not wish to say to the disciples because they could not bear them.

For example, suppose I were to say that what we read in the first chapter of this Gospel—“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was the Word; he was in the beginning with God” (John I, 1–2)—and the other things that follow are among those things the Lord did not wish to say at that time because the disciples could not bear them. They were written later, and it is not reported that Jesus the Lord said them while he was present in the flesh; rather, one of his Apostles wrote them down after they had been revealed to him by the Spirit [Note: [Col. 1875] The printed editions read *ipso ac Spiritu ejus* (“by him himself and by his Spirit”). *Ipso* is absent from the manuscripts.]. Who would listen to me saying such things so rashly?

But if, in the place where we read these words, we also read that they were among the things the Lord then did not wish to say, who would not believe so great an Apostle?

### 3

It also seems to me extremely absurd to say that the disciples were then unable to bear those things concerning invisible and exalted realities that we find in the Apostolic Letters, which were written afterward and which are not reported as having been spoken by the Lord when he was visibly present with them.

Why could they not bear at that time what everyone now reads and bears in their books, even if they do not understand it? Unbelieving people certainly fail to understand some things in the holy Scriptures when they read or hear them, and they cannot bear what they have read or heard.

The pagans cannot bear that the world was made through the one who was crucified. The Jews cannot bear that the Son of God is the one who, in the manner in which they themselves observe the Sabbath, violated the Sabbath. The Sabellians cannot bear that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are a Trinity. The Arians cannot bear that the Son is equal to the Father, and the Holy Spirit equal to the Father and the Son. The Photinians cannot bear that Christ is not merely a human being like us, but also God equal to God the Father. The Manichaeans cannot bear that Christ Jesus, through whom we are to be liberated [Note: [Col. 1875] The printed editions read *liberati* (“have been liberated”), but the manuscripts read *liberandi* (“are to be liberated”).], graciously consented to be born in flesh and from flesh.

And all the other people belonging to perverse and diverse sects certainly cannot bear whatever is found in the holy Scriptures and in the Catholic faith that is brought forward against their errors, just as we cannot bear their sacrilegious vanities and lying insanities.

For what does “unable to bear” mean except not to possess an even temper toward something? But of all the things written with canonical truth and authority after the Lord’s ascension, what faithful person—or even catechumen, before receiving the Holy Spirit in baptism—does not read and hear them with an even temper, even if he does not yet understand them as he ought?

How, then, could the disciples have been unable to bear any of the things written after the Lord’s ascension, even before the Holy Spirit had been sent to them, when catechumens now bear all these things without having received the Holy Spirit?

For although the mysteries of the faithful are not disclosed to them, this is not because they cannot bear them; rather, it is so that they may desire them all the more ardently, in proportion as they are concealed from them with greater honor.

### 4

Therefore, dearly beloved, do not expect to hear from us what the Lord then did not wish to say to the disciples, because they could not yet bear it. Rather, advance in the love that is poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit, who has been given to you (Rom. 5:5), so that, fervent in spirit and loving spiritual things, you may be able to know the spiritual light and the spiritual voice—which carnal people cannot bear—not through some sign appearing to bodily eyes, nor through some sound resounding in bodily ears, but through inward sight and hearing. For what is wholly unknown is not loved. But when something is loved because it is known in however small a part, love itself brings it about that it is known better and more fully.

If, then, you advance in the love which the Holy Spirit pours into your hearts, he will teach you all truth—or, as other manuscripts read, “he will lead you into all truth” [Note: [Col. 1876] Greek: *hodēgēsei*]—whence it is said, “Lead me, Lord, in your way, and I shall walk in your truth” (Ps. 85:11). Thus it will come about that you will not learn from external teachers those things which the Lord then did not wish to say, but that you will all be “teachable by God” (John 6:45). Then you will be able to contemplate inwardly those very things which you have learned and believed through readings and externally supplied sermons: that God’s nature is not corporeal, nor enclosed in any place, nor stretched out like a mass through infinite expanses of space, but is wholly and perfectly everywhere and infinite—without the gleams of colors, without the shapes and lines of figures, without the marks of letters, without the succession of syllables.

Behold, I have said something which perhaps comes from that source, and yet you have received it; and you have not only been able to bear it, but have also heard it willingly. But if that inward Teacher, who, while still speaking outwardly to the disciples, said, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” wished to say inwardly to us what I have said concerning God’s incorporeal nature, in the manner in which he says it to the holy angels, who always see the face of the Father (Matt. 18:10), we would still be unable to bear it.

Accordingly, when he says, “He will teach you all truth,” or, “He will lead you into all truth,” I do not think that this can be fulfilled in anyone’s mind in the present life. For who, living in this body “which is corrupted and weighs down the soul” (Wis. 9:15), could know all truth, when the Apostle says, “We know in part”? But because this comes about through the Holy Spirit, from whom we have now received a pledge (2 Cor. 1:22), we shall come even to that fullness. Concerning it the same Apostle says, “Then face to face”; and, “Now I know in part, but then I shall know just as I also am known” (1 Cor. 13:9, 12). It is not that in this life anyone knows the whole of what the Lord has promised will come to us, through the love of the Spirit, in that perfection, when he says, “He will teach you all truth,” or, “He will lead you into all truth.”

### 5

Since this is so, dearly beloved, I urge you in the love of Christ to beware of seducers and of sects of impure and obscene depravity, concerning which the Apostle says, “The things that are done by them secretly it is shameful even to mention” (Eph. 5:12). Beware lest, when they begin to teach horrifying impurities which human ears, however constituted, cannot bear, they say that these are the very things the Lord meant when he said, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” and assert that through the Holy Spirit it becomes possible to bear those filthy and abominable things.

There are evils which no human modesty, however great, can bear, and there are good things which the smallness of the human understanding cannot bear. The former are enacted in shameless bodies; the latter are removed from all bodies. The former is committed with impure flesh; the latter is scarcely perceived by a pure mind.

“Be renewed therefore in the spirit of your mind” (Eph. 4:23), “and understand what the will of God is: what is good, acceptable, and perfect” (Rom. 12:2), “so that, rooted and founded in love, you may be able, with all the saints, to comprehend what is the length, breadth, height, and depth; and to know also the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge, so that you may be filled unto all the fullness of God” (Eph. 3:17–19). In this way the Holy Spirit will teach you all truth, as he pours love more and more abundantly into your hearts.

## TRACTATE XCVII

### On the same reading

#### 1

The Holy Spirit, whom the Lord promised that he would send to his disciples to teach them all truth—which they could not bear at the time when he was speaking with them—this same Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Apostle says that we have now received a pledge (2 Cor. 1:22), by which words we understand that his fullness is reserved for us in the life to come, now teaches the faithful as much of spiritual truth as each person is able to receive. He also kindles their hearts with a greater desire, if each person advances in that love by which he loves what he has learned and desires what remains to be learned. Thus, even concerning those things which he now knows in some fashion, he knows that he does not yet know them as they ought to be known in that life “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2:9).

If the inward Teacher wished to say those things now—that is, to open and show them to our minds—human weakness could not bear them. Hence your Beloved remembers that I already spoke about this when we were discussing the words of the holy Gospel, where the Lord says, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.”

Let us not imagine that these words of the Lord refer to some exceedingly hidden secrets which, although they can be spoken by a teacher, cannot be borne by a learner. Rather, the very things which we read and write, hear and say, as part of the teaching of religion and within the knowledge of all kinds of people—if Christ wished to say them to us in the manner in which he says them to the holy angels, in himself, the only-begotten Word of the Father, coeternal with the Father—what human beings could bear them, even if they were already spiritual, such as the Apostles were not yet when the Lord spoke these words to them, but such as they later became when the Holy Spirit came?

For whatever can be known concerning creation is less than the Creator himself, who is the supreme, true, and immutable God. And who is silent about him? Where is he not named—by readers, debaters, questioners, respondents, praisers, singers, people speaking in every conceivable way, and finally even by blasphemers themselves? Yet although no one is silent about him, who grasps him as he ought to be understood, when he does not depart from human mouths and ears? Whose mind’s vision approaches him? Who would have known that he is Trinity unless he had wished to make himself known in this way? And what human being now keeps this Trinity silent? Yet who among human beings understands the Trinity as the angels do?

The very things openly and publicly spoken without interruption concerning God’s eternity, truth, and holiness are understood well by some and badly by others; indeed, they are understood by some and not understood by others. For one who understands badly does not understand. Even among those by whom they are understood well, they are perceived by some with less and by others with greater liveliness of mind, and no human being grasps them as the angels do.

In the mind itself—that is, in the inner person—we grow in a certain way, not only so that we pass from milk to food, but also so that we consume that food in ever greater measure. We do not grow by spatial bulk, but by luminous understanding, because intelligible food itself is light.

Therefore, in order that you may grow and grasp him, and that the more you grow, the more and more you may grasp him, you must ask and hope for this not from the teacher who sounds in your ears—that is, who plants and waters by working outwardly—but from the one who gives the increase (1 Cor. 3:6).

#### 2

Accordingly, as I warned you in my previous sermon, beware—especially those of you who are little ones and still need milk as nourishment—lest, on the pretext that the Lord said, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” you lend a curious ear to deceived and deceiving men in order to learn what is unknown, while your minds are still too weak to distinguish truth from falsehood.

Beware especially of the most obscene impurities which Satan has taught unstable and carnal souls, with God permitting this so that his dreadful judgments may be everywhere manifest, and so that, in comparison with impure wickedness, the purest discipline may become sweet; and also so that the person who did not fall into those evils while that ruler governed, or who rose from them when that ruler lifted him up, may give honor to God and reserve fear or shame for himself.

Beware through fear and prayer lest you fall into Solomon’s riddle, where the foolish and bold woman, having become destitute of bread, calls out to passers-by, saying, “Touch secret bread gladly, and the sweetness of stolen water” (Prov. 9:13–17).

This woman is the vanity of the impious, who, although they are exceedingly foolish, imagine that they know something, just as it is said of this woman that she became destitute of bread. Though she is destitute of bread, she promises bread—that is, though she is ignorant of truth, she promises knowledge of truth.

Yet she promises secret bread, which she says should be touched gladly, and the sweetness of stolen water, so that people may hear and do more gladly and sweetly those things which are forbidden to be said and believed openly in the Church. Through this very concealment, wicked teachers season their poisons for the curious, so that they imagine themselves learning something great because it has been granted to them as a secret; and they drink in more sweetly the foolishness which they suppose to be knowledge, whose forbidden hearing they have, as it were, stolen.

#### 3

For this reason also she commends her wicked rites to people deceived—or to be deceived—by sacrilegious curiosity through the teaching of magical arts. For this reason those unlawful divinations—whether by inspecting the entrails of slaughtered animals, by the sounds and flights of birds, or by the manifold signs of demons—are whispered into the ears of doomed people through conversations with the lost.

Because of these unlawful and punishable secrets, that woman is called not only foolish but also bold. Yet these things are alien not only to the reality itself but also to the name of our religion.

What shall we say of the fact that this foolish and bold woman, under the Christian name, has established so many criminal heresies and invented so many abominable fables? If only they were like those which are sung, danced, or mocked with theatrical buffoonery in the theaters—and not certain others of such a kind that we grieve that she could have invented them against God with such foolishness that we marvel at her boldness.

All the most foolish heretics who wish to be called Christians attempt to cloak the boldness of their inventions—things which the human mind especially abhors—under cover of the Gospel saying in which the Lord says, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now.” They act as though these very things were what the disciples then could not bear, and as though the Holy Spirit taught those things which an unclean spirit blushes to teach and proclaim openly, however great the boldness with which it is carried away.

#### 4

Foreseeing these people in the Holy Spirit, the Apostle says [Note: [Col. 1879] So read Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice: “The Apostle, foreseeing this …” M.]: “For there will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their own desires they will heap up teachers for themselves, having itching ears; and they will indeed turn their hearing away from the truth, but they will turn to fables” (2 Tim. 4:3–4).

That mention of secrecy and theft—“Touch secret bread gladly, and the sweetness of stolen water”—produces an itching in the ears of those who spiritually fornicate by listening, just as the integrity of chastity is corrupted in the flesh by a certain itching of lust.

Listen, therefore, to the Apostle foreseeing such things and healthfully warning that they must be avoided: “Avoid profane novelties of words,” he says, “for they advance greatly toward impiety, and their speech spreads like a cancer” (2 Tim. 2:16–17). He does not say merely “novelties of words,” but adds “profane.”

For there are also novelties of words appropriate to religious teaching, as is shown by the written record of when the very name “Christians” began to be used. In Antioch, after the Lord’s ascension, the disciples were first called Christians, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 11:26). Later, hospices and monasteries were also called by new names. The realities themselves, however, existed before their names and are confirmed by the truth of religion, by which they are also defended against the wicked.

Against the impiety of the Arian heretics, they also coined the new name *Homoousion* (“of the same substance”) for the Father. But they did not designate a new reality by that name. For *Homoousion* means what is expressed by, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), namely, of one and the same substance.

For if every novelty were profane, the Lord would not say, “I give you a new commandment” (John 13:34); nor would it be called the New Testament; nor would the “new song” be sung throughout the whole world.

But novelties of words are profane when the foolish and bold woman says, “Touch secret bread gladly, and the sweetness of stolen water.”

The Apostle also forbids this promise of false knowledge in the passage where he says: “O Timothy, guard the deposit, avoiding profane novelties of words and oppositions of falsely named knowledge, which some professing have fallen away from the faith” (1 Tim. 6:20–21).

For these people love nothing so much as promising knowledge and mocking, as though it were ignorance, the faith in true things which little ones are commanded to believe.

#### 5

Someone may say: “Do spiritual men have nothing in their teaching which they keep silent about before carnal people but explain to spiritual people?”

If I answer, “They do not,” someone will immediately quote to me from the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Corinthians: “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. Indeed, you are not even now able, for you are still carnal” (1 Cor. 3:1–2). He will also quote, “We speak wisdom among the perfect,” and, “Comparing spiritual things with spiritual things; but the natural person does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him” (1 Cor. 2:6, 13–14).

What all this means, lest, because of these words of the Apostle, people again seek secrets in profane novelties of words, and lest it be said that carnal people cannot bear what the spirit and body of the chaste ought to avoid, must be discussed in another sermon, if the Lord grants it, so that we may at last bring this one to a close.

## TRACTATE XCVIII

### On the same reading

#### 1

I remember that I postponed the difficult question which arose from the words of our Lord, where he says, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” so that it might be treated more leisurely, because the appropriate limit of time compelled me to end the sermon [Note: [Col. 1880] Almost all manuscripts read, “so that it might be discussed after an interval.”].

Now, therefore, since it is time to fulfill what was promised, let the question be examined as the Lord himself grants it, since he placed it in our heart to propose it.

The question is this: Do spiritual people have something in their teaching which they keep silent about before carnal people but say to spiritual people?
