For if we say, “They do not,” we shall be answered: “What, then, is the meaning of what the Apostle wrote to the Corinthians? ‘I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal, as infants in Christ. I gave you milk to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. Indeed, you are not even now able, for you are still carnal’” (1 Cor. 3:1–2)?

But if we say, “They do,” we must fear and beware lest, under this pretext, wicked things be taught secretly, and, under the name of spiritual matters, they appear to be not merely whitened by an excuse, as things which carnal people cannot grasp, but even praised through proclamation.

#### 2

First, therefore, Your Beloved must know that Christ himself crucified [Note: [Col. 1880] The printed editions read, “that Christ himself is crucified.” “Is” is wrongly added; the manuscripts lack it.], whom the Apostle says he fed the little ones as though with milk—and his very flesh, in which his true death occurred and true wounds were pierced, and his blood, which was struck—are not conceived in the same way by carnal people as by spiritual people; to the former he is milk, to the latter food, because even if they do not hear more, they understand more.

For even what is received equally by both in faith is not equally grasped by the mind. Thus Christ crucified, preached by the Apostles, was “a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles,” but to those who are called, both Jews and Greeks, “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:23–24). The carnal little ones held to him merely by believing, whereas the more capable spiritual people perceived him also by understanding: to the former he was like milk to drink, to the latter like solid food.

This was not because the former learned him one way among the crowds and the latter another way in private rooms, but because, when the same thing was said openly, each received it according to his capacity.

Since Christ was crucified in order to pour out his blood for the remission of sins, and divine grace is commended through the passion of the only-begotten Son, so that no one may glory in a human being, how did those who still said, “I belong to Paul,” understand Christ crucified (1 Cor. 1:12)? Did they understand him as Paul himself did, who said, “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6:14)?

Thus, concerning Christ crucified, Paul himself took food according to his capacity, while he nourished them with milk according to their weakness.

Finally, knowing that the things he wrote to the Corinthians could be understood one way by the little ones themselves and another way by those with greater capacity, he said: “If anyone among you is a prophet or spiritual, let him recognize that the things I write to you are the Lord’s commandment. But if anyone does not know, he will not be known” (1 Cor. 14:37–38).

He plainly wished the knowledge of spiritual people to be solid, so that not only faith would be supplied but certain understanding held. Accordingly, the little ones believed the very things which spiritual people additionally recognized.

“He will not be known,” he says, “who does not know,” because it has not yet been revealed to him that he should know what he believes. When this takes place in a person’s mind, that person is said to be known by God, because God makes him one who knows, as he says elsewhere: “But now, knowing God—or rather, being known by God” (Gal. 4:9). For God did not then begin to know them, since they had been foreknown and chosen before the foundation of the world (Eph. 1:4); rather, he then made them know him.

#### 3

Once this has been established first—that spiritual and carnal people hear the very same things together, but grasp them each according to their measure: the former as little ones, the latter as more mature; the former as nourishment of milk, the latter as solid food—there seems to be no necessity for some secret doctrine to be kept silent and hidden from faithful little ones, to be spoken separately to the more mature, that is, to those with greater understanding. Nor should this be thought necessary because the Apostle said, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal.”

For he could not speak to them as spiritual people, but as carnal, even in the very matter where he judged that he knew nothing among them except Jesus Christ, and him crucified (1 Cor. 2:2), because they were unable to grasp it as spiritual people.

Whatever spiritual people there were among them grasped spiritually the same thing which the others heard as carnal people. Thus the statement, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal,” is to be understood as though he had said, “You were not able to grasp what I was saying as spiritual people, but only as carnal people.”

The natural person—that is, one who thinks according to the human level—is called natural from *anima*, “soul,” and carnal from *caro*, “flesh,” because the whole human being consists of soul and flesh—“does not perceive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:14). That is, he does not perceive what grace the cross of Christ bestows on believers, and he thinks that the cross accomplished only this: that, while we struggle for the truth even to death, it should provide us with an example to imitate.

For if such people, who refuse to be anything but human, knew how Christ crucified became for us “wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption,” so that, as it is written, “the one who glories should glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1:30–31), they would certainly not glory in a human being, nor say carnally, “I belong to Paul,” “I to Apollos,” or “I to Cephas,” but spiritually, “I belong to Christ” (1 Cor. 1:12).

#### 4

Yet the passage in the Letter to the Hebrews still raises a question: “Although by this time you ought to be teachers, you again need someone to teach you the elementary principles of the words of God; and you have become people needing milk, not solid food. For everyone who is nourished on milk is inexperienced in the word of righteousness, for he is an infant. But solid food belongs to the perfect, to those who through habit have their senses trained to distinguish good from evil” (Heb. 5:12–14).

Here we see what he calls the solid food of the perfect defined, and this appears to be what is written to the Corinthians: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6). He then explains whom he wishes to be understood here as perfect, saying, “Those who through habit have their senses trained to distinguish good from evil.”

Those who cannot do this with a weak and untrained mind are easily led to vain and sacrilegious fables by the promise of knowledge unless they are held by a certain milk of faith, so that they believe both the invisible things which they do not see and the intelligible things which they do not yet understand.

They consequently think of good and evil only through bodily images, suppose that God himself is nothing but some kind of body, and cannot conceive of evil except as a substance. Rather, evil is a certain defect, in mutable substances, from the immutable substance; and that immutable and supreme substance, which is God, made those mutable substances from nothing.

Whoever not only believes this but also understands, perceives, and knows it with the trained inner senses of the mind need no longer fear being led astray by those who, by supposing evil to be a substance which God did not make, make God himself a mutable substance, as do the Manichaeans, or whatever other plagues fall into such folly.

#### 5

But to little ones in mind, whom the Apostle says must be nourished with milk because they are carnal, every discourse on this subject—one intended not merely to make them believe what is said but also to make them understand and know it—is burdensome, since they cannot grasp such things, and it weighs them down more easily than it feeds them.

Consequently, spiritual people do not altogether keep these matters silent from carnal people, because the Catholic faith must be preached to everyone. Yet neither do they discuss them in such a way that, by trying to bring them within the understanding of those who cannot receive them, they make the word of truth more easily despised than the truth is understood through the word.

For this reason he writes to the Colossians: “Although I am absent in body, I am with you in spirit, rejoicing and seeing your orderliness and what is lacking in your faith in Christ” (Col. 2:5) [Note: [Col. 1883] For *to stereōma*, “firmness,” he read *to hysterēma*, “what is lacking.” So too in the letter to Paulinus, now numbered 149.]. And to the Thessalonians: “Night and day we pray most earnestly that we may see your face and supply what is lacking in your faith” (1 Thess. 3:10).

They must evidently have been catechized first in such a way that they were nourished with milk, not solid food. The abundance of this milk is recalled in the Letter to the Hebrews for those whom he wished already to nourish with solid food. For this reason he says: “Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us press on to perfection, not laying again a foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith in God, of the teaching of washings and of the laying on of hands, of the resurrection of the dead and of eternal judgment” (Heb. 6:1–2).

This is the abundance of milk, without which those who already use reason sufficiently to be able to believe do not live, although they cannot distinguish good from evil—not merely by believing, but also by understanding, which pertains to solid food.

The “teaching” which he included in his mention of milk is the teaching handed down through the creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

#### 6

But far be it from us to suppose that this milk is opposed to the food of spiritual realities, which must be grasped through firm understanding and which was lacking—and needed to be supplied—in the Colossians and Thessalonians. For when what was lacking is supplied, what was already present is not condemned.

Even in the foods we consume, solid food is so far from being opposed to milk that it itself becomes milk, so that it may be suitable for infants, to whom it reaches through the flesh of the mother or nurse. So too the Wisdom itself, which in the heights is solid food for angels, deigned in a certain way to become milk for little ones when “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:1, 14).

Yet Christ the man himself, who is called the pure milk of little ones because of his true flesh, true cross, true death, and true resurrection, is found, when rightly grasped by spiritual people, to be the Lord of angels.

Therefore little ones must not be given milk in such a way that they never understand Christ as God; nor must they be weaned in such a way that they abandon Christ as man.

The same point can be expressed in another way: they must not be nourished with milk in such a way that they never understand Christ as Creator; nor must they be weaned in such a way that they ever abandon Christ as Mediator.

In this matter the comparison with maternal milk and solid food is not appropriate; the comparison with a foundation is more suitable. For when a child is weaned, so that he withdraws from the foods of infancy, he does not return among solid foods to the breast which he used to suck. Christ crucified, however, is both milk for those who suck and food for those who advance.

The comparison with a foundation is more appropriate because, for the building to be completed, the structure is added; the foundation is not removed.

#### 7

Since this is so, whoever you are—and without doubt many of you are little ones in Christ—advance toward solid food for the mind, not for the belly. Advance toward distinguishing good from evil, and cling more and more closely to the Mediator through whom you are freed from evil. Evil is not to be separated from you spatially; rather, it must be healed within you.

If anyone says to you, “Do not believe that Christ was truly human,” or, “The body of any human being or any living creature was not created by the true God,” or, “The Old Testament was not given by the true God,” or anything of this sort—for these things were not previously said to you while you were being nourished with milk because your heart was not yet suited to grasp the truth—such a person is not preparing food for you but poison.

Therefore the blessed Apostle, addressing those who already seemed to themselves to be perfect, although he himself had said that he was imperfect, says: “As many as are perfect, let us think this way; and if you think differently about anything, God will reveal this also to you.” Lest they perhaps fall in with seducers who wished to turn them away from the faith by promising knowledge of the truth, and lest they think that this was what the Apostle meant by “God will reveal this also to you,” he immediately adds, “Nevertheless, in whatever we have attained, let us walk in it” (Phil. 3:15–16).

If, then, you have understood something which is not contrary to the rule of Catholic faith—to which you have attained as to a road leading you to your homeland—and if you have understood it in such a way that you ought not to doubt it at all, add the building, but do not abandon the foundation.

Those who are more mature should teach the little ones in such a way that they do not say that Christ, Lord of all, or the Prophets and Apostles, who are far greater than they themselves, ever lied.

You must beware not only of empty talkers and seducers of minds who chatter fabulously and falsely, promising what they call profound knowledge in those vanities against the rule of faith which you have received as Catholic. You must also flee, as a more treacherous plague than the others, those who truly discuss the immutability of the divine nature or the incorporeal nature of the creature or the Creator, and prove what they say by entirely certain evidence and arguments, yet attempt to turn you away from the one Mediator between God and human beings.

Such people are those of whom the Apostle says, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” (Rom. 1:21).

For what benefit is it to possess true understanding of the immutable good for one who does not hold fast to the one through whom he may be freed from evil?

Let the warning of the blessed Apostle never depart from your hearts: “If anyone preaches to you a gospel other than what you received, let him be accursed” (Gal. 1:9). He does not say “more than what you received,” but “other than what you received.” For if he had said the former, he would have condemned himself, since he desired to come to the Thessalonians to supply what was lacking in their faith.

But one who supplies adds what was lacking; he does not remove what was already present. One who goes beyond the rule of faith does not advance along the way but withdraws from the way.

#### 8

Therefore, when the Lord says, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now,” what needed to be added to them was what they did not know, not what they had learned overturned.

As I explained in my previous sermon, he could say this because, if he wished to open to them the very things he had taught in the manner in which they are conceived by angels, the human weakness in which they still remained could not bear it.

But any spiritual person can teach another human being what he knows, if the Holy Spirit makes the other person more capable through progress; and the same Spirit could enable the teacher himself to learn something more, so that both might be “taught by God” (John 6:45).

Even among spiritual people, some are certainly more capable and better than others, so that one of them may have attained things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak.

Taking this as an occasion, certain vain people fabricated, with the most foolish presumption, an Apocalypse of Paul which the sound Church does not receive and which is full of I know not what fables. They say that this is the writing in which Paul said that he had been caught up into the third heaven and had heard ineffable words which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12:2, 4).

Their boldness would be tolerable in some way if they had said that they heard things which it is not yet permitted for a human being to speak. But since he said, “things which it is not permitted for a human being to speak,” who are these people who dare to speak of them shamelessly and disastrously?

But I shall now bring this sermon to a close with this conclusion: I desire you to be wise in what is good and innocent with respect to evil.

## TRACTATE XCIX

### On “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak”

Chapter 16, verse 13

#### 1

What does the Lord mean when, promising that the Holy Spirit would come and teach his disciples all truth, or lead them into all truth, he says, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak”?

This resembles what he himself said concerning himself: “I cannot do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge” (John 5:30). But when we explained that passage, we said that it could be understood according to his humanity (above, Tractates XIX–XXII), so that the Son might be seen to have foretold his obedience, by which he became obedient even to the death of the cross (Phil. 2:8), and also the judgment in which he will judge the living and the dead [Note: [Col. 1885] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read, “and the judgment to come.” M.]. For he will accomplish this through what he is as the Son of Man.

For this reason he said, “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son,” because at the judgment it will not be the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father and cannot be seen by the wicked, that will appear, but the form of man, in which he was made a little lower than the angels. Although he will come already in glory, not in his former humility, he will nevertheless be visible to both the good and the wicked.

Hence he also says, “He gave him authority to execute judgment, because he is the Son of Man” (John 5:22, 27).

These words of his make clear that the form to be presented at the judgment will not be the form in which, while existing as such, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized, but the form which he received when he emptied himself. “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2:6–7). In this form he seems also to have commended his obedience for the execution of judgment when he said, “I cannot do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge.”

For Adam, through whose one man’s disobedience many were made sinners, did not judge as he heard. He transgressed what he heard and did the evil he did from himself, because he did not do God’s will but his own.

But Christ, through whose one man’s obedience many are made righteous (Rom. 5:19), was not only obedient even to the death of the cross, on which he was judged alive by the dead; he also promised that he would be obedient in the very judgment by which he will judge the living and the dead: “I cannot,” he says, “do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge.”

But concerning the Holy Spirit, when it is said, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak,” shall we dare to suppose that this was said according to his humanity or according to the assumption of some creature?

For only the Son in the Trinity took the form of a servant, and that form was joined to him in the unity of person—that is, so that the Son of God and the son of man might be one Jesus Christ. Otherwise we would proclaim not a Trinity but a quaternity, which God forbid.

Because of this one person, consisting of two substances, divine and human, he sometimes speaks according to what he is as God, as in the saying, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30); and at other times according to what he is as man, as in the saying, “For the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

According to this distinction, we understand that the words now under discussion were spoken by him: “I cannot do anything from myself; as I hear, I judge.”

But in the person of the Holy Spirit, how are we to understand the statement, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak,” since in him there is no other substance of divinity and another of humanity, or of any other creature? Here a great difficulty arises.

2. For that appearance in bodily form in which the Holy Spirit appeared like a dove (Matt. 3:16) was a vision made and completed for the moment; just as, when he came upon the disciples, tongues divided like fire appeared to them, and one settled upon each of them (Acts 2:3). Therefore, whoever says that the dove was joined to the Holy Spirit in personal unity, so that from it and God—for the Holy Spirit is God—one person of the Holy Spirit consisted, is compelled to say the same also about that fire, and thus to understand that he ought to say none of these things. For these manifestations, which came before the bodily senses of human beings and passed away in whatever manner was necessary to signify something concerning God’s substance, were made by divine action for the moment from a serving creature, not from the ruling nature itself—the nature that, remaining in itself, moves what it wills and, without being changed, changes what it wills.

So also that voice from the cloud certainly reached bodily ears, and that bodily sense which is called hearing (Luke 9:35); yet we must in no way believe that the Word of God, which is the only-begotten Son, is confined to syllables and sounds merely because he is called the Word. For not all sounds can resound simultaneously when speech is being made; rather, like things being born as others die, whatever sounds succeed one another in their order, so that the whole of what we say is completed in the final syllable. Far be it from us to suppose that the Father speaks in this way to the Son—that is, God to his Word, who is God. But this is for those to grasp as far as a human being can grasp it, those to whom milk does not belong, but solid food.

Since, then, the Holy Spirit has not become a human being by assuming humanity, nor an angel by assuming angelic nature, nor a creature by assuming any creature whatsoever, how are we to understand concerning him what the Lord says: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak”? A difficult question—exceedingly difficult. May the Spirit himself be present, so that we may at least be able to express it as we are able to conceive it, and so that, according to the capacity of my modest powers, it may reach your understanding.  
[Col. 1887]

3. You must first know—and those of you who can must understand, while those who cannot yet understand must believe—that in that substance which is God, the senses are not distributed as though through the mass of a body into their proper locations, as in mortal flesh among animals: sight is in one place, hearing in another, taste in another, smell in another, while touch extends throughout. Far be it from us to believe this of that incorporeal and unchangeable nature.

Thus, to hear there and to see are the same thing. Smell, too, is spoken of with reference to God; hence the Apostle says: “Just as Christ also loved us and gave himself for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a pleasing fragrance” (Eph. 5:2). Taste also can be understood, according to which God hates those who are bitter and vomits the neither-cold-nor-hot, but lukewarm, from his mouth (Rev. 3:16); and Christ God says: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me” (John 4:34). There is also that divine touch, concerning which the bride says of the bridegroom: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me” (Song 2:6).

These things are not in God through different bodily locations. For when he is said to know, all these things are there: to see, to hear, to smell, to taste, and to touch—all without any change in his substance, without any mass that is greater in one part and smaller in another. Indeed, when God is conceived in this manner, he is conceived with a childish mind even by old people.

4. Nor should you be surprised that God’s ineffable knowledge, by which he knows all things, is designated through various modes of human speech by the names of all these bodily senses. For our own mind also—that is, the inner human being—to which these five bodily messengers uniformly convey diverse reports, when it understands, chooses, and loves immutable truth, sees the light of which it is said, “He was the true light”; hears the word of which it is said, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:9, 1); takes in the fragrance of which it is said, “We will run after the fragrance of your ointments” (Song 1:3); drinks from the fountain of which it is said, “With you is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35:10); and enjoys the touch of which it is said, “But for me, to cling to God is good” (Ps. 72:28)—not one thing and another, but a single understanding is designated by so many names of the senses.

When, therefore, it is said of the Holy Spirit, “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak,” we must understand or believe all the more that there is a simple nature there, where it is most truly simple—a nature that far surpasses, in height and depth, the nature of our mind.

For our mind is changeable: by learning it perceives what it did not know, and by unlearning it loses what it knew; it is deceived by resemblance to truth, so that it approves what is false in place of what is true, and it is hindered by its own obscurity, as though by certain darknesses, from reaching the truth. Therefore our substance is not truly simple, since for it to be is not the same as for it to know: it can exist without knowing. But that divine substance cannot, because what it has is what it is.

Accordingly, it does not possess knowledge in such a way that its knowledge by which it knows is one thing and its essence by which it is another; both are one. Indeed, we should not even speak of both, since they are simply one. As the Father has life in himself, and he is not something other than the life that is in him, so he gave the Son to have life in himself (John 5:26)—that is, he begot the Son, who himself also is life.

Thus we must understand what was said of the Holy Spirit: “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak,” so that we may understand that he is not from himself. For the Father alone is not from another. The Son was born from the Father, and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father; but the Father was neither born from another nor does he proceed from another.

Yet human thought should not on that account encounter any inequality in that supreme Trinity. The Son is equal to him from whom he was born, and the Holy Spirit is equal to him from whom he proceeds. But what difference there is between proceeding and being born would take a long time to investigate and explain, and after explaining it, it would be rash to define it. For even to grasp this in some fashion with the mind, and, if the mind should happen to grasp anything concerning it, to explain it with the tongue, is exceedingly difficult—regardless of how great the teacher or how attentive the hearer may be.

Therefore, “He will not speak from himself,” because he is not from himself. “But whatever he hears, he will speak”: he will hear from him from whom he proceeds. For hearing is knowing for him; and knowing is being, as was discussed above. Since, therefore, he is not from himself but from him from whom he proceeds, from him he has his essence, and from him he has his knowledge; therefore from him he has his hearing, which is nothing other than knowledge.

5. Nor should it trouble us that the verb is placed in the future tense. It was not said, “Whatever he has heard,” or “Whatever he hears,” but, “Whatever he will hear, he will speak.” For that hearing is eternal, because it is eternal knowledge. In what is eternal, without beginning and without end, a verb of any tense—past, present, or future—is not used falsely.

Although that immutable and ineffable nature does not admit “was” and “will be,” but only “is”—for it truly is, because it cannot be changed, and therefore it alone could rightly say, “I am who I am,” and, “You shall say to the children of Israel, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. 3:14)—nevertheless, because of the mutability of the times in which our mortality and mutability exist, we do not speak falsely when we say “was,” “will be,” and “is.” He was in ages past, he is in the present, and he will be in the future. He was, because he was never absent; he will be, because he will never be absent; he is, because he always is.

For he does not, like one who no longer exists, perish with the past; nor, like one who does not remain, slip away with the present; nor, like one who did not exist before, arise with the future. Therefore, since human speech varies according to the sequence of times, whatever tense is used concerning him who could not, cannot, and will not be absent from any time is spoken truly.

The Holy Spirit, then, always hears, because he always knows; therefore he has known, knows, and will know. Consequently, he has heard, hears, and will hear; for, as we have already said, hearing for him is the same as knowing, and knowing for him is the same as being. Therefore he has heard, hears, and will hear from him from whom he is; he is from him from whom he proceeds.

6. At this point someone may perhaps ask whether the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son. The Son is the Son of the Father alone, and the Father is the Father of the Son alone; but the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of one of them, but of both.

You have the Lord himself saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20). You also have the Apostle: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts” (Gal. 4:6). Are there two spirits, one of the Father and another of the Son? Far be it from us. “For one body,” he says, signifying the Church; and immediately he adds, “and one Spirit.” See how he completes the Trinity there: “Just as you were called in one hope of your calling. One Lord”—here he plainly wished Christ to be understood. It remains for him also to name the Father. He therefore continues: “One faith, one baptism; one God and Father of all, who is over all, and through all [Note: [Col. 1889] The printed editions have “through all things” (*per omnia*). But the manuscripts have “through all” (*per omnes*), and only a few add “us” (*nobis*) at the end of the verse. In Greek there is *dià pantôn*, of uncertain gender; and at the end *hymîn*, “you,” because the Vulgate in the ancient Corbie Bibles agreed in its wording.], and in us all” (Eph. 4:4–6).

As, then, there is one Father and one Lord—that is, the Son—so there is also one Spirit. He certainly belongs to both, since Christ Jesus himself says, “The Spirit of your Father who speaks in you,” and the Apostle says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts.”

In another place the same Apostle says: “But if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you” (Rom. 8:11). Here he plainly wished the Spirit of the Father to be understood; yet elsewhere he says: “But whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Rom. 8:9). There are many other testimonies by which it is clearly shown that the Spirit who in the Trinity is called the Holy Spirit belongs both to the Father and to the Son.

7. I think that he is not called “Spirit” for any other reason than this: even if we are asked about each individually, we can call both the Father and the Son “spirit,” since “God is spirit” (John 4:24)—that is, God is not a body but spirit. Since, therefore, what they are each called commonly is what he ought to be called properly, he is called “Spirit” properly because he is not one of them, but the one in whom the community of both appears.

Why, then, should we not believe that the Holy Spirit also proceeds from the Son, since he is himself also the Spirit of the Son? For if he did not proceed from him, after the resurrection he would not have breathed upon his disciples when he presented himself to them, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). What else did that breathing signify except that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him also?

The same applies to what he said concerning the woman who suffered from a flow of blood: “Someone touched me; for I perceived that power had gone out from me” (Luke 8:46). That the Holy Spirit is also called “power” is clear in the passage where the angel answered Mary, who said, “How will this happen, since I do not know a man?”: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1:34–35).

The Lord himself, promising the Spirit to his disciples, said: “But you remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24:49); and again: “You will receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you will be my witnesses” (Acts 1:8). The evangelist should be understood to have spoken of this power when he says: “Power went out from him and healed them all” (Luke 6:19).

8. If, then, the Holy Spirit proceeds both from the Father and from the Son, why did the Son say, “He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26)? Why do you think, except that he customarily refers even what belongs to him to the one from whom he himself is? Hence he says: “My teaching is not mine, but his who sent me” (John 7:16).

If, then, this teaching is understood to be his, although he said that it was not his but the Father’s, how much more must the Holy Spirit be understood to proceed from him also in the passage where he says, “He proceeds from the Father,” without saying, “He does not proceed from me”?

From the one by whom the Son has it that he is God—for he is God from God—he certainly has it that the Holy Spirit proceeds from him also. Therefore, the Holy Spirit has from the Father himself that he should proceed from the Son just as he proceeds from the Father.

9. From this, as far as it can be understood by people such as we are, we can also grasp why the Holy Spirit is not said to have been born but rather to proceed. For if he too were called “Son,” he would necessarily be called the Son of both, which is utterly absurd. A son is of two persons only when he is of a father and a mother. Far be it from us, however, to suspect anything of this sort between God the Father and God the Son.

For not even a human son proceeds simultaneously from his father and his mother. When he proceeds into the mother from the father, he does not then proceed from the mother; and when he proceeds from the mother into this light, he does not then proceed from the father.

But the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father into the Son and from the Son toward the sanctification of creation; rather, he proceeds simultaneously from both, although the Father gave this to the Son: that, just as he proceeds from the Father himself, so he should proceed from the Son also.

For we cannot say that the Holy Spirit is not life, while the Father is life and the Son is life. Therefore, just as the Father, having life in himself, gave the Son to have life in himself, so he gave him to have life proceeding from him, just as it proceeds from the Father himself.  
[Note: [Col. 1890] Augustine transferred this passage from section 8 into Book 15 of *On the Trinity*, chapter 27.]

The Lord’s words that follow are these: “And he will announce to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you. Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.” But since this discourse has already become lengthy, these words must be deferred to another sermon.

**TRACTATE 100. On the final words of the same reading. Chapter 16, verses 13–15.**

1. When the Lord promised that the Holy Spirit would come, he said: “He will teach you all truth”; or, as is read in some manuscripts, “He will lead you into all truth.” “For he will not speak from himself, but whatever he hears, he will speak.” We have already discussed what the Lord granted us concerning these evangelical words; now attend to what follows.

“And he will announce to you the things that are to come.” There is no need to linger here, since the meaning is plain: there is nothing requiring an explanation from us. But what he adds—“He will glorify me, because he will take from what is mine and announce it to you”—must not be passed over carelessly.

For what he says, “He will glorify me,” can be understood in this way: by pouring charity into the hearts of believers and making them spiritual, the Spirit showed them how the Son was equal to the Father, although previously they had known him only according to the flesh and had thought of him as a human being like other human beings.

Or certainly it can be understood in this way: because, through that very charity, they were filled with confidence [Note: [Col. 1891] Four manuscripts read: “because, filled by him with charity and confidence.”], and fear was driven away, they proclaimed Christ to human beings; and thus his fame was spread throughout the whole world.

Thus he may have said, “He will glorify me,” as though he were saying: “He will take fear away from you and give you love, so that, by proclaiming me more ardently, you will spread the fragrance of my glory throughout the whole world and commend my honor.”

What they were going to do in the Holy Spirit, he said that the same Spirit would do. The same is true of the saying: “For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks in you” (Matt. 10:20).

The Greek word *doxasei* (δοξάσει) has been rendered by Latin translators in their respective translations as “he will glorify” (*clarificabit*) and “he will glorify” (*glorificabit*), because the Greek word *doxa* (δόξα), from which *doxasei* is derived, is interpreted both as “splendor” (*claritas*) and as “glory” (*gloria*). For a person becomes renowned through glory, and glorious through renown; accordingly, what is signified by both words is the same.

As the most distinguished ancient authors of the Latin language have defined it, glory is widespread fame concerning someone, accompanied by praise. When such fame concerning Christ arose in this world, it should not be thought to have conferred anything great upon Christ, but upon the world. For praising what is good benefits not the one praised but those who praise.

2. There is also false glory, when those who praise are deceived by error, whether concerning things, persons, or both. They are deceived concerning things when they think something good that is evil; concerning persons when they think someone good who is evil; and concerning both when a vice is thought to be a virtue and the person praised on that account does not possess what is believed of him, whether he is good or evil.

To give one’s possessions to actors is a monstrous vice, not a virtue; and you know how widespread is the fame of such people, accompanied by praise, since, as it is written: “The sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the one who acts unjustly is blessed” (Ps. 9:3). Here those who praise are not deceived concerning the persons but concerning the things: what they believe to be good is evil.

Those who are vicious because of this evil generosity are, of course, the sort of people whom those who praise them do not imagine them to be, but see them to be.

Again, if someone pretends to be just when he is not, and does not do everything that he appears to do laudably before human beings for God’s sake—that is, for the sake of true justice—but seeks and loves only glory from human beings, while those among whom his fame is widespread and accompanied by praise think that he lives laudably only for God’s sake, they are not deceived concerning the thing but concerning the person.

What they believe to be good is good; but the one whom they believe to be good is not good.

Suppose, for example, that skill in magical arts were thought to be good, and that someone believed to have freed his country by those very arts, although he knows nothing of them at all, gained among impious people widespread fame accompanied by praise—that is, the glory so defined. Those who praise him are mistaken in both respects: concerning the thing, because they think what is evil to be good; and concerning the person, because he is not what they think.

Therefore glory is false in these three categories.

But when, concerning someone who is just through God and for God’s sake—that is, truly just—there is, on account of his justice itself, widespread fame accompanied by praise, the glory is indeed true. Nevertheless, we must not believe that the just person is made blessed by it; rather, those who praise him should be congratulated, because they judge rightly and love the just person.

How much more, then, did the Lord Christ’s glory benefit not himself but those whom his death benefited?

3. Yet among heretics his glory is not true, although among them he appears to have widespread fame accompanied by praise. It is not true glory because they are mistaken in both respects: they think something good that is not good, and they think Christ to be something that Christ is not.

It is not good to believe that the only-begotten Son is not equal to the one who begets him; it is not good to believe that the only-begotten Son of God is merely human and not God; it is not good to believe that the flesh of the Truth is not true flesh.

Of these three opinions, the first is held by the Arians, the second by the Photinians, and the third by the Manichaeans. But since none of these things is good, and Christ is none of these things, they are mistaken in both respects. They do not give true glory to Christ, although among them widespread fame concerning Christ appears to exist, accompanied by praise.

Indeed, all heretics—whose names it would take too long to enumerate—who do not think rightly about Christ are in error because they do not think truly about good and evil things.

The pagans, too, although many of them are praisers of Christ, are themselves mistaken in both respects. They say that he was a magical practitioner, not according to the truth of God but according to their own suspicion. They reproach Christians as though they were ignorant, but praise Christ as though he were a magician, and thus reveal what they love.

They do not love Christ, because they love what Christ was not. Therefore they are mistaken in both respects: being a magician is evil, and Christ was not a magician, because he is good.

Since, then, nothing need be said here about those who reproach and blaspheme Christ—for we are speaking of the glory by which he was glorified in the world—the Holy Spirit glorified him with true glory only in the holy Catholic Church. Elsewhere—that is, either among heretics or among certain pagans—his true glory on earth cannot exist, even where widespread fame concerning him appears to exist, accompanied by praise.

Thus his true glory is sung by the prophet in the Catholic Church: “Be exalted above the heavens, O God, and your glory above all the earth” (Ps. 107:6). Since, therefore, the Holy Spirit was to come after Christ’s exaltation and glorify him, this is what the sacred Psalm promised, and what the only-begotten Son himself promised would happen—a promise that we see fulfilled.

4. As for what he says, “He will take from what is mine and announce it to you,” hear it with Catholic ears; receive it with Catholic minds. The Holy Spirit is not therefore inferior to the Son, as certain heretics have thought—as though the Son received from the Father and the Holy Spirit from the Son, according to certain gradations of natures.

Far be it from us to believe this; far be it from us to say this; far be it from Christian hearts to think this.

Finally, he himself immediately resolves the question and explains why he said this: “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and announce it to you.”

What more do you want? The Holy Spirit receives from the Father what the Son receives, because in this Trinity the Son is born from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father. The Father alone is born from no one and proceeds from no one.

But how the only-begotten Son said, “Everything that the Father has is mine”—for this is certainly not in the same way as it was said to that son who was not the only-begotten, but the elder of two: “You are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31)—will, if the Lord wills, be treated with careful consideration in the passage where the only-begotten Son says to the Father: “Everything that is mine is yours, and everything that is yours is mine” (John 17:10). Thus this discourse may be brought to a close, since what follows requires another beginning from which it may be discussed.

**TRACTATE 101. On what the Lord says, “A little while, and you will no longer see me,” up to, “And on that day you will ask me nothing.” Chapter 16, verses 16–23.**

1. The Lord’s words—“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me, because I am going to the Father”—were so obscure to the disciples before what he said was fulfilled that, as they asked one another what he meant, they openly confessed that they did not know at all.

The Gospel continues: “Therefore some of his disciples said to one another, ‘What is this that he says to us, “A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me; and because I am going to the Father”?’ They said therefore, ‘What is this that he says, “A little while”? We do not know what he is saying.’”

This was what troubled them: he had said, “A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me.” Previously, when he had not said “a little while” but had said, “I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (John 16:10), he seemed to have spoken plainly to them, and they did not ask one another anything about it.

What was then obscure to them and soon became clear is now certainly clear to us. For shortly afterward he suffered, and they did not see him; then, after a little while, he rose again, and they saw him.

As for what he said, “You will no longer see me”—since by the word “now” he wished it to be understood that they would not see him thereafter—we explained there how it should be understood, where he said, “The Holy Spirit will convict the world concerning righteousness, because I am going to the Father, and you will no longer see me” (above, Tractate 95): namely, that they would no longer see Christ in his mortal condition.

2. Jesus knew, as the Evangelist next says, that they wanted to ask him, and he said to them: “Are you asking one another about this, because I said, ‘A little while, and you will not see me; and again a little while, and you will see me’? Amen, amen, I say to you, you will weep and lament, but the world will rejoice; you will be sorrowful, but your sorrow will become joy” [Note: [Col. 1893] So the manuscripts. The printed editions have, “will be turned into joy.”].

This can be understood in the following way: the disciples were sorrowful over the Lord’s death and immediately rejoiced over his resurrection. But the world—by which the enemies who killed Christ are signified—rejoiced at that time when the disciples were sorrowful, namely, when Christ had been killed.

By “the world,” the wickedness of this world can be understood—that is, the people who are friends of this world. Hence the Apostle James says in his Epistle: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is constituted an enemy of God” (James 4:4). It was because of this enmity toward God that they did not spare even his only-begotten Son.

3. Then he adds and says: “A woman, when she is in labor, has sorrow because her hour has come; but when she has given birth to the child, she no longer remembers her distress because of the joy that a human being has been born into the world. So you also now have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you.”

This comparison does not appear difficult to understand, since he himself explains plainly why it was made. Labor is compared with sorrow, and childbirth with joy; the joy is customarily greater when a boy rather than a girl is born.

By what he says, “No one will take your joy from you,” since Jesus himself is their joy, what the Apostle says is signified: “Christ, rising from the dead, no longer dies, and death will no longer rule over him” (Rom. 6:9).

4. Up to this point in the Gospel chapter on which we are discoursing today, everything has proceeded as though it were easy to understand. A sharper attention is necessary in what follows.

What, then, does he mean by saying, “And on that day you will ask me nothing”? The word translated “ask” signifies not only to request but also to question. The Greek Gospel from which this was translated has a word that can bear both meanings, so that the ambiguity is not resolved even there [Note: [Col. 1894] Greek: *erōtēsēte* (ἐρωτήσετε).]. Even if it were resolved, however, the question would not thereby disappear.

For after Christ the Lord rose again, we read both that he was questioned and that he was asked. He was questioned by the disciples as he was about to ascend into heaven: when would he restore the kingdom to Israel? (Acts 1:6). But when he was already in heaven, the holy Stephen asked him to receive his spirit (Acts 7:58).

Who would dare either to think or to say that Christ seated in heaven should not be asked, while Christ remaining on earth should have been asked? That the immortal should not be asked, while the mortal ought to have been asked?

Rather, beloved, let us ask him to dissolve this knot of the question himself, by shining in our hearts so that we may see what he says.

5. For I think that what he says—“I will see you again, and your heart will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you”—does not refer to the time when he rose again and showed them his flesh to see and touch (John 20:27), but rather to that of which he had already said: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14:21).

John the Apostle himself, whose Gospel this is, said in his Epistle, after Christ had already risen, had already shown himself to them in the flesh, and was already seated at the right hand of the Father: “Beloved, we are now children of God, and it has not yet been manifested what we shall be. We know that when it is manifested, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

This vision does not belong to the present life but to the future; not to a temporal life but to an eternal one [Note: [Col. 1895] Three manuscripts read, “not temporal, but eternal.”]. This is the eternal life of which Life itself says: “That they may know you, the one true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3).

Concerning this vision and knowledge the Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma, but then face to face; now I know in part, but then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Cor. 13:12–13).

The Church is now in labor with the fruit of all her toil, desiring it; then she will give birth to it by seeing. Now she is in labor with groaning; then she will give birth with rejoicing. Now she is in labor by praying; then she will give birth by praising.

And therefore it is a male child, because all the duties of action are directed toward this fruit of contemplation. For it alone is free, because it is desired for its own sake and is not referred to anything else. Action serves it; whatever is done well is referred to it, because it is done for its sake. It itself, however, is held and possessed not for the sake of something else but for its own sake.

There, then, is the end that is sufficient for us. It will therefore be eternal; for no end is sufficient for us unless it has no end.

This was inspired in Philip when he said: “Show us the Father, and it is sufficient for us.” The Son also promised himself in that showing when he said: “Do you not believe that I am in the Father and the Father is in me?” (John 14:8, 10).

Concerning this, then, which is sufficient for us, we rightly hear: “No one will take your joy from you.”

6. I also think that the words said above—“A little while, and you will no longer see me; and again a little while, and you will see me”—are better understood in reference to this.

For “a little while” is the entire span during which the present age flies past. Hence the same Evangelist says in his Epistle: “It is the final hour” (1 John 2:18).

That is why he added, “because I am going to the Father.” This must be referred to the first statement, where he says, “A little while, and you will no longer see me,” not to the later one, where he says, “and again a little while, and you will see me.”

By going to the Father, he was going to bring about their not seeing him. Thus the saying was not spoken because he was going to die and, until he rose again, withdraw from their sight; rather, it was spoken because he was going to go to the Father—which he did after he had risen again and had spent forty days with them before ascending into heaven (Acts 1:3, 9).

Therefore he said to those who were then seeing him bodily, “A little while, and you will no longer see me,” because he was going to the Father and they would no longer see him as a mortal, in the condition in which they saw him while he was speaking these words.

But when he added, “and again a little while, and you will see me,” he made this promise to the whole Church, just as he promised to the whole Church: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28:20).

The Lord does not delay his promise. A little while, and we shall see him, when we shall no longer ask anything or question anything, because nothing to be desired will remain and nothing to be sought will be hidden.

This little while seems long to us because it is still in progress. When it has ended, we shall perceive how short it was.

Therefore, let our joy not be like that which the world has, of which it was said, “But the world will rejoice.” Nevertheless, let us not be sorrowful without joy in the labor of this desire; rather, as the Apostle says, let us be “rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation” (Rom. 12:12). For the woman in labor to whom we have been compared rejoices more over the offspring that will soon come than she is sorrowful over her present pain.

But let this be the end of this discourse. The matters that follow contain a very troublesome question and should not be compressed by brevity, so that, if the Lord wills, they may be explained more suitably.

**TRACTATE 102. On what the Lord says, “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you,” up to, “Again I leave the world and go to the Father.” Chapter 16, verses 23–28.**

1. We must now discuss these words of the Lord: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you.”

It has already been said in earlier parts of this discourse of the Lord, for the sake of those who ask the Father for certain things in Christ’s name but do not receive them, that whatever is asked against the reason of salvation is not asked in the name of the Savior (above, Tractate 73).

For when he says, “in my name,” this must not be understood as referring to the sound of letters and syllables, but to what that sound signifies and what is rightly and truly understood by it.

Therefore, whoever holds a view of Christ that ought not to be held of the only-begotten Son of God does not ask in his name, even if he does not remain silent about Christ in letters and syllables; for when he asks, he asks in the name of the one whom he has in mind.

But whoever holds concerning him what ought to be held asks in his name; and he receives what he asks if he does not ask against his own eternal salvation. He receives it, however, when he ought to receive it. For some things are not denied but postponed, so that they may be given at the appropriate time.

Thus what he says, “he will give it to you,” must be understood to signify those benefits that properly concern those who ask. For all the saints are heard when they ask for themselves, but they are not heard in every case when they ask for all their friends, or enemies, or anyone else. For he did not simply say, “he will give,” but, “he will give it to you.”

### 2

“Until now,” he says, “you have asked nothing in my name. Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” By “complete joy” he surely means not bodily but spiritual joy; and when it is such that nothing further can be added to it, then without doubt it will be complete. Whatever, therefore, is asked that pertains to attaining this joy is to be asked in Christ’s name, if we understand divine grace and truly seek the blessed life. Whatever else is asked, nothing is asked—not because the thing itself is altogether nothing, but because, compared with so great a thing, whatever else is desired is nothing.

For a human being is not altogether nothing, concerning whom the Apostle says: “Whoever thinks that he is something, when he is nothing” (Gal. 6:3). Compared with the spiritual person, who knows that by God’s grace he is what he is, whoever presumes upon vanities is nothing. Thus, too, the saying “Amen, amen, I say to you, if you ask the Father anything in my name, he will give it to you” can rightly be understood in this way: “anything” does not mean just anything whatsoever, but something which, in comparison with the blessed life, is not nothing [Col. 1897]. And what follows, “Until now you have asked nothing in my name,” can be understood in two ways: either because you have not asked in my name, since you have not known that name as it ought to be known; or because you have asked nothing, since, in comparison with the thing you ought to have asked for, what you asked for must be regarded as nothing.

Therefore, so that they may ask in his name not nothing but complete joy—for if they ask for anything else, that same “anything” is nothing—he exhorts them, saying: “Ask, and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete.” That is: “Ask this in my name, so that your joy may be complete, and you will receive it.” For if his saints persevere in asking for this good, divine mercy will certainly not defraud them of it.

### 3

“These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly.” I might say that the hour of which he speaks ought to be understood as the age to come, when we shall see openly what blessed Paul says, “face to face”; so that “These things I have spoken to you in figures” would correspond to what the same Apostle says: “Now we see through a mirror, in a riddle” (1 Cor. 13:12). But “I will announce” means that the Father will be seen through the Son, in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “No one knows the Father except the Son, and the one to whom the Son wills to reveal him” (Matt. 11:27).

Yet this interpretation seems to be obstructed by what follows: “On that day you will ask in my name.” For in the age to come, when we have reached the kingdom where we shall be like him, since we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2), what shall we ask for, when our desire shall be satisfied with good things (Ps. 102:5)? Hence another psalm also says: “I shall be satisfied when your glory is revealed” (Ps. 16:15). Petition belongs to some need; but there will be no need where this satisfaction exists.

It remains, then, as far as I can understand, that Jesus is to be understood as having promised to make his disciples spiritual instead of carnal or animal, although not yet such as we shall be when we also possess a spiritual body. They would be like the one who said: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. 2:6); and, “I could not speak to you as spiritual people, but as carnal” (ibid. 3:1); and, “We have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit who is from God, so that we may know the things granted to us by God; and these things we speak, not in words taught by human wisdom, but in words taught by the Spirit, comparing spiritual things with spiritual things. [Note: [Col. 1897] Er.: “taught by the Spirit from spiritual people.” Lugd. and Ven.: “taught by the Spirit [to] spiritual people.” M.] But the animal person does not perceive the things of God’s Spirit.”

Thus the animal person, not perceiving the things of God’s Spirit, hears whatever he hears about God’s nature in such a way that he cannot conceive of anything other than a body—however immense, however vast, however luminous and beautiful, still a body. Therefore all statements of wisdom concerning incorporeal and unchangeable substance are figures to him—not because he reckons them as figures, but because he thinks in the manner of those who habitually hear figures without understanding them.

When, however, the spiritual person begins to judge all things, while he himself is judged by no one (1 Cor. 2:12–15), even though in this life he still sees as through a mirror and in part, he nevertheless perceives—not by any bodily sense, nor by any imaginary thought that grasps or fabricates likenesses of bodies of whatever kind [Note: [Col. 1898] Lov. lacks the particle “that” [quae], although it is required for the sense and is found in the manuscripts.], but by the mind’s most certain understanding—that God is not a body but spirit. Thus the Son announces the Father openly, so that the one who announces him is seen to be of the same substance.

Then they ask in his name, because in the sound of that name they understand nothing other than the reality itself which is called by that name. They do not fabricate, through mental vanity or weakness, the Father as if in one place and the Son standing before the Father in another, pleading for us, each occupying his own spatial bulk; nor do they imagine the Word speaking words on our behalf to the One whose Word he is, with an interval between the mouth of the speaker and the ears of the hearer; nor any other such notions which animal and likewise carnal people construct in their hearts.

Whatever of this kind occurs to those who think spiritually about God because of their familiarity with bodies, they drive away from their inner eyes by denying and rejecting it, as though they were unwelcome flies. They rest in the purity of that light which, as witness and judge, proves that these very bodily images invading their inner vision are wholly false.

Such people can, to some extent, think of our Lord Jesus Christ as interceding with the Father for us insofar as he is human; but insofar as he is God, they can think of him as hearing us together with the Father. I believe he signified this when he said: “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you.” To perceive how the Son does not ask the Father, but the Father and the Son together hear those who ask, the mind’s spiritual eye alone rises.

### 4

“For the Father himself,” he says, “loves you, because you have loved me.” Does he love us because we love him—or rather, do we love because he loves? Let the Evangelist himself answer from his Epistle: “We love,” he says, “because he first loved us” (1 John 4:10). Thus it happened that we loved because we were loved. It is altogether God’s gift to love God. The one who loved without having been loved gave himself to be loved. We were loved while displeasing, so that there might be in us something by which we could please him.

For we would not love the Son unless we also loved the Father. The Father loves us because we love the Son, although we have received from the Father and the Son the ability to love both the Father and the Son. For the Spirit of both pours love into our hearts (Rom. 5:5); through that Spirit we love the Father and the Son, and we love that Spirit together with the Father and the Son.

God therefore made our devout love by which we worship him, and he saw that it was good; for this reason he himself loved what he had made. But he would not make in us something he could love unless he loved us before he made it.

### 5

“And you have believed,” he says, “that I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.”

We have indeed believed. It ought not seem incredible because, in coming into the world, he came forth from the Father without abandoning the Father, and in leaving the world and going to the Father, he leaves the world without abandoning it.

He came forth from the Father because he is from the Father. He came into the world because he displayed to the world his body, which he assumed from the Virgin. He left the world by a bodily departure; he proceeded to the Father by the ascent of his humanity; yet he did not abandon the world in the governance of his presence.

## TRACTATE CIII

Concerning the passage that follows, “His disciples say to him: Behold, now you are speaking openly,” through “But take courage; I have overcome the world.” Chapter 16, verses 29–33.

### 1

What Christ’s disciples were like when he spoke with them before his Passion—speaking great things with little ones, but as was fitting, since great things had to be spoken to little ones because they had not yet received the Holy Spirit, whom they received after his resurrection, either when he himself breathed upon them or from above—is shown by many indications throughout the Gospel. Hence this too is what they said in the present passage.

The Evangelist says: “His disciples say to him: Behold, now you are speaking openly, and saying no figure. Now we know that you know all things, and that you have no need for anyone to question you; by this we believe that you came forth from God.”

A little earlier the Lord himself had said: “These things I have spoken to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures.” How, then, do they say, “Behold, now you are speaking openly, and saying no figure”? Had the hour already come when he had promised that he would no longer speak in figures?

The continuation of his words plainly shows that this hour had not yet come. It runs as follows: “These things,” he says, “I have spoken to you in figures; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will announce the Father to you openly. On that day you will ask in my name; and I do not say to you that I will ask the Father for you, for the Father himself loves you, because you have loved me and have believed that I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16:25–28).

Throughout these words he is still promising the hour when he will no longer speak in figures but announce the Father to them openly. In that hour, he says, they will ask in his name, and he will not ask the Father for them, because the Father himself loves them, since they have loved Christ and believed that he came forth from the Father and came into the world, intending again to leave the world and go to the Father.

Since, then, the hour in which he will speak without figures is still being promised, why do they say, “Behold, now you are speaking openly, and saying no figure”? It is because they understand so little that the things which he knows are figures to those who do not understand, that they do not even understand that they themselves do not understand. They were little ones and did not yet judge spiritually what they heard concerning realities belonging not to the body but to the spirit.

### 2

Finally, warning them that, according to the inner person, they were still little and weak, he said: “Jesus answered them: Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—indeed it has come—when you will be scattered, each to his own, and you will leave me alone. And I am not alone, because the Father is with me.”

A little earlier he had said: “I leave the world and go to the Father”; now he says: “The Father is with me.” Who goes to the one who is with him? But this is a word to one who understands, and a figure to one who does not understand. Nevertheless, what the little ones do not yet understand is somehow sucked in; and although it does not provide solid food, because they cannot yet grasp it, it does not deny them at least milk-like nourishment.

This nourishment consists in the fact that they knew he understood all things and had no need for anyone to question him. Why they said this, however, may be asked. It would seem that they ought rather to have said, “You have no need to question anyone,” not, “You have no need for anyone to question you.”

For they said: “We know that you know all things.” Now one who knows all things is ordinarily questioned by those who do not know, so that those who ask may hear what they wish from the one who knows all things; it is not he who knows all things who must question, as though he wished to learn something.

What, then, is the meaning of this? Although they seemed to have to say to the one whom they knew to know all things, “You have no need to question anyone,” they thought it better to say, “You have no need for anyone to question you.” Moreover, we read that both things happened: the Lord questioned, and was questioned.

This is quickly resolved: it was not he but rather they who needed this—those whom he questioned or by whom he was questioned. He did not question anyone in order to learn something from them, but rather in order to teach them. And those who questioned him, wishing to learn something from him, surely needed to know certain things from the one who knew all things. Thus, plainly, there was no need for anyone to question him.

For when we are questioned by those who wish to learn something from us, we discover from their very questions what they wish to learn. We therefore need to be questioned by those whom we wish to teach something, so that we may know what inquiries require an answer. But he, who knew all things, did not even need this; nor did he need to discover through someone’s question what that person wished to know from him, because before he was questioned he already knew the will of the one who was going to question him.

He nevertheless allowed himself to be questioned so that he might show, either to those who were then present or to those who would later hear these sayings or read them in writing, what kind of people those were who questioned him. In this way we might know either by what deceits he could not be ensnared or by what approaches progress could be made with him.

To foresee the thoughts of human beings, and therefore not need anyone to question him, was not a great thing for God; but it was a great thing for the little ones who said to him: “By this we believe that you came forth from God.” Much greater was the matter toward which he wished them to extend and grow in understanding. When they had said—and had said truly—“You came forth from God,” he replied: “The Father is with me,” lest they should think that the Son had come forth from the Father in such a way as to suppose that he had also departed from him.

### 3

Then, bringing this great and lengthy discourse to a close, he says: “I have spoken these things to you so that you may have peace in me. In the world you will have distress; but take courage, I have overcome the world.”

That distress was to have its beginning at the point where, in order to show that they were little ones—since, while they still did not understand and were taking one thing for another, all the great and divine things he had said were in a sense figures to them—he said above: “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming—indeed it has come—when you will be scattered, each to his own.”

Behold the beginning of the distress, but not the way in which it would continue. For when he added, “and you will leave me alone,” he did not mean that they would be such during the subsequent distress which they were to have in the world after his ascension, that they would abandon him; rather, they were to remain in him and have peace in him.

For when he was arrested, they abandoned not merely his flesh with their flesh, but also faith in him with their minds. This is what belongs to his saying: “Do you now believe? Behold, the hour is coming when you will be scattered, each to his own, and you will leave me”—as though he were saying: “Then you will be so disturbed that you will abandon even what you now believe.”

They came to such despair, and, so to speak, to the death of their former faith, as appeared in Cleopas, who, after the Lord’s resurrection, spoke with him without knowing who he was and, recounting what had happened to him, said: “We were hoping that he was the one who was going to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). See how they had abandoned him, abandoning even the faith by which they had previously believed in him.

In the distress which they endured after his glorification, once they had received the Holy Spirit, they did not abandon him. Although they fled from city to city, they did not flee from him. Having distress in the world, they held peace in him; they were not fugitives from him, but had him rather as their refuge.

When the Holy Spirit had been given to them, what is now said to them was accomplished in them: “Take courage, I have overcome the world.” They took courage and overcame. In whom, if not in him? For he would not have overcome the world if the world were overcoming his members.

Hence the Apostle says: “Thanks be to God, who gives us the victory,” and immediately adds, “through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Cor. 15:57)—the one who had said to his own: “Take courage, I have overcome the world.”

## TRACTATE CIV

On the passage that follows, “Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.” Chapter 17, verse 1.

### 1

Before these matters which, with the Lord’s help, we are now about to discuss, Jesus had said: “I have spoken these things to you, that you may have peace in me.” We should understand this not merely of the things said by him a little earlier, but of all that he had said to them, whether from the time he began to have them as disciples, or at least from the time when, after supper, he began this wonderful and lengthy discourse. For he stated such a reason for having spoken to them that either everything he said to them, or especially those things he said when he was about to die for them—like final words, after the one who was to betray him had left the holy meal—must most rightly be referred to that end.

For he set forth this reason for his discourse: that they might have peace in him. This is the whole purpose of our being Christians. This peace will have no end in time, but will itself be the end of all our pious striving and action. For its sake we are imbued with his sacraments; for its sake we are instructed by his wonderful works and words; for its sake we have received the pledge of his Spirit; for its sake we believe and hope in him, and are kindled, insofar as he grants it, by his love. By this peace we are comforted in all afflictions; by it we are delivered from all afflictions. For its sake we endure every tribulation bravely, that in it we may reign happily without any tribulation.

Rightly, then, he closed with it the words which were figures to the disciples who understood little, but which would be understood when he had given them the promised Holy Spirit, of whom he said above: “I have spoken these things to you while remaining with you. But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of all that I have said to you” (John 14:25–26). That, indeed, was to be the hour in which he promised that he would no longer speak in figures, but would announce the Father openly. For the same words of his, when understood through the Holy Spirit’s revelation, would no longer be figures to them. The only-begotten Son was not going to be silent when the Holy Spirit spoke in their hearts; he had said that in that hour he would openly announce the Father to them, which would certainly not be a figure to them once they understood. But even this—how both the Son of God and the Holy Spirit, indeed the Trinity itself which works inseparably, speak together in the hearts of their spiritual people—is a word to those who understand, but a figure to those who do not.

### 2

Therefore, after he had said why he had spoken all these things—namely, that they might have peace in him while having affliction in the world—and had exhorted them to take courage because he had overcome the world, he ended his discourse to them and then directed words to the Father, beginning to pray. For the Evangelist continues: “Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting up his eyes to heaven, said: Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son.” The Lord, the only-begotten and coeternal with the Father, could, in the form of a servant and from the form of a servant, have prayed silently if that had been necessary; but he wished to present himself to the Father as a suppliant so as to remember that he was our teacher.

Accordingly, he made known to us the prayer which he made for us, since the address of so great a teacher not only to his disciples, but also his prayer to the Father for them, is instruction for disciples: certainly for those who were present and were to hear these words, and also for us who were to read them when written down. Therefore, when he says, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” he shows that every time, and what he would do or allow to be done at each time, is ordered by him who is not subject to time. For the things that were to happen at successive times have their effective causes in God’s wisdom, in which there are no times.

Therefore we must not suppose that this hour came under the compulsion of fate, but rather by God’s ordering. No stellar necessity bound Christ to his Passion; far be it that the stars should compel the maker of the stars to die. Thus time did not drive Christ to die, but Christ chose the time at which he would die. He also appointed with the Father the time at which he was born of the Virgin—he who was born of the Father without time. In accordance with this true and sound teaching, the Apostle Paul too says: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4:4); and God says through the Prophet: “In an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you” (Isa. 49:8); and again the Apostle says: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6:2).
