Let him therefore say, “Father, the hour has come,” who arranged all hours with the Father—as though saying: Father, the hour which we jointly appointed, for the sake of human beings and among human beings, for my glorification, has come; glorify your Son, that your Son also may glorify you.

### 3

Some understand the Son’s glorification by the Father to be this: that he “did not spare him, but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:32). But if he is said to have been glorified by his Passion, how much more by his resurrection? For in the Passion his humility rather than his glory is commended, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross.” Then he continues, now speaking of his glorification: “Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.” This is the glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ, which took its beginning from his resurrection.

Thus, in the Apostle’s discourse, his humility begins where he says, “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant,” and reaches as far as death on a cross. His glory begins where he says, “Therefore God also exalted him,” and reaches as far as “is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2:7–11). For if the Greek manuscripts are examined—the language from which the apostolic Epistles were translated into Latin—the word read here as *gloria* is there δόξα (*doxa*); from this is derived the Greek verb δόξασον (*doxason*), which the Latin translator rendered *clarifica* (“make glorious”), though he could also have said *glorifica* (“glorify”), which has the same meaning. Therefore, in the Apostle’s Epistle, where *gloria* occurs, *claritas* (“glory, splendor”) could also be used; and it would have the same force.

Yet, lest one depart from the sound of the words: just as *clarificatio* is derived from *claritas*, so *glorificatio* is derived from *gloria*. Therefore, for Christ Jesus, the human mediator between God and humanity, to be glorified by resurrection, he was first humbled by the Passion; for he would not have risen from the dead if he had not died. Humility is the merit of glory; glory is the reward of humility. But this occurred in the form of a servant. In the form of God, glory always was and always will be; indeed, it did not “was” as though it no longer is, nor “will be” as though it is not yet, but is always, without beginning and without end.

Therefore, when he says, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” it should be understood as though he had said: The hour for sowing humility has come; do not delay the fruit of glory. But what is meant by what follows: “That your Son may glorify you”? Did God the Father also undergo the humility of flesh or Passion, from which he would have to be glorified? How, then, was the Son to glorify him whose eternal glory could neither be seen as less because of the human form nor become greater in divine perfection? But I do not wish to confine this question to the present discourse or make it longer on this account.

## TRACTATE CV

From the Lord’s words, “That your Son may glorify you,” through “with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” Chapter 17, verses 1–5.

### 1

That the Son was glorified by the Father according to the form of a servant, which the Father raised from the dead and placed at his right hand, the fact itself shows, and no Christian doubts it. But because he did not merely say, “Father, glorify your Son,” but also added, “that your Son may glorify you,” it is rightly asked how the Son glorified the Father, since the Father’s eternal glory was neither diminished in the human form nor capable of increase in his divine perfection.

In itself, the Father’s glory can neither diminish nor increase. Among human beings, however, it was undoubtedly less when God was known only in Judaea (Ps. 75:2); the children did not yet praise the name of the Lord from the rising of the sun to its setting (Ps. 112:1, 3). But because this came about through Christ’s Gospel, so that the Father became known to the nations through the Son, the Son certainly glorified the Father. If the Son had merely died and had not risen, he would undoubtedly neither have been glorified by the Father nor have glorified the Father. But now, glorified by the Father through his resurrection, he glorifies the Father by the preaching of his resurrection. The very order of the words makes this clear: “Glorify your Son,” he says, “that your Son may glorify you”—as though saying: Raise me up, that through me you may become known to the whole world.

### 2

Then, more and more unfolding how the Son glorifies the Father, he says: “As you gave him authority over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all that you have given him.” By “all flesh” he means every human being, signifying the whole by a part; just as, conversely, the whole human being is signified by the higher part when the Apostle says: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers” (Rom. 13:1). For what did he mean by “every soul” except every human being?

Moreover, the authority over all flesh given by the Father to Christ must be understood according to his humanity. For according to his divinity all things were made through him (John 1:3), and all things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, were created in him (Col. 1:16). Therefore, “As you gave him authority over all flesh,” he says, “so may your Son glorify you”: that is, make you known to all flesh that you have given him. For you gave it in this way: that he may give eternal life to all that you have given him.

### 3

“And this,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” The order of the words is: that they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent as the only true God. Consequently the Holy Spirit is understood as well, because he is the Spirit of the Father and the Son, being the substantial and consubstantial love of both. For the Father and the Son are not two gods, nor are the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit three gods; but the Trinity itself is the one only true God. Yet the Father is not the same as the Son, nor the Son the same as the Father, nor the Holy Spirit the same as the Father and the Son; for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three, but the Trinity itself is one God.

Therefore, if the Son glorifies you in the way that you gave him authority over all flesh, and gave it in such a way that he gives eternal life to all that you have given him, and if eternal life is this, that they may know you, then the Son glorifies you by making you known to all whom you have given him. Moreover, if the knowledge of God is eternal life, we tend toward life all the more as we advance more in this knowledge. But we shall not die in eternal life. Therefore, the knowledge of God will then be perfect, when there is no death. Then God’s glorification will be supreme, because glory is supreme—glory which in Greek is called δόξα (*doxa*). Hence δόξασον (*doxason*), which some Latin translators have rendered *clarifica* (“make glorious”), and others *glorifica* (“glorify”).

But the ancients defined the glory by which people are called glorious thus: “Glory is widespread favorable report about someone.” But if a human being is praised when his reputation is believed, how will God be praised when he himself is seen? For this reason it is written: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house; they will praise you for ages upon ages” (Ps. 83:5). There will be unending praise of God where there will be full knowledge of God; and because it is full knowledge, there will be supreme glorification or glory.

### 4

But God is first glorified here, while he becomes known by being announced to human beings and is preached through believers’ faith. Therefore he says: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do.” He does not say, “which you commanded,” but “which you gave,” where evident grace is commended. For what does even human nature have in the Only-begotten that it has not received? Did it not receive the ability to do nothing evil but to do all things well when it was assumed by the Word into unity of person—the Word through whom all things were made?

But how did he complete the work which he received to do, when the experience of the Passion still remained, in which he especially furnished his martyrs with an example to follow? Hence the Apostle Peter says: “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example that we might follow in his footsteps” (1 Pet. 2:21). Is it not because he calls completed what he most certainly knows that he will complete? Thus long before, in prophecy, he used words in the past tense concerning what would happen many years later: “They pierced my hands and feet; they counted all my bones” (Ps. 21:17–18); he did not say, “They will pierce and count.” And in this same Gospel he says: “I have made known to you all that I heard from my Father” (John 15:15), although he later says to them: “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12). For he who predestined all future things by fixed and unchangeable causes has done whatever he will do; indeed, it is said of him through the Prophet: “Who made the things that are to be” (Isa. 45:11, LXX).

### 5

According to this same principle he says what follows: “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” Earlier he had said: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.” In that order of words he had shown that the Son was first to be glorified by the Father, so that the Son might glorify the Father. But now he says: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do; and now glorify me”—as though he himself had first glorified the Father, from whom he then asks to be glorified.

We must therefore understand that in the earlier words he used the future tense, and in the order in which the events would occur: “Glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.” But now he uses the past tense concerning a future event when he says: “I have glorified you on earth; I have completed the work which you gave me to do.” Then, by saying, “And now, Father, glorify me with yourself,” as though he who had first glorified the Father were afterward to be glorified by the Father, what does he show except that, when he said above, “I have glorified you on earth,” he spoke as though he had done what he was going to do? Here he asks the Father to do that by which the Son would do the former thing: that is, that the Father might glorify the Son, by whose glorification the Son would also glorify the Father.

Finally, if we use a future-tense verb for the future event for which he himself used the past tense, no obscurity will remain in the statement: as if he had said, “I shall glorify you on earth; I shall complete the work which you gave me to do; and now, Father, glorify me with yourself.” Surely this is as plain as the earlier saying, “Glorify your Son, that your Son may glorify you.” It is precisely the same sense, except that here the manner of this glorification is stated, whereas there it was unstated—as though the former were explained by the latter for those whom the question might trouble, how the Father glorifies the Son, and especially how the Son glorifies the Father.

For by saying that he glorified the Father on earth, and that he himself was glorified by the Father with the Father, he certainly showed the manner of each glorification. He glorified the Father on earth by preaching him to the nations; the Father glorified him with himself by placing him at his right hand. But afterward, when speaking of glorifying the Father in the words, “I have glorified you,” he preferred to use the past tense in order to show that, in predestination, what was most certainly to happen had already been done and should be regarded as done: namely, that, glorified by the Father with the Father, the Son might glorify the Father on earth.

### 6

But he opened this predestination more clearly in his own glorification, by which the Father glorified him, when he added: “With the glory which I had with you before the world existed.” The order of the words is: “which I had with you before the world existed.” This is the force of his saying: “And now glorify me”—that is, as then, so now; as then in predestination, so now in fulfillment. Do in the world what had already been with you before the world; do in its own time what you appointed before all times.

Some have thought this should be understood as though the human nature assumed by the Word were changed into the Word, and the human being transformed into God; indeed, if we consider their opinion more carefully, the human being would perish in God. For no one will say, as a result of this transformation of the human being, that the Word of God is doubled or increased, so that either two should be what was one, or more should be what was less. But if human nature, changed and transformed into the Word, becomes all that the Word of God was and is, where is the human being, if he does not perish?

### 7

But with regard to this opinion, which I plainly do not see to accord with the truth, nothing compels us to accept it if, when the Son says, “And now glorify me, you, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed,” we understand this as referring to the predestination of the glory of the human nature that is in him—a nature that, from mortal, was destined to become immortal with the Father—and understand that what was to occur in the world at its proper time had already been accomplished by predestination before the world existed.

For if the Apostle said of us, “He chose us in him before the foundation of the world” (Ephesians 1:4), why should it be thought contrary to the truth that the Father glorified our Head at the time when he chose us in him, so that we might be his members? Thus we were chosen in the same way as he was glorified, because before the world existed neither we nor the mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus, existed (1 Timothy 2:5).

But he who, through him insofar as he is his Word, also made the things that were to come, and calls things that do not exist as though they existed (Romans 4:17), plainly glorified him, insofar as he is the human being who is the mediator between God and human beings, before the foundation of the world. For the Father did this if he chose us in him at that time. What, then, does the Apostle say?

“We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose. For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters; and those whom he predestined, he also called” (ibid. 8:28–30).

### 8

Unless, perhaps, we are afraid to say that he himself was predestined, because the Apostle appears to have said only of us that we would be conformed to his image. As though anyone who faithfully considers the rule of faith would deny that the Son of God was predestined, when he cannot deny that he is human.

It is rightly said that he was not predestined according to what he is as the Word of God, God with God. Why would he be predestined, since he already was what he was—eternal, without beginning and without end? But that which did not yet exist had to be predestined, so that it might come to be at its proper time in the manner in which it had been predestined before all times to come to be.

Whoever, therefore, denies that the Son of God was predestined denies that this same one is the Son of Man. But for the sake of contentious people, let us hear the Apostle on this matter from the beginning of his writings. For in the first of his Epistles, the one addressed to the Romans, the very beginning of the Epistle reads:

“Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God, which he had promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined as the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification by the resurrection of the dead” (ibid. 1:1–4).

According to this predestination, therefore, he was also glorified before the world existed, so that his glory might be, with the Father, from the resurrection of the dead, at whose right hand he sits. When he therefore saw that the time had already come for that predestined glorification of his to take place, so that what had already been done in predestination might now be accomplished in its fulfillment, he prayed, saying:

“And now glorify me, you, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed.”

It was as though he were saying: “The glory which I had with you—that is, the glory which I had with you in your predestination—it is time for me to have with you also while living at your right hand.”

But since our discussion of this question has detained us for a long time, what follows must be treated in another discourse.

## TREATISE 106

On the passage in which the Lord says, “I have manifested your name to the people,” up to the passage, “And they believed that you sent me.” Chapter 17, verses 6–8.

### 1

In this discourse, as he grants us the ability, we shall discuss the Lord’s words, which are as follows:

“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world.”

If he says this only of those disciples with whom he dined and to whom he spoke so extensively before beginning to pray, then it does not pertain to that glorification—or, as others have interpreted it, that clarification—of which he was speaking above, by which the Son clarifies or glorifies the Father. For how great, or of what kind, is the glory that he should have become known to twelve—or rather, eleven—mortal men?

But if, when he says, “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world,” he intended all people to be understood, including those who would believe in him and belong to his great future Church from all the nations, of which it is sung in the Psalm, “In the great assembly I will give thanks to you” (Psalm 34:18), then this is plainly the glorification by which the Son glorifies the Father, when he makes his name known to all nations and to so many generations of human beings.

What he says here, “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world,” is therefore like what he had said shortly before, “I glorified you on earth” (John 17:4): in both places he uses the past tense with reference to the future, as one who knew that it had been predestined that it would occur, and therefore says that he has done what he would certainly do without any doubt.

### 2

But that he was speaking not of all who would believe in him, but of those who were already his disciples, is more credibly demonstrated by what follows. When he had said this, he added:

“They were yours, and you gave them to me, and they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you; for the words that you gave me I have given to them, and they received them, and truly understood that I came forth from you, and believed that you sent me.”

Although all these things could also have been said of all future believers, with hope already regarded as accomplished [Note: Three manuscripts read *spe perfecta*; the others, together with the printed editions, read *specie perfecta*.], while they were still future, it is more compelling that he should be understood as speaking of those disciples whom he then had because he says shortly afterward:

“When I was with them, I kept them in your name. Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them was lost except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled.”

He was referring to Judas, who betrayed him; of that group of twelve apostles, he alone was lost.

Then he adds:

“But now I am coming to you.”

From this it is clear that, when he said, “When I was with them, I kept them,” he was speaking of his bodily presence, as though that presence would no longer be with them. For in this way he wished to signify his ascension, which was soon to occur and of which he said, “But now I am coming to you”—namely, going to the right hand of the Father, from which he will come to judge the living and the dead, likewise in bodily presence, according to the sound rule of faith and teaching.

For he was certainly going to be with them spiritually after his ascension, and with his whole Church in this world until the consummation of the age (Matthew 28:20). Therefore the words “When I was with them, I kept them” cannot rightly be understood as referring to anyone except those who had begun to believe in him and whom he had begun to guard by his bodily presence, and whom he was going to leave by his bodily absence, so that he might guard them with the Father by his spiritual presence.

After this he adds the rest of his own, saying:

“I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.”

Here he shows more clearly that, in the earlier passage beginning, “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me,” he was not speaking of all who belonged to him, but only of those who were hearing him when he said these things.

### 3

From the very beginning of his prayer, therefore, when he lifted his eyes toward heaven and said, “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son, so that your Son may glorify you,” up to what he says shortly afterward, “And now glorify me, you, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed,” he intended all his own people to be understood—those to whom he glorifies the Father by making him known.

For when he had said, “so that your Son may glorify you,” he immediately showed how this would happen, saying:

“As you have given him authority over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him. And this is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:1–20).

The Father cannot be glorified by human beings’ knowledge unless the one through whom he is glorified is also known—that is, the one through whom he is made known to the peoples.

This is the glorification of the Father. It did not take place only among those apostles, but takes place among all people for whom Christ is the head among his members. Nor can the words, “As you have given him authority over all flesh, so that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him,” be understood of the apostles alone, but certainly of all those who, by believing in him, are given eternal life.

### 4

Let us now see what he says about those disciples who were then hearing him. “I have manifested,” he says, “your name to the people whom you gave me.”

Did they not, then, know the name of God, since they were Jews? And what of the words that are written, “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Psalm 75:2)?

He therefore means: “I have manifested your name to these people whom you gave me out of the world, who are hearing me say these things.” He does not mean that name by which you are called God, but that by which you are called my Father—the name that could not be manifested without the manifestation of the Son himself.

For insofar as God is called the God of the whole creation, this name could not have been wholly unknown even to all the nations before they believed in Christ. The power of true divinity is such that it cannot be entirely and completely hidden from a rational creature already using reason.

Except for the few in whom nature has been excessively corrupted, the whole human race confesses God to be the creator of this world. Insofar as he made this world visible through heaven and earth, God was known to all the nations before they were instructed in the faith of Christ.

Insofar as he is not to be worshiped together with false gods to his own dishonor, “God is known in Judah.” But insofar as he is the Father of this Christ, through whom he takes away the sin of the world, his name was previously hidden from all, and he has now manifested it to those whom the Father himself gave him out of the world.

But how did he manifest it, if the hour of which he had spoken above had not yet come—the hour when, as he says, “I will no longer speak to you in figures, but will speak openly to you about my Father” (John 16:25)?

Or will an announcement be considered open if it is made in figures? Why, then, was it said, “I will speak openly to you,” unless it is because speech in figures is not open? Whatever is not concealed in figures but is made clear in words is undoubtedly spoken openly.

How, then, did he manifest what he had not yet spoken openly? It must therefore be understood that the past tense is used with reference to the future, as in the statement, “Everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (ibid. 15:15). He had not yet done this, but spoke as though he had done it, because he knew that what he would do had been immutably decreed.

### 5

What, then, does “whom you gave me out of the world” mean? It was said of them that they were not of the world. But regeneration, not generation, brought this about for them.

What also does the following mean: “They were yours, and you gave them to me”? Were they at some time the Father’s, when they were not the only-begotten Son’s? Did the Father ever possess anything without the Son? Far be it from us to think so.

Nevertheless, God the Son once possessed something that the Son as human being did not yet possess, because he had not yet become human from his mother, although he already possessed everything with the Father.

Therefore, when he said, “They were yours,” God the Son did not separate himself from them—as though the Father had ever possessed anything without him—but he customarily attributes everything that he can do to the one from whom he himself is. From the one from whom he has being, he has the ability to act; and he has always possessed both simultaneously, because he never existed without the ability to act.

Whatever the Father could do, therefore, the Son could always do with him, since the one who never existed without the ability to act was never without the Father, and the Father was never without him.

Thus, just as the Father is eternal and omnipotent, so the Son is coeternal and omnipotent; and if omnipotent, then certainly *omnitenens*, “all-holding.” For if we wish to translate literally the word the Greeks call *pantokrator* (παντοκράτωρ), this is the more exact rendering. Our translators would not have rendered it as “omnipotent” unless they understood *pantokrator*—“all-holding”—to have the same force.

What, then, could the eternal all-holder ever possess that the coeternal all-holder did not possess together with him? When he says, therefore, “And you gave them to me,” he shows that, as a human being, he received authority to have them, because the one who had always been omnipotent had not always been human.

Accordingly, although he appears to attribute to the Father the fact that he received them from him—since everything that exists in him is from the one from whom he is—he also gave them to himself. That is, Christ God, with the Father, gave human beings to Christ as human being, who did not have with the Father what he received as human being.

Finally, when he says here, “They were yours, and you gave them to me,” he had already said to these same disciples above, “I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19).

Let carnal thinking be crushed here and perish. The Son says that the Father gave him out of the world the human beings to whom, in another passage, he says, “I chose you out of the world.”

Those whom God the Son chose out of the world with the Father, that same Son as human being received from the Father out of the world. For the Father would not have given them to the Son unless he had chosen them.

Thus the Son did not separate the Father from himself when he said, “I chose you out of the world,” since the Father chose them together with him. Nor did he separate himself from them when he said, “They were yours,” since they also belonged equally to the Son himself.

But now that same Son as human being received those who were not his, because the same God received the form of a servant, which was not his by nature.

### 6

He continues and says:

“And they have kept your word. Now they know that everything you have given me is from you”—that is, they have understood that I am from you.

The Father gave everything simultaneously when he begot the one who possessed everything.

“For the words,” he says, “that you gave me, I have given them, and they received them”—that is, they understood and retained them. For the word is received when it is apprehended by the mind.

“And they truly understood,” he says, “that I came forth from you, and believed that you sent me.”

Here too “truly” must be supplied. By saying, “They truly understood,” he wished to explain this by adding, “and believed.” What they truly believed, therefore, they truly understood. For “I came forth from you” means “you sent me.”

When he had said, “They truly understood,” lest anyone should think that this knowledge had already been obtained by sight rather than by faith, he explained it by adding, “and believed.” We must therefore supply “truly” and understand the statement “They truly understood” to mean “They truly believed.”

This is not the sense indicated shortly before when he said, “Do you believe now? The hour is coming—indeed it has come—when you will be scattered, each one to his own, and you will leave me alone” (ibid. 16:31–32).

Rather, they truly believed—that is, in the manner in which one ought to believe: unwaveringly, firmly, steadfastly, and courageously—not to return again to their own things and abandon Christ.

The disciples, therefore, were not yet such as he describes them through words in the past tense, as though they already were, foretelling what they would become after receiving the Holy Spirit, who, as had been promised, would teach them everything.

Before they received him, how did they keep his word, as he said of them as though they had done so, when their foremost member denied him three times (Matthew 26:69–74), even after hearing from his mouth what would happen to anyone who denied him before human beings (ibid. 10:33)?

He therefore gave them the words, as he said, which the Father had given him. But when they received those words spiritually, not outwardly in their ears but inwardly in their hearts, then they truly received them, because then they truly understood. They truly understood because they truly believed.

## 7

But how the Father gave the Son the words that he gave him—what human being could explain it? The question certainly seems easier if we believe that, insofar as he is the Son of Man, he received those words from the Father.

Yet who can recount when and how he learned them after being born from a Virgin? Who can even recount when and how he was born from the Virgin?

But if he is thought to have received these words from the Father insofar as he was begotten from the Father and is coeternal with the Father, let no one imagine any temporal sequence, as though previously he did not have them and received what he lacked in order to have it. Whatever God the Father gave to God the Son, he gave by begetting him.

For the Father gave the Son those things without which the Son could not be the Son, just as he gave him being itself. How otherwise could he give words to the Word, in whom he ineffably spoke all things?

But what follows must be awaited in another discourse.

## TREATISE 107

On the passage in which Jesus says, “I pray for them,” and so forth, up to the passage, “That they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.” Chapter 17, verses 9–13.

### 1

When the Lord was speaking to the Father about those whom he already had as disciples, among other things he also said:

“I pray for them; I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me.”

By “the world” he now wishes those who live according to the desire of the world to be understood, those who do not belong to that company of grace by which they are chosen out of the world.

He therefore says that he prays not for the world, but for those whom the Father gave him. For the fact that the Father had already given them to him brought it about that they no longer belonged to the world for which he does not pray.

### 2

Then he adds:

“Because they are yours.”

For although the Father gave them to the Son, he did not lose those whom he gave. The Son continues:

“And all mine are yours, and yours are mine.”

Here it is sufficiently clear how everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the only-begotten Son: namely, because he too is God and was born equal from the Father and is from the Father.

This is not like what was said to one of two sons, namely the elder:

“You are always with me, and everything that is mine is yours” (Luke 15:31).

That statement concerned all those creatures that are beneath the holy rational creature and are subject to the Church. The whole Church is understood there as the two sons, the elder and the younger, together with all the holy angels, to whom we shall be equal in the kingdom of Christ and of God (Matthew 22:30).

But here it is said, “All mine are yours, and yours are mine,” so that the rational creature itself is also included, being subject only to God, so that all things beneath it may be subject to it.

Since this rational creature belongs to God the Father, it would not also belong to the Son unless the Son were equal to the Father. It was of this creature that he was speaking when he said:

“I do not pray for the world, but for those whom you have given me, because they are yours, and all mine are yours, and yours are mine.”

It is not permissible for the saints of whom he spoke here to belong to anyone except the one by whom they were created and sanctified. Consequently, everything that belongs to them must belong to the one to whom they themselves belong.

Since, therefore, they belong both to the Father and to the Son, they demonstrate that the Father and the Son are equal, since those who belong to them belong equally to both.

But when, speaking of the Holy Spirit, he said, “Everything that the Father has is mine; therefore I said that he will take from what is mine and declare it to you” (John 16:15), he was speaking of those things that pertain to the very divinity of the Father, in which the Son is equal to him by possessing everything that the Father has.

For the Holy Spirit was not going to receive from the creature that is subject to the Father and the Son what Christ meant by “he will take from what is mine.” Rather, he would receive it from the Father, from whom the Spirit proceeds and from whom the Son was born.

### 3

“And I have been glorified in them,” he says.

He speaks of his glorification as though it had already occurred, although it was still future. Above, however, he was asking the Father that it might occur.

Whether this is the same glorification of which he had said, “And now glorify me, you, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” (John 17:1, 5), must certainly be investigated.

For if it was “with you,” how was it “in them”? Or was it in them because this very thing was made known to them and, through them as his witnesses, to all who believe?

We can certainly understand the Lord to have said of the apostles that he had been glorified in them. By saying that it had already happened, he showed that it had already been predestined and wished it to be regarded as certain that it would occur.

### 4

“And now,” he says, “I am no longer in the world, and they are in the world.”

If one attends carefully to the precise hour at which he was speaking, both were still in the world: he himself and those of whom he was speaking.

We cannot and should not understand this according to an advance in heart and life, as though they were said still to be in the world because they continued to think worldly thoughts, while he was no longer in the world because he thought divine thoughts.

For one word placed here entirely prevents us from understanding it in that way. He does not say, “I am not in the world,” but, “I am no longer in the world,” thereby showing that he had been in the world and was now no longer in it.

Is it permissible, then, to believe that he had once thought worldly thoughts and, having been freed from that error, no longer thought them? Who would clothe himself in so impious an understanding?

It remains, therefore, that, according to the fact that he himself had previously been in the world, he said that he was now no longer in the world. He was plainly indicating that his bodily absence from the world would very soon occur, while theirs would occur later, by saying that he was already no longer here whereas they were here, even though he too was still here and they were still here.

Thus he spoke as a human being in a manner suited to human beings, according to the human custom of speech. Do we not say every day of someone who is about to leave shortly, “He is no longer here”? This is especially said of those who are dying.

The Lord himself, moreover, as though foreseeing what might trouble his readers, added:

“And I am coming to you.”

In this way he explained, as it were, why he had said, “I am no longer in the world.”

### 5

He therefore commends to the Father those whom he is going to leave by his bodily absence, saying:

“Holy Father, keep them in your name, those whom you have given me.”

Certainly, as a human being he asks God for his disciples, whom he received from God. But consider what follows:

“That they may be one,” he says, “as we are.”

He does not say, “That they may be one with us,” or, “That we and they may be one, as we are one.” Rather, he says, “That they may be one as we are.”

They are to be one in their nature, just as we are one in our nature. He would unquestionably not say this truthfully unless he were speaking according to the fact that he is God of the same nature as the Father, according to what he said elsewhere, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30).

He did not mean this according to the fact that he is also human, for according to that he said, “The Father is greater than I” (ibid. 14:28).

But since one and the same person is God and human being, we understand the human being in the fact that he prays; we understand God in the fact that he and the one to whom he prays are one.

There is still a place in what follows where this matter must be discussed more carefully.

### 6

Here he continues:

“When I was with them, I kept them in your name.”

He means: “When I come to you, keep them in your name, in which I myself kept them when I was with them.”

The human Son kept his disciples in the Father’s name while he was present with them in human presence. But the Father also kept those whom he heard asking in the Son’s name. For the same Son had said to them:

“Truly, truly, I say to you, if you ask anything of the Father in my name, he will give it to you” (ibid. 16:23).

We must not understand this too carnally, as though the Father and the Son took turns guarding us, their guardianship alternating so that one would succeed the other when one departed. The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, who is the one true and blessed God, guard us together.

But Scripture does not lift us up unless it first descends to us, just as the Word became flesh and descended in order to lift us up; he did not fall in order to lie prostrate.

If we have recognized him descending, let us rise with the one who lifts us up, and understand that, when he speaks in this way, he distinguishes the persons but does not separate the natures.

Therefore, when the Son was guarding his disciples by bodily presence, the Father was not waiting to take over the guardianship when the departing Son left. Both were guarding them by spiritual power.

And when the Son withdrew his bodily presence from them, he retained spiritual guardianship with the Father.

For when the Son as human being received them to guard, he did not remove them from the Father’s guardianship. And when the Father gave them to the Son to guard, he did not give them without the one to whom he gave them. He gave them to the human Son, but not without that same Son as God.

### 7

The Son continues and says:

“Those whom you gave me I guarded, and none of them was lost except the son of perdition, so that Scripture might be fulfilled.”

The betrayer of Christ is called the son of perdition, predestined for destruction, according to the Scripture that prophesies about him especially in Psalm 108.

### 8

“But now,” he says, “I am coming to you; and I am saying these things in the world, so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves.”

Behold, he says that he is speaking in the world, although shortly before he had said, “I am no longer in the world.” We explained why he said this there; indeed, we showed that he himself explained it.

Therefore, because he had not yet departed, he was still here; and because he was soon to depart, he was in a certain sense already no longer here.

What this joy is of which he says, “so that they may have my joy fulfilled in themselves,” was already made clear above when he said, “That they may be one as we are.”

He says that this joy of his—that is, the joy bestowed on them by him—is to be fulfilled in them. For this reason he said that he had spoken in the world.

This is that peace and blessedness in the age to come, for the attainment of which one must live temperately, justly, and piously in this present age.

## TREATISE 108

On the passage in which Jesus says, “I have given them your word,” up to the passage, “That they themselves also may be sanctified in the truth.” Chapter 17, verses 14–19.

### 1

The Lord, still speaking to the Father and praying for his disciples, says:

“I have given them your word, and the world hated them.”

They had not yet experienced this in their sufferings, which followed afterward; but in his customary manner he speaks in the past tense while foretelling the future.

Then, supplying the reason why the world hates them, he says:

“Because they are not of the world, just as I am not of the world.”

This was granted to them by regeneration. By generation they were of the world, which is why he had already said to them, “I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19).

They were therefore given the privilege that, like him, they too should not be of the world, because he freed them from the world.

He himself, however, was never of the world, because even according to the form of a servant he was born from the Holy Spirit, from whom they were reborn. For if they are no longer of the world because they were reborn from the Holy Spirit, he was never of the world because he was born from the Holy Spirit.

### 2

“I do not ask,” he says, “that you take them out of the world, but that you keep them from evil.”

Although they were no longer of the world, they still needed to be in the world.

He repeats the same statement:

“They are not of the world, just as I am not of the world. Sanctify them in the truth.”

For this is how they are kept from evil, which he prayed above would happen.

But one may ask how they were already no longer of the world if they had not yet been sanctified in the truth; or, if they already were, why he asks that they become so.

Is it because those who are sanctified in the same sanctity also progress in sanctity and become more holy? Nor does this occur without the assistance of God’s grace; rather, it occurs through him who sanctifies their progress, just as he sanctified their beginning.

Hence the Apostle also says:

“He who began a good work in you will bring it to completion until the day of Christ Jesus” (Philippians 1:6).

The heirs of the New Testament are therefore sanctified in the truth. The sanctifications of the Old Testament were shadows of that truth. And when they are sanctified in the truth, they are certainly sanctified in Christ, who truly said, “I am the way, and the truth, and the life” (John 14:6).

Likewise, when he said, “The truth will make you free,” he shortly afterward explained what he had said:

“If the Son makes you free, then you will truly be free” (ibid. 8:32, 36).

In this way he showed that what he had first called “the truth” he later called “the Son.”

What else, then, did he say here by “Sanctify them in the truth” except “Sanctify them in me”?

### 3

Finally, he continues and does not cease to express this more clearly:

“Your word,” he says, “is truth.”

What else did he say than, “I am the truth”?

For the Greek Gospel has *logos* (λόγος), the same word that is read in the passage:

“In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.”

We know, of course, that the Word itself is the only-begotten Son of God, who became flesh and dwelt among us (ibid. 1:1, 14).

Thus here too it could be—and in certain manuscripts it is—written, “Your Word is truth,” just as in certain manuscripts the passage there is also written, “In the beginning was the speech.”

But in the Greek, without any variation, the word is *logos* in both places.

The Father therefore sanctifies his own heirs and their fellow heirs in the truth—that is, in his Word, in his only-begotten Son.

### 4

But he is still speaking about the apostles, for he continues:

“As you sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world.”

Whom did he send except his apostles? For the very name “apostles,” since it is Greek, means nothing other than “those who have been sent” in Latin.

God therefore sent his Son not in sinful flesh, but in the likeness of sinful flesh (Romans 8:3); and the Son sent those whom he sanctified from the stain of sin, though they had been born in sinful flesh.

### 5

But because Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, became the head of the Church, and they are his members, he says what follows:

“And for them I sanctify myself.”

For what does “And for them I sanctify myself” mean except “I sanctify them in myself,” since they too are myself?

For those of whom he said this, as I have stated, are his members, and Christ is one, head and body. The Apostle teaches this when he speaks of the seed of Abraham:

“If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed.”

He had said above:

“He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as though referring to many, but as though referring to one, ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Galatians 3:29, 16).

If, then, the seed of Abraham is Christ, what else was said to those to whom it was said, “Therefore you are Abraham’s seed,” except, “Therefore you are Christ”?

For this reason the same apostle says elsewhere:

“Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I complete in my flesh what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ” (Colossians 1:24).

He did not say, “what is lacking in my afflictions,” but “what is lacking in the afflictions of Christ,” because he was a member of Christ. In his persecutions, such as Christ had to suffer in his whole body, he too, according to his portion, completed Christ’s afflictions.

To make this certain also in the present passage, consider what follows. When he had said, “And for them I sanctify myself,” so that we might understand him to have said that he sanctifies them in himself, he immediately added:

“That they themselves also may be sanctified in the truth.”

What else does this mean except “in me,” according to the fact that the Word itself, which was God in the beginning, is the truth?

In him the Son of Man himself was sanctified from the beginning of his creation, when the Word became flesh, because the Word and the human being became one person.

At that time, therefore, he sanctified himself in himself—that is, he sanctified himself as human being in himself as the Word—because Christ is one, Word and human being, sanctifying the human being in the Word.

But on account of his members he says, “And for them I”—that is, for their benefit also, because they too are myself, just as it benefited me in myself that I am human being apart from them—“sanctify myself.”

That is, I sanctify them in myself as myself, because in me they too are myself.

“That they themselves also may be sanctified in the truth.”

What does “they themselves also” mean except “in the same way as I”? And what does “in the truth” mean except “in what I myself am”?

He then begins to speak not only of the apostles but also of his other members. With his help, this must be treated in another discourse.

## TREATISE 109

On the passage, “I do not ask for these only, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.” Chapter 17, verse 20.

### 1

The Lord Jesus, with his passion already approaching, had prayed for his disciples, whom he also called apostles, with whom he had eaten the final supper, from which his betrayer went out after being revealed by the morsel, and with whom, after the betrayer’s departure and before praying for them, he had spoken at length.

He then added the rest who would believe in him and said to the Father:

“I do not ask for these only”—that is, for the disciples who were then with him—“but also,” he says, “for those who will believe in me through their word.”

Here he wished all his own people to be understood, not only those who then existed in the flesh, but also those who were to exist in the future.

For all who believed in him afterward believed without doubt through the word of the apostles, and they will continue to believe until he comes. For he had said to them:

“You also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning” (John 15:27).

Through them the Gospel was administered even before it was written. Indeed, everyone who believes in Christ believes the Gospel.

We should therefore not understand only those as included whom he says would believe in him through their word—those who heard the apostles while they were living in the flesh—but also those who believed after the apostles’ death, including us, born long afterward, who believed in Christ through their word.

For those who were then with him preached to others what they had heard from him. In this way their word reached us, so that we too might believe, wherever his Church exists; and it will reach those who come after us, wherever and whenever they are to believe in him.

## 2

Jesus’ prayer may therefore appear not to have been offered for certain of his own people, unless we examine his words in that same prayer carefully. For if he first prayed for those who were then with him, as we have already shown, and afterward also for those who were to believe in him through their word, it might be said that he did not pray for those who were neither with him when he said these things nor afterward came to believe through their word, but who had already believed in him—whether through them or by some other means.

For was Nathanael with him then? Was Joseph of Arimathea, who asked Pilate for his body, and whom this same evangelist John testifies to have already been his disciple (John 19:38)? Was Mary his mother, and the other women whom we learn from the Gospel had already been his disciples at that time? Were those with him then of whom the same evangelist John often says, “Many believed in him” (ibid. 2:23; 4:39; 7:31; 8:30; 10:42)?

For where did that multitude come from—those who, some going before and others following, accompanied him as he sat upon the animal, carrying branches and saying, “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,” together with the children, concerning whom he himself said that it had been foretold, “Out of the mouths of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise” (Matthew 21:7, 16; Psalm 8:3)? Where did the five hundred brothers come from, to whom he appeared all at once after the resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:6), unless they had already believed in him? Where did the one hundred and nine come from, who, together with those eleven, made one hundred and twenty when they assembled together after his ascension, waiting for and receiving the promised Holy Spirit (Acts 1:15; 2:4)? Where did all these people come from, unless from those of whom it was said, “Many believed in him”?

Therefore the Savior did not pray for them at that time, since he prayed for those who were then with him and for others who had not yet believed in him through their word but were going to believe. These people, however, were neither with him then nor had they not yet believed in him: they had already believed.

I omit mentioning the aged Simeon, who believed in him as an infant; Anna the prophetess (Luke 2:25–38); Zechariah and Elizabeth, who prophesied about him before he was born of the Virgin (ibid. 1:41–45, 67–79); and their son John, his forerunner and the friend of the bridegroom, who recognized him in the Holy Spirit, proclaimed him while he was absent, and, when he was present, pointed him out to others so that they might recognize him (John 1:19–36; 3:26–36). I omit these because it may be answered that one did not need to pray for such people after their death, since they had departed this life with their great merits and were resting in their reward; the same answer is given concerning the righteous of ancient times.

For who could have been saved from the condemnation of the entire mass of perdition, which came about through one man, unless, by revelation of the Spirit, he had believed in the one Mediator between God and human beings who was to come in the flesh? But was it necessary for him to pray for the Apostles, while it was not necessary for him to pray for so many who were still in this life, were not then with him, and had already believed? Who could say this?

## 3

We must therefore understand that they had not yet believed in him in the manner in which he wanted people to believe in him. For even Peter himself, to whom he had borne such great testimony when Peter confessed and said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God,” preferred that he should not die rather than believing that, after dying, he would rise again; and for this reason he was immediately called “Satan” by him (Matthew 16:16, 23).

Thus those who had already died are found to have been more faithful, since they certainly did not doubt—through the revelation of the Spirit—that Christ would rise again, than those who had believed that he himself would redeem Israel but, when they saw his death, lost the entire hope they had placed in him.

We therefore believe nothing more appropriate than that, after his resurrection, when the Apostles had received the Holy Spirit, had been taught and strengthened, and had first been appointed teachers in the Church, other people came through their word to believe in the manner in which it was necessary to believe in Christ—that is, so that they would hold fast to faith in his resurrection. Consequently, all those who already appeared to have believed in him belonged to the number of those for whom he prayed when he said, “But I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word.”

## 4

But blessed Paul the Apostle, and that robber—cruel in crime but faithful on the cross—remain for us as we continue to resolve this question.

The Apostle Paul says that he was made an Apostle “not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ”; and, speaking of his own Gospel, he says, “For I did not receive it from a human being, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (Galatians 1:1, 12). How, then, was he among those of whom it was said, “They will believe in me through their word”?

That robber, however, believed at the very time when the faith that had existed, of whatever kind it was, failed in those teachers themselves. He too therefore did not believe in Christ Jesus through their word. Yet he believed in such a way that, although he saw him crucified, he confessed not only that he would rise again but also that he would reign, saying, “Remember me when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23:42).

## 5

It therefore remains that, if we are to believe that the Lord Jesus prayed in this prayer for all his own people—for all who were either then in this life, which is a time of testing upon the earth (Job 7:1), or were to come afterward—we should understand the expression “through their word” in such a way that we believe it refers here to the very word of faith that they preached throughout the world.

It is called “their word” because it was first and above all preached by them. It was already being preached on earth by them when Paul received that same word through a revelation of Jesus Christ. For this reason he also laid the Gospel before them, lest he should have run, or be running, in vain; and they gave him the right hand of fellowship, because in him too they found—although it had not been given to him through them—their own word, which they were already preaching and upon which they had been established (Galatians 2:2, 9).

Concerning this word of Christ’s resurrection the same Apostle says, “Whether it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed” (1 Corinthians 15:11); and again: “This is,” he says, “the word of faith which we preach: that if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved” (Romans 10:8–9).

And in the Acts of the Apostles we read that God established faith in Christ for all by raising him from the dead (Acts 17:31).

Because this word of faith was preached principally and first of all through the Apostles who had adhered to him, it was therefore called “their word.” It is not, however, for that reason not the word of God, since the same Apostle says that the Thessalonians received from him not the word of human beings but, as it truly is, the word of God (1 Thessalonians 2:13).

It is therefore God’s word because God gave it; but it is called their word because God first and above all entrusted this word to them to be preached. Consequently, that robber too possessed their word in his faith: it was called theirs because preaching it belonged first and above all to their office.

Finally, when a complaint arose concerning the distribution of food to the widows of the Greeks, before Paul had believed in Christ, the Apostles who had adhered to the Lord beforehand replied, “It is not right for us to abandon the word of God and serve tables” (Acts 6:1–4). They then arranged for deacons to be appointed, so that they themselves would not be diverted from the duty of preaching the word.

Thus the word of faith, through which all who have believed in Christ—regardless of where they heard it, or who will hear and believe it—was rightly called “their word.”

Therefore, in that prayer our Redeemer prayed for all whom he redeemed, whether then living in the flesh or destined to come afterward, when, while praying for the Apostles who were then with him, he added also those who were to believe in him through their word.

What he says next, after adding those people, must be treated in another discussion.

# Treatise 110

## On the passage that follows, “That they all may be one,” and so forth, up to “And you loved them as you loved me.” Chapter 17:21–23

### 1

When the Lord Jesus had prayed for his disciples whom he then had with him, and had added his other people, saying, “But I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,” as though we were asking what or why he prayed for them, he immediately continued, saying:

“That they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so that they too may be one in us.”

Earlier, when he was still praying only for the disciples whom he had with him, he had said, “Holy Father, keep them in your name, whom you have given me, so that they may be one as we are” (John 17:11).

Therefore he has now prayed for us also for the same thing for which he then prayed for them: that all of us—that is, both we and they—may be one.

Here we must carefully observe that the Lord did not say, “That we all may be one,” but, “That they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you” (with “we are one” understood, which is expressed more clearly later). For earlier too he had said concerning the disciples who were with him, “That they may be one as we are.”

Accordingly, the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father in such a way that they are one, because they are of one substance. We, however, can be in them, but we cannot be one with them, because we and they are not of one substance, insofar as the Son is God with the Father. For insofar as he is human, he is of the same substance as we are.

But for the present he wished rather to commend what he says elsewhere: “I and the Father are one” (ibid. 10:30), where he signified that the Father and he have the same nature.

Consequently, when the Father and the Son—or even the Holy Spirit—are in us, we must not suppose that they are of one nature with us. Thus they are in us, or we in them, in such a way that they are one in their own nature, while we are one in ours. They are in us as God is in his temple; we are in them as a creature is in its Creator.

### 2

Then, after saying, “So that they too may be one in us,” he added, “So that the world may believe that you sent me.”

What does this mean? Is the world going to believe at the time when we are all one in the Father and the Son? Is that not the everlasting peace, and rather the reward of faith than faith itself? For we will be one not in order to believe, but because we have believed.

Yet even if in this life, because of the common faith itself, all of us who believe in the One are one, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement, “For you are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28), even so we are one not in order to believe, but because we believe.

What, then, does “Let them all be one, so that the world may believe” mean?

All those people are themselves the believing world. For those who will be one are not one group, while another is the world that will believe because they are one; for he unquestionably says, “That they all may be one,” concerning those of whom he had said, “I pray not only for these, but also for those who will believe in me through their word,” immediately adding, “That they all may be one.”

What, then, are all these people except the world—not the hostile world, but the faithful world?

For behold: he who had said, “I do not pray for the world” (John 17:9) prays for the world that it may believe. There is a world of which it is written, “So that we may not be condemned with this world” (1 Corinthians 11:32). He does not pray for this world, for he does not fail to know what it has been predestined to be.

There is also a world of which it is written, “For the Son of Man did not come to judge the world, but so that the world might be saved through him” (John 3:17). Hence the Apostle says, “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5:19).

It is for this world that he prays when he says, “That the world may believe that you sent me.” Through this faith the world is reconciled to God, when it believes in Christ, who was sent by God.

How, then, are we to understand his words, “So that they too may be one in us, so that the world may believe that you sent me,” unless he did not make their unity the cause of the world’s believing—as though the world believed because it saw them to be one—since the world itself consists of all those who become one by believing?

Rather, in praying he said, “That the world may believe,” just as in praying he said, “That they all may be one,” and in praying he said, “That they too may be one in us.”

For “that they all may be one” is the same as “that the world may believe,” since by believing they become one—perfectly one, although by nature they were one, and through disagreement with the One they were not one.

Finally, if we supply the word “I pray” three times, or, better, place it everywhere so that the meaning may be made fuller, the interpretation of this statement will be clearer:

“I pray that they all may be one, just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you; I pray that they too may be one in us; I pray that the world may believe that you sent me.”

He therefore added the words “in us” so that we might understand that the unity into which we are brought by the most faithful love is to be attributed to God’s grace, not to ourselves. Thus, when the Apostle had said, “You were once darkness, but now you are light,” he added, lest they should attribute this to themselves, “in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

### 3

Then, by praying to the Father, our Savior demonstrated that he was human. Now, demonstrating also that he himself, together with the Father, is God, he does what he asks:

“And I have given them the glory that you gave me.”

What glory could this be except immortality, which human nature was to receive in him?

For he himself had not yet received it, but, according to his customary way of speaking, because of the immutability of predestination, he expresses future events in the words of the past. He was to be glorified—that is, raised up—by the Father, and at the end he himself was to raise us to that glory.

This is similar to what he says elsewhere: “As the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom he wishes.” And whom does he give life to except the same people to whom the Father does? For whatever the Father does, the Son does not do something different, but the same; nor does he do it differently, but similarly (John 5:21, 19).

Consequently, he also raised himself. For this is the meaning of his words, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid. 2:19).

Accordingly, the glory of immortality that he says was given to him by the Father must also be understood to have been given by him to himself, even though he does not say so. He so often attributes alone to the Father what he himself does with the Father in order to show that whatever he is, he receives from the One from whom he is.

Yet sometimes, with the Father left unmentioned, he also says that he does what he does with the Father. We are thereby to understand that the Son is not to be separated from the Father’s work when, without mentioning himself, he says that the Father performs some action, just as the Father is not separated from the Son’s work when, with the Father left unmentioned, the Son is said to do something which nevertheless they perform together.

Thus, when the Son leaves his own activity unmentioned in the Father’s work, he commends his humility, so that he may be more beneficial to us; but when, in turn, he leaves the Father’s activity unmentioned in his own work, he commends his equality, lest he be believed inferior.

In this way, therefore, even here he does not separate himself from the Father’s work, although he said, “The glory that you gave me,” because he himself also gave it to himself. Nor does he separate the Father from his own work, although he said, “I gave it to them,” because the Father too gave it to them.

For the works of the Father and the Son—and also of the Holy Spirit—are inseparable.

Just as, because he prayed to the Father for all his own people, he wanted this to happen: “That they all may be one,” so also, through this benefit of his own, expressed in the words, “The glory that you gave me, I have given them,” he likewise wanted the same thing to happen. For he immediately added, “So that they may be one, as we are one.”

### 4

Then he added:

“I in them, and you in me, so that they may be perfected into one.”

Here he briefly indicated that he is the Mediator between God and human beings.

For this was not said as though the Father were not in us, or we were not in the Father, since elsewhere he also said, “We will come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14:23). Nor, a little earlier here, did he say, “I in them and you in me,” as he has said now, or “They in me and I in you,” but, “You in me and I in you, and they in us.”

What he now says—“I in them and you in me”—is therefore spoken from the person of the Mediator, just as the Apostle says, “You are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s” (1 Corinthians 3:23).

His addition, “So that they may be perfected into one,” shows that the reconciliation brought about through the Mediator is directed toward this end: that we may enjoy perfect blessedness, to which nothing can be added.

For this reason, I do not think that the following words, “So that the world may know that you sent me,” should be understood as though he had again said, “So that the world may believe.” For sometimes “to know” is used with the meaning “to believe,” as in the words he spoke somewhat earlier: “They truly knew that I came from you, and they believed that you sent me” (John 17:8). What he subsequently called “they believed,” he had previously called “they knew.”

But here, since he is speaking about perfection, the knowledge must be understood as the kind that will exist through sight, not the kind that now exists through faith.

The order seems therefore to have been preserved in what he said shortly before: “So that the world may believe”; here, “So that the world may know.”

There, although he said, “That they all may be one,” and “that they may be one in us,” he did not say, “that they may be perfected into one,” but then added, “so that the world may believe that you sent me.”

Here, however, he says, “So that they may be perfected into one,” and afterward does not add, “so that the world may believe,” but, “so that the world may know that you sent me.”

For as long as we believe what we do not see, we are not yet perfected in the way we will be when we are deemed worthy to see what we believe.

Thus it is entirely correct that there he says, “So that the world may believe,” and here, “So that the world may know.” Yet both there and here he adds, “that you sent me,” so that we may recognize that, with respect to the inseparable love of the Father and the Son, we now believe what we strive, by believing, to know.

If he had said, “So that they may know that you sent me,” it would have had the same meaning as his present statement, “So that the world may know.”

For these people are the world—not the world that remains hostile, such as the world predestined to condemnation, but the world that has been made a friend from an enemy, for whose sake God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.

Therefore he said, “I in them and you in me,” as though he were saying, “I in those to whom you sent me, and you in me, reconciling the world to yourself through me.”

### 5

For this reason the following statement also follows:

“And you loved them as you loved me.”

The Father loves us in the Son, because in him he chose us before the foundation of the world (Ephesians 1:4). For the one who loves the Only-Begotten certainly loves his members also, whom he adopted in him and through him.

Nor are we thereby equal to the Only-Begotten Son through whom we were created and recreated—[Note: In the printed editions, “reconciled.” But in the manuscripts, “recreated.”]—because it is said, “You loved them as you loved me.”

For the person who says, “As this is, so also is that,” does not always signify equality. Sometimes he means only, “Because this exists, that also exists,” or, “Because this exists, that too may exist.”

Who could say that the Apostles were sent into the world by Christ in precisely the same manner in which he himself was sent by the Father?

To say nothing of other differences, which it would take too long to mention, they were certainly sent when they were already human beings; he, however, was sent in order to become human. Yet earlier he said, “As you sent me into the world, so I sent them into the world” (John 17:18), as though he were saying, “Because you sent me, I sent them.”

So also here: “You loved them,” he says, “as you loved me,” which means nothing other than, “You loved them because you also loved me.”

For the one who loves the Son would not fail to love the Son’s members; nor is there any other reason for loving his members except that he loves him.

He loves the Son according to his divinity because he begot him equal to himself. He also loves him according to his humanity, because that same Only-Begotten Word became flesh, and the flesh of the Word is dear to him because of the Word.

But he loves us because we are members of the one whom he loves; and he loved us for this purpose before we existed, so that we might become his members.

### 6

Therefore the love with which God loves is incomprehensible and does not change.

He did not begin to love us only from the time when we were reconciled to him through the blood of his Son. Rather, he loved us before the foundation of the world, so that together with his Only-Begotten we too might be his sons, before we existed at all.

Therefore, when we say that we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, this must not be heard or understood as though the Son reconciled us to him so that God would then begin to love those whom he had hated, as an enemy is reconciled to an enemy so that afterward they may become friends and love one another, having previously hated one another.

Rather, we were reconciled to the One who already loved us, although because of sin we were at enmity with him.

The Apostle bears witness to whether this is truly what I say: “God,” he says, “demonstrates his love for us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8–9).

He therefore had love for us even when, acting in hostility toward him, we were committing iniquity. Yet it was also most truly said to him, “You hate all who work iniquity” (Psalm 5:7).

Thus, in a wondrous and divine manner, even when he hated us, he loved us. For he hated us insofar as we were what he had not made; and because our iniquity had not wholly destroyed his work in us, he knew that in each of us there was simultaneously something he hated—what we had done—and something he loved—what he had made.

This may indeed be understood of all people in relation to the one to whom it is truthfully said, “You hate nothing of the things you have made” (Wisdom 11:25).

For he would not have wished anything to exist that he hated, nor would anything exist at all that omnipotence had not wished to exist, unless even in what he hates there were something he loved.

He rightly hates and, as something foreign to the rule of his art, rejects vice; yet even in the vicious he loves what is his own: either a benefit by healing or a judgment by condemning. [Note: So the manuscripts: “by healing, a benefit; or by condemning, a judgment.” The printed editions instead read: “the benefit of healing, or the judgment of condemnation.”]

Thus God hates nothing of what he has made. For he is the creator of natures, not of vices; the evils that he hates he himself did not make. Yet from those same evils, either by healing them through mercy or by ordering them through judgment, the things he does are themselves good.

Since, then, he hates nothing that he has made, who could adequately express how greatly he loves the members of his Only-Begotten, and how much more greatly he loves the Only-Begotten himself, in whom all visible and invisible things were created—things which, ordered in their kinds, he loves in the most orderly manner?

By the generosity of his grace he brings the members of the Only-Begotten to equality with the holy angels. But the Only-Begotten, although he is Lord of all, is unquestionably Lord of the angels. By the nature in which he is God, he is equal not to the angels but rather to the Father; and by the grace in which he is human, how could he not surpass the excellence of any angel, since flesh and the Word are one person?

### 7

There are, however, some who even place us above the angels, saying, “Christ died for us, not for the angels.”

What is this other than a desire to glory in impiety?

For Christ, as the Apostle says, “at the appointed time died for the ungodly” (Romans 5:6). Here, then, our merit is not commended, but God’s mercy.

What kind of praise is it to want to be praised because, through our own fault, we became so detestably sick that we could be healed only by the death of the physician? This is not the glory of our merits, but the medicine for our diseases.

Or do we place ourselves above the angels because, although the angels also sinned, nothing of this kind was provided for them by which they might be healed? As though something, even something small, had been provided for them, but something greater for us.

And even if this had happened, it could still be asked whether it happened because we had stood more excellently, or because we had fallen into greater despair.

But when we know that the Creator of all good bestowed no grace for the restoration of the evil angels, why should we not rather understand that their guilt was judged all the more condemnable because their nature was more exalted?

For they ought to have sinned less than we did by as much as they were better than we.

But in offending their Creator they became all the more detestably ungrateful because they had been created with greater beneficence; nor was it enough for them to become deserters from him unless they also became our deceivers.

This, then, is the great good he will confer upon us who loved us as he loved Christ: for the sake of the one whose members he willed us to be, we shall be equal to the holy angels (Luke 20:36), although we were created inferior to them by nature and made less worthy than they by sin, though we ought to become their companions, whatever their rank.

# Treatise 111

## On what the Lord says, “Father, those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they too may be with me,” up to “So that the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” Chapter 17:24–26

### 1

The Lord Jesus raises his own people to a great hope—indeed, to one that cannot possibly be greater.

Listen, and rejoice in hope, because this life should not be loved but endured, so that in its tribulation you may be able to endure patiently (Romans 12:12).

Listen, I say, and attend so that our hope may be lifted up.

Christ Jesus speaks—the Only-Begotten Son of God, coeternal and equal with the Father, speaks. He who for our sake became human, but did not become a liar like every human being (Psalm 115:11), speaks. The Way, the Life, and the Truth speaks (John 14:6). He who conquered the world (ibid. 16:33) speaks concerning those whom he conquered.

Listen, believe, hope for, and desire what he says:
