“Father,” he says, “those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they too may be with me.”

Who are these people whom he says were given to him by the Father?

Are they not those concerning whom he says elsewhere, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (ibid. 6:44)?

If we have made any progress in this Gospel, we already know how the things that he says are done by the Father are also done by him together with the Father.

These, then, are the people whom he received from the Father, whom he himself also chose from the world, choosing them so that they would no longer be of the world, just as he himself is not of the world. Yet they too are the believing and knowing world—that Christ was sent by God the Father, so that the world might be liberated from the world, and so that the world to be reconciled to God would not be condemned together with the most hostile world.

For at the beginning of this prayer he says:

“You gave him authority over all flesh”—that is, over every human being—“so that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17:2).

Here he shows that he received authority over every human being, so that he might free whom he wished and condemn whom he wished, since he will judge the living and the dead; but that those were given to him to whom he would give eternal life.

For this is what he says: “So that he might give eternal life to all whom you have given him.”

Accordingly, those to whom he will not give eternal life were not given to him, although authority over them too was given to the one to whom authority over all flesh—that is, over every human being—was given.

Thus the world reconciled from the hostile world will be liberated when he exercises his authority over that hostile world, sending it into eternal death; but he makes this other world his own, granting it eternal life.

Therefore the good Shepherd promised all his sheep, and the great Head promised all his members, this reward: that where he is, we too may be with him.

Nor can it fail to happen, since the almighty Son said that he desired this of the almighty Father.

For the Holy Spirit too is there, likewise eternal and likewise God, the one Spirit of the two and the substance of their will.

The statement that is reported as having been made when the Passion was approaching—“Yet not what I will, but what you will, Father” (Matthew 26:39)—as though the Father’s will were one thing and the Son’s another, or had been another, is the sound of our weakness, though it is faithful weakness, which our Head transformed into himself when he also bore our sins.

That the Father and the Son have one will, since they also have one Spirit, by whose addition we recognize the Trinity—even if weakness does not yet allow us to understand it—let piety believe.

### 2

Since we have already said, as briefly as the discourse permitted, to whom he made this promise and how firm the promise itself is, let us now consider, as far as we are able, what it is that he graciously promised:

“Those whom you have given me,” he says, “I desire that where I am, they too may be with me.”

With respect to the creature in which he was made from the seed of David according to the flesh (Romans 1:3), he himself was not yet where he was to be. Yet he could say, “Where I am,” in the sense that we should understand him to have been about to ascend into heaven soon, so that he could already say that he was where he was shortly going to be.

He could also have spoken in the sense in which he had already spoken to Nicodemus: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John 3:13).

For there too he did not say, “will be,” but “is,” because of the unity of the person in which God is human and the human being is God.

He therefore promised that we would be in heaven. For the form of a servant that he assumed from the Virgin was raised there and placed at the Father’s right hand.

Because of the hope of so great a good, the Apostle also says:

“But God, who is rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us, even when we were dead in sins, made us alive together with Christ, by whose grace we have been saved; and he raised us up together and made us sit together in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (Ephesians 2:4–6).

This, then, may be understood as what the Lord said: “That where I am, they too may be with me.”

He said of himself that he was already there; concerning us he said that he desired us to be there with him, but he did not show that we were already there.

The Apostle, however, spoke of what the Lord said he desired to happen as though it had already happened. He did not say, “He will raise us up and make us sit in the heavenly places,” but, “He raised us up and made us sit in the heavenly places,” because he does not recklessly but faithfully regard as already accomplished what he does not doubt will happen.

As for the form of God, in which he is equal to the Father, if we wish to understand according to it what was said, “I desire that where I am, they too may be with me,” let every thought of bodily images depart from the mind.

Whatever presents itself to the mind as long, broad, thick, or colored by any bodily light, extended through any intervals of place, whether finite or infinite, let the mind turn the focus of its contemplation or attention away from all these things as far as it can.

Let no one ask where the Son, equal to the Father, is, since no one finds where he is not.

But if anyone wishes to seek, let him seek rather to be with him—not everywhere as he is, but wherever it is possible for him to be.

For when he said to the man hanging under punishment but confessing for his salvation, “Today you will be with me in paradise” (Luke 23:43), according to the human nature he possessed, his soul was to be in the underworld that very day and his flesh in the tomb; but according to the divine nature he possessed, he was certainly also in paradise.

Thus the robber’s soul, freed from its former crimes and already blessed through Christ’s gift, could not be everywhere as Christ was; yet even on that very day it could be with him in paradise, from which the one who is always everywhere had not departed.

For this reason it was clearly not enough for him to say, “I desire that where I am, they too may be”; he added, “with me.”

To be with him is a great good.

For the wretched too can be where he is, since wherever anyone may be, he also is. But only the blessed are with him, because they cannot be blessed except through him.

Is it not truthfully said to God, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; and if I descend into the underworld, you are present” (Psalm 138:8)? Or is Christ not the Wisdom of God, which reaches everywhere because of its purity (Wisdom 7:24)?

Yet “the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it” (John 1:5).

Accordingly, to take some kind of example from a visible thing, though it is very dissimilar: just as a blind person, even if he is where the light is, is not himself with the light but is absent from what is present, so an unbeliever and an impious person—or even someone who is faithful and devout but not yet capable of contemplating the light of wisdom—even though he cannot exist anywhere where Christ is not, is nevertheless not with Christ, at least not through sight.

For a human being who is devout and faithful is undoubtedly with Christ through faith; hence he says, “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Matthew 12:30).

But when he said to God the Father, “Those whom you have given me, I desire that where I am, they too may be with me,” he was speaking wholly of that sight in which we shall see him as he is (1 John 3:2).

### 3

Let no one disturb this perfectly clear meaning with a cloud of contradiction; let what follows bear witness to what precedes. For after saying, “I will that where I am, they also may be with me,” he immediately added, “That they may behold my glory which you have given me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world.” He said, “That they may behold,” not, “That they may believe.” This is the reward of faith, not faith itself. For if faith is rightly defined in the Epistle to the Hebrews as “the conviction of things that are not seen” (Heb. 11:1), why should the reward of faith not be defined as “the vision of the things hoped for because they were believed”?

For when we shall behold the glory which the Father gave the Son—even if in this passage we understand it not as the glory which the Father gave him by begetting him as equal to himself, but as the glory which, after the death of the cross, he gave him as the Son made man [Note: [Col. 1927] Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice read: “gave it to the Son made man.” M.]—when, then, shall we behold the glory of the Son? Surely at that time the judgment of the living and the dead will take place; at that time “the ungodly will be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord” (Isa. 26:10). And what glory can this be except that by which he is God?

“For blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8); and the ungodly are not pure in heart, and therefore they shall not see him. Then they themselves “will go into everlasting punishment”; for thus “the ungodly will be taken away, that he may not see the glory of the Lord,” while “the righteous will go into everlasting life” (ibid. 25:46). And what is everlasting life? “That they may know you,” he says, “the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3). Not, certainly, as those knew him who, although not pure in heart, were nevertheless able to see him judging in the glorified form of a servant; but as he must be known by the pure in heart: the only true God, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, the Son, because the Trinity itself is the only true God.

If, then, we understand the saying, “I will that where I am, they also may be with me,” according to the fact that the Son of God is God, equal and coeternal with the Father, we shall be with Christ in the Father; but he will be there as he is, and we as we are, wherever we may be in bodily location. For if places must be spoken of—even places that do not contain bodies, and if every thing has a place where it is—the eternal place of Christ, where he always is, is the Father himself, and the place of the Father is the Son, because he says, “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (ibid. 14:10). And in this prayer he says, “As you, Father, are in me, and I in you”; and our place is in them, because he continues, “That they also may be one in us” (ibid. 17:21). We too are God’s place, because we are his temple; thus he prays for us who died for us and lives for us, that we may be one in them, because “his place was made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion” (Ps. 75:3), which is us.

But who is capable of conceiving these places, or what is in these places, without spatial extensions and bodily masses? Yet some progress is made if whatever of this sort presents itself to the eye of the heart is denied, rejected, and condemned; and if that light in which these things are seen to be denied, rejected, and condemned is contemplated as best one can; if its certainty is recognized and loved, so that from it one may rise and press onward to what is more inward. When the feeble mind, being less pure than those realities, cannot penetrate them, let it not be driven away from them without groans of love and tears of longing; but let it patiently endure while it is purified by faith and prepared by holy conduct to be able to dwell there [Note: [Col. 1928] Erasmus, Lyon, Venice, and Lovaniensis read: “may be prepared.” M.].

### 4

How, then, shall we not be with Christ where he is, when in the Father we shall be with him in whom he is? Nor did the Apostle remain silent about this, although we do not yet possess the reality but bear its hope. For he says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, sitting at the right hand of God. Set your minds on the things that are above, not on the things that are upon the earth. For you have died,” he says, “and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Behold, meanwhile, by faith and hope our life is where Christ is; it is with him, because it is with Christ in God. Behold, it is as though what he prayed might come to pass has already happened, when he said, “I will that where I am, they also may be with me”—but now by faith. When, however, will it happen by sight? “When Christ,” he says, “your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:1–4). Then we shall appear as what we shall be then, because then it will become evident that we did not believe and hope in vain before we were made.

He will accomplish this—the one to whom the Son, after saying, “That they may behold my glory which you have given me,” immediately added, “Because you loved me before the foundation of the world.” For in him he loved us also before the foundation of the world, and then predestined what he would accomplish at the end of the world [Note: [Col. 1928] Most printed editions differ here among themselves. Erasmus reads: “May the Son accomplish this, who, after saying …” Lovaniensis reads: “before we were made: to whom the Son, after saying …” Lyon and Venice read: “which before we were. He accomplished it, when the Son said …” M.].

### 5

“Righteous Father,” he says, “the world has not known you.” Because you are righteous, therefore the world did not know you. For that world which was predestined to condemnation did not know him deservedly; but the world which he reconciled to himself through Christ knew him not through merit but through grace. For what is it to know him except to have eternal life? He did not give this to the condemned world, but he gave it to the reconciled world.

Therefore the world did not know you because you are righteous, and according to its merits you granted that it should not know you; and the reconciled world knew you because you are merciful, and to enable it to know you, you came to its aid not because of its merit but by grace. Finally, it follows: “But I have known you.” God is by nature the source of grace; man, however, is from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin by ineffable grace. Finally, because of him—because “the grace of God is through Jesus Christ our Lord”—he says, “And these have known that you sent me.” This is the reconciled world. But because you sent me, they knew; therefore they knew by grace.

### 6

“And I have made known to them,” he says, “your name, and I will make it known.” I have made it known through faith; I will make it known through sight. I have made it known to those traveling toward their goal; I will make it known to those reigning without end.

“That the love,” he says, “with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” This is not the usual Latin expression: “the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.” Ordinarily one would say, “the love by which you loved me.” This has indeed been translated from the Greek, but there are similar expressions in Latin also, as when we say, “He served a faithful service” and “he served a vigorous military service,” although it might seem that one ought to say, “He served with faithful service” and “he served with vigorous military service.”

The expression “the love with which the Father loved the Son” is of the same kind as that used by the Apostle: “I have fought the good fight” (2 Tim. 4:7). He does not say, “with a good fight,” which would be more customary and apparently more correct. But how is the love with which the Father loved the Son also in us, except because we are his members and are loved in him, when he himself is loved in his entirety—that is, head and body? Therefore he added, “and I in them,” as though he were saying, “because I am also in them.” For he is in us in one way as in his temple; but in another way because we ourselves are he, since, according to the fact that he became man in order to be our head, we are his body.

The Savior’s prayer is ended; his passion begins. Therefore let this discourse also end, so that what he himself grants concerning the passion may be discussed in other discourses.

## TRACTATE CXII

On the passage that follows, “When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples,” and so forth, up to “They seized Jesus and bound him.” Chapter 18:1–12.

### 1

After the Lord had finished the great and lengthy discourse which, after supper, he delivered to the disciples who were then with him, being near to pouring out his blood for us, and after adding the prayer which he directed to the Father, the evangelist John thus began his account of the passion:

“When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he entered, he and his disciples. Now Judas also, who betrayed him, knew the place, because Jesus often met there with his disciples.”

The Lord’s entry with his disciples into the garden, which John narrates here, did not take place immediately after that prayer of his had ended, to whose words he refers by saying, “When Jesus had said these things.” Certain events are interposed which, having been omitted by John, are found in the other evangelists; just as many things found in John are likewise omitted by the others in their accounts. Whoever wishes to know how all these accounts agree with one another, and how one does not contradict the truth reported by another, should seek the answer not in these discourses but in other laborious writings; and should learn it not by standing and listening, but rather by sitting and reading, or by giving the keenest attention of mind and ear to someone who is reading it [Note: [Col. 1930] He refers them to his books On the Harmony of the Evangelists.].

Let him nevertheless believe, before he knows—whether he is able to know this also in the present life or is prevented by some impediment—that nothing has been written by any evangelist, insofar as concerns those whom the Church has received into canonical authority, which could be contrary either to his own or to another’s equally truthful account.

Now, therefore, let us examine the account of this blessed John, which we have undertaken to expound, without comparing it with the others, and without dwelling on matters that are clear, so that we may do so when the occasion requires. Let us not, then, understand his words, “When Jesus had said these things, he went out with his disciples across the brook Cedron, where there was a garden, into which he entered, he and his disciples,” as though he entered that garden immediately after those words. Rather, let the statement “When Jesus had said these things” serve to prevent us from supposing that he entered before he had finished those words.

### 2

“Judas also,” he says, “who betrayed him, knew the place.” The order of the words is: “He who betrayed him knew the place.” “Because,” he says, “Jesus often met there with his disciples.” There, then, the wolf clothed in a sheep’s skin, and tolerated among the sheep by the profound counsel of the master of the household, learned where he might, for a brief time, scatter the flock by attacking the shepherd through treachery.

“Judas, therefore,” he says, “having received a cohort, and officers from the chief priests and Pharisees, came there with lanterns and torches and weapons.” The cohort was not a Jewish cohort but a military one. It should therefore be understood as having been received from the governor, as though for the arrest of a criminal, in accordance with the proper order of legitimate authority, so that no one would dare resist those making the arrest. Yet such a large force had also been assembled and came so heavily armed that it might either terrify or even resist anyone who dared to defend Christ.

Thus his power was concealed and his weakness displayed, so that these things seemed necessary to his enemies against one upon whom nothing could prevail except what he himself willed—being good and making good use of evils, and making good things out of evils, in order to make good people out of evil people and distinguish good people from evil people.

### 3

“Jesus therefore,” as the Evangelist continues, “knowing all that was to come upon him, went forth and said to them, ‘Whom do you seek?’ They answered him, ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ Jesus said to them, ‘I am.’ Judas also, who betrayed him, was standing with them. When therefore he said to them, ‘I am he,’ they went backward and fell to the ground.”

Where now is the military cohort, and the officers of the chief priests and Pharisees? Where are the terror and the protection of their weapons? Surely, with a single utterance—“I am”—he struck, repelled, and felled, without any weapon, so great a crowd, savage in hatred and terrifying in arms.

For God was hidden in the flesh, and everlasting day was so concealed within human limbs that it was sought by lanterns and torches in order to be killed by darkness. “I am he,” he says, and casts down the ungodly. What will he do when he comes to judge, who did this when he was being judged? What will he be able to do when he reigns, who was able to do this when he was about to die?

And now, throughout the Gospel, Christ says, “I am he”; and the Jews await the Antichrist, so that they may go backward and fall to the ground, because, abandoning heavenly things, they desire earthly things.

Certainly the persecutors came with the betrayer to seize Jesus. They found the one they were seeking and heard him say, “I am.” Why did they not seize him, but went backward and fell, unless it was because he willed this—he who could do whatever he willed? Yet if he had never allowed himself to be seized by them, they would not indeed have done what they came to do, but neither would he have done what he came to do.

For they sought him in their fury in order to kill him; but he also sought us by dying. Therefore, because he displayed his power to those who wanted to seize him but were unable to do so, let them now seize him, so that he may accomplish his will through those who do not understand.

### 4

“Again therefore he asked them, ‘Whom do you seek?’ And they said, ‘Jesus of Nazareth.’ Jesus answered, ‘I told you that I am. If therefore you seek me, let these go their way.’ This was to fulfill the word which he had spoken, ‘Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none.’”

“If you seek me,” he says, “let these go their way.” He sees enemies, and they do what he commands; they allow those to go whom he does not wish to perish. But were they not destined to die later? Why, then, would he have lost them if they had died at that time, unless it was because they did not yet believe in him in the manner in which all who do not perish believe?

### 5

“Simon Peter, therefore, having a sword, drew it and struck the servant of the high priest, and cut off his right ear. The servant’s name was Malchus.”

John alone among the evangelists also gives the servant’s name, just as Luke alone records that the Lord touched and healed his ear (Luke 22:51). Malchus is interpreted as “the one who will reign.”

What, then, does the ear cut off for the Lord and healed by the Lord signify except hearing renewed after the oldness has been cut away, so that it may exist “in the newness of the spirit and not in the oldness of the letter” (Rom. 7:6)? Whoever receives this from Christ—who would doubt that he will reign with Christ?

The fact that he was found to be a servant also pertains to that oldness which gives birth to slavery, which is Hagar (Gal. 4:24). But when healing came, freedom was also represented.

Nevertheless, the Lord disapproved of Peter’s action and forbade him to proceed further, saying: “Put the sword into its sheath. Shall I not drink the cup which the Father has given me?”

In his action that disciple wished to defend his master; he did not consider what the action signified. He therefore had to be admonished toward patience, and the event had to be written down for the sake of understanding.

When he says that the cup of suffering was given to him by the Father, it is surely what the Apostle says: “If God is for us, who can be against us? He who did not spare his own Son but delivered him up for us all” (Rom. 8:31–32). Yet he who drank this cup is himself also its author. Hence the same Apostle says again: “Christ loved us and delivered himself up for us, an offering and sacrifice to God for a sweet-smelling fragrance” (Eph. 5:2).

### 6

“Then the cohort, the tribune, and the officers of the Jews seized Jesus and bound him.”

They seized the one to whom they did not draw near, because he was the day, while they remained darkness; nor did they hear, “Draw near to him and be enlightened” (Ps. 33:6). For if they had drawn near in this way, they would have seized him not to be killed by their hands but to be received in their hearts.

But when they seized him in that manner, they then withdrew farther from him; and they bound the one whom they ought rather to have desired to set free. Perhaps there were among them some who then placed their bonds upon Christ and were afterward freed by him, saying, “You have broken my bonds” (Ps. 115:16).

Let this suffice for today. What follows will, God willing, be discussed in another discourse.

## TRACTATE CXIII

On the passage beginning, “And they led him first to Annas,” and ending, “Peter therefore denied again, and immediately the cock crowed.” Chapter 18:13–27.

### 1

After the persecutors, with Judas betraying him, had seized and bound the Lord—who loved us and delivered himself up for us (Eph. 5:2), and whom the Father did not spare but delivered up for us all (Rom. 8:32)—so that Judas may be understood to be condemned not because the usefulness of this betrayal was praiseworthy, but because the intention of his crime was damnable, “they led him,” as the evangelist John narrates, “first to Annas.”

He does not conceal the reason why this was done: “For he was,” he says, “the father-in-law of Caiaphas, who was high priest that year.” “Now Caiaphas,” he says, “was the one who gave counsel to the Jews that it was expedient that one man should die for the people.”

Accordingly, when Matthew wished to narrate the matter more briefly, he mentions that Jesus was led to Caiaphas (Matt. 26:57), because he was first led to Annas precisely because Annas was Caiaphas’s father-in-law. Here we must understand that Caiaphas wanted this same thing to be done.

### 2

“Simon Peter,” he says, “was following Jesus, and so was another disciple.” Who this disciple was should not be asserted rashly, because it is not stated. John usually identifies himself in this way and adds, “whom Jesus loved” (John 13:23; 19:26). Perhaps, then, this was the same disciple. Whoever he was, let us examine what follows.

“That disciple,” he says, “was known to the high priest, and entered with Jesus into the courtyard of the high priest; but Peter stood outside at the door. Therefore the other disciple, who was known to the high priest, went out and spoke to the doorkeeper and brought Peter in. The maid who kept the door therefore said to Peter, ‘Are you also one of this man’s disciples?’ He said, ‘I am not.’”

Behold, the firmest pillar trembled at the breath of a single breeze. Where is that boldness of his promise, and his excessive confidence in himself? Where are those words he spoke when he said, “Why cannot I follow you now? I will lay down my life for you” (John 13:37)? Is this following the master—to deny that one is a disciple? Is one’s life laid down for the Lord in such a way that one fears a maid’s voice lest it happen?

But what wonder is it if God foretold the truth while man presumed falsely? Certainly, in this denial of the Apostle Peter, which has now begun, we must observe that Christ is denied not only by the one who says that he is not the Christ, but also by the one who, although he is a Christian, denies that he is a Christian.

For the Lord did not say to Peter, “You will deny that you are my disciple,” but, “You will deny me” (Matt. 26:34). He therefore denied Christ when he denied that he was his disciple. And what else did he deny in this way except that he was a Christian?

Although Christ’s disciples had not yet begun to be called by this name—for it was only after his ascension that they first began to be called Christians at Antioch (Acts 11:26)—the reality itself already existed, destined to receive that name later. They were already disciples who would afterward be called Christians, and they transmitted this common name, as they did the common faith, to those who came after them.

Therefore, the one who denied that he was Christ’s disciple denied the reality whose name is to be called Christian. How many later—not only old men and old women, in whom the satiety of this life could more easily enable them to despise death for confessing Christ, nor only young people of both sexes, from whom courage seems appropriately to be demanded at that age, but even boys and girls—were able, and an innumerable company of holy martyrs entered the kingdom of heaven with courage and violence! Yet this man, who had received the keys of that kingdom (Matt. 16:19), could not do so at that time.

Behold why it was said, “Let these go their way,” when he who redeemed us by his blood delivered himself up for us, so that the word he had spoken might be fulfilled: “Of those whom you gave me, I have lost none.” For surely, if Peter had departed from here after denying Christ, what else would he have done but perish?

### 3

“Now the servants and officers were standing beside a charcoal fire, because it was cold, and they were warming themselves.” It was not winter, but it was cold; this can sometimes happen even around the spring equinox.

“Peter was also with them, standing and warming himself. The high priest therefore questioned Jesus about his disciples and about his teaching. Jesus answered him: ‘I have spoken openly to the world; I have always taught in the synagogue [Note: [Col. 1933] The manuscripts read: “in the synagogues.”] and in the temple, where all the Jews meet, and I have said nothing in secret. Why do you question me? Ask those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.’”

A question arises here that must not be passed over: how did the Lord Jesus say, “I have spoken openly to the world,” and especially what he said, “I have said nothing in secret”? Did he not, in this very recent discourse which he delivered to his disciples after supper, say to them: “These things I have spoken to you in proverbs; the hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs, but will announce to you openly concerning the Father” (John 16:25)?

If, then, he did not speak openly even to his closer disciples but promised an hour when he would speak openly, how did he speak openly to the world? Moreover, even to those very disciples of his, as the authority of the other evangelists also testifies, he spoke much more plainly in comparison with those who were not his disciples when he was alone with them, away from the crowds. For then he opened to them the parables which he presented to others in closed form.

What, then, does “I have said nothing in secret” mean? It must be understood as though he had said: “I have spoken openly to the world,” meaning, “Many have heard me.” That which was open was open in one sense, but in another sense it was not open. It was open because many heard; and again it was not open because they did not understand.

What he spoke privately to his disciples, however, he certainly did not speak in secret. For who speaks in secret when he speaks before so many people, especially when it is written, “In the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deut. 19:15)? This is especially true if he speaks to a few what he wishes through them to become known to many, as the Lord himself said to those whom he still had as a small number: “What I tell you in darkness, speak in the light; and what you hear in the ear, preach upon the housetops” (Matt. 10:27).

Therefore, even that which seemed to be spoken secretly by him was, in a certain sense, not spoken in secret, because it was not spoken in such a way that those to whom it had been said should keep silent about it, but rather in such a way that it should be preached everywhere.

Thus something can be said both openly and not openly, or both in secret and not in secret, just as it is said, “That seeing they may see, and not see” (Mark 4:12). For how do they see except because it is openly, not in secret? And how do those same people again not see except because it is not openly, but in secret?

Yet the very things they had heard without understanding were such that they could not justly and truthfully accuse him. And whenever they tried to find, by questioning him, some basis for accusing him, he answered them in such a way that all their deceptions were blunted and their slanders frustrated.

Therefore he said, “Why do you question me? Ask those who heard what I said to them. Behold, they know what I said.”

### 4

“When he had said these things, one of the officers standing nearby struck Jesus on the face, saying, ‘Do you answer the high priest in this way?’ Jesus answered him: ‘If I have spoken wrongly, bear witness concerning the wrong; but if I have spoken rightly, why do you strike me?’”

What could be truer, gentler, or more just than this answer? He is the one of whom the prophetic word had gone before: “Proceed, prosper, and reign, because of truth, gentleness, and righteousness” (Ps. 44:5).

If we consider who it was that received the blow, would we not wish the one who struck him either to be consumed by heavenly fire, swallowed up by the opening earth, seized by a demon and thrown about, or punished by some similar and even more severe penalty? What could he not have commanded by his power, through whom the world was made, if he had not preferred to teach us the patience by which the world is conquered?

Someone may say: Why did he not do what he himself commanded (Matt. 5:39)? For he should not have answered the one striking him in this way, but ought to have offered the other cheek also [Note: [Col. 1935] Ten manuscripts read: “to prepare.”].

But what of the fact that he answered truthfully, gently, and justly, and not only prepared the other cheek to be struck again, but prepared his whole body to be fastened to the wood? By this he demonstrated more clearly what had to be demonstrated: namely, that those great commandments of his concerning patience are to be fulfilled not by displaying the body but by preparing the heart.

A person may visibly offer the other cheek and yet be angry. How much better, then, is it to answer truthfully while calm, and to become ready in a tranquil spirit to endure greater things? Blessed is the one who, in all that he unjustly suffers for righteousness, can truthfully say, “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready.” From this comes what follows: “I will sing and make melody” (Ps. 56:8), which Paul and Barnabas [Note: [Col. 1935] Perhaps “Silas” should be read here, according to Acts 16:25.] were also able to do in the harshest imprisonment.

### 5

But let us return to what follows in the Gospel narrative.

“Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest.” According to Matthew, he was being led to Caiaphas from the beginning, because Caiaphas himself was the chief priest of that year. We must understand that the two high priests—that is, the chief priests—who were at that time, Annas and Caiaphas, customarily held office in alternate years.

Luke the Evangelist mentions them when he narrates the time at which John, the Lord’s precursor, began to preach the kingdom of heaven and gather disciples. For he says: “In the days of the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John the son of Zechariah in the wilderness” (Luke 3:2), and so forth.

Accordingly, these two high priests held office in alternate years, and it was Caiaphas’s year when Christ suffered. Therefore, according to Matthew, when Jesus had been seized, he was led to Caiaphas. But according to John, they first came with him to Annas, not because Annas was his colleague, but because he was his father-in-law.

We must believe that this was done according to Caiaphas’s wishes, or perhaps that their houses were situated in such a way that Annas could not properly be passed by those going through.

### 6

After the Evangelist had said that Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas, he returned to the point in the narrative where he had left Peter, in order to explain what had happened in the house of Annas concerning Peter’s threefold denial.

“Now Simon Peter,” he says, “was standing and warming himself.” This repeats what he had already said earlier; then he joins to it what followed.

“They therefore said to him, ‘Are you also one of his disciples?’ He denied it and said, ‘I am not.’” He had already denied him once; behold, a second time.

Then, so that the third denial might be completed, “one of the servants of the high priest, a relative of the man whose ear Peter had cut off, said, ‘Did I not see you in the garden with him?’ Peter therefore denied again, and immediately the cock crowed.”

Behold, the physician’s prediction has been fulfilled, and the sick man’s presumption has been exposed. For what Peter had said did not happen: “I will lay down my life for you”; but what the Lord had foretold did happen: “You will deny me three times” (John 13:38).

Now that Peter’s threefold denial has been completed, let this discourse also come to an end, so that we may consider in another beginning what was done concerning the Lord before Pontius Pilate the governor.

## TRACTATE CXIV

On the passage beginning, “They therefore led Jesus to Caiaphas into the praetorium,” and ending, “That the word of Jesus might be fulfilled which he spoke, signifying by what death he was going to die.” Chapter 18:28–32.

### 1

Let us next examine what happened to our Lord Jesus Christ, or concerning him, before Pontius Pilate the governor, insofar as the evangelist John indicates. He returns to the point in his narrative where he had left it in order to explain Peter’s denial.

For he had already said, “And Annas sent him bound to Caiaphas the high priest” (John 18:24). From there, after returning to the place where he had left Peter warming himself at the fire in the courtyard, and after completing the account of his entire threefold denial, he says: “They therefore led Jesus to Caiaphas [Note: [Col. 1936] The same reading is found in Book 3 of On the Harmony of the Evangelists, chapter 7. But the sacred Scriptures now read: *apo tou Caipha*, “from Caiaphas.”] into the praetorium.”

He had said that Annas had sent him to Caiaphas, his colleague and father-in-law. But if he was led to Caiaphas, why was he led into the praetorium? This must mean nothing other than the place where the governor Pilate lived.

Either, then, because of some urgent circumstance, Caiaphas had gone from the house of Annas—which both had entered in order to hear Jesus—to the governor’s praetorium, and had left Jesus with his father-in-law to be heard; or Pilate had taken possession of the praetorium in the house of Caiaphas, and the house was so large that it could accommodate its master living in one part and the judge in another.

### 2

“Now it was morning,” and they—that is, those who were leading Jesus—“did not enter into the praetorium,” that is, into the part of the house occupied by Pilate, if it was indeed the house of Caiaphas.

Explaining why they did not enter the praetorium, he says: “So that they would not be defiled, but might eat the Passover.” They had begun to observe the days of Unleavened Bread; during those days they considered it a defilement to enter the dwelling of a foreigner.

O impious blindness! They would supposedly be defiled by entering a foreigner’s dwelling, but not by their own crime. They feared being defiled by the praetorium of a foreign judge, but did not fear the blood of an innocent brother—to say nothing for the moment of the fact that their conscience was already held guilty of evil.

For that the Lord himself was the one whom their impiety was leading to death, and that the giver of life was being killed, should be attributed not to their conscience but to their ignorance.

### 3

“Pilate therefore went out to them and said, ‘What accusation do you bring against this man?’ They answered and said to him, ‘If he were not a criminal, we would not have handed him over to you.’”

Let those freed from unclean spirits, the sick who were healed, the lepers who were cleansed, the deaf who heard, the mute who spoke, the blind who saw, and the dead who rose again be questioned and answer whether Jesus was a criminal. And, surpassing all these, let the foolish who became wise answer.

But they were saying these things of whom he himself had already foretold through the prophet: “They repaid me evil for good” (Ps. 34:12).

[Col. 1937]

### 4

“Pilate therefore said to them, ‘Take him yourselves and judge him according to your law.’ The Jews therefore said to him, ‘It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.’”

What is this that their deranged cruelty is saying? Were they not killing the one whom they were presenting to be killed? Or does the cross perhaps not kill? Thus do those who do not follow wisdom go astray while persecuting it.

What does “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” mean? If he is a criminal, why is it not lawful? Did not the Law command them not to spare criminals, especially seducers such as they thought him to be, who led people away from their God (Deut. 13:5)?

But it must be understood that they said it was not lawful for them to kill anyone because of the sanctity of the feast which they had already begun to celebrate—the same feast on account of which they feared being defiled by entering the praetorium.

Have you become so hardened, false Israelites? Have you lost all understanding through excessive wickedness, so that you think yourselves undefiled by the blood of an innocent man merely because you handed him over to another to shed it?

Will Pilate, to whose authority you bring him to be killed, kill him with his own hands? If you did not want him killed, if you did not plot against him, if you did not purchase his delivery with money, if you did not seize him, bind him, and bring him, if you did not present him to hands to be killed and demand it with your voices, then do not boast that he was killed by you.

But if, in addition to all those preceding actions of yours, you also shouted, “Crucify, crucify!” (John 19:6), hear what the prophet cries against you: “The teeth of the sons of men are weapons and arrows, and their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56:5).

Behold with what weapons, with what arrows, and with what sword you killed the righteous man when you said that it was not lawful for you to kill anyone.

This is why, when the chief priests did not come themselves to seize Jesus but sent others, Luke the Evangelist nevertheless says at the same point in his narrative: “Jesus said to those who had come against him, the chief priests, the magistrates of the temple, and the elders, ‘Have you come out as against a robber?’” (Luke 22:52), and so forth.

Therefore, just as the chief priests came not in person but, through those whom they had sent to seize Jesus, came in the power of their own command, so all those who shouted with impious voices that Christ should be crucified killed him—not indeed by themselves, but nevertheless through the one who was driven to this crime by their shouting.

5. But what the evangelist John adds—“in order that the saying of Jesus might be fulfilled, signifying by what death he was going to die”—if here we wish to understand the death of the cross, as though the Jews had said, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone,” because killing is one thing and crucifying another, I do not see how this can consistently be understood, since they were responding to Pilate’s words, by which he had said to them, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your Law.” Could they not, then, take him and themselves crucify him, if they wished to avoid killing anyone by such a form of punishment? Who does not see how absurd it is that they should have been allowed to crucify anyone when they were not allowed to kill anyone? Moreover, the Lord himself calls this same death of his—that is, the death of the cross—“killing,” as we read in Mark, where he says:

> “Behold, we are going up to Jerusalem, and the Son of Man will be handed over to the chief priests and the scribes, and they will condemn him to death, and hand him over to the Gentiles; and they will mock him, and spit upon him, and scourge him, and kill him, and on the third day he will rise again” (Mark 10:33–34).

Therefore, plainly, by saying these things the Lord signified by what death he was going to die—not that here he wished the death of the cross to be understood, but that the Jews would hand him over to the Gentiles, that is, to the Romans. For Pilate was a Roman, and the Romans had sent him as governor to Judaea. Thus, in order that this saying of Jesus might be fulfilled—that is, in order that the Gentiles might kill him after he had been handed over to them, as Jesus had foretold would happen—Pilate, who was a Roman judge, when he wished to return him to the Jews so that they might judge him according to their Law, they refused to take him, saying, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone.” And so the saying of Jesus was fulfilled, the saying he had foretold concerning his death: that the Gentiles would kill him after he had been handed over by the Jews. They did so with a lesser crime than the Jews, who wished in this way to make themselves appear strangers to his killing—not so that their innocence might be shown, but so that their madness might be exposed.

# TRACTATE CXV

On the passage: “Pilate therefore entered the praetorium again,” up to: “Now Barabbas was a robber.” Chapter 18, verses 33–40.

1. What Pilate said to Christ, and what Christ replied to Pilate, must be considered and examined in this discourse. For after it had been said to the Jews, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your Law,” and they had replied, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone,” Pilate entered the praetorium again, called Jesus, and said to him: “Are you the king of the Jews?” And Jesus answered: “Do you say this of your own accord, or have others told you about me?”

The Lord certainly knew both what he himself asked and what the other was going to answer. Yet he wished it to be said—not so that he himself might know, but so that what he wished us to know might be written down.

“Pilate answered: ‘Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me. What have you done?’ Jesus answered: ‘My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews; but now my kingdom is not from here.’”

This is what the good Teacher wished us to know. But first the false human opinion concerning his kingdom had to be exposed—whether the opinion of the Gentiles or of the Jews, from whom Pilate had heard it—as though he were being punished by death because he had unlawfully sought a kingdom; or because rulers are accustomed to envy those who are about to rule, and it was evidently necessary to beware lest his kingdom be hostile either to the Romans or to the Jews.

The Lord could have answered Pilate’s first question—when he said to him, “Are you the king of the Jews?”—with the words, “My kingdom is not of this world.” But by in turn asking whether Pilate said this of his own accord or had heard it from others, and by Pilate’s response, he wished to show that the Jews had presented this accusation to him as though it were a crime. In this way he disclosed to us the thoughts of human beings, which he himself knew to be vain: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” (Psalm 93:11). Then, after Pilate’s reply, he answered the Jews and Gentiles in a way that was more timely and appropriate: “My kingdom is not of this world.”

If he had immediately answered Pilate’s question, he might have seemed to be replying concerning himself only to the Gentiles who held this opinion of him, and not also to the Jews. But since Pilate answered, “Am I a Jew? Your nation and the chief priests handed you over to me,” he removed from himself the suspicion that he had said on his own initiative that Jesus was king of the Jews, showing that he had heard this from the Jews. Then, by saying, “What have you done?” he sufficiently demonstrated that this had been brought against him as a crime—as though he were saying: “If you deny that you are a king, what have you done to cause you to be handed over to me?” It would be no wonder if someone who called himself a king were handed over to a judge for punishment; but if he did not say this, one ought to ask him what else he might have done for which he deserved to be handed over to a judge.

2. Hear, therefore, O Jews and Gentiles; hear, circumcision; hear, uncircumcision; hear, all earthly kingdoms: “I do not hinder your dominion in this world. My kingdom is not of this world.” Do not fear with that utterly empty fear with which that Herod, when Christ’s birth was announced, was terrified and killed so many infants so that death might reach him (Matthew 2:3, 16)—more cruel in fear than in anger. “My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world.” What more do you want? Come to the kingdom that is not of this world; come by believing, and do not rage through fear.

The Lord says in prophecy concerning God the Father: “Yet I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain” (Psalm 2:6). But that Zion and that mountain are not of this world. For what is his kingdom except those who believe in him, to whom he says, “You are not of the world, just as I am not of the world”? Yet he wished them to be in the world; and for this reason he said concerning them to the Father: “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you preserve them from evil” (John 17:16, 15).

Thus here also he did not say, “My kingdom is not in this world,” but, “It is not of this world.” And when he proved this by saying, “If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight so that I would not be handed over to the Jews,” he did not say, “Now my kingdom is not here,” but, “It is not from here.”

For his kingdom is here until the end of the age, with the tares mixed among it until the harvest. The harvest is the end of the age, when the reapers will come—that is, the angels—and will gather from his kingdom all scandals (Matthew 13:38–41). This certainly would not happen if his kingdom were not here. Yet it is not from here, because it is a pilgrim in the world. To his kingdom he says: “You are not of the world, but I chose you out of the world” (John 15:19).

They were therefore of the world when they were not his kingdom, but belonged to the prince of the world. Everything, then, that is human is of the world: it was indeed created by the true God, but generated from Adam’s corrupted and condemned stock. But whatever has been regenerated in Christ has become a kingdom no longer of the world. For God has rescued us from the power of darkness and transferred us into the kingdom of the Son of his love (Colossians 1:13). Concerning this kingdom he says: “My kingdom is not of this world,” or, “My kingdom is not from here.”

3. Pilate therefore said to him: “So you are a king?” Jesus answered: “You say that I am a king.”

This was not because he was afraid to confess himself a king. Rather, the expression “You say” is so balanced that he neither denies himself to be a king—for he is a king whose kingdom is not of this world—nor admits that he is such a king as would be thought to have a kingdom of this world. For Pilate understood him in this way when he said, “So you are a king?” To him the answer was given: “You say that I am a king.” For “You say” was spoken as though it were “You, being carnal, speak carnally.”

4. Then he adds: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, to bear witness to the truth.”

The syllable of this pronoun in the phrase “For this I was born” must not be prolonged, as though he had said, “For this matter I was born,” but shortened, as though he had said, “For this purpose I was born,” or, “For this I was born,” just as he says, “For this I came into the world.” For in the Greek Gospel there is no ambiguity in this expression: *eis touto* (“for this,” “for this purpose”). [Note: [Col. 1940] Greek: *eis toûto*.]

It is therefore clear that here he recalled his temporal birth, by which he came into the world incarnate, not that birth without beginning by which he was God, through whom the Father made the world. He therefore said that he was born for this—that is, born for this purpose—and had come into the world for this purpose, namely, by being born of a Virgin, to bear witness to the truth.

But because faith does not belong to everyone (2 Thessalonians 3:2), he added and said: “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” He hears, certainly, with the inner ears—that is, he obeys my voice. It would have the same meaning if he said, “He believes me.”

When Christ therefore bears witness to the truth, he plainly bears witness to himself; for his voice is: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). And elsewhere he says: “I bear witness concerning myself” (John 8:18).

But by saying, “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice,” he commended the grace by which he calls according to his purpose. Concerning this purpose the Apostle says: “We know that all things work together for good for those who love God, who are called according to his purpose” (Romans 8:28)—the purpose, namely, of the one who calls, not of those who are called. Elsewhere this is stated more clearly: “Share in the Gospel according to the power of God, who saved us and called us with a holy calling, not according to our works, but according to his own purpose and grace” (2 Timothy 1:8–9).

For if we consider the nature in which we were created, since the truth created us all, who is not of the truth? But not to all is it granted by the truth itself to hear the truth—that is, to obey the truth and believe in the truth. This is granted with no preceding merits whatsoever, lest grace cease to be grace.

For if he had said, “Everyone who hears my voice is of the truth,” someone would be thought to be called “of the truth” because he obeys the truth. But he did not say this. He said, “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.” Accordingly, he is not of the truth because he hears its voice; rather, he hears because he is of the truth—that is, because this gift has been bestowed upon him by the truth. What else is this than that, Christ granting it, he believes in Christ?

5. Pilate said to him: “What is truth?” And he did not wait to hear the answer. But after saying this, he went out again to the Jews and said to them: “I find no case against him. But you have a custom that I should release one person to you at the Passover. Do you therefore want me to release the king of the Jews?”

I believe that when Pilate said, “What is truth?” the custom of the Jews immediately came to his mind—the custom by which one person was accustomed to be released to them at the Passover. For this reason he did not wait for Jesus to answer him concerning what truth was, lest there be delay, since he had recalled the custom by which someone could be released to them at the Passover. It is clear that he very much wished to do this.

Yet he could not remove from his heart the conviction that Jesus was king of the Jews, as though truth itself—the truth about which he had asked what it was—had fixed this there, just as it was fixed in the inscription.

But when they heard this, “they all cried out again, saying: ‘Not this man, but Barabbas.’ Now Barabbas was a robber.”

We do not reproach you, O Jews, for releasing a guilty man at the Passover, but for killing an innocent man—although unless this had happened, the true Passover would not have taken place. The Jews, who were in error, held the shadow of the truth, and through deceitful human beings, by a wondrous dispensation of divine wisdom, the truth of that same shadow was fulfilled, because, for the true Passover to take place, Christ was sacrificed like a sheep.

What follows concerns the insults inflicted upon Christ by Pilate and his cohort; these must be treated in another discourse.

# TRACTATE CXVI

On the passage: “Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him,” up to: “But they took Jesus and led him away.” Chapter 19, verses 1–16.

1. When the Jews had cried out that they did not want Jesus released to them by Pilate at the Passover, but Barabbas the robber; not the Savior, but the murderer; not the giver of life, but its taker—“Then Pilate took Jesus and scourged him.”

We must believe that Pilate did this for no other reason than that the Jews, satisfied with his humiliations, might think that enough had been done and cease raging against him until his death. To this also belongs the fact that the same governor permitted his cohort to do what follows—or perhaps even ordered it, although the evangelist has not said so. For he related what the soldiers did afterward, but did not say that Pilate ordered it.

“And the soldiers,” he says, “plaiting a crown of thorns, placed it on his head, and clothed him in a purple garment. And they came to him and said: ‘Hail, king of the Jews.’ And they gave him slaps.”

Thus were fulfilled what Christ had foretold concerning himself. Thus the martyrs were trained to endure whatever persecutors might wish to do. Thus, while his dreadful power was hidden for a little while, the patience that was first to be imitated was commended. Thus the kingdom that was not of this world conquered the proud world not by the violence of fighting, but by the humility of suffering. Thus the seed that was to multiply was sown amid dreadful contempt, so that it might spring forth in wondrous glory.

2. Pilate went out again and said to them: “Behold, I am bringing him out to you, so that you may know that I find no case against him.” Jesus therefore came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment. And he said to them: “Behold the man.”

Here it is evident that Pilate was not unaware of what the soldiers had done, whether he ordered it or permitted it. The reason was the one we stated above: that Christ’s enemies might drink in these mockeries of his with the greatest pleasure and no longer thirst for blood.

Jesus comes out to them wearing the crown of thorns and the purple garment—not glorious in authority, but full of disgrace—and it is said to them: “Behold the man.” If you envy a king, now spare him, because you see him cast down. He has been scourged; he has been crowned with thorns; he has been clothed in a mocking garment; he has been derided with bitter insults; he has been struck with slaps. Shame burns; let envy grow cold.

But it does not grow cold; rather, it blazes and increases.

3. “Therefore, when the chief priests and the attendants saw him, they cried out, saying: ‘Crucify, crucify him.’ Pilate said to them: ‘Take him yourselves and crucify him, for I find no case against him.’ The Jews answered him: ‘We have a Law, and according to the Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.’”

Behold another, greater envy. The former had seemed a small matter, as though it concerned an attempt, by unlawful presumption, to acquire royal power. Yet Jesus falsely claimed neither of these things for himself; rather, both are true: he is the only-begotten Son of God, and he was established by God as king upon his holy mountain Zion.

Both of these would now be demonstrated, were it not that the more powerful he was, the more he preferred to be patient.

4. When Pilate heard this saying, he became more afraid. He entered the praetorium again and said to Jesus: “Where are you from?” But Jesus gave him no answer.

This silence of our Lord Jesus Christ is found to have occurred more than once when the accounts of all the evangelists are compared: before the chief priests; before Herod, to whom Pilate sent him to be examined, as Luke indicates; and before Pilate himself (Matthew 26:63; 27:14; Mark 14:61; 15:5; Luke 23:7–9; John 19:9). Thus the prophecy did not precede him without reason: “As a lamb before the one who shears it was without a voice, so he did not open his mouth” (Isaiah 53:7)—namely, at those times when he did not answer his interrogators.

Although he often answered certain questions, nevertheless, because of those to which he did not wish to respond, the comparison with a lamb was given for this purpose: so that in his silence he might be regarded not as guilty, but as innocent. When he was being judged, wherever he did not open his mouth, he did not open it like a lamb—not like one who was conscious of evil and was being convicted of his own sins, but like the meek one who was being sacrificed for the sins of others.

5. Pilate therefore said to him: “Do you not speak to me? Do you not know that I have authority to crucify you, and authority to release you?” Jesus answered: “You would have no authority against me at all unless it had been given to you from above. Therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.”

Behold, he answered; yet wherever he did not answer, he did not open his mouth like a guilty or deceitful man, but like a lamb—that is, like one simple and innocent. Thus, where he did not answer, he was silent like a sheep; where he answered, he taught like a shepherd.

Let us therefore learn what he said, which he also taught through the Apostle: “There is no authority except from God” (Romans 13:1). And let us learn that the one who, through envy, hands over an innocent person to a power so that he may be killed sins more greatly than the power itself if it kills him through fear of another, greater power.

God had given Pilate such authority that he was also under Caesar’s authority. Therefore, he says, “You would have no authority against me,” that is, whatever authority you have, however little it may be, unless this very thing—whatever it is—had been given to you from above.

But since I know how great it is—for it is not so great that you are free to do absolutely anything—“therefore the one who handed me over to you has the greater sin.” He handed me over to your authority through envy, whereas you are going to exercise that same authority against me through fear.

Even through fear, a human being ought not to kill another human being, especially an innocent one. Yet to do this through envy is much worse than to do it through fear. Therefore the truthful Teacher did not say, “The one who handed me over to you has the sin,” as though the other had none; rather, he said, “has the greater sin,” so that Pilate might understand that he too had sin. For the fact that one sin is greater does not make the other nonexistent.

6. From then on Pilate sought to release him.

What does the expression “from then on” mean, as though he had not sought to release him earlier? Read what precedes, and you will find that for a long time already he had been seeking to release Jesus.

“From then on” should therefore be understood as “because of this,” that is, “for this reason”: so that he would not incur the sin of killing an innocent man handed over to him, although he was less guilty than the Jews who had handed him over to be killed.

“From then on,” therefore—that is, so that he would not commit this sin—means that he had been seeking to release him not only now for the first time, but from the beginning.

7. But the Jews cried out, saying: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself a king speaks against Caesar.”

They thought they would instill a greater fear in Pilate by frightening him with Caesar and thus make him kill Christ than they had earlier, when they said: “We have a Law, and according to the Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God.”

He did not fear their Law so as to kill him. Rather, he feared the Son of God, lest he kill him. But now he could not disregard Caesar, the source of his authority, in the way he could disregard the Law of a foreign nation.

8. Yet the evangelist continues and says: “When Pilate heard these words, he brought Jesus outside and sat down on the tribunal, at the place called Lithostrotos, but in Hebrew Gabbatha. Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour.”

At what hour the Lord was crucified—because of the testimony of another evangelist, who said, “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:25), and because a major dispute commonly arises from this—when we reach the place where his crucifixion is narrated, we shall discuss it as far as we can, if the Lord wills. [Note: [Col. 1943] See below, Tractate 117, §§1–2.]

When Pilate had therefore sat down on the tribunal, he said to the Jews: “Behold your king.” But they cried out: “Take him away, take him away; crucify him.” Pilate said to them: “Shall I crucify your king?”

He was still trying to overcome the terror they had instilled concerning Caesar, wishing to break them by their own disgrace when he said, “Shall I crucify your king?” He had not been able to soften them toward Christ by reminding them of their disgrace; but he is soon overcome by fear.

[Col. 1944] 9. For the chief priests answered: “We have no king but Caesar.”

Then he handed him over to them to be crucified.

He would plainly appear to be acting against Caesar if, when they professed that they had no king but Caesar, he wished to impose another king by releasing the one they had handed over to him to be killed for this very reason.

He therefore handed him over to them to be crucified. But had he not wanted this earlier as well, when he said, “Take him yourselves and crucify him,” or even above, “Take him yourselves and judge him according to your Law”?

Why, then, had they so emphatically refused, saying, “It is not lawful for us to kill anyone” (John 18:31), and insisting in every way that he be killed not by them but by the governor? Why had they refused to take him for killing if now they take him to be killed?

Or, if this is not what happened, why is it said, “Then he handed him over to them to be crucified”? Is there some distinction here?

There certainly is. For it was not said, “Then he handed him over to them so that they might crucify him,” but, “so that he might be crucified”—that is, so that he might be crucified by the judgment and authority of the governor.

But the evangelist said that he was handed over to them in order to show that they were entangled in the crime from which they were trying to distance themselves. Pilate would not have done this unless he wished to fulfill what he saw them desiring.

As for what follows—“But they took Jesus and led him away”—this may refer to the soldiers, the governor’s attendants. For later it is stated more explicitly: “The soldiers therefore, when they had crucified him” (John 19:23). Yet even if the evangelist attributes the whole act to the Jews, he does so rightly: they took what they had demanded with the greatest eagerness, and they did whatever they had forced to be done.

But these subsequent matters must be treated in another discourse.

# TRACTATE CXVII

On the passage: “And bearing his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull,” up to: “Pilate answered: What I have written, I have written.” Chapter 19, verses 17–22.

1. When Pilate had judged and condemned the Lord Jesus Christ from the tribunal, at about the sixth hour they took him and led him away. “And bearing his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him.”

What, then, does the evangelist Mark mean when he says, “It was the third hour, and they crucified him” (Mark 15:25), except that the Lord was crucified at the third hour by the tongues of the Jews, and at the sixth hour by the hands of the soldiers?

We are to understand that the fifth hour had already passed and that something of the sixth had begun when Pilate sat on the tribunal, which John calls about the sixth hour. As he was led away, fastened to the wood with two robbers, and the events narrated took place near his cross, the sixth hour was completed. From that hour until the ninth, while the sun was darkened and darkness came over the earth, the authority of the three evangelists—Matthew, Mark, and Luke—bears witness (Matthew 27:45; Mark 15:33; Luke 23:44).

But because the Jews attempted to transfer the crime of Christ’s killing from themselves to the Romans—that is, to Pilate and his soldiers—Mark, suppressing the hour at which Christ was crucified by the soldiers, which had already begun to be the sixth hour, instead recalled and expressly recorded the third hour. At that hour they are understood to have been able to cry out before Pilate, “Crucify, crucify him” (John 19:6). Thus not only are those found to have crucified Jesus who hung him on the wood at the sixth hour, namely the soldiers, but also the Jews, who cried out at the third hour that he should be crucified.

2. There is another solution to this question: that the sixth hour here should not be understood as the sixth hour of the day. For John does not say, “It was about the sixth hour of the day,” or simply, “about the sixth hour”; rather, he says, “It was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour” (John 19:14).

“Preparation” is the Latin meaning of the Greek word *parasceve*. But the Jews more readily use this Greek word in such observances, even those who speak Latin more than Greek.

It was therefore the Preparation of the Passover. Our Passover, as the Apostle says, is Christ sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7). If we reckon the preparation for this Passover from the ninth hour of the night—for it was then, apparently, that the chief priests pronounced the Lord worthy of death, saying, “He is deserving of death” (Matthew 26:66), while he was still being heard in the high priest’s house—we may appropriately understand the preparation of the true Passover to have begun from that point. The Passover of the Jews was its shadow: the preparation, namely, for Christ’s sacrifice, beginning from the moment when the priests pronounced that he should be sacrificed.

From that hour of the night, which is conjectured then to have been the ninth, until the third hour of the day, when the evangelist Mark testifies that Christ was crucified, there are six hours: three of night and three of day.

Thus, in this Preparation of the Passover—that is, in the preparation for Christ’s sacrifice, which had begun at the ninth hour of the night—it was about the sixth hour. In other words, the fifth hour had been completed and the sixth had begun to run when Pilate ascended the tribunal. For the same preparation, which had begun at the ninth hour of the night, was still continuing until the sacrifice of Christ that was being prepared took place.

That sacrifice occurred, according to Mark, at the third hour—not the third hour of the preparation, but of the day. It was the same sixth hour, not of the day but of the preparation, the six hours being reckoned from the ninth hour of the night to the third hour of the day.

Of these two solutions to this difficult question, let each person choose whichever he wishes. But the better choice will be judged by the one who has read what has been discussed at great length concerning the Harmony of the Evangelists (Book 3 of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*, chapter 13, §§40–50). And if other solutions to it can also be found, the stability of evangelical truth will be defended even more fully against the accusations of faithless and impious folly.

Now let us return to the narrative of the evangelist John after this brief treatment.

3. “They took Jesus,” he says, “and led him away. And bearing his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him.”

Jesus therefore went to the place where he was to be crucified, carrying his own cross.

A great spectacle: but if impiety looks upon it, a great mockery; if piety, a great mystery. If impiety looks upon it, a great proof of disgrace; if piety, a great foundation of faith. If impiety looks upon it, it laughs at the king carrying the wood of his punishment in place of a royal scepter; if piety, it sees the King carrying the wood on which he was to be fastened, and which he was also going to fix upon the foreheads of kings.

He was to be despised by the eyes of the impious in the very thing in which the hearts of the saints would glory. For when Paul was going to say, “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14), Christ, carrying his own cross upon his shoulder, was commending that very cross. He was carrying the lamp that was to burn and was not to be placed under a bushel, but upon a lampstand (Matthew 5:15).

“Bearing his own cross, he went out to the place called the Place of the Skull, in Hebrew Golgotha, where they crucified him; and with him two others, one on either side, and Jesus in the middle.”

These two were robbers, as we learn from the accounts of the other evangelists, with whom Christ was crucified and between whom he was fastened (Matthew 27:38; Mark 15:27; Luke 23:33). Concerning this the preceding prophecy had said: “He was numbered among the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12).

4. “Pilate also wrote an inscription and placed it upon the cross. It was written: Jesus the Nazarene, King of the Jews. Many of the Jews therefore read this inscription, because the place where Jesus was crucified was near the city. And it was written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin: King of the Jews.”

These three languages were prominent there above the others: Hebrew, on account of the Jews who gloried in the Law of God; Greek, on account of the learned among the Gentiles; and Latin, on account of the Romans, who already at that time ruled over many, indeed almost all, nations.

5. The chief priests of the Jews therefore said to Pilate: “Do not write, ‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am king of the Jews.’”

Pilate answered: “What I have written, I have written.”

O ineffable power of divine action, even in the hearts of those who were ignorant! Was not some hidden voice sounding inwardly in Pilate, in a certain—if one may put it so—loud silence, what had been prophesied so long before in the words of the Psalms: “Do not corrupt the inscription of the title” (title of Psalms 56 and 57)?

Behold, he does not corrupt the inscription of the title; what he has written, he has written.

But what did the chief priests, who wished this to be corrupted, say? “Do not write,” they said, “‘King of the Jews,’ but that he himself said, ‘I am king of the Jews.’”

What are you saying, madmen? What are you opposing being done, when you cannot change it in any way? Will it not be true because Jesus said, “I am king of the Jews”? If what Pilate wrote cannot be corrupted, can what the truth said be corrupted?

But is Christ king only of the Jews, or also of the Gentiles? Indeed, also of the Gentiles. For when he had said in prophecy, “Yet I have been established as king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain,” proclaiming the commandment of the Lord, lest anyone say that he had been established king on account of Mount Zion for the Jews alone, he immediately added:

> “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:6–8).

Therefore he himself, now speaking through his own mouth among the Jews, says: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold. I must bring them also, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

Why, then, should we wish to understand a great sacrament in this title, in which it was written, “King of the Jews,” if Christ is also king of the Gentiles? Because the wild olive became a participant in the richness of the olive tree; the olive tree did not become a participant in the bitterness of the wild olive (Romans 11:17).

For in the fact that the title “King of the Jews” was truthfully written concerning Christ, who are to be understood as the Jews except the seed of Abraham, the children of promise, who are also the children of God? For, as the Apostle says, “Not the children of the flesh are the children of God, but the children of promise are counted as seed” (Romans 9:7–8).

And it was to Gentiles that he said: “If you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to the promise” (Galatians 3:29).

Christ is therefore king of the Jews—but of Jews by circumcision of the heart, in spirit and not in letter, whose praise is not from human beings but from God (Romans 2:29). They belong to Jerusalem, our free mother, eternal in the heavens—the spiritual Sarah, who casts out the slave woman and her children from the house of freedom (Galatians 4:22–31). For this reason Pilate wrote what he wrote, because the Lord said what he said.

# TRACTATE CXVIII

On the words: “When the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments,” and so forth. Chapter 19, verses 23–24.

1. Let us treat, insofar as he enables us, what took place near the Lord’s cross after he had already been crucified.

“Therefore, when the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and the tunic. Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout. They therefore said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be.’ Thus the Scripture might be fulfilled which says: ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and for my clothing they cast lots.’”

What the Jews wanted was done: not by the Jews themselves, but by the soldiers who obeyed Pilate when he judged, Jesus was crucified. Yet if we consider their intentions, their plots, their efforts, their betrayal, and finally their clamorous demands, then the Jews certainly crucified Jesus more truly.

2. But the division and casting of lots for his garments must not be passed over without discussion. Although all four evangelists remember this event, the others speak more briefly than John, while John speaks more fully and explicitly.

Matthew says: “After they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots” (Matthew 27:35).

Mark says: “And when they had crucified him, they divided his garments, casting lots over them, who should take what” (Mark 15:24).

Luke says: “And dividing his garments, they cast lots” (Luke 23:34).

But John also stated how many parts they made of his garments—namely, four—so that they might take one each. From this it appears that there were four soldiers who obeyed the governor in crucifying him.
