For he plainly says: “Therefore, when the soldiers had crucified him, they took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier, and the tunic.” The words “they took” must be supplied again, so that the sense is: “They took his garments and made four parts, a part for each soldier; and they also took the tunic.”

He spoke in such a way that we understand no lot to have been cast for the other garments, but for the tunic, which they took together with the others but did not divide in the same way.

Explaining this, he continues: “Now the tunic was seamless, woven from the top throughout.” And when he recounts why they cast lots for it, he says: “They therefore said to one another: ‘Let us not tear it, but let us cast lots for it, whose it shall be.’”

It is therefore evident that in the other garments they had equal portions, so that there was no need to cast lots. But in the one tunic they could not each have a separate portion unless it were torn, so that they would take its pieces uselessly. To avoid this, they preferred by casting lots that it should come to one of them.

The prophetic testimony also agrees with the evangelist’s account. John immediately adds: “In order that the Scripture might be fulfilled, saying: ‘They divided my garments among themselves, and over my clothing they cast lots.’”

For it does not say, “They cast lots,” but, “They divided”; nor does it say, “Casting lots, they divided,” but, without mentioning any lot at all in the other garments, it afterward says, “And over my clothing they cast lots,” on account of that remaining tunic.

Concerning this I shall say what he himself grants, after first dispelling the objection that might arise—as though the evangelists disagreed with one another—and demonstrating that the words of none of the others are contrary to John’s account.

3. For Matthew, by saying, “They divided his garments, casting lots,” intended the tunic also to be understood as belonging to the total division of the garments, since, in dividing all the clothing—including that tunic—they necessarily cast lots for it. Luke likewise says, “Dividing his garments, they cast lots”: in dividing, they came to the tunic for which the lot was cast, so that the entire division of his garments among them might be completed. What difference is there, then, whether one says, “Dividing, they cast lots,” as Luke says, or “They divided, casting lots,” as Matthew says—except that Luke, by saying “lots” in the plural, used the plural number for the singular? Such usage is not unfamiliar in the Holy Scriptures, although some manuscripts are found to read “the lot” rather than “lots.”

[Note: [Col. 1948] Thus today in the Greek, *klēron*.]

Mark alone, therefore, appears to introduce some difficulty. For by saying, “Casting a lot over them, to determine who should take what,” he seems to have spoken as though the lot had been cast over all the garments, not over the tunic alone. But here too brevity produces obscurity. For it is said, “Casting a lot over them,” as though it had been said, “Casting a lot while they were being divided”—and this is what happened. The division of all his garments would not have been completed unless the lot had made clear who was also to take that tunic, so that the contention of those dividing them might be ended, or rather might never arise.

Therefore, when he says, “Who should take what”—since this was assigned to the lot—it should not be referred to all the garments that were divided. The lot was cast to determine who should take that tunic. Since he omitted to relate what kind of tunic it was and how, after the garments had been divided into equal shares, it alone remained, so that it might come by lot rather than be torn apart, he therefore added the words, “Who should take what,” that is, “who should take it”—as if the whole passage were expressed in this way:

[Col. 1949] “They divided his garments, casting a lot over them to determine who should take the tunic that had remained after the shares had been made equal.”

4. Perhaps someone may ask what is signified by the division of the garments into so many parts and by the casting of lots for that tunic. The fourfold garment of the Lord Jesus Christ prefigured his fourfold Church, spread throughout the entire world—which consists, of course, of four parts—and distributed equally, that is, harmoniously, among all those parts. Therefore elsewhere he says that he will send his angels to gather his elect from the four winds (Matthew 24:31). What does this mean except from the four regions of the world: east, west, north, and south?

But that tunic for which the lot was cast signifies the unity of all the parts, held together by the bond of love. Speaking of love, the Apostle says, “I show you a still more excellent way” (1 Corinthians 12:31); and in another place, “To know also the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge” (Ephesians 3:19); and again elsewhere, “Above all these things, love, which is the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3:14). If, then, love has a more excellent way, surpasses knowledge, and is commanded above all things, it is rightly said that the garment signifying it was “woven from above.”

It was seamless so that it might never be undone; and it came to one person because it gathers all into one. Thus, among the Apostles, although their number was also twelve—that is, four groups of three—and all had been questioned, Peter alone answered, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” And he is told, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:15–16, 19), as though he alone had received the power of binding and loosing. Yet he said the former on behalf of all, and received the latter with all the others, representing the unity itself: one on behalf of all because unity exists in all.

Accordingly, here too, after saying “woven from above,” he added, “throughout.” If we refer this to what it signifies, no one is excluded from it who is found to belong to the whole. From this whole, as the Greek language indicates, the Church is called *catholic*.

[Note: [Col. 1949] Greek *holon*, “the whole.”]

And what is commended by the lot except the grace of God? In this way it comes to all in one, when the lot pleased everyone, because the grace of God likewise comes to all in unity. And when the lot is cast, the decision is entrusted not to the person or merits of any individual, but to the hidden judgment of God.

5. No one should therefore say that this signified nothing good because it was done by evil men—not by those who followed Christ, but by those who persecuted him. What, then, shall we say about the cross itself, which was likewise made and inflicted on Christ by enemies and wicked men? Yet it is rightly understood to signify what the Apostle says: “What is the breadth, and length, and height, and depth” (Ephesians 3:18).

It is broad in the transverse beam, where the hands of the one hanging are extended; and it signifies good works in the breadth of love. It is long from the transverse beam down to the earth, where the back and feet are fastened; and it signifies perseverance through the length of time, even to the end. It is high in the upper projection, where the transverse beam extends upward; and it signifies the heavenly end to which all works are directed, since all that is done well and perseveringly in breadth and length must be done for the sake of the height of divine rewards. It is deep in the part fixed into the earth; for there it is hidden and cannot be seen, while all its visible and elevated features rise from it—just as all our good works proceed from the depth of God’s grace, which cannot be comprehended or judged.

But even if the cross of Christ signifies only what the Apostle says—“Those who belong to Jesus Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires” (Galatians 5:24)—what a great good that is! Yet this is done only when the good spirit desires what is against the flesh, although it was the enemy, that is, the evil spirit, who made Christ’s cross.

Finally, what is the sign of Christ, known to everyone, except the cross of Christ? If that sign is not applied either to the foreheads of believers, or to the water in which they are regenerated, or to the oil with which they are anointed in chrism, or to the sacrifice by which they are nourished, none of these is rightly performed. How, then, can nothing good be signified through what the wicked do, when through Christ’s cross—which the wicked made—every good thing is signified to us in the celebration of his sacraments?

But enough of this. What follows we shall examine in another place, as God grants us aid.

# TREATISE 119

From the passage, “And the soldiers indeed did these things,” up to the passage, “And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.” Chapter 19:24–30.

1. After the Lord had been crucified and the division of his garments, including the casting of the lot, had been completed, let us see what the Evangelist John next relates.

“And the soldiers indeed,” he says, “did these things. Standing near the cross of Jesus were his mother, and his mother’s sister, Mary of Clopas, and Mary Magdalene. When Jesus therefore saw his mother and the disciple standing whom he loved, he said to his mother, ‘Woman, behold, your son.’ Then he said to the disciple, ‘Behold, your mother.’ And from that hour the disciple took her into his own household.”

This surely is that hour of which Jesus had spoken to his mother when he was about to turn water into wine: “What is there between me and you, woman? My hour has not yet come” (John 2:4). He had foretold this hour, which had not yet come then: the hour in which, while dying, he would acknowledge the woman from whom he had been born as a mortal.

At that time, when he was about to perform divine works, he rejected as though unknown the mother not of his divinity but of his weakness. Now, however, while suffering human things, he commended her with human affection—the one through whom he had been made human. Then the one who had created Mary was making himself known by his power; now what Mary had borne was hanging on the cross.

[Note: [Col. 1950] See above, Treatise 8.]

2. A moral lesson is therefore being conveyed. He does what he urges others to do, and by his example the good teacher instructed his followers that dutiful care should be provided by children for their parents—as though the wood on which the limbs of the dying man were fixed had also been the chair of the teacher instructing them.

From this sound teaching the Apostle Paul had learned what he taught when he said: “If anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever” (1 Timothy 5:8). For whom does anyone have more as members of his household than parents for their children, or children for their parents?

The teacher of the saints therefore established an example of this most wholesome commandment in himself, when he provided, not for the woman whom God had created and governed as a servant, but for the mother from whom he had been created as a human being and whom he was leaving, by appointing, in a sense, another son in his place.

For why he did this is indicated by what follows. The Evangelist says, “And from that hour the disciple took her into his own household,” speaking of himself. For he habitually recalled that he was the disciple whom Jesus loved—who certainly loved them all, but loved him above the others and with greater intimacy, so that at the supper he made him recline upon his breast (John 13:23). I believe this was so that, in this manner, he might more profoundly commend the divine excellence of the Gospel that he was to preach through him.

3. But into what household of his own did John receive the Lord’s mother? Surely he was among those who had said to him, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you.” Yet there too he had heard, “Everyone who has left these things for my sake will receive a hundredfold in this age” (Matthew 19:27, 29).

That disciple therefore had a hundred times more than he had left, into which he could receive the mother of the one who had granted those things. But blessed John had received the hundredfold in that fellowship where no one said that anything was his own, but everything was held in common, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles. For the Apostles were “as having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Corinthians 6:10).

How, then, did the disciple and servant of his teacher and Lord receive his mother into his own household, where no one called anything his own? Or should we understand that, since shortly afterward we read in the same book, “All who owned fields or houses sold them and brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the Apostles’ feet; and distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts 4:32–35), what was necessary was distributed to this disciple in such a way that a portion was also assigned there for blessed Mary as his mother? Should we rather understand the words, “From that hour the disciple received her into his own household,” to mean that whatever was necessary for her care belonged to him?

He therefore received her into his household—not estates, which he possessed as no private property, but duties, which he undertook to fulfill through his own stewardship.

4. He then continues:

“After this, Jesus, knowing that all things had been accomplished, so that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, ‘I thirst.’ A vessel full of vinegar had been placed there; and they put a sponge full of vinegar around hyssop and brought it to his mouth. When Jesus had received the vinegar, he said, ‘It is finished.’ And, bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.”

Who can arrange what he does in such a way as this man arranged what he suffered? Yet he was the man who is the mediator between God and human beings—the man of whom it is written, “And he is a man, and who will recognize him?” For the people through whom these things were done did not recognize the man who was God.

A man was visible, while God was hidden. The one who was visible suffered all these things, and the very same one who was hidden arranged them all.

[Col. 1952] He saw, therefore, that all the things that had to occur before he received the vinegar and gave up his spirit had been accomplished. And so that this too might be fulfilled which the Scripture had foretold, “In my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (Psalm 68:22), he said, “I thirst”—as though he were saying, “You have omitted this; give me what you are.”

The Jews themselves were the vinegar, degenerating from the wine of the patriarchs and prophets. And, as though from a full vessel, they had been filled from the iniquity of this world, possessing hearts like a sponge, fraudulent through its cavernous and twisting hiding places.

The hyssop around which they placed the sponge full of vinegar, because it is a humble herb and cleanses the chest, we appropriately understand as signifying Christ’s humility. They surrounded him with it, and thought that they had circumvented him. Hence the words in the psalm: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm 50:9). For we are cleansed by Christ’s humility, because unless he had humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross (Philippians 2:8), his blood would not have been poured out for the remission of sins—that is, for our cleansing.

5. Nor should it trouble anyone how a sponge could have been brought to his mouth when he had been lifted up from the earth on the cross. As we read in the other Evangelists, who supply what John omitted, this was done on a reed (Matthew 27:48; Mark 15:36), so that such a drink might be raised in the sponge to the height of the cross.

The reed signified Scripture, which was being fulfilled by this act. Just as one speaks of a Greek or Latin tongue, or any other tongue, meaning the sound expressed by that tongue, so a letter may be called a reed because it is written with a reed. We very commonly call the sounds signified by human speech “tongues.” But since it is less customary to call Scripture a reed, it is all the more mystically represented by that term.

The impious people were doing these things; the merciful Christ was suffering them. The one who did them did not know what he was doing. But the one who suffered not only knew what was happening and why it was happening; he also himself brought good out of those who were doing evil.

6. When Jesus had therefore received the vinegar, he said, “It is finished.” What else was finished except what prophecy had foretold so long before?

Then, because nothing remained that had still to be done before he died, like one who had power to lay down his life and power to take it up again (John 10:18), after completing everything whose completion he awaited, “bowing his head, he gave up his spirit.”

Who sleeps in such a way whenever he wishes, as Jesus died whenever he wished? Who lays aside his garment whenever he wishes, as he stripped off his flesh whenever he wished? Who departs whenever he wishes in the way he died whenever he wished? How great a power must be hoped for or feared in the Judge, if such power appeared in the one who was dying!

# TREATISE 120

From the passage, “The Jews therefore, because it was the preparation,” and so forth, up to the passage, “For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead.” Chapter 19:31–42, and chapter 20:1–9.

1. After the Lord Jesus, having completed everything that he knew had to be completed before his death, gave up his spirit when he wished, let us see, as the Evangelist relates, what followed.

“The Jews therefore,” he says, “because it was the preparation, so that the bodies might not remain upon the cross on the Sabbath—for that Sabbath was a great day—asked Pilate that their legs might be broken and that they might be taken away.”

It was not the legs that were to be taken away, but those whose legs were broken for this purpose: that they might die and be removed from the wood, lest, hanging on the crosses, they should defile the great festival day by the horror of their continuing torment.

[Note: [Col. 1953] Lov. reads “continuing”; other manuscripts read “daily.”]

2. “The soldiers therefore came, and broke the legs of the first, and of the other who had been crucified with him. But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs. But one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately blood and water came out.”

The Evangelist used a vigilant expression: he did not say, “He struck his side,” or “wounded it,” or anything else, but “opened it,” so that there might somehow be opened there the door of life, from which the sacraments of the Church flowed, without which one does not enter into the life that is true life.

That blood was poured out for the remission of sins. That water makes the saving drink wholesome; it provides both washing and drinking.

This was prefigured when Noah was commanded to make a door in the side of the ark (Genesis 6:16), through which the animals that were not destined to perish in the flood might enter—animals that prefigured the Church. For this reason the first woman was made from the side of the sleeping man (Genesis 2:22), and she was called “life” and “mother of the living” (Genesis 3:20). She signified a great good, before the great evil of transgression.

[Note: [Col. 1953] In three manuscripts, and in Alcuin, after the words “before the great evil of transgression,” there is added: “in the posture of one lying down and sleeping.”]

Here the second Adam slept on the cross, bowing his head, so that from what flowed from the side of the sleeping one a spouse might be formed for him. O death, from which the dead come back to life! What is purer than this blood? What is more healing than this wound?

3. “And the one who saw it,” he says, “has borne witness, and his testimony is true; and he knows that he tells the truth, so that you also may believe.”

He did not say, “so that you also may know,” but “so that you may believe.” The one who saw knows; the one who did not see believes the testimony of the one who saw. Believing belongs more properly to faith than seeing does. For what else is believing except to give one’s faith?

“For these things happened,” he says, “so that the Scripture might be fulfilled: ‘You shall not break a bone of him.’ And again another Scripture says, ‘They shall look upon him whom they pierced.’”

He supplied two testimonies from the Scriptures, one for each of the things he narrated as having occurred. For when he had said, “When they came to Jesus, and saw that he was already dead, they did not break his legs,” the testimony “You shall not break a bone of him” applies to this. That command was given to those who were ordered to celebrate the Passover by sacrificing a sheep under the old Law, which had gone before as a shadow of the Lord’s Passion. Hence “Christ our Passover was sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7). The prophet Isaiah had also foretold concerning him, “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53:7).

Likewise, because he had added, “But one of the soldiers opened his side with a lance,” the other testimony applies: “They shall look upon him whom they pierced,” where Christ was promised as coming in the very flesh in which he was crucified.

[Col. 1954]

4. “After these things Joseph of Arimathea, who was a disciple of Jesus, but secretly because of fear of the Jews, asked Pilate to take away the body of Jesus; and Pilate permitted it. He therefore came and took the body of Jesus. Nicodemus also came, who had first come to Jesus by night, bringing a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds.”

The passage should not be punctuated so that we say, “first bringing a mixture of myrrh,” but rather so that the word “first” belongs to the preceding sense. For Nicodemus had come to Jesus by night at an earlier time, as John himself related in the earlier parts of his Gospel (John 3:1–2). Thus we should understand that Nicodemus came to Jesus not only then, but then for the first time; afterward he came repeatedly, so that by listening he might become a disciple. This is certainly now being disclosed to almost all peoples in the discovery of the body of blessed Stephen.

[Note: [Col. 1954] They date the discovery in which the body of Nicodemus himself was also found to the end of the year 415, relying on the authority of the presbyter Lucian, in a booklet written on this subject.]

They therefore took the body of Jesus and bound it in linen cloths with spices, as is the custom of the Jews in burying. It does not seem to me that the Evangelist wished to say without reason, “as is the custom of the Jews in burying.” Thus, unless I am mistaken, he reminded us that, in such services performed for the dead, the custom of each people should be observed.

5. There was a garden in the place where he was crucified, and in the garden a new tomb in which no one had yet been placed. As no one before him and no one after him was conceived in the womb of the virgin Mary, so no one before him and no one after him was buried in this tomb.

“There therefore, because it was the preparation of the Jews and because the tomb was nearby, they placed Jesus.” He intends us to understand that the burial was hastened, lest evening come, when, because of the preparation—which the Jews more commonly call in Latin among us the *coena pura* (“pure meal”)—it was no longer permitted to do such a thing.

6. “On the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came early, while it was still dark, to the tomb, and saw that the stone had been removed from the tomb.”

The first day of the week is the day that Christian custom now calls the Lord’s Day because of the Lord’s resurrection. Matthew alone among the Evangelists called it the first of the Sabbath (Matthew 28:1).

She therefore ran and came to Simon Peter and to the other disciple whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord from the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.”

Some Greek manuscripts also read, “They have taken my Lord,” which may be understood as spoken with a more ardent affection of love or service. But in the greater number of manuscripts available to us, we did not find this reading.

7. Peter therefore went out, and the other disciple, and they came to the tomb. The two were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and came first to the tomb.

Here we should notice and commend the recapitulation—how the narrative returns to what had been passed over, yet is added as though it followed directly. For after saying, “They came to the tomb,” he returned to explain how they came, and said, “The two were running together,” and so forth.

There he shows that the other disciple, who reached the tomb first, arrived before him. By this other disciple he means himself, but narrates everything as though he were speaking about another.

[Note: [Col. 1955] Erasmus, the Lyons edition, and Venice read: “but narrates everything as though speaking about another, in the manner of Holy Scripture.” The words “in the manner of Holy Scripture” do not appear to belong to the text and are enclosed in brackets in Erasmus, Guillermus, and Lovaniensis. M.]

8. “And when he had stooped down,” he says, “he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and entered the tomb; and he saw the linen cloths lying there, and the napkin that had been around his head, not lying with the linen cloths, but separately rolled up in one place.”

Should we think that these things signify nothing? I would certainly not think so. But we are hastening toward other matters in which we are compelled to linger by the necessity of some question or obscurity. For with regard to these things, which are clear in themselves, it is indeed a delightful exercise to ask what each one may also signify, but it belongs to those who have leisure—which we do not have.

9. Then the other disciple, who had come first to the tomb, also entered. He came first, and entered afterward. This too is surely not without significance, but I have no time for it here.

“And he saw,” he says, “and believed.” Some, paying insufficient attention, think that John believed that Jesus had risen. But what follows does not indicate this. For what does the statement immediately added mean: “For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead”?

He therefore did not believe him to have risen when he did not know that he had to rise. What, then, did he see? What did he believe? Clearly, he saw the tomb empty and believed what the woman had said: that he had been taken away from the tomb.

“For they did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead.” And therefore, when they heard this from the Lord himself, although it was stated most openly, because they were accustomed to hearing parables from him, they did not understand and believed that he was signifying something else.

But let us defer the matters that follow to another discourse.

# TREATISE 121

On the passage, “The disciples therefore went away again to their own homes,” up to the passage, “Blessed are those who have not seen and have believed.” Chapter 20:10–29.

1. Mary Magdalene had announced to the disciples Peter and John that the Lord had been taken from the tomb. When they came, they found only the linen cloths in which the body had been wrapped. What else could they believe except what she had said and what she herself had believed?

“The disciples therefore went away again to their own homes”—that is, to the place where they lived and from which they had run to the tomb.

“But Mary stood outside near the tomb, weeping.” When the men had returned, the weaker sex was held in that same place by a stronger affection. And the eyes that had sought the Lord and had not found him were now filled with tears, grieving more that he had been taken from the tomb than that he had been killed on the wood, since no memory even remained for them of so great a teacher, whose life had been taken away.

This grief therefore kept the woman near the tomb. “As she wept, she stooped down and looked into the tomb.” I do not know why she did this. She surely did not fail to know that the one she sought was no longer there, since she herself had announced that he had been taken away, and they had come to the tomb and had sought the Lord’s body not merely by looking but also by entering, and had not found it.

What, then, does it mean that, while weeping, she stooped down and looked again into the tomb? Was it because she was suffering such excessive grief that she found it difficult to believe what neither her own eyes nor theirs had seen? Or rather, was it brought about in her mind by divine prompting that she should look?

She looked, “and saw two angels in white, sitting one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been placed.” Why was one sitting at the head and the other at the feet? Perhaps because those who are called *angels* in Greek are called *messengers* in Latin, and in this way they signified that the Gospel of Christ was to be proclaimed from head to foot, from beginning to end.

They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “Because they have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.”

The angels were stopping her tears. What else were they announcing in a certain way except future joy? For they said, “Why are you weeping?” as though they were saying, “Do not weep.”

But she, thinking that they had asked because they did not know, disclosed the reasons for her tears. “Because they have taken away,” she said, “my Lord”—calling the lifeless body of her Lord “her Lord,” signifying a part by reference to the whole. Thus we all confess Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, our one Lord, although this is at once the Word, the soul, and the flesh; yet he was crucified and buried with only his flesh buried.

“And I do not know,” she said, “where they have laid him.” This was the chief cause of her grief: she did not know where she should go to console her sorrow. But the hour had now come when joy would succeed the tears—what had in a certain way been announced by the angels when they forbade her to weep.

2. Finally, “when she had said this, she turned back and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her, ‘Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?’ Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, ‘Lord, if you have taken him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him.’ Jesus said to her, ‘Mary.’ She turned and said to him, ‘Rabboni,’ which means ‘Teacher.’”

Let no one accuse the woman because she called the gardener “lord” and Jesus “Teacher.” There she was asking; here she was recognizing. There she honored a human being from whom she was requesting a favor; here she recalled the teacher from whom she was learning to distinguish human and divine things.

She called him “lord” whose servant she was not, so that through him she might reach the Lord whose servant she was. Thus she used “Lord” in one way when she said, “They have taken away my Lord,” and in another when she said, “Lord, if you have taken him away.”

The prophets too called people who were human “lords,” but in another way he is called Lord of whom it is written, “The Lord is his name” (Psalm 67:5).

But how is this woman, who had already turned back to see Jesus when she thought he was the gardener and was certainly speaking with him, said to have turned again in order to say to him, “Rabboni,” unless it is because she had then turned physically and thought him to be what he was not, whereas now, turned in her heart, she recognized what he was?

3. “Jesus said to her, ‘Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father. But go to my brothers and say to them, “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.”’”

There is something in these words that we must examine briefly but attentively. Jesus was teaching faith to the woman who had recognized and called him “Teacher.” When she answered him, that gardener was sowing in her heart, as in his own garden, a mustard seed.

What, then, does “Do not touch me” mean? And as though the reason for this prohibition were being asked, he added, “For I have not yet ascended to my Father.” What does this mean? If he cannot be touched while standing on earth, how could human beings touch him seated in heaven?

Yet before he ascended, he offered himself to be touched by the disciples, saying—as the Evangelist Luke testifies—“Touch me and see, for a spirit does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have” (Luke 24:39). Or consider when he said to the disciple Thomas, “Put your finger here and see my hands, and bring your hand and put it into my side.”

Who could be so absurd as to say that, before ascending to the Father, he wished to be touched by the disciples but did not wish to be touched by women until after he had ascended to the Father? But even someone who wished to speak foolishly would not be permitted to do so.

For we read that women also touched Jesus after the resurrection and before his ascension to the Father. Among them was Mary Magdalene herself. Matthew relates that Jesus met them and said, “Greetings.” “They came,” he says, “and took hold of his feet and worshiped him” (Matthew 28:9). John omitted this, but Matthew truly reported it.

It remains, therefore, that some sacramental meaning lies hidden in these words. Whether we discover it or are entirely unable to discover it, we must nevertheless have no doubt that one is present.

Either, then, the words “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to my Father” were spoken so that in this woman the Church from the Gentiles might be represented—the Church that did not believe in Christ until he had ascended to the Father—or Jesus wished to be believed in this way: spiritually touched as the one who is one with the Father.

He rises, in a certain sense, to the Father in the deepest perceptions of the person who progresses in him so as to recognize him as equal to the Father. In no other way is he rightly touched—that is, in no other way is he rightly believed in.

Mary could have believed in such a way as to think him inferior to the Father. This is forbidden when he says to her, “Do not touch me”—that is, “Do not believe in me in the way you still understand; do not extend your understanding only as far as what I became for you, without passing on to that through which you were made.”

For how could she not yet believe in him in a carnal manner, when she was weeping for him as a human being?

“For I have not yet ascended,” he says, “to my Father.” You will touch me there, when you have believed that, as God, I am not inferior to the Father.

“But go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father.’” He did not say, “Our Father.” Thus he is my Father in one way and your Father in another: mine by nature, yours by grace.

“And to my God and your God.” Here too he did not say, “Our God.” Therefore here also he is my God in one way and your God in another: my God, under whom I too am human; your God, among whom I am also mediator.

4. “Mary Magdalene came announcing to the disciples, ‘I have seen the Lord,’ and that he had said these things to her.

“When it was evening on that day, the first day of the week, and the doors were shut where the disciples were gathered because of fear of the Jews, Jesus came and stood in the midst and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’ And when he had said this, he showed them his hands and his side.”

Nails had fastened his hands, and a lance had opened his side. The traces of the wounds were preserved there to heal the hearts of those who doubted.

But the mass of the body in which the divinity was present was not hindered by closed doors. For he was able to enter without the doors being opened, just as, when he was born, the virginity of his mother remained inviolate.

The disciples therefore rejoiced when they saw the Lord. He said to them again, “Peace be with you.” The repetition confirms the promise. He himself gives, through the prophet, the promised “peace upon peace” (Isaiah 26:3).

“As the Father sent me,” he says, “so I send you.” We know the Son to be equal to the Father, but here we recognize the words of the Mediator. He shows himself to be in the middle when he says, “He sent me, and I send you.”

When he had said this, he breathed on them and said to them, “Receive the Holy Spirit.” By breathing on them he signified that the Holy Spirit is not the Spirit of the Father alone, but also his own.

“Whose sins you forgive,” he says, “they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” The love of the Church, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, forgives the sins of those who share in it; but it retains the sins of those who do not share in it.

Therefore, after saying, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” he immediately added this concerning the remission and retention of sins.

5. Thomas, however, one of the Twelve, who is called Didymus, was not with them when Jesus came. So the other disciples said to him, “We have seen the Lord.” But he said to them, “Unless I see in his hands the mark of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe.” And after eight days his disciples were again inside, and Thomas was with them. Jesus came when the doors were shut, stood in the midst, and said, “Peace be with you.” Then he said to Thomas, “Put your finger here, and see my hands; and bring your hand and put it into my side; and do not be unbelieving, but believing.” Thomas answered and said to him, “My Lord and my God.”

He saw and touched the man, and confessed the God whom he neither saw nor touched; but through what he saw and touched, he already believed that other reality, with his doubt removed. Jesus said to him, “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” He did not say, “Because you have touched me,” but, “Because you have seen me,” since sight is, in a certain sense, the general sense. For the other four senses too are sometimes designated by it, as when we say, “Hear and see how well it sounds; smell and see how fragrant it is; taste and see how good it tastes; touch and see how warm it is.” Everywhere “see” is used, although sight properly pertains to the eyes. Hence here too the Lord himself says, “Put your finger here, and see my hands”: what else does he say than, “Touch and see”? Yet he did not have eyes in his finger. Therefore, whether by looking or even by touching, he says, “Because you have seen me, you have believed.” Although it may be said that the disciple did not dare to touch him when he offered himself to be touched—for it is not written, “And Thomas touched”—nevertheless, whether he saw and believed merely by looking, or also by touching, what follows proclaims and commends the faith of the nations even more: “Blessed are those who have not seen, and have believed.” He used the verbs in the past tense, as though the one who knew what was still future in his predestination already regarded it as accomplished.

But this discourse must now be restrained from further length. May the Lord grant that we discuss the remaining matters on another occasion.

# TRACTATE CXXII

On the passage that follows, “Jesus indeed did many other signs,” through “And although they were so many, the net was not torn.” Chapter XX, verses 30–31, and chapter XXI, verses 1–11.

## 1

After the account of the event in which the disciple Thomas, when the places of Christ’s wounds were offered to him for touching in the flesh, saw what he had been unwilling to believe and believed it, the evangelist John inserts these words and says:

“Jesus indeed did many other signs in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book. But these have been written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God; and so that, believing, you may have life in his name.”

This passage seems to indicate the end of this book. Yet afterward there is an account of how the Lord manifested himself at the Sea of Tiberias and, in the catching of fish, commended the sacrament of the Church—what it will be at the final resurrection of the dead [Note: [Col. 1959] Er., Lugd., and Ven. read “the resurrection of the dead.” M.].

I therefore think that, for the purpose of commending this matter, the passage has been placed as though it were the end of the book, while also serving as a kind of prologue to the narrative that follows and giving it, in a certain way, a more prominent position. That narrative begins as follows:

“After this Jesus manifested himself again at the Sea of Tiberias; and he manifested himself in this way: Simon Peter and Thomas, who is called Didymus, and Nathanael, who was from Cana of Galilee, and the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together. Simon Peter said to them, ‘I am going fishing.’ They said to him, ‘We are coming with you.’”

## 2

People commonly ask about this fishing expedition of the disciples: why did Peter and the sons of Zebedee return to what they had been before they were called by the Lord? For they were fishermen when he said to them, “Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men” (Matt. 4:19).

At that time they followed him so that, leaving everything behind, they might adhere to his teaching. Thus, when that rich man went away sorrowful, to whom he had said, “Go, sell what you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; and come, follow me,” Peter said to him, “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (ibid. 19:21, 22, 27).

What, then, does it mean that now, as though they had abandoned the apostolate, they become what they had been and take up again what they had left behind, as though they had forgotten what they had heard: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1960] (Luke 9:62)?

If they had done this after Jesus’ death, before he had risen from the dead—which indeed they could not have done, since the day on which he was crucified held all their attention until his burial, which took place before evening; and the following day was the Sabbath, when, observing their ancestral custom, they were not permitted to work—then, on the third day, the Lord rose and recalled them to the hope which they had already begun to lose in him. Even so, if they had acted then, we might have thought that they had done so out of the despair that had occupied their hearts.

But now, after he had been returned alive to them from the tomb; after he had offered to their eyes and hands the unmistakable reality of his risen flesh, not merely to be seen but also to be touched and handled; after they had examined the places of the wounds, even to the confession of the apostle Thomas, who had declared that he would not otherwise believe; after receiving the Holy Spirit through his breathing upon them; after hearing words spoken by his mouth into their ears—“As the Father sent me, I also send you. Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them, and whose sins you retain are retained” (John 20:21–23)—they suddenly become what they had been: not fishers of human beings, but fishers of fish.

## 3

To those whom this troubles we must answer that they were not forbidden, while preserving the integrity of their apostolate, to seek the necessities of life through their trade, which was lawful and permitted, if at some time they had no other means of subsistence.

Unless, perhaps, someone will dare to think or say that the apostle Paul did not belong to the perfection of those who left everything and followed Christ, because, so as not to burden any of those to whom he preached the Gospel, he supported himself by the work of his own hands (2 Thess. 3:8). In this he more fully fulfilled what he says: “I labored more than all of them”; and he added, “Yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (1 Cor. 15:10).

Thus it is also shown that this too must be attributed to God’s grace: that he was able, in soul and body, to labor so much more than all the others that he neither ceased preaching the Gospel nor, like them, supported this life from the Gospel, even though he sowed it among so many nations where the name of Christ had not been foretold [Note: [Col. 1960] Lov. reads “spread abroad.” But Am., Bad., and the manuscripts read “foretold”]—and sowed it much more widely and fruitfully.

There he showed that living from the Gospel, that is, obtaining one’s sustenance from it, was not imposed upon the apostles as an obligation but granted to them as a right. The same apostle recalls this right when he says:

“If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things? If others share in your right, do we not even more? But,” he says, “we have not used this right.”

And a little later:

“Those who serve at the altar share in the altar; so also the Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live from the Gospel. But I have used none of these things.”

It is therefore sufficiently clear that the apostles were not commanded, but were given the authority, to live only from the Gospel and to reap material things from those among whom, by preaching the Gospel, they sowed spiritual things—that is, to receive the support of this bodily life and, like soldiers of Christ, the pay owed to them [Col. 1961], just as Christ’s soldiers received it from the provinces [Note: [Col. 1961] Soldiers therefore received their pay from the provinces. This seems to refer to the passage above, Tractate 13, no. 17: “For sometimes even a deserter frightens a provincial; but whether he is in the camp and is of some benefit to him, the one who does not wish to be frightened and deceived considers this: the character with which he has been marked.”].

A little earlier, therefore, that same distinguished soldier had said concerning this matter: “Whoever serves as a soldier at his own expense?” (1 Cor. 9:7, 11–15).

Yet Paul himself did this because he labored more than all the others. If blessed Paul, in order not to use with the others the right that he certainly possessed along with the other preachers of the Gospel, but to serve as a soldier at his own expense, learned a trade that he had not known, so that while the teacher supported himself by his own hands no listener would be burdened—lest his teaching offend nations utterly alien to the name of Christ, as though it were being sold—how much more did blessed Peter, who had already been a fisherman, do what he knew, if at that particular time he found no other means by which to live?

## 4

Someone may reply: Why did he not find another means, when the Lord had promised, saying, “Seek first the kingdom and the righteousness of God, and all these things will be added to you” (Matt. 6:33)?

Indeed, in this way too the Lord fulfilled what he had promised. For who else supplied fish to be caught? We must believe that he brought them into their poverty for no other reason than that, by compelling them to go fishing, he wished to display a miracle that had been arranged in advance: so that he might both feed the preachers of his Gospel and enhance the Gospel itself through the great sacrament that was to be commended by the number of the fish.

We must now also speak of what he himself supplied in this matter.

## 5

So Simon Peter says, “I am going fishing.” Those who were with him say, “We are coming with you.” And they went out and got into the boat; and that night they caught nothing.

When morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore; yet the disciples did not recognize that it was Jesus. Jesus therefore said to them, “Children, do you have anything to eat?” They answered him, “No.” He said to them, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.” So they cast it, and now they were unable to haul it in because of the multitude of fish.

The disciple whom Jesus loved therefore said to Peter, “It is the Lord.” When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he girded his tunic around himself—for he was naked—and threw himself into the sea. But the other disciples came in the boat, for they were not far from land, about two hundred cubits, dragging the net of fish.

When they had come ashore, they saw burning coals laid out, and a fish placed upon them, and bread. Jesus said to them, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught.” Simon Peter went up and dragged the net ashore, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three. And although there were so many, the net was not torn.

## 6

This is a great sacrament in the great Gospel of John; and, so that it might be commended more forcefully, it was written at the very end.

The fact that seven disciples were present at this fishing—Peter, Thomas, Nathanael, the two sons of Zebedee, and two others whose names are not given—signifies by that number seven the end of time. For all time revolves through seven days.

To this also belongs the fact that, when morning had come, Jesus stood on the shore [Col. 1962], because the shore is also the end of the sea and therefore signifies the end of the age. The same end of the age is shown by the fact that Peter hauled the net onto land, that is, onto the shore.

The Lord himself disclosed this when, elsewhere, he gave a likeness drawn from a net cast into the sea: “They drag it,” he says, “onto the shore.” Explaining what the shore meant, he said, “So it will be at the consummation of the age” (Matt. 13:48–49).

## 7

But that is a parable in words, not an event that actually occurred. In the actual event, as this passage indicates how things will be at the end of the age, the Lord signified through another fishing what the Church is like now.

The fact that he performed the first fishing at the beginning of his preaching and this one after his resurrection shows that the former catch signifies the good and the wicked whom the Church now contains, whereas this one signifies only the good whom it will possess forever, once the resurrection of the dead has been completed at the end of this age.

Finally, in the former event Jesus did not stand on the shore as he does here when he ordered the fish to be caught. Instead, he boarded one boat, which was Simon’s, and asked him to move out a little from the land; then, sitting in it, he taught the crowds. When he had finished speaking, he said to Simon, “Put out into the deep and let down your nets for a catch.” There the catch of fish was in the little boats, not, as here, hauled ashore.

Through these signs, and through any others that may be found, the Church is represented there as it is in this age, but here as it will be at the end of the age. That is why the former event occurred before the Lord’s resurrection, and this one afterward: there Christ signified us as called, here as raised from the dead.

There the nets were not cast on the right side, lest they signify only the good, nor on the left, lest they signify only the wicked. Rather, he said without distinction, “Let down your nets for a catch,” so that we might understand the good and the wicked mixed together. Here, however, he says, “Cast the net on the right side of the boat,” to signify those who will stand at the right hand, the good alone.

There the net was torn in order to signify schisms. Here, however, because at that time there will be no schisms in the supreme peace of the saints, the evangelist appropriately says, “And although there were so many—that is, so large a number—the net was not torn,” as though he were looking back to the place where it was torn and commending this good in contrast with that evil.

There the catch contained so many fish that the two boats were filled and began to sink (Luke 5:3–7), that is, they were pressed down toward submersion; for they did not actually sink, but they were endangered. From what else do the many things arise that we lament in the Church, unless it is that the immense multitude cannot be resisted, when it enters to all but submerge discipline with customs utterly alien to the path of the saints?

Here, however, they cast the net on the right side, and now they were unable to haul it in because of the multitude of fish. What does “they were unable to haul it in” mean except that those who belong to the resurrection of life—that is, to the right hand—and who die within the nets of the Christian name, will appear only on the shore, that is, at the end of the age, when they have risen?

For this reason they were unable to haul the nets in such a way as to place in the boat the fish they had caught, as happened with all those for whom the net was torn and the boats were weighed down.

The Church has these people of the right hand, after the end of this life, in the sleep of peace [Col. 1963], as though lying hidden in the deep, until the net that was being dragged reaches the shore, as if after two hundred cubits.

What was represented there by the two little boats, on account of circumcision and uncircumcision, I think is represented here by the two hundred cubits, on account of the elect of both kinds, of circumcision and uncircumcision, as one hundred and one hundred; for, in its totality, the number one hundred passes to the right hand.

Finally, in that fishing the number of fish is not stated, as though what had been foretold through the prophet were fulfilled there: “I have proclaimed and spoken; they have been multiplied beyond number” (Ps. 39:6). Here, however, there are none beyond the number, but the number is definite: one hundred and fifty-three. The meaning of this number must be explained with the Lord’s help.

## 8

For if we establish a number that signifies the Law, what number will it be except ten? We know with complete certainty that the Decalogue of the Law—that is, those ten most famous commandments—was first written by the finger of God on two stone tablets (Deut. 9:10).

But when the Law is not aided by grace, it makes transgressors, and exists only in the letter. For this reason the apostle says most emphatically, “The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life” (2 Cor. 3:6).

Let the Spirit therefore be added to the letter, lest the letter kill one whom the Spirit does not make alive; but let us fulfill the commandments of the Law not by our own strength but through the gift of the Savior.

When grace is added to the Law—that is, when the Spirit is added to the letter—the number seven is, in a certain way, added to the number ten. The testimonies of the sacred Scriptures that must be considered show that the Holy Spirit is signified by this number, seven.

Holiness, or sanctification, properly belongs to the Holy Spirit. Thus, although the Father is spirit and the Son is spirit, since “God is spirit” (John 4:24), and although the Father is holy and the Son is holy, nevertheless the Spirit of both is called the Holy Spirit by his proper name.

Where, then, did sanctification first resound in the Law, if not on the seventh day? God did not sanctify the first day, on which he made light; nor the second, on which he made the firmament; nor the third, on which he separated the sea from the land, and the land produced grass and trees; nor the fourth, on which the stars were created; nor the fifth, on which he made the animals that live in the waters and fly through the air; nor the sixth, on which he made the living creature of the earth and the human being. Rather, he sanctified the seventh day, on which he rested from his works (Gen. 1 and 2:3).

The Holy Spirit is therefore appropriately signified by the number seven.

The prophet Isaiah also says, “The Spirit of God will rest upon him”; and then, commending him through a sevenfold operation or gift, he says, “the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety, and the spirit of the fear of God will fill him” (Isa. 11:2–3).

What of the Apocalypse? Are not seven spirits of God mentioned (Rev. 3:1), although there is one and the same Spirit, distributing his own gifts to each as he wills (1 Cor. 12:11)? But the sevenfold operation of the one Spirit was called this by the same Spirit, who was present with the writer, so that seven spirits might be spoken of.

When, therefore, the Holy Spirit is added to the ten of the Law through the number seven, the result is seventeen. This number [Col. 1964], calculated by adding together all the numbers from one through itself, reaches one hundred and fifty-three.

For if you add two to one, the result is three; if to these you add three and four, the total is ten. Then, if you add all the successive numbers up to seventeen, the sum reaches the number mentioned above.

That is, if you add five to ten—the number to which you had arrived by counting from one through four—the result is fifteen. Add six to this, and the result is twenty-one; add seven, and it is twenty-eight; add eight, nine, and ten, and it is fifty-five; add eleven, twelve, and thirteen, and it is ninety-one; add fourteen, fifteen, and sixteen, and it is one hundred and thirty-six. Add to this the number still remaining, the one under discussion—seventeen—and the number of fish is completed.

Therefore not merely one hundred and fifty-three saints who will rise to eternal life are signified, but thousands of saints who belong to the grace of the Spirit. Through this grace the Law of God is reconciled with what seems to be its adversary, so that, when the Spirit gives life, the letter does not kill; rather, what is commanded through the letter is fulfilled with the Spirit’s help, and whatever is lacking is forgiven.

All who belong to this grace are represented by this number; that is, they are figuratively signified by it.

This number also contains three times the number fifty, with three added because of the mystery of the Trinity. The number fifty is completed by multiplying seven by seven and adding one: seven times seven makes forty-nine. One is added to signify that the one who is demonstrated through the number seven on account of the sevenfold operation is one.

And we know that the Holy Spirit was sent on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s ascension; the disciples had been commanded to await the promise (Acts 2:2–4; 1:4).

## 9

The fish, therefore, were not said to be so many and so large without reason—that is, one hundred and fifty-three and large. For it is written:

“And he drew the net onto the land, full of large fish, one hundred and fifty-three.”

When the Lord had said, “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it,” intending to give the Spirit through whom the Law could be fulfilled, as though he were going to add seven to ten, he inserted a few words and said:

“Therefore whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

This person, then, may belong to the number of the large fish.

But that least person who abolishes by his deeds what he teaches in words can exist in the kind of Church signified by that first catch of fish, which contains both good and wicked people, since it too is called the kingdom of heaven. For this reason he says:

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” [Note: [Col. 1964] The printed editions read, “gathering fish of every kind.” The word “fish” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek] (Matt. 13:47).

There he wishes both the good and the wicked to be understood; he says that they will be separated on the shore, that is, at the end of the age.

Finally, to show that these least ones are reprobate—those who teach good things in speech but abolish them by evil living, and who will not be least in eternal life but will not be there at all—after saying, “He will be called least in the kingdom of heaven,” he immediately added:

“For I say to you, unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” [Col. 1965] (Matt. 5:17–20).

The scribes and Pharisees are certainly those who sit on Moses’ seat, concerning whom he says, “Do whatever they tell you; but do not do what they do, for they speak but do not act” (ibid. 23:2–3). They teach in their words what they abolish in their conduct.

It follows, therefore, that the one who is least in the kingdom of heaven—as the Church is now—will not enter the kingdom of heaven as the Church will then be. Since he teaches what he abolishes, he will not belong to the company of those who do what they teach. Thus he will not be among the large fish, since “whoever does and teaches will be called great in the kingdom of heaven.”

And because this person will be great, he will be there, where that least one will not be. Indeed, the great will be so great there that the one who is least there will be greater than the one greater than whom no one is here (ibid. 11:11).

Nevertheless, those who are great here—that is, those who, in the kingdom of heaven where the net gathers the good and the wicked, do the good things they teach—will themselves be greater in that eternal kingdom of heaven. These are represented by the fish that belong to the right hand and to the resurrection of life.

What follows concerns the Lord’s meal with these seven disciples, what he said after the meal, and the conclusion of the Gospel itself. May we discuss these matters as God grants; but this discourse must not be extended any further.

# TRACTATE CXXIII

On what Jesus says, “Come, dine,” through “But he said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God.” Chapter XXI, verses 12–19.

## 1

With the third manifestation of the Lord to his disciples after his resurrection, the Gospel of the blessed apostle John comes to an end. We have now treated, as best we could, the earlier part of it, up to the passage where it was narrated that the disciples to whom he showed himself caught one hundred and fifty-three fish, and that, although they were large, the nets were not torn.

The passages that follow must now be considered and, with the Lord’s help, discussed as the matter requires.

After that fishing had been completed, Jesus says to them, “Come, dine.” And none of those reclining at table dared ask him, “Who are you?” because they knew that it was the Lord.

If they knew, then what need was there for them to ask? But if there was no need, why does the text say that they did not dare, as though there were a need but that some fear prevented them from daring?

The meaning, therefore, is this: such was the evidence of the truth with which Jesus appeared to those disciples that no one dared either to deny or even to doubt that he was the Lord; for if anyone had doubted, he ought certainly to have asked.

Thus it is said, “No one dared ask him, ‘Who are you?’” as though it had been said, “No one dared doubt that it was he.”

## 2

“And Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise.”

Behold, it has also been stated what they ate for their meal. We too shall say something pleasant and wholesome about that meal, if he feeds us as well.

It was narrated above that when these disciples came down onto the land, they saw burning coals laid out, and a fish placed upon them, and bread. It should not be understood that the bread too had been placed upon the coals; rather, the verb “they saw” must be understood as applying to it as well.

If we repeat that verb where it must be understood, the whole sentence can be expressed as follows: “They saw burning coals laid out, and a fish placed upon them, and they saw bread.” Or, better: “They saw burning coals laid out and a fish placed upon them; they also saw bread.”

At the Lord’s command they also brought some of the fish that they themselves had caught. Although the narrator did not explicitly state that they did so, he did not fail to state that the Lord commanded it. For he says, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught” (John 21:9–10). Who could believe that they did not do what he commanded?

The Lord therefore prepared a meal for those seven disciples from the fish that they had seen placed upon the coals, adding to it some of those they had caught, and also bread, which they are likewise said to have seen.

The roasted fish is Christ who suffered. He is also the bread that came down from heaven (ibid. 6:41). The Church is incorporated into him in order to share in everlasting blessedness.

For this reason it was said, “Bring some of the fish that you have just caught,” so that all of us who hold this hope, represented by that number seven of the disciples through which our universal fellowship can be understood in this passage, might know that we share in so great a sacrament and are joined to the same blessedness.

This is the Lord’s meal with his disciples, with which John concludes his Gospel, although he had many other great things concerning Christ to say, as I think, after contemplating realities of such magnitude.

Here the Church as it will exist among the good alone is signified by the catch of one hundred and fifty-three fish; and, through this meal, participation in so great a blessedness is demonstrated to those who believe, hope, and love these things.

## 3

“This,” he says, “was now the third time that Jesus manifested himself to his disciples after he had risen from the dead.”

We must refer this not to the manifestations themselves but to the days—that is, the first day, when he rose; after eight days, when the disciple Thomas saw and believed; and today, when he performed this action concerning the fish. The number of days after which he did this is not stated.

For on that very first day he was seen more than once, as the combined testimony of all the evangelists demonstrates. But, as has been said, his manifestations must be counted according to the days, so that this is the third.

The first manifestation must be regarded as the same and as one because it occurred on one day, regardless of how many times and to whom he showed himself on the day on which he rose. The second was after eight days; this is the third; and thereafter he appeared as often as he wished until the fortieth day, when he ascended into heaven, although not all these appearances have been written down.

## 4

“When therefore they had dined, he said to Simon Peter, ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’

“He said to him again, ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me?’ He said to him, ‘Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my lambs.’

“He said to him a third time, ‘Simon, son of John, do you love me?’ Peter was grieved because he said to him a third time, ‘Do you love me?’ And he said to him, ‘Lord, you know all things; you know that I love you.’ He said to him, ‘Feed my sheep.

“‘Amen, amen, I say to you: when you were younger, you girded yourself and walked where you wished; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.’ But he said this, signifying by what death he would glorify God.”

This was the end found by that man who had denied and loved: exalted by presumption, cast down by denial, cleansed by weeping, tested by confession, and crowned through suffering.

This was the end he found: to die in perfect love for his name, with whom he had perversely and hastily promised that he would die.

Strengthened by Christ’s resurrection, let him do what he had rashly promised to do when he was weak. For it was necessary that Christ should first die for Peter’s salvation, and afterward Peter for the preaching of Christ.

The order that truth had established made it perverse for human presumption to attempt what Peter had begun to dare. Peter thought that he would lay down his life for Christ (John 13:37), as one who was to be liberated for the Liberator, when Christ had come to lay down his life for all his own [Note: [Col. 1967] Two manuscripts read, “for his own sheep”], among whom Peter also was included. And behold, this has now happened.

Now, with the Lord himself granting it, let true firmness of heart be assumed for accepting death in the Lord’s name; let it not be falsely presumed by us in our error.

Now is the time not to fear the death of this life, because, with the Lord’s resurrection, an example of the other life has gone before us.

Now, Peter, is the time not to fear death, because the one whose death you mourned is alive, and the one whom, through carnal affection, you tried to prevent from dying for us (Matt. 16:21–22).

You dared to go before your guide; you feared his persecutor. Now that the price has been paid for you, it is time for you to follow the one who bought you—and to follow him all the way to the death of the cross.

You heard the words of the one whom you have now proved truthful; he himself foretold that you would suffer, just as he had foretold that you would deny him.

5. But first the Lord asks what he knew—not once, but twice and a third time—whether Peter loves him; and the Lord hears nothing else so many times from Peter than that he is loved, while he commends nothing else so many times to Peter than the feeding of his sheep. A threefold confession is returned for the threefold denial, so that the tongue may serve love no less than fear, and so that impending death may not seem to have drawn more words from him than present life. Let it be the duty of love to feed the Lord’s flock, just as it was an indication of fear to deny the shepherd.

Those who feed Christ’s sheep with the intention that they should be theirs, not Christ’s, prove that they love themselves, not Christ: they are driven by the desire either for boasting, or for domination, or for acquisition, rather than by the charity of obedience, assistance, and pleasing God. Against such people, therefore, this oft-repeated saying of Christ keeps watch—those whom the Apostle laments as seeking their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ (Philippians 2:21). For what else is “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” than if he had said: “If you love me, do not think of feeding yourself, but my sheep; feed them as mine, not as yours; seek my glory in them, not yours; my authority, not yours; my gains, not yours; so that you may not be among those who belong to the perilous times, lovers of themselves, and the other vices joined to this beginning of evil”?

For when the Apostle had said, “For people will be lovers of themselves,” [Col. 1968] he continued: “Lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, irreligious, without affection, slanderers, incontinent, savage, without kindness, traitors, reckless, blinded, lovers of pleasures rather than of God, having the appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Timothy 3:1–5). All these evils flow, as it were, from that one source: the first thing he mentioned, that they are lovers of themselves.

It is rightly said to Peter, “Do you love me?” and he replies, “I love you”; and he is told, “Feed my lambs.” This is repeated a second and a third time. Here it is also demonstrated that love and affection are one and the same: for at the end the Lord does not say, “Do you feel affection for me?” but, “Do you love me?” Let us therefore love not ourselves but him, and in feeding his sheep let us seek what belongs to him, not what belongs to us.

For in some inexplicable way, whoever loves himself rather than God does not love himself; and whoever loves God rather than himself is the one who loves himself. Whoever cannot live from himself certainly dies by loving himself; therefore he does not love himself who loves himself in order not to live. But when he is loved from whom life is received, the person loves himself more by not loving himself, so that he may love him from whom he lives.

Let those who feed Christ’s sheep therefore not be lovers of themselves, lest they feed them as their own rather than as his. Let them not seek to extract their own gains from them, like lovers of money; nor dominate them, like the boastful; nor glory in the honors they receive from them, like the arrogant; nor advance so far as even to create heresies, like the blasphemers. Let them not resist the holy fathers, like the disobedient to parents; nor repay evil for good to those who wish to correct them because they do not wish them to perish, like the ungrateful. Let them not destroy their own souls and those of others, like the wicked; nor tear apart the maternal entrails of the Church, like the irreligious; nor fail to sympathize with the weak, like those without affection; nor attempt to stain the reputation of the saints, like slanderers; nor fail to restrain their worst desires, like the incontinent; nor engage in quarrels, like the savage; nor know how to offer assistance, like those without kindness; nor disclose to the enemies of the godly what they have learned must be kept secret, like traitors; nor disturb human modesty by shameless provocation, like the reckless; nor understand either what they say or the matters about which they assert things, like the blinded (1 Timothy 1:7); nor prefer carnal pleasures to spiritual joys, like lovers of pleasure rather than of God.

For these and similar vices, whether they all occur in one person or different vices dominate different people, spring in some manner from that root: people being lovers of themselves. This vice must be especially avoided by those who feed Christ’s sheep, lest they seek their own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ, and devote to the uses of their desires those for whom Christ’s blood was shed.

The love of Christ in the one who feeds his sheep must grow into so great a spiritual ardor that it conquers even the natural fear of death—the fear by which we do not wish to die, even when we wish to live with Christ. For the Apostle Paul says that he has the desire to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1:23); yet he groans under his burden and does not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed over, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life (2 Corinthians 5:4).

And to this lover of his, [Col. 1969] the Lord says: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go.” By this he indicated the death by which Peter would glorify God. “You will stretch out your hands,” he says—that is, you will be crucified. But in order that you may reach this point, “another will gird you and lead you,” not where you wish, but where you do not wish.

First he said what would happen, and then how it would happen. For he was led where he did not wish to go, not as one already crucified, but as one who was to be crucified. Once crucified, he did not go where he did not wish, but rather where he did wish. Released from the body, he wished to be with Christ; but, if it could be, he desired eternal life apart from the distress of dying. He was led unwillingly to that distress, but led out of it willingly; unwillingly he came to it, but willingly he conquered it. He retained this weakness of feeling—that no one wishes to die—as something so natural that even old age could not remove it from blessed Peter, to whom it was said, “You will be led where you do not wish.”

For our consolation the Savior himself also represented this feeling in himself, saying, “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matthew 26:39). He had certainly come to die, and he did not have a necessity of death but a will to die, having the power to lay down his life and the power to take it up again. Yet however great the distress of death may be, the force of love by which he is loved who, although he is our life, nevertheless chose to endure death for us must conquer it. For if death had no distress, or only a slight one, the glory of the martyrs would not be so great.

But if the good shepherd, who laid down his life for his sheep (John 10:18, 11), made so many martyrs for himself from those very sheep, how much more ought those to contend for the truth unto death and against sin unto blood to whom he entrusts the sheep themselves to be fed—that is, taught and governed? Accordingly, in view of the example of his preceding passion, who does not see that shepherds ought all the more to cling to the shepherd by imitation, if many sheep also imitated him? Under this one shepherd, in one flock, the shepherds themselves are sheep. For he made all of them his sheep, for all of whom he suffered; indeed, in order to suffer for all, he himself became a sheep.

## TRACTATE 124

From the passage, “And when he had said this, he says to him, ‘Follow me,’” and so forth, to the end of the Gospel (chapter 21, verses 19–25).

### 1

It is no small question why, when the Lord manifested himself to the disciples for the third time, he said to the Apostle Peter, “Follow me,” but concerning the Apostle John, “I wish him to remain until I come; what is that to you?” We devote the final discourse of this work to this question, so far as the Lord himself grants either that it may be discussed or that it may be solved.

After the Lord had foretold by what death Peter would glorify God, he said to him, “Follow me.” Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—the one who also reclined at supper upon his breast and said, “Lord, who is the one who will betray you?” When Peter had seen him, therefore, he said to Jesus, “Lord, but what about this man?” Jesus said to him, “I wish him to remain until I come; what is that to you? You follow me.” [Col. 1970]

Thus this saying went out among the brothers: that that disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say to him, “He will not die,” but, “I wish him to remain until I come; what is that to you?” Behold how far the question extends in this Gospel—a question whose depth exercises the mind of the one examining it to no ordinary degree.

Why, then, is Peter told, “Follow me,” while the others who were present together are not? Certainly the disciples were following him as their teacher. But if this is to be understood with reference to passion, did Peter alone suffer for Christian truth? Was not there among those seven another son of Zebedee, the brother of John, who after the Lord’s ascension was openly put to death by Herod (Acts 12:2)?

Someone might say that because James was not crucified, it was rightly said to Peter, “Follow me,” since he experienced not merely death but death on a cross, as Christ did. Let this be accepted, if nothing more suitable can be found.

Why, then, was it said of John, “I wish him to remain until I come; what is that to you?” and why was it repeated, “You follow me”—as though he would not follow because Christ wished him to remain until he came? Who would readily believe that something other than what the brothers who were then present had understood was said: namely, that this disciple would not die, but would remain alive until Jesus came? Yet John himself removed this opinion, openly declaring that the Lord had not said this.
