Why else would he add, “Jesus did not say, ‘He will not die,’” unless it were to prevent what was false from taking root in human hearts?

### 2

But let anyone who prefers continue to resist and say that what John says is true: that the Lord did not say that this disciple would not die, but that this was nevertheless signified by the kind of words John reported him to have spoken. Let him assert that the Apostle John is alive, and contend that in his tomb, which is at Ephesus, he is sleeping rather than lying dead. Let him take as evidence the claim that the earth there gradually bubbles up and, as it were, boils over; and let him affirm, whether consistently or obstinately, that this happens through John’s breathing.

There can be no shortage of people who believe this, since there are also people who assert that Moses is still alive because Scripture says that his tomb was not found (Deuteronomy 34:6), and because he appeared with the Lord on the mountain, where Elijah too was present (Matthew 17:3)—although we read that Elijah did not die but was taken up (2 Kings 2:11).

As though Moses’ body could not have been hidden somewhere in such a way that people were entirely unaware where it was, and then divinely raised for a time when he and Elijah were seen with Christ! In the same way, many bodies of the saints rose for a time when Christ suffered and appeared to many in the holy city, as it is written (Matthew 27:52–53).

Nevertheless, to return to what I began to say: if some deny that Moses died, although Scripture itself—where we read that his tomb was nowhere found—testifies without any ambiguity that he died, how much more, on account of these words in which the Lord says, “I wish him to remain until I come,” is John believed to be sleeping alive beneath the earth?

They even report—something that is found in certain writings, although [Col. 1971] apocryphal—that when he ordered a tomb to be made for himself, he was present in good health; and after it had been dug out and most carefully prepared, he placed himself there as though in a bed and immediately died. But, according to those who understand the Lord’s words in this way, he did not lie down dead but like one who was dead; and when he was thought to be dead, he was buried while sleeping. He remains there until Christ comes, and indicates his life by the bubbling of the dust. They believe that this dust, as it rises from the bottom to the surface of the tomb, is driven upward by the breath of the one resting there.

I consider it unnecessary to argue against this opinion. Let those who know the place see whether the earth there does or suffers what is said, since we have indeed heard this from people who are not frivolous.

### 3

For the moment let us yield to an opinion that we cannot refute by certain proofs, lest another question arise to be asked of us: why the earth itself over a buried corpse appears in some manner to live and breathe.

But is this great question thereby solved, if, by a great miracle of the sort the Almighty can perform, a living body remains in sleep beneath the earth until the end of the age? On the contrary, the question becomes greater and more difficult: why would Jesus grant a long sleep in the body as a great gift to the disciple whom he loved above the others, so much that he was worthy to recline upon his breast, while he released blessed Peter from the burden of that very body through the immense glory of martyrdom and granted him what the Apostle Paul said and wrote that he desired: “To depart and be with Christ” (Philippians 1:23)?

But if the more credible view is that the holy John said that the Lord did not say, “He will not die,” so that no one would think that by the words he did say the Lord meant this, and if John’s body lies lifeless in his tomb like the bodies of other dead people, then it remains that, if what rumor has spread about the earth really occurs—namely, that when it is removed it grows back—this either happens so that his precious death may be commended in this way, since martyrdom does not commend it—for no persecutor killed him for the faith of Christ—or it happens for some other reason unknown to us.

The question nevertheless remains: why did the Lord say of a man who was going to die, “I wish him to remain until I come”?

### 4

Even in these two apostles, Peter and John, who would not be moved to ask why the Lord loved John more, when Peter loved the Lord more?

Whenever John mentions himself, so that he may be understood without naming himself, he adds that Jesus loved him—as though Jesus loved him alone—so that by this sign he might be distinguished from the others, whom he certainly loved. What, then, did he wish to be understood by saying this, except that he was loved more? Far be it from us to think that he said this falsely.

What greater indication of his greater love for John could Jesus have given him than this: although he was a human being sharing with his fellow disciples in so great a salvation, he alone reclined upon the breast of the Savior himself?

Now that the Apostle Peter loved Christ more than the others can indeed be demonstrated by many proofs. But, without going far afield, it appears sufficiently clearly in the preceding reading concerning this third manifestation of the Lord, which comes before the present passage. There, when the Lord questioned him, [Col. 1972] he said, “Do you love me more than these?” He knew this, certainly, and yet he asked, so that we too, who read the Gospel, might know Peter’s love for the Lord, both through the Lord’s question and through Peter’s answer.

When Peter answered, “I love you,” he did not add, “more than these,” because he answered according to what he knew about himself. He could not know how much he was loved by anyone else, since he could not see another person’s heart. Nevertheless, by saying in his earlier replies, “Yes, Lord, you know” (John 21:15–16), he himself sufficiently declared that the Lord, who knows, had asked what he asked.

The Lord therefore knew not only that Peter loved him, but also that Peter loved him more than the others. Yet if we put the question and ask which of the two is better: the one who loves Christ more, or the one who loves him less—who would hesitate to answer that the one who loves more is better?

Again, if we ask which of the two is better: the one whom Christ loves less, or the one whom Christ loves more—we shall undoubtedly answer that the one loved more by Christ is better.

In the first comparison I proposed, therefore, Peter is preferred to John; in this second one, John is preferred to Peter.

Let us therefore propose a third question: which of the two disciples is better—the one who loves Christ less than his fellow disciple but is loved by Christ more than that fellow disciple, or the one whom Christ loves less than his fellow disciple although he himself loves Christ more than his fellow disciple? Here the answer plainly hesitates, and the question grows greater.

As far as I myself understand, I could readily answer that the one who loves Christ more is the better, while the one whom Christ loves more is the happier—if I could see how to defend the justice of our Liberator, who loves less the one by whom he is loved more, and loves more the one by whom he is loved less.

### 5

I shall therefore undertake, within his manifest mercy, whose justice is hidden, to discuss the solution of so great a question, according to the strength that he himself grants. Up to this point the question has been proposed, not explained.

The beginning of its explanation shall be this: let us remember that in this corruptible body, which weighs down the soul (Wisdom 9:15), we live a miserable life. But since we have already been redeemed through the Mediator and have received the Holy Spirit as a pledge, we possess blessed life in hope, even though we do not yet possess it in reality.

“Hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25). Patience is necessary in the evils that each person suffers, not in the good things that he enjoys.

This life, then, concerning which it is written, “Is not human life upon earth a trial?” (Job 7:1), and in which we cry out daily to the Lord, “Deliver us from evil” (Matthew 6:13), a person is compelled to endure even with sins forgiven—although sin was originally the cause of his entering this misery. Punishment lasts longer than guilt, lest guilt be thought insignificant if punishment ended together with it.

Accordingly, whether to demonstrate the misery that is owed, to correct a life that is prone to fall, or to exercise [Col. 1973] the patience that is necessary, punishment temporarily holds a person whom guilt no longer holds liable to eternal condemnation.

This is the condition of these days, which we spend in this mortality and call evil, although in it we desire to see good days—a condition to be mourned, but not condemned. It comes from the just anger of God, concerning which Scripture says: “A human being born of woman is short-lived and full of anger” (Job 14:1). The anger of God, however, is not like human anger—that is, the disturbance of an agitated mind—but the tranquil establishment of a just punishment.

In this anger of his, God did not restrain his mercies, as it is written (Psalm 76:10). Among the other consolations for the miserable that he never ceases to provide for the human race, in the fullness of time, when he himself knew that this was to be done, he sent his only-begotten Son (Galatians 4:4), through whom he created all things. Remaining God, the Son became human, and was the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5).

Those who believe in him, through the bath of regeneration, with the guilt of all sins removed—both original sin, which generation transmits and against which regeneration was especially instituted, and the other sins contracted by wrongdoing—would be freed from everlasting condemnation. They would live in faith, hope, and charity, journeying in this world, and amid its laborious and dangerous temptations proceeding toward his presence by God’s bodily and spiritual consolations, keeping to the way of which Christ became their way.

And because even those who walk in him are not without sins that creep in through the weakness of this life, he gave the saving remedies of almsgiving, by which their prayer might be assisted. There he taught them to say, “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors” (Matthew 6:12).

This is what the Church does in this troubled life, possessing blessed hope. The Apostle Peter, because of the primacy of his apostleship, represented this Church in a figurative and universal manner.

In what properly belonged to him, he was by nature one human being, by grace one Christian, and by more abundant grace one and the same person, the chief apostle. But when he was told, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven,” he represented the universal Church, which in this world is shaken by various temptations as by rains, rivers, and storms, yet does not fall, because it has been founded upon the rock from which Peter received his name.

For the rock is not named from Peter, but Peter from the rock; just as Christ is not named from Christian, but Christian from Christ. For this reason the Lord said, “Upon this rock I will build my Church,” because Peter had said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16:16–19). “Upon this rock,” he said, “which you have confessed, I will build my Church.”

For Christ was the rock (1 Corinthians 10:4), and upon this foundation Peter himself was built. “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

The Church, therefore, which is founded in Christ, received from him the keys of the kingdom of heaven in Peter—that is, the power of binding and loosing sins. [Col. 1974] What the Church is in Christ by proper reality, Peter is in the rock by signification; and by this signification Christ is understood as the rock, Peter as the Church.

This Church, which Peter signified, so long as it dwells amid evils, is freed from evils by loving and following Christ. It follows him more fully in those who contend for the truth unto death. But the command, “Follow me,” is addressed to the universal Church, for whose sake Christ suffered. Concerning him Peter himself says, “Christ suffered for us, leaving us an example, so that we might follow his footsteps” (1 Peter 2:21).

Behold why he was told, “Follow me.”

There is another life, however, an immortal life that is not amid evils. There we shall see face to face what here is seen through a mirror and in a riddle (1 Corinthians 13:12), when we make great progress in contemplating the truth.

The Church therefore knows two lives divinely proclaimed and commended to her: one in faith, the other in sight; one in the time of pilgrimage, the other in the eternity of dwelling; one in labor, the other in rest; one on the way, the other in the homeland; one in the work of action, the other in the reward of contemplation; one turns away from evil and does good, the other has no evil from which to turn and has a great good to enjoy; one fights with an enemy, the other reigns without an enemy; one is strong in adversity, the other experiences no adversity; one restrains carnal desires, the other is free for spiritual delights; one is anxiously concerned with conquering, the other is secure in the peace of victory; one is helped amid temptations, the other rejoices in the Helper himself without any temptation; one comes to the aid of the needy, the other is where it finds no needy person; one forgives the sins of others as its own sins are forgiven, the other neither suffers anything that it must forgive nor does anything for which it must ask forgiveness; one is scourged by evils lest it be lifted up by good things, the other, through such fullness of grace, is free from every evil and clings to the highest good without any temptation to pride; one distinguishes good and evil, the other sees only what is good.

The first, therefore, is good but still miserable; the second is better and blessed. The first was signified by the Apostle Peter, the second by John.

The first is lived out here until the end of this age, and there it finds its end. The second is postponed until after the end of this age, but in the age to come it has no end.

Therefore the one is told, “Follow me”; while concerning the other it is said, “I wish him to remain until I come; what is that to you? You follow me.”

What does this mean? As far as I understand and grasp it, what else does it mean than this: “You follow me by imitating the endurance of temporal evils; let him remain until I come to bestow eternal goods”?

It may be stated more plainly in this way: “Let perfected action follow me, formed according to the example of my passion; but let contemplation, begun here, remain until I come, to be perfected when I come.”

For the fullness of devoted patience follows Christ by reaching even unto death; but the fullness of knowledge remains until Christ comes, when it will be revealed. Here the evils of this world are endured in the land of the dying; there the goods of the Lord will be seen in the land of the living.

When he says, “I wish him to remain until I come,” this should not be understood as though he had said “to stay” or “to continue,” but “to wait.” For [Col. 1975] what is signified by him will not be fulfilled now, but when Christ comes. What is signified by the one who was told, “You follow me,” must be enacted now; otherwise we shall not reach what is awaited.

In this active life, the more we love Christ, the more easily we are freed from evil. But he loves us less as we now are; and for this reason he frees us, so that we may not always remain as we are. There, however, he loves us more, because we shall not possess what displeases him and what he removes from us. He loves us here for no other reason than to heal us and transfer us from the things he does not love.

Here, therefore, he loves us less, where he does not wish us to remain; there, he loves us more, to where he wishes us to pass and from which he does not wish us to perish. Let Peter therefore love him, so that we may be freed from this mortality; let John be loved by him, so that we may be preserved in that immortality.

### 6

This explanation, however, shows why Christ loved John more than Peter, not why Peter loved Christ more than John.

For if Christ loves us more in the age to come, where we shall live with him without end, than in this age from which we are rescued so that we may be there forever, it does not follow that we shall then love him less, when we shall be better. We cannot be better except by loving him more.

Why, then, did John love him less than Peter, if he signified that life in which Christ is to be loved much more? Is it not because this was said of him—“I wish him to remain,” that is, to wait, “until I come”—since we do not yet possess the love that will then be much greater, but await it as something future, so that when he comes we may possess it?

For as the same apostle says in his Epistle, “It has not yet appeared what we shall be; we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). Then, therefore, we shall love more what we shall see.

The Lord himself, knowing what our future life will be like in us, loves it more by predestination, so that by loving us he may bring us to it.

Accordingly, since “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24:10), we know our present misery because we feel it; and therefore we love more the mercy of the Lord that we desire to be shown to us for deliverance from misery, and we ask for and receive it daily, especially for the forgiveness of sins.

This was signified by Peter, who loves more but is loved less, because Christ loves us less as miserable than as blessed.

But we love less the contemplation of truth as it will be then, because we do not yet know or possess it. This was signified by John, who loves less and therefore waits until the Lord comes, both for that life itself and for the fulfillment in us of the love due to it. Yet he is loved more, because what is represented by him makes a person blessed.

### 7

Nevertheless, let no one separate these distinguished apostles. Both were present in what Peter signified, and both were destined to be in what John signified. In signification one followed and the other remained; but in faith both endured the present evils of this misery, and both awaited [Col. 1976] the future goods of that blessedness.

Nor is this done by them alone. The whole holy Church, the bride of Christ, does this: it is to be rescued from these temptations and preserved in that happiness.

The two lives that Peter and John represented, each one representing one, were nevertheless both lived by them temporally through faith, and both will be enjoyed eternally through sight.

For all the saints who belong inseparably to the body of Christ, the chief of the Apostles, Peter, received the keys of the kingdom of heaven for the governance of this stormiest life, for binding and loosing sins. For all the same saints, the evangelist John reclined upon Christ’s breast, signifying the most secret and peaceful bosom of that life.

For neither does Peter alone bind and loose sins—the whole Church binds and looses them—nor did John alone drink from the spring of the Lord’s breast those sublime truths about Christ’s divinity and about the Trinity and unity of the whole Godhead, which he would pour forth by preaching: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God,” and the other truths that are to be contemplated face to face in that kingdom but are now, until the Lord comes, seen through a mirror and in a riddle.

Rather, the Lord himself spread the Gospel throughout the whole world for all his people to drink, according to each person’s capacity.

There are some who have thought—and they are not contemptible interpreters of sacred eloquence—that the Apostle John was loved more by Christ for this reason: that he neither married nor, from early boyhood, lived otherwise than most chastely (Jerome, *Against Jovinianus*, book 1). This is not clearly evident in the canonical Scriptures; nevertheless, it too greatly supports the appropriateness of the interpretation, since John signified that life in which there will be no marriages.

### 8

“This is the disciple who bears witness to these things and wrote these things; and we know that his testimony is true.” He then says: “There are also many other things that Jesus did, which, if they were written one by one, I do not think that the world itself could contain the books that would be written.”

We should not suppose that the world could not contain them because of the extent of physical space. How could the things be written in the world if the world could not hold what was written? Rather, perhaps they could not be comprehended by the capacity of readers—although, while the truth of events is preserved, words often seem to exceed the truth of what is being said.

This does not happen when something obscure or doubtful is explained by supplying its cause and reason. It happens when something clear is either magnified or diminished, without departing from the path of signifying truth. Words then exceed the matter indicated in such a way that the intention of the speaker, who does not deceive, remains evident; for he knows how far the hearer should believe, even when something is diminished or magnified in speech beyond what ought to be believed.

The teachers of both Greek and Latin literature call this manner of speaking by the Greek name *hyperbole* (“hyperbole”). This manner of speech is found here, as well as in several other passages of the divine Scriptures, such as: “They have set their mouth against heaven” (Psalm 72:9), and “The crown of the head of those who walk in their sins” (Psalm 68:22), along with many similar expressions that are not absent from the holy Scriptures, just as other figures of speech—that is, other modes of expression—are not absent.

I would discuss these matters at greater length, if the Evangelist, by bringing his Gospel to an end, had not also compelled me to bring my discourse to an end.

[Col. 1977]

## TEN TRACTATES OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE EPISTLE OF JOHN TO THE PARTHIANS

[Note: [Col. 1977] Written around the year 416 after Christ.]

[Note: [Col. 1977] The following manuscript codices were used to correct these tractates: two from the Bigot library; two from the Michael and German libraries; three from the Remi library; one, the oldest and of excellent quality, from the Theoderic library; and one each from the libraries of Benignus, Vendôme, Fleury, and Vincent; one from the Church of Laon; one from the Abbey of Saint-Quentin at Beauvais; and another from the Church of Beauvais, which is noted at the end as having been written in the twelfth year of King Chlothar. Also used were the variant readings which the Doctors of Louvain excerpted from five Belgian manuscripts. Finally, the editions of Amerbach, Badius, Erasmus, and Louvain were consulted.]

[Note: [Col. 1977] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of volume 1 of the *Retractations* and *Confessions*. M.]

### Prologue.

[Col. 1977] Your Holiness remembers that we are accustomed to expound the Gospel according to John in the order of the readings. But because the solemnity of these holy days has now intervened—days on which certain readings from the Gospel must be recited in the Church, readings that recur annually in such a way that there can be no others in their place [Note: [Col. 1977] This is also attested in Sermon 232, §1, and Sermon 239, §1, *On the Season*: it had become customary for the account of the Lord’s resurrection to be recited for seven or eight days during the Paschal solemnity, according to all the Evangelists; and not always in the same order, but so that Luke was sometimes placed after Mark. Indeed, this second Tractate, which the very ancient Theoderician manuscript assigns to the second day of Easter, is shown by its opening to have been delivered on the day when Luke’s account of Christ’s appearance to the two disciples going to Emmaus had been read. Easter fell on 2 April in the year 416, to which one may reasonably assign these Tractates; for Augustine says in the Prologue that he delivered them after he had already begun his exposition of John’s Gospel, interrupting it for a short while. There is no mention of them in the work *Retractions*, in which he reviewed only books among his own works, hoping to publish another work on his Epistles and popular Tractates, as he writes to Quodvultdeus in Letter 224. But in Possidius’s *Catalogue*, chapter 9, they are recorded in these words: “Ten Sermons on the Epistle of John to the Parthians.” In all the manuscripts they are attributed to Augustine; but in some fewer copies they are entitled *Tractates*, in others *Sermons* or *Homilies*, with the title *On Charity* added in some. Finally, in the manuscripts the Prologue forms part of the first Tractate and is not separated from it by any mark or title of its own, as it is in the printed editions.], that order which we had undertaken has been interrupted for a little while by necessity, not abandoned. When I was considering what, in keeping with the joyfulness of these present days, I might discuss with you from the Scriptures during this week—something that, as much as the Lord grants, could be completed in these seven or eight days—the Epistle of blessed John occurred to me. Thus, although we have interrupted his Gospel for a short time, by expounding his Epistle we may not depart from him; especially since in this Epistle charity is commended sufficiently to all whose heart has a sound palate, where God’s bread may be tasted, and sufficiently memorably in the holy Church of God. He spoke much—indeed, almost everything—about charity. Whoever possesses within himself the capacity to hear must necessarily rejoice at what he hears.

For such a person this reading will be like oil upon a flame: if there is something there to be nourished, it is nourished, grows, and endures. For others it ought to be like a flame applied to tinder, so that, if they were not burning, they may be kindled when the discourse approaches. In some, what already exists is nourished; in others, what is lacking is kindled, so that we may all rejoice in one charity. Where there is charity, there is peace; and where there is humility, [Col. 1978] there is charity. Now let us hear him himself; and concerning his words, as the Lord suggests them, let us speak also to you, so that you may understand them well.

## TRACTATE I

On what John writes: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard and which we have seen,” and so forth, up to “Because the darkness has blinded his eyes.” Chapter 1 and chapter 2, verses 1–11.

### 1

“That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, and which our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life.” Who is it that handles the Word with his hands, unless it is because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us”? This Word, which was made flesh in order to be handled with the hands, began to be flesh from the Virgin Mary; but the Word did not then begin, since he said, “That which was from the beginning.” See whether his Epistle does not bear witness to his Gospel, where you have just heard: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:14, 1).

Perhaps someone may understand “the Word of life” as a certain discourse about Christ, and not Christ’s very body, which was handled with the hands. See what follows: “And the life itself was manifested.” Christ, therefore, is the Word of life. And from where was he manifested? He was from the beginning, but he had not been manifested to human beings; he had, however, been manifested to the angels who saw him and, as it were, were nourished by him as by their bread. But what does Scripture say? “A human being ate the bread of angels” [Col. 1979] (Psalm 77:25).

Therefore that very life was manifested in the flesh, because it was presented in manifestation so that what can be seen by the heart alone might also be seen by the eyes, in order to heal hearts. The Word is seen by the heart alone; flesh, however, is seen by bodily eyes. There was something from which we could see the flesh, but there was nothing from which we could see the Word. The Word became flesh, which we could see, so that in us that by which we might see the Word could be healed.

### 2

“And we have seen, and we are witnesses.” Perhaps some of the brethren who do not know Greek are unaware of what “witnesses” is in Greek; yet it is a familiar and religious word to everyone. Those whom we call *witnesses* in Latin are called *martyrs* in Greek. Who, indeed, has not heard of martyrs, or in whose Christian mouth does the name of martyrs not dwell daily? Would that it might dwell in the heart as well, so that we might imitate the sufferings of the martyrs, rather than persecute them with kicks.

Therefore he said: “We have seen, and we are witnesses”—we have seen, and we are martyrs. By giving testimony from what they had seen, and by giving testimony from what they had heard from those who had seen, when the testimony displeased the people against whom it was spoken, they suffered everything that martyrs suffer. The martyrs are God’s witnesses. God wanted human beings to have witnesses, so that human beings might also have God as their witness.

“We have seen,” he says, “and we are witnesses.” Where did they see? In manifestation. What is “in manifestation”? In the sun—that is, in this light. But how could he who made the sun be seen in the sun, unless it was because he placed his tabernacle in the sun, and he himself, like a bridegroom coming forth from his bridal chamber, rejoiced like a giant to run his course (Psalm 18:6)?

He was before the sun, he who made the sun [Note: [Col. 1979] Three manuscripts read: “But he was the sun who made the sun.” Two others: “Now that sun who made the sun.”], before the morning star, before all the stars, before all the angels—the true Creator, since “all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made” (John 1:3). In order to be seen by fleshly eyes, which see the sun, he placed his own tabernacle in the sun; that is, he displayed his flesh in the manifestation of this light.

The bridal chamber of that bridegroom was the Virgin’s womb, because in that virginal womb the two were joined: bridegroom and bride, the bridegroom being the Word and the bride being flesh. For it is written: “And the two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2:24); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh” (Matthew 19:6). Isaiah too rightly recalls that the two are one. For he speaks in the person of Christ and says: “As a bridegroom he placed a mitre upon me, and as a bride he adorned me with an ornament” (Isaiah 61:10).

One person appears to speak, and he made himself both bridegroom and bride, because they are not two but one flesh; because “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” The Church is joined to that flesh, and the whole Christ comes to be, head and body.

### 3

“And we are witnesses,” he says, “and we announce to you the eternal life which was with the Father and was manifested among us”—that is, it was manifested among us; more plainly, it would be said: “It was manifested to us.” Therefore, “what we have seen and heard, we announce to you.”

Let your Charity pay attention: “What we have seen and heard, we announce to you.” They saw the Lord himself present in [Col. 1980] the flesh, and they heard words from the Lord’s mouth, and they announced them to us. We too, therefore, have heard, but we have not seen. Are we then less blessed than those who saw and heard? And how does he add: “So that you too may have fellowship with us”?

They saw, we did not see, and yet we are companions, because we hold the common faith. For one person, by seeing, did not believe; he wanted to touch and thus to believe, and said: “I will not believe unless I put my fingers into the place of the nails and touch his scars.” And he presented himself in that moment to be handled by human hands, although he always presents himself to be seen by the eyes of angels. That disciple touched him and exclaimed: “My Lord and my God.” Because he touched the human being, he confessed God.

And the Lord, consoling us who cannot now touch him with our hands as he sits in heaven, but can touch him by faith, said to him: “Because you have seen me, you have believed; blessed are those who do not see and yet believe” (John 20:25–29). We have been described; we have been designated. Therefore let the blessedness which the Lord foretold come to be in us. Let us hold firmly what we do not see, because those who saw announce it.

“So that you too,” he says, “may have fellowship with us.” And what great thing is it to have fellowship with human beings? Do not despise it; see what he adds: “And our fellowship may be with God the Father and with Jesus Christ his Son.” And “we write these things to you,” he says, “so that your joy may be full.” He speaks of full joy in that very fellowship, in that very charity, in that very unity.

### 4

“And this is the announcement which we have heard from him and announce to you.” What does this mean? They themselves saw and handled with their hands the Word of life. He was from the beginning; for a time he became visible and tangible, the only-begotten Son of God.

For what purpose did he come, or what new thing did he announce to us? What did he wish to teach? Why did he do what he did: why did the Word become flesh, why did God endure from human beings things wholly unworthy of him, why did he bear blows from the hands he himself had formed? What did he wish to teach? What did he wish to show? What did he wish to announce?

Let us hear. For without the fruit of the commandment, hearing about an event—because Christ was born and because Christ suffered—is a distraction of the mind, not its strengthening. What great thing are you hearing? Look to the fruit with which you hear [Note: [Col. 1980] The Louvain edition reads: “What great thing do you hear, with what fruit might you hear? See.” Erasmus: “What great thing do you hear, with what fruit might you hear? See, etc.” Lyons: “What great thing do you hear, with what fruit might you hear? See,” and so forth. Venice: “What great thing do you hear? Look to the fruit with which you hear; see what he wished to teach.” M.].

What did he wish to teach? What did he wish to announce? Listen: “God is light,” he says, “and there is no darkness in him at all.” He has named light, but the words are still obscure. It is good for us that the light he has named should illuminate our hearts, so that we may see what he said.

This is what we announce: that God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all. Who would dare to say that there is darkness in God? Or what is this light? Or what is darkness? Perhaps he is speaking of things that concern these eyes of ours. “God is light,” someone says; “the sun is light, the moon is light, and a lamp is light.” This must be something far greater than these, far more excellent, and far more exalted.

As much as God is above creation, as much as the Creator is above what has been created, as much as wisdom is above what was made through wisdom, so far beyond all things must this light be [Col. 1981]. Perhaps we shall be near to it if we learn what this light is and attach ourselves to it, so that we may be illuminated by it; for in ourselves we are darkness, and when illuminated by it we can be light, and not be ashamed because of it, since we are ashamed because of ourselves.

Who is ashamed of himself? The one who knows himself to be a sinner. Who is not ashamed because of it? The one who is illuminated by it. What is it to be illuminated by it? It is to see that one is already darkened by sins, to desire to be illuminated by it, and to approach it. Hence the Psalm says: “Approach him, and be enlightened, and your faces shall not be ashamed” (Psalm 33:6).

But you will not be ashamed because of it [Note: [Col. 1981] The Louvain edition reads: “But you are ashamed because of it.” The majority of manuscripts, supported by the Basel edition, read: “But you will not be ashamed.”], if, when it shows you how foul you are, your foulness displeases you, so that you may receive its beauty. This is what he wishes to teach.

### 5

And perhaps we are saying this too hastily. Let him himself make it clear in what follows. Remember at the beginning of our discourse that this Epistle commends charity: “God is light,” he says, “and there is no darkness in him at all.” And what had he said earlier? “So that you may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with God the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.”

Now, if God is light and there is no darkness in him at all, and we must have fellowship with him, darkness must be driven away from us so that light may come to be in us; for darkness cannot have fellowship with light. Therefore see what follows: “But if we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie.”

You have the Apostle Paul also saying: “Or what fellowship has light with darkness?” (2 Corinthians 6:14). You say that you have fellowship with God, and you walk in darkness; yet God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all. How, then, can light and darkness have fellowship?

Let the human being say to himself: “What shall I do? How shall I become light? I live in sins and iniquities.” A certain despair and sadness seem to steal upon him. There is no salvation except in fellowship with God. “God is light, and there is no darkness in him at all.” But sins are darkness, as the Apostle says that the devil and his angels are “the rulers of this darkness” (Ephesians 6:12). He would not call them rulers of darkness unless they were rulers of sins and masters of the unrighteous.

What, then, shall we do, my brothers? We must have fellowship with God; there is no other hope of eternal life. But God is light, and there is no darkness in him; iniquities are darkness, and we are weighed down by iniquities, so that we cannot have fellowship with God. What hope, then, is there?

Did I not promise to say something during these days that would bring joy? If I do not provide it, this is sadness. God is light, and there is no darkness in him; sins are darkness. What will become of us? Let us listen, in case he may console us, raise us up, and give us hope, so that we may not fail on the road. For we are running, and we are running toward our homeland; and if we despair of reaching it, we fail through that very despair. But he who wishes us to arrive, so that he may preserve us in our homeland, feeds us on the road.

Let us listen, then: “But if we say that we have fellowship with him and walk in darkness, we lie and do not practice the truth.” Let us not say that we have fellowship with him if we walk in darkness.

“But if we walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, we have fellowship with one another.” Let us walk in the light, as he himself is in the light, so that we may be able to have fellowship with him.

And what shall we do about sins? Hear what follows: “And the blood of Jesus Christ his Son will cleanse us from every sin.” God has given great security. Rightly do we celebrate Easter, where the Lord’s blood was poured out, by which we are cleansed from every sin.

Let us be secure. The devil held against us a bond of slavery, but it has been erased by Christ’s blood. “The blood,” he says, “of his Son will cleanse us from every sin.” What does “from every sin” mean? Pay attention. Already, in the name of Christ, through his blood [Note: [Col. 1982] The printed editions read: “through the blood of the Lord’s cross, which these persons have now confessed.” We, with several manuscripts, read: “through his blood, which,” and so forth.], all their sins have been cleansed—those now confessing him who are called infants.

The old entered; the new went out. What does “the old entered, the new went out” mean? The elderly entered; the infants went out. For old age is a decayed, ancient life, whereas infancy is the new life of regeneration.

But what shall we do? Past sins have been forgiven, not only for them but also for us. Yet after the forgiveness and abolition of all sins, while living in this world amid temptations, perhaps some sins have been contracted. Therefore let a person do what he can: let him confess what he is, so that he may be healed by the one who always is what he is. For he himself always was and is [Note: [Col. 1982] The Louvain edition reads: “for he is and is.” In the other books: “for he always was and is.”]; we were not, and now we are.

### 6

See what he says: “But if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” Therefore, if you confess yourself to be a sinner, the truth is in you; for the truth itself is light. Your life has not yet shone forth perfectly, because sins remain in it; nevertheless, you have already begun to be illuminated, because confession of sins is present in you.

See what follows: “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all iniquity.” Not only from past sins, but also from any that we may perhaps have contracted in this life, because as long as a human being bears the flesh, he cannot fail to have at least minor sins.

But do not despise these minor sins that we mention. If you despise them when you weigh them, be afraid when you count them. Many small things make one great thing: many drops fill a river; many grains make a mass.

And what hope is there? Above all, confession: let no one consider himself righteous and, before the eyes of God who sees what he is, let a human being who was not and now is raise his neck in pride.

Above all, therefore, confession; then love. For what has been said about charity? “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8). Let us now see whether he commends charity itself on account of sins that creep in, since charity alone extinguishes sins.

Pride extinguishes charity; humility therefore strengthens charity, and charity extinguishes sins. Humility belongs to confession, by which we confess that we are sinners. This is humility—not merely to say it with the tongue, as though out of arrogance, lest we displease people if we say that we are righteous.

The impious and the insane do this: “I know that I am righteous, but what shall I say before human beings? If I call myself righteous, who will bear it, who will tolerate it? Let my righteousness be known to God; nevertheless, I will say that I am a sinner—not because I am one, but so that I may not be found hateful through arrogance.”

Tell people what you are; tell God what you are. For if you do not tell God what you are, God condemns what he finds in you. You do not want him to condemn it? You condemn it yourself. You want him to forgive? Acknowledge it yourself, so that you may be able to say to God: “Turn your face away from my sins.”

Say to him also those words in the same Psalm: “For I acknowledge my iniquity” (Psalm 50:5, 11). “But if we confess our sins, he is faithful and just, who forgives us our sins and cleanses us from all iniquity.”

“If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us.” If you say, “I have not sinned,” you make him a liar while wishing to make yourself truthful. How can God be a liar and a human being truthful, when Scripture contradicts this: “Every human being is a liar; God alone is truthful” (Romans 3:4)? Therefore God is truthful through himself; you are truthful through God, for through yourself you are a liar.

### 7

And lest he seem to have granted impunity for sins, because he said, “He is faithful and just, who cleanses us from all iniquity,” and people should say to themselves, “Let us sin; let us do whatever we wish without fear. Christ cleanses us; he is faithful and just; he cleanses us from every iniquity”—he removes your evil security and inserts a useful fear.

You wish to be secure in the wrong way? Be concerned. He is faithful and just to forgive us our sins if you always displease yourself and are changed until you are perfected.

Therefore what follows? “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin.” But perhaps sin steals upon us from human life. What, then, will happen? What? Will there now be despair? Listen: “And if anyone sins,” he says, “we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he himself is the propitiation for our sins.”

He is therefore the advocate. Take care that you do not sin. If sin should steal upon you through the weakness of this life, immediately see it, immediately let it displease you, immediately condemn it; and when you have condemned it, you will come confidently to the Judge. There you have an advocate. Do not fear that you will lose the case of your confession.

For if in this life a person sometimes entrusts himself to an eloquent tongue and does not perish, and you entrust yourself to the Word—will you perish? Cry out: “We have an advocate with the Father.”

### 8

See John himself preserving humility. Certainly he was a righteous and great man, who drank the secrets of the mysteries from the Lord’s breast—he, he who, by drinking from the Lord’s breast, belched forth the divinity: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1:1).

Such a man did not say, “You have an advocate with the Father,” but, “If anyone sins,” he says, “we have an advocate.” He did not say, “You have”; nor did he say, “You have me”; nor did he say, “You have Christ himself.” Rather, he set forth Christ, not himself; and he said “we have,” not “you have.”

He preferred to place himself among sinners, so that he might have Christ as his advocate, rather than to put himself forward as an advocate in Christ’s place and be found among the proud who are condemned.

Brothers, we have Jesus Christ the righteous himself as our advocate with the Father; he himself is the propitiation for our sins. Whoever holds to this has not made a heresy; whoever holds to this has not made a schism.

For from where have schisms arisen? When people say, “We are righteous”; when people say, “We sanctify the unclean, we justify the ungodly; we ask, we obtain.”

But what did John say? “If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.”

But someone will say: “Then do the saints not pray for us? Then do bishops and superiors not pray for the people?” Attend to the Scriptures and see that the superiors also commend themselves to the people. For the Apostle says to the people: “Praying together also for us” (Colossians 4:3). The Apostle prays for the people; the people pray for the Apostle. We pray for you, brothers; but you too pray for us. Let all the members pray for one another; let the head intercede for all.

Therefore it is not surprising that what follows here closes the mouths of those who divide the Church of God. He who said [Note: [Col. 1984] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read: “because he said.” M.], “We have Jesus Christ the righteous, and he himself is the propitiation for our sins”—because of those who were going to divide themselves and say, “Here is Christ, there he is” (Matthew 24:23), and who wanted to display him in a part, although he purchased and possesses the whole—immediately continued: “Not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world.”

What does this mean, brothers? Surely we find “her in the fields” [Note: [Col. 1984] Four manuscripts read: “What does this mean? Attend to the Psalm: ‘We found her in the fields.’”] (Psalm 131:6); we find the Church among all nations.

Behold, Christ is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world. Behold, you have the Church throughout the whole world. Do not follow false justifiers and true cutters-off [Note: [Col. 1984] The printed editions read: “precipitators.” The manuscripts read: “true cutters-off.”]. Remain on that mountain which filled the whole earth (Daniel 2:35), because Christ is the propitiation for our sins—not for ours only, but also for the sins of the whole world, which he purchased with his own blood.

### 9

“And by this,” he says, “we know him, if we keep his commandments.” Which commandments? “Whoever says that he knows him and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.”

But you still ask: “Which commandments?” “Whoever,” he says, “keeps his word, truly in him the love of God has been perfected.” Let us see whether the commandment itself is called love.

We were asking which commandments, and he says: “Whoever keeps his word, truly in him the love of God has been perfected.” Attend to the Gospel, whether this is not the commandment: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John 13:34).

“By this we know that we are in him, if we have been perfected in him” [Note: [Col. 1984] This phrase, “if we have been perfected in him,” is found here in all the manuscripts, but is absent from the sacred biblical text.].

He calls them perfect in love. What is the perfection of love? To love enemies, and to love them so that they may become brothers.

For our love must not be carnal. To wish someone temporal health is good; but even if it is lacking, let the soul be safe. You wish your friend life? You do well. You rejoice at the death of your enemy? You do wrong.

But perhaps that life which you wish for your friend is useless, and the death over which you rejoice in the case of your enemy was beneficial. It is uncertain whether this life is useful or harmful to someone; but the life that is with God is undoubtedly useful.

Love your enemies in such a way that you wish them to be brothers; love your enemies in such a way that they may be called into your fellowship. For he loved in this way who, hanging on the cross, said: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

He did not say, “Father, let these people live for a long time. They are killing me, but let them live.” What did he say? “Forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” With a most merciful prayer and most excellent power, he was driving eternal death away from them.

Many of them believed, and the blood of Christ that had been poured out was forgiven to them. First they poured it out while raging; now they drank it when they believed.

“By this we know that we are in him, if we have been perfected in him.” Concerning this perfection in loving enemies, the Lord admonishes us and says: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matthew 5:48).

Therefore, whoever says that he remains in him ought himself also to walk just as he walked. How, brothers? What does he admonish us? Whoever says that he remains in him—that is, in Christ—ought himself also to walk just as he walked.

Perhaps he admonishes us to walk upon the sea? Certainly not. Rather, he admonishes us to walk in the way of righteousness.

On what way? I have already mentioned it. He was fixed upon the cross, and on that very way he walked. That is the way of charity [Note: [Col. 1985] Four manuscripts read: “The way itself is charity.”]: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.”

Therefore, if you have learned to pray for your enemy, you are walking in the Lord’s way.

### 10

“Beloved, I am not writing a new commandment to you, but an old commandment which you had from the beginning.” What commandment did he call old? “Which you had,” he says, “from the beginning.”

It is therefore old because you have already heard it; otherwise he would contradict the Lord, who says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.”

But why is the commandment old? Not because it belongs to the old human being. Why, then? “Which you had from the beginning.” The old commandment is the word which you heard. It is therefore old because you have already heard it.

And he shows that the same commandment is new when he says: “Again, I am writing a new commandment to you.” It is not another commandment; it is the very same one which he called old, and it is also new. Why? “Because it is true in him and in you.”

You have heard why it is old: because you already knew it. Why is it new? “Because the darkness has passed away, and the true light is already shining.”

There is the reason why it is new: darkness belongs to the old human being, whereas light belongs to the new. What does the Apostle Paul say? “Put off the old human being, and put on the new” (Colossians 3:9–10). And again what does he say? “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5:8).

### 11

“Whoever says that he is in the light”—now he makes clear everything he has said—“and hates his brother is in darkness until now.”

Come, my brothers, how long shall we say to you, “Love your enemies” (Matthew 5:44)? See what is worse: do not still hate your brothers.

If you loved only your brothers, you would not yet be perfect. But if you hate your brothers [Note: [Col. 1986] Here and in various places in the Tractates, the printed editions now read *oditis*, “you hate,” and now *oderitis*, “you will hate.” Erasmus has *oditis* here. Louvain has *oderitis*, but four of its manuscripts have *oditis*, and one manuscript has *odistis*. Lyons and Venice read *si autem auditis*, “but if you hear.” M.], what are you? Where are you?

Let each person look into his own heart. Let him not hold hatred against his brother because of some harsh word, because of a dispute over land, lest he become earth. For whoever hates his brother must not say that he walks in the light.

What did I say? He must not say that he walks in Christ. Whoever says that he is in the light and hates his brother is in darkness until now.

Someone who had been a pagan has become a Christian. Pay attention: he was in darkness when he was a pagan; now he has become a Christian. Thanks be to God; everyone rejoices. The Apostle is read, rejoicing on his behalf: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord.”

He worshiped idols; now he worships God. He worshiped what he made; now he worships the one who made him. He has been changed. Thanks be to God; all Christians rejoice.

Why? Because now he is a worshiper of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and a despiser of demons and idols. John is still concerned about this person; though many rejoice, he is still viewed with suspicion.

Brothers, let us willingly embrace this maternal concern. The mother is not concerned about us without reason, even when others rejoice. I call charity the mother; for charity itself dwelt in John’s heart when he said these things.

Why, unless he fears something in us, even while people are already rejoicing over us? What does he fear? “Whoever says that he is in the light”—what does this mean? Whoever now says that he is a Christian—“and hates his brother is in darkness until now.”

There is no need to explain this; rather, there is need to rejoice if it does not happen, and to weep if it does.

### 12

“Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him.”

I beseech you through Christ: God feeds us; we are going to refresh our bodies in the name of Christ. They have been refreshed somewhat and must be refreshed again; but let our mind be fed.

I do not say this because I am going to speak for a long time—for behold, the reading is already coming to an end—but so that perhaps, because of weariness, we may not listen attentively enough to what is especially necessary.

“Whoever loves his brother remains in the light, and there is no scandal in him.” Who are those who suffer scandal, or cause it? Those who are scandalized by Christ and by the Church.

Those who are scandalized by Christ are burned, as it were, by the sun; those who are scandalized by the Church are burned, as it were, by the moon. But the Psalm says: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 120:6). That is: if you hold fast to charity, you will suffer scandal neither in Christ nor in the Church; you will abandon neither Christ nor the Church.

For whoever abandons the Church—how is he in Christ, since he is not among Christ’s members? How is he in Christ, since he is not in Christ’s body?

Those, then, suffer scandal who abandon either Christ or the Church. How do we understand that the Psalm said, “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night,” because it wants that burning to be understood as scandal? First, attend to the comparison itself. Just as someone who is burned says, “I cannot bear it; I cannot endure it,” and withdraws himself, so those who cannot endure certain things in the Church and withdraw themselves either from the name of Christ or from the Church suffer scandal.

See how those carnal people suffered scandal, as though burned by the sun, to whom Christ preached his flesh and said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” Nearly seventy people said: “This is a hard saying,” and departed from him; and the twelve remained.

The sun burned all those people, and they departed, unable to bear the force of the word. The twelve, therefore, remained. And lest people perhaps think that they themselves were doing Christ a favor by believing in Christ, rather than receiving a benefit from him, when the twelve had remained the Lord said to them: “Do you also wish to leave?” This was so that you might know that I am necessary to you, not you to me.

But those whom the sun had not burned answered through Peter’s voice: “Lord, you have the word of eternal life; where shall we go?” (John 6:54–69).

But whom does the Church burn like the moon by night? Those who have made schisms. Hear the very word placed in the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burned?” (2 Corinthians 11:29).

How, then, is there no scandal in the one who loves his brother? Because whoever loves his brother endures everything for the sake of unity; for brotherly love consists in the unity of charity.

Someone—whether bad, or bad in your opinion, or bad according to your invention—offends you, and you abandon so many good people? What kind of brotherly love is that? What did it appear to be among those people [Note: [Col. 1987] Among the Donatists.]? When they accused the Africans, they abandoned the whole world.

Surely there were no saints in the whole world? Or could they be condemned without being heard by you? But if only you loved your brothers, there would be no scandal in you.

Hear what the Psalm says: “There is abundant peace for those who love your law, and there is no scandal for them” (Psalm 118:165). He said that those who love God’s law have abundant peace, and therefore there is no scandal for them.

Those, then, who suffer scandal lose peace. And whom did he say do not suffer scandal, or do not cause it? Those who love God’s law. Therefore they are established in charity.

But someone says: “He spoke of those who love the law of God, not of brothers.” Hear what the Lord says: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” What is the law, if not a commandment?

And how do they not suffer scandal, unless by enduring one another? As Paul says: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4:2–3).

And because this is the law of Christ, hear the same Apostle commending that law: “Bear one another’s burdens,” he says, “and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2).

13. For whoever hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going. A great matter, brothers; pay attention, I beg you. Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes. What is as blind as those who hate their brothers? For, so that you may know that they are blind, they have stumbled against the mountain. I say the same things, so that they may not slip from your memory. Is not this stone, cut from the mountain without hands, Christ, from the kingdom of the Jews without the work of marriage? Did not that stone shatter all the kingdoms of the earth—that is, all the dominions of idols and demons? Did not that stone grow and become a great mountain and fill the whole world (Dan. II, 34–35)? Do we point out this mountain with a finger, as the moon is pointed out to people on the third day of the lunar month [Note: [Col. 1988] See *Tractatus in Evangelium Ioannis* 4, no. 4.]? For example, when people want to see the new moon, they say, “Look, the moon—look, there it is”; and if there are people who cannot direct their gaze and say, “Where?”, a finger is pointed out to them so that they may see. Sometimes, when they are ashamed lest they be thought blind, they say that they have seen what they have not seen. Do we point out the Church in this way, my brothers? Is it not open? Is it not manifest? Has it not taken hold of all nations? Is not fulfilled what was promised so many years ago to Abraham: “In your seed all the nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18)? It was promised to one faithful man, and the world has been filled with thousands of faithful people. Look: a mountain filling the whole face of the earth; look: the city of which it was said, “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matt. V, 14). Yet they stumble against the mountain. And when they are told, “Climb up,” they say, “There is no mountain”; and they more easily dash their faces against it than seek a dwelling place there.

Isaiah was read yesterday; whoever among you was attentive perceived—not merely with his eyes, but with his ear, and not with the bodily ear but with the ear of the heart—“In the last days the mountain of the house of the Lord shall be manifest, prepared on the summit of the mountains.” What is as manifest as a mountain? Yet there are also unknown mountains, because they are situated in one region of the earth. Who among you knows Mount Olympus? How can those who live there not know our Giddabam [Note: [Col. 1988] Six manuscripts have *Gibbam*. Two have *Gibam*. Three have *Giblam*.]? Such mountains are confined to particular regions. But that mountain is not like this, because it has filled the whole face of the earth; and of it it is said, “Prepared on the summit of the mountains.” It is a mountain above the summits of all mountains. “And all nations,” he says, “shall gather to it” (Isa. II, 2). Who goes astray on this mountain? Who shatters his face by stumbling against it? Who is ignorant of the city set upon a mountain?

But do not be surprised that it is unknown to those who hate their brothers, because they walk in darkness and do not know where they are going, because darkness has blinded their eyes. They do not see the mountain; do not be surprised—I tell you, they have no eyes. Why do they have no eyes? Because darkness has blinded them. How do we prove it? Because they hate their brothers: when they are offended by the Africans, they separate themselves from the whole world, because they do not tolerate, for the peace of Christ, those whom they slander [Note: [Col. 1988] Namely, Caecilianus and those who ordained him.], while they tolerate, for the party of Donatus, those whom they condemn [Note: [Col. 1988] Namely, the Maximianists. See Letters 51, 108, etc.].

# TRACTATE II

From the verse, “I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven through his name,” up to, “But whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as he himself remains forever.” Chapter II, verses 12–17.

## 1

Everything that is read from the holy Scriptures ought to be heard attentively, for our instruction and salvation. Above all, however, those things must be entrusted to memory that are especially effective against heretics, whose snares never cease to entrap the weaker and more negligent.

Remember our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, and that he both died for us and rose again: he died because of our sins and rose again because of our justification (Rom. IV, 25). As you have just heard, the eyes of the two disciples whom he encountered on the road were held back from recognizing him. He found them despairing of the redemption that was in Christ, supposing that he had already suffered and died like a human being, and not thinking of him as the Son of God, who lives forever; believing that he had died in the flesh in such a way that he would not live again, but as one of the prophets. You heard their words a little earlier, you who were attentive.

Then he opened the Scriptures to them, beginning with Moses and continuing through all the prophets, showing them that everything he had suffered had been foretold. Otherwise they might have been more disturbed if the Lord had risen, and might have believed him less if these things had not previously been foretold about him. The firmness of faith consists in this: that everything that happened in Christ was foretold.

The disciples therefore did not recognize him except in the breaking of the bread. And truly, whoever eats and drinks without bringing judgment upon himself (1 Cor. XI, 29) recognizes Christ in the breaking of the bread. Later the eleven themselves thought that they were seeing a spirit. He offered himself to be touched, he who had offered himself to be crucified: to be crucified by enemies, to be touched by friends; yet he was the physician of all—of the impiety of the former and the unbelief of the latter [Note: [Col. 1989] Four manuscripts have: “and he healed the impieties of the former and the unbeliefs of the latter.”].

For you heard, when the Acts of the Apostles were being read, how many thousands of Christ’s killers believed (Acts II, 41). If those who had killed him later believed, would those who hesitated for a little while not believe? Yet even to them—something you ought especially to observe and commit to memory, because God willed to establish a stronghold in the Scriptures against treacherous deceivers, and no one dares speak against the Scriptures who wishes in any way to appear Christian—even after he had offered himself to be touched, it was not enough for him unless he confirmed the hearts of believers from the Scriptures. For he was looking ahead to us, who do not have Christ present to touch, but do have what we can read.

If they believed for this reason, that they held and touched him, what shall we do? Christ has now ascended into heaven; he will come only at the end, to judge the living and the dead. From where, then, shall we believe, unless from the same source by which he wished even those who touched him to be confirmed? For he opened the Scriptures to them and showed them that it was necessary for Christ to suffer and for everything written about him in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms to be fulfilled.

He embraced the whole ancient text of the Scriptures. Whatever belongs to those Scriptures speaks of Christ—provided it finds ears willing to hear. And he opened their understanding, so that they might understand the Scriptures. Therefore we too must pray that he himself may open our understanding.

## 2

What, then, did the Lord show to have been written about himself in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms? What did he show? Let the Evangelist himself say. He set this down briefly, so that we might know what we ought to believe and understand amid the vast extent of the Scriptures. Certainly there are many pages and many books, but all contain what the Lord briefly said to his disciples. What is this? “That it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise again on the third day.”

You already have what concerns the bridegroom: that it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise again. The bridegroom has been commended to us. Let us see what he says about the bride, so that when you have recognized the bridegroom and the bride, you may not come to the wedding without reason. For every celebration is a celebration of a wedding: the wedding of the Church is being celebrated.

The son of a king is going to take a wife, and he himself is the king’s son and king; and those who attend are themselves the bride. It is not as in bodily weddings, where some attend the wedding and another woman is married. In the Church, those who attend—if they attend well—become the bride. For the whole Church is the bride of Christ, whose beginning and firstfruits is the flesh of Christ: there the bride was joined to the bridegroom in the flesh.

Rightly, when he commended that very flesh [Note: [Col. 1990] Six manuscripts: “Rightly, in order to commend that very flesh.”], he broke bread; and rightly, in the breaking of the bread, the eyes of the disciples were opened and they recognized him.

What, then, did the Lord say was written about himself in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms? “That it was necessary for Christ to suffer.” If he had not added, “and to rise again,” those whose eyes were held back would rightly have mourned; but his rising again was also foretold. And why was this necessary? Why was it necessary for Christ to suffer and rise again? Because of that psalm that we commended to you especially on Wednesday, at the first station of the last week: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his presence” (Ps. XXI, 28).

For so that you may know that it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise again, notice what he added here, in order that after commending the bridegroom he might also commend the bride: “And that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” [Note: [Col. 1990] Erasmus and the Lyon and Venetian editions: “beginning”; manuscript M.: “beginning,” with a different grammatical form.].

You have heard, brothers; hold fast to it. Let no one doubt concerning the Church, because it is among all nations. Let no one doubt, because it began from Jerusalem and filled all nations. We recognize the field where the vine was planted; but when it has grown, we do not recognize it, because it has occupied everything. Where did it begin? From Jerusalem. Where did it reach? To all nations. A few remain, but it will hold all.

Meanwhile, while it holds all, some branches appeared useless to the gardener and had to be cut off; and they made heresies and schisms. Do not let those cut-off branches draw you in, so that you too may be cut off; rather, exhort what has been cut off to be grafted in again.

It is manifest that Christ suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven. The Church too has been manifested, because repentance and forgiveness of sins are preached in his name among all nations. Where did it begin? “Beginning from Jerusalem.”

A foolish, empty, and—what more shall I say?—blind person hears this, one who does not see so great a mountain, who closes his eyes against a lamp placed on a lampstand.

## 3

When we say to them, “If you are Christian Catholics, join in communion with that Church from which the Gospel is spread throughout the whole world; join in communion with that Jerusalem,” when we say this to them, they answer us, “We do not join in communion with that city where our king was killed, where our Lord was killed,” as though they hated the city where their Lord was killed.

The Jews killed the one whom they found on earth; these people repudiate the one who sits in heaven. Which are worse: those who despised him because they thought he was a human being, or those who insult his sacraments, although they now confess him to be God? Yet they evidently hate the city in which their Lord was killed.

Pious and merciful people! They grieve greatly that Christ was killed, and they kill Christ in human beings! But he loved that city and had mercy on it. From there he said that his preaching should begin: “Beginning from Jerusalem.” There he made the beginning of the preaching of his name; and you recoil from communion with that city [Note: [Col. 1991] Printed editions: “you recoil from communication with that city.” Manuscripts: “communion.”]?

It is no wonder that, having been cut off, you hate the root. What did he say to his disciples? “Remain seated in the city, because I am sending my promise upon you” (Luke XXIV, 13–49). See what city they hate.

Perhaps they would love it if the Jews who killed Christ lived there. For it is manifest that all the killers of Christ—that is, the Jews—were expelled from that city. The city that once held people raging against Christ now holds people worshiping Christ. This is why they hate it: because Christians are there.

There he wished his disciples to remain seated, and there he wished to send them the Holy Spirit. Where was the Church begun, if not where the Holy Spirit came from heaven and filled the one place where one hundred and twenty were sitting? That number twelve had been multiplied tenfold.

One hundred and twenty people were sitting, and the Holy Spirit came and filled the whole place. There was a sound as if a mighty wind were being carried along, and divided tongues appeared as though of fire. You heard the Acts of the Apostles; that very reading was read today [Note: [Col. 1991] The book of Acts was read annually after the Lord’s Passion; see *Tractatus in Evangelium Ioannis* 6, no. 18.]. “They began to speak in tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance.”

And all those who were present there—Jews coming from different nations—each recognized his own language. They marveled that those uneducated and inexperienced men had suddenly learned not one or two languages but absolutely those of all nations (Acts I, 15, and II, 1, 12).

Where, then, all languages were already sounding, it was shown that all languages would believe. But these people, who love Christ greatly and therefore refuse communion with the city that killed Christ, honor Christ in such a way as to say that he remained only among two languages, Latin and Punic—that is, African. Does Christ possess only these two languages? These two languages alone exist in the party of Donatus; they have no more.

Let us awake, brothers. Let us rather see the gift of God’s Spirit, believe what was previously said about it, and see fulfilled what was previously spoken in the Psalm: “There are no languages or speeches whose voices are not heard.” And lest perhaps those languages came to one place, rather than the gift of Christ coming to all languages, hear what follows: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world.” Why is this? “Because he placed his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. XVIII, 4–6), that is, in what is manifest.

His tabernacle is his flesh; his tabernacle is his Church. It has been placed in the sun: it is not in the night but in the day.

But why do they not recognize it? Return to the reading at which we finished yesterday, and see why they do not recognize it: “Whoever hates his brother walks in darkness and does not know where he is going, because darkness has blinded his eyes.”

Let us therefore examine what follows and not be in darkness. How shall we not be in darkness? If we love our brothers. How is it proved that we love brotherhood? Because we do not divide unity, because we hold fast to love.

## 4

“I write to you, little children, because your sins are forgiven through his name.” You are called little children because, your sins having been forgiven, you are born anew. But through whose name are sins forgiven? Through Augustine’s? Then not through Donatus’s name either. Let it be seen who Augustine or who Donatus is: sins are forgiven neither through Paul’s name nor through Peter’s.

For when those who divide the Church among themselves and attempt to make parties out of unity are doing this, motherly love, laboring in the Apostle to give birth to little ones, exposes its entrails, tears its breasts apart, so to speak, with its words, mourns the children whom it sees being carried away, calls back to one name those who wanted to make many names for themselves, drives them away from its love so that Christ may be loved, and says: “Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” (1 Cor. I, 13).

What does he say? “I do not want you to belong to me in order that you may belong with me” [Note: [Col. 1992] Erasmus: “but that you may be with me.” The Lyon and Venetian editions: “but in order that you may be with me.” Manuscript M.: “but that you may be with me.”]. Be with me; we all belong to the one who died for us, who was crucified for us. Hence here too: “Your sins are forgiven through his name,” not through the name of any human being.

## 5

“I write to you, fathers.” Why are they first called children? Because their sins are forgiven through his name, and they are regenerated into a new life; therefore they are children. Why fathers? Because they have known him who is from the beginning; for “beginning” belongs to fatherhood.

Christ is new in the flesh, but ancient in divinity. How ancient do we think he is? How many years old? Do we think he is older than his mother? Certainly older than his mother: for all things were made through him (John I, 3). If all things were made through him, then he who is ancient made his own mother also, from whom the one who was new was to be born.

Do we think he existed only before his mother? He existed also before his mother’s ancestors. Abraham was his mother’s ancestor, and the Lord says, “Before Abraham was, I am” (ibid. VIII, 58).

Before Abraham, you say? Heaven and earth were made before human beings existed. The Lord existed before these things—indeed, he exists. For he did not say, “Before Abraham I was,” but, “Before Abraham I am.” What is said to have been is no longer; what is said to be is not yet. He knows only being. Insofar as he is God, he knows being; he does not know having been or being destined to be.

There is one day there, but it is everlasting. Yesterday and tomorrow do not place that day in the middle: yesterday ends, today begins, and tomorrow will bring today to its end. That one day is there without darkness, without night, without intervals, without measure, without hours. Call it whatever you wish: if you wish, it is a day; if you wish, it is a year; if you wish, it is years. For it was said of him [Note: [Col. 1992] In manuscript B.: “of that day.” Erasmus, the Lyon and Venetian editions, and Lov.: omit the word “day,” rightly, according to M.], “Your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI, 28).

When was he called “day”? When it was said to the Lord, “Today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7). Begotten by the eternal Father, begotten from eternity, begotten in eternity: with no beginning, no end, no interval of extension; because he is what he is, because he is the one who is.
