He declared this name of his to Moses: “You shall say to them, ‘He who is has sent me to you’” (Exod. III, 14).

What, then, existed before Abraham? What before Noah? What before Adam? Hear Scripture: “Before the morning star I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3). Finally, before heaven and earth. Why? Because all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (John I, 3).

Therefore, fathers, recognize him: fathers are made by recognizing him who is from the beginning.

## 6

“I write to you, young men.” They are children, fathers, and young men: children because they are born; fathers because they recognize the beginning. Why young men? Because they have conquered the evil one.

In children there is birth; in fathers, antiquity; in young men, strength. If the evil one is conquered by young men, he fights with us. He fights, but he does not overcome. Why? Because we are strong—or because he is strong in us, who was found weak in the hands of those who persecuted him?

He made us strong, he who did not resist his persecutors. “For he was crucified in weakness, but he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. XIII, 4).

## 7

“I write to you, children.” Why children? Because you have known the Father.

“I write to you, fathers.” He commends this and repeats it [Note: [Col. 1993] The repetition is absent from the Vulgate and from the Greek.]: “Because you have known him who is from the beginning.” Remember that you are fathers. If you forget him who is from the beginning, you have lost your fatherhood.

“I write to you, young men.” Consider again and again that you are young men: fight so that you may conquer; conquer so that you may be crowned; be humble so that you may not fall in battle.

“I write to you, young men, because you are strong, and the word of God remains in you, and you have conquered the evil one.”

## 8

All these things, brothers—because we have known what is from the beginning, because we are strong, because we have known the Father—commend knowledge, as it were, but do they not commend love? If we have known, let us love; for knowledge without love has not saved us. “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (1 Cor. VIII, 1).

If you wish to confess but not love, you begin to become like demons. The demons confessed the Son of God and said, “What have we to do with you?” (Matt. VIII, 29), and they were driven away. Confess and embrace. They feared because of their iniquities; you should love the one who forgives your iniquities.

But how shall we be able to love God if we love the world? Therefore he prepares us to be inhabited by love [Note: [Col. 1993] Erasmus: “But how shall we be able to love God if we love the world? If we love the world, it separates us from the love of God. Therefore it prepares us to inhabit love.” The Lyon edition: “If we love the world? If we love the world, it separates us from the love of God. Therefore it prepares us to inhabit love.” Manuscript M.: “It prepares us to inhabit love.”].

There are two loves: the love of the world and the love of God. If the love of the world dwells within, there is no room for the love of God to enter. Let the love of the world withdraw, and let God’s love dwell there; let the better take its place.

You loved the world; do not love the world. When you have emptied your heart of earthly love, you will draw in divine love, and love will already begin to dwell there, from which no evil can proceed.

Hear, then, the words of one who is now cleansing. He finds the hearts of human beings like a field—but how does he find it? If he finds a forest, he uproots it; if he finds a cleared field, he plants. He wishes to plant there a tree: love. And what forest does he wish to uproot? The love of the world.

Hear the one who uproots the forest: “Do not love the world”—for this follows—“or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

## 9

You have heard that if anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. Let no one say in his heart that this is false, brothers. God says it; the Holy Spirit spoke through the Apostle; nothing is truer: “If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

Do you wish to have the love of the Father, so that you may be a co-heir of the Son? Do not love the world. Exclude the evil love of the world, so that you may be filled with the love of God.

You are a vessel, but you are still full. Pour out what you have, so that you may receive what you do not have.

Certainly our brothers have already been born again from water and the Spirit, and we too were born again from water and the Spirit some years ago. It is good for us not to love the world, lest the sacraments remain in us for condemnation rather than supports for salvation.

The support of salvation is to have the root of love, to have the strength of devotion, not merely its outward form. The form is good, the form is holy; but what good is the form if it does not hold the root? Is not a branch that has been cut off thrown into the fire?

Have the form, but in the root. How are you rooted so that you are not uprooted? By holding fast to love, as the Apostle Paul says: “Rooted and founded in love” (Eph. III, 17).

How will love be rooted there amid so many wooded thickets of love for the world? Uproot the forests. You are about to plant a great seed; let there be nothing in the field that chokes the seed.

These are the words that uproot, which he spoke: “Do not love the world, or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.”

## 10

“For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.” He named three things that are not from the Father but are from the world.

“And the world passes away, and its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as he himself remains forever.”

Why should I not love what God made [Note: [Col. 1994] The words “Why should I not love what God made?” are absent from Ambrosian and Baptist manuscripts and from nine other manuscripts.]? What do you want? To love temporal things and pass away with time, or not to love the world and live forever with God?

The river of temporal things carries us away; but, as it were, beside that river a tree has been planted—our Lord Jesus Christ. He assumed flesh, died, rose again, and ascended into heaven. He wished, in a certain way, to plant himself beside the river of temporal things.

Are you being swept headlong? Hold on to the wood. Does the love of the world whirl you away? Hold on to Christ. For your sake he became temporal, so that you might become eternal; for he too became temporal in such a way that he remained eternal. Something was added to him from time; nothing was taken away from his eternity.

You, however, were born temporal, and through sin you became temporal. You became temporal through sin; he became temporal through the mercy by which he forgives sins.

What a difference there is, when two people are in prison, between the prisoner and the one who visits him! A man sometimes comes to a friend and enters to visit him, and both appear to be in prison; but they are very different and distinct. One is oppressed by the reason for his imprisonment; the other was brought there by humanity.

So, in this mortality, we were held by guilt; he descended through mercy. The redeemer entered to the captive, not as an oppressor.

The Lord shed his blood for us, redeemed us, and changed our hope. We still bear the mortality of the flesh, but we anticipate future immortality. We are tossed on the sea, but we have already fixed the anchor of hope on land.

## 11

But let us not love the world, nor the things that are in the world. For the things that are in the world are the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age.

There are these three things, lest someone perhaps say, “The things that are in the world God made”—that is, heaven and earth, the sea, the sun, the moon, the stars, and all the adornments of the heavens. What are the adornments of the sea? All crawling creatures. Of the earth? Animals, trees, and birds.

These things are in the world; God made them. Why, then, should I not love what God made?

Let the Spirit of God be in you, so that you may see that all these things are good. But woe to you if you love created things and abandon the Creator. They are beautiful to you; but how much more beautiful is he who formed them?

Let your Love pay attention. You can be instructed by comparisons, lest Satan insinuate himself among you, saying what he usually says: “May things go well for you in God’s creation; why did he make them, unless so that things might go well for you?” And people become intoxicated, perish, and forget their Creator. By using created things not temperately but greedily, they despise the Creator.

The Apostle speaks of such people: “They worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever” (Rom. I, 25).

God does not forbid you to love these things, but he forbids you to love them for blessedness. He permits you to approve and praise them so that you may love the Creator.

For example, brothers, suppose a bridegroom made a ring for his bride, and she loved the ring she had received more than the bridegroom who made it for her. Would not the bride’s soul be exposed as adulterous in that very gift, even though she loved what the bridegroom had given? Certainly she loved what the bridegroom had given; yet if she said, “This ring is enough for me; I no longer wish to see his face,” what would she be like? Who would not detest such madness? Who would not convict her of an adulterous heart?

You love gold in place of your husband; you love a ring in place of your bridegroom. If this is in you—that you love the ring in place of your bridegroom and do not wish to see your bridegroom—he gave you the pledge for this purpose: not to make you a pledge, but to turn you to himself. Surely the bridegroom gives the pledge so that he himself may be loved in his pledge.

Therefore God gave you all these things; love him who made them. Greater is what he wishes to give you: namely, himself, who made these things.

But if you love these things, although God made them, and neglect the Creator and love the world, will your love not be judged adulterous [Note: [Col. 1995] Manuscripts: “and if you love the world, you sin.” Ambrosian and Baptist manuscripts and Erasmus: “and if you love the world, you lose the Creator who made the world.”]?

## 12

For “world” refers not only to this structure that God made—heaven and earth, the sea, visible and invisible things—but the inhabitants of the world are also called “world,” just as a house refers both to its walls and to those who inhabit it.

Sometimes we praise a house and blame its inhabitants. We say, “A good house,” because it is faced with marble and beautifully coffered; and in another sense we say, “A good house,” because no one there suffers injury, and no robberies or oppressions occur there.

In the latter case we are not praising the walls but the inhabitants of the walls. Yet it is called a house in either case.

All lovers of the world, because they inhabit the world through love, are called “world,” just as those whose heart is above inhabit heaven while they walk in the flesh on earth. Therefore all lovers of the world are called “world.”

They have nothing but these three things: the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age. For they desire to eat, drink, have intercourse, and use these pleasures.

Does this mean there is no limit in such things? Or when it is said, “Do not love these things,” is the meaning that you should not eat, drink, or beget children? That is not what is being said. Rather, let there be moderation for the sake of the Creator, so that these things do not bind you through love, lest you love for enjoyment what you ought to possess for use.

You are not tested unless two things are set before you: this or that. “Do you want justice, or profits?” “I have no means by which to live; I have no means by which to eat or drink.” But what if you cannot have these things except through wrongdoing? Is it not better to love what you do not lose than to commit wrongdoing?

You see the profit of gold but do not see the loss of faith. This, then, he says, is the desire of the flesh—that is, the desire for things that pertain to the flesh, such as food, intercourse, and other things of this kind.

## 13

“And the desire of the eyes.” By “the desire of the eyes” he means every kind of curiosity. How widely does curiosity extend? It is found in spectacles, in theaters, in the sacraments of the devil, in magical arts, and in sorceries.

Sometimes it even tempts God’s servants, so that they want, as though to perform a miracle, to test whether God will hear them in miracles. This is curiosity, that is, the desire of the eyes; it is not from the Father.

If God has given you the gift, perform it; he has offered it so that you may perform it. For those who have not performed such things will not therefore fail to belong to the kingdom of God.

When the Apostles rejoiced because demons were subject to them, what did the Lord say to them? “Do not rejoice in this, but rejoice that your names are written in heaven” (Luke X, 20). He wanted the Apostles to rejoice in what you too rejoice in. For woe to you if your name is not written in heaven.

Is there woe for you if you have not raised a dead person? Is there woe for you if you have not walked on the sea? Is there woe for you if you have not driven out demons? If you have received the means to do such things, use them humbly, not proudly.

For the Lord also said concerning certain false prophets that they would perform signs and wonders (Matt. XXIV, 24). Therefore let there be no ambition of the age. The ambition of the age is pride. A person wishes to display himself in honors; he seems great to himself, whether because of riches or because of some power.

## 14

These are the three things, and you find no way in which human desire is tempted except by the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, or the ambition of the age.

By these three things the Lord was tempted by the devil. He was tempted by the desire of the flesh when it was said to him, “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves,” when he was hungry after fasting. But how did he repel the tempter and teach the soldier how to fight? Notice what he said to him: “Human beings do not live by bread alone, but by every word of God.”

He was also tempted by the desire of the eyes, through a miracle, when the devil said to him, “Throw yourself down, for it is written, ‘He has commanded his angels concerning you, that they may receive you, lest you strike your foot against a stone.’”

He resisted the tempter. For if he had performed a miracle then, it would have seemed that he had done so either because he yielded or because he acted out of curiosity. He performed miracles when he wished, as God, but as one healing the weak. If he had done it then, he would have seemed merely to have wanted to perform a miracle.

But so that people would not think this, notice what he answered. And when such a temptation comes to you, say this too: “Get behind me, Satan; for it is written, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God’”—that is, “If I do this, I shall tempt God.” He said what he wanted you to say.

When the enemy suggests to you, “What kind of person are you, what kind of Christian? Have you ever performed even one miracle? Have the dead risen through your prayers, or have you healed the feverish? If you truly had any standing [Note: [Col. 1997] The old Theoderician manuscript has “merit.”], you would perform some miracle,” answer and say, “It is written, ‘You shall not tempt the Lord your God.’ Therefore I shall not tempt God, as though I belonged to God if I performed a miracle and did not belong to him if I did not.”

And what of his words, “Rejoice because your names are written in heaven”?

How was the Lord tempted by the ambition of the age? When the devil raised him up on high and said to him, “All these things I will give you if you fall down and worship me.” By the exaltation of an earthly kingdom he wished to tempt the King of the ages [Note: [Col. 1997] Three manuscripts have “of the heavens.”]. But the Lord, who made heaven and earth, was trampling on the devil.

What great thing was it for the Lord to conquer the devil? What, then, did he answer the devil, except what he taught you to answer? “It is written, ‘You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve’” (Matt. IV, 1–10).

Holding fast to these things, you will not have desire for the world. Without desire for the world, neither the desire of the flesh, nor the desire of the eyes, nor the ambition of the age will subjugate you. And you will make room for love as it comes, so that you may love God.

For if the love of the world is present, the love of God will not be present. Hold fast rather to the love of God, so that just as God is eternal, you too may remain forever. For each person is such as his love is.

Do you love earth? You will be earth. Do you love God? What shall I say? Shall I say, “You will be God”? I do not dare to say this on my own; let us hear the Scriptures: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High’” (Ps. LXXXI, 6).

If, then, you wish to be gods and sons of the Most High, do not love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him.

For everything that is in the world is the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the ambition of the age, which is not from the Father but from the world—that is, from human beings who love the world.

And the world passes away, and its desires; but whoever does the will of God remains forever, just as God remains forever.

# TRACTATE III

Concerning what follows, “Children, it is the last hour,” up to, “His anointing teaches you about everything.” Chapter II, verses 18–27.

1. “Little children, it is the last hour.” In this reading he addresses the little ones, urging them to hasten to maturity, because it is the last hour. Bodily age does not depend on the will. Thus no one grows according to the flesh whenever he wishes, just as no one is born whenever he wishes; but where birth depends on the will, growth also depends on the will. No one is born of [Col. 1998] water and the Spirit unless he wills it. Therefore, if he wills it, he grows; if he wills it, he diminishes. What does it mean to grow? To make progress. What does it mean to diminish? To fail. Whoever knows that he has been born should hear that he is a child and an infant; let him eagerly cling to his mother’s breasts, and he will quickly grow. The mother is the Church; and her two breasts are the two Testaments of the divine Scriptures. From them let him suck the milk of all the mysteries accomplished in time for our eternal salvation, so that, nourished and strengthened, he may arrive at eating the food which is: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). Our milk is Christ in his humility; our food is that same Christ, equal to the Father. He nourishes you with milk so that he may feed you with bread: for to touch Jesus spiritually with the heart is to know that he is equal to the Father.

2. For this reason he also forbade Mary to touch him, saying to her: “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father.” What does this mean? He offered himself to the disciples to be touched, yet avoided Mary’s touch? Is he not the one who said to the doubting disciple, “Put your fingers here, and touch the scars” (ibid. 20:17, 27)? Had he by then ascended to the Father? Why, then, does he forbid Mary and say, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father”? Are we to say that he did not fear being touched by men but feared being touched by women? His touch cleanses every flesh. Did he fear being handled by those to whom he first wished to reveal himself? Was not his resurrection announced to the men through women, so that the serpent might be conquered by a contrary strategy? For since he had first announced death to the first man through a woman, life was announced to men through a woman. Why, then, did he not wish to be touched, unless he wished that touch to be understood spiritually? Spiritual touch comes from a pure heart. He touches Christ from a pure heart who understands him to be coequal with the Father. But whoever does not yet understand Christ’s divinity comes only as far as the flesh; he does not reach as far as the divinity. What great thing is it to reach only as far as those who persecuted and crucified him reached? The great thing is to understand that the Word was God with God in the beginning, through whom all things were made: to know him as he wished to be known when he said to Philip, “Have I been with you for so long a time, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

3. But so that no one may be sluggish about making progress, let him hear: “Little children, it is the last hour.” Make progress, run, grow: it is the last hour. That last hour is prolonged; nevertheless, it is the last hour. For he used “hour” to mean the final period, because our Lord Jesus Christ will come in the last times. But some will say: “How is it the final period? How is it the last hour? Surely the Antichrist will come first, and then the day of judgment will come.” John saw these thoughts. Lest they become secure and therefore think that it was not the last hour because the Antichrist was going to come, he said to them: “And just as you heard that the Antichrist is coming, now many antichrists have arisen.” Could there be many antichrists unless it were the last hour?

4. Whom did he call antichrists? He goes on and explains: “From this we know that it is the last hour.” From what? “Because [Col. 1999] many antichrists have arisen.” “They went out from us”: behold the antichrists. “They went out from us”: therefore we mourn the loss. Hear the consolation: “But they were not of us.” All heretics, all schismatics, went out from us—that is, they go out from the Church—but they would not go out if they were of us. Before they went out, therefore, they were not of us. If, before they went out, they were not of us, many are inside who have not gone out and yet are antichrists. Do we dare say this? Why else, unless so that each person, while he is inside, may not be an antichrist? For he is about to describe and identify the antichrists, and we shall see them now. Each person ought to question his own conscience whether he is an antichrist.

In Latin, *Antichristus* means “one opposed to Christ.” It does not mean what some understand: that he is called Antichrist because he will come before Christ—that is, that Christ will come after him. It is not said or written in that way; rather, Antichrist means “opposed to Christ.” Now you understand who is opposed to Christ, with him himself explaining it, and you understand that those who are antichrists alone can go out; whereas those who are not opposed to Christ cannot possibly go out. For whoever is not opposed to Christ clings to his body and is counted as a member. Members are never opposed to one another. The integrity of the body consists in all its members. And what does the Apostle say about the harmony of the members? “If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it” (1 Corinthians 12:26). If, then, the other members rejoice in the glorification of one member, and all the members suffer in its suffering, the harmony of the members has no antichrist.

There are also those who are inside the body of our Lord Jesus Christ in the manner of harmful fluids, since his body is still being healed and perfect health will not come until the resurrection of the dead. They are in the body of Christ as bad humors. When they are vomited out, the body is relieved; so also, when the wicked go out, the Church is relieved. And the body says when it vomits them out and casts them away: “These humors went out from me, but they were not of me.” What does “they were not of me” mean? They were not cut away from my flesh; rather, while they were within me, they pressed upon my breast.

5. “They went out from us”; but do not be sad: “they were not of us.” How do you prove it? “For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” Let your Charity therefore see that many who are not of us receive the Sacraments with us; they receive Baptism with us; they receive with us what the faithful know they receive: the Benediction, the Eucharist [Note: [Col. 1999] In two manuscripts: “the Benediction of the Eucharist”]; they receive with us participation in the altar itself, and yet they are not of us. Temptation proves that they are not of us. When temptation comes upon them, they fly out as though driven by a gust of wind, because they were not grain. All, however, will then fly away—as must often be said—when the Lord’s threshing floor begins to be winnowed on the day of judgment.

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” Now, beloved, do you wish to know how certainly this is said, so that those who perhaps have gone out and return may not be antichrists, may not be opposed to Christ? Those who are not antichrists [Note: [Col. 2000] In most manuscripts: “so that those who perhaps have gone out may not be antichrists. Let them return, and they are not opposed to Christ: for these are the antichrists. It cannot happen that they remain,” etc.] cannot remain outside. But each person is, by his own will, either an antichrist or in Christ. We are either among the members or among the harmful fluids. Whoever changes himself for the better is a member in the body; whoever persists in wickedness is a harmful fluid, and when he goes out, those who were being oppressed are relieved.

“They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us”—but this happened “so that they might be shown not all to be of us.” He added “so that they might be shown,” because even while they are inside they are not of us; nevertheless, they are not manifest, but by going out they are revealed. “And you have an anointing from the Holy One, so that you yourselves may be manifest to yourselves.” The spiritual anointing is the Holy Spirit himself, whose sacrament is present in visible anointing. Christ says that all who possess this anointing recognize the wicked and the good, and that they do not need to be taught, because the anointing itself teaches them.

6. “I write to you, not because you do not know the truth, but because you know it, and because every lie is not from the truth.” Behold, we have been instructed how to recognize the Antichrist. What is Christ? Truth. He himself said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Every lie, however, is not from the truth. Therefore all who lie are not yet of Christ. He did not say that one kind of lie is from the truth and another kind is not from the truth. Attend to the sentence; do not flatter yourselves, do not fawn upon yourselves, do not deceive yourselves, do not mock yourselves: “Every lie is not from the truth.”

Let us therefore see how the antichrists lie, since there is not only one kind of lie. “Who is the liar but the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?” Jesus has one meaning, Christ another. Although Jesus Christ our Savior is one, “Jesus” is nevertheless his proper name. As Moses is called by his proper name, and Elijah, and Abraham, so our Lord has “Jesus” as a kind of proper name. “Christ,” however, is the name of a sacrament. As he is called a prophet, or a priest, so Christ is proclaimed as the anointed one, in whom the redemption of the whole people of Israel would reside.

This Christ was expected by the Jewish people to come; and because he came in humility, he was not recognized. Because he was a small stone, they stumbled over him and were broken. But the stone grew and became a great mountain (Daniel 2:35). And what does Scripture say? “Whoever stumbles over that stone will be shattered; and upon whomever that stone falls, it will crush him” (Luke 20:18). The words must be distinguished: he said that the one who stumbles will be shattered, but that the one upon whom it falls will be crushed. First, because he came in humility, people stumbled over him; because he will come in exaltation to judgment, he will crush the one upon whom he falls. But when he comes, he will not crush the one whom he did not shatter when he came. Whoever did not stumble over him in his humility will not fear him in his exaltation.

In brief, brothers, you have heard: whoever did not stumble over him in his humility will not fear him in his exaltation. For Christ is a stone of stumbling to all the wicked; whatever Christ says is bitter to them.

7. Indeed, listen and see. All who leave [Col. 2001] the Church and are cut off from the unity of the Church are antichrists; let no one doubt it. He himself identified them: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” Whoever therefore does not remain with us but goes out from us is plainly an antichrist.

And how are the antichrists proved? By a lie. “Who is the liar but the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ?” Let us question the heretics: which heretic do you find who denies that Jesus is the Christ? Let your Charity see the great sacrament. Attend to what the Lord God has inspired in us and what I wish to convey to you. Behold, they went out from us and became Donatists. We ask them whether Jesus is the Christ; immediately they confess that Jesus Christ is the Christ. If, then, the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ is an antichrist, they cannot call us antichrists, nor can we call them antichrists, because both we and they confess it. If neither they call us antichrists nor we call them antichrists, then neither they went out from us nor we from them.

If, then, we did not go out from them, we are in unity. If we are in unity, what are two altars doing in this city? What are divided households doing, divided marriages? What is a shared bed doing with Christ divided? He admonishes us; he wishes us to confess what is true. Either they went out from us, or we from them. But far be it from us to have gone out from them: we possess the testament of the Lord’s inheritance, we read it, and there we find ourselves: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2:8).

We hold Christ’s inheritance; they do not hold it. They do not share in the whole world; they do not share in the entire people redeemed by the Lord’s blood. We have the Lord himself, risen from the dead, who offered himself to the hands of his doubting disciples to be touched. And while they still doubted, he said to them: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and forgiveness of sins to be preached in his name. Where? In what place? To whom? Among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47). We are secure concerning the unity of the inheritance. Whoever does not share in this inheritance has gone outside.

8. But let us not be saddened: “They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.” If they went out from us, they are antichrists; if they are antichrists, they are liars; if they are liars, they deny that Jesus is the Christ.

Again we return to the difficulty of the question. Ask each one individually; they confess that Jesus is the Christ. A narrow understanding constrains us in this Epistle. You certainly see the problem. This question disturbs both us and them if it is not understood. Either we are the antichrists, or they are the antichrists. They call us antichrists and say that we went out from them; we say the same of them. But this Epistle has identified the antichrists: whoever denies that Jesus is the Christ is himself the antichrist.

Let us then ask who denies it, and let us not attend to the tongue but to deeds. For if all are questioned, all confess with one voice that Jesus is the Christ. Let the tongue be silent for a little while; question the life. If we discover this—if Scripture itself tells us that [Col. 2002] denial is made not only with the tongue but also by deeds—then certainly we find many antichrists who profess Christ with their mouths but disagree with Christ in their conduct.

Where do we find this in Scripture? Listen to the Apostle Paul. Speaking of such people, he says: “For they profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). We find these people to be antichrists as well: whoever denies Christ by his deeds is an antichrist. I do not listen to what sounds from his mouth; I see how he lives. His works speak, and we still ask for words? For what wicked person does not wish to speak well? But what does the Lord say to such people? “Hypocrites, how can you speak good things when you are evil?” (Matthew 12:34). You bring your voices to my ears; I inspect your thoughts. I see an evil will there, and you display false fruits. I know from what I gather; I do not gather figs from thistles, nor grapes from thornbushes. “Each tree is known by its fruit” (ibid. 7:16).

The antichrist is more truly a liar when he professes with his mouth that Jesus is the Christ but denies him by his deeds. He is a liar because he says one thing and does another.

9. Now, brothers, if deeds are to be questioned, we find not only that many antichrists have gone outside, but also that many who have not yet been revealed have not gone outside at all. All the perjurers, deceivers, sorcerers, consultors of fortune-tellers, adulterers, drunkards, usurers, slave-dealers, and all the others whom we cannot count—whatever is contrary to the doctrine of Christ is contrary to the word of God; and the Word of God is Christ. Whatever is contrary to the Word of God is in the Antichrist. For the Antichrist is opposed to Christ.

And do you wish to know how openly these people resist Christ? Sometimes it happens that they do something wicked and begin to be reproved. Because they do not dare to blaspheme Christ, they blaspheme his ministers, by whom they are reproved. But if you show them that you are speaking Christ’s words, not your own, they try as hard as they can to convince you that you are speaking your own words, not Christ’s. If it becomes clear that you are speaking Christ’s words, they turn against Christ and begin to criticize Christ: “How and why,” they say, “did he make us such people?”

Do people convicted of their deeds not say this every day? Perverted by a depraved will, they accuse the craftsman. The craftsman cries out to them from heaven—for he himself made us, the one who remade us: “What did I make you? I made a human being, not greed; I made a human being, not robbery; I made a human being, not adultery.”

You have heard that my works praise me. From the mouths of the three young men came the hymn itself that protected them from the fires (Daniel 3:24–90). The works of the Lord praise the Lord: heaven praises him, earth praises him, the sea praises him; everything that is in heaven praises him; angels praise him, stars praise him, the heavenly lights praise him; whatever swims, whatever flies, whatever walks, whatever crawls—all these things praise the Lord.

Have you ever heard that greed praises the Lord? Have you heard that drunkenness praises the Lord, that lust praises him, that frivolity praises him? Whatever you do not hear there praising the Lord, the Lord did not make. Correct what you yourself made, so that what God made in you may be saved. But if you are unwilling, and love and embrace your sins, you are opposed to Christ. Whether you are inside or [Col. 2003] outside, you are an antichrist; whether you are inside or outside, you are chaff. But why are you not outside? Because you have not found an opportunity for the wind.

10. These things are now clear, brothers. Let no one say: “I do not worship Christ, but I worship his Father, God.” Everyone who denies the Son has neither the Son nor the Father; and whoever confesses the Son has both the Son and the Father.

He addresses you as grain; let those who were chaff hear and become grain. Each person, examining his conscience, should change if he is a lover of the world; let him become a lover of Christ, so that he may not be an antichrist. If someone tells him that he is an antichrist, he becomes angry and thinks that an insult has been inflicted upon him. Perhaps he even threatens a lawsuit if he hears from an adversary that he is an antichrist. Christ says to him: “Be patient. If you have heard something false, rejoice with me, because I too hear false things from the antichrists. But if you have heard something true, confront your conscience; and if you are afraid to hear it, be more afraid to be what it says.”

11. Therefore, let what you heard from the beginning remain in you. If what you heard from the beginning remains in you, you too will remain in the Son and in the Father. This is the promise that he himself made to us.

Perhaps you were seeking a reward and said: “Behold, I preserve and obey what I heard from the beginning. For this perseverance I endure dangers, labors, and temptations. What fruit will I receive? What reward? What will he give me afterward, since in this world I see myself laboring amid temptations? I do not see any rest here. Mortality itself weighs down the soul, and the body that is subject to decay presses it toward lower things. Yet I endure everything so that what I heard from the beginning may remain in me, and I will say to my God: ‘Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways’” (Psalm 16:4).

What reward, then? Listen, and do not fail. If you were failing in your labors, be strong because of the promised reward. Who works in a vineyard and allows the reward he is going to receive to depart from his heart? Make him forget his reward, and his hands grow weak. The memory of the promised reward makes him persevere in his work—and a human being made the promise, a human being who can deceive you.

How much stronger ought you to be in God’s field, when the one who made the promise is Truth, whom no successor can replace, who cannot die, and who cannot deceive the person to whom the promise has been made?

And what has been promised? Let us see what he promised. Is it gold, which people greatly love here? Or silver? Or estates, into which people pour gold, although they love gold so much? Or pleasant farms, spacious houses, many slaves, and numerous animals? This is not the kind of reward to which he exhorts us, so that we may endure in our labor. What is this reward called? Eternal life.

You heard it, and you cried out with joy. Love what you heard, and be freed from your labors into the rest of eternal life. Behold what God promises: eternal life. Behold what God threatens: eternal fire. What does he say to those placed on the right? “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world.” And to those on the left? “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:34, 41). If you do not yet love the former, at least fear the latter.

12. Remember, therefore, my brothers, that Christ promised us eternal life: “This is the promise that he himself made to us: eternal life.” “I have written these things to you concerning those who are leading you astray.” Let no one lead you astray [Col. 2004] into death; desire the promise of eternal life.

What can the world promise? Let it promise whatever it likes; perhaps it is making a promise to someone who will die tomorrow. And with what face will you go out to meet the one who remains forever? “But a powerful person threatens me so that I will do something evil.” What does he threaten? Prisons, chains, fires, tortures, wild beasts—but not eternal fire? Fear what the Almighty threatens; love what the Almighty promises; and the whole world becomes worthless, whether it promises or frightens.

“I have written these things to you concerning those who are leading you astray, so that you may know that you have an anointing, and that the anointing which we received from him” [Note: [Col. 2004] Two manuscripts read: “and that you have the anointing which you received from him,” omitting “so that you may know that you have an anointing.”] “may remain in us.”

The sacrament of anointing is the invisible power itself. The invisible anointing is the Holy Spirit. The invisible anointing is that love which, wherever it exists, will be like a root for the person in whom it is found; although the sun burns fiercely, it cannot wither. Everything that is rooted is nourished by the sun’s heat and does not wither.

13. “And you have no need for anyone to teach you, because his anointing teaches you about everything.” What, then, are we doing, brothers, since we teach you? If his anointing teaches you about everything, it seems that we labor in vain. And why do we shout so loudly? Let us leave you to his anointing, and let his anointing teach you.

But now I pose a question to myself, and I pose it to that same Apostle. May he deign to hear a little one asking him a question. I say to John himself: “Did those to whom you were speaking have the anointing?” You said: “His anointing teaches you about everything.” Why, then, did you compose such an Epistle? What were you teaching them? What were you instructing? What were you building up?

Here, brothers, see the great sacrament: the sound of our words strikes the ears, but the teacher is within. Do not suppose that anyone learns anything from a human being. We can admonish through the noise of our voice; but if there is not one within who teaches, our noise is empty. Indeed, brothers, do you wish to know? Have you not all heard this sermon? How many will leave here still unlearned?

As far as I am concerned, I have spoken to everyone; but those to whom that anointing does not speak within, those whom the Holy Spirit does not teach within, return unlearned. External teaching is a kind of assistance and admonition. The one who teaches hearts has his chair in heaven. Therefore he himself also says in the Gospel: “Do not call anyone your teacher on earth; one is your teacher, Christ” (Matthew 23:8–9).

Let him therefore speak to you within, when no human being is there; for even if someone is beside you, no one is in your heart. And let your heart not be empty [Note: [Col. 2004] Three manuscripts read: “And let no one be in your heart.” One reads: “And let no one be in your heart.” Another: “And let no one be in your heart.”]: let Christ be in your heart; let his anointing be in your heart, so that your heart may not be thirsty in solitude and lack springs by which it can be watered.

The inner teacher, then, is the one who teaches. Christ teaches; his inspiration teaches. Where his inspiration and his anointing are absent, words resound externally to no purpose. These words that we speak externally, brothers, are like the farmer in relation to the tree. Externally he works; he supplies water and the care of cultivation. But can he form the fruit? Can he clothe the nakedness of the branches with the shade [Col. 2005] of leaves? Does he do anything of this kind within? Who does it, then? Listen to the Apostle as farmer, see what we are, and listen to the inner teacher: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3:6–7).

This, then, is what we say to you: whether we plant or water by speaking, we are nothing; rather, it is God who gives the growth—that is, his anointing, which teaches you about everything.

## TREATISE IV

On what follows, “And he is true, and there is no lie”; up to “For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, to destroy the works of the devil.” Chapter II, verses 27–29, and chapter III, verses 1–8.

1. You remember, brothers, that yesterday’s reading ended at the point that you have no need for anyone to teach you, but that the anointing itself teaches you about everything. I am sure that we explained this to you as follows: we who speak externally to your ears are like laborers who cultivate a tree externally, but cannot give it growth or form its fruits. He, however, who created you, redeemed you, and called you, dwelling in you through faith and through his Spirit—unless he speaks to you within, we make our noise in vain.

How does this become evident? Because although many hear, what is said does not persuade everyone, but only those to whom God speaks within. He speaks within to those who give him room; and they give God room who do not give room to the devil. For the devil wishes to inhabit the hearts of human beings and to speak there everything that can lead them astray.

But what does the Lord Jesus say? “The ruler of this world has been cast out” (John 12:31). From where has he been cast out? Surely not outside heaven and earth? Surely not outside the structure of the world [Note: [Col. 2005] The printed editions add here “No,” a word absent from the manuscripts]? Rather, outside the hearts of believers. Once the invader has been cast out, let the redeemer dwell within [Note: [Col. 2005] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Venetian edition read: “let him dwell”; manuscript M reads: “he dwells”]; for the one who created is himself the one who redeemed. The devil now attacks externally but does not conquer the one whom Christ possesses within. He attacks externally by sending various temptations; but the person to whom God speaks within, and whose anointing you have heard of, does not consent.

2. “And it is true,” he says—that same anointing; that is, the Spirit of the Lord himself, who teaches human beings, cannot lie. “And it is not a lie. Just as it taught you, remain in it” [Note: [Col. 2005] Two manuscripts read: “in him.”]. “And now, little children, remain in him, so that when he is manifested we may have confidence in his presence and not be put to shame by him at his coming.”

You see, brothers [Note: [Col. 2005] Erasmus, the Lyon edition, Lovanius, and the Venetian edition read: “See, brothers.” Manuscript M reads: “You see, brothers.”]: we believe in Jesus whom we have not seen. Those who saw him, touched him, and heard the word from his mouth announced him; and in order to persuade the human race of these things, they were sent by him and did not dare to go on their own.

Where were they sent? You heard it when the Gospel was read: “Go, preach the Gospel to every creature under heaven” (Mark 16:15). The disciples were therefore sent everywhere, [Col. 2006] with signs and wonders bearing witness so that people might believe them, because they were saying what they had seen.

We believe in him whom we have not seen, and we await his coming. Whoever awaits him in faith will rejoice when he comes; those who are without faith will be ashamed when what they do not now see comes. That shame will not last for one day and then pass, as happens when people are found guilty of some offense and are mocked by others. That shame will lead the ashamed to the left, so that they may hear: “Go into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25:31).

Let us therefore remain in his words, so that we may not be put to shame when he comes. For he himself says in the Gospel to those who had believed in him: “If you remain in my word, you are truly my disciples.” And as though they were saying, “With what benefit?” he continues: “And you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8:31–32).

For now our salvation is in hope, not yet in reality. We do not yet possess what has been promised; we hope for what is to come. But the one who promised is faithful; he does not deceive you. Only do not fail; await the promise. Truth does not know how to deceive. Do not be a liar, professing one thing and doing another. Keep faith, and he will keep his promise. But if you do not keep faith, you have defrauded yourself, not the one who made the promise.

3. “If you know that he is righteous, know also that everyone who does righteousness has been born from him.” Our righteousness now comes from faith. Perfect righteousness exists only in the angels—and scarcely even in the angels, if they are compared with God. Nevertheless, if there is any perfect righteousness among the souls and spirits whom God created, it is in the holy, just, and good angels, who have not turned away through any lapse or fallen through pride, but remain always in contemplation of the Word of God and find nothing else sweet except the one by whom they were created. In them there is perfect righteousness.

In us, however, righteousness has begun according to the Spirit, from faith. You heard it when the Psalm was read: “Begin with confession to the Lord” (Psalm 146:7). “Begin,” he says. The beginning of our righteousness is confession of sins. You have begun not to defend your sin; you have already begun righteousness. It will be perfected in you when nothing else gives you pleasure, when “death is swallowed up in victory” (1 Corinthians 15:54), when no desire will titillate you, when there will be no struggle with flesh and blood, when there will be the crown of victory and triumph over the enemy. Then righteousness will be perfect.

For now we are still fighting. If we are fighting, we are in the arena; we strike and are struck. But the one who will conquer is awaited. He conquers, however, who does not presume upon his own strength even in striking, but relies upon God, who exhorts him [Note: [Col. 2006] Seven manuscripts read: “who protects him.”]

The devil alone fights against us. If we are with God, we conquer the devil; but if you fight the devil alone, you are conquered. He is an experienced enemy. How many victories has he had? Consider whom he cast down: in order that we might be born mortal, he first cast our very origin out of paradise.

What, then, must be done, since he is experienced? Let the Almighty be invoked against the experienced devil. Let the one who cannot be conquered dwell in you, and you will safely conquer the one who is accustomed to conquer. But whom does he conquer? Those in whom God does not dwell.

For, so that you may know, brothers, Adam, placed in paradise, despised God’s command [Col. 2007] and raised his neck, as though wishing to be in his own power and unwilling to submit to the will of God; and he fell from that immortality and that blessedness (Genesis 3:6). But another human being, already experienced, born mortal, while he sat upon a dungheap full of rotting worms, conquered the devil. Adam himself also conquered—in Job, because Job was of Adam’s race. Therefore Adam, defeated in paradise, conquered on the dungheap.

When he was in paradise, Adam listened to the persuasion of the woman whom the devil had incited against him. But when he was on the dungheap, he said to Eve: “You are speaking as one of the foolish women speaks” (Job 2:10). There he lent his ear; here he gave an answer. When he was happy, he listened; when he was scourged, he conquered.

Therefore see what follows, brothers, in this Epistle, because it commends to us that we should indeed conquer the devil, but not from ourselves. “If you know that he is righteous,” he says, “know also that everyone who does righteousness has been born from him”—from God, from Christ. And because he said, “He has been born from him,” he exhorts us. Now, then, because we have been born from him, we are perfect.

4. Listen: “See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God—and that we are.” For those who are called but are not what they are called, what benefit is there in a name where the reality is absent? How many are called physicians who do not know how to heal? How many are called watchmen who sleep all night? In the same way, many are called Christians but are not found to be so in reality, because they are not what they are called to be—in life, conduct, faith, hope, and love.

But what did you hear here, brothers? “See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God—and that we are. For this reason the world does not know us, because it did not know him, and the world does not know us.”

The whole world is Christian, and the whole world is impious; for throughout the whole world there are impious people, and throughout the whole world there are godly people. The former do not recognize the latter. How do we understand “they do not recognize”? They mock those who live well.

Attend and see, for perhaps such people are even among you. Whoever among you now lives piously, despises worldly things, does not wish to go to the spectacles, does not wish to become drunk as though it were a solemn celebration—and, what is worse, does not wish, with the patronage of holy days added, to become defiled—if he refuses to do these things, how is he mocked by those who do them? Would he be mocked if they recognized him? Why, then, is he not recognized? The world does not recognize him.

What is “the world”? The inhabitants of the world, just as a house is named after its inhabitants. These things have often been said, and we do not repeat them to you with disgust [Note: [Col. 2007] The printed editions read: “And we do not repeat them with you today.” Three manuscripts more suitably read: “we do not repeat them to you with disgust.” Thus also below, Treatise 7, no. 1: “Nor should it be feared, he says, that by saying it often it will become hateful.”].

When you hear “the world” in a negative sense, understand nothing except those who love the world, because they inhabit it through love and have deserved to bear the name of that which they inhabit.

“For this reason the world did not know us, because it did not know him.” The Lord Jesus Christ himself also walked among them. God was present in the flesh, hidden in weakness. Why was he not recognized? Because he reproved all sins in human beings. By loving the pleasures of sins, they did not recognize God; by loving [Col. 2008] what the fever urged, they wronged the physician.

5. What, then, are we? We have already been born from him; but because we are still in hope, he says, “Beloved, now we are children of God.” Now? What, then, are we waiting for, if we are already children of God? “And it has not yet been manifested,” he says, “what we shall be.” What else shall we be, then, except children of God? Hear what follows: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Let Your Charity understand. A great matter: “We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” Now consider what is called “is.” You know what is called “is.” It is what is called “is,” and it is not merely called so, but truly is; it is unchangeable, always remains, knows no alteration, and is in no way corrupted. It does not advance, because it is perfect; it does not decline, because it is eternal. And what is this? “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). And what is this? “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped” (Philippians 2:6).

The wicked cannot see Christ in this form of God—the Word of God, the Only-Begotten equal to the Father. But insofar as “the Word became flesh,” even the wicked will be able to see him, because on the day of judgment the wicked too will see him: he will come to judge in the same manner in which he came to be judged. In that very form he is human, yet God; for “cursed is everyone who places his hope in a human being” (Jeremiah 17:5). A human being came to be judged; a human being will come to judge.

And if he will not be seen, what is meant by the text, “They will look upon him whom they pierced” (John 19:37)? It was said of the ungodly that they will see and be put to shame. How will the ungodly not see him, when he places some at his right hand and others at his left? To those placed at his right hand he will say, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom”; to those placed at his left he will say, “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25:34, 41). They will see the form of a servant; they will not see the form of God. Why? Because they are ungodly. The Lord himself says, “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5:8).

Therefore, brothers, we shall behold a certain vision “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart” (1 Corinthians 2:9): a vision surpassing every earthly beauty—the beauty of gold and silver, of woods and fields, the beauty of the sea and air, the beauty of the sun and moon, the beauty of the stars, the beauty of the angels—surpassing all things, because from it all things are beautiful.

6. What, then, shall we be when we see this? What has been promised to us? “We shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.” As far as the tongue could, it has spoken; let the rest be contemplated in the heart. What could John himself say in comparison with the One who is, or what can be said by us, whose merits are so far inferior to his?

Let us return, then, to that anointing of his; let us return to that anointing which inwardly teaches what we cannot express. And because you cannot yet see, let your task be one of longing. The entire life of a good Christian is holy longing. What you desire, you do not yet see; but by desiring, you become capable of being filled when what you are to see arrives.

For just as, if you wished to fill some container and knew how great the gift would be, you would stretch out the opening of a sack, a wineskin, or some other vessel—you would know how much you were going to put in and see that the opening was too narrow, and by stretching it you would make it more capacious—so God, by delaying, stretches desire; by desire he stretches the soul; by stretching it, he makes it capable. Let us long, then, brothers, because we are to be filled.

See Paul stretching out his capacity so that he may receive what is to come. He says: “Not that I have already received it, or am already perfect; brothers, I do not consider myself to have grasped it. But one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue according to my intention toward the prize of the heavenly calling” (Philippians 3:13–14). He said that he was stretched out, and that he pursued according to his intention. He felt himself too small to receive what “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart.”

This is our life: to be exercised by longing. Holy longing exercises us only insofar as we have cut away our desires from love of the world. We have said before: “Empty out what is to be filled” [Note: [Col. 2009] This should be read in this way, as supported by the Ambrosian, the Basle edition, and eight manuscripts, except that the punctuation of the words is worse in all the manuscripts: “We have said before that what is to be filled must be emptied out.”].

You are to be filled with good; pour out evil. Suppose God wishes to fill you with honey: if you are full of vinegar, where will you put the honey? What the vessel contained must be poured out; the vessel itself must be cleansed. It must be cleansed, even with labor and grinding, so that it may become fit for its purpose.

Let us call it the sea, let us call it gold, let us call it wine; whatever we call what cannot be adequately named, whatever we wish to say, it is called God. And when we say “God,” what have we said? Are these two syllables the whole of what we await? Whatever, therefore, we are able to say is less than the reality. Let us stretch ourselves toward him, so that when he comes, he may fill us. “For we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is.”

7. “And everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself.” You see that he has placed us in hope. You see how the Apostle Paul agrees with his fellow apostle: “We were saved in hope.” “But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with patience” (Romans 8:24–25).

That very patience exercises desire. Remain where you are, for he remains; persevere in walking, so that you may arrive, because the one toward whom you are journeying will not move away. See: “Everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure.”

See how he has not taken away free will, since he says, “He purifies himself.” Who purifies us except God? But God does not purify you against your will. Therefore, by joining your will to God, you purify yourself. You purify yourself—not from yourself, but from him who comes to dwell in you. Nevertheless, because you do something there by your will, something is also attributed to you.

It is attributed to you so that you may say, as in the Psalm, “Be my helper; do not abandon me” (Psalm 26:9). If you say, “Be my helper,” you are doing something; for if you were doing nothing, how would he help you?

8. “Everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity.” Let no one say, “Sin is one thing, iniquity another”; let no one say, “I am a sinful human being, but I am not iniquitous.” For “everyone who commits sin also commits iniquity.” Sin is iniquity.

What, then, shall we do about our sins and iniquities? Hear what he says: “And you know that he was manifested in order to take away sins; and there is no sin in him.” The one in whom there is no sin came to take away sin. For if there were sin in him, it would have to be taken away from him; he would not himself take it away.

“Everyone who remains in him does not sin.” To the extent that he remains in him, to that extent he does not sin. “Everyone who sins has not seen him, nor has he known him.” This is a great question: “Everyone who sins has not seen him, nor has he known him.”

It is not surprising. We have not seen him, but we shall see him; we have not known him, but we shall know him. We believe in one whom we have not known. Or perhaps we have known him through faith, though we have not yet known him by sight? Yet in faith we have both seen and known him. For if faith does not yet see, why are we called enlightened?

There is an enlightenment through faith, and there is an enlightenment through sight. Now, while we are pilgrims, “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). Therefore our righteousness too is by faith, not by sight. Our righteousness will be perfect when we see by sight.

For now, let us not abandon that righteousness which comes from faith, since, as the Apostle says, “the righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1:17). “Everyone who remains in him does not sin.” For “everyone who sins has not seen him, nor has he known him.” The one who sins does not believe; but if he does believe, then insofar as his faith is concerned, he does not sin.

9. “Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.” When we hear that we are righteous, just as he is, should we think that we are equal to God? You ought to know what “just as” means. A little earlier he said, “He purifies himself, just as he is pure.” Is our purity, then, equal and identical to God’s purity, and our righteousness equal to God’s righteousness? Who could say this?

But “just as” is not always used to indicate equality. For example, if someone saw this basilica, which is large, and wished to make a smaller one while preserving its proportions—if, for instance, this one were one unit wide and two units long, and he made another one one unit wide and two units long—it would appear that he had made it “just as” this one is. But this one might be one hundred cubits, while the other was thirty; it would have the same proportions, yet it would not be equal.

You see that “just as” does not always refer to parity and equality. Consider, for example, the difference between a human face and its image in a mirror: the face is a face in the body, and the image is an image by imitation; the body exists in truth. What do we say? As there are eyes here, so there are eyes there; as there are ears here, so there are ears there. The things are unequal, but “just as” refers to likeness.

We too have the image of God, but not the image possessed by the Son, who is equal to the Father. Nevertheless, in our own measure, if we were not “as he is,” we would not be called similar in any respect.

Therefore he purifies us “just as he is pure,” but he is pure in eternity, while we are pure through faith. We are righteous “just as he is righteous,” but he is righteous in his own unchangeable perpetuity, while we are righteous by believing in the one whom we do not see, so that one day we may see him.

And when our righteousness has been perfected, when we have become equal to the angels, even then we shall not be equal to him. How far, then, are we from him now, when even then we shall not be his equal?

10. “Whoever commits sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning.” To be “of the devil”—you know what this means: to imitate the devil. The devil made no one, begot no one, created no one. But whoever imitates the devil becomes, as it were, born from him and becomes the devil’s child by imitation, not by literal birth.

How are you a son of Abraham? Did Abraham beget you? How did the Jews, Abraham’s children, who did not imitate Abraham’s faith, become children of the devil? They were born from Abraham’s flesh, but they did not imitate Abraham’s faith.

If, then, those who were born from him were disinherited because they did not imitate him, you, who were not born from him, become his child by imitation, and so you will be his child by imitating him. And if you imitate the devil—because he was proud and ungodly against God—you will be a child of the devil by imitation, not because he created or begot you.

11. “For this purpose the Son of God was manifested.” Come, brothers: all sinners are born from the devil insofar as they are sinners. Adam was made by God; but when he consented to the devil, he was born from the devil, and he begot all his descendants in the condition in which he himself was.

We were born with that very concupiscence; and before we add our own debts, we are born under that condemnation. For if we are born without any sin, why are infants brought hastening to baptism so that they may be freed?

Consider, brothers, two births: Adam and Christ [Note: [Col. 2011] Lov. reads “Adam and of Christ.” But the Ambrosian, Basle, and the manuscripts have “Adam and Christ.”]. There are two human beings, but one of them is merely human, while the other is the God-human. Through the human being who is merely human, we are sinners; through the human being who is God, we are justified.

That birth cast us down into death; this birth raised us up to life. That birth carries sin with it; this birth frees from sin. For this reason Christ came as a human being: to release human beings from sins. “For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, to destroy the works of the devil.”

12. I commend the rest to Your Charity, lest I burden you. The very question in which we are laboring to find a solution is this: we call ourselves sinners, for if anyone says that he is without sin, he is a liar.

In John’s own Epistle we find: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves.” You must remember what came earlier: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

And again, in what follows, you hear: “Whoever is born of God does not sin”; “Whoever commits sin has not seen him, nor has he known him”; “Everyone who commits sin is of the devil.” Sin is not from God.

Once again he terrifies us. How have we been born from God, and how do we confess ourselves to be sinners? Shall we say that we have not been born from God? And what, then, do these sacraments accomplish in infants?

What did John say? “Whoever is born of God does not sin.” The same John said again: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

This is a great and difficult question, and I have set Your Charity to work upon solving it. Tomorrow, in the name of the Lord, we shall discuss what he grants us from that passage.

## TREATISE V

On the passage that follows, “Everyone who is born of God does not commit sin,” up to “Let us not love in word and tongue only, but in deed and truth.” Chapter 3:9–18.

1. Listen attentively, I beg you, because no small matter is at issue here. I do not doubt that you attended carefully yesterday, and that today you have gathered with still greater attention.

There is no small question in how he says in this Epistle, “Whoever is born of God does not sin,” and how earlier in the same Epistle he said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8).

What is the person to do whom both statements from the same Epistle have enclosed in their midst? If he confesses himself to be a sinner, he fears that it will be said to him, “Then you were not born from God,” because it is written, “Whoever is born from God does not sin.” But if he says that he is righteous and has no sin, he receives a blow from the other passage in the same Epistle: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

Placed between the two, the person does not know what to say, confess, or profess. To profess that one is without sin is dangerous—and not only dangerous, but false: “We deceive ourselves,” he says, “and the truth is not in us,” if we say that we have no sin.

But would that you had no sin and said so! You would be speaking the truth, and in proclaiming the truth you would have no reason to fear even a trace of iniquity. But you do wrong if you say it because you are speaking a lie: “The truth is not in us,” he says, “if we say that we have no sin.”

He does not say, “We have not had sin,” lest it perhaps appear that he was speaking of past life. This person did have sins; but from the time he was born from God, he began not to have them. If that were the case, no question would trouble us. We would say: “We were sinners, but now we have been justified; we had sin, but now we do not have it.”

He does not say this. What does he say? “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

A little later he says again, “Whoever is born from God does not sin.” Was John himself not born from God? If John was not born from God—John of whom you heard that he reclined upon the Lord’s breast—would anyone dare promise himself a regeneration that he did not merit, when John merited to recline upon the Lord’s breast? Was the one whom the Lord loved more than the others (John 13:23) the only one whom he had not begotten by the Spirit?

2. Consider these words now. I still commend our difficulties to you, so that through your attention—which is prayer both for us and for you—God may enlarge them and grant a way out, lest anyone find in his word an occasion for his own destruction. That word was preached and written only for healing and salvation.

“Everyone,” he says, “who commits sin also commits iniquity.” Do not perhaps distinguish between them: sin is iniquity. Do not say, “I am a sinner, but I am not iniquitous.” Sin is iniquity.

“And you know that he was manifested for this purpose, to take away sins; and there is no sin in him.” What benefit is it to us that he came without sin? “Everyone who does not sin remains in him; and everyone who sins has not seen him, nor has he known him.”

“Little children, let no one deceive you. Whoever practices righteousness is righteous, just as he is righteous.” We have already discussed this, since “just as” is ordinarily spoken according to a certain likeness, not according to equality.

“Whoever commits sin is of the devil, because the devil has been sinning from the beginning.” We have also discussed this: the devil created and begot no one, but his imitators are born, as it were, from him.

“For this purpose the Son of God was manifested, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:4–8). Therefore, to take away sins [Note: [Col. 2013] The printed editions add here the word “he came,” which is absent from all the manuscripts]—he who has no sin.

Then follows: “Everyone who is born from God does not commit sin, because his seed remains in him; and he cannot sin, because he has been born from God.” He has bound the matter tightly. Perhaps he said “does not sin” with respect to a certain sin, not every sin. Thus, when he says, “Whoever is born from God does not sin,” understand a particular sin which the person born from God cannot commit.

And that sin is such that, if someone commits it, he confirms the other sins; but if someone does not commit it, he removes the other sins. What sin is this? Acting against the commandment.

What commandment? “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34). Pay attention. This commandment is called love of Christ; through this love sins are removed. If this is not maintained, it is both a grave sin and the root of all sins.

3. Pay attention, brothers. We have brought forward something by which the question has been resolved for those who understand well. But are we walking the road only with the swift? Those who walk more slowly must not be abandoned. Let us turn this over in whatever words we can, so that it may reach everyone.

I think, brothers, that every person is concerned for his soul—one who does not enter the Church without reason, who does not seek temporal things in the Church, who does not enter for the purpose of conducting worldly business, but enters so that he may hold fast to something eternal promised to him, something to which he may attain. It is necessary for him to consider how he walks along the road, lest he remain behind, turn back, go astray, or fail to arrive because he limps.

Whoever is concerned, whether he is slow or swift, must not leave the road. I have said this because “whoever is born from God does not sin” perhaps was intended to refer to a certain sin; otherwise it would contradict the passage, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

The question can therefore be resolved in this way. There is a certain sin which the person born from God cannot commit. When it is not committed, the other sins are removed; when it is committed, the other sins are confirmed.

What sin is this? Acting against the commandment of Christ, against the new testament. What is the new commandment? “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another.”

Whoever acts against charity and against brotherly love must not dare to boast and say that he has been born from God. But whoever is established in brotherly love has certain sins which he cannot commit—especially this one: that he should hate his brother.

What, then, does he do about the other sins, concerning which it was said, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us”? Let him hear assurance from another passage of Scripture: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (1 Peter 4:8).

4. We therefore commend charity; this Epistle commends charity. After the resurrection, what else did the Lord ask Peter except, “Do you love me?” And it was not enough to ask once; again he asked nothing else, and a third time nothing else. When Peter was already troubled by the repetition, as though the Lord did not know what was taking place within him, the Lord nevertheless asked him this first, second, and third time.

Fear denied three times; love confessed three times (John 21:15–17).

Behold, Peter loves the Lord. What is he to render to the Lord? For he too was not unmoved by that Psalm: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me?” The one who said this in the Psalm considered how much had been granted to him by God, and he sought what he might render to God, but he could not find it. Whatever you wish to render, you received from him in order to give it back.

And what did he find to render? What he had received from him, as we have said, he found that he could render. “I will receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord” (Psalm 115:12–13). For who had given him the cup of salvation except the one to whom he wished to render something?

To receive the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord is to be satisfied with charity—and to be so satisfied that you not only do not hate your brother, but are prepared to die for your brother. This is perfect charity: to be prepared to die for your brother.

The Lord himself displayed this in himself, dying for all, praying for those by whom he was being crucified, and saying: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34).

But if he alone had done this, he would not have been a teacher, since he would not have had disciples. His disciples followed him and did the same. Stephen was being stoned, and, kneeling, he said: “Lord, do not hold this sin against them” (Acts 7:59). He loved those by whom he was being killed, because he was dying for them as well.

Hear the Apostle Paul too: “I myself,” he says, “will be spent for your souls” (2 Corinthians 12:15). He was among those for whom Stephen was pleading when he died at their hands.

This, then, is perfect charity. If someone has such charity that he is prepared even to die for his brothers, charity is perfect in him. But is it already entirely perfect as soon as it is born? It is born in order to be perfected; once born, it is nourished; once nourished, it is strengthened; once strengthened, it is perfected. When it reaches perfection, what does it say? “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain. I long to depart and be with Christ, for that is far better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Philippians 1:21–24). He wished to live for those for whom he was prepared to die.

5. And so that you may know that this is perfect charity, which the person born from God does not violate and against which he does not sin, the Lord says to Peter: “Peter, do you love me?” [Col. 2015] And he replied, “I love you.”

He did not say, “If you love me, serve me.” For when the Lord was in mortal flesh, he hungered and thirsted. At the time when he hungered and thirsted, he was received as a guest; those who had means ministered to him from their own substance, as we read in the Gospel (Luke 8:3).

Zacchaeus received him as a guest; having received the physician, he was healed of his illness. What illness? Greed. He was very rich and a chief tax collector. Consider how he was healed of the illness of greed. “Behold,” he said, “I give half of my possessions to the poor; and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I will repay fourfold” (Luke 19:6–8).
