He kept the other half, not for his own enjoyment, but to repay what he owed.

At that time, therefore, he received the physician as a guest, because the Lord’s flesh was subject to weakness, and human beings could offer him this service. He accepted it because he wished to benefit those who served him; it benefited those who served, not him. For he whom the angels served—did he require the service of human beings?

Nor did Elijah, his servant, ever need this, although he sent him bread and meat by a raven; yet, so that a religious widow might be blessed, the servant of God was sent, and the widow fed the one whom God was secretly feeding (1 Kings 17:4–9).

Nevertheless, although those who consider the needs of these servants of God thereby provide for themselves—because of the reward most clearly set forth by the Lord in the Gospel, “Whoever receives a righteous person in the name of a righteous person will receive the reward of a righteous person; and whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward; and whoever gives one of these little ones even a cup of cold water only in the name of a disciple, truly I say to you, he will not lose his reward” (Matthew 10:41–42)—although, then, those who do such things provide for themselves, not even this could be offered to the one who was about to ascend into heaven.

What could Peter, who loved him, render to him? Hear what: “Feed my sheep”—that is, “Do for your brothers what I have done for you. I have redeemed them all with my blood. Do not hesitate to die for the confession of truth, so that the others may imitate you.”

6. But this, as we have said, brothers, is perfect charity; the one who is born from God possesses it. Let Your Charity pay attention; see what I am saying.

Behold, a baptized person has received the sacrament of birth. He possesses the sacrament—and a great sacrament, divine, holy, ineffable. Consider what kind it is: it makes a new person through the forgiveness of all sins.

Yet let him attend to his heart, to see whether what has been done in the body is perfect there. Let him see whether he has charity, and then let him say, “I have been born from God.” But if he does not have charity, he certainly bears the mark, but wanders about as a deserter. Let him have charity; otherwise, let him not say that he has been born from God.

“But I have the sacrament,” he says. Hear the Apostle: “If I know all the sacraments and have all faith, so that I could move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:2).

7. If you remember, we commended this when we began reading this Epistle: nothing in it is commended to us in the same way as charity. And although it may appear to say one thing here and another there, it continually returns to that point, and wishes everything it says to be referred to charity.

Let us see whether it does the same here. Pay attention: “Everyone who is born from God does not commit sin.” We ask what sin is meant. For if you understand it as every sin, it will contradict the passage, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”

Let him therefore state what sin it is; let him teach us, lest I have rashly said that this sin is a violation of charity, since earlier he said: “Whoever hates his brother is in darkness, and walks in darkness, and does not know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11).

But perhaps he said something later and mentioned charity [Note: [Col. 2016] Four manuscripts read, “and did not mention charity.”]. See that this circuit of words has this end and this conclusion.

“Everyone who is born from God does not sin, because his seed remains in him.” The seed of God is the word of God; hence the Apostle says, “Through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4:15). “And he cannot sin, because he has been born from God.”

Let him say this; let us see in what respect he cannot sin. “By this the children of God and the children of the devil are revealed. Everyone who is not righteous is not from God, and neither is the one who does not love his brother.”

Now it is certainly clear what he means when he says, “the one who does not love his brother.” Love alone distinguishes between the children of God and the children of the devil.

Let everyone sign himself with the sign of Christ’s cross; let everyone answer, “Amen”; let everyone sing, “Alleluia”; let everyone be baptized; let everyone enter the churches; let them build the walls of the basilicas. The children of God are not distinguished from the children of the devil except by charity.

Those who have charity have been born from God; those who do not have it have not been born from God. A great indication, a great distinction. Have whatever you wish: if you lack this one thing, nothing benefits you. If you lack other things but have this, you have fulfilled the Law. For, as the Apostle says, “Whoever loves another has fulfilled the Law,” and “Love is the fullness of the Law” (Romans 13:8, 10).

I think this is the pearl which the Gospel describes the merchant as seeking: he found one pearl, sold everything he had, and bought it (Matthew 13:46). This is the precious pearl, charity, without which whatever you possess benefits you nothing; if you possess charity alone, it is sufficient for you.

Now you see through faith; then you will see by sight. For if we love when we do not see, how shall we embrace when we do see? But where should we exercise ourselves? In brotherly love.

You can say to me, “I have not seen God.” Can you say to me, “I have not seen a human being”? Love your brother. For if you love the brother whom you see, you will at the same time see God as well, because you will see charity itself, and God dwells within.

8. “Whoever is not righteous is not from God, and neither is the one who does not love his brother.” For this is the announcement. See how he confirms it: “For this is the announcement which we heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.”

He has made clear that he is speaking of this: whoever acts against this commandment is in that wicked sin into which those fall who are not born from God. “Not as Cain, who was of the evil one and killed his brother.” And for what reason did he kill him? “Because his works were evil, but his brother’s were righteous.”

Therefore, wherever there is envy, brotherly love cannot exist. Let Your Charity pay attention. Whoever envies does not love. The devil’s sin is in him, because the devil also cast down through envy. He fell, and envied the one who stood. He did not wish to cast him down so that he himself might stand, but so that he would not fall alone.

Keep in mind, from what he added here, that envy cannot exist in charity. You have it plainly when charity itself is praised: “Charity does not envy” (1 Corinthians 13:4).

There was no charity in Cain; and unless there had been charity in Abel, God would not have accepted his sacrifice. When both offered—one the fruits of the earth, the other the offspring of sheep—what do you think, brothers? Did God disregard the fruits of the earth and love the offspring of sheep?

God did not look at the hands [Note: [Col. 2017] The Ambrosian, Basle, Erasmus, and five manuscripts read “at the gift.”]; he saw the heart. The one whom he saw offering with charity—his sacrifice he regarded; the one whom he saw offering with envy—from his sacrifice he turned his eyes away.

Thus Abel’s good works signify nothing other than charity; Cain’s evil works signify nothing other than hatred of his brother. It is not merely that he hated his brother and envied his good works: because he refused to imitate him, he wished to kill him. From this it became evident that he was the devil’s son, while the other was shown to be righteous before God.

This, then, is how people are distinguished, my brothers. Let no one look merely at words, but at deeds and the heart [Note: [Col. 2017] Ten manuscripts read, “but at deeds. If he does not act well.”]. If he does not act well toward his brothers, he reveals what he has within himself. People are tested by temptations.

9. “Do not be surprised, brothers, if the world hates us” [Note: [Col. 2017] Thus the manuscripts. The sacred Bibles read, “you.”]. Must I often tell you what the world is? It is not heaven, nor earth, nor these works which God made, but the lovers of the world.

By saying this repeatedly I have become burdensome to some; but I do not say it without reason, since some are asked whether I have said it and do not answer. Let something, then, at least by repetition, remain fixed in the hearts of those who hear.

What is the world? When “world” is used in an evil sense, it means the lovers of the world. When it is used in praise, “world” means heaven and earth and the works of God in them; hence it is said, “And the world was made through him” (John 1:10).

The world also means the fullness of the earth, as John himself said: “He is not only the propitiation for our sins, but also for those of the whole world” (1 John 2:2). By “world” he means all the faithful scattered throughout the earth.

But the world in the evil sense means the lovers of the world. Those who love the world cannot love their brother.

10. “If the world hates us, we know.” What do we know? “That we have passed from death to life.” How do we know? “Because we love the brothers.”

Let no one question another person; let each return to his own heart. If he finds brotherly love there, let him be confident that he has passed from death to life. He is already on the right hand; let him not be concerned that his glory is now hidden. When the Lord comes, then his glory will appear.

He is alive, but it is still winter; the root is alive, but the branches appear dry. Within is the living sap; within are the leaves of the trees; within is the fruit. But they are waiting for summer.

Therefore we know that we have passed from death to life, because we love the brothers. Whoever does not love remains in death.

Do not think, brothers, that hating or failing to love is a light matter. Hear what follows: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer.” If someone had regarded brotherly hatred with contempt, will he also regard murder in his heart with contempt? He does not move his hands to kill a person, but he is already held by the Lord as a murderer. The other person lives, yet this one is already judged a killer.

“Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer. And you know that no murderer has eternal life abiding in him.”

11. “By this we know love.” He speaks of the perfection of love, the perfection we have commended. “By this we know love, that he laid down his life for us; and we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers.”

This is where the question came from, Peter: “Do you love me? Feed my sheep.” For so that you may know that he wished his sheep to be fed in such a way that the shepherd would lay down his life for the sheep, he immediately said to him:

“When you were young, you girded yourself and went wherever you wished; but when you are old, another will gird you and take you where you do not wish to go. And this,” says the Evangelist, “he said to signify by what death he would glorify God” (John 21:15–19).

Thus, to the one to whom he had said, “Feed my sheep,” he taught him to lay down his life for his sheep.

### 12

Where, then, does love begin, brothers? Pay a little attention: you have heard to what point it is perfected; the Lord himself commended that same end and that same measure in the Gospel: “No one has greater love,” he says, “than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Thus he showed its perfection in the Gospel, and here its perfection has been commended. But you ask yourselves and say: “When will we be able to have this love?” Do not quickly despair of yourself: perhaps it has been born, but it is not yet perfected. Nourish it, lest it be choked.

But you will say to me: “And how do I know?” We have heard to what point it is perfected; let us hear where it begins. The text continues and says: “But whoever has the world’s means, and sees his brother hungry, and closes his heart against him—how can the love of God remain in him?” This is where love begins. If you are not yet capable of dying for your brother, become capable now of giving your possessions to your brother. Let love already strike your heart, so that you do not act out of ostentation, but from the innermost richness of mercy; so that you consider him placed in poverty.

For if you cannot give your brother what is superfluous, can you lay down your life for your brother? Money lies in your purse, which thieves can take from you; and even if thieves do not take it, you will abandon it when you die, even if it does not abandon you while you live. What are you going to do with it? Your brother is hungry; he is placed in need. Perhaps he is being held in suspension, or is being pressed by a creditor. He has nothing; you have something. He is your brother; you were bought together; your price is one and the same; both of you were redeemed by the blood of Christ. See whether you have mercy, whether you have the world’s means.

“What concern is that of mine?” you perhaps say. “Am I to give away my money so that he will not suffer hardship?” If your heart gives you this answer, the love of the Father does not remain in you. If the love of the Father does not remain in you, you were not born of God. How can you boast that you are a Christian? You have the name, but not the deeds.

But if the deed follows the name, let someone call you a pagan, and by your deeds show that you are a Christian. For if you do not show by your deeds that you are a Christian, even if everyone calls you [Col. 2019] a Christian, what benefit is the name when the reality is not found?

“But whoever has the world’s means, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him—how can the love of God remain in him?” And it continues: “Little children, let us not love in word only and with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.”

### 13

I think that the great and necessary secret and mystery has been made clear to you, my brothers. All Scripture commends the value of love, but I do not know whether it commends it anywhere more strongly than in this Epistle. We ask and beseech you in the Lord to keep in memory what you have heard, and to come attentive and listen attentively to what still remains to be said until the Epistle itself is finished.

Open your hearts to good seeds. Uproot the thorns, lest what is sown in you be choked; rather, let the crop grow, and let the farmer rejoice and prepare a granary for you as for grain, not a fire as for straw.

## TREATISE VI

On the passage, “And by this we know that we are from the truth,” up to, “And this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard,” etc. Chapter III, verses 19–24, and chapter IV, verses 1–3.

### 1

If you remember, brothers, yesterday we closed our sermon with this sentence, which without doubt ought to remain—and ought now to remain—in your hearts, because it was the last thing you heard: “Little children, let us not love in word only and with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.”

Then it continues: “And by this we know that we are from the truth, and before him we persuade our heart; because if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart, and he knows all things.”

He had said: “Let us not love in word only and with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.” We are asked in what deed and in what truth the one who loves God, or who loves his brother, is recognized.

Above he had already said to what point love is perfected, as the Lord also says in the Gospel: “No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). And this writer had said: “As he laid down his life for us, so we ought to lay down our lives for our brothers.” This is the perfection of love, and nothing greater can be found.

But because love is not perfect in everyone, and the person in whom it is not perfect ought not to despair if what is to be perfected has already been born—and certainly, if it has been born, it must be nourished and brought to its own perfection by certain forms of nourishment—we asked where love begins, where its beginning lies, and there we immediately found it: “If anyone has the world’s means, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him, how does the love of the Father remain in him?” (1 John 3:16–17).

Therefore, brothers, this love begins here: that one gives from his surplus to a needy person placed in some distress, and, from what he possesses in abundance for the present, frees his brother from temporal affliction. This is the beginning of love. If you nourish love, once begun in this way, with the word of God and the hope of future life, you will reach that perfection at which you are ready to lay down your life for your brothers.

### 2

But because many such things are done by those who seek other ends and who do not love their brothers, let us return to the testimony [Col. 2020] of conscience. How do we prove that many such things are done by those who do not love their brothers? How many people in heresies and schisms call themselves martyrs! They seem to themselves to be laying down their lives for their brothers. If they were laying down their lives for their brothers, they would not separate themselves from the whole brotherhood.

Again, how many people give and donate many things for the sake of ostentation, seeking nothing there except human praise and popular glory, full of wind and made firm by no stability! Since there are such people, where is brotherly love to be proved? He wished it to be proved and, admonishing us, said: “Little children, let us not love in word only and with the tongue, but in deed and in truth.”

We ask: “In what deed, and in what truth?” Can there be a more evident deed than giving to the poor? Many do this out of ostentation, not love. Can there be a greater deed than dying for one’s brothers? Many also want it to be thought that they do this out of ostentation, to acquire a reputation, not from the depths of love.

It remains, then, that the one who loves his brother is the one who, before God—where God alone sees—persuades his own heart and asks his heart whether he is truly doing this for love of his brother. The eye that penetrates the heart bears witness to him, though a human being cannot attend to it.

Therefore the Apostle Paul, because he was ready to die for his brothers and said, “I myself will spend myself for your souls” (2 Corinthians 12:15), nevertheless, because God saw this in his heart, not the people to whom he was speaking, said to them: “But it is a very small thing for me to be judged by you or by a human tribunal” (1 Corinthians 4:3).

He also showed in another place that such things are often done from empty ostentation, not from the firmness of love. For, speaking of the commendation of love itself, he says: “If I distribute all my possessions to the poor, and deliver my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13:3).

Can someone do this without love? Yes. For those who do not have love have divided unity [Note: The Donatists.].

Look there, and you will see many giving many things to the poor; you will see others ready to undergo death, even throwing themselves down when the persecutor desisted. These people unquestionably do this without love.

Let us therefore return to conscience, concerning which the Apostle says: “For this is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1:12). Let us return to conscience, about which he says again: “Let each one test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself and not in another” (Galatians 6:4).

Let each one of us therefore test his own work, to see whether it flows from the vein of love, whether the branches of good works sprout from the root of love. “Let each one test his own work,” he says, “and then he will have glory in himself and not in another”—not when another’s tongue bears witness to him, but when his own conscience bears witness.

### 3

This, then, is what he commends here: “By this we know that we are from the truth,” when we love in deed and in truth, not in words and with the tongue only. “And before him we persuade our heart.” What does “before him” mean? Where he himself sees.

Thus the Lord says in the Gospel: “Beware of practicing your righteousness before human beings in order to be seen [Col. 2021] by them; otherwise you will have no reward with your Father who is in heaven.” And what does “Let not your left hand know what your right hand is doing” mean (Matthew 6:1, 3), except that the right hand is a pure conscience and the left hand is worldly desire?

Many do wondrous things through worldly desire: the left hand is working, not the right. The right hand ought to work while the left is unaware, so that worldly desire does not mix itself in when we do something good out of love.

And where do we recognize this? You are before God; question your heart. See what you have done and what you desired there: your salvation, or the windy praise of human beings. Look within, for a person cannot judge what he cannot see. If we persuade our heart, let us persuade it before him.

“For if our heart condemns us”—that is, if it accuses us within because we are not acting with the disposition with which we ought to act—“God is greater than our heart, and he knows all things.”

You hide your heart from a human being; hide it from God, if you can. How will you hide it from him to whom a certain sinner, fearing and confessing, said: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your presence?” He was seeking where he might flee in order to escape God’s judgment, but he could not find it. For where is God not present? “If I ascend into heaven,” he says, “you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psalm 138:7–8).

Where will you go? Where will you flee? Do you wish to hear advice? If you wish to flee from him, flee toward him. Flee toward him by confessing, not by hiding from him. You cannot remain hidden, but you can confess. Say to him: “You are my refuge” (Psalm 31:7), and let love be nourished in you—the love that alone leads to life.

Let your conscience bear witness to you that you are from God. If you are from God, do not wish to boast of it before human beings, because neither human praise lifts you to heaven nor their reproaches bring you down from there. Let the one who crowns see; let the one before whom you are judged to be crowned be your witness.

“God is greater than our heart, and he knows all things.”

### 4

Beloved, if our heart does not condemn us, we have confidence before God. What does it mean for our heart not to condemn us? It means that it answers us truthfully: that we love, and that genuine love is in us—not feigned, but sincere, seeking our brother’s salvation and expecting no advantage from him except his salvation.

We have confidence before God. And whatever we ask, we shall receive from him, because we keep his commandments. Therefore this is not before human beings, but where God himself sees in the heart.

We have confidence before God, then, and whatever we ask, we shall receive from him—but because we keep his commandments. What are his commandments? Must this always be repeated? “I give you a new commandment: that you love one another” (John 13:34).

He speaks of love itself; he commends love itself. Whoever, therefore, has brotherly love, and has it before God—where God sees—and whose heart, when questioned under a just examination, gives no other answer than that the genuine root of love is there, from which good fruits arise, has confidence before God and will receive from him whatever he asks, because he keeps his commandments.

### 5

A question arises, because it is not merely this or that person—you or I—of whom, if I ask something from the Lord our God [Col. 2022] and do not receive it, anyone can easily say: “He does not have love.” The same can easily be said of any person in this present age, and let each person think whatever he wishes about another person.

But the question is made more difficult by those men who are clearly known to have been saints when they wrote and now to be with God. Who has love if Paul did not have it? He said: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted by us” (2 Corinthians 6:11–12). He said: “I will gladly spend myself for your souls” (ibid. 12:15). Such grace was in him that it was evident that he had love.

Yet we find that he asked and did not receive. What are we to say, brothers? It is a question. Be attentive to God. This too is a great question.

Just as, concerning sin, where it is said, “Whoever is born of God does not sin” (1 John 3:9), we find that the sin meant is the violation of love, and that this is specifically designated in that passage, so now we ask what he has said.

If you attend to the words, it seems clear; if you attend to the examples, it is obscure. Nothing is clearer than these words: “Whatever we ask, we shall receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him in his sight. Whatever we ask,” he says, “we shall receive from him.”

This greatly narrows the matter. It would also be restrictive there if he were speaking of every sin. But for that reason we find a place for explanation: he spoke of a particular sin, not of every sin, but of a certain sin which everyone born of God does not commit. And we find that this particular sin is the violation of love.

We have a clear example from the Gospel, when the Lord says: “If I had not come, they would not have sin” (John 15:22). What then? Had he come to innocent Jews, since he speaks in this way? Therefore, if he had not come, they would have had no sin? Did the physician’s presence make the sick person sick, rather than remove the fever? Who, even if insane, would say this? He came only to cure and heal the sick.

Why, then, did he say, “If I had not come, they would not have sin,” unless he wanted a particular sin to be understood? The Jews would not have had a certain sin—the sin by which they did not believe in him, by which they despised him while he was present.

Therefore, just as there he called something “sin,” and it does not follow that we should understand every sin, but a particular sin, so here too he does not mean every sin—lest he contradict the passage where he says, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (1 John 1:8)—but a particular sin, namely, the violation of love.

Here, however, he has bound us more tightly: “If we ask,” he says, “if our heart does not accuse us and declare before God that true love is in us, whatever we ask, we shall receive from him.”

### 6

I have already said to your Charity, brothers: let no one attend to us. For what are we? Or what are you? What, except the Church of God, which is known to all? And if it pleases him, we are in it; and if we remain in it with love, let us persevere there, if we wish to show the love that we have.

Nevertheless, what evil are we going to think about the Apostle Paul? Did he not love [Col. 2023] his brothers? Was the testimony of his conscience not present before God? Was that root of love not in Paul, from which all good fruits proceeded? Who would say this, unless insane?

Where, then, do we find that the Apostle asked and did not receive? He himself says: “So that I might not be exalted because of the greatness of the revelations, a thorn in my flesh was given to me, an angel of Satan, to strike me. For this I asked the Lord three times that he remove it from me; and he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (2 Corinthians 12:7–9).

Look: he was not heard so that the angel of Satan might be removed from him. But why? Because it was not beneficial to him. Therefore he was heard for salvation, though he was not heard according to his will.

Let your Charity know this great mystery, which we commend to you so that it may not escape you in your trials. The saints are heard in all things for salvation; they are always heard for eternal salvation. This is what they desire, because according to this they are always heard.

### 7

But let us distinguish God’s answers. We find some who are not heard according to their will but are heard for salvation; and again we find some who are heard according to their will but are not heard for salvation.

Understand this distinction; hold fast to the example of the one who was not heard according to his will but was heard for salvation. Listen to the Apostle Paul, for God showed him this very answer for salvation: “My grace is sufficient for you,” he says, “for power is perfected in weakness.”

“You asked, you cried out, you cried out three times. The one time you cried out, I heard you; I did not turn my ears away from you. I know what I will do. You want the medicine by which you are being burned to be removed; I know the illness by which you are burdened.”

Thus he was heard for salvation but was not heard according to his will.

Whom do we find heard according to their will but not heard for salvation? Do we suppose that we find some wicked or impious person heard by God according to his will but not for salvation? If I give the example of some human being, perhaps you will say to me: “You call him wicked, but he was righteous; if he were not righteous, God would not hear him.”

I am going to propose someone whose wickedness and impiety no one can doubt. The devil himself asked for Job, and received him (Job 1:11–12). Have you not also heard concerning the devil that “whoever commits sin is from the devil” (1 John 3:8)? Not because he created him, but because the sinner imitates him.

Was it not said of him, “He did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44)? Is he not that ancient serpent who, through the woman, first offered poison to the first human being (Genesis 3:1–6)? He also preserved Job’s wife for this reason: so that she would not console her husband, but tempt him (Job 2:9).

The devil himself asked that the holy man be tested, and received him. The Apostle asked that the thorn in his flesh be removed, and did not receive this. But the Apostle was heard more than the devil. The Apostle was heard for salvation, even though not according to his will; the devil was heard according to his will, but for condemnation.

For this man was allowed to be tested so that, once Job had been proved, the devil might be tormented.

But, brothers, we find this not only in the ancient Books, but also in the Gospel. The demons asked the Lord, when he was driving them out of a man, that they be permitted [Col. 2024] to enter the pigs. [Note: [Col. 2024] Er., Lugd., and Ven.: “Nonne.” M.] Could the Lord not have told them not even to approach there? If he had not wished it, they would not have rebelled against the King of heaven and earth.

Nevertheless, for the sake of a certain mystery and by a certain dispensation, he allowed the demons to enter the pigs (Luke 8:32), in order to show that the devil dominates those who live the life of pigs.

Were the demons, then, heard, while the Apostle was not heard? Or rather, let us say what is truer: the Apostle was heard, while the demons were not heard. Their will was carried out; his healing was perfected.

### 8

Accordingly, we should understand that even if God does not grant our will, he grants what serves our salvation. For what if you ask for something that harms you, and the physician knows that it harms you? The physician does not fail to hear you when perhaps you ask for cold water: if it benefits you, he immediately gives it; if it does not benefit you, he does not give it.

Did he not hear you, or rather did he hear you for your healing because he opposed your will?

Let love be in you, brothers; let it be in you, and be secure. And when what you ask is not given to you, you are heard—but you do not know it.

Many have been handed over into their own hands, to their harm. The Apostle says of them: “God handed them over to the desires of their heart” (Romans 1:24). Someone asked for a great deal of money and received it to his harm. When he did not have it, he was little afraid; once he began to possess it, he became prey to someone more powerful.

Was he not heard to his own harm, who wanted to have something that would make him a target for a robber, while no one sought the poor man?

Learn to ask God in such a way that you entrust to the physician what he himself knows to do. You confess the illness; let him apply the medicine. Only hold fast to love.

For he wishes to cut; he wishes to burn. If you cry out and are not heard during the cutting, the burning, and the tribulation, he knows how far the corruption extends. You now want him to withdraw his hand, but he is attending to the depth of the wound; he knows how far it reaches.

He does not hear you according to your will, but he hears you for your healing.

Be certain, therefore, my brothers, that what the Apostle says is true: “We do not know what we ought to pray for, but the Spirit himself intercedes with unutterable groanings, because he himself intercedes for the saints” (Romans 8:26–27).

What does “the Spirit himself intercedes for the saints” mean except that it is love itself, which has been produced in you through the Spirit? For this same Apostle says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Romans 5:5).

Love itself groans; love itself prays. The one who gave it does not know how to close his ears against it. Be secure: let love pray, and there are God’s ears.

What you want does not happen, but what is beneficial does. Therefore, he says, “Whatever we ask, we shall receive from him.”

I have already said: if you understand this as referring to salvation, there is no question. If not to salvation, there is a question—and a great one—which makes you accuse the Apostle Paul.

“Whatever we ask, we shall receive from him, because we keep his commandments and do what pleases him in his sight.” In his sight: inwardly, where he sees.

### 9

And what are those commandments? “This is his commandment,” he says: “that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another.”

You see that this is the commandment. You see that whoever acts against this commandment commits the sin [Col. 2025] from which everyone born of God is free.

“As he gave us a commandment: that we love one another. And whoever keeps his commandment”—you see that nothing else is commanded of us except that we love one another—“whoever keeps his commandment remains in him, and he in him.”

“And by this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us.”

Is it not clear that the Holy Spirit does this in a human being: that love and charity are in him? Is it not clear what the Apostle Paul says: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us”?

He was speaking about love and saying that we ought to question our heart before God. If our heart does not condemn us—that is, if it confesses that whatever is done in a good work is done from love of one’s brother—then this is added.

When he spoke about the commandment, he also said this: “This is his commandment: that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, and love one another. And whoever keeps his commandment remains in him, and he in him. By this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us.”

For if you find that you have love, you have the Spirit of God for understanding. This is an exceedingly necessary matter.

### 10

In the earliest times the Holy Spirit fell upon those who believed, and they spoke in languages they had not learned, just as the Spirit gave them utterance. These were signs appropriate to that time.

For it was necessary that the Holy Spirit be signified in all languages, because the Gospel of God was going to travel throughout the whole world in all languages. This was signified, and it passed away.

Is it now expected that those upon whom hands are laid so that they may receive the Holy Spirit should speak in tongues? When we laid hands on these infants, did each of you attend to whether they spoke in tongues? And when you saw that they did not speak in tongues, were some of you so perverse in heart as to say: “These have not received the Holy Spirit, for if they had received him, they would speak in tongues as happened then”?

If, then, the presence of the Holy Spirit is not now testified by these miracles, how does anyone know that he has received the Holy Spirit? Let him question his heart. If he loves his brother, the Spirit of God remains in him.

Let him see and test himself before the eyes of God. Let him see whether the love of peace and unity is in him, the love of the Church spread throughout the whole world.

Let him not think that he loves only the brother whom he sees before him. We do not see many of our brothers, and yet we are joined to them in the unity of the Spirit.

What is surprising if they are not with us? We are one body; we have one head in heaven.

Brothers, our eyes do not see one another, as though they did not know one another. Or do they not know one another in the love of the body’s joining? To show you that they know one another in the union of love: when both are open, the right eye is not permitted to attend to something that the left does not attend to. Direct the right eye’s gaze without the other, if you can. They move together; they are directed together. Their focus is one, though their locations are different.

Therefore, if all who love God with you have one intention with you, do not attend to the fact that you are separated from them in bodily location. You have fixed the gaze of your hearts together upon the light of truth.

If you wish to know that you have received the Spirit, then question your heart [Col. 2026]. Take care lest you have the sacrament but not the power of the sacrament [Note: Erasmian, Lyon, and Venetian editions: “lest, while you have the sacrament, you should not have the power of the sacrament.” Louvain prints *habeas* twice. M.].

Question your heart. If the love of your brother is there, be secure. Love cannot exist without the Spirit of God, because Paul cries out: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us.”

### 11

Beloved, do not believe every spirit. He had said: “By this we know that he remains in us, from the Spirit whom he gave us.” But pay attention to how the Spirit himself is recognized: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.”

And who is the one who tests the spirits? He has set before us a difficult matter, my brothers. It is good for us that he should say himself how we are to distinguish them. He is going to say it; do not be afraid.

But first look and pay attention. See that this brings out the point over which vain heretics make accusations. Pay attention; see what he says: “Beloved, do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God.”

The Holy Spirit has been called by the name of water in the Gospel, when the Lord cried out and said: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink. Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

The Evangelist explained what he meant. For he continued: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive.” Why did the Lord not baptize many? But what does he say? “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:37–39).

Since, therefore, they had Baptism but had not yet received the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord sent from heaven on the day of Pentecost, the glorification of the Lord was awaited so that the Spirit might be given.

Before he was glorified and before he sent the Spirit, however, he invited people to prepare themselves to receive the water about which he said: “Whoever thirsts, let him come and drink,” and, “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.”

What are “rivers of living water”? What is that water? Let no one ask me; ask the Gospel. “Now he said this,” it says, “about the Spirit whom those who were going to believe in him were going to receive.”

The water of the sacrament is therefore one thing, and the water that signifies the Spirit of God is another. The water of the sacrament is visible; the water of the Spirit is invisible. The former washes the body and signifies what takes place in the soul; through that Spirit the soul itself is cleansed and nourished.

This is the Spirit of God, whom heretics cannot have, nor those who cut themselves off from the Church. And those who do not cut themselves off openly, but who have been cut off through iniquity and roll about inside like straw, not being grain, do not have this Spirit.

This Spirit was signified by the Lord under the name of water. And we have heard from this Epistle: “Do not believe every spirit.” The words of Solomon also bear witness: “Keep away from strange water.”

What is water? The Spirit. Does water always signify the Spirit? Not always. In some passages it signifies the Spirit; in some passages Baptism; in some passages peoples; in some passages counsel. In one place you have the words: “The fountain of life is counsel to those who possess it” (Proverbs 16:22).

Thus, throughout the various passages of Scripture, the name “water” signifies various things [Col. 2027]. But here you have heard the Holy Spirit named as water, not from our interpretation, but from the testimony of the Gospel, where it says: “Now he said this about the Spirit whom those who believed in him were going to receive.”

If, therefore, the Holy Spirit is signified by the name of water, and this Epistle says to us, “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God,” let us understand that the words, “Keep away from strange water, and do not drink from a foreign fountain” (Proverbs 9:18, according to the Septuagint), have been spoken with this meaning.

What does “Do not drink from a foreign fountain” mean? Do not believe a foreign spirit.

### 12

The examination therefore remains: how is it proved that a spirit is the Spirit of God? He did indeed give a sign, and perhaps it is difficult. Let us nevertheless see.

We are going to return to that love. It is love that teaches us, because love is the anointing. But what does he say here? “Test the spirits to see whether they are from God, because many false prophets have gone out into this world.”

All heretics and all schismatics are already there. How, then, do I test the spirit? It continues: “By this the Spirit of God is recognized.”

Raise the ears of your hearts. We were laboring and saying: “Who knows? Who distinguishes?” Look: he is going to give the sign.

“By this the Spirit of God is recognized: every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God. And every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not from God. And this is the Antichrist, of whom you have heard that he is to come, and now he is in this world.”

Our ears seem to be raised for distinguishing the spirits, and yet we have heard something from which we still cannot distinguish them. For what does he say? “Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is from God.”

Then the spirit found among the heretics is from God, because they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? At this point they may perhaps rise up against us and say: “You do not have a spirit from God, but we confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.” Yet he declared that those who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh do not have the Spirit of God.

Ask the Arians: they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Ask the Eunomians: they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Ask the Macedonians: they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Ask the Cataphrygians: they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. Ask the Novatians: they confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Do all these heresies therefore have the Spirit of God? Then they are not false prophets? There is no deception there, no seduction there? Certainly they are antichrists, who went out from us, but they were not of us.

### 13

What then are we to do? How do we distinguish them? Pay attention. Let us go together in heart and knock. Love itself is awake, because love itself is going to knock and love itself is going to open. You will now understand this in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Above you heard that it was said: “Whoever denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh, this is the Antichrist” (1 John 2:19, 22). There we asked who denies this, because neither do we deny it nor do they deny it.

And we found that some deny it by their deeds (see above, Treatise 3, nos. 7–9). We brought forward the testimony of the Apostle, who says: “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16). [Col. 2028]

So now let us seek in deeds, not on the tongue. What spirit is not from God? The one that denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. And what spirit is from God? The one that confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh.

Who is the one who confesses that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh? Come, brothers, let us attend to deeds, not the clamor of the tongue. Let us ask why Christ came in the flesh, and we will find those who deny that he came in the flesh.

For if you attend to their words, you will hear many heresies confessing that Christ has come in the flesh. But the truth convicts them.

Why did Christ come in the flesh? Was he not God? Was it not written of him: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1)? Was he not himself feeding the angels, and does he not himself feed the angels? Did he not come here in such a way that he did not depart from there? Did he not ascend in such a way that he did not abandon us?

Why, then, did he come in the flesh? Because it was necessary for the hope of the resurrection to be shown to us. He was God, and he came in the flesh. God could not die; flesh could die. Therefore he came in the flesh so that he might die for us.

How, then, did he die for us? “No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). Love therefore brought him to the flesh.

Whoever does not have love denies that Christ came in the flesh.

Now ask all the heretics: “Did Christ come in the flesh?” “He came; I believe this; I confess this.” No, you deny this. “How do I deny it?” “You hear that I say this.” No, I prove that you deny it. You say it with your voice, but deny it in your heart; you say it in words, but deny it in deeds.

“How,” you ask, “do I deny it in deeds?” Because Christ came in the flesh for this reason: so that he might die for us. He died for us because he taught great love: “No one has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends.”

You do not have love, because for the sake of your own honor you divide unity.

Therefore, from this understand what spirit is from God. Knock; touch the clay vessels, lest they have perhaps cracked and give a bad sound. See whether they sound whole; see whether love is there.

You remove yourself from the unity of the whole world; you divide the Church through schisms; you tear apart the body of Christ. He came in the flesh in order to gather; you cry out for this reason: to scatter.

Therefore, the Spirit of God is the one who says that Jesus came in the flesh—the one who says it not with the tongue but by his deeds, not by making a sound but by loving.

But the spirit that denies that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is not the Spirit of God. It too denies—not with the tongue, but by its life; not in words, but in deeds.

It is clear, then, how we recognize them, brothers. Many are inside, as though inside; but no one is outside unless he is truly outside.

14. So that you may know that he referred to deeds: “And every spirit,” he says, “that dissolves Christ as having come in the flesh, is not from God.” [Note: [Col. 2028] In Er., Lugd., and Ven., the words “to have come in the flesh” are absent, although Lov. maintains that they are found in the manuscripts. M.] “To dissolve” is understood by deeds. What does he show you? “The one who denies,” because he said, “dissolves.” [Note: [Col. 2028] Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov.: “What does he show you who denies, because he said: ‘He dissolves’?” M.] He came to gather; you come to dissolve. You want to tear apart the members of Christ. How can you not be denying that Christ came in the flesh when you divide the Church of God, which he gathered? [Col. 2029] You therefore come against Christ; you are antichrist. Whether you are inside or outside, you are antichrist; but when you are inside, you remain hidden, and when you are outside, you are exposed. You dissolve Jesus and deny that he came in the flesh; you are not from God.

Therefore he says in the Gospel: “Whoever dissolves one of these least commandments and teaches others to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” What does it mean “to dissolve”? What does it mean “to teach”? It is dissolved by deeds and taught, as it were, by words. “You preach against stealing, yet you steal” (Rom. 2:21). Thus the one who steals dissolves it in deed and, as it were, teaches in this way; he will be called least in the kingdom of heaven—that is, in the Church of this present time. Of such people it was said: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matt. 23:3). “But whoever does and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (ibid. 5:19). What he said here, “does,” he expressed there in opposition as “dissolves”—that is, does not do, yet teaches others to do so. The one who does not act, then, is the one who dissolves.

What does he teach us except that we should question deeds and not believe words? The obscurity of these matters compels us to say much, especially so that what the Lord deigns to reveal may reach even our slower brothers, since all have been purchased by Christ’s blood. And I fear that this Epistle itself will not be completed during these days, as I promised; but whatever pleases the Lord, it is better to preserve the remains than to burden hearts with excessive food.

# TRACTATE VII

From the passage that follows, “Now you are from God, little children,” up to “No one has ever seen God.” Chapter 4, verses 4–12.

## 1

This world is for all faithful people who seek their homeland what the wilderness was for the people of Israel. They were still wandering and seeking their homeland; but with God as their guide, they could not go astray. God’s command was their road. [Note: [Col. 2029] Thus in the manuscripts. But in the printed editions, “the vision of God.”] For although they wandered for forty years, the journey itself could be completed in very few stages, and it is known to everyone. They were delayed because they were being tested, not because they were being abandoned.

What God promises us, therefore, is ineffable sweetness and goodness, as Scripture says—and you have often heard it when we have recalled it—that “the eye has not seen, nor the ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart” (Isa. 64:4; 1 Cor. 2:9). We are exercised by temporal hardships and instructed by the temptations of the present life. But if you do not wish to die of thirst in this wilderness, drink love. It is a spring that the Lord wished to place here so that we would not fail on the way; and we shall drink from it more abundantly when we have reached our homeland.

The Gospel has just been read. To speak from the very words with which the reading ended, what else did you hear except about love? We made a covenant with our God in prayer: if we wish him to forgive us our sins, we too must forgive the sins committed against us (Matt. 6:12). But he forgives only where there is love. Take love away from the heart: hatred remains, and it does not know how to forgive. Let love be there; it forgives securely, because it is not constricted.

As for this Epistle, which we have undertaken to expound for you, see whether it commends anything other than this one love. Nor should we fear that repeated mention of it will provoke hatred. For what is loved, if love itself provokes hatred? By what love other things are rightly loved, how should love itself be loved? Therefore, the thing that must never depart from the heart should not depart from the mouth either. [Col. 2030]

## 2

“Now you are from God,” he says, “little children, and you have conquered him”—whom, if not the Antichrist? Earlier he had said: “Everyone who dissolves Jesus Christ and denies that he came in the flesh is not from God” (1 John 4:3). We explained, if you remember, that all who violate love deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh. Jesus would not have needed to come except because of love. For the love he commends to us is the very love that he himself commends in the Gospel: “No one can have greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).

How could the Son of God lay down his life for us unless he assumed flesh, in which he could die? Therefore, whoever violates love—whatever his tongue may say—by his life denies that Christ came in the flesh. And wherever he may be, wherever he may enter, he is antichrist.

But what does he say to those who are citizens of the homeland for which we sigh? “You have conquered him.” And by what means did they conquer? “Because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.” So that they would not attribute the victory to their own strength and be conquered by the arrogance of pride—for the devil conquers anyone whom he makes proud—he wished to preserve them in humility. What does he say? “You have conquered him.”

Now every person who hears, “You have conquered,” lifts his head and raises his neck; he wants to be praised. Do not exalt yourself; see who conquered in you. Why did you conquer? “Because the one who is in you is greater than the one who is in the world.” Be humble; carry your Lord. Be the beast of burden for your rider. It is good for you that he himself rule and lead you. For if you do not have that rider, you can raise your neck and kick; but woe to you without a guide, because this freedom sends you among beasts to be devoured.

## 3

“These are from the world.” Who are they? The antichrists. You have already heard who they are. And if you are not among them, you recognize them; but whoever is one of them does not recognize them. “These are from the world; therefore they speak from the world, and the world listens to them.”

Who are those who speak from the world? Pay attention to those who speak against love. You have heard the Lord say: “If you forgive people their sins, your heavenly Father will also forgive you; but if you do not forgive, neither will your Father forgive your sins” (Matt. 6:14–15). It is a sentence of truth. Or, if truth is not speaking, contradict it. If you are a Christian and believe Christ, he himself said: “I am the truth” (John 14:6). This sentence is true and firm.

Now listen to people who speak from the world. “Are you not going to avenge yourself? He will say that he did it to you.” “Rather, you should realize that he has business with a man.” [Note: [Col. 2030] Er.: “but has business.” Lov. reads the word “business” in the manuscripts; M. confirms it.] These things are said every day. Those who say them speak from the world, and the world listens to them. They say such things only because they love the world, and such things are heard only by those who love the world.

And whoever loves the world and neglects love—you have heard that he denies that Jesus came in the flesh. Or did the Lord himself do that in the flesh? When he was struck, did he wish to be avenged? When he hung upon the cross, did he not say: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34)? If he who had the power did not threaten, why do you threaten, why do you puff yourself up, set as you are under another’s power? He died because he willed to die, and he did not threaten. You do not know when you will die, and yet you threaten?

## 4

“We are from God.” Let us see why. See whether it is for any reason other than love. “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this we know the spirit of truth and the spirit of error.” For whoever listens to us has the spirit of truth; whoever does not listen to us has the spirit of error.

Let us see what he advises, and let us listen to him advising us in the spirit of truth—not to the antichrists, not to the lovers of the world, not to the world. If we have been born from God, “Beloved,” he continues above; see what follows: “We are from God. Whoever knows God listens to us; whoever is not from God does not listen to us. By this the spirit of truth and the spirit of error are recognized.”

He has therefore made us attentive: whoever knows God listens; whoever does not know him does not listen. This is the distinction between the spirit of truth and the spirit of error. Let us see what he is about to advise, in what matter we ought to listen to him.

“Beloved, let us love one another.” Why? Because a human being advises us? “Because love is from God.” He has greatly commended love by saying that it is from God. He is going to say more; let us listen attentively. Just now he said: “Love is from God.” And: “Everyone who loves has been born from God and knows God. Whoever does not love does not know God.” Why? “Because God is love.”

What more could be said, brothers? If nothing were said in praise of love throughout all these pages of this Epistle, if nothing at all were said throughout the other pages of Scripture, and we heard only this one statement from the voice of God’s Spirit—“God is love”—we should seek nothing further.

## 5

Now see that acting against love is acting against God. Let no one say, “When I do not love my brother, I sin against a human being”—pay attention—“and it is easy to sin against a human being; provided only that I do not sin against God.” How do you not sin against God when you sin against love? God is love.

Are we the ones saying this? If we were saying, “God is love,” perhaps one of you would be scandalized and say: “What did he say? What did he mean by saying that God is love? God gave love; God bestowed love. Love is from God: God is love.” Here you have, brothers, the Scriptures of God. This Epistle is canonical; it is read among all nations and held by the authority of the whole world. It has itself built up the whole world. Here you hear from the Spirit of God: “God is love.” If you dare, then, act against God and do not love your brother.

## 6

How, then, did he say earlier, “Love is from God,” and now, “Love is God”? For God is Father, Son, and Holy Spirit: the Son is God from God; the Holy Spirit is God from God; and these three are one God, not three gods. If the Son is God and the Holy Spirit is God, and the one in whom the Holy Spirit dwells loves, then love is God—but God because it is from God.

You have both statements in the Epistle: “Love is from God,” and “Love is God.” Scripture does not know how to say of the Father alone that he is from God. When you hear “from God,” either the Son or the Holy Spirit is understood. Since the Apostle says, “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5), let us understand that the Holy Spirit is present in love.

He is the Holy Spirit whom the wicked cannot receive. He is that spring of which Scripture says: “Let the spring of your water be your own, and let no stranger share it with you” (Prov. 5:16–17). For all who do not love God are strangers; they are antichrists. And although they enter basilicas, they cannot be counted among the children of God; that fountain of life does not belong to them.

A wicked person can possess Baptism; a wicked person can possess prophecy. We find that King Saul possessed prophecy: he was persecuting holy David, and he was filled with the spirit of prophecy and began to prophesy (1 Kings 19). A wicked person can receive the Sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood; for of such people it was said: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself” (1 Cor. 11:29). A wicked person can possess the name of Christ—that is, a wicked person can be called a Christian. Of such people it was said: “They profaned the name of their God” (Ezek. 36:20).

A wicked person can therefore possess all these sacraments; but he cannot possess love and remain wicked. This, then, is the proper gift; it is the singular fountain. The Spirit of God urges you to drink from it; the Spirit of God urges you to drink from him.

## 7

“In this the love of God was manifested among us.” Behold, we have an exhortation to love God. Could we love him unless he first loved us? If we were slow to love, let us not be slow to return love. He loved us first, yet we do not love him in return.

He loved the unrighteous, but he removed their unrighteousness; he loved the unrighteous, but he did not gather them into unrighteousness. He loved the sick, but he visited them to heal them. God, then, is love.

“In this the love of God was manifested among us, because he sent his only-begotten Son into this world so that we might live through him.” As the Lord himself says: “No one can have greater love than to lay down his life for his friends.” And Christ’s love for us was proved there, because he died for us.

How was the Father’s love for us proved? Because he sent his only Son to die for us. Thus the Apostle Paul also says: “He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all, how will he not also give us everything with him?” (Rom. 8:32).

Behold, the Father handed Christ over; Judas handed him over. Does this not seem to be, as it were, a similar deed? Judas is a betrayer; therefore is God the Father also a betrayer? “God forbid,” you say. I am not saying it; the Apostle says it: “He who did not spare his own Son but handed him over for us all.”

The Father handed him over, and he handed himself over. The same Apostle says: “He loved me and handed himself over for me” (Gal. 2:20). If the Father handed over the Son, and the Son handed himself over, what did Judas do? The Father handed him over; the Son handed him over; Judas handed him over. One deed was done. But what distinguishes the Father handing over the Son, the Son handing himself over, and Judas the disciple handing over his master?

The Father and the Son did this in love; Judas did it in betrayal. You see that we must consider not what a person does, but with what intention and will he does it. In the same deed we find God the Father and Judas; we bless the Father and detest Judas. Why do we bless the Father and detest Judas? We bless love and detest wickedness.

How much benefit came to the human race from Christ’s being handed over! Did Judas think of that when he handed him over? God thought of our salvation, by which we were redeemed; Judas thought of the price for which he sold the Lord. The Son himself thought of the price he gave for us; Judas thought of the price he received in order to sell him.

Thus different intentions made the deeds different. Although there was one deed, when we measure it by the different intentions, we find one thing to be loved and the other to be condemned; one to be glorified and the other to be detested. Such power does love have. See that love alone distinguishes; see that love alone separates human deeds.

## 8

We have said this concerning similar deeds. In different deeds, we find a harsh person acting from love and a flattering person acting from wickedness. A father beats a child, while a pimp flatters him. If you put two things before someone—beatings and flatteries—who would not choose the flatteries and flee the blows? But if you consider the persons, love beats and wickedness flatters.

See what we are commending: human deeds cannot be distinguished except by the root of love. For many things can be done that have a good appearance but do not proceed from the root of love. Thorns also have flowers. Other things appear harsh and savage, yet they are done for discipline at love’s command.

One brief command, then, is given to you: Love, and do what you will. Whether you are silent, be silent out of love; whether you cry out, cry out out of love; whether you correct, correct out of love; whether you spare, spare out of love. Let the root of love be within; nothing but good can arise from that root. [Note: [Col. 2033] Most manuscripts: “Whether you are silent, be silent out of love; whether you cry out, cry out out of love.” And consistently they have “you correct” and “you spare.”]

## 9

“In this is love. In this the love of God was manifested among us, because God sent his only-begotten Son into this world so that we might live through him.”

“In this is love”: not that we loved him, but that he loved us. We did not love him first; rather, he loved us for this purpose, so that we would love him.

“And he sent his Son as a propitiator for our sins”—a propitiator, a sacrificer. He sacrificed himself for our sins. Where did he find a sacrifice? Where did he find the victim that he wished to offer, pure as it was? He found none other; he offered himself.

Beloved, if God loved us in this way, we too ought to love one another.

“Peter,” he says, “do you love me?” And he said, “I do.” “Feed my sheep” (John 21:15–17).

## 10

“No one has ever seen God.” He is invisible; he must be sought not with the eye but with the heart. But just as, if we wished to see the sun, we would purify the bodily eye by which light can be seen, so, if we wish to see God, let us purify the eye by which God can be seen.

Where is this eye? Hear the Gospel: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8).

But let no one, because of the desire of his eyes, imagine God for himself. One person makes for himself an immense form; another stretches some immeasurable size through places, like the light he sees with these eyes, enlarging it across the fields as much as he can; another makes for himself an old man of some venerable appearance. Imagine none of these things.

There is something you should imagine if you wish to see God: “God is love.” What face does love have? What form? What stature? What feet? What hands? No one can say. Yet it has feet, for they lead to the Church; it has hands, for they extend themselves to the poor; it has eyes, for by them one recognizes the person in need: “Blessed is the one who understands concerning the poor and needy” (Ps. 40:2). It has ears, of which the Lord says: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear” (Luke 8:8).

These are not distinct bodily members located in different places; but whoever has love sees everything at once through understanding. Possess it, and you will be possessed; remain, and it will remain in you.

For, my brothers, who loves what he does not see? Why, when love is praised, do you rise up, applaud, and praise? What have I shown you? Have I brought forth colors? Have I placed gold and silver before you? Have I dug gems out of treasures? What such thing have I shown to your eyes? Has my face changed as I speak? I wear flesh; I am in the same form in which I came; you are in the same form in which you came. Love is praised, and you cry out. Certainly you see nothing.

But just as it pleases you when you praise it, so may it please you to keep it in your hearts. Pay attention to what I say, brothers. As the Lord grants, I exhort you to a great treasure.

If some embossed, gilded, elaborately crafted vessel were shown to you, attracting your eyes, drawing your heart’s attention to itself, and you admired the craftsman’s hand, the weight of the silver, and the brilliance of the metal, would not each of you say, “If only I had that vessel”? Yet you would say this in vain, because it was not in your power. Or if someone wished to possess it, he might consider stealing it from another’s house.

Love is being praised to you. If it pleases you, possess it and own it. You do not need to steal from anyone; you do not need to think of buying it. It is obtained freely. Hold it; embrace it. Nothing is sweeter than it. If it is so pleasing when it is recalled, what must it be like when it is possessed?

## 11

If any of you, brothers, wish to preserve love, above all do not think that it is preserved in a degraded and idle manner, or by some gentleness—or rather, not gentleness but laxity and negligence. It is not preserved in that way.

Do not think that you love your servant when you do not beat him, or that you love your son when you do not discipline him, or that you love your neighbor when you do not correct him. That is not love but weakness.

Let love burn for correction and amendment. If their conduct is good, let it delight you; if it is bad, let it be amended and corrected. Do not love the error in a person, but the person. God made the person; the person himself made the error. Love what God made; do not love what the person himself made. When you love the person, you remove the error; when you cherish the person, you correct the error.

Even if at times you act harshly, do so because of love for correction. For this reason love was shown by the dove that came upon the Lord (Matt. 3:16). [Note: [Col. 2035] Lov.: “The dove is the form.” M.] That form was the form of a dove, in which the Holy Spirit came, so that love might be poured into us.

Why this form? A dove has no gall; yet it fights with its beak and wings for its nest. It is fierce without bitterness. A father does the same when he disciplines his son: he disciplines him for instruction. As I said, the seducer flatters with bitterness in order to sell; the father disciplines without gall in order to correct.

Be like this toward everyone. See, brothers, a great lesson and a great rule. Everyone has children, or wishes to have them; or, if he has firmly decided not to have children physically, he desires to have them spiritually. Who does not correct his son? What father does not discipline his son? (Heb. 12:7). And yet he seems to act harshly. Love acts harshly; love is fierce. It is fierce, in a certain way, without gall, in the manner of a dove, not a raven.

Why does it come to mind, my brothers, to tell you that those violators of love made a schism? Just as they hate love itself, so they hate the dove. But the dove convicts them. It comes from heaven; the heavens are opened, and it remains over the Lord’s head. Why is this? So that he may hear: “This is the one who baptizes” (John 1:33).

Withdraw, robbers; withdraw, invaders of Christ’s possession. In your possessions, where you wish to rule, you have dared to fix the titles of the powerful. He recognizes his own titles; he claims his own possession. He does not erase the titles, but enters and possesses.

Thus, when someone comes to the Catholic Church, the Baptism is not erased, so that the emperor’s title may not be erased. But what happens in the Catholic Church? The title is recognized; the possessor enters under his own titles, whereas the robber entered under titles belonging to another.

# TRACTATE VIII

On the passage that follows, “If we love one another, God will remain in us,” up to “God is love; and whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” Chapter 4, verses 12–16.

## 1

Love is a sweet word, but a sweeter deed. We cannot always speak about it. For we do many things, and different activities occupy us, so that our tongue does not always have leisure to speak about love; yet our tongue could do nothing better.

Although we cannot always speak about it, we can always preserve it. Just as we sing “Alleluia” now: do we always do this? We scarcely sing “Alleluia” for the whole span of an hour, but only for a small part of it, and then we turn to something else. [Note: [Col. 2035] In one manuscript: “and we are called to something else.”] As you already know, “Alleluia” means “Praise God.”

The one who praises God with his tongue cannot do so always; the one who praises God by his conduct can do so always. Works of mercy, the affection of love, the holiness of devotion, the integrity of chastity, and the moderation of sobriety must always be maintained—whether we are in public or at home, before people or in our room, speaking or silent, doing something or at leisure. All these things must always be maintained, because all these virtues I have named are within.

But who is sufficient to name them all? They are like an army belonging to an emperor who sits within your mind. Just as an emperor accomplishes whatever pleases him through his army, [Note: [Col. 2036] Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov.: “whatever pleases him.”] so the Lord Jesus Christ, beginning to dwell in our inner person—that is, in our mind through faith (Eph. 3:17)—uses these virtues as his ministers.

Through these virtues, which cannot be seen with the eyes and yet, when named, are praised—for they would not be praised unless they were loved, nor loved unless they were seen; and if they are loved only because they are seen, they are seen with another eye, that is, with the inner sight of the heart—through these invisible virtues, visible limbs are moved: feet for walking, but where? Where the good will moves them, a good emperor’s soldier. Hands for working, but what do they do? What love commands, love inspired within by the Holy Spirit.

The limbs are therefore seen when they move, but the one who commands within is not seen. And who commands within, only the one who commands and the one within who is commanded nearly know.

## 2

For, brothers, you heard just now when the Gospel was read—certainly if you gave it not only the ear of the body but also that of the heart. What does it say? “Beware of practicing your righteousness before people in order to be seen by them” (Matt. 6:1).

Did he mean that we should hide whatever good we do from human eyes and fear being seen? If you fear spectators, you will have no imitators. Therefore, you should be seen. But you should not act for the purpose of being seen. The end of your joy should not be there, nor the limit of your happiness, so that you think you have obtained the entire fruit of your good work when you have been seen and praised.

That is nothing. Despise yourself when you are praised; let the one who works through you be praised in you. Do not therefore do the good you do for your own praise, but for the praise of the one from whom you have the ability to do good. You have the ability to do evil from yourself; you have the ability to do good from God.

But observe how perverse and inverted wicked people are. They want to attribute to themselves what they do well; if they do evil, they want to accuse God. Turn around this distorted and inverted thing, as though setting it upside down: make what is above below, and what is below above. Do you want to put God below and yourself above? You are being thrown down, not raised up; for he is always above.

What then? You do good, and God does evil? Rather, if you wish to speak more truthfully, say: “I do evil; he does good; and whatever I do well, I do well through him. For from myself, whatever I do is evil.”

This confession strengthens the heart and establishes the foundation of love. For if we ought to hide our good works so that they may not be seen by people, where is the Lord’s statement in the sermon he delivered on the mountain? In the very place where he said this, he also said shortly before: “Let your good works shine before people.” And he did not stop there or make that the end; he added: “And let them glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

And what does the Apostle say? “I was unknown by face to the churches of Judea that are in Christ; they had only heard that the one who formerly persecuted us now proclaims the faith that he once destroyed; and they glorified God in me” (Gal. 1:22–24).

See how he too, because he became known in this way, did not end with his own praise but with the praise of God. As far as he himself was concerned, he was a destroyer of the Church, an envious persecutor, and a wicked man. He himself confesses this; we are not insulting him. Paul loves having his sins mentioned by us, so that the one who healed such a sickness may be glorified.

The physician’s hand cut away the magnitude of the wound and healed it. That voice from heaven cast down the persecutor and raised up the preacher; it killed Saul and gave life to Paul (Acts 9). Saul was a persecutor of the holy man (1 Kings 19); this man had that name when he was persecuting Christians. Later he became Paul from Saul (Acts 13:9).

What does “Paul” mean? “Little.” Thus, when Saul, he was proud and exalted; when Paul, humble and little. This is why we say, “I shall see you shortly”—that is, after a little while.

Hear that he became little: “I am the least of the Apostles” (1 Cor. 15:9); and elsewhere: “To me, the least of all the saints” (Eph. 3:8). Thus he was among the Apostles like the fringe of a garment. But the Church of the Gentiles touched him as a woman suffering from a hemorrhage, and she was healed (Matt. 9:20–22).

## 3

Therefore, brothers, let me say this—I say it now, and if I could I would not be silent about it: let those particular works be present in you at the appropriate time, according to the hours and the days. Are we always to speak? Are we always to be silent? Are we always to refresh the body? Are we always to fast? Are we always to give bread to the needy? Are we always to clothe the naked? Are we always to visit the sick? Are we always to reconcile those who are at odds? Are we always to bury the dead?

Now one thing, now another. These activities begin and cease; but that emperor neither begins nor ought to cease. Let love within never be interrupted; let the services of love be offered according to the time. Therefore, as it is written, “Let brotherly love continue” (Heb. 13:1).

## 4

Perhaps some of you have been troubled, since we have been expounding this Epistle of blessed John for you, as to why he commends nothing so emphatically except brotherly love. “Whoever loves his brother,” he says (1 John 2:10); and, “We have been given the commandment that we should love one another” (ibid. 3:23).

He has repeatedly named brotherly love. But he has not named the love of God—that is, the love with which we ought to love God—with equal frequency, although he has not been entirely silent about it. As for the love of enemies, he is almost completely silent throughout the whole Epistle.

Although he vigorously preaches and commends love to us, he does not tell us to love our enemies; he tells us to love our brothers. But just now, when the Gospel was read, we heard: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?” (Matt. 5:46).
