What, then, is the meaning of John the Apostle’s commending brotherly love to us as a great thing, leading toward a certain perfection, while the Lord says that it is not enough for us to love our brothers, but that we must extend this love until we reach our enemies?

The one who reaches his enemies does not leap over his brothers. As with fire, it must first occupy what is nearest and then extend itself to what is farther away. Your brother is nearer to you than some unknown person. Again, the person whom you did not know but who nevertheless does not oppose you is more closely attached to you than an enemy who also opposes you.

Extend love to those near you, but do not call that extension. For you love those near you when you love those who adhere to you. Extend it to strangers who have done you no harm. Go beyond even them; reach the point of loving your enemies. Certainly this is what the Lord commands.

Why, then, has John remained silent about love of the enemy?

## 5

Every dilectio [love]—including what is called carnal, which is customarily called not dilectio but rather amor [love/affection], since the name dilectio is more commonly used and understood of better things—nevertheless has, dearest brothers, a certain goodwill toward those who are loved.

For we ought not, nor can we, love people in the way that gluttons say, “I love thrushes.” You ask why? So that he may kill and consume them. He says that he loves them, and he loves them for this purpose: so that they may cease to exist, so that he may destroy them. Whatever we love as food, we love so that it may be consumed and we may be refreshed.

Are people to be loved as though they were to be consumed? Rather, there is a friendship of goodwill, so that at times we may benefit those whom we love. [Note: [Col. 2038] Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov.: “but a friendship of goodwill, so that.” M.]

What if there is nothing we can give them? Goodwill alone is sufficient for the one who loves. We should not wish people to be miserable so that we may exercise works of mercy. You give bread to the hungry; but better would be that no one were hungry and you gave to no one. You clothe the naked; would that all were clothed and there were no such need! You bury the dead; would that the life in which no one dies should one day come! You reconcile those who quarrel; would that the eternal peace of Jerusalem should one day exist, where no one disagrees!

All these are services required by necessity. Remove the miserable, and the works of mercy will cease. When the works of mercy cease, will the ardor of love also be extinguished? You love a happy person more genuinely when there is nothing you need to give him; that love will be purer and much more sincere.

For if you benefit a miserable person, perhaps you wish to exalt yourself over him and want him to be subject to you, the one who is the source of his benefit. He was in need; you gave. You seem greater because you gave than the one who received the gift. [Col. 2039] Wish him to be your equal, so that both of you may be under the one to whom nothing can be given.

6. For in this the proud soul exceeded measure and was, in a sense, greedy, because “the love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6:10). And again it is said, “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10:15). Sometimes we ask how these two statements agree: “The love of money is the root of all evils,” and “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” If pride is the beginning of every sin, then pride is the root of all evils. Yet certainly the love of money is the root of all evils: and we find greed also in pride, for a person has exceeded measure. What is it to be greedy? To go beyond what is sufficient.

Adam fell through pride: “Pride is the beginning of every sin,” it says. Was this not greed? What was greedier than one for whom God could not suffice? Therefore, brothers, we read how humanity was made in the image and likeness of God—and what did God say about it? “And let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the heavens, and over all the animals that creep upon the earth” (Gen. 1:26). Did he say, “Let them have dominion over human beings”? “Let them have dominion,” he said: he gave a natural dominion. Over what were they to have dominion? Over the fish of the sea, the birds of the heavens, and all the creeping things that creep upon the earth.

Why is this the human being’s natural dominion in these matters? Because humanity has dominion by virtue of having been made in the image of God. Where, then, was humanity made in the image of God? In understanding, in the mind, in the inner person—in that by which one understands truth, distinguishes justice from injustice, knows by whom one was made, can understand one’s Creator, and praise one’s Creator. Whoever possesses prudence possesses this understanding.

Therefore, since many, through evil desires, were wearing away the image of God in themselves and, in a sense, extinguishing the very flame of understanding through perverse conduct, Scripture cried out to them: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, which have no understanding” (Ps. 31:9). This is to say: “I have set you above the horse and the mule; I made you in my image and gave you dominion over these creatures. Why? Because wild beasts do not possess a rational mind; but you, with a rational mind, grasp the truth and understand what is above you. Submit yourselves to the one who is above you, and those over which you have been placed will be beneath you.” But because through sin humanity abandoned the one under whom it ought to be, it has been subjected to those over which it ought to have been.

7. Pay attention to what I say: God, the human being, the animals. For example, God is above you; the animals are beneath you. Acknowledge the one who is above you, so that what is beneath you may acknowledge you. Thus, when Daniel acknowledged God above himself, the lions acknowledged him as above themselves (Dan. 6:22).

But if you do not acknowledge the one who is above you, you despise your superior and are subjected to your inferior. Therefore, how was the pride of the Egyptians subdued? By frogs and flies (Exod. 8). God could also have sent lions, but a certain kind of great person must be terrified by a lion. The more proud they were, the more their evil neck was broken by contemptible and lowly creatures.

But the lions acknowledged Daniel because he was subject to God. What, then? The martyrs who fought with wild beasts and were torn by the bites of animals—were they not subject to God? Or were the three young men servants of God, while the Maccabees were not servants of God? The fire acknowledged the three servants of God whom it did not burn and whose garments it did not damage (Dan. 3:50); did it not acknowledge the Maccabees? It acknowledged the Maccabees; it acknowledged these men also, brothers (2 Macc. 7).

But a certain scourging was necessary, with the Lord permitting it—he who says in Scripture, “He scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6). Do you suppose, brothers, that iron would have pierced the Lord’s entrails unless he himself had permitted it, or that he would have remained fixed to the wood unless he himself had willed it? Did his own creation not acknowledge him? Or did he set before his faithful an example of patience?

Thus God visibly delivered some and did not visibly deliver others; yet he delivered all spiritually and spiritually abandoned no one. Visibly he seemed to have abandoned some and seemed to have rescued others. Therefore he rescued certain people, so that you would not think he was unable to rescue them. He gave testimony that he can, so that where he does not act, you might understand a more hidden will rather than suspect an inability.

But what, brothers? When we have escaped all these snares of mortality, when the times of temptation have passed, when the river of this age has run its course, and we have received that first garment—the immortality that we lost through sin—when “this corruptible has put on incorruption,” that is, when this flesh has put on incorruption, and “this mortal has put on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53–54), then, as perfected children of God, when there is no need to be tested or scourged, every creature will acknowledge us. Everything will be subjected to us, if here we are subject to God.

8. Thus a Christian ought to be such that he does not glory over other human beings. God has given you dominion over beasts—that is, he has made you better than beasts. This is natural to you: you will always be better than a beast.

If you wish to be better than another human being, you will envy him when you see that he is your equal. You ought to wish all human beings to be your equals; and if you surpass someone in prudence, you ought to wish that he too may become prudent.

As long as he is slow to understand, he learns from you; as long as he is uneducated, he needs you; and you appear to be the teacher, while he is the learner. You are therefore superior because you are the teacher, and he inferior because he is the learner. Unless you wish him to be your equal, you always want him to remain a learner. But if you always want to have a learner, you will be an envious teacher. If you are an envious teacher, how will you be a teacher? I beg you, do not teach him your envy.

Hear the Apostle speaking of the depths of love: “I would that all people were as I myself am” (1 Cor. 7:7). How did he wish all to be equal? He was superior to all because, through love, he desired all to be equal.

Humanity therefore exceeded measure: it wanted to be greedier, so as to be above human beings, although it was made above the animals. And this is pride.

9. And observe how many works pride performs. Consider in your heart how similar they are, and almost equal, to the works of love. Love feeds the hungry, and pride feeds them too—love so that God may be praised, pride so that pride itself may be praised. Love clothes the naked, and pride clothes them too. Love fasts, and pride fasts too. Love buries the dead, and pride buries them too.

All the good works that love wishes to do and does, pride drives forward against it, and, as it were, drives its own horses. But love is inward: it removes the place of pride when pride is badly driven—not from the one who drives badly, but from the one badly driven.

Woe to the person whose charioteer is pride; he must go headlong. But, so that pride may not be what drives good deeds, who knows? Who sees? Where is this found? We see the actions: mercy feeds, and pride feeds too; mercy welcomes a guest, and pride welcomes a guest too; mercy intervenes on behalf of the poor, and pride intervenes too.

What is this? In the actions we do not distinguish them. I dare to say something—but not I; Paul said it: love dies, that is, a person who has love confesses the name of Christ and undergoes martyrdom; pride also confesses and undergoes martyrdom. One possesses love; the other does not.

But let the one who does not possess love hear from the Apostle: “If I distribute all my goods to the poor, and if I give my body to be burned, but do not have love, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13:3).

Divine Scripture therefore calls us back inward from the display of this outward appearance, from this surface that is paraded before human beings. Return to your conscience; question it itself. Do not attend to what flourishes outwardly, but to what root lies in the earth.

Is desire rooted there? There may be the appearance of good deeds, but the deeds cannot truly be good. Is love rooted there? Be secure: nothing evil can proceed from it.

Pride flatters; love rages. One clothes; the other beats. For the former clothes in order to please human beings; the latter beats in order to correct through discipline. The blow of love is received more readily than the almsgiving of pride.

[Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions present this passage as follows: “Pride flatters . . . that one clothes . . . for that one clothes.” M.]

Return inward, then, brothers; and in everything you do, look upon God as your witness. See whether he sees with what disposition you act. If your heart does not accuse you of acting for the sake of display, good: be secure.

But do not be afraid to do good lest another see it. Fear doing it for this reason: that you may be praised. Let another see it so that God may be praised. For if you hide it from human eyes, you remove it from human imitation and take praise away from God.

There are two people to whom you give alms: two are hungry; one for bread, the other for righteousness. Between these two hungry people—since it is said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matt. 5:6)—you, the good worker, have been placed. If love acts through you, it has compassion on both and wishes to help both.

One seeks something to eat; the other seeks something to imitate. You feed the one; present yourself to the other. You have given alms to both: you made the one grateful for the hunger that was ended; you made the other an imitator through the example set before him.

[Note: Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain read praebes, “you present,” rather than praebe, “present.” M.]

10. Be merciful, therefore, as merciful people, because in loving your enemies also you love your brothers. Do not think that John gave no command concerning love of the enemy, because he did not remain silent about brotherly love: you love your brothers.

“How,” you ask, “do we love our brothers?” I ask why you love your enemy: why do you love him? So that he may be healthy in this life? What if that is not good for him? So that he may be rich? What if he will be blinded by those very riches? So that he may marry? What if he will suffer a bitter life because of it? So that he may have children? What if they will be evil?

These things that you seem to wish for your enemy because you love him are therefore uncertain; they are uncertain. Wish him to have eternal life with you; wish him to be your brother.

If, then, you wish this—by loving your enemy—that he may be your brother, when you love him, you love a brother. For you do not love in him what he is, but what you wish him to be.

I said to your Charity once before, if I am not mistaken: a piece of wood lies before the eyes; an excellent craftsman sees the unworked timber, cut from the forest, and loves it. I do not know what he intends to make from it. He does not love it so that it may always remain as it is. In his craft he saw what was to be, not in his affection what was; and he loved what he was going to make from it, not what it was.

So God loved us sinners. We say that God loved sinners, for he says, “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick” (Matt. 9:12). Did he love sinners so that we would remain sinners? The craftsman saw us as timber from the forest and conceived the building he was going to make from it, not the forest that it had been.

So you look upon your enemy opposing you, raging, biting with words, provoking with insults, and attacking with hatred; you attend to the fact that he is a human being. You see all these hostile things done by a human being, and you see in him what was made by God. That he was made human was God’s work. That he hates you, God did not make; that he envies, God did not make.

And what do you say in your heart? “Lord, be merciful to him; forgive him his sins; strike him with fear; change him.” You do not love in him what he is, but what you wish him to be.

Therefore, when you love your enemy, you love your brother. Perfect love is consequently love of the enemy; and this perfect love is contained in brotherly love.

Let no one say that the Apostle John gave us a lesser command and the Lord Christ a greater one: John instructed us to love our brothers; Christ admonished us to love even our enemies (Matt. 5:44). Consider why Christ admonished you to love your enemies. Was it so that they would always remain enemies? If he instructed you to love them so that they would remain enemies, you hate them; you do not love them.

Consider how he himself loved them—that is, because he did not wish persecutors to remain as they were. He said, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). Those for whom he wished forgiveness, he wished to be changed; those whom he wished to be changed, he graciously made brothers from enemies—and truly he did so.

He was killed, buried, rose again, ascended into heaven, and sent the Holy Spirit to his disciples. They began to preach his name with confidence and performed miracles in the name of the crucified and slain man. His killers saw them; those who had shed his blood in rage drank it in faith.

11. I have said these things, brothers, at some length; yet because love itself had to be commended to your Charity with greater force, it had to be commended in this way. For if there is no love in you, we have said nothing. But if it is in you, we have added oil to the flames; and in one in whom it was not present, perhaps it has been kindled by our words.

In one person what was already there has grown; in another, what was not there has begun to exist. We have said these things, therefore, so that you will not be slow to love your enemies.

Does a person rage against you? He rages; you pray. He hates; you show mercy. The fever of his soul hates you. He will be healthy, and he will thank you.

How do physicians love the sick? Do they love them as sick? If they loved them as sick, they would want them always to be sick. They love the sick not so that they may remain sick, but so that from being sick they may become healthy.

And how much they often endure from the deranged! What insults in words! They are often struck as well. The physician persecutes the fever and forgives the person. And what shall I say, brothers? Does he love his enemy? Rather, he hates his enemy’s illness. He hates the illness itself and loves the person by whom he is struck; he hates the fever.

By what is he struck? By disease, by sickness, by fever. He removes what is hostile to the person, so that what can bring joy may remain.

So also you: if your enemy hates you, and hates you unjustly, know that worldly desire rules in him; that is why he hates you. If you hate him in return, you repay evil for evil.

What does repaying evil for evil accomplish?

[Note: Louvain reads, “What are you doing, repaying evil for evil?” These words are absent from Erasmus’s Frobenian edition and are placed in brackets in Erasmus’s, Guillaume’s, Lyons, and Venice editions. M.]

I was weeping over one sick person who hated you; now I lament over two, if you also hate. But he attacks your property; he takes from you things you possess on earth. Therefore you hate him, because he causes you distress on earth. Do not endure distress: move upward into heaven. You will have your heart where there is breadth, so that you may suffer no distress in the hope of eternal life.

Consider what he is taking from you. He would not take even that unless the one who scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. 12:6) permitted it. In a certain sense your enemy is God’s instrument by which you are healed. If God knows that it is useful for you to be stripped, he permits him to do so; if he knows that it is useful for you to be beaten, he permits him to beat you. Through that person he is treating you. Wish, then, that he may be healed.

12. “No one has ever seen God.” See, beloved: “If we love one another, God will remain in us, and his love will be perfected in us.” Begin to love, and you will be perfected. Have you begun to love? God has begun to dwell in you. Love the one who has begun to dwell in you, so that by dwelling more perfectly he may make you perfect.

“In this we know that we remain in him and he in us, because he has given us of his Spirit.” Good; thanks be to God. We know that he dwells in us. And how do we know this—because we know that he dwells in us? Because John himself said this: “Because he has given us of his Spirit.”

How do we know that he has given us of his Spirit? This very fact—that he has given you of his Spirit: how do you know it? Question your inmost being. If it is full of love, you possess the Spirit of God.

How do we know that you know from this that the Spirit of God dwells in you? Ask the Apostle Paul: “Because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

13. “And we have seen and testify that the Father sent his Son as Savior of the world.” Be confident, you who are sick: such a physician has come, and you despair? The diseases were great, the wounds incurable, the illness beyond hope. You attend to the magnitude of your evil but do not attend to the omnipotence of the physician?

You are beyond hope; but he is omnipotent. Those who were first healed and announce the physician are witnesses of this; yet even they were healed more in hope than in reality. For the Apostle says, “For in hope we were saved” (Rom. 8:24).

We have therefore begun to be healed in faith; but our salvation will be perfected when “this corruptible puts on incorruption, and this mortal puts on immortality” (1 Cor. 15:53–54). This is hope, not yet the reality. But whoever rejoices in hope will also possess the reality; whoever has no hope will not be able to arrive at the reality.

14. “Whoever confesses that Jesus is the Son of God, God remains in him, and he in God.” Let us now say this of not many: whoever confesses—not in word, but in deed; not with the tongue, but with life. For many confess with words but deny with deeds.

“And we have known and believed the love that God has for us.” Again, how did you come to know it? “God is love.” He already said this above; behold, he says it again. Love could not have been commended to you more fully than by saying that God is love.

Perhaps you were about to despise God’s gift. And do you despise God? God is love. “And whoever remains in love remains in God, and God remains in him.” They dwell mutually in one another—the one who contains and the one who is contained.

You dwell in God, but so that you may be contained; God dwells in you, but so that he may contain you, lest you fall. Do not perhaps imagine that you become God’s house in the way that your house carries your body. If the house in which you are withdraws from you, you fall; but if you withdraw yourself, God does not fall.

He is whole when you abandon him; whole when you return to him. You are healed; you contribute nothing to him. You are cleansed, restored, corrected. He is medicine for the sick, a rule for the crooked, light for one in darkness, a dwelling for one abandoned. Everything is conferred upon you.

See that you do not think anything is conferred upon God when you come to him—not even, so to speak, a slave. Will God therefore have no servants if you do not wish it, and if no one wishes it? God does not need servants; servants need God. Therefore the Psalm says, “I said to the Lord, ‘You are my God’” (Ps. 15:2). He is the true Lord.

And what does he say? “You have no need of my good” (Ps. 15:2). You need the good of your servant. A servant needs your good so that you may feed him; you also need the good of your servant so that he may help you.

You cannot fill your own water, cook for yourself, run before your own horse, or care for your own animal. You see that you need the good of your servant; you need his service. You are therefore not a true lord when you need one who is beneath you.

He is the true Lord who asks nothing from us; and woe to us if we do not seek him. He asks nothing from us, yet he sought us when we were not seeking him. One sheep had gone astray; he found it and, rejoicing, carried it back on his shoulders (Luke 15:4–5).

Was the sheep necessary to the shepherd, and not rather the shepherd necessary to the sheep? The more gladly I speak of love, the less I wish to bring this Epistle to an end. Nothing more fervently commends love. Nothing sweeter is preached to you, nothing more wholesome is drunk—but only if by living well you confirm God’s gift in yourselves.

Do not be ungrateful for the greatness of his grace: although he had an Only-Begotten Son, he did not wish him to remain alone, but adopted brothers for him, who would possess eternal life with him.

# TREATISE IX

On the passage that follows, “In this love is perfected in us,” up to, “And we have this commandment from him, that whoever loves God should love his brother also.” Chapters 4–5, verses 17–21.

[Col. 2045]

1. Your Charity remembers that the final part of the Epistle of the Apostle John remains for us to treat and expound to you, insofar as the Lord grants it. We therefore remember this obligation; you ought to remember the demand you make. For the same love that is commended, chiefly and almost exclusively, in the Epistle itself makes us most faithful debtors and makes you sweetest exactors.

I called you sweetest exactors because where love is absent, the exactor is bitter; but where love is present, the one who demands is sweet. And the one from whom something is demanded, even if he undertakes some labor, finds that very labor made almost nothing and light by love itself.

Do we not see even among dumb and irrational animals—where there is not spiritual love, but carnal and natural affection—that young creatures nevertheless draw milk from their mother’s breasts with great feeling? And although the suckling strikes the breast with force, it is still better for the mother than if it did not suck and demand what love requires.

Often we see the breasts of cows struck on the head even by rather large calves, and the bodies of the mothers almost lifted by the force of the blow; yet they do not drive them away with a kick. And if the son who should suck is absent, they call him to their breasts by lowing.

If, then, that spiritual love is in us of which the Apostle says, “I became a little child among you, like a nurse cherishing her own children” (1 Thess. 2:7), then we love you when you make demands. We do not love the sluggish, because we fear for the languishing.

Certain solemn readings for feast days intervened and interrupted the text of this Epistle; they could not be omitted from reading or from treatment. Let us now return to the order we passed over, and let your Holiness listen attentively to what remains.

I do not know whether love could be commended to us more magnificently than by saying, “God is love.” A brief praise, and a great praise: brief in expression, great in meaning. How quickly one says, “God is love”! This is brief: if you count, it is one word; if you weigh it, how great it is! “God is love.”

“And whoever remains,” he says, “in love remains in God, and God remains in him” (1 John 4:16). Let God be your house, and be God’s house. Remain in God, and let God remain in you. God remains in you to contain you; you remain in God so that you do not fall, because the Apostle says of love itself, “Love never falls” (1 Cor. 13:8). How can the one whom God contains fall?

2. “In this love is perfected in us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgment, because as he is, so are we in this world.” He explains how each person may prove how far love has advanced in him—or rather, how far he himself has advanced in love.

For if God is love, God neither advances nor declines. Love is said to advance in you because you advance in it. Ask, then, how far you have advanced in love, and what your heart answers you, so that you may know the measure of your progress.

He promised to show us the way by which we know him, and said, “In this love is perfected in us.” Ask, “In what?” “That we may have confidence on the day of judgment.” Whoever has confidence on the day of judgment has perfect love in him.

What does it mean to have confidence on the day of judgment? Not to fear that the day of judgment will come.

There are people who do not believe in the day of judgment. These cannot have confidence on a day that they do not believe will come. Let us set them aside. May God awaken them so that they may live; why speak of the dead? They do not believe that the day of judgment will come; they neither fear nor desire what they do not believe.

Someone begins to believe in the day of judgment. If he begins to believe, he also begins to fear. But because he still fears, he does not yet have confidence on the day of judgment; love is not yet perfected in him.

Should we nevertheless despair? When you see a beginning, why despair of the end? “What beginning do I see?” you ask. Fear itself. Hear Scripture: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Ecclus. 1:16).

He has therefore begun to fear the day of judgment. By fearing, let him correct himself; let him keep watch against his enemies—that is, against his sins. Let him begin to revive inwardly and to mortify his members that are upon the earth, as the Apostle says: “Mortify your members that are upon the earth.” He calls the works of spiritual wickedness members upon the earth, for he continues and explains: “Greed, uncleanness” (Col. 3:5), and the other things he lists there.

To the extent that this person, who has begun to fear the day of judgment, mortifies his earthly members, to that extent his heavenly members rise and grow strong. The heavenly members are all good works.

As the heavenly members rise, he begins to desire what he once feared. He feared that Christ might come and find an ungodly person whom he would condemn; he desires Christ to come because he will find a godly person whom he will crown.

When the chaste soul begins to desire Christ’s coming—the soul that longs for the embraces of the bridegroom—it renounces the adulterer and becomes inwardly a virgin through faith, hope, and love. It now has confidence on the day of judgment. It does not struggle against itself when it prays and says, “Your kingdom come” (Matt. 6:10).

For whoever fears that God’s kingdom may come fears that his prayer may be heard. How does one pray who fears that the prayer may be heard? Whoever prays with the confidence of love already desires that it may come.

A certain person spoke of this desire in a Psalm: “And you, Lord, how long? Turn, Lord, and deliver my soul” (Ps. 6:4–5). He groaned because the coming was delayed.

Some people die patiently; there are also certain perfect people who live patiently. What did I say? Whoever still desires this life, when the day of death comes, patiently endures death. He struggles against himself so as to follow God’s will; he does inwardly what God chooses rather than what human will chooses. Desire for the present life becomes a struggle with death; he applies patience and courage so that he may die with an even mind. Such a person dies patiently.

But whoever desires, as the Apostle says, “to depart and be with Christ,” does not die patiently; rather, he lives patiently and dies gladly. See the Apostle living patiently—that is, patiently not loving this life here, but enduring it. “To depart,” he says, “and to be with Christ is much better; but to remain in the flesh is necessary for your sake” (Phil. 1:23–24).

Therefore, brothers, work inwardly; act upon yourselves within, so that you may desire the day of judgment. Perfect love is not proved in any other way than when that day begins to be desired. The person who desires it is the one who has confidence in it; and the person who has confidence in it is the one whose conscience does not tremble in perfect and sincere love.

3. “In this his love is perfected in us, that we may have confidence on the day of judgment.” Why will we have confidence? “Because as he is, so are we in this world.”

You have heard the reason for your confidence: “Because as he is,” he says, “so are we in this world.” Does he not seem to have said something impossible? Can a human being be like God?

I have already explained to you that “as” is not always spoken with reference to equality; it can be spoken with reference to a certain likeness. For how do you say, “As I have ears, so does an image have ears”? Is it altogether so? Yet you say, “as.”

If, then, we have been made in the image of God, why are we not like God? Not in equality, but according to our measure.

How, then, is confidence given to us on the day of judgment? “Because as he is, so are we in this world.” We must refer this to love itself and understand what has been said.

The Lord says in the Gospel: “If you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same?” What, then, does he wish us to do?

[Note: Venice adds, “to love.” M.]

“But I say to you, love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you.” If, then, he commands us to love our enemies, from whom does he give us an example? From God himself. For he says, “So that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.”

How does God do this? He loves his enemies, “for he makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5:44–46).

If, then, God invites us to this perfection, that we love our enemies as he himself loved his, our confidence on the day of judgment is grounded in this: “As he is, so are we in this world.” For as he loves his enemies by making his sun rise on the good and the evil and sending rain on the just and the unjust, so we, since we cannot bestow sun and rain upon our enemies, bestow tears when we pray for them.

4. Now, then, consider what he says about confidence itself. How is perfect love understood? “There is no fear in love.” What, then, shall we say of the person who has begun to fear the day of judgment? If love were perfect in him, he would not fear.

Perfect love would produce perfect righteousness, and he would have no reason to fear; rather, he would have reason to desire that iniquity pass away and God’s kingdom come.

Therefore, “there is no fear in love.” But in what kind of love? Not in love that has merely begun. In what kind, then? “Perfect love,” he says, “casts out fear.”

Let fear begin, then, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.” Fear, as it were, prepares a place for love. But when love begins to dwell there, the fear that prepared its place is driven out. As love grows, fear diminishes; as love becomes more inward, fear is driven outward. Greater love, lesser fear; lesser love, greater fear.

But if there is no fear at all, there is no way for love to enter. Just as we see thread introduced by a bristle when something is sewn: the bristle enters first, but unless it exits, the thread does not follow. So fear first occupies the mind; yet fear does not remain there, because it entered in order to introduce love.

Once security has been made in the soul, what joy is ours either in this age or in the age to come? And in this age, who will harm us when we are full of love?

See how the Apostle exults in love itself: “Who,” he says, “will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or danger, or the sword?” (Rom. 8:35). And Peter says, “Who can harm you if you are zealous for what is good?” (1 Pet. 3:13).

“There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear, because fear has torment.” The conscience of sins torments the heart; justification has not yet been completed. There is something there that tickles and pricks.

Therefore, what does the Psalm say about the perfection of righteousness itself? “You have turned my mourning into joy; you have removed my sackcloth and girded me with gladness, so that my glory may sing to you and I may not be pricked” (Ps. 29:12–13).

What does “I may not be pricked” mean? May there be nothing to sting my conscience. Fear stings; but do not fear. Love enters and heals what fear wounds.

The fear of God wounds like a physician’s instrument: it removes the corruption, and seems, as it were, to enlarge the wound. When corruption was in the body, the wound was smaller but dangerous. The physician’s instrument approaches; the wound hurt less before than it does now when it is cut. It hurts more when it is being healed than if it were not being healed. But it hurts more when the medicine arrives so that, when health follows, it may never hurt again.

Let fear therefore occupy your heart, so that it may introduce love; let the scar follow the physician’s instrument.

[Note: Printed editions read, “fear, and when love has been introduced, let the scar follow.” Three manuscripts read, “so that it may introduce love; let the scar follow.” Two others read, “so that it may introduce love, and let the scar follow.” M.]

Such is the physician that not even scars appear. Only submit yourself to his right hand. For if you are without fear, you cannot be justified. Scripture has spoken the sentence: “Whoever is without fear cannot be justified” (Ecclus. 1:28).

It is therefore necessary that fear first enter, through which love may come. Fear is medicine; love is health.

“But whoever fears is not perfect in love.” Why? “Because fear has torment”—just as a physician’s incision has torment.

### 5

There is another statement that seems contrary to this one, if it does not have an interpreter. For in one place in the Psalm it says: “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever” (Ps. XVIII, 10). It presents us with a certain eternal fear, but a pure one. Now if that passage presents us with eternal fear, does it perhaps contradict this Epistle, which says, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear”? Let us question both utterances of God. The Spirit is one, even if the books are two, even if the mouths are two, even if the languages are two. This was spoken through John, that through David; but do not suppose that the Spirit is another. If one breath fills two pipes, can one Spirit not fill two hearts and move two tongues? [Col. 2049] But if two pipes filled by one spirit—that is, by one breath—sound in harmony, can two tongues filled by the Spirit of God sound discordantly? There is therefore a certain consonance and a certain harmony, but it requires a hearer. Behold: the Spirit of God inspired and filled two hearts, two mouths, and moved two tongues. From one tongue we heard, “There is no fear in love, but perfect love casts out fear”; from the other we heard, “The fear of the Lord is pure, enduring forever and ever.” What is this? Do they seem to be discordant? No: clear your ears and attend to the melody. It was not without reason that here he added “pure,” while there he did not add it: it is because there is one fear called pure, and another that is not called pure.

Let us distinguish these two fears and understand the harmony of the pipes. How do we understand or distinguish them? Let Your Charity attend. There are people who fear God for this reason: lest they be sent into Gehenna, lest they perhaps burn with the devil in eternal fire. That is the fear that introduces love; but it comes in order to depart. For if you still fear God on account of punishments, you do not yet love the one whom you fear in this way. You do not desire good things, but avoid bad ones. Yet by avoiding bad things, you correct yourself and begin to desire good things. When you have begun to desire good things, there will be in you a pure fear. What is pure fear? Fear lest you lose those very good things.

Pay attention. It is one thing to fear God lest he send you into Gehenna with the devil; it is another to fear God lest he depart from you. The fear by which you fear being sent into Gehenna with the devil is not yet pure; for it does not arise from love of God, but from fear of punishment. But when you fear God lest his presence abandon you, you embrace him and desire to enjoy him.

### 6

Nothing can explain better the difference between these two fears—one which love casts out, and the other, pure fear, which endures forever and ever—than to set before you two married women. Suppose that one of them wishes to commit adultery and takes pleasure in wickedness, but fears that her husband may condemn her. She fears her husband, but because she still loves wickedness, she therefore fears her husband. Her husband’s presence is not pleasing but burdensome to her; and if she lives wickedly, she fears that her husband may come. Such are those who fear lest the day of judgment come.

Now suppose that the other loves her husband, owes him chaste embraces, and does not defile herself with any pollution of adultery; she longs for her husband’s presence. How are these two fears distinguished? That woman fears, and this woman also fears. Ask them: they seem to give one answer. Ask the one, “Do you fear your husband?” She replies, “I fear him.” Ask the other whether she fears her husband; she replies, “I fear him.” The voice is one, but the mind is different. Let them now be asked, “Why?” The one says, “I fear my husband lest he come”; the other says, “I fear my husband lest he depart.” The one says, “I fear lest I be condemned”; the other says, “I fear lest I be abandoned.” Place this in the minds of Christians, and you have found [Note: [Col. 2049] *Invenisti*, according to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov. M.] the fear which love casts out, and the other, pure fear, enduring forever and ever.

### 7

Let us therefore first address those who fear God as that woman does who takes pleasure in wickedness: she fears her husband lest he condemn her. Let us first address such people. [Col. 2050] O soul that fears God lest God condemn you, as the woman who takes pleasure in wickedness fears her husband lest her husband condemn her: just as that woman displeases you, so let yourself displease you. If you have a wife, would you want your wife to fear you in this way—to fear lest you condemn her—so that wickedness would delight her, but the weight of your fear would restrain her, rather than the condemnation of her iniquity? You want her to be chaste so that she may love you, not so that she may fear you. Present yourself to God as you want your wife to be toward you. And if you do not yet have a wife but wish to have one, this is the kind of wife you wish to have.

And what shall we say, brothers? That woman who fears her husband because she fears being condemned by him perhaps does not commit adultery lest somehow it come to her husband and he take this temporal light from her. Yet that husband can also be deceived, for he is a human being, just like the woman who can deceive him. She fears the one outside whose sight she can be: do you not always fear the face of the husband who is above you? “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil” (Ps. XXXIII, 17).

She seeks the absence of her husband and is perhaps stirred by the pleasure of adultery; yet she says to herself, “I will not do it.” He is indeed absent, but it is difficult for the matter not to reach him somehow. She restrains herself lest it come to a man who can both be unaware and be deceived, who can even think good of what is bad, and can even suppose that a chaste woman is faithful when she is an adulteress. Do you not fear the eyes of the one whom no one can deceive? Do you not fear the presence of the one who cannot turn away from you?

Ask God to look upon you and to turn his face away from your sins: “Turn your face away from my sins.” But how do you deserve that he should turn his face away from your sins? If you do not turn your face away from your sins. For that very voice says in the Psalm: “For I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me” (Ps. L, 11, 5). You acknowledge it, and he forgives.

### 8

We have addressed the woman who still possesses a fear that does not endure forever and ever, but which love excludes and casts out. Let us also address the woman who already possesses pure fear, enduring forever and ever. Do we think that we have found her, so that we may address her? Do you think she is in this assembly? Do you think she is in this hall? Do you think she is in this land? She cannot fail to exist, but she is hidden. It is winter; within, there is greenness in the root. Perhaps we have found her ears [Note: [Col. 2050] Er., Lugd., Ven.: “and her ears.” M.]. But wherever that soul is, would that I might find her—not so that she would lend me her ears, but so that I might lend her mine! Let her teach me something, rather than learn from me.

A certain holy, fiery soul, desiring the kingdom of God: it is not I who address her, but God himself, and he thus consoles her as she patiently lives on this earth: “You already wish me to come, and I know that you already wish me to come. I know what you are like, so that you may await my coming without fear. I know that it is a burden to you. But wait still longer; endure. I am coming, and I am coming quickly.” But to one who loves, delay is long.

Hear her singing like a lily amid thorns; hear her sighing and saying: “I shall sing and understand in the way of the undefiled: when will you come to me?” (Ps. C, 1–2). But in the undefiled way she rightly does not fear, because perfect love casts out fear. And when she comes into his embrace, [Col. 2051] she fears, but securely. What does she fear? She will beware of and guard herself against her iniquity, lest she sin again—not lest she be sent into the fire, but lest she be abandoned by him. And what will there be in her? Pure fear, enduring forever and ever.

We have heard two pipes sounding together. The one speaks of fear, and the other also speaks of fear; but one speaks of the fear by which the soul fears being condemned, while the other speaks of the fear by which the soul fears being abandoned. The former is the fear that love excludes; the latter is the fear that endures forever and ever.

### 9

Let us love, because he first loved us. For how could we love, unless he had first loved us? By loving, we became friends; but he loved enemies in order that we might become friends. He first loved us and granted us the ability to love him. We did not yet love him; by loving, we become beautiful.

What does a disfigured man with a distorted face do if he loves a beautiful woman? Or what does a disfigured, distorted, dark-skinned woman do if she loves a handsome man? By loving, can she become beautiful? And can he become handsome by loving? He loves a beautiful woman; and when he sees himself in a mirror, he is ashamed to raise his face toward the beautiful woman whom he loves. What will he do in order to be beautiful? Does he wait for beauty to come? Rather, by waiting, old age is added and makes him uglier. There is therefore nothing to do, no advice to give him, except that he restrain himself and not dare, unequal as he is, to love one who is his equal—or, if perhaps he loves her and wishes to marry her, that he love chastity in her, not the beauty of her flesh.

But our soul, my brothers, is ugly through iniquity; by loving God it becomes beautiful. What kind of love is this, which makes the lover beautiful? God, however, is always beautiful, never deformed, never changeable. He who is always beautiful loved us first; and what sort of people did he love, if not ugly and deformed ones? Yet not in order to leave us ugly, but to change us and make the deformed beautiful.

How shall we become beautiful? By loving him who is always beautiful. As love grows in you, beauty grows also, because love itself is the beauty of the soul. Let us love, because he first loved us.

Hear the Apostle Paul: “But God demonstrates his love toward us, in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Rom. V, 8–9)—the just for the unjust, the beautiful for the ugly.

How do we find beautiful Jesus? “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men; grace is poured upon your lips” (Ps. XLIV, 3). From where? See again from where he is beautiful: “You are beautiful in form beyond the sons of men,” because “in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I, 1).

But because he assumed flesh, he assumed, as it were, your ugliness—that is, your mortality—in order to adapt himself to you, correspond to you, and rouse you to love the beauty within. From where, then, do we find that Jesus is ugly and deformed, just as we find that he is beautiful and fair beyond the sons of men? Ask Isaiah: “And we saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” (Isa. LIII, 2).

These are the two pipes, as it were, sounding differently; but one Spirit fills them both. Here it is said, “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men”; [Col. 2052] there it is said in Isaiah, “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty.” Both pipes are filled by one Spirit; they do not sound discordantly. Do not turn away your ears; apply your understanding.

Let us ask the Apostle Paul, and let him explain to us the harmony of the two pipes. Let “Beautiful in form beyond the sons of men” sound for us: “Who, though he was in the form of God, did not regard equality with God as something to be grasped” (Phil. II, 6). Behold: beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.

Let “We saw him, and he had neither appearance nor beauty” sound for us also: “He emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings, and being found in appearance as a human being” (Phil. II, 6–7). He had neither appearance nor beauty in order to give you appearance and beauty.

What appearance? What beauty? The love of charity, so that, loving, you may run, and running, love. You are already beautiful; but do not fix your attention on yourself, lest you lose what you have received. Fix your attention on him by whom you were made beautiful. Therefore be beautiful so that he may love you. Direct your entire attention toward him; run toward him; seek his embrace; fear to depart from him, so that there may be in you pure fear, enduring forever and ever.

Let us love, because he first loved us.

### 10

“If anyone says, ‘I love God’”—which God? Why do we love? Because he first loved us and granted us the ability to love. He loved the ungodly in order to make them godly; he loved the unjust in order to make them just; he loved the sick in order to make them healthy. Therefore let us also love, because he first loved us.

Ask each person to tell you whether he loves God. He shouts out and confesses, “I love him”; he himself knows. There is another question by which he must be examined. “If anyone says,” he says, “I love God,” and hates his brother, he is a liar. How do you prove that he is a liar? Hear this: “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV, 20).

What then? Does the one who loves his brother also love God? He must love God; he must love love itself. Can he love his brother and not love love? He must love love.

What then? Does the one who loves love therefore love God? Certainly. By loving love, he loves God. Have you forgotten what you said shortly before: “God is love” (John IV, 8, 16)? If God is love, whoever loves love loves God.

Love your brother, therefore, and be secure. You cannot say, “I love my brother, but I do not love God.” Just as you lie when you say, “I love God,” while you do not love your brother, so you deceive yourself when you say, “I love my brother,” if you think that you do not love God. Whoever loves his brother must love love itself; and love is God. Therefore whoever loves his brother must love God.

But if you do not love the brother whom you see, how can you love God whom you do not see? Why does he not see God? Because he does not possess love itself. He does not see God because he does not possess love; he does not possess love because he does not love his brother. Therefore he does not see God because he does not possess love.

For if he possesses love, he sees God, because God is love. And that eye is cleansed more and more by love, so that it may see that unchangeable [Col. 2053] substance, whose presence it may always enjoy and in which it may delight forever, joined to the angels. But let it run now, so that one day it may rejoice in its homeland.

Let it not love its exile; let it not love the road. Let everything be bitter except the one who calls, until we cling to him and say what was said in the Psalm: “You have destroyed all who commit fornication away from you.” And who are those who commit fornication? Those who depart and love the world. But what of you? It follows and says: “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 27–28).

All my good is to cling freely to God. For if you ask and say, “Why do you cling to God?” and he says, “So that he may give me something,” what will he give you? He himself made heaven; he himself made earth. What is he going to give you? You already cling to him; find something better, and he gives it to you.

### 11

“For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” And we have this commandment from him: whoever loves God must love his brother also.

You spoke magnificently when you said, “I love God,” and yet you hate your brother! O murderer, how do you love God? Have you not heard earlier in this very Epistle: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer”?

“But I truly love God, even though I hate my brother.” You certainly do not love God if you hate your brother. And now I prove it by another testimony. He himself said, “He gave us the commandment that we should love one another” (I John III, 15, 23). How do you love the one whose commandment you hate?

Who would say, “I love the emperor, but I hate his laws”? The emperor understands that you love him by whether his laws are observed throughout the provinces. What is the emperor’s law? “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII, 34).

You therefore say that you love Christ: keep his commandment and love your brother. But if you do not love your brother, how do you love the one whose commandment you despise?

Brothers, I am not satisfied speaking about love in the name of Christ. To the extent that you possess an appetite for this matter, to that extent we hope that love itself grows in you and casts out fear, so that pure fear may remain—the fear enduring forever and ever.

Let us endure the world; let us endure tribulations; let us endure the scandals of temptations. Let us not depart from the way. Let us hold fast to the unity of the Church; let us hold fast to Christ; let us hold fast to love. Let us not be torn away from the members of his bride; let us not be torn away from the faith, so that we may glory in his presence. And we shall remain secure in him: now through faith, then through sight; of him we have, as so great a pledge, the gift of the Holy Spirit.

# TREATISE X

On the passage in which John writes, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God,” up to, “For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments.” Chapter V, verses 1–13.

### 1

I believe that those of you who were present yesterday remember how far our exposition had reached in the course of this Epistle: namely, “For whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see? And we have this commandment from him, that whoever loves God must love his brother also.” Up to this point the discussion had proceeded. Let us therefore examine what follows in order. [Col. 2054]

“Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.” Who is the one who does not believe that Jesus is the Christ? The one who does not live as Christ commanded. For many say, “I believe”; but faith without works does not save. The work of faith is love itself, as the Apostle Paul says: “Faith which works through love” (Gal. V, 6).

Your past works, before you believed, were either nonexistent or, if they seemed good, they were empty. If they were nonexistent, you were like a man without feet, or unable to walk because his feet were injured. But if they seemed good, before you believed you were indeed running, but because you were running outside the way, you were wandering rather than arriving.

We must therefore both run and run on the way. Whoever runs outside the way runs in vain; indeed, he runs toward labor. The more he runs outside the way, the more he wanders. What is the way on which we run? Christ said, “I am the way.” What is the homeland toward which we run? Christ said, “I am the truth” (John XIV, 6). Through him you run; toward him you run; in him you rest.

But so that we might run through him, he extended himself even to us. For we were far away and wandering far off. It is little to say that we were wandering far away: we were weak and unable to move ourselves. The physician came to the sick; the way was extended to exiles. Let us be saved by him; let us walk through him.

This is what it means to believe that Jesus is the Christ: to believe as Christians believe who are Christians not in name only, but also in deeds and life—not as the demons believe. For the demons also believe and tremble, as Scripture says (James II, 19).

What more could the demons have believed than to say, “We know who you are, the Son of God”? What the demons said, Peter also said. When the Lord asked who he was and whom people said that he was, the disciples answered him: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets.” And he said to them: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered and said: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.”

And he heard from the Lord: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jona, because flesh and blood did not reveal this to you, but my Father who is in heaven.” See what praises follow this faith: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matt. XVI, 13–18).

What does “Upon this rock I will build my Church” mean? Upon this faith; upon what was said, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” “Upon this rock,” he says, “I will establish my Church.” Great praise!

Peter therefore says, “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The demons also say, “We know who you are, the Son of God, the Holy One of God.” Peter says this, and the demons say it too: the words are the same, but not the disposition.

And how is it evident that Peter said this with love? Because the faith of a Christian is with love, while the faith of a demon is without love. How is it without love? Peter said this in order to embrace Christ; the demons said it in order that Christ might depart from them. For before they said, “We know who you are; you are the Son of God,” they said, “What have we to do with you? Why have you come before the time to destroy us?” (Matt. VIII, 29; Mark I, 24).

It is therefore one thing to confess Christ in order to hold fast to Christ; [Col. 2055] it is another thing to confess Christ in order to drive Christ away from you. Thus you see that when he says here, “Whoever believes,” this is a particular kind of faith, not belief in the same way as the many believe.

Therefore, brothers, let none of the heretics say to you, “We also believe.” For this reason I set before you the example of the demons: so that you would not rejoice at the words of those who believe, but would examine the deeds of those who live.

### 2

Let us therefore see what it means to believe in Christ, and what it means to believe that Jesus himself is the Christ. It follows: “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God.” But what does it mean to believe that? “And everyone who loves the one who begot him loves the one who was begotten by him.”

He immediately joined love to faith, because faith without love is empty. The faith of a Christian is with love; the faith of a demon is without love. Those who do not believe are worse than demons and slower than demons. Some person does not wish to believe in Christ; he does not yet even imitate the demons.

Now he believes in Christ, but hates Christ. He possesses a confession of faith out of fear of punishment, not out of love for the crown—for the demons also feared punishment. Add love to this faith, so that it becomes the faith of which the Apostle Paul says, “Faith which works through love” (Gal. V, 6). You have found a Christian; you have found a citizen of Jerusalem; you have found a citizen of the angels; you have found an exile sighing on the way. Join yourself to him: he is your companion. Run with him, if indeed you are also such a one.

“Everyone who loves the one who begot him loves the one who was begotten by him.” Who begot? The Father. Who was begotten? The Son. What, then, does he say? Everyone who loves the Father loves the Son.

### 3

“In this we know that we love the children of God.” What does this mean, brothers? A little earlier he was speaking about the Son of God, not about the children of God. Behold: Christ alone has been set before us for contemplation, and it was said to us, “Everyone who believes that Jesus is the Christ has been born of God”; and “everyone who loves the one who begot him”—that is, the Father—“loves the one who was begotten by him”—that is, the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.

And it follows: “In this we know that we love the children of God,” as though he were going to say, “In this we know that we love the Son of God.” He said “the children of God” of the one about whom he had just been speaking as the Son of God, because the children of God are the body of the only Son of God; and when he is the head and we are the members, there is one Son of God.

Therefore whoever loves the children of God loves the Son of God; and whoever loves the Son of God loves the Father. No one can love the Father unless he loves the Son; and whoever loves the Son also loves the children of God.

Which children of God? The members of the Son of God. By loving, a person himself becomes a member and, through love, becomes part of the joined structure of Christ’s body; and there will be one Christ loving himself. For when the members love one another, the body loves itself. And if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and if one member is glorified, all the members rejoice with it. And what does he say next? “But you are the body of Christ and members” (I Cor. XII, 26–27).

A little earlier he was speaking about brotherly love and said, “Whoever does not love the brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (I John IV, 20). But if you love your brother, perhaps you love your brother and do not love Christ? [Col. 2056] How could that be, when you love the members of Christ?

When, therefore, you love the members of Christ, you love Christ; when you love Christ, you love the Son of God; when you love the Son of God, you also love the Father. Love cannot be separated. Choose what you will love; the rest follow you.

You say, “I love God alone, God the Father.” You lie: if you love God, you do not love God alone; but if you love the Father, you also love the Son [Note: [Col. 2056] This passage is variously read in the printed editions. Lugd. and Ven. present it thus: “You lie. If you love God, you do not love God alone; but if you love the Father, you also love the Son.” Two manuscripts in Lov. read: “You lie. If you love, you do not love the Father alone,” etc. M.].

“Behold,” you say, “I love the Father and I love the Son—but only these: God the Father, and God the Son, and our Lord Jesus Christ, who ascended into heaven and sits at the right hand of the Father; that Word through whom all things were made, and the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I, 3, 14). “This alone I love.”

You lie. For if you love the head, you also love the members. But if you do not love the members, neither do you love the head. Do you not fear the voice of the head crying from heaven on behalf of the members: “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts IX, 4).

He called the persecutor of his members his own persecutor; he called the lover of his members his own lover. You already know what his members are, brothers: it is the Church of God.

“In this we know that we love the children of God, because we love God.” And how? Are the children of God something other than God? But whoever loves God loves his commandments. And what are God’s commandments? “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII, 34).

Let no one excuse himself by one kind of love from another kind of love. This love holds everything together entirely: just as it is joined together into one, so it makes all the things that depend upon it one, and as it were melts them together like fire.

It is gold; it is melted into a mass and becomes one thing. But unless the heat of love kindles it, many things cannot be melted into one. Because we love God, we know from this that we love the children of God.

### 4

And how do we know that we love the children of God? Because we love God and do his commandments.

Here we sigh because of the difficulty of doing God’s commandment. Hear what follows. “Human being, why do you labor in loving?” In loving greed [Note: [Col. 2056] Lov. has: “Human being, you who labor in loving greed, with toil.” Er., Lugd., Ven. have *homo qui laborabas*, “human being, you who were laboring,” and the rest as Lov. M.].

What you love is loved with toil; God is loved without toil. Greed commands labors, dangers, threshings, tribulations, and you are going to obey. To what end? So that you may have something with which to fill your chest, while losing your security. Perhaps you were more secure before you possessed anything than when you began to possess it.

See what greed commanded you: “Fill the house”—you filled it, and thieves are feared. “Acquire gold”—you acquired it, and lost sleep. See what greed commanded you: “Do it,” and you did it.

What does God command you? “Love me.” You love gold; you will seek gold and perhaps will not find it. “Whoever seeks me, I am with him.” You will love honor and perhaps will not attain it. “Who has loved me and not come to me?”

God says to you: “You wish to make someone your patron or a powerful friend; you court another who is inferior.” “Love me,” God says to you. No one is courted through another in order to reach me; love itself makes me present to you. What is sweeter than this love, brothers?

Not without reason did you hear in the Psalm just now: “The unjust have told me of delights, but not like your law, O Lord” (Ps. CXVIII, 85).

What is the law of God? God’s commandment. What is God’s commandment? That new commandment, which is called new because it renews: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.”

Hear that this itself is the law of God. The Apostle says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ” (Gal. VI, 2). Love is the completion of all our works. There is the end; for this we run; toward it we run. When we have reached it, we shall rest.

### 5

You heard in the Psalm: “I have seen the end of every completion” (Ps. CXVIII, 96). He said, “I have seen the end of every completion.” What had this man seen? Do we suppose that he had climbed to the summit of some very high and sharply pointed mountain, looked out from it, and seen the circuit of the earth and the circles of the entire world, and therefore said, “I have seen the end of every completion”?

If this is praiseworthy, let us ask the Lord for such sharp bodily eyes that we may seek some very lofty mountain on earth, from whose summit we may see the end of every completion.

Do not go far away. Behold, I tell you: climb the mountain and see the end. Christ is the mountain. Come to Christ; from there you see the end of every completion.

What is this end? Ask Paul: “The end of the commandment is love from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I, 5); and in another place, “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XIII, 10).

What is as complete and finished as fullness? Indeed, brothers, he fittingly uses the word “end.” Do not suppose that it means destruction, but completion.

For one says differently, “I finished the bread,” and “I finished the tunic.” I finished the bread by eating it; I finished the tunic by weaving it. In both cases “finished” is said, and in both cases “end” is sounded; yet bread is finished so that it is consumed, while a tunic is finished so that it is completed. Bread is finished so that it no longer exists; a tunic is finished so that it is perfect.

Understand “end” in this way also when the Psalm is read and you hear, “A Psalm of David, toward the end.” You hear this continually in the Psalms, and you ought to know what you hear.

What does “toward the end” mean? “For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X, 4). And what does “Christ is the end” mean? Because Christ is God, and the end of the commandment is love, and God is love; because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one.

There is your end; elsewhere there is the way. Do not cling to the way and fail to arrive at the end. Whatever else you reach, pass through it until you arrive at the end.

What is the end? “But it is good for me to cling to God” (Ps. LXXII, 28). You have clung to God; you have finished the way; you will remain in your homeland.

Pay attention. Someone seeks money; let it not be your end. Pass through it [Note: [Col. 2057] Er., Lugd., and Ven.: “let the end not be there. He passes through.” Lov.: “let the end not be there. Pass through.” M.] as an exile. Seek where you may pass through, not where you may remain. But if you love money, you are entangled by greed; greed will be a chain on your feet, and you cannot go farther. Pass through this also, then; seek the end.

You seek bodily health; do not yet remain there. For what sort of bodily health is this, which death destroys and illness weakens—trivial, mortal, fleeting? Seek it lest poor health perhaps impede your good works. Therefore the end is not there, because it is sought for the sake of something else.

Whatever is sought for the sake of something else is not the end; whatever is sought for its own sake and freely is the end.

You seek honors; perhaps you seek them in order to accomplish something, so that you may do something and please God. Do not love the honor itself, lest you remain there.

You seek praise. If you seek God’s praise, you do well; if you seek your own, you do badly—you remain on the way. But behold, you are loved and praised. Do not rejoice when you are praised in yourself; praise in the Lord, so that you may sing, “In the Lord my soul shall be praised” (Ps. XXXIII, 3).

You speak some good sermon, and your sermon is praised. Let it not be praised as yours; the end is not there. If you place the end there, you will be finished—not finished as though you were perfected, but finished so as to be consumed.

Therefore let your sermon not be praised as coming from you, as yours. How should it be praised? As the Psalm says: “In God I shall praise the word; in God I shall praise the speech.” From this comes what follows in you: “In God I have hoped; I will not fear what a human being can do to me” (Ps. LV, 5, 11).

For when everything of yours is praised in God, you do not fear that your praise may perish, because God does not fail. Therefore pass through that as well.

### 6

See, brothers, how many things we pass through in which there is no end. We use them as on a road; as in stations or inns, we refresh ourselves and pass on. Where, then, is the end?

Beloved, we are children of God, and what we shall be has not yet appeared. It was said here [Note: [Col. 2058] Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov.: “this.” M.], in this Epistle. We are therefore still on the way. Wherever we have arrived, we must still pass through, until we reach some end.

“We know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (I John III, 2). This is the end: there is perpetual praise, there is always an unfailing Alleluia.

Therefore he said of this very end in the Psalm: “I have seen the end of every completion.” And as though he were asked, “What is the end that you saw?” he answered: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Ps. CXVIII, 96).

That is the end, the breadth of the commandment. The breadth of the commandment is love, because where there is love there are no narrow places. The Apostle was in this breadth when he said: “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians; our heart is enlarged. You are not restricted in us” (II Cor. VI, 11–12).

Therefore, “your commandment is exceedingly broad.” What is the broad commandment? “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another.” Love is therefore not restricted.

Do you wish not to be restricted on earth? Live in the broad place. Whatever another person does to you does not restrict you, because you love what another person cannot harm. You love God; you love the brotherhood; you love the law of God; you love the Church of God. It will be eternal.

You labor on earth, but you will reach the promised fruit. Who can take away from you what you love? If no one takes away what you love, you sleep securely—indeed, you keep watch securely, lest by sleeping you lose what you love.

For it was not said without reason: “Enlighten my eyes, lest I ever sleep in death” (Ps. XII, 4). Those who close their eyes against love fall asleep in the desires of carnal pleasures. Wake up, therefore.

For there are pleasures: eating, drinking, luxuriating, playing, hunting. All evils follow these empty displays. Do we not know that they are pleasures? Who would deny that they give pleasure? But the law of God is loved more [Note: [Col. 2059] The printed editions have *diligatur*, “let it be loved.” Nine manuscripts have *diligitur*, “it is loved.” Two others have *delectat*, “it gives pleasure.”].

Cry out against such persuaders: “The unjust have told me of delights, but not like your law, O Lord.” This delight remains. It does not merely remain as something to which you may come; it also calls back the one who is fleeing.

7. For this is the love of God, that we keep his commandments. You have already heard: “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets.” How did he not want to divide you among many pages? “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets.” On which two commandments? “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind”; and, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” “On these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. 22:37–40).

Behold the commandments about which this entire Epistle speaks. Therefore hold fast to love, and be secure. What are you afraid of—that you might do harm to someone? Who harms the one whom he loves? Love, and it cannot happen except that you do good. But perhaps you rebuke someone? Love does this, not cruelty. But perhaps you strike someone? You do it for discipline, because the love of love itself does not allow you to neglect one who is undisciplined. And what is in a certain way a different and contrary fruit comes about: sometimes hatred flatters, and love acts harshly.

Someone hates his enemy and pretends friendship toward him. He sees him doing something evil and praises him; he wants him to plunge headlong, he wants him to go blindly over the precipices of his desires, from which perhaps he will not return. He praises him: “For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul” (Ps. 9:3). He applies to him the ointment of his flattery. Behold: he hates, and he praises. Another sees his friend doing something of this kind and calls him back. If he does not listen, he even uses words of correction, rebukes him, argues with him; sometimes one is driven to the necessity of arguing. Behold: hatred flatters, and love argues.

Do not attend to the words of the flatterer, or regard as cruelty the words of the rebuker; examine the vein, seek the root from which they proceed. The one flatters in order to deceive; the other argues in order to correct. Therefore, brothers, there is no need for your heart to be stretched apart through us; ask God to enable you to love one another.

Love all people, even your enemies—not because they are brothers, but so that they may become brothers; so that you may always burn with brotherly love, whether toward one who has become a brother or toward an enemy, so that he may become a brother through your loving him. Wherever you love a brother, you love a friend. He is already with you; he is already joined to you in Catholic unity. If you live rightly, you love a brother made from an enemy.

But you love someone [Note: [Col. 2059] Erasmus, Lyons, and Venice read “if” for “but”; and a little below, Louvain reads “you love.” M.] who has not yet believed in Christ—or, if he has believed in Christ, has believed as the demons believe [Note: [Col. 2059] Erasmus, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain have “has believed.” M.]; you reproach his vanity [Note: [Col. 2059] Several manuscripts have “he reproaches his unity.”]. You love him—love him with brotherly love. He is not yet a brother, but for that very reason you love him, so that he may become a brother.

Therefore all our love is brotherly love toward Christians, toward all his members. The discipline of love, my brothers, is strength, flowers, fruit, beauty, delight, nourishment, drink, food, an embrace without satiety. If we are so delighted while we are strangers and travelers, how shall we rejoice in our homeland?

[Col. 2060] 8. Let us run, then, my brothers; let us run and love Christ. Which Christ? Jesus Christ. Who is this? The Word of God. And how did he come to the sick? “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

Thus what Scripture foretold was fulfilled: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day.” Where does his body lie? Where are his members laboring [Note: [Col. 2060] Erasmus: “Where does his body lie? His members labor.” M.]? Where must you be, so that you may be beneath the head? “And that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:46–47).

Let your love be spread there. Christ and the Psalm—that is, the Spirit of God—say: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad”; and someone places the boundaries of love in Africa! Extend your love throughout the whole world, if you wish to love Christ, because Christ’s members lie throughout the world.

If you love one part, you are divided. If you are divided, you are not in the body. If you are not in the body, you are not beneath the head. What does it profit that you believe and blaspheme? You adore him in the head, but blaspheme him in the body. He loves his body. If you have cut yourself off from his body, the head has not cut itself off from its body.

“Without cause you honor me,” the head cries to you from above; “without cause you honor me.” It is as if someone wished to kiss your head while trampling your feet—perhaps he would crush your feet with hobnailed boots—while wanting to hold your head and kiss it. Would you not, amid the words of the one honoring you, cry out and say, “What are you doing, man? You are trampling me”? You would not say, “You are trampling my head,” because he was honoring the head. But the head would cry out more loudly on behalf of the trampled members than on its own behalf, because it was being honored. Does not the head itself cry out, “I do not want your honor; do not trample me”?
