Now say, if you can, “Why have I trampled you?” Say to the head, “I wanted to kiss you; I wanted to embrace you.” But do you not see, fool, that what you wish to embrace reaches, through a certain bond of unity, the thing you are trampling? Above, you honor me; below, you trample me. What you trample suffers more than what you honor rejoices, because what you honor suffers on behalf of those whom you trample.

How does the tongue cry out? “It hurts me.” It does not say, “It hurts my foot,” but says, “It hurts me.” O tongue, who touched you? Who struck you? Who pricked you? Who pierced you? No one—but I am joined to those who are being trampled. How do you want me not to suffer, when I am not separated from them?

9. Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ, when he ascended into heaven on the fortieth day, commended his body—where he was to leave it lying—because he saw that many would honor him because he had ascended into heaven; and he saw that their honor was useless if they trampled his members on earth. And lest anyone should go astray and, while adoring the head in heaven, trample the feet on earth, he said where his members would be.

As he was about to ascend, he spoke his final words; after those words he did not speak on earth. The head, about to ascend into heaven, commended the members on earth and departed. You no longer find Christ speaking on earth; you find him speaking, but from heaven. And why from heaven itself? Because his members were being trampled on earth.

For he said from above to Saul the persecutor, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?” (Acts 9:4). “I have ascended into heaven, but I still lie on earth. Here I sit at the right hand of the Father; there I still hunger, thirst, and am a stranger.”

How, then, did he commend his body on earth as he was about to ascend? When the disciples asked him, “Lord, is it at this time that you will restore the kingdom to Israel?” he replied, as he was about to depart: “It is not yours to know the times which the Father has placed in his own authority; but you shall receive power when the Holy Spirit comes upon you, and you shall be my witnesses.”

See through what places he spreads his body; see where he does not wish to be trampled: “You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem, and throughout all Judea and Samaria, and to the whole earth” (Acts 1:6–8). Behold where I lie, I who ascend. I ascend because I am the head; my body still lies here. Where does it lie? Throughout the whole earth. Take care not to strike it; take care not to violate it; take care not to trample it. These are Christ’s final words as he was going into heaven.

Consider a man lying sick in bed, lying in his house, weakened by illness, near death, gasping, already holding his soul, so to speak, between his teeth. Perhaps he is concerned about something dear to him, something he loves greatly; it comes to his mind, and he calls his heirs and says to them, “I beg you, do this.” In a certain sense he holds his soul back by force, lest it depart before those words have been confirmed. When he has dictated those final words, he breathes out his soul; the corpse is carried to the tomb.

How do his heirs remember the final words of the dying man? What if someone should appear and say to them, “Do not do it”? What would they say to him? “So I am not to do what my father, as he breathed out his soul, finally commanded me—what last sounded in my ears as my father departed from here? I can regard any other words of his differently; his final words hold me more firmly. I have not seen him again, nor heard him speaking.”

Brothers, consider with Christian inward feeling: if words spoken by one going into the tomb are so sweet, so welcome, and so weighty to heirs, what ought the final words of Christ’s heirs to be—of one who is not going back into the tomb, but ascending into heaven?

For the one who lived and died is carried away, his soul to other places, while his body is laid in the earth. Whether those words are fulfilled or not does not concern him; he is now doing or suffering something else: either he rejoices in Abraham’s bosom, or in eternal fire he desires a little water (Luke 16:22 and following). But in his tomb lies the [Col. 2062] senseless corpse, and his final words as a dying man are guarded.

What do those people hope for who do not guard the final words of one seated in heaven, who sees from above whether they are disregarded or not—of the one who said, “Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me?”—the one who reserves for judgment whatever he sees his members suffering?

10. “And what have we done?” they say. “We have suffered persecution; we have not inflicted it.”

You have inflicted it, wretched people: first, because you divided the Church. The sword of the tongue is greater than one of iron. Sarah’s maidservant Hagar was proud, and because of her pride she was afflicted by her mistress. That was discipline, not punishment. Therefore, when she had withdrawn from her mistress, what did the angel say to her? “Return to your mistress” (Gen. 16:4–9).

So, if the carnal soul, like a proud maidservant, has perhaps suffered certain troubles for the sake of discipline, why are you raving? Return to your mistress; hold fast to the Lord’s peace.

Behold, the Gospels are brought forth; we read how the Church is spread abroad. They argue against this and say to us, “Traitors.” Traitors to what? Christ commends his Church, and you do not believe him; am I to believe you when you curse my parents? Do you want me to believe you concerning traitors? First believe Christ yourself.

What is worthy of belief? Christ is God; you are a human being. Whom ought one to believe first? Christ has spread his Church throughout the whole world. I say, “Despise it”; the Gospel speaks, “Beware.”

What does the Gospel say? “It was necessary for Christ to suffer, and to rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins should be preached in his name.” Wherever there is forgiveness of sins, there is the Church.

How is there a Church? For to him it was said, “I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven, and whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven” (Matt. 16:19). Through what places is this forgiveness of sins spread? “Among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24:47). Behold, believe Christ.

But because you understand that, if you believe Christ, you will have nothing to say about traitors, you want me to believe you when you curse my parents, rather than believe Christ when he preaches [Note: [Col. 2062] Several manuscripts have: “that I should believe, and my parents.” And almost all, instead of “when you curse,” have “when you preach,” which is the final word.]. [Note: [Col. 2062] Here the treatise ends in all the manuscripts.]

[EXPOSITION OF CERTAIN PROPOSITIONS FROM THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS]

[Col. 2063]

EXPOSITION OF CERTAIN PROPOSITIONS FROM THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, BY SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO. [Note: [Col. 2061] See Book 1, chapter 23, of the Retractions, col. 620, from the words “When I was still a presbyter,” no. 1, through col. 622, no. 4, ending with the words “in Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.”] [Note: [Col. 2063] This present Exposition was collated with two Victorine manuscripts, one Vatican manuscript, the Thuaneus, Corbeiensis, Germanensis, Colbertinus, Jolyensis, Navarricus, and one belonging to the Bernardine College of Paris; with the variant readings of Louvain from three Belgian manuscripts; and with the editions of Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain. In these editions we observe that the division of the propositions is not suitable, since one and the same proposition has often been divided into two or more. It was not possible now to introduce another division together with a change in the numerical markings, lest confusion should result.] [Note: [Col. 2063] We also compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of the Retractions and Confessions, vol. 1. M.] (C)

One book [Note: [Col. 2063] Written about A.D. 394—that is, while Augustine was still a presbyter—according to Book 1 of the Retractions, chapter 23, no. 1.].

These are the meanings in Paul the Apostle’s Epistle to the Romans. First of all, one must understand that in this Epistle the question concerns the works of the Law and grace.

PROPOSITION ONE. [ROM. CHAPTER 1, VERSE 4]

When he says, “According to the Spirit of sanctification by the resurrection of the dead,” that is, because they received the gift of the Spirit after his resurrection, he mentions the resurrection of the dead because in him we were all crucified and rose again.

II. [Ibid. 1:11]

When he says, “That I may impart to you a spiritual gift,” he means the love of God and of neighbor, so that through the love of Christ they might not envy the Gentiles who were called to the Gospel.

III. [Ibid. 1:18]

When he says, “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness,” and so forth, Solomon also speaks concerning the wise men of the world: “If they were able to know so much that they could estimate the age, how did they not more readily find its Lord and Creator?” (Wis. 13:9).

But those whom Solomon rebukes did not know the Creator through the creature. Those whom the Apostle rebukes did know him, but they did not give thanks; and, “claiming to be wise, they became fools,” and fell into the worship of images (Rom. 1:21–23). That the wise men of the Gentiles did find the Creator is clearly shown by the same Apostle when he spoke to the Athenians. For after saying, “In him we live and move and have our being,” he added, “As some of your own poets have said” (Acts 17:28).

He first rebukes the ungodliness of the Gentiles with this purpose: to prove from this that those who are converted can also attain to grace. For it is unjust that they should suffer the punishment of ungodliness and not receive the reward of faith.

[Col. 2064] IV. [Ibid. 1:21]

When he says, “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks,” this is the beginning of sin, concerning which it is said, “The beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10:15). If they had given thanks to God, who had given them this wisdom, they would not have attributed anything to themselves through their own thoughts. Therefore they were handed over by the Lord to the desires of their hearts, so that they might do what was not fitting.

V. [Ibid. 1:24]

When he says, “He handed them over,” this is understood as “he abandoned them to the desires of their hearts.” He says that they received from God a reciprocal recompense: they were handed over to the desires of their hearts.

VI. [Ibid. 1:28–29]

When, finally, he says, “God handed them over to a reprobate mind,” and so forth, and says that they were “filled with all iniquity,” it is understood that the things he now mentions pertain to doing harm—that is, to crimes. Earlier he was speaking of corruptions called disgraceful acts, from which one proceeds to crimes, since anyone who follows the destructive sweetness of disgraceful acts, while attempting to remove those who impede him, advances into crime.

This same distinction is found in that passage of Solomon’s Wisdom where, after enumerating the earlier disgraceful acts, he says: “Let us circumvent the righteous poor man, because he is of no use to us” (Wis. 2:12), and so forth.

VII–VIII. [Ibid. 1:32; 2:1]

When he says, “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them,” he indicates that whatever they did, they did not unwillingly [Note: [Col. 2063] The printed editions have: “they did not unwillingly do them. For when they consent to evil…” But all the manuscripts have: “not unwillingly, but when…,” except one Victorine manuscript, which reads: “they did not unwillingly do them, but when…”], but, when they consent to evil deeds, they also approve the things they have done [Note: [Col. 2063] The printed editions have: “the things they have not done.” The word “not” is absent from eight manuscripts.]. And therefore, speaking of sins already completed, he says: “Therefore you are inexcusable, O every human being who judges.”

When he says “every,” he now begins to show that this applies not only to the Gentile, but also to the Jew who wished to judge the Gentiles according to the Law [Col. 2065].

IX. [Ibid. 2:5]

When he says, “You are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath,” he everywhere uses “the wrath of God” to mean vengeance. That is why he says, “of the just judgment of God.” It should be noted that God’s wrath is also mentioned in the New Testament. When people who oppose the Old Law read of it in the Old Testament [Note: [Col. 2065] The Manichaeans.], they think that the Old Law should be condemned, although God, like us, is certainly not subject to disturbances, as Solomon says: “But you, Lord of hosts, judge with tranquility” (Wis. 12:18). Thus, as has been said, “wrath” is used in the sense of vengeance.

X. [Ibid. 2:15]

When he says, “Their conscience bearing witness,” he speaks in accordance with what the Apostle John says: “Beloved, if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our conscience,” and so forth (1 John 3:20).

XI. [Ibid. 2:29]

When he says, “In spirit, not in letter,” this means that the Law is to be understood according to the spirit, not according to what the letter contains. This certainly happened in the case of those who received circumcision more carnally than spiritually.

XII. [Ibid. 2:29]

When he says, “Whose praise is not from human beings but from God,” this applies to the one of whom he says, “who is a Jew in secret.”

XIII–XVIII. [Ibid. 3:20]

When he says, “For no flesh shall be justified before him by the Law; for through the Law comes knowledge of sin,” and similar statements, which some think are offered as an insult to the Law, they must be read with sufficient care, so that the Law does not appear to be rejected by the Apostle, nor free choice taken away from the human being.

Accordingly, let us distinguish four stages of the human being: before the Law, under the Law, under grace, and in peace.

Before the Law, we follow the desire of the flesh. Under the Law, we are dragged along by it. Under grace, we neither follow it nor are dragged along by it. In peace, there is no desire of the flesh.

Before the Law, therefore, we do not fight, because we not only desire and sin, but also approve our sins. Under the Law, we fight but are defeated; for we acknowledge that the things we do are evil, and by acknowledging them to be evil we certainly do not want to do them, but because grace is not yet present, we are overcome.

At this stage it is shown to us how we lie prostrate; and while we wish to rise and fall, we are afflicted more grievously. Hence it is said here, “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound” (Rom. 5:20). Hence also the present statement: “For through the Law comes knowledge of sin.”

It is not the removal of sin, for sin is removed through grace alone. The Law, therefore, is good, because it forbids what must be forbidden and commands what must be commanded. But when someone thinks that he can fulfill it by his own strength, not through the grace of his Liberator, this presumption does him no good. Rather, it harms him so greatly that he is carried away by an even stronger desire for sin and is found to be a transgressor even in his sins. “For where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15).

Thus, when someone who lies prostrate recognizes that he cannot rise by himself, let him implore the help of his Liberator. Grace therefore comes: it grants forgiveness of past sins, helps the one who strives, bestows love of righteousness, and removes fear.

[Col. 2066] When this happens, although certain desires of the flesh, while we are in this life, fight against our spirit in order to lead it into sin, the spirit nevertheless does not consent to these desires, because it is established in the grace and love of God, and so it ceases to sin. We do not sin in the evil desire itself, but in our consent.

This is the force of what the same Apostle says: “Therefore, let not sin reign in your mortal body, so that you obey its desires” (Rom. 6:12). For by this he shows that there are desires to which, by not obeying them, we do not allow sin to reign in us.

But because these desires arise from the mortality of the flesh, which we draw from the first sin of the first human being, from whom we are carnally born, they will not end unless, through the resurrection of the body, we merit that transformation which is promised to us. There perfect peace will exist, when we are established in the fourth stage [Note: [Col. 2066] Amerbach and Erasmus: “there will be perfect peace, which we establish in the fourth stage.”].

The peace is perfect because nothing will resist us when we do not resist God. This is what the Apostle says: “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness. And if the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:10–11).

Free choice, therefore, was perfect in the first human being. In us, however, before grace, free choice does not exist so that we do not sin, but only so that we do not wish to sin. Grace makes it possible not only for us to wish to do what is right, but also to be able to do it—not through our own strength, but through the help of our Liberator, who will also grant us perfect peace in the resurrection. This perfect peace follows upon a good will. “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will” (Luke 2:14).

XIX. [Ibid. 3:31]

When he says, “Do we then abolish the Law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the Law,” that is, we confirm it. But how was the Law to be confirmed except through righteousness? And what righteousness except that which comes through faith? For the very things that could not be fulfilled through the Law have been fulfilled through faith.

XX. [Ibid. 4:2]

When he says, “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God,” this means that Abraham, while without the Law and not seeking glory from the works of the Law—as though he were fulfilling the Law by his own strength, when that Law had not yet been given—has glory that belongs to God, not to himself. For he was justified by faith, not by his own merit as though by works, but by the grace of God.

XXI. [Ibid. 4:4]

When he says, “To the one who works, the reward is not reckoned according to grace but according to debt,” he speaks of the way human beings pay wages to human beings. God, however, gave through grace, because he gave to sinners so that they might live righteously through faith—that is, might do good works.

Therefore, the fact that we do good works after having received grace is to be attributed not to us but to him who justified us by grace. For if he wished to repay a debt owed, he would repay the punishment owed to sinners.

XXII. [Ibid. 4:5]

When he says, “Who justifies the ungodly,” this means that he makes the ungodly godly, so that thereafter he may remain in that godliness and righteousness [Col. 2067], because he was justified in order to be righteous, not in order to suppose that he is permitted to sin.

XXIII. [Ibid. 4:15]

When he says, “For the Law brings about wrath,” he signifies vengeance, and this pertains to the stage at which someone is under the Law.

XXIV. [Ibid. 4:17]

When he says, “Before God in whom he believed,” he signifies that faith is in the inner person, in the sight of God, not in the display made before human beings, as is the case with circumcision of the flesh.

XXV. [Ibid. 4:20]

When he says of Abraham, “Giving glory to God,” this is directed against those who sought their own glory from the works of the Law before human beings.

XXVI. [Ibid. 5:3]

When he says, “And not only this, but we also glory in tribulations,” and gradually leads the argument onward through the rest to the love of God, when he says that we possess this love through the gift of the Spirit, he shows that all the things we might attribute to ourselves must be attributed to God, who graciously chose to give grace through the Holy Spirit.

XXVII–XXVIII. [Ibid. 5:13]

When he says, “For until the Law, sin was in the world,” this is to be understood as “until grace should come.” It was said against those who think that sins could have been removed through the Law.

The Apostle says that sins were made manifest through the Law, but not removed, when he says, “Sin was not reckoned when there was no Law.” He does not say, “It did not exist,” but “it was not reckoned.” Nor, when the Law was given, was sin removed; rather, it began to be reckoned—that is, to become apparent.

Therefore, we should not think that “until the Law” was said as though sin no longer existed under the Law. Rather, “until the Law” was said so that you should count the entire period of the Law up to the end of the Law, which is Christ.

XXIX. [Ibid. 5:14]

When he says, “But death reigned from Adam to Moses, even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression” [Note: [Col. 2067] In Amerbach and Erasmus, approximately forty lines are omitted after the words “in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” and this lacuna is filled by these three words: “here it has less,” which undoubtedly entered the text from the margin. Consequently, another proposition, which began with the words “But not as the trespass,” became confused with Proposition Twenty-Nine.], this can be distinguished in two ways.

Either: “Death reigned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression,” because even those who did not sin died from the mortality inherited from Adam.

Or certainly: “Death reigned even over those who did not sin in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, but sinned before the Law.” Those who received the Law are understood to have sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression, because Adam also sinned after receiving the law of the commandment.

It is also clear that “until Moses” is to be understood as the whole period of the Law. Adam is called a type of the one who was to come, but by contrast: just as death came through him, so life comes through our Lord.

[Ibid. 5:15–19] When he says, “But the gift is not like the trespass,” the gift surpasses it in two ways: either because grace abounds much more, since through it one lives eternally, whereas death reigned temporarily through Adam’s death [Col. 2068]; or because through Adam the condemnation of one trespass brought death upon many, whereas through our Lord Jesus Christ, by the gift concerning many trespasses, grace was given unto eternal life.

He explains another difference in this way: “And the gift is not like what happened through one who sinned” [Note: [Col. 2068] So the manuscripts read, in accordance with the Greek, δι’ ἑνὸς ἁμαρτήσαντος (*di’ henos hamartēsantos*). But the printed editions have “through one sin.”]. “For judgment from one led to condemnation; but grace from many trespasses led to justification.”

When he says “from one,” “trespass” is understood, because what follows is, “but grace from many trespasses.” Therefore the difference is this: in Adam one trespass was condemned, whereas by the Lord many trespasses were forgiven.

The statement that follows contains both differences, and it is to be explained as follows: “For if, because of one trespass, death reigned through one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and righteousness reign in life through the one Jesus Christ.”

What he said, “They will reign much more,” pertains to eternal life; what he said, “They receive an abundance of grace,” pertains to the gift concerning many trespasses.

After explaining these differences, he returns to the pattern from which he had begun, whose order he had interrupted when he said, “Just as through one man sin entered into this world, and through sin, death” (Rom. 5:12). He now returns to this when he says: “Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings, so through one justification justification of life came upon all human beings. For just as through the disobedience of one man many were made sinners, so through the obedience of one many will be made righteous.”

This is the pattern of the one who was to come, Adam, about whom he had begun to speak earlier but had postponed the order by inserting certain differences concerning him. Returning now to that order, he concluded by saying, “Therefore, just as through one trespass condemnation came upon all human beings,” and so forth.

XXX. [Ibid. 5:20]

When he says, “The Law entered in so that transgression might abound,” the very word sufficiently indicates that the Jews did not know the dispensation according to which the Law was given. It was not given as something able to give life, since grace gives life through faith. Rather, the Law was given to show by how many and how tight bonds of sins those who presumed on their own strength to fulfill righteousness were constrained.

Thus sin abounded when desire became more ardent because of prohibition, and when the guilt of transgression was added to those who sinned against the Law. This is understood by the one who considers the second stage among those four stages [Note: [Col. 2068] Above, Proposition 13.].

XXXI. [Ibid. 6:1–2]

When he says, “What shall we say, then? Shall we remain in sin so that grace may abound? By no means. We who have died to sin, how shall we live in it?” he shows that this was done concerning past sins so that they might be forgiven, and that grace abounded in this respect: that past sins might be forgiven [Note: [Col. 2068] The manuscripts have: “so that transgressing sins might be forgiven.”].

Therefore, whoever still seeks an increase of sin in order to experience an increase of grace does not understand that he is acting so that grace may accomplish nothing in him. For it is the work of grace that we die to sin.

[Col. 2069] XXXII–XXXIV. [Ibid. 5:6]

When he says, “Knowing this, that our old person was crucified together with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed,” this refers to what was said through Moses: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree” (Deut. 21:23). The crucifixion of the old person was signified in the Lord’s cross, just as the restoration of the new person was signified in the resurrection.

It is clear that we act according to that old person who was cursed. Because of him, no one doubts that Scripture also said concerning the Lord that he bore our sins (Isa. 53:11), that he was made sin for us (2 Cor. 5:21), and that, because of sin, he condemned sin (Rom. 8:3).

What does it mean to destroy the body of sin? He himself explained: “So that we might no longer serve sin.” And when he says, “If we have died with Christ,” this means, “if we have been crucified with Christ.” For elsewhere he says: “Those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires” (Gal. 5:24).

Moses therefore did not curse the Lord; rather, he prophetically foretold what his crucifixion would signify.

XXXV. [Ibid. 6:14]

When he says, “For sin shall not rule over you; for you are not under the Law but under grace,” this certainly pertains already to that third stage, in which a person serves the Law of God with the mind, although with the flesh he serves the law of sin (Rom. 7:25).

He does not obey the desire of sin, although desires still trouble him and urge him toward consent, until the body also is given life and death is swallowed up in victory (1 Cor. 15:54). Therefore, because we do not consent to evil desires, we are in grace, and sin does not reign in our mortal body. Indeed, from the place where he says, “We who have died to sin, how shall we live in it?” (Rom. 6:2, 12), he describes the one who has been established under grace.

But the one over whom sin rules, although he wishes to resist sin, is still under the Law, not yet under grace.

XXXVI. [Ibid. 7:2]

When he says, “For a woman who is under a husband is bound by the law while her husband lives; but if her husband dies, she is released from the law of her husband,” and so forth, it must be observed that this comparison differs from the reality for which it was introduced in this respect: here he says that the husband dies, and that the woman marries whom she wishes, having certainly been freed from the law of her husband.

There, however, he presents the soul as a woman and the husband as the passions of sins, which operate in the members so as to bear fruit for death—that is, so that offspring worthy of such a union may be born. The Law [Note: [Col. 2069] Perhaps: “and the law of the husband, as the law which …”] was given not to remove sin or to free from sin, but to show sin before grace. Through this it happened that those placed under the Law were carried away by a more vehement desire to sin and sinned even more through transgression.

Thus, although there too there are three elements—the soul as the woman, the passions of sins as the husband, and the Law as the law of the husband—he does not say there that the soul is freed when sins die, as though the husband had died. Rather, he says that the soul itself dies to sin and is freed from the Law, so that it may belong to another husband, namely Christ, once it has died to sin, although sin itself still remains, as it were, alive.

This happens when, although desires and certain impulses toward sin still remain in us [Col. 2070], we nevertheless do not obey or consent to them, serving the Law of God with the mind, because we have died to sin.

Sin, too, will die when the body has been transformed in the resurrection, concerning which he later says, “He will give life to your mortal bodies because of the Spirit dwelling in you” (Rom. 8:11).

XXXVII. [Ibid. 7:8, 13]

When he says, “But sin, taking opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every desire,” this must be understood not to mean that there was no desire at all before it was increased by prohibition. For desire increases through prohibition when the grace that liberates is absent.

Therefore, not all desire exists before it is prohibited. But once it has been prohibited, when grace, as we have said, ceases to be present, desire increases so greatly that it becomes “all” desire in its own kind—that is, it becomes complete—so that it even acts against the Law and accumulates the guilt of transgression.

When he says, “For apart from the Law sin was dead,” he does not say “dead” because it does not exist, but because it is hidden. He makes this clear in what follows when he says, “But sin, so that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through what is good.” The Law is good, but without grace it merely reveals sins; it does not remove them.

XXXVIII. [Ibid. 7:9–10]

When he says, “I was once alive apart from the Law,” this is to be understood as, “I seemed to be alive,” because before the commandment sin was hidden.

And when he says, “When the commandment came, sin revived, but I died,” this is to be understood as, “Sin began to appear, but I came to know that I was dead.”

XXXIX. [Ibid. 7:11]

For what he says, “For sin, having taken occasion through the commandment, deceived me, and through it killed me,” is said for this reason: the fruit of a forbidden desire is sweeter. Hence all sins committed secretly are also sweeter, although this sweetness is deadly. This is why, in Solomon, a woman seated under the guise of deceptive teaching and inviting the foolish to come to her is written as saying: “Eat hidden bread gladly, and drink stolen water sweetly” (Prov. 9:17). This sweetness is the occasion for sin discovered through the commandment; and when it is desired, it certainly deceives and turns into greater bitterness.

### XL. [Book VII, 13]

When he says, “What then? Was that which is good made death to me? By no means; but sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through that which is good,” he clearly shows why he had said above, “For without the Law sin is dead” (Rom. 7:8): namely, because it is hidden. For now he says that it was not that good thing—that is, the Law—that was made death to him, but that sin worked death through the good of the Law, that is, so that the sin which was hidden without the Law might appear. For each person recognizes that he is dead when he confesses that what was rightly commanded cannot be fulfilled by him; and by the guilt of transgression he sins more than if he had not been forbidden.

This is what he says below: “So that sin might become exceedingly sinful,” or “the sinner might become exceedingly sinful,” through the commandment. [Note: [Col. 2070] The printed editions have *peccator peccans*, “the sinful sinner.” But the manuscripts have *peccator aut peccatum*, “the sinner or sin.” [Col. 2071] Elsewhere Augustine says that perhaps the Greek read *ē hamartia* (ἡ ἁμαρτία, “the sin”).] Before the commandment it was less, because where there is no law, there is no transgression.

### XLI. [Book VII, 14]

When he says, “We know that the Law is spiritual, but I am carnal,” he sufficiently shows that the Law cannot be fulfilled except by spiritual people, such as the grace of God makes. [Note: [Col. 2071] *On Retractions*, chapter 23, no. 1.] For anyone made similar to the Law itself easily fulfills what it commands; nor will he be under it, but with it. Such a person is no longer captivated by temporal goods or terrified by temporal evils.

### XLII. [Book VII, 14]

When he says, “Sold under sin,” it is to be understood that each person sells his soul to the devil by sinning, receiving as though it were the price the sweetness of temporal pleasure. Hence our Lord is also called our Redeemer, because in this way, as has been said, we were sold.

### XLIII. [Book VII, 15, 13]

When he says, “For what I do, I do not understand,” this may seem, to those who understand less well, contrary to the statement in which he said, “Sin, in order that it might appear as sin, worked death in me through that which is good.” For how does it appear if it is not understood?

But “I do not understand” is said here in the sense of “I do not approve.” For just as darkness is not seen, but is perceived by comparison with light—and to perceive darkness is to fail to see—so sin, because it is not illumined by the light of righteousness, is discerned through failure to understand, just as darkness is said to be perceived through not seeing. To this also belongs what is said in the Psalm: “Who understands his offenses?” (Ps. 18:13).

### XLIV. [Book VII, 19, 20]

When he says, “For I do not do the good that I desire, but I do the evil that I do not desire. But if I do what I do not desire, I agree with the Law, that it is good,” the Law is indeed sufficiently defended from every accusation. Yet care must be taken lest anyone think that these words remove from us the free choice of the will, which is not the case.

For the human being is now described as placed under the Law before grace. He is then overcome by sins, while he tries to live justly by his own strength, without the help of the grace of God that liberates. But in free choice he has the ability to believe in the Liberator and receive grace, so that, once the one who grants and assists him has liberated him, he may no longer sin. Thus he ceases to be under the Law, but is with the Law or in the Law, fulfilling it through the love of God, which he could not fulfill through fear.

### XLV–XLVI. [Book VII, 23–25]

When he says, “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin which is in my members,” he calls the custom of sin by which anyone entangled in a carnal habit is bound the law of sin. He says that this wars against the law of his mind and takes him captive under the law of sin. From this it is understood that the person described is not yet under grace. [Note: [Col. 2071] The same work.]

For if carnal habit merely resisted and did not take him captive, there would be no condemnation. Condemnation consists in this: that we obey and serve wicked carnal desires. But if such desires arise and are not absent, while we nevertheless do not obey them, we are not taken captive and are already under grace. He will speak of this after crying out and imploring the help of the Liberator, so that through grace love may accomplish what fear could not accomplish through the Law.

For he said, “Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?” And he added, “The grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord.” Then he begins to describe the person established under grace, which is the third stage among the four that we distinguished above (Prop. 13). To this stage already belongs what he immediately adds: “Therefore I myself with my mind serve the Law of God, but with my flesh the law of sin.” For although carnal desires exist, the person established under grace no longer serves them by consenting to commit sin; with his mind he serves the Law of God, but with his flesh the law of sin.

He calls the law of sin the mortal condition resulting from Adam’s transgression, through which we became mortal. For from this stain of the flesh carnal desire troubles us; and in accordance with this he says elsewhere: “We too were by nature children of wrath, like the rest” (Eph. 2:3).

### XLVII. [Book VIII, 1]

When he says, “There is therefore now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,” he sufficiently shows that there is no condemnation if carnal desires exist, but only if they are obeyed for the purpose of sinning. This occurs in those who are under the Law, not yet under grace. For those under the Law not only have concupiscence resisting them, but are also led away captive when they obey it. It does not occur, however, in those who with their minds serve the Law of God.

### XLVIII. [Book VIII, 3, 4]

When he says, “For what was impossible for the Law, in that it was weakened through the flesh, God sent his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and concerning sin condemned sin in the flesh, so that the righteousness of the Law might be fulfilled in us who walk not according to the flesh but according to the spirit,” he teaches most clearly that the very commandments of the Law were not fulfilled, although they ought to have been fulfilled, because those to whom the Law was given before grace were devoted to carnal goods and desired to acquire happiness from them. They feared nothing except when adversity threatened such goods; and therefore, when those temporal goods were disturbed, they easily withdrew from the commandments of the Law.

The Law was therefore weakened by the failure to fulfill what it commanded—not through any fault of its own, but through the flesh, that is, through those people who, desiring carnal goods, did not love the righteousness of the Law but preferred temporal advantages to it.

Therefore our Liberator, the Lord Jesus Christ, by taking mortal flesh, came in the likeness of sinful flesh. Death is owed to sinful flesh. But the Lord’s death was the result of condescension, not of obligation. Nevertheless, the Apostle also calls this assumption of mortal flesh “sin,” although it was not sinful flesh, because, when it dies, it makes the immortal one appear as though he were sin.

“But on account of sin,” he says, “he condemned sin in the flesh.” For the Lord’s death accomplished this: that death should no longer be feared, and that temporal goods should no longer be desired or temporal evils feared—the things in which that carnal wisdom existed through which the commandments of the Law could not be fulfilled.

When this wisdom was destroyed and removed in the Lord’s human nature, the righteousness of the Law is fulfilled, when one does not walk according to the flesh but according to the spirit. Hence it was said most truthfully: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5:17). The fullness of the Law, therefore, is love (Rom. 13:10). And love belongs to those who walk according to the spirit. For this pertains to the grace of the Holy Spirit. When there was not the love of righteousness but fear, the Law was not fulfilled.

### XLIX. [Book VIII, 7]

When he says, “Because the wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God; for it is not subject to the Law of God, nor indeed can it be,” he shows what he meant by “hostile,” lest anyone think that, as though arising from an opposing principle, some nature which God did not create exercises hostility against God.

The enemy of God, then, is the person who does not obey his Law, and does so through the wisdom of the flesh—that is, when he desires temporal goods and fears temporal evils. For the definition of wisdom is usually explained in terms of seeking goods and avoiding evils.

Therefore the Apostle rightly calls that wisdom “of the flesh” by which these things are sought as great goods, although they do not remain with a person, and by which one fears losing things that must eventually be lost. Such wisdom cannot obey the Law of God. But the Law is obeyed when this wisdom has been extinguished, so that the wisdom of the spirit may take its place—a wisdom in which our hope is not in temporal goods, nor our fear in temporal evils.

For the same nature of the soul possesses the wisdom of the flesh when it pursues lower things, and the wisdom of the spirit when it chooses higher things, just as the same nature of water freezes through cold and is melted by heat. Thus it is said that the wisdom of the flesh is not subject to the Law of God—nor indeed can it be—just as one might rightly say that snow cannot be made warm—nor indeed can it be. But when heat is applied, it dissolves, and the water becomes warm; no one can then call it snow.

### L. [Book VIII, 10]

When he says, “The body indeed is dead because of sin, but the spirit is life because of righteousness,” the body is called dead in the sense of mortal. For from its mortality the need for earthly things troubles the soul and arouses certain desires; yet the person who already serves the Law of God with his mind does not obey these desires by sinning.

### LI. [Book VIII, 11]

When he says, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus Christ from the dead dwells in you, he who raised Jesus Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit dwelling in you,” he now indicates the fourth stage among the four that we distinguished above (Prop. 13).

But this stage is not found in the present life. It belongs to the hope by which we await the redemption of our body, when this corruptible body will put on incorruption and this mortal body will put on immortality (1 Cor. 15:53–54). There peace is perfect, because the soul suffers no distress from the body, which has already been given life and changed into a heavenly condition.

### LII. [Book VIII, 15, 16]

When he says, “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery into fear” [Note: [Col. 2073] The printed editions have *in timore*, “in fear.” But the manuscripts have *in timorem*, “into fear,” in accordance with the Greek *eis phobon* (εἰς φόβον), to which the ancient Corbie Bibles also conform in having *in timorem*.], “but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father,’” the distinct periods of the two Testaments are made most evident. The former belongs to fear, but the New belongs to love.

Yet it may be asked what the spirit of slavery is. For the Spirit of adoption as sons is certainly the Holy Spirit. The spirit of slavery, therefore, in fear, is the one who has the power of death. For through this fear those who lived under the Law, not under grace, were subject to slavery throughout their whole life.

It is not surprising that they received this spirit through divine providence, since they pursued temporal goods—not because the Law and commandment belong to him. For “the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good” (Rom. 7:12). But the spirit of slavery is certainly not good, since those receive it who cannot fulfill the commandments of the Law that was given, while they serve carnal desires and have not yet been taken up by the grace of the Liberator into the adoption of sons.

For the spirit of slavery itself has no one in its power unless that person has been handed over to it according to the order of divine providence, with God’s justice assigning each person his due. The Apostle had received such authority when he says concerning certain people, “Whom I have handed over to Satan, that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20); and again concerning another: “I have already judged,” he says, “to hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the soul may be saved” (1 Cor. 5:3, 5).

Those, therefore, who are not yet under grace but are established under the Law, and are overcome by sins so as to obey carnal desires, increasing the guilt of their crimes through transgression, have received the spirit of slavery—that is, the spirit of him who has the power of death.

But if we understand the spirit of slavery as the human spirit itself, then the Spirit of adoption also begins to be understood as that same spirit changed for the better. Since, however, we understand the Spirit of adoption to be the Holy Spirit—as he clearly shows when he says, “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit”—it remains that we understand the spirit of slavery as the one whom sinners serve.

Thus, just as the Holy Spirit delivers from fear of death, so the spirit of slavery, which has the power of death, holds the guilty in the terror of that same death, so that each person may turn to the help of the Liberator—even against the will of the devil himself, who always desires to keep that person in his power.

### LIII. [Book VIII, 19–23]

When he says, “For the expectation of creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God. For creation was subjected to futility, not willingly,” and so forth, up to the point where he says, “And we ourselves groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, the redemption of our body,” this is to be understood in such a way that we neither suppose that trees, plants, stones, and other creatures of this kind possess the capacity to feel pain and groan—for this is the error of the Manichaeans—nor think that the holy angels were subjected to futility or that they will be liberated from slavery to corruption, since they are certainly not destined to perish.

Rather, without any forced interpretation, we should understand all creation in the human being itself. For no creation can exist except as spiritual, which excels in the angels; animal, which is sufficiently evident even in the life of beasts; or bodily, which can be seen or touched. All of these are also present in the human being, because the human being consists of spirit, soul, and body.

Therefore creation awaits the revelation of the sons of God—whatever now labors in the human being and is subject to corruption—namely, that manifestation of which the same Apostle says: “For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God. When Christ, your life, appears, then you also will appear with him in glory” (Col. 3:3–4).

John also says: “Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be. But we know that when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Creation, then, which is now subject to futility in the human being, awaits this revelation of the sons of God, for as long as it is devoted to temporal things, which pass away like a shadow. Hence it is also said in the Psalm: “Man has become like vanity; his days pass away like a shadow” (Ps. 143:4).

Solomon also speaks of this futility when he says: “Vanity of those who are vain” [Note: [Col. 2075] The printed editions have *Vanitas vanitatum*, “Vanity of vanities.” But the manuscripts have *Vanitas vanitantium*, “Vanity of those who are vain,” as Augustine testifies that he once read it in Book I of the *Retractions*, chapter 7.], “and all is vanity. What abundance does a man have in all his labor by which he labors under the sun?” (Eccl. 1:2–3). David likewise says: “Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. 4:3).

He says that creation was subjected to futility not willingly, because this subjection is penal. For just as the human being sinned willingly, so he was not condemned willingly; yet this condemnation was inflicted upon our nature not without the hope of restoration.

Therefore he says, “Because of him who subjected it in hope.” For creation itself will also be liberated from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God—that is, even that which is merely creation and has not yet been joined through faith to the number of God’s children.

Nevertheless, in those who were going to believe, the Apostle saw what he says: that creation will be liberated from slavery to corruption, so that it will not serve corruption, to which all sinners are enslaved. For it was said to the sinner: “You shall surely die” (Gen. 2:17).

It will be liberated into the freedom of the glory of the children of God—that is, it will itself also attain the freedom of the glory of the children of God through faith. When faith was not yet present in it, it was called merely creation. To this same creation he refers in what follows: “For we know that the whole creation groans together and suffers in labor pains until now.”

There were still those who were going to believe, and who were also subject in spirit to burdensome errors. But lest anyone think that this was said only of their labor, he adds something also about those who had already believed.

Although in spirit—that is, in mind—they served the Law of God, nevertheless, because in the flesh one serves the law of sin (Rom. 7:25), for as long as we suffer the troubles and enticements of our mortality, he therefore added, saying: “And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the first fruits of the Spirit, groan within ourselves.”

Thus, he says, not only does that which is called merely creation in human beings who have not yet believed—and therefore have not yet been placed among the number of God’s children—groan together and suffer; but we ourselves also, who believe and have the first fruits of the Spirit, because we already adhere to God in spirit through faith and therefore are called not creation but children of God, nevertheless groan within ourselves, awaiting adoption, [Col. 2076] the redemption of our body.

For this adoption, which has already taken place in those who believe, has taken place in spirit, not in the body. For the body has not yet been transformed into that heavenly change, just as the spirit has already been changed through the reconciliation of faith, turned from errors to God.

Therefore, even in those who have believed, that manifestation is still awaited which will come through the resurrection of the body. This pertains to that fourth stage, where peace will be perfect in every respect and there will be eternal rest, with no corruption resisting us in any part or distress troubling us. [Note: [Col. 2076] See Prop. 13.]

### LIV. [Book VIII, 26, 27]

When he says, “Likewise the Spirit also helps our weakness; for we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should,” it is clear that he is speaking of the Holy Spirit. This becomes clear in what follows, where he says, “Because he intercedes for the saints according to God.”

We therefore do not know what we ought to pray for as we should for two reasons: first, that what we hope for in the future, and toward which we are striving, has not yet appeared; and second, that in this present life many things may seem advantageous to us which are disadvantageous, and things disadvantageous which are advantageous.

For when tribulation comes upon God’s servant for testing or correction, it sometimes seems useless to those who understand less well. But if it is referred to what was said, “Give us help in tribulation; human salvation is vain” (Ps. 59:15), it is understood that God often helps us through tribulation, and that salvation is sought in vain when it is sometimes disadvantageous, because it entangles the soul in delight and love of this life.

Hence there is also the statement: “I found tribulation and sorrow, and I called upon the name of the Lord” (Ps. 114:3–4). When he says, “I found,” he indicates something beneficial. For we do not rightly rejoice that we have found something unless it is what we were seeking.

Therefore we do not know what we ought to pray for as we should. For God knows both what is beneficial for us in this life and what he will give us after this life. But the Spirit himself intercedes with inexpressible groanings.

He says that the Spirit groans because he makes us groan through love, stirring up desire for the life to come. Thus he says, “The Lord your God tests you, to know whether you love him” (Deut. 13:3)—that is, to make you know. For nothing is hidden from God.

### LV. [Book VIII, 28–30]

When he says, “Those whom he called, he also justified,” this may cause difficulty, and it may be asked whether all who have been called are justified. But elsewhere we read: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22:14).

Yet since the chosen themselves were certainly also called, it is clear that no one is justified except those who have been called, although not all who have been called, but those who have been called according to the purpose, as he said above. The purpose, however, must be understood as God’s purpose, not theirs.

He himself explains what “according to the purpose” means when he says: “For those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son.” For not all who were called were called according to the purpose. This purpose pertains to God’s foreknowledge and predestination; nor did he predestine anyone whom he did not foreknow would believe and follow his calling. These he also calls chosen.

For many do not come when they have been called; but no one comes who has not been called.

### LVI. [Book VIII, 29]

When he says, “So that he might be the firstborn among many brothers,” he sufficiently teaches that our Lord is to be understood in one way as only-begotten and in another way as firstborn.

Where he is called Only-Begotten, he has no brothers and is by nature the Son of God, the Word in the beginning, through whom all things were made (John 1:1, 3). But according to his assumption of humanity and the dispensation of the incarnation, through which he also deigned to call us, who are not sons by nature, into the adoption of sons, he is called firstborn with the addition of brothers.

For where someone is called first, he is certainly not alone, but has brothers who are to follow him into that place where he went before them. Hence elsewhere he is also called “the firstborn from the dead, so that he himself might hold first place” (Col. 1:18). For before him there was no resurrection of the dead so that they would no longer die; after him, however, there is the resurrection of many saints, whom he is not ashamed to call brothers because of their sharing in humanity.

### LVII. [Book VIII, 35]

When he says, “Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or distress, or persecution?” and so forth, this depends upon the preceding statement, where he says: “If indeed we suffer with him, so that we may also be glorified. For I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy of comparison with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Rom. 8:17–18).

For the whole intention of this passage is directed toward that exhortation: that those to whom he speaks should not be broken by persecutions if they lived according to the wisdom of the flesh, by which temporal goods are desired and temporal evils feared.

### LVIII. [Book VIII, 38]

When he says, “For I am sure,” and does not say, “For I suppose,” he held with complete faith that neither any death, nor any promise of temporal life, nor the other things that follow can turn a believer away from the love of God.

No one, therefore, separates him—not even one who threatens death, because whoever believes in Christ, even if he dies, will live; nor one who promises life, because Christ gives eternal life. The promise of temporal life is to be despised in comparison with eternal life.

Nor does an angel separate, because even if an angel, he says, descends from heaven and announces to you something other than what you received, let him be accursed (Gal. 1:8–9).

Nor does a principality separate—that is, an opposing principality—because he himself stripped off the principalities and powers, triumphing over them in himself (Col. 2:15).

Nor do present things or future things separate—that is, temporal things, whether they delight, oppress, offer hope, or inspire fear.

Nor does power separate. Here too a hostile power must be understood, in accordance with the statement: “No one can plunder the goods of the strong man unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12:29).

Nor height nor depth. For an empty curiosity about things that cannot be discovered—or that are discovered in vain—whether in heaven or in the abyss, often separates people from God, unless love prevails. Love invites people to certain spiritual realities, not through the vanity of outward things but through the truth within. [Note: [Col. 2077] Four manuscripts have *sed interno homine invitat*, “but invites through the inner person.” The editions of Amerbach and Erasmus have *sed interno volumine invitat*, “but invites through an inner volume.” The manuscript of Germanus has *sed intra hominem invitat*, “but invites within the person.”]

Nor does any other creature separate. This can be understood in two ways: either “visible creature,” because we too—that is, the soul—are a creature, but invisible; so that he may have said that no other creature separates us, namely, the love of bodily things. Or it may mean that no other creature separates us from the love of God, because there is no other creature between us and God that can oppose itself and exclude us from his embrace.

For above human minds, which are rational, there is no creature but God.

### LIX. [Book IX, 5]

When he says, “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh,” and adds, “who is God over all, blessed forever,” he commends the fullness of faith most completely. For we confess our Lord both as Son of Man according to his assumption of flesh and as the Word in the beginning, God according to eternity, blessed above all forever.

The Jews are refuted by the Lord because they held only part of this confession. For when he asked them whose son they said Christ was, they answered, “David’s.” This was according to the flesh. But concerning his divinity, that he is God, they answered nothing.

Therefore the Lord said to them, “How then does David, in the Spirit, call him Lord?” (Matt. 22:42–43). He wanted them to understand that they had confessed only that Christ is the son of David, while they had remained silent about the fact that Christ is David’s Lord. The former is according to the assumption of flesh; the latter according to the eternity of divinity.

### LX. [Book IX, 11–13]

When he says, “For before the children were born or had done anything good or evil, so that God’s purpose according to election might remain—not from works but from him who calls—it was said to her, ‘The elder shall serve the younger,’ as it is written, ‘Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated,’” this troubles some people, leading them to think that the Apostle Paul removed free choice of the will, by which we please God through the good of devotion or offend him through the evil of impiety.

For they say that before either had performed any works, whether good or evil, and while the two were not yet born, God loved one and hated the other. We answer that this occurred through God’s foreknowledge, by which he knows what each person will be like even before birth.

But lest anyone say, “Then God chose the works of the one he loved, although they did not yet exist, because he foreknew that they would exist” [Note: [Col. 2078] In B., “because he foreknew that they were going to exist.” We have followed Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition. M.], and ask, “If he chose works, how does the Apostle say that election was not from works?”—it must therefore be understood that good works are performed through love, while love exists in us through the gift of the Holy Spirit, as the same Apostle says: “God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us” (Rom. 5:5).

No one, therefore, ought to glory in works as though they were his own, when he possesses them through God’s gift and when love itself is what produces the good in him.

What, then, did God choose? For if he gives the Holy Spirit to whomever he wishes, through whom love produces good, how did he choose whom to give it to? If there was no merit, there is no election; for all are equal before merit, and election cannot be named among things that are entirely equal.

But since the Holy Spirit is given only to believers, God did not choose the works that he himself bestows when he gives the Holy Spirit, so that we may perform good works through love; nevertheless, he chose faith. For unless a person believes in him and persists in the will to receive him, he does not receive God’s gift, that is, the Holy Spirit, through whom, once love has been poured out, he can perform good.

God therefore did not choose, in his foreknowledge, anyone’s works that he himself was going to give; rather, he chose faith in his foreknowledge, so that the person whom he foreknew would believe he might choose as the one to whom he would give the Holy Spirit, so that through doing good he might also obtain eternal life.

For the same Apostle says: “It is the same God who works all things in all” (1 Cor. 12:6). But nowhere is it said, “God believes all things in all.” What we believe, therefore, is ours; but the good that we do belongs to him who gives the Holy Spirit to those who believe in him. [Note: [Col. 2079] In *On Retractions*, chapter 23, no. 2, and in Book I of *On the Predestination of the Saints*, chapter 3, he says that he had erred here.]

This example was directed against certain Jews who believed in Christ and gloried in works performed before grace. They said that they had earned the grace of the Gospel itself through their preceding good works, although good works cannot exist in anyone except one who has received grace.

Grace consists in the call being granted beforehand to the sinner [Note: [Col. 2079] The printed editions have *ut vocatio peccatoris prorogetur*, “so that the sinner’s call may be postponed.” The manuscripts more correctly have *peccatori praerogetur*, “that the call may be granted beforehand to the sinner.”], although no merits preceded him except those deserving condemnation.

If the person called follows the one who calls—which already belongs to free choice—he will also merit the Holy Spirit, through whom he can perform good works. By remaining in this Spirit—which likewise belongs to free choice—he will also merit eternal life, which no stain can corrupt.

### LXI. [Book IX, 11–15]

When he says, “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show compassion to whom I show compassion,” this demonstrates that there is no injustice with God. Some people may say this when they hear, “Before they were born, I loved Jacob but hated Esau.”

“For I will have mercy,” he says, “on whom I have mercy.” First, God had mercy on us when we were sinners, in order to call us. “On whom I will have mercy,” he says, “so that I may call him, I will continue to have mercy on him when he believes.”

But how could he continue to have mercy except by giving the Holy Spirit to the one who believes and asks? Once he has given the Spirit, he will show compassion to the one toward whom he has been compassionate—that is, he will make him compassionate, so that he can perform good through love.

Let no one, therefore, dare to attribute to himself the merciful acts he performs, because God has given him love through the Holy Spirit, without which no one can be compassionate.

God therefore did not choose those who were already doing good, but rather those who believed, so that he himself might make them do good. It is ours to believe and to will; it is his to give those who believe and will the ability to do good through the Holy Spirit, through whom God’s love is poured into our hearts, so that he may make us compassionate. [Note: [Col. 2079] The same work, no. 3.]

### LXII. [Book IX, 15–21]

But when he says, “So then it depends not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who has mercy,” he does not abolish freedom of will; rather, he says that our willing is not sufficient unless God helps us, making us merciful so that we may do good through the gift of the Holy Spirit. He refers this to what he said above: “I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will show mercy to whom I show mercy.” For we cannot even will unless we are called; and when, after the call, we have willed, our will and our running are not sufficient unless God both supplies strength to those who run and brings them to the place to which he calls them. It is therefore evident that what we do well belongs not to the one who wills or runs, but to God who has mercy—although our will is also present, a will that by itself could accomplish nothing.

Hence he next introduces the testimony concerning Pharaoh’s punishment, when Scripture says of Pharaoh: “For this very purpose I raised you up, that I might show my power in you, and that my name might be proclaimed throughout the whole earth.” For, as we read in Exodus, “the heart of Pharaoh was hardened” (Exod. X, 1), so that he was not moved by such evident signs. Thus, the fact that Pharaoh then did not obey God’s commands already arose from punishment. No one, however, can say that this hardening of his heart happened to Pharaoh undeservedly, but rather by God’s judgment, which repaid his unbelief with the punishment it deserved. Therefore, what is charged against him is not that he did not obey at that time—for with his heart hardened he could not obey—but that he had made himself worthy for his heart to be hardened through his earlier unbelief.

For just as, in those whom God chooses, faith rather than works begins the basis of merit, so that by God’s gift they may do good, so in those whom he condemns, unbelief and godlessness begin the basis of punishment, so that through that very punishment they may also do evil. The same apostle says above: “And because they did not approve of retaining God in their knowledge, God handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is improper” (Rom. I, 28).

Accordingly, the Apostle concludes in this way: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” For the one on whom he has mercy he makes able to do good; and the one whom he hardens he leaves to do evil. Yet that mercy is attributed to a preceding merit of faith, and that hardening to preceding godlessness [Note: [Col. 2080] On this and the preceding passages, see *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 23, §§3–4.], so that we do good through God’s gift and evil through punishment, while human freedom of will is nevertheless not taken away—whether for believing in God, so that mercy may come upon us, or for godlessness, so that punishment may come upon us.

Having drawn this conclusion, he introduces a question as though raised by an objector. For he says: “You will say to me, then, ‘Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?’” He answers this inquiry in such a way that we understand the following to be open to spiritual people, who no longer live according to the earthly human being: how God, in his foreknowledge, chooses those who will believe and condemns unbelievers—not choosing the former on the basis of works, nor condemning the latter on the basis of works, but granting the faith of the former so that they may do good, and hardening the godlessness of the latter by abandoning them, so that they may do evil.

Because this understanding, as I have said, is open to spiritual people but is far removed from carnal judgment [Col. 2081], he refutes the questioner in such a way that the latter understands that he must first put off the human being of clay, in order to deserve to investigate these matters through the Spirit. Thus he says: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, ‘Why did you make me this way?’ Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, from the same lump to make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?”

“As long as you are a thing formed,” he says, “and belong to the lump of clay, not yet brought to spiritual things so that you may be spiritual, judging all things and judged by no one, you ought to restrain yourself from such inquiry and not answer back to God.” Anyone who wishes to know his counsel must first be received into his friendship; and this cannot happen except to spiritual people, who already bear the image of the heavenly human being. For he says: “I no longer call you servants, but friends; for everything that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John XV, 15).

Therefore, as long as you are a clay vessel, that very thing in you must first be crushed by the iron rod of which it is said: “You will rule them with an iron rod, and like a potter’s vessel you will crush them” (Ps. II, 9). Then, when the outer human being has been corrupted and the inner human being renewed, you will be able, being rooted and grounded in love, to comprehend its breadth, length, height, and depth, and also to know the surpassing knowledge of the love of God (Eph. III, 16–19).

Now, then, when from the same lump God makes some vessels for honor and others for dishonor, it is not yours to investigate this, whoever you are who still live according to this lump—that is, who think in an earthly and carnal way.

LXIII. [On Rom. IX, 22.]

When he says, “He endured with much patience vessels of wrath, made ready for destruction,” he sufficiently indicates that the hardening of heart which occurred in Pharaoh arose from the merits of a prior, hidden godlessness. Yet God patiently endured him until he should be brought to the time when vengeance might suitably proceed against him, for the correction of those whom he had undertaken to free from error and to bring, by calling them in piety, to his worship [Note: [Col. 2081] All our manuscripts: “and to bring them back to his worship and piety”], providing help for their prayers and groans.

LXIV. [On Rom. IX, 24–25.]

When he says, “Whom he also called—us, not only from the Jews but also from the Gentiles, as he says also in Hosea, ‘I shall call not my people, my people,’” etc., he brings the purpose of this whole discussion to this point: since he has taught that our doing good belongs to God’s mercy, the Jews are not to glory as though on the basis of works. Having received the Gospel, they thought it was to be attributed to their own merits and did not wish it to be given to the Gentiles. They should now cease from this pride, understanding that, if we are called to believe not on the basis of works but by God’s mercy, and believers are enabled to do good, this mercy is not to be begrudged to the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 2081] *Retractions* I, ch. 23, §4], as though there were some prior merit of the Jews—which there is not.

LXV. [On Rom. IX, 27.]

When he says, “But Isaiah cries out concerning Israel: ‘Though the number of the children of Israel [Col. 2082] be as the sand of the sea, a remnant shall be saved,’” he shows how God is the cornerstone, joining both walls in himself (Eph. II, 20). For the testimony of the prophet Hosea was spoken for the Gentiles: “I shall call not my people, my people, and not beloved, beloved” (Hos. II, 24); while Isaiah’s testimony was spoken for Israel: “For a remnant shall be saved” (Isa. X, 22), so that those who believed in Christ may be reckoned as Abraham’s seed. Thus he makes the two peoples harmonious, in accordance also with the Lord’s testimony in the Gospel concerning the Gentiles: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; them also I must bring, and there shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John X, 16).

LXVI. [On Rom. X, 1.]

When he says, “Brothers, the good will of my heart and my prayer to God is for their salvation,” he now begins to speak of the hope of the Jews, lest the Gentiles too dare to be proud against the Jews. For just as the pride of Jews who gloried as though from works had to be refuted, so provision must be made for the Gentiles, lest they be proud as though preferred to the Jews.

LXVII. [On Rom. X, 8–10.]

When he says, “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; that is, the word of faith which we preach: because if you confess with your mouth that Jesus is Lord, and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you shall be saved. For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation,” this entire passage refers to what he said above: “For the Lord will perform a consummating and shortening word upon the earth” (Rom. IX, 28). For, after the innumerable and manifold sacraments by which the Jewish people was burdened had been removed, it came about through God’s mercy that we might attain salvation by the brevity of the confession of faith.

LXVIII. [On Rom. X, 19.]

When he says, according to Moses’ testimony, “I shall provoke you to jealousy by that which is not a nation; by a foolish nation I shall provoke you,” in saying “a foolish nation” he explained what he meant by “not a nation”: as though a foolish people ought not even to be called a nation. Yet he says that the Jewish people is to be provoked by that people’s faith, because they laid hold of what the Jews rejected. Or certainly, “by that which is not a nation, by a foolish nation,” because, although every people that worshipped idols was a foolish nation, it nevertheless laid aside Gentile status by believing. Hence also this: “If therefore the uncircumcision keeps the righteous requirements of the Law, shall not his uncircumcision be reckoned as circumcision?” (Rom. II, 26). Thus the sense is: I shall bring you to jealousy by the one which has become not a nation, having laid aside Gentile status through faith in Christ, though it had been a foolish nation by worshipping idols.

LXIX. [On Rom. XI, 11.]

When he says, “Has God cast off his people? By no means. For I too am an Israelite, of the seed of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin,” this refers to what he said above: “But the word of God cannot fail. For not all who are from Israel are Israelites; nor, because they are Abraham’s seed, are they all children; but ‘In Isaac shall seed be called for you’”—that is, from the Jewish people itself, those who believed the Lord are reckoned as seed. Again he says above concerning this, “A remnant shall be saved” (Rom. IX, 6, 7, 27).

[Col. 2083] LXX. [On Rom. XI, 11.]

When he says, “I say then, Have they stumbled so as to fall? By no means. But through their transgression salvation has come to the Gentiles” [Note: [Col. 2083] The printed editions add *has come*, which is absent from the manuscripts and the Greek; the Vatican manuscript has *came* in its place], he does not say this because they did not fall, but because their fall was not fruitless, since it profited the Gentiles for salvation. Therefore they did not so transgress as to fall—that is, merely to fall, as though only for their own punishment—but so that their very falling might benefit the Gentiles toward salvation. Then from this point he begins to commend the Jewish people, even in respect of the fall of unbelief, so that the Gentiles may not be proud; for even the fall of the Jews is considered so precious for the salvation of the Gentiles. Rather, the Gentiles should beware lest, while being proud, they too fall in like manner.

LXXI. [On Rom. XII, 20; 14; 17.]

When he said, “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he thirsts, give him drink; for in doing this you will heap coals of fire upon his head,” this may seem to many contrary to the saying in which the Lord commanded us to love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us (Matt. V, 44), or also to that which the same apostle said above: “Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse”; and again, “Repaying no one evil for evil.” For how does anyone love a person to whom he gives food and drink precisely in order to heap coals of fire on his head, if coals of fire here signify some severe punishment? Therefore it must be understood as said in order that, when we do good to one who has injured us, we may summon him to repentance for his deed. For these coals of fire serve for burning—that is, for the tribulation of the spirit, which is as it were the head of the soul. In it all malice is burned up when a human being is changed for the better through repentance. Such are the coals of which it is said in the Psalms: “What shall be given you, or what added for you, against a deceitful tongue? Sharp arrows of the mighty, with desolating coals” (Ps. CXIX, 3–4).

LXXII. [On Rom. XIII, 1.]

When he says, “Let every soul be subject to the higher authorities; for there is no authority except from God,” he very rightly warns us that no one, because called by his Lord into freedom and made a Christian, should exalt himself in pride and suppose that, in the course of this life, he need not preserve his proper order or be subject to the higher authorities to whom, for the time being, the administration of temporal affairs has been entrusted. Since we consist of soul and body, and while we are in this temporal life make use also of temporal things as aids for living it, we ought, in that part of ourselves which belongs to this life, to be subject to authorities—that is, to people who administer human affairs with a certain rank. But in that part by which we believe God and are called into his kingdom, we ought not to be subject to any human being seeking to overthrow in us that very thing which God has deigned to grant for eternal life.

If, then, anyone thinks that because he is a Christian he need not pay customs or tribute, or render due honor [Col. 2084] to the authorities who administer these things, he is in great error. Likewise, if anyone thinks he ought to be so subject that he considers one who excels in some high position in the administration of temporal matters to have power even over his faith, he falls into a still greater error [Note: [Col. 2084] This sentence, “Likewise, if anyone . . . falls into a still greater error,” found in all the manuscripts, was omitted in the Amerbach and Erasmus editions]. But the rule must be observed which the Lord himself prescribes: that we render to Caesar what is Caesar’s and to God what is God’s (Matt. XXII, 21).
