Although we are called to that kingdom where there will be no authority of this kind, nevertheless, during this journey, until we attain the age in which every rule and authority is abolished, let us endure our condition for the sake of the order of human affairs, doing nothing deceitfully and, in this very matter, obeying not so much human beings as God, who commands these things.

LXXIII. [On Rom. XIII, 3–4.]

When he says, “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it,” some may be troubled when they consider that Christians have often suffered persecution from these authorities. Did they then not do good, since they were not merely not praised by those authorities but were also punished and killed? Therefore the Apostle’s words must be considered. For he does not say, “Do good, and the authority will praise you”; rather, he says, “Do good, and you will have praise from it.” Whether it approves your good deed or persecutes you, you will have praise from it: either when you have won it to obedience to God, or when you have deserved a crown through its persecution. This is also understood in what follows, when he says, “For it is God’s minister to you for good,” even if it is for evil to itself.

LXXIV. [On Rom. XIII, 5.]

When he says, “Therefore be subject by necessity” [Note: [Col. 2084] Amerbach, Erasmus, and six manuscripts here and below read “necessity”], this means that we should understand it to be necessary, on account of this life, that we be subject, not resisting if they wish to take anything over which they have been given authority among temporal things. Since these things pass away, this subjection is to be located not among goods as though permanent, but among necessities for this time. Yet because he said, “Be subject by necessity,” lest anyone be subject to authorities of this kind without a whole heart and pure love, he added: “Not only because of wrath, but also because of conscience”—that is, not only to avoid wrath [Note: [Col. 2084] All our manuscripts: “to remove it”], which can also be done deceitfully, but so that in your conscience you may be certain that you do it out of love for the one to whom you are subject by the command of your Lord, who “wills all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth” (I Tim. II, 4). For when the Apostle said this, he was speaking of the authorities themselves. This is what he advises servants elsewhere: “Not serving to the eye, as pleasing people” (Eph. VI, 6), so that, in being subject to their masters, they may not hate them or desire to win favor by deceits.

LXXV. [On Rom. XIII, 8, 10.]

When he says, “For the one who loves another has fulfilled the Law” [Note: [Col. 2084] Printed editions: “loves his neighbor.” But the manuscripts read “another,” following the Greek, *ton heteron*], he shows that the fulfillment [Col. 2085] of the Law is situated in love—that is, charity. Hence the Lord too says that the whole Law and all the Prophets hang upon those two commandments, namely love of God and neighbor (Matt. XXII, 37–40). Thus he who came to fulfill the Law bestowed love through the Holy Spirit, so that what fear could not previously fulfill, charity might afterward fulfill. Hence too the same apostle’s saying, “The fullness of the Law is charity,” and: “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I, 5).

LXXVI. [On Rom. XIII, 11.]

When he says, “And this, knowing the time, that it is already the hour for us to rise from sleep,” he refers to what was said: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (II Cor. VI, 2). For the time of the Gospel is signified, and that opportunity for making believers in God saved.

LXXVII. [On Rom. XIII, 14.]

When he says, “And make no provision for the flesh in its lusts” [Note: [Col. 2085] Vatican manuscript: “make excessive provision.” The other manuscripts: “make provision”], he shows that provision for the flesh is not blameworthy when provision is made for what serves the necessity of bodily health. But if it is for superfluous pleasures and luxuries, so that one may delight in what the flesh desires, one is rightly reproved because one makes provision for the flesh in its lusts. For “the one who sows in his flesh shall reap corruption from the flesh” (Gal. VI, 8), that is, the one who delights in fleshly pleasures.

LXXVIII. [On Rom. XIV, 1–3.]

When he says, “Receive the weak in faith, not for judging thoughts,” he means that we should receive one weak in faith and bear that person’s weakness by our own strength, and should not judge that person’s thoughts—that is, should not dare, as it were, to pronounce judgment on another’s heart, which we do not see. Therefore he goes on to say: “One person indeed believes he may eat all things, but one who is weak may eat vegetables.” For at that time many were already strong in faith and knew, according to the Lord’s saying, that not what enters a person but what goes out defiles (Matt. XV, 11–20); they ate foods indiscriminately with a safe conscience. But some weaker people abstained from meat and wine, lest even unknowingly they fall into things sacrificed to idols. For every sacrificial animal was then sold in the market, and the Gentiles poured libations from the first fruits of wine to their images and performed certain sacrifices in the winepresses themselves. The Apostle therefore commands both those who used such food with a safe conscience not to despise the weakness of those who abstained from such food and drink, and those weak persons not to judge as defiled people who did not abstain from meat and drank wine. This is the point of what he says next: “Let the one who eats not despise the one who does not eat, and let the one who does not eat not judge the one who eats.” For the strong contemptuously despised the weaker, and the weak rashly judged the strong.

LXXIX. [On Rom. XIV, 4.]

When he says, “Who are you to judge another’s servant?” he says this so that in matters [Col. 2086] which can be done with either a good or a bad intention we may leave judgment to God and not dare to pronounce a verdict about another’s heart, which we do not see. But in matters so comprehended that it is evident they cannot be done with a good and chaste intention, it is not disapproved if we judge. Thus, in speaking of food, because it is unknown with what intention it is done, he does not wish us to be judges, but God. But concerning that impious fornication, in which a certain man had his father’s wife, he commanded that judgment should be made (I Cor. V, 1). That man could not say that he had committed so enormous a disgrace with a good intention. Therefore all deeds which are so manifest that one cannot say, “I did it with a good intention,” must be judged by us; but those done in such a way that the intention is uncertain are not to be judged, but reserved for God’s judgment, as it is written: “Secret things belong to God; but things openly revealed shall belong to you and your children” (Deut. XXIX, 29).

LXXX. [On Rom. XIV, 5–6.]

When he says, “One indeed judges alternate days, while another judges every day,” setting aside for the moment a better consideration, this seems to me to be said not of two human beings but of a human being and God. For the one who judges alternate days is a human being: today one can judge one thing, tomorrow another. That is, a person whom today one condemns as convicted or confessing evil may tomorrow be found good after correction; conversely, one whom today one praises as righteous may tomorrow be found depraved. But the one who judges every day is God, because he knows not only what each person is like but also what that person will be like on every future day. Therefore, he says, “Let each one abound in his own understanding”: that is, let each person dare to judge only as much as has been granted to human understanding, or to that person. “The one who regards the day,” he says, “regards it for the Lord”: that is, one who judges the present day well thereby regards it for the Lord. To judge with reference to the day is to know that one whose fault you have judged manifest in the present is not to be despaired of concerning future correction.

LXXXI. [On Rom. XIV, 22; 16.]

When he says, “Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves,” this should especially be referred to what he said above: “Therefore let not our good be blasphemed.” This is also what he says immediately before this sentence: “The faith which you have, have it before God within yourself.” Since this faith, by which we believe that all things are clean to the clean (Tit. I, 15), is good, and in that faith we approve ourselves, let us use our own good well. Otherwise, if we misuse that good to the offense of weak brothers, we may sin against the brothers and judge ourselves in that very good when we scandalize the weak—the good in which we approve ourselves when the faith itself pleases us.

LXXXII. [On Rom. XV, 8–9.]

When he says, “For I say that Christ Jesus became a minister of the circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises to the fathers, while the Gentiles glorify God for mercy,” he says this so that the Gentiles may understand that the Lord Christ was sent to the Jews and may not be proud. When the Jews rejected what had been sent to them, it came about that the Gospel was preached [Col. 2087] to the Gentiles. This is written most clearly in the Acts of the Apostles, when the Apostles say to the Jews: “To you it was necessary that the word be preached first; but since you have judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII, 46). This agrees also with the Lord’s own testimonies, when he says, “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel,” and again, “It is not good to cast the children’s bread to dogs” (Matt. XV, 24, 26). If the Gentiles consider this well, they understand that by their faith, through which they now believe that all things are clean to the clean, they ought not to insult those who may perhaps be weak from the circumcision [Note: [Col. 2087] All manuscripts: “weak of themselves”] and who, because of participation in idolatry, dare not touch any meat at all.

LXXXIII. [On Rom. XV, 16.]

When he says, “That I may be a minister of Christ Jesus among the Gentiles, consecrating the Gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may become acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit,” this means that the Gentiles are offered to God as an acceptable sacrifice when, believing in Christ, they are sanctified through the Gospel. Thus he says above as well: “Therefore I beseech you, brothers, through the mercy of God [Note: [Col. 2087] Here the worklet ends in the Amerbach and Erasmus editions, which omit the eighty-fourth Proposition [Col. 2088], the last one in the Louvain edition and in all the manuscripts], that you present your bodies [Col. 2088] as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God” (Rom. XII, 1).

LXXXIV. [On Rom. XVI, 17–18.]

When he says, “I beseech you, brothers, to watch those who cause dissensions and scandals contrary to the teaching which you learned,” he is understood to speak of those concerning whom he also wrote to Timothy: “As I urged you to remain at Ephesus when I was going to Macedonia, so that you might charge certain persons not to teach differently, nor give heed to myths and endless genealogies, which furnish questions rather than the edification of God which is in faith” (I Tim. I, 3–4); and to Titus: “For there are many unsubmissive, vain talkers and deceivers of minds, especially those of the circumcision, whom it is necessary to refute. They overthrow whole households, teaching what they ought not, for shameful gain. One of their own, their own prophet, said: ‘Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy bellies’” (Tit. I, 10–12). For this is the point of what he says here also: “For such persons serve not Christ the Lord, but their own belly”; concerning them he says elsewhere: “Whose god is their belly” (Phil. III, 19).

[EXPOSITION BEGUN OF THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS.]

[Col. 2087]

[Note: [Col. 2087] On the following work, see *Retractions*, book I, chapter 25, from col. 623, beginning “Also, the Epistle to the Romans,” through col. 624, ending “he wrote to the Romans.” M.] THE EXPOSITION BEGUN OF THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS, BY SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO. [Note: [Col. 2087] This present Exposition was not found in our manuscripts; but it has now been purged of many errors with the help of a Vatican manuscript, and collated with the Amerbach, Erasmus, and Louvain editions.] [Note: [Col. 2087] We further compared all the editions mentioned at the beginning of vol. 1 of the *Retractions* and *Confessions*.] (C)

One book [Note: [Col. 2087] Written about A.D. 394, namely when Augustine was still a presbyter, according to *Retractions*, book I, chapters 23 and 25]. In it only the salutation is explained, and the sin against the Holy Spirit is discussed.

1. In the Epistle which the apostle Paul wrote to the Romans, so far as can be understood from its text, he has this question: whether the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ came to the Jews alone because of the merits of works of the Law; or whether, with no prior merits of works, the justification of faith which is in Christ Jesus came to all the Gentiles, so that people did not believe because they were righteous, but, justified by believing, thereafter began to live righteously. He therefore intends to teach that the grace of the Gospel of our Lord [Col. 2088] Jesus Christ came to all. He shows that it is called grace precisely because it was not rendered as a debt of justice, but freely given.

For certain people who had believed from among the Jews had begun to make an uproar against the Gentiles, and especially against the apostle Paul, because he admitted the uncircumcised, free from the bonds of the old Law, to the grace of the Gospel, preaching to them that they should believe in Christ while imposing no yoke of fleshly circumcision. But he proceeds with such moderation that he permits neither the Jews to be proud as though by merits of works of the Law [Col. 2089], nor the Gentiles to be inflated against the Jews by the merit of faith because they themselves received Christ whom the Jews crucified. For, as he says elsewhere, acting as an ambassador for the Lord himself (II Cor. V, 20)—that is, for the cornerstone (Eph. II, 20)—he joins both peoples, Jews and Gentiles alike, in Christ through the bond of grace, taking from both every pride in merits and joining both, to be justified, in the discipline of humility.

2. Thus he began the Epistle: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God” (Rom. I, 1). Briefly, in two words he distinguishes the dignity of the Church from the antiquity of the Synagogue. For the Church is named from calling, whereas the Synagogue is named from gathering together. To be called together is more fitting for human beings; to be gathered together, more fitting for cattle—hence herds are properly said to be of cattle. Although in many places in Scripture the Church itself is called God’s flock, God’s sheepfold, and God’s herd, nevertheless, when human beings are called cattle by comparison, they belong to the old life. Such people evidently are content not with the food of everlasting truth but with temporal promises as with earthly fodder. Paul, then, was called as a servant of Christ Jesus and apostle; this calling enrolled him in the Church. But he was set apart for the Gospel of God—whence, if not from the flock of the Synagogue, provided the meaning of the Latin words in every respect agrees with the Greek interpretation?

3. Certainly he commends by the authority of the Prophets the Gospel of God, for which he recalls that he was set apart. Thus, since he had preferred to the Jews those who believe Christ, among whom he was called, and from whom he had said he was set apart, he in turn warns the Gentiles not now to be proud. For the Prophets were from the Jewish people, through whom he testifies that the Gospel—by faith in which believers are justified—was promised beforehand: “Set apart,” he says, “for the Gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his Prophets” (Rom. I, 1–2). For there were also prophets who were not his, in whom certain things are found which proclaimed what they had heard concerning Christ, as is also said of the Sibyl. I would not readily believe this, had not a certain poet, most famous in the Roman language, before uttering matters about the renewal of the age which seem sufficiently to accord and agree with the kingdom of our Lord Jesus Christ, prefaced the verse:

> Now comes the last age of the Cumaean song. (*Virgil, Eclogue* 4, v. 4.)

No one could doubt that the Cumaean song is Sibylline. The Apostle therefore knew that testimonies to truth are found in the books of the Gentiles, as he showed most plainly when speaking to the Athenians in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XVII, 28). He therefore did not merely say “through his Prophets,” lest someone be led into some impiety by false prophets through certain confessions of truth; he added also, “in the holy Scriptures.” He intended, of course, to show that the writings of the Gentiles, full as they are of superstitious idolatry, should not on that account be considered holy because something pertaining to Christ is found in them.

4. And lest someone perhaps produce prophets remote [Col. 2090] and alien from the Jewish people, in whom there was no worship of images—so far as concerns images made by human hands; for every error deceives its followers by the images of their own imaginations—and yet, producing something of this kind because Christ’s name is displayed there, assert that those rather than the Scriptures divinely entrusted to the Hebrew people are holy Scriptures, it seems to me quite fitting that, after saying “in the holy Scriptures,” he adds what follows: “concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh” (Rom. I, 3). David, certainly, was king of the Jews. It was fitting that Christ’s prophetic announcers should arise from the people from which he whom they announced was to assume flesh.

But the impiety of those also had to be met who understand our Lord Jesus Christ only according to the humanity which he assumed, and do not understand that the divinity in him is distinct from the fellowship of all creation. Such are the Jews themselves, who suppose Christ to be merely the son of David, unaware of the excellence by which he is the Lord of David himself, according to that in which he is the Son of God. Hence in the Gospel he rebukes them by the prophecy uttered through David’s own mouth. For he asks them how the one whom David himself calls Lord can be his son (Matt. XXII, 42–45). They ought, of course, to answer that according to the flesh he was David’s son, but according to divinity the Son of God and David’s own Lord.

Because the apostle Paul had now learned this, after saying, “for the Gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his Prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David,” he added “according to the flesh,” lest they should think that what was made according to the flesh was the only thing and the whole of Christ. By adding “according to the flesh,” therefore, he preserved its proper dignity for divinity. It can be attributed not only to David’s seed, but not even to the generation of any angelic or other most excellent creature, since he himself is the Word of God through whom all things were made. This Word was made flesh from the seed of David and dwelt among us (John I, 1, 3, 14), not changed and converted into flesh, but clothed in flesh so that he might appear suitably to fleshly people. Accordingly, the Apostle distinguished humanity from divinity not only by the phrase “according to the flesh,” but also by saying “was made.” For he was not made according to that in which he is the Word of God. For all things were made through him; nor could the one through whom all things were made be made with all things. Nor was he made before all things in order that all things might be made through him. For if, apart from him, he had already been made before those things, then not all things would be those made through him; nor could all things truly be said to have been made through him if he himself were not among them, were he himself also made. Therefore, when the Apostle says that Christ was made, he adds “according to the flesh,” to show that according to the Word, which is the Son of God, he was not made by God but begotten.

### 5

He plainly says that this very same one who was made according to the flesh from the seed of David was predestined to be the Son of God in power—not according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit; and not according to just any spirit, but according to the Spirit of sanctification, through the resurrection of the dead (Rom. 1:4). For in the resurrection the power of the one who died is manifested, so that he might be said to have been predestined in power according to the Spirit of sanctification through the resurrection of the dead.

Then sanctification produced a new life [Note: [Col. 2091] The Vatican Manuscript reads: “Then sanctification produced our new life.”], which was signified in the resurrection of our Lord. Hence the same apostle says elsewhere: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated at the right hand of God” (Col. 3:1).

The order of the words may indeed also be understood in such a way that we do not join “through the resurrection of the dead” to “the Spirit of sanctification,” but rather to “he was predestined,” so that the order is: “who was predestined through the resurrection of the dead,” with the words “the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification” inserted between them. And this order certainly seems more precise and better, so that he is the son of David in weakness according to the flesh, but the Son of God in power according to the Spirit of sanctification.

He was therefore made from the seed of David—that is, he became the son of David from a mortal body, and for this reason he also died. But he was predestined to be the Son of God and the Lord of David himself through the resurrection of the dead. Insofar as he died, this pertains to his being the son of David; but insofar as he rose from the dead, it pertains to his being the Son of God and the Lord of David himself. Thus the same apostle says elsewhere: “For even if he was crucified because of weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (2 Cor. 13:4)—so that weakness pertains to David, but eternal life to the power of God.

Therefore, in these very words David designates him as his Lord, saying: “The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies beneath your feet” (Ps. 109:1). For because he rose from the dead, he sits at the right hand of the Father.

Thus, seeing in the Spirit that he had been predestined through the resurrection of the dead to sit at the right hand of the Father, David would not dare to call him his son, but his Lord. Accordingly, the Apostle then adds here, “Jesus Christ our Lord,” after saying “through the resurrection of the dead,” as though reminding us why David testified that he was his Lord rather than his son.

He does not say that he was predestined “from the dead,” but “through the resurrection of the dead.” For it is not by his resurrection itself that he appears as the Son of God, in that proper and most eminent dignity by which he is also the head of the Church, since the other dead will likewise rise. Rather, the Son of God was predestined with a certain primacy of resurrection: from the resurrection of all the dead he was himself predestined—that is, designated to rise before the others and above the others.

Thus, the expression “the Son of God,” placed after “he was predestined,” serves as evidence of such great sublimity. For no one ought to have been predestined in this way except the Son of God, insofar as he is also the head of the Church. Hence elsewhere he calls him “the firstborn from the dead” (Col. 1:18).

It was fitting that the one who had gone before as an example should come to the judgment of those who rise—not as an example for all who rise, but as an example for those who will rise in such a way that they may live and reign with him forever; and he is also their head, as they are members of his body.

For from the resurrection of these people also he was predestined, so that he might become their leader. But for the others who rise in accordance with their own condition, he is not leader but judge. He was therefore not predestined from the resurrection of those dead whom he is going to condemn.

The Apostle wishes “predestined through the resurrection of the dead” to be understood as “predestined to precede the resurrection of the dead.” He preceded those who will follow him to that heavenly kingdom to which he went before them.

For this reason he does not say: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God through the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord,” but rather: “through the resurrection of the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord,” as though he were saying: “Who was predestined to be the Son of God through the resurrection of his dead”—that is, of those who belong to him in eternal life. It is as if he were asked, “Whose dead?” and answered, “Those of Jesus Christ our Lord.”

For he was not predestined through the resurrection of the other dead, whom he did not precede into the glory of eternal life and who will certainly not follow him, since the ungodly will rise for their punishments.

Therefore, as the only-begotten Son of God, he was also predestined as the firstborn from the dead, through the resurrection of the dead. Whose dead, if not those of our Lord Jesus Christ?

### 6

“Through whom,” he says, “we have received grace and apostleship.” Grace he received together with all the faithful, but apostleship not together with all. And therefore, if he had said only that he had received apostleship, he would have shown himself ungrateful for the grace by which his sins were forgiven; for he would appear to have received apostleship on account of the merits of his earlier works.

He therefore maintains the order of causation very well, so that no one dares to say that he was brought to the Gospel by the merits of his former life. For not even the Apostles themselves, who excel the other members after the head of the body, could have received apostleship properly unless they had first received, together with the others, the grace that heals and justifies sinners.

When he adds, “for obedience to the faith among all the nations for his name,” he says that he received apostleship for this purpose: that obedience might be rendered to the faith for the name of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, that all who desire to be saved may believe in Christ and be marked with his name.

He now shows that this salvation did not come only to the Jews, as some who had believed from among them supposed, when he says, “among all the nations,” among whom, he says, “you also are called by Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:5–6). That is, you too belong to this Jesus Christ, who is the salvation of all nations, although you are found not among the number of the Jews but among the number of the other nations.

### 7

Up to this point he has stated who the person is who writes the Epistle. The one who writes the Epistle is Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called as an apostle, set apart for the Gospel of God.

But since the question arose, “What Gospel?” he replied, “Which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son.”

Again, since the question arose, “Concerning which Son of his?” he replied, “Who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh, who was predestined to be the Son of God in power according to the spirit of sanctification through the resurrection of the dead, Jesus Christ our Lord.”

And as though it were said to him, “How do you belong to him?” he replied, “Through whom we have received grace and apostleship, for obedience to the faith among all the nations for his name.”

Again, as though it were said, “What reason, then, is there for you to write to us?” he replied, “Among whom you also are called by Jesus Christ.”

He now adds, as is customary in an epistle, to whom he is writing: “To all who are in Rome, beloved of God, called as saints.”

Here too he indicated God’s kindness rather than their merit. For he did not say “those who love God,” but “beloved of God.” He loved us first, before any merits, so that we too, having been loved, might love him (1 John 4:19).

Hence he also added, “called as saints.” Although someone may attribute to himself the fact that he obeys the one who calls, no one can attribute to himself the fact that he was called. “Called as saints” should not be understood to mean that they were called because they were already holy, but that they became holy because they were called.

### 8

It remains, then, for him to offer a greeting, so that the customary beginning of an epistle may be completed—as though he were saying “greetings to you.” Instead of saying “greetings,” he says: “Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (Rom. 1:7).

For not every grace is from God. Even wicked judges offer favor when they are led by some desire to accept persons or terrified by fear. Nor is every peace God’s peace, or from him. Hence the Lord himself distinguishes them when he says: “I give you my peace,” adding that he does not give such peace as this world gives (John 14:27).

Grace, then, is from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ: through it our sins are forgiven, sins by which we were opposed to God [Note: [Col. 2093] The Vatican Manuscript reads: “were estranged from God.”]. Peace, however, is that by which we are reconciled to God.

When, through grace and the forgiveness of sins, our enmity has been removed, it remains for us to cling in peace to the one from whom our sins alone had separated us. As the prophet says: “His ear is not burdened so that he cannot hear; but your sins separate between you and God” (Isa. 59:1–2). When these sins have been forgiven through faith in our Lord Jesus Christ, there will be peace, with no separation intervening.

### 9

Perhaps someone may wonder how the justice of God the judge is to be understood when he grants grace by forgiving sins. But this is plainly just before God: it is truly just that those who repent of their sins, at a time when the manifest terror of punishments has not yet appeared, should mercifully be separated from those who stubbornly seek defenses for their sins and do not wish to be corrected by any repentance.

For it is unjust that they should be joined and united in penal fellowship with those who have not despised God when he called them, but have become displeasing to themselves because they sinned, so that, just as God hated their sins, they too might hate their own.

This, then, is the discipline of human justice: to love nothing in oneself except what belongs to God, and to hate what is one’s own; neither to approve one’s sins nor to condemn another person in them, but oneself; not to think it sufficient for one’s sins to be displeasing, unless they are thereafter avoided with the most watchful determination; and, in avoiding them, not to consider one’s own strength sufficient unless one is helped by God.

It is therefore just before God that whatever such people previously committed should be forgiven, lest—which would be most unjust—they be confused and mixed together with those who are not such people.

Consequently, the fact that such people are not forgiven is an expression of God’s justice; and the fact that they are forgiven is grace. God’s grace is therefore just, and his justice welcome, since even the merit of repentance is preceded by grace: no one would repent of his sin except through some admonition arising from God’s call.

### 10

Moreover, the constancy of divine justice is so great that, although spiritual and eternal punishment is remitted for the repentant, bodily afflictions and sufferings—which we know even the martyrs have endured in training—and finally death itself, which our nature deserved through sinning, are remitted to no one.

For the fact that even just and devout people undergo these punishments must be believed to proceed from God’s just judgment. This is what is also called discipline in the sacred Scriptures, and no just person is permitted to escape it.

For it exempted no one when it said: “For whom God loves, he corrects; and he scourges every son whom he receives” (Heb. 12:6).

Hence Job himself, who suffered so many things precisely so that it might become evident to human beings what kind of man he was and how great a servant of God, nevertheless often testifies that he is paying the bodily penalties for his sins.

The apostle Peter also, exhorting the brethren to endure sufferings for Christ’s name, speaks as follows:

“Let none of you suffer as a murderer, or a thief, or a slanderer, or as one meddling in the affairs of others. But if as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; rather, let him glorify God in this name. For the time has come for judgment to begin from the house of God. And if it begins with us, what will be the end of those who do not believe the Gospel of God? And if the righteous person is scarcely saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (1 Pet. 4:15–18).

He plainly shows that the very sufferings endured by the righteous pertain to God’s judgment, which he said begins from the house of God, so that from this one may infer how great punishments are being reserved for the ungodly.

Hence Paul himself also says to the Thessalonians:

“So that we ourselves boast of you in the churches of God, because of your patience and faith in all your persecutions and afflictions that you endure, as an example of the just judgment of God” (2 Thess. 1:4–5).

This refers altogether to what Peter said: that the time has come for judgment to begin from the house of God; and also to what he inserted from the prophet: “And if the righteous person will scarcely be saved, where will the sinner and the ungodly appear?” (Prov. 11:31).

For this reason it also seems to me that those things which God threatened through the prophet Nathan to King David, although he immediately forgave him when he repented, nevertheless happened for this purpose (2 Sam. 12): to demonstrate that the forgiveness granted spiritually was given with a view to the future judgment of punishments awaiting those who do not wish to be corrected in the present time.

Peter says elsewhere:

“For this reason the Gospel was preached even to the dead, so that although they might be judged according to human standards in the flesh, they might live according to God in the spirit” (1 Pet. 4:6).

I have said this to show, insofar as I can and insofar as the opportunity offered by the present passage of Scripture permits, that God’s grace and peace, when they are mentioned, should not be understood in such a way that people suppose God can depart from justice.

For when the Lord promised peace itself, he said: “I have said these things to you so that in me you may have peace; in the world you will have affliction” (John 16:33).

But when tribulations and troubles are imposed upon sins through God’s justice, they do not turn the good and righteous—those to whom their sins themselves are already more displeasing than any bodily punishment—back toward sinning; rather, they cleanse them completely from every stain.

Perfect peace will also be granted to the body at its proper time [Note: [Col. 2095] So reads the Vatican Manuscript. The printed editions have “will be strengthened.”], if now our spirit holds firmly and unchangeably to the peace which the Lord has deigned to give through faith.

### 11

But when the Apostle says that grace and peace are from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, without adding the Holy Spirit as well, I see no other explanation than that we should understand the Holy Spirit himself to be the gift of God. For what else are grace and peace than the gift of God?

Therefore, grace by which we are freed from sins and peace by which we are reconciled to God cannot in any way be given to human beings except in the Holy Spirit.

Thus the Trinity, and likewise the unchangeable unity, is recognized in this greeting.

I believe this especially because, apart from the Epistle which he wrote to the Hebrews—where he deliberately omitted the introductory greeting so that the Jews who angrily attacked him would not, offended by his name, read what he had written for their salvation with a hostile disposition, or not care to read it at all; for this reason some were afraid to receive it into the canon of Scripture—apart from this Epistle, however that question may stand, all the others which the Church, without any doubt, establishes as belonging to the apostle Paul contain such a greeting.

The only exception is that in both Epistles to Timothy he inserts “mercy.” For he writes:

“Grace, mercy, and peace from God the Father and Jesus Christ our Lord” (1 Tim. 1:2; 2 Tim. 1:2).

Writing to Timothy with greater familiarity and therefore, in a certain sense, more sweetly, he inserted that word by which it is clearly opened and shown that the Holy Spirit is given to us not according to the merits of our former works, but according to the mercy of God, so that both the abolition of our sins—which separated us from God—and our reconciliation, by which we cling to him, may take place.

### 12

Nor do the other Epistles of the Apostles, which ecclesiastical usage accepts, give us little reminder of this Trinity in their beginnings.

For Peter says: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you.” He immediately adds: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1:2–3). Thus, once the Holy Spirit is understood through grace and peace, the mention of the Father and the Son reminds the mind of the Trinity.

And in another place he says: “May grace and peace be multiplied to you in the knowledge of God and of Jesus Christ our Lord” (2 Pet. 1:2).

John, however, omitted such a beginning, for some reason I do not know. But he too plainly did not neglect the mention of the Trinity, inserting fellowship in place of grace and peace:

“What we have seen,” he says, “we announce also to you, so that you too may have fellowship with us, and our fellowship may be with the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ” (1 John 1:3).

In the second Epistle he agrees with the Epistles to Timothy, saying: “May grace, mercy, and peace be with you from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father” (2 John 1:3).

At the beginning of the third Epistle the Trinity is entirely unmentioned, I believe because the Epistle is extremely brief. For it begins:

“The elder to the most beloved Gaius, whom I love in the truth” (3 John 1:1).

I think that “the truth” is put for the Trinity itself.

Jude, having named God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, places three words in order to indicate the Holy Spirit—that is, the gift of God. For he begins as follows:

“Jude, servant of Jesus Christ and brother of James, to those beloved in God the Father and preserved in Jesus Christ and called: may mercy, peace, and love be multiplied to you” (Jude 1:1).

For grace and peace cannot be understood without mercy and love.

James, however, gave his Epistle its most customary opening, writing:

“James, servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes that are in the dispersion: greetings” (James 1:1).

I believe that he considered salvation to exist only in the gift of God [Note: [Col. 2096] The Vatican Manuscript reads: “in the house of God.”], where grace and peace are found.

Although he had already named God and our Lord Jesus Christ before this word, nevertheless, because people are saved by no grace and no peace except that which is from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, it seems to me that just as John placed “truth” for the Trinity in the third Epistle, so James placed “salvation” for the same Trinity.

### 13

At this point I certainly do not think that we should pass over what Father Valerius noticed with amazement in a conversation between certain country people.

When one of them had said to another, “Salus” (“salvation”), he asked someone who knew both Latin and Punic what “salus” meant. The answer was, “Three.” Then, recognizing with joy that our salvation is the Trinity, he thought that the correspondence of the languages had not sounded this way by chance, but through the most hidden arrangement of divine providence: when “salvation” is named in Latin, the Punic word for “three” is understood; and when the Punic people name “three” in their language, “salvation” is understood in Latin.

For the Canaanite woman—that is, the Punic woman—who came out from the region of Tyre and Sidon and who represents the Gentiles in the Gospel, was asking salvation for her daughter. The Lord answered her: “It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

She did not deny the charge; rather, as though she would obtain salvation for her daughter—that is, for her new life—through confessing her sins, she said: “Yes, Lord, for even the dogs eat from the crumbs that fall from the table of their masters” (Matt. 15:22–27).

For in the language of that woman, who was a Canaanite, “three” is called “salvation.” Hence, when our country people are asked what they are and answer in Punic, “Chanani,” with one letter altered, as commonly happens in such matters, what else do they answer than “Canaanites”?

Therefore, in asking for salvation, she was asking for the Trinity. For the Roman language, in which the name for salvation sounds like the Punic word for “three,” was found to be the head of the nations at the Lord’s coming; and we have said that the Canaanite woman represents the Gentiles.

When the Lord calls “bread” the very thing that the woman was asking for, what else does this attest than the Trinity? For elsewhere he most clearly teaches that the same Trinity is to be understood in the three loaves.

But whether this correspondence of words happened by chance or was providentially arranged, one should not contend stubbornly to force everyone to agree with it. It should be accepted only insofar as the interpreter’s elegance is admitted by the hearer’s good humor.

### 14

It plainly appears that we must consider with the greatest attention and embrace with all the strength of devotion the following point: if the Apostle places “grace and peace” in order to complete the mention of the Trinity, as though he had named the Holy Spirit, then the person sins against the Holy Spirit who, despairing of or mocking and despising the preaching of grace by which sins are washed away and of peace by which we are reconciled to God, refuses to repent of his sins, decides that he must persist in a certain impious and deadly pleasure in them, and persists in it to the end.

What the Lord says must therefore not be heard carelessly: that a person will be forgiven if he has spoken a word against the Son of Man, but if he has spoken a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come, and he will be guilty of an eternal sin.

Let us suppose that someone ignorant of the Latin language hears another person pronounce the words “the Holy Spirit” and asks what reality is signified by this sound of syllables. Suppose that some deceitful or impious mocker answers something else—anything cheap and contemptible—in order to deceive the questioner, as such people commonly do for the sake of ridicule. Suppose that the ignorant person, not knowing what the name signifies, despises it and even hurls some abuse at it.

I do not think anyone could be so foolish and thoughtless as to accuse this person of any crime of impiety.

But if, with the name kept silent, the reality itself is conveyed to the questioner’s understanding in whatever words are possible, and he then speaks or acts insultingly against such great holiness, he will be held guilty.

Since this is so, I think it is clear that someone who, upon hearing this name, believes that it signifies one thing rather than another, and speaks against the thing he believes the name signifies, does not sin in such a way that he is judged to have spoken a word against the Holy Spirit.

Likewise, if someone asks what the Holy Spirit is and hears from an ignorant person that he is the Son of God, through whom all things were made, who was also born of a virgin at a definite time, was killed by the Jews, and rose again, and, having heard this, denies or mocks what has been said, he should not be thought to be held guilty as though he had spoken a word against the Holy Spirit. Rather, he has spoken against the Son of God, or against the Son of Man, as he deigned both to be called and to be.

For it is not what was presented to the ignorant person by the sound of the word that must be considered, but what was explained by reasoning. When that person uttered curses, he was cursing the one whom he contemplated in his thought as having been described to him.

Whatever name it might have been called, the question is whether the reality itself should be revered, denied, or condemned.

In the same way, if someone asks who Jesus Christ is, and in answer to his question is told things that apply not to the Son of God but rather to the Holy Spirit, and, having heard them, he blasphemes, he will not be held to have spoken against the Son, but against the Holy Spirit [Col. 2098].

### 15

But if we attend only briefly and carelessly to what was said—“If anyone speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12:32)—who could be found to whom God has granted forgiveness of sins?

For even those called pagans, although they are now prevented from attacking our entire religion with the sword and slaughter, pursue it with curses and insults. Whatever we say about the Trinity itself, they despise by denying and blaspheming it.

They do not make an exception of the Holy Spirit, whom they might revere while raging against the rest. Rather, with as much fury of impiety as they can, they bark against everything we carefully say about the majesty of the triune God [Note: [Col. 2098] The Vatican Manuscript reads: “whatever we say about the Trinity,” omitting “carefully.”].

For they neither hold worthy thoughts about God the Father himself, whom some of them entirely deny, while others confess him in such a way that, by inventing falsehoods about him, they revere not him but their own fabrications.

Much more, therefore, they have preferred, according to their impious custom, to mock what we say about the Son of God or the Holy Spirit rather than worship him in our devout fellowship.

Nevertheless, insofar as we can, we exhort them to know Christ and persuade them that through him they must serve God the Father [Note: [Col. 2098] The Vatican Manuscript reads: “and through him serve God the Father and the highest [God].”], the highest and true Emperor. We invite them to faith by promising forgiveness of all their past sins.

In this matter we judge that even if they have spoken anything against the Holy Spirit in their sacrilegious superstition, it is forgiven without any obscurity of doubt once they have become Christians.

The Jews, however, and the way they behaved against the Holy Spirit, are testified to by Stephen, whom they stoned while he was full of the Holy Spirit, although the Spirit himself had spoken all the things that Stephen said against them.

Among his words it is most plainly said to the Jews: “You always resist the Holy Spirit” (Acts 7:51).

Among those Jews who resisted the Holy Spirit and stoned Stephen, his vessel, for no other reason than that Stephen was full of the Spirit, was also the apostle Paul, in the hands of all those whose garments he guarded.

Later, when he was already filled completely with that same Spirit against whom he had first resisted while utterly empty of him, he rebuked himself in repentance. He was now ready to be stoned for the kinds of words whose preacher he himself had previously stoned.

What of the Samaritans? Do they not oppose the Holy Spirit in such a way that they attempt to extinguish entirely the prophecy administered through the Holy Spirit?

Yet the Lord himself also bears witness to their salvation: in the case of the one of the ten cleansed lepers who alone returned to give thanks, although he was a Samaritan (Luke 17:15–16); and in the case of the woman with whom he spoke at the well at the sixth hour, or of those who believed through her (John 4:7–42).

After the Lord’s ascension, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, with what great joy did Samaria receive the word of God from the saints?

The apostle Peter also rebuked Simon the magician because he had thought so wrongly about the Holy Spirit that, considering the Spirit to be for sale, he asked to purchase him for money. Yet Peter did not despair of him so completely as to leave him no possibility of forgiveness; rather, he kindly urged him to repent (Acts 8:9–22).

Finally, the Catholic Church’s authority is so distinguished that, fruitful throughout the whole world in the same gift of the Holy Spirit and the mother of all the saints, it has never cut off from any heretic or schismatic the hope of liberation if he corrects himself, nor has it closed the way to appeasing God.

Does it not call all of them back with tears to its breasts, which they abandoned in proud disdain?

Who, either among the leaders or among the groups of heretics, is found who does not oppose the Holy Spirit? [Note: [Col. 2099] The printed editions have “who would not be found among the kings of the heretics.” The Vatican Manuscript has “who would not be found among the groups of heretics.”]

Unless perhaps someone thinks so perversely that he supposes a person who has said something against the Holy Spirit is held guilty, but one who has done many things against the Holy Spirit is not held guilty.

Who fight so openly against the Holy Spirit as those who rage against the peace of the Church with the most arrogant disputes?

But if the question concerns words, I ask whether they say nothing against the Holy Spirit when some of them assert that he does not exist at all as something proper to himself, but that there is one God in such a way that the Father himself, the Son himself, and the Holy Spirit himself are called one and the same [Note: [Col. 2099] The Sabellians].

Others indeed confess that the Holy Spirit exists, but deny that he is equal to the Son or that he is God at all [Note: [Col. 2099] The Arians].

Others acknowledge that there is one and the same substance of the Trinity, but hold such an impious view of that divine substance that they consider it changeable and corruptible. They also falsely claim that the Holy Spirit, whom the Lord promised he would send to his disciples, came through a human being not on the fiftieth day after his resurrection, as the Acts of the Apostles attest (Acts 2:1–4), but almost three hundred years later [Note: [Col. 2099] The Manichaeans].

Others likewise deny the coming of the Spirit which we affirm and contend that he chose prophets in Phrygia through whom he would speak so much later [Note: [Col. 2099] The Cataphrygians].

Others mock his sacraments and do not hesitate to baptize again those who have been baptized in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 2099] The Donatists].

But not to proceed through each case, since they are innumerable: when all these people whom I have briefly mentioned as circumstances required return to the bride of Christ and condemn their error and impiety through repentance, no Catholic discipline has judged that the peace of the Church should be denied them or that the bowels of mercy should be closed.

### 16

But if someone thinks that a word is spoken against the Holy Spirit only when it is spoken by someone whose sins have already been forgiven through Baptism, let him observe that even such people are not deprived of the opportunity for repentance through the holiness of the Church.

For if he believes that forgiveness is not granted to such a person because, having already received the grace of faith and the sacraments of the faithful, he cannot be said to have sinned through ignorance, let him see that one reason is involved when it is said that forgiveness is withheld because the sin was not committed in a time of ignorance, and another reason when it is said that forgiveness is withheld because the person spoke a word against the Holy Spirit.

If ignorance alone merits forgiveness, and ignorance is recognized only before someone has been baptized, then not only if he has spoken against the Holy Spirit, but also if after Baptism he has spoken a word against the Son of Man—or if after Baptism he has stained himself with fornication, murder, or any disgraceful or criminal act—he cannot be healed by repentance.

Those who held this view have been excluded from Catholic communion, and it has been judged sufficiently that, in such cruelty, they cannot share in divine mercy.

But if it is thought that only the word spoken against the Holy Spirit is unforgivable after Baptism, then first, when the Lord spoke of this matter, he made no exception concerning time, but said in general: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come.”

Furthermore, Simon, whom I mentioned shortly before, had already received Baptism when he believed that the Holy Spirit had been subjected to the most disgraceful commerce. Yet Peter rebuked him and still gave him the counsel to repent.

What shall we say about those who received the sacrament of Baptism as children or even infants and were later brought up negligently, leading a most shameful life through the darkness of ignorance, knowing nothing at all about what Christian discipline commands or forbids, what it promises or threatens, what must be believed, hoped for, or loved?

Would we dare to attribute their sins to something other than ignorance merely because they sinned after being baptized, when they sinned in complete ignorance and, as the saying goes, did not know at all where their head was? [Note: [Col. 2100] The Vatican Manuscript reads: “not knowing at all where the head was.”]

### 17

But if someone is said to have sinned knowingly at the time when he knows that what he is doing is evil and nevertheless does it, why is this judged unforgivable only when committed against the Holy Spirit, and not also when committed against the Lord Jesus Christ?

Or if this is believed to be what it means to sin or speak a word against the Holy Spirit—namely, to commit any sin knowingly—so that whatever people sin through ignorance is judged to be sin against the Son, while whatever they sin knowingly is judged to be sin against the Holy Spirit, I ask: who does not know that it is evil, for example, to violate another man’s wife’s chastity—or at least knows it from the very fact that he would not wish to endure such a thing with his own wife; or to defraud someone in business; or to deceive by lying; or to oppress by false testimony; or to lie in wait in order to take away another person’s property and kill him; or, in general, to do anything to another which he does not want done to himself and which, if he perceives it being done, he unhesitatingly condemns with his whole heart?

But if we say that such things are done by the ignorant, what can we find in which people appear to sin knowingly?

It follows, then, that if sinning against the Holy Spirit means sinning knowingly, the possibility of repentance must be denied for the sins I have mentioned, since by sinning against the Holy Spirit the Lord removed every hope of forgiveness.

But if Christian teaching rejects this and continually calls all who sin in this way to correction of life, we must still seek to determine what it means to sin against the Holy Spirit—the sin for which no forgiveness is granted.

[Col. 2101] **18.** Or should one not be said to sin knowingly who knows that sin itself is evil, yet sins while ignorant of God and his will? For this seems to be what he says to the Hebrews when he writes: “For if we sin deliberately after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins” (Heb. 10:26). It would have been insufficient if he had said only, “If we sin deliberately,” unless he added, “after receiving the knowledge of the truth,” in which God and his will are certainly known.

This knowledge seems to correspond to that saying of the Lord: “The servant who did not know his master’s will and did things deserving of blows will receive few blows; but the servant who knew his master’s will and did things deserving of blows will receive many blows” (Luke 12:47–48). We might take “he will receive few blows” to mean that, having been lightly corrected, he will attain pardon; whereas in “he will receive many blows” we might understand the eternal punishment threatened to those who sin against the Holy Spirit, to whom he says that sin can never be forgiven. Thus, to sin against the Holy Spirit would mean to sin knowingly against the will of God.

If this is so, we must first consider and examine when the will of God is known. Some people have known it even before receiving the sacrament of Baptism. For the centurion Cornelius certainly learned the will of God through the teaching of the apostle Peter, and, with the clearest signs bearing witness, received the Holy Spirit before he was baptized. Yet he did not therefore despise those sacraments; rather, he was baptized all the more certainly, so that he would not in any way delay receiving those most holy seals themselves, whose reality had preceded in him, for the completion of his knowledge of the truth (Acts 10).

Many, however, do not take care to learn the will of God even after receiving Baptism. Therefore, whoever has sinned after knowing God’s will before Baptism—we cannot say, nor can we in any way believe, that when such a person approaches Baptism, all the sins he has committed are not forgiven.

Furthermore, the will of God is briefly conveyed to believers in the love of God and of neighbor, so that the whole Law and all the Prophets depend upon these two commandments (Matt. 22:37–40). The Lord himself commends love of neighbor to us—that is, love of the human being extending even to love of one’s enemy (Matt. 5:44). Yet we see how many people, already baptized, both acknowledge these things as true and revere them as the Lord’s commandments; but when they have suffered hostility from someone, they are so swept away by the desire for revenge and burn with such fires of hatred that they cannot be appeased even when the Gospel is brought forth and read aloud.

The churches are full of such baptized people. Nevertheless, spiritual men do not cease to admonish them fraternally and diligently instruct them in a spirit of gentleness (Gal. 6:1), so that they may be prepared to meet and resist temptations of this kind, and may prefer to love reigning in the peace of Christ rather than rejoice in the downfall of an enemy. This would be done in vain if no hope of pardon and no remedy of repentance remained for such sins.

And certainly those who hold this view should take care lest they assert that David the patriarch—approved and praised by divine election—was ignorant of the will of God when, struck by love for another man’s wife, he arranged that her husband should be deceived and killed. Yet, after he had been condemned first by his own voice and then by the prophet’s, he was freed through the humility of repentance and confession of his sin. But he certainly “received many blows” (2 Sam. 11–12), and by his example taught that what the Lord said—“The one who knew his master’s will and did things deserving of blows will receive many blows”—refers not to eternal punishment but to more severe discipline.

**19.** For those who examine the passage to the Hebrews more carefully understand it in this way: the statement, “There no longer remains a sacrifice for sins,” should not be taken as referring to the sacrifice of a contrite heart through repentance, but to the sacrifice about which the Apostle was then speaking—namely, the holocaust of the Lord’s passion, which each person offers for his sins at the time when, through faith in that same passion, he is consecrated and instructed by being baptized in the name of Christians. The Apostle therefore meant that someone who has sinned afterward cannot be cleansed by being baptized again.

On this interpretation, the opportunity for repentance is not shut off—provided, of course, that we acknowledge that those who have not yet been baptized have not yet received the full knowledge of the truth. From this it follows that everyone who has received the knowledge of the truth is also understood to have been baptized. But not everyone who has been baptized has also received the knowledge of the truth, because of the later progress or pitiable negligence of some. Nevertheless, the sacrifice of which he was speaking—the holocaust of the Lord, which is offered in a certain sense for each person when that person is marked in baptism—cannot be offered again if he has sinned afterward.

Those who have been baptized once cannot be baptized again, even if after Baptism they have sinned through ignorance of the truth. Thus, since no one is rightly said to have received the knowledge of the truth without Baptism, whoever has received it has no sacrifice for sins remaining—that is, he cannot be baptized again. Yet not everyone who has not received the knowledge of the truth through instruction should therefore suppose that the sacrifice can be offered for him if it has already been offered—that is, if he has already received the sacraments of that same truth through Baptism, he cannot be baptized again.

It is as though we were to say that not every human being is a quadruped; but it does not follow that every animal which is not a human being is also a quadruped. We say that those who have already been baptized are healed better through repentance, not renewed; for renewal takes place in Baptism. Repentance certainly operates there, but as upon a foundation. While the foundation remains, the building can be restored; but if someone wishes to lay the foundation again, the entire building must necessarily be overturned.

For this reason he says to the Hebrews, who seemed to have turned from the New Testament toward the old priesthood: “Therefore, leaving the word of the beginning of Christ, let us press on toward completion, not again laying the foundation of repentance from dead works and faith in God, of the doctrine of washings, the laying on of hands, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment” (Heb. 6:1–2). All these things are handed down in Baptism, and he denies that they are to be repeated—certainly in the consecration of the faithful. In the exposition and teaching of the word of God, however, they must be stated not merely once but often, as the circumstances of the matters under discussion require.

**20.** Or will this objection now arise: that one is not judged to be without pardon merely because he knowingly commits any sin, but only if he knowingly commits specifically the sin against the Holy Spirit? At this point it may be asked whether the Jews knew that the Lord acted through the Holy Spirit when they blasphemously said that he cast out demons by the prince of demons (Matt. 9:34).

I wonder, however, how they could recognize the Holy Spirit in him when they did not know that the Lord himself was the Son of God—amid that blindness which has occurred in part to Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter (Rom. 11:25). With the Lord’s help and permission, this will be treated more suitably in its proper place.

Next, if “the discernment of spirits” is understood to mean the discernment by which someone determines whether the Holy Spirit or a deceptive spirit is at work in a person, and if this discernment is given to the faithful by the Holy Spirit at a particular time, as the same Apostle says elsewhere (1 Cor. 12:10), how could the unbelieving Jews, without this gift, discern whether the Lord was acting through the Holy Spirit?

Yet in them, so that they might be struck by a just punishment, the clearest signs of evil intent became evident: when they procured false witnesses against him (Matt. 26:59–60); when they sent men pretending to be sincere in order to trap him in his words (ibid. 22:15–17); and when, after the terrible wonders that occurred at his resurrection had been reported to them, they tried, by bribing the guards, to spread a false report and conceal the truth (ibid. 28:13). Other signs of a malicious and poisonous spirit also appeared in them, as far as the Gospel narrative makes clear.

**21.** Hence it now begins to become apparent that the person sins against the Holy Spirit who, with an evil disposition, opposes the works performed through the Holy Spirit. Although he may not know whether that Spirit is the Holy Spirit, nevertheless, if he is disposed to prefer that the works at which he is envious should not be the works of the Holy Spirit—not because they are evil, but because he envies them, and because through his malice he is opposed to goodness itself—he is rightly judged to sin against the Holy Spirit.

Yet if someone from that very group of people against whom the Lord brought this charge should come to faith in Christ, subdue his envy through the torments of repentance, and seek salvation with tears—as some of them may in fact have done—I ask whether anyone could become so hardened in error as to deny that such people ought to have been admitted to Christ’s Baptism, or to maintain that they were admitted in vain.

For if someone, through envy, blasphemes the works of God because by his malice he resists the good things of God—that is, the gifts of God—and is therefore to be considered to sin against the Holy Spirit and to have no hope of pardon, let us consider whether the apostle Paul belonged to that number. He says: “Although I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and an insolent man, I received mercy because I acted ignorantly in unbelief” (1 Tim. 1:13).

Or perhaps he did not belong to this class of crime because he was not envious? Let us hear what he says elsewhere: “For we too were once foolish and unbelieving, wandering astray, serving various pleasures and desires, living in malice and envy, hateful and hating one another” (Titus 3:3).

**22.** If, then, access to Christ’s Baptism is not closed to pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics who have not yet been baptized, when they condemn their former life and change it for the better—even though before being washed in the Christian sacraments they resisted Christianity and the Church of God, and also resisted the Holy Spirit with all the hostility they could muster; and if even those who, up to the reception of the sacraments, had received the knowledge of the truth, but afterward fell and resisted the Holy Spirit, are not denied the help of mercy when they return to health and seek the peace of God through repentance; and finally, if even some of those against whom the Lord brought the charge of blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, when they came to their senses and fled to the grace of God, were without doubt healed—what remains except to understand that the sin against the Holy Spirit, which the Lord says is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come, is nothing other than perseverance in wickedness and malice together with despair of God’s pardon?

For this is to resist that grace and peace from which our present discussion arose. From this it may also be understood that even for those Jews whose blasphemy the Lord rebuked, the opportunity for correction and repentance had not been closed. In that very rebuke the Lord said to them: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad” (Matt. 12:31–33). He would certainly not have said this to them in any way if, because of that blasphemy, they could no longer change their minds for the better and produce the fruits of right conduct, or if they would produce them in vain without receiving the forgiveness of their sin.

**23.** Therefore, because the Lord was casting out demons by the Spirit of God and healing the other diseases and infirmities of human bodies, he did this for no other reason than that people might believe him when he said: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (ibid. 3:2). Sins are forgiven invisibly; he prepared faith in that forgiveness through visible miracles, as is demonstrated most clearly in the case of the paralytic.

When he had first offered him the visible gift for which he had come—for the Son of Man had not come then to judge the world but to save the world (John 3:17)—and had therefore said, “Your sins are forgiven,” the Jews murmured indignantly because he seemed to be arrogating such authority to himself. He said: “Which is easier, to say, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Rise and walk’? But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins”—then he said to the paralytic—“I say to you, rise, take up your bed, and go to your house” (Mark 2:3–11).

By this act and by these words he sufficiently showed that he did such things in bodies so that people might believe that he freed the souls of sinners through the forgiveness of sins—that is, so that visible power might earn faith in invisible power.

Because he did all these things through the Spirit of God in order to bestow grace and peace upon human beings—grace in the remission of sins, peace in reconciliation with God [Note: [Col. 2105] See *Retractions*, book 1, chapter 25], from whom sins alone separate—when the Jews said that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, he mercifully wished to warn them not to speak a word or blasphemy against the Holy Spirit (Matt. 12:22–33). That is, he warned them not to resist the grace and peace which he had come to grant through the Holy Spirit.

He did not mean that they had already committed the sin that would not be forgiven them either in this age or in the age to come; rather, he warned them lest, by despairing of pardon, or presuming upon their own righteousness and therefore failing to repent, or persevering in their sins, they should commit it. In this way they would “speak a word,” that is, blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, through whom the Lord performed those signs in order to bestow grace and peace, if by persevering in their sins they resisted grace and peace themselves.

“To speak a word” does not seem to be used here so that only what we form with the tongue is meant, but rather what is conceived in the heart and also expressed in action. For just as those who confess God only with the sound of their mouths, and not also through good works, do not confess God—for it is said of them, “They profess to know God, but by their deeds they deny him” (Titus 1:16)—so it is clear that something is said by deeds, just as it is clear that something is denied by deeds.

Likewise, when the Apostle says, “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3), this cannot rightly be understood unless “to say” is understood in terms of deeds. For we must not suppose that those are saying this in the Holy Spirit to whom the Lord himself says: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46), and, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7:21).

Thus, whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit the word which the Lord intends to be understood as unforgivable—that is, whoever, despairing of the grace and peace he grants, says that he must persevere in his sins—must be understood to speak it by his deeds. Just as those people deny the Lord by their deeds, so these people say by their deeds that they will persevere in their evil life and ruined morals, and so they act—that is, they persevere.

If they do this, who would be surprised, or who would fail to understand, that the Lord Jesus Christ, through that warning, called the Jews to repentance so that he might grant grace and peace to those who believed in him; but that to those who resisted this grace and peace, and in this way spoke a word and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit—that is, to those who persevered in their sins through a despairing and impious obstinacy of mind and acted proudly against God without humble confession and repentance—pardon can be granted neither in this age nor in the age to come?

If these things are so, then, on the occasion of treating the grace and peace that we have from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ, a great and very difficult question has been resolved by that same Lord’s generosity. Whoever still desires more careful consideration and treatment of so important a matter should know that he must seek it in an exposition of the Gospel and in the words of the Evangelists. Let him remember that we have now undertaken to treat the Epistle of the apostle Paul to the Romans; and, if the Lord wills, we shall pursue the continuing text of that Epistle in other volumes, so that this may at last be the conclusion of the present work.

(C)

## PREFACE

**1.** The reason why the Apostle writes to the Galatians is that they may understand that the grace of God brings about this: they are no longer under the Law.

For when the grace of the Gospel had been preached to them, certain people from the circumcision appeared. Although they bore the name of Christians, they did not yet hold to the actual benefit of grace, and still wished to remain under the burdens of the Law that the Lord God had imposed—not upon those serving righteousness, but upon those enslaved to sin. He gave a just Law to unjust people in order to demonstrate their sins, not to remove them. For sins are removed only by the grace of faith that works through love.

Thus, although the Galatians had already been established under this grace, those people wished to place them under the burdens of the Law, asserting that the Gospel profited them nothing unless they were circumcised and undertook the other bodily observances of the Jewish rite. For this reason they began to regard the apostle Paul with suspicion, since he had preached the Gospel to them, as though he did not hold to the discipline of the other Apostles, who were compelling the Gentiles to Judaize.

The apostle Peter had yielded to the scandals caused by such people and had been led into dissimulation, as though he too thought that the Gospel profited the Gentiles nothing unless they fulfilled the burdens of the Law. The apostle Paul recalls him from this dissimulation, as he teaches in this very Epistle (Gal. 2:14).

A similar question is also found in the Epistle to the Romans. Nevertheless, there seems to be some difference: there he resolves and settles the very dispute that had arisen between those who had believed from the Jews and those who had believed from the Gentiles. The former thought that the reward of the Gospel had been paid to them on account of the merits of the works of the Law, and did not want this reward given to the uncircumcised as though they were undeserving; the latter, in turn, were eager to place themselves above the Jews, as though above the killers of the Lord.

In this Epistle, however, he writes to those who had already been disturbed by the authority of people from the Jews who were compelling them to observe the Law. They had begun to believe those people, as though the apostle Paul had not preached the truth because he had refused to circumcise them.

Thus he began: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring from him who called you into the glory of Christ to another Gospel.” In this opening he briefly indicated the question at issue.

Moreover, even in the greeting itself, when he says that he is an apostle “not from men nor through a man” (Gal. 1:6, 1), something found in no other Epistle, he sufficiently shows both that those who were offering such persuasion were not from God but from men, and that he should not be regarded as inferior to the other Apostles insofar as the authority of evangelical testimony is concerned. For he knows that he is an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.

Accordingly, beginning at the very entrance of the Epistle, we have undertaken, with the Lord’s permission and the help of his support for our study, to consider and discuss each point in this way.

**2. [Gal. 1:1–2.]** “Paul, an apostle not from men nor through a man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead; and all the brothers who are with me, to the churches of Galatia.”

He who is sent by men is a liar; he who is sent through a man may be truthful, because the truthful God can also send through a man. Therefore, whoever is sent neither from men nor through a man, but through God, is truthful because of the one who sends him; and God also makes truthful those who are sent through a man.

The earlier Apostles, then, are truthful: they were sent not from men but by God through a man, namely, through Jesus Christ while he was still mortal. The last Apostle is also truthful: he was sent through Jesus Christ, who after his resurrection was already wholly God [Note: [Col. 2107] *Retractions*, chapter 24, no. 1].

The other Apostles are earlier, through Christ who was still partly human—that is, mortal. The last is the apostle Paul, through Christ who was already wholly God—that is, immortal in every respect. Let the authority of his testimony therefore be equal; in his honor the Lord’s glorification makes up for whatever the order of time seemed to lack.

For this reason, after saying “and God the Father,” he added, “who raised him from the dead,” so that he might briefly indicate from this also that he had been sent by the glorified Christ.

**3. [Gal. 1:3–5.]** “Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The grace of God is that by which our sins are forgiven so that we may be reconciled to God; peace is that by which we are reconciled to God.

“Who gave himself for our sins, so that he might rescue us from the present evil age.” The present age is to be understood as evil because of the evil people who are in it, just as we call a house evil because of the evil inhabitants within it.

“According to the will of God and our Father, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

How much less, then, should human beings arrogantly attribute to themselves whatever good they do, when even the Son of God himself said in the Gospel that he did not seek his own glory (John 8:50), and that he had not come to do his own will but the will of the one who sent him (ibid. 6:38)?
