The Apostle now recalled that will and glory of the Father so that he too, following the example of the Lord by whom he was sent, might indicate that he did not seek his own glory or do his own will in preaching the Gospel, as he says shortly afterward: “If I were pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ” (Gal. 1:10).

**4. [Gal. 1:6–9.]** “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring from him who called you into the glory of Christ to another Gospel, which is not another.”

For if the Gospel is another Gospel besides that which the Lord gave either directly or through someone else, it can no longer rightly be called the Gospel.

He carefully said, “You are transferring from him who called you,” and added, “into the glory of Christ,” which those people wished to nullify, as though Christ had come in vain if circumcision of the flesh and similar works of the Law had such value that human beings could be saved through them.

“Except that there are some who are disturbing you and want to turn the Gospel of Christ into another form.” They do not turn the Gospel of Christ in the same way as they disturb these people, because the Gospel remains entirely firm. Nevertheless, they want to turn it because they divert the attention of believers from spiritual things back to bodily ones. When the believers turn toward these things, the Gospel remains unturned. Therefore, after saying “disturbing you,” he did not say “and turning it,” but “wanting,” he says, “to turn the Gospel of Christ.”

“But even if we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you a gospel contrary to what we preached to you, let him be accursed.” Truth is to be loved for its own sake, not on account of the human being or angel through whom it is announced. For whoever loves it on account of its announcers may also love lies, if those announcers should happen to put forward some of their own.

“As we have said before, and now I say again: if anyone preaches to you a gospel contrary to what you received, let him be accursed.” Either he had said this earlier in the present Epistle, or, because he repeated what he had said, he wished to say, “As we have said before.” In any case, the repetition very beneficially stirs the mind toward firmly retaining the faith that is commended in this way.

**5. [Gal. 1:10.]** “Am I now persuading human beings, or God? Or am I seeking to please human beings? If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

No one persuades God, because everything is manifest to him. But a person persuades human beings well when he does not wish to please them personally, but wishes to please the truth itself that he recommends.

Whoever pleases human beings without seeking his own glory from them, but seeking God’s glory so that they may be saved, no longer pleases human beings but God. Or, certainly, when he pleases both God and human beings, he does not please human beings in the same sense. For it is one thing to please human beings, and another to please both God and human beings.

Likewise, when someone pleases human beings because of the truth, it is no longer the person himself who pleases them, but the truth.

He said, “I would please,” insofar as it depended upon himself and concerned his will—as though he were saying, “I would wish to please.” For if someone pleases another without his own action, as though for his own sake rather than for the sake of God and the Gospel he preaches, this should be attributed to the pride of the person who is pleased in a perverse way, not to his error.

The sense, then, is this: “Am I now persuading human beings, or God? Or, because I persuade human beings, am I seeking to please human beings? If I were still seeking to please human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

For he commands his servants to learn from him to be gentle and humble in heart (Matt. 11:29). No one can do this if he seeks to please human beings for his own sake—that is, for the sake of his own supposedly private and personal glory.

He says elsewhere as well: “We persuade human beings, but we are manifest to God” (2 Cor. 5:11), so that you may understand that when he says here, “Am I persuading human beings, or God?” it is human beings, not God, who are to be persuaded.

Therefore, let it not disturb us that he says elsewhere: “Just as I also please everyone in everything.” For he added: “Not seeking what benefits me, but what benefits many, so that they may be saved” (1 Cor. 10:33).

But it benefits no one to be saved if a human being pleases that person for his own sake. He pleases beneficially only when he pleases for the sake of God—that is, so that God may please and be glorified when his gifts are recognized in a human being or received through the ministry of a human being. When a human being pleases in this way, it is no longer the human being but God who pleases.

Both statements, then, can rightly be made: “I please” and “I do not please.” If there is a good interpreter and a devout knocker, both will become clear, and no contradiction between them will repel the one seeking entrance.

**6. [Gal. 1:11–12.]** “For I make known to you, brothers, the Gospel that was preached by me: it is not according to man. For I neither received it from a human being nor learned it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ.”

A Gospel that is according to man is a lie. For “every human being is a liar” (Ps. 115:11), because whatever truth is found in a human being comes not from the human being but from God through the human being.

Therefore, what is according to man should no longer be called the Gospel. Such was the Gospel brought by those who were drawing into slavery from freedom people whom God was calling from slavery into freedom.

**7. [Gal. 1:13–14.]** “For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism: how beyond measure I persecuted the Church of God and devastated it; and I advanced in Judaism beyond many of my contemporaries among my own people, being more abundantly zealous for my ancestral traditions.”

If Paul advanced in Judaism by persecuting and devastating the Church of God, it is evident that Judaism is opposed to the Church of God—not that spiritual Law which the Jews received, but their carnal manner of life in slavery.

And if Paul persecuted the Church of God as a zealot—that is, an imitator—of his ancestral traditions, then his ancestral traditions are opposed to the Church of God. The fault, however, does not belong to that Law, for “the Law is spiritual” (Rom. 7:14), nor does it compel itself to be understood carnally. Rather, the fault belongs to those who interpret carnally both the things they received and the many things they themselves handed down, “setting aside the commandment of God for the sake of their traditions,” as the Lord says (Matt. 15:3).

**8. [Gal. 1:15–19.]** “But when it pleased God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace, to reveal his Son in me so that I might proclaim him among the Gentiles, immediately I did not yield to flesh and blood.”

Someone is, in a certain sense, set apart from his mother’s womb whenever he is separated from the blind custom of carnal parents. Whoever assents to the carnal persuasion of his carnal relatives and blood relations, however, yields to flesh and blood.

“And I did not go up to Jerusalem to those who were Apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and again I returned to Damascus. Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to visit Peter, and I remained with him fifteen days.”

If Paul preached the Gospel in Arabia and afterward saw Peter, he did not do so in order to learn the Gospel through Peter; for he would certainly have seen him before preaching it. Rather, he did so in order to strengthen brotherly love through bodily acquaintance as well.

“But I saw none of the other Apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.” James, the Lord’s brother, is to be understood either as one of Joseph’s sons by another wife, or as a relative of Mary, his mother.

**9. [Gal. 1:20–24.]** “Now concerning what I am writing to you, behold, before God, I am not lying.”

Whoever says, “Behold, before God, I am not lying,” certainly swears an oath. And what oath is holier than this? Yet an oath that arises from evil is not contrary to the commandment—not from the evil of the one who swears, but from the unbelief of the person whom he is compelled to convince by swearing.

From this it is understood that the Lord prohibited swearing in such a way that, insofar as it depends upon each person, no one should swear. Many people do this while having an oath constantly on their lips, as though it were something great or pleasant.

The Apostle certainly knew the Lord’s commandment, and yet he swore. We must not listen to those who deny that such expressions are oaths. For what will they do with the statement, “I die daily, by your glory, brothers, which I have in Christ Jesus our Lord” (1 Cor. 15:31)? The Greek manuscripts show most clearly that this is an oath [Note: [Col. 2110] See *On the Sermon on the Mount*, book 1, chapter 17, no. 51].

Thus, insofar as it depends upon him, the Apostle does not swear; he does not seek an oath out of desire or pleasure in swearing. An oath is more than “Yes, yes; No, no,” and therefore “comes from evil” (Matt. 5:37), namely, from the weakness or unbelief of those who are not moved to faith in any other way.

“Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia. I was personally unknown to the churches of Judaea that are in Christ.” It should be observed that Jews did not believe in Christ only in Jerusalem, nor were they so few that they were mixed into the churches of the Gentiles; rather, they were so numerous that churches were formed from them.

“They were only hearing: ‘The one who once persecuted us now preaches the faith that he once tried to destroy’; and they glorified God in me.” This is what he meant when he said that he did not please human beings for his own sake, but so that God might be glorified in him. This is also what the Lord says: “Let your works shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

**10. [Gal. 2:1–2.]** “Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus also.”

He acts as though he were presenting multiple witnesses when he names these men as well.

“I went up according to a revelation,” so that they would not be disturbed about why he had gone up at that time, after not having gone up for so long. Therefore, since he went up in accordance with a revelation, it was then beneficial for him to go up.

“And I set before them the Gospel that I preach among the Gentiles, but privately before those who seemed [to be something].”

[Note: [Col. 2111] The Louvain editors, on the authority of the Amandus manuscript, restore: “before those who seemed to be something” (*his qui videbantur esse aliquid*). In the other books, however, *esse aliquid* is absent; the Vulgate also lacks it in the ancient Corbie Bibles. There it reads *his qui videbantur*, and likewise three manuscripts here; eight others, as well as the Amiatine and Erasmian manuscripts, read *his qui videntur*. In Greek the reading is τοῖς δοκοῦσι (*toîs dokoûsi*), that is, “to those who are prominent in the Church,” as Augustine interprets it.]

That he set the Gospel privately before those who were prominent in the Church, after he had already set it before everyone, does not mean that he had said anything false and therefore told the truth privately to a smaller group. Rather, he had omitted certain things that the still immature were unable to bear, just as he says that he gave the Corinthians milk, not solid food (1 Cor. 3:2).

It is never permissible to speak falsely; but sometimes it is useful to withhold something true. The other Apostles needed to know the fullness of his teaching. For it did not follow that, if someone was faithful and held the true and correct faith, he therefore had already to be an apostle.

The statement he adds—“lest I should be running, or should have run, in vain”—is to be understood not as spoken to those with whom he discussed the Gospel privately, but to those to whom he is writing, as though by way of a question. From this it would appear that he was not running, nor had he run, in vain, because, now with the testimony of the other Apostles as well, he was shown to dissent in nothing from the truth of the Gospel.

### 11. [Book II, 3–5]

“But not even Titus, who was with me,” he says, “although he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.” Although Titus was a Greek, and no custom or family connection required his circumcision, as it did Timothy’s, the Apostle would nevertheless readily have allowed him to be circumcised as well. For he was not teaching that salvation was taken away through such circumcision; rather, he was showing that, if hope of salvation were placed in it, this was contrary to salvation. He could therefore tolerate it calmly as something superfluous, in accordance with what he said elsewhere: “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments” (1 Cor. 7:19).

But Titus was not compelled to be circumcised on account of the false brothers who had slipped in; that is, they could not force him to be circumcised. He says that those who had slipped in were scrutinizing their liberty very closely, and wanted Titus to be circumcised so that they might proclaim circumcision as necessary for salvation, now with the testimony and agreement even of Paul himself, and thus, as he says, bring them into slavery—that is, recall them under the burdensome obligations of the Law. He says that he did not yield to their subjection even for an hour—that is, not even for a time—in order that the truth of the Gospel might remain among the Gentiles.

### 12. [Book II, 6–9]

They were also casting suspicion upon the Apostle Paul and wanted him to be regarded with distrust, because he had once been a persecutor of the churches. Therefore he says: “But from those who seem to be something”—whatever they once were—“it makes no difference to me.” For those who seem to be something seem to be something to carnal people; in reality they are not themselves anything. Even if they are good ministers of God, Christ is something in them, not they themselves in their own right. For if they were something in their own right, they would always have been something.

“Whatever they once were”—that is, since they too had been sinners—he says makes no difference to him, because God does not accept a person’s status; that is, without respect of persons he called everyone to salvation, not counting their offenses against them. And therefore, while those who had first become apostles were absent, Paul was perfected by the Lord, so that when he conferred with them there was nothing they could add to his perfection. Rather, they saw that the same Lord Jesus Christ, who saves without respect of persons, had given Paul to minister to the Gentiles what he had also given Peter to minister to the Jews.

They were therefore not found to disagree with him in anything, so that, when he said that he had received the perfect Gospel, they would deny this and wish to add something to him as though he were imperfect. On the contrary, instead of being reprovers of his imperfection, they were approvers of his perfection. And they “gave the right hands of fellowship”—that is, they agreed to fellowship and obeyed the Lord’s will, consenting that Paul and Barnabas should go to the Gentiles, while they themselves went to the circumcision, which seems to be opposed to uncircumcision, that is, to the Gentiles.

For what he says, “On the contrary,” may also be understood in this way, with the order being: “For those who seemed to be something added nothing to me” [Note: [Col. 2112] Am. and Er., together with ten manuscripts, read: “For those who seem to be something added nothing to me”; they do not have “something.”], “but, on the contrary, they agreed that we should go to the Gentiles, who are opposed to circumcision, while they themselves should go to the circumcision; they agreed with me and Barnabas—that is, they gave us the right hands of fellowship.”

### 13

Nor should anyone think that he said “those who seem to be something, whatever they once were, makes no difference to me” as an insult to his predecessors. They too, as spiritual men, wanted to resist those carnal people who thought that the apostles themselves were something, rather than Christ in them. They rejoiced greatly when people were persuaded that they themselves, Paul’s predecessors, like Paul himself, had been justified by the Lord from among sinners, since God does not accept a person’s status. For they sought God’s glory, not their own.

But because carnal and proud people become angry and take as an insult anything said about their former life, they judge the Apostles according to their own disposition. Peter, James, and John, however, were more honored among the Apostles, because the Lord revealed himself to those three on the mountain as a sign of his kingdom, after saying six days earlier: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Matt. 16:28).

Yet even they were not pillars; they only seemed to be. For Paul knew that Wisdom had built herself a house, not establishing three pillars but seven (Prov. 9:1). This number either refers to the unity of the churches—for it is commonly used to signify the whole, as in the Gospel where it is said, “He will receive seven times as much in this age” [Note: [Col. 2113] Perhaps the Greek had *heptaplasiona* (“sevenfold”).] (Matt. 19:29), as though he were saying, “As having nothing, yet possessing everything” (2 Cor. 6:10). Hence John also writes to seven churches (Rev. 1:4), which certainly represent the universal Church [Note: [Col. 2113] Am. and Er., with ten manuscripts agreeing: “which certainly represent the Church as a whole.”].

Or, more probably, the number seven of the pillars refers to the sevenfold operation of the Holy Spirit: wisdom and understanding, counsel and strength, knowledge and piety, and fear of God (Isa. 11:2–3). By these operations the house of the Son of God—that is, the Church—is upheld.

### 14. [Book II, 10]

As for what he says, “Only that we should remember the poor, which very thing I was eager to do,” this was a common concern of all the Apostles: the poor among the saints who were in Judaea, who had placed the prices of their sold possessions at the Apostles’ feet (Acts 4:35).

Thus Paul and Barnabas were sent to the Gentiles so that the churches of the Gentiles, which had not done this, might, at their exhortation, minister to those who had done it. As he says to the Romans:

> “But now I am going to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have been pleased to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem. They have been pleased to do so, and they are their debtors. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Rom. 15:25–27).

### 15. [Book II, 11–16]

Paul had therefore fallen into no pretense, because everywhere he preserved what he saw to be appropriate, whether for the churches of the Gentiles or for those of the Jews. He did not abolish any custom whose observance did not hinder the attainment of the kingdom of God, while warning that no one should place hope of salvation in superfluous things, even if he wished to preserve such customs on account of the offense of the weak.

As he says to the Corinthians:

> “Was anyone called while circumcised? Let him not seek uncircumcision. Was anyone called while uncircumcised? Let him not be circumcised. Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but the keeping of God’s commandments. Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called” (1 Cor. 7:18–20).

He referred this to those customs or conditions of life that do no harm to faith and good morals. For if someone was a robber when he was called, he ought not to remain in robbery.

When Peter came to Antioch, Paul rebuked him—not because he preserved the custom of the Jews in which he had been born and brought up, although he did not observe it among the Gentiles—but because he wanted to impose it upon the Gentiles when he saw that certain people had come from James, that is, from Judaea; for James presided over the church at Jerusalem.

Therefore, fearing those who still thought that salvation consisted in these observances, Peter separated himself from the Gentiles and hypocritically agreed with them in imposing upon the Gentiles those burdens of slavery. This is sufficiently clear from the words of the rebuke itself. For Paul does not say, “If you, although you are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you return again to the Jewish custom?” Rather, he says, “How do you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?”

That he said this to him publicly was required so that all might be healed by the rebuke. It was not useful to correct in secret an error that was openly harmful.

Moreover, Peter’s firmness and charity—he to whom the Lord had three times said, “Do you love me? Feed my sheep” (John 21:15)—most willingly endured such a rebuke from a later shepherd for the sake of the flock’s salvation. For the man who was rebuked was himself more admirable than his rebuker and more difficult to imitate.

It is easier to see what must be corrected in another and to correct it by criticizing or rebuking him than to see what must be corrected in oneself and willingly accept correction—especially from another, and especially from one who is later, and especially in the presence of everyone.

This provides a great example of humility, which is the supreme discipline of Christianity. Charity is preserved through humility, for nothing violates it more quickly than pride. Therefore the Lord did not say, “Take my yoke and learn from me, because I raise four-day corpses from the tombs, drive all demons and diseases from human bodies, and perform other things of this kind.” Rather, he said: “Take my yoke and learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11:29).

Those other signs signify spiritual realities; but to be gentle and humble, the preserver of charity, is itself a spiritual reality [Note: [Col. 2114] The manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “the preservation of charity is itself”; then, “the realities themselves,” and so forth.]. Through those signs people are led to these realities—people devoted to the bodily senses, who, because they can no longer seek faith in familiar and customary things, seek it in new and sudden visible events.

If those who compelled the Gentiles to Judaize had learned to be gentle and humble in heart, as Peter had learned from the Lord, then, at least when such a great man was corrected, they would have been moved to imitate him. They would not have thought that the Gospel had been given to them as a due payment for their own righteousness. Rather, knowing that a person is not justified by works of the Law except through faith in Christ Jesus—so that, with his weakness helped, he might fulfill the works of the Law, not by his own merit but by God’s grace—they would not have demanded from the Gentiles the carnal observances of the Law. Instead, through that same grace of faith, they would have understood that the Gentiles could fulfill the spiritual works of the Law.

For when someone attributes the works of the Law to his own strength rather than to the grace of the merciful God, “no flesh”—that is, no human being, or all who think carnally—“will be justified” by those works.

Therefore those who were already under the Law and believed in Christ came to the grace of faith not because they were righteous, but in order to be justified.

[Col. 2115]

### 16. [Book II, 15–18]

The Jews had imposed the name “sinners” upon the Gentiles, through a certain ancient pride, as though they themselves were righteous, seeing the speck in another’s eye and not the beam in their own.

The Apostle spoke according to their manner of expression when he said, “We are Jews by nature, and not sinners from the Gentiles.” That is: We are Jews by nature, although we were not Gentiles, whom they call sinners even though they themselves are sinners. “Yet we,” he says, “although Jews by nature, believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ.”

They would not have sought justification unless they were sinners. Or did they sin because they wanted to be justified in Christ? For if they were already righteous, then certainly they sinned by seeking something else. “But if this is so,” he says, “then Christ is a minister of sin.”

They certainly cannot say this, because even those who wanted the Gospel to be given only to circumcised Gentiles had believed in Christ. Therefore, when he says, “Certainly not,” he says it not alone but together with them.

He destroyed the pride that gloried in the works of the Law, a pride that both ought to be and could be destroyed, lest the grace of faith seem unnecessary if the works of the Law were believed capable of justifying even without it.

Therefore he is a transgressor if he rebuilds those things again, saying that the works of the Law justify even without grace, so that Christ is found to be a minister of sin.

Someone might therefore object to him when he says, “If I rebuild the very things I destroyed, I establish myself as a transgressor”: “What then? Since you formerly opposed the faith of Christ, which you now build up, do you establish yourself as a transgressor?”

But he did not destroy that faith, because it cannot be destroyed. He had truly destroyed, and steadfastly continued to destroy, that pride, because it could be destroyed.

Therefore the transgressor is not the person who, after attempting to destroy something true and later recognizing it as true and indestructible, preserves it in order to build upon it. The transgressor is the person who, after destroying something false because it can be destroyed, builds it up again.

### 17. [Book II, 19–21]

He says that he died to the Law so that he might no longer be under the Law, yet through the Law. This is either because he was a Jew and had received the Law as a pedagogue, as he later makes clear (Gal. 3:24), or because, through the Law understood spiritually, he died to the Law so that he would not live under it carnally.

For this is the way in which he wanted them to die to the Law through the Law when he said to them shortly afterward: “Tell me, you who desire to be under the Law, have you not read the Law? For it is written that Abraham had two sons” (Gal. 4:21–22), and so forth. Thus, by understanding the same Law spiritually, they were to die to the carnal observances of the Law.

When he adds, “so that I might live for God,” the person who is under God lives for God, while the person who is under the Law lives for the Law. A person lives under the Law to the extent that he is a sinner—that is, to the extent that he has not been changed from the old man. For he lives his own life, and therefore the Law is above him; whoever does not fulfill it is beneath it.

For the Law is not imposed upon the righteous (1 Tim. 1:9)—that is, it is not placed above them. Rather, he is in the Law instead of under the Law, because he does not live his own life, upon which the Law must be imposed for its restraint.

To put it this way, the person who lives justly with love of righteousness, rejoicing not in a private and passing good but in a common and lasting good, lives in a certain sense by the Law itself [Note: [Col. 2116] Several manuscripts read this way. The printed editions have: “he lives the Law itself in a certain sense.”].

Therefore the Law did not need to be imposed upon Paul, who says, “But now it is no longer I who live; rather, Christ lives in me.” Who, then, would dare impose the Law upon Christ, who lives in Paul? No one dares say that Christ does not live rightly, so that the Law must be imposed upon him for his correction.

“But what I now live,” he says, “in the flesh”—for he could not say that Christ still lives mortally, while life in the flesh is mortal—“I live in faith in the Son of God.” Thus Christ also lives in the believer, dwelling through faith in the inner person (Eph. 3:16–17), so that afterward he may perfect him through vision, when what is mortal has been swallowed up by life (2 Cor. 5:4).

To show that Christ lives in him, and that, while living in the flesh, he lives in faith in the Son of God, he makes clear that this is not his own merit but Christ’s grace: “who loved me,” he says, “and gave himself for me.”

For whom did he give himself, if not for a sinner, in order to justify him? And this is said by one who had been born and brought up as a Jew and had been more abundantly zealous for his ancestral traditions. Therefore, if Christ gave himself even for such people, they too were sinners.

Let them not say, then, that what need not be given to the righteous was given on account of their merits of righteousness. For the Lord says, “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. 9:13)—that is, so that they may no longer be sinners.

“If Christ loved me and gave himself for me, I do not nullify the grace of God by saying that righteousness comes through the Law. For if righteousness comes through the Law, then Christ died for nothing”—that is, he died without cause, since righteousness could exist in human beings through the Law, that is, through the works of the Law in which the Jews trusted.

Yet even those whom he refutes do not say that Christ died for nothing, since they wanted to be regarded as Christians. They were therefore wrong to persuade people that Christians are justified by those works of the Law.

### 18. [Book III, 1]

To them he rightly says, “O foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you?” This would not rightly be said of people who had never made progress, but of people who had fallen away after making progress.

“Before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified.” That is, before the eyes of those people Jesus Christ lost his inheritance and possession—lost it through those very people who expelled the Lord from it. They were turning those who had believed, through the grace of faith by which Christ possesses the Gentiles, back to the works of the Law, thereby taking away his possession: namely, those in whom he had dwelt by right of grace and faith.

The Apostle wants this to be understood as having happened in the Galatians themselves. This is the force of his saying, “before whose eyes.” For what occurred as visibly before their eyes as what occurred in themselves?

After saying, “Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed,” he added, “crucified,” in order to move them especially when they considered at what price he had purchased the possession that he was losing in them. It was not enough that he had died for nothing, as he had said above. For that earlier statement sounds as though he had never obtained the possession for which he gave his blood.

But from one who has been proscribed, even what he held is taken away. This forfeiture does not harm Christ, who is still Lord of all through his divinity; it harms the possession itself, which lacks the cultivation of this grace.

### 19

From this point he begins to demonstrate how the grace of faith is sufficient for justification without the works of the Law, lest someone say that he does not attribute the whole of human justification solely to the works of the Law, but also does not attribute it solely to the grace of faith, claiming instead that salvation is completed from both.

But for this question to be treated carefully, so that no one is misled by ambiguity, he must first know that the works of the Law are of two kinds. Some belong to rites, others to morals.

To the rites belong circumcision of the flesh, the temporal Sabbath, new moons, sacrifices, and all the innumerable observances of this kind. To morals belong: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not bear false witness” (Exod. 20:13–16), and other commandments of the same kind.

Can the Apostle therefore be so indifferent to whether a Christian is a murderer or adulterer, or chaste and innocent, as he is indifferent to whether he is circumcised in the flesh or uncircumcised?

He is now treating chiefly the works that belong to rites, although he indicates that he sometimes introduces those other works as well. Near the end of the Epistle, however, he will treat separately the works that belong to morals: the former briefly, the latter at greater length.

These rites are rather burdens that he forbids being imposed upon the Gentiles—or perhaps, according to the uncertain reading, that he “rather explains” [Note: [Col. 2117] Perhaps: “he forbids them to be imposed,” or “rather explains them.”]. Their usefulness lies in their interpretation. For all these things are explained to Christians so that they may understand what they signify, not so that they may be compelled to perform them.

In observances, if they are not understood, there is only slavery, such as existed among the Jewish people and continues to exist even now. But if they are both observed and understood, they not only do no harm but also provide some benefit when they are appropriate to the time. Thus Moses himself and the Prophets observed them, because they suited that people, for whom such slavery was still useful, so that they might be kept under restraint through fear.

Nothing terrifies the soul so piously as an unintelligible sacrament. Once understood, however, it produces holy joy and is freely celebrated if the time requires it; if it is not required, it is read and discussed only with spiritual delight.

Every sacrament, when understood, refers either to the contemplation of truth or to good morals. The contemplation of truth is founded upon the love of God alone; good morals upon love of God and neighbor. Upon these two commandments hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22:37–40).

Let us now see how circumcision of the flesh and the other works of this kind from the Law are not necessary where the grace of faith is already present.

### 20. [Book III, 2–9]

“This alone,” he says, “I wish to learn from you: Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the Law, or from the hearing of faith?”

The answer is: Certainly, from the hearing of faith. Faith was preached to them by the Apostle, and in that preaching they certainly experienced the coming and presence of the Holy Spirit. At that time, in the newness of the invitation to faith, the presence of the Holy Spirit also appeared through perceptible miracles, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts 2).

This had taken place among the Galatians before those people came to corrupt and circumcise them. The sense, therefore, is this: If your salvation were found in those works of the Law, the Holy Spirit would not have been given to you until you had been circumcised.

Then he adds: “Are you so foolish that, having begun with the Spirit, you are now being completed in the flesh?” This is what he had said above at the beginning: “Unless there are some who are troubling you and wanting to turn you toward another Gospel of Christ” (Gal. 1:7).

Troubling is contrary to order. The order is to rise from carnal things to spiritual things, not to fall from spiritual things to carnal things, as had happened to them. This is the Gospel’s being turned backward; because this is not good, it is not the Gospel when such a thing is announced.

When he says, “Did you suffer so many things?” they had already endured much for the sake of faith—not through fear, as though they were under the Law, but because in their very sufferings they had overcome fear through love, since “God’s love has been poured into their hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to them” (Rom. 5:5).

“You have suffered so many things for nothing,” he says, if you wish to fall back from the love that sustained so much in you into fear. “If indeed you suffered so many things for nothing.”

For something said to have been done for nothing is superfluous; what is superfluous neither benefits nor harms. But it must be considered whether this may actually be harmful. For not rising is not the same as falling, although they had not yet fallen but were already inclining toward a fall.

For the Holy Spirit was still working in them, as he says next: “Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works mighty deeds among you do so from the works of the Law, or from the hearing of faith?” The answer is certainly: From the hearing of faith, as was discussed above.

Then he introduces the example of the father Abraham, about whom he has argued more fully and clearly in the Epistle to the Romans (Rom. 4:3). The chief point by which he triumphs in Abraham’s case is that, before he was circumcised, his faith was counted as righteousness. To this the statement most appropriately refers: “In you all nations will be blessed” (Gen. 22:18)—namely, through the imitation of his faith, by which he was justified even before receiving the sacrament of circumcision, which he accepted as the sign of faith [Note: [Col. 2118] Nine manuscripts read: “which he accepted as the sign of faith,” omitting “as the seal of faith.”], and before the whole servitude of the Law, which was given much later.

### 21. [Book III, 10–12]

When he says, “For all who are of the works of the Law are under the curse of the Law,” he wants this understood as being under fear, not in freedom. Thus those who did not continue in everything written in the book of the Law, so as to do it, were punished by bodily and present vengeance; and, in addition, in the very punishment of their bodies they feared the disgrace of the curse.

But the person who is justified before God is the one who worships him freely—not from desire to obtain something from him apart from him, nor from fear of losing something. In God alone our true and perfect blessedness exists. Since he is invisible to bodily eyes, he is worshiped by faith as long as we live in this flesh, as he said above: “But what I now live in the flesh, I live in faith in the Son of God” (Gal. 2:20). This itself is righteousness.

This is the point of the statement, “The righteous person lives by faith.” He wanted to show from this that no one is justified in the Law, because it is written that the righteous person lives by faith.

Therefore we must understand that “in the Law,” in the statement he now makes about “the works of the Law,” refers to those who are occupied with circumcision of the flesh and similar observances. Whoever lives in these is in the Law in such a way as to live under the Law.

But, as was said, he has now used “Law” for the works of the Law themselves, as becomes clear later. For he says: “The Law is not of faith, but the one who does them will live by them.”

He does not say, “The one who does it will live in it,” so that you may understand “Law” in this passage as referring to the works themselves.

Those who lived in these works certainly feared that, if they did not perform them, they would suffer stoning, crucifixion, or something of that kind. Therefore, “the one who does them,” he says, “will live by them”—that is, he will receive a reward and will not be punished by such a death.

He does not, therefore, live by faith before God, whose most immediate reward someone will possess after departing this life if he has lived by faith in this life [Note: [Col. 2119] Lov. reads: “he will possess the most excellent reward.” Other codices read: “the most immediate reward.”].

Whoever desires or fears present visible things does not live by faith, because faith in God concerns invisible things, which will be given afterward.

There is, then, a certain righteousness in the works of the Law, since it is not left without its own reward: the person who does them lives by them.

Hence he also says to the Romans: “For if Abraham was justified by works, he has glory, but not before God” (Rom. 4:2).

It is one thing not to be justified; it is another not to be justified before God. The person who is not justified at all preserves neither those things that have a temporal reward nor those that have an eternal one. But the person who is justified in the works of the Law is not justified before God, because he expects from them a temporal and visible reward.

Nevertheless, as I have said, this too is a certain—so to speak—earthly and carnal righteousness. For the Apostle himself calls it righteousness when he says elsewhere: “According to the righteousness that is in the Law, I lived without reproach” (Phil. 3:6).

### 22. [Book III, 13–14]

For this reason the Lord Jesus Christ, now about to give freedom to believers, did not observe the letter of certain of those ordinances. Thus, when the disciples plucked ears of grain on the Sabbath because they were hungry, he answered those who were indignant that the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath (Matt. 12:1–8).

By not observing those ordinances carnally, he therefore inflamed the hostility of carnal people. He accepted the punishment prescribed for those who did not observe them, but he did so in order to free believers in him from fear of such punishment.

To this belongs what he adds: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.’”

For those who understand the sacrament spiritually, this statement is a sign of freedom. For those who understand it carnally, if they are Jews it is a yoke of slavery; if they are pagans or heretics, it is a veil of blindness.

Some of our people, less instructed in the Scriptures, fear this statement too greatly. While approving the ancient Scriptures with the reverence owed to them, they do not think that it was said about the Lord, but about Judas, his betrayer [Col. 2120]. They say that the text does not read, “Cursed is everyone who is fastened to a tree,” but “who hangs on a tree,” because it does not signify the Lord here but the one who hanged himself with a noose.

They are greatly mistaken and fail to notice that they are arguing against the Apostle, who says: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us, because it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.’”

The one who became a curse for us certainly hung on a tree: Christ, who freed us from the curse of the Law, so that we would no longer be justified by fear in the works of the Law, but by faith before God—a faith that operates not through fear but through love.

The Holy Spirit, who spoke this through Moses, provided for both things [Note: [Col. 2120] The printed editions read “foresaw.” The manuscripts more appropriately read “provided.”]: that those who were not yet able to live by faith in invisible realities should be guarded by fear of visible punishment, and that he himself should remove this fear by taking upon himself what was feared. Once fear had been removed, he could give the gift of love.

Nor should it be considered an insult to the Lord that the one who hangs on a tree is called accursed. He hung on the tree in that part of him that was mortal. The origin of mortality is known to believers: it comes from the punishment and curse of the first man’s sin, which the Lord assumed and carried our sins in his body upon the tree (1 Pet. 2:24).

If it were said, “Death is accursed,” no one would recoil. But what hung on the tree except the Lord’s death, so that by dying he might overcome death? The very thing that was conquered was therefore accursed.

Likewise, if it were said, “Sin is accursed,” no one would be surprised. But what hung on the tree except the sin of the old man, which the Lord assumed for us in the mortality of that very flesh?

Hence the Apostle was neither ashamed nor afraid to say that Christ was made sin for us, adding: “in order that, through sin, he might condemn sin” (Rom. 8:3).

For our old man would not also have been crucified, as the same Apostle says elsewhere, unless the representation of our sin hung in the Lord’s death, so that the body of sin might be destroyed and we might no longer serve sin (Rom. 6:6).

As a figure of this sin and death, Moses also lifted up the serpent on a tree in the wilderness (Num. 21:9). Through the persuasion of the serpent, the human being fell into the condemnation of death. Therefore the serpent was appropriately lifted up on a tree as a sign of death itself. For in that figure the Lord’s death hung on the tree.

Who would recoil if it were said, “Cursed is the serpent that hangs on a tree”? Yet the serpent, prefiguring the death of the Lord’s flesh, hung on a tree. The Lord himself attested to that sacrament when he said: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up above the earth” (John 3:14).

No one would say that Moses did this as an insult to the Lord, since he knew that such great salvation for human beings was present in that cross. He ordered the serpent to be raised for no other reason than that those who looked upon it—those who had been bitten by serpents and were dying—might immediately be healed.

Nor was that bronze serpent made for any other reason than to signify the faith in the Lord’s passion that would endure. For things whose number remains are commonly called “bronze.” If human beings had forgotten, and the event had been erased from the memory of time, that Christ died for humanity, they would truly perish. But now the faith of the cross remains like bronze, so that, while some die and others are born, they may nevertheless find that same exalted cross enduring, and may be healed by looking upon it.

It is therefore no wonder that he conquered a curse through a curse, who conquered death through death, sin through sin, and the serpent through the serpent. Death was accursed, sin was accursed, and the serpent was accursed; all these were triumphed over on the cross.

“Cursed, therefore, is everyone who hangs on a tree.”

Because Christ justifies those who believe in him not through the works of the Law but through faith, the fear of the curse of the cross has been removed. The charity of Abraham’s blessing, on account of the example of faith, remains for the Gentiles.

“So that,” he says, “we may receive the proclamation of the Spirit through faith”—that is, so that not what is feared in the flesh, but what is loved in the spirit, may be proclaimed to those who believe.

### 23. [Book III, 15–18]

For this reason he also mentions a human testament, which is certainly much weaker than the divine one. “Yet,” he says, “once a human testament has been confirmed, no one annuls it or adds a codicil to it.”

When a testator changes a testament, he does not change one that has already been confirmed, for it is confirmed by the testator’s death.

The fact that the testator’s death confirms his testament, because he can no longer change his decision, corresponds to the immutability of God’s promise, which confirms the inheritance of Abraham, whose faith was counted as righteousness (Rom. 4:9).

Therefore the Apostle says that the seed of Abraham to whom the promises were made is Christ—that is, all Christians who imitate Abraham by faith. He reduces this to the singular in order to emphasize that it was not said, “and to seeds,” but, “and to your seed.” For there is one faith, and those who live carnally from works cannot be justified in the same way as those who live spiritually from faith.

He then argues that the Law had not yet been given and could not, after so many years, have been given in such a way as to invalidate the ancient promises made to Abraham. If the Law justifies, Abraham, who lived long before the Law, was not justified. Since they cannot say this, they are compelled to admit that a person is justified not by the works of the Law but by faith.

At the same time, this compels us to understand that all the ancients who were justified were justified by that same faith. What we believe partly as past—that is, the Lord’s first coming—and partly as future—that is, the Lord’s second coming—we are saved by believing. They believed the whole as future: both comings were future for them, revealed to them by the Holy Spirit, so that they might be saved.

Hence there is also the statement: “Abraham longed to see my day; he saw it and rejoiced” (John 8:56).

### 24. [Ib. III, 19, 20.]

A sufficiently necessary question follows: If faith justifies, and the earlier saints who were justified before God were justified by faith itself, why was it necessary for the Law to be given? He introduced this question for discussion [Col. 2122] by asking and saying, “What then?” Up to this point there is a question; what follows is the answer: “The Law was put forward because of transgressions, until the seed should come to whom the promise was made, ordained through angels in the hand of a mediator. Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one” [Note: [Col. 2122] *Retractationes*, book 1, chapter 24, §2.].

That the mediator is Jesus Christ according to his humanity becomes clearer from another statement of the same apostle, where he says: “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus” (1 Tim. 2:5). A mediator, therefore, could not be between God and God, since God is one; but “a mediator is not of one,” because he stands in the middle between several parties.

The angels, moreover, who have not fallen from the presence of God do not need a mediator by whom they might be reconciled. Likewise, the angels who fell by spontaneous transgression, without anyone persuading them, are not reconciled through a mediator. It remains, therefore, that the one who was cast down through the persuasion of the proud mediator, the devil, is raised up through the humility taught by the humble mediator, Christ.

For if the Son of God had wished to remain in natural equality with the Father and had not emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), he would not have been the mediator between God and human beings. For the Trinity itself is one God, the same in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, with the eternity and equality of the divine nature remaining constant.

Thus the only Son of God became mediator between God and human beings when the Word of God, God with God, both lowered his majesty to the level of human beings and raised human humility to the level of divine things, so that he might be a mediator between God and human beings—a human being, yet through God beyond human beings. For he is “beautiful beyond the sons of men, and anointed with the oil of gladness beyond his companions” (Ps. 44:3).

Therefore all human beings who loved Christ’s humility, and by loving it imitated it—believing it through revelation before it occurred, and through the Gospel after it occurred—were healed from the impiety of pride so that they might be reconciled to God.

But this righteousness of faith, because it was given to human beings not on account of merit but through God’s mercy and grace, was not widespread before God, as man, was born among human beings. The seed to whom the promise was made signifies the people—not those very few who, seeing by revelations that this righteousness would come, were saved through that same faith but could not thereby save the people as a whole.

That people, if considered throughout the whole world—for from the whole world the Church gathers the heavenly Jerusalem [Note: [Col. 2122] Three manuscripts read, “the Church gathers the heavenly Jerusalem.” One has, “the Church in Jerusalem is gathered into the heavenly [Jerusalem].”—]—are few, because the narrow way belongs to the few. Yet, gathered into one, all who have been able to exist since the Gospel began to be preached, and all who will be able to exist among all nations until the end of the age, together with those—however few—who, through faith in the Lord and prophetic faith [Note: [Col. 2122] So the manuscripts. Lovaniensis reads, “through faith in the Lord by prophecy.”—] before both his advents received the salvation of grace, fill the most blessed state of the saints in the eternal city.

Therefore the Law was imposed upon the proud people so that, since they could not receive the grace of love [Col. 2123] unless they had been humbled—and without this grace they could in no way fulfill the commandments of the Law—they might be humbled by transgression, seek grace, and not suppose that they could be saved by their own merits, which would be prideful. Thus they would be righteous not by their own power and strength, but in the hand of the mediator who justifies the ungodly.

The entire administration of the Old Testament, moreover, was ministered through angels, with the Holy Spirit and the Word of truth himself acting through them—though not yet incarnate, yet never withdrawing from any true administration. Because that administration of the Law was arranged through angels, who at times acted in their own person and at times in the person of God, as is also the custom of the prophets, and because through that Law, which displayed but did not remove diseases, pride was crushed by the guilt of transgression, the seed was ordained through angels in the hand [Note: [Col. 2123] So several manuscripts. The printed editions read, “through angels, but in the hand.”—] of the mediator. Thus he himself might free from sins those who, already compelled by transgression of the Law to confess their need of the Lord’s grace and mercy, required their sins to be forgiven and to be reconciled to God in a new life through him who had shed his blood for them.

### 25. [Ib. III, 21, 22.]

For among these people pride had to be shattered through transgression of the Law. They gloried in their father Abraham and boasted that they possessed righteousness by natural descent, putting their merits in circumcision before those of the other nations with all the more danger because they did so with greater arrogance.

The nations, however, could be humbled quite easily even without this kind of transgression of the Law. For the evangelical grace found human beings who saw that they derived no origin of righteousness from their parents enslaved even to idols. It could not be said to the Jews, as it could be said to those others, that the righteousness of their ancestors in worshiping idols was not what they imagined it to be; for it could not likewise be said to the Jews that the righteousness of their father Abraham was false.

Therefore it is said to the former: “Produce, then, fruit worthy of repentance, and do not say to yourselves, ‘We have Abraham as our father.’ For God is able to raise up children for Abraham from these stones” (Matt. 3:8–9). But to the latter it is said:

“Therefore remember that formerly you were Gentiles in the flesh, those who are called uncircumcision by what is called circumcision in the flesh made by hand; that at that time you were without Christ, alienated from the commonwealth of Israel and strangers to the covenants of promise, having no hope of the promise and being without God in this world” (Eph. 2:11–12).

Finally, there the unbelievers are shown to have been broken off from their own olive tree, while here the believers are shown to have been grafted from a wild olive into their olive tree (Rom. 11:17).

Their pride, therefore, had to be worn down through transgression of the Law. Thus, after enlarging upon their sins with the words of Scripture, he says to the Romans: “But we know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are under the Law, so that every mouth may be stopped and the whole world may become guilty [Col. 2124] before God” (Rom. 3:19)—the Jews through transgression of the Law, and the Gentiles through impiety without the Law.

Hence he says again: “For God has shut up all things in unbelief, so that he may have mercy on all” (Rom. 11:32). He says the same thing here, reopening the very question: “Is the Law therefore against the promises of God? Certainly not. For if a law had been given that could give life, righteousness would indeed have come from the Law. But Scripture shut up all things under sin, so that the promise might be given to believers through faith in Jesus Christ.”

The Law, therefore, was not given to remove sin, but to shut up all things under sin. The Law showed that there was sin where people, blinded by habit, might have supposed there was righteousness. In this way, once humbled, they would recognize that their salvation was not in their own hand but in the hand of the mediator.

For humility especially recalls us from the place to which pride cast us down. And humility itself is suited to receiving the grace of Christ, who is the unique example of humility.

### 26. [Ib. III, 23.]

No one here, however ignorant, should say: Why, then, did it not benefit the Jews that the Law, ministered through angels, was ordained in the hand of the mediator?

It benefited them to an extent that cannot be expressed. For what else were those churches of the Gentiles who sold their possessions and placed the proceeds at the apostles’ feet, as so many thousands of people did so suddenly (Acts 4:34)? Nor should the crowds of unbelievers be taken into consideration; for every threshing floor has far more chaff than grain.

And what else can those words of the same apostle to the Romans concern except the sanctification of the Jews? “What then? Has God rejected his people? Certainly not. For I too am an Israelite, from the seed of Abraham, from the tribe of Benjamin. God has not rejected his people whom he foreknew” (Rom. 11:1–2).

When he praised the Church of the Thessalonians above the other churches of the Gentiles, he said that they had become like the churches of Judea, because they had suffered many things from their fellow countrymen for the faith, just as those churches had suffered from the Jews (1 Thess. 2:14).

This is also what I mentioned shortly before, where he says to the Romans: “If the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things” (Rom. 15:27).

Consequently, he also says of those Jews: “Before faith came, we were being kept under the Law, shut up for the faith that was afterward to be revealed.” The fact that they were so near, and that by selling their possessions they approached God so closely—as the Lord commanded those who wished to be perfect (Matt. 19:21)—was accomplished by the Law itself, under which they were guarded, shut up for the faith that was afterward to be revealed: that is, for the coming of that faith which was afterward revealed.

Their being shut up at that time was the fear of the one God. And the fact that they were found to be transgressors of that very Law benefited those who believed, not to their destruction but to their advantage. For awareness of a greater illness made them desire the physician more intensely and love him more ardently. “The one to whom more is forgiven loves more” (Luke 7:43, 47).

### 27. [Ib. III, 24–27.]

“Therefore,” he says, “the Law was our pedagogue in Christ”—that is, what he says elsewhere: “Under the Law we were being guarded, shut up in it” (Gal. 3:23).

After faith came, we are no longer under a pedagogue. He is therefore now reproving those who nullify the grace of Christ: as though the one who called them to freedom had not yet come, they still wish to remain under a pedagogue.

When he says that all are children of God through faith because all who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ, this [Col. 2125] serves to prevent the Gentiles from despairing because they had not been kept under a pedagogue and therefore might not think themselves children. By putting on Christ through faith, all become children—not by nature, as the only Son is, who is also the Wisdom of God; nor through the overwhelming power and singularity of his assumption by which he naturally possesses and enacts the person of Wisdom, as that mediator himself became one with the Wisdom that assumed him, without the intervention of any other mediator.

Rather, they become children through participation in wisdom, prepared and bestowed by the faith of the mediator. He now calls this grace of faith a garment, so that those who have believed in Christ may have put on Christ and therefore become children of God and brothers of the mediator.

### 28. [Ib. III, 28, 29.]

In this faith there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female; for insofar as all are believers, all are one in Christ Jesus.

And if faith accomplishes this—faith through which one walks righteously in this life—how much more perfectly and abundantly will sight itself accomplish it when we see face to face (1 Cor. 13:12)?

For now, although we possess the firstfruits of the Spirit, who is life, on account of the righteousness of faith, nevertheless, because the body is still dead on account of sin (Rom. 8:10, 23), this distinction—whether of nations, social condition, or sex—has indeed been removed from the unity of faith, but remains in mortal conduct.

The apostles command that its order be preserved on the journey of this life, and they also provide very salutary rules concerning how Jews and Greeks should live with one another according to their difference of nation; masters and slaves according to their difference of condition; and husbands and wives according to their difference of sex [Note: [Col. 2125] So the readings near Erasmus, Lyon, and Venice. In B., “of wives.”—], along with whatever other such cases arise. The Lord himself first said: “Give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matt. 22:21).

There are things that we preserve in the unity of faith without any distinction, and other things that belong to the order of this life as to a road, so that the name of God and the teaching may not be blasphemed.

This is done not only because of wrath, so that we may avoid offending people, but also because of conscience, so that we do not do these things deceitfully, as though merely for human eyes, but with a pure conscience of love for the sake of God, who wishes all human beings to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth (1 Tim. 2:4).

“Therefore,” he says, “you are all one in Christ Jesus.” And he added, “But if”—so that the sentence should be divided and understood in this way: “You are one in Christ Jesus; and if you are one in Christ Jesus, then you are Abraham’s seed.”

The meaning is therefore: “You are all one in Christ Jesus; but if you are one in Christ Jesus, then you are Abraham’s seed.”

For above he had said: “He does not say, ‘And to seeds,’ as of many, but as of one, ‘And to your seed,’ which is Christ” (Gal. 3:16).

Here, therefore, he shows that Christ is the one seed. Yet Christ is not to be understood as the mediator alone, but also as the Church, of whose body he is the head. Thus all may be one in Christ and, according to the promise, receive the inheritance through faith—the faith into which the people had been shut up: that is, into whose coming the people were guarded under a pedagogue [Col. 2126] until the appropriate time of maturity, when those who had been called according to the purpose within that people were to be called to freedom—namely, those who were found to be grain on that threshing floor.

### 29. [Ib. IV, 1–3.]

For to this he adds:

“But I say, as long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave, although he is lord of all; but he is under guardians and administrators until the time appointed by the father. So also we, when we were children, were enslaved under the elements of this world.”

It may be asked how, according to this comparison, the Jews were under the elements of this world, since through the Law they received they were commended to worship the one God who made heaven and earth.

There may, however, be another way of understanding this passage. Above he made the Law a pedagogue (Gal. 3:24), under whom the Jewish people existed; now he may call the elements of the world the guardians and administrators under whom the Gentiles were enslaved.

Thus the child, that is, the people belonging through one faith to the one seed of Abraham—for it has been gathered from both Jews and Gentiles—was partly under the pedagogue of the Law during the time of its childhood, namely, insofar as it was gathered from the Jews; and partly under the elements of this world, which it served as though they were guardians and administrators, insofar as it was gathered from the Gentiles.

Accordingly, when the apostle includes himself, saying not, “When you were children, you were enslaved under the elements of this world,” but, “When we were children, we were enslaved under the elements of this world,” this does not pertain here to the signification of the Jews, from whom Paul derived his origin, but rather to that of the Gentiles, since in this passage he can appropriately connect himself with those to whom he was sent to preach the Gospel.

### 30. [Ib. IV, 4, 5.]

Then he says that, when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son to free the child-heir who was enslaved—partly to the Law as to a pedagogue, and partly to the elements of this world as to guardians and administrators:

“God sent,” he says, “his Son, made from a woman.”

He used “woman” in place of “female,” according to the idiom of the Hebrews. For when it was said of Eve, “He formed her into a woman” (Gen. 2:22), she had not yet experienced intercourse with a man; Scripture does not say that she did so until after they had been expelled from paradise.

He said “made” on account of the assumption of created nature. For those who are born from females are not then born from God, but God nevertheless makes them so that they can be born in this way, like every creature.

He said “made under the Law” because he was circumcised and a lawful offering was presented for him (Luke 2:21, 24).

Nor is it surprising that he also endured those works of the Law from which he was to free those who were held by them in servitude. He also endured death in order to free from death those who were held by mortality.

“So that we might receive,” he says, “adoption as sons.”

He says “adoption” so that we may clearly understand the unique Son of God. We are children of God by his kindness and merciful favor; he is Son by nature, being what the Father is.

He did not say “let us receive,” but “let us receive again,” signifying that we had lost this in Adam, from whom we are mortal.

Therefore, when he says “to redeem those who were under the Law [Col. 2127],” this refers both to freeing the people who were children serving under the pedagogue and to what he had said, “made under the Law.”

But when he says “so that we might receive adoption as sons,” this refers to what he had said, “made from a woman.” For from this we receive adoption: the Only-Begotten did not disdain participation in our nature, being made from a woman, so that he might be not only the Only-Begotten, where he has no brothers, but also the Firstborn among many brothers (Rom. 8:29).

He set forth two things: “made from a woman” and “made under the Law”; but he answered them in a changed order.

### 31. [Ib. IV, 6.]

Then, joining to them the people who were children serving under guardians and administrators—that is, under the elements of this world—so that they would not think themselves to be children because they were not under a pedagogue, he says:

“But because you are sons, God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

He used two words, so that he might interpret the first by the second; for “Abba” means “Father.”

It is elegantly understood that he did not use two words from two languages signifying the same thing without reason. This was on account of the whole people, called into the unity of faith from Jews and Gentiles: the Hebrew word was directed to the Jews, the Greek word to the Gentiles, while the identical meaning of both words belonged to the unity of the same faith and Spirit.

Likewise, when a similar question concerning peace in Christ between Jews and Gentiles is treated in the Epistle to the Romans, he says: “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Rom. 8:15).

He rightly wished to prove from the presence and gift of the Holy Spirit that the Gentiles belonged to the promised inheritance. For the Gospel was not preached to the Gentiles until after the Lord’s ascension and the coming of the Holy Spirit.

The Jews had already begun to believe while the Son of God was still bearing mortal humanity on earth. Thus it is written in the Gospel that, although he himself praised the faith of the Canaanite woman (Matt. 15:28) and that of the centurion, of whom he said that he had not found such faith in Israel (Matt. 8:10), it is nevertheless sufficiently clear from the Lord’s own words that at that time the Gospel was specifically being preached to the Jews.

For when the Canaanite woman pleaded with him, he said that he had not been sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel (Matt. 15:24). And when he sent out the disciples, he said: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go first to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:5–6).

He called the Gentiles another sheepfold when he said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these also I must bring, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16). When could this have occurred, except after his glorification?

After the resurrection, moreover, he also sent the disciples to the Gentiles, ordering them meanwhile to remain in Jerusalem until, according to his promise, he sent them the Holy Spirit (Acts 1:4).

Therefore, when the apostle had said, “God sent his Son, made from a woman, made under the Law, to redeem those who were under the Law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Gal. 4:4), it remained for him to show that the Gentiles, who were not under the Law, nevertheless belonged to the same adoption as sons [Col. 2128].

He teaches this from the gift of the Holy Spirit, who was given to all. For this reason Peter also defended himself before the believing Jews concerning the uncircumcised centurion Cornelius, saying that he could not withhold water from those who had clearly already received the Holy Spirit (Acts 10:47).

Paul had also used this most weighty proof earlier when he said: “I wish to learn only this from you: Did you receive the Spirit from the works of the Law or from hearing with faith?” And shortly afterward: “Therefore, does he who supplies the Spirit to you and works powers among you do so from the works of the Law or from hearing with faith?” (Gal. 3:2, 5).

So here too: “Because you are sons of God,” he says, “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’”

### 32. [Ib. IV, 7, 8.]

Then he most clearly shows that he is speaking also of those who had come to faith from the Gentiles, to whom he was writing the Epistle:

“Therefore,” he says, “you are no longer a slave but a son,” referring to what he had said: “As long as the heir is a child, he differs in nothing from a slave.”

“And if a son,” he says, “then also an heir through God”—that is, through the mercy of God, not through the promises made to the fathers, since he was not born carnally from them as the Jews were. Yet he was a son of Abraham according to the imitation of faith, and through the mercy of the Lord he obtained the grace of that faith.

“But at that time,” he says, “when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods.”

Since he is not writing to Jews but to Gentiles, and does not say “we served” but “you served,” it is sufficiently probable that what he said above also concerned the Gentiles: that they were enslaved under the elements of this world, as under guardians and administrators (Gal. 4:1–3).

For the elements themselves are certainly not gods by nature, “whether in heaven or on earth, as there are many gods and many lords; yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:5–6).

When he says, “You served those who by nature are not gods,” he sufficiently demonstrates that the one true God is God by nature. By this name the Trinity is understood within the most faithful and catholic embrace of the heart.

He calls those who are not gods by nature guardians and administrators above because there is no creature—whether one that remains in truth and gives glory to God, or one that has not stood in truth and seeks its own glory—that does not, willingly or unwillingly, serve divine providence.

The one who is willing does what is good together with it [Note: [Col. 2128] Lovaniensis, on the authority of three manuscripts, reads: “the one willingly does what is good when something good is done through it.” In the earlier editions of Erasmus and Amerbach it read: “the one willingly does what is good with it”—understand, “with divine providence.” All our manuscripts except the Albiniensis support this reading; the Albiniensis has, “the one willingly does it when he does what is good.”—]; with regard to the other, what is just is done.

For if the transgressing angels themselves, with their prince the devil, were not rightly called guardians or administrators of divine providence, the Lord would not call the devil the ruler of this world; nor would apostolic authority use him to correct human beings, as the same Paul says elsewhere: “I have handed them over to Satan, so that they may learn not to blaspheme” (1 Tim. 1:20).

And elsewhere, for salvation, he says:

“Although absent in body but present [Col. 2129] in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, the one who has done this. In the name of our Lord Jesus, when you are assembled, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus, hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord Jesus” (1 Cor. 5:3–5).

Even a magistrate under an appointed emperor [Note: [Col. 2129] Amerbach, Erasmus, and ten manuscripts read, “under so great an [emperor].”—] does nothing except insofar as he is permitted to do so; and the guardians and administrators of this world do nothing except insofar as the Lord allows.

For nothing is hidden from him, as it is from a human being; nor is he less powerful in any respect, so that guardians and administrators who are under his power might accomplish something among those subject to them according to their rank without either his permission or his knowledge.

Yet they are not repaid according to what is justly done through them, but according to the intention with which they themselves act. For God neither denied free will to his rational creature, nor did he surrender the power by which he justly orders even the unjust.

We have often treated this subject at greater length and more fully in other books (*On Free Will*) [Note: [Col. 2129] The word “often” is absent from Erasmus, Amerbach, and seven manuscripts.].

Whether, therefore, the Gentiles worshiped the sun, moon, stars, heaven, earth, and other things of this kind, or demons, they are rightly understood to have been under guardians and administrators.

### 33. [Ib. IV, 9.]

Nevertheless, what follows again seems to entangle the question as though it had already been explained.

Throughout the entire Epistle he shows that no one other than those who came from circumcision had troubled the faith of the Galatians—people who wished to lead them toward the carnal observances of the Law, as though salvation were found in them. Yet in this one passage he seems to be speaking to those who were trying to return to the superstitions of the Gentiles.

For he says:

“But now, having come to know God—or rather, having been known by God—how are you turning back again to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved again as before?”

When he says “you are turning back,” and is speaking not to the circumcised but to Gentiles, as is evident throughout the Epistle, he certainly does not mean that they are turning back to circumcision, in which they had never been. Rather, he says, they are turning back “to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved again as before.”

We are compelled to understand this as referring to the Gentiles. For above he had said to them: “At that time, when you did not know God, you served those who by nature are not gods” (Gal. 4:8). He signifies that they wish to return to this slavery when he says: “How are you turning back to the weak and impoverished elements, to which you wish to be enslaved again as before?”

### 34. [Ib. IV, 10, 11.]

What he adds—“You observe days and months and seasons and years; I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored over you in vain” [Note: [Col. 2129] The printed editions here and below read *in vobis*. The manuscripts read *in vos*, in accordance with the Greek.]—may seem more strongly to confirm this interpretation.

This is an extremely common error among the Gentiles: in conducting affairs or awaiting the outcomes of their lives and business, they observe days, months, years, and seasons marked out by astrologers and Chaldeans.

Nevertheless, perhaps we should not understand this as referring to the error of the Gentiles, lest we seem suddenly and rashly to be twisting the argument, which he took up at the beginning and carries through to the end, toward something else [Col. 2130]. Rather, we should understand it as referring to those things against which he appears to be warning throughout the Epistle.

The Jews also observe days, months, years, and seasons in a servile manner: in the carnal observance of the Sabbath and the new moon, of the month of new things, and of every seventh year, which they call the “Sabbath of Sabbaths.”

Because these things were shadows of future realities, they remained as superstition after Christ had come, being observed as though they were salvific by those who did not know to what they should be referred.

It is as though the apostle had said this to the Gentiles:

“What benefit is it that you escaped the slavery in which you were held when you served the elements of the world, if you return again to such things, led astray by those who, still failing to recognize the time of their freedom, serve the seasons among the other works of the Law that they understand carnally? You too wish to serve them again as before, and to observe with them the days, months, years, and seasons which you served even before you believed in Christ.”

For it is clear that the cycles of time are administered through the elements of this world—that is, through heaven and earth and the movements and order of the stars.

He calls them “weak” because they vary in a weak and unstable appearance; and “impoverished” because they lack the supreme and stable form of the Creator, so that they can exist as they do.

### 35.
