Let the reader therefore choose whichever of these interpretations he wishes, provided that he understands that superstitious observance of times concerns such great danger to the soul that the apostle added at this point: “I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored over you in vain.”

Although this passage is read throughout the churches of the world with such great prominence and authority, our meeting places are full of people who receive from astrologers the times for actions.

Indeed, when something is to be begun—whether a building or any work of this sort—they often do not hesitate to warn us against beginning it on the days they call Egyptian days, not knowing, as the saying goes, where they are going.

If this passage is to be understood as referring to the superstitious observance of the Jews, what hope do they have, when they wish to be called Christians, steering their shipwrecked lives by an almanac?

For if they were observing times according to Jewish custom from the divine books that God once gave to the carnal people, the apostle would say to them: “I fear for you, lest somehow I have labored over you in vain.”

And yet, if someone is discovered—even a catechumen—observing the Sabbath according to the Jewish rite, the Church erupts in commotion.

But now innumerable people from the number of the faithful say to us with great confidence to our faces: “On the day after the Calends, I do not set out.”

We scarcely and gently forbid these practices, smiling lest they become angry and fearing lest they be astonished as though we were introducing something new.

Woe to the sins of human beings, which we dread only when they are unusual! But those customary sins, for the cleansing of which the Son of God’s blood was poured out—however great they may be, and even though they entirely close the kingdom of God against those who commit them—we are often compelled to endure merely because we see them so often, and sometimes even to commit some of them because we tolerate them!

Would that, O Lord, we did not do everything that we cannot prevent [Note: [Col. 2130] Augustine transferred this passage, “Woe to the sins,” and what follows, into the *Enchiridion*, chapter 80.]!

[Col. 2131]

### 36. [Ib. IV, 9.]

But let us now examine what follows.

We had indeed passed over the words: “But now, having come to know God, or rather, having been known by God.”

It certainly seems that in this passage the apostolic manner of speaking also wishes to accommodate itself to human weakness, lest it appear that the style of divine speech descends to earthly human thoughts only in the books of the Old Testament.

Since he corrected what he had said—“having come to know God”—this should not trouble us. For it is clear that as long as we walk by faith and not by sight (2 Cor. 5:7), we have not yet come to know God; rather, we are cleansed by that faith so that at the proper time we may be able to know him.

But when he says, in the very correction, “or rather, having been known by God,” if this is taken literally, God will seem to know something in time that he had not known before.

The statement is therefore spoken figuratively, so that we understand the eyes of God to be his very love, which he demonstrated by sending his only Son to be killed for the ungodly. For we customarily say of those who are loved that they are held before our eyes.

Thus, “having come to know God, or rather, having been known by God,” means what John also said: “Not that we loved God, but that he loved us” [Note: [Col. 2131] Lovaniensis reads, “he loved us first.” Manuscript M.] (1 John 4:10).

### 37. [Ib. IV, 12–18.]

He says: “Become as I am,” since although I was born a Jew, I now despise these carnal things through spiritual discernment.

“For I too am as you are”—that is, I am a human being.

Then, appropriately and fittingly, he makes them recall his affection, so that they will not regard him as an enemy. For he says:

“Brothers, I beg you, you have done me no wrong.”

It is as though he were saying: “Therefore do not think that I wish to harm you.”

“You know that it was because of an infirmity of the flesh that I formerly preached the Gospel to you”—that is, while I was suffering persecution.

“And you did not despise or reject your trial in my flesh.”

They were tested when the apostle was suffering persecution: would they abandon him through fear, or embrace him through love?

“And you did not despise,” he says, “that trial as though it were useful”—nor did you reject it by refusing to share in my danger.

“But you received me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.”

Then, expressing admiration, he commends their spiritual work so that, by keeping it in view, they might not fall into carnal fear.

“What, then,” he says, “was your blessedness? For I bear you witness that, if it had been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.”

“Therefore have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?”

The answer is certainly: “No.”

But what truth was he telling except that they should not be circumcised?

And so see what he adds:

“They are zealous for you, but not rightly”—that is, those who wish to make you carnal instead of spiritual envy you; they are zealous, but not rightly.

“But they wish to shut you out,” he says, “so that you may be zealous for them”—that is, imitate them. And how could this be except by their keeping you under the yoke of slavery, just as they themselves are kept under it?

“But it is good,” he says, “to be zealous for what is good always” [Note: [Col. 2131] So the manuscripts, in accordance with the Greek. The printed editions read, “but it is good to be zealous.”—].

For he wants them always to imitate him. Therefore he adds: “And not only when I am present with you.”

For when they wished to give him their eyes while he was present, they were certainly attempting to imitate the one whom they loved in this way.

### 38. [On chapter IV, verse 19]

For this reason he also says, “My little children,” so that they might imitate him as a parent: “whom I am again in labor with,” he says, “until Christ is formed in you.” He spoke this more particularly in the person of Mother Church; for elsewhere also he says, “I became a little one in your midst, as a nurse cherishes her children” (1 Thess. II, 7).

Christ is formed in the believer through faith in the inner person, called into the freedom of grace, gentle and humble of heart, not boasting of the merits of works—which are nothing—but with grace itself beginning some sort of merit in him, so that the one who said, “Whatever you did for one of the least of mine, you did for me” (Matt. XXV, 40), may call him his least one, that is, himself.

[Note: [Col. 2132] Two manuscripts read: “his least one, that same person, he who says.”]

For Christ is formed in the one who receives Christ’s form; and he receives Christ’s form who clings to Christ through spiritual love. Through this he becomes, by imitating Christ, what Christ is, insofar as his own degree permits. For John says, “Whoever says that he remains in Christ ought himself to walk as he walked” (1 John II, 6).

But since human beings are conceived by mothers so that they may be formed, while, once formed, they are brought forth in labor so that they may be born, the statement “whom I am again in labor with, until Christ is formed in you” may seem puzzling. Unless we understand this labor as referring to the anguish of anxieties with which he labored to bring them forth so that they might be born in Christ—and then labors again because of the dangers of seduction by which he sees them disturbed. His concern for such anxieties about them, by which he says that he is, in a sense, again in labor, can last until they attain “the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,” so that they are no longer “tossed about by every wind of doctrine” (Eph. IV, 13–14).

Thus the words “whom I am again in labor with, until Christ is formed in you” were spoken not because of the beginning of faith, by which they had already been born, but because of their strength and perfection. He also commends this labor elsewhere in other words, where he says: “My daily burden is the anxiety for all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I am not burning?” (2 Cor. XI, 28–29).

### 39. [On chapter IV, verse 20]

But when he adds, “I would like now to be present with you and to change my tone, because I am perplexed about you,” what else can be understood except that, since he had called them his children, he perhaps spared them in writing, lest they, provoked by a harsher rebuke, should easily be led by those deceivers—against whom, while absent, he could not resist—to hate him?

“I would like,” he says, “now to be present with you and to change my tone,” that is, to deny that you are children, “because I am perplexed about you.” For parents also commonly disown bad children, lest they be ashamed of them.

### 40. [On chapters IV, verses 21–31]

Then he adds: “Tell me, you who desire to be under the Law, do you not hear the Law?” What he says about Abraham’s two sons is readily understood, for he himself interprets this allegory. Abraham had these two sons when the two Testaments were signified. The sons whom he fathered from another wife after Sarah’s death do not belong to this symbolism. Therefore many who read the Apostle but do not know the book of Genesis suppose that Abraham had only two sons.

The Apostle mentions only these two because he had only them when these things were signified, which he proceeds to explain. The son born from the slave woman, whose name was Hagar, signifies the Old Testament—that is, the people of the Old Testament—because of the slavish yoke of carnal observances and earthly promises. Entangled in these, and hoping from God only for such things, they are not admitted to the spiritual inheritance of the heavenly patrimony.

It is not enough, however, that Isaac was born from a free woman to signify the people who are heirs of the New Testament. What is more important here is that he was born according to the promise. A son could also be born from a slave woman according to the flesh, and from a free woman according to the flesh, as Abraham later fathered sons from Keturah, whom he subsequently married—not according to the promise, but according to the flesh (Gen. XXV, 1–2).

Isaac, however, was wondrously born through the promise when both parents had grown old. If, relying on the confidence supplied by the Apostle, who most plainly shows that those two are to be understood allegorically, someone should also wish to discern in Keturah’s sons some figure of future realities—for these events concerning such persons were not recorded under the administration of the Holy Spirit without reason—he may perhaps find heresies and schisms signified.

Those sons were born from a free woman, as these are from the Church; nevertheless, they were born according to the flesh, not spiritually through the promise. If this is so, they too are found not to belong to the inheritance, that is, to the heavenly Jerusalem, which Scripture calls barren because for a long time she bore no children on earth.

She is also called desolate because people, abandoning heavenly justice and pursuing earthly things, had deserted her, as though that earthly Jerusalem had a husband, since it had received the Law.

[Note: [Col. 2133] Three manuscripts read: “with people abandoning justice for heavenly things.”]

Thus Sarah signifies the heavenly Jerusalem, which for a long time was deserted from intercourse with her husband because her barrenness was known. For men such as Abraham did not use women for the gratification of lust, but for the succession of offspring. Old age had been added to barrenness, so that, amid complete hopelessness, the divine promise might grant great merit to those who believed.

Therefore, certain of God’s promise, he approached the duty of begetting when already advanced in age, an age from which he had withdrawn from bodily intercourse during his more vigorous years. For no other reason does the Apostle, with the symbolic meaning of those women added, interpret what was said through the prophet: “For the children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband,” even though Sarah died before her husband and no divorce had occurred between them.

How, then, was one desolate and the other a woman with a husband, except that Abraham had transferred his effort to beget offspring to the fertility of the slave woman Hagar, away from the barrenness of his wife Sarah? Yet Sarah herself permitted this and voluntarily offered that her husband should father children by the slave woman.

For the ancient rule of justice is that which the same Apostle commends to the Corinthians: “A wife does not have authority over her own body, but her husband does; likewise, a husband does not have authority over his own body, but his wife does” (1 Cor. VII, 4). For such obligations, like everything else that is owed, belong to the authority of those to whom they are owed. Whoever does not defraud that authority preserves the rights of conjugal chastity.

The old age of Isaac’s parents is relevant to this symbolism because, although the people of the New Testament are new, their predestination with God—and the heavenly Jerusalem itself—is ancient. Hence John says to the Parthians:

[Note: [Col. 2134] Six manuscripts read “to the Parthians”; Lovaniensis reads “to the fathers”; Amerbach and Erasmus read “to the parents.”]

“I write to you, fathers, because you have known what was from the beginning” (1 John II, 13).

The carnal people who are in the Church, from whom heresies and schisms arise, received from the Gospel the opportunity to be born; but the carnal error in which they were conceived and which they carry with them does not belong to the antiquity of truth. Therefore they were born from a young mother and an old father without the promise.

For the Lord appeared in the Apocalypse with a white head for no other reason than the antiquity of truth (Rev. I, 14). Such people, then, were born from the occasion of ancient truth within a new and temporal falsehood.

The Apostle therefore says that we are children of the promise according to Isaac. Thus Isaac suffered persecution from Ishmael, just as those who had begun to live spiritually suffered persecution from carnal Jews. Yet this was in vain, since according to Scripture the slave woman and her son are cast out, and the son of the slave woman cannot be an heir with the son of the free woman.

“But we,” he says, “brothers, are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman.” For this freedom must now be set against the yoke of slavery under which those who were trying to draw these people toward circumcision were held through the works of the Law.

### 41. [On chapter V, verses 1–3]

When he says, “Stand firm, therefore,” he indicates that they have not yet fallen; for he would more appropriately have said, “Rise.” But when he adds, “And do not again be held by the yoke of slavery,” since no other yoke can be understood here by which he does not want them to be held except circumcision and similar Jewish observances, he continues:

“Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

How are we to understand his saying, “Do not again be held by the yoke of slavery,” when he is writing to people who had never been Jews? For his purpose is certainly to prevent them from being circumcised. Here, however, the interpretation about which we argued above is clearly revealed and confirmed.

I find no other meaning that he could have intended here for Gentiles except that they should benefit from having been freed through faith in Christ from the slavery of their superstition, and should not again wish to become slaves under the yoke of carnal observances—even though these were under God’s Law, they bound a carnal people in servile fashion.

He says that Christ will profit them nothing if they are circumcised, but in the manner in which these people wanted them circumcised: that is, if they placed their hope of salvation in circumcision of the flesh. Christ did indeed profit Timothy, although Paul himself circumcised that young man after he had become a Christian; he did this because of the scandal among his own people (Acts XVI, 3), without pretending anything, but in accordance with the indifference expressed in the words, “Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing” (1 Cor. VII, 19). For circumcision does no harm to one who does not believe that salvation is found in it.

In accordance with this interpretation he also adds: “I testify again to every person who circumcises himself”—that is, who desires this circumcision as a means of salvation—“that he is a debtor to do the whole Law.” He says this so that, perhaps out of fear of the innumerable observances written among the works of the Law, they might refrain from those things under which these people wished to subjugate them, lest they be compelled to fulfill them all. Neither the Jews nor their ancestors were able to fulfill them, as Peter says in the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XV, 10).

### 42. [On chapter V, verses 4–12]

“You have been severed from Christ,” he says, “you who are justified in the Law.” This is the proscription by which he previously said that Christ had been proscribed (Gal. III, 1): when these people are severed from Christ—that is, when Christ departs from them as from a possession that he held—the works of the Law are brought into that possession as into an empty one.

Because this harms not Christ but them, he adds, “You have fallen away from grace.” For the grace of Christ acts to free those who were debtors to the works of the Law from that debt; but these people, ungrateful for so great a grace, wish to be debtors to the performance of the entire Law.

This had not yet happened, but because their will had begun to turn in that direction, he speaks in many places as though it had already happened.

“For we,” he says, “through the Spirit, by faith, await the hope of righteousness.” Here he shows that those things belong to the faith of Christ which are awaited spiritually, not those desired carnally, such as the promises by which that slavery was held captive. As he says elsewhere: “We do not look to the things that are seen, but to the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. IV, 18).

Then he adds: “For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any force,” to declare that indifference and to show that circumcision is not harmful in itself, except when salvation is expected from it.

He therefore says that in Christ circumcision and uncircumcision have no force, but faith, which works through love. Here too he touches on the fact that under the Law slavery operates through fear.

“You were running well,” he says; “who hindered you from obeying the truth?” This is what he said above: “Who has bewitched you?” (Gal. III, 1).

“This persuasion of yours,” he says, “does not come from the one who called you.” For this persuasion is carnal, whereas he called them into freedom. He called what was being urged upon them “their persuasion.”

He calls the few who came to them to urge these things “leaven,” because they were small in number compared with the multitude of the Galatian believers. But they will receive this leaven, and the whole lump—that is, their entire Church—will in some way be leavened into the corruption of carnal slavery if they honor such persuaders by receiving them as just and faithful.

“I am confident in you in the Lord,” he says, “that you will think nothing otherwise.” From this it is clear that they had not yet been possessed by such people.

“But the one who is troubling you,” he says, “will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.” This is that disturbance contrary to order, by which spiritual people become carnal.

Since it must be understood that there were some who wanted to persuade them to this slavery but saw them being recalled by the authority of the Apostle Paul, they may also have said that Paul himself held this view but did not wish to disclose his opinion openly to them. Therefore he most appropriately adds:

“But as for me, brothers, if I still preach circumcision, why am I still suffering persecution?”

For he also suffered persecution from those who were trying to persuade them of such things, although they already appeared to have accepted the Gospel. He touches on them elsewhere when he says, “In dangers from false brothers” (2 Cor. XI, 26), and here at the beginning of the Epistle, where he says:

“Because of the false brothers who had been secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy out our freedom, which we have in Christ Jesus, in order to reduce us to slavery” (Gal. II, 4).

Therefore, if he preached circumcision, they would cease persecuting him. Yet, so that those to whom Christian freedom was being announced would not fear them—or think that they themselves were to be feared by the Apostle—he had earlier, full of confidence, openly declared his name, saying:

“Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V, 2).

It is as though he were saying, “Behold me: imitate me, so that you will not be afraid; or, if you are afraid, attribute the cause to me.”

When he says, “Then the offense of the cross has been abolished,” he repeats the statement, “If righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died for nothing” (Gal. II, 21). But since he mentions the offense here, he recalls that the Jews were especially offended at Christ because they repeatedly observed him disregarding and despising those carnal observances which they believed they possessed for salvation itself.

Thus he spoke as though saying: “The Jews therefore crucified Christ, though he despised these things, for no reason, if such things are still being urged upon those for whom he was crucified.”

With a most elegant ambiguity, he then adds what appears under the guise of a curse but is in fact a blessing:

“I wish that those who are troubling you would even cut themselves off.”

“Let them not merely be circumcised,” he says, “but also cut themselves off.” Thus they will become eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIX, 12), and will cease sowing carnal things.

### 43. [On chapter V, verse 13]

“For you,” he says, “brothers, were called into freedom.” For that disturbance, which was dragging them back from spiritual things to carnal things, was leading them into slavery.

But from this point he begins to discuss those works of the Law which, as I said above, he would discuss at the end of the Epistle (above, no. 19). No one doubts that these also belong to the New Testament, but with a different purpose: they are to be performed by free people, that is, by those who hope for the eternal rewards of love and await them through faith.

This is not like the Jews, who were compelled to fulfill these things through fear—not through that chaste fear which endures forever and ever (Ps. XVIII, 10), but through fear for their present life. Therefore they fulfilled certain works of the Law belonging to the sacraments, but they could not fulfill at all those pertaining to good morals. For no one fulfills these except through love.

If someone does not kill another because he fears being killed in turn, he does not fulfill the commandment of righteousness. But if he does not kill because killing is unjust, even if he could do so with impunity—not only before human beings but also before God—then he fulfills it.

So David, when God had placed King Saul in his power, could have killed him with impunity, since neither human beings would have avenged Saul—for David himself was greatly loved by them—nor God, who had said that he had given David this very power, so that he might do to Saul whatever he wished (1 Sam. XXIV, 4–8).

David therefore, loving his neighbor as himself, spared not only one who had persecuted him, but one who would persecute him, because he preferred to correct him rather than kill him. He was a man under the Old Testament, but not a man of the Old Testament: faith in the future inheritance of Christ, revealed and believed, saved him and called him to imitation.

Therefore the Apostle now says: “You were called into freedom, brothers; only do not turn freedom into an opportunity for the flesh,” that is, do not suppose, on hearing the name of freedom, that you may sin with impunity.

“But through love,” he says, “serve one another.” For whoever serves through love serves freely. He obeys God without misery, doing through love what he is taught, not through fear what he is compelled to do.

### 44. [On chapter V, verse 14]

“For the whole Law,” he says, “is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

By “the whole Law” he now means those works that pertain to good morals. For even those things that belong to the sacraments, when properly understood by free people and not observed carnally by slaves, must necessarily be referred to those two commandments: love of God and love of neighbor.

It is therefore rightly understood that this is also what the Lord meant when he said, “I have not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V, 17): he was going to remove carnal fear and give spiritual love, through which alone the Law can be fulfilled.

For “the fullness of the Law is love.” Since faith obtains the Holy Spirit, through whom the love of God is poured into the hearts of those who do righteousness (Rom. V, 5), no one should boast of good works apart from the grace of faith.

Therefore the Apostle refutes those who boast of the works of the Law by showing that the ancient sacramental works were shadows of future things, which, after the Lord’s coming, he showed were no longer necessary for the free heir. But works pertaining to good morals are fulfilled only through love, through which faith works (Gal. V, 6).

Thus, if some works of the Law are superfluous after faith and others are worthless before faith, “the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. II, 4), so that, strengthened by the light burden of Christ (Matt. XI, 30), he may cast off the heavy burden of slavery and not go beyond the boundaries of righteousness, obeying the gentle yoke of love.

[Note: [Col. 2137] Printed editions read “the light yoke”; manuscripts read “the gentle yoke.”]

### 45. [On chapter V, verses 15–16]

It may be asked why the Apostle here too mentions only love of neighbor, by which he says that the Law is fulfilled, while in the Epistle to the Romans, when discussing the same question, he says:

“Whoever loves another has fulfilled the Law. For, ‘You shall not commit adultery,’ ‘You shall not murder,’ ‘You shall not steal,’ ‘You shall not covet,’ and if there is any other commandment, it is summed up in this saying: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself.’ Love of neighbor does no evil. Therefore love is the fullness of the Law” (Rom. XIII, 8–10).

Since love is perfect only in the two commandments of love of God and love of neighbor, why does the Apostle in both this Epistle and that one mention only love of neighbor? Is it not because people can lie about their love of God, since fewer temptations put it to the test, whereas in love of neighbor they are more easily shown not to possess it when they act unjustly toward others?

It follows that whoever loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind also loves his neighbor as himself, because this is commanded by the one whom he loves with all his heart, all his soul, and all his mind.

Likewise, who can love his neighbor—that is, every human being—as himself unless he loves God, by whose command and gift he can fulfill love of neighbor?

Since the two commandments are such that neither can be kept without the other, it is often sufficient, when discussing works of righteousness, to mention one of them; but it is more appropriate to mention the one by which a person is more easily exposed.

Hence John says: “Whoever does not love his brother whom he sees, how can he love God whom he does not see?” (1 John IV, 20). For some claimed to have love of God, but were shown by their hatred of their brothers not to possess it. This is easy to judge from daily life and conduct.

“But if you bite and devour one another,” he says, “take care that you are not consumed by one another.” For this vice of contentiousness and envy especially nourished destructive disputes among them: they spoke evil of one another and each sought his own empty glory and victory. By such pursuits the fellowship of the people is consumed as it is divided into factions.

How, however, can they avoid these things unless they walk by the Spirit and do not fulfill the desires of the flesh? For the first and greatest gift of the Spirit is humility and gentleness.

Thus the Lord cries out in the passage I have already mentioned: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. XI, 29). And the prophet says: “Upon whom does my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. LXVI, 2).

### 46. [On chapter V, verse 17]

When he says, “For the flesh desires against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; for these oppose one another, so that you do not do the things you wish,” people suppose that the Apostle is here denying that we possess freedom of the will. They do not understand that he says this to those who do not wish to hold fast to the grace of faith they have received, through which alone they can walk by the Spirit and not fulfill the desires of the flesh. If they do not wish to hold fast to it, they will not be able to do what they wish.

They wish to perform the works of righteousness that are in the Law, but they are overcome by the desire of the flesh. By following it, they abandon the grace of faith.

Hence he also says to the Romans: “The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God, for it is not subject to the Law of God; nor indeed can it be” (Rom. VIII, 7).

Since love fulfills the Law, while the wisdom of the flesh, pursuing temporal advantages, opposes spiritual love, how can it be subject to the Law of God—that is, willingly and obediently fulfill righteousness and not oppose it—when, even while it tries, it must be overcome whenever it finds that it can gain a greater temporal advantage through wrongdoing than by preserving justice?

The first life of a human being is before the Law, when no wickedness or evil is prohibited and no resistance is offered from any side to perverse desires, because there is no one to prohibit them.

The second is under the Law, before grace, when a person is indeed prohibited and attempts to abstain from sin, but is overcome, because he does not yet love righteousness for God’s sake and for the sake of righteousness itself; rather, he wants to make righteousness serve him in acquiring earthly things.

Thus, when he sees righteousness on one side and temporal advantage on the other, he is dragged by the weight of temporal desire and abandons righteousness. He had tried to hold on to it precisely so that he might possess what he now sees he will lose if he holds on to righteousness.

The third life is under grace, when no temporal advantage is preferred to righteousness. This cannot happen except through the spiritual love that the Lord taught by his example and granted by his grace.

In this life, even if desires of the flesh arise from the mortality of the body, they do not subject the mind to consent to sin. Thus “sin no longer reigns in our mortal body” (Rom. VI, 12), although it cannot fail to dwell in it as long as the body is mortal.

At first sin does not reign when with the mind we serve the Law of God, although with the flesh we serve the law of sin (Rom. VII, 25)—that is, the penal habit—from which desires arise, though we do not obey them. Later it is extinguished entirely.

For if the Spirit of Jesus dwells in us, the one who raised Jesus Christ from the dead “will also give life to our mortal bodies, because of his Spirit who dwells in us” (Rom. VIII, 11).

For now, then, the stage under grace must be brought to completion, so that we may do by the spirit what we wish, even if we cannot do it by the flesh. That is, we must not obey the desires of sin by presenting our members to it as weapons of unrighteousness (Rom. VI, 13), even if we are unable to prevent those desires from arising.

Although we are not yet in that eternal peace which is perfect in every part of the human being, we must already cease to be under the Law, where the mind is held guilty of transgression while the desire of the flesh leads it captive into consent to sin. We must instead be under grace, where there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus (Rom. VIII, 1), because punishment follows not the one who is fighting, but the one who has been defeated.

### 47. [On chapter V, verse 18]

Accordingly, he adds most orderly: “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law.” We are to understand that those are under the Law whose spirit so desires against the flesh that they do not do what they wish—that is, they do not remain unconquered in the love of righteousness, but are defeated by the flesh that desires against them.

[Note: [Col. 2139] See *Retractions*, chapter 24, no. 2.]

The flesh not only resists the law of their mind but also takes them captive under the law of sin that is in their mortal members (Rom. VII, 23).

For those who are not led by the Spirit must consequently be led by the flesh. It is not suffering opposition from the flesh that constitutes condemnation, but being led by the flesh.

Therefore he says, “But if you are led by the Spirit, you are no longer under the Law.” For above he did not say, “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not have the desires of the flesh,” but, “You will not fulfill them” (Gal. V, 16).

For not to have them at all is no longer the contest but the prize of the contest, if we win by persevering under grace. Only the transformation of the body into an immortal state will have no desires of the flesh.

### 48. [On chapter V, verses 19–21]

Then he begins to enumerate the works of the flesh, so that they may understand that, if they consent to their carnal desires in order to perform these works, they are being led by the flesh, not by the Spirit.

“The works of the flesh,” he says, “are manifest: fornications, impurities, the service of idols, sorceries, enmities, contentions, hostilities, rivalries, dissensions, heresies, envies, drunkennesses, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Those do these things who, consenting to carnal desires, decide that they ought to be done, even if they are not given the ability to carry them out. But those who are touched by such impulses and remain unmoved in greater love—not only failing to offer the members of their bodies for evil action, but also not consenting even by a nod of the will to offer them—do not do these things, and therefore they will possess the kingdom of God.

For sin no longer reigns in their mortal body so that they obey its desires, although sin dwells in their mortal body, since the impulse of the natural habit by which we were born mortal has not yet been extinguished, nor has the character of our own life, by which, through sinning, we ourselves increased what we had inherited from the origin of human sin and condemnation.

It is one thing not to sin; another not to have sin. In the one in whom sin does not reign, there is no sinning—that is, he does not obey its desires. But in the one in whom these desires do not exist at all, he not only does not sin but also does not have sin.

Even if this can be achieved in many respects during this life, it must nevertheless be hoped for in every respect only in the resurrection of the flesh and its transformation.

It may be puzzling that he says, “I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God,” if we ask where he warned them before, since no such statement is found in this Epistle. Either he had warned them of this when he was present, or he knew that the Epistle sent to the Corinthians had reached them.

For there he says:

“Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who have intercourse with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor slanderers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God” (1 Cor. VI, 9–10).

### 49. [On chapter V, verses 22–23]

After enumerating the works of the flesh, which close the kingdom of God, he also adds the works of the Spirit, which he calls the fruit of the Spirit.

“But the fruit of the Spirit,” he says, “is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, self-control.” And he adds, “Against such things there is no law,” so that we may understand that those are under the Law in whom these things do not reign.

For those in whom these things reign use the Law lawfully, since the Law was not imposed upon them for restraint. Their delight in righteousness is greater and more powerful.

Thus he says to Timothy:

“We know that the Law is good, if one uses it lawfully, knowing this: that the Law is not laid down for the righteous, but for the unrighteous and the disobedient, the ungodly and sinners, the wicked and defiled, murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, murderers, fornicators, men who have intercourse with males, kidnappers, liars, perjurers, and whatever else is opposed to sound doctrine” (1 Tim. I, 8–10).

The implied meaning is that the Law is laid down for such people.

These spiritual fruits therefore reign in the person in whom sins do not reign. These good things reign when they delight us so greatly that, amid temptations, they hold the mind back from falling into consent to sin.

For we necessarily act according to whatever delights us more. For example, the appearance of a beautiful woman comes before us and arouses the delight of fornication. But if the inner and sincere beauty—the beauty of chastity—delights us more through the grace that is in the faith of Christ, then we live and act according to it.

Thus, while sin does not reign in us so that we obey its desires, righteousness reigns through love, and with great delight we do whatever we know pleases God in accordance with it. What I have said about chastity and fornication, I wish to be understood about the other matters as well.

### 50

Nor should it cause concern either that he did not enumerate the works of the flesh in precisely the same number and order in this Epistle as in the Epistle to the Corinthians, or that he set fewer spiritual goods against a greater number of carnal vices, or that he did not arrange them correspondingly—for example, chastity against fornication, purity against impurity, and so on.

His purpose was not to teach how many there are, but in what category some are to be avoided and others desired. By the terms “flesh” and “Spirit,” he was declaring that we must be converted from the punishment of sin and from sin itself to the grace of the Lord and to righteousness.

Otherwise, by abandoning the temporal grace through which the Lord died for us, we will not attain the eternal rest in which the Lord lives for us. Nor, by failing to understand the temporal punishment in which the Lord deigned to subdue us through the mortality of the flesh, will we fall into the everlasting punishment prepared for those who persist in pride against the Lord.

When, after mentioning many works of the flesh, he added “and things like these,” he sufficiently showed that he had not arranged them according to a carefully examined number, but had set them forth in freer speech.

He did the same with the spiritual fruits. For he did not say, “Against these there is no law,” but “Against such things”—that is, whether these or other things of the same kind.

### 51

Nevertheless, those who examine the matter carefully will see that the opposition between carnal and spiritual works is not entirely disordered and confused. The reason it is concealed is that fewer or individual virtues are set against several vices.

For since he placed fornications at the head of the carnal vices and love at the head of the spiritual virtues, who could be a student of the divine Scriptures without being moved to investigate the rest?

If fornication is love released and wandering away from legitimate marriage, pursuing the freedom to satisfy lust, what is joined more legitimately to spiritual fruitfulness than the soul to God? The more firmly it clings to him, the more incorrupt it is. It clings through love.

Love is therefore rightly opposed to fornication, since the preservation of chastity is found in love alone.

Impurities are all the disturbances conceived from that fornication; joy, with its tranquility, is opposed to them.

The service of idols is the final fornication of the soul. For its sake the most furious war was also waged against the Gospel and those reconciled to God; although its remnants have long since been worn down, they still still smolder.

Peace is therefore opposed to it—the peace by which we are reconciled to God. When that same peace is also preserved with human beings, the vices of sorceries, enmities, contentions, rivalries, hostilities, and dissensions are healed in us.

So that these matters may be rightly managed among those with whom we live, patience serves for enduring, kindness for caring, and goodness for forgiving.

Against heresies there is faith; against envy, gentleness; against drunkenness and revelry, self-control.

### 52

Let no one suppose that envy is the same as rivalry. They are close to one another, and because of that closeness either term is often used for the other: rivalry for envy, or envy for rivalry.

But since both are used here in their respective places, they certainly demand that we distinguish them.

Rivalry is pain of mind when another person attains something that two or more people desired and that cannot be possessed by more than one of them. Peace cures this, because we desire what, if all who desire it attain it, makes them one in it.

Envy, however, is pain of mind when someone seems unworthy to attain something that you yourself did not desire. Gentleness cures this when a person refers the matter to God’s judgment,

[Note: [Col. 2142] Three manuscripts read: “recalling himself.”]

does not resist God’s will and trusts more that the matter has been rightly done than that it was unworthy, as he had supposed.

### 53. [Galatians V, 24]

They have crucified their flesh with its passions and desires, as he goes on to say, those who belong to Christ Jesus. And by what means have they crucified it, unless by that chaste fear which endures for ever and ever (Psalm XVIII, 10), through which we take care not to offend the one whom we love with our whole heart, whole soul, and whole mind? An adulterous woman does not fear that she may be guarded by her husband in the same way as a chaste woman fears that she may be abandoned by him: the presence of her husband is grievous to the former, his absence to the latter. And therefore the former fear is corrupt and does not wish this age to pass away; the latter, however, endures for ever and ever. It is of this fear that the prophet desires to be crucified when he says: “Pierce my flesh with nails, because of your fear” (Psalm CXVIII, 120). This is the cross of which the Lord says: “Take up your cross and follow me” (Matthew XVI, 24).

### 54. [Galatians V, 25]

“If we live by the Spirit,” he says, “let us also follow the Spirit.” It is certainly clear that we live according to that which we have followed; and we shall follow that which we have loved. Therefore, if two things stand opposed to one another—the commandment of righteousness and carnal habit—and both are loved, we shall follow that which we have loved more. If both are loved equally, we shall follow neither of them; rather, whether through fear or unwillingly, we shall be dragged toward one side or the other. Or, if we fear both equally as well, we shall undoubtedly remain in danger, shaken by the alternating fluctuation of love and fear. “Let the peace of Christ therefore prevail in our hearts” (Colossians III, 15).

Then God does not despise prayers and groans, the right hand of his mercy invoked for aid, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart; rather, through the peril from which he has delivered them, he kindles a greater love for himself. They were mistaken in this respect: they could not deny that they ought to follow the Holy Spirit, the defender and leader of their freedom; but, having turned carnally toward servile works, they did not understand that they were trying to go backward. For this reason he does not say, “If we live by the Spirit, let us follow the Spirit,” but, “Let us follow the Spirit.” They admitted that they ought to serve the Holy Spirit, but wished to follow him not by their spirit, but by their flesh; they did not obtain God’s grace spiritually, but placed their hope of salvation in carnal circumcision and other practices of the same kind.

### 55. [Galatians V, 26]

“Let us not become desirous of empty glory,” he says, “envying one another and provoking one another.” This is stated with truly magnificent and altogether divine order. After instructing them against those by whom they were being led into the servitude of the Law, he warns them against this danger: that, having become better instructed and now wishing to answer the accusations of carnal people, they might devote themselves to quarrels and, while no longer serving the burdens of the Law, might serve empty desires through their appetite for empty glory.

### 56. [Galatians VI, 1]

Nothing proves a spiritual person so clearly as the treatment of another’s sin: whether he considers that person’s restoration rather than his humiliation, assistance rather than abuse, and undertakes as much as his ability permits. Therefore he says: “Brothers, even if someone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person.”

Then, lest anyone think that he is restoring another even while arrogantly attacking and mocking the sinner, or proudly detesting him as incurable, he adds: “In a spirit of gentleness, keeping watch over yourself, lest you also be tempted.” Nothing inclines us so greatly toward mercy as consideration of our own danger. Thus he wished them neither to fail in correcting their brothers nor to devote themselves to combat. Many people, when awakened from sleep, want to quarrel; or, conversely, when forbidden to quarrel, want to go back to sleep.

Therefore, through consideration of their common danger, peace and love must be preserved in the heart.

**Note:** [Col. 2143] Am. Er.: “and may consideration of the common danger be preserved in the heart.” The manuscripts likewise read this, with only one exception.

The manner of speech—whether it is delivered more severely or more gently—must be moderated according to what the health of the person whom you are correcting appears to require. For in another place he says: “The servant of the Lord must not quarrel, but must be gentle toward all, teachable, patient.” And lest anyone think from this that he must cease correcting another’s error, observe what he adds: “Correcting with modesty those who hold contrary opinions” (2 Timothy II, 24–25).

How can one correct “with modesty,” and yet be “correcting,” unless we retain gentleness in our heart while applying some medicinal sharpness through the word of correction? Nor do I see how the following statement in the same Epistle should be understood otherwise: “Preach the word; be urgent in season and out of season; reprove, exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching” (ibid. IV, 2).

For being “out of season” is certainly contrary to being “in season,” and no medicine heals unless it is applied at the proper time. Nevertheless, the passage may also be divided in this way: “Be urgent in season,” with the next sense being, “Reprove out of season,” and then the remaining words joined together: “Exhort, rebuke with all patience and teaching.” In that case, you are considered timely when you press forward by building up; but when you tear down through reproof, you should not care even if you seem untimely, provided that what is untimely to such people is necessary.

Thus the two following expressions may each be referred to one of the two preceding ones: “Exhort when you are urgent in season; rebuke when you reprove out of season.” Then the final two may likewise be referred to them, but in reverse order: “with all patience,” in order to endure the indignation of those whom you are tearing down; and “with teaching,” in order to instruct the purposes of those whom you are building up.

Yet even if the passage is divided in the more customary manner—“Be urgent in season; and, if this does not advance you, out of season”—it should be understood in such a way that you never abandon what is timely. Thus you should understand “out of season” to mean that you seem untimely to the person who does not willingly hear what is said against him. You, however, should know that it is timely for him, and you should maintain toward him in your mind love and concern for his health, with gentleness, modesty, and brotherly feeling.

Many people later, reflecting on what they have heard and how justly they have heard it, have reproached themselves more gravely and severely. Although they may seem to depart from the physician more agitated, they are gradually healed as the force of the word penetrates to their innermost parts. This would not happen if we always waited for a person in danger, with his limbs already decaying, to decide when he was willing either to be burned or cut.

Even physicians of the body, who treat people with a view to earthly payment, do not observe such a rule. For who is found who has not experienced their knife or fire while bound? And those who willingly submit to being bound are the rarer ones. Many resist, declaring that they would rather die than be treated in that way; and the physicians, scarcely leaving the tongue itself free, bind all their limbs—not according to their own wishes, nor according to the resistance of the patient, but according to the judgment of the art itself. Yet the physician’s spirit is neither disturbed by the insults and reproaches of those who suffer, nor does his hand cease its work.

But the ministers of heavenly medicine either wish to see the splinter in their brother’s eye while a beam of hatred remains in their own (Matthew VII, 3), or they prefer to see a sinner’s death, which they can more easily bear, than to hear the word of one who is indignant. This would not happen if, in treating another’s soul, we brought as healthy a spirit to the work as those physicians bring healthy hands to the treatment of another’s limbs.

### 57.

The task of reproving another’s sin must therefore never be undertaken unless, after examining our conscience through inward questioning, we have clearly answered before God that we are acting out of love. If the abuse, threats, or even persecutions of the person whom you are reproving have wounded your spirit, and if he still appears capable of being healed through your efforts, say nothing until you have first been healed yourself. Otherwise, you may perhaps consent, through your carnal impulses, to do harm and may present your tongue as a weapon of unrighteousness to sin (Romans VI, 13), returning evil for evil or abuse for abuse (1 Peter III, 9).

Whatever you say with a wounded spirit is the thrust of one who is punishing, not the love of one who is correcting. Love, and say whatever you wish: what has sounded outwardly like a curse will in no way be a curse, if you remember and realize that, through the sword of God’s word, you wish to be the person’s liberator from the siege of his vices.

But if, as often happens, you undertake such an action out of love and approach it with a loving heart, yet during the process something creeps in while resistance is offered—something that turns you away from striking the person’s vice and makes you hostile to the person himself—then afterward you must wash away such dust with tears. It will be much more salutary to remember how we ought not to pride ourselves over the sins of others, since we sin while reproving those sins, and since the anger of the sinner more easily makes us angry than his misery makes us compassionate.

### 58. [Galatians VI, 2]

“Bear one another’s burdens, and so you will fulfill the law of Christ”—the law, certainly, of love. If the person who loves his neighbor fulfills the Law, and love of neighbor is also strongly commended in the earlier Scriptures (Leviticus XIX, 18), and if the same apostle says elsewhere that all the commandments of the Law are summed up in this love (Romans XIII, 8–9), it is clear that the Scripture given to the earlier people is also the law of Christ, which he came to fulfill through love (Matthew V, 17), since it was not fulfilled through fear.

The same Scripture and the same commandment are therefore called the Old Testament when they restrain slaves who desire earthly goods, but the New Testament when they raise up free people who burn with desire for eternal goods.

### 59. [Galatians VI, 3–5]

“For if anyone,” he says, “thinks that he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself.” His admirers do not deceive him; he himself does so, because he is closer to himself than they are and prefers to seek himself in them rather than in himself.

But what does the Apostle say? “Let each person test his own work, and then he will have glory in himself alone, and not in another”—that is, inwardly in his own conscience, and not in another, that is, when another praises him.

“For each person,” he says, “will bear his own burden.” Our admirers therefore do not lessen the burdens of our conscience. Indeed, would that they did not also increase them, since we often neglect to heal them when they are offended, lest our praise be diminished, or we ostentatiously display something of our own to them rather than show it with steadfastness.

I pass over the things people fabricate and falsely claim about themselves for the sake of human praise. What is more obscurely blind than this: to seek a person’s error in order to obtain the emptiest glory, while despising God as witness in one’s heart? As though the error of the person who thinks you good could in any way be compared with your error when you strive to please someone through a false good and displease God through a true evil.

### 60. [Galatians VI, 6]

I think the remaining matters are quite plain. For it is also a customary command that the preacher of God’s word should receive the necessities of life from the person to whom he preaches. They were to be urged toward good works, so that they might minister even to Christ in his need and stand at his right hand with the sheep; so that the love produced by faith might operate more powerfully in them than the fear of the Law could.

No one ought to command this with greater confidence than this apostle, who supported himself by the work of his own hands (Acts XVIII, 3; XX, 34; 1 Corinthians IV, 12; 1 Thessalonians II, 9; 2 Thessalonians III, 8). He did not wish these things to be done for him, so that he might demonstrate to everyone that he was admonishing them more heavily for the benefit of those who provided such things than for the sake of those for whom they were provided.

### 61. [Galatians VI, 7–10]

As for what he adds next—“Do not be deceived: God is not mocked; for whatever a person sows, that he will also reap”—he knows amid what sayings of lost people those struggle who are established in faith in things they do not see. They see the sowing of their works, but they do not see the harvest.

Nor is a harvest such as is usually rendered here promised to them, because “the righteous person lives by faith” (Habakkuk II, 4). “For the one who sows in his flesh,” he says, “will reap corruption from the flesh.” He says this of those who love pleasures more than God. A person sows in his flesh when he does everything—even if what he does appears good—for the sake of being well off in a carnal way.

“But the one who sows in the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.” Sowing in the Spirit means serving righteousness from faith with love and refusing to obey the desires of sin, even though these desires arise from mortal flesh.

The harvest of eternal life will come when the final enemy, death, has been destroyed; when what is mortal has been swallowed up by life; and when this corruptible body has put on incorruption. In this third state, therefore, in which we are under grace, we sow in tears whenever desires arise from the animal body. By refusing to consent to them, we resist them, so that we may reap in joy when, after the body has also been transformed, no trouble or danger of temptation will afflict us in any part of our being.

The animal body itself is also counted as seed. “A natural body is sown,” he says elsewhere; the addition, “a spiritual body will rise,” belongs to the harvest (1 Corinthians XV, 26, 44). To this judgment the prophet also sings in harmony when he says: “Those who sow in tears will reap in joy” (Psalm CXXV, 5).

To sow well—that is, to do good—is easier than to persevere in doing so. The fruit usually consoles the labor, but our harvest is promised at the end; and therefore perseverance is necessary. “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew X, 22). And the prophet cries: “Wait for the Lord; act manfully; let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm XXVI, 14).

This is what the Apostle now says: “While doing good, let us not grow weak; for at the proper time we shall reap without weariness. Therefore, while we have the opportunity, let us do good to all, but especially to those who belong to the household of faith.”

Who are we to understand by these people except Christians? Eternal life is to be desired for all with equal love, but the same acts of love cannot be shown to everyone.

### 62. [Galatians VI, 11–14]

Then, after teaching that the works of the Law themselves—which are beneficial and pertain to good morals—can be fulfilled only through the love that arises from faith, and not through servile fear, he returns to the point on which the whole matter turns:

“You see with what large letters I have written to you with my own hand.” He takes care lest anyone deceive the unwary under the name of his Epistle.

“Those who wish to please in the flesh,” he says, “compel you to be circumcised, only so that they may not suffer persecution for the cross of Christ.” For the Jews persecuted greatly those who appeared to abandon such inherited observances. The apostle shows clearly that he himself does not fear them when he wished to write such a letter with his own hand.

He therefore teaches that fear was still at work in those who, as though established under the Law, were compelling the Gentiles to be circumcised. For those who are circumcised do not keep the Law. He calls keeping the Law such things as not killing, not committing adultery, and not bearing false witness, together with any similar commands that plainly pertain to good morals. It has already been said that these cannot be fulfilled except through love and hope of eternal goods, which are received through faith.

“But they wish you to be circumcised,” he says, “so that they may glory in your flesh”—that is, so that they may not only avoid persecution from the Jews, who could scarcely tolerate the Law’s being proclaimed among the uncircumcised, but may also glory before them in having made so many proselytes. For the Lord said that the Jews used to travel around sea and land to make one proselyte (Matthew XXIII, 15).

“But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.” “The world has been crucified to me,” he says, “so that it may not hold me; and I to the world, so that I may not hold it.” That is, the world cannot harm me, nor do I desire anything from the world.

Whoever glories in the cross of Christ does not wish to please in the flesh, because he does not fear the persecutions of carnal people. Christ first endured these persecutions in order to be crucified and to provide an example for those who follow his footsteps.

### 63. [Galatians VI, 15–16]

“For neither circumcision is anything, nor uncircumcision.” He preserves to the end the principle of indifference, so that no one might think that he acted deceitfully in circumcising Timothy, or that he might do so in anyone’s case if some such reason should arise. For he shows that circumcision itself does not harm believers, but rather the placing of the hope of salvation in such observances.

In the Acts of the Apostles, too, they are found persuading people to circumcision in precisely this way: they deny that those who have believed from among the Gentiles can be saved otherwise (Acts XV, 1). The Apostle therefore refutes not the danger of the act itself, but the ruinous error attached to it.

“Neither circumcision, therefore, is anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” By “new creation” he means a new life through faith in Jesus Christ. The word deserves attention. It is difficult to find people called “creation” even when, through believing, they have already entered into adoption as sons. Yet he says elsewhere: “If anyone is therefore a new creation in Christ, the old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new; and all things are from God” (2 Corinthians V, 17–18).

But when he says, “The creation itself will also be delivered from the slavery of corruption,” and afterward, “And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit” (Romans VIII, 21, 23), he distinguishes those who have believed from the designation “creation.” In this way he sometimes calls the same people human beings and sometimes not human beings.

For in one place he reproaches the Corinthians by saying that they were still human beings: “Are you not human beings, and do you not walk according to human standards?” (1 Corinthians III, 3–4). Likewise, in one place he calls the same Lord not human even after the resurrection, as at the beginning of this Epistle, where he says, “Not from human beings, nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ” (Galatians I, 1); elsewhere he calls him human, as where he says, “For there is one God, and one mediator between God and human beings, the human being Christ Jesus” (1 Timothy II, 5).

“And whoever,” he says, “follows this rule, peace and mercy be upon them, and upon the Israel of God”—that is, upon those who are truly being prepared for the vision of God, not upon those who are called by this name but, through carnal blindness, do not wish to see the Lord, since they reject his grace and desire to be servants of the times.

### 64. [Galatians VI, 17]

“As for the rest,” he says, “let no one cause me trouble.” He does not wish, through turbulent disputes, to be wearied by arguments about a matter sufficiently explained both in the Epistle he wrote to the Romans and in this one.

“For I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body”—that is, I have other conflicts and struggles with my flesh, which fight alongside me in the persecutions that I suffer.

The word *stigmata* refers to certain marks of servile punishments. Thus, if a slave, for example, had been placed in fetters because of an offense—that is, because of a fault—or had suffered something of this kind, he was said to bear marks; and for that reason he belonged to an inferior rank under the law of manumission.

The Apostle therefore wished to call the punishments he endured through persecution “marks,” as though they were signs of penalties. He knew that these had been imposed on him because of the guilt of the persecution with which he had persecuted the churches of Christ, just as the Lord himself said to Ananias when Ananias feared him as a persecutor of Christians: “I will show him what he must suffer for my name” (Acts IX, 16).

Nevertheless, because of the forgiveness of sins, in which he had been baptized, all those tribulations did not lead him to destruction but advanced him toward the crown of victory.

### 65. [Galatians VI, 18]

The conclusion of the Epistle is plainly in the form of a subscription, for he uses it in several other Epistles as well:

“The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers. Amen.”

---

# Appendix to the Third Volume of the Works of Saint Augustine

Containing several treatises on Scripture formerly and falsely attributed to him, namely:

- Three books *On the Marvels of Sacred Scripture*.
- *On the Blessings of the Patriarch Jacob*.
- *Questions on the Old and New Testaments*, formerly included in Volume IV.
- An exposition *On the Apocalypse of John*, formerly included in Volume IX.

**Note:** [Col. 2149] Certain other short works formerly contained in the Appendix to Volume III, since they do not pertain to Sacred Scripture, have been transferred to other volumes: *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, *On Faith to Peter*, *On Spirit and Soul*, and *Short Questions on the Trinity* to Volume VIII; and *The Sentences of Prosper* to Volume IX.

[Col. 2149]

# [ON THE MARVELS OF SACRED SCRIPTURE]

[Col. 2149]

## NOTICE ON THE WORK THAT FOLLOWS IMMEDIATELY (C, G, S)*

This short work corresponds neither in style nor in intellectual character to Saint Augustine, according to the judgment of Erasmus and the theologians of Louvain. Saint Thomas had already understood this long ago; in Part III, Question 45, Article 3, he does not wish these books to carry authority and says that they are falsely attributed to Augustine.

In the manuscripts and earlier editions—except Erasmus’s edition—the work is preceded by a preface in epistolary form. From this alone it can be established that the author of these books is not Augustine of Hippo but another person of the same name, who dedicates the work here to bishops and presbyters, especially those of Carthage.

Yet below he seems to indicate that he was an Englishman or Irishman, in Book I, Chapter 7. There, while making an incidental observation about islands, he names Ireland as the only one among them; shortly afterward he calls the tides *Ledon* and *Malina*, terms in use among the English and neighboring inhabitants of the British Sea, especially in Bede’s age.

Then, in Book II, Chapter 4, he records the death of a certain Manichaean among the Irish. Moreover, when discussing the cycles in that passage, he clearly shows that he wrote these books after the year 660 of Christ. We suspect that they were dedicated not to presbyters of Carthage but to those of monasteries in Canterbury, Wales—if the word was already in use—or Kilkenny, and so forth.

[Col. 2149]

# THREE BOOKS ON THE MARVELS OF SACRED SCRIPTURE

To the most venerable bishops and presbyters of cities and monasteries, especially those of Carthage,

**Note:** [Col. 2149] Perhaps “those of Canterbury.”

Augustine, entirely subject to you, wishes salvation in Christ.

Most blessed men, constrained by the command of my father Eusebius, who was still living, for the undertaking of this work, and also urged on by your Christian exhortations—above all compelled by the authority of the most venerable master of the empire—I have composed, with the Lord’s favor, three books on the marvels of Sacred Scripture of the Old and New Testament, in historical exposition and with as much brevity as I could. In them, the boldness of undertaking the work will be excused by the authority of those who commanded it.

For although I saw that I was unequal to the matters under discussion, I did not dare to resist the commands of those giving orders or turn aside in another direction, knowing with complete certainty that a greater punishment follows one who evades a command in disobedience than the accusation of those who censure a person who obeys a command yet is unequal to the task imposed.

The prophet Jonah found greater danger when he fled amid the waves of the sea (Jonah II, 1) than the censure he feared he would have endured from his people had he carried out what was commanded. Likewise, the prophet of the altar at Bethel, because he did not undergo the hunger and thirst of the arduous journey as he had been commanded, soon encountered death on the road, having eaten his fill, as the punishment of disobedience (1 Kings XIII).

Jeremiah, moreover, was still a boy and, when he was sent by the Lord to prophesy, possessed neither literary learning nor the strength of mature judgment. But because he had obeyed the command, he deserved to receive knowledge that he had not possessed (Jeremiah I, 4–9).

I therefore do not consider the poverty of my small ability, but rather the prudent authority of those who commanded me. For if you did not believe that there was some spark of light in me, you would in no way have imposed upon me the ingenious labor of so important a work.

The arrangement of these volumes is such that the first is designated as dealing with the Pentateuch of Moses, the second with the Prophets,

**Note:** [Col. 2151] An old codex of the monastery of Saint-Ouen at Rouen reads “with prophecy.”

and the third with the New Testament.

The chief purpose of all this labor is to show that in all matters in which something appears to have happened outside the ordinary course of daily administration, God is not making a new nature there, but governing the very nature that he established in the beginning.

Moreover, in this work we have taken care to set aside, for the present, interpretations of figures and to explain only the account and sequence of the events themselves. For the passages in which we have touched upon certain matters in historical narrative possess a multiplicity of meanings; and if we were to discuss each of these individually, we would provide readers with many books and the labor of a much longer work.

We have judged it right to omit this especially because all the authors who have undertaken to explain these passages have adhered to the mystical interpretation of allegories—that is, to the figurative exposition found in them.

Whether this work perishes or survives depends upon your judgment. From one of you, namely Bathanus,

**Note:** [Col. 2152] The Audoenian manuscript reads “Barbanus.” Perhaps “Baithanus,” who was a Scottish bishop, according to Bede, Book II of the *History*, Chapter 19.

after my father Manchianus,

**Note:** [Col. 2152] The Audoenian manuscript reads “Manchianus.”

I received whatever understanding I have added; and from another, as I believe, I received from the utterance of his mouth the cause of this labor in place of his exertions [the reading is uncertain]. From all readers generally, however, our prayer and request earnestly asks that they not, for any reason, become disgusted before they understand what has been said by reading it through.

# BOOK ONE  
## On the Pentateuch of Moses

[Col. 2151]

## CHAPTER ONE  
### On God the Creator and the Establishment of Creatures

With the help of almighty God, when we desire to undertake a discourse on the marvels of things, where should we more suitably begin and take our point of departure than from the very Creator of all things, of whom Scripture often testifies, saying: “He does great and inscrutable things and marvelous things, of which there is no number” (Job IX, 10)?

He established what may be called the principal foundation of all these marvels when he made all the creatures that he had created from nothing.

The eternal and almighty Creator of things, always remaining triune and undivided, without any diminution of his power, alone preceded all creatures outside time. Then, so that he might also display through creatures the immeasurable goodness, power, and benevolence that he had previously possessed in himself alone, from formless matter—which he himself had first created from nothing—he divided the manifold forms of all visible and invisible things, that is, of sensible and insensible things, of intellectual things and things lacking intellect.

As the authority of the Book of Genesis confirms, this is shown to have been accomplished through the succession of six days, so that it is firmly declared that on the sixth day he completed everything pertaining to the establishment and instruction of creation. For it is written:

“God completed all his works on the sixth day, and he blessed the seventh day, because on it he rested from all his works” (Genesis II, 2).

From this it is understood that God perfected all things on the sixth day, so that on the seventh day he appears to have ceased not from labor but from creating.

But when the Lord Jesus answered the Jews who were questioning him about the rest of the Sabbath, “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V, 17), we believe that he completed everything on the sixth day and rested on the seventh, yet we do not doubt that he continues to work until now.

How the same God is understood to have completed his work then and to be working now must be investigated more subtly. On the sixth day he perfected the natures of creatures, which he has not ceased to govern even now. On the seventh day he rested from the work of creation, but he never ceases from the administration of governance.

God is therefore to be understood as Creator then and Governor now. Consequently, even if we see something new arising among creatures, we must think that God is not creating a new nature there, but governing one created long ago.

Yet the one who created the creature is so powerful in governing it that he seems to create a new nature when he draws forth from the hidden recesses of nature what lay concealed within it.

Therefore, when things display the will and power of their governor through an unusual act of governance—something they do not accomplish through the effectiveness of daily administration—such events are called marvels in Scripture.

But since we shall discuss these marvels more extensively later, when we come to their several passages, let this remain fixed for the present: after completing the creation of the natures, God rested from his work on the seventh day, and thereafter, throughout all time, he does not cease governing the whole of creation.

Although it is said that all creation was established through the succession of six days, this succession of days is not to be understood as a period of time; rather, it indicates the succession of works. For afterward the narrator of the history divided in speech what God did not divide in the completion of his work.

God created all things together (Ecclesiasticus XVIII, 1), when by one will he ordained that the manifold variety of all species should come into being. In that one will he made all things together and outside time, although from their origin he does not cease to administer them through time.

## CHAPTER TWO  
### On the Dissimilar Sin of Rational Natures
In this ordering of all things, therefore, spiritual and invisible creation came forth first in its original state. Then, lest what was interior not also be exterior in God’s works, corporeal and visible creation likewise began to come into being. In it, according to the principal and general division of all things, the Creator established two rational natures: one spiritual, the other corporeal—namely, angels and human beings—and, in accordance with the difference between their natures, he also distinguished the places of their habitation. For he granted heaven as a dwelling-place to the angels and earth to human beings.

After these beings had been established, the sin of both natures followed—of angels, that is, and of human beings. But the transgression of the commandment that occurred among human beings is narrated in the history of the book of Genesis. To those who consider it, however, a very considerable question presents itself: for what reason Scripture’s testimonies conceal how the sin of the angels occurred.

For although, under the person of the king of Babylon, the prophet sets forth words concerning that angelic fall, saying, “I shall sit upon the mountain of the Testament, on the sides of the north; I shall ascend above the heights of the clouds, and I shall set my throne toward the north, and I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. 14:13–14), these words can very easily be understood historically of the king of Babylon, unless perhaps, by a figurative interpretation, the words are transferred allegorically from the body to the head. [Col. 2153] Hence the question raised here is not resolved, since the cause of the fall, its sentence, and its punishment are not disclosed historically in the Gospel itself.

Unless perhaps someone should say, as others believe, that his original sin consisted in the deception of humanity through the serpent, by which he also received the sentence of punishment, when the Lord said, “Cursed are you above all cattle and all the beasts of the earth; upon your breast you shall walk, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14). But far be it from us to think that an angel could persuade a human being to sin on earth unless he had first sinned himself in heaven, as the Lord says: “I saw Satan falling like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10:18). For how could he himself have envied human happiness unless he had first lost his own blessedness?

Therefore, it must be believed that the devil’s fall preceded not only human sin but also that perfection of creation which took place on the sixth day, when the Lord pronounced concerning those who were to be condemned on the last day: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25:41). When, then, was that fire prepared, unless at the perfection of all creation? Unless perhaps we say that God created something after the perfection of the sixth day—which God forbid, lest we make Scripture, or rather ourselves, liars.

Therefore, the sin of the one for whom a prison was prepared in that ordering of creation originally preceded those creatures. For, as Scripture says, “He was a liar from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth” (John 8:44).

It remains, therefore, that we explain the angelic fall, whose cause was concealed by the Lord, while we do not doubt that the angel who was the beginning of God’s creatures fell. The true physician did not wish to disclose how the angelic wound had occurred, since he did not intend to heal it afterward. Nor did he disclose by what sentence of punishment the angel had been expelled, since he did not recall him by repentance.

But how the human sin occurred is made known, because there is hope that the human being may at some time merit pardon. And God preferred to disclose how the human being had been expelled, since he restored him again to his former state at the last. Nor did he conceal how the human being received the sentence of punishment, since he did not refuse at some time to grant him satisfaction through the pardon of his mercy.
