Considering this difference between human beings and angels, the Apostle says: “For God did not take hold of angels, but of the seed of Abraham” (Heb. 2:16). For when the merciful Creator, remaining in that supreme and unchangeable substance of God the Father, willed to empty himself by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2:7), he took hold not of an angelic nature but of a human one.

But another question also arises. Since God did not spare the sinning angels, yet released the sinning human being from guilt by assuming human flesh, why, then, was the highest angel struck down with an irrevocable punishment, while the human being, though sinning and transgressing the commandment of his Creator, was afterward recalled to repentance with pardon, with John, the Lord, and Peter crying out: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Luke 3:3; Matt. 4:17; Acts 2:38)?

The angel, therefore, established in the highest rank of his honor, had no change into a more excellent state available to him except that, being confirmed by contemplation of his Creator, he should remain in the condition in which he had been created. For this reason he could not be recalled after falling, since he fell from the most exalted state of his order.

But the human being, still placed on earth, appointed to the duty of generation and assigned to the consumption of food, would have received a change into a higher, better, and spiritual life without death if, for as long as he remained in this condition, he had persevered in keeping the commandment. Before he reached that higher state, sin snatched him away; and therefore he immediately fell from that lower order of his, namely, the immortality of his body, as the Lord says: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. 3:19).

By the Creator’s mercy, therefore, the human being is recalled through the Lord’s Passion to that blessedness which he had not yet attained while sinning. If he had fallen from it as the angel did, he would never again have been recalled, since he would never again have reached that order—that is, the immortality of his body—unless, after the death of all things had been accomplished, that blessedness to which we are recalled should be restored through the resurrection.

Yet the restoration will not be to that order or condition from which the first human being had fallen, but to another and higher one, which he hoped for, as the Lord says: “They will be like the angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22:30).

Moreover, as an addition to the accumulation of the devil’s sin, this also occurred: immediately after he sinned, he fell into the pit of despair. For if he had not despaired of obtaining pardon for his offense, he would never have sought to bring about the loss of salvation for the human being who consented to him. Whoever desires pardon for an earlier sin does not in any way prepare to add another.

Through this, therefore, he found the pit of destruction not only for himself but also became, through his agency, the cause of destruction for the sinning human being. Yet this occurred for the alleviation of the human being’s offense: not only did he not discover the transgression of the commandment by himself alone, but he consented to the serpent’s persuasion; moreover, he did not lead another rational creature into offense against God. Thus he found the door of repentance more easily opened. Whoever does not enter through it will be subject to the loss of eternal life; but whoever washes away sins through repentance will be a companion of angelic blessedness forever.

## CHAPTER III—Abel and Enoch, holding primacy in human righteousness

To show that, from the very beginning of the human race after original sin, human beings could at some time merit pardon, God chose a few people to whom he would reveal knowledge of his friendship. In the course of time he would visit progressively more of them, until, at his coming, he would enlighten the whole human race throughout the entire world.

Among these few, Abel is chosen as the first prince of all human righteousness, and Enoch, second after him, as the most distinguished before the Flood. To these two the highest righteousness is entrusted at the beginning and at the end of the world. One of them, immediately at the beginning of his righteousness and at the very beginning of the world, was crowned amid the triumph of his own blood and seized by martyrdom (Gen. 4:8). The other, still without death (Gen. 5:24), is reserved as a witness for the last age.

To this Abel, then, the Lord Jesus Christ assigned primacy among human beings in righteousness, saying: “From the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah” (Matt. 23:35). In saying “from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah,” and not adding “righteous” after Zechariah, he showed that Zechariah holds the inheritance of Abel’s righteousness.

The same is written in the genealogy of the Savior: “Jesse begot David the king, and David the king begot Solomon” (Matt. 1:5–6). The word “king” is not added to Solomon, although Solomon held a greater dominion in his father’s kingdom. From this, however, it is understood that Solomon possessed the kingdom of his father David by hereditary right, and that the honor of the kingdom belongs more particularly to David because he was the first of that generation to obtain the kingdom. So too Abel held primacy in human righteousness because he was the first righteous person to begin to exist on earth.

Thus, as though by hereditary right, descendants succeed their fathers, and all the righteous take up Abel’s footsteps in every aspect of righteousness. Yet, properly stirred by this inquiry, someone might perhaps ask: “Why, then, since Abel held primacy in righteousness, did God not preserve him without death as a witness for the last age, so that at the end of the world he himself might become a teacher of truth, who at the beginning had been the author of the perfect work?”

A fitting answer can nevertheless be made by one who knows that righteousness consists of three parts. For the whole of righteousness is virginity, priesthood, and martyrdom. This threefold righteousness was found first in Abel: he offered gifts pleasing to God, left no offspring of his race in the world, and earned the crown of martyrdom by the shedding of his blood.

If Abel had remained for a longer period, like Enoch, he would without any doubt have entered into marriage. For he would have lived under the law of that time which said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth” (Gen. 1:28). If he had fulfilled that commandment, he would certainly not have remained a virgin. And if God had preserved him without death, he would never have received primacy in martyrdom.

It was therefore fitting that, in the one who was chosen as the first righteous person on earth, the form of all righteousness should be preserved, and that to the first among human beings after the offense should be granted the privilege of bearing the figure of the Savior, who appears as virgin, priest, and martyr.

Enoch, however, is kept apart from human society for almost the whole duration of the world’s age and is preserved without death, so that in him it might be shown how human beings, if they had not sinned, would have been transformed through the generation of offspring into spiritual life without death. Although he has been preserved for a long time and still lives, he will nevertheless not be able to avoid the debt of death which we all assumed in Adam.

Certainly, this also gives rise to the matter from which the opportunity for writing about marvels seems to have been taken: why, contrary to nature, is this life stretched out for such a very long time beyond the limits of the human lifespan? Yet in this case no new nature is generated for one human being; rather, the original and general condition of all human beings is governed.

For those who consider the history of the book of Genesis, it appears that it was implanted in every human being at the first creation that he should live not only for a long time but forever, unless death, through the sting of sin, had destroyed the limits of nature.

## CHAPTER IV—The fact that only earthly animals were killed in the Flood

As time proceeded, human beings advanced into offense against God through their own pursuits after original sin and fell into forgetfulness of their Creator. When giants had arisen through enormous sin and great bodily stature, God prepared to wash away the crime of the whole earth with water. Having found a man perfect in his generation—namely Noah, son of Lamech—he alone disclosed the mystery of his plan to him and commanded him to construct an ark over a long period of time, so that either Noah, through this deed, might be delivered with his household from the impending death, or those who saw the approaching destruction might be moved by fear and recalled to repentance for their sins (Gen. 6).

But when that judgment was stubbornly and negligently despised, God, offended at an unforeseen time, covered all the spaces of the earth alike with water for the common destruction of the whole world. Except for those whom the ark had enclosed, he destroyed with water brought from heaven everything that can live only on earth—human beings and the other animals (Gen. 7:17–23).

But he did not touch all those creatures that can live in water; he killed only the earthly animals. Here an apparently subtle question, requiring a solution, comes to the aid of those who inquire: why do earthly animals succumb to human punishment more than aquatic animals, when the latter are not supported by a greater number of sinful deeds?

Yet in the sin of the first human being, the earth from which he had tasted was immediately cursed. For the divine oracle declares: “Cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3:17), and so forth. In this matter it should be observed that the very animals that ate the cursed earth could not be free from the curse, especially since the earth was cursed together with its animals.

Again, another question arises: why did God not also curse the waters in Adam’s curse? The answer is very easy: the human being did not drink water contrary to the Lord’s prohibition, but ate of the fruit of the earth.

Apart from these reasons, God spared the waters from Adam’s curse because he had prepared to wash away that curse through water, which was accomplished in the Flood and is now granted through Baptism. For in water and the Holy Spirit all human bodily and spiritual crimes alike are cleansed.

Aquatic creatures, then, do not succumb to the curse of punishment because they do not share in the curse. Accordingly, when the Lord had laid aside the curse of human death by rising again, he ate not the flesh of earthly but of aquatic animals, when, for the confirmation of his resurrection, he took and ate before the disciples a portion of roasted fish and a honeycomb (Luke 24:42–43).

## CHAPTER V—How the animals that can live neither only on land nor only in water escaped the Flood

[Col. 2156]

[Note: This is found in Alcuin, *Book of Questions on Genesis*, question 123.]

A question is also raised concerning the animals that can live neither only on land nor only in water: how did they escape the Flood? Such are otters, sea-calves, and many kinds of birds, which seek their food in the waters but sleep, are nourished, and rest on the sand.

If they were enclosed in the ark, they could not live without the support of the waters; and if they remained outside the ark, when the waters covered everything, where and how could they rest?

Concerning these creatures, then, as I said above, the question is debated: whether by his power God modified one or the other of their natures until the Flood had passed, so that at that time they could live either only in moisture or only on dry land.

But if he had wished to preserve Noah with his household through the ark and not through his power, how would he have wished to preserve these creatures through his power? Or could there have been some refuge for them somewhere among the crags? But how could even those have helped them, when the water covered all the mountains, being twelve cubits higher than they (Gen. 7:20)?

Or could some place of rest for them have been available outside on the roof of the ark? Its length was three hundred cubits, its height thirty, and its breadth fifty; all of this contracted upward on every side to a single cubit, it formed a broad and stable space, so that what preserved those remaining inside without danger might also have served as a refuge for creatures wandering in danger over the deep?

[Note: Ms. Aud.: “sailing.”]

## CHAPTER VI—The bursting forth of the waters of the Flood

Concerning the bursting forth of the waters of the Flood, it is reported: “All the fountains of the great deep were broken open, and the cataracts of heaven were opened, and rain was made for forty days and forty nights” (Gen. 7:11–12). It is added afterward: “The fountains of the deep were closed, and the rains from heaven were restrained” (Gen. 8:2).

We are prevented by the smallness of our knowledge from explaining the difficulty of this matter with a fixed judgment. Nevertheless, let us set forth in impartial speech what the intention of teachers has been able to devise in these matters, assigning greater authority to none of the differing opinions. With regard to these accounts and their individual alternatives, we grant freedom to judge whether they should be approved or rejected.

Inquiry asks whether rivers existed from springs before the Flood. Concerning these, no definite statement at the beginning of creation shows whether they were made or not, except that one spring rose from the earth and, divided into four heads, watered the regions (Gen. 2:6).

Unless perhaps someone should say that even then all the other springs bubbled forth everywhere throughout the entire extent of the earth from that one spring, so that the mention of that original great spring would suffice for the separate identification of all the others.

Or did they not exist before the Flood, until, in that extremely abundant bursting forth of the waters, the channels of all the springs burst forth where they had not previously existed—something we often see happening even now?

Yet it is not said that the springs of the earth, but that the springs of the deep, were broken open: “The springs of the deep were broken open.” But this may be understood generally of springs. For how could the earth have water unless, with the deep lying beneath it, it received through hidden passages the channels of springs? Thus the springs of the deep can also be called the springs of the earth.

But what will those who understand the matter in this way say about what is added shortly afterward, once the forty days of flooding had been completed: “The springs of the great deep were closed, and the rains from heaven were restrained”?

If those springs which now flow through the lands were opened in the Flood, how are they again declared to have been closed? Unless they do not declare that all the springs were closed, but only those through which the outlet of this passage was provided.

They also affirm that this was said only with reference to that time. For the following account declares that the springs which had been closed were afterward opened again, when the waters “went and returned” (Gen. 8:3). Where did they return, unless to the place from which they had come?

Through springs, therefore, that had been opened, the waters had burst forth; afterward, so that the bursting might cease, they were closed. But when the water was called back again, the springs that had been closed were also reopened. For how could the waters, unable to come through closed doors, have gone back in again unless the passages had been opened?

The statement “the cataracts of heaven were opened, and rain was made” likewise involves a question requiring no less careful attention, and it is known to have been debated among investigators according to different opinions.

Some think that these cataracts were opened in the clouds, which are often called heaven in the divine Scriptures. Thus we read: “The heavens will give rain, and the earth will give its fruit” (Jer. 14:22; Ps. 84:13); “He gave them bread from heaven” (Ps. 77:24); “The birds of heaven can dwell there” (Mark 4:32); and “The birds of heaven have nests where they rest” (Luke 9:58).

Those mentioned above therefore think that the cataracts were made in heaven—that is, in the clouds—so that rain might come, just as the whole world acknowledges that such a service is even now carried out through the clouds. But Scripture recalls that the cataracts of heaven were then opened because an unusually great outpouring of rain had occurred.

Others, however, say that these cataracts had first been made in that highest firmament which God had made in the beginning in order to divide the waters from the waters. They say that God had prepared for such a service the waters he had placed above the firmament.

In this ordering of both the upper and lower waters, they perceive, by figurative interpretation, the ministry of holy Baptism: through the rain from heaven they understand the Holy Spirit, and through the flood of the deep the water of Baptism. Thus, just as the upper and lower water washed away the sins of the world’s first life, so the Holy Spirit and water remit the offenses of our former life.

But since in this work we have taken up the meaning of the events themselves rather than a figurative interpretation, let us pursue what pertains to the present subject.

Those, then, who hold that the waters of the firmament came down for the Flood do not believe that rains existed in the world before the Flood. They have been led to this opinion by the rainbow that was established in the clouds after the Flood, investigating the matter from the nature of the creatures themselves. For if any clear rain had fallen before the Flood, the rainbow—that is, that arc—would have appeared in the clear clouds. It is produced by the sun through moist and clear clouds, and it is seen to be produced not only by the sun but sometimes also by the moon in clear clouds.

The first age of the world, newly created, could therefore have been nourished by morning and evening dew without any changes of turbulent air or rains. Just as it had human beings long-lived and vigorous in bodily health, so the world itself, not yet disturbed by any upheavals, could have continued to bear suitable fruits for those who fed upon them. From the second age onward, however, it could have begun to live and flourish amid turbulent movements and stormy disturbances of nature.

This is comparable to what still occurs in the land of Egypt, which is nourished not at all by rains from the clouds but by the moisture of the earth itself, the temperateness of the air, and the rising of the Nile.

But learned and catholic men may determine with certainty how this investigation should be understood.

## CHAPTER VII—The withdrawal of the waters of the Flood

Let us likewise set forth, without presuming upon any authority of our own, what learned and ingenious teachers think concerning the withdrawal of the waters of the Flood. Here a tangled question presents itself to diligent minds: if the waters of the Flood left any empty space when they occupied the earth’s expanse, and if they had left no such space, what did they fill when they withdrew?

Concerning this inquiry, there are two opinions among the teachers regarding the waters that flowed down from the cataracts of heaven.

Either, as some believe, they were recalled through those same cataracts; and just as the clouds customarily draw watery rains from the sea, so the space of that upper firmament could recall to itself from the clouds the waters that it had sent forth. For Scripture says: “The waters went and returned.” Where, then, did they go, unless to the place from which they had come?

If, therefore, the waters had flowed down from that exalted firmament, as we said according to the opinion of some, and if they abandoned the space they had occupied because they were recalled there, what is surprising if they filled the very spaces they had left?

Or, certainly, if it is granted that the same abundance of rain was shown to have come from the clouds, what conflicts with an intelligent understanding if it turned back again toward the clouds, just as it is observed to occur in the daily administration of things, when rain appears to be sent forth from the clouds and then drawn back again?

Those, moreover, who do not allow that rain existed before the Flood hold a different view concerning the withdrawal of the waters. Although they declare that the waters were diffused from the firmament, they nevertheless affirm that they returned only to the clouds. That excess which the water flowing down from above had supplied still produces, throughout all time, turbulent movements of the air and different hemispheres in the clouds. Through reciprocal changes, the same cloudy air now releases itself into the lower regions of the world—that is, earth and sea—and now gathers itself back from those same places, sea and earth.

The same thing occurs in the human breast: through reciprocal changes, the breath is drawn back again to be resumed in the same manner in which it is released.

Among these various opinions and the many complications of the teachers, we accept this as fixed in our minds: whatever water had come down from above, so that the earth might be stripped of its waters, was licked up by the wind. For it is written: “The Lord sent a wind over the earth, and the waters were diminished” (Gen. 8:1).

Whether the wind had gathered the watery seas into the clouds, or whether the space of the upper firmament had taken them back, the learned may determine with certainty.

But those waters that had poured forth abundantly from the broken springs of the deep returned again, at the Lord’s command, by the same routes through which they had come.

Yet another common question arises for us here, one that seemed to have been resolved in the other matters: if, when the waters had flooded the earth, they left some space, what space was it? And if they had no such space, what did they fill when they returned?

Others discuss this question as follows: by the command of God, the sea could then grow beyond its customary measure through the opening of those springs, overflow its boundaries in an extraordinary inundation across all the spaces of the earth, and then take back into itself what it had lost. It could also carry into the space of the earth what belonged to the lower waters.

For the earth is accustomed to absorb the waters placed above it and draw them back into itself through the springs; nor do we see anything contrary to custom when even very small things grow larger. Nor is it contrary to the nature of the earth that it should continually consume the moisture placed upon it, especially since God has granted this power even to his saints, as he gave it to Elijah and Elisha (3 Kings 18:44–45; 4 Kings 3:20).

[Note: Ms. Aud.: “he gave it to widows.”]

Seas also are accustomed to grow beyond their ancient boundaries and diminish and cut away areas of land, as old men still living in our time confirm that they have seen.

Thus they also create islands which, as many assert, did not exist from the beginning of the created world, when they separate nearby promontories from the mainland by marine boundaries.

From this it is understood that those wild creatures enclosed within the circuits of islands are proved to have been found there at the separation of the islands from the mainland, not transported there through human care. For who, for example, would transport wolves, deer, wild boars, foxes, badgers, hares, and sesquivoli to Ireland? Or, if they were domestic animals at that time, how could they have escaped the hand of the person carrying them so that all these kinds now appear to wander through the forests?

Some authors, however, say that the earth itself produces these kinds of beasts and wild animals. They think that the animals enclosed on the islands were created not from the ark but from the earth itself.

Even if someone should judge this opinion of theirs concerning the withdrawal of the Flood’s waters to be acceptable and sufficient, the question nevertheless remains entangled in our minds. For it is continually reborn through the daily inundations and withdrawals of the Ocean.

Just as we do not know from where this inundation comes or where it withdraws, so we do not know the withdrawal of the Flood. For this daily inundation always takes place twice a day, at regular intervals, over a period of twenty-four hours, and alternates in successive weeks between Ledo and Malina.

[Note: Bede, *On the Nature of Time*, chapter 28: “He chose to call the rising tides Malinas, but the ebbing tides Ledones,” speaking as though these terms had only recently begun to be used for this purpose. In Marcellus Empiricus, who lived in Gaul during the reign of Theodosius the Elder, one reads *Liduna* and *Malina* in chapters 16 and 25, though with somewhat different meanings, as the illustrious V. Cl. D. du Cange observes in the *Glossary*. In Bede, in the aforementioned work, chapter 8, and here in our author, *Ledo* is the gentler sea tide that occurs for almost four days both before and after the second and final quarter of the moon each month; *Malina*, however, is the more violent tide, occurring on the other days at the new moon and at the full moon.]

Ledo has six hours of flooding and an equal number of hours of withdrawal. Malina, however, swells greatly for five hours and for seven hours uncovers the backs of the shores.

It displays such agreement with the moon that it always begins three days and twelve hours before the moon rises, and customarily continues for another three days and twelve hours after the beginning of the rising moon. Similarly, it begins three days and twelve hours before the full moon and ends after the same span of time.

According to lunar reckoning, each common year has six Malinas in each of the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—that is, twenty-four in all. Intercalary years are excepted, since they contain twenty-six Malinas.

Of each of the periods mentioned above, the middle two—that is, those at the equinoxes—and the others, whenever day or night completes its course, customarily become stronger than usual and higher in inundation. After intervening intervals, an equal period of Ledo is always inserted.

Yet the destination of this rationally constant inundation is hidden from our minds. For those who do not know, human knowledge prepares no lesser benefit. Whoever desires true wisdom should strive to hasten toward the eternal kingdom, where there is no ignorance, and meanwhile say with the distinguished teacher of the nations: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Cor. 13:9).

Indeed, we scarcely know in part all the things that we possess. The surface of the earth on which we labor, by which we are nourished, in which we live, and by which we are sustained appears before our eyes; yet we still do not know how it itself is sustained.

The sun is given during the day for the service of our needs, but what service it performs at night is hidden from our knowledge. Who is capable of understanding the causes of the entire change by which the moon waxes for fifteen days and wanes for an equal period?

We are permitted to observe the swelling of the inundating sea, but we are deprived of understanding its withdrawal. Within ourselves, we know and remember the day of our birth; but when the day of death will come, although it will certainly come, we do not know.

Even bodily things that we see we can consider only in part. Thus we know in part for as long as we are in this world. But if we come to that light of the Father of lights, there will be nothing in creation that we do not know.

But, to follow our purpose in this great miracle of the Flood among God’s creatures, nothing is shown to have occurred contrary to nature, since nothing appears to have been added that God had not made in the first creation of creatures—except that a greater-than-usual abundance of sea and rain was brought together.

I would establish none of these matters by authority, lest I become contentious in defending any one opinion. But if some better understanding of these things should perhaps occur to another’s more capable intellect, it may perhaps also please my own little mind.

For whatever the learning of any teachers contributed to this subject, I have communicated in these brief writings. If anything in them appears faulty or to reflect an insufficiently sound intention, the hesitation is mine, not theirs.

## CHAPTER VIII—The course of the sun and moon during the Flood

[Col. 2160]

Although the question concerning the boundaries and the return of the sun and moon during the Flood strikes the minds of many as famous and difficult, the course of the year in which the Flood occurred shows that the Flood altered nothing in the customary services of the luminaries or the stars.

For Noah entered the ark with all who belonged to him on the seventeenth day of the second month (Gen. 7:11, 13). After one hundred and fifty days, on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, the same ark came to rest upon the mountains of Armenia. On the first day of the tenth month the summits of the mountains appeared. On the first day of the first month the waters had diminished.

After the circle of the year had elapsed, on the twenty-seventh day of the second month, the earth was seen to have dried. On that day, at the Lord’s command, Noah and all his household went out of the ark (Gen. 8:4–18).

From these indications it is shown most clearly that, in those matters pertaining to the completion of the annual cycle, after the full course of the days and nights had elapsed in the services of the luminaries, nothing appears to have been diminished.

For if the courses of the luminaries—of the sun and moon, that is—had faltered in any respect, first the alternation of days and nights, and then the whole cycle of the year, would have appeared disrupted. But since the annual cycle returns to itself without being disturbed in any way, it is clear that the course of the luminaries was not disturbed in the preceding year.

## CHAPTER IX—The dispersion of languages
After the general purification of the whole world by water had been completed under God’s governance, and the earth had again been exposed when the waters receded at the same command, the offspring of Noah, the sole righteous man at that time, quickly multiplied and spread out to fill all the regions of the world (Gen. IX–X). But before they had been divided among all the lands, an impious and arrogant thought insinuated itself into everyone’s mind: they resolved, by building an exceedingly high tower reaching to heaven, to magnify their own name collectively rather than that of God the Creator, so that through all subsequent generations, governments, and the entire duration of the age they might be famous by the unceasing praise of all posterity.

But once again God was angered by this rashness and arrogant presumption. Yet, because of the common guilt of the whole race, he did not wish to destroy the entire people utterly by the destruction of all alike, as he had recently done to human beings—especially since no righteous person had been found who might remain. Nevertheless, since up to that time the whole people had possessed one language, he divided the languages of all who had come for such a work into different forms of speech (ibid. XI, 1–9), so that, by the perfectly just judgment of the righteous arbiter, those who in the lofty swelling of their pride had despised God might feel the punishment of speech in the most fragile member of their substance.

And this event did not occur only among those fathers themselves; the condition of such vengeance passed through all the descendants of their sons, so that those who sought an everlasting reputation for themselves in posterity might find, throughout all the future ages of those posterities, the punishment of that very presumption abiding among them.

Afterward, too, this division of languages occurred by God’s dispensation, so that the mystery of the divine Scriptures might be guarded by the language of one chosen people from among many until the appointed maturity of time. When, at the predetermined time, he wished to disclose to all nations the sacrament of his dispensation, he sent the Holy Spirit from on high to the ministers appointed for that sacrament, bringing knowledge of all languages. Through the Apostles they proclaimed God’s mighty works, which that people had sung in one language until then, as though for the consecration of all languages at the Spirit’s first coming.

Thus those whom God had gathered at that time in Jerusalem from all the nations, as though for the verification of this event, said: “We hear them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God” (Acts II, 4–11). In this way apostolic humility, through the gift of the Holy Spirit, gathered together what arrogant presumption and the desire for empty glory had scattered.

Most authorities agree that those languages were seventy-two, because they say that so many fathers had gathered for the construction of that tower in the land of Shinar, which is now Babylon. Hence the Gospel is also said to report that the Lord chose seventy-two disciples, apart from the chief Apostles, through whom the same Gospel would afterward be preached among all nations (Luke X, 1). As a prefiguration of them, Moses’ spirit was also distributed among seventy elders; and to the other two who had remained in the camp, namely Eldad and Medad, the gift of prophecy from that spirit was granted (Num. XI, 24–26).

As their quasi-hereditary successors, seventy wise men descended from the stock of Israel were sent to Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Alexandria, by the priests—Eleazar, namely, and the others who at that time presided over the Jewish people—and they translated the Scriptures of the ancient Law into Greek.

At the time of the New Testament, however, primacy among all these languages was assigned to three languages, namely Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, because the title of Christ’s cross is reported by the authority of the Gospel to have been written in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin letters (John XIX, 20).

Yet in this God did nothing contrary to the nature of human speech, which he had formerly established, by dividing and confusing human languages and forms of speech. The nature of speech itself remains in human beings; only differing custom teaches languages to diverge from one another, not naturally but conventionally. A Latin or Greek person born or raised among barbarians speaks barbarically; conversely, the son of a barbarian, taught by Greeks or Latins, speaks in graceful language. From this it is understood that God did not change human nature or create something new in them, but divided only the modes and forms of speaking among different peoples.

## CHAPTER X — On the Punishment of Sodom

After a great interval of time had passed, five cities situated on the border of Arabia and Palestine—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, Zeboiim, and Zoar—enjoying a most fertile soil and abundance of every good, were convicted of immoderate luxury and desire in the accumulation of grain and thereby opened the way for the Lord’s vengeance. Thus the whole region, drenched with rains of fire and sulfur, burned in flames together with its inhabitants, animals, and cities (Gen. XIX).

It was fitting that those who by common purpose had offended God should perish together in the assault of a common punishment; that those who, contrary to human custom, had burned with the practice of shameful desire should be consumed not by the customary death of human beings or by earthly punishment, but by the pouring down of heavenly fires; and that those who had made their sin public not only by committing it but also by proclaiming it should end their infamous life in a punishment equally notorious.

This punishment has not yet departed from their land, since it shows the penalty to which those who do such things will be subject. Between these two chief punishments in the world, namely the Flood and that of Sodom, the following difference is discerned: one land appears to have been punished by water, the other by fire. The one was washed by the dew of heaven and the flood of the abyss; the other was condemned by a fiery rain and a deluge of sulfur. In the one case, after a single annual cycle had elapsed, the earth was exposed; in the other, the earth was long afflicted even after the cessation of the event. In the one, a natural crime in human beings was punished; in the other, the invention of desire contrary to custom was avenged. In this punishment of Sodom, however, God is seen to have done nothing contrary to nature, since the heat of an unusual desire was kindled from above through that ignited expanse of air.

## CHAPTER XI — On Lot’s Wife, Who Was Changed into a Pillar of Salt

From this plague of sinners, Lot, God’s servant, was rescued by the Angels. But his wife, who had been ordered not to look back, looked back and was solidified into a pillar of salt (Gen. XIX, 17, 26), so that she whose gaze was not free from participation in guilt could not escape death, although she had been rescued from the conflagration because of her association with the righteous man.

But since we have undertaken to maintain that nothing in God’s creation is contrary to nature, and that implanted nature is always governed in all things, how was the nature of the human body governed in this transformation when Lot’s wife was changed into a pillar of salt?

No one who has observed the saltness of tears doubts that the nature of salt exists in the human body. Tears, emerging from disturbed bile, as physicians say, disclose even by their taste the nature of salt, which they conceive in the hidden recess of nature and release as they flow from the eyes. Not only in tears, but also in phlegm and in the sputum expelled by coughing, the salty quality of the chest is perceived, showing that the nature of salt is inserted throughout the human body.

Therefore, when the powerful governor of things wishes to turn the whole into what had been a part, he spreads throughout the whole what had been hidden in a small part. Thus, when he wished to turn Lot’s wife into a pillar of salt, that very fine portion of salt which was present in the flesh infected the entire body. And so it came about that he who completed the establishment of all natures on the sixth day did not gather anything from one nature into another, but governs each nature within itself, just as he had established it in the first creation.

## CHAPTER XII — On Sarah, a Woman of Ninety, Giving Birth to a Son

At approximately the same time, Sarah, the barren wife of Abraham, who had been chosen from among a multitude of nations for friendship with God, bore a son named Isaac when she was already ninety years old (Gen. XXI, 1–2), although she had remained barren throughout the whole span of her life up to that age.

This was entirely fitting. Since the son whom she was bearing prefigured Christ, who would be born from a Virgin alone without any desire for human pleasure, she should bear him not at the age when women ordinarily give birth—that is, from the twelfth year up to the forty-ninth—but beyond the limits of that customary period. Thus the child would be born not merely after the fiftieth year, when the function of childbirth has ended, but also in the ninetieth year, when the desire for pleasure had ended.

Although this happened contrary to custom, it did not happen contrary to nature. For even if it is contrary to custom for an old woman to give birth, it is not contrary to nature for a son eventually to be born in a woman’s womb.

## CHAPTER XIII — On the Well Seen by Hagar after She Had Been Cast Out with Her Son

After the birth and weaning of the son, the slave-woman Hagar was cast out with her son Ishmael, who had been born first. As she wandered through the desert with the child, the water failing and death from thirst approaching, she wept. But when the angel called to her and said, “The Lord has heard the voice of the boy,” her eyes were opened, and she saw a well in the wilderness (Gen. XXI, 9–19).

The account of this well is given in such a way that either it then burst forth and emerged from the earth, or, if it had been there previously, Hagar’s eyes were then opened so that she might see what she had previously been unable to see.

## CHAPTER XIV — On the Ram That Abraham Offered for His Son

So that it might also become clear to human beings how faithfully Abraham remained in friendship with God, God commanded him to offer his son Isaac, when he was already grown, as a burnt offering upon one of the mountains that God had shown him. Obedient, he quickly went to the place God had shown him, took up his son, and had already begun to sacrifice him. But when the angel cried out that he should do no harm to his son, he saw a ram caught by its horns among the brambles, and at the angel’s command immediately offered it as a burnt offering in place of his son (Gen. XXII, 1–13).

But inquiry is made concerning where this ram had been in the wilderness. Was it, as some assert, produced by the earth at that hour, just as at the beginning it produces animals? Or, so that God may not be said to have created something from the earth after the sixth day, should we believe that the angel brought this ram from elsewhere, just as the angel transported Philip from the eunuch to Azotus (Acts VIII, 39), and, as is reported, an angel carried Habakkuk to Daniel in Babylon, to the lions’ den (Dan. XIV, 35)?

## CHAPTER XV — On Jacob and Joseph: Why One Was Buried in the Promised Land and the Other in Egypt

Then Isaac fathered Jacob and Esau (Gen. XXV, 25), and Jacob fathered the twelve Patriarchs (ibid. XXXV, 22–26). Ten brothers, envious of Joseph, sold him into Egypt (ibid. XXXVII, 28). There, in the land of his exile and captivity, he brought salvation to the nations to which he came and received the administration of the whole Egyptian kingdom and dominion over the land of Egypt. He even invited his father and his entire household to Egypt. After Jacob had lived there for sixteen years, when the day of his death was already approaching, he adjured his son Joseph to carry him to the tomb of his fathers, to the land of promise where Abraham and Isaac lay with Sarah and Rebekah, and where Leah had also been buried.

Joseph fulfilled this adjuration in deed: he carried his father’s body to the tomb of his fathers, to the ancestral burial place (Gen. XLIX–L). Yet when Joseph himself later died in Egypt, he did not wish immediately after his death to be carried to the ancestral tomb. Instead, he accepted a place of burial in Egypt for the time being, and afterward he commanded the people departing from Egypt concerning his bones, saying: “Carry my bones away with you from here” (ibid. L, 24).

Why, then, is one carried immediately to Abraham’s tomb in the land of promise, while the other is buried in the land of Egypt, to be carried away at a later time?

Jacob did not mingle with women of a foreign nation, except with those who had come with him from Mesopotamia; therefore, after his death, he was immediately carried with his body intact to the ancestral tomb. Joseph, however, took as his wife Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis (ibid. XLI, 45), and had been mixed with foreign blood. Therefore, after his death, he was buried in foreign soil.

Why, then, did he afterward wish to be carried to the land of promise, when he had first been buried in Egypt? Joseph, as a prophetic man, foresaw that the Egyptian nation, devoted to idolatry, would someday wish to worship the very man who had been the author of earthly generosity toward them and had freed them from the danger of famine. And so they did. For they set up an image of an ox beside Joseph’s tomb, since the ox assists a man in agriculture.

For the same reason, when the children of Israel wished to worship an idol in the wilderness, they made no other statue than a calf—that is, an ox—especially because that animal was worshiped in Egypt beside Joseph’s tomb.

Therefore, lest Joseph succumb to Egyptian idolatry, foreseeing the departure of the children of Israel, he said: “God will surely visit you; carry my bones away with you from here.” I have set forth this explanation here not because it should be counted among the miracles, but lest I leave unmentioned so great a span of time between Abraham and Moses without something worthy of remembrance.

## CHAPTER XVI — On Moses and the Bush at Horeb

After Joseph’s death, the Egyptian people began to oppress the children of Israel under the harshest yoke of slavery, even ordering their male infants to be thrown into the river and killed by various forms of death, lest the nation grow beyond measure (Exod. I, 14, 22).

At that time Moses, son of Amram, born amid that crisis and a man of the tribe of Levi, rose up to avenge his people. Seeing an Egyptian oppressing an Israelite, he killed him. When the matter became known to the king of the Egyptians, Moses fled from Egypt and lived as an exile for forty years, tending sheep in the land of Midian (ibid. II, 11–15).

When the period of the promise made to the fathers had elapsed, as he was driving the flock through the pastures on Mount Horeb, a burning bush appeared that was not consumed by its fire. When he wished to investigate this vision—to learn why the bush was not consumed although it was burning—the Lord spoke from the midst of the bush: “I am the Lord, the God of your fathers. I will send you into Egypt, so that you may free their descendants, who are oppressed by the yoke of slavery” (ibid. III, 1–10).

In this astonishing vision, the first question arising for our present work is how the fire appeared to burn while the thing in which it burned was nevertheless not consumed. If the fire had drawn nourishment from that material, why was the material from which it grew not consumed? And if the visible flame had not arisen from that material, why was it necessary for it to be displayed in a bush?

A certain kind of shrub is said to possess the property that the more intensely it burns, it is not merely not consumed, but by burning becomes purer. Saint Jerome, in his explanation of the wooden altar shown by the Lord in a vision to Ezekiel in the city (Ezek. XLI, 22), reports that this wood has something like the color of flax, though he kept silent about its name while indicating its nature.

If, then, that fire shown to Moses burned in the bush of that tree, what is surprising if the bush was not consumed? Thus the nature of both elements—fire and tree—is preserved: fire naturally burns from the tree, and the tree, naturally burning in the fire, is not consumed.

Or certainly, the fire seen in that bush was not the fire hostile to the tree; rather, it was that fire of which it is said: “Who makes his angels spirits and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. CIII, 4). An incorporeal fire is therefore manifested in the bush. Since it was shown to a corporeal human being, however, it was necessary that some corporeal material be displayed.

## CHAPTER XVII — On the Two Signs: the Hand Turned into the Bosom and the Rod Changed into a Serpent

Then, as he proceeded toward Egypt, a twofold sign was granted to him, so that the word might stand upon three witnesses: Moses himself and the two signs. The rod that Moses, still a shepherd of sheep, had carried in his hand became a serpent when he threw it upon the ground. His hand, when he put it into his own bosom, emerged leprous the first time; when he put it back into the same bosom a second time, it appeared healthy (Exod. IV, 1–7).

But nothing contrary to nature appears to have occurred either in the hand or in the wood. Human flesh retains within itself both leprosy and health, as is often demonstrated by their alternation. Yet the frequent alteration of the same hand—healthy, then white with leprosy, and again healthy at once—provided observers with the miracle of a most remarkable sign.

The rod’s being changed into a serpent, and the serpent’s being changed back into a tree, therefore presents a difficulty to investigators of nature. Unless, that is, it is clearly taught that both the rod and the serpent were made from the earth. Whatever arises from the same material is, by the power of God the governor, changed alternately into the other.

But if everything made from the earth is granted to be capable of being changed back and forth into everything else—an animal into a tree, bread into stone, a human being into a bird—we would seem to grant that nothing could remain firmly within the limits of its own nature, and we would appear to assent to the ridiculous tales of magicians who say that their ancestors flew through the ages in the substance of birds. Consequently, we would call God not the governor but the changer of natures. Far be it from us to believe that, after the first establishment of all natures, he made something new that its own nature does not retain.

“For there is nothing new under the sun.” Nor can anyone say, “Behold, this is new” (Eccl. I, 10). Therefore many teachers say that the true rod, which always remained a branch held in Moses’ hands, was only imaginatively changed into the form of a serpent on several occasions as a sign, especially since it was necessary for no other use than the display of the sign.

For if it had been a real serpent, it would have remained a serpent after the signs. The true rod, after all, was the one with which Moses began to scourge Egypt with plagues; it was never changed into a serpent but always remained a rod. With it the sea was divided (Exod. XIV, 21), and the rocks at Horeb and Kadesh were struck (ibid. XVII, 6; Num. XX, 11).

If, then, that imaginary serpent was displayed only in the signs, why were the other serpents of the magicians devoured before Pharaoh by it (Exod. VII, 12)? Learned men will easily be able to answer this objection by saying that the serpents devoured by it were themselves imaginary; therefore the imagination of the divine sign could devour what had been produced imaginatively through the magicians’ diabolical incantations.

According to this interpretation, then, the rod was not changed into the nature of a serpent, but was imaginatively changed into its likeness for the sake of the sign. For nothing in the nature of a tree is found that could make a serpent. Thus, except at the moment of the sign, what was naturally a rod is seen specifically as a serpent.

[Note: [Col. 2164] Ms. Aud., “the rod is always specifically seen.” Very good.]

## CHAPTER XVIII — On the Water Changed into Blood

As Moses proceeded into Egypt and performed signs before Pharaoh as the Lord had commanded him, declaring to the king God’s sentence that he should release the Israelite people, the king himself in no way consented to God’s command. At the Lord’s order, Moses scourged the land of Egypt with ten plagues.

First, he struck the waters and changed them into blood, so that all the waters throughout Egypt, transformed into blood, brought death to the creatures that were in them and, through the destruction of the waters, inflicted a deadly punishment of thirst upon human beings (Exod. VII, 20–21).

This first vengeance appropriately befell the Egyptians and their king: those who had ordered the infants of God’s people to be thrown into the river would receive death from drinking the water of that same river after it had been changed into blood, while those who did not drink it would nevertheless suffer punishment.

But this too must be examined, since it relates to the purpose of the present work: how did God, the governor of nature, change water into blood naturally?

Water, the material of every liquid, is daily changed into different forms through the administration of things themselves, since it is incessantly and naturally drawn together for the nourishment and renewal of each nature. When it is poured through the vine, it is changed into the taste and color of wine. When it rises through the wood of the olive to its lofty branches, the same water produces the richness of oil. When bees gather it into honeycombs, it produces the sweetness of honey. When it is processed through the strength of palm trees, it produces dates and, when pressed, attains the pleasantness of fermented drink. When it is assigned to nourish different animals, it is distinguished through the same flesh into various substances of blood.

It also prepares in the breasts, for the nourishment of offspring, milk of white color and most pleasant sweetness, while throughout the remaining members of the flesh it darkens into the red color of blood. Moreover, there are many kinds of blood in the same flesh, which physiologists enumerate up to twenty-three; from these, they declare, urine, semen, black and red bile, saliva, tears, and other substances arise. Through daily operations in various things, water prepares these according to their own natures.

What, then, prevents receptive minds from accepting that what nature accomplishes over a longer period could be effected in a moment, naturally, at the command of the most powerful Governor? Thus, when water was changed into blood, nothing contrary to nature occurred. What it would have produced over time in other things, it immediately produced within itself at the Lord’s command.

## CHAPTER XIX — On the Other Plagues of the Egyptians

Concerning the other plagues with which God through Moses, and Moses through Aaron, chastised Pharaoh, his land, and his servants, the simple account of the plagues itself shows that nothing exceeded the boundaries of nature.

Although frogs then appeared in greater numbers than usual, frogs always arise from water. Gnats arise from dust in the heat of the sun during summer. Locusts and flies, strengthened by the sun’s heat, gather from every direction. Animals, dying for their customary variety of causes, reach the end of their lives. Dust stirred up from the earth often darkens the clear air; and the air produces blisters, followed by ulcers, in infected human beings and animals. Hail and lightning fall from freezing and violently disturbed clouds. The absence of light impedes the sight of the eyes, and the farther light withdraws, the more deeply darkness obstructs them. Death, first sown in Adam, rules over all his children; through it the firstborn offspring of all the Egyptians were then condemned with particular severity.

Although all these things were implanted in the natures of things, they occurred among the Egyptians as plagues intended to restrain their infidelity—suddenly and in greater numbers than usual.

The order of the plagues grew both in the distinction of the things affected and in that of their ministers. The first three plagues of all were brought about through Aaron. First, when he struck the water, it was immediately changed into blood. When he again stretched the same rod over the water, an inundation of frogs filled the land. When he stretched the rod a third time over the dust of the earth, gnats boiled forth (ibid. VII, 20; VIII, 6–17). These three plagues were brought about through Aaron.

The next three were administered through Moses’ word. At his command, locusts and flies came, and the death of the animals followed.

The final three were not commanded by speech alone, but summoned through Moses’ action. Moses took dust from the furnace and scattered it into the air; blisters and ulcers broke out on human beings and animals, and running sores appeared like dust throughout the land of Egypt. Afterward he took the rod and stretched it toward heaven, and an extraordinary abundance of hail and lightning fell upon the earth. Again Moses directed the same rod toward heaven and brought upon the land a darkness lasting three days and as many nights, so dense that it could be felt and exceedingly dreadful (Exod. X, 13–14; VIII, 24; IX, 6, 10, 23–25; X, 22).

The final plague occurred through neither Aaron nor Moses. Rather, the angel of the Lord passed through Egypt and destroyed all the firstborn of the Egyptians (ibid. XII, 29).

Whenever vengeance is drawn from the earth, therefore, it is carried out through Aaron as the minister of a lower order. When punishment is drawn from flying creatures and from the death of animals—which themselves fly, as it were, upon the earth—it is carried out through Moses’ command. When chastisement is summoned from the clouds above, it is brought down through the extension upward of Moses’ hand. But when the end of human life is administered by God, that ministry is entrusted not to a human being but to an angel, so that those who had been less frightened by the scourges of the things they possessed might at least fear the common destruction that followed through the loss of their most distinguished possession.

The scope of these plagues also corresponded in every direction—that is, through earth, waters, animals, air, fire, clouds, heaven, and angels—so that it might be shown that the entire world arms itself together against those who rebel and resist God.

Just as every creature grows angry with those whom God wishes to punish, so every creature supports those to whom he grants aid. Indeed, the Red Sea divided these two peoples: for one of them it was the end of all oppression, and for the other the beginning of every blessing.

## CHAPTER XX — On the Retreat and Drying of the Red Sea

When the Egyptians, worn down by so many plagues, had compelled the Israelite people to leave them, they were again driven by evil regret. The entire army, with its king, pursued them in order to bring back into slavery those whom they had dismissed.

Then, when Israel had been hemmed into the narrow gulf of the Red Sea, Moses stretched his rod over the waters, and suddenly the wave of the Red Sea was divided. As the people entered on dry feet and the enemies followed, the way widened. When the wind was sent forth, God kept the divided sea dry throughout the whole night. He also placed between the two peoples a dark cloud that separated them and a pillar that illuminated the night itself.

Pharaoh’s army entered the sea after Israel. But what was a refuge for one was a snare for the other. Therefore that cloud was dark to the Egyptians, so that throughout the night they could not join those going ahead; but it illuminated the night for Israel, so that they could walk along a bright road through the depths of the sea.

At dawn, protected from both dangers—the enemy and the sea—the entire people of God escaped to the fields of the wilderness. Pharaoh’s entire army, without even a messenger escaping, was overwhelmed in the gravel of the deep when the waters returned to their proper limits (Exod. XIV).

In this remarkable miracle among God’s works, the question required by the purpose of our present undertaking is how an explanation can be preserved for the sea’s drying and retreat from its shores. With God’s help, we think that we can discover this without great difficulty, since we very often observe the surfaces of ponds covered with ice when their waters freeze.

What is naturally produced in water when the violence of winds and rains ceases and the lower regions of the air are seized by frost was then brought about by God’s command through a freezing wind suddenly pressing upon the sea.

[Note: [Col. 2166] Perhaps, “stiffening.”]

But just as the sea was suddenly made dry at the Lord’s command, so, at the same command, it melted and was released from the dry ground into flowing waves. We have already mentioned the daily operation by which that sea recedes, since we regularly observe it occurring through the tidal inlets of the Ocean. From this we can conclude that just as the sea naturally abandons its shores every day, so then, although in a far different and dissimilar manner, God governing it, it uncovered its own shores without acting contrary to nature.

## CHAPTER XXI — On the Harmonious Song of the Children of Israel

Considering the mighty power that the Lord had exercised in their liberation, the children of Israel all together sang a song to the Lord in harmonious chant, with Moses leading (Exod. XV, 1–22).

Here a miracle occurred worthy of sufficiently immense admiration: all the elders together with the children, and every age group, inspired by the same breath, sang in unison, as though from one mouth, the same letters or syllables harmoniously, without having been instructed beforehand.

But the investigator of nature is secure at this point, since the singers’ hearts and mouths were inspired not by the custom of human ingenuity but by the divine Spirit.

Nevertheless, the same Spirit is not discerned to have done anything contrary to nature in these singers, in whom breath and voice were moved through mouths and tongues to form words. What they themselves could have done through speech and practice, the Lord granted them to accomplish in a single moment: all of them sang a harmonious song together. The same one who shortly before had opened the deep before them afterward governed their tongues and minds in such a song.

## CHAPTER XXII — On the Sweetening of the Waters at Marah

From there they traveled through a barren wilderness devoid of birds. Exhausted by the continuous labor of three days, and complaining in the burning heat of thirst, they found exceedingly bitter waters at Marah. Prevented by their saltness, they were utterly unable to find relief for their thirst.

But the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood. When it touched the water, the bitter water of the stream was sweetened. Thereafter the people laid aside the burning thirst that had ceaselessly wearied them up to that point, having quenched it with the water’s sweet taste (Exod. XV, 23–25).

But how will the investigator of nature approve as natural the claim that bitter water was immediately sweetened in an instant by the touch of wood? What sort of nature, or what degree of sweetness, could that wood have possessed, so that once dipped into the stream, it would make the exceedingly bitter water pleasant and flavorful? If someone were now to throw a honeycomb into bitter water, would the honeycomb not become bitter rather than the water become flavorful?

From this it is understood that the wood did not then make the water sweet by its own nature. Rather, at the command of the Creator and governor of nature, he changed the liquid into a different taste.

The rod with which Moses struck the Red Sea, and scourged river, heaven, and earth when the land of Egypt was afflicted by various plagues, did not possess this power within itself by nature when Moses or Aaron raised it to perform these things—whether to turn the river water into blood, to raise gnats from dust, or to bring darkness down from heaven.

If someone other than Moses, and without God’s command, had struck the sea again with that rod, Thetis would certainly not have yielded to his blow. And if he had struck the waters again by chance, he would certainly never have changed them into blood.

Likewise, if someone dipped that tree by which the salt water at Marah was sweetened into a bitter liquid, without the same God commanding it as he had at first, it certainly would not change that saltness into a pleasant taste.

It must therefore be understood that God did not command these woods—or the dust from the furnace in those miracles—to be involved so that anyone might think that something had been accomplished in them through their own nature or operation. Rather, he established them as signs prefiguring the mysteries of future things, so that a wise teacher might determine by figurative interpretation what these things now accomplish in the progress of the Church.

But once we have established that the wood did nothing naturally in this event, it remains for us to explain how it happened through nature. Whatever is discovered in a thing through painstaking effort, even over a long period, is not brought into it from elsewhere by transferring an alien nature through human industry. Rather, when it is hidden in the secret recess of nature, the labor of time first entangles it and makes it an aid to another nature.

Whatever is produced through human effort—or even through the operation of things themselves—by prolonged cultivation, nature itself produces at God’s will whenever necessary.

Sailors frequently prove that bitter waters, even waters that are exceedingly salty, can be changed into a sweet taste. They pour them through good soil, and by this technique, having sweetened them, often relieve their thirst. Clouds likewise raise vapors of salty liquid from the sea, but when they rain, they provide the same vapors as fresh water for earthly uses. The defect of saltness that the waters acquire within themselves is removed through their infusion into earth or clouds.

Similarly, fresh waters become salty, with a taste stronger than that of the Ocean, when people draw them through the ashes of sea plants. Water therefore possesses this change naturally within itself, but it produces it more quickly at the command of the Creator than through the effectiveness of human care or the operation of the things themselves.

Human diligence, through the aid of another thing, or the operation of each thing itself, changes the surface of a nature. But the Creator and governor of creatures strips bare within the thing itself the hidden nature that would otherwise have to be manifested through another thing.

Just as bitter water would now reveal the sweetness that it had secretly contained within its nature after being cleansed of bitterness through earth or cloud, so, at the command of the most powerful governor of natures, it displays that sweetness by itself, without the aid of another thing.

## CHAPTER XXIII — On the Manna Raining from Heaven
So, after entering the wilderness, God satisfied for forty years with manna—that is, with heavenly bread—the nearly six hundred thousand foot soldiers of this people, excluding the camp followers, that is, the innumerable mixed multitude who had come up from Egypt (Exod. XII, 37–38). Finally, recalling that bread, the Psalmist later said: “He gave them the bread of heaven; man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXVII, 25). It descended every night, except on the night of the Sabbath, together with the dew, displaying the whiteness of snow around the camp. “For,” says Scripture, “it was like coriander seed, and its appearance was like the appearance of bdellium, white like snow” (Num. XI, 7). It could not endure the rising of the sun, but immediately melted; yet, when gathered, ground in a mill, and turned about, it endured the heat of fire in the baking of bread. If anyone left any of it until the morning of the following day, it swarmed with worms; nevertheless, a measure of manna, an omer, remained sound in the Ark even after a long period of time (Exod. XVI, 32).

In this sign, both marvelous and necessary, apart from those matters that pertain to figurative interpretation, points arise that assist attentive minds, which require the Lord’s help for the illumination of their explanation. First, it is asked whether it is bread; then, how it is called the bread of angels; and, if that food is described as having had nothing of earthly nature, how people, still situated on earth and subject to bodily weaknesses, were sustained by it. For in the Psalmist’s aforementioned verse it is written, as we have said, that it is heavenly bread, which is supplied from the clouds together with the rain; and, as we have already said, these clouds are called “heavens” throughout Scripture.

That food is called the bread of angels, not because angels, who have no need of food, were satisfied by it, but because such a service was performed through the ministry of angels, just as the Law and the other things were provided to the people—things arranged through angels and given into the hand of the Mediator (Gal. III, 19). How, then, could it have sustained human beings of whatever kind, unless it possessed something earthly in its substance? But how will manna raining from the clouds be shown to have an earthly substance, unless perhaps the lower part of the air itself is shown to retain some earthly nature? For how could it have been able to support the bodies of flying birds, if the air did not contain something of earthly solidity?

Therefore that substance, and the clouds supported by the nature of the earth itself, also freeze into snow and hail, which acquire almost the hardness of stones. What, then, is so contrary to minds capable of understanding, if, just as clouds conceive small stones of hail, they were likewise able to produce grains of manna—especially since, [Col. 2169] when it came down to earth, like a substance related to dew, if the rising sun found it, it would perish like hail melting on the ground? In this way it could happen that manna, generated in the earthly regions of this air, supplied earthly human beings with food for nourishment.

For this lower part of the air is also called “earth” in divine Scripture. In the hundred and forty-eighth Psalm, all creatures are stirred by the prophetic Spirit to praise the Lord the Creator. Thus, after completing those things that pertain to the adornment of the upper heavens, when it comes to the lower regions of this air, the passage continues as follows: “Praise the Lord from the earth,” and so forth, “which carry out his word.” Behold: the Prophet has now called the air, which is thicker and interwoven with clouds and vapors, “earth,” before he reaches the regions of the lower earth that are mentioned afterward.

In that upper part of the earth, therefore, where hail and snow are generated, manna was born, and through angels was administered as food to the human beings of the lower part of the earth. From this it is readily discerned that God did not seek it from somewhere outside nature, but prepared nourishment from the earth. This does not mean that God could not also have supplied them with ordinary bread every day in the wilderness; rather, it was so that a human being fed from the clouds might know that “man lives not by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deut. VIII, 3). For just as he commanded nature that a human being should be filled with bread, so, if he should command it, a person will have sound nourishment from any thing whatsoever, just as at that time he had rain from the clouds.

## CHAPTER XXIV — On the rock struck at Horeb

That same people, thirsting in the wilderness, requested refreshment with drink. Therefore Moses the leader, at God’s command, struck the rock at Horeb with his staff and brought water out of the rock (Exod. XVII, 6). Here the investigator of nature is brought into difficulty: how is the nature of water concealed in a hard stone? But how does one who does not hesitate to say that stones were made from water in the beginning fail to understand this—one who knows that the nature of crystal, when snow freezes for a long time, develops into the unchangeable hardness of stone? This is especially so since we often observe clods formed not from the soil of the earth itself but from the first growth of grass upon the tops of trees or rocks; and in them we find small stones generated by the infusion of rains and by the movement of the grass itself into earth.

We have also seen certain clayey soils, overspread by the customary flow of running waters, transformed into the hardness of stones. Embedded in them we have noticed stones still harder, as though of an earlier age, which the soil itself had previously contained within it. We likewise see hollow oyster shells embedded in some stones—shells that had been interposed when the soil was still soft, but which now appear incorporated into their natural hardness.

In other objects that the sea, after a very long period, cast upon the land, crusts called *nagarbae* appear superimposed [Note: [Col. 2169] Ms. Aud., *roccae nagarba*]; by observation itself we establish that these were not lifted from the gravel of the sea, but were formed from the very quality of marine moisture and from the hardened outer skin of those bodies. Many marine creeping creatures are also covered with shells as old as tortoises, in which the hardness appears greater than that of very many stones.

From all these clear proofs, every educated person acknowledges that stones are now generated from water alone, and others from water and soil together, just as the nature and ordinary behavior of tearful marble indicate. Nature itself is often observed to turn liquid into stone hardened by congealing, and again to dissolve it into liquid. A stone also, as the history of the Book of Job relates, when dissolved by heat, is converted into bronze (Job XXVIII, 2); but this cannot happen unless it is first changed into the nature of liquid. Moreover, every metal, whatever its hardness, although it may not reveal itself to be of a liquid nature, melts when dissolved by fire.

Since, therefore, it is proved that the nature of stones is generated from the moisture of water, what prevents a stone from being changed into water by the will of God the Governor, so that nature may hasten to return to its origin, when God commands water to be supplied from the rock to his people? [Col. 2170]

## CHAPTER XXV — Why the sons of Moses were deprived of priestly leadership

After these events, when Moses’ kinsman had brought Zipporah, Moses’ wife, and his two sons, Moses hastened to go out through the wilderness to meet him. Although a foreigner, by his advice, when they came to the place of the camp, tribunes, centurions, commanders of fifty, and decurions were appointed among God’s people (Exod. XVIII, 5–7, 21–22).

But a question arises concerning Moses’ sons: why are they not heirs to their father’s leadership of the people, and why are they at least deprived of the priesthood, when the Psalmist says, “Moses and Aaron among his priests” (Ps. XCVIII, 6)? Yet this question is resolved by giving the reason: Moses’ sons were born of a foreign mother, during the period of his wandering. For thus it is reported of Moses when he fathered his firstborn: “And he called his name Gershom, saying, ‘For I was a sojourner in a foreign land’” (Exod. II, 22).

## CHAPTER XXVI — On the forty-day fast

Meanwhile Moses, summoned by God’s command, fasted for forty days. After God’s people had been delivered from the ten plagues of the Egyptians, on the fiftieth day from the celebration of Passover in Egypt, he brought down from Mount Sinai the law of the ten commandments on two stone tablets (Exod. XXIV, 12; XXXI, 18). When he was angered by the offense of the sinful people, he broke them at the foot of the mountain (Exod. XXXII, 19). After an equal number of tablets had been restored from the same material, he again fasted for forty days and, by the gift of God the giver, deserved to receive the same commandments (Exod. XXXIV, 28).

During this period, however, contrary to ordinary human custom, twice, as I have said, he ate no food of earthly life and was not wearied by the labor of hunger, because, supported by fellowship with the divine word, he was able to endure so long a fast without hunger.

## CHAPTER XXVII — On the people’s demand for meat

Moreover, a portion of the faithless people, burning with desire for meat, murmured and preferred the pots of Egyptian meat to the heavenly manna. But when this seemed intolerable even to Moses, the Lord said: “Sanctify the people tomorrow, for I will satisfy them with meat for an entire month.” Moses, stirred by human weakness, replied to him: “Six hundred thousand foot soldiers are counted among this people, apart from its innumerable multitude. Shall an immense number of cattle and sheep be slaughtered, or shall the fish of the sea be gathered together in one place to satisfy an innumerable crowd?”

And so, to ensure that nothing of what Moses’ frail, human mind had grasped would contribute to the people’s food, a wind going forth from the Lord carried quail, seized from across the sea, to the place of the camp; and it inserted the *ortygometra* among them, with the birds flying about the camp at a height of two cubits, as far as could be covered in a single day [Note: [Col. 2170] *Ortygomêtra*, a species of quail of remarkable size]. The people gathered them and ate them for an entire month, that is, for thirty days.

But punishment overtook the unbelievers for their murmuring. For at that place, before the people departed, those who had desired the meat were struck down by the Lord’s anger and buried (Num. XI). [Col. 2171] Certainly nothing new or contrary to nature is contributed by the Lord in this event: he appears to provide, in the need of his people, a creature of birds that he had long ago created and stored away in some hidden corner of the world.

Although it is written in the Book of Wisdom, “They saw a new creation of birds” (Wis. XIX, 11), this means one recently displayed, not recently created. What God had created long ago, together with the other creatures, he supplied to his people in a time of need.

Nevertheless, for this reason he brought quail again for such a service—quail that, when previously supplied together with the manna, had caused no harm to those who ate them—so that no one might think that bird food had brought death upon the people because of the fault of murmuring. For in this punishment also, it preserved those who ate with a sound conscience unharmed; and when it was given together with the manna, it caused no injury to the entire multitude.

## CHAPTER XXVIII — On Moses’ Ethiopian wife and the leprosy of the murmuring Miriam

[Col. 2171]

Later, because of his Ethiopian wife, Aaron and Miriam spoke insolent words against Moses, whom the words of the Holy Spirit describe as the meekest of all the human beings then living on earth. But when he had summoned only the three of them to the tabernacle, Aaron, rebuked by God’s word, was defended from punishment by the oil of anointing; Miriam’s body, however, was afflicted with the whiteness of leprosy, and therefore she was also ordered to remain outside the camp. But when Moses prayed for her, she was restored, healed, on the seventh day (Num. XII).

Concerning this Ethiopian wife of Moses, however, there is a twofold opinion among the teachers: whether he had taken her from Ethiopia while he was in Pharaoh’s household, from which he departed at the age of forty, and whether she had awaited him through the many days of his wandering; or whether, at the time of the signs, when he returned to Egypt after his wandering, he had joined an Ethiopian woman to himself as wife, whom he brought with him from Ethiopia and led through the wilderness; or whether it is likewise said of Zipporah that she was Ethiopian, since in many places in the histories of Scripture they describe another Ethiopia in the region north of the Red Sea, where the Ethiopians had previously lived.

Ecclesiastical history states concerning this region that it adjoins India in part.
