In the Canonical Chronicles of Eusebius it is reported [Note: [Col. 2171] Under the year of the world 3580] that Ethiopians, rising from the River Indus, settled near Egypt. From this it is understood that the land in which the Ethiopians first lived could have been called Ethiopia; and if Moses had taken his wife from that Ethiopia, she was therefore called Ethiopian.

## CHAPTER XXIX — On Korah, Dathan, and Abiram

Korah, son of Izhar, of the tribe of Levi, a cousin of Moses and Aaron; Dathan and Abiram, sons of Eliab; On, son of Peleth, of the tribe of Reuben; and, in addition, two hundred and fifty distinguished men of the assembly, who were called by name at the time of the council, stood against Moses and Aaron with the haughty swelling of pride.

Korah had wanted to claim the priesthood for himself, while the others contended over leadership of the people. But him, who had attempted to offer the fire of a burnt offering to God without God’s command, heavenly fire consumed at the time of the burnt offering, together with those who belonged to him. Those who, exalting themselves on high, had begun to resist God’s ordinance, the earth beneath their feet split open and, with open mouth, swallowed them into the underworld (Num. XVI, 1–36).

In these events it is clearly shown that both sentient and insentient creatures obey God’s command to an equal degree: just as living creatures come swiftly at his command, so things that do not live, as though living, carry out what is ordered.

Yet although the earth performs this work of punishment as though alive, nothing contrary to nature occurs in it. For the earth is unquestionably recognized as possessing an insensible life, through which the fruits of trees and plants growing within it appear to move. Thus, just as veins of blood course through living flesh and pulse, streams of living waters flow through the earth. Through this insensible life, at God’s command, the earth opened its mouth when, serving in the ministry of punishment as though it were a servant, it swallowed the tents of sinful human beings.

## CHAPTER XXX — On the plague that descended upon the people when Moses fled into the Tabernacle

On the following day, the whole people rose up against Moses and Aaron as though they were guilty of blood, and wanted to kill them in vengeance for those who had been punished. But both of them—Moses and Aaron—fled to the tabernacle of God, and heavenly flame again raged among the rebellious people.

Then, at Moses’ command, Aaron filled a censer with fire from the altar, went out among the people, and the punishment did not pass beyond the boundary separating the living from the dead. A proper measure was accomplished in both respects: those who had burned inwardly with the fire of anger against just rulers were consumed outwardly by the flame of most just punishment; and the fire sent from heaven did not dare to burn those who had been protected at the boundary of one who had mercifully forgiven [Col. 2172] the faults of his neighbors in his heart. On that day the fire consumed fourteen thousand people (Num. XVI, 41–49).

## CHAPTER XXXI — On Aaron’s staff, which had blossomed

Those who remained were also pressed more heavily by the guilt of rebellion. Yet when the tumult had ceased, so that each person might know more clearly whom the Lord had chosen for the priesthood, Moses requested staffs from the leaders of each of the twelve tribes, with their names inserted. For the Levitical tribe he received Aaron’s staff, with his name inserted. He placed them for one night in the presence of the Lord, beneath the covering of the tabernacle.

On the following morning, Aaron’s staff displayed buds of almond blossoms, by which it was evident that God had chosen Aaron for the priesthood above all the others (Num. XVII, 1–8). Yet even in this the staff is not shown to have accomplished anything contrary to nature.

## CHAPTER XXXII — On the rock struck twice at Kadesh

After some time, the thirsty people in the wilderness of Zin at Kadesh raised a serious uproar against Moses and Aaron with their murmuring. When this matter was reported to the Lord through Moses, he commanded that the rock be struck with the staff. But Moses, moved by the murmuring of the faithless people, also faltered in faith concerning the Lord’s command; and, in the presence of the people, he struck the rock twice with Aaron, and the thirsty people drank the waters that flowed forth abundantly. Because of this, Moses did not enter the promised land (Num. XX, 2–12).

At Horeb the rock was struck once, where only the people’s unbelief is indicated (Exod. XVII, 6). But at Kadesh in the wilderness of Zin the rock is struck twice: there unbelief is discerned both in the people and in the leader.

## CHAPTER XXXIII — On the bronze serpent

Likewise, when the people murmured, the Lord sent fiery serpents among them, burning them with their breath; their breath killed many of the murmurers whom they had scorched. But the rest, terrified by the punishment of those who were dying and inclined by a repentant spirit toward making satisfaction, cried out to Moses and to the Lord that this plague might cease from them.

Therefore, yielding to the tears of the repentant, the Lord commanded Moses to raise a bronze serpent on a staff before the people. When this had been done, the bronze serpent was immediately set up, and by looking upon it the wounds inflicted by the earlier serpents were healed (Num. XXI, 5–9).

Nevertheless, as we have said concerning the staff and the tree by which the bitter water was sweetened, salvation was not held in the serpent but in the Lord’s command. Whatever he had ordered would at that time have been salvation for the people. Yet the history of the preceding events contains the power of the present mystery in figure, in Christ and in the Church.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — On Balaam and his she-ass

When Balak son of Zippor learned that Israel had come into his land, he sent messengers to invite Balaam the diviner, so that he might curse the people of Israel. As Balaam traveled seated on a she-ass, the animal saw an angel standing in a narrow place with a drawn sword and was afraid; after being beaten three times, it finally stopped before its master.

Then, beaten still more, it spoke in human fashion and in human speech, like a complaining maidservant. While it was speaking, Balaam’s eyes were immediately opened so that he could see the angel (Num. XXII).

In this astonishing sign, although the she-ass utters words appropriate to it, it does not speak by its own mind or feeling. Rather, the Lord—of whom it is said, “And the Lord opened the mouth of the she-ass”—just as he opened its mouth for speech, also directed its tongue and palate into words. The she-ass had absolutely no knowledge of what or how it should speak, or even whether it would say anything.

For human beings also who speak while filled with another spirit do not know what they are saying even while they speak, and remember nothing of it when they recover their senses. But the one who has often found ways of speaking in clouds and in fire also guided the tongue of a mute animal, like a plectrum, into words.

From this we understand that the Lord changed nothing in the nature of the she-ass, but, through the air of its mouth, restrained the prophet’s ignorance, although the animal itself was unaware, so that Balaam would not become puffed up with pride, even if the Spirit of the Lord were speaking within him. He would have discovered that the same Spirit often spoke through insensible things and through a brute, mute, and subject animal.

“For the Spirit of God blows where it wills” (John [Col. 2173] III, 8), even when this is less suitable to the will of the one who speaks. Thus Saul, who wanted to kill the prophets and had come driven by an evil intention, was nevertheless seized by the Spirit of the Lord and prophesied among those whom he was pursuing (I Kings XIX, 24). Balaam likewise, brought there to curse and desiring to accomplish that purpose, was unable to curse God’s people; instead, against his will, he was compelled by the Lord’s Spirit to bless them (Num. XXIII).

For these two reasons, then, Balaam was permitted by the Lord to come: so that his foolishness might be refuted through the mute animal, and so that the coming of Christ might be written in God’s law through a gentile prophet—the one who was to be the Savior of the nations.

Throughout all the journeying of the people of Israel, the pillar of cloud by day never failed, nor did the pillar of fire by night stand absent before the people (Exod. XIII, 21–22), so that, protected from the cold of night and illumined amid the darkness, they might proceed with the fire. By day they were protected from the heat of the sun beneath the cloud. The Lord, the guardian of Israel, truly protects them: neither the sun by day nor the moon by night ever scorches them.

## CHAPTER XXXV — On Moses’ ascent of Mount Abarim

In the fortieth year after the sons of Israel departed from Egypt, at the forty-second encampment, the people settled in the plains of Moab beside the Jordan. There Moses proclaimed Deuteronomy, that is, the repetition of the Law [Col. 2174] (Deut. I ff.). Afterwards, having appointed Joshua son of Nun, of the tribe of Ephraim, as leader of the people in his place (Deut. XXXI, 7), he alone ascended, by the Lord’s command, Mount Abarim (“of the crossings”), Mount Nebo.

There, at the age of one hundred and twenty, with his teeth unmoved, his eyes undimmed, and his body unimpaired, he paid the common debt of the entire human race (Ibid., 34). As the wise say, there were two reasons why no one knew of his death or burial: so that no one might see that face, which had shone through its fellowship with the Lord’s speech, subdued by the grief of death; and so that the people of Israel, if they knew where his tomb was, would not worship it.

For this reason, as many think, he also took away with him the staff by which he had performed signs, so that it would not be worshiped; for afterward the sons of Israel worshiped the serpent that he had made.

His entire life is divided into three periods of forty years. For forty years, from childhood, he learned letters in Pharaoh’s house in Egypt. For forty years, as an exile from Egypt, he lived in the house of the priest of Midian. And for forty years he provided leadership to the people through the wilderness.

Certainly, after completing what we have included in historical narrative from the Pentateuch, it is fitting to make here the end of the first book, *On Miracles*, so that the second, extracted from Prophecy, may begin with Joshua son of Nun and the Jordan.

# BOOK TWO — On Prophecy

[Col. 2173]

## CHAPTER I — On Joshua son of Nun and the Jordan divided at the people’s crossing

When Moses had departed and Joshua son of Nun had assumed the governance of God’s people, strengthened by the Lord’s word, he ordered the camp to move from the plains of Moab to the River Jordan. Then, when the priests, adorned with the burden of the ark of the covenant and preceding the rest of the people, entered the first waters, from the place where they stood as far as the sea the entire riverbed was immediately stripped of its waters. The upper mass of water, which was being increased by the springs, mounted upward into the air until all Israel had crossed the riverbed on dry feet (Josh. III, 14 ff.).

As testimony to this miracle, twelve stones, as large as twelve men could carry, were brought from the lowest gravel of the Jordan to the place of the camp; and an equal number, of equal size, were taken from those that the dry land had contained and placed in their stead (Josh. IV, 9–10).

Certainly here too, in accordance with the purpose of our work, the question arises how the river, by its natural behavior, does not allow the Lord’s ark to pass through. For the portion of the waters that flowed toward the sea follows the customary course of its nature: leaving the higher places, it gradually descends along the slopes in the river’s own manner.

Yet we read and hear how human ingenuity has stripped riverbeds of their waters. Cyrus, emperor of the Persians, is said to have encamped his army upon the River Ganges, which is second in size only to the Euphrates, during the expedition in which he conquered Babylon. There, the whirlpool of the rushing channel submerged a rider especially valued by men and horsemen, who had been persuaded by the boldness of crossing the river [the corrupt wording is uncertain].

After this, the king, moved by an astonishing fury of anger against the river, decided to exact vengeance upon it as though it were a sentient creature. By means of an immense channel he divided the great river, with all his strength, into four hundred and sixty ditches over the course of a full year; and, with its bed laid bare, he left it passable even to women whose knees were scarcely wetted.

Therefore, when the same army and king were besieging Babylon in the same expedition, and had been repulsed from the attempt to conquer it by the lofty obstruction of its walls, they turned toward the upper fords of the flowing Euphrates. Taught by the aforementioned method, they diverted the river through another channel, entered beneath Babylon’s wall through its exposed bed, and captured the city.

What human ingenuity accomplished through laborious effort, God performed more easily through the power of his might. But perhaps someone will answer differently and say that the two events are not comparable: “There, digging ditches diverted the waters into lower channels; here, standing water ascended into the heights of the air without anything resisting it.”

But does human diligence not often accomplish this as well, forcing waters to rise from opposing valleys into high places and, when they encounter an obstruction, to return to their sources? What human beings, as earthly creatures, frequently do with thick earthly material—how could angels, through whose ministries all these miracles are performed, not have done it through the air?

For it is the natural work and proper function of air to retain waters in the clouds. As learned and unlearned alike know, it retains them through its daily administration. Thus then, at God’s command, it restrained the river’s course so that God’s ark and the priests might pass through its waters.

## CHAPTER II — On the sandals and clothing of the sons of Israel

After entering the promised land following the labor of a long journey, the multitude of the people ate the produce of the region of Canaan, and the food of manna from the clouds ceased to be supplied (Josh. V, 42). On this very long journey, something worthy of admiration occurred: for forty years no sandal or garment failed for anyone among the entire people (Deut. XXIX, 5).

In this matter the Lord did not create a new nature in sandals and clothing, but preserved one that he had created long before.

## CHAPTER III — On the overthrow of Jericho

After leaving the bank of the Jordan, the city of Jericho was the first of the cities of Canaan to appear. Circled for seven days, it quickly collapsed, as though terrified by the approach of the Lord’s ark and army. In this circuit the victorious people used no assistance from weapons; rather, at the sound of a shout resounding around it, the wall was demolished down to its foundations (Josh. VI, 20).

The event itself shows that nothing contrary to nature occurred there. Scripture frequently declares that such things are brought about by earthquakes. Thus, in that famous earthquake, one hundred cities of Libya collapsed, and in the earthquake at the Lord’s passion eleven cities in Thrace were overthrown. [Col. 2175]

Moreover, what human activity gathers together through its effectiveness is consumed either by another force that destroys it or even by the passage of old age. Yet in saying these things, we do not show that the fall of Jericho’s walls occurred by chance; nor will we show that it occurred contrary to nature, as though it were something performed among miracles. For, just as we have indicated that the other events were administered through angelic work, we do not doubt that this too was accomplished at God’s command.

## CHAPTER IV — On the sun and moon standing at Joshua’s command

After this, when the five kings of the Canaanites had gathered together to fight against the sons of Israel, and the forces met one another face to face, victory was granted to God’s people. Joshua son of Nun, leader of the people of Israel, commanded the sun in the middle of the day not to move, and the moon to remain where it had been, until God’s people had avenged themselves upon their enemies. And it happened.

For the sun enclosed two days within one, and the moon did not appear during the span of that day. In this command the heavenly lights did not rest through the authority of a human ruler; they obeyed the command of the Lord who ordered them to stand. For God’s creatures do nothing because of the word of the commanding human being; rather, because the Lord, obeying the prayer of his servant, commanded it, they accomplish it.

Thus it is written: “The sun stood still against Gibeon, and the moon over the valley of Aijalon, while the Lord obeyed the voice of a man” (Josh. X, 12–14). From this it is understood that God obeys the prayers of his servants and governs his creatures suitably for their need.

This delay of the heavenly lights introduced nothing new into nature, even if it displayed something variable in its service. Nor did that variation disturb the course of the year or of the remaining days, since the sun and moon alike rested each in its own order. If one luminary had continued moving while the other rested in the meantime, it would have disrupted the customary course of days, months, and years. But since both underwent this delay, each proceeded, as though after an ordinary day, to the limit of its setting.

For the command to stand was not given so that the moon might then contribute light to the battle in the presence of the sun, but so that nothing might be destroyed in the proper movement of the luminaries by the rest of one and the course of the other.

Since we have also clearly shown that the motion of the sea corresponds in every respect to that of the moon, and that the sea too rested at that time, even though this is left unmentioned in the words of Scripture, does not the observable movement of those things itself declare it? The moon, moreover, did not merely rest in this station; during that interval it could not carry out its customary increase or decrease. If, while the moon stood still, it nevertheless underwent its increases or decreases, that lunar increase would disturb the calculations of the cycles beyond the solar course.

Since that day produced nothing longer than usual in the course of the circle returning upon itself, it is then clear that, when the evening supervened, the moon underwent the increase of one day, as it does every day. To make this clear through evident demonstrations, we shall briefly set out the recurrences of the cycles from the beginning of the created world. We shall show that every five hundred and thirty-two years, with the sun as at the beginning and the moon agreeing in every respect, they return to the point from which they began, without any intervening impediment.

In the fifth cycle from the beginning of the world, in the one hundred and fourteenth year, the universal flood of the whole world came under Noah; it ended in the four hundred and eighteenth year after the flood. From that point another cycle began, the sixth, and ended in the eighth year of Abraham’s life.

In his ninth year the seventh cycle began, and it concluded in the thirty-fifth year after the sons of Israel departed from Egypt, five years before Moses’ death. After it came the eighth cycle, in which the sign involving the sun and moon occurred: beginning in the thirty-sixth year after Israel’s departure from Egypt, it fell in the thirty-first year of Asa, king of Judah.

In the thirty-second year of Asa, the ninth cycle began. In it another sign involving the sun is recorded as having occurred in the time of King Hezekiah, which we shall discuss shortly. It completed the span of its course in the one hundred and eighth year after the restoration of the Temple, which took place under Darius.

Then the tenth cycle arose and was completed in the ninety-second year after the Savior’s [Col. 2176] passion, when Alia and Sparsa were consuls [Note: [Col. 2176] For *Aviola and Pansa*].

After this, the eleventh cycle, running from the consulship of Paternus and Torquatus down to our own times, was completed in its final year, when Manichaeus of Hibernia died among the other wise men. The twelfth cycle is now in its third year and, presenting itself to the knowledge of future events, leaves us ignorant of what end it will have.

Each cycle, with a uniform configuration, after five hundred and thirty-two years turns back upon itself, that is, into the beginning of the following cycle—namely, after each has completed nineteen solar cycles of twenty-eight years and twenty-eight lunar cycles of nineteen years.

After these cycles, once the lunar reckoning has been carefully counted through the common twelve months and seven intercalations, through the eight-year and eleven-year periods, and through the lunar increase that computists call the “leap”; and once the solar reckoning has been counted through the quarters and leap days; then, when the two luminaries have the same number of days and all the lines of their courses agree in orderly harmony, the year of the world’s creation is renewed, as it were.

Since, therefore, the total recurrences of these circles return fittingly upon themselves, and after those cycles in which signs of the sun and moon’s delay or return—such as are read to have appeared under Joshua or Hezekiah—are described as occurring, they return without any variation, it is clearly understood that neither that delay nor that return left anything obstructed or unusual in the customary course of the luminaries and the seasons.

Rather, after completing the span of that day, which was longer than usual, they ran, as I said above, through the entire day toward the limit of their setting. It therefore appears that the long day contributed no amount of time to the length of the following night, since its ruler, the moon, rested during the day together with the sun, the ruler of the day.

## CHAPTER V — On Gideon and the two signs
Therefore, after the region of Canaan had been cleansed of its destructive inhabitants, the land itself was granted by the Lord into the possession of God’s people. Later, when that people had relaxed into the leisure of peace, it spread throughout the land’s idolatrous worship, as well as that of the surrounding nations. For this reason, the Lord often granted power to the nations whose idols Israel itself worshiped, and delivered Israel into slavery to them. But afflicted by the harshest labors of captivity and servitude, Israel frequently begged God’s forgiveness through repentance. The one who had been appeased by the tears of the penitent then raised up judges, who, rescuing the people from the yoke of servitude, presided not by the rule of power but by the authority of judgment (Judg. II–IV). While the people were serving the Midianites in the days of these judges, a heavenly messenger appeared to Gideon, son of Joash, and, after the idolatrous rite had been destroyed, instructed him concerning the liberation of his people. While Gideon was preparing an offering in the messenger’s presence and pouring the broth of the flesh over it, heavenly fire from above consumed the burnt offering. And again, when he asked for a sign, there was dryness over all the ground but dew on the fleece; and then, conversely, dryness on the fleece but dew over all the ground (Judg. VI). Yet although these events are counted among miracles, they seem to display nothing new in the administration of things. For heavenly fire frequently consumes earthly things, as we have often said and shall say; and in the world rain alternately falls upon different regions. Nevertheless, many such matters arise from the miracles of Scripture which, although they do not demand careful explanation as historical events, are nevertheless filled with prefigurations of spiritual realities. But since in this work we intend to pursue only the meaning of events as they happened, we shall immediately insert this account historically among the miracles, for the sake of memory. Even if such things often occur by chance through God’s will, they were nevertheless governed and manifested more terribly, swiftly, certainly, and wondrously through the Lord’s command in the display of a sign. Thus, when historically, in this burning of the sacrifice, it was shown not by earthly fire but by a heavenly flame that the war then impending would prosper not through human strength but through heavenly assistance, the dew previously shown upon the fleece demonstrated that divine mercy, which at that time had been upon Israel as a fragile and pliant people, could extinguish the burning anger of the nations just as water extinguishes fire.

## CHAPTER VI — On Samson’s Strength in His Hair

Again, when the Israelite people were serving the Philistines, the angel of God appeared first to the barren wife of Manoah, son of Saruch, from the tribe of Dan, and then to Manoah himself, in prophetic guise. He instructed them concerning the son who was to be born to them and how he was to be raised: a razor was never to pass over his head, and he was not to drink strong drink, wine, or anything capable of causing intoxication. When Manoah, not knowing that he was an angel, wished to offer him a meal, the angel said, “I shall not eat of your food; but, if you wish, prepare a burnt offering for the Lord.” When Manoah had prepared it at his command, the angel immediately ascended into heaven in the fire of the sacrifice before their eyes (Judg. XIII). Here too the fire of the earthly sacrifice, ascending from earth to heaven, had shown that God had prepared the liberation of the people through the strength of the man who was to be born.

Samson was therefore born and raised according to the Lord’s command, and he possessed immense strength in the seven locks of his head. This was certainly proved when, after he had once been deprived of them, he also lost his strength. For when he loved Delilah, a foreign woman from the region of the Philistines, in the valley of Sorek, and she had accepted from the Philistine leaders, to whom Samson had done much harm, the price of his betrayal, he revealed to her, when she asked, that the secret of his strength lay in preserving his hair. She summoned a barber and shaved his head while he slept on her lap.

Samson was then taken by the Philistines, blinded, and made to turn a millstone by hand until his hair grew back to its former length. Afterwards, while the Philistines were feasting, he was brought in so that Samson might be mocked during their banquet. He told the boy guiding his steps to lead him to the two pillars upon which the whole house rested, so that, weary as he was, he might lean against them. Grasping both pillars with either hand and calling upon God for help, he shook the entire house. It soon collapsed and brought down with him three thousand Philistines (Judg. XVI).

But for those investigating the nature of things, this raises a considerable question: how did the entire sensible body possess the motion of strength in an insensible hair, whose loss caused no sensation of pain when the barber severed it from the rest of the body with the point of his instrument? Concerning Samson, therefore, before he was born the Lord commanded that his hair should never be cut by the edge of iron or by the point of any instrument (Judg. XIII, 5). As long as he remained in the keeping of the divine commandment, he possessed immense strength through the gift of the Holy Spirit. Thus, when through a woman’s persuasion he devised a transgression of the Lord’s commandment, the spiritual gift of strength that he had possessed immediately departed.

It was not that strength resided in an insensible hair lacking bone, flesh, and blood, and possessing none of these things. Rather, obedience to the Lord’s commandment preserved the gift of strength. But perhaps someone will say: Why did his strength grow again along with his hair, if he had not previously possessed strength in his hair as well? Yet even on this occasion he was not so much recovering, through the length of his hair, the strength he had lost as gradually obtaining, through the growth of his hair and under the affliction of repentance, the spiritual gift that he had lost through negligence. This was especially so because, although he could in some measure be excused in the transgression of this commandment—since, while he did not refuse to disclose the secret of his strength to Delilah when she asked, he was nevertheless not shorn with his knowledge, permission, or consent. Thus, later in his affliction, he more easily obtained from God what he had lost not willingly but after being deceived in sleep.

## CHAPTER VII — On the Lord’s Ark in the Land of the Philistines

After some considerable time, when the children of Israel were offending God by transgressing his commandments, the Philistine forces were stirred up and assembled to fight against them. The Israelites, trusting nothing in themselves, brought the ark of the Lord’s covenant with their army into battle against their adversaries. But the ark of the Law does not protect transgressors of the Law; rather, after part of the people had been defeated and destroyed, the ark itself was captured by foreigners.

Rejoicing in the gift of victory, they carried the captured ark into their own land and, as though it were the author of their triumph, placed the ark of Israel’s God beside their god Dagon in his temple. On the first day Dagon was found prostrate before the ark, but he was restored to his place. On the following day he was found broken into a hundred pieces at the threshold, with his head, hands, and backbone severed. This showed that the worship of idolatry, fleeing at the arrival of the Lord’s law, had been overthrown. Those who flee turn their backs to their pursuer.

Moreover, all Philistia was struck by a most repulsive plague: their *extales* [the reading is uncertain] protruded outward, and an enormous and unprecedented number of mice spread throughout the entire province (1 Sam. IV–V). The Lord had fittingly imposed both punishments upon them, as the appropriate logic of the events themselves demanded: those who venerated wretched animals with divine worship were to be chastised, at the coming of the Lord’s law, through the most wretched animals; and those who had dragged the inner things of the Lord’s tabernacle—namely, the ark—outside their proper bounds were to be afflicted by the disgusting calamity of their own inner organs protruding outward.

Therefore, when they allowed the ark, placed upon a new cart and drawn by two milch cows that had never before borne a yoke, to return to their borders, while their tender calves lowed at home, they placed beside it in a small chest five mice and an equal number of golden rings, tokens of their plagues, so that they would not send it back empty (1 Sam. VI, 10–11). But multiple interpretations of figures lie hidden in these events, and they require the diligent labor and leisure of a work devoted to them.

## CHAPTER VIII — On the Roar of Heaven by Which the Allophyli Were Terrified

Again, an immense host of Philistines, as innumerable as the sand of the sea, poured across the plains of the land of Israel. The Lord, in response to Samuel’s prayer, terrified them before the face of the Israelites with a great roar from heaven (1 Sam. VII, 10), so that Israel might understand that it had not conquered by its own strength and the enemies might know that God’s protection and assistance were with this people.

## CHAPTER IX — On the Voices and Rains When Saul Was Appointed

Likewise, when Samuel invoked the Lord, while the people were asking for a king and the prophet, commanded by God’s decree, was appointing Saul, son of Kish, from the tribe of Benjamin, the Lord thundered through rains and terrifying voices. The people who heard them were thereby to understand that they had rejected the Lord from reigning over them. The Lord, at Samuel’s renewed supplication, restrained these thunderclaps after he had seen the people’s inward repentance concerning this matter (1 Sam. XII, 18–19).

## CHAPTER X — On Saul Prophesying among the Prophets

Saul, stirred by the goad of envy and often seized by an evil spirit, wished to kill David. At that time David himself was prophesying with Samuel and the company of the other prophets. Saul sent messengers and ordered them to seize David from among the prophets and kill him. But as soon as they arrived, the spirit that was speaking in the prophets seized them. Saul himself, setting out after them as though he were going to carry out the task assigned to his servants, came among the prophets and prophesied (1 Sam. XIX, 20 ff.).

We said, when we discussed Balaam and the she-ass, that the words of the Holy Spirit are not assessed according to the merit of those who speak them, but are uttered by the Spirit’s own will wherever it wishes. Yet the merits of those who utter them are not thereby increased for the better if they do not possess good works, as in the cases of Balaam, Saul, and Caiaphas the high priest. Accordingly, such prophets will answer the Lord at the judgment when condemned: “Did we not prophesy in your name?”—and nevertheless they will undergo fellowship with eternal fire among the other impious (Matt. VII, 22–23).

Some, however, think in this passage that Saul prophesied throughout that entire day not by the divine Spirit but by that evil spirit by which he was often seized, until David too escaped, by the Lord’s dispensation, from the threatening danger of death, while Saul himself was seized by his own spirit [Note: [Col. 2178] Ms. Aud., *arrepto*, “having been seized”]. But how can this be understood when it is written: “And the spirit of the Lord came upon him, and as he walked he prophesied”? Unless perhaps in this passage “the spirit of the Lord” is understood in the same way as in another passage “the evil spirit of the Lord” seized Saul (1 Sam. XVI, 14).

Nevertheless, wherever Scripture speaks without qualification of “the Spirit of God,” “the Spirit of the Lord,” “the Spirit of Christ,” or “the Spirit of Jesus,” no sound understanding doubts that the Holy Spirit is meant. But wherever, with an added qualification, it says “the evil spirit of the Lord,” as in the Book of Samuel, the devil is understood: he seems to be called “of the Lord” because of his ministry, and “evil” because of his vice. Often, too, when simply “spirit” is found without the addition of “holy,” “of God,” or some other expression belonging to the designation or indication of the Holy Spirit, the opposing spirit—that is, the devil—or any subordinate subject to him among those who serve demons, is recognized.

## CHAPTER XI — On Samuel Raised by the Pythoness

Later, when Saul was in distress and the enemy’s attack pressed upon him, and the Lord gave him no answer, although he sought one through prophets, priests, or dreams, Saul, king of Israel, went to a pythoness so that she might raise someone from the dead for him by the incantations of her art. When she asked him which dead person he wished to have released from the sleep of death, he replied that he wished Samuel to be raised. The raised Samuel then foretold to Saul what would happen, saying: “At this hour you and your sons shall be with me; and I shall deliver Israel with you into the hand of its enemies” (1 Sam. XXVIII, 5–19).

How, then, is Samuel said to have been raised by the pythoness, when the pythoness appears to use demonic incantations and magic tricks? And how did Saul, who had found no answer from God through the living prophets, deserve to hear a prophet raised from the dead? It is therefore more readily understood that this was not that perfect prophet Samuel, but that the devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. XI, 14), should be regarded as appearing in Samuel’s apparition.

This is rightly discerned from his words, for he said to the condemned Saul, “You and your sons shall be with me.” If that true Samuel had appeared here, he would in no way have called an unrighteous king his companion in merit after death.

If, then, the devil is shown by the pythoness, why is Samuel said in divine Scripture to have been raised? In many passages of sacred Scripture, names belonging to real things are often assigned to imagined things. Thus the rod imagined in the likeness of a serpent, the fantastic serpents of the Egyptian magicians (Exod. VII, 10, 12), and the bronze serpent in the wilderness are all called serpents (Num. XXI, 9). Two cherubim are also said to overshadow the mercy seat by their likeness (Exod. XXXVII, 7). Five mice and five golden tumors from the land of the Philistines are reported as being in a small chest with the ark of the Lord (1 Sam. VI, 11). Twelve oxen are placed beneath the bronze sea (1 Kings VII, 25), and fourteen lions upon Solomon’s ivory throne (ibid. X, 19–20). Cherubim, palm trees, pomegranates, and nets are described as depicted in the construction of the temple (ibid. VI, 32), although all these things receive these names not from the literal reality of the objects themselves but from their resemblance.

Nevertheless, Scripture itself names these things without any reservation of uncertainty, as though they were real objects. Thus Samuel’s apparition is announced as having been shown as Samuel himself, just as the men shown in the visions of the prophets and in the Apocalypse of John are announced as men.

## CHAPTER XII — On Uzzah’s Striking

Not long afterward, while David held the kingship, the ark of the covenant was brought from the house of Abinadab to Jerusalem by the king and all the people. Uzzah, son of Abinadab, followed the ark and, when he touched it as though supporting it, was struck by sudden death and suffocated (2 Sam. VI, 2–7).

In this act, the presumption of Uzzah himself is condemned, since, although he was not of Aaron’s lineage, he touched the ark; and the whole people are admonished that they ought to act cautiously in divine matters. Some, however, think that some preceding sin in Uzzah was punished through this offense, since it often happens that lesser faults bring down vengeance for earlier sins.

## CHAPTER XIII — On David’s Counting the People

Similarly, when the people of Israel had sinned, the Lord moved David to count the people. As a result, the sinful people suffered punishment for its earlier offenses through the king’s small fault. For the angel of the Lord killed seventy thousand men throughout Israel as far as Beer-sheba and seemed about to destroy the city of Jerusalem (2 Sam. XXIV). This was not because the Lord wished to destroy the city, but so that the angel, shown ready to execute vengeance, might inspire the king who saw him with an appropriate repentance.

From this it is understood that David committed a lesser fault than the people: he wiped out his sin through repentance alone, whereas the people’s offense deserved the severity of death upon its leaders.

## CHAPTER XIV — On the Two Signs beside the Altar at Bethel

Afterward, when through Solomon’s sin the one kingdom of the people of Israel was divided into two, Jeroboam son of Nebat, king of the ten tribes in the northern region, fearing that the people might again be joined to Rehoboam, son of Solomon, by visiting the temple that was in Jerusalem, set up idols and altars at Dan and Bethel (1 Kings XII).

At the dedication of the altar that was at Bethel, however, a man from Judah was sent by the Lord to prophesy against that altar. When he arrived, two terrifying signs were displayed. For at the very hour of the sacrifice the altar was immediately split into two parts, and the king’s own withered hand dried up (ibid. XIII, 1–5).

These two signs aptly corresponded to the event and to its purpose, clearly showing what had then happened in the king himself. It was fitting that the man who had divided the worship of God—which had existed in a single altar and temple—should see the altar that he had made for himself split and dried up in this way; and that the man who had made the hand of God’s people withered, so that it could not offer sacrifices and burnt offerings to its Lord, should have his own hand appear withered at that schismatic sacrifice.

## CHAPTER XV — On the Drought of Three Years and Six Months

Furthermore, while Ahab son of Omri was committing many crimes at the instigation of his wife Jezebel, Elijah the Tishbite from Gilead said in the word of God: “There shall be neither dew nor rain during these years, except according to the word of my mouth” (ibid. XVII, 1). At his prayer rain was withheld, and it did not fall for three years and six months, so that those who had provoked God on earth by their evil deeds might be deprived of heaven’s mercy and the air’s beneficial abundance.

Many teachers think that this plague afflicted only the land of Israel. But it is customary for Scripture to name indiscriminately the whole land when it means the province of which it speaks. This is fittingly demonstrated later in Elijah’s conversation with Ahab. When Ahab saw Elijah, he is reported to have said, “Are you the one who troubles Israel?” Elijah answered him and declared that the fault which had provoked this plague lay in Israel alone: “It is not I who trouble Israel,” he said, “but you and your father’s house, because you have forsaken the law of the Lord and served Baal” (ibid. XVIII, 17–18).

Through both these statements, the agreement of the words demonstrates that the fault and the plague concerned Israel alone. For if that plague had scourged the whole world, Ahab would not have said merely, “You who trouble Israel,” but, “You who trouble the whole world.”

During the drought, the Lord told Elijah to hide himself in the cave of the torrent Carith, where, with ravens ministering bread and meat, he would be satisfied with the water of the torrent (ibid. XVII, 2–4). This served a double purpose: that he might have nourishment during the famine and escape the savage anger of his persecutors, who were eagerly seeking him.

The prophet was commanded to be served by ravens so that the bird might appear to purge the fault it had committed on earth in the Flood, becoming a faithful minister to Elijah although it had previously been negligent and deceitful toward Noah. Moreover, this ministry also showed how, if human beings had not sinned, they would even now make use of the ministries of unproductive animals.

But let the one who entrusted the raven with such a duty determine from where that raven carried the meat and bread. Yet it must be observed that the ravens received these things through the activity of certain human beings, knowingly or unknowingly, who prepared baked bread and various kinds of meat in whatever manner.

## CHAPTER XVI — On the Widow at Zarephath of Sidon

When the water of the torrent failed because of the excessive drought, God commanded Elijah to go to a widow at Zarephath, so that he might be fed there. When she received him familiarly into her house and supplied him with his daily food, the little jar of oil and the jar of flour in which she had found a one-day ration at his arrival did not diminish until the Lord visited his people (1 Kings XVII, 8–16).

This did not happen because the Lord’s hand was weak, as though, after the torrent’s water had failed, he were unable to supply Elijah with water, bread, and meat from elsewhere. Rather, the prophet was sent to be fed at Zarephath of Sidon so that through him the good and faithful widow might be fed.

Nor should anyone be troubled by the fact that the land of Sidon suffered this same plague along with Israel, since Jezebel, the persecutor of the prophets and the cause of the entire vengeance and crime, was the daughter of the king of Sidon and derived her paternal origin from that land.

Certainly, this sign too shows that what was being governed by the Lord was not something new but ordinary nature, with an extraordinary abundance, just as is recalled concerning the shoes and clothing of Israel. For in all the miracles mentioned above, nothing departs from the order of nature, as the outcome of events itself frequently shows.

## CHAPTER XVII — On the Widow’s Only Son, Who Was Dead and Whom Elijah Raised

At that time, while Elijah was staying in this widow’s house, her son died of a severe illness. Elijah restored him to life through his prayer (1 Kings XVII, 17–22). The Hebrews relate that this was the prophet Jonah, whom the Lord later released from the belly of the swallowing whale after three days had passed (Jonah II). For the Lord, who can kill his enemy wherever he is in a secure place, is able to rescue his servant from any distress he wishes.

But the famous question concerning the raising of the dead is reserved by us until Lazarus.

## CHAPTER XVIII — On the Sacrifice on Mount Carmel

When the time of the drought had passed and the Lord wished to give rain upon the earth, he ordered the prophet Elijah to go out to meet King Ahab. Ahab gathered all Israel and the four hundred and fifty prophets of the idols on Mount Carmel.

When they had assembled, holy Elijah proposed that two oxen be slaughtered as burnt offerings—one to the Lord and the other to Baal—one by himself and the other by the prophets of the idols, so that the god who answered through fire might himself be the God of the whole people.

When this had been agreed, the priests of Baal first killed their ox. Until midday they called upon Baal in distress to consume the sacrifice by fire. But Baal, who had rather been handed over to the power of fire, was unable to send fire upon the sacrifice.

Elijah, however, cut his ox into pieces and divided it limb by limb. He then placed it upon the altar that had been built and that he himself had repaired, and drenched it abundantly with water. As he prayed, fire suddenly fell from heaven and consumed the ox together with the altar, the stones, and the water. Afterwards he killed the priests of Baal, who had been delivered into his power, at the torrent Kishon, and all the people confessed and believed that the Lord was God (1 Kings XVIII, 19–40).

In this event too the fire did nothing contrary to nature. Descending from above through the fiery region of the air, it consumed, by the command of God who governed it, the material for its nourishment that it found on earth. That fire’s nature is more abundant in the region above is also declared by the fire burning on earth, which ardently attempts to climb upward toward the place where its nature exists. For just as it is the nature of water always to descend to lower places, so it is proper to fire to seek what is high.

Water too, however, is often seen to ascend to high places without acting contrary to its nature. It does not do this by itself through its own substance, which is heavy, but through the lighter nature of the air, by which the tiniest drops of water are drawn together in vapor. These minute drops, ascending toward the heights of the air in the manner of smoke, come together within denser clouds. They cannot remain suspended above the nature of the air, but, under the pressure of the wind, they descend to earth in a heavier mass.

If frost seizes them in the clouds before they have fallen, the rigor of cold brings those same drops down, congealed into little stones of hail solidified by ice. If the frost finds them more fluid and not yet condensed, it makes snow. If icy cold does not touch them, free drops of water return to the lower regions from which they came.

Just as water does not ascend by itself except through another substance, as we have shown, so fire does not descend below except through another substance. Thus, when the Lord rained fiery showers upon the five cities about which we spoke in the first book (ch. 5), this too occurred through sulfur, so that fire might burn in the sulfur and, through the heavier nature of sulfur, descend to earth.

Here, therefore, where fire descended upon the altar for the sacrifice, it descended either through air or through sulfur, since fire cannot descend by itself unless God commands it to mingle with some heavier material.

Elijah, the servant of God, therefore killed the priests of the idols without incurring the guilt of homicide, since he belonged to the Law that says, “You shall not allow a blasphemer to live” (Lev. XXIV, 16). No human being worships an idol without having become a blasphemer against God. Accordingly, by slaughtering the worshipers of idolatry, he was cleansing the earth of blasphemers and sacrilegious persons.

After all this, the man who by prayer had withheld rain from watering the earth for three years and six months obtained from God, through the same service of prayer, abundant and gentle rain for the thirsty earth within a short period of time. This rain would never have come upon the earth unless he had cleansed it by killing the worshipers of Baal.

## CHAPTER XIX — On the Forty-Day Fast

When Jezebel learned that Elijah had killed them, she terrified the prophet with threatening words concerning his own death. Elijah therefore went sorrowfully into the land of Judah, sat beneath a broom tree, and fell asleep. The angel of the Lord touched him, awakened him from sleep, and, feeding him with bread and water, satisfied his hunger and refreshed his thirst.

Strengthened by that food, he walked in its power for forty days and forty nights, eating nothing, until he reached Horeb, the mountain of God. There, having enjoyed the company of the word of the Lord, he returned again to the land of Israel (1 Kings XIX).

We reserve for those who know from what source the nature of these things derives the task of explaining the meaning of the bread and water provided by angelic service, whose strength carried the prophet through the labor of hunger for forty days [Note: [Col. 2182] Ms. Aud., “protected.”]. In this bread we observe something resembling human workmanship, since it was baked like bread; yet we do not understand it to have possessed the power of earthly bread, by which a single meal could satisfy the need of forty days.

Unless, perhaps, through angelic workmanship it was made from some earthly material and, nourishing the soul of a human being dwelling on earth, rendered it stronger than ordinary human bread. Although this bread, by concealing its own nature, causes the attentive reader difficulty, it nevertheless makes the forty-day fast intelligible and reassuring: through the power of one meal, the prophet lived for so long without requiring any food.

## CHAPTER XX — On the Fire Descending upon the Captains of Fifty

After some interval of time had passed, while the prophet was sitting on the mountain, the king ordered a captain of fifty, together with those under his command, to bring him to the king. Inflated in mind with arrogance—that is, with proud swelling—he said, “Man of God, the king, Ochozias, that is, the son of Ahab, commands you to go out to him with us.”

Elijah answered him: “If I am a man of God, as you say, let heavenly flame now consume you and those who are with you.” This occurred. The king then ordered another man of the same rank, with as many companions [Col. 2183], to go to him. When this man repeated words agreeing with those of the first, the same judgment consumed him with the same vengeance.

After this, the third captain of fifty, sent into the same danger with his men, humbly bent his knee before the Lord’s prophet and begged him in supplicatory words to come before the king. “Go down with him,” the angel of the Lord said to Elijah. He rose immediately and went with him, after the proud men had been killed, to the king with the humbled and suppliant captain (2 Kings I, 9–15).

In this passage, as in the sacrifice mentioned above, the fire obeyed the prophet’s spoken word and fulfilled what it was commanded to do. Here too, as we stated earlier concerning Uzzah and the census of the people, the avenging flame perhaps punished a more serious crime committed previously.

## CHAPTER XXI — On Elijah and Elisha Crossing the Jordan

Finally, when the Lord wished to raise Elijah up, he and Elisha, son of Shaphat, his servant, crossed the divided river Jordan on dry foot, Elijah’s cloak having divided it, just as we previously said occurred at the crossing of the children of Israel (ibid. II, 8).

For explaining this event, what was said earlier from the Book of Joshua is sufficient for this work. Although the events mentioned above correspond in many of these wondrous deeds of power, and although the explanations of the miracles may diverge in their figurative interpretation, the explanations demanded by nature in the historical understanding of the events nevertheless require the same account.

Before we begin to weave a little garland of discourse concerning all the miracles of divine Scripture, it is worthwhile also to explain, as they occurred, those matters in which, because of their resemblance to preceding events, no further explanation is necessary—especially since I have resolved to omit nothing among the miracles of Scripture’s Lord in which they appear to excel the ordinary service of daily things.

## CHAPTER XXII — On Elijah’s Ascension

When both men had come up from the bank of the Jordan, Elijah said to his servant: “Ask me what you wish before God commands me to pass away from you and be received.” Elisha answered, “I beg that your spirit may rest upon me in double measure.”

Elijah replied again: “You have asked for a difficult thing; nevertheless, if you are present with me at the hour of my reception and see me, the outcome will fulfill this request.”

In making this request, Elisha did not desire, out of an impulse toward pride, to rise above his master. Rather, seeing the countless sins of the people, he foresaw that they could be restrained by the prophet who would remain not with Elijah’s single spirit but with a double spirit.

If he had asked for what he requested through the fault of a mind wishing to exalt itself, he would certainly not have obtained what he asked from the Lord and from Elijah himself.

After these words, then, while Elisha watched, Elijah was snatched away in a fiery chariot, as though to heaven (ibid., 9–12). To this day he, like Enoch, is preserved without death as a testimony for the last age, so that the word of the final testimony may stand in the mouth of these two witnesses at the end of time, shortly before Satan is condemned—the one who will crush the human race in open war.

It was therefore fitting that Elijah, whose zeal for divine love had blazed in his soul with fiery ardor, who had performed many wondrous signs through fire, should be carried by the Lord into a higher state through a fiery chariot, transformed from the condition of human beings. Moreover, let us see whether what we said earlier in the first book concerning Enoch also applies to Elijah.

## CHAPTER XXIII — On the Miracles of Elisha
Meanwhile, the sorrowful heir of Elijah, Elisha, gathered up the garments falling to the ground and, invoking the God of Elijah as well, crossed the Jordan on dry foot. Coming to Jericho, he healed the bitter and barren waters by putting salt into the spring, just as Moses did through the wood in the wilderness. It is sufficient to have discussed this matter in that place. From there, when he came to Bethel, the bald Elisha was mocked by little boys. When he cursed them in the name of the Lord, forty-two boys were torn apart by two bears coming out of the forest (ibid., 12–24). At this point the Prophet did not curse the boys because he had been angered by a personal insult; rather, he inflicted just vengeance upon the children of those who had turned away from the Lord [Col. 2184] and the law of their fathers—people who sacrificed to idols at Bethel—since perhaps the boys themselves had also been dedicated to idols, as was customary at that time. For at Bethel one of the two calves that Jeroboam son of Nebat had made—the one who caused Israel to sin—had been set up (3 Kings 12:29). By worshiping these idols, the people of the ten tribes of Israel turned away from the Lord and sinned.

Moreover, the Prophet, foreseeing what the insolent Jewish people would suffer long afterward when mocking Christ crucified on Calvary, meanwhile enacted what fittingly corresponded to them in a figurative manner. Then, during the expedition in which Joram king of Israel, Jehoshaphat king of Judah, and the king of Edom had gone out against the sons of Moab, when the entire army had been exhausted by hardship and was suffering from thirst in the wilderness, Elisha obtained from God that water should come through the dried-up torrent without rain. There he ordered the people to make trenches and wells, on account of the Israelites and the Gentiles who were in the same army (4 Kings 3:9–20).

When he had returned from that expedition and reached the land of Israel, the widow of one of the prophets cried out to him tearfully: “Behold,” she said, “my creditor wants to take my two sons, whom I bore to my husband, your servant, to serve him, because I have nothing else with which to repay him.” Elisha said to her: “Tell me, what do you have in your house?” She answered: “I have a little oil stored in a vessel, enough to anoint myself.” Elisha therefore said: “Go and borrow from all your neighbors empty vessels—not a few.” When she had done this, she filled them all from that small amount of oil as it increased (ibid. 4:1–6).

Through the Prophet’s power, this small quantity of oil could increase into something greater without violating nature. For it is fitting that the whole magnitude of created things should always grow from small beginnings, especially since this is more particularly seen in the nature of liquid: in the art of the cupbearer, certain kinds of vessels are known to overflow and swell from a small amount of material into an abundance of liquid.

The same man often passed through the city of Shunem. When he had frequently been received with generous hospitality by a certain wealthy but barren woman, he foretold that she would conceive by her own husband. But after the child had been born and raised, he was struck by the severe and customary illness of pain and died while still a boy. Elisha, however, restored him to life in a figurative sequence and returned him alive to his mother (ibid., 8–37).

At another time, driven by famine, the sons of the prophets gathered wild herbs and, failing to recognize among them deadly and very bitter colocynths, cooked them in a stew. When one of them had tasted it, he cried out that there was death in the pot. But when Elisha put a little flour into the same pot with his own hand, the power of that flour, through its tasty, pleasant, and healthy flavor, overcame the insipid and deadly wild colocynths (ibid., 38–41).

He also ordered twenty loaves to be divided among a hundred men; they satisfied the crowd, and the attendants gathered up and retained an overflowing quantity of fragments (ibid., 42–44). We shall explain more carefully the meaning of this power when, if the Lord permits, we discuss in the Gospel the five loaves and two fish, and again the seven loaves and a few small fish.

## CHAPTER XXIV — The Healing of Naaman’s Leprosy and Its Clinging to Gehazi

After these events, Naaman, commander of the army of the king of Syria, was a leper. When he learned that in the land of Israel there was a remarkable prophet endowed with the gift of healing, he went first to the king of Israel, accompanied by a crowd of soldiers and having taken gifts and letters from his master. The king himself instructed him to proceed to the house of Elisha.

When Naaman stood before the door, Elisha sent word through a servant that he should wash himself seven times in the Jordan. He would have scornfully rejected the messenger altogether if the words of his companions had not persuaded him to undertake so easy a task. Yielding to them, he washed seven times in the Jordan, as Elisha had commanded, and his entire skin was restored healed—soft and tender like that of a child.

For this benefit of healing, he attempted to offer gifts to the man of God. Elisha refused them, preferring to bestow freely what he had received freely. From this it is most clearly [Col. 2185] shown, as I said earlier, that in the word of the commanding God, according to the Prophet’s command, the sacrament of the power does not reside in some material object. For if Naaman had washed in the Jordan without the Prophet’s command—or rather, without God’s command through the Prophet—he would in no way have received the cleansing of his leprosy so quickly.

Gehazi, the servant of the man of God, then considered that his master Elisha had spared Naaman for no apparent reason. Taking two boys with him, he hurried after Naaman, as though sent by his master. Through a contrived lie, he obtained money from him and brought back part of it on horses, although Elisha had altogether refused to accept or possess it.

Afterward, when his master asked Gehazi where he had been, he falsely pretended that he had gone nowhere. But the Prophet exposed the hidden lie with manifest judgment: “Was not my spirit present with you when the man descended from his chariot to meet you? While the unhappy thought of greed deceived you into doing and saying this, the leprosy of Naaman shall cling to you and to your offspring forever” (4 Kings 5).

Behold: by the same power by which the prophet Elisha removed Naaman’s leprosy from his body, he commanded that the same leprosy should cling to Gehazi’s flesh and household. It must therefore be clearly understood that all these miracles are accomplished not through the effects of the things themselves but through the command of the one who commands them. Nevertheless, it is certain that nothing contrary to nature is brought about in the operation of either those or these things. In their accomplishment, however, the will of the commanding God—whether by himself, through angels, or through human beings—summons those things which he foresees to correspond fittingly in every respect to the figures of future events.

## CHAPTER XXV — The Floating of the Iron

At another time, while the sons of the prophets were making a place for themselves in the presence of Elisha, the iron blade of an axe slipped from the handle in the hand of one of them and fell into the Jordan River. Since he had lost the borrowed tool, he was deeply distressed. Moved by the man’s cry and by his grief, Elisha sought the submerged place where the iron had fallen. After marking the spot and throwing a piece of wood there, he brought the iron up from the depths, making it float to the surface of the water (4 Kings 6:5–6).

The thin substance of water cannot support the heavy nature of iron. Yet the one who later solidified the nature of the sea beneath Peter’s feet (Matt. 14:29) first commanded the iron to rise from the depths.

Water, although more fragile than earth, nevertheless appears more solid than air. It is shown to possess less power than earth because metals and stones are less readily supported by it. But it retains more than air, since it can support the floating bodies of human beings and other animals, as well as wood. Thus, although water does not support metal completely, it nevertheless bears it in part along with those carrying it. A stone which, as is often proved, two men can scarcely lift in the air, can be held in water by one person when suspended from a rope.

It is therefore apparent that water, although it does not support metal entirely, can support it in part; and that God naturally commands a thing to follow through the whole what it possesses in part. For this reason the nature of water could support floating iron, because God commanded that what the creature itself habitually does in part should be accomplished completely.

## CHAPTER XXVI — Victory through Elisha

During wartime, the king of Syria arranged ambushes for the king of Israel in many places. The prophet Elisha always revealed them to the king of Israel, so that he might act cautiously in those places. When the king of Syria learned for certain that this was being done through Elisha, he sent a well-equipped army with numerous chariots and horses against the city of Dothan, where Elisha was.

When the servant of the man of God rose early and saw this, he came to Elisha terrified and shaken with fear. The Prophet encouraged him: “There are more helpers on our side than enemies.” And so that the boy’s mind would not remain excessively terrified at the sight of the great multitude of enemies, he made visible to him phalanxes of angels equipped with fiery chariots and horses, standing all around him throughout the mountain.

Then, going out to meet the enemy [Col. 2186], he obtained from the Lord that he would strike that people with blindness, just as formerly at the doors of Lot (Gen. 19:11). Promising that he would lead the blinded enemies to the man they were seeking, he brought them into the city of Samaria and there opened their eyes. When the king of Israel saw them, he asked Elisha whether he should kill them. But the man of God commanded him not to kill them; instead, he was to feed the enemies and let them depart (4 Kings 6:8–23).

This people, therefore, was not struck with blindness in such a way that they could not see the light of day. Rather, recognition of the present Elisha and of the places through which they were walking was hidden from their eyes. For if they had been blinded so that they could not see daylight, such a great multitude could never have followed Elisha alone as he led them into Samaria. They were therefore struck with a kind of blindness: they saw him but could in no way recognize him.

In the same way, the man of God opened the eyes of his servant—not so that he might see the daylight by which he could see the enemies, but so that his vision might be directed toward the angels, whom he had not previously seen.

During this same war, Ben-hadad king of Syria came into the land of Israel with an innumerable multitude, besieged Samaria for many days, and forced the inhabitants, enclosed in such extreme distress that mothers were eating their own children, to submit to the necessity of the siege. Therefore the king of Israel, driven by this shameful disgrace, came to Elisha’s house full of fury and resolved to behead him, since he believed that Elisha could relieve the present distress.

For this reason the Prophet, as though concerned for his own life, replied firmly: “Tomorrow at this very hour, a measure of fine flour will be sold for one shekel, and two measures of barley for one shekel, at the gate of this city.” But one of the king’s two officers, chattering in disbelief, said: “Even if the Lord were to make windows in heaven, could what you say happen?” Elisha answered him: “You shall see it with your own eyes, but because of your unbelief you shall not eat of it.”

Then, during the following night, the Lord caused the sound of a brazen crash to be heard in the Syrian camp. This drove all the enemy forces into flight at once. When the people discovered this, they poured out in groups through the city gate and crushed to death that unbelieving officer. He saw these things but, in accordance with Elisha’s word, could not eat of them (ibid. 24 and following; 7:1–7, 17 and following).

Of all these miracles, which we have briefly touched upon in order to preserve the origin of the marvels of divine Scripture, we have either noted similar examples earlier in the first book or reserved some for explanation in the third book, in which we shall discuss the Gospel and the New Testament, if the Lord grants life and assistance.

Meanwhile, after the death of Elisha, the servant of God, his attendants were one day carrying a dead man when, seeing raiders, they became afraid and threw the corpse into the nearby tomb of Elisha. When it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came back to life and stood up (ibid. 13:21).

Some say that the saying previously mentioned was fulfilled in this sign: “Let the spirit that is in you be doubled in me.” This necessarily had to be fulfilled. Elijah, therefore, is recorded as having raised one dead person during his lifetime, before he was taken away (3 Kings 17:22), and Elisha likewise is now seen to have done the same (4 Kings 4:35). But he also appears to have restored another person—namely, this man—to life after his own death, in the tomb.

Yet even in this event a double grace does not seem to be evident. For what Elijah had done once, he could have repeated twice or three times, if necessary. Rather, the double grace of Elijah in Elisha is shown by the fact that Elisha commanded by giving orders what Elijah obtained by praying and asking.

Or, as others say, it consists in this: Elisha possessed the gift of miracles and prophecy with great honor and worldly distinction, whereas Elijah, as a fugitive and persecuted man, living in mountains and caves and cast out by human beings, retained it under such conditions.

## CHAPTER XXVII — The Captivity of the People and Sennacherib’s Coming into Judaea

For a long period afterward, the people of Israel transgressed the law of God and the sayings of the Prophets, despising the Lord himself by worshiping idols—even though he had led their fathers out of the land of Egypt. Having been handed over to the nations [Col. 2187], after many massacres of the people and the destruction of besieged cities, the Lord utterly cast away from his presence the ten tribes that were in the region of Samaria.

The kings of the Assyrians—namely, Shalmaneser and Tiglath-pileser [Note: [Col. 2187] Ms. Aud., Teglaphalnasar.]—to whom he had handed them over to be taken captive and transported, gathered Samaritans in their place as guardians, that is, people from many nations and cities, so that the land would not remain uncultivated. Because these people did not fear the Lord, lions tore them apart at his command.

Word therefore quickly reached King Tiglath-pileser through messengers that the nations he had settled in the land of Israel, not knowing the worship of the God of the land, were being torn apart by lions. Accordingly, the king sent one of the priests of the Levitical line and caused those nations to worship God. Once this had been done, although little of their Gentile superstition had been abandoned, the plague of the lions ceased (4 Kings 17).

But God still preserved the tribe of Judah and the city of Jerusalem, which he had chosen, together with all who belonged to them. At that time their kingdom was governed by Hezekiah, a righteous king who feared God.

Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, however, seeing that his fathers had destroyed the kingdom and rule of Israel in Samaria, summoned an army and ordered it to attack Jerusalem in the land of Judah, under the command of Rabshakeh, whom the Hebrews call the son of the prophet Isaiah and a Judean refugee who had migrated to the Assyrians.

But in the very attempt, God—the defender of his people and humbler of the proud—sent a soldier from the heavenly army, namely an angel, against the camp of the Assyrians. In the course of one night he killed 185,000 of Sennacherib’s army. Thus routed from the land of Judah, Sennacherib scarcely escaped, fleeing with a few men to his own city, Nineveh. There, while he was found in the temple of his idols, he fell dead from the wound inflicted by his own sons (ibid. 18–19).

## CHAPTER XXVIII — Hezekiah’s Illness and Sign

A short time later, King Hezekiah of Judah, lest he should be elated by so great a victory—and perhaps also because he had been deficient in thanksgiving—fell into a very serious illness. The prophet Isaiah came to visit him in his illness and said: “Set your house in order, for you shall live no longer; you shall surely die.”

Immediately distressed by this very sorrowful message, the king turned his face toward the wall and poured out before the most merciful and compassionate Lord a tearful prayer for his life. This was not because, as a perfect man, he was uncertain of his own merit before his Creator, but because he had not abandoned the lineage of his race in the generation of the Christ who was to come, nor the lamp on the throne of David.

When the pious Lord had been moved to mercy by the tears of the king and his servant, the prophet Isaiah was again sent, impelled by the pure divine will. He had scarcely gone halfway across the court when he announced that health, kingship, and peace would belong to the king and the city on every side, and confirmed by the word of God that fifteen years would be added to his life from that very day.

But since Isaiah had uttered two prophecies contrary to one another in the same hour [Note: [Col. 2187] Ms. Aud., “day.”], it was necessary that he confirm the one that was to be fulfilled by the display of a sign. Therefore, so that the king might believe what had been said without doubt, God turned the sun back along its course from setting toward rising for ten hours. Thus it began again, as if at dawn, to hurry forward after it had completed the span of the entire day except for two hours.

During those two hours, as many think, it returned rapidly from setting to rising, so that the whole day might again be renewed at the rising of the sun without the intervention of night, and so that two days might, even on this occasion, be enclosed within a single light (4 Kings 20:1–11).

Just as under Joshua son of Nun the sun had delayed during the war mentioned earlier, so it is beyond doubt that on this occasion the moon also returned, lest, as we said, anything be disturbed in the courses of the cycles. For this reason it is not denied that the very alternation of the sea was also interrupted, so that thereafter it might suitably accompany the courses of the moon, as it does every day.

In this return, the sun’s nature did not change; rather, it obeyed naturally in all things [Col. 2188] the command of its Creator. Just as the sun possesses by nature the qualities of shining and heating, so whatever the Lord’s command might order—whether to run, stand still, or run back—it possesses naturally.

Such a sign fittingly and most appropriately occurred for a king placed in expectation of death. The Lord arranged for it to take place through the sun by a suitable dispensation. For just as the sun, poised at the threshold of its setting, is brought back to the beginning of the day, so the king, situated in expectation of death, is recalled, as it were, to the joys of life’s beginning.

The Lord also said that he would add fifteen years to his life, so that the son who was to be born at that time would, after those years had passed, be able to govern the kingdom of his deceased father.

As for the considerable question concerning this event—whether God had determined that the end of Hezekiah’s life should occur then if he did not weep—many authors have raised it. When, if the Lord permits, we speak about Lazarus, who had been dead four days, we wish to make the matter known from the authority of the Gospel itself. The same judgment that must be stated about this man, recalled from the gate of death, must also be stated about those who, having been raised from death’s sleep, later die again.

## CHAPTER XXIX — The Babylonian Captivity

After Hezekiah’s death, when the kings of Judah and the rest of the people multiplied their crimes, and the Lord foretold through the Prophets that he would hand Jerusalem over to the Chaldeans, together with its kings and peoples, for destruction, subsequent events confirmed this prophecy, since the entire people had altogether despised the words of the Prophets.

When Pharaoh, king of Egypt, came to fight against the Assyrians and Chaldeans, Josiah, a sufficiently righteous king of Judah, met him in the field of Megiddo with his army. In that conflict Josiah was defeated, wounded, and killed, and his son Jehoahaz was appointed king in his place by the people of the land of Judah.

But after Necho had defeated the army of the Assyrians and Chaldeans, and had appointed commanders at the city of Carchemish to protect the kingdom he had seized, he returned to Jerusalem with a great army three months after Josiah had been killed. Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah, had been appointed king without Necho’s knowledge. Necho replaced him with his brother Eliakim, and Jehoahaz was bound in chains and taken with him to Egypt.

After Necho’s death, and after the commanders left at Carchemish had been defeated in battle, in the third year of Jehoiakim, king of Judah, who had remained allied with Necho until then, Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged Jerusalem with his army as though it were a colony of Egypt.

Jehoiakim voluntarily surrendered to him and, after giving hostages—Daniel, Hananiah, Azariah, and Mishael—and part of the vessels of the temple of the Lord, was nevertheless left in his own kingdom. Later, oppressed by the burden of a very severe servitude, he again turned toward the king of Egypt. An army was sent from Babylon, and he was captured and dragged away. Before reaching the city, he was killed in the fields of Babylon in the eleventh year of his reign.

Meanwhile, his son Jehoiachin, who is also called Jeconiah, was appointed king in Jerusalem by the people in his father’s place. In the third month of his reign, when the Chaldean army returned and besieged the city of Jerusalem, the prophet Jeremiah advised him not to allow the city to be burned. King Jehoiachin therefore surrendered to the people of the Chaldeans, together with his mother Nehushta, all the tribes of the people, the soldiers, the craftsmen, and the smiths. They led him, with all his migration, into the land of the Chaldeans, that is, into Babylon.

After him, his uncle Zedekiah, son of Josiah king of Judah, was appointed by the Chaldeans and obtained the kingdom of Jerusalem. In the ninth year of his reign, he too defected from the Chaldeans to the king of Egypt. This gave King Nebuchadnezzar the opportunity, while he himself was seated at Riblah in the land of Hamath, now Antioch, to besiege and conquer Jerusalem through his army.

When Nebuchadnezzar captured Zedekiah himself in the eleventh year of his reign, he burned the temple and the entire city, killed very many people, took the rest captive, deprived Zedekiah of both his sons and his eyes, and led him with him to Babylon (4 Kings 23:26 and following; 24–25).

## CHAPTER XXX — Daniel Shining in Babylon

At that time Daniel, whom we mentioned at the beginning of the captivity [Col. 2189] as one of the hostages, was shining in Babylon with distinguished renown among the Jewish people. Since he was full of the Spirit of God and had been endowed with the gift of prophecy, God revealed to him what remained unknown to other human beings.
