Thus it happened that King Nebuchadnezzar saw a dream, but, when he awoke, no memory of the dream remained, even in part. God revealed to Daniel not only the dream itself but also the circumstance of the dream—what had occurred before the king went to sleep (Dan. 2).

This happened so that Daniel might introduce the knowledge of the supreme Creator to the king, and so that the people placed in servitude and captivity might possess at least some small help and consolation.

## CHAPTER XXXI — The Three Boys Who Escaped the Torment of Fire Unharmed

But that king became so hardened in mind and fell so deeply into forgetfulness of God that, after erecting an excessively tall golden statue in the plain of Dura in the province of Babylon, he commanded it to be consecrated and worshiped under his own name.

For the dedication of this statue, all the officials of the provinces and peoples from every direction were summoned. By common decree, they were compelled, whether they wished it or not, to worship the image. A punishment was announced in the presence of those who refused: anyone who declined to obey was to be burned in the great flames of the furnace.

It therefore happened that three officials of the Babylonian region—Sidrach, Misach, and Abdenago, descended from the Jewish people, whom we said had been taken to Babylon together with Daniel at the beginning of the captivity (above, chap. XXIX)—were accused by the Chaldeans before the king. They had been unwilling to worship either the patron gods of the king himself or the image that had recently been consecrated.

To ensure that the accusation did not arise from someone’s hatred rather than from a just complaint, the king ordered them to be summoned before him. He questioned them to determine whether what he had heard from others was indeed true.

He pressed the matter further: “Enough has been said about the past. Now, in my presence, carry out my commands and worship the golden statue that I have erected. But if you do not wish to execute the command, you must necessarily undergo the burning heat of the furnace.”

They replied with one unanimous judgment: “We do not merely refuse to worship any of your gods; we also absolutely refuse to worship the newly erected statue that stands visibly before us. We willingly and with common as well as personal devotion worship only the heavenly Creator of all things. By his power, whoever preserves a pure faith, unharmed by any evil deed, is protected from every kind of distress.

“Therefore, O king, we do not fear the flames of the furnace now before us, nor do we fear in any way the threats and punishments of your power. For the most powerful Creator and Governor of all things can entirely free his servants from the heat of fire and from whatever wound your hand may inflict.”

The king was therefore inflamed with incredible anger. He ordered the furnace to be heated more intensely than usual and, in a savage decree, commanded that these men be thrown into the fire by the strongest soldiers of his army, with their garments and ornaments.

But when they had been thrown into the furnace and had fallen into the midst of the flames, they felt the heat of the fire opposing them in no way. For an angel of God descended into the furnace with them at that same moment. He drove the heat and flames of the fire outward from the furnace, while preserving those within, as though they had been covered by a gentle dew, unharmed and without any distress.

The fire consumed all the Chaldeans whom it found around the furnace guilty of their destruction and death. Looking into the furnace, King Nebuchadnezzar said: “Behold, I see four men unbound in the midst of the flame, and the fourth surpasses the others in the excellence of his appearance.” He immediately called the three whom he had thrown into the fire by their proper names.

All the assembled peoples observed that nothing harmful had happened to them from their experience in the furnace. Not only had their bodies suffered no wounds from the heat and scarcely any marks at all, but their clothing and even their hair showed no sign of scorching or the heat of fire (Dan. 3).

In this marvelous event, the investigator of nature asks how fire gently cherished those enclosed in the furnace [Col. 2190], while the same fire, at the same moment, burned the men standing around it, who were of the same substance. How, then, did fire at that time possess gentleness in one part of itself, when in another part its fierce heat killed the enemies of the kingdoms [Note: [Col. 2190] Perhaps, “servants.”] of God?

The substance or nature of fire can live in nothing except water or some liquid material, since it is understood to be of incorporeal nature. Hence, when it burns in wood, it consumes everything in the wood that belongs to moisture; and when it reaches the dry ash that has again been returned to the earth, the lack of liquid extinguishes the fire.

The voracity of the heat likewise does not consume the nature of liquid altogether. As it strives to rise upward, where there is an abundance of that nature, it lifts itself again into the air. Thus the familiar vapor, when raised to the heights of the air, condenses into a cloudy form and is again supplied to the earth through rains, from which it had arisen.

This is often confirmed by the burning of devastated provinces and demonstrated by the frequent vapors of mountains set on fire, which draw down abundant dew. Fire therefore persists in any earthly material only so long as it either consumes all the liquid within it or sends upward into the air whatever remains from its nourishment.

But if a small fire encounters sufficiently moist material, it is overcome as the weaker by the stronger and yields to the abundance of moisture. Moreover, when it is nourished by a watery substance, as I said above, its life is in no way preserved except through the air. For if it is kindled in oil or in any other fuel, but the air surrounding it does not reach it everywhere, it is immediately extinguished.

Therefore, as long as fire burns in any earthly material, its life consists in air and moisture. The powerful Governor therefore wished to divide the nature of fire between enemies and servants: he turned its heat toward the enemies, but converted the airy and moist substance of air and water into the service of his servants. Thus the enemies were kindled and burned by its consuming nature, while the servants experienced no adversity in the airy and watery vapor.

For this reason Scripture says: “The angel of the Lord descended with Azariah and his companions into the furnace, drove the flame of fire out of the furnace, and made the middle of the furnace like a wind blowing with dew” (Dan. 3:49–50). From the air he found breath, and from the water he found dew within the fire itself. Behold, he brought about this division, as he did the other miracles, through the angel who, as I said above, descended into the fire together with the servants of God.

## CHAPTER XXXII — Daniel Resting in the Lions’ Den

Daniel, likewise, a worshiper of the true God, whom we mentioned at the beginning of the captivity, had been appointed one of the three officials of the kingdom of the Persians and Medes. Through the Lord’s favor, he had become dearer than all the others to King Darius, son of Astyages.

But since affection is followed by honor, and great honor arouses envy, the other officials of the Medes and Persians envied him bitterly. Unable to find any pretext against him except in the law of his God by which they could deliver him to death, they established a law, confirmed by the authority of the Persians and Medes, through a deception of which the king was unaware:

“No one may make any petition to any god or human being for thirty days, except to the king. If anyone is found to oppose this decree, he shall be thrown without mercy or clemency into the lions’ den, to be devoured.”

After the decree had been confirmed, they carefully watched Daniel without ceasing. They discovered him kneeling in his house three times every day, according to his customary practice, before his true God.

They therefore accused him severely, and the king wished to rescue him from their hands. But the established law of the Medes and Persians did not permit it. Accordingly, with the king grieving sorrowfully, Daniel was sentenced to be devoured and was placed in the lions’ den.

But an angel of God shut the lions’ mouths so that the innocent man would not perish. After a sleepless night, the king came tearfully to the den in the morning and found Daniel safe, lying among the lions [Col. 2191] with an untroubled mind.

By the king’s command, Daniel was immediately taken out of the lions’ den, and his accusers were thrown in instead, to be devoured. The lions, whom Daniel’s fasting had made hungry, received the guilty bodies of the offenders and their blood (Dan. 6).

In this equally remarkable event, the nature of the lions was not changed. Rather, what had been implanted in them from the beginning of their creation was governed by God through the angel according to his will. They displayed toward Daniel the gentleness and tenderness that lions show toward their cubs, while they displayed toward the devoured sinners the savagery and ferocity that they exercise against prey.

It is therefore certain that the Lord does not cause any creature to act contrary to the boundaries of its nature. Rather, he governs the parts of nature as necessity requires—either for the defense and consolation of those whom he protects or for the harm of those whom he oppresses.

The account of the den and of Habakkuk being transported again, in the stories of Bel and the dragon, is not included in this sequence because those stories are not found in the authoritative divine Scriptures (ibid. 14:30 and following).

## CHAPTER XXXIII — Ezra Restoring the Law

Meanwhile, when the period of captivity had been completed, which the Lord had foretold through the Prophets would be fulfilled (Jer. 25:12; 29:10; Dan. 9:2), he prepared the return of his people and the release from captivity through the clemency of King Cyrus.

At that time Ezra, the priest of God, restored the Law, which had been burned by the Chaldeans, in the temple archives (1 Esdras 6–7). He was, of course, filled with the same Spirit by whom it had previously been written.

## CHAPTER XXXIV — The Principal Wars Accomplished with the Lord’s Aid
I have set forth in summary, by historical exposition, the marvelous order of the Holy Scriptures of the Old Testament—namely, of the Law and the Prophets—in these two books. If the keen investigation of some superior intellect should add anything to them, I do not refuse even now to become a disciple. But we have omitted here only those principal wars accomplished with the Lord’s assistance that have been inserted into the text of Holy Scripture, because, although they are worthy of admiration on account of the help from heaven and contain many mysteries in their figurative meaning, nevertheless they leave nothing uncertain in the understanding of what happened. We know that Amalek was defeated by Jesus son of Nun while Moses was praying (Exod. XVII, 11–13); and that Israel’s people killed Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, men of great stature (Num. XXI, 24, 33, and XXII, 5). Phinehas son of Eleazar, with an army, killed Balak son of Zippor, king of Midian, together with Balaam, that distinguished astrologer. Jesus son of Nun struck down thirty-one kings of Canaan in many battles (Josh. XII, 7). Gideon son of Joash, with three hundred men, killed innumerable thousands of Midianites by means of trumpets and lamps (Judg. VII, 19–23). Jephthah the Gileadite freed the people from the power of the Gentiles by right of war (ibid. XI, 32). Samson, that strongest of the Hebrews, broke apart a lion that met him while he had nothing in his hands; afterward he took and ate a honeycomb from its mouth and head (Judg. XIV, 6, 8); and, capturing three hundred foxes, he set them on fire and released them into the Philistines’ crops (ibid. XV, 4, 5). With the jawbone of an ass he alone killed a thousand men in a single attack (ibid. 15). When Philistines were sitting all around the city where he had fallen asleep, he seized both leaves of the gate, together with the doors, lintels, locks, and bars, and carried them away, leaving them on the summit of the mountain that looks toward Beersheba (ibid. XVI, 3). The entire tribe of Benjamin, except for six hundred men, was destroyed by all the people of Israel after three wars because of the crime that had been committed (ibid. XIX–XX). Jonathan son of Saul and his armor-bearer struck the Philistine garrison (I Sam. XIV, 13). David son of Jesse, still a boy and a shepherd of sheep, rescued prey from the mouths of bears and lions that he had killed, and struck down the Philistine Goliath with a sling-stone (ibid. XVII, 34, 49). Later, by the virtue of patience, he twice spared Saul, his enemy, when he had been caught (ibid. XXIV, 8; XXVI, 10, 11). Afterward, when he had become king, he defeated the Philistine forces in three very severe battles and made them tributary (II Sam. V, 20; and VIII, 1). David alone killed eight hundred in a single attack (ibid. XXIII, 8). Abishai son of Zeruiah raised his spear against three hundred and killed them (ibid., 18). Three mighty men broke through the Philistine ranks in order to bring King David a drink from the cistern of Bethlehem, which was in the midst of the enemy (ibid., 16). Benaiah son of Jehoiada killed two lions in Moab and a lion in a cistern on a snowy day (ibid., 20, 21). He also, holding a staff in his hand, killed an Egyptian who bore a spear worthy of notice. The battle of the mighty men at Gibeon also turned out favorably for David’s army (II Sam. XXI, 15 ff.). Besides these, many great wars of King David against the surrounding regions were successfully conducted, with the Lord’s help and favor, either by David himself or often by his army. The civil war in the forest of Ephraim, within Israel itself, restored the kingdom of Samaria to David as an inheritance (ibid. XVIII, 6, 7). There were many battles against the Syrians and the kings of Damascus, now tending this way, now that, with alternating success. All these events came about wondrously because of assistance from heaven. Yet they cannot contribute an addition suitable to our work, since they show nothing unusual in the daily administration of affairs, being accomplished through the arrangements and strength of human beings and even of angels. In the books of the Maccabees, although something may be found that would fittingly be included among the number of miracles, we shall not weary ourselves with concern over it, because we have proposed to do only this: to touch, in some small measure, upon a historical exposition of the miracles of the divine canon, even though it exceeds the capacity of our little talent. Therefore let this present little book also reach its conclusion at this point, so that the third, concerning the New Testament, may take its beginning from the start of the Gospel—namely, from John and the Lord.

## Book Three: Concerning the New Testament

[Col. 2191]

### Chapter I — Concerning Zechariah’s vision and the birth of John the Baptist

In the forty-first year of Octavian Augustus Caesar, the priest Zechariah, of the division of Abijah, was offering a burnt offering in the temple according to the order of his service. The angel Gabriel, one of those who stand in the presence of the Lord, brought him an answer with swift announcement, adding these words: “Your wife Elizabeth, hitherto barren and already quite advanced in age, will conceive and bear you a son named John, a prophet and forerunner of the Most High.” But the priest, unbelieving in mind and scarcely granting faith in his heart to what had been said, replied: “How can this happen, since I am already quite old, [Col. 2192] and my wife, deprived of this capacity in her youth, has advanced in age through her days?” Nevertheless, the angel was not at all repelled by this excuse. He did not withdraw the gift because of the unbelief that had been expressed; rather, so that what had been said by the Lord might be fulfilled, he left the priest mute, subject to an appropriate punishment of his mouth, until, when the child was afterward born, the bond that had confined his tongue was released. When he tried to write the child’s name, he said, “John is his name” (Luke I, 5–27, 57–64).

It was fittingly arranged that John, who afterward would provide human beings with examples of repentance in food, clothing, and place of habitation, and who would preach repentance, should also, from the time of his conception, have his father endure the discipline of repentance imposed upon him by the angel until he was born. This sign also occurred appropriately in another sense: while the one who would preach the kingdom of heaven was being conceived for birth, the priest, preacher of the ancient Law and the Prophets, was condemned to silence, because “the Law and the Prophets were until John” (Matt. XI, 13), but from that time the kingdom of God is proclaimed by the Gospel. While John, still remaining in his mother’s womb before he was born, sensed the entrance into the house where he was of Mary, the mother of the Lord, he prophesied through his mother’s mouth, by spiritual utterance, concerning Christ the Lord who was to be born from her (Luke I, 41). When the spirit of Moses was distributed among seventy-two counselors (Num. XI, 25), what wonder is it if the spirit of a child still remaining in the womb spoke through his mother?

### Chapter II — Concerning the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and his birth from the Virgin Mary

Meanwhile, a messenger brought such words to Joseph’s betrothed, the virgin Mary, of the line of David, foretelling that she would bear a son without intercourse with a man, through the gift of the Holy Spirit: “When he is born,” he said, “this one whom the oracles of all the Prophets promise will be great in the sight of the Lord, and forever will be called the Son of the Most High by the mouths of all believers. For to him he gave the throne of his father David, and he will hold the sovereignty of the house and kingdom of Jacob forever, without end and without an heir succeeding him.” At these words the rejoicing virgin, with fitting faith, consented, without offering any objection of unbelief or disobedience (Luke I, 26–38).

But the sight of his wife Joseph’s swelling womb, which he himself had never known, made his mind troubled. So that he would not be wearied by this thought, the same angel informed him about the child conceived and to be born, and about receiving the virgin as his wife (Matt. I, 19–24). In due time the virgin gave birth to the son whom she had conceived without a man’s seed and without the pleasure of carnal desire, without any injury to her virginity.

Although in this event a work accomplished without a man’s seed is shown, contrary to the custom of the conception of all human beings, nevertheless the substance of flesh taken from a woman’s womb was not born outside nature. He who naturally received nature from nature imparted a true and complete human substance of flesh from his mother—although from flesh alone—through the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, except for the passions of sin. Lest we leave this matter as something new among God’s creatures, without any example from nature, we can demonstrate that many living creatures are generated without the union of parents. Bees, for example, grow without fathers, nourished only by the fostering of a maternal body; and all flying creatures of that kind conceive their offspring in this manner. Many birds can also produce eggs without males. Natural philosophers say that such conception exists in many kinds of fish. A worm is likewise born in flesh alone, without a father; for this reason the Lord does not disdain to compare himself to it through the prophet (Ps. XXI, 7). If, then, the Lord performs something according to the customary order in many things, what is there contrary to nature if, whenever he wished, a son was born in a virgin’s womb through the dispensation of the Holy Spirit, without intercourse with a man?

### Chapter III — Concerning the shepherds to whom the angels announced the infant’s birth

When he was born in the city of Bethlehem of David, shepherds assigned to guard the flocks were instructed by angels that the King of heaven had then deigned to assume flesh on earth from a human being, according to the law of birth among human beings. Then, when the shepherds had heard this announcement, the angels sang a hymn appropriate to it; afterward they returned, ascending again to heaven (Luke II, 8–15).

A fitting order carried out by the angels is also perceived in this: first the Lamb who had been born and the Shepherd of the flocks was announced to shepherds. In these two children, John and Jesus—the forerunner and the Lord—the order of their births is extended with historical appropriateness: one is generated from an old woman, the other from a virgin girl. John, the forerunner of Christ in all things, had to be born of an aged mother because he was, as it were, the final son and the end of the Old Law. Christ, however, assumed a body from a virgin girl. He is the beginning of the New [Col. 2194] Testament and became the origin of the children who were to be born from the New Law.

Therefore, in the forty-second year of Octavian Augustus Caesar, in the time of Herod, king of the Jews, when all power of rule had been removed from the Jews, the Lord Jesus Christ was born in the town of Bethlehem of Judea, from the line of David, from the virgin Mary. This fittingly occurred when the succession of kings and high priests descending from the line of Jacob had come to an end: then was born the one who is king and priest forever.

### Chapter IV — Concerning the Magi from the East and the star as their guide

When that child was born whom the Prophets of both peoples, Israel and the Gentiles, had foretold would be the savior of both peoples, Magi were led from the land of Hevilath by a star and came to him with gifts, after a very long journey. Having presented their gifts and worshiped the child for a time, they returned—not by the same route on which they had come, but, warned by a divine message, they took care to return to their homeland by another way (Matt. II, 1–12).

The Gospel’s words explain this star as having served as a guide for the Magi traveling from Jerusalem to Bethlehem. Those, however, who think that the Magi had this star as their guide from their own country all the way to Jerusalem cannot establish their view from the authority of the Gospel. For while the Magi were still in their own land, they saw a star surpassing the other stars. Understanding—whether from their own knowledge or from an angelic warning—that it belonged to God and to the king who, according to the prophecies both of their own people and of the Church (Num. XXIV, 17), was to be born from Israel, they came to the land of Israel. When they arrived at Jerusalem, where the capital of the whole province had been, they inquired about the king who had been born and was also God. Accordingly, when they found the oracles of the Israelite prophets concerning the one who had been born and the place where he was to be born (Mic. V, 2), they proceeded eagerly at the prompting of the king, whose speech was deceitful. After leaving the city, they soon reached Christ by following the star as their guide.

As for this star, whether it should be understood simply as a star, or as an angel, or as the Holy Spirit: although none of these interpretations conflicts with Catholic understanding, once each has been discussed, the measure of our little talent leaves the freedom of choosing to greater judges.

If someone prefers to understand it simply as a star, how did it depart from the other stars in this guidance? Their nature, created from the beginning, is known to have been established in the firmament of heaven, as the authority of the book of Genesis makes clear (Gen. I, 17). If it remained in the firmament of heaven, how could it become a guide for travelers between Bethlehem and Jerusalem? And if it flew through the air like an arrow, though somewhat more slowly because of those who followed it, it would meanwhile abandon its accustomed place and course in the firmament. Scripture does not describe even the greater luminaries as doing this, when they stood still or turned back at signs.

Unless perhaps that aerial fire which received such a ministry was called a “star” because of its resemblance, as we have said in many cases. Or if an angel performed this ministry in the appearance of a star, what objection is there, since angels transform themselves into many forms when they show themselves to human beings? Thus the angel spoke to Moses at Horeb with a fiery appearance from the bush (Exod. III, 2), and appeared to Jesus son of Nun outside the camp at Gilgal like an armed soldier (Josh. V, 13). At Elijah’s ascension, angels are represented in the form of a chariot and fiery horses (II Kings II, 11). When Elisha opened the eyes of his servant, angels were manifested in those same forms (ibid. VI, 17). They presented themselves to Abraham and Lot in the form of guests (Gen. XVIII, 2; XIX, 1), and Manoah and his wife saw an angel speaking to them in prophetic form (Judg. XIII, 9).

Surely on this occasion also an angel became the guide of the Magi, transforming himself for the astrologers into the likeness and radiance of a most brilliant star. Even though this concerns the image of things spoken to John in his Apocalypse by way of a vision, it does not oppose this understanding: “The seven stars are the seven angels of the churches” (Apoc. I, 20). Therefore, although they are called stars in spirit, what objection is there if the star in this passage is also understood to have been called an angel?

Or certainly, if this star is recognized as neither an angel, nor a star of the firmament, [Col. 2195] nor any other kind of fire, let it then be granted that the Holy Spirit became this star. Just as afterward he descended in bodily form like a dove upon the Lord Jesus in the Jordan (Matt. III, 16; Luke III, 22), so, in the form of a star, the Holy Spirit led the Gentiles who worshiped to the cradle of the Lord who had been born in the flesh. Balaam the astrologer spoke of him in a parable: “A star shall rise out of Jacob” (Num. XXIV, 17)—namely, the radiant light of Christ’s spiritual grace, by which the night of the Gentiles’ unbelief is illuminated. Therefore, just as he later descended upon the Apostles in the upper room of Zion in the form of fire (Acts II, 3), so the Holy Spirit led the Magi to the Lord in the form of a star.

### Chapter V — Concerning Christ’s baptism

This child therefore surpassed his age in knowledge until, when he was thirty years old, he came to the Jordan. There he was baptized by John, whom we mentioned above, the son of Zechariah, who at that time was baptizing the people who would believe in the one who was to come. The Lamb himself first received baptism and washed away what had to be confessed in the waters of the Jordan. The Holy Spirit descended upon him in the form of a dove, and he heard the Father speaking from heaven concerning him: “This is my beloved Son, in whom my soul is well pleased.” With these signs he saw heaven opened, and thus, baptized, he rose from the washing of the river (Luke III, 21, 22).

The Lord Jesus went out to baptism—not because he, who had no guilt of personal or original sin, needed the sacrament and washing of baptism, but in order to cleanse the waters which, although God had not cursed them because of Adam’s transgression, had been infected by the curse upon the earth that contained them. He also entered the waters of baptism so that no one would neglect the sacrament of Baptism, since the one who was without sin had entered its waters. And he sought to be plunged into the waters of baptism by his servant so that no one would think it beneath him to be baptized by one inferior to himself. Moreover, he did this so that, while he concealed himself from the devil until the temptation was completed, the devil might see him being washed in water as though he needed cleansing, among those polluted by sins.

He saw the Holy Spirit descending upon him at his baptism, heard the Father’s voice from heaven confessing him as his Son, and saw heaven opened before him. This was not because the Son of God did not possess all these things before his baptism, but so that he might show what the sacrament of Baptism accomplishes. For it was not then that he began to receive the Spirit, who is believed to have the same substance as the Holy Spirit. Nor was it then that the Father first declared him to be his Son, to whom he had said, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you” (Ps. CIX, 3)—that is, before every angelic creature, which is often called “morning star” throughout the Scriptures. Nor did the heavenly chamber begin then to be opened to him who says, “Heaven is my throne, but the earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. LXVI, 1).

The Holy Trinity gathered all these things together at the Lord’s baptism so that each of us might know what gift he receives in the mystery of sacred Baptism. For then, cleansed from the filth of sins, each person receives the Holy Spirit; then, by the grace of adoption, he begins to be acknowledged by God the Father as a son; then he understands that the gate of the kingdom of heaven is opened to him and that he is a citizen of the heavenly homeland and a companion of the holy angels.

Although the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the Lord in bodily form, there is no doubt that he did not take a dove from among the birds, but formed it from the air. It was by no means necessary for the Holy Spirit to assume a body from birds, since birds have in no way transgressed the law of nature established for them [Note: [Col. 2195] Perhaps, “established.”]. But if they had transgressed it in some way, they would have had no such merit in this respect, being neither eternal nor rational creatures, that the Spirit should assume flesh from them in order to release them from punishment for sin.

Since the person of the Son was being clothed in a bodily form of human flesh, it was fitting that the person of the Holy Spirit should descend upon him in a bodily form, and that the bodily voice of the Father should be heard through the air by bodily ears from a cloud. Moreover, the Father and the Holy Spirit came to the baptism in a cloud and in the image of a dove because those forms possessed something of an aquatic nature. Since the Son, on earth, had chosen the creature of water for the mystery of baptism, it was necessary that the Father also should thunder through an aquatic cloud and that the Holy Spirit should represent that body—which in the beginning was made from water (Gen. I, 20)—as received from that cloud, so that the whole Trinity might display the same will that it possesses.

### Chapter VI — Concerning Christ’s temptation and fasting

When the Lord Jesus had been baptized in the water, he immediately came up in order to give the devil an opportunity to tempt him. He sought the remote places of the desert, where he fasted for forty days and an equal number of nights, supported by no human provision of food. There he was tempted in the three matters by which the first man had been deceived, and by three replies he overcame Satan, who was tempting him (Matt. IV, 1–11).

In the devil’s three proposals there was the whole of iniquity; in Christ’s three replies, by which the devil is resisted, there was the whole of righteousness. When the enemy is condemned and conquered, freedom and redemption are prepared for the human race. For in this, when Satan wished to raise himself above his creator [Note: [Col. 2196] Ms. Aud., “higher.”], the one who had been under him until then—that is, the human being—grew beyond him through the help of the victorious Lord.

When he attempted to bind the one who had been free from every impediment [Note: [Col. 2196] Ms. Aud., “sacred.”], meanwhile the one whom he himself held in prison laid aside the chains by which he had been held. And when he tried to resist one stronger than himself, meanwhile the one who had been weaker was strengthened against him. The Lord also ordered him who until then had been cast from heaven only to earth to migrate in terror [Note: [Col. 2196] Manuscripts: “in error.”] from earth to the underworld.

The incarnation of the Lord could endure the hunger of forty days without danger to life, because the Lord’s Word, which twice renewed Moses through the air for forty days, was inwardly irrigating Christ’s limbs and sinews. Why, then, is the Lord Jesus described as becoming hungry after the forty days and forty nights had been completed, when Moses and Elijah are not said to have suffered hunger during a fast of such duration (Exod. XXIV, 18; XXXIV, 28; III Kings XIX, 8)?

Our Redeemer endured hunger and toil after completing so many days so that he might both offer the tempter an opportunity to tempt him and make known how truly he bore the substance of human flesh. Thus, even in this fast, he did nothing outside human practice or anything new, since he did not exceed the length of time for which human beings had previously fasted.

### Chapter VII — Concerning the Gospel’s miracles up to the walking upon the sea

After defeating the adversary and completing a fast of forty days, he called the Israelite people throughout Judea and Galilee to the way of salvation, and from among all people he set apart twelve chief soldiers for himself through the special gift of election (Matt. IV, 17 ff.; Luke VI, 13–16). In order to make the hearts of all firm concerning the invisible and inward substance—namely, the health of souls—he also visibly restored bodies afflicted by illness, with no resisting force, in the power of a servant [Note: [Col. 2196] Ms. Aud., “of hell.”].

Thus, while preaching the Gospel of the kingdom of God, he traveled throughout Galilee and saw the common crowd oppressed by various illnesses. Some were deprived of the joy of the present light by the failure of their eyes; others had been disfigured by leprosy spread over the whole surface of the body; and some, deprived of the proper form of their feet, he healed.

In the paralytic carried by four men, three divine works are seen: his sins are forgiven, the wound of his present illness is then loosed by a word, and he receives an answer to his thoughts from the one who, as God, searches all things (Matt. IX, 2–6; Mark II, 3–12). In this man it is shown that some suffer because of the stains of the soul.

How could the mute speak, when the Word of God the Father was asking answers from him? He who found eloquence in the mouth of an ass—how could he fail to strengthen a human tongue, even though it was mute, for speech? When the light of righteousness, which came into the world, appeared, how could the blind person fail to see? And by what power could the devil remain in a human being, when Christ came to cast him out—the human being whom the devil, while he sinned, had expelled from heaven?

In the five loaves and two fish that satisfied five thousand people, three things worthy of wonder are contained: the smallness of the material, the multitude of the people who were satisfied, and the abundance of the fragments (Matt. XIV, 15–21).

### Chapter VIII — Concerning the Lord walking upon the waves

When the Lord was seeking his disciples from the land, he necessarily had to walk upon the waves. The reason for this was Peter’s faith: namely, lest, if Christ alone had done it, he should leave the reality of his flesh in doubt. Since Peter, the son of a man and a woman, did this through the assistance of Christ who commanded him, he leaves no room for doubt that the Son came from the flesh of a Virgin (Matt. XIV, 26, 29).

But it may be asked whether the nature of the Lord’s and Peter’s bodies was made lighter, so that the water could support them, or whether the substance of the water was solidified, so that it could sustain human bodies. Even if both occurred, it would not be contrary to nature, when the Lord commanded it, for him either to solidify the water or to lighten human flesh by his command. Thus, those serving in the regions of Scythia, as the ancients relate, disport themselves even on the shores [printed: “ears”] of the sea; trained also in the art of swimming, they scarcely sink into the depths when their middles are submerged. If this is possible for human beings, what wonder is it if flesh was lightened at the Lord’s command? Especially since, at the resurrection, bodies will be so lightened that they will be supported not only by dense water but also by clouds and air, as the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air” (I Thess. IV, 16).

Alternatively, if someone chooses to understand that the nature of the water was solidified, this is possible because water has an earthy density: when it is gripped by frost, it becomes rigid with a solidity harder than that of earth itself and is able to bear a multitude of things, while afterward warm air dissolves it. Or certainly, if nature did not harden liquid waves, the quality implanted in water, which ordinarily supports great pieces of wood, human bodies, the bodies of other animals, and Liburnian ships floating upon it, would suffice. That solidity was produced at the Lord’s command. It is therefore no wonder if it did not even support Peter when he doubted, just as, when the Lord willed, the earth did not support unbelievers, such as Dathan and Abiram (Num. XVI, 31).

### Chapter IX — Concerning the other miracles of our Lord Jesus Christ

In the natural administration of things, two kinds of principles are discerned. The lower principle is understood as the daily administration of things: for example, water becomes blood in animals, and salty water is sweetened through clouds or through the infusion of earth. The higher principle is an unusual governance, recognized in miracles, as when God changed water into blood in Egypt in an instant, and changed it into sweetness by means of a piece of wood immersed in it (Exod. VII, 20; XV, 25).

### Chapter X — Concerning the loaves and fish that satisfied thousands of people

Therefore, according to the lower principle, he produces bread from a small seed into a great crop through the administration of a long period, for the nourishment of innumerable people; according to the higher principle, he multiplies it in an instant from a small amount of material through blessing. In the same way he multiplies fish through the first blessing, when it was said, “Increase and multiply, and fill the waters of the sea” (Gen. I, 22). Their flesh is now multiplied through the cause of the higher principle, by a present blessing, to satisfy the crowds (Matt. XIV, 19; John VI, 11).

### Chapter XI — Concerning the Lord’s vision on the mountain, with Moses and Elijah speaking with him

Although in this manifestation the Lord’s face shone with the splendor of the sun (Matt. XVII, 2 ff.), it was not the flesh itself that shone; rather, the divinity hidden in the body granted those outside to see a portion of its light, as much as they were able. Why, then, did the garments have the whiteness of snow, when they came neither from the flesh nor from the divinity? Perhaps, just as the divinity shone outward through the flesh, so the flesh, illuminated by the divinity, radiated through the garments.

Moses and Elijah are brought forward especially for such a manifestation either as the leaders of the Law and Prophecy, leading them to their conclusion, or so that, when compared with Christ, the horned face of Moses—which the children of Israel could not gaze upon (Exod. XXXIV, 35; II Cor. III, 13)—and Elijah, carried away in a fiery chariot (IV Kings II, 11), might be overshadowed.

Scripture records that these men fasted for forty days; but concerning Jesus the Lord alone, in their presence, it records the testimony of the Father declaring him. Yet if Elijah, still remaining in his body, had come for such a leading forth, what should be said about Moses? Was he present in his body once again for this manifestation, or was he assuming a simulated form made from air, as Samuel appeared?

And if he came clothed in his own body, did he on this occasion complete his resurrection, which for the others will occur only at the end? On this question, the authorities, expressing one and the same judgment, speak without disagreement. Since the Lord was meeting with his three disciples and Elijah—not with imagined but with real bodies—and since Moses himself appears to have been taken up from the grave in his true body, this is their view.

But if the Lord Jesus is rightly believed to be “the firstborn of the dead” (Apoc. I, 5), Moses’ body was afterward entrusted again to burial, so that he might take it up on the last day, when the dead rise [Note: [Col. 2198] Ms. Aud., “may be expected.”].

### Chapter XII — Concerning Lazarus and the other dead who were raised

With unchanging will, God predetermined the lives of all things to a definite end and limit. Accordingly, the life of some people appears to be terminated by death not so that they may die, but so that those who raise them may thereby be regarded as more glorious and, as beloved by God, also honored among human beings.

Thus the Lord says to the disciples concerning Lazarus himself: “This illness is not unto death, but for the Son of Man to be glorified through it.” Behold, after this statement Lazarus soon dies; nevertheless, through the Son of God, who is glorified in him, he is raised on the fourth day (John XI, 4, 44). This did not establish the duration of his life; rather, because the Lord had determined without alteration what he would do, he often pretended to withdraw it, just as he delayed the giving of offspring to the wives of Abraham and Isaac, so that the gift might be more pleasing.

The Lord also provides occasions for someone to be asked to grant what he himself wishes to give. For if one of the saints were to ask for something he had not determined, he would by no means permit it to happen—for example, that Moses should enter the promised land (Deut. XXXIV, 4), or that the angel of Satan should depart from Paul (II Cor. XII, 8, 9); and those who asked did not obtain what they sought.

Thus, concerning all the dead in general, something of this kind is understood: they die the first time so that through them those who are worthy may be glorified. Among the eight dead whom divine Scripture of the Old and New Testaments records as having been raised, this should be considered: concerning the first of them, namely the widow’s son whom Elijah raised, it says: “Let the soul of the child, I beg you, return” (III Kings XVII, 19). Concerning the last, namely Eutychus in the Acts of the Apostles, it says: “He was lifted up and found dead.” When Paul had gone down to him, he bent over him, embraced him, and said: “Do not be troubled, for his soul is in him” (Acts XX, 9, 10).

Both statements must be understood carefully. The widow’s son was dead, and the Prophet asked that his soul return; the other was dead, and Paul said that his soul was in him. In both cases Scripture is true, because it cannot lie. But how can it be accepted that a dead person’s soul could be hidden in the members of the body? Unless perhaps the soul, which is incorporeal, is believed to be secretly present in the body.

Some, however, avoiding the difficulty of interpretation, say concerning Eutychus that he died after releasing his soul, but that, when the soul returned after a short interval, Paul is thought to have said, “His soul is in him.” Yet Scripture is silent as to whether the soul departed or returned. The other six dead, of whom neither departing nor returning souls are reported, clearly and without any ambiguity demonstrate here that they were dead and were raised by divine operation.

### Chapter XIII — Concerning the eclipse of the sun during the Lord’s Passion

The sun’s failure occurred according to the flesh not as it usually does, when the moon is illuminated, but at the full moon—namely, on the fifteenth day of the month—so that what happened would not be thought to have occurred by chance. Darkness obscured the sun’s light at midday to such an extent that during those three hours of the eclipse the stars were seen in the sky (Luke XXIII, 44, 45).

### Chapter XIV — Concerning the bodies of the saints coming from their tombs after the Lord’s resurrection

The saints came from their tombs after the Lord’s resurrection (Matt. XXVII, 52, 53), but they entered the tombs again, as I also mentioned concerning Moses. There they await the final resurrection of all, as the Apostle says: “All these, having been approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise, since God had provided something better for us, so that they might not be made perfect without us” (Heb. XI, 39, 40).

If, then, these men and Moses are to be believed to have risen twice—once in this manifestation and once in the final resurrection of all—although they had tasted death once, imposed upon them through Adam’s sin, let it be far from the Catholic faith to believe that one who dies once rises twice. Unless perhaps someone says that Moses and these men died twice.

But nowhere is it written that those who appeared in this way rose again. They are said either to be alive, to have appeared, or to have come out of their tombs. The name “resurrection” is applied either to the Lord alone, or to the future resurrection of all, in the case of those who after death have lived in this present life. Such an appearance of these men belongs neither to human life nor to the future resurrection. Rather, it moves minds toward confirmation of the Lord’s resurrection and belief in the resurrection of souls from the underworld.

Just as in the case of the dead who were raised, only a likeness—not continuing death—is seen, so in these men a likeness of resurrection, not resurrection itself, was displayed. For from continuing death no one returns to unfailing life until the last day except the Lord; and from the true resurrection no one will ever again be thrust back into death.

### Chapter XV — Concerning the Lord’s food after the resurrection

Learned men ask how the flesh of the resurrection received this bodily food, since all believers know that bodies destined for resurrection are spiritual, as it is said: “The spiritual body will rise” (I Cor. XV, 44). Therefore, with sound understanding, it is believed that resurrected bodies will possess the ability to eat food, if necessity required it, though they will not taste it.

The examples of God do not at all deny this, as in the case of the angels near the oak of Mamre (Gen. XVIII, 8, 9). They do not, however, transfer food that has been chewed into the stomach and intestines as we do; rather, as soon as they receive it, they taste it—as they appear to do—and transform it wholly, not partially, into a spiritual nature.

### Chapter XVI — Peter restores a paralytic

The fitting correspondences involving the Holy Spirit—in a dove over Christ and in fire over the Apostles—have been written down. We also spoke of the division of tongues and of the Apostles’ miracles after receiving the Spirit, in the discussion of the excuse of almsgiving and the profession of poverty, when Peter said to the paralytic, “Rise and walk” (Acts III, 6), keeping the Master’s command, “Do not possess gold or silver” (Matt. X, 9). Since he served God alone and had been freed from unrighteous mammon, he quickly released by a word of command the man bound by illness.

### Chapter XVII — Peter’s power
Behold how great was the apostolic power in Christ: when Peter rebuked the healthy Ananias, he bound him to death by the mere authority of his word (Acts 5:4–5); and Tabitha, bound by the bond of death, he released by that same power of command (ibid. 9:40). Therefore Ananias and Sapphira first died suddenly in the sight of the Church, so that the extent of apostolic authority might be displayed; the enormity of the sin of taking back from the Church what had been offered might be shown; and the others might be corrected by their example.

[ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCH JACOB.]

[Col. 2199]

ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK. (G,S)*

This exposition, historical and allegorical, of the question concerning the blessings of the patriarch Jacob is not Augustine’s but Alcuin’s, clearly extracted from his own book *Questions on Genesis*. Nevertheless, in Jerome also, under the same title and in almost exactly the same words, one may find the earlier exposition in a work likewise entitled *Questions on Genesis*; while the final part of the later exposition is found in Gregory’s books of the *Morals on Job*. Indeed, both expositions in their entirety, though in a somewhat different order and with several words altered, are found in the third book of the *Commentaries on Genesis*, formerly and falsely attributed to Eucherius of Lyons and published in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.

[Col. 2199]

ON THE BLESSINGS OF THE PATRIARCH JACOB

What are we to understand by the blessings with which the patriarch Jacob blessed his sons? Are they to be understood historically or allegorically, when he says, “Gather yourselves together, sons of Jacob, that I may announce to you what will happen in the last days” (Gen. 49:2)? And if these words seem to convey allegory more than history, what is the answer?

Both are intended: history and allegory—history concerning the division of the Promised Land, whose portions were to be divided among their descendants [Col. 2200], and allegory concerning Christ and the Church, which would come into being in the last times. But first the foundations of the history must be laid, so that the summit of the allegory may more suitably be placed upon the earlier structure.

“Reuben, my firstborn, you are my strength and the beginning of my grief; foremost in gifts, greater in authority. You have been poured out like water; do not increase, because you went up onto your father’s bed [Col. 2201] and defiled his couch” (Gen. 49:3–4).

[Note: [Col. 2201] From Jerome, *Questions on Genesis*.]

The meaning is this: You are my firstborn, greater in offspring, and, according to the order of your birth, you ought to have received the inheritance due by right to the firstborn, the priesthood, and the kingship. This is indicated by the honor you bore and your great strength. But because you sinned and, like water that cannot be held in any vessel, were poured out in the rush of pleasure, I therefore command you not to sin any further, but to remain among your brothers, paying the penalty of your sin because you forfeited the rank of the firstborn.

[“The beginning of grief is every firstborn, because on his account the parents’ inward parts are stirred.”]

[Note: [Col. 2201] This is not Jerome’s.]

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of warring iniquity. Let my soul not enter their counsel, and let my glory not be in their assembly, because in their fury they killed a man and in their self-will they undermined a wall. Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn, and their indignation, because it was harsh. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel” (ibid. 5–7).

He indicates that it was not by his counsel that they killed Shechem and Hamor, men joined to them by treaty, and contrary to what was right shed innocent blood in a time of peace and friendship; and that, carried away by a kind of fury and cruelty, they overthrew the walls of the hospitable city (ibid. 34:26). Hence he says, “Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn,” and what follows.

“And I will scatter them in Israel.” Levi did not receive a separate inheritance, but in all the tribes he had only a few cities in which to dwell (Josh. 21). Concerning Simeon, it is written in the book of Joshua that he too did not receive his own allotment, but received something from the tribe of Judah (ibid. 19:1–2).

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be on the necks of your enemies; your father’s sons shall worship you. Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion and like a lioness. Who will rouse him?”

Since Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” it is rightly written concerning Judah, “Your brothers shall confess to you,” or “shall praise you.” Although this contains a great mystery concerning Christ, according to the literal sense it signifies that kings would be born from the stock of David and that all the tribes would worship him. For he does not say, “Your mother’s sons,” but “your father’s sons.”

What follows, “You have gone up to the prey, my son,” shows that he would lead captive peoples away; and, according to the more sacred understanding, that he had ascended on high and led captivity captive. Alternatively—and this seems preferable—captivity signifies the Passion, and ascent the Resurrection.

“Binding his colt to the vine, and his she-ass to the vine.”

He evidently joined the colt of the she-ass on which Jesus sat (John 12:14)—that is, the people of the Gentiles—to the vine of the Apostles, who are from the Jews; and to the vine, or, as it is found in Hebrew, *Soreth*,

[Note: [Col. 2201] Read *Sorec*: this is how “vine” is called in Hebrew.]

that is, the chosen vine, he bound the she-ass on which he sat, the Church gathered from the nations.

When he says, “My son,” he turns to Christ from Judah himself,

[Note: [Col. 2201] Ms. Corb.: “When he says, ‘My son,’ he makes an apostrophe to Judah himself.”]

because Christ would accomplish everything.

[“The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49:8–11): this signifies that rulers would not fail from the tribe of Judah until the time when Christ was born, he who, sent by the Father, is the expectation of the nations.]

[Note: [Col. 2201] These are not Jerome’s.]

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, reaching as far as Sidon. Issachar is a strong ass, lying between the boundaries; he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent, and he placed his shoulder under the burden; he became a tribe serving others” (ibid. 13–15).

Since above he had said of Zebulun that it would possess the shores of the Great Sea and would also touch Sidon and the remaining Phoenician cities, he now returns to the inland province [Col. 2202] and, by his blessing, makes Issachar, who would possess the most beautiful region in Galilee beside Naphtali, its inhabitant.

He calls him a bony or strong ass and says that he placed his shoulder under the burden, because he would labor greatly in working the land and transporting to the sea the things that grew within his borders, also carrying tribute to the kings.

The Hebrews say that, metaphorically, this signifies that, meditating on the Holy Scriptures day and night, he devoted himself to labor; and therefore all serve him, carrying gifts to him as to a teacher.

“Dan shall judge his people as also the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path, biting the horse’s heels so that its rider may fall backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord” (Gen. 49:16–18).

Samson, a judge in Israel, was from the tribe of Dan (Judg. 13:2). Thus he says: Now, seeing in the spirit your Nazarite Samson nourishing his hair and triumphing over his enemies after striking them down—he who, like a serpent and a basilisk lying in wait, prevents anyone from passing through the land of Israel; and even if some reckless man, trusting in his own strength as in the speed of a horse, should wish to plunder it like a brigand, he will not be able to escape.

He speaks throughout by the metaphor of the serpent and the horseman. Seeing, therefore, your Nazarite so strong, and that he himself died because of a prostitute and, in dying, killed our enemies (ibid. 16:30), I thought, O God, that he was your Christ, your Son. But because he died and did not rise again, and Israel was once more led into captivity, another Savior of the world and of my people must be awaited, that the one to whom it has been reserved may come, and he himself may be the expectation of the nations.

“Gad, girded, shall fight before him, and he himself shall be girded behind” (Gen. 49:19).

This signifies that Gad, Reuben, and half the tribe of Manasseh, returning after fourteen years to the sons whom he had left beyond the Jordan in possession, would encounter a great battle against the neighboring nations and would fight bravely after conquering their enemies. Read Joshua and Chronicles.

“Naphtali is a hind let loose, giving words of beauty;” or, “Naphtali is a watered field” (ibid. 21).

The Hebrew expression *Aiala Seluha* signifies both. It means that hot springs arise in that very tribe, or that it was watered by the course of the Jordan beside the Lake of Gennesaret. The Hebrews, however, wish “watered field” and “words of beauty” to be prophesied because of Tiberias, which seemed to possess knowledge of the Law.

The released hind signifies seasonal crops and the speed of a more fertile land. But it is better if we refer everything to the teaching of the Savior, because the Savior taught there above all, as it is also written in the Gospel (Matt. 4:15–16).

“My son Joseph is increasing, my son is increasing and beautiful in appearance; daughters ran along the wall. But they provoked him, quarreled with him, and envied him, having arrows. His bow remained firm, and the bonds of his arms and hands were loosened by the hands of the Mighty One of Jacob. From there the shepherd went forth, the stone of Israel” (Gen. 49:22–24).

O son of Joseph, who are so beautiful that the whole crowd of the girls of Egypt looks upon you from the walls, towers, and windows: they envied you, and your brothers provoked you to anger, wounded by the arrows of envy and the darts of jealousy.

But you placed your bow and weapons of warfare in God, who is a mighty warrior; and your bonds, with which your brothers had bound you, were loosened and broken by him, so that from your seed the tribe of Ephraim might arise, strong and steadfast, harder and unconquerable like a stone, and also ruling over the ten tribes of Israel.

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf; in the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the spoils” (ibid. 27).

It is clear to everyone what an unmistakable prophecy these words contain concerning the apostle Paul: in his youth he persecuted the Church, and in his old age he became a preacher of the Gospel.

The Hebrews, however, explained it as follows: The altar on which sacrifices were offered, and at whose base the blood of the victims was poured, was in the territory of the tribe of Benjamin. This, they say, signifies that the priests sacrifice victims in the morning and in the evening divide among themselves what has been granted to them by the Law. They interpret the bloodthirsty, devouring wolf as the altar, and the divider of spoils as the priests, who, serving the altar, live from the altar.

[Col. 2203]

[Note: [Col. 2203] Up to this point from Jerome.]

These matters concern the historical sense.

Spiritually, however, Reuben represents the earlier people of the Jews, to whom the Lord says, “Israel is my firstborn” (Gen. 49:3; Exod. 4:22). For, according to what was due to the firstborn, it belonged to Israel to receive the priesthood and the kingship.

He adds, “You are my strength.” Certainly, from that people came the foundation of faith, and from that people came the Power of God, who is Christ.

But how is Israel itself “the beginning of grief,” unless because it continually inflicted injury upon God the Father, turning its back toward him and not its face?

It is “foremost in gifts,” because the oracles of God were first entrusted to it (Rom. 3:2), as were the legislation and the Testament, or promise.

It is “greater in authority,” certainly because of the greatness of its strength, since that same people reigned more extensively than the others in this world.

But it was poured out like water by sinning against Christ, like water that cannot be held in a vessel; it was poured out in the rush of pleasure. Therefore he added, “Do not increase,” because after that people had been scattered throughout the whole world, it was greatly diminished.

But why did it deserve such things? He added: “Because you went up onto your father’s bed.” He proclaims the audacity of the firstborn of the people, who went up onto his father’s bed and defiled his couch when he seized and hung upon the cross the Lord’s body, in which the fullness of divinity rested (Col. 2:9), and stained it with iron.

“Simeon and Levi are brothers, instruments of warring iniquity.”

By Simeon and Levi are understood the scribes, Pharisees, and priests of the Jewish people. The scribes of the Jews came from Simeon, while from the tribe of Levi came the chief priests, who formed a plan to seize Jesus by deceit and kill him.

Of this plan he says, “Let my soul not enter their counsel,” for he abhorred the great crimes that the Jews would commit in the last times.

“Because in their fury they killed a man”—that is, Christ, of whom it is said, “Behold, a man, whose name is the Rising One” (Zech. 6:12); and elsewhere, “A woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31:22).

“They undermined a wall”—that is, they pierced with a lance that strongest spiritual wall which guards Israel.

“Cursed be their fury, because it was stubborn”—certainly because, inflamed with fury and anger, they delivered Christ to Pontius Pilate, saying, “Crucify, crucify.”

“And their indignation, because it was harsh”—when they asked for the robber Barabbas and demanded that the Prince of Life be crucified.

“I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel”—because some of them believed, while others remained in unbelief. Those who separate from them and come to faith are said to be divided; those whose homeland and temple had been overthrown, and whose unbelieving race was scattered throughout the world, are said to be dispersed.

“Judah, your brothers shall praise you.”

Through this Judah the true confessor, Christ, is expressed, who according to the flesh was born from his tribe. His brothers shall praise him: namely, the Apostles and all his fellow heirs, who through adoption by the Father have become children of God and, by grace, brothers of Christ, while he himself is their Lord by nature.

“Your hands shall be on the necks of your enemies.”

By those same hands and by the same trophy of the cross he both sheltered his own and bent down his enemies and the opposing powers. In accordance with this the Father also promises him, saying, “Sit at my right hand until I place your enemies as a footstool for your feet” (Ps. 109:1–2).

“Your father’s sons shall worship you.”

This happens when many of Jacob’s sons worship him, having been saved through the election of grace (Rom. 11:5).

“Judah is a lion’s cub.”

This is when, by being born, he became little, as it is written, “A little one has been born for us” (Isa. 9:6).

“You have gone up to the prey, my son.”

That is, ascending the cross, you redeemed captive peoples; and those whom the adversary had invaded, you rescued by dying. Finally, returning from the underworld, you ascended on high and led captivity captive (Ps. 67:19; Eph. 4:8).

“Resting, you have lain down like a lion.”

Christ most clearly lay down in his Passion when, bowing his head, he handed over his spirit; and when in the tomb he rested securely, as though in a kind of sleep of the body [Col. 2204].

But why “like a lion,” and “like a lion’s cub”? In his sleep he was a lion, because he completed this not by necessity but by power, as he himself says: “No one takes my life from me, but I lay it down” (John 10:18).

What he adds, “And like a lion’s cub,” means that he died from the same source from which he was born. Christ therefore rested well like a lion: he not only did not fear the bitterness of death, but even in death conquered death’s dominion.

When he says, “Who will rouse him?” this means that no one will do so except he himself, in accordance with his own words: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (ibid. 2:19).

“The ruler shall not fail from Judah,” and what follows. This most clearly refers to Judah. For a long time the succession of kings among the Jews remained undefiled from his seed, until Christ was born, as we said above.

“Binding his colt to the vine.”

His colt is the people from the Gentiles, upon whom the burden of the Law had never yet been imposed. He joined it to the vine—that is, to the Apostles who are from the Jews. For “the vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel” (Isa. 5:7).

“And his she-ass to the vine.”

He himself says, “I am the true vine” (John 15:1). To this vine, therefore, he binds his she-ass: namely, the sluggish synagogue, weighed down by the heavy burden of the Law.

“He washed his garment in wine”—or his flesh in the blood of the Passion, or the holy Church in that wine which “will be poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins.”

“And his cloak in the blood of the grape.”

The cloak is the Gentiles, whom he joined to his body, as it is written, “As I live, says the Lord, unless I clothe all these as a garment.”

“His eyes are more beautiful than wine.”

The eyes of Christ are the Apostles and Evangelists, who provide the Church with the light of knowledge. Their commandments surpass the austerity of the wine of the ancient Law, because they are far lighter.

“And his teeth are whiter than milk.”

The teeth are the holy teachers, who cut people away from error and, as though consuming them, transfer them into the body of Christ. The teachers of the Church have become whiter than the milk of the old Law.

“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships.”

Zebulun is interpreted as “dwelling of strength” and signifies the Church. It dwells on the shore of the sea and at the station of ships, so that it may be a refuge for believers and show the harbor of faith to those in danger.

With unshaken firmness it observes shipwreck amid all the storms of the world, as well as the tempests of the Jews and heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Although it is battered by the waves, it is not broken.

It reaches as far as Sidon—that is, as far as the Gentiles. It is also read in the Gospel that some Apostles were taken from there and that the Lord often taught in those places, as it is written: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the people sitting in darkness, saw a great light” (Isa. 9:1–2; Matt. 4:15ff.).

Sidon is interpreted as “hunter” or “huntress.” Who are the hunters except the Apostles? As we said above, they were taken from those places of which it is said, “I will send many hunters, and they will hunt you on every mountain” (Jer. 16:16).

“Issachar is a strong ass.”

Issachar, which is interpreted as “reward,” refers to the people of the Gentiles, whom the Lord purchased at the price of his blood. This Issachar is written to be a strong ass because formerly the Gentile people, like a brutish and lustful animal, stood firm by no rational principle; but afterward it willingly bore the yoke of evangelical discipline.

“Lying between the boundaries, he saw that rest was good and that the land was excellent.”

[Note: [Col. 2204] From Gregory, *Morals*, book 1, chapter 6.]

To lie between the boundaries is to rest while awaiting the end of the world and to seek nothing of the things now passing in the midst of it, but to desire the final things.

The strong ass sees rest and the best land when the simple Gentile people raise themselves to the strength of good works for this reason: because they are making their way toward the homeland of eternal life.

Therefore it also places its shoulder under the burden, because, desiring to reach the promised rest, it willingly bears all the burdens of the commandments.

Thus it became a servant to tribute—that is, offering gifts of faith and good works to Christ [Col. 2205], the king of its faith.

“Dan shall judge his people as the other tribes in Israel. Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent on the path,” and what follows.

[Note: [Col. 2205] From Gregory, *Morals*, book 31, chapter 10.]

Some say that by these words the Antichrist is also foretold and that he will arise from this tribe, because here Dan is asserted to be both a serpent and a biter, and because among the tribes of Israel Dan was the first to encamp toward the north (Num. 2:25), signifying the one who says that he will sit on the sides of the north, and of whom the prophet figuratively says, “From Dan the snorting of his horses was heard” (Jer. 8:16).

He is called not only a serpent but also a *cerastes*. For κέρατα (*kérata*) in Greek means “horns.” That serpent is therefore said to be horned, by which the Antichrist is fittingly represented, because against the life of the faithful he will be armed not only with the poisonous bite of his preaching but also with the horns of power.

Who does not know that a path is narrower than a road? Thus Dan becomes a serpent in the road because he urges those to walk in the broadness of the present life to whom he fawningly shows favor as though sparing them. But he bites on the road because he consumes with the poison of his error those to whom he grants freedom.

He becomes [Col. 2206] a horned serpent on the path because, when he finds people faithful and constraining themselves within the narrow ways of the heavenly commandment, he attacks them not only with the wickedness of crafty persuasion but also oppresses them with the terror of power; and, during the exhaustion of persecution, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of power.

This horse, whose heels the horned serpent is said to bite, signifies this world, which in its pride foams along in the course of passing times.

And because the Antichrist strives to seize the final moments of this world, this horned serpent is said to bite the horse’s heels. To bite the heels of the horse is to reach the final things of the age by striking them.

“So that its rider may fall backward.”

[Note: [Col. 2206] In Ms. Corb. it ends as follows: “The rider of the horse is everyone who is lifted up by the iniquities of this world; he is said to fall backward.”]

The unbelieving Jewish people, caught in the snares of their error, await the Antichrist in place of Christ.

Jacob rightly, in the same passage, suddenly turned into the voice of the elect, saying, “I shall await your salvation, Lord”—that is, not the Antichrist, as the unbelievers do, but, I faithfully believe, Christ, who will come for our redemption. Amen.

[QUESTIONS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS.]

[Col. 2205]

ADMONITION CONCERNING THE BOOK OF QUESTIONS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS

All learned men reject this work as Augustine’s. And certainly not without reason, since its subject matter and method of teaching—quite apart from the difference in style—are far removed from the genius and faith of the holy Doctor.

In the second question God is said to have created matter, which was a confusion of things, from which he would make the world, so that he might destroy the devil’s presumption not by power but by reason.

In Question 13 it is stated absolutely that the infants who perished with their parents in Sodom are free from Gehenna because they were killed in another person’s cause. In this passage the author of the *Questions*, whoever he may be, seemed, in Bellarmine’s judgment, to deny original sin.

Indeed, in answering this very question, Alcuin, in his work on Genesis, question 103, although he otherwise uses the same words found here, nevertheless did not conceal the guilt of original sin: “Was it not provided for them,” he says, “that, living for a long time, they should not follow the example of their parents, and that, since they were killed in another person’s cause, they might be punished less severely in the future—or not at all?”

In Question 21 and Question 45 the author argues that woman was not created in the image of God, contrary to Augustine’s teaching in book 3 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 22.

Question 23 contains nothing difficult concerning the origin of the soul, according to Augustine.

Question 27 asserts that Samuel was not raised by the pythoness, but that his apparition—or the devil—appeared to Saul, in such a way as to insist that the contrary opinion is false and absurd. Yet Augustine, in book 2 of the *Questions to Simplicianus*, shows that this other opinion accords beautifully with the Holy Scriptures.

Question 41 argues against understanding the words of Genesis, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” as referring to the Holy Spirit, whereas Augustine frequently explains them in that way.

Question 43 strongly disapproves of Jephthah’s vow, calling him a criminal and saying that he possessed no testimony of righteousness, although he is nevertheless praised among distinguished men in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 11.

In Question 46 it condemns as ignorance or folly those who say that Samuel exercised the office of priest—an opinion that Augustine himself shares with many others in book 17 of *The City of God*, chapter 4.

In Question 48 it speaks of the Son of God in the manner of the Arians.

Question 56 says that it seems unjustly to some people—although it also seemed so to Augustine—that Joseph was the son of Heli and Jacob, one according to nature and the other according to the Law.

Question 59 wishes the Lord’s words in John, “The Spirit blows where it wills,” to be interpreted of the wind, not of the Holy Spirit, whereas Augustine interprets them otherwise.

Question 108 attacks with many insults those who wish the Hebrews to have been named from Heber, not from Abraham; but Augustine, in book 2 of the *Retractations*, chapter 16, and in book 16 of *The City of God*, chapter 11, follows that opinion.

Question 109 labors to persuade the reader that Melchizedek was not a human being but the Holy Spirit, and it rejects the statement that he is called the high priest in the offering.

Question 115 says that Abraham worshiped idols with his father, contrary to Augustine’s position in book 16 of *The City of God*, chapter 13.

In Question 116 the author thinks that the Passover was named from the Passion, whereas Augustine, in Letter 53 to Januarius, section 2, thinks it was named from the Hebrew word meaning “passing over.”

Moreover, in the judgment of the theologians of Louvain, several questions reflect the Pelagian heresy, such as Questions 79, 80, 83, and others.

Finally, very few of the questions do not conflict in some respect with Augustine’s teaching. It would therefore be superfluous to add that the holy Doctor makes no mention of this lengthy work in his books of the *Retractations*, although there he carefully reviews other books of questions.

[Col. 2207]

It remains for us to submit to the examination and judgment of readers an opinion approved today by very many learned men: namely, that these *Questions* belong to the same author to whom the *Commentaries on the Apostle*, published under the name of Ambrose, are attributed.

For, when the two works are compared with one another—Question 24 with the *Commentary on 1 Corinthians* 11:5; Question 74 with the *Commentary on 2 Corinthians* 5:21 and on Galatians 3:13; Question 102 with the *Commentary on 2 Timothy* 2:20; Question 108 with the *Commentary on Philippians* 3:5; Question 113 with the *Commentary on Ephesians* 3:10; and so forth—they have discovered an extraordinary agreement in subject matter, ideas, and even the very words.

Moreover, they think that both works were completed at nearly the same time: the *Commentaries* while Pope Damasus, who died toward the end of the year 384, was governing the Roman Church, as their author testifies in the *Commentary on 1 Timothy* 3:15; and the *Questions* about the year 300 after the destruction of Jerusalem, according to Question 44, “Against the Jews,” although some believe that this year is counted from Christ’s coming.

Furthermore, the writer of the *Commentaries* is thought to have been identified by Augustine in book 4 of *To Boniface*, chapter 4, where he presents under the name of Hilary an opinion that is contained word for word in the same *Commentaries* on Romans 5:12.

But since these *Commentaries* differ greatly in style and doctrine from Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, they are thought to belong to another Hilary: namely, Hilary the deacon, who likewise lived under Pope Damasus, the man said to have been a Luciferian by sect and a Sardinian by nationality.

Here, without pronouncing anything concerning the author of the *Commentaries*, we are pleased to observe concerning the Questions that we have detected among the manuscript codices a variety capable of reviving and strengthening the opinion of Erasmus and others. They had initially suspected that the work of Questions was not by one man, because the same matters are repeated and the same question is treated again under different titles; because a different style of expression is employed; and because the doctrines defended are not consistently the same but plainly contradictory.

There are, in fact, two classes of manuscript codices.

Some contain the 127 questions that were first published: namely, 47 from the Old Testament and all the rest from the New Testament. They differ from the printed editions only in that they nowhere possess the third title, “Mixed from Both,” which the printers prefixed to the final thirty questions.

Two manuscripts of this first class are in the Sorbonne Library, two likewise in the Victorine Library, and one—much older, written approximately 700 years ago—in the Colbertine Library.

We found no more than three manuscripts of the second class: one Sorbonic, another Victorine, and a third our Germanic manuscript. Although these contain 151 questions—56 from the Old Testament and 95 from the New—and are therefore 24 questions longer than the codices of the first class, they do not contain most of the treatises and sermons first published from those codices.

What is relevant here is that they lack Question 44, “Against the Jews,” and Question 115, “Against the Mathematicians,” as well as several others from which the author’s age and homeland were thought to be ascertainable.

From this second class of manuscripts Jacob Haemer extracted the second collection of questions, which were published later.

Finally, we give here a double list of the questions, in which the difference between the manuscripts can be understood at a glance. We have marked with an asterisk the questions proper to codices of either the first or the second class.

[Col. 2207]

[QUESTIONS OF THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS. (C,G,S)*]

LIST OF QUESTIONS

[Col. 2207] FROM MANUSCRIPT CODICES OF THE FIRST CLASS.
