[Note: [Col. 2207] This series contains all the questions first published.]

QUESTIONS OF THE OLD TESTAMENT

I. What is God?

II. Why did God make the world?

III. Why was it necessary to explain through Moses, and not earlier, the beginning of the world and the order of creation?

IV. Why did he not give the Law at the beginning?

V. Why was Abel’s sacrifice accepted and Cain’s rejected?

VI. Whether Lamech killed Cain, as is supposed.

VII. What were the ten words given on the tablets, and so forth.

VIII. Why did Moses, descending from the mountain, have a radiant face?

IX. If God made all things good, what does it mean that he says to Noah concerning clean and unclean animals, “Bring in with you,” and so forth?

X. When God says that the children of Israel would come out of Egypt in the fourth generation, why does Moses say that they came out in the fifth generation?

XI. If the will of a righteous man is good, why did Isaac bless not Esau, whom he wished to bless, but Jacob, whom he did not wish to bless?

XII. Why did Abraham receive circumcision as the sign of his faith?

[Col. 2209]

XIII. If God’s judgment is just, why were the infants in Sodom burned?

XIV. What does it mean that God, who is proclaimed just, says that the sins of the fathers are repaid to their children?

XV. Although the Law proclaims a man just, why does Solomon say, “Do not be excessively righteous”?

XVI. Why was the angel who wished to kill Moses on the way appeased by the circumcision of the infant?

XVII. What does it mean that he calls accursed those who have not left offspring in Israel?

XVIII. Why did Saul, when he sinned, ask that prayer be made for him, and could not obtain it, whereas David received the opposite treatment?

XIX. Whether Adam had an immortal body or a mortal one.

XX. What does it mean that “man ate the bread of angels,” since angels have no need of food?

XXI. What does it mean that God made man in his image and likeness, and whether woman is the image of God?

XXII. What does Solomon mean when he says, “Justify your soul before your death,” and so forth?

XXIII. Whether souls, like bodies, are propagated by descent.

XXIV. What does it mean that the man is the image of God and not the woman?

XXV. Why did Joseph adjure the children of Israel to carry his ashes out of Egypt?

XXVI. Concerning Elisha: whether he obtained what he boldly asked from Elijah.

XXVII. Whether the pythoness raised Samuel.

XXVIII. What should be answered to those who say that the world is eternal?

XXIX. Why was it commanded that circumcision be performed on the eighth day?

XXX. In Proverbs he says, “The righteous man is his own accuser.” How can he be righteous if he is a sinner?

XXXI. Whether the serpent naturally spoke with the woman, or whether the serpent was named from the act, or whether it was the devil.

XXXII. We read in Solomon, “The rich and the poor met one another, but the Lord made them both.” How, then, is there no partiality with God?

XXXIII. Solomon says, “The years of the wicked will be shortened,” although we see some wicked people living to an advanced age.

XXXIV. In Solomon it says, “God did not make death”; and elsewhere, “Good and evil, life and death, are from God.”

XXXV. For what reason did David call Saul, after God had departed from him, “the Lord’s anointed,” and so forth?

XXXVI. If “the soul that sins shall itself die,” what does it mean that thirty men were killed in the case of Achan?

XXXVII. What does it mean that, when death was sent into Jacob, it came upon Israel?

XXXVIII. If the horse and the mule have no understanding, how much less does the earth? Why, then, is the earth said to bless the Lord?

XXXIX. What does it mean when we read in Solomon, “There is hope in darkness. A living dog is better than a dead lion”?

XL. What does the prophet mean when he says, “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear,” and so forth?

XLI. Whether the Spirit who was borne over the waters is to be understood as the Holy Spirit.

XLII. Why did the angel appear to Moses both in fire and in the bush?

XLIII. * Since Abraham was forbidden to sacrifice his son, why was Jephthah not forbidden to sacrifice his daughter?

XLIV. * Against the Jews.

XLV. * How man was made in the image of God, and whether woman was also made so.

XLVI. * Whether Samuel was one of the sons of Aaron, and whether he was a priest.

XLVII. * Concerning what is read in Isaiah: “And seven women shall seize,” and so forth.

QUESTIONS OF THE NEW TESTAMENT.

XLVIII. God is perfection: what need, then, was there for Christ to be born?

XLIX. Why was the Savior baptized?

L. If the Savior was baptized in order to provide an example, why was this not likewise done in circumcision?

LI. How is the statement understood: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you”?

LII. If Christ was born of the Holy Spirit, why is it said, “Wisdom built herself a house”?

LIII. What does it mean that the Savior is said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January?

LIV. If Christ, the Son of God, was made from the seed of David—that is, was already born—why, when he is baptized, does he hear: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”?

LV. What was the reason that the Lord allowed himself to be crucified on the eighth day before the Kalends of April?

LVI. Why is Joseph’s father written as Jacob in Matthew, but as Heli in Luke, and so forth?

LVII. What does it mean that, although it is written in Malachi, “Behold, I send my angel,” Mark says that it is in Isaiah?

LVIII. How does John deny that he knew Christ before the baptism, when he proves that he knew him beforehand?

LIX. If Baptism is a heavenly mystery, why does the Lord say to Nicodemus, “If I have told you earthly things,” and so forth?

LX. If the Law and the Prophets lasted until John, why does the Savior send offerings to the priests to be presented?

[Col. 2211] LXI. What does it mean that, when the Jews were accusing the disciples, the Lord brought forward David as an example, by which they seem to become guilty together with David?

LXII. What does it mean that, when Leah’s sons have been killed, Rachel is said to mourn her sons?

LXIII. How did the Magi understand from the star that Christ had been born king of the Jews?

LXIV. How is it proved that the Savior rose after three days and nights?

LXV. If the Evangelists spoke with one voice, why did three say that the Lord suffered at the sixth hour, while Mark said the third?

LXVI. Mark said that the demons knew the Lord, but the Apostle says of the rulers of this age, “If they had understood,” and so forth.

LXVII. What does it mean that, on the cross, the Lord says, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know,” and so forth? For if they do not know, what is being forgiven?

LXVIII. We are taught to pray for our enemies; why, then, do the souls of the slain ask to be avenged?

LXIX. If the Law ceased when John preached, how does the Savior say, “I did not come to abolish the Law, but to fulfill it”?

LXX. * The Lord certainly wants us to be enemies of the devil; why, then, does he say, “Be in agreement with your adversary”?

LXXI. Jacob was called “a man who sees God”; how, then, is it said, “No one has ever seen God”?

LXXII. What does it mean that it is said in the Apocalypse, “Go and take the book and eat it,” and so forth?

LXXIII. What does Simeon mean when he says to Mary, the mother of the Lord, “This one has been appointed for the fall,” and so forth?

LXXIV. What does Isaiah mean when he says of Christ, “He committed no sin,” while the Apostle says, “For our sake he made him sin”?

LXXV. Why did the Savior pay the didrachma only for himself and Peter?

LXXVI. In the Gospel it says, “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Christ.” Was truth, then, not present before? Therefore neither was the Law.

LXXVII. What does it mean that it is said in Mark, “Entering into a house, he did not want anyone to know, and he could not remain hidden”?

LXXVIII. * It is read in John that, although Jesus denied that he had gone up to the feast, he nevertheless went up.

LXXIX. If we live by our own free choice, why did the Savior say, “No one comes to me unless the Father draws him”?

LXXX. Certainly everyone is either a son of God or of the devil; what, then, we are born as must be investigated.

LXXXI. The Apostle says, “We are Jews by nature.” He therefore shows that Jews are born from Jews, not from proselytes, and so forth.

LXXXII. The pagans are subject to the elements; why, then, does the Apostle say, “We were subject to the elements,” and so forth?

LXXXIII. If salvation and true knowledge come through Christ, why did he not come earlier, and so forth?

LXXXIV. Why, while observing the moon’s course in determining Easter, do we condemn the pagans because they observe lunar days and the moon’s movement?

LXXXV. What does it mean that, although there are seventeen generations from David to the Babylonian captivity, the Evangelist says fourteen?

LXXXVI. What proves that the mother of the Lord was from the tribe of David?

LXXXVII. If there is one God, why is the hope of salvation in three?

LXXXVIII. * If grace is greater in the New Testament, why does the Lord appear seated in the Old and standing in the New?

LXXXIX. How should we understand what the Savior says about the Holy Spirit: that, when he comes, he will convict the world, and so forth?

XC. If Satan is the devil, why does he say to the Jews, “You are born from the father, the devil,” and so forth?

XCI. Against Photinus, who says that Christ did not exist before Mary.

XCII. How is what the Lord says understood: “I give you my peace,” and so forth?

XCIII. Did the Apostles possess the Holy Spirit while the Lord was present in the flesh?

XCIV. Did Judas Iscariot burst open while hanging before the Lord’s passion?

XCV. From where did the observance of Pentecost originate?

XCVI. Is Easter interpreted as “Passover”?

XCVII. Against Arius.

XCVIII. If Satan is the devil, why does the Savior say to the Jews, “You are from the father, the devil”?

XCIX. What does “Let no temptation overtake you except what is human” mean?

C. * Concerning what is read in the Gospel of Matthew: “I confess to you, Father,” and so forth.

CI. * Concerning the boastfulness of the Roman Levites.

CII. * Against the Novatians, who deny saving repentance.

CIII. * Since it is clear that God commanded in Leviticus that sacrifices be offered, why does he elsewhere deny and reject them?

CIV. * Why did the Lord order that a sword be prepared, and afterward forbid striking?

CV. + How prophecy corresponds with the Gospel concerning the darkening of the sun, and so forth.

[Col. 2213] CVI. * How the things read in Genesis concerning the work of the six days are to be understood.

CVII. * Concerning the order of day and night: which comes first?

CVIII. * Concerning the Hebrew language: from where did it receive its name?

CIX. * Concerning Melchizedek: how he blessed Abraham, and so forth.

CXI. * Concerning the Twenty-Third Psalm.

CXII. * Concerning the Fiftieth Psalm.

CXIII. * Why the Son of God was sent, and not another.

59. Why did the Savior pay the didrachma only for himself and Peter?

60. * Why does the Apostle Paul rebuke Peter for practicing circumcision, when he himself circumcised Timothy?

61. * What spirit does the Apostle assert is to be saved when he says that such a person is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, “so that the spirit,” and so forth?

62. * Why does the Savior pray and say, “May your flight not be in winter or on the Sabbath,” when the time of this persecution cannot be postponed?

63. Certainly everyone is either a son of God or of the devil; what, then, we are born as must be investigated.

64. The Apostle says, “We are Jews by nature.” He therefore shows that Jews are born from Jews, not from proselytes, and so forth.

65. * What does the Apostle mean by saying, “No one can say, ‘Lord God,’ except in the Holy Spirit,” when Photinus, Marcion, Manichaeus, prostitutes, and filthy persons say it?

66. * If no one is justified by the Law, why is the one who has not fulfilled the Law called accursed?

67. * If all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are in Christ, how does he say that he does not know the day and hour of judgment?

70. * What does it mean that the Savior says to Mary, “Do not touch me,” and so forth, when other women are read to have touched him?

71. * What does “All who came before me are thieves,” and so forth, mean, since it seems to strike at the Prophets?

72. * The Apostle says that Christ died for everyone, but the Lord himself says that he gives his life as a redemption for many.

## Questions from the Old Testament

[Col. 2213]

### QUESTION ONE.—What is God?

This is what no opinion reaches. For he is more than anything that can be said or conceived. Let us nevertheless say something which, although unequal to him, may nevertheless correspond in some respect to what seem worthy of God. For each nature forms its conception of God according to its capacity, so that, as one nature differs from another, so one judgment differs from another in determining what God is. Since he is above all things, he must surpass the minds of all.

Human beings, insofar as they can extend the gaze of their mind, discern what God is by opinion, not by definition. Angels, who are superior to human beings, undoubtedly have a greater conception of God; Archangels have a greater one still. The Cherubim and Seraphim, which are said to be powers close to God, have greater conceptions of God, yet they do not fully comprehend what God is. For no one knows the Father except the Son, nor does anyone know the Son except the Father (Matt. 11:27).

Therefore God is, as he appears to human beings, a simple spiritual nature, inaccessible light, invisible, immeasurable, infinite, perfect, needing nothing, eternal, wholly immortal; from whom all things have received their beginning; worthy of reverence, love, and fear; outside whom nothing exists, or rather, in whom are all things that exist, both above and below, highest and lowest. He is almighty, holding all things, truly rich in all things, because there is nothing that does not belong to him; good, just, and merciful.

He is good because he caused what did not exist to come into existence; just because whatever he made for progress was left to its own free choice. Yet because his creatures are not so perfect that they cannot fall, he decreed that the seeds of the law should be naturally present in them, adding the assistance of the law once it had been made manifest, so that his authority might be perfect for human beings. He is merciful because he does not quickly repay sinners, but endures them so that he may forgive those who turn back.

He is also severe, so that what he has well established may be preserved through fear of him, lest negligence bring about the ruin of life. And, not to omit something still more wonderful, his clemency is so great that, though he suffers insults from those whom he made, he endures them and is the first to call them to peace. Is this not a greater virtue than creating a creature? If his excessive goodness persisted in this way, it would harm the creature. Therefore he wishes at times to be loved and at times to be feared, lest those who stray from him perish.

This is why, lest his patience be thought worthy of contempt—not indeed to his harm, but wholly to ours—he says: “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isa. 42:14).

God, then, is good, and everything he made is good. From where, therefore, does evil come? Nothing is evil except the transgression of the good, when either what is forbidden is presumptuously undertaken or what is permitted is done disorderly: so that what is commanded in one circumstance becomes sin in another. Thus what is permitted with a wife is done with a prostitute; what ought to be offered to God is offered to the devil; someone does not take what is his own but another’s; and when a transgressor ought to be killed, an innocent person is killed.

No nature, therefore, is shown to be evil. The will, however, is an accident of nature, conceived from causes that are wrongly moved, when it exceeds the proper measure and does what is not according to its nature. The causes of transgression arise from the senses, when we see or hear something wrongly. This error occurs because a human being is not God, who alone cannot err.

Human nature has therefore been entrusted and left to its own free choice, so that it may do what it wills. If it improves the good of its nature through its own exercise, it is more honorable; but if it weakens its vigor, it is considered worthy of disgrace. For it does what is against itself. It is no small gift granted to a human being that, when following what is right, he may rejoice in himself because through his own work he sees himself becoming better—or at least blame himself because, when he could have done so, he did not strive to make himself better through good deeds.

But if a human being were not master of himself, he would be subject to necessity, so that he would have neither the glory of a good work nor the punishment of an evil one, but would be one of the beasts. Since, therefore, we have been made capable of either course, so that through negligence we may sin if we hear and see wrongly—that is, outside the norm [Note: [Col. 2215] Manuscripts read “nature.”] and reason—what we ought to hear and see rightly, while through vigilance we may preserve the good of nature, we cannot always be cautious. For, as I have said, we have been made capable of both.

If we sin, however, we are not yet condemned unless we sin again, now as though we were traitors. Whoever has sinned once must restore himself so as not to sin again, lest he be equal to the one who overcame him; if he does not sin again, he is then considered superior. For the one who has once been struck down will triumph twice.

This is justice: since there is a struggle in the world, the one who is more inclined to sin is crowned if he does not sin. Nothing, therefore, is evil in God’s work. But if certain things are called evil by some—such as poison or darkness, because our bodies cannot withstand the force of poison—then they should also call fire or water evil, and iron or lead evil because they are far inferior to gold.

They condemn darkness by comparison with light, although they know that darkness is necessary in its proper place, just as lead or baked clay are necessary. For these things certainly provide rest after labor. Therefore everyone who struggles in the world must strive in such a way that, when defeated in a difficult matter, he does not depart guilty, barely or slowly restoring himself; for death may intervene during this process, and he may leave this life with his sin.

Whoever resists with every strength, if he is perhaps struck down, falls like a man. No one is angry with him; rather, someone restores his spirit with a kind of encouragement. For they see that he intended to win and hope that one who was struck down by his enemy only after great exertion may advance to victory.

Whoever is easily defeated has no will to resist. He is not defeated but consents. Such a person sins more grievously. One of this kind is scarcely [Note: [Col. 2216] The manuscripts of the second type read “not.”] to be admitted to forgiveness, since he has the desire to sin. Whoever takes thought not to sin does not sin gravely even if he does sin. For smaller sins sometimes steal upon the more diligent. The smaller they are, the subtler they are; and while they are despised, they are not avoided. Greater sins are plainly visible. Accordingly, whoever sins in greater matters bears the guilt of his will.

Since, as we said above, sins take their beginning from the senses, when we look at or hear something contrary to the command of the law or to reason—for example, if, seeing the sun, we think that it should be worshiped because of its beauty—we then see wrongly. This is an insult to the common Creator, since what is owed to him alone is attributed to a creature, especially when the law has forbidden it.

Or when we see well-formed and beautiful bodies, or something belonging to our neighbor, and desire it, looking at it differently from what the law commands, we then commit the sin called evil.

Someone might perhaps say: “Then nothing beautiful ought to have been made, lest we sin, so that our protection might depend on the deformity of others.” If that were so, iron ought not to exist, lest murders be committed with it. Nor should a lamp be used, lest thieves use its light for breaking in, so that what is greatly useful to everyone would be absent because of the empty talk of some.

It is clear that we always look at everything, but do not always desire everything; for the fault is not theirs but ours when we are negligent. This is clear from the fact that the distinction is created by an interval, because we are not what God is.

We likewise hear wrongly if, when hearing that idols are gods, we assent, or if we lend an ear to those singing shameful songs. We hear rightly, however, if, when hearing that God is one, we take delight. If someone hears something contrary to the law and assents to it, he sins; and this is to hear wrongly.

### II.—Why did God make the world?

He made it because he is a maker; or let it be denied that he is one, if he is not. But the works themselves show that he is. He therefore made it so that what previously did not exist might exist, because without doubt it is better to exist than not to exist.

If someone says, “Was there perhaps some empty space in which he could make it, or what existed previously where he made it?” the Chosen Vessel resolves this briefly. For, speaking of God, he says: “In him we live and move and are” (Acts 17:28). This means that all things are in God, because he is everywhere, and before all things he alone is eternal, invisible to every creature.

And lest we appear to have omitted the mystery—or rather, to have been ignorant of why the world was made—we say that the devil’s apostasy drew many angels, that is, spiritual powers, with him into transgression, when he wished to defend a kingdom for himself through impious presumption. The prophet Isaiah signifies this when he says: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning” (Isa. 14:12), that is, you who appeared brighter than the others.

For he was as if a prince of many, among whom he was the more illustrious, and with whose fellowship he descended into an impious contest. Seeing many spiritual powers beneath him—especially since in the paradise of God he excelled in knowledge of the heavenly mystery—he was puffed up by this very pride [Col. 2217] and wished to be called god.

The same reasoning can be seen in an example from the present life: some people, elated by the sight of soldiers gathered around them, with their attendants providing fuel for conspiracy in this matter, have wished to claim power for themselves. Therefore God, in order to destroy his presumption not by force but by reason, created matter that would be a confusion of things, from which he would make the world.

For things that had been confused together, once distinguished, produced the ordered world that we see. When substances had been separated from one another and joined together, the result is called the world, because each thing appeared in the world separated from another.

Thus this human being, placed here and created from what is above and what is below—that is, from heavenly and earthly things—might display the dominion of the one God not only by his voice but also by his image, since one human being was made by one God, from whom the others would arise. For one made one in order to teach that all things are from one, and therefore that there is one God, so that the higher creature might learn the truth, to its own confusion, in the human being who was formed from earth.

For this reason the devil became the enemy of the human being. He foresaw that the human being had been made for his accusation. Therefore, through his cunning, he worked to lead the human being into the same transgression into which he himself had fallen, so that he might make his accuser a participant in his condemnation.

Through transgression he promised him divinity, which, while he himself desired it, he had been cast away from. And because every nature is free from guilt, it receives names from what happens to it. First there is the thing, and afterward its designation. Accordingly, “Satan” and “devil” are names formed from his action, signifying not his nature but his will.

Therefore, so that God’s purpose—what he had decreed concerning the created human being—might remain, and so that the devil’s deed, by which he deceived the human being, might increase his guilt, Christ deigned to come from the holy dwellings even to earth. He came both to free the human being from the sentence of transgression and to display the devil’s future destruction, so that no one might imitate his deed.

For this reason the Apostle John said: “The Son of God came for this purpose, to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8). If the devil were evil by nature, it would be either madness or injustice to promise him punishment. For who would accuse one whom he saw doing something in no other way than his nature permits?

Can fire be reproached because it burns, or water because it cools, when they do this not by will but by nature? Likewise, if the devil were evil by nature, he would have no will. He could not distinguish, but would thrust himself upon everyone in one and the same manner, like a blind man [Note: [Col. 2217] The Colbertine and German manuscripts read “immerse himself.”].

Yet he acts with a certain judgment. He spares those who do his will; he pretends not to notice certain novices; he places obstacles and impediments before those who wish to flee to God’s aid; he lays ambushes for God’s servants; and he is more hostile to those who are more zealous in God’s service.

It is therefore clear that his will is guilty. For this reason the Apostle Peter says: “Be sober and vigilant, because your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8).

He does not seek pagans; he does not seek Jews; he does not seek people of evil life and conduct. He seeks God’s servants and Christ’s attendants, whom he knows to be his enemies, because they condemn his deed and his presumption.

Finally, when the Law was given, his envy burned more fiercely against those who were under the Law, because he knew that the teaching of the Law handed down belief in one God and good conduct to human beings.

Therefore, if he is thought to do this by nature, he cannot be held guilty, because he does what belongs to his nature and can do, and does not do what he cannot do because it does not belong to his nature. Thus he should be neither praised nor condemned. He should not be praised because what he does is harmful, but he should not be condemned because he does it not by will but by the impulse of nature.

For we know that some people have suddenly become deranged and have harmed others with clubs, iron, stones, and bites, even killing some; but when they were seized and brought before judges, they were not considered guilty, because they had done these things not willingly but under the compulsion of some unknown force, without knowing what they were doing. For how can one be held guilty who does not know what he has done?

So too, if the devil does not know the good, why should he be considered worthy of condemnation for not doing what he does not know? Indeed, if it could be so, he ought to be praised, because he does what he does not know.

We, however, are rightly held guilty because we do not do what we know we ought to do, or because we do what we know we ought not to do.

But because throughout all Scripture we see that the devil is held guilty, and because we read that Gehenna has been prepared for him, we know that he is to be condemned according to the laws. For although he knew and was able to do good, he did evil.

God, who is just, would not condemn him because he had failed to do good that he did not know; he condemned him because he had done evil that he knew.

It therefore seems to me to have been demonstrated that no nature ought to be called evil, because, as has become clear, all evil arises from the will, which comes to nature through the senses.

### III.—Why was it necessary for Moses to explain the beginning of the world and the order of creation later, and not earlier?

It should not have been described earlier, because until then such great error had not yet arisen among human beings from this cause. But when error had already grown among the human race, so that even the children of Israel in Egypt were hearing arguments opposed to this account from the Egyptian philosophers—philosophers from whom Moses himself had also learned all Egyptian learning, which claims that a certain Apis [Note: [Col. 2218] German manuscript, Saclam. Colbert manuscript, Salam.] created this present world through evil angels and that he himself appeared to be the ruler of the world, that is, Satan—then this too had to be explained. Marcion followed this opinion and rushed into death. The Manichaeans likewise say that humanity was made by the same Satan [Note: [Col. 2218] German and Colbert manuscripts, Saclam.], though not this world, and are therefore more foolish than the others. Since it is agreed that the world was fashioned for humanity’s sake, they say that the world was made for humanity by God, though from another’s material, while humanity itself was created by the Adversary, so that one master might have been placed in another’s house.

Moses therefore had to expose and remove this error by making it clear that God is the author of the world and of the human being who was fashioned. Having received authority through the signs and wonders that he performed, he taught that what he delivered with signs as witnesses was certainly true. For who would not believe one whose deeds contained such great signs? Hence those who hold opinions contrary to this teaching are known to err: they strive to support their assertion with bare words.

Therefore, in order to teach that nothing is coeternal with God, he sets forth the order of created things. By mentioning that the smaller things were made first and the greater things afterward, he shows that none of these things is uncreated. For those that are smaller in time are greater in power. Thus, if the former should try to claim priority on the basis of their being earlier in time, they are refuted by the very weakness through which they are subject to the later things; or if the latter, presuming upon their power, should claim primacy for themselves, they are humbled by their later origin, so that none of them appears not to have been subject to a beginning.

First, heaven and earth were made; then light, which serves the function of day [Note: [Col. 2218] Manuscripts, *dies* (“day”).]; afterward the firmament, which was called heaven, and the gatherings of waters, which he called seas, so that the earth on which it would be possible to live might appear. When he says that the earth was made after heaven, he does not intend earth alone to be understood, but signifies matter—that is, all the lower things that developed into the whole appearance of the world. He maintains that heaven was made in the beginning, not this bodily heaven but that higher, spiritual one. Thus, by saying that heaven was made first and earth afterward, he signifies that God created all invisible things in heaven and all visible things on earth. For he comprehends the totality of the highest and lowest of all nature, so that whatever lies between them must certainly also be believed to have been made.

He asserts that the lights established to govern the world were made on the fourth day, so that, although they are greater in power, they might be later in time [Col. 2219]. He established humanity on the sixth day, in order to introduce an inhabitant into a house that had already been made. Yet humanity is greatly superior, since it is declared to have been made on the sixth day. I called humanity superior for this reason: its inner nature is invisible and capable of understanding. But the sun is greater in strength, and the moon is more powerful in light, than the earth.

This is why some are displeased by the statement, “And he saw the light, that it was good.” Since they claimed that everything had been made by the evil one and therefore could not be believed good, Moses, in order to prove that the things made were good, showed that the things made were pleasing to God himself, so that he might make the one to whom they were displeasing guilty. For how could the one who said, “Let there be light,” and light came to be, be unaware of light? Or who does what he does not know? When the light had been made, it pleased the one who made it. What craftsman does not rejoice in his work? Thus it is said, “God saw the light, that it was good” (Gen. I, 3–4). Yet there are also those who say that it is evil. What if it had been left without testimony?

Accordingly, after describing the structure of the world, he follows the lineage of the human race from the origin of the first man through Seth, who was given in place of Abel, and in due order arrives at Abraham, the father of the Jews. This was to show that Abraham believed in this God, who is the creator of the world, and that this same God gave the Law, in which Christ was promised as one who would free the human race from the dominion of the devil.

From these considerations our faith is shown to be reasonable [Note: [Col. 2219] German manuscript, “by reasons.”]. The recorded genealogy bears witness to it, because the race of Christians exists from the beginning. From Seth, the son of Adam, one comes to Enoch; from Enoch to Noah; from Noah to Abraham; from Abraham one descends to David; from David to Mary; and from Mary Christ is born of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, in retrospect, all who have had faith in the one God whom the Savior preached ought rightly to be called Christians. For from the beginning it was promised that the Savior would come. Hence John says in the Apocalypse, “The Lamb who was slain from the foundation of the world” (Apoc. XIII, 8). Thus Christians have always existed. All those whom I mentioned above, from the first human being created in the world through whom the lineage extends to the Savior, had faith in this God, of whom Christ spoke, saying: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John XVII, 3) [Note: [Col. 2219] The remainder is missing in the manuscripts of the second class.].

It may be objected: If they too were Christians before Christ, what knowledge did Christ bring? Christ’s coming brought this advance in understanding, because the proclamation of the one God revealed the mystery, showed what belonged to each person, and, in order to fulfill the justice of the Law, added what had been reserved.

### IV.—Why did God not give the Law at the beginning?

[Note: [Col. 2219] Compare Alcuin, *Questions on Genesis*, question 14.]

First, the Law ought not to have been given in written form, because it was, in a certain sense, implanted in nature itself, and knowledge of the Creator was not hidden through the lineage of humanity. For who does not know what belongs to a good life, or who is unaware that he ought not to do to another what he does not want done to himself?

But when the natural law had vanished, suppressed by the habit of sinning, then the Law had to be revealed, so that through the Jews all human beings might hear it. Not because it had been completely erased, but because people lacked its greatest authority: idolatry was being practiced. There was no fear of God on earth. Fornication was practiced. Greedy desire was directed toward the property of one’s neighbor.

The Law therefore had to be given so that the things already known might have authority and those that had begun to be forgotten might be made manifest. For we find that before Moses sins had not only been known but also punished. Accordingly, many righteous people are found who, knowing that God was an avenger, feared to sin. When this began to be neglected, the natural law had to be revealed, so that everyone might know plainly that God would call human actions to account.

Although punishment is recorded through the Flood and against Sodom and Gomorrah (Gen. VII, XIX), the forgetfulness of antiquity had covered these events. Therefore Moses recalled them as a source of terror, to correct conduct and restore faith in God. Hence the Apostle also says concerning the righteous, “The Law is not laid down for the righteous but for the unrighteous, for those who worship idols, fornicators” (I Tim. I, 9), and others of this kind.

Now let us see whether it is fitting for those who laugh when they hear of God’s future judgment: whether it will benefit them or harm them, whether it is supported by truth or lacks rational foundation. The Law was indeed given to the world, but we see it cease to operate among many. It therefore does not seem just that those who sin here through power should be secure. Some mock the laws; the poor are oppressed; accusations are fabricated against the just; those who act well are subjected to reproach; the devout are in need; the wicked flourish; the unjust and corrupt are honored; the greedy and plunderers grow rich; the judge is for sale.

Would it not seem unjust if the Creator of all things did not call these matters to account—so that those who have been unjustly oppressed here might be restored; those who have suffered want while living well might be rewarded; and those who were reproached on account of justice might be honored? Meanwhile, those who through power have despised the laws or mocked them by evasions while pursuing iniquity, and who have gloried in these things as though they were insulting justice itself, should be humbled and subjected to punishments in the presence of those whose misfortunes and humiliation they used to enjoy—so that those people too might rejoice over their punishment and give thanks to God, before whom alone there is no partiality (Rom. II, 11).

### V.—Why was Abel’s sacrifice accepted and Cain’s rejected? [Note: [Col. 2220] Alcuin, *Questions on Genesis*, question 15.]

This can be gathered from the words of the passage itself, because the narrative is not veiled by literary artifice. The language of Scripture itself indicates that Abel was prudent and devoted, while Cain was negligent, careless, and consequently less devout.

Abel therefore chose the better of the tame animals to present to the Lord his Creator, offering him the finest of the things he had created, so that by this he might demonstrate both his act of dedication and his merit, and might show both his own reverence and God as the author. Cain, like a peasant, was unable to offer this. Since he had implanted his whole mind in the earth, he could not raise the eyes of his mind toward heaven to see what was worthy of the Creator; he offered God gifts of whatever sort.

This same cause—an oblique attitude of mind—is also found among the Jews. They were often reproved when they carelessly offered their gifts on God’s altar, things that would not even have seemed worthy of human beings. The Lord says: “You offer me the blind and the lame; I will not accept these from your hands. Offer them to your governor or ruler, and see whether he will accept them” (Mal. I, 8). Yet everyone agrees that the greatest gifts ought to be offered to a person of high rank.

Cain’s gifts were therefore rejected, and the Lord said to him: “Why are you sorrowful, and why has your face fallen? If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be still. Its turning is toward you, and you will rule over it” (Gen. IV, 6–7). You see, then, that division incurs sin: because he did not consider what was worthy of God, he reserved the better things for his own use.

He was therefore not reproved because he offered, but because he offered things unworthy. Nor was he condemned merely for this, but because, after being admonished, he refused to correct what he had done. “Its turning,” he says, “is toward you, and you will rule over it.” That is: since I have not accepted it, the offering you made has turned toward your dominion, so that henceforth you may know what to do.

At this, envy flared up in him, so that he killed his brother—so that the one who had first displayed justice might be killed by the unjust, and a bad example might be given to humanity. Blinded by jealous rivalry, he not only failed to give thanks that he had not been made guilty, and that he had learned how to correct the matter, but added another and more serious offense by which he deserved to be condemned.

Such is the case of careless and fratricidal Cain, like that of the wicked servant who, though he had gone unrecognized by his master, became ungrateful and went out and strangled his fellow servant. Thus he was condemned without excuse both for the earlier offense unknown to him and for the impiety he committed against his fellow servant (Matt. XVIII, 27 ff.).

Yet Cain was not immediately condemned. Rather, he was put to shame and sent away under accusation and fear upon the earth, so that, if he repented, he might be forgiven. Finally, fearing that someone might kill him for this deed, he said to the Lord: “My guilt is greater [Col. 2221] than can be forgiven; forgive me [Note: [Col. 2221] Manuscripts, “forgive.”]. If you drive me away today from your face, I shall hide from your face and from the face of the earth, and I shall be groaning and trembling upon the earth. And everyone who finds me will kill me.”

Terrified by the words of the just Judge, Cain fears being despised by the Lord, so much so that he thinks he must flee even from the sight of human beings, certain that one who lives under an angry God can also be killed by a human being.

But what does the Lord answer him? “Not so,” he says. That is: I have not sent you away, though you do not deserve to live, so that you might be killed by someone, but so that you might groan and tremble, as one who first gave a bad example upon the earth, while the fruit does not answer the labor of your hands.

“And everyone who kills Cain,” he says, “shall pay sevenfold vengeance.” This sentence shows that Cain was rightly condemned. When he saw that a law had been given with such a threat, lest anyone imitate his deed, he began to fear more greatly, knowing what evil he had committed.

He therefore promises sevenfold vengeance if anyone should attempt such a crime, so that, seeing from Cain’s case that the offender had been made guilty, and that even before the Law had been revealed he would suffer sevenfold punishment if he did not avoid the deed, the knowledge of the Law might add six blows beyond what Cain had deserved, so that Cain’s wound would be counted as seven acts of vengeance.

By this same number those who leave everything and follow the Lord are to be rewarded, and in the future they will have eternal life. This is the sign that the Lord placed upon Cain, lest everyone who found him kill him (Gen. IV, 13–15). For a law was established in the case of the parricide: if anyone committed homicide—for every parricide is homicide—he would be guilty seven times as Cain had been, so that the others, terrified by this severity, might restrain themselves from such a crime.

### VI.—Did Lamech kill Cain, as is supposed?

Those who think this are mistaken. They suppose that Lamech spoke of Cain when he said, “I have killed a man for my bruise, and a young man for my wound.” Lamech had already been born in the fifth generation from Cain—that is, he was Cain’s great-great-grandson through Methuselah.

Lamech recalls this in order to show that the one who sins after the Law has been revealed must be bound by a more severe penalty. If, after Cain, sevenfold vengeance was exacted upon his imitator, how much more must vengeance be exacted upon one whom neither Cain’s deed and correction, nor the sentence subsequently pronounced against him, terrified enough to turn his will away from so impious and cruel a crime?

After Cain, therefore, Lamech committed this homicide. Without doubt, in accordance with what has been said above, he paid sevenfold vengeance. He also showed what would happen after Lamech to anyone who followed this deed, saying: “But for Lamech, seventy-sevenfold” (Gen. IV, 23–24). Since the evil deed is not followed by repentance, let him be struck by seventy-seven blows of punishment. Hence the Savior also commanded that the one who sins seventy-seven times, provided he turns back, should be forgiven (Matt. XVIII, 22).

But lest anyone think that another person committed homicide after Cain and before Lamech, because it says, “Vengeance was taken for Cain” (Gen. IV, 24, according to the Septuagint), as though the deed had already been committed, consider how Lamech could speak of himself as having been punished when the homicide he confessed to having committed was still recent. Every deed, however, is understood to contain its sentence within itself. When no other expectation remains except what is known to be due after the deed has been completed, what is future is treated as though it were already accomplished.

Thus it was said to Adam and Eve, “On the day on which you eat, you shall die” (Gen. II, 17). They did not die immediately, but after a long interval. Yet, because they had already lost the hope of immortality, the future death was spoken of as present, since it had already begun to exist in expectation.

Therefore, when Lamech confesses that he killed a young man, and Cain, as has been shown, could not have lived until that time—or, if he did reach it, which seems impossible, he was already older—Lamech did not kill him.

### VII.—What were the ten words given on the tablets, and what and how many words did each tablet contain?

He called ten pronouncements “ten words,” because the Savior also used “word” to signify a meaning. Among other things, he said to the Jews: “I too will ask you one question; answer me: the baptism of John, was it from heaven or from human beings?” (Matt. XXI, 24). He called this meaning a word.

In the same way, the ten words written on the two tablets are said to be ten meanings. Thus he says: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” This is the first word. He then added the second: “You shall not make for yourself any likeness in heaven above, or on earth below, or in the water beneath the earth.” Then he added the third: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” For the Lord will not cleanse the one who takes his name in vain—that is, “You shall not take the name of your God in a lie, so as to swear falsely by it.”

Next, in the fourth place, he says: “You shall keep the Sabbath of the Lord your God, and you shall do no servile work on it.” These four words properly concern God and are contained on the first tablet.

The remaining words are these. The first is: “Honor your father and your mother.” The second: “You shall not kill.” The third: “You shall not commit fornication.” The fourth: “You shall not steal.” The fifth: “You shall not give false testimony.” The sixth: “You shall not covet anything belonging to your neighbor” (Exod. XX, 3–17).

The apostle Paul proves that these were written on the second tablet when he says: “Honor your father and mother,” which is “the first commandment with a promise” (Eph. VI, 2). For how could it be first unless it began with it on the second tablet? He says “with a promise” because he immediately adds: “So that you may be long-lived upon the earth, and that it may be well with you.” This is the promise made to those who keep the commandments.

Thus you have both the commandments distinguished, their number completed, and an account of what and how many were written on each tablet.

### VIII.—Why did Moses, when descending from the mountain with the tablets, have a radiant and unbearable face?

Having received authority over sinners, he descended from the mountain with honor and a glorious face. For the Law was given against sinners. Since Moses had not sinned, he appeared glorious, so much so that sinners could not look upon him. It was shown in his case that sinners do not deserve to behold the glory of God.

After the image of the cast calf and the breaking of the tablets on which the Law had been given, Moses again ascended the mountain with tablets. When he descended with the Law he had received on them, his face had become glorious, so that the children of Israel could not look upon his face, nor could Aaron, because he too had sinned. But he spoke to them with a veil placed between them, so that they might remain unworthy of the glory of God as long as they continued in sins (Exod. XXXIV, 29 ff.).

Hence the Apostle says, “When he turns to God, the veil will be removed” (II Cor. III, 16), so that, washed by God’s gift, they might become worthy to contemplate the glory of God.

By the breaking of the tablets that he had previously received, he signified the Jewish people as rejected, because, devoted to sins, they were destined to become unworthy of God’s promise. The repetition of the Law signified that another people would arise, for whom the Law given on the mountain would be beneficial.

### IX.—If God made all things good and very good, why did he say to Noah, “Take with you into the ark those that are clean and unclean” (Gen. VII, 2), when something unclean cannot simply be called good?

Because words have several meanings, they give rise to questions. If they are referred to the matter at hand, however, there will be no question, because the things themselves disclose their meaning in due order.

Sometimes we call something “common” because it is undivided; sometimes we call something “common” because it is unclean. The word is used in two ways. Thus the apostle Peter says: “Nothing common or unclean has ever entered my mouth” (Acts X, 14). The apostle Paul says: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. XIV, 23); and elsewhere he says, “The Law is not from faith” (Gal. III, 12), yet the Law is not sin.

You see, therefore, that one and the same expression does not always signify the same thing. Accordingly, when something is called “unclean,” one must consider the reason for which it is called so. Sometimes it is called unclean by comparison with something better; sometimes the word refers to filthy actions, so that evil is understood.

No substance, therefore, is evil. Things that are called unclean in their substance are unclean only by comparison with extremely beautiful things. A dog is called unclean in comparison with a sheep; lead is unclean in comparison with gold; a raven in comparison with a peacock. Even though the members belong to one body, some are called honorable and others dishonorable, although they are known not to be evil.

Thus all things are good in their own nature, because they are useful.

### X.—When God says to Abraham concerning the children of Israel that they would leave the power of the Egyptians in the fourth generation (Gen. XV, 16), why does the Law say, “The children of Israel left the land of Egypt in the fifth generation”?

As far as the words are concerned, there appears to be a contradiction. But if the meaning is sought, it will be found not to be different. The Law speaks in such a way that it can be understood by the diligent and attentive, so that the reasoning of truth reveals itself not to the careless but to the concerned.

God certainly said, “In the fourth generation,” and Moses wrote, “In the fifth generation,” although Moses reported both statements, and it is impossible that he should deceive us, since such power worked through him. The meaning must therefore be investigated, because divine Scripture does not speak anything without purpose or carelessly.

The two men each mentioned one part. God signified four generations that were born in Egypt. Moses, adding to these the one from which they originated when they entered Egypt, said: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel left.” He embraced together the generation that entered Egypt and the four that were born there.

From Abraham to the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt there were eight generations. For they lived 215 years in Canaan from the promise made to Abraham, and 215 years in Egypt. These are the years included by the Apostle when he says to the Galatians: “After 430 years the Law was made” (Gal. III, 17).

These four generations, therefore, were born in Canaan: one in Isaac, another in Jacob, the third in Levi, and the fourth in Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. When the children of Israel entered Egypt, Kohath begot Amram; this was the first generation produced in Egypt. Amram begot Aaron, Moses, and Miriam; this was the second generation produced in Egypt. Aaron begot Eleazar and his brothers; this was the third generation. Eleazar begot Phinehas, the fourth generation.

These are the four generations produced in Egypt. Hence the Lord said to Abraham: “Your seed will be a sojourner, and they will oppress them in servitude; but I will free them, and in the fourth generation they will leave there.”

See whether it is not clear that God signified nothing other than what took place in Egypt. Moses, however, in order to include also the generation that entered Egypt with its father Jacob, from which these four originated, said: “In the fifth generation the children of Israel left the land of Egypt.”

### XI.—If the will of a righteous man is good, why did Isaac bless not Esau, whom he wished to bless, but Jacob, whom he did not wish to bless (Gen. XXVII, 27)?

[Note: [Col. 2223] Found in Alcuin, question 228 on Genesis.]

The will of a righteous person is good as far as his conscience is concerned; but as far as foreknowledge is concerned, it is free from things that may go wrong. God alone judges concerning the future.

Accordingly, Isaac, who was righteous as regards present human understanding, thought that his elder son was more worthy to be blessed. But God, who knows hidden things, showed that the younger deserved the blessing, so that in the blessing it might be shown to be a benefit not of humanity but of God. For the dignity of office, not human merit, is what God’s blessing follows.

Thus God said in Numbers to Moses and Aaron, the priests: “Place my name upon the children of Israel; I, the Lord, will bless them” (Num. VI, 27). The transmission of grace through the ministry of the one who gives the blessing therefore conveys it to human beings; the priest’s will can neither hinder nor help, but the merit belongs to the one asking for the blessing.

Let us consider from this how great is the dignity of the priestly order. Among other things, it is said of the wicked Caiaphas, the killer of the Savior: “He did not say this from himself; but, since he was high priest that year, he prophesied” (John XI, 51). This shows that the spirit of grace follows neither the person, whether worthy or unworthy, but the order of the transmitted office [Note: [Col. 2224] Manuscripts of the second class, “the order of the transmitted office.”]. Even if someone has good merit, he cannot bless unless he has been ordained to perform the office of ministry. It belongs to God to grant the effect of the blessing.

### XII.—Why did Abraham receive the sacrament of circumcision as the sign of his faith (Gen. XVII, 10)?

If you pay attention, you will see that what you think differs from reason is not inappropriate [Note: [Col. 2224] Alcuin, question 174 on Genesis.].

Believing that he would have a son in whom all nations would be blessed, and from whom holiness would arise, he received the sign on that part through which the generation of children both begins and ceases, so that it might be more holy.

But if this seems to some a disfigurement, let them observe that Abraham rejoiced in it and that his children were glorified by this testimony. Achior, one of the leaders of the Gentiles, seeing that there was such power in the God of Abraham that he enabled Holofernes, commander of the Assyrian army, whose power made the whole earth tremble, to be beheaded by the hand of a woman with his own sword, circumcised himself voluntarily, thinking that by this very act he had acquired dignity for himself (Judith XIV, 6).

Would anyone not display it if he lost an eye or some other limb for the name of Christ? Would he not present that very part to human faces so that he might appear glorious? To lose something temporarily for the sake of faith is to gain profit.

Thus Abraham, receiving the sign of his faith, was not disfigured but improved [Note: [Col. 2224] The remainder is missing in the manuscripts of the second class.].

Spiritually, however, this signified that the cloud of flesh had to be circumcised from human hearts through faith in Christ. Carnal error stood in the way, bringing darkness to human hearts so that they would not recognize the Creator. Since Christ was also promised to arise from Abraham’s seed, and since he would wipe away this darkness, Abraham was circumcised because he believed that he would have a son who would cut away this error.

Now consider whether it was not appropriate that he received such a sign on that particular part.

### XIII.—If God’s judgment is just, why were infants burned together with their parents in Sodom (Gen. XIX, 25)?

So that the exceedingly impious crime of the Sodomites might be recognized, their sin reached even to the death of their own children, lest any trace of them remain through their offspring. Was provision not made for them, so that they would not live long and follow the examples of their fathers? They are free from hell, having been killed in another’s cause [Note: [Col. 2224] Alcuin, more cautiously, question 183 on Genesis: “And so that they might suffer less, or not at all, having been killed in another’s cause.”].

The parents are guilty both for themselves and for their children, because their entire offspring was wiped out so that their deeds might be obliterated. Just as children rejoice in the goodness of their parents, since their parents’ distinction commends them, so they cannot complain about the death inflicted because of their parents’ evils. For just as they share in profit, so they must also share in loss.

Likewise in Egypt the children were punished for the offenses of their fathers, but so that this might contribute to their correction: since they had refused to believe and honor God, who was present in Moses, for other reasons, they might be terrified by this plague and confess with repentance, lest they experience this guilt more severely.

The death of the children, therefore, is the crime of the fathers. In whatever manner the children rendered their indebted spirit, they would become future accusers of their parents, because the parents could not overcome their unbelief even through the blood of their children.

The evils of the parents therefore came upon the children not for the future but for the present. Nor is it any small benefit not to be glorious and yet not to be guilty [Note: [Col. 2224] Alcuin states the point more clearly in question 183 on Genesis: “It is some kind of benefit not to be guilty, even though one is not glorious.”].

For if some, while placed at the end of life, strive with prayers to come to the true faith, so that, if they do not deserve a crown, they may at least deserve forgiveness, how could those with whom matters were arranged in such a way complain about this? There was neither anything from which they could ask forgiveness nor any greatness to which they could attain, since they had not labored at all.

Now compare the torment of a single moment with punishment lasting a long time. Consider also that many labor, and because they cannot persevere, not only lose the result of their labor but are also punished. Add that those born from evil people and brought up or associated among the most wicked can scarcely direct their minds toward following God’s discipline.

See, therefore, whether things were not handled more favorably for the children of the lost.

### XIV.—Why did God, who is proclaimed just, promise to repay the sins of fathers upon their children to the third and fourth generation (Exod. XX, 5)?

Anyone who doubts that God does or says anything unjust is insane. Therefore, if the Lord’s words are not suppressed, but everything relevant to the same question is set forth, what seems obscure will become clear, and what is considered not at all just will be judged pious.

For one who suppresses words relevant to a question is either ignorant or evasive, concerned more with slander than with instruction.

The Lord did indeed promise that he would repay the sins of fathers upon their children, but upon those who hate him—that is, those who, continuing in their fathers’ evils, serve idols just as their fathers did. The enemy of God is the one who assigns the honor of his name to a created thing.

Just as the children of the righteous, themselves righteous, ennoble their lineage within themselves, being exalted by both their fathers’ justice and their own, so the children of the most wicked, themselves most wicked, increase the evil, because they are children of evil people and have imitated their wickedness for the destruction of many.

God appears to have spoken with terror, but there is truth in it, and it is reasonable. Who does not hate an evil person and the child of an evil person by a double measure? And how does one not judge a good person and the child of a good person worthy of honor by a double reward?

He promised to repay the sins to the third and fourth generation so that, if after an evil father the son did not follow his father’s unbelief, but the grandson imitated his grandfather in evil, he might know that he would not escape the severity of the sentence. Or if the grandson, perhaps not following the grandfather but the father’s footsteps, loved God’s Testament, he would know that the sentence would reach his great-grandson if he were an imitator of his great-grandfather’s unbelief.

By revealing this law, God wished to deter impious fathers, so that, recognizing how much evil the practice of idolatry produced, they might be recalled to reverence for the Creator by affection for their children; or so that children, fearing to incur their fathers’ sins, might obey God’s Law.

But by adding to their wickedness, they began to interpret this differently, saying: “Our fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth were set on edge.” Thus, secure in their belief that the sins would be repaid to their children, they had no piety either of spirit or of flesh.

Therefore it is said to them: “The son shall not die for the father, nor the father for the son; but the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. XVIII, 2, 4). They were to learn that this would not be without punishment for them, but that the sins of fathers were repaid to children in such a way that those who followed their parents’ impiety and imitated evils that ought to have been erased would be punished more severely.

After showing what evil idolatry produces, God immediately added what good follows those who love him, saying: “And showing mercy to thousands of thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments” (Exod. XX, 6). Thus the good of a father is repaid not merely to a great-grandchild but to thousands of thousands.

For example, if someone from the seed of David loves God—and it is agreed that David lived long ago, more than a thousand years in the past—God’s mercy is added to him, so that in his need, with two causes supporting him, he may deserve to receive mercy: both because he himself worships God and because he descends from one who loved God.

In this too God’s clemency is praiseworthy: toward those who hate him, he repays to the third and fourth generation, but not to thousands of thousands. Thus, if evil has been carried into the fifth generation, it begins again there as from a new head, so that it may be counted from that point to the third and fourth generation.

But someone may say: It seems more just that more should be repaid to the originator than to the imitator. Vengeance is appropriately inflicted upon the originator; but when he says that more is repaid to the children, this is the punishment of the fathers. If you ask the reason, sinners become more guilty as the Law approaches, as happened with Lamech and after Lamech.

Some, however, think that the sins of fathers were repaid to their children when they were led into captivity on account of their fathers and remained there until the fourth generation. If this is true, he repaid the sins of fathers not only to those who hated him but also to those who loved his name, because Daniel was taken away, as were the three youths, Baruch, and Ezekiel, while Ezra was born there.

It is therefore plainly evident that what we said above fits the question under discussion.

### XV.—Since the Law praises the just person, and the one who possesses complete justice is truly just, how could Solomon say, “Do not be exceedingly just” (Eccl. VII, 17)?

Excessive justice incurs sin, while moderated justice makes people perfect. For one who is exceedingly just is not free from malice: if you respond to sinners on every occasion, there will be no lack of an occasion on which you sin.

God’s justice, accordingly, is moderated. At times he forgives sinners; at times he is angry; at times he does not repay them according to what they deserve. For he bears with them so that there may be people who make progress.

Since the Law cannot soften itself, it must be moderated by us so that it may benefit those who live under it. The just person, therefore, is not “exceedingly just” when he imitates God.

### XVI.—Why was the angel who wanted to kill Moses on the way appeased by the circumcision of the child (Exod. IV, 24)?

What Moses had done without deliberation, the angel’s threatening appearance corrected. Indeed, when he saw that what had been neglected through negligence was being carried out, he ceased from his anger. Thus Moses saw the angel hostile to him and ready to exact vengeance because the fault of a man of high standing is a grave sin. For the higher the person’s rank, the graver his offense. What is done, therefore, by a man of the highest position—especially by the leader of the people—is an especially bitter sin.

He was proceeding to the children of Israel, sent by the God of Abraham, but he was not carrying the sign of Abraham’s righteousness, in which he knew the Jews gloried. Thus he would either be called a tempter himself, or would appear not to have been sent by the same God who had chosen Abraham. While living in Midian, he had not circumcised his sons at all. He ought either not to have taken them with him to Egypt, since he was going there to lead the others out, or at least he ought to have taken them circumcised, for the reasons stated above.

Therefore Zipporah, Moses’ wife, understanding—as Scripture expresses it briefly—the reason why the angel appeared hostile to her husband, took a stone, circumcised her son, and the angel departed. The anger was appeased by the same means by which it had been aroused. For Scripture sometimes speaks briefly, intending what follows to be understood from the stated circumstances. So also, among other things, the Savior says to the Jews:

“Why do you also transgress the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition? For God said, ‘Honor your father and your mother’; and, ‘Whoever curses father or mother, let him die the death.’ But you say, ‘Whoever says to his father or mother, “Whatever gift I might give you will profit you,” and does not honor his father or his mother’” (Matt. 15:3–6).

Without doubt the Savior spoke by way of summary, so that the Jewish priests might be understood to have despised God’s Law while pursuing greed. In an impious conspiracy they advised their sons that, if they cursed their father or mother, whatever they offered as a gift to God would release the sentence pronounced against those who cursed. Thus, having been made secure, the sons disregarded their parents contrary to God’s command.

So too, when Moses saw that the angel was hostile to him, he understood the cause and showed his wife what had to be done so that the angel who sought to kill him would depart. This is implicit in the present account, just as is what we said above concerning the priests.

### XVII.—Why does the Law call those accursed who leave no offspring in Israel, while Isaiah says that this does no harm to eunuchs, because they cannot beget children (Exod. 23:26; Deut. 7:14; Isa. 56:3–5)?

Because the statement had begun to be understood differently from what had been intended, the prophet Isaiah later showed in what sense it had been spoken. Since this had been set down as a sentence arising from God’s displeasure—because those who abandoned God were struck by it, lest, taking wives, they should leave offspring—human error seized upon it in such a way that people thought themselves guilty before God if they either did not want wives or, having taken them, were unable to beget children, as though God sought nothing except offspring [Note: [Col. 2227] Manuscripts of the second class: “forbade”], just as they are reproved through the prophet Malachi. [Col. 2227]

Therefore Isaiah, to console those whom a mistaken interpretation had distressed, taught that it did no harm if someone either could not have children or did not wish to, provided that he kept God’s Law. The curse applied to those who, although they could and wished to have children, were sterile because of the divine judgment, so that they might not possess the fruit of God’s creation, which they despised. Thus, when they saw that they could not beget children or could not retain those born to them, they would recognize that this was the anger of an indignant God and, turning back, make satisfaction.

Indeed, holy men who desired children but did not obtain them thought that sins stood in the way and grieved, unaware that this was God’s providence, by which they were being reserved for them. Thus, through God’s providence, Hannah conceived and bore Samuel (1 Sam. 1:20), Elizabeth bore John (Luke 1:57), and the wife of Manoah bore Samson (Judg. 13:24).

The spiritual meaning in this matter is that those are considered accursed who have left no offspring who may see God—that is, who have not instructed a son, servant, or neighbor to teach the fear of God upon the earth.

### XVIII.—Why did Saul, when he sinned, ask that prayers be offered for him so that he might be forgiven, but was unable to obtain it, whereas David, when he sinned, made his request and received pardon (1 Sam. 15:24–26; 2 Sam. 12:13)?

God’s judgment must not be reconsidered. Human weakness and ignorance ought to be instructed by God’s judgment in what they do not understand, so that from God’s sentence they may recognize the truth and see that nothing else ought to have happened than what they see God doing—God whom they know to be no respecter of persons (Acts 10:34).

If David’s prayer was accepted and Saul’s rejected, we must not conclude that God did anything unjust. For, knowing the mind with which each spoke, he accepted the petition of the one whom he saw asking forgiveness with a contrite heart, but rejected the other because the pain of repentance had not touched his soul. God is more a hearer of the heart than of the voice. Hence it is said, “Man sees in the face, but God in the heart” (1 Sam. 16:7). We too are deceived because pretense in words and appearance misleads us; we cannot see what is in the heart.

Therefore we ought to follow God’s judgment, for he examines each person according to the heart, in which each person’s decision lies. We also find that the Savior did this. He did not accept a scribe who offered himself (Matt. 8:19), but he called Levi, sitting at the tax booth (Matt. 9:9; Luke 5:27), because the scribe’s heart did not follow his words, whereas Levi, though silent, held in his heart what the scribe held in his words. Jesus, who, as it is written, “knew what was in man” (John 2:25), chose Levi. [Note: [Col. 2227] The remainder is missing in manuscripts of the second class.]

Moreover, David did not wish someone else to humble himself on his behalf, as Saul did; he himself, with a contrite heart, suppliantly begged for forgiveness.

### XIX.—It must be asked whether Adam, when he was made, had an immortal or a mortal body.

God made man so that, as long as he did not sin, he would flourish in immortality, making himself responsible either for life or for death. By guarding himself from sin, he would rejoice through his own labor that he was immortal; but, having become negligent, he would blame himself because he had begun to be mortal.

As long as he remained in the law of the Creator, he was worthy to eat from the tree of life, so that he could not die. His body was not of such a kind that it seemed impossible for it to dissolve; rather, eating from the tree of life prevented the body’s corruption. Indeed, even after sin he could have remained indissoluble, if only he had been permitted to eat from the tree of life. For how could he have had an immortal body if it was sustained by food? [Col. 2228] An immortal being does not need food or drink. Food supplied strength, while the tree of life, as medicine, prevented all corruption. Thus it was for man like an impregnable wall.

### XX.—What does it mean that “man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. 77:25), when angels have no need of food, since they are simple by nature and vigorous in spiritual power?

The bread which he calls the bread of angels is manna. Manna is interpreted as “What is this?” For when the children of Israel saw something white falling upon the ground like coriander seed, they said to one another, “What is this?” (Exod. 16:15). In the Hebrew language this is said, *Man hu?*—“What is this?”

This bread or food, therefore, was not created according to the world’s order through the combination of the elements; rather, it came from above, provided by a spiritual arrangement. [Note: [Col. 2228] Manuscripts of the second class: “for the just.”] It was not actually kept in the heavenly places, since it was created by God’s power for the momentary nourishment of bodies. It was called the bread of angels because it was created by the power by which the angelic nature subsists and lives. For apart from God there is no life.

Because it is said to have come from heaven, therefore, it was called the bread of angels. In order to recall how great and how many God’s benefits toward man are, he spoke in such a way that they might give thanks to God when they recognized that he governs his servants with such care that, while they are still placed in the flesh, he supplies them, when necessary, with what angels live by.

Among other things the Apostle said, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4), because water flowed from the rock by Christ’s power (Exod. 17:6), and therefore the rock was called Christ. In the same way, because manna came from heaven by his power, it is called manna—that is, bread—so that what happened then might be understood as a figure of that which is now offered in the Church: so that human beings, that is, the Jews, might eat the bread of the Christian people, whom Scripture signified by angels.

And because grace is now greater than it was among the prophets, and freedom was given through Christ—for “where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom” (2 Cor. 3:17)—Christians, in comparison with those former times and graces, are called angels. The Jews, whom he called human beings, were filled with their bread, which is Christ. For Christ belongs especially to those to whom he has been revealed and who are judged worthy to be called by this name.

The question stated above can therefore be understood in two ways: the bread may be called the bread of the heavenly angels, and it may also be called the bread of Christians, according to what has been said.

### XXI.—What does it mean that God made man “in his image and likeness” (Gen. 1:27), and is woman also the image of God?

Man was made in the image of God in this respect: one made one, so that just as all things are from one God, so the whole human race is from one man. The likeness consists in this: just as the Son is from the Father, so woman is from man, so that the authority of one origin might be preserved.

But the Son was born from God the Father ineffably and incomprehensibly; woman, on the other hand, was made bodily from man, as we read (Gen. 2:21–22), so that through her birth might arise. The Son of God was born so that creation might come into being through him. In this respect, therefore, the cases differ. For God was born from God, whereas woman came from man, because in the former there is simplicity, and from the simple only the simple could be born: spirit from Spirit, God from God.

Thus man is the image of God. For it is written, “God made man; in the image of God he made him.” Hence the Apostle also says, “A man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but woman,” he says, “ought to veil her head” (1 Cor. 11:7, 6). Why? Because she is not the image of God. Hence the Apostle says again, “I do not permit a woman to teach or to have dominion over a man” (1 Tim. 2:12).

### XXII.—What does it mean when Solomon says, “Justify your soul before your death,” while in the Psalm it says, “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Eccli. 14:17; Ps. 142:2)?

He justifies his soul before death who, through hope of the future life, obtains faith so that he may not die impious. [Col. 2229] But Solomon speaks of one who lives under the Law and does not conduct himself justly. If such a person corrects his mind so that he walks in the ways of righteousness, he justifies his soul before death.

Solomon gave this counsel with the future judgment in view, so that no one, careless about himself, might die in sins. David, however, spoke of the perfection of righteousness, because no one will be justified before God, so as to be worthy of the promise, unless he dies in righteousness. For as long as he lives, he does not yet possess the full merit of what is to come. Hence the Savior says, “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22; 24:13).

### XXIII.—Are souls derived by generation, as bodies are?

I consider it disgraceful to say that souls are generated along with bodies, so that soul is born from soul, which is not even fitting for the soul itself. Alternatively, if each of the heavenly powers was made individually and the others were born from them, it might seem credible that the other souls were born from Adam’s one soul. But this is not fitting, because it was possible for God alone to generate what is simple; this was not granted to others.

This matter is so mysterious in the case of the Savior that it is considered incredible not only by pagans and Jews but even by those who call themselves Christians. For the Photinians and Arians reject this belief and do not believe that God generated.
