If, at the time when the body is conceived, the soul too is generated from soul, we read that a rib was taken from Adam, but not that a soul was born from soul. If the rib had a soul with it, then that soul was not born but removed as a part. Yet this also is not written.

For among other things the prophet Zechariah says, “Who formed the soul of man within him” (Zech. 12:1). Isaiah, agreeing with him, says, “Thus says the Lord God who made you and formed you in the womb” (Isa. 44:2). If the soul is formed in the womb, then it is attributed to a body already formed. When it fills all the body’s members, it is said to have been formed in the body.

Just as water, although without shape, appears shaped when poured into a vessel, so the soul, although incorporeal and simple by nature, is, as it were, formed in the body, giving life to its individual members.

Moses handed down the matter more plainly, saying, “If anyone strikes a woman who is pregnant and she miscarries: if the fetus is formed, he shall give life for life; but if it is unformed, he shall be fined money” (Exod. 21:22). Thus he showed that the soul is not present before formation.

Therefore, if the soul is given to a body already formed, it is not born at the conception of the body through derivation with the seed. For if both seed and soul exist from soul, many souls perish each day when the seed, through some kind of discharge, does not advance to birth.

But if we look more closely, we shall see what we ought to follow. Let us contemplate Adam’s creation. In Adam an example was given, so that from him it might be understood that the already formed body received a soul. For God could have mixed the soul into the clay of the earth and thus formed the body. But it was formed according to reason, because first the house had to be joined together and then the inhabitant introduced.

Since the soul is spirit, it certainly cannot dwell in what is dry; therefore it is carried in the blood. When the body’s features have not yet been joined together, where will the soul be? Does it wander outside until it is put in, when reason teaches that it is given in order to animate the body, not to wander idly?

But let those who think otherwise say from what it is given: from the male or from the female? [Note: [Col. 2229] Manuscripts of the second class: “Some think that it is given from the male, others from the female.”]

If from the female, this does not fit, because the example says something else. They propose that the soul was given from the man along with the rib. We have shown that this is weakened by many arguments. Hence it might perhaps seem to be given from the woman, especially because of the Savior, whom we know to have been born from a woman by the Holy Spirit, without bodily union.

But if they think this, they attribute more to women: they transfer the authority of the man to the woman. For when they say that the origin of both body and soul is from the man, they reverse themselves and say that what is superior—the soul—is from the woman, while what is inferior—the body—is from the male, although it is clear that the order of the example handed down by God cannot be changed. [Col. 2230]

### XXIV.—What does it mean that, although man and woman are one flesh, man is the image of God and woman is not?

Man and woman are indeed of one substance, both in soul and in flesh. But man is greater in rank because woman is from him, as the Apostle says, “The head of woman is man” (Eph. 5:25; 1 Cor. 11:3). The cause, not the substance, made man greater. For even within one body there are larger and smaller members, not by nature but by arrangement. [Note: [Col. 2230] Manuscripts of the second class: “by order.”]

### XXV.—Why, after prophesying, did Joseph adjure the children of Israel to carry his ashes out of Egypt when they were liberated by God (Gen. 50:24)?

It is clearly not without purpose that Joseph gave this command to the children of Israel. For one who could prophesy should not be thought to have spoken without foresight.

Since he was especially devoted to the worship of God the Creator, and knew that the Egyptians honored him because of the administration by which he governed Egypt during its great famine, he requested after his death that the error be removed, being certain that the common people were more likely to venerate the dead as gods than the living, lest the honor due to the Creator be paid to him.

Thus he showed himself free from the vain superstition of the Egyptians when he commanded that his ashes be carried away, so that this would not contribute to an insult against God.

We find that the Apostles followed this example. When Paul and Barnabas saw that people wished to sacrifice to them, knowing that this was hateful to God, they tore their garments and said, “What are you doing? We are human beings like you,” and so restrained the crowds (Acts 14:10–17).

### XXVI.—It must be asked whether Elisha obtained what he is said to have requested harshly from Elijah (2 Kings 2:10).

Elisha, eager to perform mighty deeds and attracted by his teacher’s example, was given the opportunity to ask for whatever he wished. Greedy for what was good, he asked that he might have twice as much spirit as his teacher possessed.

The man of God, Elijah, said to him, “You have asked for a hard thing.” In his eagerness he did not consider that a disciple is not above his teacher (Matt. 10:24). Yet Elijah, knowing that he had not asked this out of ambition for present glory, answered, “Nevertheless, if you see me when I am taken from you, it shall be so for you.”

This meaning must be weighed carefully. Although he had spoken with some indignation, saying, “You have asked for a hard thing,” he added, “If you nevertheless see me when I am taken away, it shall be so for you”; nor did he seem to have denied the request. He showed that it would happen to him as was fitting, not as he himself had requested.

Scripture often wishes much to be understood implicitly, so that the meaning gathered from its words may not be contrary to religious reason. A hard request ought certainly also to have forfeited the merit; but because he eagerly sought what was good, God, who knows what ought to be given to each person, did not allow him to be deprived of the good things due to his merits.

Let us therefore see whether Elijah’s merit would permit Elisha to deserve a double gift. For the Holy Spirit said through Zechariah what merit John would possess: “He will come,” it says, “in the spirit and power of Elijah” (Luke 1:17). Thus it shows John to be Elijah’s equal. The Lord also says, “No one has arisen among those born of women greater than John the Baptist” (Matt. 11:11). He did not say, “He is greater than everyone,” but, “No one is greater than he”: that is, he has an equal, but no greater.

Elijah, therefore, is his equal, certainly inferior to no one. How, then, is Elisha greater than Elijah, when John, than whom no one is greater, is Elijah’s equal?

Moreover, when Elisha came to the crossing of the waters, he did not receive honor from them so that he could cross until he invoked the God of Elijah (2 Kings 2:14). By this it seemed that the hard request had been rebuked, since he was heard only in the name of Elijah, lest he be thought to have received what he had harshly requested, as though the allotment of the spirit granted to Elijah according to the merit of his time were insufficient.

### XXVII.—Did the Pythoness raise Samuel, and was he seen by her and speak to Saul, as the account relates in the Book of Kings (1 Sam. 28:7–20)?

[Col. 2231] I consider it an unworthy deed to assent to the account according to its words. For how could a man both holy by birth and righteous in the deeds of his life be summoned by magical art? Or, if he was not summoned, did he consent? To believe either of these things about a righteous man is absurd.

If he was brought there unwillingly, his righteousness provides no protection; but if he came willingly, he lost the spiritual merit that he had acquired while living in the flesh. This is extremely absurd, because one who departs from this life righteous remains righteous.

Moreover, this is a deception of Satan, by which, in order to deceive as many as possible, he pretends that even good people are in his power. The Apostle says, among other things, “Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light” (2 Cor. 11:14).

In order to produce an error in which he himself would also glory, he disguised himself in the appearance and name of a righteous man, so that he might falsely claim that the hope preached to God’s worshipers was of no benefit, when he pretended that the righteous who departed this life were in his power.

Some are deceived by the fact that he did not lie about Saul’s death and that of his sons, as though it were a great thing for the devil to foresee the body’s end before its day, when certain signs often appear in those who are about to die, especially when God’s protection seems to have been removed from them.

How much more could the devil foresee this, of whom the prophetic oracles testify that he was exalted by angelic majesty, and concerning whose greatness the Apostle says, “Do you not know the depths of Satan?” (2 Cor. 2:11). What is surprising, then, if he could foresee an imminent death, since this is the means by which he deceives and seeks to have himself worshiped in God’s place?

Saul had been driven to such madness and dullness that he fled to the Pythoness. Corrupted by the cause of his sin, he resorted to the very things he had condemned.

But if someone thinks that, for the sake of the historical account and the things expressed in words, nothing should be omitted lest the historical narrative be pointless, he will do well—provided that he does not drag this matter into the realm of truth, but treats it as a matter of appearance and understanding.

For Saul, having become rejected, could not possess a sound understanding. The historian described Saul’s mind and Samuel’s appearance, expressing what was said and seen while leaving aside whether these things were true or false.

What does he say? When Saul heard in what appearance the figure had been raised, “he understood,” he says, “that this was Samuel.” He reported what Saul understood; and because Saul did not understand correctly, he worshiped someone other than God, contrary to Scripture. Thinking it was Samuel, he worshiped the devil, so that Satan might obtain the fruit of his deception. For this is what he strives for: to be worshiped as God.

If Samuel had truly appeared to him, surely the righteous man would not have permitted himself to be worshiped, since he had taught that God alone must be worshiped. And how could the man of God, who was with Abraham in repose, say to a man of destruction, worthy of the fire of Gehenna, “Tomorrow you will be with me”?

Through these two details the imprudent Satan exposed the subtlety of his deception: he allowed himself to be worshiped under another’s appearance and in Samuel’s name, contrary to the Law; and he falsely claimed that a man weighed down by sins would be with the most righteous Samuel, although there is a great difference between sinners and the righteous.

The statement may seem true if Samuel’s name is left out, because Saul was to be with the devil. He passed over to the one whom he worshiped. The devil, always hiding beneath a veil, reveals himself when he fabricates things that are inconsistent with the persons through whom he tries to deceive.

### XXVIII.—What must be said in response to those who claim that this world has moved naturally from eternity and is subject neither to a beginning nor to destruction?

It is implausible and impossible to say that the world has existed from eternity and owes subjection to no one. We see it existing with such a diversity of bodies, although nothing divine or eternal can be other than simple, in which no diversity is visible but only unity.

It does not even preserve the regular cycles of the seasons, so that it is not merely varied in time or composed of contrary substances, but is also variable within the very cycles of time. An eternal thing rejects diversity and cannot be apprehended by touch or sight, since it is incorporeal. This world, however, is subject to change: water resists fire, and if fire becomes stronger it overcomes water; earth, being dry and cold by nature, suffers burning, as a bodily thing does.

It is therefore inappropriate to call eternal a world which, when we see it [Col. 2232] subject to change and weakened by old age through the ages, we believe will also come to an end. What should be thought of a person who considers the world eternal?

Certainly man began in the world. Without man, then, for whose benefit did the world’s annual fertility operate? Or did it generate without any providence? And how could an eternal thing generate corruptible and mortal things, when from what is eternal something eternal ought to exist?

That which is visible, perceptible, and tangible—by what audacity is it called eternal? And that which is governed by the cycles of time, so that the seasons themselves sometimes fail to perform their functions—how can it be called eternal? Eternity is neither corrupted nor changed.

### XXIX.—Why was circumcision commanded on the eighth day (Gen. 17:12)?

It was commanded that circumcision take place on the eighth day after birth because, following the number and cycle of the seven days, that day is found again to be the first, as it were, after the Sabbath. Thus it is no longer regarded as the eighth day but as the first.

Because future salvation through Christ had been predestined for the first day—the day called the Lord’s Day because the Lord rose on it—which comes after the Sabbath, the figure of this salvation was therefore given in circumcision, so that the future renewal might be recognized as though in the law of circumcision.

And because human beings were to be saved through faith, which was confirmed on the first day by the Lord’s resurrection, the figure of this was given in circumcision on the first day, which would also be a sign of Abraham’s faith.

The whole matter therefore coheres: the sign of the faith previously marked out on the first day was a figure of the future faith established on the first day.

### XXX.—In Proverbs it says, “The righteous is his own accuser at the beginning of his speech” (Prov. 18:17). How can he be righteous if he is a sinner?

Every truth is righteousness. Since he confesses what is the case, he is righteous, for he speaks the truth. But sinners who defend their offenses cannot be justified. Hence such a person is rightly called righteous, because, declaring his sin, he asks that it be forgiven him, imploring God’s mercy.

For he knows that it is said in the Law, “Confess your sins, so that you may be justified” (Isa. 43:26). What does it mean to confess “at the beginning of his speech” except to confess without compulsion, voluntarily?

For who, even while fearing God, is without sin, when offenses are mixed even into thought and we sometimes sin unwillingly? Yet this may also be said or understood of the one called a catechumen, who approaches the faith so that he may be justified. When he asks to be changed, he plainly confesses himself to be a sinner so that he may be justified.

### XXXI.—Did a serpent by nature speak with the woman, or did the serpent called the devil seduce her by an act of cunning [Note: [Col. 2232] Perhaps, “by craft.”] (Gen. 3:1)?

As far as the historical account is concerned, the serpent is said to have been an animal by nature, more cunning than the other beasts that the Lord God had made upon the earth. Indeed, God also pronounced judgment upon the serpent.

For what is surprising if the devil was more intelligent than the beasts, of whom the Apostle says, among other things, “Do you not know the depths of Satan?” (2 Cor. 2:11)?

The serpent was so truly an animal by nature that it was said to it, “Upon your breast and belly you shall crawl, and you shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Gen. 3:14). These things are far removed from the nature of Satan, because he is neither corporeal nor mortal.

And if the sentence is examined more closely, it will appear that the judgment pronounced did not harm the serpent. Rather, it was commanded to remain in the condition in which it had been made. Since it had become Satan’s servant for subjugating man, to whom God had subjected everything, God therefore, through the subjection by which he had subjected all things to man, restrained the serpent’s pride, through which it had begun to be an instrument of arrogance.

For man appeared to have been made subject to the serpent, through whom, after receiving counsel, he despised the law that had been given.

That serpents are prudent is confirmed by the Lord in the Gospel, when he says, “Be shrewd as serpents” (Matt. 10:16). Since it is therefore clear that the serpent truly spoke with Eve, it remains to determine whether it could have been so prudent and cunning as to deceive her by trickery.

Although it was more prudent than the other beasts, it was not more prudent than human beings, since no animal is rational except man. Therefore it was impossible for the serpent to devise this subtlety. Although it is called prudent, it is not prudent beyond its nature; it does not deliberate, devise, or form a plan.

There is therefore no doubt that it was the devil who, through the serpent, circumvented the woman. By mingling himself with the serpent, he acted through it as through an instrument, so that the woman, knowing the serpent to be cunning, would not perceive the trickery of the hidden devil.

Thus, although the sentence was given bodily, it fell spiritually upon Satan, because the sentence holds the guilty party. The sentence was not given by a human being, who might perhaps have destroyed an innocent person through error or ill will, but by God, who certainly cannot be deceived, so that his sentence might hold only the one who was guilty.

Since Satan is invisible but carried out his deception bodily, the sentence appears to have been given bodily, so that it might hold spiritually the one whose deed brought about the sentence.

For the most shameless Satan, cast from the most sacred seats of heaven, is hurled about upon the earth, always groaning.

But someone might ask, “In what language, do you suppose, did the serpent speak to the woman?” In the mouth of the serpent, certainly. If today there are people who understand the barking of dogs, the howling of wolves, the trumpeting of elephants, and the crowing of roosters, why could the woman, still inexperienced, not have known and understood the hissing of serpents, when we know that many people distinguish the voices of birds? [Note: [Col. 2233] The remainder is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

It is also established that the devil uses the tongue of whatever creature’s body he has entered; otherwise he could not have deceived the woman. Thus he spoke through the serpent, with the serpent’s mouth.

### XXXII.—We read in Solomon, “The rich and the poor meet one another; the Lord made them both” (Prov. 22:2). How, then, is there no partiality with God?

Let this impious assertion be far from the minds of the faithful. Scripture, in order not to teach that the poor should be despised and the rich honored, shows that God is the maker of both—not with respect to poverty and riches, but with respect to what they are.

Although they differ from one another in possessions, they do not differ in the substance of their nature. The fact that certain opportunities of increase make some prosperous in wealth and others unfortunate in poverty does not mean that those whom God has not humbled should be despised, or that those to whom the truth has given no testimony should be honored.

Those who corrupt morals and commit sacrilege against God’s Law are certainly to be despised; those who love God and cultivate discipline are to be honored. Those are considered rich with God who possess good conduct, and the more contemptible they are in the world, the more honorable they are in heaven.

Those who have received the benefit of the present age in increasing their possessions, if they recognize themselves and understand God’s will—God who gave the earth to all and commands his sun to rise for everyone and pours down impartial rains (Matt. 5:45)—should minister to those whom the injustice of the age, chance circumstances, or need deprives of what God gave to all. By fulfilling God’s will, they may be rich not only in this world but also in heaven, lest the riches of a brief time exclude eternal riches.

But those whom people think should be despised because of poverty, if they contemplate God’s future judgment, will always be rich there, where the rich of this age will be in need, repenting that they were not poor.

### XXXIII.—Solomon says, “The years of the wicked will be shortened” (Prov. 10:27). How, then, do we see some wicked people living to an old age?

It would indeed have been fitting for all wicked people not only to be deprived more quickly of this light, but also not to enjoy life for a single moment, since, forgetting their Creator, they attribute the authority of the whole of life to creation.

But Scripture addresses those wicked people who, while living under God’s Law, were more inclined toward idols. They are worse than other wicked people: although they know God, they despise him and obey his servants.

The Apostle proves that this was said about such people when he says, “We know that [Col. 2234] whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are under the Law” (Rom. 3:19). Gentiles, however, are not counted among the living.

### XXXIV.—How can the same Solomon say, “God did not make death,” when elsewhere he says, “Good and evil, life and death, poverty and honor are from God” (Wis. 1:13; Eccli. 11:14)?

No one doubts that all good things are from God. But the evils he mentioned are evils only in the sense that punishment is inflicted upon us. For although punishment is imposed justly, it nevertheless appears evil to the person who suffers it.

Thus God also speaks through the prophet to sinners, saying, “I will bring evils upon you”—that is, “I will punish you.”

Life and death are from God in this sense: he gave a law that promises life to those who keep it, but death to those who despise it—the death called the second death. When he assigns to each person what he deserves, it comes from him, whether acquittal unto life or guilt unto death.

He is therefore not the inventor of death but its judge, because sin is the author of death. How could God have made death, when he does not know how to sin? Yet when he repays sins, death is said to be from him, although it does not come from him but from the one who sinned.

By the same reasoning, poverty and riches are from God. Some people, possessing the fear of God, despise luxury, shun a wasteful life, and do not turn their eyes away from the needy and poor. Such people increase their good things. For it is written in Proverbs, “Discipline removes poverty and dishonor” (Prov. 13:18).

But those who do not have the fear of God, living more carelessly and despising the needy, will, as it is written, be in poverty. They are not only negligent and improvident concerning themselves but also despisers of the law that was given.

In this way God makes the poor and the rich: when violation of the law produces poverty, it is said to be made by God, the author of the law; and when some people preserve the discipline of the law through fear, they become rich through God, the author of the law.

### XXXV.—For what reason does David call Saul, after God had departed from him, “the Lord’s anointed,” and show him honor (1 Sam. 26:16, 18 ff.)?

David, aware that a divine ordinance belongs to the office of royal rank, therefore honors Saul, who was still established in that same ordinance, lest he seem to do injury to God, who decreed honor for such ranks. For the king bears the image of God, just as the bishop bears that of Christ. Therefore, so long as he remains in that ordinance, he is to be honored, if not for his own sake, then for the sake of the office. Hence the Apostle says, “Be subject to the higher authorities. There is no authority except from God; and those that exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. 13:1). This is why we honor even a Gentile placed in authority, although he himself may be unworthy and, while holding God’s order, give thanks to the devil. Authority demands this, because it deserves honor.

For this reason the dream of the coming famine was revealed to Pharaoh (Gen. 41:1–37), and, while others stood with Nebuchadnezzar, he alone saw the Son of God in the furnace of fire (Dan. 3:92)—not, certainly, on account of his own merit, since he wished to be worshiped in an idol, but on account of the dignity of royal office.

### XXXVI.—If the soul that sins shall itself die, how is it that Achar son of Charmi sinned, and thirty men [Note: [Col. 2234] Manuscripts of the second class read, “thirty-six men.” And this is more accurate. M.] were killed because of him (Josh. 7:24, 5)?

Scripture spoke in a different sense from the one proposed. For it did not speak of that death which is common to all, but of the one called the second death. This receives sinners. As for those who died in the battle, Achar’s sin was not repaid to them; rather, it harmed them by preventing them from prevailing over their enemies with divine protection. They were not weakened because of Achar, but, being deprived of God’s help, they were killed because they were unable to fight valiantly. They were few against many, and so they are known to have been defeated.

There is therefore no injustice in God’s will. He has the power to help if he wishes: if he is present, he is merciful; if he does not wish to help, he is just. In such matters he is not a debtor who can be held liable. This is why Jesus son of Nave, having been saddened, tore his garments (ibid. 6), [Col. 2235] understanding that God had withdrawn his help for a reason.

[Note: [Col. 2235] The same question, from manuscripts of the second class, was hitherto the fourteenth among those appearing after the published books of the Old Testament.] Charmi indeed sinned and died by stoning. But the thirty-six men who died in the battle were not, strictly speaking, struck down by God; they were simply not helped. Because of their own weakness, they were killed when they could not fight valiantly. Charmi therefore brought this about or caused the harm, because those who ought to have been helped were neglected by God. Hence Jesus son of Nave was saddened and tore his garments, because he understood that God had withdrawn his help in that place.

### XXXVII.—How is it that death, having been sent, came upon Jacob in Israel, when Jacob himself is said to have been called Israel (Isa. 9:8, according to the Septuagint)?

He gave one people two names, so that their merits might be understood from the names. For the one who was surnamed Israel had previously been called Jacob. While wrestling with the Savior, he understood that the one whom he saw in bodily form was God; therefore he was called “a man seeing God” (Gen. 32:24–28).

The people whom he calls Jacob therefore signifies here and in this matter the carnal people, just as names are given to children by their parents. But these people—that is, the Jews—because of their evil works were not called Israelites, since they sacrificed to calves and groves in Samaria, through the zeal and command of King Jeroboam. That people, however, which offered sacrifices in Jerusalem in the Lord’s temple through God’s priests, was called Israel.

Samaria, then, because of its impiety, was handed over to captivity and death; but Jerusalem was preserved because it had kings who loved God. When Jerusalem itself followed Samaria’s impiety, however, the sentence pronounced against Samaria also overtook it. Thus it was said, “God sent death upon Jacob,” that is, upon the people of Samaria, who lived carnally, as we have said above; “and it came upon Israel,” that is, upon the people of Jerusalem, because it followed idolatry and imitated Samaria, so that it too might be led into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, just as Samaria was by Salmanasar, king of the Assyrians.

The meaning is clear: a sentence pronounced against the wicked also overtakes the good when they cease to be righteous. Death sent upon Jacob, as has been shown above, reached Israel—not by passing over Samaria, but because, when the cause for which it had been sent to Samaria was found in Jerusalem, it came there also to the place where the same matter existed. For vengeance follows the cause and does not distinguish persons.

[Note: [Col. 2235] Ibid. The thirteenth question.] He gave one people two names. For the one who was first called Jacob later received the name Israel when he wrestled with the Son of God and saw him through understanding, “a man seeing God.” The people whom he calls Jacob is therefore understood in this place and in this matter not to see God, but is regarded as carnal, because of its good works [Note: [Col. 2235] Perhaps, “not good.”]: so that, just as Jacob was not called an Israelite before he saw God Christ, so these, while they are called Jacob as a people, may be designated as not seeing God.

By Israel, however, he calls the people who, having been made worthy through the works of God, are considered fit to see God. Thus the people of Jacob, because it relied on carnal assistance and despaired of God’s help—for it loved idols—was handed over to death when the king of the Assyrians was stirred up against it.

This is understood to have been said about Samaria by the prophet Isaiah. It had first done evil before God, establishing calves for sacrifice and introducing new priesthoods through Jeroboam. Death was therefore sent against them. They were the first to be captured and deported by Salmanasar, king of the Assyrians, as an example to the people of Judah and Benjamin and Levi—the two tribes and the half-tribe that remained in Jerusalem under Rehoboam, son of Solomon, and that sacrificed in the Lord’s temple through the Lord’s priests.

These, then, he calls the people of Israel because of the tribe of Judah and Levi. Although they too, frightened by Samaria’s example, ought to have acted rightly, they acted wickedly by serving idols. Nevertheless, there were some kings in Jerusalem who, after Solomon and his son Rehoboam had departed, followed the way of David and walked rightly before God. All the kings of Samaria, however, acted wickedly before the Lord until their deportation. Hence they were designated by a carnal name.

And because Jerusalem followed their impiety, it too was handed over into captivity to Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. This is what it means that death was sent upon Jacob and came upon Israel. It was sent to Samaria; but when the cause for which it had been sent to Samaria was found in Jerusalem, it came there as well, to the place in which the same matter existed. Vengeance does not follow the place, but the cause.

### XXXVIII.—If horse and mule have no understanding, how much more is the earth a thing without sense? How, then, can the earth be said to bless the Lord (Ps. 31:9; Dan. 3:74)?

This is not to be understood according to the sound of the words. For a work, although mute, is said to cry out the praise of its Creator: it urges those who behold it to bless its maker, just as every well-constructed vessel praises its craftsman.

For we read in the Psalms, “Will dust give thanks to you, or will it declare your truth?” (Ps. 29:10). Thus, in every insensible substance, it is not the will—which certainly does not exist—but the works that bless their author.

If, however, you wish to understand this spiritually, take the earth as signifying the human being, according to the prophet’s statement: “Remember, Lord, that we are earth” (Ps. 102:14). The works of creation urge him to burst forth in praise of his Creator.

[Note: [Col. 2236] The same question, from manuscripts of the second class, is the sixteenth among those appearing after the published books of the Old Testament.] “Let the earth bless the Lord,” he says; that is, “let it praise and confess your truth.” How, then, does he say in the Psalms, “Will dust give thanks to you, or will it declare your truth?” This is not to be understood as it is read and as the words sound. For the earth has no understanding by which it can give thanks to its Creator.

If you understand this spiritually, however, take the earth as signifying the human being, according to the prophet’s statement, “Remember, Lord, that we are earth.” The works of the created world exhort that person to burst forth in praise of his Creator, so that he may attain confession of his truth. Though it is silent, the earth is said to cry out the praise of its Creator, whose work it is. This, then, is why the earth is said in the account of creation to bless God.

### XXXIX.—What does Solomon mean when he says, “There is hope in the darkness. A living dog is better than a dead lion” (Eccl. 9:4)?

“Darkness” signifies paganism and ignorance. He wishes it to be understood that there is greater hope in the pagan people than in the apostate, by what he adds: “A living dog is better than a dead lion.” For just as the lion is stronger than all wild animals, so Christianity is stronger than all sects. If anyone falls away from it, he loses salvation, so that he becomes worse than a pagan. A pagan may believe and acquire the salvation that the apostate has lost. But if he does not believe, the apostate is still worse, because it is worse to have lost salvation than never to have possessed it.

The Savior shows that the dog signifies the pagan when he says, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs” (Matt. 15:26).

[Note: [Col. 2236] Ibid. The nineteenth question.] “Darkness” signifies ignorance and paganism, because there is hope rather in the pagan than in the apostate. The latter he calls “a dead lion,” that is, a Christian apostate: for as long as he remained in the faith, he was a lion; but once he withdrew, he is called dead.

The dog, however, he calls the pagan, in whom there is hope that he may believe. As long as he lives, he is held in hope; but the other’s hope will perish. The Savior shows that the dog signifies the pagan when he says, “It is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

### XL.—What does the prophet mean when he says, “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband” (Isa. 54:1)?

Since the children of earthly Jerusalem apostatized from God, joy cannot be attributed to her, but rather sorrow. Therefore, as a reproach to this Jerusalem, the prophet says that the Jerusalem above ought to rejoice, the one whom the Apostle calls “our mother” (Gal. 4:26). For without groaning or labor pains she has many more children than this Jerusalem, which gives birth carnally and with tears to the Jews, while the other gives birth spiritually, through faith, to Christians.

He calls her “deserted” because she is the life that the first Adam abandoned and followed death. When human beings are regenerated, they return to the life they had abandoned. This life is Christ, because he himself says, “I am the life” (John 14:6). God the Father is also life, because the Lord says, “Just as the Father has life, so he has given the Son to have life” (John 5:26). Without doubt the Holy Spirit is also life, as the Lord says, “He will receive from what is mine” (John 16:15). Whoever receives from life is life. Thus the three are one life.

This is the life through faith in which we are regenerated. It is our mother, as we read in Genesis, since she—that is, Life—is “the mother of all the living” (Gen. 3:20). Who are those who live except those who believe?

[Note: [Col. 2237] The same question, from manuscripts of the second class and among those appearing after the published books of the Old Testament.] We understand two mothers in this passage, a heavenly and an earthly one: that is, the Jerusalem that is free, of which the Apostle says, “She is our mother,” and this Jerusalem, which he says is enslaved with her children, that is, the Jews.

The prophet, proclaiming the Lord’s advent and calling upon the time full of grace with an exultant voice, urges the heavenly Jerusalem to rejoice. She is called deserted because she had no inhabitants—children generated through faith. The time had come for her to have the children long ago foretold, and many more than this Jerusalem had had, because the Christians surpassed the number of the Jews.

She is therefore called barren because she is a virgin who does not generate a son through intercourse and embrace, but spiritually through faith alone. Hence she is not said to travail, since the woman who travails suffers pains. This one cries out in joy at the salvation of humanity.

Earthly Jerusalem is said to have had a husband because she generated carnally. The city is signified as a mother, just as that heavenly dwelling to which we are called is called our mother.

### XLI.—Is the Spirit who was borne over the waters to be understood as the Holy Spirit, since it is said, “The Spirit of God was borne over the waters” (Gen. 1:2)?

If it seems that he has erred in this interpretation, what he said must not be accepted. Some therefore suppose that this is the Holy Spirit because he is read to be the Spirit of God. But the assertion is weak and empty. Not only does the order of the passage reject it and reason oppose it, but the words themselves prove inadequate to establish this interpretation.

For in the Law we frequently find these words signifying something else. Among other things, the Lord God says, “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” And in what follows: “But I will destroy,” he says, “all things, from man to beast” (Gen. 6:3, 7). Since he was about to bring the Flood upon the earth, can the Holy Spirit be understood here? Is he not speaking about souls? For not only are our souls called spirits, but those of animals as well. Thus it is written, “And all flesh in which there was the spirit of life died in the water” (Gen. 7:22).

And in the prophet Ezekiel it is said, when God promises the restoration of human beings: “Thus says the Lord God to these bones: I will stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live” (Ezek. 37:5). Was he speaking of the Holy Spirit and not of the soul?

All heavenly beings are indeed spirits, but they differ from one another. God is spirit (John 4:24; 2 Cor. 3:17), but in a very different way. Every spirit is therefore God’s; yet not every spirit is God, except the Spirit who is from him. The indication of this is that he is called holy.

Human beings too are called children of God, and Christ is called the Son of God; but there is a distinction, because he is the true Son, while they are adopted. So also there is a distinction among the spirits of God. The Holy Spirit is from God and consubstantial with him; the other spirits are called God’s, but they are creatures.

Nor is it consistent with the order of things to understand the Holy Spirit as borne over the waters, since reason teaches that a spiritual creature was over the waters, and that above it there was another, more excellent creature, because “one creature differs from another in glory” (1 Cor. 15:41). Whatever approaches near the dwelling of God has more glorious ministries.

Hence the angel Raphael says, among other things, “I am one of the seven holy angels who stand and move about before the majesty of God” (Tob. 12:15).

[Note: [Col. 2238] The same question, from manuscripts of the second class and among those appearing after the published books of the Old Testament, the second.] If some suppose that this is the Holy Spirit because he is read to be God’s spirit, the assertion is weak and empty. Not only does the order of the passage reject it and reason oppose it, but the words themselves prove inadequate to establish this interpretation.

For these words frequently signify something else in the Law. The Lord God says, “My spirit shall not remain in these men, because they are flesh.” And in what follows: “But I will destroy all things, from man to beast.” He says this because he was going to bring the Flood upon the earth. The Holy Spirit can never be understood here. He spoke about souls. For not only are our souls called spirits, but those of animals as well.

Thus it is written, “And all flesh in which there was the spirit of life died in the water.” And in the prophet Ezekiel it is said, when God promises the restoration of human beings: “Thus says the Lord to these bones: I will stretch skin over you, and I will put my spirit in you, and you shall live.” The Holy Spirit should certainly not be understood from the fact that the Lord said, “I will put my spirit in you,” since God clearly spoke of the soul.

This is common to every spirit and to the Holy Spirit: every spirit is similarly called the spirit of God. Understanding is therefore necessary here, to distinguish things that bear one name. For God is called spirit; the human soul is called spirit; and so are wind, air, the soul of an animal, angels, and all things that have received life through their own substance.

But you already distinguish through understanding that God is called spirit in one way and a creature in another, just as you understand Christ to be called the Son of God in one way and human beings to be called children of God in another. Whenever Scripture wishes to signify the Spirit who is properly from God, it adds the designation “Holy Spirit,” so that he may not be understood as a creature, but may be believed, because he is from God, to be nothing other than what God is.

When Moses was describing the material creation—that is, the confusion of things, which is certainly without rational perception—he said that the spirit of God was borne over the earth, the abyss, and the darkness, so that from the spirit itself and from the place over which it was borne, the higher creature, which we call spiritual, might be recognized.

Moreover, by saying that it was borne over them, he signified it as a creature, because every creature is borne by the power of God, from whom it received existence. For what order would there be in the Holy Spirit’s being borne over the waters, when it is certain that he is above every creature? If Christ is at the right hand of God, above all the heavens (Col. 3:1), the Holy Spirit is there also. Things of one dignity and nature ought to be together.

Although it is not denied that God is everywhere—that is the power of the Trinity—due honor is nevertheless preserved, so that he is said to be above every creature, as something proper to him. Hence we say, “Our Father, who are in heaven” (Matt. 6:9), and “who dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6:16).

### XLII.—Why did the angel sent to speak with Moses appear on the mountain in fire and in a bush (Exod. 3:1–2)?

God is exalted. It was therefore fitting that he should appear in a high place, namely, in a place close to heaven. And because fire always seeks what is above, rising upward toward heaven, the Lord of heaven ought to appear in it, since from the earth it strives toward the heights.

He chose to appear in a bush because of sins. Since he had descended to give the Law because of sins—and thorns signify sins, for he says, “I waited for it to produce grapes, but it produced thorns” (Isa. 5:2)—and since the Law had not come immediately to punish but first to make manifest, therefore the fire did not burn up the bush. That is, the Law, when given, did not make sinners guilty for the past.

Moreover, since sins are not part of nature but arise accidentally, the material of the bush—that is, of the thorns—does not have a root armed with thorns. It was therefore done for a reason that the Lord appeared to Moses in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 2239] The same question, from manuscripts of the second class, is the seventh among those appearing after the published books of the Old Testament.] Angelic nature is simple in itself; its substance seeks what is above, not what is below. Therefore the Lord appeared in fire, whose nature always tends upward, where Christ is.

He appeared in a bush because the bush has thorns that cause harm and is easily consumed, yet was not consumed by the fire. Let the fire represent the Law, since it is fire to sinners. The bush signifies sins, because the Savior used the bush to represent a bad tree in comparison with the others; and sins are nothing other than wickedness.

Thus, when the fire appeared in the person of the Law, it did not burn up the bush. In the same way, the Law was given because of past sin, but did not immediately exact punishment; rather, it restrained the force of its justice, so that later, if it were despised after being given, it might punish. For this reason the Lord appeared in fire and in a bush: in the bush, the fire signified the Law.

### XLIII [Note: [Col. 2239] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]—Since Abraham was forbidden to sacrifice his son, why was Jephthah not forbidden to offer the sacrifice of his daughter (Gen. 22:11–12; Judg. 11)?

There is a great difference between Abraham’s case and Jephthah’s. First, Abraham was legitimately born, whereas Jephthah was illegitimate, for he was the son of a prostitute. In addition, Abraham was of exemplary conduct, whereas Jephthah was a leader of brigands. Abraham was a righteous man, tested in trial; Jephthah, however, had no testimony to his righteousness.

Abraham was therefore commanded to offer his son to God, so that it might be shown to human beings how greatly Abraham trusted God: when God commanded him, he did not hesitate even to kill his own son. For the one who had been able to make him be born contrary to the world’s hope, from a barren and aged woman, could without doubt raise him from the dead contrary to the world’s reason (Heb. 11:19).

By doing this Abraham’s righteousness was increased. For God showed that he had not demanded the boy’s blood, but that his servant Abraham might be made greater through this deed. He wishes those who love him to suffer something, so that he may appear just in advancing them.

Jephthah, however, a criminal and thoughtless man, promised a gift to God in foolish devotion, saying, “Whatever meets me when I return from the slaughter before the doors of my house, I will offer to God.” Was he forced to make this vow? Or did he understand how a vow ought to be made? What if a dog or an ass had met him—something that the Lord forbade to be offered—or another man’s son, or his wife, so that he might fulfill his vow while rejoicing in another’s grief?

Therefore, what he had rashly devoted to another’s destruction was turned back against that very man by divine judgment. Jephthah was so senseless that even afterward he did not recognize that he had made a foolish vow, so that the error which had begun with him might be corrected through him.

He ought to have understood that God is not pleased by such a sacrifice, to have prayed for his foolishness, and to have offered something else that was not contrary to the Law. But he showed himself faithful by becoming a parricide, although it is clear that foolish faith not only profits nothing but does harm.

In the matter of his daughter, therefore, he himself was struck down; hence God refrained from preventing such a sacrifice. For if he had forbidden it, Jephthah would have seemed to wish to offer something else to him, even though he knew that, as an unworthy offering, it ought not to be made.

His daughter, however, gained an advantage. Since she died innocent amid her father’s evils, she escaped the punishment of the underworld, which perhaps she could not have attained had she lived longer.

As for Jephthah’s victory, neither his merit nor that of the people brought it about. For we do not read that they implored God to give them a defender. Or did the Lord himself send Jephthah, or speak to him? Rather, because the Allophyli praised their gods, as though those gods had made the children of Israel subject to them, and reproached the God of Abraham, God avenged the honor of his name upon the Allophyli, if not for the sake of these people, then for the sake of Abraham’s merit and his own majesty.

Or, because the spirit of the Lord rushed upon Samson while he was consorting with a prostitute (Judg. 14:6, 19; 15:14), should he therefore be called worthy, when it is understood that this was done for the destruction of the Allophyli?

### XLIV [Note: [Col. 2240] Against the Jews. This is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]—How could it be shown from the testimony of the Prophets, already received in the New Testament by the Gentiles, that the promise God made to Abraham was fulfilled through Christ’s coming?

It is written in the prophet Isaiah, “My house shall be called a house of prayer for all nations” (Isa. 56:7). But perhaps the Jews will say, “The house of God,” that is, the synagogue, is open to all. We do not object to this—provided, however, that those who are circumcised are thereby attached to the Law, as has always been the case. For their law is that by which they were commanded to be circumcised according to the custom of Abraham. Nothing new, then, will seem to be contained in this example of the prophet, since no one coming from any nation has been forbidden from joining himself to the Law from the very beginning of Judaism. Nothing new can be thought to have been said by the prophet; indeed, it would be superfluous, if Gentiles had always been admitted to serve the God of Abraham and are found never to have been forbidden to do so. And this is true, since those who submit themselves to the Law are shown never to have been rejected.

If this is so, then the prophet seems to have given a superfluous warning about something that, once handed down, has always been observed. And could anyone be found so dull-witted as to say that so great a prophet spoke about something superfluous and empty? I do not know to whom it would be safe even to hear this and not forbid it. For when the Jewish people, because of the sins they were committing against God, sought help from idols, were often rebuked by the prophets, and refused to enter upon the path of repentance so as to return to God, God signified, to their reproach, that he would open his house to all nations for prayer, showing that, after rejecting the Jews, he would put others in their place.

For if the nations had always been admitted to the Law, as was said above, how could the prophet say that this would happen, unless he signified something different from what had previously been commanded? He could not speak of something that was happening every day as though it were still future. Hence it is clear that this prophecy works toward the destruction of the Jews, to whom the prophet showed that, when they had been removed, others would be called and would receive the house of God’s grace—what had been promised to the Jews.

But what the promise is, the prophet Isaiah teaches, saying, “He shall come from Zion, the one who will deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob; and this shall be my covenant with them” (Isa. 59:20–21). This covenant, therefore, is the abolition of sins. This is the New Covenant that was promised through Jeremiah, who says:

“Behold, the days are coming, says the Lord, and I will complete a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; because they did not remain in my covenant, and I disregarded them, says the Lord” (Jer. 31:31–32).

This was their transgression: when they made the image of the calf, they then corrupted his covenant. Therefore the tablets on which the Law had been given were broken beneath the mountain (Exod. 32:4, 19), because they deserved to receive more severe commandments.

[Col. 2241] But because God is gracious and merciful, he promised through the prophets that he would change the Law and give another covenant, one different from that which he had previously given. Thus not only what was burdensome would be changed, but also those things that had been given in figure—that is, the Sabbath and circumcision—so that, since they had long been oppressed, they might be relieved in every respect and offer grateful thanks to God in supplication.

And because they persisted in their ancestral transgression and refused to turn their minds away from idols, he bears witness that the nations, together with the remnant who kept the faith, would enjoy the covenant that he had said was to come, so that the faithless Jews, burdened in two ways, might be tormented. For they were burdened by the commandments for a time, and in the future they will pay the penalties appropriate to them, because they were found faithful neither in the Old nor in the New Covenant.

He therefore said that he would give a New Covenant, so that the Old Covenant, which had been given to the fathers, might cease. Accordingly, whoever serves God in this covenant observes neither the Sabbath, nor new moons, nor circumcision, nor distinctions among foods, but has only fear of God in faith. For he will not be justified by the Law but by faith, as the prophet Habakkuk says: “For the righteous shall live by faith” (Hab. 2:4). Thus he no longer uses many commandments to win God’s favor, but few.

Isaiah again speaks of this same meaning, saying: “If the number of the children of Israel should be like the sand of the sea, their remnant shall be saved. For he is completing and abridging his word in righteousness, because the Lord will make an abridged word throughout the whole world” (Isa. 10:22–23). To the remnant who have persevered in faith in the promise, while the others have disbelieved, he shows the abridged word of the Law. This is the New Covenant that he promised.

It would not otherwise be called a covenant unless this covenant too were confirmed in a similar way by the testimony of blood, as was the Old Covenant, so that the two might have one name. But in the Old Covenant there are many commandments, while in the new there are few, as he promised.

And because he had said that Abraham would become the father of many nations (Gen. 17:4–5), the children might be justified in the same way as the father had been justified. Once those things that had begun after Abraham’s faith had ceased, those who received the faith by which Abraham himself had been justified would be children of Abraham, as was said by the Lord.

Indeed, it is neither astonishing nor unheard-of that people should be justified without observing the Sabbath, circumcision, and the other commandments of this kind. For it was not by this that Enoch pleased God and was taken away; nor was Noah found alone righteous in the flood because he observed this; nor was Abraham himself justified after he had been circumcised. “Abraham believed God,” it says, “and it was counted to him as righteousness” (Heb. 11:5, 7, 8; Rom. 4:3).

He was circumcised afterward, so that this might be a sign in him, because, when he was already advanced in age, he believed that he would have a son. Circumcision, therefore, does not commend Abraham; faith does. Hence faith is sufficient for believers unto justification, so that they may be children of Abraham in faith, not in circumcision, since they have no need of circumcision. For what Abraham believed is not what they believe.

The Jews, however, were commanded to be circumcised so that they might have the sign of Abraham’s faith—not of their own faith—but so that they might be known as his children according to the flesh. If they believe, however, they will also be his children in justification.

For what benefit is there in calling someone the son of a powerful man when he is powerless himself, except that it is rather harmful? It is a disgrace to be the son of someone illustrious and glorious without honor. Indeed, circumcision of the flesh is so completely without merit that God says through the prophet Jeremiah that he will punish all those who are circumcised in the foreskin if they have not been circumcised in heart (Jer. 4:4).

He does not condemn those who are circumcised in heart but uncircumcised in the flesh, because no one has pleased God without circumcision of the heart. Therefore, all who are circumcised in the flesh signify Abraham’s race according to the flesh; but those who are circumcised in heart signify God’s race according to faith, because, circumcised from every worldly error, they confess God as their Father.

What benefit, then, is there in circumcision of the flesh if, when faith is lacking in a Jew, he cannot attain to Abraham’s merit? Or what harm is there in uncircumcision, since no one attains to Abraham’s righteousness unless he is an imitator of Abraham’s faith? They therefore boast uselessly of circumcision of the flesh when they see that it has no merit before [Col. 2242] God.

And if, as has been shown, it is better to have faith than circumcision, the Gentiles are better than the Jews, because the former have faith, while the Jews have circumcision. And whom do you think Abraham recognizes more readily as children: those who resemble him according to the flesh, or those who resemble him in faith?

Abraham’s faith bears witness. Accordingly, he does not glory in the flesh but in faith. Therefore he received as children those whom he sees to be imitators of his glory. For how can he call those his children from whom he sees that the very thing by which he pleased God and was justified is absent? He will therefore judge them not his children but his enemies. They appear to be envious of him, scorning the faith by which he was glorified.

Nor is it surprising that the Jews are found to disbelieve and refuse to accept the New Covenant, since we know that they were not faithful even in the Old. For they were always rebellious and insolent toward God, and therefore they received such commandments as would weigh down their necks, which were inflexible. They never wished to hope for good from God, although they had recognized his many benefits and such wondrous powers.

For this reason, among other things, the prophet Ezekiel says:

“I lifted up my hand in the wilderness among them, that I might scatter them among the nations and disperse them throughout the regions, because they did not perform my judgments and rejected my commandments.”

And in what follows:

“I gave them commandments that were not good, and my judgments, in which they shall not live” (Ezek. 20:23–25).

He shows for what reason such numerous and harsh commandments were given to them: because, having proved ungrateful for such great benefits, they were, in accordance with justice, weighed down by more severe commandments.

For this reason he called them “not good,” although they were just: they did not contribute to their justification but to their destruction. And although punishment may have been deservedly inflicted, it is nevertheless not good for the one who suffers it.

After this, however, because God is compassionate, he promised that he would give a New Covenant in which the abbreviation of the Law would justify believers, just as Abraham had been justified. Thus, when new moons, the Sabbath, circumcision, and the other commandments had ceased—not those belonging to the natural law, such as murder, adultery, and the like—they would be justified as Abraham was.

With Abraham’s faith renewed, he wished everything else to cease, so that the time might be like that in which Abraham believed.

But perhaps the Jews will say: “If the things given through Moses are said to cease through the abbreviation of the Law, was circumcision given through Moses so that it too should cease? Accordingly, we possess the sign of our father because we are children of Abraham, and this sign ought not to cease, since it bears witness to our descent.”

Circumcision was indeed to be observed in its own time—that is, before the New Covenant was given, which had been promised. But when, by God’s gracious provision, the burdens of the Law were commanded to cease, what need is there for circumcision?

The new Law, that is, the spiritual Law, was therefore given so that carnal things might cease, and those who received it might accept its sign. Just as in the Old Covenant they had the sign of Abraham, from whom the Old Covenant began, so in the New Covenant they should have the sign of the Savior, who established the New Covenant.

For just as the Hebrews were named from Abraham, so Christians are named from Christ. Therefore, all who are still called Hebrews have not received the New Covenant that God promised, rendering God’s benefit and mercy ineffective. God no longer wished his people to be designated by the name of a man; he graciously established them under the name of his Son.

With what audacity, then, do the Jews say that we do not use our Law but theirs, when David says, “I will confess to you among the nations” (Ps. 17:50), and again, “Rejoice, nations, with his people”? And to the prophet Jeremiah the Lord says: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came forth from the womb, I sanctified you, and I appointed you as a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1:5).

Judaism certainly has its own proper designations. For this people is signified either by Jacob, or by Samaria, or by Jerusalem, or by Judea, or by Israel. But it is clear that the nations are signified in another way than the Jews are.

Jeremiah, therefore, is our prophet. Although God has shown in all the prophets that the nations share in his [Col. 2243] gift, he says particularly to Jeremiah that he gave him to us as a prophet. For Jeremiah signified the future New Covenant, which would benefit the nations more than the Jews, as now appears to have been made clear.

Since the preaching of the New Covenant extends throughout the whole earth, a faithful Jew is found so rarely and with such difficulty that all the churches of the New Covenant are called churches of the nations, as had been said through the prophet Hosea: “I will call ‘my people’ those who were not my people, and ‘beloved’ her who was not beloved” (Hos. 2:24; Rom. 9:25).

Therefore, after the Jews had been rejected, he calls the nations by that mercy and grace by which he also deigned to call Abraham. For Abraham did not come to know the Lord without being called. Thus the one who deigned to call Abraham also deigned to call the nations.

Why, then, do they say, “The Law is ours,” when it is clear that God’s gift belongs to all who desire it? Let this reckless claim of appropriation cease, because God’s grace is common to all.

With what shame, then, do they deny that our Christ was promised in the Law, when they see in him all the signs that the Law had foretold would come? For, in accordance with the promise made to Abraham, all nations are justified by believing in him (Gen. 22:18); and, according to the prophet Isaiah, he was born of a virgin (Isa. 7:14) in Bethlehem, from the tribe of Judah, as had been promised through the seed of David (Mic. 5:2).

And, in accordance with what Jeremiah prophesied (Jer. 31:31–32), he proclaimed the New Covenant that God had then promised would come. After all the signs of his powers had been displayed, he humbled himself according to the words of the prophets. Having suffered all that had been foretold, he rose on the third day, just as it is written in the prophet.

And if they demand the time of the promise, as it was shown in the prophet Daniel (Dan. 9:24 ff.), they will find that it was fulfilled at the time when Christ was born and suffered. For from the first year of Darius, king of the Persians, up to the birth and passion of the Lord and the destruction of Jerusalem, which was carried out by Vespasian, ruler of the Roman Empire, the seventy weeks were completed—that is, four hundred and ninety years. This calculation is clear from the succession of kingdoms and rulers.

It can also be found calculated by Tertullian in the book that he wrote against the Jews. Because he calculated correctly, and so that this might not redound to his injury, we have passed it over.

And who could doubt this number, when approximately three hundred years have now been added beyond it? It is therefore shameless, after so many years have been added beyond the number appointed for the Savior’s coming, to say, “He has not come.”

Among the Apostles, or during the time when the Lord lived among human beings, malicious contradiction could conceal itself and oppose the truth. Although they saw all the signs of the promised Christ in the Savior, they could still claim to doubt the time in order to conceal their faithlessness.

But afterward, when many years began to accumulate beyond the promised number, what shamelessness is it to deny that he came, when it is known that the event was fulfilled both by the signs and by the times?

When something is full but does not overflow, a contentious person may say that it is not full. But an overflow closes the mouth of the contentious person. In the same way, at the time of the Savior the Jews could have said, even if deceitfully, that the calculation from the time of Darius to Christ had not been made correctly, so that he himself might be said to be the one who had been promised. For we make mistakes in the years, months, and days of emperors, and do not calculate them with complete precision.

But once the periods have grown beyond the prescribed number of years for the promised Christ, no excuse can be offered for denying that the Christ who came is the one who was promised—unless, God forbid, the one who promised is said to have lied.

For when the time of the promise has elapsed and the one who was promised is denied, what else is the one who promised accused of than falsehood? But all the signs that were foretold concerning Christ and are known to have been found in Christ teach that the one who promised is truthful.

The Jews, however, while ashamed to correct their error, do not consider the judgment to come. For nothing is worse than for someone to deny as true what he understands not to be false.

### XLV

[Note: [Col. 2244] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

How was man made in the image of God, and whether this was for dominion, and whether the woman also was made in that image?

“Let us make man,” he says, “according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26). Some think this should be understood from another passage of Scripture, namely, the one in which we read that God said, “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages” (Gen. 11:7). For, as it appears on the surface, the wording is similar: it is one speaker speaking in the plural. But the meaning differs, because the reasoning is also different.

In the first passage he speaks of creating man, whom God wishes to be created according to his image and likeness. But the statement, “Come, let us go down and confuse their languages,” concerns preventing human beings from understanding one another. Hence God may appear to have been speaking to the angels, as a commander speaks to an army.

He speaks collectively because he was going to accomplish this through them, as their Creator; hence he says, “Let us confuse their languages.” But when he says, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” it cannot be said that he was speaking to angels, because it cannot be said that there is one image of God and of the angels, as there is one image of an emperor and his attendants. For where there is one image, the dignity or nature cannot be different.

Finally, he adds: “And God made man; according to the image of God he made him” (Gen. 1:27), so that God both spoke and God acted—not another god or a different one, but the same God.

For what one person said to another did not signify another nature but a person. Although God is one, there are nevertheless three persons. God is therefore one because, whether in the Son or in the Holy Spirit, there is the substance of the one God; for that which is from God cannot fail to be what God himself is.

It is therefore the person of God the Father who says, “Let us make”; it is the Son who makes man according to the image of God. Whether according to the Father’s image or his own makes no difference, because the image of both is one. The Son made him through the Holy Spirit. For just as the Father is said to make through the Son, so the Son makes through the Holy Spirit, as he himself says: “I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. 12:28).

Thus the image of the three is one, because whether Father, Son, or Holy Spirit is named, there is one God. Accordingly, man was made according to the image of the one God.

Man is the image of God in this respect: just as there is one God in heaven, from whom all spiritual things subsist, so there should be one man on earth, from whom the others would have their bodily origin.

Some, however, think that man was made in God’s image with respect to dominion, because Scripture says, “And let him rule over the fish of the sea, and the birds of the air, and the whole earth,” even though these things are seen to be subject not only to the man but also to the woman, who plainly does not possess the image of God.

This view is irrational in two ways. First, it would mean that God did not say to the Son, “Let us make man according to our image and likeness,” but to the heavenly dominions whom the Apostle mentions, if man possesses the image of God through dominion. Second, it would grant this image to the woman as well, so that she too would be the image of God—which is absurd.

For how can it be said of the woman that she is the image of God when she is plainly subject to the authority of the man and possesses no authority? She cannot teach, testify, give a profession of faith, or judge; how much less can she rule?

### XLVI

[Note: [Col. 2244] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

Whether Samuel was one of the sons of Aaron, and whether he should be considered to have been a priest?

There are some among us who, partly occupied with worldly affairs and partly insufficiently devoted to the sacred Scriptures, fall into error by thinking that Samuel was a priest—that is, that he derived his origin from Aaron. For the Lord God ordained that priests should be born from Aaron’s descendants, not made priests from elsewhere. No one except his sons was permitted to place incense upon the altar.

Some who err still further deny that Samuel was of Aaron’s lineage—that is, they say that he was not born [Col. 2245] a priest—and nevertheless assert that he exercised the priesthood. We must answer these people first. For it is worse to deny that Samuel was born a priest and yet assert that he exercised the priesthood than to say that he was a priest from the sons of Aaron. In the former case there is foolishness; in the latter, ignorance.

Once those who think he was born a priest have learned that he was not one of Aaron’s sons, they will plainly understand that he was not a priest, being unaware that no one was permitted to exercise the priesthood except one who was descended from Aaron.

They know the evidence. It is clear that when Korah, who was not one of Aaron’s sons, wished to place incense upon the altar, he was swallowed up by the opening of the earth together with his companions (Num. 16:1–34). King Uzziah, although he was not descended from Aaron but belonged to the tribe of Judah, presumed to exercise the priesthood. While standing before the altar, he was struck with leprosy on his forehead and died in that condition (2 Chron. 26:16–21).

Those who say that Samuel was not born a priest and nevertheless assert that he exercised the priesthood are speaking quite foolishly; and persuading a fool of what is good is a matter of the greatest difficulty.

How dull-witted they are, that when the sun is shining upon the earth they say that it is night! Although they read—and read in more than one place—that God decreed that no one should exercise the priesthood except Aaron and his sons, they stubbornly insist that Samuel was a priest.

They do not understand that if Samuel was not born a priest but exercised the priesthood, he is called a usurper, because God established that priests should be born, not made. And I think it unsafe to hold this view of Samuel. How could a man who was praiseworthy and commended by God’s testimony have done what he knew was forbidden?

He had also certainly witnessed the punishment of such presumption, which had occurred once and again. He could not have aspired to this by God’s judgment, since he knew God to be unchangeable. If he had somehow heard such a command, he would rather have believed himself to be undergoing a test, knowing that God could in no way revoke his own decree.

He could more readily have believed that this was being done to him under the appearance and name of God so that he might be deceived by the opposing side than that God could change his judgment.

Finally, when Balaam had been forbidden by God to go to Balak and afterward asked again whether he should go, God became angry with him and rebuked him through the mouth of the donkey. The donkey, seeing the angel who was forbidding the journey, did not wish to continue on the road (Num. 22:28).

But Balaam, although God had forbidden him to go, asked again whether God wished him to go, and thus judged God as though he were a human being who, through ignorance, is changeable and inconsistent. Balaam, however, is commended by no divine testimony, for he was a diviner.

But Samuel was a man beloved by God and knew that God’s judgments were fixed. How could he believe that something ought to be done other than what he knew had been established by God?

“But when Eli and his sons, who were priests, had died,” they say, “Samuel began to exercise the priesthood.” Neither does the text teach this, nor does reason admit it.

Those who say this think that there was no one at that time to exercise the priesthood, so that, once these three had died, the priesthood would have ceased unless Samuel had offered the people’s gifts. Such an assertion is hostile to God. It judges God to be improvident, as though he did not know what he was doing, when he established something that could not continue.

Why did he establish that no one but the sons of Aaron should exercise the priesthood forever—that is, until the time of Christ’s coming—if he knew that the priesthood would fail? If he did not know, God forbid that this should be said, he was improvident. And therefore it could have happened that Samuel was not a priest even when those men had died.

But if God is provident and foreknowing, what he established continued. And if what he established continued, Samuel did not exercise the priesthood, since he was not God’s priest.

In the Old Law God decreed that priests should be born; in the New, the Lord commanded that priests should be made. Let them now choose one of two alternatives: either prove that Samuel was born a priest or that he was made one.

They agree that he was not born a priest, because they know that he was not one of Aaron’s sons. Therefore, if Samuel was not born a priest, and it is neither read nor proved that he was made one—since God had not established that priests should be made—it is absolutely clear that Samuel was not a priest.

But the opponents, with their eyes closed, [Col. 2246] say: “If he was not a priest, he nevertheless acted in the place of a priest, since he is read to have offered a sacrifice to God.”

Who would dare deny what Scripture proves to have been written (1 Sam. 7:9)? Samuel did offer a sacrifice to God, but from this it is not known that he acted in the place of a priest.

The person whose offerings they are is always said to offer them, although the priest places them upon the altar. Saul also offered in this sense—that is, through the priest—as offerings are made now. David offered, Solomon offered, and the others likewise offered. Did they all therefore act in the place of priests?

Although a priest performs his own office, the person in whose name the priest acts is nevertheless said to offer. The offering is credited to the person whose gifts are offered.

And if someone was not a priest, how could he act in the place of a priest? Can a deacon act in the place of a priest? An administrator can act in the place of an administrator, and a praetor in the place of a praetor; but a private individual cannot act in the place of someone possessing an authority. How much less can someone act in the place of a priest who is not himself a priest?

With what intention would he dare to aspire to something he knows is not permitted to him? For if a priest is absent somewhere, a priest from another place may be asked to come and act in his place. But a prophet, even if he leads a holy life, cannot do what he knows has not been granted to him.

It is one thing to live well and another to receive the authority of an office. Just as one who is a priest should not think that his life is thereby approved, so one who lives a holy life should not on that account claim the priesthood for himself.

Although the priesthood is good, it will be evil for the person to whom it has not been granted if he presumes to exercise it.

If we consider what is written about the holy Samuel, we will see what testimony Scripture gives him. It says: “And it became known to all the people that Samuel was a faithful prophet of the Lord” (1 Sam. 3:20). And in the Psalm: “Let Moses and Aaron be among his priests, and Samuel among those who call upon his name” (Ps. 98:6).

Who would fail to notice from this distinction that the persons are divided according to their dignities, so that Moses and Aaron are known to have attained priestly dignity, while Samuel is understood to have proved worthy of God among the prophets who called upon God in prayer to protect his people, as Scripture records?

Indeed, it is proved that priests were by no means lacking, since, after the ark had been brought back from the Philistines, the men of Beth-shemesh, who were Levite bearers, offered sacrifices to God in Samuel’s absence.

After Saul had become king, Ahimaaz, a great-grandson of Eli the priest, carried the ephod.

“But from this,” they say, “Samuel appears to have been a priest, because he was clothed in an ephod.” As though deacons today were not clothed in dalmatics, just as bishops are.

We also read that David wore an ephod, and a double ephod (2 Sam. 6:14). Samuel, while still a very small boy, was girded with an ephod (1 Sam. 2:18). Could a very small boy offer the people’s gifts to God?

You see, then, that ephod is one name, but does not always signify one thing. The priests carried the ephod; they were not clothed in it. Kings and the Levite Samuel, however, wore the ephod.
