Sometimes, therefore, ephod signifies a garment; sometimes it signifies something like a small chest—[Note: [Col. 2246] Manuscript of Colbert: “armiliolum.”]—which the priests carried in order to inquire of the Lord.

As far as can be seen, it has been proved that Samuel was not a priest but a prophet. We now answer those who, being unaware that Samuel was not one of the sons of Aaron the priest, think that he was a priest; for they say that it was not lawful for one descended from Aaron’s line not to be a priest.

First, I want them to understand that if Samuel was a priest, then without a doubt his father Elkanah was also a priest. It would also have been fitting for his sons to have been priests. Since they were not priests, he appointed them judges over the children of Israel (1 Sam. 8:1), just as Samuel himself was.

For we read that “he judged the children of Israel.” But Elkanah, Samuel’s father, because he was not a priest, “went up,” [Col. 2247] it says, “from year to year from his city, Ramathaim, to worship and sacrifice to the omnipotent God Sabaoth [of hosts]. And Eli and his two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, the priests of the Lord, were there” (1 Sam. 1:3).

What could be clearer? Elkanah came at the proper time to offer his gifts before the Lord through the priests, in accordance with what Moses had established: that three times each year they should offer their gifts and tithes wherever the ark of the Lord and the priests were.

Moreover, he had two wives at one time, something unlawful for priests. He was a Levite, as the genealogical order is set out in the book of Chronicles (1 Chron. 6:33).

At that time the Levites did not yet have an established order of ministry concerning the priests and the ark of the Lord. In his kingdom David arranged the courses of priests and Levites so that, from the age of twenty and above—and, according to the Law, from twenty-five and above—they would begin to perform service in the ceremonies of the Lord.

There were twenty-four priestly courses descended from Aaron—that is, from the line of Phinehas and Ithamar—which performed their duties at appointed times. The Levites were appointed as gatekeepers of the tabernacle, bearers of the ark of the Lord, watchers of the guard, custodians of the vessels, and receivers of miscellaneous offerings.

Twenty-four courses of singers, harpists, and other musicians were also established, so that all the Levites likewise had assigned periods of service. For it was necessary that they also have time to care for their households.

Not only does this support the case stated above, namely, that Samuel was not one of Aaron’s sons; the same is shown by what his mother said to the Lord: “If you give me a son,” she said, “I will devote him to the Lord for all the days of his life” (1 Sam. 1:11).

She would not have said this if he had been born a priest, for he would have been obliged to serve at the altar. But because he was a Levite, and the law for the Levites had not yet been established, each person acted according to his own will, so that those who went astray presumed to do what was unlawful.

Jonathan, the son of the son of Moses, although he had been counted among the Levites, presumed to exercise the priesthood for the tribe of Dan. Accordingly, we read in the book of Judges: “Everyone,” it says, “did what seemed right to him, because there was no king in Israel” (Judg. 17:6).

For this reason Hannah made her vow, saying, “I will devote him to the Lord,” so that he would not go astray along with the others.

And so that the question may be examined more fully, let us also discuss what was said about Elkanah: that he came year after year to offer his gifts and tithes. How could he offer tithes when he possessed nothing?

The Levites did not receive fields, because they obtained their sustenance from the tithes given by the people. But it could have happened—and this is how the matter may be understood—that he had a possession belonging to his wife, or one that he had purchased. For they took wives from the other tribes, not only the Levites but also the others, so that even priests took wives from the other tribes.

For Jehoiada the high priest married a woman from the tribe of Judah, the daughter of King Jehoram (2 Chron. 22:11).

### XLVII

[Note: [Col. 2247] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

How does the statement in Isaiah, “And seven women shall take hold of one man,” and so forth (Isa. 4:1), signify the seven catholic churches?

“And seven women,” he says, “shall seize one man, saying, ‘We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; nevertheless, let your name be invoked over us; take away our disgrace.’” The matter is clear: by the seven women, the seven Churches are signified. For although the Church is one, it is called sevenfold, so that one body may consist of members numbered sevenfold. For not only are we members of the Church, but also the heavenly citizens, whose head is Christ (Eph. V, 23). Therefore, whether the Churches are called one or seven, there is no contradiction. It is called one because it has one head, who is Christ; but seven because, just as the members are diverse, so also the spiritual powers—including those among whom we are reckoned—are diverse virtues. For this reason they are also called aerial. [Note: [Col. 2247] The Colbert Manuscript reads *egere*.]

They are diverse so that no single one can do everything, but that all together may be the body of Christ, because he is “the head of the body, the Church” (Col. I, 18), from whom the whole body subsists—that is, from whom all things in heaven and on earth have their origin. In this Church, therefore, which is on earth, mention has been made of all the Churches, because when the mystery of the Creator is preached to this Church, this teaching is also made known to the heavenly beings. For when it is disclosed to those below, it is necessary that those above also hear it. Hence the Apostle says:

“To me, the least of all the saints, this grace was given: to preach among the Gentiles the incomprehensible riches of Christ, and to enlighten all concerning the administration of the mystery hidden from the ages in God, who created all things, so that through the Church the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places” (ibid. 23 ff.).

Through this Church, therefore, the heavenly beings are taught, because, as he says, “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Ps. LXXXIV, 12). Thus, in order that mention might be made of those above, seven Churches are now named within one people, and the prophet presents these seven Churches as supplicants before the Savior who became man. For they understood that Christ had been born for this purpose: to remove disgrace, first that of those living under his Law, and then that of the others. They had in mind that it was written, “He will come from Zion, who will deliver and turn away ungodliness from Jacob” (Isa. LIX, 20).

These seven Churches, therefore, seized one man—that is, Christ who had been born—and said, “We shall eat our own bread and wear our own garments; nevertheless, let your name be invoked over us; take away our disgrace.”

What is the meaning of their petition? If they use their own bread and put on their own garments—that is, if they are alive and are not naked—what do they lack? If bread signifies life, and clothing signifies being clothed with God, because one who is without God is called naked—for the Apostle says, “You who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III, 27), and again, “If indeed we have been stripped, we shall not be found naked” (II Cor. V, 3)—what is it that they ask to have removed from them as disgrace? It is because this people is signified by the number of the seven Churches: living under the Law, it awaited the promised Christ, who would abolish sins.

Therefore they say, “We shall eat our own bread”—that is, “We shall be nourished by the words of the Law, which proclaim the one God,” because “man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. VIII, 3; Matt. IV, 4). And, “We shall be covered with our own garments”—that is, “We shall be designated by the name of our Creator,” because each person is said to be clothed with what he is and professes. Indeed, senators and officials are understood from their garments to be what they are.

But because these things are not sufficient for winning God’s favor, he also ordained that, through the mystery of the knowledge of the one God, man should become heir to the kingdom of heaven. For, washed from sins through faith and freed from the second death—which, by the sentence passed in Adam, held human beings among the dead—he proceeds, with no one restraining him, into the paradise of God the Father, in which the Lord said to the thief that he would be with him (Luke XXIII, 43).

Although the aforementioned people, signified through the seven Churches, lived under God’s Law and were clothed in devotion to the purification both of their own sin and of their ancestral sin [Note: [Col. 2248] The Colbert Manuscript reads: “and with devotion, from the very origin of the world, he was then clothed in purification both of his own, etc.” (text uncertain).]—for “all have sinned and lack the glory of God” (Rom. III, 23)—the Churches mentioned above therefore pray that their disgrace may be removed through the invocation of Christ’s name, because those who bear his sign, by which he conquered death, cannot be held by the enemy.

And not only do these Churches pray that Christ’s name be invoked over them, but so also do the spiritual beings above who dwell in the heavens. For although they are spiritual and heavenly powers, they are nevertheless subject to disgrace if they have been alienated from their Creator; nor will they be members of the body if, failing to know their head, they wander astray.

The prophet testifies in the following words that the matter is no different from what we have explained:

“But on that day God will enlighten with counsel upon the earth.” [Col. 2249] And he added, “For the Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and daughters, and will purge the blood from their midst” (Isa. IV, 2, according to the Septuagint).

What could be clearer than that, on that day—that is, when God’s promise was fulfilled and the mystery of faith was revealed to human beings—they were enlightened so that, purified through knowledge of the Creator, those who had been liable to death might become heirs of eternal life?

The prophet therefore spoke indiscriminately, to signify that all needed God’s gift, so that both sinners and the righteous might be understood to have awaited God’s mercy: sinners on account of their own transgressions, so that they might be snatched from the jaws of death; but the righteous, absolved from ancestral sin, with the sentence passed in Adam erased—the sentence by which all were held by death—might enter God’s kingdom after receiving freedom, having now become not servants but sons of God.

## QUESTIONS FROM THE NEW TESTAMENT

[Col. 2249]

### XLVIII. — God is certainly perfection and lacks nothing; why, then, was it necessary for Christ the Savior to be born from God, and for God to have a Son through whom he would make all things?

When God wished things that did not exist to come into existence, and knew that this work was by no means worthy of his majesty, he first generated from himself—although he is simple and incorporeal in nature—a Son who differed in nothing from him, so that the effect might correspond to his greatness. For what greater thing could he do than generate from himself another who is perfect? This, therefore, is the perfect work, than which nothing greater can appear.

[For all other things are lesser: for the more excellent Christ is than all these things, the more inferior their creation is to his generation. There is also another point.] [Note: [Col. 2249] The material enclosed in brackets is omitted in manuscripts of the second type. After the word “generated,” the question ends as follows: “Through whom he would make what has been made, so that he might reveal to creation the mystery that lay hidden in him from eternity, as the Apostle says.”]

For God, from whom all things exist, wishing to establish creation, first generated the Word that he held in mystery with himself—that is, he caused it to exist. He therefore called this Word “Son,” to show that he had come forth from him and was consubstantial with him; so that the law by which sons come from parents might make this believable, and through it he might reveal to creation the mystery that had lain hidden in him from eternity.

### XLIX. — Why was the Savior baptized, although he was born holy and was called Christ the Lord at his very birth, when baptism is for purification and for sin (Luke II, 11; Matt. III, 16)?

It is true and evident that the Savior did not need baptism, because Christ was not made but born, as the angel said to the shepherds: “Behold, today a Savior has been born for you, who is Christ the Lord.” Finally, John, knowing his holiness, tried to prevent him from being baptized. But the Savior insisted that it had to be done—not on account of his own sin, certainly, but to fulfill righteousness.

For it was fitting that he himself should be an example for the future sons of God, whom he taught to become sons of God through Baptism. And since he promised that the Holy Spirit would be given by God to believers, he ought visibly to demonstrate this in himself, so that, having perceived it, believers might hope that they too could possess the Holy Spirit invisibly.

For the Savior, since he was born from the Holy Spirit, certainly had a purified body. Spiritual anointing was given to his flesh in the Virgin’s womb. The Holy Spirit purified what proceeded from the virgin Mary into the Savior’s body; and this is the anointing of the flesh of the Savior’s body.

Therefore Christ was also called “the Anointed.” What God used to grant through the ministry of the prophets to those who were anointed as kings by means of the anointing of oil, the Holy Spirit granted to the man Christ, with an explanation added. For Christ’s predecessors received through anointing only the power of rule; but the Savior, as a man born, received power and was born purified.

For it was incongruous that the Son of God should be born in a body subject to sins. Therefore, taking up the cause of humanity, [Col. 2250] and teaching through regeneration that human beings become sons of God, he had to be baptized, so that he might establish this as valid in himself. What is said is easily proved and made persuasive if it is seen to be done by the teacher. In the same way, the signs of his virtues had to be performed, so that, now appearing as the Son of God, he might provide healing for the sufferings of the body through the mystery of regeneration and become an example for future brothers, because through regeneration each person receives the power of virtue.

### L. — If the Savior was baptized to be an example, why, after being circumcised, did he forbid the others to be circumcised?

Circumcision is a commandment belonging to the past age. It had to retain authority until Christ, and was to continue only as long as Christ, who had been promised to Abraham, was born; thereafter circumcision was to cease, once the promise had been fulfilled.

Isaac was promised as a figure of Christ. For God said to him, “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII, 18)—and that seed is Christ. The faith that Abraham had received was restored by Christ, so that all nations might be blessed in Abraham’s seed, which is Christ, just as had been promised to Abraham.

Circumcision, therefore, was a sign of the promised Son of God—that is, of Christ. Once he had been born, the sign of the promise had to cease; yet the promised one himself, when he came, received the sign of his father, so that it might be known that he was the one who had been promised to justify all nations through faith in the circumcision of the heart.

For just as the bodily sign of circumcision was the mark of the son born carnally to the father Abraham, so the circumcision of the heart is the spiritual sign of those who are born spiritually. Therefore, after Christ, it was rightly no longer necessary to be circumcised carnally.

[Note: [Col. 2250] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, twenty-second in order among the post-Vulgate questions from the New Testament.]

Circumcision was granted until Christ. Abraham received circumcision with Christ promised, so that circumcision would continue only as long as Christ, who had been promised to Abraham and who would justify all nations through faith, was born, just as Abraham had been justified. He therefore had to be circumcised so that he himself might be proved to be the one who had been promised to Abraham; thereafter circumcision was to cease, the promise having been fulfilled.

Baptism, however, ought not to cease, because the form of rebirth was begun by Christ. It was not given earlier and brought to completion up to Christ; rather, beginning in Christ’s time, it continues until the consummation of the world.

### LI. — How is it to be understood that, when Mary said to the angel, “And how shall I know this, since I do not know a man?” the angel Gabriel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke I, 34–35)?

When Mary was uncertain about conception, the angel proclaimed its possibility, saying, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.” That is: “Do not doubt because you do not know a man. What I said—that you will conceive—the Holy Spirit, coming upon you, will accomplish, so that you may conceive without a man.”

“And the power of the Most High,” he says, “will overshadow you.” The power of the Most High is undoubtedly Christ, for this pertains to his person. Therefore, when the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin, he sanctified her, producing from her a holy body in which the Power called the Son of God would be born.

His overshadowing of the Virgin means that something of the immensity of the divinity was present in the Virgin’s womb, insofar as human nature could contain it. This was called an overshadowing, as though from splendor; it was the power of God—which power is also God. For nothing of God exists that is not called God. This is unlike bodily things, where something can be in the flesh without being called flesh, such as hair, bones, sinews, and the rest.

[Note: [Col. 2251] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, thirty-eighth in order among the post-Vulgate questions from the New Testament.]

When Mary was uncertain about conception, and so forth: “The power of the Most High is undoubtedly Christ.” The statement pertains to his person; for “the power of God” is a sign of the Son of God. According to divinity, however, the Father is also power, and the Holy Spirit is power, and these three are one power because they are one substance.

The Holy Spirit therefore made flesh from the Virgin for the Savior. But the power of the Most High—that is, Christ—overshadowed it, coming into the flesh made by the Spirit, so that the power of the Son might lie hidden in body and soul. His lying hidden means that, for a time, he was not understood.

The meaning of “overshadowing” must be considered carefully. If the force of the word is expressed as “the overshadowing of the power of God,” some kind of incursion is understood, so that, while the body is overshadowed, it is recognized as receiving something from God’s power. But this “something” is the whole, because divinity cannot be divided.

The passage continues: “Therefore also the holy thing that will be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” For what was born from the Holy Spirit, having in itself the overshadowing of God’s power—which is the Son of God—was undoubtedly born holy; that is, it was the body of the Son of God. The body of the Holy One is holy. Therefore the holy Son of God was born in a holy body.

Thus David spoke of Christ’s flesh: “You will not permit your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XVI, 9), so that he might himself be signified in a holy body.

### LII. — If Christ was born from the Holy Spirit—that is, if through the Spirit’s action he was made flesh from Mary—why is it said, “Wisdom built herself a house” (Prov. IX, 1), when Wisdom is certainly Christ?

This question can be understood in two ways. First, Christ’s house is the Church, which he built for himself with his blood. Second, his body can also be called his house, just as it is called his temple. If it is called God’s temple because of his dwelling in it, it will not improperly be called his house as well, just as we read in the Law.

But if the body was made through the action of the Holy Spirit, and we consider that it can be called a house, why is it referred to the person of Christ? The work of the Son is the work of the Father, because the power of both is one. In the same way, the work of the Holy Spirit is also the work of the Son of God, because of the unity of nature and will.

For whether the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit acts, it is the Trinity that acts; and whatever the Three do is the operation of the one God.

[Note: [Col. 2251] The same question from manuscripts of the second type.]

The work of the Son is the work of the Father, because the power of the Father and the Son is one. Likewise, the work of the Holy Spirit is the work of Christ, because the Spirit received from him. According to his person, therefore, Christ was made flesh through the action of the Holy Spirit—that is, he was born a man. According to his divinity, however, Christ acted in the Virgin so that flesh might be made. For the Holy Spirit and Christ have one divinity; consequently, the work of the Holy Spirit is the work of Christ.

### LIII. — If all things were made with reason, why is the Savior said to have been born on the eighth day before the Kalends of January?

No one could be so dull as to deny that God does everything with reason. Therefore Christ, descending from the holy dwellings to grant salvation to the world, wished to be born at the time when he would also teach that the world itself and its seasons had been established by him: when the diminution of the human race begins to be increased toward God, at the time when, after a great diminution, the light—which is day—begins to grow.

Thus the time of his birth corresponds rationally to the divine teaching, which began to multiply human beings from the shadow of death toward life.

### LIV. — If Christ, the Son of God, was made from David’s seed according to the flesh—that is, if he was already the Son of God in both respects because he was born holy—why, after he had been baptized, was it said to him by the Lord God, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. II, 7)?

Christ is the Son of God from eternity according to the Spirit of holiness. According to the flesh, however, the Son of God was born from David’s seed, so that in both respects he should be regarded not as made the Son of God but as born.

What he hears at his baptism concerns the mystery, not his own case. For this is heard by all who are baptized. He alone, however, is demonstrated by it, so that from this it may appear that God is present in a human being through virtues. The others are strengthened because from that moment they begin to be sons of God, when they receive the Holy Spirit.

Although the Lord’s body was born holy, the man Christ had not yet been established as the Son of God by the sacrament of regeneration unless he had received the Holy Spirit, according to the decree concerning the gift of rebirth. The Jews, too, were called sons of God in devotion, but not through the sacrament that now operates, by which, after receiving the remission of sins through the coming of the Holy Spirit, they are called sons of God.

The Savior, therefore, was both born the Son of God according to the flesh and afterward established as such in the mystery. For what was born from the Holy Spirit could not fail to be born from God. But, so that the purpose of the mystery might be fulfilled, when the Spirit came upon him he was not diminished but increased.

[Note: [Col. 2252] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, forty-fifth in order among the post-Vulgate questions from the New Testament.]

Christ is the Son of God according to the Spirit from eternity; according to the flesh, he is the Son of God from David’s seed by birth. He was not made so through Baptism, because, being born from the Holy Spirit, he had a purified body. In Baptism he therefore hears, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” to show that through the mystery of Baptism people become sons of God.

Finally, when the Spirit descended and remained upon him, he heard these words, because before receiving the Holy Spirit they are not sons of God. He therefore hears them not for himself but for us, so that in him we might learn how we can become sons of God.

For he was not baptized for himself but for us, just as the Lord himself says elsewhere: “This voice has not come for me but for you, so that you may believe” (John XII, 30). This too was done so that it might become a pattern for us.

### LV. — Why did the Lord permit himself to be crucified at the time when the Jews were going to celebrate Passover on the eighth day before the Kalends of April?

The Savior did everything in its proper place and time. To teach that he had rightly established all things by the will of the Father, he wished to redeem and restore the world through his passion at the time when he had created it—namely, at the equinox, from which the world began and the day begins to increase over the night.

Therefore, since he was living under Roman rule, he had to suffer on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, when the Romans have the equinox. For then this part of the world was first illuminated, and from that time the day began to increase.

Therefore, through the Savior’s passion, it was then led from darkness to light. No reproach of the Creator can therefore appear when he restored the fallen creation at the time when he had also made it. Nor can the beginning of creation be blamed for the fallen state of the thing, since its restoration returns it to that beginning.

On the same day he wished the joy of renewal to occur on which the dedication had occurred. [Note: [Col. 2252] In manuscripts of the second type the conclusion is as follows: “Therefore this mystery contains the fact that salvation was restored to the world at the time when it had received it.”]

### LVI. — Why is Joseph’s father written as Jacob in Matthew and as Heli in Luke, so that he is clumsily described as having two fathers, or at least so that it is unknown who his true father was (Matt. I, 16; Luke III, 23)?

There is no ambiguity that Jacob was Joseph’s father. For the line proceeding from David through Solomon follows its proper course and arrives at Jacob, whose son is Joseph. Heli, however, the son of Matthat, follows the line from David through Nathan, David’s son, until the time when the Savior came. [Note: [Col. 2253] Manuscripts of the second type read: “until the time when Joseph lived. For these two sons—Joseph and Heli—of the two brothers Solomon and Nathan, each descended through the successive generations of his own brother until the time when the Savior came.”]

Thus each Evangelist, tracing from David the line of descent of one of the brothers, made something like a fork: Matthew descended from David through Solomon to Joseph; Luke, however, ascended from Heli, who lived at the time of the Savior, through Nathan, the son of David. He joined the tribe of both—Heli and Joseph—showing that both belonged to one lineage. Thus, by associating Joseph with Heli, he showed that they did not differ in their descent but were brothers.

Consequently, the Savior is not only the son of Joseph but also the son of Heli. For the same reasoning by which the Savior is called Joseph’s son also makes him the son of Heli and of all the others who belong to the same tribe. Hence the Apostle says, “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh” (Rom. IX, 5).

Luke was moved by divine providence to ascend from Heli through Nathan to David, and through Terah, his father, to Shem, the son of Noah; then to pass beyond the Flood to Seth, the son of Adam, who was given in place of Abel. By the same reasoning he made the Savior the son of Adam by which he was said to be the son of Joseph and Heli.

Then, rising above Adam, he assigned Christ, before all flesh, as the Son of God.

Some think that Heli had taken Jacob’s wife, in accordance with the Law’s command that if someone died without children, his brother or relative should take his wife and raise up his brother’s offspring (Deut. XXV, 5). Thus, they say, Heli begot Joseph through Jacob’s wife, whom he had taken, and in this way the genealogies were joined, so that Joseph might rightly be called Heli’s son. This is neither plausible nor useful for any purpose.

What was said above, however, both joins the two brothers, the sons of one father, through their descent and shows that Christ was the Son of God before every generation.

The Evangelist, reporting the matter, says: “And Jesus himself was beginning to be about thirty years old, being the son, as was supposed, of Joseph, who was of Heli.” That is, Jesus was considered Joseph’s son; and he was not only Joseph’s son but also Heli’s. He does not say that Joseph was Heli’s son; rather, in the same way that Jesus was called Joseph’s son, he was also Heli’s son. This was because Joseph and Heli were the sons of two brothers, Solomon and Nathan, the sons of David.

Thus, ascending through David to Abraham, Noah, Seth, and Adam himself, and beyond Adam, he teaches that Christ is the Son of God. For when he says, “who was the son of Seth, who was the son of Adam, who was the Son of God,” he calls Christ the son of Adam in the same way that he was called the son of Joseph.

Mary said to him, “Son, why have you treated us so? Behold, your father and I have been searching for you in sorrow and grief” (Luke II, 48).

Above Adam he joined Christ to God the Father, so that the one who was called the son of these persons—from Adam down to Joseph and Heli—might be understood as the true Son of God before them all. This was to confound Photinus, who maintained that Christ came only from Mary and did not exist beforehand.

The one whose son he was not was called his son, while the one whose true Son he was—God—was denied.

For if, as is improbable and serves no purpose, Joseph is called Heli’s son, according to what we said above, Luke would not appear to have said of Christ that he was the Son of God, but rather of Adam. For, proceeding through the order of individual sons and setting down each one’s father, he comes to Enos, whose father he says was Seth; he says Adam was Seth’s father, and God Adam’s father. I do not know what benefit there would be in asserting this.

But if, as we have said, the individual fathers of Christ are named in order, just as he was called Joseph’s son—because it was said, “whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh”—then in that same order he is read to be the son of Seth and the son of Adam. Above all these he is assigned as the Son of God, so that he is said to exist before those whose son he is called.

### LVII. — How is it that, although it is written in the prophet Malachi, “Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way before you,” the Evangelist Mark asserts that this was written in the prophet Isaiah (Mal. III, 1; Mark I, 2)?

Mark could not have been unaware of what he was writing. For he was not unfamiliar with reading, having been imbued with and trained in the divine Scriptures and in the Law from childhood, especially since he followed the Apostles.

Knowing that all statements had to be referred back to their author, he attributed this to Isaiah, who had earlier expressed this meaning, saying, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. XL, 3).

Finally, after the words of Malachi, the Evangelist immediately added, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness,” so that he might join the words of both prophets, which referred to one meaning, under the person of the earlier prophet.

### LVIII. — How can John deny that he knew Christ before the Baptism, when, as Christ came to him for baptism, he said, “I ought to be baptized by you, and you come to me” (John I, 31, 33; Matt. III, 14)? How could he be ignorant of the one whom he forbade, humbling himself before him?

John possessed such holiness, even from the very cradle, that he cannot be thought either to have been deceived or to have deceived others, nor to have been ignorant of his Lord, who had enlightened him in the womb through the Holy Spirit.

Consequently, it is true that he recognized him when the Spirit descended upon him, and that he had not been ignorant of him before he came for baptism. For he knew him, but he did not know whether he was the one who would administer the gift of God formerly promised to the patriarchs.

This is what he professes to have learned at that time, when he saw the Spirit descend upon him. For John says that he was instructed by God in this way: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending and remaining upon him, he is the one who baptizes in the Holy Spirit.”

The Apostle also bears witness to this: “For I say that Christ became a minister of circumcision for the truth of God, to confirm the promises made to the patriarchs” (Rom. XV, 8).

This is what John did not know about the Lord. Although he was not ignorant of his greatness, it remained hidden from him that through him Abraham’s faith was to be fulfilled.

### LIX. — If Baptism is a heavenly mystery, why did the Lord say to Nicodemus, who was doubting about Baptism, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John III, 12)?

The person who thinks that Baptism consists in a carnal matter is not spiritual. Nor can one obtain the heavenly gift who does not believe that he is changed, not through water but through faith. Water is visible, but the unseen Spirit works so that faith may be present in him.

For just as water washes bodily filth, so the Spirit washes the soul from sins, so that just as visible things benefit visible things, the Spirit may benefit spiritual things. Therefore a spiritual meaning is operative in Baptism. For what is heard there is greater than what is seen.

When Nicodemus, instructed in carnal reasoning, was therefore doubtful, the Savior used an appropriate example to draw him toward faith: to establish an invisible matter, he provided a visible example, one that rests on hearing alone, not sight, and is not denied. Yet it is earthly because it accomplishes a work of the world.

The Lord therefore said to Nicodemus, persuading him: “The Spirit blows where it wishes, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So is everyone who is born again of water and the Holy Spirit.”

Just as the voice of the approaching spirit—that is, the wind—is heard but not seen, as has been said, so the meaning of Baptism is heard in what is spoken, although how it occurs through the Spirit is not seen. It is nevertheless heard when what is to happen is proclaimed by the one who explains the words, so that what is heard may be believed to occur, although the explanation of how it occurs is not given.

When Nicodemus was not led to faith even by the example, he then heard from the Savior: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?”

He called those words earthly which he had offered as an example. That is: “If you do not believe, on the basis of an earthly example, that the spirit—that is, the wind—can act, because how it acts cannot be seen, how could you believe if I offered heavenly examples, which you certainly do not know?”

What a person does not know can be made persuasive through what he does know. For example, God says of Christ that he is his true Son; how this is so cannot be comprehended. But because we know according to the flesh how sons come to be, we believe that God said, “Christ is my true Son,” in order to signify that he came from himself.

In the same way, the Savior wished to commend something that cannot be explained either in words or in the mind through what is perceptible and heard by the ears—namely, through the example of the spirit, which is wind. The senses grasp it and the ear hears it, but one does not know where it comes from. Thus he wished to make credible the work of the Holy Spirit, which cannot be comprehended.

The same thing is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind, and it filled the whole house” (Acts II, 2), and so forth.

See how plainly, by the example of wind, he indicates that the Holy Spirit came from heaven and made a sound, just as a strong wind does upon the earth. Jeremiah also calls the wind “spirit,” saying, “The wind blows throughout every region.” Because it is in this world and is carried through different places, we do not know where it comes from or where it goes. The Holy Spirit, however, comes from heaven, as we read, in order to enlighten believers.

How, then, do some think that the Savior was speaking of the Holy Spirit when he said, “The Spirit blows where it wishes, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes,” when it is clear that the Savior spoke this as an example?

Finally, he added, “So is everyone who has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit.” What could be clearer than that he signified the spirit of the wind?

They think that the wind is not signified because he says, “Where it wishes it blows,” as though every creature were not, under the law imposed upon it, nevertheless released to its own will. We too go and do what we wish while acting under the law; therefore we shall also give an account.

Or is it considered possible—and not foolish—that, wishing to convey the working of the Holy Spirit, he should have offered that very spirit as an example? I therefore believe that the question has been resolved in every respect.

[Note: [Col. 2255] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, sixteenth in order among the post-Vulgate questions from the New Testament.]

What he said—“If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe”—does not refer to Baptism, because we know that our Baptism is spiritual, although it is celebrated through water; the meaning there is heavenly. For it is not water that purifies, but God, invisibly and incomprehensibly.

Rather, it refers to the imitation of the example given—that is, to what he said: “The Spirit blows where it wishes, and you hear its voice, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes.” Through this example he wished to instruct Nicodemus toward faith, so that he would believe that a person is reborn through water and the Spirit, although he could not comprehend how it happens. For it happens spiritually.

Thus you hear the voice of the spirit—that is, of the wind—which is a sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So, too, you do not know how the person who is reborn is changed, although you perceive that it happens, because you perceive the change itself.

For if the wind blows where it wishes, how much more does the Spirit who is from God sanctify whomever he wishes?

He said, “Where it wishes it blows,” because every creature, although it is governed under the law, has nevertheless been left to its own will.

But if someone thinks that this spirit is to be understood as the Holy Spirit, the interpretation does not stand, since he introduced this spirit as an example through which he persuaded Nicodemus—who did not believe—that a human being had to be reborn through water and the Spirit. For an example is one thing, and that which is confirmed by the example is another.

If, therefore, it was given as an example, it is not the Holy Spirit but the worldly spirit called wind. Wishing to persuade unbelieving Nicodemus of the spiritual meaning, he gave the example of the spirit, so that through it the meaning and operation of the Holy Spirit might be believed.

We nevertheless know that the Holy Spirit comes from heaven to pour himself into believers, just as we read that it happened at the beginning to the Apostles, and that the sound was then called a voice. For it is said, “And suddenly there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind.” In what follows he calls this sound a voice.

By the example of the spirit—that is, the wind—he displayed the work of the Holy Spirit, so that the Savior’s statement might remain valid. For what else does it mean when he says, “And there came from heaven a sound as of a rushing mighty wind,” than that the Holy Spirit descended and made a sound like a strong wind?

He therefore gave this spirit as an example. Finally, he says, “So is everyone who is reborn.” Here too we do not know whence he comes; but the Holy Spirit comes from heaven.

### LX. — If the Law and the Prophets lasted until John, why does the Savior send a leper to the priests to offer gifts for his cleansing (Matt. VIII, 4; Mark I, 44; Luke V, 14)?

This, indeed, was not done because the time [of the Law] had come, but for the condemnation of the Jews: so that, when they failed to understand that the summit of truth, belonging to the better age, had been made for their salvation, truth might stoop to accuse them. For since they regarded the Savior as an enemy of the Law, because out of mercy he wished to free them from the burden of the Law, just as had been foretold by the prophet Jeremiah—for among other things he says, “And I will give them a new covenant, not like the covenant that I gave to their fathers” (Jer. XXXI, 31–32)—the Savior, lest he appear to be an enemy, as they supposed, by proclaiming something new, sent the man who had been cleansed of leprosy to the priests to offer gifts for his cleansing, just as Moses had commanded (Lev. XIV, 2). And to show that this served for their condemnation, he said, “For a testimony to them”: so that this matter might stand as a witness against them in the judgment, since they called the Savior an enemy of the Law.

The apostle Paul followed this example too. For although he was already preaching that no one ought to be circumcised, he circumcised Timothy because of the scandal of the Jews (Acts XVI, 3). For he preferred to do something superfluous rather than provoke an uproar from false brothers—a course of action that did, indeed, serve the Jews’ error. For they were satisfied for the moment by that through which they would err forever.

[Note: [Col. 2256] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from the New Testament, twenty-eighth.]

The apostle Paul followed this example. For although he was preaching that no one ought any longer to be circumcised, he himself circumcised Timothy because of the scandal of the Jews. For he preferred to do something superfluous rather than become a cause of scandal to the unlearned, some of whom might be saved. The Lord acted in nearly the same way, in order to remove from the Jews the opinion they held about him—for they said that he was an enemy of Jewish tradition. He therefore ordered the leper to offer gifts for his cleansing, just as Moses had commanded, and added, “For a testimony to them,” so that this matter might stand as a witness against them, since the Savior was not an enemy of the Law. Thus something was done that ought already to have ceased. But since superfluous things, once they have ceased, ordinarily do no harm, it was done so that it might benefit those who held a false opinion: they were to satisfy themselves that the Savior was not an enemy of the Law.

### LXI. What does it mean that, when the Jews accused the disciples because they were violating the sabbath by rubbing ears of grain in their hands and eating them, the Savior brought forward the example of David, because he ate the loaves that no one except the priests was permitted to eat (Matt. XII, 1–4)—which seems not to excuse them, but to make them guilty along with David, especially since David did not do this on the sabbaths either?

The Savior wished to expose the hypocrisy of the Jews through many examples, showing that greater offenses had been committed under the Law without anyone daring to accuse the perpetrators. He wished to demonstrate not only that the sabbath had been violated once and again under the Law, but also that the priestly bread had been illicitly taken with the priest’s own permission—and, what is more serious, by men possessing the highest authority under their Law.

For first, Jesus son of Nave, by divine command, did not observe the sabbath; and as a result the walls of Jericho fell of their own accord (Josh. VI, 15–20). How much good came from not keeping the sabbath, but keeping faith! The Maccabees too, after having previously been struck down, fought on the sabbaths and triumphed over their enemies (1 Macc. II, 38, 41). And the priests, in order to perform the rites belonging to the Lord, disregarded the sabbath in the temple.

David, already anointed as king, after stripping the Philistine—who had been killed by the power of God—of his weapons, was traveling and suffered the necessity of hunger. He received from the priest bread that he was not permitted to eat (1 Sam. XXI, 6). Yet apart from necessity it was not permitted; it was permitted if necessity demanded it. Accordingly, when the priest saw the necessity, he did not refuse, and David, chosen by God, accepted without hesitation. The same reason applies to the sabbath, which is why circumcision is not prohibited on the sabbath.

These matters, which are not dangerous, were commanded to be observed in such a way that no harm results if they are undertaken out of necessity, because they were commanded not for salvation but for reverence. What is altogether unlawful, however, is always unlawful, and no necessity mitigates it so that its commission does no harm. For whatever the laws prohibit because it is criminal is always illicit.

The former matters, which we have said are sometimes permitted, are like the lawful fasts that, when set aside in a time of necessity, do not make people guilty if the reason is an ailment of the stomach or a feverish illness. Knowing this, the Jews maliciously accused the disciples, as though they were violating the sabbath, as has been stated above. The Savior, however, did not wish to prejudge them concerning the time when the Law had been fulfilled, lest they rush even further into madness. Instead, by reference to the past—from which they thought the sabbath should more particularly be vindicated—he showed them to be slanderers. They were confounded not only in the matter of the sabbath but also concerning the priestly bread, as has been shown above.

[Note: [Col. 2257] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from the New Testament, in the twenty-third position.]

The Savior did not wish to prejudge the Jews concerning the time when the sabbath had been fulfilled. He plainly judged them unworthy to hear the truth directly, since they were unbelievers. Rather, he wished to convict them concerning what they themselves had presumed—that is, concerning the period when the sabbath still seemed to retain its force—when they accused the disciples of plucking ears of grain on the sabbaths, rubbing them with their hands, and eating them, even though the time for observing the sabbath had already been fulfilled.

Setting this aside, he showed them that even at the time when the law of the sabbath still remained, the sabbath had been violated on account of necessity. David did what was not permitted; Jesus son of Nave did what had been forbidden when he ordered armed men to march around the walls of Jericho for seven days; the Maccabees did what was prohibited when they defended themselves on the sabbaths; and, he says, “In the temple the priests violate the sabbath and are without guilt.”

By these examples, therefore, he showed that the disciples were accused by the Jews more out of malice than out of error. Although they knew that all these things had been done on the sabbaths by willing agents, and indeed by holy men, they accused the innocent. The sabbath was commanded to be observed in such a way that, if necessity nevertheless arose, the person who violated it would not be guilty.

For this reason circumcision was not prohibited on the sabbaths, since necessity required that it be performed. Thus, when the disciples were hungry, they plucked ears of grain. This was not permitted according to the former observance, but necessity arising from hunger made it lawful—just as David did what was not permitted when he was hungry, knowing that hunger would excuse it.

The same principle applies here as applies today to lawful fasts. If a sick person breaks a fast, is he declared guilty? Certainly not, because there is no danger. Such a thing is sometimes permitted, just as the sabbath was among the ancients. What is never permitted has no excuse based on necessity.

### LXII. Why, when the sons of Leah, who belonged to the tribe of Judah, had been killed, is Rachel said to mourn her sons (Matt. II, 18)?

As far as the historical sense is concerned, Rachel’s sons are the tribe of Benjamin. Long ago, however, because of their own crimes—namely, the deeds of the Sodomites and the violation they had committed against the Levite’s concubine—they were destroyed and wiped out by the other tribes (Judg. XIX–XX). For this reason she is said to refuse consolation, knowing that there was no hope for those who were known to have perished.

The sons of Leah, however, were killed in the earliest years, on account of the Savior. Therefore he does not wish their fate to be attributed to mourning, since they were killed both innocently and for God, by whom, undoubtedly, through the gift of reward, they were granted eternal life. Accordingly, he says that mourning belongs to Rachel’s sons, who were wiped out both in the present and in the future. Those were mourned carnally but consoled spiritually. Rachel’s sons, however, having lived according to the flesh, will be consumed by spiritual flames.

The Evangelist therefore testifies that Rachel’s mourning was fulfilled when Leah’s sons were killed because Rachel then began to mourn her sons [Note: [Col. 2258] Manuscripts of the second type read: “to mourn her sons more”], when she saw the sons of her sister killed in such a way that they would become heirs of eternal life. For when something adverse befalls one person because of another’s happiness, he laments his own misfortune all the more miserably.

### LXIII. By what reasoning did the Chaldean Magi understand from the appearance of a star that Christ had been born as king of the Jews, when a star customarily indicates a temporal king (Matt. II, 1–2)?

These Chaldean Magi did not observe the course of the stars out of malicious intent, but from a desire to investigate reality. As may be understood, they were following the tradition of Balaam. When he had been summoned by Balak to curse the people of God, he began, by divine prompting, to bless them.

From his account, therefore, they had learned that, by God’s providence, one who would reign was to arise from Jacob. For this reason he prophesied—as is not hidden—saying, “A star shall arise from Jacob,” and so forth (Num. XXIII–XXIV). Following this tradition, the Magi saw a star outside the ordinary course of the universe and understood it to be the star that Balaam had prophesied would indicate the king of the Jews.

This occurred, indeed, against the enemies of religion. Testimony came from the very source by which religion is usually rejected, for astrologers are enemies of the truth.

[Note: [Col. 2258] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from the New Testament, thirty-ninth.]

These Chaldean Magi did not observe the stars out of malicious intent, and so forth. “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a man shall rise up from Israel; he shall crush the leaders of Moab, and shall plunder all the sons of Seth, and Edom shall be his inheritance,” and so forth. This, then, is Balaam’s prophecy—not because he was a prophet, but because God acted on behalf of his people through him, not willingly but against his will. The same is found in those sent by Saul to capture David, who are reported to have prophesied, and likewise in Saul himself, when it was said, “Is Saul also among the prophets?” (1 Sam. XIX, 20–24).

Through this God wished to demonstrate how great is the majesty of the God of the Jews: Balaam had come to curse, but God turned him so that it seemed good to him to bless the people of God. For he could not fear Balaam’s curse when he held Balaam’s heart in his power.

It may therefore be understood that this prophet disclosed this to his associates. Since they were curious about the stars, when they saw an unfamiliar star shining with extraordinary brilliance—so that it surpassed the sun in brightness, for it appeared during the day—they discussed the matter among themselves and realized that it was the star Balaam had said would appear.

### LXIV. How is it proved that the Savior rose from the dead after three days and three nights?

If in this matter you seek the number of days and nights in strict sequence, you will not arrive at the intended understanding. Moses fasted for forty days and forty nights (Exod. XXXIV, 28), yet the complete number is not found there either. For when he ascended during the day and descended during the day, he did not in fact complete the entire number. But because where there is a day the night is counted, and where there is a night the day is also counted, forty days and forty nights are spoken of by taking a part for the whole.

The same applies to what the Savior said: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea creature three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. XII, 40). Since there are three nights, three days should also be understood.

The night is mentioned so that this may not appear novel or contrary to reason, as though the night depended upon the day. For it is beyond doubt that before the light was made—from which the day received its name—the evening that follows, from which the night was established, had not yet been instituted. Thus it is not absurd that the Lord’s passion is said to take its beginning from the night.

For just as light—that is, day—is an image of life, so night is an image of death, that is, darkness. This is clearly shown in Scripture by the sons of light and, conversely, the sons of darkness. Nor is it surprising that, although everywhere day precedes night and light precedes darkness, here alone what follows should be placed before what precedes; or that in such a matter the order of events should be confused and altered, as we indicated above.

For the night seems to belong more to death than the day does. The beginning is therefore taken from the night because the prince of darkness could be entered only through the night—that is, he could not otherwise be overcome—and so that the Lord of light, that is, of eternal life, might for a time be subjected to the prince of darkness or of death, in order to free from death both those who had preceded him and those who would come afterward.

For death would not have been utterly emptied, nor would the gloom of darkness ever have been dispelled, if it had not seen the Lord entering it. By such great light the secret place of death, in which it held dominion, vanished. Yet it cannot be completely overcome unless the one who is captured is captured either in his own person or in his members.

Rightly, therefore, in such an affair the night alone is given precedence, so that it might lose its power; and so that the unbelieving Jews might remain in perpetual night, and the day—not the author of so great a crime, or rather sacrilege—might not be responsible, the day is subordinated to the preceding night contrary to the order of things, just as God and Lord of all things was subordinated to the author of wicked death, in order to release everyone from the snares of death.

If this still seems contrary to anyone, let him consider carefully lest he begin to judge more harshly that God, taking upon himself the role of a servant—I do not say merely of a human being—gave himself over to death. Why, then, do you seek order here, when you see that everything is contrary? For what is the light that was in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it (John I, 5)? It is the Lord of light, who was also seized.

For whoever knows that he is being seized so that he may be struck counts that time as belonging to his death. There is also the following day, on which he was heard and crucified. There is also the night that falls upon the sabbath, and the sabbath itself. There is also the evening after the sabbath—that is, what Moses commanded the Jews figuratively, that in the evening they should enter into the sabbath—in which the Lord rose. This includes the Lord’s Day, because night is not counted without day, nor day without night.

By this reckoning, the Lord rose after three days and three nights.

[Note: [Col. 2259] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from the New Testament, eighteenth.]

The Savior, foreknowing everything that was to happen to him, declared these things in advance. He knew that he was to be seized by the Jews so that he might be killed, and that he would not resist their impiety, although he could certainly have mocked them. Indeed, after he had already been arrested, he restored the ear of the high priest’s servant, which the apostle Peter had cut off with a drawn sword, in order to show that he had been humbled not through weakness but had yielded for a time to their will by a certain providence, so that through this he might destroy the kingdom of hell.

The devil, lacking foresight, entered the minds of the Jews and inflamed them to kill the Savior, as though it would benefit him if the one who showed the way of truth were removed from life, not knowing what would come against him. For when he triumphed over the captivity of humanity because of sin, he himself was found guilty because he killed Christ, who was innocent, in order to hold among sinners the one who knew no sin. Thus it happened that he also lost those whom he had been justly holding in hell.

Knowing these things beforehand, therefore, the Savior counted as well the night in which he was seized. Anyone who has been arrested and does not believe that he will escape the judge’s hands already calls himself dead before he is struck. Add to this the day on which he suffered, and the following night. Add also the sabbath and the night that dawns into the Lord’s Day, together with the Lord’s Day itself, and you have completed the mystery of the Lord’s words.

For during the last night, while darkness still remained and the day was beginning to rise, he rose between light and darkness, so that both night and day might be counted and the number foretold by the Savior might be found complete.

### LXV. If the Evangelists spoke with one voice and in one sense, how did it happen that three of them—Matthew, Luke, and John—say that the Lord was crucified at the sixth hour, while Mark, in contrast, says that the Savior was crucified at the third hour (Matt. XXVII, 45; Luke XXIII, 44; John XIX, 14; Mark XV, 25)?

It is not good to envelop the truth in obscurity. The three Evangelists had one meaning, but Mark wished to disclose a matter that they had omitted, knowing it to be necessary. For one who followed the examples of the authors could not have been mistaken: he learned with great devotion and diligence what he wrote, and he did not do so without the Holy Spirit.

What, then, did he wish to show by this? It must be explained. We must therefore observe that the Savior was crucified not by Pilate but by the Jews. For, as far as Roman laws were concerned, Pilate pronounced the Savior innocent. Pilate said to the Jews, “I find no cause in him.” When they said, “Crucify him,” he replied, “For what evil has he done?” Finally, persisting and wishing to take him out of their hands, he suffered their accusation when they said, “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend. Everyone who makes himself king contradicts Caesar.” Thus it happened that he handed him over to their judgment (John XIX, 4–13).

Pilate therefore did not give the sentence; the Jews did. Accordingly, they had been forewarned, he says, by the chief priests to say, “Let him be crucified.” Mark wishes this sentence to be understood as having been given at the third hour. After they had persisted in their repeated cries, and after an interval of nearly three hours, during which they went to and returned from Herod, they crucified the Savior.

For everyone who is condemned to death is counted as already dead from the moment he receives the sentence. Mark therefore made clear that the Savior was not crucified by the sentence of the judge. For it is difficult to prove innocent someone who is punished by a judge’s sentence. He therefore allowed himself to differ in wording, in order to teach that what began at the third hour was completed at the sixth—not by the laws, but by the continuing malice of the Jews.

[Note: [Col. 2260] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from the New Testament, twenty-first.]

It is not good to envelop the truth in obscurity. The very agreement of the three Evangelists testifies that they spoke the truth. But the matter itself makes clear that Mark wished to disclose some hidden meaning. For he could not have been mistaken, since he followed the examples of the authors and learned with great devotion and diligence what he wrote.

What, then, did he wish to disclose by this statement? It must be investigated with attentive diligence. For he did not allow himself to differ idly in wording from the three Evangelists. Let us consider whether those who said that the sentence was given at the third hour—and therefore that the Savior was crucified at the third hour—were speaking truly, although they were unable to prove it. Perhaps they know the meaning but do not know how to defend it.

Let us therefore temporarily set aside Pilate’s role and see from what point the sentence against the Savior began. Then it will appear whether what we are saying can be considered true. It is established that the Jewish leaders had instructed the Jews to ask that the robber Barabbas be released to them on the feast day, while Jesus was to be crucified.

Pilate resisted this for a long time, wishing to release the Savior. He repeatedly went in and out to the Jews, saying that he saw no cause of death in him. But they persisted, saying, “Let him be crucified.” From this delays arose: he was mocked by the soldiers, led out, clothed in purple, crowned with thorns, worshiped, spat upon, scourged, and struck with blows on the palms. For this reason he was placed on the cross at the sixth hour.

He had been brought to Pilate. Then Pilate went outside to them, since they themselves did not enter the praetorium; he addressed them and heard their false accusations, sent him to Herod, and he returned. He questioned Jesus again, and Jesus in turn answered him. Afterward he went out again to the Jews and spoke with them, saying that there was no cause of death in the Savior.

Meanwhile, through these delays, the third hour had arrived. Then the Jews said to Pilate, who wished to release him, “Let him be crucified.” Pilate resisted them for a long time, but when he could not prevail, he handed Jesus over to their sentence at about the sixth hour. For it is written, “Then he handed him over to their will.”

It was therefore rightly said that the sentence was given at the third hour, because it was given not by Pilate but by the Jews. Pilate, however, appears to have consented unwillingly, chiefly because of the envy expressed in their words: “If you release this man, you are not Caesar’s friend.”

Let us see, then, what Mark intended by following this account. He wished to show that the Savior was not killed by the sentence of a judge, since one who receives a judge’s sentence appears difficult to regard as having been killed unjustly.

### LXVI. How does Mark the Evangelist say that the demons recognized Jesus and declared him, while the Apostle, on the contrary, denies that the princes and powers of this age knew the divinity of the Lord Jesus? Mark says, among other things, “They knew that he himself was the one”; but the Apostle says, “None of the princes of this age knew him. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty” (Mark I, 34; 1 Cor. II, 8). If the demons knew, how did the princes remain ignorant?

Some think that “the princes of this age” signifies the leading men of the Jews, in accordance with what the apostle Peter says: “For you know, brothers, that you did this evil through ignorance, as did your rulers” (Acts III, 17). They were therefore rulers of the Jews, but they were not rulers of this age. Hence he says “your rulers,” not “the rulers of the age,” since they had said that they had Caesar as king, under whose authority they had been placed.

The rulers in question are those whom the Apostle signifies elsewhere when he says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers and powers of this world, against the rulers of this darkness” (Eph. VI, 12).

The question is therefore rightly raised: if these rulers did not know Jesus, how could it happen that the demons recognized him? But it is one thing for the demons to have known Christ, and another for the Apostle to deny that the rulers of this age knew him. The demons knew that he was the one who had been promised through the Law. For they saw in him all the signs that the Prophets had said would occur: that the redeemer of Israel would come from David’s seed and from a virgin. But they did not know the mystery of his divinity, just as their rulers did not.

Accordingly, the devil asks the Savior, though deceitfully, “If you are the Son of God,” and so forth (Matt. IV, 3). At one time he saw divine power in him, and at another human weakness; uncertain what was true, he was tormented.

The Scriptures therefore agree according to what has been revealed. For it is impossible that men of one Spirit should disagree.

[Note: [Col. 2261] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from the New Testament, forty-eighth.]

Some think that by “the princes and powers of this age” he meant the leading men and rulers of the Jews, who, according to the words of the apostle Peter, did not know what evil they had done. He says, “I know, brothers, that you did this evil through ignorance, as did your rulers.” These were rulers of the Jews, but they could not be called rulers of this age, since they had been brought under Roman authority and professed that they had no king but Caesar.

These, however, are the rulers whom the Apostle signifies elsewhere, saying, “Our struggle is not against flesh, but against the rulers of this world and the rulers of this darkness.” If these are the rulers who, not knowing that Christ was the Lord of majesty, crucified him, how could he have been known by the demons?

The demons knew him in no other way than the rulers of this age knew him. They knew that he was the one promised in the Law through the signs of prophecy, but they did not know his mystery, by which he was the Son of God from eternity, nor the sacrament of the incarnation.

### LXVII. What does the Savior’s saying on the cross mean: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke XXIII, 34)? For if they do not know, what is being forgiven, especially since King Abimelech says to God, “Will you destroy an ignorant nation?” (Gen. XX, 4).

Not everyone who is ignorant is free from punishment. The ignorant person who can be excused from punishment is the one who found no one from whom he could learn. But the Savior asks forgiveness for those who had someone from whom they could learn, yet made no effort. Such people are not permitted to be ignorant. They will therefore receive forgiveness if they convert.

[Note: [Col. 2262] The same question from manuscripts of the second type, among the questions published later from both Testaments, fourth.]

Not everyone who is ignorant is free from punishment. The person who could have learned but made no effort made himself guilty. He had both the opportunity to learn and someone from whom he could learn; but having become more negligent through luxury or malice, he is inexcusable in his crime.

Hence the Savior says, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin” (John XV, 22). But the person who is ignorant through no fault of his own—because there was no one from whom he could learn and he had not even heard by report of the doctrine—is entirely free from condemnation.

For this reason, if they convert, the Lord asks the Father to forgive them: although the truth was being preached so that they might learn it, they made no effort, and through ignorance they killed its author. Hence the apostle Peter says in Acts, “Repent, so that your sins may be blotted out” (Acts III, 19).

### LXVIII. Since the Lord taught that we should pray for our enemies, what does it mean that in the Apocalypse the souls of those who had been killed ask to be avenged, requesting vengeance from God (Matt. V, 44; Rev. VI, 10)?

The souls of those who have been killed cry out and ask to be avenged in the same way that Abel’s blood cried out from the earth (Gen. IV, 10). The causes are therefore said to cry out, although they cannot speak. For what else does spilled blood ask than to be avenged, crying out not with a voice but by reason?

An artist’s work is also said to praise its maker by the very fact that it delights the one who sees it. The saints are not so impatient that they demand that what they know will occur at the appointed time should happen already—something that can neither be brought forward nor delayed.

By this statement he wished to show that God will avenge the blood of his saints, lest, because he now appears so patient, the wicked war waged against the saints should be thought to remain unpunished. He wished both to strike terror into those who persecute God’s servants and to encourage those who suffer for his sake.

The soul of one who suffers is relieved when it hears that it will be avenged by the powerful. It offers hope: if a person hears that his death displeases the judge, he then knows with certainty that he is innocent.

God is indeed merciful and patient, but moderately so. He waits for the wicked to believe and for sinners to amend themselves. If they do not, they will be punished because they have despised God’s long-suffering.

He also displayed an example of this even during the time when mercy was being preached, so that he would not appear not patient but insensible, unmoved by anyone’s grief or compassion. Hence he says through the prophet, “I have been silent; shall I always be silent?” (Isa. XLII, 14). And the Lord says, “Will God not avenge his servants who cry out to him day and night?” (Luke XVIII, 7).

They cry out in precisely the way we have described above. Therefore, if a Christian takes revenge in the present life, without bitterness and without bloodshed, he does not sin. Yet he will act better if he leaves the matter to God the judge.

[Note: [Col. 2262] The same question, number twelve.]

The Apocalypse, while testifying that future evils and tribulations would arise because of unbelief and an evil life, also demonstrates, by visible proof, the penalties corresponding to each sin, proving that no impiety or cruelty would remain unpunished. It says that the souls of those who have been killed ask day and night to be avenged.

This is not contrary to the foregoing. For God, who gave this law, promised that he would avenge them on the day of judgment. Thus the commandment given for the present may be understood to excuse the souls of those who have been killed if, already placed there, they ask for the day of vengeance.

Yet, to speak more accurately, it should be understood that it is the cause that cries out. It does not remain silent but continually demands vengeance, just as God says to Cain, “The blood of your brother cries out to me from the earth.” What does this mean except that the cause of the crime cries out, desiring to be avenged?

For if we say, because of a work, “The earth praises the Lord,” although it has neither a voice nor understanding, so blood is said to cry out because of evil works. They were certainly not so impatient, nor so ignorant, as to ask to be avenged before the future day of judgment, demanding that something occur which they knew could not take place before the appointed time.

The Savior likewise says, “Will God not avenge his chosen ones who cry out day and night?”

### LXIX. If the Law ceased when John or the Savior was preaching, how can the Savior say, “I did not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them” (Matt. V, 17)? For if it was prohibited [Note: This is how the Colbertinus manuscript reads. Manuscripts of the second type have: “For if it ceased.” The printed editions have: “The prophecy has ceased.”], how was it not abolished, since it lost its authority to prescribe conduct?

Everything that was said about Christ has been fulfilled. The Lord himself therefore fulfilled the Law and the Prophets when he did everything that had been written about him, abolishing nothing but confirming everything. For the Law and the Prophets continued until him. The Prophets spoke about him; therefore what they said concerning this matter—that is, concerning Christ—cannot extend beyond him. Nor could the Prophets find anything of this kind after him, since they had no one about whom to speak, and the one of whom they spoke had already come.

For in their books they embraced and revealed everything: his incarnation, his way of life, his passion, his resurrection, the manifestation of his divinity, and his future judgment. Consequently, when the work of the dispensation had been fulfilled, the Prophets ceased.

The Law ceased in two ways, though not in its entirety. For even what has ceased may remain in force if the condition is observed. One thing ceased in its sentence, another in the Law itself.

When John preached a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins, the sentence of the Law that held sinners guilty ceased; the burdens of the Law also ceased—those imposed on account of the hardness of the Jewish heart concerning foods, new moons, sabbaths, and other matters. When mercy arrived, vengeance ceased.

The burdens of the Law, therefore, have ceased forever. Its sentence, however, ceases and is abolished for those who remain in the benefit they have received. For those who return to the old human being, the authority of the Law is renewed, since, forgetful of the benefits, they return under the sentence of the Law.

Circumcision and the sabbath remained valid until the commandment of the new Law was preached. They were given in such a way that, when the law of faith arrived, they would cease. Hence the Apostle says, “Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. X, 4).

Daniel also signifies this when he prophesies both the Lord’s coming and the times of the weeks: the anointing, the judgment, the sacrifice, and the city itself were all to cease (Dan. IX, 24–27).

When the spiritual Law arrived, therefore, it was necessary for carnal observances to cease. Formerly God was served in bodily form; now, in the soul. Formerly visibly; now invisibly. Then in the flesh; now in the mind. For God, who is spirit, must be served in spirit (John IV, 24).

The Law was not therefore abolished because it ceased; it was succeeded by another when its time had been fulfilled. Nor is its administration or judgment accused when indulgence is granted to sinners. Rather, it is shown to have been given rightly and justly, because those over whom it ruled are not denied to have been sinners. For, he says, “The Law is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. I, 9).

Let no one therefore think that, because mercy is to be preferred, justice should be despised. If justice were not held in reverence, mercy itself would bear no fruit. For unless they preserve justice after receiving mercy, indulgence will profit them nothing.

The Law says, “You shall not make an idol for yourself, nor worship what is above in heaven or what is below on earth”; and, “You shall not swear falsely”; and, “Honor your father and your mother”; and, “You shall not kill”; “Nor shall you commit adultery”; “Nor shall you steal”; “You shall not give false testimony”; “Nor shall you desire anything belonging to your neighbor” (Exod. XX, 4–17).

Can these commandments be said to have ceased? Certainly not. Without them, who could be judged worthy even in this life? Accordingly, the other things we mentioned above have ceased: new moons, sabbaths, the law of foods, sacrifices, circumcision, and so forth.

This is why the Apostle says, among other things, “Rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it” (Rom. XIII, 3).

When observed, these commandments make people good, though not perfect. Hence the Savior says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V, 20).

By adding better things to these commandments, the Savior certainly did not abolish the Law, but fulfilled it. The meaning of the Law pertains to human salvation. For example: “An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth” (Lev. XXIV, 20), so that a person, fearing that he might suffer what he had been forbidden to inflict on another, would restrain himself from wickedness.

The Savior, however, added a higher righteousness to this meaning, saying, “But I say to you, do not resist evil; rather, if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matt. V, 39), so that, by not returning evil for evil, a person might be perfect.

To return an equivalent is justice, but not complete justice. If, however, one overlooks the injury, that is complete and abundant justice. To repay is to rejoice for a time; to forgive, however, provides joy in the future.

Thus the Savior fulfilled the Law: those whom the Law taught justice, he made more just—something the Law itself could not do. Therefore the Law rejoices, because its disciples have become more learned.
