He would plainly have destroyed the Law if he had taught people to sin with impunity. Instead, he suspended its sentence, so that the one who does evil here might have time to repent. If he does not, the sentence returns upon him with greater force, because he did not understand that he had been released for the purpose of reforming himself.

[Note: [Col. 2264] The same question from second-class manuscripts, among those placed after the commonly published questions from the New Testament, the thirteenth.]

The sayings of the Prophets concerning the Savior’s coming were fulfilled when he came; for when what had been foretold has happened, it is regarded as fulfilled. The Law, however, which we have said was given for a time, ceased together with that period in which it was forbidden to transgress it; for what is fulfilled comes to an end. It would have lost its authority and appeared to have been destroyed if it had not ceased at the appointed time. For if a successor is given to someone holding office, is he therefore said to have been destroyed? The Law would truly have been destroyed if it were accused during the time in which it had force.

Moreover, he did not say that he had fulfilled the Law or the Prophets, but that he was fulfilling them. To fulfill means nothing other than to add fully. But what is it to add to the Prophets except to establish the worship of God under the name of the Trinity? Although the Prophets taught and rebuked the people in the name of God, this mystery nevertheless lay hidden.

To fulfill the Law, then, is to add new things to what has gone before while the earlier things remain. For example, he says: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, Do not resist evil; rather, if someone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also.” This was to fulfill it. He did not destroy it, but added better things—not so that the one who exacts vengeance might appear to sin, but so that the one who does not retaliate might be better. He therefore intended nothing other than what the Law contains in its meaning, but he perfects its purpose.

For since the Law taught a person righteousness and through it saved him, it commanded that if anyone removed another’s eye, he should lose his own eye, so that, terrified by this fear, people would not do what they did not want done to themselves, and through this might have salvation. But since the human race is frail and inclined to sin, it consequently happens that a person suffers what he does not wish to be done to himself.

Thus, by changing the wording, the Savior taught what would benefit salvation, [Col. 2265] so as to fulfill the meaning of the Law: because they could not be saved through fear of the Law, they might be corrected through the victory of patience, reforming themselves. This commandment was given so that they might not live insolently on the patience of good people, since the latter do not repay them what they deserve; so that, if they wish to be corrected, the good may derive benefit from this, while they receive a double punishment.

Righteousness, then, was not destroyed, as we see it also exercised through the Apostles. For the Apostle Peter maintained it in the case of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5:1–10). Nor did the chosen Vessel reject it, but he used it when he blinded Elymas the magician, who resisted the way of the Lord (ibid. 13:8–11).

There is also another way in which the Law was fulfilled. The Lord says: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’” This is justice. But the Lord says: “But I say to you, Love your enemies” (Matt. 5:43–44). He certainly adds something—and this is what it means to fulfill—for he did not destroy the old things, but, in order to make people perfect, commanded better things.

Since he could not correct and reform enemies—that is, evil people—through the repayment prescribed by justice, he wished them to be saved through love and service, which the Law also contained in its meaning. For the Law wished to remove hostility in such a way that people, terrified by retribution, would cease to be enemies. But because, in their boldness, people despised the fear of the Law and of nature and increased in evil, the Savior wished hostility to be conquered through humility, so that people might in this way be bent toward goodness when they saw that their hostility was not repaid. Those who nevertheless remained hostile would have to be treated more severely, because they had not been overcome even by the humility of the one whose retaliation they ought to have experienced.

Justice, then, was not blotted out in vengeance, but suspended for both purposes: it ceased with regard to the one who recognized himself; otherwise it would punish the obstinate.

### LXX

[Note: [Col. 2265] This question is absent from second-class manuscripts.]

The Lord certainly commanded us to become enemies of the devil. What, then, does it mean that he says in the Gospel, “Agree with your adversary quickly” (ibid. 5:25)? Who is a person’s adversary except the devil?

No one doubts that the devil is humanity’s enemy, especially the enemy of the faithful. For he sharpens his weapons more fiercely against God’s servants. Just as he is therefore the enemy of the good, so the Law is opposed to the wicked. For who would not oppose one who despises him?

The Lord therefore addresses the sinner, telling him to agree with the commandments that condemn him for disobedience, to submit himself to their will, and to become a friend from an enemy. For the despiser of the Law is also its enemy, since he resists its will.

Therefore the Lord urges the sinner, by doing good, to reconcile himself to the Law, lest on the day of judgment it accuse him before the Judge and, once condemned, he suffer the penalties of the Law he has despised. For, he says, to everyone who wishes to act wickedly the Lord’s discipline seems hostile. Unless he agrees with it, he will be sent into Gehenna, which has been prepared for the devil, who is truly the enemy of the human race.

### LXXI

Jacob was called “the man who sees God,” and Moses saw God face to face; Isaiah also says, “I saw the God of Sabaoth with my eyes.” John the Evangelist, on the other hand, says, “No one has ever seen God” (Gen. 32:28; Exod. 33:11; Isa. 6:5; 1 John 4:12). This appears, at least apparently, to be contradictory.

As far as the truth of the faith is concerned, no one has ever seen God at all, neither the Father nor the Son. When someone is said to have been seen, this refers to understanding: he was seen as in an image. Just as, when we do not know emperors personally, we see them in an image, not in reality, so God was seen in such a way that it was understood that the one appearing was God—through reason, not through substance—for God cannot be seen in his own nature.

And, to disclose more truly the hidden matter of the question proposed, let us attempt to explain the Evangelist’s meaning. John wished to reveal something hidden, which he knew belonged to salutary teaching. Therefore he says: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son, who is in the bosom of the Father; he himself has declared him.”

Let us observe the Evangelist’s meaning. To demonstrate that it is true that no one has ever seen God, he teaches that the Son declared this—one who certainly cannot be deceived, because he is in the bosom of the Father. What, then, is the bosom of the Father except the affection of the true Father, through the unity of nature, toward the Son?

Therefore no one has seen God except the one Son. The Apostle John heard the Son of God say this, among other things: “Not that anyone has seen the Father, except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.” Thus, in order to contribute to the condemnation of the Jews, who were unwilling either to hear or to believe that Christ was the Son of God, the Evangelist showed that this was the Christ who had appeared to the Fathers as God, [Note: [Col. 2266] “as God” is absent from second-class manuscripts.] whereas the one who is the Father had never been seen except by the Son.

For when he denies that God the Father has been seen, while confessing that God appeared to the Fathers, the Son of God wishes to make clear that he himself was always seen by the Fathers as God. Hence, among other things, he says to the Jews concerning the Father: “You have never heard his voice, nor have you seen his form” (John 5:37). Behold: it is not contradictory that God has both been seen and not been seen.

### LXXII

When it is read in John’s Apocalypse, “Go and take the book from the hand of the angel and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey” (Rev. 10:8–9), what is this book that makes the stomach bitter although it is sweet?

All the divine books are bitter—but only to the treacherous and the carnal. For it is unpleasant to idolaters when they hear that one God is proclaimed in Christ. Photinus also recoils in terror when he hears this. Sabellius is ashamed when he hears that the Father is one who cannot be called the Son, because all things are from him; whereas the Son is called Son precisely because he is not the Father himself, but is from the Father, and because all things are not from him but through him.

Arius too is refuted when he reads that Christ is truly the Son of God; for he could plainly not be called true unless he were properly from God. Marcion is also convicted when he learns that “the Word became flesh,” since he thinks that flesh must be denied to Christ. The wicked Manichaean is likewise reproved when he sees the Evangelist’s statement that the Savior not only honored the vows of marriage by his presence, but also dignified them with wine (John 2:1–11), whereas he bars the entrance to marriage and urges promiscuous intercourse.

These things are contained in the book which the Apostle was given to eat. This book is the Gospel entitled κατὰ Ἰωάννην (“According to John”), which is bitter not only to those who hold erroneous opinions, but also to the undisciplined, who refuse correction and therefore advance toward worse things.

This revelation was made at the time when the Apostle John was on the island of Patmos, exiled by the emperor Domitian on account of the faith. He was then in the Spirit, so that he could see heavenly things. While things were being shown to him—things that would occur on account of impiety, sexual immorality, and other offenses—the book was given to him. It was sweet in the mouth, but it made the stomach bitter. Thus, to those who appear to constitute one human body, [Note: [Col. 2266] The Colbert Manuscript reads, “to human beings who constitute one body.”] it was sweet; they are signified by the mouth because they belong to an undivided confession. For what is sweet in the mouth is that which is one. But to those who live or think carnally through heretical perversity—because they are signified by the stomach—it was bitter. For on the day of God’s judgment it will accuse them.

After the revelation, therefore, he was commanded to write the Gospel because of the things we have mentioned above. The prophet Ezekiel was likewise told to take a book that would be sweet in his mouth when he was sent to rebuke the people’s treachery (Ezek. 3:1).

[Note: [Col. 2266] The same question from second-class manuscripts, among those placed after the commonly published questions from the New Testament, the sixty-fifth.]

Frequently, the person who seeks brevity is accustomed to go astray. Why do you not set forth everything said for the matter at hand, but suppress certain things and thereby make the meaning more obscure? For John was told: “Go and take the book that is in the angel’s hand and eat it; it will be sweet in your mouth like honey, but it will make your stomach bitter.” And he says: “You must prophesy again before many peoples and nations.”

Therefore, insofar as concerns the truth of the matter, it is demonstrated that he wrote the Gospel after his exile. While he was in exile on the island of Patmos, to which he had been banished by the emperor Domitian, he saw the revelation, as he says, “on the Lord’s day.” Afterwards, as I said, he wrote the Gospel, which is bitter to heretics, whom he signified by the stomach. For they are carnal because they understand Christ wrongly.

As for the statement, “In your mouth it will be sweet like honey,” he makes one body of all Christians, so that each individual may be a member of the others. Thus, by the mouth—which is certainly a part of the head—he signifies those who are more honorable and more faithful, to whom the truth concerning Christ is sweet. By the stomach he signifies heretics, because they are carnal. For the truth that proclaims Christ the true God is bitter to them.

The whole Gospel of John is directed against heretics. Against Photinus, who denies that Christ existed before Mary, it proves that the Savior descended from heaven. Against Arius it shows that Christ has no beginning: “In the beginning was God, Christ the Son of God, with God the Father,” and because nothing was made without him, he cannot be called a creature. For if he were a creature, something would have been made without him; but since nothing existed without him, he always existed.

It refutes Sabellius, who understands the Father and the Son as a unity, so that one individual is called by two names, by saying: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice because I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). Here he manifested two persons, when the Son calls the Father greater. For a single individual cannot be greater than himself.

He also convicts Marcion, who denies Christ’s flesh. For he says: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (ibid. 1:14). By this same meaning he rebukes the Manichaean, who does not know that Christ came in the flesh and bars the entrance to marriage, unaware that the Savior honored the marriage feast.

In a similar way, the angel also told the prophet Ezekiel to take the scroll (Ezek. 3:1), eat it, and let it be sweet in his mouth but fill his stomach. This was said to the prophet when he was sent to rebuke a treacherous and undisciplined people, who were likewise signified by the stomach because they were carnal.

Among these are those whom Scripture, in the prophet Isaiah, calls “brothers,” although they are wicked. For it says: “You who fear God, say to those who hate you and do not heed my commandments, ‘You are our brothers’” (Isa. 66:5, according to the Septuagint).

### LXXIII

What does Simeon mean when, among other things, he says to Mary, the mother of the Lord: “Behold, this one is appointed for the fall and rising of many in Israel; and a sword,” he says, “will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed” (Luke 2:34–35)?

Simeon, a holy man commended by divine oracles, spoke through the Holy Spirit about what would happen to people because of Christ: he would be a fall for those who seemed to themselves to stand through observance and knowledge of the Law, but who would fall through disbelief in Christ’s works, having been severed from the promise made to the Fathers. But for those who possessed almost no standing in the Law, yet believed in Christ, he would be a resurrection in Israel.

[So that those who had previously been unworthy and useless might become worthy of God, while those who thought themselves to be something would be rejected. [Note: [Col. 2267] This passage is absent from second-class manuscripts.]]

This is what the Lord says elsewhere: “For judgment I have come into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39). In the end, it was not the teachers of the Law, nor the Pharisees, nor the scribes who followed Christ, but fishermen—uneducated and rustic men.

Hence the Lord says: “Father, I thank you because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and have revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11:25).

As for what he added, “And a sword will pass through your own soul, so that the thoughts of many hearts may be revealed,” this certainly signified that Mary too, through whom the mystery of the Savior’s incarnation had been accomplished, would doubt at the Lord’s death, yet in such a way that she would be strengthened by the honor and power of his resurrection.

For everyone doubted in a certain astonishment at the Lord’s death. Yet they did not remain in doubt. Thus the sword passes through the soul if doubt does not remain in the mind, but is driven away when its former strength returns and restores it.

[For who would not have hesitated on seeing the one who called himself the Son of God humbled so far as to descend even to death? And since, as I said, all uncertainty was to depart at the Lord’s resurrection, he said that the sword would pass through, not fall upon or touch some passing limb. Just as a sword hurled past a person produces fear but does not strike, so doubt would produce sorrow but would not kill, because it did not settle in the soul but passed through, touching the hearts of the disciples as if by a shadow.

Finally, Cleopas and another disciple, going to Emmaus, [Note: [Col. 2268] The Colbert Manuscript reads, “Cleopas and Amaus going.”] said to the Lord himself on the road, sadly and without knowing that he was the Lord: “We had hoped that he was the one who was beginning to redeem Israel” (Luke 24:21). They doubted, but as soon as they recognized the Lord, their doubt passed away. [Note: [Col. 2268] This passage is absent from second-class manuscripts.]]

It was also said of Joseph that “iron passed through his soul” (Ps. 104:18). Although he was innocent and had been held in prison for a long time, it is not surprising that he doubted concerning God’s judgment about him. But because he hoped in God more strongly, he did not remain in uncertainty.

A person is judged according to that toward which he is more inclined. John’s Apocalypse confirms this. For it says: “The portion of the doubtful and unbelieving will be in the lake of fire and sulfur” (Rev. 21:8). Therefore the one who does not remain in doubt is rescued from death. [Note: [Col. 2268] The remainder is absent from second-class manuscripts.] That is, he escapes death, because to doubt God or Christ is death. Consequently, whoever ceases to doubt escapes death.

### LXXIV

What does the prophet Isaiah mean when he says of Christ, “He committed no sin,” whereas the Apostle says, “He who knew no sin, he made sin for us” (Isa. 53:9; 2 Cor. 5:21)?

As far as the meaning is concerned, the questions are different, though the words are similar—similar in one respect and different in another. “He made” and “he did not make” are contrary; “he did not know” and “he did not commit” are similar.

The Prophet therefore spoke from the person of Christ: “He committed no sin, nor was deceit found in his mouth.” The Apostle, however, speaks of the person of God the Father, who made him—that is, Christ, who knew no sin—sin for us.

This should be understood in two ways. First, he made him sin when he willed him to become incarnate, so that he who was untouched by the lot of sin might receive a body from sinful flesh, through which he is said to have been made sin. Second, when he offered him for sins, he made him sin. For in the Law the victim offered for sins was called “sin.”

Christ therefore did not commit sin, as the Prophet says; rather, he himself was made sin by the Father, as has been shown.

But what does it mean to offer Christ for us except to give power to those who wished to kill him? This was permitted because it was to be beneficial: he would descend to the underworld in order to strip Tartarus of its souls. For it is an excessive and unheard-of sin to have killed one who not only had not sinned in any way, but had also given life to many. Having been made guilty of this sin, the devil lost the audacity to contradict.

A similar passage is read in the Epistle to the Galatians. Among other things, he says: “He was made a curse for us” (Gal. 3:13). By whom was he made one, except by the Father? By God’s judgment, the cross of Christ is the curse of the Jews, for the death of the Savior cries out against their sin.

He therefore permitted himself to be crucified so that his passion might benefit us, and so that, going forth from this life with his sign, we might not be held by the second death. For death fears even the servants of him by whom it was conquered.

[Note: [Col. 2268] The same question from second-class manuscripts, among those placed after the commonly published questions from the New Testament, the fortieth.]

As far as the matter proposed is concerned, not only do the words differ, but the persons are also different. “He made” and “he did not make” are contrary. But since the one who is denied to have made him is not understood to be the one who made him, this cannot be called contradictory.

The Prophet’s statement concerns the person of Christ, whereas the Apostle’s concerns the person of the Father. For God the Father reconciled the world to himself through Christ, and thus it happened that he made him—that is, Christ—sin.

To make him sin means to place him in the virgin’s womb, so that he might be born as a human being and, in respect of the flesh, be made sin, because flesh is sinful—this being the human being whom neither lot nor condition touched. For this purpose he was born: to be offered as a sacrifice for sinners.

He is therefore said to have been made sin because, according to the Law, the victim offered for sins was called “sin.”

There is a similar passage elsewhere in the Apostle, where he says of the Savior to the Galatians, “He was made a curse for us.” The meaning is the same: he was made sin, or a curse, for our sake by God the Father, who permitted him to be killed by the Jews, so that they might be deprived on account of their unbelief and we might be brought into their place, as the Savior says: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21:43).

For everything God permits is said to be done by him, because if he did not permit it, it would not happen. Hence the Lord says to Pilate: “You would have no power over me unless it had been given to you from above” (John 19:11).

Therefore, it is not by actively bringing about but by permitting that he is said to give power. When an evil mind receives power to carry out its will, it becomes guilty—as did the Jews, who, by killing the Savior, made him their curse by God’s judgment.

For the Savior’s cross is the curse of the Jews. It was not like the victim offered for sins, which cleansed the one making the offering. Rather, the Savior, once offered, became the stain and sin of those who offered him. The justification, however, belongs to those who dissent from them, so that the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus. For the Jews’ offering benefited the Gentiles who did not withdraw from faith in Jesus Christ.

### LXXV

Why did the Savior pay the didrachma for himself and Peter alone, and not also for the other Apostles (Matt. 17:26)? Since all of them had followed him after abandoning all their possessions, it would seem that he ought to have paid for all of them.

The didrachma is understood as a tax imposed per head, not on landed property [which is now called “ragged gold,” because even the poor are assessed. [Note: [Col. 2269] This passage is absent from the Colbert Manuscript.]] For the Savior possessed nothing in the world, although he is the Lord of the world. He is buried at the expense of others, while we, for whom the world is foreign, wish to increase our possessions, so that when we die we may testify—not only by word but also in writing—that we have invaded the world, and by our own confession be condemned by the one whose world it is.

Hence the Lord says: “Whoever does not abandon all his possessions and follow me cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14:26).

[Whoever therefore possesses his goods in such a way that he places no hope in them, but is ready to cast them away for the faith, walks the road that leads to Christ our Lord. [Note: [Col. 2269] This passage is absent from second-class manuscripts.]]

The didrachma, then, was to be exacted from those who conducted some business or practiced some trade. Since the Savior concerned himself with none of these things, nor did his disciples, it should not have been demanded from them.

But because the hostile devil was always lying in wait, seeking an opportunity, if possible, to bring down the Savior, he occupied the minds of the collectors of the didrachma, so that they would do his will. They approached Peter, who was first among the Apostles, and said that their master, who was free from such burdens, ought to pay the didrachma.

For they were doing nothing in the world that belonged to the world. Since there was no source from which he could pay, he might either become a stumbling block to them or, through the humility of requesting assistance, seek someone from whom the money could be obtained.

Then, to show that the careless devil was always plotting against himself, the Lord commanded the Apostle Peter to go to the sea, open the mouth of the fish he caught, and find there the coin owed for the tax.

[Note: [Col. 2269] Second-class manuscripts add: “since he had entrusted the care of the household to him.”]

[Col. 2270] Once it had been paid, there would not only be no scandal for the collectors, nor would the Savior be brought low by seeking the required assistance; he would also demonstrate a great sign of power. Through it he would draw to himself those captured by the devil, so that the devil would be tormented by his own argument and cunning.

The collectors of the didrachma therefore say to the Apostle Peter, “Does your teacher not pay the didrachma?” and so forth. By saying this, they summoned the master to pay on behalf of all the disciples.

But when the Savior commands payment for himself and Peter, he appears to have paid for all, because just as all were included in the Savior on account of his status as teacher, so after the Savior all are included in Peter. For he appointed him as their head, to be the shepherd of the Lord’s flock. [Note: [Col. 2270] Second-class manuscripts read: “For he left him as shepherd after himself, to be the shepherd of the Lord’s flock.”]

Among other things, he says to the disciples: “Watch and pray, lest you enter into temptation” (Matt. 26:41). And he says to Peter: “Behold, Satan demanded to sift you all as wheat; but I prayed for you, that your faith may not fail. And you, when you have turned again, strengthen your brothers” (Luke 22:31–32).

What is there to question? Was he praying for Peter but not for James and John, to say nothing of the others? It is clear that all are contained in Peter: by praying for Peter, he is recognized as having prayed for all.

For the people are always either rebuked or praised in their leader. Elsewhere also he says: “I pray for those whom you have given me, Father; and I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17:9, 24).

### LXXVI

John says in the Gospel: “The Law was given through Moses; grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (ibid. 1:17). Therefore grace and truth did not exist previously. How, then, is the Law said to have been given by God, when it contained no truth?

This must not be passed over casually; rather, we must consider what it means. “The Law was given through Moses.” Through Moses the Law was given with commandments that are clear; but he also wrote history, which is itself called the Law.

Let us see what in its commandments is not true. Perhaps what it says, “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal” (Exod. 20:13–15)? And the other commandments are of the same kind.

As for its history, however, it is clear that before Christ’s coming its truth was not present. For what the things hidden under a veil signified was uncertain. But when it was revealed through Christ whose person it was that said in Genesis, “Let us make a human being according to our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26), and who it was that made him; and who it was that was seen by the Patriarchs in the bush (Exod. 3:2); and who worked in the rock that gave water in the desert—for he says, “The rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10:4)—then truth came through Christ, when Christ showed what the things that had been hidden or called into question signified.

Among other things, the Lord says: “Moses wrote about me” (John 5:46). This had previously remained hidden; error prevailed. For the one who was the Son was thought to be God the Father, and the one who was considered an angel was recognized as the Son of God.

A promise had also been made to Abraham. As long as it was not fulfilled, it remained uncertain; but when it was fulfilled at Christ’s coming, it became truth—when both what had been promised was given and it began to be known what had been promised. For the faithfulness of the one who makes a promise is then shown to be true when he fulfills the promise.

[Note: [Col. 2270] The same question from second-class manuscripts, among those placed after the commonly published questions from the New Testament, the thirtieth.]

We must see what is meant by “The Law was given through Moses.” The Law given through Moses contains clear commandments; and what is not true in it? “You shall not kill”; “you shall not commit adultery”—and the other commandments are of the same kind.

But he also wrote history in which, until the Savior’s coming, what the truth was had not been revealed. When, therefore, it is revealed through Christ whose person says, “Let us make,” and who it is that makes; and who it was that appeared in the bush or to the Patriarchs; and who worked in the rock when he himself produced the water—for he says, “The rock was Christ”—then truth comes through Christ, when what the things that had been in doubt signify is understood.

Thus the Law given through Moses made sinners guilty; [Col. 2271] but the grace promised in the Law, when it came, deprived sinners of death by forgiving their sins. The order, therefore, was first to give the Law and afterward mercy, which then becomes grace when it forgives sins.

Previously there was a promise, which afterward becomes grace. For he says: “From Zion the one who rescues and turns ungodliness away from Jacob will come” (Isa. 59:20, according to the Septuagint). This promise became grace through Christ, when he freely forgives sins.

But how could he forgive sins if he had not first given the Law, through which he would grant forgiveness to those made guilty? For he would give only what was owed to him. But it could not be owed unless the Law had preceded it.

### LXXVII

What does Mark the Evangelist mean when he says of Christ: “Entering a house, he wanted no one to know, and he could not remain hidden” (Mark 7:24)? If he both wanted this and could not accomplish it, his will appears to have been weakened.

It is utterly impossible that the Savior’s will should not be fulfilled. Nor can he wish for something that he knows ought not to happen. Therefore, what happened must be said to be what he willed. His will is never outside his nature. Just as his nature cannot be reproached, neither can his will.

The event proposed is recorded as having taken place in the territory of Tyre. He entered a house and wanted no one to know. The question now is how or why he wanted no one to know.

It must be observed that this occurred in the territory of the Gentiles, to whom it was not yet time to preach. Indeed, when sending out his disciples he commanded them: “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter the cities of the Samaritans; but go rather to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:5–6).

Therefore he did not want it to be disclosed by his own people that he was in the house. But he did not refuse to be sought; rather, he willingly received those who came. Although it was not yet time to preach to the Gentiles, it would nevertheless have been envy not to receive those who came of their own accord to the faith.

Thus it happened that, while the Savior did not have his presence in the house disclosed by his disciples, he was nevertheless disclosed by others who had seen him enter. It began to be known that he was in the house, so that those who wished to obtain his benefits might enter.

He therefore did not want his own people to announce that he was in the house. He did want to be sought, and this happened. For he did not remain hidden once others had shown that he was in the house.

Finally, when the Canaanite woman heard about him, she entered and begged him to drive the demon out of her daughter. Unless she had first submitted herself to the God of the Jews, she would not have obtained the benefit.

The Savior’s will, therefore, was fulfilled according to the explanation we have given. When we examine what the Evangelist, intent on brevity, compressed, we discover what had been hidden.

[Note: [Col. 2271] The same question from second-class manuscripts, among those placed after the commonly published questions from the New Testament, the twenty-fifth.]

The abbreviated form of the question conceals more of its meaning. The event is recorded as having taken place in the territory of Tyre, because when the Savior reached the territory of Tyre, he entered a house.

And because it was not yet appropriate to preach to the Gentiles, he ordered no one to announce his arrival to anyone. This is what is meant by “he wanted no one to know”: he did not want his own people to announce to anyone that he was in the house.

He did not wish to be sought, because it was not yet time to offer grace to the Gentiles. Finally, a woman came, having learned from others who had seen him enter the house, and begged him to drive the demon out of her daughter.

But the Savior, knowing that it was not yet time to give grace freely to the Gentiles, said: “Let the children first be satisfied; for it is not right to take the children’s bread and throw it to the dogs.”

Then the woman agreed with the Savior’s words and received the benefit she desired. By agreeing, she joined herself to the God of the Jews.

For this reason he did not want his presence in the house to become known through his own people, and thus it happened as he wished.

### LXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2271] This question is absent from second-class manuscripts.]

It is read in John’s Gospel that, when the Savior had denied that he would go up to the feast, he went up (John 7:8, 14). This appears to be the behavior of an inconsistent person.

You always conceal the meaning by abridging the proposition. For the event you call into question happened when he was in Galilee and, because of the disturbance among the Jews, was being urged by his brothers—who still did not believe in him—to go up to Judea, since the feast of the Jews was approaching and he was to suffer sedition.

He answered them: “You go up to this feast, because the world does not hate you; but it hates me, because I testify against its works. I am not going up to this feast, because my time has not yet been fulfilled.”

Then his brothers went up to the feast, while he remained in Galilee. Afterwards he too went up to the feast.

What contradiction is there, when he did not go up at the time he denied that he would, but went up afterward—and went up not as though to a feast, but as though to a conflict? They all went up joyfully, as if to enjoy the pleasures of the feast.

It is therefore certain that he did not go up to the feast. For the Savior, that was the feast day on which, through his passion, he redeemed the world. Hence he says: “Now the Son of Man has been glorified, and God has been glorified in him” (John 13:31). This is his feast day, on which he conquered death.

### LXXIX

[Note: [Col. 2272] The author of this and the following question appears to incline toward Pelagianism.]

If we live by our own free choice, why did the Savior say, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (ibid. 6:44)? And the Apostle, agreeing with this, says: “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”; and, “He has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens” (Rom. 9:16, 18). How is the freedom of the will genuine when a person is led by another’s will either toward good or toward evil?

The matter is otherwise than it has been stated. For this question does not mean what you claim. For in no way can the case for free will be disturbed by these passages; indeed, if you attend carefully to the meaning of what was said, you will know that the position of free will is rather strengthened by them.

These words were spoken against the malicious Jews. For when, through deceitful pretense arising from envy, they asserted that Joseph was the Savior’s own father and that his sons were the Savior’s brothers, so that he might not be believed to be the Son of God, the Savior then said: “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.” But how did the Father draw people to the Son except through the works that he performed through him? For he says: “The Father who remains in me, he himself does the works” (John 14:10), so that these works might draw people to faith in Christ.

The miracles that the Savior performed themselves persuaded people that God was Christ’s Father, so that one who said Christ had another father would not be drawn by God to Christ. God therefore worked through Christ so that faith might be given to his words, in which he said that he was the Son of God. This is attraction—not compulsion, but God’s testimony in Christ; and whoever believed in him is said to have been drawn by him to Christ. For no one believes the Savior except one who says that his Father is God.

The Apostle did not say the things you have brought back into question in order to strike at free will, but to prevent God’s judgment from being challenged. He proclaimed God to be just, for God knows whom he ought to pity. The examiner of the heart perceives the mind of the one asking, whether that person deserves to receive. Hence he says through the prophet: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isaiah 29:13).

It is therefore just that the heart of a pretender be hardened. For whoever, not through error but through malice, calls what is true false—who, while understanding what is good, pretends not to know what is good in order to turn it into evil—ought to be dealt with in such a way that he truly does not understand the good, lest he be saved when he does not wish to be saved. Nor is it just that one be saved against his will who rejects salvation not through ignorance but through malice or envy. These considerations therefore confirm free will rather than destroy it, so that each person receives an answer according to his own choice.

*[Note: [Col. 2272] This same question, from manuscripts of the second class, is listed among those published later from the New Testament as question thirty-two.]*

In no way can the case for free will be disturbed by these passages. For if you relate the statements to the matter about which they were spoken, you will know that the position of free will is rather strengthened by them.

*[Col. 2273]* When the Jews, out of the deliberate malice of their opposition, said about the Savior, “Is this not the son of Joseph, whose father we know? How then does this man say, ‘I have come down from heaven’?” Jesus answered: “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him.”

Now we must consider how the Father draws. Let the Savior’s own word be taken: “The works that I do, the Father does.” “Believe that I am in the Father and the Father in me.” If, then, the Father works in the Son, while the works invite people to faith, he rightly said that no one comes to him except the one whom the Father has drawn. He draws when he works through the Son.

For how does one who wishes to be believed remove the will of free choice? And how does one who reproves the unbeliever draw someone unwilling? He said this, of course, to the Jews, who claimed that the Savior had another father than the one who truly is his Father. For no one believes the Savior except one who says that his Father is God.

The Apostle likewise did not say the things now proposed in order to strike at free will, but to show that God’s judgment is just, since he cannot be mistaken in granting or withholding mercy. One person asks and does not deserve to receive; another asks and deserves to receive. The latter entreats not with words alone but with deeds, while the former does so only with his tongue; the latter does so with a contrite heart, and such a person can obtain what he asks.

Finally, what is said in the Law? “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” If, then, two people ask and only one of them receives, it must be understood that the one who received asked in such a way as to be worthy of receiving, because God, who is just, gives only to one whom he knows should be given what is requested. You see, therefore, that free choice was not denied but strengthened. For if you heard two people asking with one mind and one action, and saw one of them heard while the other was disregarded, you would rightly conclude both that there was no free choice and that God was a respecter of persons.

### LXXX

Certainly every person is either a son of God or a son of the devil; therefore he is always a son—at one time of God, at another of the devil. We must therefore inquire what we are born as.

When the children of Israel repeatedly sinned after being led out of Egypt, the Lord became angry and pronounced that none of them would enter the promised land except Caleb and Joshua son of Nun, who had previously been called Auses. But he said that those who had been born in the wilderness would enter, because they did not know good or evil.

Not knowing good or evil is a kind of natural simplicity, which has not been instructed in evil. This is ignorance without malice. We are born without understanding, but our nature has this good quality: it is capable of learning the truth.

A son of the devil, however, is one who, having been born and imbued with evil practices, devotes himself to things hostile to the Creator, asserting that there are many gods and that sacrifices must be offered to them as rulers of the world. If such a person comes to his senses and thinks according to his nature, turning himself toward the Creator, he will be a son of God.

Accordingly, those who are born are neither sons of God nor sons of the devil. For what does the Savior say to the Jews? “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires” (John 8:44). You see, therefore, that sons of the devil are made so by their works and profession; while those are sons of God who confess that God is properly the Father of Christ and conduct themselves rightly.

God established our race in such a way that we are born without understanding, yet have the possibility of learning either good or evil, so that we ourselves may acquire either evil or good; so that we may rejoice in ourselves when, acting rightly, we are rewarded, or blame ourselves when, following wicked things, we are condemned.

*[Note: [Col. 2273] This same question, from manuscripts of the second class, is listed among those published later from the New Testament as question forty-one.]*

When the children of Israel repeatedly sinned after being led out of Egypt, the Lord became angry and allowed none of them to enter the promised land except Caleb and Joshua son of Nun. But he said that their children, who had been born in the wilderness, would enter, because they did not know good or evil.

Not knowing good or evil is a certain natural simplicity that has not been instructed either in good or in evil—that is, ignorance without malice. We are born without understanding, but our nature is capable of learning the truth.

A son of the devil is one who, having been born and imbued with evil practices, devotes himself to things opposed to the Creator, saying that there are many gods and that sacrifices must be offered to them as rulers of the world. If such a person comes to his senses, returns to natural justice, and receives faith in Christ, he will be a son of God. Accordingly, those who are born are neither sons of God nor sons of the devil.

For what does the Savior say to the Jews? “You have been born from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires.” You see, therefore, that sons of the devil are brought forth by works and profession.

God established our race in such a way that, although born without understanding, we can nevertheless be instructed in either direction, so that we ourselves in some sense become the authors of good or evil for ourselves: that we may rejoice in ourselves when, acting rightly, we are rewarded, or blame ourselves when, following wicked things, we are subjected to punishments.

For this reason he left us to our own judgment, so that we would neither complain about evils nor rejoice vainly about ourselves if we are crowned, just as through faith people become sons of God. God, the creator and author of our substance, willed that we should possess something properly our own, so that we might not boast undeservedly about the faith we have in God. For whoever is not master of his own power—whatever he possesses belongs to another—cannot boast about good things or be held guilty for evil ones.

### LXXXI

The Apostle says, “We are Jews by nature” (Galatians 2:15). He therefore shows that Jews are born from Jews; I am not speaking of proselytes, who are plainly made Jews. Indeed, those who were born in the wilderness were not circumcised, and yet they were Jews. Circumcision, therefore, does not make a Jew; rather, it is birth produced under devotion to God the Creator. If Jews are born from Jews, why are Christians not also born from Christians? For Pagans too are born from Pagans.

Not everything that is born is identical with that from which it is born. Gold is born from the earth, yet it is not earth; likewise gems and many other things. Food is produced from wood, and a chick from an egg.

The reason Pagans are born as Pagans is that every Pagan is in ignorance, and one who is born from such a person is without understanding; both are ignorant. But there is this difference between them: the one who begets is undoubtedly a blasphemer and therefore is a son of the devil, whereas the infant who is born does not know how to blaspheme, just as he does not know how to bless. Nevertheless, he is a Pagan because he is without understanding.

A Jew is born a Jew because he is generated under devotion to the Creator. As Adam said concerning Cain, “I have produced a man through God” (Genesis 4:1). Just as Pagans, who are not devoted to the Creator, give thanks to demons for everything they do, so Jews, as suppliants of God the Creator, praise him in all their actions. They are blameworthy in this respect: they do not know Christ, through whom all things exist.

In this way, too, a Jew is born from a Jew. It is not, as some think, because circumcision makes a Jew. Circumcision is a sign of Judaism, not Judaism itself. For Abraham’s circumcision is not righteousness but a sign of righteousness, so that those born from Abraham might possess a sign by which they could be shown to be Abraham’s sons.

Indeed, they were called by this name from Judah Maccabee, so that not only those descended from Judah but also the others descended from all the sons of Jacob would be called Jews, because Judah had been their leader. Thus those born Jews receive the sign, so that those who are Jews may be recognized.

A Christian is not born from a Christian because the one who begets was not born a Christian but became a Christian. Therefore the one who is born from him must also become a Christian. He is not born through substance but through faith, which is added to those already born. Ignorance is born along with the flesh, but faith is afterward implanted through spiritual understanding.

But someone may object: “If the one who begets has indeed been made a Christian, he ought already to beget what he himself is, so that the dignity he has received may be transmitted. Senators beget senators.”

Yet the dignity of senators has no merit before God. Nor does nature itself—that is, substance—receive the benefit; rather, the dignity exists only in reputation and speech. Accordingly, the reputation passes through the transmission of the flesh, but it contributes nothing except an opinion of dignity, just as those who are consuls or are honored with statues take pleasure in vanity.

When Christians are made, however, dignity is added to nature itself, so that the very essence of the human being may possess the eternal benefit of incorruptibility. Thus it is not merely an opinion but a reality in its effect before God.

This is like the case of an eloquent poor man who is praised but lacks bread and other necessities. True praise would be present if the dignity he had acquired benefited him so far that he lacked nothing—if this were granted to his nature so that he could live by himself and live well without seeking anyone’s support. That is, he would truly become rich and glorious.

*[Note: [Col. 2275] This same question, from manuscripts of the second class, is listed among those published later from the New Testament as question fifty-six.]*

Not everything that is born is identical with that from which it is born. For gold is born from the earth, and so forth. Yet he is a Pagan because he is without understanding, possessing neither merit of his own nor another’s.

A Jew is born a Jew for the reason already given, and so forth.

But someone may object: “If the one who begets has indeed been made a Christian, he ought to beget what he himself is, so that the dignity he has received may now be transmitted—just as among the Jews, because Abraham was made a worshiper of God from a Pagan, and the origin of the Jews came from him; and just as those who have been made senators already beget senators.”

Yet the dignity of senators has no merit before God, nor does nature itself—that is, substance—receive the benefit. Rather, the dignity exists only in reputation and speech; consequently, reputation passes through the transmission of the flesh, contributing nothing except an opinion of worldly dignity.

Why a Jew is born from a Jew has already been said. But when a Christian is made, the dignity of the good is added to nature itself, so that the substance constituting the human being receives the benefit, so that it is not merely an opinion but also a reality in its effect before God.

Finally, once the remission of sins has been received, the whole human being is purified, so that he is also adopted as a son by God. Therefore all who are born must be reborn, because God’s mercy gives grace to each person individually. For one person cannot receive remission on behalf of another.

The soul that is born in the body, or with the body, is subject to the death discovered by Adam; unless it receives the sign of conquered death, it does not escape Tartarus, the underworld. Each person receives the benefit for himself, not also for one who does not yet exist.

If a person who had been made a Christian were already immortal, then someone born from him would rightly be what the parent is. Those who become Christians receive the sign so that they will not be held by the second death; nevertheless, they do not escape the present death that Adam discovered.

Infants are therefore baptized, although they are innocent, so that the unformed soul born in the body may possess the sign of conquered death and may not be held by it. Abraham did not have this sign, nor did the prophets, because their time had not yet arrived. It was reserved for the Son of God, who, when he came, would conquer death and grant this grace to believers.

Hence the Lord says to the Jews: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56). For Abraham knew that Christ had been promised for the liberation of the human race, and that it was always necessary for his coming to be awaited by those held in the underworld. When he saw in the spirit that Christ had been born, he rejoiced, certain that he would soon be rescued from the underworld and brought into heaven.

How, then, should Christians be born from Christians, when one who has not believed or has not been baptized will not be a Christian?

### LXXXII

There is no doubt that Pagans are subject to the elements. What, then, does the Apostle mean when he says, “We too were slaves under the elements of this world” (Galatians 4:3)? If the Jews too were servants of the elements, how did they differ from Pagans?

It is clear that the meaning can be perverted by the addition, subtraction, or alteration of a single syllable. Everyone knows that Pagans worship the elements; but the Jews served God, not the elements, while being under the elements, because of new moons, Sabbaths, circumcision, and other such practices. For these things are carnal. Whatever is visible is carnal and belongs to the elements.

But because these practices were commanded by God, God was being served, so that people might pass from visible things to invisible things, and by this progress become capable of grasping greater matters, so that, trained through these practices, they might become worthy of spiritual promises.

Accordingly, in the respect I mentioned above, the Jews served while under the elements; in another respect they possessed a spiritual law, which both forbids sin and exhorts them to love the Lord God, who had been promised to come to them to forgive sins.

*[Col. 2276]* Pagans do not serve while under the elements but serve the elements themselves. They worship the stars, the sun, the moon, and the constellations—these in the firmament; below, the earth and water; in the sea, Neptune; in the underworld, Pluto. They openly worship the world’s creation, having passed over the Creator.

The Jews, however, served God while under the elements in this way, because he himself had given these commandments. They observe new moons, Sabbaths, and sacrifices of animals. At the beginning of the seventh month they sound the trumpet; on the fifteenth day of the seventh month they carry the marrow of palms, thick branches of trees, and willow branches, and dwell in booths for seven days.

In observing these things, they are rightly said to have served while under the elements, for these things come from the elements.

Christians, however, serve God not under the elements but above the elements, hastening toward the heavenly Jerusalem. They worship God in spirit, not in visible and worldly things; they possess the worship of God in the soul and serve the invisible One invisibly, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming when true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23).

This, then, is the truth: to serve God in spirit, in the soul more than in the body; and since God is spirit, to honor him spiritually.

The Apostle says that the Jews were subject under the elements in the respect I have mentioned above. In another respect, however, the Law had a spiritual meaning: it prohibited sin, commanded that the Lord be loved with all the heart, and taught them to have hope in Christ.

But when the Apostles preached these things, the Jews defended more strongly what had been given in carnal form. The Apostle recalls these matters in order to expose the Jews, who, while disparaging the spiritual Law, were subject to visible things. He also indicates that these things were truly weak in comparison with the law of faith, even introducing the person of one who had been particularly their partisan.

After coming to know Christ, he judged these things contemptible, because the grace of God through Christ differs greatly from the law of works.

### LXXXIII

If salvation and true and perfect knowledge come through Christ, why did he not come earlier, so that our predecessors, who were in ignorance, might learn the truth? After Christ’s coming, many were saved—more than before. Therefore, if he had come earlier, many more would have been saved. If this is so, it appears blameworthy.

No one ought to bring an accusation against one who shows mercy. For it is in the power of the giver to have mercy whenever and upon however many he wishes. A person of this kind should be encouraged and moved by prayers, not driven away from a good work by argument.

Perhaps no objection would be made if, for this mercy, some return were made to him. Would anyone accuse a physician who freely supplies his medicines and his services? Or would his delay be blamed by those who did not ask for him?

We have spoken thus according to reason, but the Savior’s goodness does not take such things into account, because of human weakness. He follows his own nature in showing mercy. He therefore came when he ought to come, following the rationale of his own will, not our merits. For if you weigh our merits, he ought not to have come.

He came, therefore, when he knew that help ought to be given and that the benefit would be appreciated. If assistance is given beforehand to someone threatened by necessity, it will indeed be appreciated, but he will not be able to understand very well what has been done for him. If, however, you bring help to someone placed in the midst of necessity, he will know what sort of benefit he has received.

A person rescued from trouble will give greater thanks—just as when you offer bread to someone who is hungry; if you offer it when he is not hungry, it will certainly not be as welcome. It was therefore rightly done that the Lord did not come earlier.

First, he left the human race to use its own will, not without testimony to himself. For through the very structure of the world, and through the annual gifts that he decreed should be supplied for human use by the ministry of the elements, he wished his divinity to be understood and feared.

Knowledge of him also existed on earth through the lineage of the first man, and afterward through Enoch and Noah. But when, through a certain weakness of the human race, knowledge of God among human beings began to fade and customs changed, he was pleased to choose Abraham, in whom there might be a pattern of renewed knowledge of God and renewed conduct.

When reverence was still too sluggish, he later gave the Law through Moses in writing, so that it would neither grow obsolete nor fail to inspire fear. Fear is greater where authority is manifest.

And because the nations despised the Law they had received, refusing to submit to it, while those who had received it did not keep it, the Lord, moved by mercy, sent his Son. Offering himself for them, destroying death, and granting forgiveness of sins to all, he offered them justified to God the Father.

For he could not descend to the underworld except through death. Neither order nor reason required one who had not died to enter the gates of Tartarus.

If someone wishes to deceive barbarians in their own country, does he not change his clothing so that he may be thought one of them, and thus investigate how to overthrow them? The same thing happened with the devil. Because he had overthrown the human being by evil practice, a remedy was found so that the human being would not remain in death: those whom he held wrongly might be lost to him, and entry might be gained against him. The one whom he thought he had killed as a human being, he discovered in the underworld to be God.

When this had happened, he was found guilty and lost all whom he held; thereafter the way to heaven was opened.

See how much the Savior’s coming accomplished, so that people, knowing from what danger they had been freed, might give him thanks without ceasing.

But perhaps someone may object: “If many before and after the Law, oppressed by sins, gave themselves entirely to the flesh and were worthy to remain in Tartarus, there were certainly some who restrained their lives through devotion and reverence for the Creator according to the law of nature. Were even these, when stripped of this life, not held in the underworld? If Christ had come earlier, after Adam’s death, he could have freed Adam, who had sinned first, and opened the way to heaven for the others, so that those who had lived well, having recognized the Creator, might be received into heaven after death. Is it therefore a loss that Christ did not come earlier?”

It is plainly a loss, but ask whether it is just or unjust. Losses can be just, and one may not complain about them. When a thief is caught and condemned under the law to repay fourfold, does he dare to complain?

Accordingly, the loss suffered by the human race was justly inflicted, and therefore it was permitted. The Savior therefore ought not to have come at the very beginning.

For when the devil became proud, the human being made by God was placed as his enemy, so that, protected by God’s help, he might resist him, although he was unequal to him, after receiving the command.

But the devil, with his customary cunning, pretended not to know what God had commanded, and found Eve unstable. Then, promising her that if they touched what had been forbidden he would grant them divinity, he deceived them.

The devil then triumphed over the defeated human being; and the defeated human being subjected his race to sin. Therefore it would have been unjust to take the spoils violently from the victor, because whatever God does, he does justly.

Moreover, since the human being sinned grievously by consenting to become God against the Creator’s command, he committed idolatry, thereby sinning against God. Therefore he ought not to have been helped immediately, since he had neither repented nor would mercy have been welcome to him if he had not known what he deserved.

Although God can do all things, he does what accords with reason, so that he may remain beyond reproach.

*[Note: [Col. 2277] The Colbert manuscript reads “expuncti” (“erased”) instead of the preceding form.]*

*[Note: [Col. 2277] This same question, from manuscripts of the second class, is listed among those published later from the New Testament as question fifty-eight.]*

If assistance is given beforehand to someone threatened by necessity, it will indeed be appreciated, but he will not be able to understand very well what has been done for him. If, however, you bring aid to someone placed in the midst of necessity, he will know what sort of benefit he has received. For one rescued from trouble gives greater thanks—just as when you offer bread to someone who is hungry; but if you offer something to one who is not hungry, what gratitude will there be?

It was therefore rightly done that the Lord did not come earlier.

First, he left the human race to use its own will, not without testimony to himself, because through the very structure of the world, by means of the annual gifts that he decreed should be supplied for human use through the ministry of the elements, he wished his divinity to be known and feared.

Afterward, when knowledge of God on earth began to fade and customs changed, he was pleased to visit the human race, so that, by giving or restoring the Law—for it existed in nature but had begun to be neglected—he might restore both knowledge of himself and the authority of the Law. Once God had been recognized and the Law recalled, people would begin to fear, certain that the one who gave the Law would judge human actions.

And because, although they could have done so, they were unable to restrain themselves from sins after receiving the Law, even though they had long been admonished through the prophets, God, moved by mercy, sent his Son. Offering himself for them, destroying death, and granting them forgiveness of sins, he offered them justified to God the Father, so that, knowing from what danger they had been rescued, they might give thanks to God without ceasing—even if necessity required them to pour out their blood for him, and yet they would not claim that they had repaid him in full.

How welcome and precious, therefore, do they consider the benefit that they do not think it can be repaid even by death?

But perhaps someone may object: “If many before the Law and after the Law, oppressed by sins, gave themselves entirely to the flesh, there were certainly some who, devoted to God the Creator, restrained themselves from vices. Come, then: were these, when erased from life, not also descended into the underworld? If Christ had come earlier, after Adam’s death, he could have freed Adam, who was held by his own sin, from death, and made a path to heaven for the others who believed, so that those who had lived well here might, as grateful to the Creator and Restorer, be received into heaven after death. Is it therefore a loss that Christ did not come earlier?”

It is plainly a loss. But ask whether it is just or unjust. Losses can be just. When a thief is caught and condemned under the law to repay fourfold, does he not suffer a loss? Yet it is just; and thus the loss that the human race suffered arose justly and was therefore permitted.

The Savior therefore ought not to have come at the very beginning.

For when the devil became proud and the human being, made by God, was set as his enemy, the human being was to resist him, protected by God’s help, although inferior in strength, after receiving the command to display on earth the image of the one God, so that error might be removed through the fact that one was made from one, from whom the others descended.

But the devil, with his customary cunning, pretended not to know what God had commanded. He found Eve unstable and afterward promised them that if they tasted what had been forbidden they would become gods; thus he deceived them.

So the devil triumphed after defeating the human being, and the defeated human being sold his race into sin. It was therefore not just to take the spoils violently from the victor at once, because whatever God does, he does justly.

Moreover, since the human being sinned grievously—for by consenting to become God he committed idolatry, that is, he sinned against God—he ought not immediately to have been helped, since he had not repented.

Afterward Satan inflicted many evils on the just: Job, Joseph, Jeremiah, Isaiah, Zechariah, and the other prophets and righteous people. Therefore Christ was entrusted by God his Father with the task of conquering him and revealing himself, taking away his kingdom through reason, not power. Although God can do all things, he does what accords with reason, so that he may remain beyond reproach.

### LXXXIV

Why, when we observe the course of the moon in determining Easter, do we criticize Pagans because they observe lunar days and the moon’s movement?

Far be it from Christians to be said to venerate the stars, since they have been granted spiritual worship, so that, despising the things that are seen, they may be joined to things invisible and above the heavens, and, in the future, transcend all these things together with the angels of God.

For those who worship the stars will either be with the stars themselves or beneath them. How could anyone be above the things he worships?

Pagans, therefore, do not observe the moon’s calculation but venerate the moon itself as a goddess. Thinking that they have grasped the effects of its courses, they decide what must be done or avoided on particular days, subjecting their life and conduct to its rule according to a certain order. Because they have dared to usurp these matters outside God’s ordinance, we frequently find them deceived.

For God established these lights as signs for the seasons. Therefore we too observe the moon’s number; we do not worship the moon itself. We observe the calculation of Easter from the fourteenth moon, which according to the Law is the first for us.

God established everything in fullness. Therefore we have been permitted to celebrate Easter from the fourteenth through the twenty-first, during those seven days, so that some of these days may fall between the Preparation and the Lord’s resurrection. Thus neither the thirteenth is to be the day of the Passion, nor the fourteenth the day of the resurrection, nor the fifteenth, lest Christ’s Passion occur before the first moon according to our reckoning, or his resurrection fail to occur on the first day, on which the world began.

For all the seasons of the world are counted according to the course of one week, because during these days God formed the members and ornaments of the world. In six days he fashioned the world, and on the seventh he ceased, calling it the Sabbath.

The order and number of the whole world are contained in these seven days. For, always returning into themselves, they multiply the number of times. After the Sabbath, the count always begins again from the first day and continues through the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath, so that it may be understood that the Lord’s resurrection occurred on the first day of the world’s beginning; this day is called the Lord’s Day.

The Lord made this day one with evening, and when it has completed the number seven it begins again, so that after the week it is first. This was decreed from the beginning because of the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, Passion, and resurrection. In the Lord’s body nearly the whole world rose again and was restored.

It has been established, then, that we do not worship the moon but observe the number established through the moon’s course.

The devil, who is Satan, wishing to give some authority to his deception and to color his invented lies with an appearance of truth, knew that the Lord’s mysteries were to be celebrated in the first month. Since he is not without considerable power, he established for the Pagans mysteries to observe, so as to hold their souls in error for two reasons: because deception preceded the truth, the deception might appear to be something better, as though its antiquity gave it precedence over the truth.

And because the Romans have the equinox in the first month, as we do, the Pagans observe this same practice, even saying that expiation is accomplished through blood, just as it is among us through the cross.

By this trick he keeps the Pagans in error, so that they may think our truth appears to be an imitation rather than truth, as though it had been invented through rivalry and a kind of superstition. For they say that what was invented later cannot be considered true.

But because among us the truth is certain, and has existed from the beginning, signs of powers and wonders bear witness to it, so that, with power as witness, the devil’s wickedness may become known.

Because power alone is what readily persuades, it was set against the devil’s cunning and prior imitation, so that it might expose his pretense. No one, even among our enemies, would dare deny that truth is present wherever power appears.

*[Note: [Col. 2279] He speaks as though he were writing somewhere other than Rome; therefore he is not the same author as the author of Question 115, written at Rome.]*

### LXXXV

How is it that, although it is established that from David to the deportation to Babylon there are seventeen generations, the Evangelist says there are fourteen (Matthew 1:17), omitting Ahaziah, who came after Jehoram son of Jehoshaphat, Joash son of Ahaziah, and Amaziah son of Joash?

It should be considered credible that the Evangelist followed the meaning of the Law. Therefore these men were not without reason removed by the Evangelist from the number of the others.

Their wickedness continued in such a way that there was no interval in their evil. Beginning with Jehoram, the wickedness proceeded uninterruptedly as far as Uzziah son of Amaziah, so that there was no intervening branch through which any of them might remain in the number of the kings by virtue of the merit of his father.

Jehoram was included in the number because of the merit of Jehoshaphat, who had preceded him; and Uzziah was retained in the number because of the merit of Jotham. But the continuous wickedness of those three was directed against God.

Solomon too was restored to the kingdom because of the merit of his father; and Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, who acted wickedly, was left in the number of the kings because of the merit of Asa. Those three, however, enclosed in the midst of wicked men, acted wickedly and were therefore erased.

For the example of the destruction of a race is worse when wickedness continually unfolds itself. And, to speak precisely, they were omitted because Joseph did not descend from their line. For the Evangelist followed the generations from Abraham, from whom Joseph derives his origin; Mary, who bore Christ, was betrothed to him.

*[Note: [Col. 2280] The remainder is missing in manuscripts of the second class.]*

### LXXXVI

What proves that Mary, the mother of the Lord, was from the tribe and lineage of David?

We shall produce the words of a reliable witness. For among other things the angel says to Mary: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father, and he will reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there will be no end” (Luke 1:32–33). How could David be called his father by a reliable witness if Mary his mother were not from the lineage of David?

### LXXXVII

If there is one God, why is the hope of salvation in three, and not in two or four, or certainly in the one himself? And why was the Trinity not proclaimed from the beginning?

Almost nothing new has been brought about: for the Trinity is preached in such a way that one God is believed. Therefore nothing has been added; rather, the mystery of the one God has been revealed. It was not proper, however, for it to be made manifest at the very beginning, because what is to be preached must first be preached, and afterward what has been preached must be revealed: so that you may know that the Father is he from whom all things are; that the Son is he through whom all things exist; and that the Holy Spirit is he through whom all things that are indeed from the Father but through the Son are regenerated for faith in the one God.

These three, then, do exist, but there is one divinity. Reason therefore establishes that there are three, neither more nor fewer. For every number reaches as far as nine, because when three are mutually within one another, they produce the number nine: there are three in one, and three are one. Whoever sees one sees three, since one does not differ from another. Thus three are one, and three times three are one. This is perfection in the number nine, insofar as number is concerned, because everything is from one. For when one is added—from which, or in which, the three being counted become nine—they become ten or twenty. Nevertheless, one always comes as far as nine and one is added, because the nine are one, so that the fullness of unity may exist.

[Note: [Col. 2280] The same question from manuscripts of the second class, placed ninth among those following the questions from the Old Testament.]

There is indeed one God, but he is not solitary. From eternity, in mystery, he has another who exists with another. And since God the Father has within himself another with another, as I have said, it was fitting first to preach one, without revealing the mystery that was within him: for the Father is the head of the Son, and the Son is the head of the Holy Spirit, because he received from him; and just as the Father sent the Son, so also the Son sent the Holy Spirit.

After the God from whom all things exist had become known, he then revealed his Son to those who knew him, whom he had had with himself from eternity. Once revealed, the Son showed that the Father was the one who had previously been preached as the one God. When this had become known, he openly made it clear that the Holy Spirit also exists—third from the Father, but second from Christ according to the ordering of the number—while according to substance one does not exist apart from or differ from another. This, too, had existed from eternity in the mystery of God, who is to be worshiped in the Trinity.

For he wills that what is from him be received in the same honor in which he himself is received, from whom it is. This is fitting, because in him were all things made through the Son and enlightened through the Holy Spirit, so that salvation may be preached in the Trinity, while the order of the persons is preserved and the undivided power of the one divinity is worshiped.

That there should therefore be three, neither more nor fewer, reason establishes, because every number reaches as far as three. For since the three are mutually within one another, the Trinity is proclaimed from every side: there are three in one, and three are one. Whoever sees one sees three, since one does not differ from another. Thus three are one, and one is three. This is the Trinity, perfect in every respect. And this is the understanding of the Trinity, which is perfect when they are called one.

### LXXXVIII.—[Note: [Col. 2281] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.] If grace is greater and understanding more manifest in the New Testament than in the Old Testament, why did the prophet Isaiah see the Lord of hosts seated upon the throne of majesty, who, according to the interpretation of John the Evangelist, is Christ? Among other things he said: “Isaiah said these things when he saw his majesty, and he spoke about him” (Isa. 6:1; John 12:41). In the New Testament, however, Stephen, the first martyr, says that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God (Acts 7:55). What does this mean—that here he appears subordinate after his triumphs, while there he appears almost as Lord before he had conquered?

The Lord showed himself according to what the circumstance required. To the prophet he appeared as a king correcting the people; and he showed himself as what he was—that is, seated. The circumstance concerned his divinity in a condition of peace. But the calumny of the Jews caused him to appear standing to Stephen. In Stephen, the cause of the Savior was suffering violence. Therefore, while God the judge was seated, he appeared standing, as one pleading his case; and because his case is just, he was at the judge’s right hand. Everyone who pleads a case must stand.

### LXXXIX.—The Savior says, among other things, concerning the Holy Spirit: “When he comes,” he says, “he will convict the world concerning sin, and concerning righteousness, and concerning judgment. Concerning sin, indeed, because they did not believe in me; concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father, and you will no longer see me; and concerning judgment, because the ruler of this world has been judged” (John 16:8–11). He appears to have stated the reason for convicting the world, but the passage requires explanation.
