Since the Jews and the worldly powers did not believe in the Savior—for he wished to reveal himself not only to human beings but also to the rulers and powers in the heavenly places, as the Apostle teaches in his Letter to the Ephesians (Eph. 3:10)—he showed that after his passion he would prove that the Holy Spirit had spoken truly. This is what it means to convict the world: to show it that the things it refused to believe are true.

The world refused to believe that the Savior had come from God. But the Savior, maintaining righteousness, did not hesitate to return to the one who had sent him; and by returning he proved that he had come from him. For he says: “No one has ascended to God except the one who descended from God” (John 3:13). When the powers therefore saw him ascending, they were confounded, seeing to be true what they had rejected as false. Thus this righteousness convicted them: he was shown to be righteous because he returned to the place from which he had come.

He convicted them of sin in this way also: they not only refused to believe in him, but even killed him. He convicted them concerning judgment by showing that the ruler of this world had been made guilty and seized by the one whose faith they had not shared. For when they saw souls going from the underworld to the heavens, they understood that the ruler of this world had been condemned, so that, having been made guilty in the case of the Savior whom he had held, he might justly lose them.

These things were seen when the Savior ascended; but when the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples, they were openly and plainly manifested. The true conviction occurred when, after the passion and resurrection, as testimony to the Savior, the dead were publicly seen rising among the unbelieving, the lame running, lepers cleansed, paralytics strengthened, the blind seeing, the deaf hearing, the mute speaking, the demon-possessed purified, and the sick giving thanks after recovering their health. In this way the Holy Spirit convicted the world, because in the name of the Savior—who had been rejected by the world—he performed the powers of every kind of healing.

[Col. 2282] ### XC.—If the devil himself is Satan, what does the Savior mean when, among other things, he says to the Jews: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own things, because he is a liar, just as his father is” (John 8:44)?

“Devil” is not a special name but a common one, shared with others. For in whomever the works of the devil are found, that person must undoubtedly be called a devil. It is the name of an action, not of a nature.

Accordingly, in this passage “the father” of the Jews signifies Cain. Wishing to be his imitators, the Jews killed the Savior. He therefore says that Cain, because he stained himself with the murder of his brother and made himself guilty of death, did not stand in the truth. From him the pattern of fratricide was first given.

He says of this same one that, when he speaks falsehood, he speaks from his own things, to show that each person sins only by his own will. But because he is an imitator of the devil, he adds: “Because he is a liar, just as his father is.” For when the devil wished to condemn the first human being to death, he pretended not to know what God had commanded him. So Cain, when questioned, pretended not to know where his brother Abel was, whom he had killed (Gen. 4:9).

In this passage, therefore, he said that Cain was the devil; and his father was the devil whose works he followed. For the son of a devil is a devil. But that devil who is Satan has no father in his wickedness. He himself is the author of his evil. He himself sinned first; consequently, all who imitate him will be called his sons, and he will be called their father.

For we have Abraham as our father in faith, because he himself first believed God; consequently, we are designated by his name. We are called believers, just as he was.

### XCI.—It must be asked how one should answer the arguments of Photinus, who says that Christ did not exist before Mary.

Let us first question John the Baptist, whom the Savior himself declared to be his witness. Among other things, he says concerning the Lord: “He who comes from above is above all; but he who is from the earth is from the earth and speaks from the earth. He who comes from heaven bears witness to what he has seen and heard, and no one accepts his testimony” (John 3:31–32).

Behold, John calls everyone together with himself earthly in comparison with the Lord: he bears witness that the Lord came from heaven, while all the others are from the earth—that is, from the lower regions.

The Lord himself also says the same thing, among other statements: “For I have not descended from heaven to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 6:38).

Again, the Lord speaks in this sense, saying: “And I do not say to you that I will ask the Father. For the Father himself loves you, because you love me and believe that I came forth from God. I came forth from the Father and came into this world; again I leave the world and go to the Father.”

Then, seeing that he had spoken openly, the disciples say to him: “Behold, now you are speaking plainly and saying no proverb. Now we know that you know all things, and you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God” (John 16:26–30).

These words require no interpretation. For this is the sum of our religion: that we believe Christ existed in heaven with God before the flesh, as the Son with the Father.

If, on account of a righteous way of life and heavenly teaching, he said that he had come from heaven and from God and had come into the world, all the prophets and apostles ought to have said the same about themselves. And because he said, “Again I leave the world and go to the Father,” could this perhaps be said to mean that the teaching which had come from God returned to God after leaving the world? They have no other explanation to offer.

For if “to have come from heaven,” “to have come forth from God,” and “to have come into this world” refer to the cause of virtue and teaching, and not to the person of the Savior, when he says, “Again I leave the world and go to the Father,” he certainly returns to the place from which he came. But we see that after the Lord’s departure both virtue and teaching remained in the world.

You see, therefore, that the Lord was not speaking of virtue and teaching, but specifically of himself. If you say that these words concern the virtue that operated in Christ, this very virtue calls God its Father. Behold, you fall into what you fear: for if the virtue of God is the Son of God, then it is certainly the virtue of God concerning which the Apostle says, “Christ the power [virtue] of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). This came forth from God and returned to him again.

Thus this very Power, who is Christ, testifies that he casts out demons by the Spirit of God (Matt. 12:28). The Spirit worked through the apostles, so that you may know that the Holy Spirit, through whom the Lord worked, worked in the world through the apostles after the Lord’s departure. This makes it clearer that the Lord spoke of his own person, because, after leaving the world, he returned to God.

Or if you think that this Power is not Christ, there will be two powers and two sons of God. And where is the statement that is written: “The only-begotten Son of God, who is in the bosom of the Father” (John 1:18)? And again: “For God so loved this world,” he says, “that he gave his only Son for it” (John 3:16)?

You perceive now that the power of God which operated bodily in the world is one and the same as that which is called both the Power of God and the Son.

Let us see what the apostles believed, or in whom they believed, when they heard the Lord say: “Behold, again I leave the world and go to the Father.” For they replied: “Behold, now you are speaking plainly and saying no proverb. Now we know that you know all things, and you have no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.”

Let us now see whether the disciples were uncertain about whether the virtues had come forth from God, when they had seen Lazarus, already foul-smelling on the fourth day, raised (John 11:44); the eyes of the man blind from birth restored (John 9:7); the woman freed from her flow of blood by touching the fringe of his garment (Matt. 9:20–22); and the nature of water changed into wine (John 2:9).

But no one plainly doubted the Lord’s person, or the virtues, since some said that he was Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets (Matt. 16:14). For when the Jews wished to stone him, Jesus answered them: “I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of these works are you stoning me?” The Jews answered him: “We are not stoning you for a good work, but for blasphemy, and because, although you are a man, you make yourself God” (John 10:31–33).

If the Jews therefore did not doubt that these were works of God, were the apostles in doubt?

Since all doubt concerned the person of the Savior—for it was an unheard-of matter, one that did not enter human understanding, and it caused people astonishment when they heard him say that he had come forth from God and that God was his own Father—the disciples, confessing that the Lord’s words had given them sufficient evidence, said to him: “Now we know that you know all things, and there is no need for anyone to question you. By this we believe that you came forth from God.”

For if he did not truly come forth from God, the faith of the apostles is emptied of meaning. But that cannot be, because the Savior himself confirmed it. For he answered them: “Do you now believe?”—that is, although you were seeing such great signs, you did not believe.

Thus it was proved to the apostles that Christ had come forth from God and had come, so that through this coming forth it would not be doubtful that he was to be believed as the Son of God.

For if no one has seen God except the one who is from God—this one has seen God (John 6:46)—and if no one knows the Father except the Son (Matt. 11:27), this means that he truly was with God the Father, came forth from him, and came into the world.

No one else could come forth from God except the one who was with God in the beginning (John 1:1), because no one else knew or had seen God. Therefore it is not incredible for us to believe that this is the true Son of God.

As John says in his First Letter: “And let us be in his true Son Jesus Christ. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5:20). The Apostle says: “He did not spare his own Son” (Rom. 8:32). And the Evangelist says that “he called God his own Father” (John 5:18).

If Christ is therefore the true Son of God, how is he merely a human being? He would not be called the true Son unless he had been properly begotten by him.

Let Photinus say why he is believed to be the true Son of God if he is not true. Or what need would there have been to believe this man to be the Son of God if he were merely one of the other holy men who are worthy to be called sons of God?

Or is there some indignity in him by which he could not be believed to be the Son of God as the others are, and is he therefore called Son so that the one who seems incredible may be believed to be the Son of God? For if he is superior to the others, what need is there to say, “Believe that Christ is the Son of God,” if he were merely one of the others—unless it is because one must believe something different about him from what one believes about the others?

Since there are many who are called sons of God on account of their holiness, this one alone is to be believed the true Son of God; hence he is also called the only one.

For what holy person would have dared to call himself the Son of God—not to mention the only Son [Note: [Col. 2284] Colbert manuscript: “true”]—except the Savior, conscious of his birth from God?

How, moreover, would he have allowed himself to be worshiped if he did not know himself to be from God, since it is written: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Deut. 6:13)? Indeed, the angel rebuked John because he wished to worship him, saying: “Do not do this, for I am your fellow servant; worship God” (Rev. 19:10; 22:9).

And although Scripture testifies that one must serve God alone, the Apostle nevertheless says: “Whoever serves Christ is pleasing to God” (Rom. 14:18). Why? Because God and Christ, Father and Son, are one.

The Apostle acknowledges himself to be Christ’s servant, and he says to the Corinthians: “Do not become servants of human beings” (1 Cor. 7:23). And to the Galatians: “Paul, an apostle, not from human beings nor through a human being, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Gal. 1:1). He openly shows Christ to be God and human, demonstrating that his apostleship was not from a human being but from Christ, insofar as Christ is God, and from God the Father.

Finally, in what follows he says: “For I did not receive it from a human being, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ” (ibid., 1:12).

What could be clearer? He says that he obtained the teaching of God not through a human being, but was taught by God himself. For we receive God’s teaching through human beings; but the chosen vessel proves that he received nothing from the apostles—that is, from human beings.

For if, because it is God’s teaching, it is not learned through a human being, what praise does the Apostle claim for himself if he learned it in the same way as the other apostles? Why does he say, “I did not receive it from a human being, nor was I taught it, but through a revelation of Jesus Christ”? Who could doubt that Christ is signified as God in this passage?

But what wonder is this, when among other things he says to the Romans: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom is Christ according to the flesh, who is God over all, blessed forever” (Rom. 9:5)?

What does “from whom is Christ according to the flesh” mean? He would not say this unless Christ also existed according to God, so that according to the flesh Christ is from the fathers, but according to divinity he is from God, God over all.

But perhaps this is said to refer to the person of the Father. Yet in this passage there is no mention of the name “Father.” Therefore, if it is denied that this was said of Christ, let the person to whom it applies be identified.

Why should it not apply to Christ, to whose name every knee bows—those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2:10)? This means that he is God over all. For apart from these there are no others.

Let Photinus now say whether these beings bow the knee to a human being, or whether God decreed that those heavenly powers and holy angels should worship him as a human being. But far be such a thought: God decreed nothing foolish, especially since worship is permitted only to God—how much more so in heaven?

A king is worshiped on earth as God’s representative. But Christ, after fulfilling the dispensation of representation, is worshiped in heaven and on earth.

For we read that “the Word became flesh” (John 1:14): that is, through the ministry of the Holy Spirit this Word was made incarnate from Mary; that this Word was in the beginning with God and was God; and that this same one is also called the Son of God.

How, then, can what was in the beginning and was God not have existed before Mary? Even if, blinded, you deny that this is God, you nevertheless do not deny that he is the Word; nor are you unaware that this Word is called the Son of God and that he was with God in the beginning.

By what reasoning, then, do you say that what you read existed in the beginning came into existence after Mary?

In the Apocalypse we read concerning Christ: “And his name is the Word of God” (Rev. 19:13). This word has many interpretations. For nothing that is from God is not called God; but, on account of the authority of the one God, he called what was born from him “the Word,” so that, guided by the principle that we know our words to come only from ourselves, we might believe that Christ is from God.

Nor could he appropriately have been called otherwise, so that he might be believed to be from him and not outside him. Likewise he is called the Power and Wisdom of God, so that he may be understood according to the same principle to be from him.

For if he had said “God and God,” he would not have signified that the second was from him, but would have made two gods, which is contrary to unity. This is the principle found in the divine books: when Christ is signified as God, the measure of the one God is not exceeded.

But how foolish is that distinction of yours, Photinus, by which you so divide the opening of John’s Gospel that the Word may not be called God? For you read it this way: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and God was.” This Word was in the beginning with God.

What is the meaning of this distinction? What sense does it convey? What principle of piety does it signify, except hostility toward the Son of God?

For what does the statement of one who says, “And the Word was with God, and God was,” signify? Is this the wisdom of our law, that it should teach that there is a God? What language, what people, what land, what sect denies that God exists?

And why does he add, “And the Word was with God”? What is this Word intended to mean, unless it displays his rational principle? The Gospel is not written on account of God, about whom no one doubts, but on account of the Word, concerning whom questions arise.

The mystery of God is believed precisely because it is not manifest to everyone. Therefore Scripture insists on teaching what the Word is, saying: “And the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God.”

This agrees with reason, and the statement is complete. It shows that this Word, who was in the beginning with God and was God, is to be believed, within the sacramental mystery of the eternal God—unknown throughout the ages and generations—to have been God the Word with God the Father.

And because this has become doubtful to those who wish Scripture to speak according to the capacity of their own understanding, faith has been established so that, by following the sense of Scripture, it may deserve its reward.

When Solomon had asked God for wisdom, the Lord answered him: “Behold, I have given you a wise and understanding heart, such as there was none before you and no man like you shall arise after you” (1 Kings 3:12).

What shall we say? Is what God promised true? Indeed, it is true. No human being, therefore, will be like Solomon.

And what shall be thought concerning Christ, who among other things says: “The Queen of the South came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and behold, something greater than Solomon is here” (Matt. 12:42)?

Now choose, Photinus, whether you believe God or Christ, the Father or the Son. If you believe the Father, you accuse the Son; if you believe the Son, you accuse the Father.

For if Christ is merely human, he has set himself above Solomon in vain, contrary to God’s promise. But if he is understood to be God as well, he rightly placed himself before Solomon, and God’s promise remains undefiled, because no human being like Solomon arose.

Christ showed himself superior for this reason: he is God.

O Photinus’s folly! He refuses to acknowledge Christ before Mary, although he hears Christ himself testify that he existed before Abraham. For when the Jews were discussing his age with him, saying, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” he answered them: “Amen, amen, I say to you, before Abraham came to be, I am” (John 8:57–58).

He did not say, “I am better,” but answered what they had asked: he existed before the time the Jews supposed.

Photinus plainly cannot escape the curse of the Law, because he places his hope in Christ, whom he says is merely human, while he reads: “Cursed is the human being who places his hope in a human being” (Jer. 17:5).

But the Apostle, knowing that Christ is God, says that hope is in him both in the present and in the future: “If in this life only we have hope in Christ,” he says, “we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15:19).

He is therefore not merely human, in whom we are taught to place our hope, because hope in a human being is vain.

We have said these few things out of many; they would be sufficient if he were sound-minded. For Photinus, this final point alone would have sufficed.

[Col. 2286] ### XCII.—How is the Savior’s statement to be understood: “I give you my peace; my peace I leave you; not as this world gives do I give you” (John 14:27)?

Whoever receives the Savior’s peace will incur the world’s hostility. Unless one breaks with the devil, one will not have peace with Christ. For no one can serve two masters (Matt. 6:24).

The person who faithfully keeps God’s law is therefore at odds with the world. Armed with Christ’s peace, he suppresses the weapons of every adversary. For who would dare to act against one whom he knows to be the king’s friend?

The world, however, gives peace differently from the way the Savior promised to give it. The world gives peace either through fear or through entreaty. But the Savior, being the strongest of all and fearing no one, gives peace without being asked.

This, then, is the Savior’s peace: it is given as a defense against enemies. It is called by one name, “peace,” but the peace of God and the peace of the world are separated by a great distance.

The one is fragile, the other strong; the one carnal, the other spiritual; the one earthly, the other heavenly; the one imposed by necessity, the other offered willingly. For Christ, needing nothing, offers peace to the weak and unarmed; the Lord offers it to servants, the good to the wicked, God to human beings.

He therefore rightly says: “Not as this world gives do I give you.” By saying this, he wished the generosity of his good will to be understood. Since everyone gives peace for his own advantage, he—that is, the Savior—gives it so that it may benefit not himself but those to whom he gives it.

The world therefore gives peace differently from the way the Savior gave it. The world’s peace does not teach a good life, persuade one to patience, summon one to justice, encourage mercy, or promise eternal life.

Whoever receives Christ’s peace will be alien to the vices of this world, which wage war against the soul.

### XCIII.—It must be asked whether the apostles possessed the Holy Spirit at the time when they were on earth with the Lord. For among many other statements the Evangelist says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39). And elsewhere he says: “If you love me, keep my commandments, and I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, so that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth, whom the world cannot receive, because it neither sees nor knows him; but you see him and know him, because he remains with you and is with you” (John 14:15–17).

What does this mean? He denies that the Spirit was given before the passion, but promises that he will ask the Father to send him. Then he adds that the Spirit was with them and remained among them.

After the resurrection, however, we read that he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). At Pentecost, moreover, the Holy Spirit is said to have descended upon the apostles (Acts 2:1–4).

I see such great difficulties in this matter that I do not know what should be held.

In all the passages presented, the reason is not one and the same. The forms of the individual reasons are briefly indicated, because the Spirit is one but has many gifts.

When the Holy Spirit is mentioned, therefore, his function must also be understood, in which he is signified. Since he was with them and was also to come, this is not false—provided that it is not referred to his person but to his nature.

Christ promised that another would come from the Father, so that, since their divinity is undivided, the Holy Spirit would not be thought absent in Christ’s presence, and Christ also would be considered present in the coming and manifestation of the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, when he promises that the Spirit will come, he says: “You will see him, because he will remain with you and will be with you,” so that the apostles might be secure, knowing that after the Lord’s ascension they would have a shepherd or king for their protection who was neither lesser nor inferior.

There is no doubt that the Spirit was not given to believers until, as the Evangelist testifies, the Lord had conquered death, risen, and been glorified.

For these are the words of the triumphant Lord himself: “John indeed baptized with water, but you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit, whom you will receive not many days from now” (Acts 1:5). He appears to have said this at the time when he had decided to ascend to the Father.

But when the Lord is read to have breathed upon the disciples a few days after his resurrection and to have said, “Receive the Holy Spirit,” this is understood to mean that ecclesiastical authority was conferred.

Since everything in the Lord’s tradition is carried out through the Holy Spirit, when the rule and form of this discipline were handed down to them, he therefore said: “Receive the Holy Spirit.”

And because this truly pertains to ecclesiastical jurisdiction, he immediately added: “Whose sins you retain, they are retained; and whose sins you remit, they are remitted” (John 20:23).

This breathing, therefore, is a kind of grace infused through tradition into those who are ordained, by which they may be held in higher regard. Hence the Apostle says to Timothy: “Do not neglect the grace that is in you, which was given to you through the laying on of the hands of the presbyterate” (1 Tim. 4:14).

It was therefore necessary that this happen once, so that thereafter this tradition would be believed not to exist without the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Just as a visible form was given in the Savior, so that after his baptism there would be no doubt that the Holy Spirit was thereafter given invisibly to believers, so also in the matter mentioned above a form was given at the beginning, so that from that point onward the Holy Spirit would be believed to be infused into ecclesiastical tradition.

For the apostles to perform miracles in the Lord’s presence, authority was given, just as it had previously been given to the prophets.

Thus three forms of the offices of the gift of the Holy Spirit were shown in the apostles.

The first is that which pertains to ecclesiastical jurisdiction in regeneration and in the other offices. The second is that which was given at Pentecost and is general. For the Holy Spirit fell not only upon the apostles but also upon all believers. The third form is that which was granted to the apostles alone for the performance of signs and miracles, until the seeds of faith should be sown for its growth.

For the seeds of faith are the miracles performed through the apostles. They were appointed as overseers of this truth, so that through signs and wonders they might testify that our faith is not irrational. For no proof of truth is greater than a miracle.

This is what condemns all earthly philosophy, because it has always devoted itself to words alone and has not possessed the testimony of power to demonstrate that what had been constructed in words was stable.

The Holy Spirit, therefore, is given once, generally, to all believers, through whom they are proved to be sons of God, while he remains in them.

But in the performance of signs and wonders he does not remain in a person; he comes when called, or supplies what is necessary, and then departs. Likewise, in tradition or ordination, he bestows grace outwardly and also brings protection to those devoted to the faith.

[Note: [Col. 2287] The same question from manuscripts of the second class, placed forty-second among those following the questions from the New Testament.]

In all the passages presented, the reason is not one and the same. In brief, and so forth. For there is no doubt that the Spirit was not given to believers until the Lord, having conquered death, had been glorified.

Before his ascension, the Lord gave the disciples the form of how those baptized should receive the Holy Spirit, which is now preserved by bishops.

Thus three forms of the offices of the gift of the Holy Spirit were given to the apostles.

The first is the general form, which was given at Pentecost. For the Holy Spirit fell not only upon the apostles but also upon all believers, so that people of one nation might speak of the mighty works of God in different languages.

The second form is special. For it does not pertain to all believers, but only to bishops, so that by the laying on of hands they may give the Holy Spirit to those who have been baptized. Among bishops this may be called general.

The third form is that which was granted to the apostles alone for the performance of signs and miracles for the increase of faith. For the miracles performed through the apostles are the seeds of faith.

Thus the Holy Spirit was given to the apostles according to the order of these offices: first, he fell upon them at Pentecost, as he did upon the other believers; then, as the first priests, they gave the Holy Spirit to believers by laying on hands, as bishops do.

The performance of miracles through the apostles was a grace of the time, not of their persons. [Col. 2288] Yet they were blessed because they lived in the time when the Lord poured out his gift upon the earth, so that they might receive the power to perform miracles through the Holy Spirit as an example to believers.

But because they were sent by the Lord’s presence to cast out demons and perform other miracles, authority was given to the apostles to command demons without invoking the name, or to command the other afflictions of the sick; and the result was healing.

They exercised this authority by the same principle used by the prophets Elijah and Elisha in performing miracles.

Finally, the Savior says to his disciples: “Amen, amen, I say to you: whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you. Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and you will receive” (John 16:23–24).

Since the apostles performed miracles without invoking the name, as I mentioned above, they nevertheless did not act entirely without the authority of the name. For because they had been sent by the one who was a terror to demons and diseases, the demons were driven away and illnesses cured by fear of him. Thus the name of the Lord was working silently.

Finally, the apostle Peter says to the Jews, among other things: “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazarene, whom you denied and crucified, this man stands healthy before you” (Acts 3:16); and indeed, “no other name has been given under heaven by which we must be saved.”

### XCIV.—[Note: [Col. 2288] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.] It must be asked whether Judas Iscariot, the betrayer of the Lord, ended his life by hanging before the Savior’s passion.

Having handed over the Savior, and as the day of Preparation dawned, all the chief priests, scribes, and elders gathered in the house of Caiaphas the high priest, to which they knew that Jesus was to be brought, in order to hear him. The evangelists Matthew and Mark testify to this. None of them had yet departed from the governor’s house after completing their impious work, since all their zeal and devotion toward carrying out the Passover consisted in the Savior’s death.

Since, therefore, they were occupied with the Lord’s execution from morning until the ninth hour, how can Judas be shown to have returned to them before the Lord’s crucifixion the price of the blood which he had received, and to have said to them in the temple, “I have sinned, in that I betrayed innocent blood” (Matt. 27:1–5), when it is certainly established that all the chief priests and elders were not in the temple before the Lord’s passion? Indeed, they were even insulting him while he was hanging on the cross (ibid., 41).

This cannot be proved merely because the report is placed before the passion, since many events are shown to have happened earlier but are arranged last; and, conversely, when the context permits, what happened later may be placed first. For it is certainly clear that Psalm 50 is earlier than Psalm 3. Thus it sometimes happens that later events are anticipated.

Accordingly, although Mary is shown to have anointed the Lord’s feet with perfume at the supper six days before Passover, after her brother Lazarus had been raised, the evangelist anticipates this because of its symbolic significance, saying, among other things, “Now it was Mary who anointed the Lord with perfume” (John 11:2). He reports this before Lazarus died; unless we later discovered that it had happened afterward, we would not know when it took place.

But perhaps it happened after the ninth hour: when the impious and most cruel Judas saw the Savior killed and, because of this, saw the veil of the temple torn, the earth shaken, the rocks split, and the elements terrified, he may have been overcome by that very fear and grieved, knowing that he had betrayed an innocent man, during whose passion God the Judge had shown such indignation. The elders and chief priests, moreover, were also occupied after the ninth hour, as I think. For on that same evening they were going to celebrate the Passover; but on the Sabbath it was not permitted to carry money, according to the Law. For this reason it seems to me improbable on what day—or rather, at what time—Judas Iscariot ended his life by hanging.

## XCV. — From where did the observance of Pentecost arise, and for what reason?

There is no doubt that all the practices of our religion are strengthened by the testimony of antiquity [Note: [Col. 2288] “of truth,” according to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., M.], and marked by the prerogative of the ancient Law [Col. 2289]. For all the events of the past under the ancient Law are recognized as having been enacted and designated as figures of the future faith, so that we might have no doubt that we possess the truth, when we see that the things which we now both hear and believe were predestined before the ages and commended not only by words but also by the power of signs.

But the question now is whether we understand these things in the same way in which they were designated, so that we may properly discern from where and for what reason the day of Pentecost was derived. For the Scriptures of the Lord open their meanings to the attentive and devoted, but close them to the negligent. It was not fitting that matters reserved for the worthy and meritorious should be openly visible to everyone.

Pentecost, therefore, which is reckoned as the fiftieth day from Passover, has this significance: just as, after a week, the Lord’s day is the first day, on which the mystery of Passover was fulfilled for the redemption of human salvation—for after the cycle of seven days it is always necessary to return to the first, so that it may be shown that the age of the world is completed by the number seven and reaches rest—so also, after seven weeks, the first day is Pentecost.

Indeed, Pentecost is never on any other day than the Lord’s day, so that everything contributing to human salvation may be understood to have been both begun and fulfilled on the Lord’s day. For the world was made on the Lord’s day, and after the Fall it was restored again on the Lord’s day. The figure of this restoration was first given in circumcision, in which there was a sign of the future faith. For after the week, the eighth day is the first in the mystery. “This is the day which the Lord has made.” He made it one day, from which the other days would derive their cycles.

Accordingly, on that very day he rose, the day which he had made; and, according to the number indicated by the reasoning above, on that very day he also gave the Law on Mount Sinai through his servant Moses. Just as the lamb was a figure of the Lord’s passion in the sacrament of Passover, so the giving of the Law was a figure of evangelical preaching. For the Law was given on the same day—that is, on Pentecost—on which the Holy Spirit also descended upon the disciples, so that they might receive authority and know how to preach the evangelical law.

This event is confirmed by twofold testimony: it is shown to have been predestined, and by the manifest outpouring of the Holy Spirit it is proved to be divine and heavenly, bearing witness to our Law. For when uneducated people speak of God’s mighty works in languages unknown to them, they show that they have been divinely inspired.

The Law, therefore, was given to the children of Israel through Moses on the third day of the third month, as is contained in the book of Exodus (Exod. 19:16). This day is the fiftieth from the fourteenth day of the first month, on which the Passover took place in Egypt (ibid. 12:18)—that is, Pentecost.

Thus it happened that, at Pentecost, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles to preach the law of faith (Acts 2:1–4), so that the deeds of ancient times might be regarded as images of things to come, for the security of our faith; for what was proclaimed from the beginning cannot appear false.

For this reason the time of forgiveness and restoration is described in Psalm 50, so that it might be known that the same providence belongs to the fiftieth day as to the first. Hence it also happened that manna was given from heaven to the Jewish people on the first day, which is the Lord’s day. The continuity of six days proves this to be so: they gathered it for six days and rested on the seventh day, that is, the Sabbath (Exod. 16:22–23).

Manna, moreover, is a type of the spiritual food which, through the Lord’s resurrection, became reality in the mystery of the Eucharist. Everything, therefore, took place so that they might return unharmed to the cause of the first resurrection, and Satan might not boast but grow dull—he who cast man down through a false hope, lest he remain in what had been accomplished through Christ the Lord [Note: [Col. 2289] The remainder is absent from manuscripts of the second class.].

It remains now to prove whether the things we have said are to be understood in the manner mentioned above. The first month, in which Passover was celebrated on the fourteenth day in Egypt, had this day as a Wednesday. Hence the Law was also given on a Wednesday.

This can be understood from the fact that the fifteenth day of the second month, when the children of Israel set out, appears to have been a Sabbath. For this reason the flock of quail was not sent to them during the day but in the evening. In the morning, however, manna rained from heaven (Exod. 16:13–14), that is, on the Lord’s day, which is found as the first day in the repetition after the week. Indeed, they gathered manna for six continuous days, but on the seventh day, which is the Sabbath, they rested.

From this day, therefore, until the third day of the third month, when the Law was given, calculate, and you will find that it was a Wednesday when the Law was given. From the fifteenth day of the second month, when it was the Sabbath, until the third day of the third month, when the Law was given, there are nineteen days.

Hold on to these nineteen, then return to the fifteenth day of the second month, when it was the Sabbath, which is counted as the fourteenth day from the first; proceed as far as the first day of the second month, and you will have another fourteen days. Add these to the nineteen mentioned above, and you will find that the first day of the second month was a Sabbath.

Add further to the beginning of the first month seventeen days, because the thirteen days of the first month which preceded Passover must be subtracted: Passover took place on the fourteenth day of the first month. After subtracting the thirteen and adding the seventeen, you will find that the fourteenth day of the first month was a Wednesday.

And so that you do not become weary of reading, or examine each part of the question with excessive minuteness, I shall give a summary, so that you may be certain of the number of days from Passover to the giving of the Law, and may more easily learn from that on which day Passover took place.

The Law was given on the third day after the second month. Thus there are two months and three days. Subtract from these the thirteen days that preceded Passover, and fifty days will remain.

That the Law was given on a Wednesday is readily apparent from this. Manna was given on the first day, because they gathered it for six continuous days; that first day was the sixteenth day of the second month. From this first day, therefore, until the eighteenth day, on which the Law was given, you will find a Wednesday.

From Wednesday, whether you count forward or backward, the fiftieth day is Wednesday. Thus the Jews celebrated Passover in Egypt on a Wednesday and received the Law on a Wednesday; but on Thursday they departed from Egypt. Therefore the dedication of the Law is Pentecost.

## XCVI. — Whether Passover (*Pascha*) is interpreted as “passing over,” as it seems to the Greeks

The Apostle could not have been mistaken when he said, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5:7). This is not his own word, but the word of the Law, when Moses says, “And when your sons say to you, ‘What does this service mean?’ you shall say, ‘This sacrifice is the Passover of the Lord’” (Exod. 12:26–27).

What more is needed for testimony? The Law speaks; the Apostle confirms it. All that remains is for the contradictor to be rejected as obstinate.

It is clear that the passing over occurred after the Passover. For they placed the blood of the sacrificed lamb on the doorposts and on the lintel, so that when the angel passed through during the night, he would not strike the house in which the sign of blood was present. The blood, therefore, brought salvation, not the passing over; for the blood prevented the passing over from causing harm.

## XCVII. — How can Arius’s impiety be answered simply from the Law?

If faith is accorded to reason, the very meaning of the names “Father” and “Son” will show their unity. If you ask how, the answer is this: the true Son of God would not be called such unless he had come forth from the substance of God the Father. Nor would the truth and justice of God tolerate calling him the true Son if he were not from him. He is not the true Son of God if he is not from him.

But Scripture says, “He is true.” Therefore he is from him. Whoever denies that Christ was born from God slanders Scripture, which calls him the true Son of God precisely to signify that he was born from God. For if he is not from God but is called the true Son of God, Scripture is deceitful.

But if Scripture does not deceive, then the one who does not confess that Christ came forth from God both nullifies Scripture and denies that Christ is the true Son of God. It is not will that makes a true son, but birth.

“But,” they say, “this lies within the power of God: to make false things true.”

Rather, this is God’s power, and for this he is worthy of all praise: with him, the true is true and the false is false. For it belongs to a liar to call the false true; this is not fitting for God. God can indeed do all things, but he does only what accords with his truth and justice.

It is therefore clear that Christ is called the true Son of God so that he may be understood as the proper Son—that is, born from his substance. Hence the Apostle says, “He who did not spare his own Son” [Note: [Col. 2291] In manuscripts of the second class, the material found after this question is inserted here.] (Rom. 8:32); and in another Epistle: “Although he was in the form of God, he did not regard equality with God as something to be seized” (Phil. 2:6).

If, therefore, he did not regard it as something to be seized when he said that he was equal to God, he demonstrated that he was truly the Son of God. For he could not be equal to God unless he were from him.

Those are equal who are either both true or both false. Nor can a beginning and an eternal being admit equality or unity. By saying that he and the Father are one, Christ makes himself equal to God. For it says, “He was not only breaking the Sabbath, but also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John 5:18)—that is, making himself his equal.

Is it not clear that this equality proceeds from the uniqueness of his birth? By calling himself the proper—that is, the true—Son of God, he made himself equal to God. Hence he says, “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father also” (ibid. 14:9). Because they are consubstantial, whoever sees one sees both.

“For just as the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (ibid. 5:26). That is, the Father begot a Son equal to himself. Everything that belongs to the Father belongs to the Son, and what belongs to the Son belongs to the Father (ibid. 17:10). No one can seize anything from the hand of the Father or from the hand of the Son (ibid. 10:29).

And he added, “I and the Father are one” (ibid., 30); and, “The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself; but the Father who remains in me himself speaks, and the works which I do, he himself does. Believe me that I am in the Father and the Father is in me; otherwise, believe because of the works themselves” (ibid. 14:10–12).

Because generation is not from oneself but from the one who begot, he says that whatever he does has been done by the Father, so that through all these things it may be confirmed that Christ is called the true Son of God so that he may be believed to have been born from him [Note: [Col. 2291] The remainder is absent from manuscripts of the second class.], and so that his substance might not be thought to exist outside the nature of the one God.

His humility, therefore, is his greatest exaltation. When he appears to subject himself by saying, “The words which I speak to you I do not speak from myself; for the Father who remains in me himself speaks, and the works which I do, he himself performs,” he proves that he has his origin from God and shows that he is his Power, since he says that what he is is not from himself but from him. Through this he is commended, not diminished.

For whoever speaks from himself is not the true Son. You see, therefore, that the Arians misunderstand Christ precisely where he is to be understood correctly; and they reject him and call him false precisely where he is proved to be the true Son of God. For he asks the Father to glorify him, and promises to glorify the Father whom he asks; and where he appears to humble himself, he exalts himself.

For when the Father gives testimony to his Son, he bears witness to his own praise; but when the Son proclaims the Father, he manifests his own glory. The magnificence and nobility of the Father consist in the nobility of the true Son.

Therefore whatever is said to belong to the Father undoubtedly belongs also to the Son, and what is said to belong to the Son belongs to the Father. For the Spirit who is called the Spirit of God is also called the Spirit of Christ. The Church is called the Church of God and is also called Christ’s. God is worshiped, and Christ is worshiped. God is served, and Christ is served. The saints are called priests of God, and they are also called priests of Christ. The temple of the holy city is called God’s, and likewise Christ’s [Note: [Col. 2291] Ms. Colbert: “God, and likewise Christ.”].

The holy city is said to be illuminated by God’s light, and likewise by Christ’s. It is God’s throne, and also Christ’s. God is Judge, and Christ is also Judge, because the prophet Isaiah sees Christ, the Lord of hosts, seated on the throne of majesty (Isa. 6:1), a point which the Arians do not deny.

Of God the Father it is read that he is “King of kings and Lord of lords” (1 Tim. 6:15); the same is said of Christ, the true Son of God (Rev. 17:14; 19:16). Thus the Father and the Son are everywhere made equal in divinity, while the number of persons does not exceed the unity of God.

There is no difference between the Father and the Son except this one: the Father is unbegotten, whereas the Son is begotten; that is, the Father is from no one, while the Son is from the Father. This, indeed, is sublime in the Son. From it we learn the eternity of his nobility and that he is the true Son of the true Father.

What else is meant by the words spoken by God in Genesis, “Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1:26)? If their image and likeness are one, how are they not also one in nature? In spiritual things, where there are certainly no bodily figures, something will be similar only through substance. Therefore, where the image of two is one, how can their substance not also be one?

For this reason we read that their image and likeness are one, so that we might believe that they are one and that one does not differ from the other: that is, that Christ is the true Son of God, because his birth is not unlike that of the one who begot him.

Finally, the Jews understood that he was calling God his own Father and said to Pilate, “We have a Law, and according to the Law he ought to die, because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19:7). The Jews understood, and Christians claim not to understand? Those who did not believe understood; and those who claim to believe make themselves unable to understand?

At least they should have accepted what the prophet Isaiah said when, among other things, he wished to signify that Christ was not from himself but was God from God:

“Those bound in fetters shall follow after you, and they shall worship you, and they shall pray to you; for God is in you, and there is no God besides you. For you are God, and we did not know it, the God of Israel, the Savior” (Isa. 45:14–15).

To a sound mind these things are clear. Through them the Father is proved to be in the Son, and the Son is signified to be God of the same substance as the Father.

For in whom God is, and besides whom there is no God, and who himself is God—what else can he be said to be than what the Father God is, without differing from him in anything? This is what it means for the two to be one.

God is in him because, although he is God, he is not God from himself. He is from the Father because he is the Son. There is no God besides him because he is the Father’s only Son. He himself is God because the substance of God and of Christ is one and the same.

Nothing ambiguous, therefore, remains: the substance of the Father and the Son is to be believed one. He is the true Son of the true Father.

The same is found in the prophet Jeremiah, who says, among other things: “This is our God, and no other shall be accounted beside him. He discovered the whole way of knowledge and gave it to Jacob his servant and to Israel his beloved. After this he appeared on earth and lived among human beings” (Baruch 3:36–38).

Can this be said of one who is of inferior birth, to whom no other can be compared? Or can he be called anything other than the Father God, so that such a statement would become an insult to the Father?

If no other God can be compared with him and he is without God the Father, consider whether what follows ought to be said; for it is dangerous. He will be called greater than the Father.

Those who think they are honoring God the Father by separating the Son from him insult him instead. In their impious blindness they wish to make him lesser, but place him above the one whose authority they think he must obey.

Scripture, however, teaches that the Son differs in nothing from the Father—and he would differ if he were not true—by saying that no other is to be compared with him. For no other substance could be found similar to the substance of God, which is also the substance of Christ.

Otherwise Scripture could not teach that Christ is from God except by saying that no other is to be compared with him. Knowing that the Son could in no way be made subject to God the Father, and wishing thereby to show that he is equal, it says, “No other shall be accounted beside him,” because he is equal to God the Father, since he is God. For he is his true Son.

Thus the prophet says, “This is our God,” that is, the God of Israel. If this is he, then he is the one God. Scripture says of him, “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6:4). Certainly this is not the Father but his Son [Col. 2293].

You see, therefore, that the person of the Son does not prejudice the unity of God, if he too is called the one God, since Scripture itself testifies to this.

Why is this so, except because the Father and the Son are one—not because unity is signified by persons, but by nature? Or rather, they are not two in substance but one; not two in divinity but one God. Thus, whether the Father speaks or the Son speaks, one God is said to have spoken.

For if the Lord himself says elsewhere of man and woman, “They are no longer two but one flesh” (Mark 10:8), how much more are the Father and the Son not two gods but one substance?

The reason that the Father and Son are called two is birth; the reason that they are not two gods is the unity of divinity.

Yet with what dullness do they proclaim Christ created—that is, made—when it is written that God made nothing without Christ (John 1:3)? If nothing was made without him, he himself will not be a creature. For if he is a creature, something was made without him. But far be this from us, since nothing was made without him.

Born from God, he did not begin to exist, but always existed. Birth is nothing other than an issuing forth; an issuing forth is a manifestation. Therefore he was not made but brought forth.

To signify that Christ came forth or proceeded from the essence of God, his birth was called an issuing forth. Thus, because his birth is not unlike that of the one who begot him, there could be no doubt that Christ is consubstantial with God, and that the view which says, “There was when he was not,” should be condemned.

For he cannot at any time not have existed who, in order to signify that he had always been with God, is read to have proceeded from God. No one proceeds from God who was not there.

The Arians customarily interpret the following passage in this way when speaking about the Son of God: “Christ is called the true Son of God because he made him in such a way that he is true.” As though God made anything false!

And what will become of all those things we said above about the unity of the Father and the Son, when they have been so strongly confirmed and established? If it is thought that these matters must be understood otherwise, can many things established by divine declarations be overthrown by the testimony of one degenerate person?

Nevertheless, this must be cut off, lest in this very matter iniquity flatter itself. “Therefore,” he says, “he made him in such a way that he is true,” so that will took the place of birth and making took the place of generation.

“For this much,” they say, “must be granted to God’s power: that he can make things which do not exist as though they did.”

Since, therefore, they rely on this cunning deceit against the Son of God, we must answer them from the very points on which they presume, because they have been refuted in all the rest, so that they may plainly appear refuted in the whole matter.

As far as meaning is concerned, this proposition has no force; as far as its words are concerned, it creates darkness so that its meaning may not quickly appear. It is like an Egyptian placed in darkness, because a bad cause cannot be defended by a good interpretation.

To defend their impiety, therefore, they use sacrilegious words. If this is God’s power—to make Christ truly his Son when he was not born from him—then he made him such as he himself is, so that making supplied what generation would have supplied.

If, therefore, you say that there is no difference between God and Christ, it may perhaps be doubted [Note: [Col. 2293] Ms. Colbert: “thought.”] whether you are not making this assertion maliciously, so that what is said in words may also be present in the meaning: since he is called the true Son, he may be understood as true because he is of one substance with the Father, though not through generation but through making; since, as you say, God can do everything, so that something made may be as though it were unmade.

But if, following the line of reason, you say that something originating in time cannot be equal and consubstantial with what is eternal, you reveal the deceit of your malice. For, to evade the meaning of the word, you call Christ the true Son of God with a false voice while denying him equality with God the Father.

For he is not true if he is unequal. Can a son be called true if the father is not also called true? If the Son is true, then the Father too will be true; equality proves this truth. But if they are unequal, neither of them is true.

Since, however, the testimony of Scripture cannot be invalidated, by which Christ is proved to be the true Son of God, he must be believed to have been born from God the Father. For, to establish this truth, he is read to be on a par with God and equal to him.

But you, who proclaim God’s immeasurable power, say, “God cannot beget, because he is a simple nature.” By this you also insult God the Father himself. For you call him a liar by denying the Son whom he asserts to be his own and true; and you expose your hypocrisy by falsely proclaiming God powerful.

If you proclaim God’s power as consisting in making what is true from what is false, and thereby mock what is true, how much more ought you, if you were sound in mind, to embrace that by which what is called true is proved true and the testimony which God the Father gave concerning his Son is confirmed as true?

For the Lord says, “With God all things are possible” (Matt. 19:26), so that whatever appears impossible to human beings is possible with God.

For if one looks only to the reasoning of the flesh, neither did a virgin give birth, nor did Jonah live in the belly of the sea creature (Jonah 2:1), nor will the dead rise, nor did God beget a Son, since a simple nature cannot generate and nothing in this world is generated without mixture.

All these things must either be believed together or rejected together. If the reasoning of the world is to be maintained, it must have authority in all these matters. But if there is some spiritual reasoning, then the person who, infected by the reasoning of the world, denies that anything can happen otherwise than he knows is to be called carnal.

They also customarily propose another argument through their evasive reasoning. They ask, “Did the Father beget the Son by his will, or not?” When they hear the answer, obviously, “By his will,” they immediately respond, as enemies of the Son of God, “Then the will existed before the Son,” so that he may not appear eternal, since he would not have received his beginning through birth but would have come into existence afterward.

Yet if they think this, the will will exist not only before the Son but also before the Father, because the Father and the Son are the cause of generation.

Carnal understanding follows unbelief in everything. They introduce a cause in God as though it were a human cause, as though he first deliberated and devised a plan to beget, as though he were subject to weakness. But in God there was neither generation without will nor will without generation.

The will itself is generation. For it is certainly a common expression to say, “God made,” and “a human being made”; but God makes in one way and a human being makes in another. The same applies to the other causes. One must speak of God in a way worthy of him.

They themselves also raise another question about God the Father, saying, “Did something come to him so that he would beget, or is it in his nature always to beget?” They raise this [Note: [Col. 2294] According to Er., Lugd., Ven., Lov., “assert.” M.] so that they may both declare God a liar, since he testifies that he begot Christ, and make Christ not true but adopted.

“For if he begot,” they say, “he ought always to beget.” Since he does not always beget, they conclude that he should not be believed to have begotten Christ—just as though he must be denied to have made the world because he does not make other worlds.

What irreverence and lack of discipline it is to impose a law on God, as though, if he begot, he either must have begotten many or could not have begotten one! They do not even believe the Lord, who declared himself to be the only Son of God.

After the matters set forth above, which show the equality of the Father and the Son, let us see whether the things written about the Holy Spirit agree with these, so that the Trinity which we retain in our confession of salvation does not admit a difference of nature, any more than it has a diversity of faith. For although salvation does not exist without one of these, their power nevertheless appears to be one—the power that grants salvation to those who believe in them. Since we have brought forward the Father’s words as testimony to the Son, let us now use the Son’s words as testimony to the Holy Spirit, by which he declares that the Holy Spirit does not differ from himself: so that, since the Father is witness to the Son, and the Son to the Holy Spirit, the Trinity may be understood to be of one nature.

The Lord therefore says, among other things: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may be with you forever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16–17). When he says that another Paraclete is to be sent, he plainly proves that he himself is the Paraclete. For it is also read in the Epistle of John: “We have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, who pleads for our sins” (1 John 2:1). And again the Lord says, “I am the truth” (John 14:6). Behold the manifest unity of the Holy Spirit and the Son of God. For what the Son says about himself, he says the same about the Holy Spirit.

Now the passages of Scripture that arrange matters in this sense must be set forth. It is read [Col. 2295] in Isaiah that he saw the Lord of hosts seated upon the throne of majesty (Isa. 6:1); John the Evangelist understood this to be Christ, saying, among other things: “Isaiah said this when he saw his majesty and spoke about him” (John 12:41). The Apostle declares that this one is the Holy Spirit. For in the final part of the Acts of the Apostles he says: “The Holy Spirit spoke well to your fathers, saying, ‘You shall hear with your ear and shall not understand,’ etc.” (Acts 28:25–26). These words were spoken by the Lord of hosts.

This is one God; whether he is understood as the Father, the Son, or the Holy Spirit, there is no contradiction, because their divinity and power are one. For if, in the edict of a single prefect of the praetorium, the other prefects are also said to give orders because of the authority of the one power, how much more, in the command of one God, if one of the three has spoken, may all three appropriately be said to have spoken? Their nature and will are one.

They also customarily prejudice the Holy Spirit by arguing that he is therefore understood to be degenerate because he is placed third in the order, although there is such simplicity in the divine Scriptures that sometimes one finds the third placed first. They are placed according to the occasion. No one is wronged, for their divinity is one.

Finally, we read in Isaiah, where the Lord says: “I am the first, and I am forever; and my hand founded the earth, and my right hand established the heavens.” And in what follows: “I spoke, I called, I brought him, and I made his way prosperous. Draw near to me and hear these things: From the beginning I have not spoken in secret; when they came to be, I was there. And now the Lord has sent me, and his Spirit” (Isa. 48:12–13, 15–16).

Who do you think it is who founded the earth? For he himself says that he was sent. The Father? Far from it. It is therefore the Son who says that he was sent by God and by the Holy Spirit. Behold, the Son and the Holy Spirit are equal. For just as the Holy Spirit is read to have been sent by the Father and the Son, so Christ was sent by God and the Holy Spirit. This is peculiar to the Father alone: that he is not said to have been sent.

Hear the Apostle’s words, in which he presents the Trinity in another order. For, among other things, he says in the Second Epistle to the Thessalonians: “May the Lord direct your hearts into the love of God and into the patience of Christ” (2 Thess. 3:5). Whom do you think he calls Lord, if not the Holy Spirit? And what is surprising about this, since the one whom Isaiah saw seated upon the throne of majesty is here himself called the Holy Spirit, the Lord of hosts, as we showed above?

The Apostle John also indicates that God is to be understood in the Holy Spirit, saying, among other things: “By this we know that God remains in us: by the Spirit whom he gave us” (1 John 4:13). If, then, he himself remains in us through his Spirit, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit is of God. Nor is it doubtful that what is of God is God.

Hence the Apostle says: “No one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11). How can he know what is in God unless he is of the same divinity? For an inferior nature cannot know what exists in a superior one; how much less could a creature know what exists in its Creator?

And in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, departing from the order that exists in the tradition of faith, he begins with the Holy Spirit when he recalls the operations of graces and mysteries; then he adds the Lord Jesus, and places third God, whom he says operates in the Holy Spirit and in the Lord (1 Cor. 12:4–6), just as the Lord says: “The Father who remains in me, he performs the works” (John 14:10). For because both the Holy Spirit and Christ are from God the Father, their operation is the work of God.

Finally, he calls the Holy Spirit “Lord,” and likewise calls the Lord “God,” on account of the unity of nature. Since, therefore, in this passage he says that the same God who is also Lord operates all things in all, he concludes below in these words: “But all these things the one and the same Spirit performs, distributing to each as he wills” (1 Cor. 12:11).

What could be clearer than that the three have one operation? When one operates, three are said to operate—why, except because they are of one divinity? For it is not doubtful that the Holy Spirit properly operates the gift of graces. But in order to teach that God, the Lord, and the Holy Spirit are one because of the identity of nature, he showed that the work of the Holy Spirit is the work of the three. And to make clear that, so far as person is concerned, the work belongs to the Holy Spirit alone, he says: “But all these things the one and the same Spirit performs, distributing to each as he wills.” “As he wills,” because his will is the will of God. For he does not say, “as God wills,” but “as the Spirit wills.” A creature forces itself to do the will of God; the Holy Spirit naturally wills this.

But so that it may plainly shine forth that the Holy Spirit performs all things, the Lord says, among other things: “If I cast out demons by the finger of God, etc.” (Luke 11:20). He calls the Holy Spirit the finger of God, to prove that he is of God. Finally, he testified that the Jews who said he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, had blasphemed against the Holy Spirit.

The magicians also confess that Moses performed signs through the Holy Spirit, saying: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8:19).

For we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “As they were ministering to the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said, ‘Set apart for me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them’” (Acts 13:2). Behold, the Lord is being served, and the Holy Spirit claims this for himself. Hence it is clearly evident that he is Lord, just as God the Father is.

And Christ called Saul from heaven and sent him to preach (Acts 9:4); in like manner the Holy Spirit claims this for himself, saying, “for the work to which I have called them.” For no one is unaware that the Savior established bishops for the churches. Before he ascended into heaven, he laid hands upon the Apostles and ordained them bishops. The Apostle attributes this to the Holy Spirit when he says: “Pay attention to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit has placed you as bishops to govern the Church of the Lord Jesus” (Acts 20:28).

And among other things Peter says to Ananias: “Ananias, why has Satan filled your heart, so that you lied to the Holy Spirit?” And below: “You have not lied,” he says, “to human beings, but to God” (Acts 5:3–4). It is clear that the Holy Spirit is called God: to him whom Ananias lied, he is said to have lied to God. If he had not wanted the Holy Spirit to be understood as God, he would have said, “You have not lied to human beings, but to the Holy Spirit,” so that he would signify neither God nor a human being.

And what is surprising? For the Apostle sometimes calls a human being the temple of God (2 Cor. 6:16), and sometimes the temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Cor. 6:19), because they are one in nature. If the Holy Spirit were not understood as God, with what audacity would he say below: “The temple of God is holy, which you are” (1 Cor. 3:17)?

One God is proclaimed throughout all the Scriptures, but his mystery is worshiped in the Trinity. Therefore Scripture speaks in this way, so that under the confession of one God, those who are from him—namely, his Son and his Holy Spirit—may be understood to possess the same honor in which God himself exists. For this reason the mystery of God was revealed: so that his glory might be signified in the Trinity.

Accordingly, what is of God is not called God with full authority, lest it be believed that there is another apart from the one who is God. Yet the meaning is given so that we may believe that the salvation of the creature consists in the Trinity for this reason: their divinity is one. For the Creator and creatures, the Lord and servants, eternity and things that have a beginning could not be joined together and placed in one order, since without one of them there is salvation for no one.

It is an insult to all that is God—whether the Son or the Holy Spirit—if it is assigned outside the honor and glory of the one God. The Scriptures therefore show Christ to be God; they show the Holy Spirit to be God, so that those who see may know what is shown [Note: [Col. 2296] Erasmus, Venice, Louvain: “so that those who see may know how this is shown.” M.].

It is as though someone were displaying a gem without shouting that it was a gem: because he does not shout, would the object that is seen not be a gem? So too the Scriptures show through the matters discussed above what we ought to believe, enclosing our understanding within the faith of one God, in the mystery of the Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 2296] This same question is found in manuscripts of the second class, among the questions published after the forty-third from the New Testament.]

“If faith is accommodated to reason,” etc.

[Col. 2297]

It is therefore clear that Christ is called the true Son of God so that he may be understood as proper—that is, born from his substance. Hence the Apostle also says: “He did not spare his own Son.” For the very relationship of the names teaches that the Father and the Son are of one substance. Since human reason, because of its weakness, cannot grasp the mystery, names have fittingly been applied to sacred realities, so that through them the truth of the Father and the Son might to some extent be understood.

Nothing makes it so evident that Christ the Lord is God from God as this name by which he is called “the Son of God.” And because malignity introduces its unbelief even into the names themselves, interpreting the matter otherwise than the meaning of the name itself requires, he added “true Son,” in order to shut the mouth of what is perverse and the mind that is twisted.

Indeed, no one falls into heresy except by departing from the meaning of the names; those who remain simple, however, adhering to the meaning of the names, have remained attached to the Catholic faith. In its own simplicity, the untroubled mind understands this only as it has been handed down. But when evasiveness is added, and people raise questions about a matter rightly and simply stated, unwilling to believe what the words declare and thinking it disgraceful not to add or subtract something of their own, they are thrown down from the tradition.

For they make themselves anxious lest God ought to be believed otherwise than he has handed down. But the meaning of the names “Father” and “Son” leads to the truth of their unity. For there can be no difference between those whose one image is presented in the sacred Scriptures—a point which the Son himself confirms when he says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also.” If one who sees one of them sees both, then undoubtedly the Father and the Son have one image; and it would not be one unless the Father and the Son were consubstantial. This is certainly not doubtful in relation to human knowledge.

What else can be judged concerning the true Son than that their unity is confirmed by the very propriety of the names, that of the one who is born and the one who generates? For who could generate anything other than what he himself is?

If he were called only “Son,” and it were not added for the sake of understanding that he is true—as the Apostle John testifies when he says, “We are in the true Son Jesus Christ, who is the true God and eternal life”; and as the Apostle Paul likewise proclaims, “He did not spare his own Son”—one could doubt the bare name “Son.” But since he adds that this one is the true Son of God, those who depart from this word [Col. 2298] and meaning are their own particular enemies.

They invent matters for themselves and, through a certain persuasion of perverse opinion, assert that something other must be believed than what the rationale of faith contains—as though more should be believed about God than he himself wished to be believed about himself. If “true” had not been added, doubt could arise. He might be said to be like the Father because of the statement, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” so that, just as milk and gypsum are alike with respect to color but very unlike with respect to nature, the statement “Whoever sees me sees the Father” might likewise be understood.

But since these are the words of the true Son of God, nothing else should be admitted into their meaning except that he said this because the Father and the Son are one in nature—that is, because one does not differ from the other in anything. For if the Savior said of a man and a woman, because their substance is one, “They are no longer two, but one flesh,” how much more must the Father and the Son not be called two according to substance, lest their substance be recognized as either split or divided, or certainly unequal and unlike?

Finally, the Apostle Paul, confirming their unity of substance, says: “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God.” From where, then, will this equality come, unless from unity of substance? Hence both have one image. Thus, as the Apostle says, “He did not consider it robbery to be equal with God”; by this he demonstrated himself to be truly the Son of God. For he could not be equal to God unless he were from God.

Those are equal who are either both true or both false. Nor does what has begun and what is eternal admit equality, nor does unity. By saying that he was one with the Father, Christ made himself equal to God. For it says: “He was not only breaking the Sabbath, but also calling God his own Father, making himself equal to God”—that is, to the Father.

Is it not clear that this equality descends from the propriety of his birth? By calling himself the proper—that is, the true—Son of God, he made himself equal to God. This is the meaning of his saying, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also”: because they are consubstantial, whoever sees one sees both.

“For just as the Father has life in himself, so he also gave the Son to have life”: that is, “equal,” etc. [Note: [Col. 2298] Only a very small amount follows in the manuscripts of the first class, namely up to the words “may be believed to have been born.” The remainder is absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

# QUESTIONS MIXED FROM BOTH [Note: [Col. 2297] This title is inept, as is clear from Questions 101, 102, 114, 115, etc., and it was not found by us in the manuscripts, which have no division here. But it has thus far been received from the printed editions, so that this third part of the Questions may be cited under that title; therefore we have altered nothing here, especially in a work of no great importance.]

[Col. 2297]

## ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN

[Note: [Col. 2297] So in the manuscripts and the Regensburg edition. Other editions read: “How the devil is said in the Gospel of John to have a father.” [Note: [Col. 2297] This note appears at the foot of column 2297, but its callout number was not printed in the text.]]

### XCVIII

[Note: [Col. 2297] This second treatment of the same subject does not occur in the manuscripts of the second class; above, Question 90 concerns the same subject.]

You have heard what the most holy Gospel declares, when the Lord says to the Jews: “You are born from the father, the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth, because truth is not in him. When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own things, because he is a liar, as is also his father” (John 8:44).

No believer should doubt that the devil has no author of his apostasy. For he himself is the prince of all error. Seeing that God had made him possessed of no ordinary power, he dared to presume divinity; and because he saw that the others were inferior, he set himself above them as a god.

Finally, the names by which the devil and Satan are called are formed from his action, not from his nature. For every evil is proved by an act, so that the substance is not the source of the crime, but the will conceived from its causes. When he saw himself superior to the others, he was inflated with the desire to exercise dominion.

How, then, is he said to have a father, when he is regarded as the author of his crime? Or how is it proved that he was a murderer from the beginning? Scripture calls the one who became his imitator by his name, so that, since he received his name from his deed, everyone who has done an evil deed may rightly be called a devil.
