The Savior therefore called Cain “the devil” in this passage, because, as an emulator of his deeds, he envied his brother and committed murder, leaving an example of the cruelty of parricide. So also the devil, when he envied the human being made in the image of God, increased the wickedness of his deed, providing a model of error.

Hence Cain also became a liar. When God said to him, “Where is Abel your brother?”—having been imbued with the wickedness of his father, he burst into a lie and said, “I do not know” (Gen. 4:9), pretending not to know where the one whose life he had taken was. He was so blinded by fury that he answered God as though he were a human being whom he thought he could conceal the matter from.

Thus the Jews, having become imitators of this kind, also killed the Lord himself, wishing to have Cain the fratricide rather than God as their father, so that they might become guilty of all the blood that was shed. For by killing the author of life, they became the chief perpetrators of every crime, even binding their own children to this evil when they said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27:25).

To persuade Pilate that there was nothing evil in what they were asking, they said that the consequences would fall upon their children if it was unjust; for in order to satisfy their fury, they did not wish to spare even their children.

Since the devil is not evil by nature, it is therefore more readily said of him that punishment would not be threatened to one who had not done what he did not know. For it is unjust to punish one who does nothing other than what belongs to his nature. And the evil is even greater if you demand from someone what you know he cannot do.

Accordingly, the one who is known to be able to know and do good, yet does evil, is justly punished. This too can be understood from the Savior’s words. As was mentioned above, he says: “Your father was a murderer from the beginning, and he did not stand in the truth.” If he is a liar by nature, how is it said that he did not stand in the truth? For the one who does not remain in the truth does not stand in the truth. It is therefore established that the devil was in the truth but did not persevere.

Finally, we read the Lord speaking thus through the prophet: “If they had stood,” he says, “in my substance” (Jer. 23:22)—that is, in my law. And the Apostle says to the Galatians: “Stand firm, and do not again be held back by the yoke of slavery” (Gal. 5:1). What could be clearer? For here he commands them henceforth to remain in his commandments. For the law is a foundation for those who keep it. If the devil had kept them, he would have stood in God’s substance and law.

How, then, does it seem to some that the devil was either made evil by God or has his own origin—that is, arose from nothing—when both views appear contrary to God? Whoever says that he was made for the purpose of being evil considers God imperfect in goodness, because one who is perfectly good does not make evil. Whoever does not believe that God is the author of his origin denies his dominion to God. For, since everything belongs to God, he supposes that something exists which does not in any way pertain to God. Such people ought to suffer punishment when they see that all things are judged by God through Christ.

### XCIX. — What does the Apostle’s statement mean: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” (1 Cor. 10:13)?

Not without providence, I think, does our Apostle, the teacher of the Gentiles, desire that temptation should seize us, but only human temptation; for divine temptation produces destruction. By this temptation the Jews were seized and perished through serpents. Living under God’s law, they doubted his providence; and for this reason he exhorts us not to be seized by divine, but by human, temptation.

The one who is said to be tempted by God is the person who, acting under his name, hopes for salvation from idols, because he does not have God as one who has been tested and approved. For everything that has not been approved is tested; and what is tested is brought into question.

Accordingly, divine temptation is deadly, whereas human temptation is salutary: just as it is destructive to doubt God, so it is most beneficial, because of God’s law, not to despair of human beings. Therefore the Apostle says providently: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human,” so that, tested by human beings on account of God’s law, we may be found strong [Note: [Col. 2299] The Colbert manuscript reads: “perhaps if we are found”], while carnal human beings doubt us but we are approved by God. For those who are not approved by God are tempted so that they may be corrected.

There are therefore two kinds of temptation. Sometimes we are tempted as believers, sometimes as doubters; thus the temptation of believers is human. We are troubled by human beings on account of faith; they test us to see whether they can lead us away from the faith. But those who doubt are tempted so that, distressed and repentant, they may return to the way, as also happened to the Jews.

When they doubted God’s providence, they were tempted by serpents so that, seized by pain, they might be corrected. God tempts such people in order to correct them.

There is also another temptation by which Abraham, Job, and Tobias, servants of God, were tested. Abraham, through the tribulation of offering his only and beloved son (Gen. 22), was to possess a richer fruit of righteousness for eternal glory. Job, through the loss of all his possessions, was to be enriched with wealth in heaven and on earth (Job 1–2; 42:12–13). Tobias, having suffered blindness, was so advanced that for the present he became glorious when his eyes were restored, and for the future perpetual brightness was reserved for him (Tob. 2:11; 11:15). For the righteous are tested so that they may progress.

Therefore in temptation we ought to be strong in spirit, knowing that this contributes not to our diminution but to our increase, provided that we endure it with an even temper through Christ.

[Note: [Col. 2300] This same question is found in manuscripts of the second class, among the questions published after the fifty-second from the New Testament.]

Every question, if it is to be clarified, must be traced back to its origin. When the Apostle was complaining about the Jews’ unbelief, and about their having tempted God in the wilderness—hence he says, “Let us not tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him” (1 Cor. 10:9)—as he recalled these matters and explained what they had suffered because of such evils in order to inspire terror, so that by that very example he might recall us from the evil of temptation directed against the Lord—for divine temptation occurs if, while acting under God’s law, someone seeks help elsewhere or from idols, distrusting God—therefore the Apostle warns us to avoid this.

But he exhorts us to endure human temptation, because human temptation consists in despairing of a human being in God’s cause and in being steadfast in faith in God. This temptation is understood as distrust, so that they may not distrust the promises of God. With respect to human beings, since in every error of seduction there is human temptation [Note: [Col. 2300] The German manuscript reads: “human tradition”], it is hostile to worldly calculations and resists God’s law, despairing of his promises.

You therefore have the distinction made clear: what temptation directed against God is, and what human temptation is. We ought not to disdain the latter if we are participants in God’s faith.

## ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW

[Note: [Col. 2300] So in the manuscripts and the Regensburg edition. Other editions read: “How the statement in the Gospel of Matthew is to be understood: ‘I confess to you, Father, Lord of heaven, etc.’”]

### C

[Note: [Col. 2300] This question is absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

You have heard, dearly beloved brothers, what the Gospel declares when the Lord says: “I confess to you, Lord of heaven and earth, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones. Yes, Father, because this was pleasing before you” (Matt. 11:25–26).

If, then, we examine the meaning of these words, we shall see that the Lord spoke them as an exhortation to believers: those who, because they despise worldly wisdom, appear as little ones to the wise of the world—people who, commended by no testimony, nevertheless wish to be called wise. Therefore God deemed it unworthy to show the truth to such people; but to the humble, who presume nothing about themselves and submit to the divine will, saving truths must be revealed, as justice requires.

For the one who is prudent before God and mindful of his salvation is the person who places God’s law above his own knowledge. He sees that the law is supported not by a clamor of words but by the power of realities. Without doubt, the person who commends himself for this matter is foolish and vain, since it is fortified by no distinction of signs.

Therefore God promised the kingdom not to the learned of this age but to the faithful. He promises eternity not to those who scrutinize the stars but to those who act rightly. He gives glory not to dialecticians, who try by deceit and petty arguments to exclude the truth, but to people of good will, who are more careful in life than in speech.

God rejects those who prefer to employ brilliant eloquence rather than good deeds. For the person who thinks that he adorns God’s work with words also wishes to turn God’s glory toward himself. The realities themselves ought to please by themselves, so that it is not speech but understanding that is praised.

If understanding is the author of writing, and words were invented to signify realities, why should not the realities themselves be brought forth with pure understanding, so that they may more effectively [Note: [Col. 2300] The Colbert manuscript reads: “more easily”] stir the mind toward salvation?

Therefore our Lord chose fishermen as Apostles—simple and unlearned men—who, by preserving the faith without any deceit and by living well, might show God’s truth in themselves. Hence the Apostle Paul also says: “When I came to you, brothers, I did not come with loftiness of speech or wisdom” (1 Cor. 2:1). And among other things: “The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power” (1 Cor. 4:20), so that, because words are exposed to contradiction, power might stand as witness to God’s law, to which all loftiness of speech yields.

These things have therefore been said beforehand, dearly beloved brothers, for the sake of the simpler people, lest they perhaps consider themselves unworthy of God’s grace because they have not been trained in forensic learning, when their simplicity contributes more to their praise. What the wise of the world do not see because of the pride of their learning, these people believe—not being wise in words, but wise in counsel.

For they know that God rests in good works and seeks faith, not cultivated speech. They read the Lord saying: “In whom shall I rest, if not in the humble and gentle person who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66:2).

Therefore, so that we may be made worthy of the promised rewards, we must do what the Lord commands, confident that the Lord loves those who keep his words. For he says to his disciples: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14:15), so that, serving the Lord in these things, we may be heirs of his kingdom through Jesus Christ our Lord.

## ON THE BOASTFULNESS OF THE ROMAN LEVITES

[Note: [Col. 2301] So in the manuscripts and the Regensburg edition. Other editions read: “How one ought to argue against the Roman levites who contend that levites are equal to priests, and deacons to presbyters.”]

## CI [Note: [Col. 2301] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

While we wish to obey the commands of charity, we may perhaps fall into reproach by writing about a matter that has never been called into question by anyone; for, because we do not wish to offend a friend, we entangle an effort that ought to have served to disclose some hidden matter. Yet the charity mentioned above has imposed this task upon us because of the excessive folly of a certain person who makes the assertion that we expose below, lest, since no one had answered it for a long time, it should advance toward something worse and one who had long exercised himself in vanity should be unable to be corrected. This, indeed, is the work of charity, which does not seek what is its own.

There is therefore a certain man named Falcidius [Note: [Col. 2301] The Colbert manuscript has: “with Falsi-de-re-quaerunt [an uncertain reading] as leader,” etc.], who, led by folly and by the vainglory of the Roman city, strives to make levites equal to priests and deacons equal to presbyters. I will not say “to place them above them,” because that is more foolish and may perhaps seem incredible [Note: [Col. 2301] According to the Lyon and Venetian editions, *videtur* (“seems”) is printed.], and we might be regarded not as correctors but as slanderers.

By what law, then, or by what custom, or following what example, he dares to undertake this, I do not think anyone knows: namely, to make equal those who have been given no seat in the Church with those who, because they are God’s overseers, sit with dignity in the house of God and in the honor of Christ. What audacity is it to make ministers equal to presbyters? What presumptuous temerity is it to compare with priests the carriers of the tabernacle, the bearers of all its vessels and wood, and those who carried water? This was the duty of the levites. It is as though officials were made equal to prefects or servants to masters.

For it is written, when the Lord says to Moses: “Take the tribe of Levi from among the children of Israel, and set them before Aaron the priest, and let them minister to him” (Num. 8:13). What example could be clearer than this, which is still observed in the Church? Although the deacons of the Roman Church may appear somewhat more shameless, they nevertheless do not presume to claim the dignity of sitting in the Church.

Indeed, the multitude of clerics makes it unnecessary for them to perform every ministry of service in due order. Otherwise they would also carry the altar and its vessels and pour water into the priest’s hands, as we see done throughout all the Churches and as was established by the Lord through Moses. Or are they perhaps better than Elisha, who poured water over Elijah’s hands (IV Reg. 3:11)?

He defends the deacons against the presbyters as though deacons were ordained from presbyters, and not presbyters from deacons. But because they are ministers of the Roman Church, they are thought to be more honorable than in the other Churches, on account of the magnificence of the city of Rome, which seems to be the head of all cities. If this is so, they ought to claim the same for their priests [Col. 2302]; for if those who are inferior increase in honor because of the magnificence of the city, how much more should those who are superior be exalted? Whatever is granted to officials becomes an increase to authority, just as the honor shown to a servant advances the praise of his master.

Nevertheless, before God, the just judge, each person retains here the honor that has been decreed for the individual offices of the Churches, so that whoever is a deacon may have the honor of a deacon throughout all the Churches. For it is no ordinary honor merely to serve God’s overseer in the Church, so that a priest is regarded as worthy of the whole of ecclesiastical honor.

The higher order possesses within itself and among its own members the lower as well. For the presbyter also performs the office of deacon, exorcist, and reader. That a presbyter is understood to be a bishop is proved by the apostle Paul, when he instructs Timothy—whom he ordained as a presbyter—about what sort of person he ought to appoint as a bishop (I Tim. 3:1–7). For what is a bishop except the first presbyter, that is, the chief priest? Accordingly, here he calls them nothing other than his fellow presbyters and fellow priests. Does the bishop likewise call his ministers his fellow deacons? Certainly not, because they are much inferior.

And it is shameful to call a judge a chief officer. In Alexandria and throughout Egypt, if a bishop is absent, a presbyter consecrates [Note: [Col. 2302] The Colbert manuscript reads “appoints” (*consignat*).]

How great the dignity of the priestly order is, the example of Caiaphas demonstrates. Although he was a very wicked man, he prophesied. Why? Because, it says, “he was chief of the priests” (John 11:49).

Again, the book that we call the Acts of the Apostles proves that there is a great difference between a deacon and a priest. When the people of Samaria had believed Philip, a deacon ordained by the Apostles, as he preached, they sent, it says, to Peter and John, so that they might come and give the believers the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands (Acts 8:14–15).

But I believe that those who defend these things are ignorant of the Scriptures or forgetful of the Law. Whoever thinks that such claims ought to be upheld should therefore remember what happened to the levites when they held such opinions. When they presumed that there was no difference between priests and levites, the earth opened and swallowed up Korah and those who agreed with him, while a torrent of fire consumed two hundred and fifty men at the same time, with God as judge (Num. 16:31–35). And when King Uzziah presumed to perform a priestly function, he was covered with leprosy (II Chron. 26:19–21), so that by this example the others might be terrified and not dare to presume what had not been granted to them.

Now we see deacons rashly performing what belongs to priests at banquets and wishing in prayer to receive a response from the people, although this is permitted to priests alone. For the office of a deacon is to receive from the priest and then give to the people.

Do you see what empty presumption produces? Forgetful through pride of mind, because they see that they are ministers of the Roman Church, they do not consider what has been decreed for them by God and what they ought to observe. But they remove these matters from their memory by continual attendance at households and by official influence, which at present has considerable power through either good or bad recommendations. For either people fear that they will give bad recommendations, or they buy them so that they may give good ones.

These are the things that make them fail to consider the order of their own rank. For while they unlawfully serve such men through flattery, they drive them headlong, so that they think more is permitted to them, especially when they see that such deference is not shown to priests; and consequently they think themselves superior.

“But a presbyter is appointed on the testimony of a deacon,” they say, as though this belonged to the prerogative of rank and greatness. For we read that the apostle Peter said to the people: “Choose from among yourselves those whom we may appoint to serve the mysteries of the Church” (Acts 6:3). I do not wish to say: “to serve tables.” Behold, deacons were appointed on the testimony of laypeople.

And the Apostle also wishes the man who is said to be appointed bishop to have testimony even from Gentiles, for he says: “He must also have a good testimony from those who are outside” (I Tim. 3:7). Everyone, therefore, may give testimony, yet not everyone is worthy of this honor. Everyone may judge, yet not everyone can be what he judges.

A painter may be judged good and preferred to another by one who does not know how to paint; and one flute-player may be approved as better than another flute-player by someone skilled in a different art. Likewise, one who is inferior in rank may serve as a witness for the man being made a presbyter.

Again, in order to inflate themselves and think that much is owed to them, they say: “Those who are to be ordained are brought forward by us.” Thus, because they are surrounded by their attendants, they seem worthy of honor.

Let it be true. An official is sent by the bishop to provide attendance to the man being ordained. An emperor too, in order to appear as emperor, is attended by military service; yet the army is neither better than nor equal to the emperor. And Haman, although distinguished in military honor, was sent by the king to go in attendance upon Mordecai (Esth. 6:10), so that from such services it might be recognized how worthy Mordecai was.

In the same way, deacons are sent to serve those who are being made presbyters, so that everyone may understand that these men are made worthy to be priests. For, with the exception of the priests to whom deacons owe service, deacons are placed above everyone else.

## AGAINST NOVATIAN [Note: [Col. 2303] Thus the manuscripts and the Ratisbon edition. Other editions read: “How one should dispute against the Novatians, who deny saving repentance.”]

### CII

[Note: [Col. 2303] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

“His disciples said to Jesus, ‘Lord, do you wish us to say that fire should come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?’ And he answered them, saying, ‘You do not know of what spirit you are. For the Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them’” (Luke 9:54–56).

Although it would certainly have been appropriate to punish the Samaritans for refusing to receive him, the Lord nevertheless, who came to bestow mercy, withdrew the sentence, so that thereafter they might be corrected and reformed. The prophet Elisha, too, angered by the boys who insulted him, took vengeance on them with God as judge, so that in that place they were devoured by bears, where there is said to be no forest (2 Kings 2:23–24). The Lord, however, spared the prostitute who had been brought before him—namely, the woman whom the leading men of the Jews said they had caught in adultery (John 8:11)—so that, because the gracious preaching had begun, he might teach that she should not be condemned but forgiven.

For the Law given through Moses, since it possessed justice directed toward vengeance, exercised severity at its beginnings. Thus it took funeral vengeance on the man who went out to gather wood on the Sabbath (Num. 15:32–36); and it likewise inflicted punishment on the son of the Egyptian who had blasphemed God (Lev. 24:10–14); and in the case of the molten calf it struck the children of Israel (Exod. 32:27). Each Law, therefore, displayed its full character at its very beginning: the old Law, since it was more ready to punish, appeared harsher in its opening stages, so that by instilling fear it might make its hearers diligent and attentive.

The New Law, however, because it is gracious and readily inclined toward mercy, showed its beginnings to be most gentle and compassionate, so that by that very attractiveness and love it might summon all to forgiveness. Later, the one that had appeared harsher, because of the frailty of the human race, not only softened its rigor but also showed itself humane and gracious; and the one that had appeared merciful sometimes inflicted punishment. Ananias and his wife Sapphira were struck down by divine action (Acts 5:5, 10). Elymas the magician, unbelieving and resisting God’s Law, was blinded by the Lord’s judgment and power (Acts 13:8–11). King Herod, because he did not give honor to the God of heaven, was struck by God’s angel and died, teeming with worms (Acts 12:23).

Lest people think that, because mercy was preached, everything would remain unpunished and sin could be committed with impunity, he established fear, showing that forgiveness of sins is granted for this purpose: that those who have been, as it were, brought to life from the dead may thereafter abstain from what is contrary, and that everyone may strive to avoid departing from this life with guilt, since judgment will come. For each person is charged with the sentence under which he dies.

Since, therefore, the New Law possesses the fullness of mercy, lest it be held in contempt by lovers of sin, it inflicted punishment on those mentioned above. The Old Law, although given for vengeance, nevertheless forgave certain people, lest it be called altogether cruel; but it punished more people, because its character is ready to take revenge.

Without doubt, therefore, the grace of the New Law is greater than that of the old. If it is greater, how is it denied the ability to grant what the other granted, though the other possessed less grace? For the latter was more inclined toward severity. Thus, if the former is shown to have forgiven the penitent, how can it be that this Law, which is merciful, does not receive penitents?

The Jews, too, were called sons of God; they are read, on the authority of the apostle Paul, to have been baptized through Moses in the cloud and in the sea (1 Cor. 10:2). Since they were about to receive the Law, they were undoubtedly known to have been purified, so that thereafter they might render an account of the Law they had received and, if they sinned, reform themselves through repentance. For the Lord says through the prophet Isaiah: “Repent, you who have gone astray, and turn back” (Isa. 45:22).

But perhaps the contrary is said: repentance was indeed preached, but not forgiveness. If, then, repentance was preached by God, there will be a reward for those who repent. The Lord would not have admonished them about this in vain. Moreover, knowing that forgiveness of sins ought to be given to those who turn back, the Lord commanded this, since he said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but only that he turn back and live” [Note: [Col. 2304] In B.: “so long as he turns back and lives.” We have followed the reading of Er., Lugd., Ven., and Lov. M.] (Ezek. 18:32).

There is therefore a fruit of repentance, as became clear in the case of those who turned to God. The impious assertion devised by Novatian is consequently refuted: he reverses the meaning of the Lord’s words by saying, “The Lord said, ‘Whoever denies me, I will also deny him’” (Matt. 10:33), as though, if any Christian denied him for whatever reason, he could no longer return, or, if he did return, could in no way be received.

And where would the commandment of repentance be? For after giving this sentence, the Savior did not deny the apostle Peter when he denied him. Why? Because, when repentance followed, Peter wept most bitterly over his error (Matt. 26:75), knowing that those who turn back are forgiven and restored through repentance.

But Novatian pretends that repentance should be undertaken. Since he does not dare openly to deny that repentance should be granted, constrained by the Law, he subtly attempts to frustrate it. For when he says that whoever denies will in no way receive forgiveness, but will himself be denied in the presence of God’s angels, how does he not profess repentance deceitfully?

Here, moreover, his fraud is plainly apparent when he adds: “Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven, neither here nor in the future” (Matt. 12:32). Although the cause of sinning against the Holy Spirit is one thing, and that of denying the Lord Jesus another, Novatian nevertheless wishes the sense of the one who denies the Lord and of the one who sins against the Holy Spirit to be the same, so that by this evasion he may cut off the fruit of repentance. For if denying the Lord is the same as sinning against the Holy Spirit, no forgiveness is to be hoped for by those who deny him, nor is there any fruit of repentance, because the Lord’s oracles promise that this sin will be forgiven neither here nor in the future. Thus it is clear that Novatian deceitfully says that repentance should be undertaken. What purpose could repentance serve if he denies that the offense can be erased?

The sighs, tears, and lamentation of repentance achieve this: that a person may both merit forgiveness and receive restoration. Finally, David, repenting and confessing his sin, both obtained forgiveness (2 Sam. 12:13) and was restored to his former condition, since he remained king and afterward prophesied. This is clearly demonstrated: in the fiftieth Psalm he repented, and afterward, having suffered persecution from his son, he prophesied. For, according to the historical sequence, the third Psalm follows the fiftieth.

But perhaps it should have been appropriate to forgive a king, whereas the humble ought not to be forgiven, although it might seem more difficult to forgive those who are more powerful. Yet “God does not show partiality” (Rom. 2:11). The higher a person is, the more serious his crime, even if his sin is slight. Just as humility in a powerful person is exalted and magnificent, so his fault must be regarded as a crime.

Apart from sins that are known to be unlawful for everyone, not everything is permitted to the powerful that is permitted to the humble. It is disgraceful for a man of rank to engage in trade [Note: [Col. 2305] Ms. Colbert: “a man of rank” (*dignitoso*).], and it is conspicuous for him to enter a tavern. For senators, too, lending at interest is a disgrace. If, therefore, they are to be censured when found guilty of these minor matters, how much more must they be judged guilty if they sin?

Thus it is evident that David sinned most grievously, and indeed in two ways. Yet when he turned back, he obtained forgiveness both for murder and for adultery; and, what is more, by mourning he was restored. When the prophet Nathan reproved him, he did not dare to conceal his sin but confessed, saying, “I have sinned against the Lord.” Then the prophet answered and said, “The Lord has taken away your sin, and you will not die, because you have repented.” Since he is later found to have prophesied, there is no doubt that he was restored.

Ahab, too, when reproved by the prophet because of Naboth’s death, went away weeping, tore his garments, and girded himself with sackcloth. Then the word of the Lord came through his servant Elijah concerning Ahab, and the Lord said: “Have you seen how Ahab has been humbled before me? I will not bring evil upon him in his days” (1 Kings 21:27–29). And when the Ninevites mourned their sins, life was restored to them while death threatened (Jonah 3:10). Behold how great is the benefit of repentance!

But perhaps it may be said in opposition: forgiveness was indeed granted, but not for the crime of idolatry. For although these sins are serious, the crime of idolatry is more serious. Nevertheless, Novatian’s assertion has rightly been dismissed, at least in substantial part, since two grave crimes appear to have been granted to repentance. If fornication ought not to be forgiven, as Novatian thinks, how much more ought murder or adultery not to be forgiven?

His vanity is exposed by the fact that these more serious sins are shown to have been forgiven. Therefore it must now be investigated whether God promised that forgiveness could be granted to idolaters. Whatever is not rightly forgiven here will not be able to be forgiven in the future. For here, as the Lord said, sins are either bound or loosed (Matt. 16:19); in the future there will be nothing else but reward or condemnation. Whoever is rightly rejected here cannot be chosen or judged worthy in the future.

Let us therefore hear what the Lord says through the prophet Jeremiah concerning idolaters: “Go and say: Return to me, Israel, who have dwelt as strangers, says the Lord, and I will not set my face against you, because I am merciful, says the Lord, and I will not be angry with you forever. Nevertheless, acknowledge your guilt: you have acted impiously and have set your ways toward strangers beneath every leafy tree” (Jer. 3:12–13).

Behold what God promises to those who, after falling, turn back to him: after apostasy, when they return, he forgives their sins. Again God says through Jeremiah: “My cherished ones have walked along harsh roads; they have been led away like a flock seized by enemies. Take courage, children, and cry out to God; your remembrance will be in the place of your captivity. For just as your mind was set on straying from God, so, when you have turned back and seek him, you will multiply your efforts tenfold. For he who brought evils upon you will bring you eternal joy together with your salvation” (Baruch 4:26–29).

O the clemency of God! How he urges the fallen to rise again! How he exhorts them, after the error of idolatry, to return to him! Like a benevolent father, he promises his children everlasting joy in salvation if they correct themselves.

Likewise, in the same prophet, among other passages, he says: “I will restore them to this land, and I will rebuild them and not overthrow them; I will replant them and not uproot them” (Jer. 24:6). He had threatened, saying, “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be uprooted.” Lest those who sinned against God despair of themselves, as though those who had sacrificed to idols had already been uprooted and could not be replanted, he exhorts them: if they repent, they will be able to be restored to their former condition. The sentence remains in force only if the sin is not corrected.

Finally, it was proclaimed to the Ninevites that after three days their city would be overthrown. Why after three days, unless so that they might either repent and the sentence be withdrawn, or, remaining in their sin, perish more justly? This is what he said through the prophet: “I do not desire the death of the one who dies, but only that he turn back and live.” Thus it happened that, when death threatened the Ninevites because of their sins, they were forgiven after repentance followed.

Why do we find that the ark was built for a hundred years in the time of Noah (Gen. 5:31; 7:6), unless so that those who saw and heard what was impending might reform themselves? For God does not wish anyone to perish.

Hence we read in Solomon: “The Most High has had mercy on those who repent” (Sir. 12:3). And again: “You have mercy on all, because you can do all things, and you overlook the sins of human beings for the sake of repentance” (Wis. 11:24).

In this same spirit, the Lord, grieving over the Jews’ faithlessness, says: “Jerusalem, Jerusalem, which kills the prophets and stones those who are sent to you! How often I wanted to gather your children, as a hen gathers her chicks beneath her wings, and you were unwilling!” (Matt. 23:37).

Thus, throughout the whole Law, the Lord continually exhorts sinners to turn back to him, unwilling that his work should be handed over to destruction. The Law was given for no other reason than that human beings might turn from error to truth. Yet in the New Testament the author of the Law appears more merciful, because, at the time when he deigned to reveal the mystery of his Son, our Lord, he wished to be more generous and abundant in mercy, so that, when the Son preached, there might be more grace than there had been when servants preached.

And rightly so. It was fitting that he should bestow greater gifts through the Son than through servants. Finally, to those who turn to him in faith, he grants all their sins at once, without any intervening lamentation of repentance. Hence the apostle Paul says: “The gifts and calling of God are without repentance” (Rom. 11:29).

Afterward, however, if they sin, they will be able to merit forgiveness through repentance. Since they sinned after receiving free mercy, they can no longer attain forgiveness freely, but only through the intervention of sighs and tears.

For it is impossible for a human being not to sin. Therefore the apostle John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:8–9). David likewise merited forgiveness and restoration when he confessed his sin.

Certainly John the apostle is speaking to Christians. For he says in what follows: “My little children, I write these things to you so that you may not sin; but if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ” (1 John 2:1). He says this so that, if we sin after Baptism, we may humbly beseech our advocate to intercede for us with the Father.

If repentance had a place among our predecessors, how can it be that it has no place in the present age, when the mercy of the preaching is greater? He who had mercy on his enemies by calling them to grace—when they have become his friends, will he not have mercy on them together with their reward? For anguish of heart is the reward of the penitent.

If this were true, people would grieve that they had been made friends from enemies [Note: [Col. 2306] Thus Ms. Colbert. The printed editions continue after *penitent*: “If pardon were not granted to fallen penitents, who had been friends before their fall, what Novatian said would be true: they would grieve,” etc.]. Or how should one regard a person who gave mercy to enemies who did not repent, but refused it to friends and penitents?

Moreover, since the Lord knows that the devil raises himself up and rages more fiercely against the friends and servants of God, the apostle Peter says: “Be vigilant and sober, because your adversary the devil prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour” (1 Pet. 5:8). Since the Lord knows that we have a dreadful and powerful adversary, if we are defeated by him, he wants us to flee to his help, grieving that we have been struck down, so that, restored by his power, we may fight back bravely.

For just as, unless those days of which the Lord speaks had been shortened, no flesh would be saved (Matt. 24:22), so, if repentance is denied to human beings, no one will be able to be saved. For if “no one will boast that he has a pure heart” (Prov. 20:9), and elsewhere it says, “No one is without uncleanness, not even an infant of one day” (Job 14:4), who will be able to escape if repentance is denied?

And where is what the Lord says, that “there will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15:7)?

But, he says, greater crimes ought not to be forgiven: fornication and idolatry. Where, then, is the Lord’s declaration in which he promises that all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven human beings, but that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (Matt. 12:31)? He says plainly that all sins can be forgiven except one.

Now choose, Novatian: of whom do you wish this to have been said—of those who have not yet believed, or of those who already believe? If of those who have not believed, how is forgiveness of sins granted, since it is clear that before they believe all sin against God and against the Holy Spirit? For some call the Lord’s deeds magical arts, attributing the work of the Holy Spirit to demons.

But if you wish it to have been said of believers, your assertion is excluded, because all sins will be forgiven: “Whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man,” he says, “will be forgiven.” Therefore, whether one sins against God or against Christ, it will be forgiven human beings. For he included all sins except sin against the Holy Spirit.

Accordingly, he does not wish the sin committed against God to be understood as the same as the sin against the Holy Spirit. If it were the same, he would not have excepted it. Since, therefore, the phrase “blasphemy against the Holy Spirit” signifies another sin—for this statement concerns a person, not the nature of the Holy Spirit—all sins will be forgiven, whether to those who already believe through repentance or to those who will later believe through Baptism.

The fact that the Jews sinned against the Holy Spirit is a different matter, belonging to that particular time. Hence he shows that it will not be forgiven them, either here or in the future. For they did not sin against the Holy Spirit through error but through malice. Knowingly and deliberately, although they saw that the works performed by the Savior were God’s works, they pretended that they were the work of the prince of demons in order to turn the people away from his faith.

Therefore the Lord says to them: “You have taken away the key of knowledge; you yourselves did not enter, and you prevented those who were entering” (Luke 11:52). This sentence was therefore pronounced against the malicious, for whom no remedy by which they might be saved can be found. There is no crime more serious than this: a person pretends that something he knows to be true is false.

The Jews, who appeared to be under God’s Law and to whom the promise of Christ had been made, saw his mighty works and understood that they were what God had promised. Yet they were blinded by envy, so that they denied this; and not only denied it, but persecuted him even to death.

It is therefore not fitting that this sin should ever be forgiven those who, with their own conscience as witness, dared to resist the God to whom they claimed to be devoted.

There are different causes, however, when someone sins against God or against Christ. A person may, while envying another’s happiness, rise up against the Creator in the anguish of his own humiliation; or, having suddenly suffered some adverse event, may be provoked to anger and act abusively toward his Father.

The incarnation of Christ, however, also provokes insult [Note: [Col. 2307] Ms. Colbert: “Christ’s incarnation provokes insult.”]. When people do not understand the mystery of the incarnate Christ, they blaspheme, considering it unworthy that the Son of God, who is incorporeal and of a simple nature, should be said to have been born in human fashion. They blaspheme, therefore, because they do not understand the mystery.

For this reason, a hand should be extended to those who turn back, since they act against the truth while believing that they are acting for the truth. A person tortured and racked with claws says that this is true which he had been persecuting [Note: [Col. 2307] Ms. Colbert: “he follows.”].

Those Jews mentioned above, however, thought one thing and did another, and, without a judge or executioner, are always tortured by the testimony of their own conscience. Whoever became an enemy of the truth through error rejoices, once converted, that he has come to know the truth. The malicious person, however, has nothing to correct; for if he turns back, he will begin to say that something is true which previously he knowingly declared to be false.

There is no cause for an offense against the Holy Spirit. His activity does not produce provocation, since it appears in the power of signs and wonders. Who would dare hiss against him [Note: [Col. 2308] Ms. Colbert: “leap against him” (*insilire*).] upon seeing the dead raised? Or who would become angry with him when, through his effect, he sees the lame running, the blind receiving sight, and the deaf hearing? Or how could anyone fail to love him when he sees him cast out unclean spirits, cleanse lepers, and heal every kind of illness?

The Jews preferred to insult him, calling his work the work of demons, so long as they could fulfill their envy and hatred against the Savior [Note: [Col. 2308] Ms. Colbert: “which they exercised against the Savior.”]. Therefore he shows that this sin will not be forgiven them, either here or in the future.

But Novatian says: “Let it be proved that greater crimes are specifically forgiven—that is, idolatry and fornication after the washing. For this is why, he says, all sins are forgiven together in Baptism: so that thereafter, if they commit any serious offense, they may in no way obtain forgiveness, since, after receiving the Holy Spirit, what is contrary to the Holy Spirit ought not to be committed.”

Who would deny that one ought never to sin, if that were possible? Yet God, knowing that the human race is fragile, has always surrounded people with saving remedies, so that after sins they would have a means by which to restore themselves.

But if the Spirit who has been given prevents repentance from being granted to those who sin, then there is no providence in the New Testament, and it will appear that better provision was made for those of old, to whom this medicine was by no means denied.

And how is grace greater in the New Testament than in the Old? This would be the work of an enemy, who, knowing that human beings cannot reach salvation except through the intervention of repentance, would give the Holy Spirit so that, if an offense were committed against him through fear or error, no satisfaction could afterward restore the person. That would be to seek an opportunity to destroy people, not to save them.

But far be it from us, since the Lord says, “The Son of Man did not come to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9:56).

If God commanded us to forgive one another the sins that we commit against one another seventy times seven times, provided that we turn back (Matt. 18:22), how much more does he himself forgive those who turn back if they sin against him? For he wants every sinner to turn back.

Therefore the apostle proves that forgiveness was granted to fornicators and the impure when he says: “Otherwise, when I come, I might mourn over many of those who sinned previously and did not repent of the impurity and fornication that they committed” (2 Cor. 12:21). He proves that some repented, for whom he does not grieve but rejoices; but he indicates that others did not repent of their fornication, and for this reason he says that he will mourn over them, since they do not belong to life because they did not repent.

If repentance for such a crime had always to be undertaken in this life, he would not have said that he mourned because they “did not repent,” but because they “were not repenting.” Knowing that repentance both begins and is completed here, he says that they did not repent. For he wanted, when he came to them, to have peace in their communion.

Behold, it has been proved that fornicators are to be admitted to communion after carrying out repentance. They cannot be admitted to communion as long as they are practicing such things; but they are to be admitted when they cease, according to the judgment of the Church.

It remains to see whether we can prove specifically that forgiveness can be granted to idolaters. For we read in the Apocalypse of the blessed apostle John that repentance for idolatry is preached. The bishops are admonished—for he calls them angels, that is, messengers, just as the blessed apostle Paul says, “You received me as an angel of God” (Gal. 4:14)—so that they may impose repentance on sinners and not permit those who cause scandals in the Church to go without admonition, since they too belong to the Church.

He therefore says:

> “And to the angel of the church in Pergamum write: Thus says he who has the two-edged sword: I know where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is; and you hold fast to my name and have not denied my faith in the days when Antipas, my faithful witness, was killed among you, where Satan dwells. But I have a few things against you, because you have there those who hold the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the children of Israel, to eat food sacrificed to idols and to commit fornication. So you also have those who hold the teaching of the Nicolaitans. Repent in the same way.”

He identifies this as the teaching of the Nicolaitans, which was also that of Balaam—that is, idolatry and fornication—and he commands repentance for it.

Because he is speaking to members of the Church, he shows this by saying: “This is what the Spirit says to the churches.” What fruit repentance has, he indicates by adding: “To the one who conquers I will give to eat of the hidden manna,” as though through repentance the person conquers sins.

For what is repentance except to grieve over past actions and thereafter to refrain from those things one had committed?

And to the angel of the church in Thyatira write:

> “Thus says the Son of God, who has eyes like a flame of fire, and whose feet are like bronze from Tyre: I know your works, your love, faith, ministry, and perseverance, and that your final works are greater than the first. But I have this against you: you tolerate the woman Jezebel, who calls herself a prophetess and teaches and seduces my servants to commit fornication and to eat what has been sacrificed to idols. I gave her time to repent, but she was unwilling to repent of her fornication. Behold, I will cast her onto a bed, and those who commit adultery with her into great tribulation, unless they repent of their deeds; and I will strike her children with death. And all the churches will know that I am the one who searches minds and hearts, and I will give each of you according to your works. But I say to you and to the rest who are in Thyatira, whoever does not hold this teaching and has not known the depths of Satan, as they say, I will not lay any other burden upon you. Nevertheless, hold fast to what you have until I come. And to the one who conquers and keeps my works to the end, I will give authority over the nations” (Rev. 2:12–26).

In this one Epistle addressed to the church at Thyatira, he refutes and rejects the twofold error of the Novatian heresy. He promises a reward to those who repent of idolatry, and he shows that the wicked within one church do not contaminate the good, even though they belonged to one communion. For he was not writing to people outside the Church when he said, “Whoever has ears, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”

The apostle Paul speaks in the same way: “We know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those who are under the Law” (Rom. 3:19). And elsewhere: “What have I to do with judging those who are outside?” (1 Cor. 5:12).

Thus, among the people of one Church, he summons some to repentance and praises others, saying: “But I say to you and to the rest who are in Thyatira, whoever does not hold this teaching”—that is, the teaching of idolatry—“hold fast to what you have until I come.” This means: persevere to the end, because “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10:22). Likewise, the one who perseveres in evil will be condemned.

Accordingly, just as the righteousness of a righteous person will not save him on the day when he goes astray, so the wickedness of an unjust person will not harm him when he turns back. Therefore he said, “Whoever sacrifices to the gods shall be uprooted”; but if he turns back, he will live.

The same applies to what the Lord says: “Whoever denies me, I will deny him” (Matt. 10:33). If he turns back, he cannot be denied by the one whom he confesses.

This is why he says in the Psalm: “No living person will be justified in your sight” (Ps. 142:2). For the sentence is charged to a person according to the state in which he dies.

Because the wicked were going to remain in the Church together with the good until God’s judgment, God himself indicated this, saying:

> “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind. But when they came to shore, they separated the good into their vessels, but cast the bad outside. So it will be at the consummation of the age: the angels will go out and separate from the kingdom of God all scandals and those who practice iniquity” (Matt. 13:47–49).

The same point is signified by the man who was found among those reclining at table without a wedding garment (Matt. 22:12–13). By showing that he alone was cast out from the assembly, the Lord demonstrates that his crime of unworthiness did not pollute the others. Since this unworthiness was designated by the fact that he did not possess a wedding garment, it was evident to the others. They saw that he was dressed differently from them.

Hence the apostle Paul says: “In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver, but also of wood and clay” (2 Tim. 2:20). He said this concerning Hymenaeus and Philetus, who, although they were from the Church, held perverse opinions about the resurrection, just as some members of the church at Corinth denied the resurrection.

Novatian, however, interprets this great house as the world, not the Church, so that he will not be forced to assert that in one Church there are wicked together with good, impure together with pure. I think this can easily be overturned.

In one house everyone bears one name. Although they may differ in character, they are nevertheless reckoned under the one name of their master in their profession. The world, however, contains people of different professions, so that they profess to have different gods and lords.

You see, therefore, that this cannot have been said of the world, but of the Church, in which people dwelling under one name are diverse in conduct.

I perceive that Novatian was not unaware of this. But because he had no just complaints to make concerning his separation, and did not wish to be openly ashamed, he fabricated certain arguments for himself through a wicked interpretation of the Law, by which he might try to excuse and conceal the envious will of his malice.

Finally, he replies to what we have said: “Nor do I refuse to require repentance for the idolatry that has been committed; but I do not dare to forgive it, because this crime must be forgiven by the one against whom it was committed.”

He answers deceitfully. His own interpretations expose him, and through them his fraud becomes evident. When he says, “It is written, ‘Whoever denies me, I will also deny him,’ and the one whose words they are cannot lie,” he shows the repentance he says should be undertaken to be empty and fruitless.

For if the sentence has been given, and the one who gave it does not deceive, why do you compel a person to torment himself with lamentations and sighs when you either deny or refuse to acknowledge that these actions can achieve anything?

Everyone who gives another advice gives it for this purpose: to declare what benefit can result from it. But because you, Novatian, profess this deceitfully in order to mock people’s minds, you say that repentance should be undertaken. Knowing that this cannot openly be denied, you subtly cut off repentance—not in words, but in intention [Note: [Col. 2310] Ms. Colbert: “in effect.”].

You certainly say that everyone who has sacrificed to idols sins against the Holy Spirit, and you insist from the words of the Law that this sin will be forgiven neither here nor in the future. How, then, do you say that repentance for this offense should be undertaken, unless you are deceiving people, as I have shown above?

But you are accustomed to trying to conceal this fraud by another deceit, saying that the apostle Peter also spoke in the same sense to Simon: “Repent of this wickedness of yours, if perhaps it may be forgiven you” (Acts 8:22).

The apostle Peter, however, observed that this man’s malice was ancient, poisonous, and exceedingly bitter; therefore he gave him an uncertain answer. For what mortal ever sinned in such a way as to wish to purchase the gift of God with money?

That answer was therefore given because of malice, not because of error. Malice is what has no remedy, since it is neither error nor accompanied by any necessity that could provide an excuse and enable a person to reach forgiveness through weeping.

If, therefore, some people are found in such a condition, let them hear what Simon also heard. For this reason the apostle Peter answered him ambiguously, saying: “I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity.”

If, then, in so grave a matter, one that appears to be without remedy, the answer was given ambiguously, it is not doubtful that those who sin against God through error or some necessity can be forgiven if they undertake suitable repentance.

This has been entrusted by the author to ecclesiastical authority: that it should both impose repentance and receive people after repentance.

Novatian still makes another objection: “Why do they hand over the Lord’s body to those whom they know to be sinners?” As though those who are judges could themselves act as accusers. If the accused are brought forward and exposed, they can be expelled. For what judge assumes the role of an accuser?

If the Lord himself tolerated Judas, whom he knew to be a thief and to carry away what was put into the common purse (John 12:6), and did not cast him out because he had not been accused, we ought to follow this example, so that we may not cast out someone who has not been publicly exposed.

For it is not appropriate even for a just man to accuse another. Hence Matthew says: “Joseph, being a righteous man and unwilling to expose her, resolved to dismiss her quietly” (Matt. 1:19).

Judas, therefore, while he was among the disciples, did not contaminate them by his own corruption, since they disagreed with his thefts; and, receiving the Eucharist among them, he did not pollute the innocent. Nor did the Lord deny his body to the man whom he knew to be a robber, because, according to the apostle, “the one who receives it unworthily receives a sword against himself” (1 Cor. 11:27).

Nor did he turn himself away from the Lord’s gaze. Sinners pollute those who consent to their evil deeds. Hence it is said: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him” (Ps. 49:18).

This is why the apostle rebuked the people of Corinth: they neither corrected nor avoided the man who publicly had his father’s wife, so that he might reform himself. He says: “Do you not know that a little leaven corrupts the whole lump?” (1 Cor. 5:1, 6).

Since there was no leader or superior of the Church present, it was the responsibility of the people to correct the man whom they saw conducting himself so shamefully and disgracefully among them. Accordingly, the apostle rebukes them as though they were consenting to his crime.

There was no need for an accuser or witnesses in this matter, since he publicly kept his stepmother in the place of a wife.

Thus, insofar as our case is concerned, we have set out the reasoning—not accusing others, but defending ourselves. I appeal to the conscience of the Novatians, who always accuse us, if they know that all those who are with them are holy. Yet he is so angry with us that he even denies that we are Christians, although he knows that we were initiated into the faith on which he himself relies.

Certainly profession and life make a Christian. If, therefore, you see a person professing the same things as you and not being unlike you
in life; why do you deny that he is what you are? Certainly, whoever confesses the Lord Jesus speaks in the Holy Spirit (I Cor. XII, 3); he speaks the truth. For every truth is from God. Why do you not agree with one who speaks the truth, but deny him? Do you contradict one who confesses God—not rationally, but in fury? Do you not seem an enemy of God, resisting one who professes the truth about him? Does a pagan, on hearing someone say that idols are gods, deny that he is a pagan? Why do you deny that someone is a Christian when you hear him professing the words of the sound faith, although you read, “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X, 10)?

But you, like an enemy, resist God in what you fail to see through your anger: you deny that the one who confesses this has salvation, although the Lord says, “Whoever confesses me, I also [will confess] him” (Luke XII, 8). Does he say, “If a Novatian has confessed me”? Yet you assert this in such a way that you seem to defend the proposition that the one who is saved must be not merely a Christian, but also a Novatian. But if confession made in Christ brings salvation, then wherever and among whomever this confession remains whole, it possesses salvation. Therefore, if the tradition of this confession has been corrupted among us, or its meaning changed, you rightly accuse us. For if it remains in us just as it does in you, by denying us you appear to deny yourself also.

But you accuse the ministers of the faith. Grant that this is true, although you cannot prove it: “Those, however, heard it from them.” Is what they heard true or false? For if a vicious person speaks the truth, it does not thereby cease to be true because it was spoken by a vicious person; the conduct of one’s life is one matter, and one’s profession another. Does not the persecutor, out of hatred for the Christian name, persecute the profession, not the manner of life? In the first place, knowing that this advances religion, when we confess that we are Christians, the sacrilegious persecutor believes what we confess, which he does not wish to hear precisely because he hears it. But you, although you belong to the same profession and bear the same seal, do not believe us when we confess what you yourself confess.

If you knew that we had been reborn in a manner different from that in which you were reborn, you would rightly not believe that we are what you are. Why do I suffer persecution from a sacrilegious person if I am not what you are? For if I professed about myself what you say about me, I would not suffer persecution. And, finally, I myself must be believed concerning myself, not you. The judge seeks my profession, not your statement about me. Why, then, do you deny me when I confess, since in this case it is true that it is not another’s testimony but my own profession that must be sought, either on my behalf or against me?

I did not wish, on account of the Name, to torture you in opposition to me, [Col. 2312] [Note: Ms. Colbert: “I wished to be tortured on account of the Name.”] so that it might become evident whether you too would deny, in opposition to me, one confessing truths, or whom one should believe. For you put this forward deceitfully, so that you may appear to have a just cause for your schism. You are certainly not unaware that in this matter my testimony about myself is required, not another’s, and that what I have confessed is to be accepted as true, not what someone else has denied.

It is plainly evident that those are free who, out of love for Christ and without investigating people’s actions, hasten to attain his faith. They approve in these people what they know to be useful to themselves—that is, attaining the tradition of the faith concerning Christ. For whoever thinks that something else besides the mystery is necessary for a person in this matter does injury to the tradition; he has too low an opinion of the grace of God. Whenever he denies that the gift of God can benefit one devoted to it unless human merit is present, he makes the human being either superior or equal to the tradition itself, although human merit is far removed from this office.

As the apostle Paul says concerning this very matter: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. Therefore neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (I Cor. III, 6–7). How can anything be hoped for from a human being in this matter, when words have been given to be handed on? Let us therefore see what benefit it will bring if the one who delivers the solemn words has good merit, or what harm it will cause if he has evil merit.

The person approaching desires to hear the words of God; placing his faith in them, he believes that he receives salvation. What difference does it make in this matter whether the one who delivers the solemn words leads a good or an evil life, when what is sought is the recipient’s devoted faith, so that he may believe with his whole heart what he hears? If the one who delivers them leads an evil life, will he become an obstacle to the recipient, preventing him from believing what he hears and ought to believe? Will his sin enter the recipient’s heart so that he does not believe? Or will God, who is just, despise one devoted to him because of the sin of the person whom he himself permits to remain in the ecclesiastical order?

Even a human being does not judge in this way, although it is clear that he is often deceived or influenced by favor. If this were so, and a person were pleading his own case, would he not say to God: “I do not know who this person is for whose sake you despise me. I approached him for your sake, because he was called your bishop; I sought you, I desired you, I trusted you, and I placed no hope in the human being. Why, then, should his evil harm me, when I would not have known him except that I was seeking you? If his good could benefit me, it might perhaps seem just that his evil should also harm me. But just as his good did me no good if I believed uncertainly, so his evil ought not to harm me when I believe rightly.

“For I gave my faith to his words, which are said to have been given by you, which you inspire, which speak of you, and which promise concerning you. I believed nothing from this man concerning himself, nor from his deeds; rather, I joined myself to the faith that comes from you.” On these grounds the believer’s case is sound.

Take bishops, as you would advocates. If an advocate leads an evil life, will judgment be pronounced against the case he has undertaken? It is the advocate’s duty to plead the case of the person he has undertaken according to the order of the law. If his life is disgraceful, can it harm the case of the person whose cause he has undertaken? The advocate’s person can neither harm nor benefit the case; the response to it will be made according to the nature of the case.

So too are those who wish to become Christians: they approach the bishop and declare their vows to him; he speaks the words of ecclesiastical law. If their vows are genuine, they are accepted by the judge. In what way, then, can the bishop harm or benefit them, especially since he does not even know the case of the person whose cause he has undertaken? For God the judge alone knows who approaches and with what state of mind. The bishop’s duty, therefore, is to perform the office entrusted to him; the judge’s duty is either to accept or reject the case of the person whose cause has been undertaken.

For he himself is found to have said, “Daughter, your faith has saved you” (Matt. IX, 22). You see, then, that each person is saved by his own faith, without anyone’s assistance. For this is what God has decreed concerning faith: if it does not doubt, it obtains everything it desires.

Yet you, not as a friend but as though an enemy of Christ, have gathered the people under your own name, so that they are not Christians unless they are also Novatians. But the Apostle condemns anyone who says that he belongs to Paul or to someone else (I Cor. III, 4). You, however, judging yourself superior, have placed your own name above the name of Christ, [Col. 2313] as though he were not sufficient to protect his own Church.

### CIII [Note: [Col. 2313] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

How is it that in Leviticus the Lord commanded sacrifices and libations to be offered, whereas elsewhere he rejects them? For it is clear that in Leviticus the Lord commanded the fathers to offer libations or sacrifices, or burnt offerings. Finally, through the prophet Jeremiah he says:

> “Gather your burnt offerings together with your sacrifices, and eat meat; for I did not speak to your fathers, nor did I command them on the day when I brought them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. 7:21–22).

If you pay close attention to the matter of burnt offerings and sacrifices, there is no reason to raise a question about it; nor should you think that the Lord lied or changed his mind, commanding something and later denying it. For he is not found to have commanded anything concerning such sacrifices, libations, or burnt offerings as those about which he now declares that he spoke.

Observe, then, that there are two kinds of sacrifice: one which was commanded to be offered according to its several categories, and another which was called voluntary. In the former case—whether sacrifices for sins or for firstborn creatures—the command specified what was to be offered, what kind of offering it was, and how it was to be made. But the voluntary sacrifice was not in fact commanded, since it was left to one’s discretion: if anyone wished to offer something, he was to offer whatever seemed appropriate to him. These sacrifices were voluntary [Note: [Col. 2313] The Colbert manuscript reads “votive.”].

And because they offered these things carelessly and thoughtlessly, failing to consider that one who offers to a superior ought to offer choice gifts, they are therefore told: “I did not command you concerning these things.” Rather, if you wish to offer, you ought to offer what is worthy. Thus Cain too is found to have sinned, because he did not consider that what is best ought to be offered to God.

For while they claimed that they were offering these things to appease God, by that very act they provoked him to indignation: in the very thing they said they were doing well, they sinned by offering unworthy burnt offerings. Hence the prophet Malachi says:

> “If you bring a blind or lame or sick animal for sacrifice, it is not good. Offer it, then, to your governor or prefect: will he accept you?” says the Lord Almighty (Mal. 1:8).

For this reason God complains through Isaiah about the same matter, saying:

> “What are the sheep of your burnt offering to me? You have not honored me even in your sacrifices. For I did not make you for this purpose, that you should labor over incense or purchase for me incense with silver; nor did I desire the fat of your sacrifices. Yet in your sins and iniquities you have stood before me” (Isa. 1:11).

It is therefore clear that complaints arose because, when they offered voluntary sacrifices, they did not honor God in them, offering what was unworthy, although these offerings were not required. If they had been commanded, they would have seemed obliged to offer them, whatever their quality. But when they offered them by their own choice, they ought to have offered such things as would show their devotion to God. Since their minds, however, were wandering through desire for idols, they acted without reflection.

Thus they are reproached on two grounds: they dared to offer to God while acting wickedly, and they offered things that were unworthy. Yet wicked acts are not redeemed by sacrifices, but by lamentation and mercy. Hence David says after he had sinned:

> “If you had desired sacrifice, I would indeed have given it; you will not be pleased with burnt offerings. The sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Ps. 50:18–19).

Finally, Samuel says to Saul, who, having despised the Lord’s command, thought that God could be appeased by sacrifice:

> “God does not desire sacrifice more than that his voice should be obeyed” (1 Sam. 15:22).

And Scripture says:

> “I desire mercy more than sacrifice” (Hos. 6:6).

The Jews, being unjust and without mercy, thought that God could be made favorable through offerings; so even now some people, scorning justice, think that they win praise through offerings. An offering is therefore good if justice is preserved and mercy is not neglected, because what we ask for ourselves we must also grant to others.

## CONCERNING THE GOSPEL OF LUKE

### [Col. 2314]

### CIV [Note: This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

Knowing that a Jewish war would arise against him, the Lord told his disciples to prepare swords for themselves. Once this had been done, when the conflict began under the leadership of Judas Iscariot, the apostle Peter, seeing the enemies rising against them, drew his sword and cut off the ear of the priest’s servant. Then the Lord ordered Peter to put the sword back into its sheath:

> “For everyone who takes up the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26:51–52).

Why did he order swords to be prepared when he forbade striking, even designating as liable to death the one who struck with a sword, although the apostle does not seem to have struck unjustly? As far as Peter was concerned, he struck the man whom he saw armed against them. He ought to have resisted ungrateful servants armed to kill the Lord.

If you examine each element of the case whose meaning you wish to uncover, you will find other questions raised by these words. Why was it necessary for one who relied upon spiritual power to order carnal swords to be prepared, when previously he had commanded that on the road they should carry neither bag, nor money, nor staff (Luke 10:10), and now ordered them to possess what he had previously forbidden?

Let us therefore begin to explain why he ordered swords to be prepared but forbade them to be used for killing. He commanded weapons to be obtained for the approaching conflict not only because of his enemies, but also for the sake of his own disciples. For something new and astonishing was about to happen: the one who performed new and unheard-of signs was suddenly to be humbled, subjected both to beatings and to death.

Therefore, lest he appear to suffer these things as one unaware, or as one from whom power had perhaps departed, he foretold them all in such a way that he showed no uncertainty about them, but, knowing beforehand what was to happen, prepared himself for it. And because he was humbled by his own will, he ordered them not to resist his enemies more fiercely. He showed that he was still the one he had been by restoring, even after he had been seized, the ear that had been cut off, returning what had fallen through the action of the sword—not as a merely human physician, but as the creator of bodies, reshaping his mutilated work. For physicians cannot restore severed bodily limbs.

Thus, so that it might be seen that God’s power in him had not diminished but remained as it had been, and so that he might confirm what he had said, “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18), he ordered swords to be prepared, but not to be used for killing.

It remains to show why, observing the deed of the apostle Peter, he said that the one who used the sword would perish by the sword, when Peter does not seem to have struck unjustly. For, as Luke indicates, he struck with the Lord’s permission, and, when he was forbidden, he heard these words (Luke 22:49–50).

It was permitted for this reason: so that the Lord might appear able to defend himself, yet unwilling to do so; and so that it might be shown that the power which had been in him still remained, making it unmistakable that he could defend himself in both respects. His enemies, meanwhile, were to be convinced that power had been given them by him to do these things. For he did not appear overcome, but as one handing himself over to their will.

Why, then, was the sentence given that whoever takes up the sword should perish by the sword, except that no one is permitted to kill another with the sword unless he is a judge? The apostle Peter was permitted to go only so far as to inflict pain, not to kill. For this reason he heard the command not to strike again. Moreover, he learned that once people have become Christians, they may not kill. Those who have been placed under mercy may not harshly employ the law of civil justice entrusted to the world.

But the command that he seemed previously to have given the disciples as they went along the road—that they should take nothing with them—concerned peace, the grace of spiritual gifts, and the friendliness of teaching. What need was there to take anything along the road for those for whom everything was to be provided on account of their signs?

When, however, the time arrived in which he permitted himself to suffer, and because of which a quarrel rather than a war was threatening, he ordered the disciples to be armed—not so that he, who wished to suffer, might resist, but, as I have said, so that he might show himself foreknowing this event and possessing his own passion within his power. He would humble himself for the sake of human salvation, as will be said in its proper place.

### CV [Note: This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

How prophecy corresponds with the Gospel [Col. 2315] concerning the darkening of the sun and certain other matters.

Since it had been foretold at the Lord’s first coming that the sun would be darkened during his passion, this is proved to have happened at the very hour specified, namely at midday. For thus it is written in the prophet Amos:

> “On that day, says the Lord, the sun will set at noon, and the day of light will grow dark over the earth” (Amos 8:9).

On that day, therefore, the sun was darkened from the sixth hour until the ninth hour, and thus the prophecy of the prophet mentioned above was fulfilled.

The image of what will happen at the Lord’s second coming was displayed in the Lord’s passion. For at the end, when the Lord begins to come to judge the world, the heavenly lights will be released from their service, as the Lord says:

> “In those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light” (Matt. 24:29).

The prophet Joel likewise did not omit this, so that, when it is signified by many witnesses, it may unquestionably be believed to be fulfilled. For he says:

> “The sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and manifest day of the Lord comes” (Joel 2:31).

As far as appears, this more properly concerns the second coming. For then he will be openly manifested to all, as Scripture says:

> “Then every eye will see him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him, and those who crucified him” (Rev. 1:7).

If, therefore, this is contained in both comings, since the sun will be darkened in those days, what is the day on which Scripture sang that the sun and moon would be enlarged? For Isaiah says, among other things:

> “There will be upon every high mountain and upon every elevated place flowing water on that day, when many have perished and when towers have fallen. And the light of the moon will be like the light of the sun; and the light of the sun will be sevenfold, on the day when he heals the brokenness of his people” (Isa. 30:25–26), and so forth.

What day can be understood as the day on which the Lord promised to heal the brokenness of his people? I think it is the day that Zechariah, the father of John, indicated when he said:

> “Blessed is the Lord, the God of Israel, because he has visited and accomplished the redemption of his people. And he has raised up a horn of salvation for us in the house of David his servant, as he spoke through the mouth of his holy prophets, who have been from of old. And he will deliver us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hate us, to show mercy to our fathers” (Luke 1:68–72).

And Simeon says, among other things:

> “This one is appointed for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke 2:34).

This “fall” is that of the scribes, Pharisees, and Jewish leaders, whom the prophet signified by the towers. As these therefore fell through unbelief, others rose by believing—those who had previously seemed weak and sick because of negligence.

Hence the Savior says:

> “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9:39).
