Thus those who seemed to possess sight through their knowledge and practice of the Law were blinded through unbelief, while the blind—that is, the unlearned and tax collectors—came to see when they believed.

The prophet had foretold that the Savior would bear their infirmities (Isa. 53:11). Accordingly, this was accomplished in the Savior’s time, as it is read in the Gospel: he took our infirmities and healed our wounds (Matt. 8:17).

All these things were completed and fulfilled in the Savior’s passion. For the salvation of the human race was both redeemed and established, among those above as well as among those below, because the prophecy of the aforementioned Zechariah comprehends both. Here, among those above, people were delivered from the brokenness caused by their enemies through the intervention of mercy; there, among those below, they were rescued from Tartarus. For all who hoped in the promised Christ were awaiting his coming, so that, when death had been conquered, they might be freed from the underworld.

Hence he said, “to show mercy to our fathers.” [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, and the Louvain edition read “he showed mercy.” The Venetian edition reads “he will show mercy,” as do the Fathers’ edition of Benedictus and M.]

If someone understands this salvation also to be contained in the second coming, nevertheless at both comings, and especially at the second, “the sun will be turned into darkness, and the moon will not give its brightness.” How, then, shall we understand the sun and moon to be increased on the day when the Lord visits his people, when we read that at both times—when the people’s deliverance began and when it was completed—the sun and moon were not diminished but darkened?

Unless, quite plainly, we understand the sun and moon as compared with the saints. In another passage we read that the saints are made equal to the lights, as the apostle Paul declares: holy people appear in this world among human beings like lights. And in the Gospel he says:

> “Then the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matt. 13:43).

For the Lord calls righteous works “light.” Thus he says:

> “Let your light shine before human beings, so that, seeing your good works, they may glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matt. 5:16).

Those, therefore, who leave all they possess and follow the Lord for the sake of righteousness and holiness are compared with the sun and moon, honored sevenfold, as the Lord says:

> “There is no one who has left house, or wife, or children, or fields, who will not receive seven times as much in this age” (Luke 18:29–30).

Those, therefore, who are honored sevenfold in the present may be understood also to be believed to become seven times brighter than the others in the future, so that their resurrection may be compared with the sun and moon, while the others are like stars.

The brightness of the saints, therefore, which is honored sevenfold here, receives another sevenfold increase in the resurrection: whoever here possesses the brightness of the moon will receive the brightness of the sun in the future, while whoever is compared here with the sun is believed to receive seven times as much in the future.

The prophet Isaiah therefore foretold, by his comparison of the sun and moon, that the merits of the saints would be increased—and not without reason. For if the Lord himself is called the sun of righteousness, while the saints will be like him, as the apostle John says, “When he appears, we will be like him” (1 John 3:2), then the aforementioned prophet appropriately shows that the saints are signified by the sun, although he indicates that the sun will be seven times greater than the moon.

When he shows that the moon will be like the light of the sun, but the sun sevenfold, he plainly signifies that the moon will be increased to the measure of the sun seven times, so that the moon then will be what the sun is now. Yet although the order concerning the saints is reversed here, he has disclosed the measure of the lights in part under this explanation: after the sun and moon have been increased, one will again be greater by as much as the sun was; and as much as one saint differs from another in the present, so much will they differ in the future after their reward.

## CONCERNING THE BOOK OF GENESIS

[Note: [Col. 2316] This is how the manuscripts and the edition of Regensburg read. Other editions instead have: “How the things contained in Genesis are to be understood, especially concerning the work of the six days.”]

### CVI [Note: This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

> “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1).

If God made heaven and earth in the beginning, and heaven is the firmament, as appears in what follows, then it is not true that light was made first and the firmament afterward. For it could signify no other heaven, since it describes the creation of the world as completed through God’s activity.

Moses was therefore inspired by God to show what the true account of the world was, because human beings were being deceived by various opinions concerning it. Some thought that it had no beginning; others thought that it did have a beginning but had been fashioned by certain angels; still others likewise thought it had been made, but by some Sacla [Note: Ambrose, Erasmus, and the Louvain edition read “by a spirit”; the Regensburg edition reads “by Secla.” Several manuscripts read “by Sacla,” as here and above in the third question. The Venetian and Louvain editions have “by a certain spirit.” M.], who is also a god of opposing power. Only a few, following the true line concerning its origin, maintained that God was its maker.

Because of those who were being led astray by this false diversity of opinion, Moses was compelled to reveal the true cause of the world, lest the children of Israel, rescued from the power of the Egyptians, should nevertheless remain unliberated from their false understanding. Among other peoples, they had pursued the study of error more zealously, for from ancient times they had devoted themselves above all others to vain philosophy. Finally, Moses, because he appeared to have been adopted by Pharaoh’s daughter, was educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians (Acts 7:22).

What, then, does he mean when he says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth”? If it signifies the firmament, according to what we have shown above, [Col. 2317] let us see what he is saying.

We think that Moses, in order to remove every error concerning the lower creation and the materials employed in making the world, signified that, in the beginning, the very substances from which the world consists were made. If he had left this unmentioned, these substances might perhaps have been thought eternal, and judged to be co-eternal with God. But whoever accepts this testimony cannot doubt that the world was made, since Moses declares that the substances which contributed to the making of the world were established at the beginning.

Thus, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” that is, the heavenly and earthly substance. The heavenly substance is that of which heaven consists; the earthly substance, however, is a kind of filthy concretion which contributed to the dry land called earth and to the darkness.

Hence the prophet Isaiah says:

> “I am God, who made the light and created the darkness” (Isa. 45:6–7).

After these things had been created, he made the substance all together—that is, water, darkness, and earth—before the ages. For the ages are beneath the firmament.

The firmament, as some think, is ice formed from the waters. It is therefore called the firmament because, when the waters were divinely congealed, it was made firm. It was called heaven because it conceals or hides. Since water is the greater element, it is mentioned first, because part of it contributed to the vault of the world.

The earth is its pavement. David too acknowledges that it was created by the Holy Spirit. For he says:

> “And let the waters that are above the heavens praise the name of the Lord. For he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 148:4–5).

After these elements, and before the world was joined together, God made light, so that his works might proceed into the light. This light, in the ordered arrangement, completed the course of the day.

Night came into being according to the measure of the day. When it had likewise completed the allotted measure of its interval, it was illuminated by the arrival of the morning light. Thus the first day was completed as the second began. Night was counted as belonging to the day, so that together they are called one day. For since darkness is subjected to light, it has no authority and cannot make up a number.

Thirty days are called one month, even though nights are included in them. Thus the service of light, by which it completes the interval assigned to it, is called day. The substance of darkness, before it is illuminated, is called night. The interval between sunset and sunrise is night.

Darkness does not make night in the way that light makes day, because darkness remains in its own nature. The arrival of light makes day, and its departure makes night. Night is therefore rightly subjected to the day.

After light had been made, and the course of twelve hours had been completed, with an equal interval of night also completed, there was an equinox on the first day. From that point the day began to grow longer than the night for three months, which constitute the season of spring. Afterward, through its own increase, the day was diminished during another three months, which constitute the season of summer.

Then there was another equinox, so that from that point the night began to grow longer than the day for another three months, which constitute the season of autumn. The night then began to diminish from the length by which it exceeded the day, until the end of the fourth season, which is winter.

There is an equinox at the beginning of the first season, when God created the world. This day is understood to be the eleventh day before the Kalends of April, when the first day of Passover occurs—that is, the first day of the first month.

For in the Law it was commanded that on the evening of the tenth day of the first month they should prepare themselves to celebrate Passover on the fourteenth day of the month, that is, beginning on the eleventh. The evening of the tenth day already shines into the eleventh, so that the beginning of the first month was from the eleventh day before the Kalends of April.

In the beginning the moon was made full, on the fourteenth day, because everything was made complete. Add the three days from the evening of the tenth, and these are the three days before the lights that existed, so that the world was made on the eleventh day before the Kalends of April. For the number of the moon proceeds from the eleventh to the fourteenth, to which the complete first month was assigned for Passover, so that on the solemn day of Passover it might be neither outside the eleventh day before the Kalends of April nor outside the fourteenth day of the moon.

The world was made on the eleventh day; on the fourteenth, however, it was made brighter by the moon’s greater light. Between the beginning and the brightness by which the world was illuminated, our Savior both suffered and rose again. For he suffered under the fourteenth moon and rose on the first [Col. 2318] day, which is therefore called the Lord’s Day because the Lord himself made it—the Lord who made the months, seasons, and years increase.

In order that it might not be celebrated in exactly the same way every time, the course of the moon produces its periods of waning and waxing.

> “But the earth was invisible and unformed.”

It is clear that, after the earth was made, it was invisible and unformed. It was covered by the waters and was therefore invisible; and it was unformed because, being fluid, it was not suitable for cultivation.

> “And darkness was over the abyss.”

He says that darkness was over the abyss, that is, over the immense body of water extending in every direction.

> “And the Spirit of God was borne over the water” (Gen. 1:2).

He indicates this water as though it were the summit, over which the Spirit of God was borne, showing that darkness was over an infinite depth.

He speaks of the Spirit of God over the waters because where the Spirit of God was, there was no obscurity: as far as it could, it illuminated the water. But it could not illuminate the abyss, that is, the immeasurable depth. It illuminated the waters above, while darkness was beneath and over the abyss.

He calls this the Spirit of God not because he wishes it to be understood as the Holy Spirit, but because he wishes it to be understood spiritually as ruling over the material creation. To signify that the whole belongs to God, he calls this spirit, which was borne over the waters, God’s spirit, in order to overthrow the perverse assertion used by certain people who say that something exists which does not belong to God.

For it is neither orderly nor reasonable to say that the Holy Spirit was over the waters, since he is above every creature. Whatever is of God is above all powers and principalities, and likewise above all spiritual powers.

No one’s mind should be disturbed because it is called God’s spirit, since it is established that everything belongs to God. Among other things, when God was about to bring the flood, he says:

> “My spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh” (Gen. 6:3).

And in Ezekiel, among other passages, he says:

> “Thus says the Lord to these bones: I will extend skin over you, and I will give my spirit into you, and you will live” (Ezek. 37:5).

Do these things concern the office of the Holy Spirit, and not the soul? This spirit is indeed God’s, like all other things, but it is the governor of material substances; for it is its function to preside over them.

After light had been made, the course of the day regulated, and the second day completed, he made the firmament, that is, heaven, so that the light upon the earth might regulate the day of the firmament, as though it were a lamp in a house.

This firmament, I say, was made from the aforementioned substance of water. For now the world is joined together in visible form, so that, after the substances had been separated from the confusion of things, the individual parts might be fitted together as components contributing to the body of the world.

The substances which we have said were made first are the materials of the world. The world is therefore so called because things that had been confused and mixed together, separated from one another and brought forth into visible form, caused it to be called “the world,” since they contributed to its construction.

The firmament, therefore—that is, heaven—was made in the midst of the waters, to divide the water that was above the firmament from the water that was beneath the firmament. By God’s power the firmament stood in the middle of the waters, having water beneath it, within it, above it, and around it. It was to be hollow on the outside but fortified within, so that neither the inner nor outer waters would penetrate its hollow space, making it like a protected and strengthened house, so that those dwelling in it might be secure.

On the third day he commanded the water that was beneath heaven—that is, within the capacity of the firmament—to be gathered into one gathering, so that the dry land, which is earth, might appear; and it was so.

For, when the breadth of the earth had been emptied, a kind of channel was formed into which all the water that was within the firmament sank, and the dry land appeared. As the water withdrew, it was necessary that the earth, which had been made visible and was previously invisible, should appear.

Then the dry land was called earth, and the gatherings of the waters were called seas. And he commanded the earth to produce plants for pasture and fruit-bearing trees bearing seed upon the earth.

On the fourth day God likewise commanded lights to be made in the firmament of heaven, so that they might shine upon the earth: the greater light for the beginning of the day, the lesser light for the beginning of the night, and the stars.

These things pertain to the conception, birth, [Col. 2319] and nourishment of what is generated in the world, and to the signs of the seasons, which are necessary at their appointed intervals, as well as to the adornment of the entire world.

Just as a house is adorned when its ceiling has a coffered surface decorated with gold, so the stars provide adornment for the world, shining with varied light.

The splendor of the sun was therefore added to the light that had previously been made, so that these things might be joined and inseparable. To the night, which had been dark, a light was given. And because the moon was full when it was made, he says, “the lesser light for the beginning of the night.” For, having been made full, it shone throughout the entire night.

Thus he speaks from the part with reference to the whole when he says “for the beginning of the night,” because it does not shine every evening. The greater light, which we call the sun, remains at the beginning of the day, because it was formed together with the earlier light.

For three days the world existed without these lights. Their functions were not yet needed, since there was not yet anything for them to benefit.

But when the earth produced plants for pasture and fruit-bearing trees, things were needed that would nourish or preserve what had been produced. Since every generation is completed through their intervention, it was not appropriate that these lights should be made first, lest what had been produced from the earth be thought to have arisen through their effect. Rather, they were made beforehand so that it might be unmistakable that the earthly things had been made without them.

Then, on the fifth day, he commanded the waters to produce creeping creatures with living souls and flying creatures flying over the earth beneath the firmament of heaven; and it was so.

And among other things he says:

> “And God saw that they were good, and he said, ‘Increase and multiply’” (Gen. 1:21–22).

He added, “And God saw that they were good,” because some people say that these things are evil, so that at least in this way they may be put to shame. When they please God their creator, they ought certainly to displease no one.

For fools are accustomed to say: “He saw them and they pleased him because previously he did not know.” O dull-witted people, how could he not know? Whatever he wished was produced. Does anyone wish for what he does not know? And can one who is able to make something be said not to know what he is making?

What is more, he himself did not make them directly but commanded that they should be made. And was the one who commanded not possessed of the power to make them? Yet because all things are possible for him, when he commanded what could not act, it began to be able to act, so that it might contribute to his praise [Note: Erasmus, the Lyon edition, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition present the passage as follows: “What could not act began to exist, so that it might contribute to his praise.” M.].

There is therefore a twofold power: he commanded the insensible to produce sensible things.

On the sixth day he commanded the earth to produce living creatures: four-footed animals and beasts of the earth. It was so, and they were produced. And God saw that they were good, and very good, because all things are necessary.

On the day mentioned above, therefore, God said:

> “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness, and let him have authority,” he said, “over all that has been made upon the earth” (Gen. 1:26).

First God made the substances from which he would join the world together. After it had been joined together, adorned with every ornament, and provided with what was necessary, he then made the human being to enjoy it and all that is in it.

For although he had commanded everything upon the earth to be produced from the waters and the earth, he is nevertheless described as taking clay from the earth in his hands in order to make the human being, so that he might teach that the human being differs greatly from the things he had made.

He wishes it to belong to the honor of the human being that he is described as made by God’s hands and made according to the image and likeness of God—that is, of the Father and the Son.

What it means for the human being to be made according to the image and likeness of God, although we have discussed it elsewhere, this passage and subject require us to explain again.

For the words of the Father to the Son are:

> “Let us make the human being according to our image and likeness.”

Although the person of both—the one speaking and the one obeying—is understood in the work.

The image of God in the human being is therefore this: one person was made, as it were, lord, from whom the others would arise, possessing the authority of God as his representative. For every king bears the image of God.

For this reason the woman was not made according to the image of God. For it says:

> “And God made the human being; according to the image of God he made him.”

Hence the Apostle says:

> “A man ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman [Col. 2320] covers herself because she is not the glory or image of God” (1 Cor. 11:7).

The likeness of God in the human being is this: just as the Son is from the Father, so the woman is from the human being. There is, of course, this difference: she was made, whereas he was born.

Some people nevertheless think that God made everything all at once. “If he made it by a word,” they say, “why should it not be said that he made everything simultaneously?” For they think that making things in stages is a human custom. It therefore seems to magnify God’s power if it is said that everything was made by him in one day.

Yet we observe great providence in this work and order. He certainly could have made everything simultaneously, but a multifaceted reason prevented it. Setting all these arguments aside, we must believe the divine Scripture, which says—and says repeatedly—that:

> “In six days the Lord your God made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them” (Exod. 20:11).

At the beginning, things had to be made in such a way that they would perceive and know that they had been made. When they did not see everything existing simultaneously, but one thing today and another tomorrow, they understood that they had a beginning and could in no way suspect eternity, since they recognized themselves as existing in successive parts.

For if everything had existed at once, they would have had no sense of their own weakness, but would have thought that they had never begun. Things that suddenly come into existence simultaneously through the word of God do not perceive themselves as being made unless, by seeing one thing before them and another after them, they perceive the process.

And so that what was made first might not think itself uncreated when it saw greater things made after it, it believed about itself what it saw in something else that was superior.

Finally, the light called day has heaven and earth—that is, water and dry land—before it. When the water, dry land, and darkness themselves had been made in a confused state, they could not claim eternity, because none of these things dared claim for itself a fixed condition and distinct property.

The sun and moon, although they are the brightest things, likewise have many things before them. Thus it was arranged that, when the later and superior things see the earlier and inferior things, none of them claims eternity for itself.

Moreover, the work was completed in six days, and it contains within itself the age of the entire world, so that the works of six days might represent six thousand years. For what was to happen in each age is contained in order within the works of the six days.

For example, since in the earlier ages there was not to be such knowledge of God upon the earth, the earlier days appear without splendor. And since animals were to be made before the human being, this was because our ancestors of old, uncultivated and rustic, were going to live like animals.

On the sixth day, however, the human being was made. This signified that, in the sixth millennium of years, the coming of Christ made the human being so that he would not be subject to death.

The human being was made the image of God because, by God’s gift, he was to be conformed to the Son of God, as the apostle John says:

> “We know that when he appears, we will be like him” (1 John 3:2).

And the Chosen Vessel says:

> “Conformed to the Son of God” (Rom. 8:29).

The tree of life planted in paradise was an image of the future grace of God, which is the body of the Lord; whoever eats of it will live forever.

The tree of the knowledge of good and evil signifies the Law given through Moses. When it made known the sin that had previously lain hidden, it gave knowledge of good and evil. For it showed what was good and what was evil.

As for the fact that on the seventh day he rested from his works, this signifies that, when the six-thousandth year has been completed, he will rest in the seventh millennium, when the world has ceased from every secular work [Note: The Colbert manuscript reads “millennium” here and below.].

We have said these few things out of many in order to open a path to understanding in accordance with what we have shown above.

## CONCERNING THE ORDER OF DAY AND NIGHT
## CVII

As far as the order of the world is concerned, we read of darkness before light. For those things that contributed to the construction of the world, and that appear to have been made together, are considered to have been without light—that is, water, earth, and darkness, from which the world was joined together, as is contained in the Wisdom that is called Solomon’s, “from unseen matter” (Wisdom XI, 18), that is, from darkness. The sacred books also testify, by the very voice of the Lord through the prophet Isaiah, that both darkness and water were made: “I,” he says, “am God, who made the light and created darkness” (Isaiah XLV, 6–7). Likewise, through David, the Holy Spirit shows both that the waters were made and that the earth was established upon the waters (Psalm CXXXV, 6).

This agrees both with evangelical authority and with apostolic tradition, in which all things are read to have been made; and, so that nothing might be excepted, it says, “whether the things that are in heaven or those that are on earth” (John I, 3; Colossians I, 16). In this respect, therefore, insofar as it concerns the earth, we read of darkness before light. This is so as regards the order of the reading, not as regards dignity; for light is certainly much better than darkness. In the ordering of the world, however, light receives the name by which it is called “day,” and darkness that by which it is called “night.” This is for the following reason: while darkness is being illuminated and the light passes away, the period until the light returns is called night; and the period during which the darkness is illuminated is called day.

Thus, when night is mentioned, a future day is expected; and when day is mentioned, a future night is expected. But when these functions have ceased, as the world passes away, only darkness and light will be spoken of. For it cannot be called night when there is darkness perpetually, nor day when the light has ceased to set. Where eternity is, these names cease, because they began with the world.

Indeed, before the light that was called day came to be, Scripture does not say that there was night, but darkness. After the darkness had been illuminated and the light had passed away, they were called evening and night. Therefore, so far as appears, night is subordinate to day. For the fact that darkness is read of before light does not mean that it ought therefore to be regarded as prior in rank. Heaven existed before the sun, yet the sun is greater in brilliance; the earth existed before humanity, and cattle and the other living creatures existed before humanity, yet they are subordinate to human beings. Night, then, ought not for that reason to be preferred to day, because darkness is read of first, since it is evident that light is superior to darkness in dignity and day is superior to night in time.

For, as was shown above, when there was darkness, light was made. “And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night; and there was evening and there was morning, one day” (Genesis I, 5). For if there had been no day, there would have been no night; there was darkness, and when it had been illuminated and the day had passed through its course, evening came to be. When it had become light again after evening, the first day came to be once the night had passed, so that night followed day. This is both fitting and supported by reason: the inferior nature should in every respect be subject to the superior.

How, then, is night said to come before day, when you read its name after day? Night and evening would not have been named if the light had not made its course as day; when that course was completed, evening came to be, and evening is night. Day accordingly became evening, so that you might know that night is a part of day. Day is completed only when night, too, has passed.

Thus we say, “A year has three hundred and sixty-five days,” certainly not without its nights. When we say “days,” we count the nights there as well. Under the authority of the word “day,” we signify night also; for if night preceded day, day too would be counted under the designation “night.” What person, after all, would say, “I will see you after five nights,” and not, “after five days”? Nor do we remember reading anywhere that night is signified before day. “Moses was on the mountain forty days and forty nights,” it says (Exodus XXIV, 18). And in the Psalm: “The sun shall not burn you by day, nor the moon by night” (Psalm CXX, 6).

And, to give an example from the very beginnings, it says: “Let there be lights in the firmament of heaven, and let them shine upon the earth: the greater light for the beginning of day, and the lesser light for the beginning of night” (Genesis I, 14). But the moon cannot be preferred to the sun, just as night cannot be preferred to day. Rather, just as the moon is subordinate to the sun, so night is subordinate to day.

In the Gospel, too, nights are signified under the authority and numerical designation of days. Among other things, the Lord says: “There are some standing here who will not taste death until they see the Son of Man in his kingdom.” And he adds: “It came to pass after eight days” (Luke IX, 27), and so forth. Are not nights also included in this number? And elsewhere he says: “These things took place in Bethany beyond the Jordan, where John was baptizing. On the following day he saw Jesus coming.” Did he say, “On the following night”? Again it follows: “On the next day he desired to depart for Galilee” (John I, 28, 29, 43). And immediately afterward: “And on the third day a wedding took place at Cana of Galilee” (John II, 1). Everywhere, then, day is shown to have authority, with night subordinate to it.

For if day were contained under the name of night, night would precede day. Since the Romans possess the kingdom, however, Spaniards, Gauls, Africans, and the others who are subject to them are called Romans under their name. So also night, because it is subordinate to day, is contained under its name.

Some people are misled by the fact that the Jews are commanded to enter the Sabbath at evening, without considering why this was commanded. On the preceding day they necessarily have to buy food for themselves, prepare for the Sabbath, and bathe. Could they do these things at night and enter the Sabbath when day had risen? Certainly the Lord rose at evening, and this is counted as part of the day. The resurrection is celebrated on the day called the Lord’s Day. For you read: “This is the day which the Lord has made” (Psalm CXVII, 24); yet it is not called the Lord’s night, because day holds the primacy.

Whether the preceding day or the following day is considered, night is always subordinate, because it is inferior both in order and in nature, as the Apostle says: “You are sons of day and of light, not of night or of darkness” (1 Thessalonians V, 5).

And if we draw an inference from the consuls, we shall see that the one who is chosen first is named first. Thus it is customary to say, “Who will be consul with him?” If night, then, were before day, it would be named first. The reckoning begins with day to such an extent that, for example, if we say, “Tomorrow is the sixth day before the Kalends,” the reckoning is from morning until morning arrives again, so that after the day and night have passed, they are counted together.

The moon, too, was certainly made at the beginning of the morning as the fourteenth moon; having been made to shine through the whole night, it began the fifteenth at the next morning. Why, then, is there any doubt that beginnings are reckoned from day? Because of the disputes of some people concerning an evident matter, we have been compelled to speak at greater length, although the reading itself explains the matter, clearly signifying day before night.

All the foregoing we have said according to the origin of the world. But if we wish to speak more profoundly, raising our understanding by spiritual strength, we find it incongruous to assert that darkness was created before light. For if light is heavenly in nature and darkness earthly, it is certainly foolish to think that light was made after darkness. Moses says that light was indeed made, but in that part in which the world now exists, not as though it had then first been created. For all spiritual things were created before bodily things, so that the light which was in the things above might be made in the things below, like a lamp in a house.

But for what reason is darkness said to precede light, when darkness always appears after light? Heavenly and spiritual things are therefore believed to be light by nature, while earthly and bodily things are darkness, so that the nature of darkness seems to subsist through the power of light, since everything lowest belongs to the highest.

For if we inquire, we discover darkness in the sun itself. When you are near it, it appears so exceedingly bright that it cannot be looked at; if there is some distance, it is exceedingly bright but can be seen; if you are far away, it is less bright—and the farther away, the less bright. From this a certain diminution appears, announcing darkness, and thus one arrives at the point where darkness seems to take its origin from light.

Therefore, the one who made light created darkness in this manner, just as, in making water, he created earth at the same time: as earth is the solid condition of water, so darkness is the diminution of light. God alone does not suffer diminution. Since he is everywhere—or rather, since he contains all things within himself—he is so brilliant that he is seen by no one unless he chooses to moderate himself.

Indeed, although the Savior was in a body and was not shut in, he was nevertheless not seen at all unless he wished to be seen. For the fact that he was transfigured on the mountain and appeared in great brilliance (Matthew XVII, 1–2) was, as it were, hidden within the body; when he wished, he revealed it. How, then, was he hidden, when he was not enclosed?

For if he entered among the disciples with his body while the doors were shut (John XX, 19), how does his divinity not penetrate all things? That is, it cannot be shut in, because it suffers no diminution. Although God is absent from nowhere, he is nevertheless said to be present where he appears and wishes to be seen. Although all things are in God, because he surpasses all things—as the Apostle says, “For in him we live and move and have our being” (Acts XVII, 28)—he himself is nevertheless in nothing except that in which he wishes to be.

For by a certain mystery he is in all things, and by a certain providence he appears in whatever he wishes.

## On the Hebrew Language, and from What It Received Its Name

### CVIII

*[Note: This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]*

Everything that comes from God is rational, and a cause gives each thing its beginning, being its origin, so that it does not appear to have been named or to subsist absurdly, but so that its designation may be revealed—the designation understood to be the head or principle of the name itself.

The rationale of the human being, therefore, is the cause by which he subsists. He consists of four elements: earth, air, water, and fire, by God’s authorship alone. The fifth is the spirit, like a charioteer, so that it may direct the body once it has been compounded and formed, and like its commander. We took our beginning from the soil, and we are named from it. For we are called *homines* (“human beings”) on account of *humus* (“soil”), from which our external ancestor has his origin.

Thus cause and reason make it possible for other beings subsisting under the name of someone to be called by that same name, signifying him in themselves. Let us therefore see whether it is consistent, as some think, that the Hebrews were named from Heber. As far as the name is concerned, the origin of this designation seems to descend from him; for Heber is earlier than Abraham.

But if this were true, those who belonged to the tribe of Heber ought to have been called by the same name after him. For Abraham was born in the seventh generation from Heber (Genesis XI, 16, 26). If, then, Abraham himself, or those after Abraham, were called Hebrews, there is no doubt that the Hebrews are named from Heber. But if it is not read that they were called Hebrews before Abraham, but only after Abraham, then they are not called Hebrews from Heber but from Abraham, since Abraham’s sons are known to have first been called by this name. In Genesis, Joseph and his brothers are called Hebrews (Genesis XLIII, 32).

For they knew that Abraham had descended from Syria into Canaan (Genesis XII, 4), had multiplied, and, richly supplied with all resources because of his faith, had been called a king and a prophet and the father of many nations (Genesis XVII, 4); and that, with three hundred and eighteen of his native-born men, he had struck down five kings (Genesis XIV, 14–15). Since these things had not been done and spoken in a corner, so that they might remain hidden, they called those who were descended from his seed Hebrews.

Abraham’s order and merit, therefore, made him the head of those who derived their descent from him. For by God’s judgment he was established as prince and origin in the land of Canaan, so that those born from him might have a different profession and manner of life from that which he himself had before he descended into the land of Canaan. Having himself been renewed, he established a new people devoted to God.

This is why the Apostle Paul acknowledges himself to be a Hebrew from Hebrews (Philippians III, 5). For this appeared to be a surname of dignity. It was a testimony and nobility of lineage that those who had pleased God in many ways, and who were descended from him, should be surnamed from his name, since he was their origin.

Let it be rejected if it does not accord with reason; let it be despised if it is inconsistent; let it be torn away if it is foreign to Abraham’s merits; and let us be refuted as though we were his flatterers. What hostility toward Abraham, what rivalry, leads his enemies to disparage him—and who are these enemies except those who are called his sons? In what respect does Abraham displease them, so that this glory should be thought alien to him? And what is there in Heber that pleases them, so that he is said to possess this primacy?

If Heber’s manner of life could be investigated, perhaps he would be found to have worshiped idols, just as Terah and Nahor did, and Nahor’s father—men who are known not to have been far removed from him—as Joshua son of Nun testifies, saying that they worshiped idols (Joshua XXIV, 2).

Or let those who take the opposite position show for what reason this claim should be vindicated for Heber, lest perhaps we suppress his merit. But there is none, because the Scriptures are common to us, and what is owed to each person is evident. If they think this must be defended solely from the name, the argument is weak and implausible. His claim would rightly be vindicated by his name only if there were some causes serving as witnesses and confirming it. For some people might claim for themselves a matter that belongs to another merely because they shared the same name.

Therefore the truth is what is established not by the name alone but also by clear reasoning. Since, by God’s favor, it came about that the human race was given life again in Abraham *[Note: The Colbert Manuscript reads “was visited”]*, and that he became a saving model for human beings, no one doubts that what had been lost through the weakness of humanity was restored in him.

He was established as a certain image, so that in accordance with his likeness the human race might return to God, and so that it might recover for human use both the worship of God and the speech that had previously been given for human use. For just as in the beginning the image of God was in Adam, so that knowledge of him might exist on earth, after the ruin of the human race and the forgetfulness of the true God it was re-formed in Abraham, so that the faith in God begun through him might again sprout forth into fruit.

It is therefore not absurd that the people begun from him should derive their name from his name. But lest they be troubled by the name Heber, because the name sounds more like *Heber* with the Hebrews—since they are called *Hebraei*, not *Abrahaei*—let them recognize again that they are called *Hebraei*, not *Heberaei*: Heber is so called, not *Hebre*. If they think this is a reason for attacking the argument, they suffer from the very thing they do, and neither of us will have victory on this point, except the one who demonstrates the truth of his claim by presenting the reasoning in its proper order.

For someone who is equal in one matter must be considered to have lost if he is found unequal in another. The letter was altered on account of sound, so that they were called *Hebraei* rather than *Hebraei*, because the latter sounds better. Likewise, they are called *Judaei*, not *Judai*, from Judah. Wherever something appeared awkward, a letter was changed so that the utterance would have a well-formed sound. Thus, instead of *medio die* (“at midday”), we say *meridie*, and there are many such examples.

It therefore follows, as has been shown, that both the language and the people were called by the name of Abraham.

This, then, is the language that we say was first given to Adam and the others. Because of the presumption involved in building the tower, we believe that it was scattered and confused into many languages, so that it was no longer this one language, but many languages derived from it through changes to certain expressions. They retained one form, yet it did not perish; rather, it was wholly confused with the other languages.

This was done at that time so that human beings would not understand one another and would dare greater things (Genesis XI, 8). Thus as many languages are understood to have existed then as there were people who, after being scattered to the places in which they settled, established a language for themselves.

But if it is not thought to have been the very language that Scripture records as having then been one, the remaining possibility is that it was collected piecemeal from the other languages and joined together into the form of a single language for Abraham’s use. Since he was the father of many nations, he would then have had speech composed from many languages and would have been renewed in every respect.

But since those whom the Book of Genesis mentions as having one voice and one language (Genesis X, 31) are read to have migrated from the East, and from there were again scattered by God over the face of the whole earth, it certainly did not remain there in such a way that the language originally given failed to remain.

Finally, it has no land among human beings, as the other languages do, nor any nation except the Jews, because it was given to the first human being in paradise. After the languages had been confused, this language, now called Hebrew, was found nowhere.

If, then, it has no place or nation anywhere, while Abraham was Syrian by nationality, from where did Abraham or the rest of his descendants receive this language, unless it is either the first language or one adapted from many? For we see that some languages possess certain words resembling it.

But the former explanation accords with reason better than the latter, if it is said to be the first language. Reason demonstrates that this did not happen without purpose. Abraham ought to have had the same language that the first human being had, so that Moses, coming to describe both the creation and the human being made by God, might use the very speech in which God spoke and called the human being Adam, and in which the woman was called Eve.

Thus this word would be present in Moses’ book, as it had been among those whom he describes, so that he might truly show that the first cause and the divine benefit had been restored in every respect in Abraham.

## On Melchizedek

*[Note: Thus in the manuscripts and in the Regensburg edition. Other editions add: “How Abraham blessed him, and what the Apostle thought about him.”]*
### CIX

[Note: [Col. 2324] This is absent from manuscripts of the second class. — Bernard Vindingus [Col. 2325], in his *Critical Notes on Augustine*, writes concerning this question: “Some suspect that the author of this work is the man whom Jerome rebukes in his letter to Evagrius, asserting that Melchizedek is the Holy Spirit. I grant that the book on Melchizedek which he attacks there has been inserted into this work, just as the rest of it is plainly compiled from various authors and books. But if St. Jerome had taken this entire work from Evagrius, since it teems with many other and very serious errors, he would not have singled out only the one concerning Melchizedek, but would at least have touched upon the others in passing as well.”]

We read about Melchizedek in the Book of Genesis; and similarly, he is also mentioned in the Epistle written to the Hebrews, because, it says, “Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings, and brought out bread and wine, and offered them to him, and blessed him, saying: ‘Blessed are you, Abraham, by the Most High God, who made heaven and earth, who delivered your enemies into your hands’” (Gen. XIV, 18–20). And so that the Apostle might indicate who should be understood by Melchizedek, he added: “Without any doubt, the lesser is blessed by the better” (Hebr. VII, 7).

He certainly did not refer this to the handing down of ecclesiastical office. For who would doubt that the rule of the Lord’s ordinance, by which those subject to the Lord are blessed, is better than those who are blessed by it? The Lord’s mystery operates in those words that encompass and commemorate him. But he wished to demonstrate the person’s own merit and power. Who, then, and how great is he, in comparison with whom Abraham is called “the lesser”—Abraham who, as is evident, bears in all the faithful the sign of noble testimony and faith?

Accordingly, Melchizedek is not understood to have blessed Abraham in the manner in which human priests do, as though he were conferring a blessing by delegation through solemn words; rather, he blessed him as possessing a blessing proper to himself, which he had received not through words but substantially through nature, so that it was his own. The priests whom we call bishops, however, possess a rule ordered and handed down to them in solemn words; placing this rule over human beings, they bless them—not, however, whomever they wish, but sometimes even those whom they do not wish to bless, because the giver of the rule himself knows to whom the most sacred blessing ought to be given or infused.

But he who possesses blessing substantially by nature, whom Scripture calls the priest of the Most High God, gives blessing by his will. The words of blessing and his nature agree with his will. He does not err by willing it where he ought not, or by being unwilling where he ought; rather, to whomever he gives the words, he also gives the effect. Our priests, however, daily impose the Lord’s name and the words of blessing upon many, but the effect is found in only a few.

There is also the case when those who are superior bless others. Although one who is holy bows his head to receive a blessing, this is not the priest’s own possession but an institution of God. The priest Eli blessed Hannah, and the effect followed (I Sam. I, 17, 20)—not, to be sure, through the priest’s merit, but through Hannah’s own, whose pure heart God regarded.

Therefore Melchizedek is not called better than Abraham merely on account of the priestly office; he is also superior to him by nature, so that he must be understood as being beyond humanity. For it is utterly impossible that one who is placed above so great a friend of God—and one so faithful that, through love and fear of God, he did not hesitate to kill his dearest son—should be thought a human being. By what justice, by what works, could anyone merit more than Abraham merited? There was nothing more that could have been done for the commendation of his merits than Abraham did.

First, when he did not yet know God and had seen no sign by which he might be persuaded, God said to him, “Go out from your land, from your kindred, and from your father’s house” (Gen. XII, 1). He did not delay but immediately obeyed, fulfilling the will not only of the God who was present but also of the Lord who was to come. For the Lord says: “Whoever loves house, parents, brothers, or relatives more than me is not worthy of me” (Matt. X, 37). What kind of man, then, and of what merit, was Abraham, who fulfilled the Savior’s commands before they were proclaimed?

The Apostle teaches that hospitality should be pursued with the greatest zeal (Hebr. XIII, 2). Abraham cultivated it so faithfully and so devotedly (Gen. XVIII, 3) that the Apostle seems to have learned from him that it should be proclaimed.

[Col. 2326] Next, advanced in years, he believed that his offspring would be multiplied, though this seems foolish to the wise of the world, like the stars of heaven; so that, before judgment had been pronounced by the wise of this age, they might be seen to have been condemned by him. For afterward it was said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise” (Isa. XXIX, 14; I Cor. I, 19).

At God’s command he was circumcised—a thing that certainly does not occur without pain—and he did not resent it, so as to give his descendants an example of endurance. A son was promised him by his wife Sarah, already an old woman, and he did not doubt it (Gen. XVII, 17), in order to show future generations that God’s authority must be believed to such an extent that, even if he commands or promises things that appear irrational, one should not doubt. His person must be regarded more than his words, so that what seems weak or impossible in the words may be confirmed by his person and made to appear possible. For it is God who promises, and one must believe that he can do what appears impossible to human beings.

What offense can be judged to arise when humanity thinks more highly of God than it thinks of itself? For this reason Abraham did not hesitate to kill the son given to him by God when God himself commanded it, nor did he delay. He was not astonished that God should command the killing of the son whom, by his grace, he had given as a great gift and object of wonder. He was certain that God’s will must not be questioned by a human being, and that neither God’s command nor his act is without providence.

To fulfill the command with complete devotion and haste, he did not tell the child’s mother, his own wife, knowing that women are more vulnerable where their children are concerned and that compassion expressed through tears could obstruct this devotion. Nor was the boy himself informed until the hour of his death, so that he might obey God’s command with the full assent of his mind (Gen. XXII, 3–10). Abraham did not count this as parricide but as a holocaust carried out by the authority of a just judge.

What, then, could Melchizedek have done greater than these things, by which he might surpass Abraham, who, as we see, is nowhere found to have been disobedient?

Moses, of whom it is written that the Lord spoke with him face to face (Exod. XXXIII, 11), was sent to his people and to his brothers but was unwilling to go (ibid. IV, 1). The prophet Jonah, commanded to preach to the Ninevites, disobeyed and went toward another place to which he had not been sent (Jonah I, 1–3). Job, plainly outstanding in all things, nevertheless, moved by the loss of his children, tore his garments and shaved the hair of his head (Job I, 20). Abraham, however, is nowhere said to have grieved over the death of his beloved son, whom he himself had been commanded to kill, nor is he anywhere said to have trembled when God commanded him.

Thus it is evident from these considerations that Melchizedek is beyond humanity, since there was no way in which he could be better than Abraham unless he surpassed him by nature alone.

An impassible nature possesses blessedness substantially; human birth [Note: [Col. 2326] Thus in the manuscripts and in the Ratisbon edition. Other editions read *necessitas* (“necessity”) instead.] acquires blessedness through deeds. Because it does not possess the perfection of divinity, humanity advances through exercise and struggle in order to become better, when it overcomes more often than it is overcome.

For if it were to act in such a way—which is impossible—that it never sinned, it would become better than God. Far be it from us! For a nature that can sin, just as it can refrain from sinning, if it were always victorious, would have to be placed above that nature which does not sin because it is impassible. It would not seem a great thing not to sin when one cannot sin; but it would be magnificent not to sin when one could sin.

This, then, is the difference between the substance of God and that of humanity: God’s substance is always blessed through the secure invincibility of its eternity, whereas humanity becomes blessed substantially through labor. One kind of blessedness must belong to the impassible, and another to one who is worn down by tribulations so that he may eventually rejoice. Impassible blessedness consists in always being blessed; the blessedness of one subject to suffering consists in rejoicing after great hardships that he has escaped death. He is saddened in order to be able to rejoice, and is not perpetually secure because of the passibility of his nature.

The impassible, however, is always blessed [Col. 2327], because it neither knows sadness nor imagines that it could become sad. Human nature, although it attains blessedness through labor, will nevertheless not remain untouched, nor will it lack scars. For how could one who has often engaged in combat and has sometimes been defeated remain unwounded? The impassible, however, always remains untouched, unharmed, and inviolate.

Abraham, therefore, would not be called lesser than Melchizedek unless Melchizedek’s nature were superior to Abraham’s.

What we have said may perhaps seem to be a matter of intellectual ingenuity. But if we look to the Law, many further and more important things may be said. This Melchizedek, king of Salem, priest of the Most High God, met Abraham returning from the slaughter of the kings and blessed him. He is first interpreted as “King of righteousness,” then as “King of Salem,” which means “king of peace”; he is “without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life,” but “likened to the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.”

And to commend these matters in the places where they had been signified, Scripture added concerning him: “You see how great this man is, to whom Abraham the patriarch gave a tenth of the first fruits” (Hebr. VII, 1–4). To show with what power and how great Melchizedek is, it praises Abraham by saying that he is “the patriarch”—that is, Abraham is better than all the others, but lesser than Melchizedek.

Is it not evident that this is not a human being but one who is superior? What does it mean that Scripture says of him that he is king of peace and king of righteousness? Come closer and see. From far away, when you see the sun, you think it is a lamp; when you look at silver, you suppose it is tin.

Can any human being be called king of peace and righteousness? Peace is proclaimed to human beings, and likewise righteousness; but he is called king of peace and righteousness so that it may be understood that righteousness and peace have their origin in him. For that which is ruled by him cannot be said to be above him. Human beings are instructed by righteousness as their teacher and by peace so that they may please God. This righteousness, then, which is the teacher of humanity, has Melchizedek as its king.

How much better than a human being, then, is Melchizedek, when that which governs humanity is under him—that is, when he is king of kings? Accordingly, when he is called king of righteousness and peace, he is shown to be their author. Thus, just as the Lord Jesus is the author of life, so Melchizedek is the author of righteousness and peace, because those who live through Christ are governed by the administration of righteousness and peace. He pours righteousness and peace into the hearts of God’s servants, to adorn the Lord’s discipline.

We read in the eighty-fourth Psalm that “Righteousness and peace have embraced one another, and truth has sprung up from the earth.” And to show of what righteousness he was speaking, he says, “Righteousness has looked down from heaven” (Ps. LXXXIV, 11, 12).

Scripture shows that this concerns the time of the Savior, when God’s righteousness was given to the world through Christ, in the knowledge of the mystery of the one God that he had previously promised. For it is just that creation should know the truth of its Creator. This righteousness, manifested on earth, removed the discord that had arisen from the injustice of the unknown God and made the discordant peaceful, establishing those who had previously been divided in one faith.

Thus righteousness and peace and the truth of the One embraced one another. From the earth arose the teacher of righteousness. The incarnation of Christ showed what truth concerning God himself was to be known. This, then, is certainly God’s righteousness.

Likewise, it is also peace, as the Apostle says: “May the God of peace himself crush Satan” (Rom. XVI, 20). I do not see how this can be distinguished, since the God of peace is the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and Christ himself as well; for he says, “I give you my peace” (John XIV, 27). Yet Melchizedek is said to be king of righteousness and peace. I do not understand on what basis they are distinguished. I think that, as far as the matter itself is concerned, the king of peace differs nothing from the God of peace.

Because no one in the world ought to be called God, so that this name might be reserved for the One alone from whom all things are, he established a king who would bear his image and possess all his authority except the name of God. But because he is earthly, he is king of human beings, though not king of peace and righteousness. For he himself also has righteousness as his ruler, which he is not permitted to despise. Righteousness is his god, so to speak. Righteousness is God’s affair, and whoever transgresses it becomes liable to God’s judgment.

Melchizedek, however, as he is given to understand, is not called king in the human manner, because he has beneath him the righteousness that rules kings. No one can have righteousness beneath him unless he is of such a nature that he cannot sin. It is said to be beneath him because it was discovered by him as a rule of law by which those who can sin are governed.

Therefore the king of righteousness is the regulator of the words he himself discovered, through which one may live, believe, and be blessed in goodness. We labor long and hard, and still say too little about Melchizedek unless we return to Scripture, which itself knocks and cries out for a long time, in order to rouse those weighed down by deep sleep to understanding—not of night but of day.

It says, then, that Melchizedek is without father, without mother, and without genealogy. And lest he be understood otherwise than is fitting, it adds: “Having neither beginning of days nor end of life.” By this it shows that Melchizedek was neither born nor dead.

What does human subtlety argue against such manifest statements? What craftiness of intellect, so cunning, dares to resist what is evident, so that it does not receive the meaning from the reading but imposes a meaning upon the reading? Violence is done to the divine Scriptures, so that they even regard as enemies those who seem to bow to their authority.

Some say that Melchizedek should not be believed in the manner in which he is presented in Scripture, and thus they twist the Scriptures to fit their own interpretation. It would be better for such people openly to reject the Scriptures than deceitfully to act against them, so that war may be prepared under the name of peace and an enemy may hide beneath the cloak of friendship.

They say, then, that “without father and without mother” does not refer to Melchizedek’s nobility but to the obscurity of his lineage, because he is read to have been without father and mother. They claim that this was written in order to show that he was from foreign peoples, not from the tribe from which Abraham arose, since his lineage is not found in the Law. For this reason, they say, Scripture also added, “and without genealogy,” so that it might be understood that his origin was entirely absent from the Law, and that he should be believed to have become a good man by himself, from parents of whatever kind.

But Scripture is already so extensive that it sets down everything necessary to the matter in orderly arrangement. First it says, “without father, without mother.” Let us see whether the mothers of the others are indicated in the Law. We are not told who the wife of Nahor, Abraham’s grandmother, was, nor who Terah’s mother was; nor is Abraham’s mother named, to say nothing of the others. Are these people therefore to be said to have been without mothers?

If Scripture had said, “without father, without mother,” this might have had some appearance of reason, because the fathers of all who existed are recorded in the Law. It adds, “and without genealogy.” If it said this in order to show that his generation is not found in the Law, it would have been enough to say “without father,” because no one knows his father.

Again, and much more explicitly, Scripture says, “having neither beginning of days nor end of life.” Tell me, whoever you are who use violence against the text: how do you interpret this? What does it mean to have neither a beginning of days nor an end of life?

Certainly it would have been enough to say that his generation was not written in the Law and that, consequently, his origin should be believed to be from foreign peoples. Someone might say that he was translated, like Enoch, and therefore did not die. Let it be so. But what does it mean to have no beginning of the days of life? Perhaps you will say that his birthday was not written down. Whose birthday is written in the Law? And is this the reason that one whose birthday is not written is said to have no beginning of the days of life?

The same could therefore have been said of the others. And if he had been translated as a human being, he would nevertheless have had an end of life, because whatever is subject to the expectation of death has an end.

Desist, whoever you are who pursue contention. It is better to be defeated by truth than to defeat truth through falsehood. That is loss, not victory; for although truth may seem to lose among human beings, it nevertheless conquers before God, because its reasoning is invincible.

The mind must therefore be conquered by the Law, so that it may understand what the Law signifies, rather than impose upon the Law, by its own arbitrary judgment, a meaning that subjects the Law to violent interpretation.

And hear Zerubbabel, who says: “Above all things, truth prevails” (III Esdr. III, 12).

Melchizedek already displayed the future mystery of the Lord’s incarnation and passion when he first gave Abraham, as it were the father of the faithful, the Eucharist of the Lord’s body and blood, so that what was to be the truth in the sons might be prefigured in the father.

If he is thought to have been a human being and a priest in the manner of Aaron, or of the priests who now exist, let the place of his habitation be shown or read; or, if there was some temple or synagogue in which he gathered the people and offered their sacrifices, let it be shown, along with the people who assembled around him.

For if he was a priest on earth, he unquestionably had a people; and before Abraham, or at least in his time, there was a people serving God. How, then, did Abraham become, as it were, the head of faith, so that from him the people might receive knowledge of God? Likewise, if Melchizedek existed to teach the fear of the one God on earth, Abraham was chosen in vain so that God’s people might be named from him. There could have been people among them who gathered around Melchizedek.

And what of the passage read in the Song of Deuteronomy? “When the Most High divided the nations,” it says, “when he separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God. And the Lord’s portion became his people Jacob” (Deut. XXXII, 8, 9).

Therefore, if there was no people of God in the world except the sons of Abraham, on what grounds is another people thought to have existed, descended from the teaching of Melchizedek, when the prophet denies this? For when he names all the nations that are in the world and says that no people of God exists except the sons of Abraham, what remains except to deny that the others possessed knowledge of God? “God is known in Judah” (Ps. LXXV, 1).

Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High God, appeared to bless Abraham as a foreshadowing of the holy things to come, because in the future the blessing was to be given to God’s people through a prelate, almost a god, whom we call a priest.

Thus this Melchizedek appeared as the forerunner of the consecrated Son of God who was to come, because the one who precedes comes first in service, while the one who follows comes afterward in order.

What we have said about Melchizedek should therefore not be surprising, since Scripture, to silence those who contradict it, adds still more and says: “But, likened to the Son of God, he remains a priest forever.”

Now consider whom you persist in judging wrongly. If you do not fear him, at least fear Christ, to whom Scripture declares that Melchizedek is similar.

For Scripture proceeds gradually toward his natural merit, so that, if anyone were disturbed by the earlier statements—in which he was signified as king of righteousness and peace, and because, seen in the flesh, he had neither father nor mother, that is, appeared unbegotten, having neither origin nor end—the final statements might demonstrate the credibility of the preceding ones.

Who, unless insane, would dare to say that all these exalted statements are unsuitable to one who is designated as like the Son of God and remains a priest forever? He cannot be like the Son of God unless he is of the same nature.

And what is unbelievable if Melchizedek appeared as a human being, when it is understood that he is the third person? For if Christ, who is the second person, was frequently seen in human form, why should there be doubt about the things that have been said?

For we read in the Psalm: “You are a priest forever, according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. CIX, 4). None of us doubts that this refers to the person of Christ, because Christ is a priest forever by the same order by which Melchizedek is. But Christ is the High Priest, while Melchizedek is second.

For if Melchizedek is a human being, how is it fitting that Christ should be a priest forever according to his order? The two are already read to be similar and to belong to one dispensation, because they also belong to one nature.

Since the authority of the one God must in every way be preserved, a third person is therefore also placed under the Father’s name. Christ, however, is the Father’s vicar and bishop, and for this reason he is also called a priest. Likewise, the Holy Spirit, as a kind of bishop, is called the priest of the exalted God, not the High Priest, as our priests presume in the offering.

Although Christ and the Holy Spirit are of one substance, the order of each must nevertheless be observed. Priests, therefore, or ambassadors, are so called because they display in themselves the one whose ambassadors they are; for they are his image.

Accordingly, Christ and the Holy Spirit, naturally possessing the image of God, are called his priests. God is seen in them, as the Lord says: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV, 9).

And if the Lord was seen in the deeds of God, while the works are the deeds of the Holy Spirit—as the Lord indicates when he says, “For I cast out demons by the Spirit of God” (Matt. XII, 28)—then God was also seen in the Holy Spirit.

### ON THE FIRST PSALM

### CX

[Note: [Col. 2330] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

“Blessed is the man who has not stood in the way of sinners.” But if he has stood there, he is no longer blessed, but guilty and deserving of punishments. Yet he seems to retain some hope of correction, because he is not ungodly but a sinner. But if there is one who has not gone in the counsel of the ungodly and has not stood in the way of sinners, he is blessed in a twofold respect. For he cannot be blessed if he does not go into the counsel of sinners but stands in the way of sinners; for, if he is not liable to destruction, he is nevertheless liable to punishment.

He then added: “And has not sat in the seat of pestilence.” He says that this blessedness consists in these three stages and is secured by a threefold principle: namely, that one should neither go into the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of pestilence. But since there are only two classes, the ungodly and sinners, to which class did he wish to assign this third thing added in the foregoing enumeration, when he said, “And has not sat in the seat of pestilence”: to the ungodly, or to sinners?

But let us see what it is to sit in the seat of pestilence, and then we shall understand to which class he assigns it. We call that the seat of pestilence which exists outside God’s ordinance, devised precisely so that unjust judgments may proceed from it. It is therefore called a seat of pestilence because it is a corruption that brings forth death, just as iniquity brings condemnation. The seat of death, then, is not from God. Moses, indeed, received the seat of life. For it was given so that the authority of the righteous judge or of God the Creator might reside in it. Hence the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon the seat of Moses” (Matt. XXIII, 2). And the Apostle says: “There is no authority except from God; and those that exist have been ordained by God” (Rom. XIII, 1).

Hence he says to the ruler of the people: “You sit judging according to the Law, and contrary to the Law you order me to be struck” (Acts XXIII, 3). By saying “according to the Law,” he signified the just and salutary authority of the seat. But when he says, “contrary to the Law you order me to be struck,” he shows that the very judge was unjust, judging unjustly while sitting in God’s seat. Hence also Daniel says: “The kingdom is God’s, and he will give it to whom he wills” (Dan. IV, 14).

For just as the authority of an earthly emperor extends through all, so that he is revered by all, so God ordained that the authority of God should begin from the king himself and extend through all. Although the world often does not understand this and subjects itself to persons in authority other than those to whom it ought, the ordinance is that there should be one who is feared. Where this ordinance is absent, there is found the seat of pestilence. [Note: [Col. 2330] Manuscript Colbert: “Where this ordinance exists, there the seat of pestilence is not found.”] The authority of the one God is nowhere rejected except among those who proclaim fear and reverence for many gods. These, therefore, are those who sit in the seat of pestilence, because what their pontiffs preach is death. For this is what they demand: that worshippers of the one God, as though foolish and enemies, should either be exposed to reproach or removed from this life.

This very thing is the substance of ungodliness, which also extends into its other aspects, by which it displays the laws of its ungodliness. For at Jezebel’s command the bishops of iniquity sat in the seat of pestilence. Though they were not judges, they plotted against the innocent Naboth and, having suborned false witnesses, pronounced sentence of death (III Kings XXI, 11–13). Hence he also says in another psalm: “And I will not sit with the ungodly” (Ps. XXV, 5). For this is the judgment of him whose is also the seat of pestilence.

Accordingly, if those sitting in God’s seat oppress the innocent, the judgment will be unjust, but not the seat. Where the seat of pestilence is, however, the judgment cannot fail to be unjust [Col. 2331], although they attach to themselves certain things like veils with which they cover their ungodliness, so that those who see may be deceived. For ungodliness by itself cannot be offered, because it finds no buyer; and where the law of the devil is, if he is named, it is abhorred. But just as honey is mixed with poison so that the poison may remain concealed, so they mix certain just things into the devil’s law and apply to it the name of truth. Yet the meaning of each thing must be judged, because it sometimes makes something true appear in order to deceive, so that, when it preaches malicious things, they may be thought good.

Since we have established that the seat of pestilence is not from God’s ordinance, we also call the seat of those who have set up seats for themselves outside the Church or against the Church a seat of pestilence. For he who presumes what has not been granted is guilty; how much more so if he also corrupts the tradition of him whose seat he usurps? [Note: [Col. 2331] The Erfurt, Lyons, Venice, and Louvain editions read *inconcessa* (“what has not been granted”). In B it is written separately, *in concessa*.]

For they disturb the order begun by the apostle Peter and preserved down to this time through the succession of bishops, claiming for themselves an order without an origin—that is, professing a body without a head. It is therefore fitting to call their seat also the seat of pestilence. Nor will it be without punishment merely because they do this under God’s name. For it is evident that they conduct their own causes under God’s name. They do not do this through zeal for God, but because they wish to defend a place for themselves. We know that Korah and two hundred and fifty men, who presumptuously made an offering to God, were swallowed up by a fissure in the earth (Num. XVI, 31, 35), and that King Uzziah, when he unlawfully made an offering to God, was struck with leprosy on his forehead (IV Kings XV, 5; II Chron. XXVI, 21).

Since it has become clear that the seat of pestilence belongs to the ungodliness described above, let us pursue the remainder. For he added: “But his will was in the law of the Lord.” He says that the will of him who, having rejected the ungodly and abandoned sinners and refused the seat of pestilence, has established his will in God’s law, is in the law of the Lord. For this reason he called him blessed. And it follows: “And in his law he will meditate day and night.” It is clear that one who is free from all enticements and immune from things contrary to God’s law engages in nothing but exercise in God’s law. Confirmed by the mysteries of the Son of God, by day he persists in good works and by night in prayers. For this is he of whom he says in the Song of Songs that he sleeps and his heart watches (Song V, 2).

Hence he says: “And he shall be like a tree planted beside streams of water.” Who doubts that one who meditates on God’s law has hope of obtaining a reward? For just as a tree planted beside water cannot be barren, so one who diligently devotes himself to God’s law cannot fail to have the result of its work. And he added: “Which will give its fruit in its season.” Every planting that is well tended gives fruit at the appropriate time; so also this man who obeys God’s law will have fruit at the appointed time. For then he will receive the reward of this devotion, when the Lord Jesus Christ begins to sit in judgment on the living and the dead.

He then added: “And his leaf shall not fall.” It is clear that, in a tree whose leaves do not fall, he signified life. For the tree, nourished by the moisture of flowing water, retains its leaves. The Lord Jesus also says: “For if they do these things in the green wood, what will be done in the dry?” (Luke XXIII, 31). By the green wood he signified life and fruit. Therefore, just as a tree does not feel drought through the aid of flowing water, so this man who devotes himself to God’s law, when temptation comes, safe through God’s protection, does not lose but gains salvation. As the Apostle says: “Through many tribulations we must enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts XIV, 21).

And it follows: “And all whatsoever he does shall prosper.” What he says is clear: one who keeps faith with God’s law and eagerly follows its commandments becomes fortunate in all his deeds. So too Joseph, because he preferred the fear of God to this present life, had God make all that he did prosper in his hands. And he added: “Not so the ungodly, not so.” The repetition of the phrase signifies that what is promised will in no respect turn out otherwise: for the ungodly [Col. 2332] will have nothing prosperous in the future, but everything adverse, unto their destruction.
