Hence he says: “But like dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth.” He says that the ungodly perish in the same manner as dust which the wind casts from the face of the earth so that it may perish. For, removed from its substance, it is gradually lost as it is scattered through the air. So also the ungodly, cast from the presence of God the Creator by the angelic ministers, will perish without him, without whom one cannot live.

And it follows: “Therefore the ungodly shall not rise in judgment.” What he says is fitting. For why should those rise in judgment who preferred that no business of God should be entrusted to them, for which they might render an account? In scorning and denying God’s law, they have no basis on which to render an account, so that, questioned at the judgment according to the law entrusted to them, they might state their case. Found arrogant and rebellious toward God, they rise for this purpose: that they may see to be true what they refused to believe, and may perish because they judged God to be a liar.

And he added: “Nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous.” In this psalm the Psalmist signifies three classes of human beings: the ungodly, sinners, and righteous, in the order in which error begins. But the ungodly are strangers to these, because, as I have said, they were unwilling to live under God’s decree. Sinners, however, living under God’s law, must stand before Christ’s tribunal, separated from the righteous, in order to render an account of the commandments of the law they received [Note: [Col. 2332] Manuscript Colbert: “that they may render an account of amendment.”], in which they did not labor so as to have more praise than blame. But the righteous, found much more earnest in the exercise of fulfilling the law, are to be rewarded.

And he added: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous.” God is said to know those who, mindful of his precepts, persist in good works, so that, regarded as righteous, they may be crowned. But to those who, forgetful of him, are negligent concerning the care of the soul, he will say: “Depart from me; I do not know you, workers of iniquity” (Luke XIII, 27). And it follows: “And the way of the ungodly shall perish.” The Psalm began and ended with this, so that, its case having been discussed, the ungodly might be taught to be liable to nothing other than destruction. For, as I have said, God is said to know the way of the righteous because they walk in his law; but the way of the ungodly, because it is outside God’s law, shall perish. For all the ways of the ungodly are dark (Prov. IV, 19), as Solomon says, whereas those of the godly are most bright, with Christ our Lord as their guide.

### ON THE TWENTY-THIRD PSALM
### CXI

[Note: [Col. 2332] This question is absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

The title of the Psalm suggests its meaning. Since he is about to speak of the mystery of Christ our Lord, he marks the Lord’s day by saying, “For this David, on the first day of the week.” For when it says, “For this David,” it pertains to him whose image David here bears, concerning whom the prophet says, “And my servant David shall shepherd them” (Ezek. XXXVII, 24). “The first day of the week” is the first feria. For after the Sabbath, the first day is the Lord’s day, as the Gospel affirms when it says, “But on the first day of the week Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the tomb,” etc. (Matt. XXVIII, 1).

On the Lord’s day, therefore, he signified the mystery of the Savior. But so that the Psalm might be expounded according to the order of its meaning, he began with the person of God the Father, so that the mystery of the divine nature might be disclosed to human beings in an orderly manner. For whoever wishes to explain some cause, unless he grasps its head and origin, cannot show its proper character or teach what its truth is.

Thus the Prophet began and said: “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” He maintained the truth of the matter by saying, “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness.” For he followed the authority of the holy men of old, who said that the earth and what is in it belong to the Lord God. And he added: “The world and all who dwell in it.” Lest it be thought that he had signified something less by saying, “The earth is the Lord’s, and its fullness,” he disclosed his meaning by saying, “the world and all who dwell in it,” so that he might teach that the whole earth absolutely belongs to the Lord, together with what is in it, and that nothing is excepted which does not belong to God. This is directed against certain heretics who, according to the statement of the apostle Peter, deny God’s dominion (II Pet. II, 10); for the prophetic oracles have taught, to their condemnation, that everything belongs to God. [Col. 2333]

And it follows: “He founded it upon the seas.” This is what he signified in another Psalm when he said, “You formed the earth above the waters” (Ps. CXXXV, 6). So that the testimony might follow the faith, he showed how God had done this. For while all things were in confusion and neither earth nor water possessed its proper form, at God’s command the earth was gathered together and established above the waters, so that both earth and water might retain the character of their origin. Hence, in the Book of Kings, there is the voice of God saying, “Did I not make the waters?” And he added: “And upon the rivers he prepared it.” It was prepared upon the rivers because it contains within itself waters stored up, which, flowing as though through the channels of veins, give it density, lest it be entirely dry, fragile, and useless for cultivation. For they provide the roots of growing things with life-giving effect, and likewise serve as a relief from thirst in dry places.

And to show that confession without a good life is of little benefit, he said: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” He sets forth what the person who professes God as Creator ought to be, lest those whom he has shown to be punishable because, as I said, they deny God’s dominion think that those who confess God are exempt from punishment if they conduct themselves improperly.

Thus, by saying “the mountain of the Lord,” he signified heaven. Hence in another Psalm he says, “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Ps. CXX, 1). The Lord’s place is where he appears. Thus it is said to Jesus son of Nave when the Lord had appeared to him, “The place on which you stand is holy ground” (Josh. V, 16); and when Jacob saw God, he said, “This is the house of God” (Gen. XXVIII, 17).

And it follows: “The innocent in hands and pure in heart.” He says that such a person is worthy to ascend the mountain of the Lord—that is, into heaven—or to stand in his holy place, if he is innocent in his works and has a pure heart in the matter of God, that is, of faith. Such a person can ascend into heaven and stand in his holy place. Having died to this life, he ascends into heaven. Then, when the city Jerusalem descends from heaven at the Lord’s coming, he will be worthy to stand where the Lord will judge the living and the dead, as an innocent person. But the impious and sinners will be unworthy to stand in the holy place of God’s judgment, because the impious will rise for destruction and sinners for punishment.

For if the children of Israel could not, because of sin, look upon the glorified face of Moses as he descended from the mountain (Exod. XXXIV, 29–30), how much more will a conscience burdened with sins fear to look upon the Lord of glory himself, seated on the throne of his majesty? For they will hear, “I do not know you, workers of iniquity” (Matt. VII, 23).

And he added: “Who has not received his soul in vain.” He now touches upon the several kinds of sinners. First, this is the innocent person who has a pure heart, who is free from the fornication of idolatry. For idolatry is vanity, and whoever bows before it subjects his soul to corruption.

And it follows: “Nor has sworn deceitfully to his neighbor.” He has mentioned two principal obligations, those toward God and toward one’s neighbor, because whoever is found worthy in these will without doubt be considered approved in the others also. The Lord says:

“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength. This is the first commandment. And the second is like it: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. On these two commandments depend the whole Law and the Prophets” (Matt. XXII, 37–40).

Who, then, loving God with all his heart, would not keep his law? Or who, possessing love for his neighbor, would devote himself to sins—especially since, through fear of God, he loves his neighbor?

And he added: “He will receive blessing from the Lord and mercy from God his Savior.” He now shows what reward belongs to the person who has maintained faith and love in relation to God and humanity, to the Creator and to his neighbor: he will be blessed by the Lord, so that he may appear approved, and he will obtain mercy in those matters which he could not fulfill. For no one can be so watchful as never to go astray. But because he has been found diligent and faithful in great matters, he will receive mercy from his God even in small matters.

He is called “Savior” because he does not desire the death of the dying, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. XVIII, 32).

And it follows: “This is the generation of those who seek the Lord, of those who seek the face of the God of Jacob.” He said that there is one generation of those who seek God and those who seek the face of the God of Jacob, and this is not without significance. Although both are good, by these words he indicated two degrees. It is good to seek God; it is the fullness of goodness to seek the face of the God of Jacob. For those who stand before the face of the judge are more worthy.

This, then, is the generation of these merits: innocence and purity of heart bring one to this state, just as injustice and iniquity precede the possibility of reaching evil. [Col. 2334] For there are two generations: one from the side of iniquity, which is the mother of Cain; the other from the side of righteousness, which is the mother of Abel. The latter consists in faith and good conduct; the former in faithlessness and crooked works. These are the two laws, of good and evil, of God and the devil; and each person will be called the son of the one whom he has followed.

Accordingly, this is the generation of those who seek God: faith in God and love of one’s neighbor, as we said above. For whoever has faith in God always seeks his help; nor does he act unjustly toward human beings, since he wishes to have God favorable to him.

This is indicated when it says, “the God of Jacob,” because God is known in Judea (Ps. LXXV, 2). But why are they said to seek his face, when Moses heard, “My face shall not be seen by you” (Exod. XXXIII, 20)? If Moses also sought the face of God and could not see it, then these people are said to seek it in vain, since they are not better than Moses.

Yet no one should be said to seek the face of God in vain. They are said to seek the face of God so that it may be known whom they seek, because they are worthy also to see him. For everyone who is sought is then recognized when his face is seen. But since the face of God cannot be seen by mortals, this expression signifies the face when it says, “the God of Jacob.”

**Diapsalma.** Here the diapsalma signifies a change of person. After those matters that pertain to the person of God the Father, he adds those that pertain to the mystery of the Son of God, so that the order of the Father and the Son may remain complete.

For the Law was given through Moses, so that it might be, as it were, a pedagogue for human beings, instructing and preparing them as a teacher of righteousness, so that they might become worthy to await the year of the Lord and the day of recompense; [Note: [Col. 2334] Perhaps: “to await.”] so that those who had been faithful in hope of the future Christ might receive him and be able to escape Adam’s sin, secure concerning themselves, because the coming of the one whom they had hoped for would give them mercy concerning those things in which they had been secretly led into sin. This is what he indicated above when he said, “He will receive mercy from God his Savior.”

He therefore says: “Lift up your gates, princes.” This is the voice of the holy angels, of whom the Gospel says, “Behold, angels came and ministered to him” (Matt. IV, 11). These angels therefore say to the princes and powers against whom the Apostle tells us that we have a struggle (Eph. VI, 12) that they should lift up the gates of their prince, that is, of the devil, who is the prince of princes established in error, through which one goes into Gehenna. These gates are faithlessness and the deceit of idolatry.

And it follows: “And be lifted up, eternal gates.” Faith and hope together with love are eternal gates, because what is preached through truth cannot be destroyed. But those gates which I have said are faithlessness and the deceit of idols are temporary, because every lie does not endure. Once the truth has been revealed, it will perish.

They are therefore taught to lift up the gates of their prince of darkness—that is, when the error of many gods has been removed, the faith of the one God is to be introduced in Christ. This is what the Apostle testifies that he was sent to teach: not only to show human beings, but also princes and powers in the heavenly places, the mystery of the one God in Christ (Eph. III, 8–12).

And he added: “And the King of glory shall enter.” He says that the deceptive gates fashioned by the devil’s subtlety must be removed. These are presumption, by which he thought himself to be a god, so that the King of glory, who is Christ Jesus our Lord, may enter. For the faith of God enters no one’s mind unless that person has removed from himself the error discovered through the devil’s transgression.

And the princes mentioned above cannot receive Christ the King into faith in the one God unless they cast away from themselves the tradition by which accusation is brought against the one God. This concerns not only earthly things, [Col. 2335] but also the things in the heavenly places that have been usurped by the prince of princes, Satan. For they established here on earth the error that they had conspired among themselves there, when, under the devil’s authorship, they called themselves gods, so that this error here might be an image of that one.

And it follows: “Who is this King of glory?” Lest someone perhaps think that Christ was needlessly called the King of glory, he introduces the person of one who asks and says, “Who is this King of glory?” It is as though he were astonished or wished to be taught whether it is true and fitting to call Christ the King of glory.

And therefore they answered him: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle,” so that, by this addition, he might learn—on the basis of testimony, not bare words—that Christ is the King of glory. For the strength and power by which he subdued and crushed the devil and his attendants show that he is the King of glory.

And he added: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates.” That is: since, through the testimony of a power which it would be impious to contradict, you have learned that Christ is worthy to be called the King of glory, remove error from your minds.

And when he says, “The King of glory shall enter,” it is shown that they cannot share in the faith of Christ unless they cleanse their hearts from every impurity of idolatry. For unless a person has been renewed, the Holy Spirit will not enter him.

And it follows: “Who is this King of glory?” This repetition provides confirmation. For whatever is heard as something new is not grasped by the heart unless it is repeated. It produces wonder and astonishment when what has never before been heard is announced.

And he added: “The Lord of hosts—he is the King of glory.” By repeating the same words, he teaches that the one who is the Lord of hosts is rightly called the King of glory. For he is not improperly called the King of glory who rules over powers. Hence the Apostle says: “For if they had understood, they would never have crucified the Lord of majesty” (I Cor. II, 8).

## ON THE FIFTIETH PSALM

### CXII

[Note: [Col. 2335] This is absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

The Fiftieth Psalm is placed here not according to chronological order but according to its meaning. For its title is subject not to number but to significance. As far as the historical account is concerned, it precedes the Third Psalm. For he was rebuked by the prophet Nathan on account of his sin before his son Absalom rose up against him and sought to deprive him both of life and of his kingdom.

This, then, is the reason why it was placed as the Fiftieth Psalm, a number which clearly derives from the Law. For there it is ordained that the number fifty should signify remission. After seven weeks, it is the first number bearing the type of the Lord’s day. For just as, after seven days, the first day is the same day that was made at the beginning, which, whenever the week has been completed, is always the first day, so after seven weeks the fiftieth, being counted, is first in the mystery. It is called the Lord’s day in a twofold manner: first, because it was made by the Lord at the beginning and, always returning upon itself after the cycles of the completed week, is the first day; then because on it the Lord rose after triumphing over death, and it is therefore also called the Lord’s day.

It is therefore not without reason that remission is contained in the number fifty, which we understand to have been signified as first in the mystery. Finally, the Law was given on the fiftieth day. For beginning with the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, they were commanded to be washed on the forty-eighth day, so that, purified for two days, they might be ready on the third day to receive the Law (Exod. XIX, 10–11). What else does this washing indicate than remission taking place on the fiftieth day, so that, purified, they might receive the Law? From that point onward, with past matters erased, they would give an account of their conduct according to the Law entrusted to them.

For this reason also the Law commanded that purchased property should be released in the fiftieth year (Lev. XXV, 10). This, then, is why the Psalm was entitled the Fiftieth. In it King David requests remission according to the meaning just mentioned. Hence he says: “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.”

King David knew that he had sinned gravely, and so he makes his request, saying, “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” For mercy is great when it forgives great sins.

And he added: “And according to the multitude of your mercies, blot out my iniquity.” To make clear that he had sinned bitterly, he calls his sin “iniquity,” because iniquity is not a light sin; and whoever blots out iniquity—that is, does not impute it—is abundant in mercy.

He therefore makes no attempt to excuse anything in his case, so that he may not only soften the judge’s mind toward himself but also make the judge suffer with him. For the mind is moved to mercy when it sees the accused confessing his sins in such a way as to show that he grieves because he has sinned. Whoever does not grieve appears to mock the judge, because he prays only in order to escape, intending afterward to do the same things again.

And afterward it follows: “Wash me thoroughly,” he says, “from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.” Since he proclaims God’s abundant mercy, he prays to be completely cleansed, so that no sin or injustice may remain in him by which he might be suspected.

And so that he might be able to obtain or secure this very thing, he added: “For I know my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.” [Note: [Col. 2336] Ms. Colbertinus: “against me.”]

Because he knows that he has sinned gravely, he is anxious that not all of it may be forgiven him. Considering the magnitude of his sins, he fears, knowing that grave sins are not easily forgiven. Accordingly, he confesses with tears, keeping his sin before his eyes, so that he may make the judge favorable to him in every respect. For he knows that it is written: “Declare your iniquities first, so that you may be justified” (Isa. XLIII, 26).

And it follows: “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.” He now looks for a remedy for his guilt from another angle, so that he may bring his petition to its fulfillment. By this statement, in the first instance he calls himself innocent. [Note: [Col. 2336] The printed editions read “guilty,” and below, “against another God.” We follow the manuscripts.] For whoever sins against another god is an enemy of the God who is the author. For he chooses another in his place, to whom he attributes God’s authority.

Thus, showing himself free from this iniquity, he says, “Against you alone have I sinned, and I have done evil before you.” That is: because I sinned against you, and against no other whom I might mistakenly call God, my guilt is less than that of the others who are subject to destruction. I am not impious but a sinner, because I sinned not against you but against your law. I did not deny you, but, confessing you as God and Lord, I sinned against a human being.

Therefore, because I am not guilty in that matter which is properly yours, forgive me for sinning against a fellow servant. I sinned in such a way that I neither denied the honor of your name nor gave it to another. Thus there was a reason for the judge to be moved to mercy. For when many sin against him, and he even urges them to turn to him, while those who do not sin against him nevertheless ask pardon for other reasons, he willingly receives them. For the Lord always wishes his servants to flee to his help.

Hence he added: “So that you may be justified in your words and prevail when you are judged.” Asking for mercy, he does not pray that God alter his justice, as though justice ordinarily consisted in treating the sinless and the sinful equally—that is, in repaying each according to his works. But the innocent man does not fail to understand what he is asking in the mystery of God.

Knowing that God frequently said in the Law, “For I am merciful, says the Lord your God” (Exod. XXII, 27), he asks that this faith remain, and that God be justified in his words by remaining in what he has spoken and not being overcome by human sins, so that he would cease to have mercy.

For those who sin know what God promised to those who live well, and because they see that God remains faithful, they judge him to be a liar. They do not believe that what he promised is true, since they live badly. Therefore King David asks that God prevail over what people think and grant what he promised, so that those who, while not keeping the commandments, judge that God will not give what he promised may be put to shame.

And it follows: “For behold, I was conceived in iniquities.” By adding this, he now recalls the cause of the weakness of the human race, because it is easy for human beings to sin, so that the judge’s scrutiny of them may be softened.

He mentions the first sin, [Note: [Col. 2336] Ms. Colbertinus: “causes.”] from which Adam, by transgressing, made the human race subject to sin. Through the persuasion and deceit of the enemy, by conceiving iniquity, he subjected all his offspring to iniquity, so that all who were generated by descent from him would be liable to sin.

Therefore he added, “And in sins my mother conceived me,” so that the transmission of sin from Adam might be an impediment to those conceived and born, preventing them from living a good life. Accordingly, mercy must not be denied to the suppliant, because he has an enemy hostile to him who urges him to sin. [Note: [Col. 2337] Ms. Colbertinus: “inserted.” And immediately the same old manuscript: “for sin, which is the devil, … received power to enter into his flesh, and of those who love, etc.”] Through sin, the devil, having obtained power over the flesh of the first human being subject to him, entered into his flesh and suggested the enticements of sins through a certain subtlety, by which he strips the captured human being of life.

The teacher of the nations recalls this matter when he says, “But I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Rom. VII, 23), so that the judge, observing this, may extend his hand to the grieving person who has been deceived.

And it follows: “For behold, you have loved truth.” Because you love truth, he says, help the one who asks, the one whom you know to be setting forth the true obstacles within his heart, and to whom, once moved by mercy, you long ago determined to offer help, so that heavenly providence might correct the error committed on earth.

For this reason he added: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of the heart.” By the uncertain and hidden things of the heart he signifies those things that God arranged for the protection of the human race. Thus the Apostle also says: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II, 9).

Who are those who love God except those who consent to his law, neither concealing nor excusing their sins? These hidden things of the heart are therefore made manifest to those who love God. Since they grieved that they had been deceived by sins, they did not deny them when reproved, [Note: [Col. 2337] Ms. Colbertinus: “nor did they deny them when reproved.”] attributing them to themselves and their origin rather than transferring what they had done to God the Creator. Their hearts were illuminated by a spiritual flash, so that they might see God’s providence in Christ, because he was to come to condemn the sin that, arising from Adam’s transgression, ruled over the human race.

King David therefore prays that what God had determined for the future, seeing the human race suffering, might first help him, who was constrained by the same necessity in which God had determined to help everyone. Thus the gift that was to be gratuitous and could not be given before its time might be granted to him in response to his prayer and tears.

He does not keep silent about how this happens, saying: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed.” He rightly asks to be cleansed through the sprinkling of hyssop. For the children of Israel smeared their doorposts with blood so that they might be kept safe from death (Exod. XII, 22–23). Thus here also he prays to be cleansed from sins by the sprinkling of hyssop, so that death may not touch him.

And it follows: “You shall wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” It is clear that God’s work differs from human work. Therefore he says, “I shall be whiter than snow,” because what God has made is much better than what a human being has made.

For this reason he asks to be cleansed by the sprinkling of hyssop, so that just as a bodily substance is washed with water, the stains of souls may likewise be washed spiritually through the symbolism of hyssop. The sprinkling of hyssop is a kind of purification, so that through what is visible one may be cleansed invisibly.

And it follows: “You shall give joy and gladness to my hearing.” There is no doubt that the voice of one proclaiming remission gives joy to sinners. For who would not rejoice when he hears that pardon is being granted? When God forgives, a person is secure both in the present and in the future.

Therefore “the humbled bones shall rejoice.” The humbled bones are so in a twofold manner: first, because a person was humbled in order to sin—for no one who sins is exalted—and then in order afterward to plead humbly for forgiveness. For he was surely rolling in sackcloth and ashes as he prayed for mercy; once he obtained it, he was raised up through exultation of mind and restoration of body.

And he added: “Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.” In this form he requests remission, as it had been established for the future through faith in Christ, so that the Savior who had been promised to him spiritually might begin by granting all sins to those who turned back.

For the person whose sins are not regarded and whose iniquities are all blotted out has no basis on which to be charged, and the mouths of his enemies are closed. For whoever does not regard sins does not impute them. This is what it means to turn one’s face away from someone’s sins: not to accept an accusation against him. [Col. 2338]

But what does it mean that, when he had been reproved for two sins, he adds that he is accusing himself of many? And when he had heard from the prophet Nathan that the matter was forgiven him, why does he make such a request with persistent prayer in order to reach pardon? It is because he is not pleading only his own case; under the accusation of his sin, he recounts the sufferings of the whole people. [Note: [Col. 2338] Ms. Colbertinus: “on the occasion of his sin.”]

He prays for his own restoration, because the one who is forgiven is not without shame unless he is restored to his position, so that the dignity of his position may excuse his shame. But for the others he signified the benefit of God that was to come in Christ for the cleansing of all sins.

And it follows: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and dedicate a right spirit within me.” [Note: [Col. 2338] Thus the manuscript reads. The printed editions have “renew.”]

This is to ask for mercy with a good mind. He does not ask only concerning the past but is also concerned about the future, so that the sinner, intent on hating sin lest he sin, may be helped by God through the spirit of righteousness which he prays to be dedicated within him—that is, so that a new spirit may be placed in him for this purpose, to guard him from sins, lest he be compelled to do what he is known not to wish to do.

He can have a clean heart in this way: if he does not sin either within or without—that is, neither in deed nor in thought. But because it is nearly impossible for this to be maintained in every respect, it must at least be maintained in the matter of God, which is primary: the heart must be kept clean in the mystery of God and Christ, while their faith is preserved inviolate. For it is also said elsewhere, “Who can boast of having a clean heart, or of being free from sins?” (Prov. XX, 9).

Finally, King David had a clean heart in the matter of God, because he never sought help from vanity, which is idolatry, nor failed to fulfill anything else commanded to him by God.

Therefore he added concerning the rest: “Do not cast me away from your face, and do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” [Note: [Col. 2338] Ms. Colbertinus: “Therefore you seem to say concerning the rest: … And he added.”]

This is the meaning I mentioned above: secure concerning forgiveness, he is concerned about restoration. For the one who is merely forgiven is accustomed to being separated from the Lord’s face. Although punishment may not be inflicted upon him, his crime has nevertheless not been erased from the mind of the Lord or the judge.

Therefore he prays that his sin may be completely erased, that he may be worthy to approach the Lord’s face and prophesy again—and this did happen. For this is what he says: “And do not take your Holy Spirit from me.” This is the spirit of the prophets.

And it follows: “Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and strengthen me with a princely spirit.” He asks that the joy promised in Christ be given to him, so that, washed from every stain and restored, he might rejoice in the salvation he had sought, and might not be shaken but strengthened in the kingdom by the Holy Spirit.

He called this spirit “princely” because it is above every creature, and through it kings reign.

And he adds: “I will teach the unjust your ways, and the impious will be converted to you.” He says this so that the unjust may learn from him the piety of God, who receives sinners when they confess to him and advances them. Nor does he neglect the converted impious, but exhorts them while showing mercy to others.

And it follows: “Deliver me from bloodshed, O God, God of my salvation.” By saying this, he shows that his sin deserved death, so that he might proclaim the greatness of God’s mercy. Through this he also urges others to flee to God’s clemency.

Hence he added: “My tongue shall exult in your righteousness, O Lord.” He says that he rejoices in the Lord’s righteousness because the Lord remains in what he promised, saying, “I will not remove my mercy from them” (Ps. LXXXVIII, 34). Thus King David, joyful and secure in this respect, proclaims the righteousness of his God.

And it follows: “You shall open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” He opens his lips in this way, by not allowing the cause of sin to keep him subject. The mouth of the one who has been delivered is open; the mouth of the sinner is closed. Seized by shame and fear, he does not dare to speak; but once acquitted and delivered, he joyfully proclaims the judge’s praise.

[Col. 2339] The Apostle also testifies to this when he says, because he was free from human beings, “Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians” (II Cor. VI, 11).

And he added: “For if you had desired sacrifice, I would surely have given it.” He speaks here from certain knowledge, knowing that the holy Samuel said to King Saul, who thought that his sin could be erased not by sorrow of mind or by the compassion of tears but by the offering of sacrifice: “God does not desire sacrifice more than hearing his voice” (I Sam. XV, 22). For sacrifices of this kind can cause harm, but they cannot placate God.

God is placated when the soul, remembering its sin, laments what it has done in tribulation and sorrow of heart.

And it follows: “You will not delight in burnt offerings.” God does not delight in burnt offerings, but in matters of this kind. The mind itself must make satisfaction for itself; it must not redeem itself from without. Such things can provide assistance. For just as the mind delighted in sins, so it must be afflicted in repentance; and then it will please God to blot out its sins.

Hence he added: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit; a contrite and humbled heart God will not despise.” He shows what sacrifice God accepts for sins: no one can placate God unless the one who rejoiced against his salvation has been troubled in heart and is thus restored to life.

Finally, every restless or undisciplined person frequently goes so far as to injure the members of his body, and these cannot receive medicine for their health without pain. So sinners cannot redeem their sins unless the mind that sinned feels pain. This is just: because it rejoiced contrary to reason, it should suffer sorrow according to reason.

And it follows: “Deal kindly, O Lord, in your good will with Sion.” By saying “Sion,” he signifies the Church, so that our perseverance may not appear unacceptable. He urges God to fulfill his promise, knowing that the Church will then receive full remission when what God determined in Christ has been fulfilled: namely, that those hoping in the promised salvation should be freed from every sin, not only from their own sins but also from Adam’s sin, which has reached everyone through descent. [Note: [Col. 2339] Ms. Colbertinus: “our affirmation.”]

And he added: “And the walls of Jerusalem shall be built.” Had they been destroyed? But by “the walls of Jerusalem” he signifies the Church, which had been arranged to be built through faith in Christ. Its walls are understood to be holy people, as the Apocalypse of the apostle John teaches us, since both the city Jerusalem and its walls are to be understood as the servants of God (Rev. XXI, 12).

Knowing also that through Christ King David had been promised what was to be fulfilled for the liberation of God’s servants, he prays that it may be fulfilled—that is, that the Church may be built through faith and that those who hope for salvation through this faith may be delivered.

And it follows: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness, offerings and burnt offerings.” He says this because God would then accept offerings and burnt offerings when the Church had been built; and not indiscriminately or according to every custom, but, he says, “you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness.”

A sacrifice is just when a worthy offering is presented. Nothing, however, is so just and worthy a sacrifice as offering ourselves to God. For since God is spirit (John IV, 24), spiritual sacrifices must be offered to him, so that a living offering may be offered to the living God.

Because he had said that, in the matter of sin, God was not at all pleased with bodily sacrifices, he shows that what was to be offered spiritually would come in the future and would be accepted, because these sacrifices are worthy of God. That is: in the past they were lesser, because they were bodily; now they are greater, because they are spiritual.

And he added: “Then they will place calves upon your altar.” If he signified that spiritual sacrifices would succeed the former sacrifices once the latter had ceased, why would he say, “Then they will place calves upon your altar,” unless by these bodily things he signifies spiritual things—especially since he said that God is not pleased with bodily sacrifices?

By “calves,” therefore, he signified a new people, reborn through faith in Christ, whose devotion is daily offered upon the Lord’s altar. Since he is understood to have spoken of the Church, it must also be understood that he signified its spiritual sacrifices.

[Col. 2340]

### CXIII

[Note: [Col. 2340] This question is absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

Why was the Son of God sent, and not another?

Although everything that God does must be believed to have been done rationally and providentially, I nevertheless think it better if, after faith, the reason for what was done can also be discerned, so that what is believed may not remain unknown. Hence the Lord says: “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17:3). First, one must believe, as the Prophet said; then one must know what one believes. For the Holy Spirit already assists the faithful person who is diligent in this matter, so that, by understanding, he may grasp the rationale of faith. He then possesses the full joy of his belief, if he understands what he believes. This is the strength of faith, this is the immovable foundation of belief: to learn the mystery.

For where there is faith alone, devotion is not so pure, and deception can find an entrance. Hence the chosen vessel labors so that believers may learn the rationale of their faith. For when they have understood how great is the one in whom they have believed, and what his power is, they will permit themselves to be led away from his hope by no means and for no reason. Hence we read: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33:9), so that, having applied themselves, they may come to know the savor of his divinity, understanding that nothing is wiser than to believe in Christ.

Therefore the Teacher of the Gentiles says, among other things: “In whom are hidden all the treasures of the wisdom and knowledge of God” (Colossians 2:3); and again: “I know,” he says, “whom I have believed, and I am certain that he is able to guard my deposit” (2 Timothy 1:12). Thus this man knows the rationale of his faith and does not doubt his power who understands that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the mystery of Christ’s birth, passion, and resurrection.

While my faith remained firm, I reflected at length with myself in order to know why our Lord had come incarnate [Note: [Col. 2340] The Colbertinus Manuscript reads *incarnandus* (“about to be incarnate”).] from the holy and heavenly seats to earth—and not another of those whom the Lord himself calls holy angels. For it seems incongruous that such a work should have been undertaken by his person unless the reason for it is known.

Indeed, this is what troubles many people. For the providence of God the Father could have entrusted this task to another person, both to show the truth to human beings held in error and to restrain and strip bare the presumptuous devil, who envies salvation, together with his attendants, once he had been defeated. For the obstinacy and irreverence of the most wicked servants ought to have been checked by servant-ministers, so that the Lord of all would not himself undergo something unworthy of him.

Nor is Satan’s force and power so great that he could not have been overcome by another power of the same order, since it is clear that, with God’s assistance, he can even be defeated by human beings. Although the comparison is unequal, examples drawn from earthly matters nevertheless correspond in some measure to the argument. When a servant rebelled against King David, Joab, his fellow servant, was sent to pursue and kill him; and against Absalom, who had acted impiously toward his father, the task was assigned to servants (2 Samuel 20:6; 15:14). How much more, then, would the effectiveness of one among many have sufficed to conquer the devil’s tyranny, especially since we read that the one who resisted the archangel Michael could not persist against him but was cast down to earth (Revelation 12:7–9)?

Reflecting often upon this, I knew only this: that he himself had been sent by the Father so that it would not redound to the Father’s dishonor if a work accomplished through him were restored through another [Note: [Col. 2340] The Colbertinus Manuscript reads *reformaret* (“might restore”).] But to know this alone was very little. It did not suffice for so great and wondrous a cause unless something else were also grasped that might contribute to understanding the mystery.

Thus it happened that I recognized that the cause itself had demanded that the one who came should come in this way. For reason itself required that the one whose dignity and merit Satan had usurped should come to restrain him. After God the Father, the devil wished to be called “god,” and he still strives for this, although the matter did not concern him [Col. 2341] but belonged to the Son of God, who is second after the Father as God—not by nature, but by order.

Therefore, for undertaking this cause, no one other than Christ our Lord ought to have come. He came not only to restrain the devil but also to reveal himself to every creature, so that, once the devil’s person had been rejected, they might recognize that this was the one whose sovereignty and majesty Satan had presumptuously usurped. Thereafter, having recognized the truth, they would abandon their error, firmly holding that Christ is the Son of God, who alone is God from God, and the head or beginning of all things, whether those in heaven or those on earth.

For by the power and might with which he overcame the tyrant Satan, he revealed himself to be the one whose dominion the impious devil had presumed to claim—the one who is Satan. For when he wickedly wished to be called god, so that he might rule over spiritual powers—hence the prophet rebukes him, saying, “For you said in your heart: I will set my throne among the clouds, and I will be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14:13–14)—he deceived many, through whose conspiracy he became the leader of error.

In the Psalm they are admonished to reject falsehood and receive the truth. For it is said to them: “Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory will enter.” Unless error is removed from the minds of unbelievers, they cannot receive faith in the one God in Christ. They are taught this: that, once the gates through which one goes to death according to the unbelief begun by the devil have been lifted up [Note: [Col. 2341] The Colbertinus Manuscript reads: “to the second death, which is the unbelief begun by the devil.”], they should receive the mysteries of faith, through which one goes to life.

These are the things signified by the “eternal gates,” because the truth of faith is eternal; unbelief, however, is temporal, because falsehood is the devil’s invention. For the devil sowed on earth the transgression he had begun in heaven, persuading people to worship many gods, among whom he might hold the chief place. He wished to be the head and beginning of the others, although this was not due to him but to the Savior.

Therefore he persecutes him even to the earth, so that, by restraining him, he may display his transgression of error, made manifest in himself through the truth. Hence it is said: “Truth has sprung from the earth” (Psalm 84:12). For, having been cast down from heaven, he fled to earth in order to accomplish below what he had devised concerning divinity above. Hence the Apostle says: “So that he sits in the temple of God, displaying himself as though he were God” (2 Thessalonians 2:4). In every way he wishes to fulfill his desire, even at the cost of condemnation; for, being full of fury, he considers condemnation a lesser evil than failing to satisfy his appetite for error.

## Against the Pagans

**CXIV.** [Note: [Col. 2341] This question is absent from manuscripts of the second class.]—For what reason the Pagans dare to contend against us or attack our faith, while they think themselves acquitted, I do not see. For they possess no proof for their assertions—indeed, I would call them proofs of their superstition rather than of their religion. For they bring forward whatever safeguards they have, so that they themselves may rather be regarded as the authors and defenders of new things.

First, they assert that they worship gods, yet they provide no distinguishing signs and no testimonies of them. They call those beings gods who themselves did not dare to be called by this name, so that human beings might be regarded as the authors of gods, when God ought to be the author of human beings. Consequently, their assertion is vain and empty. For whatever is without God cannot be stable.

The books of the Pagans prove that what I say is evident. In them nothing divine is read, nothing established at God’s command; rather, they assert that individual men, for various reasons, instituted different sacrifices to the deities, so that those who seem to have possessed no merit might nevertheless be judged to have established these things worthily.

When, then, those whom they call gods are never read to have commanded any of these things, by what authority do the Pagans do them, or consider acceptable what they cannot prove to have been commanded? Even if a command could be proven, it ought first to have been examined whether it was worthy or right to obey those whose deeds [Col. 2342] displayed no signs or prodigies to commend their divinity.

But when excluded from this argument, they customarily flee to the elements, saying that they worship those by whose governance human life is directed. From these, as above, we ask whether anything was commanded or ordered by God—the very one whom they themselves acknowledge to be great and supreme, yet neglect.

If this worship ought to be offered, it should have been commanded by the one who is said to be its author. If it was not commanded by him, it is presumption and will lead to punishment, not reward. For it is an insult to the Creator that, once the Lord has been despised, servants should be worshiped, and that, after the emperor has been rejected, his companions should be adored. How could this go unpunished, when we see that even in this life such conduct is punished, and indeed more severely?

But if they should say that the command came from the elements themselves, let them show somewhere that it was prescribed; let them read something that those elements once spoke. If they cannot show this, what punishment do those deserve who are exposed as the authors of a religion presumed upon and fabricated?

The elements are free from this impiety. The very lights of the world will accuse them before God the Judge, because in this vain deliberation they do not show themselves to be its authors. Likewise, those whom they call gods, although it is established that they were human beings, will, when they begin to suffer punishment for their sins, defend themselves in this matter by denying that they are guilty and directing the accusation against those by whom they were not commanded to be worshiped as gods.

With what shame, then, can they criticize our faith or think it worthy of ridicule, when they read a law supported by testimonies of virtue, as well as the voice of the Lord and our God himself, saying: “I am God, and there is no other besides me” (Isaiah 45:21–22)?

If he had said this in bare words, he ought not to have been believed, lest we appear similar to the Pagans, who, seeing no signs of majesty in their gods, began to worship them—and, what is worse, to worship dishonorable things. For shameful acts are performed there, things which modesty forbids one to disclose; yet they call themselves wise because, concerning their law, they are mocked as by Samardacus.

Our God, however, commanded that he be worshiped with the testimony of virtue. And, so that he might leave no room for suspicion, he handed down the law itself as honorable and holy, as is worthy of God. We, whom the Pagans call foolish, would not have believed our God unless he had satisfied us also by testimonies of virtue; nor would we have accepted his law unless we had recognized it as pure and worthy by its very profession.

This is why nothing among us is done in darkness or secretly. Whatever is known to be honorable is not afraid of being made public; but what is shameful and dishonorable cannot be made public because modesty forbids it. For this reason the Pagans celebrate their mysteries in darkness, and in this they are considered wise. They are ashamed to be mocked openly. They do not wish to reveal the abominations performed there in place of a law, lest those who call themselves wise appear foolish to the people whom they call foolish.

But lest we seem foolish to them for this reason—that our law proclaims chastity, mercy, piety, and self-restraint—among them these things are foolish. For every good person is evil in the eyes of the wicked, and the wise person is senseless to the fool.

They so detest chastity that they even take pleasure in *cinaedi* (effeminate men), submitting themselves to their instruction. Unless these men are such, they themselves are not fit, if one may say so, for their religion. For this reason they are castrated and alter their clothing, so that from men they may become, as it were, women, and, subjected contrary to nature, endure the treatment of women; only then are they considered suitable and worthy ministers of their superstition.

Can one accuse someone whom the law makes such a person? For, having lost both the conduct and the appearance of a man, he is transformed into a woman so that he may licitly endure the treatment of women. What, then, are these supposed mysteries, in which what is honorable becomes dishonorable and what is incorrupt becomes corrupt? True religious worship is that which makes honorable people out of the dishonorable and disciplined people out of the undisciplined.

How can its worshipers be rivals of a good life when the mysteries of their law cannot be celebrated without *cinaedi*? If their law takes pleasure in such things, then anyone who is not such a person will be a sinner and a fool. That is why they call us fools. Those who practice these shameful things are judged wise by them; those who avoid and flee them are [Col. 2343] judged foolish.

This appears to have been cunningly and cleverly arranged by them. For they attach the name of wisdom to their law in order to conceal what is reprehensible in it, since where there is wisdom there is no accusation. They call our law foolish so as to keep people away from it.

But once the names “wisdom” and “foolishness” have been removed, and all hostility arising from the defense of both sides has been set aside, let the laws themselves contend with one another, so that it may become clear where wisdom is and where foolishness.

When the sign of the cross is present, Paganism falls silent. And if that wisdom which they call foolishness is present, their sacred rites do not dare to answer. Their entrails are restrained and concealed out of reverence for Christian majesty. It is a great thing that the thing they call wisdom fears what they call foolishness.

Let us now compare the substance of the laws. The Pagans profess in writing that they worship gods and goddesses; and what they say is true, because they worship both males and females. Janus and Saturn, Jupiter and Mercury, Apollo and the others, as well as Minerva, Isis, Fruxilla, Venus, Flora the prostitute, and the rest, are gods and goddesses, as the histories of both the Greeks and the Romans testify.

Christians, however, being poor—as the Pagans call them foolish—worship one God in the mystery from whom all things exist; nor do they venerate anything that he created. They know that he alone is sufficient and abundant for salvation, not being unaware that, if they assign his glory and name to others, they offend him. For no emperor permits tribunes and companions to be worshiped together with his name.

Let the laws now be compared, so that it may be seen where wisdom lies: with the one who worships the Creator, or with the one who worships the creature; with the one who worships the Lord, or with the one who worships servants.

Can it happen in any household that someone other than the one lord is called lord, as the Pagans, instructed in forensic literature and thinking themselves wise, worship many gods and goddesses in one world created by one God? They call the world’s administrators and authors gods, even though they are exposed as lacking foresight [Note: [Col. 2343] The Colbertinus Manuscript reads *actores* (“agents”) rather than *auctores* (“authors”).]. To assert what brings destruction is the mark of one lacking foresight and of a fool. For God must avenge his injury upon those who have bestowed the name and glory of the Lord God upon their fellow servants.

Next, let the commandments be considered. Our law, whose adherents the Pagans call foolish, orders that bishops and ministers be appointed who are suitable, blameless, holy, and irreproachable. The tradition of the Pagans, by contrast, teaches that their bishops and ministers cannot be suitable unless they are transformed from men into women, so that they may licitly and publicly endure the treatment of women, and, with their hair dishonorably loosened in water, emit a soft, broken, and shameful voice. If they did this publicly, they would be stoned by the whole people.

And there is that Cynocephalus who, constantly wandering from place to place [Note: [Col. 2343] The Colbertinus Manuscript reads *natabundus* (“swimming about”) rather than *mutabundus* (“changing about”).], searches for the limbs of the adulterer Osiris, the husband of Isis.

Behold the ministers or teachers by whom the Pagans claim for themselves the name of wisdom, although their conduct involves not merely a lack of wisdom but also crime. For it is deadly to love obscene and disgraceful things.

And what of the fact that in a cave they are mocked with covered eyes [Note: [Col. 2343] That is, “in a cavern.”]? So that they may not recoil from being dishonorably degraded, their eyes are covered. Some beat their wings like birds, imitating the voice of a raven; others growl like lions; still others, with their hands bound with chicken entrails, are thrown over pits full of water, while someone approaches with a sword and bursts open the aforementioned entrails, calling himself their liberator. There are other things even more dishonorable.

Behold in how many ways those who call themselves wise are shamefully mocked. But because they endure these things in darkness, they think that they can remain unknown. All these practices, invented and arranged by evil and dishonorable people in secret, the holy Christian faith has disclosed and exposed.

When the faith was preached, those who heard it considered what goodness and holiness were being publicly promised, and turned to the faith, abandoning those hidden, dishonorable, and shameful practices and confessing how they had been mocked through ignorance.

For previously almost everyone had been caught up in this error, and therefore [Col. 2344] seemed wise to themselves because no one existed to criticize them. Although all were wandering under the single deceptive name of idolatry, each person nevertheless arranged worship according to his own customs and manner of life, so that one error acquired variety from the depravity and conduct of its authors.

In the end, the rites they call those of Liber are dishonorable, utterly vain, and full of madness. For it is difficult for an impure person not to be irascible; indeed, he is found depicted everywhere with Priapus, with whom he lived dishonorably.

The rest of their sacred rites are of the same kind. But the fact that later generations were captured by these inventions was accomplished through Satan’s subtlety and cunning. These things were not invented without his counsel; yet, once each had been invented, he sprinkled them with certain illusions by which he might entice human beings into error.

Thus it happened that falsehood was commended through the transmission of antiquity, and a shameful invention was excused. For through custom what was shameful began not to seem shameful. When some people are dishonored, at first they blush; afterward, as custom flatters them, shame withdraws with an altered expression, especially if they see many others behaving in the same way.

The profit of dishonor arises when those who are called noble appear to be dishonored; for ennobled nobility easily finds imitators. If, then, they formerly seemed wise to themselves for this reason—that no one existed to whom these foul inventions were displeasing—now that, by God’s mercy, the human race has been enlightened and what was believed to be law has been declared a crime, while what was thought to be wisdom has been exposed as foolishness, they ought either to abandon this designation or refuse to persist in a crime that has been exposed, recognizing that the name of wisdom is alien to them.

But, to add to the accumulation of their confession of foolishness, once caught in foolishness they call fools those by whom they are convicted. Yet they accuse our faith and our posterity; nevertheless, in their principles they do not deny that nothing can be found worthy of reproach.

Those who accuse our faith do not undertake their attack against us more than against our author. They call us fools, as though we had given faith to a foolish matter; but they pronounce him a liar, a deceiver, and even malicious, as one who handed down a faith through which we were to be deceived.

Let us therefore first prove that we did not believe foolishly; afterward we shall plead the cause of its author. When we were living in the error in which the Pagans now remain, we were not attracted by any signs of virtue, but accepted their bare words, which they call sacred, thinking that what was useful was not what divinity had commended but what ancient custom had handed down. In that custom—as is not hidden—we were deceived by various vanities and recognized no hope of salvation.

For what benefit could there be in something invented by human beings? But when we approached the faith of God and believed in his Son incarnate and crucified, we were persuaded not by words but by deeds. For we saw the dead raised, lepers cleansed, eyes restored to one born blind, demons cast out, and all illnesses healed at once.

Let it now be judged when we were foolish: when we believed bare words, or when we believed deeds? Without doubt, deeds precede words, since words were invented to signify deeds. If, then, we gave credence to human tradition, with no virtue persuading us, a tradition invented to mock the minds of human beings, how much more should we believe this faith, which all the signs that invoke God testify to be divine and deifying?

Would we not rightly be judged foolish if we did not believe the works of virtue, though we had believed words? Would we not reasonably be marked as lacking foresight and judgment if we did not follow the hope that called us, when we had been subject to despair?

“But,” they reply, “what is believed is foolish. For it does not accord with reason that God should have a Son, nor that dead and dissolved bodies should be restored to life.”

All philosophers and founders of philosophical schools wounded one another in diverse arguments, yet none crossed over to the other, because each remained in the teaching with which he had been imbued. Since words are subject to contradiction, no one overcame another through them. There was no means by which one could demonstrate himself victorious; rather, they wearied one another with mutual contradictions and persuaded one another in no way.

For this reason the providence of God—whose purposes cannot be investigated—[Col. 2345] added power to its preaching, so that the truth of the preaching might be proved by the testimony of power, and that those who were prepared to contradict with words would not dare to contradict when they saw the power.

What greater testimony to truth can there be than the operation of power? But if someone denies the works of virtue while accusing the Scriptures, how can he call our faith foolish while denying the Scriptures? In the very place where it is written that Christ is to be believed as the Son of God, the testimony of power is also found.

If it seems absurd to anyone who reads that Christ, the Son of God, was crucified, let him read further and find that he rose from the dead. Let him understand that he did not die without purpose or unwillingly, since he was able to rise again, but that there was a mystery involved.

Whoever he may be will therefore either remain silent about the cross—for if he calls the cross foolish, he cannot call the resurrection foolish, since the resurrection excuses the cross—or, if he speaks about the cross, he cannot deny that providence was present in it, since he sees that it is confirmed by the testimony of the resurrection. Either both are accepted or both are rejected, so that one who does not defend them may not dare to accuse them.

The reason he permitted himself to be crucified must be reserved for those who are close to him as a mystery. But he so commended this death that he testified that he would be glorified through it. For he says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (John 10:18). He was therefore not compelled to die, since he had power both to die and to rise again.

Anyone who denies this cannot say that death was inflicted upon him by force. For if he denies this, he will not be able to affirm that Christ died, since this statement is contained in the very passage where he is read to have been handed over to death. No one condemns what comes later on the basis of what came earlier, or what came earlier on the basis of what comes later, because what belongs to one body is not contradictory.

They deceitfully say that it is foolish to believe that the dead will rise. Yet they see examples by which it may be judged credible. All seeds necessary for human use cannot be reborn unless they have first been dissolved. If God ordained this in the world for the sake of human beings, why is it considered foolish to believe that he will grant the same thing to their own bodies?

Unless it is because they themselves are foolish, refusing to grant to God the power that the world can possess, although even now the shadow of past deeds appears, since the time for performing such works is no longer present. For they had to be performed at the beginning, so that the seed of faith might grow through them.

Even now, however, demons are terrified when the cross of Christ is named; and if it is invoked more forcefully, they are driven away. The gods of the Pagans, overcome by fear and dread at the mention of the cross, cannot deliver oracles.

If Christ’s death is an insult, why does it cause terror? Something that arises from a crime ought not to be feared but despised. For who would fear a person killed for his crime? But if he were innocent, he could nevertheless not be feared, but only mourned.

Therefore, unless the demons—or the gods of the Pagans—perceived that the cross of Christ contained a mystery, they would not be terrified when it was named. To speak more plainly: unless they were guilty, they would not be afraid.

For all those who belong to the devil’s side consented to Christ’s death. Hence all demons, or gods of the nations, are shaken with terror when the cross of Christ is named. Whenever anyone is guilty of the death of an innocent person, fear seizes his heart when that person’s name is mentioned. For, as the crime is recalled, he sees himself to be guilty.

How much more, then, are the demons or gods of the nations guilty, since they are guilty of the death of the Lord and Savior of the world?

But the Pagans insist that they possess the truth on account of antiquity, because, they say, what is earlier cannot be false. As though antiquity or ancient custom could prejudice the truth!

Murderers, effeminate men, adulterers, and other criminals could use this argument to defend their unlawful practices, because they are ancient and began from the very origin of the world. Yet from this they ought rather to understand their error: what is reprehensible and shameful is shown to have begun badly; what is honorable and holy is rightly worshiped. A shameful and reprehensible thing cannot previously have been honorable and irreproachable.

Finally, it cannot be denied that the tradition of the Pagans was invented by human beings. But the fact that our Law was given by God is evident [Col. 2346]. For the majesty of God appeared on a mountain in order to give the Law to human beings.

And so that faith might be placed in this event, he first provided many signs and wonders performed in Egypt—something that the books preserved by Ptolemy in the Alexandrian library also testify to this day. Thus he deigned to give the Law in such a way that no one would doubt that it was God who had handed it down.

The majesty of God was openly and visibly seen by all, with such radiance and terror that no other God was believed to exist besides him, and whatever he commanded was considered worthy of complete observance.

And so that everything might correspond to divine reason, let the Law that was handed down be examined: whether anything unjust, dishonorable, or ridiculous is found in it.

This was the manner in which God ought to make himself known—not appearing by deceit in a corner, since he cannot be confined; nor in a mirror, where what is seen is something other than it appears, through the operation of alluring deception; nor handing down for observance things that, because they were dishonorable, were done in darkness [Note: [Col. 2346] Thus reads the Colbertinus Manuscript. The printed editions read *celaret* (“he would conceal”).]

Since knowledge of the one God had been blotted out in the world by the custom of sinning, because falsehood had provided a veil for truth, the merciful and compassionate God, unwilling to allow his work to be given over to destruction, deigned to visit the human race.

He did not appear in the manner of those who falsely wished to be called gods. Rather, just as God is Truth, so he revealed himself, in order to remove the error that had corrupted the world’s understanding through the preaching of false gods.

Indeed, more than six hundred thousand men came out of Egypt. Seeing and recognizing from the appearance of his ineffable glory that this Lord was above all others, they were afraid to approach him; instead, they bowed their knees from afar and worshiped him (Exodus 20:18).

Afterward, through the further signs that followed—[Note: [Col. 2346] The printed editions insert here: “both those which he performed in the desert.” This is redundant and absent from the Colbertinus Manuscript.]—he was manifested in all his wonders as the one God. These things became known in almost every language; these things became a terror to neighboring nations.

What comparable thing is found among the gods of the nations? To what nation or people did they display their glory? What signs or powers did they perform as testimony to their divinity? Where or when are they shown to have spoken?

But the irrational crowd began to worship as gods either visible shadows, demons, or images of the dead. Having been turned into an ancient custom, this practice thinks that the truth of reason can be defended for itself, although the rationale of truth does not come from custom, which derives from antiquity, but from God, who is proved to be God not by antiquity but by eternity.

Therefore faith is not a thing that began at some point but is without beginning. For to believe in God is something that begins with us; what is believed, however, is eternal.

How, then, do the Pagans consider themselves earlier, when what they worship is subsequent to God? Is not a work subsequent to its maker? The Pagans worship works; we worship the maker. They worship the creature; we worship the Creator.

Certainly God made the world. Did he not, by making it, reveal knowledge of himself? Or did he make human beings and not wish to be worshiped by those whom he made? That is absurd.

Once created, therefore, the human being began to venerate his Creator, because this is worthy and the reason of the matter demanded it. When this had grown obscure through human laziness, God restored it in Abraham, so that the knowledge of God that had existed in Adam might begin again in Abraham. Those born from him were to be raised under his knowledge, so that, through its transmission, there might not fail or be lacking someone who worshiped God; people from foreign nations were also summoned to this knowledge of God.

Whoever has come to know begins at the beginning; but the one who is known is beyond the beginning. By what reasoning, then, do the Pagans say that their law existed before ours? If the world existed before God—which God forbid—then Paganism could likewise be placed before Christianity.

Let no one be surprised at the name “Christianity.” For it means worshiping one God in the mystery of the Trinity. Even if the name “Christ” is thought to derive from *chrism*—anointing—the rationale of the name existed before the anointing.

Among our ancestors, those who were anointed as kings were called *christs*, possessing an image of Christ who was to come. He who was born from God the Father was rightly called Christ as king [Col. 2347], because what anointing gave to those kings, birth gave to him.

As long as the Pagans are ignorant of him, they reject him; but when they have come to know him, they worship him more devotedly, rejoicing that they have passed from evil to good.

Those who were so obstinate and vehement in a matter so frivolous and foolish—when will they be stronger and more vehement once they have learned the truth?

What sort of Christ, then, is our Christ, who, when unknown, is hated, but, when known, is loved? Every wicked person, when unknown, is loved; when known, he is hated.

How many formerly hated Christ who now love him, and who grieve that they hated what they did not know? For it belongs to the thoughtless to hate someone whom they do not know, since one must first determine whether a thing is worthy of hatred.

Indeed, those who oppose him today will defend him tomorrow, doing penance and regretting that they learned late what is true. If the matter were worthy of hatred, or contained any deception, Pagans would be made from Christians every day.

But because this is the truth, every day and every hour, without interruption, people abandon Jupiter; among them are sophists and nobles of the world who had confessed him to be God, and they flee to Christ, to whom belong honor and glory forever and ever.

## On Fate
### CXV [Note: [Col. 2347] Absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

Nothing is so contrary to a Christian as to concern himself with the art of astrology. For this is recognized as hostile to the law of God. If those who are evil are born, and, conversely, those who are good, then the law is said to have been given in vain; and not only this, but the Lawgiver will be considered unjust. For whoever, having given a law, compels people to do what is contrary to the condition in which they were born, knowing that their nature cannot be changed, appears to have given the law for this purpose: that he might have an opportunity to satisfy his cruelty by the death of a human being. Why, then, does he forbid what he knows cannot be avoided? Or how does he condemn a person who did not do what he could not do?

But if this seems unjust—as indeed it is, since it is impious to think such a thing about God—then he rightly and beneficially gave the law, knowing that a person can restrain himself from what the law forbids. Therefore, because he gave the law justly, he is certainly not unjust when he exacts punishment. Thus, if faith must be accorded to the law of God, because it is proved to have been given justly, the art of astrology must be avoided and shunned. For the devil’s cunning and subtlety invented it. Since he does not dare openly to oppose its author, he accomplishes this by evasive devices, so that he both insults God and makes a person hostile to the law, condemning him to the second death.

Whoever, therefore, yields to God’s authority and considers it impious to call his work into question obeys the law given by him, devoting himself to its teachings day and night, and turning his attention to nothing opposed to it, not doubting that a human being is able to keep his commands. For those who desire to sin seek an opportunity by which to make their sins foreign to themselves; so that, while sins seem as though they ought to be attributed to nature, the sinner may appear exempt from punishment.

This is the purpose of those who, despairing of the promised future life, desire to enjoy the present pleasure. But those who, relying on the confidence of faith, await the hope of future things, strive to fulfill what they promised at the beginning of their rebirth: to renounce the spectacles and pleasures of Satan.

With what great subtlety, then, did Satan act, in order to make a person readier to sin, thereby satisfying the wickedness of his envy? For when a person hears that he was born in such a way that he must sin, and does not fail to recognize that God is most just, he believes that he may sin with impunity, because a just judge does not condemn one who sinned under the command of nature. Indeed, his act ought not even to be called his sin, since another acted through him.

Thus the human being was deceived; for, weighed down by sins, he became liable to death. Therefore, whoever removes evil from humanity removes all human good as well. If the sinner has no punishment, neither does the just person have a crown. Why, then, are the good praised and the evil reproved? If it belongs to this nature that a person cannot sin, why do you praise in him what is not his? And why do you condemn the offense in the sinner, when you know that what he does in sinning is not his? What else can one be who praises the good and accuses the evil, but unjust?

But perhaps the contrary will be said: “I praise the good nature in a person and condemn the bad; for good wine is praised because it is good by nature, and bad wine is rejected because nature has likewise produced it.” If this were so, there would be no reason for reproach: the just person would be praised in such a way that he would not be judged worthy of a crown, nor would the unjust person be accused in such a way that he would be declared worthy of punishment.

Yet we know and read that the just are rewarded both in the present and in the future, and that the unjust are subjected to punishment and burned. This would certainly seem unjust if the one who had done what belonged to his nature suffered punishment in the avenging fire, or if another who likewise carried out what belonged to his nature received rewards.

But if the good person is to be praised because he did what belonged to his nature, the evil person too ought to be praised, because he likewise did what belonged to his nature, so that each person, remaining in the condition in which he was made, might be praised. For if a person is considered blameworthy because he remains in the condition in which he was made, the blame touches the author, who caused such a person to be born that he would be displeasing.

But if the just person is rightly to be rewarded and the unjust person condemned, then the response is no longer being made to nature but to the will; for nature is free, while the will is the determining factor. The will admits approaches and withdrawals through the senses, so that the unjust person, seeing the just crowned while he himself is condemned, may blame himself because, trusting the senses against the law, he did evil when he could have done good.

Can the sun be accused because it burns, or water because it cools? Or should water be rewarded because it refreshes people afflicted by thirst, or should the sun receive a prize because it restores people with its warmth after the cold? They do what belongs to their nature; therefore they are neither condemned nor praised, for they do not know how to do anything else.

But since the matter is not as the observers of the stars suppose, the reason underlying human actions proves it. For no one can be found who always does good or always does evil. A person would then seem to have been born in such a way as to do good if he remained irreproachable; and he would rightly be considered evil if he persisted in always doing evil. But when you see even the one whom you think was born good sometimes doing evil, and observe the one whom you say was born evil sometimes doing good, how do you prove this to be true—that the evil person is evil and the good person good? It is rather most certain that when a person has devoted his mind to something, he makes progress in it.

There are also causes that generate sins: someone may quarrel because of envy, or become hostile. Yet those things forbidden by the law they do not commit openly and publicly, but secretly. Why, unless because they respect the law? If, however, they had been born—as they assert—for the purpose of doing evil, they would not seek hiding places or show any respect for the law; rather, they would openly do whatever nature compelled them to do.
