But when you see sins being contrived and devised so that they can be committed secretly—when people choose places, persons, and times in order to carry out the intention of their evil purpose—in the same way the good also, by a kind of judgment, distinguish their good works, distributing their goodness according to the time and the circumstances. This must no longer be attributed to nature, but to the will that exists within nature.

If it were natural, judgment would cease. For if we examine the matter more fully, we will show that those who are now just were previously unjust: they were changed through deliberate action. Abraham himself, for example, is read to have been justified by faith (James II, 23, and Romans IV, 3). Therefore he was not previously just, especially since he is understood to have worshiped idols under the guidance of his father. And likewise Zacchaeus, to whom the Lord bears witness after his former public life (Luke XIX, 9). And the chosen vessel—Paul—also confesses this, saying, “We too were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest” (Ephesians II, 3), because the will takes the place of nature. For a person is judged according to the will, not according to nature.

Without doubt all the martyrs and the just became good; for they were not born faithful but reborn. And how many do we know who had disgraceful lives and were wasteful devotees of luxury, but are now self-controlled and holy? When the fear of God is added, the vices that previously dominated them are conquered.

Let us consider from this how powerful fear of the law is. Before Julian’s edict, women were unable to divorce their husbands. Once they received the power to do so, they began doing what they had previously been unable to do; every day they began freely divorcing their husbands. Where had fate been hidden for so many years? I suppose it concealed itself through fear of the law.

But how did the matter introduced by Moses enter? I suppose the fates were asleep. For so many things were handed down to them to observe, and such things as no nation possesses as commandments. And lest anyone think that this should be attributed to a region of the sky, they keep the commands of their law while dispersed throughout almost the entire world.

These commandments are contrary to fate. For they certainly did not exist for three thousand years and more from the creation of the world; afterward they were given, and they remain until the end. How, then, did what had not existed for so many thousands of years begin? The courses of the stars have existed from the creation of the world.

And what of the fact that, although there is such a multitude of Jews throughout the world, none of them is changed into a Gentile, while we see that some Gentiles, though rarely, become Jews? See how, in matters pertaining to the Jewish rite, fate is excluded: they began to exist outside fate, and they remain in that condition.

What shall we say about Sodom and Gomorrah, whose end lies before our eyes as a punishment (Genesis XIX, 24)? It happened that all those stained with the disgrace of every impurity were consumed by divine fire. In the cataclysm, all were subject to one fate, so that all might perish by one death and at the same time, except for the household of Noah (ibid., VII).

And will the entire army of Pharaoh be said to have been born under one decree [Note: [Col. 2349] So the Colbertinus manuscript. But the printed editions read: “is said to have been condemned.”], so that the foolish error of astrology might be refuted, because they were drowned in the Red Sea with their king (Exodus XIV, 24)? There are many other examples that we omit, since two examples are sufficient for our purpose—how much more so the many mysteries?

For all nations also have different institutions: what is permitted in one place is not permitted here; and again, what is permitted here is not permitted elsewhere. Here, in the city of Rome [Note: [Col. 2349] “Rome” is written here, although elsewhere the question is written as “at Rome.”] and its territories, which are called most sacred, women are permitted to divorce their husbands, although it is prescribed in the divine law that not even husbands should have this power, except on account of fornication (Matthew V, 32).

See how in this matter the barbarians are better. Nor is it impossible that this rule could be observed here, since it is shown to have been observed previously. Fate has therefore been changed, because what had formerly been forbidden has become permitted.

It is not permitted to make eunuchs in the Roman Empire, but it is permitted among other peoples. That they could also be made here is evident; for the deed is proved to occur secretly. If fear ceased, it would be done publicly. Fear, therefore, restrains fate; for fate is conquered if a person does not do what it wishes him to do.

The Persians also wear earrings in the manner of women, which here is considered dishonorable and unlawful. That it could also be done here is attested by the priests of the Mother who is called Great. And indeed she was great—but a prostitute. The difference is that these men are catamites, while those are men.

And what shall we say? Are these people alone in the whole world born under this fate, so that, after being castrated, they are transformed into women, and so that these few individuals are found throughout the entire world? It is clear that they are overcome by threats and compelled by promises of rewards to endure this pain and disgrace. But if they had been born for this purpose, they would not need to be compelled.

The Persians consider it lawful to have intercourse with their daughters. That this could also occur here is shown by the fact that some are proved to have done it. But because punishment intervened, they were seized by fear, so that they would not do what can be done but is not permitted.

Everything that is forbidden is forbidden for this reason: so that, because it can be done, it may not be done. But if it belonged to fate, it could not be done, nor would it be forbidden. For if something did not belong to fate and were nevertheless forbidden, this would indicate that what is not fated can be done. What wisdom is there in forbidding what cannot be done—as if someone should forbid anyone to fly from the city of Rome to Spain, or to carry a mountain on his shoulders?

Those things that can be done but ought not to be done are what are forbidden. Among the Moors it is customary for women to wear earrings even in their noses. Is this a matter of fate? If it were fate, those who were brought here would remain in the same condition; for if fate exists, each person carries his own fate with him. But since it is not fate, everyone who comes from there changes here, seeing that what is considered attractive there is regarded as shameful here.

Certainly, among all peoples, a number is a number; earth is earth; water is water; air is air; and fire is fire. Can earth be found anywhere that is not dry, or air that can be touched, or water that is not flowing and cold, or fire that is cold? In the same way, Jupiter is Jupiter everywhere; Saturn is Saturn; Venus is Venus. The remaining signs are likewise.

For this art is practiced everywhere according to one method. But because customs remain different among all peoples, this is not due to the reasoning of fates—which is the same everywhere, as they claim—but to human invention. Whatever seemed worthy of reason and suited to propriety to the person regarded as foremost among his people, he established for those over whom he presided. Hence each region or nation has its own practices that it preserves.

Thus Solon and Lycurgus established many things that were observed by the Greeks as laws; these gradually fell into oblivion as their kingdoms declined. The kings of the Jews preferred mules for riding; the Romans, not mules but horses; the kings of the Garamantes, who live above Tripoli in Africa, preferred bulls for riding. The kings of the Persians are carried in vehicles; for the ancient Persian kings were not even seen by the people. The kings of the Midianites delight in riding camels, so much so that their necks are adorned with golden collars. Throughout Africa, people prefer riding asses to horses.

Although everything exists everywhere, not everything is pleasing to everyone, because each person chooses what has greater favor with him. Our own preferences also differ—in clothing, food, other forms of use, and opinion itself.

Lest those who assert different fates for different people say that this too is due to fate, the matter itself proves otherwise, because our preferences frequently change. What we loved for a long time later displeases us; we begin to love what we previously did not willingly have, and after forming a habit we remain changed.

But if they say that the order of the fates is such that things are accomplished at particular times, recurring after intervals in their former pattern—for example, that what people do today they will do again after a certain period—then they are not said to remain fixed in one condition. For they are conquered by training and habit.

For a long time the use of wine was unknown to Roman women. Training, having become habit, strengthened their judgment, so that they retained what they had learned to be beneficial. Were these fates present in those times and later died, so that a practice well discovered might cease? It was not fate that discovered this, but training. But when the habit was abandoned, the discipline perished.

The ancient Romans were also so self-controlled that they rejected even gifts offered to them, considering a good reputation to be riches and preferring virtue to pleasures. Did these fates succeed to them, or did they die? It was not a matter of fate but of discipline, which is also the tutor of fate itself.

How can something belong to fate that neither existed before its time nor exists now? Indeed, I do not know why they attribute such great envy to fate, saying that it is the author of everything that happens, although it both is and is not. For where there is discipline, it is not; where there is habit, it is not; where there is chance, it is not. But where it seems to exist, it is conquered by fear of the law: desire is restrained by fear, and the pursuit of money is rejected for the sake of pleasing God.

In this respect it cannot be denied that what is conquered exists; yet it can rightly be said that, even in the very matter where it seems to exist, fate is absent, because what is conquered lacks authority. Therefore, for the person who follows God’s law and maintains the practice of a good life, all the things called fates yield.

Habit has such power that it even tames wild animals. Those who desire to live badly establish fates for themselves. For through luxury and pleasure arise intemperance and restlessness, which produce lack of self-control and anger.

Although they know that this deserves punishment, they attribute their shame to fate in order to exempt themselves from punishment. When they think about this matter, demons provide assistance; for they also arrange that those who think evil should obtain its fulfillment. These people call such things fates, not understanding that the demons are enemies of humanity.

For if sins did not enter the soul through the senses but were born from within, everything that is done wrong would rightly seem to belong to fate. But when they see that sinful desire arises through sight, hearing, and the remaining senses—with the assistance of enemies who suggest that what is contrary should be done, and with the act not being considered wrong while it is being done—for it seems sweet while it is being done or before it is done, but appears bitter once completed, why do they attribute it to fates?

That it can be conquered we understand from this: when we are thinking and troubled about some matter, the enemies are silent and desire comes to rest, for they cannot make suggestions while we are occupied. Does anyone suggest something else to a person devoted to some task? He does not, knowing either that he will not be heard or that he himself will be driven away as one making an untimely suggestion.

The same is true of the enemies whom we know to be demons. They are the gods of the pagans. When they see us occupied with divine matters, they do not intrude to suggest what is contrary, but lie in wait, seeking an opportunity to intrude.

Therefore, constant meditation on the law of God and its practice are defenses for the soul. For if they see us idle with respect to divine matters, they are aroused to trouble us. They are the ones who sow desires through flesh and blood.

Although the flesh has its own movement arising from its origin, because carnal birth is not inactive [Note: [Col. 2351] So the Colbertinus manuscript. The printed editions read “slain.”], nevertheless in this matter the assistance of demons contributes to the destruction of human beings. For demons are diverse and have unequal wills. Some, when they disturb minds, overthrow bodies; others, mingling with the blood, generate desires in the mind; others, joining themselves to the human heart, make contrary suggestions with enticing words; and some bind bodies alone with illnesses, like the daughter of Abraham whom the Lord healed (Luke XIII, 11–16).

The pagans, ignorant of all these things, call them fate, although the causes are different and these things are brought about by enemies, so that a person may be irritated by whatever cause and subjected to passions.

They call it good fate when bodies are well balanced or when people are commended for their affability, possessing a certain grace. But they say that fate is bad if people have too much heat or moisture, or if someone is not sprinkled with grace but is rather disposed toward misfortune; such people they call unfortunate.

Let us grant that these things are true. For we see them also in animals, so that some possess more heat. But animals are not rational like human beings, so that with care they might regulate their bodies. The mind is therefore the ruler of the body, so that it may govern it with the restraints of divine law.

For the divine law shows that what is suggested either by the impulse of the flesh or by an enemy is not beneficial. God gave the law for this reason: so that, when the enemy dictates evil while appearing to us as good, we may recognize him as a deceiver, because he advises something different from what the law teaches.

Thus the body is restrained: because it is hot, less is given to it, and it is held back from indulgence. For just as the heat of a feverish body increases if it receives food or drink, so bodies of this kind, burning with the heat of the blood, will blaze more fiercely unless they are governed. A fire is smothered when fuel is lacking.

It belongs to the mind to lead the body. But if it lets the body go wherever it wishes, it will hurl it headlong, like a mad horse throwing a careless rider. And because the heat of the body grows more fiercely when enemies act to deceive the soul—for it is not the body that desires, but its heat that generates desires in the soul—we must implore the assistance of our God for protection, so that he may restrain them [Note: [Col. 2351] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “ducio.”]. “For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against rulers and authorities” (Ephesians VI, 12). When these have been removed, it will be easy to suppress the movement of flesh and blood.

[Col. 2352] For a fire is extinguished if the material by which it burns is absent.

The things spoken of by astrologers happen to those who believe that what they say will occur. For the subtlety of demons brings this about: they cause the things foretold by their priests to happen, lest they be exposed as false. But with regard to those who do not place confidence in their responses, their effects do not prevail; for they are neither so intent on satisfying those who do not believe them, nor does God permit them to do what would deceive those who trust in God and do not believe the devil.

God arranged everything so that it might happen according to each person’s faith, while the freedom of the will remains. Consequently, nothing can prevail against the person who believes in God and flees to his aid. For that person is certain that what God has made is in his power, and that the demons do not dare act against one whom they see to have the common God favorable to him.

Certainly God made the world and created the sun and the stars, assigning them courses by which the human race is governed. Does he not have power to command them at some time to do something other than what has been decreed for them? He created them in such a way that they are subject to his will: they fulfill their appointed courses only when no other command has been given.

Thus, if he is asked by those whom the stars serve—when either untimely rains occur or the crops appear barren because of excessive drought—he can command the weather to be moderated. Or if people happen to live under God’s anger, as often occurs, while wandering through luxury and vanity and failing to do what pleases God, he can suspend the rains for a long time and stir up famine over the earth, as we read happened under Elijah and Elisha, and, once appeased by their satisfaction, grant that the rains irrigate the dry land (III Kings XVIII, 43).

The order of the world is analogous to secular government. Just as some people, oppressed by provincial governors, flee to the aid of the emperors in order to be restored, so human beings, when they see adverse times confronting them, should present themselves as suppliants to God, in whose power all things are.

But astrologers do not think this possible. They say that nothing can happen except what the stars fulfill according to the causes decreed for them. They can neither be recalled nor impelled toward anything else, but preserve the functions once assigned to them. This is the assertion of the astrologers: that the fates cannot be changed and that nothing can be obtained by prayers. They say that God once established the order of the whole world and handed it over to the stars as servants, so that nothing can happen either earlier or later than ordained.

This is the astrologers’ error, by which they also assault God. For by this assertion they deny that anything can happen outside the order of the world. Thus, if anything reported to have been done by God in the world differs from the law of the world, they deny that it should be believed. They affirm only what is said to have occurred according to the arrangements of the world, so that they deny that a virgin gave birth, that Aaron’s rod blossomed and produced fruit (Numbers XVII, 8), or that the aged Sarah gave birth (Genesis XXI, 2).

The order of the world does not contain these things, because they are read to have been done by God outside the order of the world. And what is surprising if the author of the world did what the world itself cannot do?

“But he would seem to have transgressed,” they say, “the order he established, if he is said to have acted differently from what he decreed for the world.” Very well: he established for the world a law of doing or generating—did he establish it for himself? Would it be humility on his part to act in the same way as the world that he created? And how would it be understood that something had been done by him, rather than by the world, if he had done it according to the law of the world? In order that it might be understood to have been done by God and not by the world, it was done according to another order.

Certainly he decreed for the sun that it should unceasingly complete its appointed distances and should have no permission to stand. Does the one who established this law for the sun not have permission to command the sun himself? Certainly judges are forbidden to revoke a sentence given against an accused person. Is the emperor himself likewise subject to this law? For he alone is permitted to revoke a sentence, release a condemned person from death, and pardon him. How much more must God be permitted to do what should not have been granted to the world, since the world is the servant of its Creator?

Finally, through the law handed down to it, the world can kill but cannot give life; through excess it can make someone blind but cannot restore his eyes; it can make someone weak and ill but cannot cure him. God reserved this for himself, so that it might be evident that he is Lord of all.

For the overthrow of fate is demonstrated by the fact that the dead rose, that the eyes of one born blind were restored, that the sick and paralytics were strengthened, and by the other things that were done, so that nothing that may belong to fate can become an obstacle to those who flee to God.

The Apostle John says: “The one who is in us is greater than the one who is in this world” (I John IV, 4). When God is entreated, he even removes what he has decreed. For he certainly decreed that vengeance should be taken upon sinners, and yet he forgives those who entreat him, because he alone has the power to bind and loose.

Therefore, although the sun alone was not granted permission to stand still, under Joshua son of Nun it was commanded to stand, and it obeyed his order (Joshua X, 12–13), contrary to what had been prescribed for it in the order of the world.

Under Hezekiah, something even greater is read to have occurred. So that Hezekiah would not doubt the truth of what had been promised to him, he received a sign that was new and unheard of by human ears. For the sun was not commanded, as before, to stand still, but to turn back (IV Kings XX, 11). When Hezekiah saw this, he could be certain that the one who had made the ninth hour become the sixth could add fifteen years to his life.

Because what was granted to Hezekiah is contrary to the astrologers—for they deny that anything can be added to life—he receives once again a sign in this matter that contradicts the astrologers. They assert that the stars can do nothing other than what has been established for them.

Certainly they say that it belongs to fate whether one has a slave or does not have one. Let it be so. Where were these fates from the beginning of the world? Until the Flood, and through the long succession of years afterward, this condition of servitude did not exist.

Or did these fates begin in the time of King Ninus, who is said to have been the first to begin making war upon neighboring peoples and reducing captives to servitude? You see, then, that this was invented later and does not belong to fate but to the activity of demons. For if it belonged to fate, it would have existed from the beginning of the world. The stars themselves were made in the beginning, and their courses remain even now.

Previously human life was rustic, and people did not pursue riches. How, then, do astrologers now say that the rich and the poor are made so through the stars? Have the stars changed? It is rather Satan’s trickery and deception, by which he says that through the stars those things are done that he accomplishes through his angels, his servants.

As the time approaches when his destruction draws near, he devises greater means by which people may sin. We know that Italy, Africa, Sicily, and Sardinia have suffered from famine. Let the astrologers say whether all these regions had one fate, when they say that not even the fates of two people out of a hundred can coincide. Let them be ashamed and keep silent, and stretch out suppliant hands to God, in whose power all things are.

But perhaps this was secretly taken away from the fates? What shall we say of Pannonia, which was so utterly destroyed that it can have no remedy? O their weakness! For they profess themselves Christians with wavering faith. While they doubt the promises, they do not consider the things that have happened.

If they considered the deeds performed by the Prophets and Apostles, they would never admit the astrologers’ fables. They would know that everything is in God’s power and would not be terrified when evil happens to the good, because they will be rewarded in the future judgment, remembering the Apostle’s words: “We must enter the kingdom of God through tribulations” (Acts XIV, 21).

The person who is content and awaits the judgment of his God will also be vindicated by receiving his reward. But if he desires to be vindicated in the present, or to enjoy present resources with every eagerness, he doubts the promised life; and consequently, in the future he will be counted among the faithless and judged worthy of punishment.

God made the world for exercise and adorned it with every resource, setting forth two conditions: the present and the future, the heavenly and the earthly, so that it might serve as a test for humanity. Whoever, despising the future life, chooses the present will be assigned to the flesh; whoever prefers the future to the present will be judged worthy of spiritual things. And whoever, unjustly oppressed by the power of the unjust, presents or entrusts his complaints to God will be relieved in the future judgment and honored with spiritual glory [Note: [Col. 2353] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “reserved.”].

Therefore, none of the saints appeared glorious in this world, nor did they love present delights. Hence the Apostle says: “Having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Timothy VI, 8).

But a person who is a Christian even grieves if he appears fortunate in this world, since the dignity and happiness of Christians were not promised on earth but in heaven. How can someone call himself a Christian who wishes to glory not where it has been promised, but here, where it has been forbidden?

For if it were advantageous to enjoy the present, heavenly things would certainly not be promised to those who despise these things. With what hope, then, do Christians lend their ears to astrologers, when they hear the Apostle John crying out and saying, “Do not love this world, nor the things that are in this world” (I John II, 15)?

Therefore, if these are the commands of our faith or law—that the world should not be loved, nor the things that are in the world—why do some of us complain, saddened by the happiness of others that exists in the world, although perhaps that happiness is unhappiness in God’s sight? They ought rather to rejoice, because the world does not provide those people with the means by which they might be held bound and made subject to human affairs.

For this happiness, having received the capacity for security, lacks concern for divine things. A person filled with all necessities must necessarily be careless concerning the divine oracles, since he has no reason to be anxious. Such people instead begin to labor under another kind of anxiety: to increase their standing in the world, which cannot be done without sin.

But if the matter is examined more closely, the world will be seen to be more the enemy of those whom it is said to make happy. Scarcely any of them thinks about heavenly things.

Christians should therefore rejoice when they are rightly conducting themselves yet are oppressed in this world. For the person who is content with whatever happens to him in this world and gives thanks to God conquers the world. If temporal things appear to be denied him here, he hopes that eternal things will be given in return.

Why did God establish a future judgment, unless so that those who are unjustly oppressed for a time might be granted eternal life, while those who, through power, despise others—or who do not believe in God’s future judgment and therefore think that crimes are unpunished—might be brought low?

But the advocates of fate deny that there will be a future judgment. If those who are good are born, and conversely those who are evil, what do you praise or accuse, when neither the good person has labored to conquer, nor the evil person has been negligent so as to be defeated?

Why do they retail fables among private persons? When sinners are brought before judges, they have never dared to excuse their crimes by appealing to fate. Rather, confessing themselves guilty, they do not deny that they rightly receive the sentence.

Thus the authority of the law tramples upon the reasoning of fate, so that fate cannot even be named when the law has begun to act. How do those who wickedly conduct themselves believe that they will escape forever, when for a time they evade the severity of the divine law by a kind of deliberate effort, without considering that the author of the law cannot conceal this from himself?

Here the law is an image; there it is the truth. Whoever mocks the image cannot mock the truth. Is there any place without God, or can anyone escape his hand?

Yet they flatter themselves, thinking that whoever escapes here is already secure. How do they consider it just that, while others are punished in such cases, they themselves should escape?

Certainly God established the world and showed what law it should use. Being attentive to his work, he showed it the way by which one proceeds to life, appointing the guides it should use, because there is also a way that leads to death.

Should he not therefore inquire whether those whom he appointed as ministers of his kingdom governed his people according to the law he established? Whether the people accepted his edict? Whether the administrators were found faithful and worthy of praise, or unfaithful and subject to punishment?

The people likewise are praised when they keep the law and condemned when they despise it. Justice demands this; the case itself requires it. Why, then, does it displease some people to believe in a future judgment?

The madness of the astrologers invented this objection. For how can they accept a future judgment when they oppose the present one, since they insist that judgment exists at birth? And because reward is attributed to birth, those very people are foolish who assert that good and evil people are not made but born, yet with a kind of natural judgment punish sinners and do not allow sins to remain unpunished [Col. 2355] [Note: [Col. 2355] The Colbertinus manuscript reads this passage as follows: “And because truth is reckoned [as] a reward, it rises again, those who, with a certain natural judgment, assert that good and evil people are not made but born, repay sinners and do not allow sins to remain unpunished.” Morel accepts this reading and judges that it should be corrected as follows: instead of “And because truth is reckoned as a reward, it rises again,” one should read, “And because truth, when it is thought to be oppressed, rises again.” No one should dare deny that this correction is extremely well suited to the sense, if not to the genuine wording, at least to the natural meaning. M.].

For inwardly they correct evil people with rods and bonds, whom outwardly they assert were born incapable of amendment. Does any prudent person correct those whom he knows cannot be changed? That would be either foolish or unjust.

But lest they say that this too occurs by fate, the person who is under fate does not do what he wishes. Thus they themselves would naturally have it that they punish those whom they know will remain naturally unchangeable. Truly, it must be said that whatever is attributed to fate should be assigned to folly.

For how foolish it is to say that someone was born evil, while not proving good the person whom they assert was born good! How can someone be judged good who is discovered to have done an unjust deed? What is more unjust than to believe someone unjust who is denied the ability to do anything other than what he did?

And if everything is under fate, how did the law enter, forbidding what belongs to fate to be done? If the law were removed, unlawful acts would be committed publicly and indiscriminately; the powerful could not be endured, and there would be no freedom, because even the person who now has no thought of evil would begin to be evil once fear had been removed.

Finally, we read that the law was given because of evil people. But perhaps this too was a matter of fate—that the law should be given? By what reasoning, then, can the fates persist if they generate something by which they themselves are destroyed?

The law contradicts the claim that whatever is fated ought to be done. Therefore they lack reason, if they are contrary to themselves …
they generate. And they are unjust, because they cause human beings to be born for damnation; and if they are unjust, they ought not to possess authority, since everything unjust is liable to punishment. Or perhaps they will say that the law is of no benefit, because one who is born in such a way as to be evil cannot be changed by the law. If this is so, the law was given in vain; and how did the fates bring into being something vain? For nothing exists without fate [Note: [Col. 2355] Thus the Colbertinus manuscript. The printed editions, however, read: “would have been of no benefit to fate.”].

Thus the fates act both on their own behalf and against themselves. But if this is so, what is inconsistent through irrationality cannot stand, since it possesses no stability. Or perhaps the fates wanted the law to exist for this reason: that those whom the fates cause to be born evil might be condemned by the law, so that it would accord with the fates for punishment to be imposed by the law? What answer can be given to this except that both laws and fates deserve to be condemned by their own judgment, if they alike contrive that those who did evil not willingly but under the compulsion of the fates should be put to death?

The law contradicts this, because by its own declaration the fates are to be condemned. For the law does not deny that those who are evil are evil because of fate; rather, it denies that their evil is attributable to fate and assigns it to their will. Therefore it rightly establishes that they are to be punished [Note: [Col. 2355] The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “it rightly establishes them as guilty.”]. Nothing, then, is held in common by the law and the fates, since the law denies what the fates assert.

For what reason, then, are those said to have been born who prohibited astrologers from the city of Rome? It is well known that this prohibition was long maintained, and certainly those who imposed it were pagans. How can things that are contrary to fate be produced by fate? But if fate exists, it does not act against itself. Those who act against fate do not possess fate; and if these people do not possess fate, fate does not exist.

“But,” they say, “there is a fate assigned to each person that determines by what death he will die.” If this is so, a murderer ought not to be accused. For he will defend himself in a twofold manner: both he himself acted under the agency of the fates, and the other person was killed under the agency of the fates. Meanwhile the law is assaulted, because it punishes the murderer who has been brought before it.

In the same way, a man is born to be an adulterer, and a woman to be an adulteress, and a third person to suffer adultery. If this too is so, the law is again compromised, since it punishes adulterers. And if this truly belonged to fate, the one whose fate it was to suffer adultery ought also to be punished. For he too is found to be a participant, since his fate allowed the adultery to take place. [Col. 2356] It would therefore have been equitable either for all to be condemned together or for all to be acquitted together. In this situation the law appears unjust.

Therefore, if the fates are from God, the law is not from God, because it is unfitting not only for God but even for a prudent person to condemn what he himself has made. But since no one has ever dared to speak against the law, or to deny that it is from God, the fates cannot be said to be from God, because God punishes these things through the law. For whenever what is done under the compulsion of the fates is condemned, the fates themselves are unquestionably condemned.

“But,” they say, “evil souls are born for the purpose of doing evil.” Granted. But evil souls ought not to be born by fate, so that the innocent might be killed by them. If those souls were evil, they ought not to have been born but to have been punished, lest they kill the innocent. Yet it is not the souls whom they imagine to be evil who kill the innocent; it is the fates, which cause human beings to be born in such a way that they are killed. Consequently, it is not the souls but the fates that are unjust; and if they are unjust, they are not from God. Therefore they are from the devil; and if they are from the devil, they must be condemned together with him.

And since the fates are said to determine for each person how he will die—by the sword, by the noose, by a fall, by shipwreck, or in some other way—and since they provide the same outcome by many different means, no one can differ alone from the fates of all others. But if someone is found to differ, it is no longer fate but chance. And if there is chance in the death of one person, there will also be chance in the deaths of many; and then it will no longer be fate.

Anaxagoras was thrown into a mortar at the king’s command, crushed, and died—a thing that happened to no other human being. And a woman drove a stake into the temple of Sisera, king of the Philistines, and thus he gave up his spirit (Judg. IV, 21). No one has died in this manner. In earlier times, too, people were fastened to crosses, but this was later prohibited by decree. If this was fate, how did it cease? For when what belongs to fate is prohibited and does not happen, fate is overcome. Or if it did not belong to fate, people were not crucified by fate but by the judgment of the law. Thus people are not condemned by fate, but, having been convicted, are condemned for their evil deeds.

Among the Etruscans [Note: [Col. 2356] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “among the Etruscans.”], a certain man is said to have been born with a face more beautiful than anyone had ever possessed. Because he was a good man, and so that no one might suspect him—since he attracted even the eyes of respectable women—he wounded his own face with seven blows, thereby condemning the beauty desired by everyone (Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 5). Behold how, if there are fates, they are overcome.

But perhaps someone will say: “It was nature’s doing that he was born handsome, but fate’s doing that his face was wounded.” If this is so, fate is no longer the cause of his birth; an accident is. And if it is an accident, it belongs not to fate but to deliberation—or perhaps to chance, insofar as the remaining circumstances are concerned. For what else is overcoming fate than changing nature? Yet if fate were so fixed that it could neither be changed nor overcome, it could not be overcome.

For it is recorded in a certain legal book that a woman once gave birth to five children. How was this taken away from the fates, so that nature decreed for this woman alone what was not decreed by fate? If it had belonged to fate, a number of women would have been burdened with this lot.

And when a certain man was setting out for foreign lands, he entrusted his wife to a friend whom he knew to be faithful—not to a boy, certainly, but to a mature man. So that he might be a more diligent guardian of her, the man castrated himself, in order that he might safely sleep with her without arousing anyone’s suspicion. What are we to think: was this a matter of fate or of deliberation? But how could something contrary to fate belong to fate? For whoever overcomes what has been born in him thereby empties fate of its force.

The same issue is certainly involved in intellectual pursuits: whether someone will know something or will be unable to comprehend it. All senators, then, have one fate, for none of the senators is uneducated; and peoples who are without literacy have one fate, while all slaves share one fate, for no slave is a senator. But if whatever is born is called fate, whatever is added will be outside fate. Or if what happens comes from fate, why does it come through labor? It would be called fate only if it happened against a person’s will.

For what occurs [Note: [Col. 2356] The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “what threatens.”] without providence is attributed to the fates. But what is devised, carefully weighed for a long time, and acquired through intervening exercises—why is it said to belong to fate? [Col. 2357] Someone is born a eunuch; others become eunuchs. Where is fate in this? I suppose it is in the one who was born so. But what is to be said about those who become eunuchs? Being born and becoming are different things. Or if those who become eunuchs were made so by fate, the one who was born a eunuch was born contrary to fate. And why is a eunuch born so rarely that it seems incredible?

There was a woman in the city of Rome who is known to have had eleven husbands; and there was another man who had twelve [Note: [Col. 2357] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “eleven.”] wives. What fates were these, which decreed such things for them? For in the time of the emperor Constantine it is evident that a girl in a region of Campania was transformed into a male and brought to Rome. What fates brought this about? There is another matter, I believe, of which you are unaware.

Oh, if only you would be silent about this word “fate,” and assign some things to chance and accidents, and concede certain things to providence! For the power and skill of minds are so great that they not only resist nature but also correct or fail to correct themselves, since they possess judgment concerning themselves.

It is related that the women of the Scythians, who were called Amazons, when their husbands were absent for a long time because they were occupied in distant warfare, joined with slaves for the sake of offspring and killed every male child that was born, preserving the females. Thus none of them devoted herself to woolworking; instead, from early childhood they were trained in wrestling and arms.

Their valor in action was so great that, reigning for many years, they subdued a number of peoples and placed all Asia under tribute. What can be said about this? Surely these events, carried out over so many years in such a way as to nullify everything thought to belong to fate, cannot have been matters of fate?

First, women ruled contrary to nature, rejecting men; second, they united with their own slaves; third, all the male children born to them were killed while the females were allowed to live. Such prosperity followed them that, without men, they established a kingdom and extended it with great forces over a long period.

Certainly nothing like this had ever happened since the foundation of the world, except in Scythia alone. Otherwise someone might say that, when the world is renewed after 1,460 years, such things come about—especially since the world is now in its sixth thousandth year—whenever anyone imitates what has been done.

Crassus was called Agelastus because he is said to have laughed only once in his life. Why was Junius surnamed Brutus? Because, through shrewd deliberation, he pretended to be foolish, so that he would not be killed by the arrogant king on account of his great wealth.

In the time of Constantine, a certain man named Samatius [Note: [Col. 2357] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “Samsucius.”] pretended for thirty years to be a jester, so that, as he himself later said, he might divert the emperor from his cares. Where is the logic of the fates, when each person does what he wishes? It has been excluded.

What, moreover, are we to make of the fact that the advocates of the fates are devoted to supplications, even though supplications are opposed to them? They entrust their years to them, and ask about marriages, journeys, purchases, and offices. But if these things belong to fate, why do you pray? Why do you make supplication for what will happen even against your will?

“But,” he says, “I am asking whether I ought to buy.” Then the matter does not rest with fate, since you say that you ought to do it if you learn that it is advantageous. For if it belongs to fate, you ask in vain: whether you wish it or not, whether you ask or do not ask, you will do it.

Yet because this assertion is not even fixed among the adherents of fate themselves, they undertake uncertain inquiries, lest they discover something other than the truth of what they are investigating. But those among them who appear more prudent say: “We do not make supplication on account of the fates, since we know that they cannot be changed; we do so on account of things that are adjacent to the fates, lest they do something contrary to us.”

Very well, then: if someone has a good fate, and something that appears contrary is situated beside it, what can happen, since they deny that a good fate can be changed, just as they deny this of an evil fate? Certainly one makes supplication that what is adjacent to fate may not cause harm; for it will cause harm unless supplication has been made. How, then, is it denied that fate can be changed, when what is close to it is feared? Indeed, it would not be feared unless it were believed capable of being changed.

But since the real issue lies in this, lest you say that fate can be changed, you are unquestionably making supplication without purpose. Take care, however, lest the very thing for which you make supplication belongs to fate, since whatever you assign to fate is ordinarily without evil. Certainly it is not an evil thing to make supplication. Why, then, should it not be said to belong to fate?

If making supplication belongs to fate, to whom does failing to obtain what one asks belong? For if it belonged to fate, one ought to obtain what one asks. But if making supplication and failing to obtain what one asks both belong to fate, fate is foolish, because it makes a person supplicate whom it knows will not obtain what he asks. And if fate does not know whether he can obtain it, although it causes him to supplicate, fate will be improvident and devoid of reason. For every ignorance is lack of wisdom, and lack of wisdom is foolishness.

All the argument of the pagans falls into this category. Let the pagans see to it, they who, surrounded by darkness, do not see the light. Enclosed by an ancient error, they refuse to lend their ears to the truth that was previously hidden.

What shall we say about certain Christians who, as though changed only in name through the Savior, defend the vanity of their former error? They are so dull that they maintain that God himself acted under fate, saying: “He himself said, ‘My hour has not yet come’” (John II, 4), as though this hour had been a necessity not of his will but of a fatal condition, when he indicated the hour of his own will—the hour at which he would allow himself to be handed over [Note: [Col. 2358] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “to suffer.”].

Finally, he says: “I have power to lay down my life, and I have power to take it up again” (ibid. X, 18). Fatal necessity therefore ceases wherever the power of the will exists.

And how is the Savior called our Savior if the things we do, or the things that happen to us, are matters of fate? He is called the Savior for this reason: because he showed us the way of salvation. Therefore, if this way was shown by him, it did not belong to fate, since it had previously been hidden.

They insist that what is said to belong to fate happens unexpectedly. But this is the merit of faith, which cannot be said to arise from fate, because what is believed had not been heard of in earlier ages. The fates are said to provide what is involved in human conduct. But how can they be said to provide what they are found not to know? This is why the Apostle says: “None of the rulers of this age knew it” (1 Cor. II, 8).

These are the rulers and powers who have evil angels under them. Under the name of the fates they accomplish their own pleasures, according to whatever they desire, just as magicians themselves are accustomed to confess. There are some whom they love, others whom they do not love, and some whom they hate. Each one suggests to each person what he loves, since they too have different pleasures: to some they bring the desire for various forms of sexual immorality, to others gifts, to others pleasure, to others insolence, to others anger, to some greed, to others profits, to others losses; to some a “charism” or special gift, to others hatred, and likewise impediments.

At times, when they have been satisfied at particular times, they rest in idleness. At other times they do not intrude, whether because of prudence or because the mind is occupied; for they do not rule but creep in, seeking an opportunity by which they may capture their victims.

The freedom of the will therefore exists. Yet when, through a certain desire, we become negligent concerning ourselves, they trouble us and persuade us toward what is harmful—especially if they discover that we are considering something that is not in accordance with divine law. They come at that very point to assist us in carrying out what the law prohibits.

For if the fear of God is present in the mind, neither flesh nor blood, neither rulers nor powers, can prevail. With God’s aid we so pursue them that they are overcome without difficulty. But if we did not possess power over ourselves, how could the Lord say, “Ask, and it will be given to you; for everyone who asks will receive” (Matt. VII, 7–8)?

If the one who wishes to ask will receive, then what is commonly said—“We do not have what we want, but what has been given”—is no longer valid. For the will is stirred by the Savior to ask, and to receive what it has asked for.

They say, however, that it belongs to fate that, whether a person asks or does not ask, he will nevertheless obtain by fate whatever is either evil or good. But the Lord excludes this when he says: “Daughter, your faith has saved you” (ibid. IX, 22). It is no longer a matter of fate when faith receives a benefit.

Again, he says: “If you believe, all things are possible for the believer” (Mark IX, 22). He placed the merit in the will, therefore, since the good belongs to faith, not to nature. Faith is something added, which arouses the will to exercise itself. Since faith is not present in nature, the will—which is present in nature—once it has received faith, assigns merit to it before God.

Human nature is like a stone: although it does not contain fire in its substance, it nevertheless contains it potentially, so that through action it may produce what it appears not to possess, because it does not exist in actuality but only, as it were, in seed. It exists potentially so that it may be generated through exercise; and if exercise is lacking, it does not come into being. For seed itself, unless it is cultivated, does not generate, but remains merely seed. Addition, therefore, makes it generate.

So too the human being does not possess faith by nature, but possesses the seed of faith. Unless this seed is summoned forth and awakened, it will produce no fruit—that is, the person will not possess faith. Those who believe in the fates of the astrologers [Note: [Col. 2359] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “fables.”] destroy the seed of faith, which bears witness both to the Creator and to his justice. For a work recognizes its maker and testifies to him by an equal right, through love and through its very accomplishment.

We warn that this art must be avoided in every way. For those who pursue it out of curiosity are enemies of God and are never free from anxiety: they are always in suspense, awaiting what they know is by no means certain.

But we, who believe that all favorable things come from God, and that if anything adverse arises it is restrained by his will, should live prayerfully and securely, confident in his protection. Yet we must not be unaware that, even if something adverse happens to us while we are acting rightly, its being endured will contribute to our crown.

# On the Meaning of Easter

[Note: [Col. 2359] So in the manuscripts and in the Regensburg edition. Other editions add: “Whence Easter was so called, and how it is mystically celebrated through blood.”]

## CXVI

[Note: [Col. 2359] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

Easter (*Pascha*), dearly beloved brothers, is named from the Passion, as the foreshadowing of this tradition teaches us, which was fulfilled in Egypt through God’s servant Moses, when Scripture says: “This is the Lord’s Passover sacrifice” (Exod. 12:11).

What, then, is the reason that the mystical sacrament [Note: [Col. 2359] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “sacred mystery.”] was celebrated through blood, and the restoration of life through death—so that, when Death thought it was increasing itself, it might flow away, diminished, upon receiving the Savior’s blood; and when it considered that it had acted with power, it might collapse, weakened?

Through divine providence, death was discovered as the work that would destroy death: because, since Death always desires evil, it was yielded to for a time, so that, once destroyed by the work of its own injustice, it could not complain that its kingdom had been taken away. For although God can do all things, he nevertheless does nothing that is contrary to reason. The justice he requires, he also carries out, making no presumption upon his power.

Great, therefore, is his providence toward the human race: while preserving justice, he would thus undo what had been justly decreed and rescue the human being from death, although the human being was not unjustly held by it. But because the devil’s envy had deceived him, it was just that he should be helped. The human being was held by God’s sentence, but Satan had brought this about. Therefore, just as it seemed just to rescue him, so it was unjust to do so by power while disregarding justice.

The human being, overcome by the devil’s persuasion, was receiving mercy; yet the devil, as accuser, was opposing it. Therefore the matter was arranged so that he who gloried in the human being’s sin might himself be found to have sinned, so that, having then become guilty, he would no longer dare to oppose it.

Thus it came about that the Son of God was born as a human being and, proclaiming righteousness, incited the devil against himself, because he was restraining human beings from the devil’s vices; with the result that the devil even killed him who knew no sin. Then he was found to have sinned—and indeed more grievously than the human being whom he accused. For although, by God’s decree, he claimed the human being for himself on account of sin, since the one who sins belongs in part to the devil, he was found to have sinned more when he killed one who had not sinned in order to seize him for himself.

Through death, therefore, destruction entered into Death: so that blood might be recovered, blood was poured out. For, as I have said, the author of death, who is the devil, since he was found to have sinned in the Savior’s death, lost his blood together with all of us: just as through one sinning Adam he held everyone in death, so through one who did not sin he lost everyone.

Therefore the Savior’s blood, unjustly shed, obtained this reward [Note: [Col. 2360] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “in the name of the reward”]: recovering with triumph the blood of its origin, it restored it to its former condition, its substance having been improved. For once Death had been conquered, it could not oppose the one who had conquered it.

Blessed, then, is the mystery of Easter, which redeemed us through blood, when death was conquered through death, just as poison is customarily overcome by poison.

# On Abraham

[Note: [Col. 2360] Some editions add: “and on his faith, by which he deserved to be called the father of believers.”]

## CXVII

[Note: [Col. 2360] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

The faith of this patriarch was so exceptional and admirable that, by God’s judgment, all other righteous people acknowledge him as the father of belief; nor is anyone worthy and beloved of God unless he has been called his son.

The distinction of his honor and merit is his faith: since he does not hesitate to give credence to incredible things, among other privileges he also proved worthy of seeing the Savior in hope [Note: [Col. 2360] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “in appearance.”] of the future Incarnation. For the Lord says and confirms to the Jews: “Abraham your father rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad” (John 8:56).

Since he became the father of believers by the merit of his faith, it was fitting that he should foresee the hope of his future sons, which, through the grace of inheritance, would flow from a human and devout father to obedient children under a merciful and provident God.

Let us now see what this faith believed, so that by divine judgment it might attain such honor and glory. We have praised his faith, but we have not yet said what it believed.

The Lord led him out, showed him the stars of heaven, and said: “Can you number them? So shall your offspring be.” And Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:5–6).

It would not be a great thing to have believed God, except that what he believed the world judges not to be believed and calls foolish, because this does not belong to the expectation of nature. Therefore Abraham, one person from the world who believed this, was separated from worldly people and justified.

His having believed this is made great by the unbelief of worldly wisdom; against that wisdom, to have believed this is of the greatest merit. The despair of worldly people is the merit and hope of Christians. For the reward of the good makes the wicked its cause. Faith is stronger and fuller when it entrusts itself more completely to things that are incredible.

A man already dried up and with an aged wife believed that he would have offspring, offspring so numerous that they could not be counted. He did not attend chiefly to what had been shown, but to the one who had shown it, considering that he could not lie. Therefore it was reckoned to him as righteousness.

For it is characteristic of a dull mind to believe an absurd thing known to be impossible, unless there is a person who persuades one to believe it. Thus Abraham is both admirable in faith and skilled in heart: he believes what is incredible and entrusts himself to one whom not to believe would be both foolish and dangerous.

This proves our faith reasonable: it believes of no one other than God that he can do what he promises. This, then, is the stronghold of faith; this is its triumph.

Some worldly wise men, observing that nature cannot do this, say that it is foolish to believe. They do not know that, according to the Apostle, “what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings” (1 Cor. 1:25). They would rightly judge us foolish if we believed this of the nature of things, which is shown to be unable to do it. But we believe that God can do the things that the nature of things cannot, if he has promised them.

What foolishness, then, can be found in this? If the work believed possible is unworthy of God, faith is rightly compared with dullness. But if it is worthy, precisely because it is impossible for creation, why should faith not be praised, since it grants the Creator as much as creation is denied the ability to do?

Great, therefore, and admirable is Abraham, who did not hesitate to believe God against the judgment of the world, because God can do what he promises.

A Chaldean by birth, he appeared as a teacher of belief. Although skilled in astrology, he nevertheless placed God above human reasoning, judging it worthy that one should believe this about God: that what he does cannot be investigated.

God’s power confirmed his weakness [Col. 2361], because, in order to proclaim the unique greatness of his majesty, he intended to do things impossible and unheard-of in the world. By this act he would show himself Lord of creation, and creation would subject itself to him whose work seemed impossible to everyone else. By their unbelief, the most faithful Abraham is exalted all the more.

His faith is the punishment of unbelievers; the unbelief of unbelievers is his glory. For he is the father of believers and the judge of unbelievers. Through his example, eternal life is granted to the good, and eternal punishments will be given to the wicked [Note: [Col. 2361] The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “and the wicked will give eternal punishments.”]

At that time, when the world was still immature in knowledge and had not been enlightened by signs and wonders that might draw it to faith, he did not deny God faith contrary to his own knowledge. Holy Abraham was therefore given to the human race as the most faithful example.

In him all nations were prefigured as coming to salvation through faith. So that the superabundant growth of his faith might be recognized, he was tested and commanded to sacrifice his son to God—a thing that had never before been done. He was neither disturbed by the novelty of the deed nor argued about whether parricide ought to be committed at God’s command, when God had threatened that homicide must not occur. Thus, fearless and secure regarding God’s will, he did not hesitate to believe that what God commanded was provident.

This was the son whom two old people had received in fulfillment of a promise, the reward of faith, the proof of his merits, and the one in whom all hope of the promised future offspring was contained.

To fulfill the command with complete devotion, he did not tell the boy’s mother, lest she should impede his devotion, knowing that, in their affection for their children, mothers are more inclined to love. Therefore he concealed it from her, without doubting that what God commanded had to be fulfilled, so that by this example we might be taught to carry out God’s commands with every care.

For if the most faithful Abraham is found obedient in a matter so grave and harsh, how much more should we obey, to whom commands are given that can be borne?

O faith devoted to God, and hope firm in the Lord, so dear and sweet that it is placed before the affections of parents and children, as Scripture says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33:9)!

Our most faithful patriarch Abraham, because he was a prophet, knew what he ought to follow. Therefore, in accordance with what the Lord has now said, he then acted, preferring God in love to his son, however dear, as the Lord says: “If anyone loves father and mother, or sons, above me, he is not worthy of me” (Matt. 10:37). Therefore the patriarch, so that he might be worthy of the Lord above all else, did not refuse even to kill his son.

# On Job

## CXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2361] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

Great is the love of almighty God toward the human race, dearly beloved brothers. When understood, it leads to the heavenly kingdoms; when not understood, it leads down to the underworld. God wants his beneficence to be received gratefully and fruitfully, so that it may benefit us and delight him in showing mercy.

Therefore, because he is good and wants all human beings to be saved, he displayed in Job, his servant, an example of righteousness, as the present reading testifies. If we follow it, we shall be able both to avoid evil and to come to the good, and not only to be freed from punishment but also to be rewarded.

How admirable, then, is the most holy Job, who, before the Law had been published in writing, displayed the pattern of the Law in his deeds! Learning no instruction from anyone else in this matter, but guided by nature itself—in which God decreed that the seeds of righteousness should naturally be present—he preserved reverence toward the Creator with devout dedication.

How much praise he deserves, and in what words his deeds ought to be exalted, since we cannot find anyone equal to him either before the Law or after the Law! Even if someone could imitate his deeds, that person would not be compared with him, nor would rightly be called like him. The achievement would not belong to that person, because he would have followed another’s example.

But holy Job, when he had seen nothing of this kind and had read nothing of it in books, made himself such that nothing of anyone else had been applied to him [Col. 2362]; rather, he supplied it to others, providing a model of marvelous deeds by which to win God’s favor.

For this reason he is commended by the Lord’s testimony, which says: “Have you paid attention to my servant Job? For there is no one like him on earth, a true worshiper of God” (Job 1:8).

Who could have deserved so much that the Lord would give such testimony, except one who is found not to be an imitator but the originator of the deeds he performed? Hence he is also asserted to be a true worshiper of God.

No fabricated pretense of truth can be seen in someone who has no such predecessor before him. For everyone who pretends imitates what he sees. Yet what is said of Job is superior to all these considerations.

In these praises there had been no trials of suffering, but only a purpose devoted to God, established in practice and observance. Because the tempter did not regard this as sufficient for the crown of his merits, he asked that he be permitted to test Job’s righteousness through various temptations, so that, bound by many trials, he might become entangled somewhere and exceed the proper measure.

For diverse punishments are usually inflicted upon sinners so that, because no one can endure every torment, some confession of the truth may be drawn from them. Thus the tempter was permitted to destroy and ruin everything belonging to Job, even to the death of his children.

The purpose was that, if he endured the loss of cattle, he might not endure the loss of sheep; or if he endured that of sheep as well, he might not endure the loss of camels, servants, or his entire property; or, if he was strong-minded and of sufficiently pure devotion and was not overcome by all these things, he might at least be broken by affection and love when all his children died together.

But because, before the Law was published, he had the Law written in his heart, no losses or bereavements made him less devoted to God. Thus he provided a model for loving God with one’s whole heart above all things.

How worthy of glory, then, is the man who observed the Law before the Law, demonstrating how the future Law was to be kept—not in words, but as the originator in deeds?

And because the irreverent tempter did not regard even this glory as sufficient for testing the righteous man, unless he devised something else against him that he knew a human being could not endure, he asked again to strike Job himself with a savage wound from head to the nails of his feet.

When this was permitted, since no trust ought to be placed in him, the tempter was commanded to preserve Job’s life for the sake of free choice and not to dare to do anything violently against one whom he could not overcome by the right of reason.

Having therefore received authority, and with his cruelty’s savagery growing fiercer within him, he struck the righteous man with a very great plague, so that there was no part of his body free from injury—something no human being could have endured except Job alone [Note: [Col. 2362] The printed editions omit “Job,” which is restored from the Colbertinus manuscript], who was able to conquer Satan.

When even then the devil’s wickedness could not draw from the righteous man any murmuring against God, Satan, remembering his former cunning by which he had deceived Adam, tried to see whether he could deceive this man as well through a woman, since a person is more easily deceived through someone in the household.

In all these efforts the most shameless Satan accomplished nothing—indeed, he suffered loss. He found not only that God’s servant was unmoved, but also that he was a teacher. In the very midst of his distress, Job not only remained firm in the fear of God, but also rebuked his wife when she offered contrary advice, teaching that everything that happens with God’s permission must be endured courageously (Job 2:1–10).

This amounted to a double punishment for the thoughtless Satan, because he neither persuaded Job to do what he wanted nor, through envying him, prevented others from learning what he did not want Job himself to know.

How greatly temptation benefits God’s servants and harms the devil, we are taught more fully by this reading. When Satan thinks he is harming them, he advances them; and when he persecutes one, he urges many toward virtue. Seeing Job protected by God’s help, many become his imitators.

Thus, wishing to make a profit, Satan suffered loss. His rage is always harmful to him. When he persecutes the righteous so that they may not be rewarded, he makes them more worthy. When he envied holy Job, he doubled his merit in heaven and on earth, because Job was increased here and received in heaven with the Savior [Col. 2363], so that all these things might advance the glory of the saints but bring punishment to the devil.

# On Tobit

## CXIX

[Note: [Col. 2363] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

Such is the Lord God’s providence toward us that, because he does not want us to go astray, he gave both the Law and examples of good works, by which life may be conducted modestly and peacefully with the fear of God.

The author of life does not want his work to be subject to death. Although nature itself is not without the Law, nevertheless, because the Lord is good and merciful, he showed in writing and by examples the things that should be followed and those that should be avoided, so that they might be more fully known, as the present reading testifies.

Therefore holy Tobit, God’s servant, was given to us as an example after the Law, so that we may know how the things we read are to be done; and, if temptations arise, may not depart from the fear of God or hope for help from anywhere other than him, remembering that it is written: “I was young, and indeed I grew old, and I have never seen the righteous forsaken, nor his offspring seeking bread” (Ps. 36:25).

No one who hopes in God with his whole mind can ever be deceived. Even if, for a time, tribulations arise through Satan’s snares, the examples of holy men teach us that God permits these things only for the increase of our merits. For if they are borne with an even temper, consolation will be given to us here with its effect, and in the future eternal life with glory.

Because our God is just and there is no partiality with him (Rom. 2:11), he permits us to be tested because he loves us, so that after our labor he may give us the greatest rewards.

Finally, when the Apostle prayed that temptations might cease for him, the Lord said: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness.” Then he added: “When I am weak, then I am stronger”; and, “I rejoice,” he says, “in my tribulations, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12:9–10).

How worthy of praise holy Tobit was, Scripture teaches us. Neither captivity diminished his devotion, nor did the loss of his eyes persuade him to stop blessing God, nor did the exhaustion of his property turn him away from the path of righteousness and truth (Tobit 1–3).

Necessity proves the righteous person; and to preserve equity in poverty is true and perfect righteousness. Where the devotion of some people diminishes, there Tobit, worthy of praise, increased his.

“For poverty,” he says, “humiliates a man; and one who is humiliated cannot preserve righteousness.” But holy Tobit’s mind, raised toward God, was neither broken by captivity nor humbled by poverty. Even in defiance of the prohibition, he buried the bodies of the dead; and, secure in God’s generosity, he was merciful from his small means, knowing that the mercy which comes from little is more pleasing to God—just as that widow acted whom the Lord highly praised in the Gospel (Luke 21:2–4).

This person is truly faithful; this person does not doubt God’s promises, who gives from little.

Comforting his spirit, therefore, with hope of future things, Tobit, devoted to God, was found strong and courageous in temptation, showing that in necessity one must be even more watchful in the fear of God. For if necessity does not drive us to God’s help, how much less will security do so?

The holy men were certain that God had reserved for himself judgment concerning all the things that happen in this world. Therefore they not only did not bear tribulations, losses, other disasters, or insults with resentment, but also accepted them gratefully, as did our Apostles, who rejoiced when they were beaten because they had been considered worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Christ (Acts 5:41).

Disasters are indications of future merits when they unjustly befall the faithful, whether in tribulations or in insults.

Thus righteous Tobit pleased God so greatly that he received the reward of his merits in two ways. In the present life, he recovered the light he had lost through the ministry of an angel and was also enriched with the resources belonging to this present life; in the future, he was made an heir of the kingdom of heaven.

By this we are taught that God often increases in this world the resources of the person who obeys God’s Law with all his heart and does not doubt his promises [Col. 2364]. In the future he grants that person eternal life [Note: [Col. 2364] The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “God cares for him.”]

There is also another matter that invites us to divine service. Holy Tobit received not only the merits of his righteousness; for it adds to the fullness of his glory that he also benefits from the goodness of those who prove to be his imitators. Examples are praised in their imitators.

This can also happen to us, if we live in such a way that it is worthy for us, too, to have imitators.

# On Fasting

## CXX

[Note: [Col. 2364] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

It is fitting, dearly beloved brothers, that the most devout priest of God and leader of Christ’s people should exhort the people placed under his care in sound doctrine, as the Apostle commands (Titus 1:9), so that, in keeping with the season, we may carry out the work of faith with every care and diligence, with an eager and devoted spirit.

For although it is not unknown what benefit the fasts now to be observed as the feast of Easter approaches provide, it should nevertheless not be left unspoken. Devotion is stirred when things that are not unknown are nevertheless recalled.

Such is the character of our nature that it becomes sluggish if the practice of reading ceases. For just as iron, unless it is used [Note: [Col. 2364] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “unless it acts”], produces rust, so the soul, unless it is exercised more frequently through divine readings, will produce sins.

This is why the Psalm calls blessed the person who meditates on the Lord’s Law day and night (Ps. 1:2). Finally, although the divine words are familiar, when they are recalled from the sacred books, the devout heart receives them as though they were new. The soul’s desire for saving works is awakened.

Therefore the Apostle says to Timothy, among other things: “That you may rekindle the grace of God which is in you” (2 Tim. 1:6).

Fasts are therefore necessary for us, like medicine for wounds. They bring healing that leads to eternal life, but only if they are commended by the testimony of two things: prayer and mercy.

Fasts moderate bodily excess, restrain contrary impulses, and remove pressure from the soul, as the Lord says: “Do not give yourselves over to eating and drunkenness, lest your hearts be weighed down” (Luke 21:34).

When the soul has been freed from excessive eating and drinking, it then recognizes itself more clearly. For just as a person does not see himself in a dirty mirror as he truly is, so, if he has been weighed down by food and drunkenness, he feels himself to be other than he is.

Then lust is aroused, anger is kindled, pride is inflamed, and wantonness is generated. Hence the Apostle says: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is wantonness” (Eph. 5:18).

But if the body is moderated by the interposition of fasting, the soul, having recovered self-knowledge, understands with what devotion it ought to serve the Redeemer.

Fasts are therefore necessary to a great extent. Under Queen Esther, when the Jewish people were placed in danger, they were delivered with the support of fasting (Esth. 4:16). When the Ninevites heard from the prophet the appointed day of their destruction, they deserved to escape by proclaiming a fast (Jonah 3:7).

Our righteous men and prophets, whenever they wished to obtain something from God, humbled themselves with fasting, as David says: “In fasting I humbled my soul” (Ps. 34:13).

The Savior himself, although he had no need of it, fasted in order to give us an example (Matt. 4:2). Therefore no one can doubt that fasts are beneficial. A person shows that he wants to obtain what he asks for when he afflicts himself with fasting.

Hence it is said: “Prayer is good with fasting” (Tob. 12:8). For prayer to be acceptable, it wants fasting as its companion [Note: [Col. 2364] The Colbertinus manuscript reads: “it wants fasting as its solace.”]

And because none of these things is firm without devotion, the text adds: “And almsgiving with righteousness,” so that almsgiving practiced with righteousness may commend prayer together with fasting.

Finally, Cornelius’s mercy commended his prayer and fasting. Although he abounded in resources [Note: [Col. 2364] Erasmus, the Venetian edition, and the Louvain edition read “abounding in wealth, or resources, he fasted”; Lyon reads “abounding in wealth, he fasted”; M.], he fasted; but he also fed those who had nothing, so that their fullness might make his fasting acceptable.

Fasting therefore needs some things [Col. 2365], and must be without some things, in order that it may deserve to obtain what it asks.

# Praise and Glory of Easter

[Note: [Col. 2365] Thus in the manuscripts and in the Regensburg edition. Other editions read: “On Easter: how praiseworthy and glorious the solemnity is.”]

## CXXI

[Note: [Col. 2365] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

O holy and saving day of Easter, worthy to be proclaimed with every praise! On this day death was conquered, the devil’s kingdom was taken away, God’s mystery was revealed, and the decree that stood against us was annulled; the gates of Tartarus were broken, the bound were released, the confined were set free, the blind were enlightened, the unlearned were given knowledge, the impious were made merciful, forgiveness of sins was granted to the wicked and unjust, enemies were reconciled, error was corrected, and truth was declared.
