From the lost, sons were acquired for God; pride was brought low, humility was exalted; the poor were enriched, the rich were drained; mountains were leveled, valleys filled, hills laid low; shamelessness was trampled down, modesty adorned [Note: [Col. 2365] The Colbertinus manuscript reads “strengthened”]; souls were given access to heaven, freedom was restored, captivity was shattered and dissolved.

Darkness grew numb, wickedness was confounded, squalor was purified, Satan was cast down; hell was emptied.

Our Lord Jesus Christ was proven to be the true Son of God; the flesh of the world was raised into heaven to confound the wise; heavenly, earthly, and infernal things were shown to belong to one God and Lord.

Therefore, dearly beloved brothers, we ought to celebrate and venerate this feast day, devoted to God with modesty of life and joy of soul, avoiding disgraceful and dishonorable things, so that through Christ our Lord we may deserve to attain the fruit of Easter. To him be honor and glory for ever and ever.

# On the Beginning
## CXXII

[Note: [Col. 2365] Absent from the same manuscripts.]

“In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1). What does “in the beginning” mean? We read in the Old Books also: “In the beginning God made heaven and earth” (Gen. 1:1). And in the Letter of the man whose Gospel this is, and whose “beginning” we are attempting to explain, the same meaning is expressed: for he says, “That which was from the beginning.” Thus the Letter and the Gospel have one meaning.

For one thing is meant when the Old Book says, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” and another when it says, “In the beginning was the Word,” and, “That which was from the beginning” (1 John 1:1). To be “in the beginning” and to be “from the beginning” signify the same thing: he who was from the beginning did not begin to exist. For whatever begins to exist was not from the beginning; and therefore it is subjected to a beginning—that is, so that it may be first among other things in order, because, having itself been made first, it began to have others after it, which were made after it.

Thus we read that “in the beginning God made heaven and earth.” He did not say, “In the beginning heaven and earth were,” because, when they did not yet exist and God was arranging to make the world, “in the beginning”—that is, first among the other things that would contribute to the world’s construction—God made heaven and earth. For a beginning is the starting point of something being initiated, which is first in order.

But when it is said that something “was in the beginning”—that is, the Word—it is signified that it existed before the beginning of the heavenly and earthly creation, so that it would certainly not be understood as having been made first among the things that were created, because it was “in the beginning,” when God was arranging to make creation. Therefore, if it was “in the beginning”—that is, it existed before all things—it always was. And therefore the Word was.

Where? “With God,” he says, so that what had always been with God would not improperly be considered subject to a beginning. For it is fitting that what was with God before all things should be subject to no beginning. Hence he added: “And the Word was God.” Now he openly shows that what was said above applies to the Word, because, he says, the Word is God; and of God one ought not to think otherwise than that he is always said to have existed. For if he began to exist, he is a creature; if he is a creature, he is not God. Whatever exists is either God or a creature; and therefore the name “God” does not belong to a creature. But because he did not begin to exist—for he was—he is rightly called God.

He is said to have always been with God [Col. 2366] because he is God not from himself but from God. Therefore his name is also called the Word of God, as the faith of that same evangelist demonstrates in his Revelation. For among other things he says: “And his name is called the Word of God” (Rev. 19:13).

Thus, so that the one from whom all things exist would not be signified, but the one through whom all things exist—that is, not the Father but the Son—he was called the Word of God. Since God cannot exist without the Word, he who is called the Word of God is believed always to have been with God. And since the word is not outside the one whose word it is, this Word which was with God is understood to be not from elsewhere but from God; and because he is from God, he is not absurdly called God.

Thus the statement that God was with God does not make two gods. For if there were two, they would differ in nature and would not have one will. If we human beings, although of one nature, nevertheless have different wills, how much more would this be so where both nature and will were different? In that case, God would not be said to be with God [Note: [Col. 2366] So the manuscripts. The printed editions read: “where there is no diversity of nature or will, God would be said to be with God.”]

For the God who was and is with God does not have from himself what makes him God. Otherwise he would not be called God with God, nor would the Word of God be called the Word-God. But because what is from God signifies nothing other than that it is God, the Word of God was named God, so that, because he is called the Word of God, he might not be referred to another God. And he is called God lest it become an insult to God if what was from God were not called God.

Thus both the unity of God has been preserved and due honor has been rendered, since he who is God from God has not been received into his own glory but into the glory of the one from whom he is God. For this reason the Gospel begins to speak about the Word before it speaks about God the Father, because the questions concern not God but the Word of God. No one doubts about God, but about him who is God from God.

Every tongue of heavenly and earthly beings confesses one God, but it is troubled by the mystery of the one God. It trembles when it hears the Word of God called God, for it is struck by bodily conceptions: a human word cannot be called a human being. Yet God is by nature simple, not composed of members; he does not have an inside and an outside, nor a before and an after, nor a highest and a lowest. Rather, if one may put it so, he is wholly and everywhere the same, nowhere varied or unlike himself; his brightness is one and immeasurable.

For if fire has no front or back, no inside or outside, how much more does its Creator? Therefore, because everything that God is is wholly one, there is no discrepancy when what is from God is called God.

The Son of God, who is the Word of God, is therefore God partly according to a human example and partly not according to a human example. In the way that human sons are human beings, the Son of God is God. But because human sons are human beings through mixture, the Son of God is not God in this respect, since he was born simply from the simple God.

And just as our word is from us, by this example the Word of God is understood to be from him. But because our word is not what we are, the Word of God is not from God in this respect, since the Word of God is a reality, not a fleeting sound.

Nor, because certain terms are common to us and to God, will the same principle apply to us and to God in the reality of things. For we read, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth.” How did he make them? Did he make them as we make works with our hand [Note: [Col. 2366] Ms. Colbertinus: “we make with the hand, by work.”]? And in what follows: “And God said, Let there be light; and there was light” (Gen. 1:3). To whom do we think God spoke? Certainly he did not speak to a human being, but to one who could make things, who was also going to make the human being, just as he did.

But how did he speak? Did he speak as we speak, by a bodily organ? Far from it. You see, therefore, that the terms are indeed common to us and to God, but differ in their effect: God acts otherwise than we act, and he is said to speak, but not in our manner.

So the Word of God is not such a word [Col. 2367] as ours, which, once it has been produced, no longer exists. That Word remains, because it is such a Word as both hears, speaks, and acts.

Moreover, he is not only the Word of God but also the Power and Wisdom of God: he is the Son of God. Insofar as the matter concerns effect, he is called the Son of God; insofar as it concerns the speech by which God addresses us through him, he is called the Word of God; insofar as it concerns the wisdom by which God teaches us his mystery through him, he is called the Wisdom of God; and insofar as it concerns the work by which God made and makes all things through him, he is called the Power of God.

These titles could belong to no one else but the Son of God. Because he is God from God, he is said to possess everything that belongs to God. By being born he obtained everything that belongs to God. For it was not fitting that the Word of God should be called degenerate, or that the Power and Wisdom of God should be called degenerate. This is God the Word, the Power, and the Wisdom.

Christ, however, because he is wholly God from the whole God, is called both the Wisdom of God, the Power, and the Word. That is, he is God from God and with God. Hence he says: “This was in the beginning with God.”

To overcome the minds of unbelievers, Scripture burst forth with insistence, showing that Christ is God, since everywhere, on account of the unity of God, it wishes Christ to be understood as God. Now, in an open declaration, it said that he is God and has always been with God. Disclosing the mystery of God, it made clear that God is not called one in order that he be considered solitary, but that, even if there are two or three, their being from one does not prejudice the unity, because what is from one is referred back to that very one, since he is one, although all things are said to be from God.

For one thing properly exists from God, and another thing, created externally by his will, belongs to God. That is, one thing proceeds from his substance, and another, which in no way previously existed, was created by his will. What proceeded from God’s substance never existed after his substance; but what was created then began to exist as a substance, when it was created. Consequently, only the Trinity has no beginning.

The disclosure of the mystery therefore diminished the rewards of faith: for the more hidden what is believed, the greater the reward of the believer and the lesser the punishment of the unbeliever. But the disclosure of the mystery, just as it made the rewards smaller for believers [Note: [Col. 2367] Ms. Colbertinus: “made believers deserving of reward.”], so it aroused greater punishments for unbelievers. For a more manifest law makes a person more guilty.

The testimony of the Savior was sufficient, by which he called God his own Father. For which believer would doubt that the Son differs in no way from the Father in substance? But because the perversity of heretics had begun to assault the rights of faith with inventions of unbelief, receiving the Son of God otherwise than he is proclaimed, it was added, to make the matter manifest, that he existed before all things with God and was God. Thus it declared what the mystery of true sonship mystically contained.

Through this, divine mercy appears to have provided for human weakness, revealing what it had reserved, closed away, for the merits of a stronger faith. Hence it added: “All things were made through him,” so that if anyone had doubted in any respect about what was said above—for human understanding is too narrow to grasp divine realities—he might be made capable of understanding by hearing, “All things were made through him.”

He would certainly not think that the Word himself was a created thing, since he hears that all things were made by God through him. If he himself were also a created thing, it would not have been said that all things were made through him by God; for he himself was not made through himself.

To state this still more clearly, he added: “And without him,” he says, “nothing was made.” By saying this, he excluded every controversy and earthly argument. Although there are still those who doubt, when he shows that nothing was made without him, he teaches that one must in no way suspect him of being a created thing.

For how can he himself be said to be a created thing, when God is said to have made nothing without him? If he did make him, Scripture lies. But far be that from us. Scripture is faithful; and, to cut off error, it uses as much disclosure as possible for the redemption of human beings.

Finally, it added: “What was made in him is life” (John 1:2–4). “In him”—that is, in the Word—it signifies that what was made has life. As the Lord himself also says: “As the Father has life in himself, so he has granted the Son also to have life in himself” (John 5:26).

This does not mean that the Word was without life and that life was later either given or made in him; rather, he wishes the Word himself to be understood as life. If it can be said of God the Father that he himself is one thing and has another thing in himself, then the same may be said of his Son, since, as the Father has life in himself, so he gave the Son to have life in himself.

Human speech is not adequate to explain divine realities. Therefore what is said seems defective: although the Son of God is not a created thing, it is said that what was made is in him [Note: [Col. 2368] Ms. Colbertinus omits “is.”] And even if it had said, “What was begotten is in him,” this too would have seemed defective.

But in order to show the substantial nature of his generation [Note: [Col. 2368] So Ms. Colbertinus. The printed editions read, “the substance of his generation.”], he indicated, by whatever expression he could use, the work accomplished in that generation through which he came into existence: his generation has life in itself.

We live, certainly, but we cannot give life to others, especially since that same life is not in our power. He, however, is said to have life in himself because he has the power to give life and to create whatever he wills to exist and live.

For this reason he is said to have been born, so that he might be able to do everything that the Father does, because he has life in himself just as the Father does. This is what it means that God made all things through him and in him: he begot him in such a way that he would have life in himself, through which he could do all things.

It is not that he himself is something other than life; rather, because his life has the power both to live and to create other things that live, he is said to have life in himself. We live, but we do not possess life itself in ourselves in such a way that we can also give life to others.

The apostle Paul recalls the same meaning, among other things, when he says: “He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn before all creation, because in him all things were established in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether Thrones or Dominions or Principalities or Powers; all things were created through him and in him” (Col. 1:15–16).

The Gospels of the two apostles, John and Paul, agree on this. They say the same thing: the Son of God was begotten before all creation, in order to create the spiritual powers, the world, and the visible things that are in it.

What John said—“What was made in him is life”—means the same as what Paul signified by saying, “In him all things were established in heaven and on earth,” and, in what follows, “All things were created through him and in him.”

He created through him because he is the same God in substance—that is, the Father in the Son. But “in him” means that he begot the Son in such a way that he would have the power to make all visible and invisible things.

He made life in him by making him such that he would both live and provide life to others—to live, understand, act, and to the other living creatures according to his will—as the image of God.

When he is called the image of God, this refers to both matters: through his clearly expressed birth he has in himself the complete likeness of the Father, and he can do whatever the Father can do. Thus it is true that the Father is seen in the Son, who is the image of the invisible God.

Did he make the Son visible merely because he called the Father invisible, when the Son is by nature whatever the Father is? And since the heavenly creation is invisible, how much more is its Creator?

But he signified what is in heaven, not what is on earth. For although the Son is invisible, he is nevertheless seen there—that is, in the heavenly realms—by the apostles and others of their kind, concerning whom he said: “Father, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, and may see my glory” (John 17:24).

And elsewhere he says: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5:8). This means the Father in the Son, God in the image: that is, God in God.

Just as the body of a physical thing is its image, so God is the image of God, because the Father is the exemplar and the Son is the exemplar from the exemplar, which he communicates to the Holy Spirit: “For he will receive from me,” he says (John 16:14).

Therefore God is seen in the Son as in his own image. Just as no one was found worthy to open the book and its seals except the Word of God (Rev. 5:4–8), so no one is worthy to see God the Father, either by nature or by merits, except his true Son.

For there is nothing intermediate that obstructs the Father and the Son, as he himself testifies to us when he says: “No one has seen the Father except he who is from God; he has seen God” (John 6:46).

But if the Father is seen in the Son, why is no one said to be worthy to see God, when he is seen in the Son, since the Son differs in nothing from the Father?

He differs in absolutely nothing in substance, because he is the true Son. But he differs in rank of causality [Note: [Col. 2369] Ms. Colbertinus: “in cause or rank”], because all power is from the Father in the Son. The Son is not lesser in substance, yet the Father is greater in authority, as the Lord himself testifies, saying: “If you loved me, you would certainly rejoice, because I go to the Father, for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28).

The apostle Paul, preserving this same order, says: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things and we in him; and one Lord Jesus, through whom are all things and we through him” (1 Cor. 8:6). Thus the first rank is the one from whom all things are; the second, the one through whom all things are; the third, the one in whom all things are.

And because none of these is degenerate, they are signified in the unity of God, as the Apostle says: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever and ever” (Rom. 11:36).

## CXXIII

[Note: [Col. 2369] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

**Did Adam have the Holy Spirit?**

I have discovered that certain of our brothers have not thoroughly examined the Scriptures, but, in the simplicity of their hearts, assert that Adam, when he was made, received the Holy Spirit, which he lost when he sinned, just as it is now given to believers.

They are led by the reasoning commonly asserted by many: that through faith the human being was restored, so that, when returned to his former state, he received everything that Adam had obtained at the beginning. And because Adam was said to have been made a perfect human being, they say that if he did not have the Holy Spirit, he was imperfect.

I, however, say that not only the human being but also all the things God made—which cannot be said to have received the Holy Spirit—were perfect. All kinds of animals are perfect in their own nature, so that they may fulfill the purpose for which they were made. Thus the human being is perfect in his own kind, so that he is able to distinguish evil from good and wrong from right.

He is a rational animal, perfect for the purpose for which he was made. He is capable of speaking, thinking, and doing, so that what he cannot accomplish by strength he may fulfill through understanding.

How, then, did they dare to say that the human being must be born perfect and know everything, when they see that he knows nothing beyond what he learns here? Whatever he does not learn here, he does not know.

Finally, because he does not learn here what he is, he does not know what he is. If, therefore, he does not know what he is, how does he know everything, when knowing oneself is less than knowing other things?

But because he learns about other things and does not learn about himself, he knows about others but does not know about himself—not what he is, nor whether he exists before the body or after the body.

For if he had been made perfect in such a way that he lacked nothing, he would not have been a human being but God; nor would he have been deceived and transgressed.

To possess the Holy Spirit, however, is beyond human nature and perfection, so that one may be capable of the things that belong to God. Did not the fact that the donkey spoke to Balaam exceed its perfection (Num. 22:28)? It received the ability to do what did not belong to its nature but to ours.

Therefore, because the human being is superior to the other animals, are those animals to be called imperfect? Or because the holy angels are not what God is, are they imperfect? Or because the luminaries and stars are less perfect than the heavenly angels, or because clouds obscure the sun and moon with their covering, are they less perfect? And because the limbs need one another—for the feet cannot do what the hands can do—will they be called imperfect?

Far from it. Everything is firm and perfect according to its place and rank, so that it may fulfill the purpose for which it was made. Thus everything is perfect, because its Creator is perfect; but in comparison with him, everything is imperfect.

For God is perfect in all things, as the source and origin of all things. Created things are indeed perfect, but perfect in relation to the purpose for which they were made; in another respect they are not perfect, because each needs the other. Thus everything is both perfect and imperfect: perfect in what it does not need, but not perfect in what it needs.

The hands need the feet, because unless the feet walk, the hands will be idle. Again, the feet need the hands, since they cannot put shoes on themselves or tend to themselves.

Although the body is perfect in its limbs, it cannot fly or carry as much as a donkey can. And although these animals are perfect, they do not know how to govern themselves or apply medicine to themselves.

Hence it is said: “Do not become like the horse and the mule, in which there is no understanding” (Ps. 31:9).

Water and fire, although they oppose each other, are perfect in their own kind, for they fulfill the purpose for which they were made. Fire cooks, consumes, purifies, and warms; water washes, cools, irrigates, and refreshes the thirsty.

Thus, although everything is perfect in its own kind, without the human being these things can do nothing; nor can the human being, although more perfect, do without them.

For this reason the Apostle calls us both imperfect and perfect. In comparison with unbelievers, we are perfect because we know God. But because we know less than we ought of what has been promised, and because in this life we cannot comprehend as much as the thing believed requires, we are imperfect.

Since, then, they think that Adam’s perfection is restored in believers, let us see whether this restoration contains no divine gift beyond what Adam had received.

When Adam was made, he was placed in paradise to work there and guard it—that is, to cultivate the earth and to keep God’s commandments. Through these he would know that he had received dominion over everything, yet that he himself was to live under the law of the Creator, lest dominion exalt him and, puffed up by pride, he forget his Creator.

He was therefore placed there so that his life might be sustained by food. Through Christ, however, it has been granted that, when we rise again, we will have no need of food or drink, because what is mortal in the human being is transformed into life.

Adam was made to dwell on earth, but faith has graciously granted that our dwelling should be in heaven.

Scripture itself testifies: “The first man Adam was made a living soul; the second man a life-giving spirit. The first man was from the earth, earthly; the second man from heaven, heavenly. As was the earthly, such are the earthly; and as is the heavenly, such are the heavenly” (1 Cor. 15:45–48).

What could be clearer than that Adam did not have the Holy Spirit? He was made a living soul; through Christ, however, the human being is made into a life-giving spirit, so that the human being might in some respect be like the Creator whom he believes [Note: [Col. 2370] Ms. Colbertinus: “and be what he believes.”].

Since the mystery of faith, which was given for salvation, is threefold, the human being becomes threefold—body, soul, and the Holy Spirit, through whom we are called sons of God. Adam, however, is by no means shown to have been called this; for he was made earthly.

Those who are born as sons of God—not carnally but spiritually—are called heavenly.

Here, then, the matter is settled: God granted human beings far more grace in the time of the Savior than Adam had received. The human being was not merely restored but improved—restored because he was cleansed from sins, and improved in the remaining respects.

Justice and reason demanded this also: that God’s mercy should then be more abundant in granting benefits, when he wished the mystery of his divinity to be made known to creation. By learning what had been unknown throughout the ages and generations—that the mystery of the one God consists in the Trinity—believers, as though in honor of the dedication of this new revelation, would not only be cleansed from sins but also justified and adopted by God, receiving the Holy Spirit, through whom they might be seen to possess the sign of adoption.

Adoption by God must bear the sign of God the Father, so that those adopted may rightly be called sons of God. This gift was also promised through the Prophets, to be given when the mystery of God was to be declared in the triumph of death’s defeat, so that creation might know that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God.

Hence the evangelist says: “The Spirit had not yet been given, because Jesus had not yet been glorified” (John 7:39).

This glorification occurs when, through his power, he is recognized to be what he testified about himself. This glorification gave the gift that had been promised through the prophet Joel. For God says: “In the last days I will pour out my Spirit upon all flesh,” and so forth (Joel 2:28).

And the Apostle says, among other things: “When the kindness and humanity of God our Savior appeared—not by works of righteousness that we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us through the washing of regeneration and renewal by the Holy Spirit, whom he poured out upon us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Savior—so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life” (Titus 3:4–7).

The Apostle confirmed what had been promised through the prophet Joel: after Jesus had been glorified, God fulfilled this by pouring out the Holy Spirit upon those who believe in Christ. And this is what it means to become heirs of eternal life: to receive the Holy Spirit. Since the Spirit is eternal, the one who receives him possesses eternal life. He is the pledge of immortality.

For whoever receives him and remains in his love, when this life has passed, proceeds to heaven, to the one whose Spirit he possesses. It is incongruous that one who departs this life possessing the Holy Spirit should be held in hell. The Spirit is the sign in a human being of Christ’s victory, by which he conquered death, so that the person in whom his Spirit is found cannot be held in the underworld.

Consequently, the Holy Spirit was not in the ancient saints as he is now in believers, because, when they departed from the world, they were in the underworld. Nor can it be said that the Holy Spirit, because of Adam’s sin—which, through the transmission of the race, subjected all his offspring to the underworld—was held under the same sentence imposed on Adam.

There is no doubt that the Holy Spirit was with the Prophets and righteous men: with the Prophets for the sake of divine dispensation, and with the righteous on account of their holiness. Thus it is read concerning the holy Simeon: “The Holy Spirit,” it says, “was with him” (Luke 2:25). This was not in him as the sign of adoption, but through the grace of his merits.

For believers first began to be sons of God when the Son of God was revealed to the whole creation after conquering death.

But if the Holy Spirit is said to have been in Adam or in the others in the same way as he is now in believers, what new gifts did God give when he established the kingdom of his Son among us? And how can the Savior’s advent be called a fortunate and blessed time above all others if he granted what had already been granted?

Where then is what the Savior says to the disciples: “Many Prophets and righteous men desired to see what you see, and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matt. 13:17)?

How, then, can it be said that the blessedness of the present time brought no greater gift than had been bestowed upon the ancients? This indeed dishonors the Savior, as though he had nothing new to give to those who received him at the beginning of his reign, even though wealthy people commonly take pains to give their guests carefully selected gifts on the festival of their birthday.

How great, then, is the insult if God is said not to have had unprecedented gifts to give to those whom he invited to a new and unheard-of festival day worthy of all praise?

And where is what the evangelist John says: “He came to his own, and his own did not receive him; but to all who received him he gave power to become sons of God—to those who believe in his name, who were born not from blood, nor from the will of the flesh, nor from the will of man, but from God” (John 1:11–13)?

How, then, is what God gave to believers in Christ not unprecedented, when he gave them power to become sons of God—that is, brothers of his own Son—not by the will of flesh or man, but from God, so that they might be born spiritually?

Or, if this grace is shown to have been granted previously, then let it be said that Christ’s advent brought nothing new.

Adam’s making was certainly carnal and earthly, not spiritual. For he was not born from God without flesh and blood; rather, he was made by God from the earth. Therefore he could not receive the Holy Spirit, since he was not spiritual, and he had not been granted to call God the Father in prayer.

Those who receive the Holy Spirit are given the power, by virtue of possessing the Holy Spirit, to call that Father—the Father of Christians—in prayer. Since this was not granted previously, the earlier generations cannot be said to have had the Holy Spirit.

Those, therefore, who think that Adam or the others had the Holy Spirit do not know what gift of God they possess; nor can they offer him appropriate thanks, since, although they received more than the others, they claim to have obtained nothing more.

## One Work Differs According to the Persons, Whether for Praise or Condemnation

### CXXIV

[Note: [Col. 2372] Absent from the manuscripts of the second class.]

The mercy shown by a rich person and by a poor person is one and the same, but it is reckoned differently to the rich person and to the poor person, because it is more deserving of praise in the poor than in the rich.

The poor person did not fear to give from his scant resources, hoping that God would repay him both in the present and in the future. For he believes the Scripture that says, “Whoever gives to the poor shall not lack” (Prov. 28:27).

Thus that poor widow [Note: [Col. 2372] Ms. Colbertinus: “poor woman.”], while the rich were contributing large amounts, alone deserved to be praised by God, because she did not fear to give from her poverty (Luke 21:2–4).

The rich give confidently from their wealth, but the poor person is confident in the Lord. The rich therefore do well when they give to the needy, but the poor do much better. Accordingly, the reward of the poor and that of the rich are different.

If the rich person does not do this, he will be punished; for so much is not demanded from the poor. Therefore the merciful poor person is praiseworthy.

Theft is one sin in a poor person and in a rich person, but it makes the rich person more guilty. The poor steal because of need, whereas the rich, although they have abundance, are not content with what is theirs and take what belongs to others. Worse still, they commonly strip the poor. Therefore the punishment of the two differs.

The justice of the poor and of the rich is one and the same, but it is more deserving of praise in the poor. To preserve justice in poverty is a magnificent thing. The rich, however, seem to preserve justice because they are strangers to want.

Both are therefore just, but it is greater to preserve justice in necessity.

Pride is one and the same, but it is more deserving of condemnation in the poor than in the rich. The rich person is lifted up by abundance, but the poor person is proud in poverty; that pertains to madness, and therefore the poor person is more guilty.

Humility is one and the same, but it is more deserving of praise in the rich. What is so remarkable if a poor person appears humble, when poverty itself makes him humble? But it is magnificent if one who is commended by dignity and wealth bows down, claiming for himself nothing that he knows he deserves.

Thus humility is good in everyone, but much more so in the rich.

The reason for learning and study is one and the same, but it is more praiseworthy in the rich. When the poor person had no distinction by which he could be commended, he applied himself so that he might have something for which he could be sought.

But the rich person, although he already had grounds for distinction, increased himself through effort, so that he might be needed for a double reason. Wealth did not distract him or withdraw his mind, so as to prevent him from flourishing by his own efforts.

Therefore he is more worthy of praise than the poor person, who, if he had not devoted himself to study, would have remained wholly insignificant. The one was made eager for study by choice, the other by necessity.

Lust is the same in the poor and in the rich, but it is more deserving of condemnation in the poor than in the rich. Poverty itself ought to recall the poor person from the desire for luxury. He ought to consider that he has no means by which to satisfy it; and while he hastens to fulfill it, he must admit many other evils, from which perhaps he will not escape even for the present. Or certainly, by consuming what he possesses on this very thing, he will remain a beggar, marked with disgrace.

The rich, however, are provoked to the pleasure of lust by the abundance of delights. Moreover, the rich are secure in their impunity, knowing that judgments are for sale and that no one will rebuke them. For who would dare to accuse a man supported by dignity and wealth?

For this reason they are inflamed all the more to act violently in this way. They are not reproved at all, but are held in great honor, and they can even glory in being such people.

If both—that is, the poor person and the rich person—are chaste, the chastity of the rich differs greatly from that of the poor. Humility may recall the poor person, preventing him from doing what he wishes, or fear of the laws may do so.

But when the rich person can be drawn toward pleasure by many forces working together, he is praiseworthy if he turns his mind away from it. The chaste rich person therefore deserves one reward, and the chaste poor person another.

If he is a king and is chaste, it is exceedingly glorious: possessing everything in his power, he does not touch what he knows he could do with impunity.

This person truly fears God; this person truly keeps his commandments: possessing power over laws, he contemplates the future judgment of God.

It is therefore a great thing when one who has no one to fear in the present conquers what delights him, since pleasure can be so powerful that he does not fear not only future things but even things in the present.

Accordingly, all who overcome this deserve much; but those deserve more who presently rule over laws and human beings. Others fear both people and laws, and therefore preserve their resolve. They refrain from what is forbidden lest they be ashamed before people, and lest they be condemned.

But for one who, because of his rule, fears neither laws nor human reproach, it is a great glory to abstain.

## Against Eusebius
CXXV [Note: [Col. 2373] Absent in manuscripts of the second class].—I remember reading in a certain little book by Eusebius, formerly an outstanding man in other respects, that even the Holy Spirit does not know the mystery of the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ; and I am astonished that a man of such learning inflicted this stain upon the Holy Spirit. For by saying this he marked Him as degenerate. For He cannot be said to be from God if He does not know the things that belong to God, since an inferior nature does not know what exists in a superior one. But if He is of the same substance and divinity, how can He fail to know what belongs to Him? Finally, because the Son of God says, “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30), on account of the unity of substance He rightly added, saying, “All things that belong to the Father are mine, and the things that are mine are the Father’s” (ibid. 16:15).

Therefore, if the Holy Spirit is of the same divinity, on what grounds is He separated so that He should not possess the same knowledge, when it is not denied that He is of the same substance? He granted what is greater while rejecting what is less [Note: [Col. 2373] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “You grant what is greater, and retain what is less.”]. A creature learns and begins to know certain things about its creator, and what it has learned will be shared with its creator; but substance or divinity cannot be shared by God and a creature. For God’s substance has nothing to learn, since there is nothing it does not know; human substance, however, does not have knowledge by nature, but has the capacity to learn. Thus knowledge happens to human nature; yet the substance is not changed, because human nature lacks knowledge. For it was constituted in such a way that through exercise it acquires knowledge.

Therefore substance is greater than knowledge, because knowledge does not acquire substance, but substance acquires knowledge; and substance exists without knowledge, though knowledge cannot exist without substance. In God, however, just as there is substance, so also there is knowledge. For a substance that has nothing to learn is itself its own knowledge. Hence everything in God is called substantial. A substance lacking nothing possesses everything substantially, because nothing has been added to it after study.

How, then, can it be said of the Holy Spirit that He does not know the birth of the Son of God, if He is consubstantial with Him? Can one and the same substance both know and not know? Certainly the Son of God did not learn the mystery of His own birth; He knows it substantially, not through instruction. On what grounds, then, is the Holy Spirit said not to know, when He likewise has nothing to learn, because He knows everything through substance? For just as the Son of God is the substance of God, so also is the Holy Spirit, since the Lord says, “All things that belong to the Father are mine,” thereby signifying that the substance of God the Father is His own substance.

[Col. 2374] He also says that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and receives from Him: “Therefore,” He says, “I said, He will take from what is mine, because all things that belong to the Father are mine.” If He proceeds from the Father and receives from the Son, how can He fail to know the Son’s birth, when His substance is the Son’s substance? For all things that belong to the Father belong to the Son. Without doubt, therefore, the substance of the Father is also in the Holy Spirit. For the Son added, saying, “And all things that are mine are the Father’s.”

Why, then, is there any doubt whether the Holy Spirit is of the same divinity, since He is of the same substance? For just as the Lord said of Himself that He proceeded from God, so He also bears witness concerning the Holy Spirit. And lest this be interpreted otherwise, He says, “He proceeds from the Father” (John 15:26), and, “He will take from what is mine” (ibid. 16:14), so that proceeding from the Father means receiving from Christ. For when it is said that He receives from the Son of God, there is no doubt that He Himself is also from God, so that it may not be doubted that the substance and divinity of the Father are in the Holy Spirit.

Therefore, whoever says that the Holy Spirit does not know the birth of the Son of God detracts from the One from whom He is said to have received. For He receives nothing other than what He Himself is, from whom He receives; because receiving from Christ signifies proceeding from God. Therefore He cannot fail to know that He is from the One from whom He received; nor should the Lord be said to be unknown to Him, since He proceeded from God.

Certainly the Son of God, because He is from God the Father, knows all things belonging to God. Why, then, should the Holy Spirit be denied knowledge of whatever belongs to Christ, when He received it from Him? Therefore, if the Son of God knows the things that are in God, there is no doubt that the Holy Spirit also does not fail to know the things that are in the Son of God. And by the fact that He knows what is in the Son, He should not be said to be ignorant of what is in God. For from the One from whom He receives, He possesses knowledge of God.

And why do we labor over this, when the Apostle is a witness in this matter, saying, “No one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God” (1 Corinthians 2:11)? Behold, with the Apostle’s help, we have completed the matter over which we labored so long. Did he thereby prejudice the Son of God, because he said that no one knows the things that are in God except the Spirit of God? Certainly not. Nor did the Son prejudice the Holy Spirit when He said, “No one knows the Father except the Son.” For He said that no one knows the things that are in God except the One who is from God, because everything that is from God knows God and the things that are in God.

The nature of God knows itself. When you understand that this nature is also in the Holy Spirit, by the fact that He proceeded from the Father and received from the Son, it is not safe to say that He does not know God the Father, whose nature you recognize in Him. Yet the Savior said, “No one knows God the Father except the Son,” in such a way as to reserve knowledge of Him for another person; for He immediately added, saying, “and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal Him” (Matthew 11:27).

To whom, do you suppose, does the Son wish to reveal Him? No one can be dearer to Him than His own Spirit. For He says, “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to Him” (Romans 8:9). How, then, do you suppose that God the Father was revealed by the Son to the Holy Spirit, unless in the manner in which the Lord Himself says, “He will take from what is mine”?

For God the Father cannot be revealed to a creature, because a creature cannot bear the nature of God unless it is of the same substance. For He dwells in an inaccessible light, inaccessible, that is, to a creature (1 Timothy 6:16).

But some think that it is rightly said that the Holy Spirit does not know the mystery of the birth of the Son of God, because He is said to search all things (1 Corinthians 2:10), and, they say, whoever searches certainly does not know. This must be understood from another passage. Among other things, God’s words say, “I am God who searches the kidneys and hearts” (Jeremiah 17:10); and in the Psalm, “God searches hearts and kidneys” (Psalm 7:10); and the Apostle says, “He who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires, because He intercedes for the saints according to the will of God.”

When the Spirit of God is said to search in these examples, He is not shown to be ignorant. He is also said to search the deep things of God. And what are the deep things of God that He is said to perceive fully? To search signifies to penetrate hidden things, so that by this it is believed that nothing is hidden from Him. For the deep things of God are God’s inner mysteries, which creatures cannot search out.

For He is also read to intercede for the saints according to the will of God, something the saints certainly do not know, since the Apostle says, “For we do not know what we ought to pray for” (Romans 8:27, 26). Therefore, to know the deep things of God and not to be ignorant of the will of God signify the same thing. For what mystery is so deep as the will of God, which is known to the Holy Spirit but unknown to all others?

We must consider how it is said that “no one knows what is in a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him” (1 Corinthians 2:11). By “spirit” he signified the soul, because no one knows what is in a human mind except that person’s mind, which is the spirit. Likewise, in God no one knows the things that are God’s except the Spirit of God—that is, God Himself.

He who is from God [Note: [Col. 2375] The printed editions read “in God,” but the Colbertine manuscript reads “from God”] is understood to be nothing other than what God is. Therefore the Spirit of God knows what is in God, because He is from God. For if no one knows human thoughts except God, how much more can no one know the secrets and will of God unless he is from God—that is, God Himself? For He alone is known to Himself.

Certainly, there are no thoughts in God. For He does not deliberate within Himself about what He should or should not do, considering whether it is expedient, because all things that are in God exist without doubt, not through accident but through substance, not through study but through nature; for He is not changed [Note: [Col. 2375] The Colbertine manuscript reads “they are not changed.”].

Accordingly, the Holy Spirit knows the mysteries of God only through substance. For one substance has one understanding and one will. He speaks of God, who is always one and unchanging, whether in the Son or in the Holy Spirit. What the Father wills, the Son also wills; and what the Son wills, the Holy Spirit wills in the same way.

Therefore He is sometimes called the Spirit of God and sometimes the Spirit of Christ: “who proceeds from God,” and “will take from what is mine.” This is why the apostle John says, “By this we know that God remains in us: by the Spirit whom He gave us” (1 John 3:24). Therefore, if God is said to remain in us when the Spirit of God remains in us, the Spirit of God is shown to be God.

Finally, this is the sign of believers, that they are sons of God: when they receive Him, they dare to call themselves sons of God. For unless they have the sign of divinity, they cannot be called sons of God. Yet no one is a true son of God so as to be wholly from the Whole, as Christ is.

By adoption, however, they become sons of God, so that, receiving the Spirit of Christ, they are called sons of God through Him, because the Spirit whom they possess within themselves is from God. For in sons, even if they are adopted, the substance of the father must nevertheless be seen in some respect.

In the world, because things are imperfect, sons adopted by human beings receive no pledge, but only a name. God, however, because He is perfect, does more: He gives His Spirit to those who are adopted, through whom they may be seen to possess some reality of adoption from Him. For names without realities are empty.

Our Apostle supports this assertion of ours, saying, “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments and inscrutable His ways!” (Romans 11:33).

What, then, does it mean that, although elsewhere he says that the deep things of God—that is, His secrets—are searchable, in this passage he denies it, saying that they are unsearchable? In this passage he spoke of the creature, because the secrets or judgments of God are unsearchable to it. But he said that all the things in God are searchable by the Holy Spirit, because He knows everything belonging to God, so that what is unknown to the creature is asserted not to be unknown to the Spirit of God.

Therefore the nature of God cannot be denied, since it knows what cannot be comprehended by a creature.

Those who call the Holy Spirit degenerate from God strike at the proposition that declared the salvation of the whole creation to consist in the divinity of the Trinity. For if He is not consubstantial with God and Christ, it is foolish to place Him in the number of the Father and the Son, so that without Him no one would possess salvation or dignity. If He is not of the same divinity, then this was done either foolishly or without reason [Note: [Col. 2375] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “or was done graciously.”]—which God forbid.

For who among the prudent would deny that the Creator cannot be numbered together with a creature, that the eternal cannot be compared with one who exists from a beginning, that the Lord cannot be equated with a servant, that the powerful cannot be ranked with the powerless, or that the knowing cannot be counted with the ignorant?

But now let the slander cease. He is third in order, not in nature; in rank, not in divinity; in person, not in ignorance. For just as the Son of God is second from the Father and is not lesser in divinity, so also the Holy Spirit follows the Son, not unequal but equal in the divinity of the substance.

Finally, what we read about the Son of God we also read about the Holy Spirit, who Himself bears witness to us. For He says, “I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Paraclete, the Spirit of truth” (John 14:16). By saying “another,” He signified Himself as the Paraclete. John makes this clear, saying that the Son of God pleads for our sins (1 John 2:2). And the Apostle Paul says, “The Spirit of God Himself pleads for us.”

Behold, Scripture shows that both are advocates. And when He called Him the Spirit of truth, He showed that He differs from Himself in nothing, because He said, “I am the truth” (John 14:6).

He said that He was sent by the Father, and He Himself promised to send the Holy Spirit. If He is not unequal to the One who sent Him, neither is the Holy Spirit unequal to Him who sends Him. For though they are three individually, they are not members one of another, so as to be able to differ. The power of the three is one, so that nothing is lacking in any one of them.

Let this be the end. For what remains concerning the indivisible unity embraced by the Trinity has already been treated more fully in the book composed against Arian impiety.

## ON THE ONE WHO RECEIVED THE FAITH OF CHRIST

[Note: [Col. 2376] Some printed editions add: “what superiority or prerogative he has for obtaining grace, beyond unbelievers.”]

CXXVI.—It is written: “For nothing will benefit the righteous man on the day when he goes astray from his righteousness; and nothing will harm the wicked man in the day when he turns away from his wickedness” (Ezekiel 18:26, 27). And the Lord says in the Gospel, “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3:18), thereby signifying that the one who believes is not subjected to judgment in order to receive a sentence, but will be worthy of praise through the merit of faith.

Therefore knowledge of God has this prerogative: that the sinner obtains forgiveness. For whoever believes that Jesus is the Son of God is found worthy to be freed from all sins. Having long wandered in error and been tossed about by the waves of ignorance through various paths, he has been enlightened and has attained the flash of truth, in which he may rest securely after excessive storms. It is fitting for him, after attaining knowledge, to restrain himself from those things he formerly did while still placed in ignorance.

For what benefit is knowledge if the former manner of life remains? A person appears to have known God by this: that he changes his life and corrects his conduct. Once God is known, He must be feared, because He is proclaimed as the One who will judge, so that the faithful may receive the fruit of their righteousness and the wicked—that is, unbelievers—may pay the punishment fitting their faithlessness.

For it is fitting that the righteous rejoice in the future, where Christ will reign with His own, so that, just as they are now a reproach and subject to injuries in this world, over which the devil is ruler, so also they may appear glorious in the kingdom of Christ, for whose sake they were judged contemptible by worldly people.

But the unrighteous, because they seem falsely to flourish while resisting the truth through deceit, should be troubled in punishment, so that those who appeared glorious through pretense may be seen, in reality, to be despised and exceedingly humbled.

Then the righteous will rejoice that they believed when they see the faithless being tortured. Nor will the faithless regret that they did not believe unless they see the glory of those whom they considered foolish and contemptible, and their own punishment.

Therefore, from the moment a person professes to be a Christian, he must strive not to sin and arm himself against vices. And because it is impossible always to conquer, if he is defeated, he must grieve so that he may not be defeated again; for the one who grieves over being defeated restores himself.

Whoever resists has grounds for excusing himself if he is defeated. For he shows that he had the desire to conquer, but was entirely unable to prevail. There is hope for such a person, because he can restore himself, so that through constant meditation he may be found more skilled and stronger in the struggle.

But whoever rises for the purpose of sinning becomes inexcusable and bears a very serious charge. For it is worse to live under the profession of God while intending to sin than for someone to be ignorant of God and to behave disgracefully and corruptly. [Col. 2377] The latter does not know whom he ought to fear; the former knowingly despises Him.

Believers therefore receive the forgiveness of sins. Yet they will not be glorious unless they live under the fear of God after receiving the faith, so that, having struggled against the enemies of the Christian name, they may win the victory and deserve the reward by conquering more often than they are conquered.

For someone who understands God but does not approach His faith in order to live as a Christian, and who wishes to receive the faith only at the end so that he may die a Christian—or who is ashamed to live as a Christian, or devotes himself to sins that he thinks can be forgiven once he has believed—such a person, I think, does not have a good case.

For he does not wish to become a Christian, or is ashamed to become one, so that he may sin as long as he is in this world. What kind of God does he expect, when he is ashamed to serve Him but wishes to receive pay from Him? Such a person is a mocker.

Knowing that he no longer has time for sinning, with death imminent he then wishes to become a Christian, so that, since he can no longer sin, he may say that he believes in Christ, who condemns sin—not because he no longer wishes to sin, but because he is no longer able to do so, since death has overtaken him.

To such people the saying must be applied: “God is not mocked” (Galatians 6:7). People of this sort are also accustomed to give such instructions, so that faith may be given to those already failing and alienated, who are only gasping for breath, lest they escape and be ashamed because they have become Christians.

To them the words of the Gospel must be recited: “Whoever,” says the Lord, “is ashamed to confess me in this generation” [Note: [Col. 2377] The Colbertine manuscript reads: “For whoever is ashamed of me,” he says, “and of my words in this…”], “the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in the kingdom of His Father” (Matthew 10:33).

But perhaps they say: “Knowing that the human condition is fragile, for this reason we wish to receive the faith at the end of life, so that we may no longer sin.” Yet faith must be received in such a way that one knows what one is receiving. For it will then possess its benefit if one knows it and professes it. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10:10).

Accordingly, how can someone who no longer knows where he is be said to receive it? The one who has received it is the person who professes that he has received it, knowing that he has received it. For if they believe that forgiveness of sins is given to believers, they must know that the person believes who believes with his heart as his witness.

For God, who made the promise, is the examiner of the heart. He receives the very person whom He sees believing in his heart. Therefore, how will the one whose heart does not heed the words of faith possess its benefit?

Thus the person who is seen to act so as not to sin easily may be regarded as becoming a Christian upon receiving the faith, not rashly. But whoever hastens to sin does not wish to receive the faith for this reason: lest he be compelled to live well, which he plainly does not wish to do. He wants to attain it at death, hoping for impunity and forgiveness of past evils, so that he may be secure both concerning the past and concerning the future, because, being about to die, he will in any event no longer be able to sin.

But this is not done with good counsel or a clean conscience: he wishes to receive the faith when he is no longer able, rather than unwilling, to sin. The saying, “Let us do evil so that good may come,” applies to such people; that is, “Let us sin now, and believe at the end, and we shall be forgiven.” Therefore he added, “Their condemnation is just” (ibid. 3:8).

For it is not worthy that forgiveness of sins be given to those who, knowingly recognizing God—who does not wish anyone to sin and hates sinners—eagerly desire to sin, refusing to acknowledge that God’s gift benefits those who sin in ignorance of God, not knowing that God will judge.

But whoever has heard, reflected upon the matter, and has the desire to sin—not because some compelling circumstance overcomes him, but because he wishes to sin—it is difficult to forgive him. For there are two grounds that obtain forgiveness of sins: one of the gift, the other of repentance, so that the one who sins after the gift may be restored through repentance.

Because he did not remain in the grace he had received, so as to persevere in freedom, but again subjected himself to sin, he obtains the blotting out of his sin through lamentation and grief. For he sinned knowingly and deliberately—not that anyone is unaware of sin, but the person who does not know that God will judge thinks that what he sins will go unpunished.

Accordingly, if a Gentile begins to grow weak and, in the very despair of life, reflects within himself upon the faith and the promised hope, he has a sound case, so that, when he believes, his sins may be forgiven and he may not be held in the underworld, carrying with him the sign of death conquered and despoiled, even though he does not possess dignity or reward.

For there ought to be some difference between the person who, provoked by love for his Lord, did not fear to fight against His enemies, arming himself with continence and watchfulness against every vice so that he might resist evil, always concerned with how he might defend the command of his Lord, and the person who, making common cause with his Lord’s enemies and standing beside them, returned to his Lord at the end of life—not to vindicate his Lord’s kingdom, but to benefit himself alone by being a citizen before becoming a soldier.

For the person who wishes to live as a Christian so that he may be rewarded after death knows that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the future glory that will be revealed in us” (Romans 8:18). Accordingly, having taken up the armor of faith, he does not hesitate to engage in battle against rulers and authorities, so that, victorious while existing in this world, he may be crowned after this world.

For it is fitting that the person who now bears witness to the kingdom of his Lord among the faithless and rebellious should receive in the future the reward for this deed. Then the enemies of God, seeing Christ’s witness appear exalted in the kingdom of God because of the truth of his confession, will grieve, ashamed that they considered false what has been shown to be true.

Likewise, those who believed late—not during life but at death, confessing God—will see how great is the glory of those who, serving as soldiers under Christ’s armor, carried on the battles of their commander devotedly and faithfully. They will regret not having lived as Christians, but having died as Christians.

For the person who did not desire to live as a Christian may appear entirely unfit to die as a Christian. Perhaps, already about to die, he wished to be called a Christian for this reason: “Perhaps what is believed is true; I wish to become a Christian, losing nothing if what is believed is false.” And because at death not the desire to sin but sin itself ceases [Note: [Col. 2378] Thus the Colbertine manuscript. The printed editions read: “not the pleasure of sinning”], he tests whether the faith might benefit him after death, when it would certainly have been useful to correct vices and sins here, where they had been committed.

For a person proves that he has condemned his past when, following the line of faith, he is seen to change his conduct and life. If he formerly sinned because he did not know God, then, once he knows Him, he ought not to sin any longer, lest it be useless for him to have known Him. For a person ought to be perfected through knowledge of God.

Before his profession, a Christian ought to understand that he must be proved by his works more than by his name. For this reason the commandments were given as superior to the other laws [Note: [Col. 2378] The Colbertine manuscript reads “purer”], and as pertaining to holiness, so that God’s worship might appear through them. Otherwise they will hear: “Why do you call me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ and do not do what I say?” (Luke 6:46).

By this He then signified that it is beneficial to call the Lord “Lord” if His commandments are kept. For the person who calls Him Lord while despising His commandments appears to be a mocker. To him the words of the Law must be recited, which say that God is not mocked. Therefore he will be condemned by his own words, because he calls Him Lord whom his works show that he does not fear at all.

## ON THE SIN OF ADAM AND EVE

[Note: [Col. 2378] Some printed editions add: “concerning their condition and gratuitous gifts.”]

### CXXVII

[Note: [Col. 2378] Absent from manuscripts of the second class.]

I think no one doubts that this world was fashioned for the sake of the human being. Although it consists of diverse substances, it is nevertheless one, fitted together from many members, so that through their reciprocal services those things might be produced which would be necessary for humanity. For the house was made for the human being together with its provisions, so that each of its parts might be made according to its kind upon the earth—that is, so that the things made might possess within themselves an implanted [Note: [Col. 2378] Thus the Colbertine Manuscript. The printed editions, however, read: “might have from this an unbounded.”] power of reproducing each of the kinds that were to be created upon the earth. For origins were established whose seed would advance toward the propagation of multiplying kinds upon the earth [Col. 2379]. Hence Scripture bears witness: “And God blessed them, saying, ‘Increase and multiply upon the earth’” (Gen. I, 22, 28).

In a similar way the human race also was blessed. We observe this meaning in the Law. For we read that it is written: “The people increased and multiplied in Egypt” (Acts VII, 17). By that blessing with which the things created for human usefulness were blessed, the human being too was blessed, so that likewise the offspring of the human race might grow and multiply upon the earth from male and female; and so that, just as seeds were to be improved through cultivation, the human race also might apply itself with care to this end: having received knowledge of the Creator, it should discipline its life so as to win his favor, so that all things together might advance toward the praise and glory of the Creator.

And since these words signify nothing else, the things themselves bear witness to it. For everything that was made has multiplied and improved upon the earth by God’s will. Nor could it happen otherwise than as God’s will and blessing decreed for the seeds. How, then, can it be said that something is badly done, or that something is unlawful, which grows by God’s blessing and with his favor?

The tradition of this matter remained in the Synagogue and is now observed in the Church: God’s creature is joined together under God’s blessing. This is certainly not presumptuous, since the form was given by the very author. But if it is thought that this must cease, then it ought to cease when those things also cease which were similarly blessed so that they might multiply. For if the generation of human beings ceases, for what purpose are the things born that have been blessed upon the earth? The world cannot act in one part and cease in another. Either it works as a whole, or it rests entirely in idleness. Is a body useful whose members are vigorous in some places and numb in others?

Why, then, do some assert that what has been blessed by the Lord is a filthy and polluted work, unless it is because in this way they are, so to speak, laying hands upon God himself? They would not criticize this unless they thought wrongly about God, the author of the work. Since they fear openly to disparage God, they nevertheless accuse him through the work he devised. For when a work is displeasing, its author is reproved.

If such people were to read—or rather, to accept—the Scriptures, they would remember Balaam saying: “How shall I curse one whom God has blessed?” (Num. XXIII, 8). For the one praised by the judge is accused in vain; indeed, he himself is his own accuser who declares guilty the one whom the laws defend. Who, then, are you, that you think something should be condemned which you read to have been blessed by God? Is it because you deny that this God exists, or because you accuse Scripture of falsehood?

There are people who, as though receiving something new, think that the old things must be rejected. But the new commandments proclaimed to the peoples through Christ do not differ from these. For when he was invited to a wedding, he did not disdain to go; and not only did he honor it by his presence, but he also supplied what was lacking for the celebration (John II, 1–11). For it is written: “Wine gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII, 15; Ecclus. XL, 20).

And to show that he had done this according to the will of God his Father, when the Jews asked whether it was lawful for a man to divorce his wife, he replied among other things:

“Because from the beginning God made male and female, and said: ‘For this reason a man shall leave father and mother and cling to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh.’ Therefore they are no longer two, but one flesh. What God has joined, let no human being separate” (Matt. XIX, 4–6).

For this reason, when invited to a wedding, he went willingly, lest he appear to weaken the work of God his Father. Showing still more clearly that the teaching of the old and new Law agrees, he not only did not forbid marriage but also deigned to attend it, bearing witness that God is its author; and he showed by a saving commandment that what has been joined by God ought neither to be forbidden nor separated.

And because birth is beneficial, when he was already leaving the world he entrusted his mother to his disciple John (John XIX, 26–27). Therefore we too, observing in every respect the commandments of the old and new Law, are taught to honor our parents (Deut. V, 16; Matt. XV, 4). Unless we do this, the Law warns that we shall incur a curse.

What kind of presumption, then, is this, or from what law does it descend, to close the way to marriage, when both the new and the old Law seem in every respect to favor it? But we read that “whatever is beyond this is from evil” (Matt. V, 37). Hence the Apostle says that such people have a seared conscience: they forbid marriage and teach abstinence from foods which God created to be received (I Tim. IV, 2–3). They are marked as doing this hypocritically, out of hostility, in order to incriminate the Law handed down by God.

Others, because they are eager to obstruct salutary commandments, stretch out hostile hands in order to commend the commands of a perverse doctrine; and for this reason they are said to have a seared conscience. For with corrupted minds they know one thing and profess another.

So also the Jews, although they knew that the deeds of the Savior were works of the Holy Spirit, said out of envy that he cast out demons by Beelzebub (Matt. XII, 24), in order to turn the people away from faith in him. Such too is the cunning of those mentioned above. To pretend that they are lovers of holiness and chastity, they say that marriage must be condemned, so that by this means they may be commended and turn the people away from the truth. And, pretending to pursue abstinence, they teach that one must refrain from foods, so that by this means they may present themselves as strangers to the world and hastening toward the heavenly kingdoms; yet afterward, by enticing human minds, they teach that unlawful things are permitted and condemn lawful things as though they were forbidden.

These are Satan’s tricks: to invert causes and, as though introducing something new, exclude the truth, in which there is nothing new, because everything is eternal. Who would not perceive that this interpretation has been devised by adversaries? For who would dare to reject something devised by God, and something that has never harmed anyone, except an enemy of the truth? In order to conceal his own impurity, he preaches the holiness he does not love, so that, while presenting himself as though of good will, he may advise unlawful things as though they were lawful.

He commends himself in order to deceive more readily, and thus, having captured the unwary, he suggests things that make them greater sinners. For in order to provide some remedy for his cause, he strongly urges human beings to sin, seeking great consolation from it: he displays many companions in his crime and considers the punishment light, as though it were less severe if he sees many with him in Gehenna.

Blind people [Note: [Col. 2380] The Colbertine Manuscript reads: “If they see many with them in sins, and not other people while they are overcome by vices.” A little later it reads: “they will defend things that ought not to be vindicated here.”], when they are overcome by vices, defend themselves either through weakness or through ignorance, failing to condemn what a contrary desire deceives them into pursuing. Or what darkness prevents the truth from being seen? For words often seem to signify one thing when they are not pronounced correctly or are improperly punctuated.

But when we read, “God made,” and “He blessed what he made,” who can argue about this? Who can doubt it? Who can think that what has been blessed is accursed, unless he is animated by another spirit? If this were said to be a human voice, perhaps some deception might be believed. But God is said to speak, and you doubt? God blessed, and you reject it?

Perhaps Moses introduced an error under God’s name? Let the signs and wonders performed through Moses in Egypt suffice for you; let the marvels performed in the Red Sea for the deliverance of the children of Israel persuade you. Hear the magicians confessing: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. VIII, 19). Agree with the Apostle, who says:

“I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, that all our fathers were under the cloud, and all passed through the sea, and all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, and all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them; and the rock was Christ” (I Cor. X, 1–4).

And from where did the Apostle speak these words? Scripture is at hand, in which we read that Christ our Lord said to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, because he wrote about me” (John V, 46).

Who would deny faith to this harmony? Who would dare to say that what is one is at variance? Who is so ill-minded as to insist that indivisible love should appear to be enmity? [Col. 2381]

Behold, you have both the testimony of words and examples of virtues, which should subjugate your mind to the truth, so that you do not regard anything as true except what the books of the Catholic Church contain.

Since, therefore, it has been proved that the God who was in the Old Testament is the same as the one who is now ours, and that he is shown to be true by many signs of his virtues, his authority must be preferred to such an extent that even what seems harsh and perhaps absurd to us must be accepted, and understood otherwise than we think, if it is commended by God’s judgment; for we ought to believe God more than ourselves.

Our weakness and ignorance often judge things harmful to be useful and regard falsehoods as truths. To suspect such a thing of God is impious. For there is no nature that can be deceived. How much less, then, should marriage be doubted, when God says: “What God has joined, let no human being separate”?

The matter is open and simple. Certainly every human being rejoices when he has attained God’s favor, and believes himself improved when he learns the Creator’s mystery—which he would certainly not attain unless he had been born. Why, then, does he lament what he rejoices in, and condemn what he boasts of having learned?

If he rejoices because he has learned, but would not have learned unless he had been born, then without doubt it is good to be born, because the fruit of birth is knowledge of the truth. But if it is evil to be born, knowledge will not be good. Of what use will knowledge be if birth is condemned? For if it is neither useful nor right to be born, it is pointless for one who is destined for condemnation to learn.

But since no one is so dull as to deny that knowledge of God benefits human beings, it is both good and useful. Through it birth itself is improved, so that improved birth merits more than was granted to Adam: believers will reign in heaven, not on earth, and in the paradise of God the Father, not in the place where Adam was bodily commanded to work.

Now, if the dedication festival was celebrated in Jerusalem—that is, if a feast was held for the dedication of God’s temple—how much more should the birthday of the human being itself be celebrated, since the human being is more truly God’s temple, and for him too a temple was fashioned by hands for giving thanks to God? For our body is the better temple: the one was constructed by God’s work, the other by human labor; and this one is under the hope of eternity, whereas the other is destined for destruction.

Therefore, whoever knows that he was born by God’s ordinance, so that he may give thanks to God, and who understands God’s mystery, ought to rejoice on his birthday, seeing that the fruit of his birth has advanced.

In truth, those should not have been born who abandon their Creator and assign his glory to others; for their birth advances toward punishment. But it is not birth that incurs guilt; it is the will.

Who are you, then, who forbid marriage? Perhaps Marcion, because you think that the body was not fashioned by God but by the devil; and you maintain that the soul, having fallen through some error, came to the regions of darkness in which the world now exists. How, then, could it be freed from here if generation were forbidden? Born into the world, you came to know your fall, and you deliberately acted so as to return to your native dwelling [Note: [Col. 2381] The Colbertine Manuscript reads “native home.”], restored to your allotted destiny. Finally, you say that you give thanks to Christ, through whom you rejoice that you have attained this knowledge. But consider: if you had not been born, knowledge would cease, and liberation would not follow.

Therefore, if you rejoice that the soul is liberated, favor birth; for if you resist birth, you are an enemy of souls.

Or if you are a Manichaean, who reject marriage as though it were contrary, I ask you: if bodies were not generated at all, how would the soul—which you assert has been poured into the region of darkness and clings to material things—be rescued from here? Your own books say that it is liberated by being born, so that the souls received by the moon and departing from bodies are handed over to the sun, whom you assert to be the god of your souls. For you rejoice when you are called Manichaeans. By this name you demand your liberation—which you certainly would not know unless you had been born.

It is therefore plainly evident that you condemn marriage hypocritically. While professing holiness, you secretly pursue impurity; and this has been exposed not only privately but also in the proclamations of emperors.

[Col. 2382]

Now listen, Catholic, and learn from the Gospel that human birth is beneficial [Note: [Col. 2382] The Colbertine Manuscript reads “as a witness.”].

When Simeon, a just man, wished to depart from the world, thinking that knowledge of the Creator was sufficient for him without knowledge of his mystery, he was not permitted to do so until he had advanced in the perception of God, so that he might receive the full reward of his faith. Finally, when he received the newborn Savior in his hands, he blessed God and said:

“Lord, now you dismiss your servant in peace, according to your word; because my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke II, 29–30).

It was plainly shown that God’s gift is present in human birth when the just man, thinking of death, was told that he would not die before he had seen the Christ of the Lord.
