For he advanced so far in life that he became worthy, even in the present, to see the one whom he hoped would be his liberator after death.

Since, therefore, he was preserved in life and not permitted to die until he had seen the fruit of his hope, so that he could be secure that he was passing from life to life, how can it be said that birth did not benefit him?

If it is evil that we are born, paradise would not be promised, nor eternal life, nor the kingdom of heaven, but punishment and the destruction of Gehenna. A person who knew that he had been born for destruction would fear to beget another; and one who knew that he had been unlawfully born would not desire to beget.

But perhaps someone will say: “The kingdom of heaven has indeed been promised, but to the faithful and those who act well.” Correct. You see, then, that human beings do not become guilty because they have been born, but because they have lived badly.

The kingdom of heaven was not promised to the unborn, so that those to whom it would not be given might attribute this to birth. Rather, it was promised to those who have been born and act well, so that birth neither benefits the one who acts badly nor harms the one who acts well. Birth is improved by the faithful and those who act well; by the faithless and those who act badly it is made worse.

Birth is like a tree that is grafted. If it is grafted with a good shoot, it will become better and be called good; but if it is grafted with a bad shoot, it will become worse and be called not good but bad. Likewise, if good teaching is added to birth, it will produce good fruits; but if bad teaching is added, it will produce bad fruits.

Therefore, just as a tree is necessary so that there may be a place for grafting, birth is also necessary so that there may be a place for advancement.

But the opposite response is made: “If birth is useful, why are we born again?” We would not be born again unless birth were useful. To be born again is to be renewed, and those who are renewed are restored. Rebirth, therefore, does not accuse birth but reforms it; and what is reformed is shown to have been rightly established from the beginning.

Thus, because we are born again, we are changed by deliberation, having received cleansing of the body, so that we may be restored to Adam’s original condition. The body was stained by the soul’s sin; when the body has been repaired and improved through faith, it is cleansed by deliberate purpose. Just as it had been polluted through contempt of God, so it is cleansed through obedience, so that it may escape the sentence given to Adam and be able to rise again.

Therefore, if sin began with the soul, why is the body’s nature accused [Note: [Col. 2382] Thus the Colbertine Manuscript. The printed editions instead read: “Why is it not the body that is accused?”], when, in Adam’s sin, there was no bodily desire, but the soul, enticed by the hope of divinity, transgressed God’s command, so that it subjected its body to sin and human beings were born under sin?

This does not harm the human being, provided that he obeys God’s law, except that he dies. For this, God’s benevolence promised a reward: since the faithful are found devoted to the Creator, while through Adam’s transgression they have been subjected to corruption and death, for this reason they will receive from God the judge [Note: [Col. 2382] Thus the Colbertine Manuscript. The printed editions instead read: “so that those who are found faithful in devotion to the Creator may be saved. But because through transgression they have been subjected to Adam’s corruption and death, for this they will receive from God the judge.”] more than had been granted to Adam: in the future they will be glorious, possess eternal life, and be called adopted sons of God, so that their birth will have been a gain.

From this point I shall return to the remaining part of the reading.

When the human being had been placed in paradise, he received these commandments:

“From every tree that is in paradise you shall eat for food. But from the tree by which good and evil are distinguished, you shall not eat from it” [Col. 2383].

All the trees that Scripture mentions are fruits for the nourishment of creatures. Finally, they are all called by the single name “trees,” but different fruits are understood. They are all trees, and the manner of eating them is one, although the things eaten are different.

Since he had created many fruit-bearing trees for human beings to eat, as I said, he forbade eating from one tree, so that those who had received everything under their power might show reverence for the Creator in some respect. One tree was reserved, permission regarding it being withheld, so that they might remember the condition imposed by the law.

But how can the kind of sin be understood from the sentence of punishment? For this sentence also applies to a murderer, a sorcerer, an adulterer, and an infamous person. Achan son of Carmi, too, when he sinned, was condemned to be destroyed together with all that belonged to him (Josh. VII, 1). How, then, can this sentence be understood as indicating the kind of sin? It can be recognized as a great offense, but not as indicating the kind of offense. For we know that others have been condemned by this sentence, although they are known to have sinned in another way.

The Amorites [Note: [Col. 2383] The Colbertine Manuscript reads “and Haman.”] and the Sodomites also are known to have perished with all that belonged to them. Thus it happens both that those guilty of a single sin are struck by different sentences and that sinners guilty of different crimes are punished by one and the same kind of punishment.

For this reason, the kind of sin cannot be understood from the sentence given to Adam and Eve. Although their sin was one, the man and the woman received sentences according to their respective persons. The serpent too received a sentence, so that they might not remain merely in the condition into which they had fallen, but that labor might also be added to them as punishment.

Since all cattle and animals had been subjected to the human being, as we read (Gen. I, 26), the serpent raised itself against this arrangement and, by deceit and trickery, subjected the human being to itself. Without doubt, whoever captures another places that person beneath himself.

Therefore, lest the serpent should gain the result of its cunning, God’s sentence reverses its position and presses it lower than it had been made, so that it would not be above the human being. Thus, through its cunning, it would suffer not only that it had accomplished nothing but also that it had made its own condition worse.

Although it is read to have been more prudent than the other beasts, after it deceived the human being it was cursed above all the beasts of the earth.

After the sentence given to the man, the sentence given to the woman, and the sentence given to the serpent, it follows that the woman whom the serpent had joined to itself in despising God’s law should also receive a sentence. He said to her:

“I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sadness you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” (Gen. III, 16).

No one confirms what he condemns himself. If children were granted because she had usurped intercourse, then usurpation accomplished more. But since he said, “In sadness you shall bear children,” if you think that generation took its beginning from this, where is the command that had been given: “Increase and multiply”?

Understand, therefore, that this was added only as a punishment: since it had previously been granted to her through joy, sadness was imposed as a penalty. And so that a harsher and multiplied punishment might continually oppress the woman, “your turning shall be toward your husband” was added, so that there might be another source from which her pain could be renewed.

If the Lord condemned intercourse, why did he add among the things subjected to punishment, “Your turning shall be toward your husband”? No one establishes as punishment the very thing he condemns, since punishment is necessarily contrary to condemnation and never proceeds from the same thing but against it. If both were the same, no one would fear condemnation.

Furthermore, someone would learn to do this from the very thing through which he saw that the law had been violated [Note: [Col. 2383] Thus the Colbertine Manuscript. The printed editions read “would learn.”]. This would be confirmation, not punishment, of the sin: if the woman’s turning toward her husband, and the thing she cultivates rather than what is true, were believed to have been imposed upon her as a punishment—although this turning had simply been granted from the beginning, together with final servitude—because through the woman, who had been granted to him, the man had become subject.

The woman certainly appeared to be superior, since the man, following her counsel, thought that what she advised would be beneficial, so that the work of God might seem to have been overturned through the serpent’s subtlety. It is restored through the sentence established by God, so that the woman, humbled before the man, might return to the condition of subjection in which she had been established. To this was added what is added as punishment, when she hears:

“I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning. In sadness you shall bear children, and your turning shall be toward your husband, and he shall rule over you” [Col. 2384].

Had it been decreed otherwise than that the woman should be subject to the man’s dominion? From this, then, it is evident that the woman was recalled to what had already been established, with an addition. Hence he says: “I will greatly multiply your sorrows and your groaning.” What fills something appears to add to what is deficient, not to work upon what does not exist.

Therefore, by this sentence—which had previously been pronounced, “Increase and multiply” (Gen. I, 22, 28)—he does not begin the act of creating, but brings destruction upon the creature that had been granted. Pain is added to the woman in bearing children, and difficulty is imposed; a new form of procreation is not established.

For if generation is rightly thought to have arisen from this, it can more readily be understood to have originated from the serpent’s decision than from the Lord’s. And it is truly as that saying has it: “Brood of vipers” (Matt. III, 7).

If anyone thinks that he was born in this way, let him consider what he deserves: because of sin, the pain of childbirth was increased for her, so that pain on account of children might increase for the woman who would otherwise have had only a small amount of pain. For children are born with groaning and sorrow, and births are not reckoned without sadness.

Now, third, a sentence of this kind is pronounced against the man:

“Because you listened,” he says, “to the voice of your wife and ate from the tree concerning which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat from it,’ cursed is the earth in your labors; in your sorrows you shall eat from it all the days of your life. Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Gen. III, 17–18).

Here too Adam is recalled to what he had been made for, but with a diminution. Previously he had been placed in order simply to work the earth, so that the result of labor would follow him. But when he rejected God’s command, believing that the serpent’s counsel would provide better for him than God had done, he was recalled to his original purpose with the cost of labor. The earth would not respond to him according to his labor; it was cursed not for his own sake but in his works, so that it might be shown that God’s purpose cannot be overturned and that no one can provide better than God.

For no one can love another’s work more than the one who made it, as the Apostle says: “No one hates his own flesh; rather, he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the Church” (Eph. V, 29).

Let us now see whether what follows in the Law agrees with its beginnings.

When Abraham had pleased God, among the other things that pertained to the reward of his faith, he was judged worthy, although advanced in years, to beget one son (Gen. XVIII, 10). How, then, can something be accused that appears to have been granted as a reward, so that God might fulfill the desire of the one who had done God’s own will? That desire would certainly not have been fulfilled unless it were innocent; nor would God fulfill what he saw being sought wrongly or foolishly, especially by one who pleased him. Such conduct would not even be fitting for a human being.

And when Hannah was barren and loved God, she asked that she might have a son, and she received one (I Sam. I). If this had been contrary to God’s will, she could have been warned by the one whom she loved not to request something harmful.

Samuel, who was born from her and was most holy, begot sons, yet did not diminish the merits of his righteousness. From his earliest age he continually advanced, so that in old age he might be commended by the more abundant testimony of God.

The priest Zechariah too, a righteous man, begot a son in his old age by God’s will; before the child was born, he was found worthy to prophesy (Luke I, 5). By what reasoning, then, is something accused that is proved not to harm anyone? And who would deny that something must be called good if it harms no one?

To say something here also about the Apostles, which bears upon the strength of the case: certainly holy John was a guardian of chastity; but his fellow disciple, holy Peter, is known to have had a wife, and his having fathered children did not prevent him from receiving primacy among the Apostles.

How, then, can something be thought condemnable that does not impede merit? Hence the Apostle shows that a man who has a wife, provided that he observes the commandments in other respects, can and ought to become a priest. If this were unlawful, he could not possibly say that a sinner ought to become a priest.

And what could be clearer? For it is the voice of this same Apostle who says: “Concerning virgins, I have no commandment of the Lord” (I Cor. VII, 25). When the Corinthians were being harassed by heretics who hypocritically taught that marriage must be condemned, they wrote to the Apostle to ask whether it was lawful to marry or to send away one’s wife [Col. 2385]. Then the Apostle commanded that a wife ought not to depart from her husband. If he had known that he ought to teach that marriage was unlawful, he had the opportunity to say so; instead, he shows that he cannot teach what had not been handed down to him.

And which of the disciples would teach what had not been handed down by the teacher? Or who would fail to hear him preaching: “I want young women to marry and bear children” (I Tim. V, 14)?

But perhaps someone will say: “If it is lawful and good to marry, why are priests not permitted to have wives? That is, why is intercourse not permitted to those who have already been ordained?”

Who does not know that each thing has its own law? There is something that is altogether and generally unlawful for everyone; there is also something lawful for some and unlawful for others; and there is something lawful at one time and unlawful at another.

Fornication is always unlawful for everyone. Conducting business, however, is lawful at one time and unlawful at another. Before someone becomes a member of the clergy, he may conduct business; once he has become one, he may not.

A Christian may at one time have intercourse with his wife, and at another time may not. On account of the days of procession, intercourse is sometimes not permitted, because even lawful things must be abstained from so that what is requested may more easily be obtained. Hence the Apostle says that abstinence should be practiced for a time by mutual consent, so that they may devote themselves to prayer (I Cor. VII, 5).

According to the Law, striking and quarreling are not permitted during a fast, but afterward they are permitted, because greater reverence is owed to matters concerning God. Is everything that is permitted before other people also permitted before the emperor? [Col. 2386] How much more is this true in matters concerning God?

Therefore his bishop must be purer than others. For he appears to bear Christ’s person and is his vicar, so that what is permitted to others is not permitted to him, because he must daily act in Christ’s place: either pray for the people, offer the sacrifice, or baptize.

And intercourse is not permitted not only to him but also to his minister, because he too must be purer, since the things he ministers are holy.

For just as, in comparison with a lamp, darkness is not merely obscure but also dirty; in comparison with the stars, a lamp is darkness; in comparison with the sun, the stars are misty; and in comparison with God’s brightness, the sun is night—so things that are lawful and clean for us are, in comparison with God’s dignity, as though unlawful and unclean. Although they are good, they do not suit God’s person.

Is not an ordinary person’s tunic, although clean, nevertheless dirty and unlawful for an emperor? Likewise, is not a Saxonician garment [*Saxonicia*] unsuitable for a senator?

Therefore God’s bishops must be purer than others, because they bear Christ’s person; and God’s ministers must be cleaner, too. No one ministers to an emperor without being carefully prepared; therefore they minister clothed in bright and clean garments. But since God is by nature supremely radiant, his ministers ought to be clean by nature rather than merely by their clothing.

To him be praise and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

---

## [The Other Questions of the Old and New Testaments]

[Col. 2385]

## Notice Prefixed to the Questions of the Old and New Testaments after Their Publication

At the beginning of the preceding book you have a double table of contents. One presents the collection of the preceding one hundred twenty-seven Questions, first published by Augustine of Regensburg, John Amerbach, and Desiderius Erasmus. The other represents a collection much larger not only in the different arrangement of the Questions but also in their number.

When Jacobus Haemer had obtained a copy of this second collection from the Victorine Library, he arranged for the following Questions to be brought to light—namely, those that he observed either had not yet been published or had certainly been treated in different words.

He himself divided them into three classes. In the printed editions the first is entitled “The Second Part of the Questions from the Old Testament.” The others are similarly called “The Second Part of the Questions either from the New Testament or mixed from both.” Yet the Victorine codex, together with other manuscripts examined by us, contains in both classes all the Questions, arranged in the same method and order as those found in the table of contents printed above.

We thought that nothing should be changed in the division established by Haemer and already confirmed by later editions, except that it seemed appropriate to transfer some Questions from there into the earlier book of the first-published collection. Thus, when Questions dealing with the same subject are placed beside one another, you may immediately perceive what differences exist between them; and you may also judge which collection is older and more reliable in the manuscripts—or rather, whether both reflect the hand of an inept interpolator.

For the rest, the theologians of Louvain wish the same judgment to be made about the work that follows as about the preceding one. It contains, they say, various matters unworthy of Augustine and alien to the truth.

[Col. 2385]

## [Questions]

### Second Part of the Questions from the Old Testament

### Against Those Who Deny That Anything Pertains to God
## QUESTION ONE  
*[Note: [Col. 2385] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Many people whom this worldly darkness has blinded are exceedingly displeased with us if we diligently observe God’s commandments, avoid opportunities for wrongdoing, strive with saving zeal to fulfill every good duty, disregard the seductive allurements of pleasures and vices, allow ourselves to be captivated by no worldly sweetness, willingly undergo torments and punishments for God’s name, and despise death itself through the strength of the spirit. This is evidently the opinion of those whom this mortal perception has persuaded that nothing which occurs is worthy either of praise or blame [Col. 2386]. For they do not wish any of these matters to pertain to God.

Some, wishing so ardently to defend their crimes and offenses, say: “It makes no difference whether you live well or badly. For God is not now concerned with such things, so as to hasten anxiously to observe you acting differently according to your own inclination and diseased condition, or at some point to stain his eyes with your foul deeds. All things celebrated as one pleases are empty. Whatever pertains to God is hidden and remote from these human affairs, and therefore he neither grows angry nor is moved. He has no contemplation of human affairs, none of our conduct. The entire course of the revolving age, and a certain inexplicable whirling of the world’s sphere, seizes and casts everything away so violently that anyone is believed foolish who supposes that he can recall himself to God’s concern [Col. 2387]. Nor is the spirit of the martyrs to be approved, since they declare God merciful but suppose that he delights in the shedding of their blood. Nothing in us is dear to him, nothing hateful; he rejoices neither at any condition of our death nor at the soundness of our health. Nor does he desire to know what is being done where. This is not because it would be impossible for the divine majesty to possess knowledge of nearly everything that has been done or is being done, but because he does not wish to know the miseries of human beings and the vanities of the world.”

Thus it is written: “Vanity of those who practice vanity [Note: [Col. 2387] The printed editions have *vanitatum* (“of vanities”), and shortly afterward *Dei jussus auctoritate* (“by the authority of God’s command”). The manuscripts have *vanitantium* (“of those who practice vanity”), and *divini sensus auctoritate* (“by the authority of the divine meaning”).], all is vanity” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

Their opinion, fortified by despair, is dissolved by the authority of the divine meaning; and it is refuted and overcome by the common sacred speech of those very people, which is most widely used. For when, amid business dealings and various contracts, good faith and treachery contend, the divinity whom they deny ever knowing what we do is summoned as witness. “God is my witness,” they say; “Let God see; let God judge; let God bring it about; let God repay.” When the necessity of an oath arises, and the mind of the person swearing fears that something may happen to him if he perjures himself, he both demands an oath and trusts that it can be repaid to him by the one who swore falsely to him. When desired health and good physical condition have been attained, thanks are returned to the divinity. When, after some object has fallen, someone escapes the impending accident unharmed, the good God is said to have granted it. When waves rise under an adverse blast of wind, the sea is thrown into turmoil, and the ship is battered and shaken on every side, the crowds of sailors raise their hands to heaven, implore God with suppliant voices, and trust that they can be heard and delivered.

How can these things be so if God has no concern for us and does not know what we are doing? This belief, then, is empty. Everything is known to God. Let no one flatter himself that the crimes he has committed will go unpunished. The greatest fruit of a good life is everlasting reward; of an evil life, perpetual punishment and eternal torments. Therefore, for us who believe that God knows all things and who devoutly hasten toward martyrdom, an immeasurable reward—perpetual life—will be granted. But for the impious, who have taught that God does not know the hidden things of their crimes and offenses, consuming flames and a fire that never ceases will be provided.

## II  
*[Note: [Col. 2387] Found above among the first published collection, beside Question 41.]*

Is the Spirit who was borne over the waters to be understood as the Holy Spirit, since it is said: “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters” (Genesis 1:2)?

If some people think that this is the Holy Spirit because the Spirit is read to be God’s Spirit, etc.

## III  
*[Note: [Col. 2387] The same subject is treated in the manuscripts of the first type, Question 123, but in an entirely different manner.]*

If Adam, when made and animated by God, received the Holy Spirit, since it is written: “God breathed into his face the spirit of life” (Genesis 2:7).

It was not appropriate for him to receive the Holy Spirit, because God reserved this for the future, so that in the last days, when the mystery of the one God had been revealed, he might be given to believers.

From the beginning the Trinity was proclaimed, but its meaning was, as it were, concealed beneath a veil. The person of God the Father was first proclaimed and manifested without hesitation or figure, because all things are from him. But the persons of his Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, and of the Holy Spirit were neither left unmentioned nor manifested. Finally, the unbelieving raise a question about the Lord, and about the Holy Spirit as well. For some madmen say that the Holy Spirit is the Father himself, just as Sabellius says that the one who is the Son is himself the Father. But no one doubts the person of God the Father.

Therefore, when the Trinity is manifested, only then is the Holy Spirit given to believers, so that his person may be manifest and those who receive him may possess a sign that they are children of God, because they have within themselves the Spirit of God, who certainly comes from God. For this is the sign of perfection, when it is known that there are both the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. This perfection bestows this gift.

For when the Son of God came, unveiling and manifesting these things, [Col. 2388] he ought to give something more, and it was fitting that he should grant this perfection to believers; for perfection or salvation is found neither in the Son alone nor in the Father alone, but in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Hence the evangelist John says that “from his fullness we have all received, grace for grace: for the Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:16–17).

It is clear that, when the Savior came, the fullness of truth was accomplished. When what had been hidden and what had been promised is revealed and manifested, the fullness of truth is brought about. Then believers, having received the Holy Spirit, become children of God.

For the inspiration said to have been made by God in Adam is the transmission of the soul. The spirit is frequently used for “soul,” as the Gospel says, among other things: “And his spirit returned to her” (Luke 8:55). And in the Psalm: “A contrite spirit and a broken heart God does not despise” (Psalm 50:19).

Nevertheless, some books do not read, “God breathed,” but “God blew into his face the spirit of life, and the human being became a living soul.” It is not because it says “the spirit of life” that it signifies the Holy Spirit. For it also says of the animals: “In which there was the spirit of life” (Genesis 7:22). It is called “the spirit of life” because it animates bodies for life.

## IV  
*[Note: [Col. 2388] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Why was Adam, when placed in the world, given a commandment or law, although he himself possessed dominion over the other creatures?

Although Adam was placed as lord in the world, since he received this not from himself but from God, he ought to receive through the law a sign of this fact: that he who appeared to be lord might through the law be subject to the one who had given him this power. Thus the authority of the Creator would inspire him with reverence through the law, lest such great dominion exalt him and make him forget God his creator.

## V  
*[Note: [Col. 2388] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Why does God say: “My Spirit will not remain in these human beings, because they are flesh; their years shall be one hundred and twenty,” etc. (Genesis 6:3)?

Since giants were upon the earth in those days—pestilential and arrogant, lifted up by their great stature, pursuing the desires of the flesh, and born as apostates—when God was displeased, he promised that he would destroy the human race by a flood and set a period of time, so that if anyone, hearing of God’s anger and indignation, wished on that account to reform himself, he might have time to amend his ways.

For this reason the ark appears to have been built over a period of one hundred years. Twenty years, however, are said to have elapsed before the construction of the ark began. But the narrative seems to obscure this, since after speaking about Noah’s number of years it adds the following. For this sentence is recognized as having been pronounced before Noah was five hundred years old. What does it say? “My spirit will not remain in these human beings”; and therefore it adds: “Because wickedness has increased upon the earth, I will destroy [Note: [Col. 2388] The manuscripts have *deleam*, “I will destroy,” rather than *delebo*.] the human being from the face of the earth, even to the animals”—which was certainly fulfilled when the flood occurred.

For we remember that after the flood human beings lived for many years; and Aaron, the brother of Moses, is recorded to have lived one hundred and twenty-three years (Numbers 33:38–39). Moses himself, however, was prevented from passing beyond one hundred and twenty years because he did not glorify God when the water was contested. For he would have entered the promised land if sin had not stood in the way (Deuteronomy 34:7; 32:48–52).

Some think that this statement refers to the time of Moses, since Jehoiada the priest is found to have lived one hundred and thirty years (2 Chronicles 24:15).

## VI  
*[Note: [Col. 2388] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

What does Jacob’s blessing, which he gave to his sons, contain (Genesis 48–49)?

He not only foretold the future of each tribe from present circumstances, but also signified future developments concerning things that did not yet have even a shadow among the Jewish people. He showed what each tribe would later be in character, faith, discipline, luxury, wantonness, and contempt of faith: although they came from one man, they would not preserve unity [Col. 2389].

Some advanced for the better, others deteriorated, and others remained as they were. Thus they could not claim for themselves any privilege based on their ancestry, since it had been foretold by that very ancestor that some of those who certainly came from his lineage would become reprobate—indeed, that many would perish—so that others would be understood to enter in and be incorporated, to the shame and condemnation of those who had fallen from the nature into which the newcomers were inserted.

He therefore declared that a mixed people would arise among all the tribes, so that through this diversity both the good, though few, and the evil, though many, might be understood. And although he gave his son Joseph the scepter for a time, he appointed Judah over all. This was not because all who came from Judah would prove worthy, but because the Savior, who is truly king, was descended according to the flesh from that tribe.

## VII  
*[Note: [Col. 2389] Found above among the first published collection, beside Question 42.]*

Why did the angel sent to speak to Moses appear in fire and in a bush?

The angelic nature is simple in itself, and its substance desires the higher things, etc.

## VIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2389] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Was the serpent the only sign that Moses openly performed before Pharaoh (Exodus 7:10)?

Let anyone who considers this blameworthy say what else ought to have been done. Certainly he made a serpent that would inspire terror but would not cause harm, since, by reason of a certain stupor, it is slower to inflict injury. For if he had made a lion, a bear, or something similar, how could those who were present have escaped? He did not wish to kill anyone, but only to instill fear and display power.

Since the first transgression began through a serpent, the remembrance of the knowledge of God and the correction of conduct would likewise come through the sign of the serpent, so that just as sin had come through it, it might also be corrected through it. In the same way, sin was committed through a woman and was taken away through a woman—namely Mary, the mother of the Lord, from whom Christ was born and condemned sin. Eve transgressed while still a virgin, just as Mary was a virgin.

Thus what had been lost was restored to its original condition. The kingdom had been lost through the taste of a tree, and it was again sought through a tree. For the Lord, it says, “reigned from the tree” (Psalm 96:10). Likewise, the world in which he was made must also be renewed in it—namely, at the beginning of the first month, which is Easter.

Therefore no nature will be evil except transgression alone, since sin was corrected through the means by which it had also been committed.

## IX  
*[Note: [Col. 2389] Found above among the first published collection, beside Question 87.]*

If there is one God, why is the hope of salvation in three, and not in two, or four, or certainly in one? And why was the Trinity not proclaimed earlier?

God is indeed one, but he is not solitary, etc.

## X  
*[Note: [Col. 2389] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Why were circumcision and commandments given to the people, when they had not existed earlier and are not now held to be authoritative?

Circumcision is the sign of Abraham’s faith, so that when this sign was seen in his sons, they might be known to be the sons of him who, believing in God, had received the sign (Genesis 17:10–11).

The commandments concerning the sabbaths were given both as a testimony to past things and as figures of future things (Exodus 20:9–11). For this sabbath, which was made in the completed week, is a figure of the future sabbath that will give rest in eternity.

The law concerning foods, however, was not given at the beginning of the Law. Rather, when, under the leadership of unbelief, they refused to give credence to God’s words and promises, they received commandments that were not good, in accordance with the hardness of their hearts, as the prophet Jeremiah says (Ezekiel 20:25). This was done so that their neck might be pressed down, for their advancement. The whole of creation ought not to be subjected to proud and stubborn people.

Afterward, however, when God’s mercy came, the freedom to eat was restored. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Why do you impose upon the neck of the brothers a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

[Col. 2390]

## XI  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

If the Jews had received harsh commandments because of their distrust and complaints, what had their children done wrong, so that they too should be bound by these commandments?

The law was given to the fathers, and it was to be an equal burden for their children. Later they sinned against God no less, and perhaps even more, than their fathers had. For God, who knew the future, gave this law more particularly to the children, because all the fathers died in the wilderness.

## XII  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Why was even Aaron commanded in the Law to offer burnt offerings for his sins, when David says: “You did not require a burnt offering for sins” (Psalm 40:7), and in the following passage: “You will not delight in burnt offerings” (Psalm 51:18)? How did he command something in which he does not delight?

It is clear that God does not delight in burnt offerings, but that forgiveness can be earned for sin through groaning and sorrow of heart, as satisfaction. He wished the sacrifice to be a testimony to sin, so that the sinner might confess through the offering of the sacrifice that he had sinned.

But he showed elsewhere how remission was obtained, saying: “Break your bread for the hungry; if you see someone naked, clothe him, and do not despise those of your own household” (Isaiah 58:7); or certainly: “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Psalm 51:19).

First, therefore, he instructed that the offense be confessed; then he showed how forgiveness might be obtained. For he never commanded a sacrifice for an obvious offense, but for offenses committed unknowingly, because a human being sins even when unaware and, when he thinks he is acting rightly, transgresses through a certain intention. He said that such sin could be cleansed through sacrifice.

## XIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Found among the first published collection, beside Question 37.]*

What does it mean that death, having been sent into Jacob, came upon Israel, when Jacob himself is Israel?

He gave one people two names. For the one who was previously called Jacob, etc.

## XIV  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Found above among the first published collection, beside Question 36.]*

If the soul that sins shall itself die, why does it appear that thirty-six men were killed because of Charmi’s sin?

Charmi indeed sinned and died by stoning. But those thirty-six men, etc.

## XV  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Same place, Question 40.]*

What does the prophet mean when he says: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not give birth; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not suffer labor, because the children of the deserted woman are more numerous than those of her who has a husband”?

In this passage we understand two mothers, the heavenly and the earthly—that is, free Jerusalem, etc.

## XVI  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Same place, Question 38.]*

“Let the earth bless the Lord,” he says—that is, “let it praise and confess your power.” How, then, does it say in the Psalms: “Will dust confess to you, or announce your power?” (Psalm 30:10).

It is not to be understood in the way it is read and in which the words sound, etc.

## XVII  
*[Note: [Col. 2390] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

“In the sun,” he says, “he placed his tabernacle” (Psalm 19:5)—that is, his body in which Christ dwelt, who was scourged by Pilate. How, then, is it said in the Psalm concerning Christ: “The scourge will not approach your tabernacle” (Psalm 91:10), when he himself said that his body was the temple?

The body of the Son of Man and of the Son of God is understood to be the temple. God, however—that is, the Son of God—although he came in the flesh, nevertheless dwelt in the soul. Therefore both the soul and the body are the tabernacle of the Son of God, although he is one God and human being, Son of God and son of man.

Accordingly, in this respect the scourge is said not to have approached his tabernacle—that is, his soul, in which his divinity dwells. It was free from the punishment of hell and from that of its rulers.

Lest anyone suppose that, because he was crucified here as though he were a sinner although he was innocent, and because his flesh suffered, his soul also suffered some sorrow among the dead, Scripture shows that his soul could not be troubled among the dead. He descended for this purpose—that is, he permitted himself to suffer—to confound the darkness and make its rulers dull and powerless.

Hence the Lord himself says: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew 26:38). He permitted it to be sorrowful, as was proper to its nature, while immediately carrying back a trophy and the spoils of those by whom it had been saddened unto death, and after death being established in eternal joy.

This may also be understood of the whole human being, because one who knew no sin could not be scourged by the Law.

## XVIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2391] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Why did Solomon possess the spirit of wisdom (1 Kings 3), although he did not lead a pure life? For he was exceedingly fond of women and consequently sinned (ibid. 11).

At first he received the spirit of prudence on account of his own merit. But after he began to associate excessively with women and thereby to sin, if he possessed the spirit of wisdom, he possessed it on account of the merit of his kingship—just as Nebuchadnezzar, on account of the merit of his kingship, saw Christ in the furnace.

[Col. 2392]

## XIX  
*[Note: [Col. 2392] Found above among the first published collection, beside Question 39.]*

In Solomon it says: “Hope exists in darkness, and a living dog is better than a dead lion.”

Darkness signifies ignorance and paganism, because there is hope in a pagan rather than in an apostate, etc.

## XX  
*[Note: [Col. 2392] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

In Wisdom it says: “He who created the world from unseen matter”; and elsewhere, in opposition to this: “We were made from nothing” (Wisdom 11:18; 2:2).

The meaning of the Scriptures declares that God created the substances while they were still confused, with darkness mixed into them. He called this confusion of things—that is, air, fire, water, earth, and darkness—“unseen matter,” just as it is read in Genesis: “But the earth was invisible and unformed” (Genesis 1:2).

From this confusion, therefore, he created the world by establishing the firmament, so that within it, after the waters had been gathered together in one place, a dwelling might be made for the human race. Having distinguished and separated the substances, he made a habitable home in the concavity.

# SECOND PART OF THE QUESTIONS FROM THE NEW TESTAMENT

[Col. 2391]

## QUESTION ONE  
*[Note: [Col. 2391] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Why were the deeds and sayings of the Lord arranged in writing in four volumes by four authors?

It was fitting that the Lord’s acceptable year, as the prophet says (Isaiah 61:2), should be contained in four volumes, as if in four seasons. For just as the year unfolds through four seasons, each requiring the others, so the Lord’s deeds and sayings were defined in four books, in such a way that each requires the other. Together, however, they are complete in their fullness.

The reason they were arranged by four authors was this: since the seasons have different names, the Gospels likewise should have different titles. And if certain things appear contrary in wording, they do not differ in meaning, because of an interpretation suited to the matter. The seasons, too, although they appear to differ in name, in air, and in the course of the stars, nevertheless do not differ in the effects of what is generated.

## II  
*[Note: [Col. 2391] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Since it is established that four books have been properly written concerning the Lord’s deeds and sayings, it should be known what their order is.

The Gospel is arranged more according to order than according to time. Matthew, therefore, must be placed first, because he took his beginning from the promise itself—that is, from Abraham, to whom the promise of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ was made.

After him comes Luke, because he narrates how this incarnation took place. Mark is third, because he testifies that the Gospel preached by Christ had been promised in the Law.

John is fourth, because he openly shows that the one who had been promised to Abraham as destined to become incarnate, and whom Luke had described as incarnate, and whose Gospel Mark had shown to have been preached according to the prophet Isaiah, is God, saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1).

## III  
*[Note: [Col. 2391] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Why, when describing the Gospel of Christ, does Matthew say: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (Matthew 1:1), when Abraham comes first?

He began in this way so that he might first speak of him, describing the genealogy of his incarnation from the promise, as the Apostle says: “Whose are the fathers, and from whom Christ is according to the flesh” (Romans 9:5).

Therefore he said, “the book [Col. 2392] of the generation,” because Christ’s incarnation consists of many and diverse people: since diverse peoples began from one, he drew bodily substance from them all. From Jews and Gentiles, from the worthy and the unworthy—for Ruth was a Moabite woman, and Bathsheba, an adulteress, was made a wife—so that, drawing all their flesh to himself, he might restore them to genuine unity.

Therefore he says, “of Jesus Christ, son of David,” although Abraham comes first, because Christ is especially called the son of David on account of his kingship, so that just as God arose from God, so also a king might arise according to the flesh from a king. For thus it was said to David: “I will place upon your throne the fruit of your womb” (Psalm 132:11).

## IV  
*[Note: [Col. 2392] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Why did the apostle Matthew divide all the generations mentioned above into three parts (Matthew 1:17)?

Causes produce divisions, as do periods of time. Therefore he distinguished the generations from Abraham to David. The first part, in terms of its cause, extends from Abraham to David, because Abraham is the father of faith and David is the father of kingship. Saul, having become unworthy, deprived himself of the kingdom.

From David to the transmigration there is another part in terms of its cause: in it the Jews lost the kingdom after becoming reprobate. After the transmigration to Babylon, from that point to Christ, there is a third part of lamentation and misery, captivity and dispersion. For although, after the Babylonian transmigration and the period of seventy years, they were released by Cyrus and returned to their own land, they nevertheless never had rest [Note: [Col. 2392] Morel maintains that *pausam* (“rest”) should be read. See *Elementa Critica*, p. 321. M.] or respite.

For afterward Judea could not rule, but they were always anxious and wandering. Indeed, at the time of Christ’s birth they were captives, saying: “We have no king except Caesar” (John 19:15).

For this reason Matthew made three stages of the generations, so that he might also show the changes of merits and causes from the promise that had been made up to Christ, while the periods of the years remained in one grace until the end.

## V  
*[Note: [Col. 2392] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Since there are forty-one generations, why does the Evangelist appear to have counted forty-two (Matthew 1:17)? For three times fourteen makes forty-two, does it not?

[Col. 2393] According to the actual number, forty-one generations are counted; according to the reckoning, however, forty-two are established.

Jechoniah, born during the transmigration—that is, made king, as is contained in Chronicles—brought the second part to an end. And because after the transmigration he remained in the kingdom by the permission of King Nebuchadnezzar, the third part begins with him and extends to Christ. Therefore Jechoniah is counted twice, so that he both concludes the second part and begins the third.

For it says: “After the transmigration to Babylon, Jechoniah begot Salathiel” (Matthew 1:12). Up to this Salathiel, those descended from Judah ruled—that is, those from whose root Joseph arose.

Jechoniah’s first son was named Assur. But since Joseph derives his origin through the root of Salathiel, Assur was passed over and Salathiel was joined to his father Jechoniah, so that the genealogy might arrive at Joseph, to whom the virgin Mary was betrothed.

Jechoniah also follows Josiah. But since one arrives at Joseph through Joachim, Jechoniah’s father, Joachim was passed over and Jechoniah was inserted, so that the number of fourteen generations would not be exceeded, and because after Jechoniah come Salathiel and his son, through whom Joseph originates.

## VI  
*[Note: [Col. 2393] This is the same as the question numbered 56 in the first published collection.]*

Why is Joseph’s father written as Jacob in Matthew and as Heli in Luke, so that either he is incompetently described as having two fathers, or else it is unknown who his true father was?

There is no ambiguity: Jacob was Joseph’s father. For the line from David, proceeding through Solomon on its own path, reaches Jacob in a direct course, etc.

## VII  
*[Note: [Col. 2393] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

It is clear that the Savior was born the Son of God and was called Christ. Why, then, after his baptism did the tempter approach him, saying: “If you are the Son of God,” etc. (Matthew 4:3)?

The Savior was born from the Virgin in such a way that he was both Christ and Son of God, not by a making but by birth. While still of lesser age, however, emptying his power—that is, concealing his authority—he did not provoke the devil’s insolence.

After he was baptized, when the Holy Spirit descended upon him and he appeared to human beings with the testimony of God the Father, the enemy, driven by jealous zeal, was led to insult him, seeing that this event worked against him. For he understood that the institution of baptism had been established for the salvation of human beings.

Therefore he approached the Savior, the originator of this matter, not to approve it but to find an opportunity to overthrow it. For temptation sometimes occurs for testing, and sometimes through deception for subversion.

He supposed that he had, as it were, elicited from the Savior a response suited to the deception of his own purpose, and that he could thus securely retain his whole kingdom: if the leader of the Savior’s teaching were brought under, no one would escape death.

## VIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2393] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Why did the Savior resist the devil who tempted him only by means of examples from the Law (Matthew 4:4–10)?

The Savior answered not only the devil who tempted him, but also the Jews, through whom the devil exercised his cruelty and impiety against the Savior. Since he knew in advance that the Jews would call him an enemy of the Law, he restrained the insolence of their father, the devil, by testimonies from the Law, so as to condemn the father through the children and the children through the father.

## IX  
*[Note: [Col. 2393] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Why did the Savior fast for forty days after his baptism and afterward become hungry (Matthew 4:2)? For one who fasted for forty days ought by then to have ceased being hungry.

It is written: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Sirach 2:1).

Therefore the Savior fasted in order to give us a pattern, so that in the same way we too, persisting in fasts, might overcome every movement of the devil directed against us with God’s help. We should know from the Savior’s example that the adversary’s snares must be guarded against especially when we approach the fear of God. For he is grieved that we have withdrawn [Col. 2394] from him; therefore he rages against us more fiercely.

The Savior did this for us, not for himself. Similarly, the fact that he became hungry was for our sake, not his. When the devil’s temptations had been overcome through fasting—temptations that are not written down because they do not contribute to the advancement of the teaching—afterward, that is, after forty days, he permitted himself to suffer hunger, as was proper to a human being.

Thus the devil, seeing in him the weakness of hunger after he had already been defeated, was provoked to tempt him again, seeing that he was a human being by whom he was being conquered.

This was the Savior’s mystery: because the devil had insulted and ruled over the human being after his defeat, he would be conquered by a human being, so that the power of God might gain victory for humanity. In this way Satan was made still more contemptible, since he saw a human being and yet did not understand the power that was not human.

He was amazed, dulled by astonishment, that there was a mystery within which remained hidden from him: there was power to approach, but no power to circumvent.

For he was tormented for two reasons. Seeing weakness, he approached, but found power, so that, seeing a human being, he became suspicious of divine power. He therefore became hungry in order to mock Satan’s cunning.

He fasted no longer so that he might correspond to Moses and Elijah.

## X  
*[Note: [Col. 2394] Absent from the manuscripts of the first type.]*

Why, although John the Baptist had previously borne witness to the Savior, did he later express doubt through his disciples, saying: “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?” (Matthew 11:3–10).

Those who think that John doubted disparage the Savior. For either they rightly assert that he doubted, or else they charge the Savior with incompetence, because, as they suppose, he praised someone who held a wrong opinion about him.

But since it is impossible for the Savior to be mistaken, John was rightly praised by him. If he was rightly praised, he did not doubt.

At the very time when John sent his disciples from prison to Jesus, saying, “Are you the one who is to come, or should we expect another?”, Jesus answered his disciples: “Go, tell John what you see and hear. The blind see, the deaf hear, lepers are cleansed, the lame walk, the dead rise, and blessed is the one who is not scandalized by me.”

After John’s messengers had departed, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John the Baptist: “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind, or a man clothed in soft garments? Behold, those who wear soft garments are in kings’ houses. But what did you go out to see? A prophet? I tell you, and more than a prophet. This is the one of whom it is written: ‘Behold, I send my angel before your face, who will prepare your way.’”

Then the tax collectors praised God, having been baptized with John’s baptism.

How great was the praise given to John, when he was said to be more than a prophet, and when the Savior called blessed the one who is not scandalized by him! How, then, is John praised if he was scandalized by doubting?

But he certainly did not doubt. The praise of the one called blessed proves this, because he was not scandalized. The Savior also burst forth at that very time in praise of John in order to show that John’s understanding was free from the doubt of his disciples.

John, wishing to strengthen his astonished disciples in faith in the Savior and knowing that his own end was near, wanted what he had said about the Savior to be confirmed by the Savior’s own mouth. Thus, in order to be a true witness, he sought the testimony of one greater, so that their agreement might remove every ambiguity.

This was John’s stratagem: he sent the doubtful to the Savior as though in his own words, so that, hearing the same things from the Savior that they had heard from John, they might be strengthened, knowing that the testimony of a fitting representative and of the heavenly Lord could not be called into question.

Therefore the Savior answered as though to John, so that they might learn the truth from the exchange between John asking and the Savior answering.

## XI  
*[Note: [Col. 2394] Absent from the same manuscripts.]*

Why do we read above that Herod had died (Matthew 2:19), but below, many years later, that Herod killed John (ibid. 14:1–11), when John survived Herod’s death?

[Col. 2395] Herod was king of Judea. He had four sons: Archelaus, Herod, Philip, and Lysanias. After their father Herod died, Archelaus succeeded him. When Archelaus died, the kingdom of the Herod mentioned above was divided into four parts, so that Pilate was admitted to one quarter of the kingdom as governor, not as king (Matthew 2:22; Luke 3:1). The sons of Herod, however, were called kings.

Later, when Philip died, his brother Herod took his wife, and John the Baptist reproved him for this. For this reason Herod, the son of the Herod mentioned above, killed John.

For what does it say? “Herod,” it says, “the tetrarch”—that is, one placed in the fourth part of the kingdom of his father Herod.

What ambiguity, then, remains, when the indication supplied by the added title shows that this is a different Herod? He is the one who also killed James, the brother of John, with the sword, and who later, after being struck by an angel of God, breathed his last, swarming with worms.

## XII  
*[Note: [Col. 2395] Found above among the first published collection, beside Question 68.]*

The Lord certainly taught that we should pray for our enemies. Why, then, do the souls of the slain ask to be avenged, requesting vengeance from the Lord?

The Apocalypse, while bearing witness that future evils and tribulations arise from distrust and evil living, with God as avenger, etc.

## XIII  
*[Note: [Col. 2395] Same place, Question 69.]*

If the Law ceased when the Savior or John began to preach, how does the Savior say: “I have not come to abolish the Law or the Prophets, but to fulfill them”? For if it ceased, how was it not abolished or destroyed, since it lost its authority to prescribe conduct?

The statements of the prophets concerning the Savior’s coming were fulfilled when he came, etc.

## XIV

[Note: [Col. 2395] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—John says to the Lord, “Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?” (Matt. 11). He acts the case of his disciples in his own person. For John was not in doubt, since he had said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Rather, in order to satisfy his disciples, he sends them with these words, so that the Savior’s own mouth might confirm what he himself was teaching about him, and so that after his departure his disciples might follow Christ without any doubt.

## XV

[Note: [Col. 2395] Absent in the same manuscripts.]

—Why are the Law and the Prophets said to have continued until John, and afterward rightly to have ceased (Matt. 11:13)? Because the one about whom they prophesied has now arrived. Why does the Law continue until John, when the Apostle says that we ought to be subject to the Law: “Whatever exists,” he says, “has been ordained by God” (Rom. 13:1)?

The Law indeed has one name, but it has a threefold meaning. The first part of the Law concerns God. For the Law is so called from *reading*, so that you may know what to choose from among many things. Placed, therefore, amid errors, they received the command to choose what is true—that is, having rejected the devil, to choose God.

The second part of the Law is that which is contained in commandments, beginning in this way: “Honor your father and mother.”

The third concerns new moons and the Sabbath, the distinguishing and choosing of foods, circumcision, and the offering of animal sacrifices. This Law, therefore, he says, is to be observed only until John, and no longer. For it was given in such a way that it would cease when its appointed time was completed. It did not exist from the beginning, but was given for a time and for a particular reason, so that when the Savior arrived the Law would cease.

Therefore, the Law concerning God remains, as does the Law of commandments and its nature, which unquestionably cannot be abolished by him. Through him one advances toward the promised reward. For fear produces anxiety.

## XVI

[Note: [Col. 2395] Found above among the first published questions, near question 59.]

—Since the Savior calls John’s baptism heavenly, why, when speaking with Nicodemus about baptism, does he say to him in his doubt, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe,” and so forth?

What he said, “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe,” does not refer to baptism, and so forth.

## XVII

[Note: [Col. 2395] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—Why did the Savior, at the beginning, deny mercy to a foreign woman—that is, a Canaanite woman (Matt. 15:22–28)—when he did not refuse the foreign centurion, or the leper whom Jesus himself called a foreigner, the benefit of salvation (Luke 7:2–10; 17:12–19)?

The very circumstances identify the appropriateness of the Savior’s action. For it would have been absurd, and would have injured the promise made to the fathers, if a woman who had not confessed the God of the Jews had received the benefit promised to a nation that confessed God. For this reason it was denied to her at first.

But when, with her neck bowed, she did not reject faith in the Savior’s words, but confessed that believing Jews were children, whereas the Gentiles were dogs or servants—thereby joining herself to the Lord’s faith, since servants indicate a master, and a master does not exist without servants—the unity of the subject and the one exercising authority was established. Thus she deserved to obtain what she had requested.

The centurion, however, who received the benefit from the Savior without hesitation, had long since devoted himself to the things of God. Indeed, the elders of the Jews say to the Lord, “He is worthy that you grant this to him, for he loves our nation, and he himself built our synagogue.”

The Lord called the leper a foreigner not because of his faith, but because of his nation. He was a Samaritan, and it is established that the Samaritans were Babylonian in origin. Yet he too did not obtain the benefit without confession. For the Lord had said to the disciples, “Do not go on the road of the Gentiles, and do not enter a city of the Samaritans, but go rather to the sheep that have perished, the house of Israel” (Matt. 10:5–6). That is, the Samaritans and Gentiles were not to be preached to before the Jews, to whom this promise had belonged.

But when the Jews began to reject faith in Christ, the Savior then offered himself also to the Samaritan woman, and after the cross to the centurion Cornelius. From the Canaanite woman, however, he accepted the request because the time had not yet come for salvation to be offered to them.

## XVIII

[Note: [Col. 2396] Found above among the first published questions, near question 64.]

—How is the Savior’s statement proved—that he would rise from the dead after three days and three nights—when he plainly suffered at the pure supper and rose at daybreak on the Lord’s Day, while it was still dark? Hence the number of days and nights seems not to correspond.

The Savior, who knew beforehand everything that would happen to him, testified to this, and so forth.

## XIX

[Note: [Col. 2396] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—Why does the Savior say, “Pray that your flight may not take place in winter or on the Sabbath” (Matt. 24:20), when the time of this persecution cannot be postponed, since the Apostle says, “He will be revealed in his own time” (2 Thess. 2:6, 8), and in Acts the Apostle says, “Determining the times and boundaries of their habitation” (Acts 17:26)? And why does he indicate that flight in winter or on the Sabbath is not expedient?

Flight is unsafe in winter. There are cold temperatures, continual rains, snow, freezing, and overflowing rivers, and therefore it is extremely difficult for those fleeing. For they cannot hide in forests, mountains, or caves.

According to the Jews, on the Sabbath one may not go far out of the city, nor climb to a great height; consequently, one cannot flee on the Sabbath.

[Note: [Col. 2396] The Germanensis manuscript has, “you cannot flee on the Sabbath.”]

Just as these seasons do not make flight safe because of the obstacles mentioned above, so our flight will not be safe if that foretold persecution finds us bound by carnal impediments. Worldly desires hold people as though in chains—that is, worldly possessions prevent them from escaping the devil’s decrees.

Therefore we must pray that, when the time comes for flight, the condition of winter and the Sabbath may not be found in us, but that God’s help may make us free from these impediments, so that nothing may enslave us to the world by capturing us through its own desirability.

Since the Savior was speaking of the final persecution, which will come from Antichrist, he therefore introduced winter because it is the final time, and likewise the Sabbath because it is the final day. Thus, just as flight is harsh and difficult in those seasons, he signified that at that time persecutions and tribulations would be so severe that scarcely anyone would be able to escape them.

## XX

[Note: [Col. 2397] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—When the Savior said that he would suffer and rise again on the third day, he added, “After I have risen, I will go before you into Galilee; there you will see me”; and the angel said the same to the women (Matt. 26:32; 28:7). Yet he is found by the women and by his disciples in Jerusalem.

It is faithless to retract the Savior’s words. But I see that you are not doubting the Savior’s words; rather, you are seeking their meaning—why, although he was seen in Jerusalem after his passion, he said that they would see him in Galilee.

He was seen in Jerusalem, but separately, in order to restore the courage of the disciples; in Galilee, however, he was seen by all together. Thus, those who were going to see him in Jerusalem in separate appearances, he appointed to meet him in Galilee so that he might appear to them all at once and give instructions for establishing discipline.

## XXI

[Note: [Col. 2397] Found above among the first published questions, near question 65.]

—Three evangelists say that the Savior was crucified at the sixth hour, whereas the evangelist Mark says that he was crucified at the third hour. But some energetic interpreters, through their own diligence, say that the sentence was pronounced at the third hour and that therefore he was crucified at the third hour. For once a sentence has been pronounced, a person is considered already dead. Yet it is established that Pilate sat on the tribunal after the fifth hour and into the sixth, and then pronounced sentence, as John shows.

It is not good to envelop obscure matters in obscurity. For the very agreement of the three evangelists testifies that they spoke the truth, and so forth.

## XXII

[Note: [Col. 2397] Same place, question 50.]

—If the Savior was baptized in order to serve as an example, why did he forbid the others to be circumcised?

Circumcision was permitted until Christ. Abraham, however, received circumcision in the Christ who had been promised, and so forth.

## XXIII

[Note: [Col. 2397] Same place, question 61.]

—When the Jews accused the disciples because they were acting against the law of the Sabbath by plucking ears of grain, the Savior cited David as an example, saying, “Do you not know what David did when he was hungry—how he took the bread of the Presence and ate it, and gave it to those who were with him, although it was lawful only for the priests?” This example seems not to excuse the disciples; rather, both they and David may appear to have been transgressors.

The Savior did not wish to prejudice the Jews concerning the time when the Sabbath had been fulfilled, and so forth.

## XXIV

[Note: [Col. 2397] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—Why did the Savior call his disciples “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17), when they seem more properly to be called sons of God? For thunder is said to be produced by the collision of clouds.

Because thunder causes terror, for this reason he called the disciples sons of thunder, as though they were sons of one who is to be feared. Although thunder is produced by the collision of clouds, it nevertheless occurs by the will of God and is terrifying.

## XXV

[Note: [Col. 2397] Found above among the first published questions, near question 77.]

—According to the account of the evangelist Mark, how was Christ’s intention not fulfilled? For, upon entering a house, he says, “He wanted no one to know, and he could not remain hidden.” If, then, he wanted to remain hidden but could not, his intention was weakened.

This has been presented in abbreviated form in order to conceal the meaning more deeply, and so forth.

## XXVI

[Note: [Col. 2397] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—In the Gospel we read that the angel said to Mary, the mother of the Lord, that there would be no end to his kingdom—that is, Christ’s kingdom (Luke 1:33). Daniel says the same thing: “Then an eternal kingdom will arise, which will never be destroyed” (Dan. 7:14). On the other hand, the Apostle says of the Lord, “When he has handed over the kingdom to God and the Father” (1 Cor. 15:24). How will he have an eternal kingdom if he is said to hand it over to God and the Father?

[Col. 2398] In the case of the Father and the Son—that is, God and Christ—“handing over” is to be understood not as abolition. Consider, for example, how the Father handed the kingdom over to the Son, with the Lord himself testifying: “All things have been handed over to me by my Father” (Matt. 11:27). If, then, the Father ceased to possess it when he handed it over, it could likewise be said of the Savior that, when he handed it over, he lost it.

But after the Son said that the kingdom had been handed over to him by the Father, still preferring the Father, he said: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17:3).

According to this meaning, therefore, the Son does not lose the kingdom when he hands it over, so that both these statements may be true, and the angel and Daniel may be said not to differ from this meaning. Whoever thinks that the testimony of these passages must be retracted is full of unbelief.

But now let us see, while remaining in this faith, what it means for the Son to hand the kingdom over to the Father. For elsewhere the Apostle says among other things: “Then he himself will also be subject to him who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all” (1 Cor. 15:28).

This subjection, therefore, is itself the handing over of the kingdom. Thus an interpretation seems necessary here, so that the Son may not be denied to be subject to the Father, while nevertheless being said to have an eternal kingdom.

This is the Son’s kingdom: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth” (Phil. 2:10). The Apostle Peter also confirms this, saying, “There is no other name given under heaven by which we must be saved” (Acts 4:12). The Lord himself likewise says to the disciples, “Until now you have asked nothing in my name; ask, and I will do it” (John 16:24).

The Son reigns in this way: all things are saved in his name, and whatever is requested is granted, until the end of the world. But after all things have confessed Christ, whether by force or willingly, and have been subjected to his power, which they had resisted, the mystery of the one God will be made manifest to all, and every thanksgiving will be rendered to the Father, from whom all things are, so that, when preaching has ceased, the one God may be known in the mystery of the Trinity.

For when all powers, principalities, and dominions have bent the knee to Christ, then the Son will show that he is not the one from whom all things are, but his Son, and that the Father is seen in him. This is the subjection and the handing over of the kingdom. By showing that the Father is the one from whom all things are, he subjected himself to him when he declared himself to be from him.

For such majesty and glory appear at the Son’s coming that all powers and choirs of angels think him to be the one unique God. But when the Savior says that he is not the one called the Father, but his Son, he hands over the kingdom, while reigning, to the Father.

In this matter both the subjection and the handing over of the kingdom are revealed, because, when he professes that he is from the Father, he confesses that whatever he has belongs to the Father, referring the whole sum of things back to him.

## XXVII

[Note: [Col. 2398] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—The Savior says, “If anyone does not leave all his own things—that is, house, field, and the rest—he cannot be my disciple.” Yet the evangelist says, “Joseph of Arimathea came, a rich man, who himself was also a disciple of Jesus, awaiting the kingdom of God” (Luke 14:33; 23:50–51). How can the evangelist declare him a disciple whom the Savior denied to be one? Zacchaeus was also rich, as was Cornelius the centurion, and so were the women who ministered to them from their possessions.

The Apostle resolves this meaning briefly, saying, “Those who have [possessions should live] as though they did not have them; those who use this world as though they did not use it; and those who buy as though they did not possess” (1 Cor. 7:30–31).

Whoever possesses these things in such a way as though he did not possess them seems to have left them. For when he does not rely upon them or boast of them, but proceeds humbly—not only in appearance but also in mind—and understands himself to be their steward and servant, he seems to have left all his possessions.

That is said to be left which has receded from desire and has no favor.

## XXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2398] Found above among the first published questions, near question 60.]

—If the Law and the Prophets continued until John, why does the Savior send people to the priests to offer gifts for cleansing?

[Col. 2399] The Apostle Paul followed this practice. For when he preached that no one ought any longer to be circumcised, and so forth—

## XXIX

[Note: [Col. 2399] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—If the Law and the Prophets continued until John, from whom the kingdom of heaven was preached (Luke 16:16), for he is the initiator of the new preaching, why did his baptism cease?

John’s baptism did not cease; rather, what was lacking was added to it. John baptized only; he did not give the Holy Spirit to believers. Thus he himself says of the Savior, “I baptize you in water for repentance, but he will baptize you in the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 3:11).

This is what he says: “Through me there is forgiveness of sins, but the Holy Spirit is not given,” so that those who have been purified may be called children. This was reserved for the Savior, as Lord, so that they would not become children of God unless they had received the Holy Spirit from the Son of God.

The effect, therefore, of John’s baptism—which secretly operated without an interrogation, though not without mention of the Savior, so that what he did might be firm—is the gift of the Trinity. The Savior’s condescension shows this, giving the form of three names, which at the beginning, under the name or person of the one God, performed one undifferentiated work.

An interpretation was therefore added to John’s baptism, together with the disclosure of the mystery that had long been hidden. An additional gift was also added, so that those baptized, having received the Holy Spirit, might be children of God. It was therefore enlarged, not emptied.

## XXX

[Note: [Col. 2399] Found above among the first published questions, near question 76.]

—In the Gospel of John it says, “The Law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” If truth came through Christ, then it did not exist before. If it did not exist before, how can the Law be said to have been given by God, when truth was not in it?

We must consider what is meant by “The Law was given through Moses.” The Law given through Moses has manifest commandments, and so forth.

## XXXI

[Note: [Col. 2399] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—The Sabbath is certainly the Law, or a part of the Law. How, then, has the Law not been abolished, when the evangelist says, “He not only broke the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father” (John 5:18)?

The Savior did indeed break the Sabbath, but without prejudice to the Sabbath that had been given. Since the time of the Sabbath had already come to an end, while the Jews still asserted that the Sabbath remained, the Savior, by working on Sabbaths and commanding the sick man to carry his bed on the Sabbath, broke the Sabbath according to the Jews’ understanding.

For, according to the truth, it is the same as saying that something had already ceased as it is to say of someone who ought to be called a former prefect that he suffered an insult because the prefecture suffered an insult.

The Sabbath, therefore, was not broken; rather, the people who shamelessly claimed authority for the Sabbath were deceived, since the new Law had already succeeded the Sabbath.

## XXXII

[Note: [Col. 2399] Found above among the first published questions, near question 79.]

—If we live by our own free choice, why does the Savior say, “No one comes to me unless the Father who sent me draws him,” and why does the Apostle, without disagreeing with this, say, “It is not of the one who wills or of the one who runs, but of God who shows mercy”? Free choice of the will seems to be disturbed by these statements. For if no one goes unless drawn, the one who does not go will not be guilty, since he was not drawn. And if the one who asks and runs does not receive, but God gives to whomever he wishes, the one who wishes but does not obtain will be without guilt and crime; rather, the crime will redound upon the one who rejects the petitioner.

The cause of free choice cannot be disturbed in any way by these statements. For you must refer the words to the matter about which they were spoken, and so forth.

## XXXIII

[Note: [Col. 2399] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—Why, when the Savior healed almost everyone by a word, did he restore the eyes of the blind man with mud made from spittle (John 9:6–7)?

The Savior did this to confound those who accuse the Creator. For when he corrected an injury occurring to the body in no other way than the Creator had made it, he commended the author of this work. He corrected it by the very means through which it had been created.

Everything that is made, if it is restored from a fall by means of what had been made, will be proved to have been made rightly. If the Savior therefore proves himself to be God by repairing the body’s losses and defects, how much more is God the one who invented the body itself?

## XXXIV

[Note: [Col. 2400] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—What does the Savior mean when he says, “I am the door; all who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John 10:7–8)? This statement seems to attack the Prophets.

Because no one goes to God the Father except through faith in Christ, the Savior therefore calls himself the door of the kingdom of heaven.

If, then, he uses the language of a door, why was it necessary for him to speak of those who came before him—“All who came before me”—when no question concerning the past was under discussion, but a present door was being asked about present matters?
