He is speaking of the Jews, who thought that they would enter the kingdom of God not through faith but through the righteousness of the Law. For those who came before the Savior—that is, who stood before him—were reviling him and contradicting him, so that they might also turn others away from faith in him. Hence they were called thieves and robbers.

These words were spoken at the time when the Pharisees were disputing with the man who had been blind and had been enlightened, whose eyes the Savior restored, though nature had denied them to him. They wanted to turn him away from faith in the Savior, saying that one could not enter through him, because he violated the Sabbath, but through the righteousness of the Law.

Then the Savior said, “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will find pasture; but if anyone wishes to enter by another way, he is a thief and a robber.”

How does this apply to the persons of the Prophets? Did the Prophets say, contrary to Christ’s teaching, that God could be pleased through the righteousness of the Law without faith, even though they knew that Christ would come in the flesh?

He therefore said this about those who were present, so that all who were before him—standing or sitting—would be understood as thieves and robbers. For by separating the man who had been blind, they wanted to turn him away from faith in the Savior, saying, “Give glory to God; we know that this man is a sinner.”

But the man rebuked them, saying, “From the beginning it has never been heard that anyone opened the eyes of one born blind. If this man were not from God, he could do nothing” (John 9:24, 32–33).

The Savior therefore spoke about him, because he persevered in faith, and about those who said, “These words are not those of one who has a demon. Can a demon open the eyes of the blind?” He said, “But the sheep did not listen to them” (John 10:8–9, 21)—namely, those whom he called thieves and robbers.

For how could the sheep have failed to listen to the Prophets, when Scripture establishes that all the good obeyed the Prophets, and the wicked obeyed false prophets?

## XXXV

[Note: [Col. 2400] Absent in the same manuscripts.]

—Why, when he was about to perform an astonishing and unknown work—namely, to raise Lazarus from the dead—did the Savior weep, or, as though unaware, ask for the place where he had been laid (John 11:34–35)?

The Savior is God and man, and therefore he always acted in two ways: because he possesses human affection, he wept; but because he was also God, he raised the one over whom he had wept. Thus one always proceeds from lesser things to greater, so that, because he was seen to be human, this might refute the idea that he was merely what he appeared to be; but he asserted through his works that he was God.

## XXXVI

[Note: [Col. 2400] Absent in the same manuscripts.]

—Although the Savior says, “I pray for those whom you have given me; I do not pray for the world” (John 17:9), the Apostle John, by contrast, says, “We have an advocate with the Father, an intercessor for our sins, and not only for ours but for the whole world” (1 John 2:1–2). This seems contradictory.

Although the meaning is not far apart, what the Savior says is one thing and what the Apostle John affirms is another. The Savior prays for the disciples so that they may be kept safe from the assault of evil. Thus he says, “I do not ask that you take them out of the world, but that you protect them from evil.”

The Apostle John, however, introduces another kind of prayer. For he says, “We have an advocate who pleads for our sins and for those of the whole world.”

Thus, in the case of Christians, prayer is offered in two ways: prayer is made both for the forgiveness of their sins and that they may be kept safe from the assault of the devil.

[Col. 2401] For those who do not believe, the only prayer is that, although they would deserve to be punished for their sins and unbelief, goodness and patience might wait for them, in case they should wish to be corrected.

It is not requested that their sins be forgiven while they remain unbelieving, but that they receive a long delay, so that, if they amend themselves, their offenses may be forgiven. This, then, is what the Savior requests for them, as we have said.

## XXXVII

[Note: [Col. 2401] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—Why, when Mary wished to touch the Savior out of joy, did he say to her, “Do not touch me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father” (John 20:1–17), when we read that he was both touched and worshiped by the other women?

The words, “Do not touch me,” are the words of one who is indignant. Although she desired the Savior, while the others believed in his resurrection, she stood weeping at the tomb, when she ought already to have been rejoicing. For she had heard from the Apostles John and Peter that the Lord had risen.

Thus the text reads: “He saw the linen cloths and the face cloth together, and believed; for he did not yet know the Scripture, that he had to rise from the dead.” But because Mary did not see him risen, she did not believe. Excessive love caused her to doubt.

Indeed, when those whom we love suffer misfortune, we do not believe that they have escaped it; but when those whom we hate are already near death, we find it incredible. Therefore, because Mary was astonished and was suffering grief through love, when she ought to have followed the disciples’ faith, the Lord first showed himself to her so that she might cease from mourning—but not without indignation.

Thus she hears, “Do not touch me.” That is: “You seek a carnal understanding; hold yourself back and follow spiritual things, which are not seen.”

“For I have not yet,” he says, “ascended to the Father.” This means: “Your heart is still pressed down toward earthly things; if you do not see, you do not believe. If you had lifted your heart to God, you would have believed with the disciples that the Lord had risen.”

This is like what blessed John the Baptist did when he sent his disciples to Jesus and said, “Go and tell him, ‘John the Baptist has sent us to you, saying, Are you the one who is to come, or are we to expect another?’” (Luke 7:19–20). He acts the case of his disciples in his own person. For John was not in doubt, since he had said, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1:29). Rather, in order to satisfy his disciples, he sent them with these words, so that the Savior’s own mouth might confirm what he himself was teaching about him, and so that after his departure his disciples might follow Christ without any doubt.

So also the Savior rebukes Mary in his own person, saying, “I have not yet ascended to the Father.”

[Note: [Col. 2401] Morel maintains that *ipse* should be read. See *Elementa Critica*, p. 156. M.]

That is: “Your heart is still weighed down toward the earth; if you do not see, you do not believe. If you had raised your heart to God, you would have believed with the disciples that the Lord had risen.”

## XXXVIII

[Note: [Col. 2401] Found above among the first published questions, near question 51.]

—How is it to be understood that, when Mary said to the angel, “And how will I know this, since I have not known a man?” the angel Gabriel replied, “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you”?

To Mary, who was uncertain about the conception, the angel proclaims its possibility, saying, and so forth.

## XXXIX

[Note: [Col. 2401] Same place, question 63.]

—By what reasoning did the Chaldean Magi understand from the appearing star that Christ, the king of the Jews, had been born, when a star indicating a temporal king is used as the sign?

These Chaldean Magi did not observe the course of the stars out of malevolence, but out of curiosity about events, and so forth.

## XL

[Note: [Col. 2401] Same place, question 74.]

—What does the prophet Isaiah mean when he says of Christ, “He committed no sin,” whereas the Apostle says, “He who knew no sin was made sin for us”?

As far as the matter at hand is concerned, not only do the words differ, but the persons are also different, and so forth.

## XLI

[Note: [Col. 2401] Same place, question 80.]

—Certainly whoever is not a son of God is a son of the devil. Therefore he is always a son, at one time of God and at another of the devil. We must therefore ask what we are born as: whether sons of God, or sons of the devil, or whether a third possibility can be admitted.

When the sons of Israel, after being led out of Egypt, frequently sinned, the Lord became angry and permitted none of them to enter the promised land, and so forth.

## XLII

[Note: [Col. 2402] Found above among the first published questions, near question 93.]

—It must be asked whether the Apostles had the Holy Spirit during the time when they were with the Lord, and so forth.

In all the matters that have been proposed, the cause is not one and the same. For the forms of the individual causes have been indicated briefly, and so forth.

## XLIII

[Note: [Col. 2402] Same place, question 97.]

—By what reasoning can Arian impiety be answered simply from the Law?

If faith is accommodated to reason, the very relationship between the names “Father” and “Son” will show their unity, and so forth.

## XLIV

[Note: [Col. 2402] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—When we profess that the Savior was born, why does the Apostle say that he was made from the seed of David (Rom. 1:3), when being made is one thing and being born another?

Although in this passage *made* can be understood as referring to birth—for being made does indeed differ from generation, though not in other matters where the nature of flesh and body is at issue—the Apostle nevertheless did not use these words without reason. For elsewhere he also says, “Made from a woman” (Gal. 4:4).

He therefore indicated something by this expression. Since the Lord’s flesh was not formed in the Virgin’s womb from human seed and made into a body, but through the operation and power of the Holy Spirit, the Apostle spoke in this way.

For it is one thing to coagulate blood by the admixture of seed and to generate, and another to produce without mixture, by power. Therefore he said *made* rather than *begotten*.

[Note: [Col. 2402] The Germanensis manuscript reads, “He said made because he was unbegotten.”]

## XLV

[Note: [Col. 2402] Found above among the first published questions, near question 54.]

—If Christ, the Son of God, was made from the seed of David according to the flesh—that is, if, having been born, he was already the Son of God in both respects, because he was born sanctified—why, after he was baptized, did God say to him, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you”?

Christ is the Son of God according to the Spirit from eternity; according to the flesh, however, he is the Son of God from the seed of David by birth, and so forth.

## XLVI

[Note: [Col. 2402] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—The Apostle calls the Law given through Moses holy, just, good, and spiritual (Rom. 7:12, 14). Elsewhere he says, “The Law produces wrath,” and, “Where there is no Law, neither is there transgression” (Rom. 4:15). To be without these things is security.

You ought to have been satisfied by comparing the statements themselves. For those who are uncertain commonly formulate questions by seeking statements from one author—statements that it is not permissible to criticize—as though they were contradictory and hostile.

If the Apostle calls the Law holy, just, good, and spiritual—a man outstanding in every praise and fortified on every side by truth—that should suffice for faith. The apparent contradiction in his words ought to have been examined without obstinacy or envy.

For this proposition seeks impunity for sin. The Apostle, when he preferred the law of faith on account of the appropriate time and grace among the Romans, who under faith in Christ had been brought into the Law, did so for a reason.

I mean not the law that is natural. For the Romans were certainly under the law that the decemvirs sent from Athens—and afterward two others—brought, the law written on the two [Note: [Col. 2402] Perhaps read, “twelve.”] tablets buried in the Capitol. Rather, I mean the law that is called the law of deeds: that people should be circumcised, observe the Sabbath and new moons, distinguish foods, be concerned with the cleansing of vessels, and observe the other matters contained in this kind of Law.

This Law, therefore, he says, produces wrath. For these things were added by an angry God so that they might be a burden to the unbelief of the Jews. From so many matters it is inevitable that something should be omitted.

Hence the Apostle Peter says, “Why are you placing a yoke upon the neck of the brothers that neither our fathers nor we have been able to bear?” (Acts 15:10).

Finally, God says through the prophet Jeremiah: “I gave them commandments that were not good” (Ezek. 20:25). After many offenses, temptations against God, insults directed against Moses, and criticisms of God, these commandments were given for them to observe, so that their stubborn neck might be pressed down and, wherever they turned, they would have the Law, leaving them no relief.

Therefore, in order to remove them from this Law, the Apostle says, “Where there is no Law, neither is there transgression,” so that, freed from this burden, they might serve God spiritually. For, he says, “If you observe the law of the Jews, you must transgress.” There are so many commandments that it is impossible to fulfill them.

For how could he have spoken of the natural law in this way? Moses wrote in order to establish its authority, not because it did not exist beforehand, since we read that punishment was exacted before Moses, but so that he might explain to the Romans that they ought no longer to live under the Law, even though it had been expedient for them to act under the Law. For otherwise they could not preserve righteousness.

Finally, he says to them, “Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good”; and, “Those who despise it acquire condemnation for themselves” (Rom. 13:3, 2).

He therefore calls this Law spiritual, and shows it to be holy, just, and good. This is the law we have called natural, which forbids sin; for it is the guide of a good life. When the law of faith is added to it, it makes the complete human being.

Because the law I have called natural and the law called the law of deeds are both designated by the common name “law,” the Apostle seems to speak against the Law. But, lest he appear to abolish this law, without which this life cannot be governed, he says, “We know that the Law is spiritual,” so that it would be understood that the law he abolishes is the law of the Sabbath, circumcision, foods, and new moons.

That law is called spiritual because it punishes all sins.

[Note: [Col. 2403] The Germanensis manuscript reads, “removes sins.”]

## XLVII

[Note: [Col. 2403] Absent in manuscripts of the first class.]

—By what reasoning is the wisdom of the flesh hostile to God, and what is this wisdom itself that is not subject to the law of God (Rom. 8:7)?

In meaning, this question does not differ from the preceding one.

[Note: [Col. 2403] This indicates the question that appears below as question 61.]

For it has been explained what is signified by “flesh,” and from this it can easily be recognized what its wisdom is.

We have therefore said that all the elements are called flesh—that is, the substances of visible things. Their nature is such that they judge that nothing can come into being without spiritual and simple mixture, recoiling from the rationale of power and judging it foolish.

Those who, distrusting spiritual things, follow carnal things have no other understanding or belief of what is true than what the nature of the elements contains. Thus they do not believe either that a virgin gave birth or that the flesh will rise again, because the reasoning of the flesh—that is, of the elements—does not accept this.

For everything that is generated in time is generated through the operation of mixture. Dead and dissolved bodies cannot be restored to life again, because each element, once separated through mixture, returns to its own nature.

Inflated by these ideas, they deny what we believe will happen or has happened. Their assertion is therefore hostile to God, since it considers foolish and empty what God has done and has promised to do.

## XLVIII

[Note: [Col. 2403] Found above among the first published questions, near question 66.]

—The Apostle says of the rulers and powers of this age that, if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory. By contrast, the evangelist Mark says of the demons, “For they knew who he was.” If the demons knew, how did the powers remain ignorant?

Some think that by “the rulers and powers of this age” he meant the elders and rulers of the Jews, and so forth.

## XLIX

[Note: [Col. 2403] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

What spirit does the Apostle [Col. 2404] assert will be saved when he says, “I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh” (etc.) (1 Cor. 5:5)?

The destruction of the flesh occurs when someone, devoted to carnal pleasures and desires, brings hell upon himself; for he acquires destruction through the work of the flesh. Through these things he becomes wholly carnal, because just as a person living according to the law becomes wholly spiritual, so that even the flesh is called what the soul is, so, if he lives according to the world’s desire and the pleasures of lust, the whole person becomes flesh, advancing toward the destruction of the flesh.

That is, just as the flesh, because it is fluid, corruptible, and mortal, is disfigured when it loses the soul and, deprived of its form, flows into destruction—for it perishes when it loses the strength of all its members—so the soul of such a body is also disfigured. Its strength had been despised in punishment together with the flesh, in which it had stained itself with vices. Thus there is no benefit to the flesh through the soul; rather, the soul suffers destruction through the flesh, because the body was not governed spiritually, although the soul had been given as queen over the flesh, but the soul itself teaches carnal works.

[Note: [Col. 2404] The printed editions read *leads*. The Germanensis manuscript reads *teaches*.]

When, therefore, the Church has cast out such a man, the Church has its spirit saved—namely, the holy Spirit, who is the guardian of the Church. For if they allow someone who has polluted his father’s wife through lust to remain among them, although they could compel him by law, so that he might not contaminate everyone and the Holy Spirit might withdraw from the Church because of the polluted man, the Church will not have its spirit saved. What is lost is not safe; and, found naked of the Spirit on the day of the Lord, they will not be able to be counted among the children of God. For the Spirit bears witness that we are children of God (Rom. 8:16).

The Apostle speaks these things to the people, because at that time bishops had not yet been appointed in every place. Therefore he commands the people to do what he would have done if a bishop had been established there: that, joining together in agreement, they should expel him from their assembly, lest they appear to consent to his works. For whoever does not rebuke someone whom he can rebuke, but receives him as though he were not in error, supplies him with encouragement to sin; and for this reason he too is contaminated, driving the Holy Spirit away from himself.

To the Thessalonians, likewise, among other things he says: “May your spirit, soul, and body be preserved blameless at the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Thess. 5:23). The meaning is the same: to be safe is to be whole. Thus the king says to Daniel, “Are the signs safe, Daniel?” and he answered, “Safe, O king” (Dan. 14:16)—that is, whole—so that our spirit may be whole when it does not abandon us.

For those whom the spirit abandons will no longer be whole in the matter of regeneration, because they do not possess him through whom they were called children of God. Nor is it contradictory if we say that the Holy Spirit abandons us when we sin and is not whole. He is not whole precisely because he abandons us, although he was our guide and ruler; for if he is our head, we are his members. When we do something contrary to him, it is not he but we who appear to abandon him; and then he appears not to be whole when he loses us. For this is true and evident: he does not turn away from us, but we turn away from him when we sin.

To the Colossians, among other things, he says: “From whom the whole body, supplied and knit together, grows with the increase of God” (Col. 2:19). If we understand this according to the sound of the words, it does not fit; for God lacks nothing that could be increased through us. But when we return to the author of our life, confess him, and he acquires us for salvation, divinity produces growth in us. Therefore, in those who withdraw from him, there is loss. Not to be whole, then, means also to suffer loss.

## L

[Note: [Col. 2404] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

Although many sins appear to be committed against the body—for everyone who in any way does violence to any part of his body certainly sins against his own body: one cuts himself, another ends his life by a noose, another thrusts a sword into himself—why does the Apostle say, “Every sin that a person commits is [Col. 2405] outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. 6:18)?

Do you think that the Apostle was inexperienced, or do you desire an explanation of the saying’s force? For when the Apostle says “body,” he does not signify one individual person, but includes the woman as well, because woman is a portion of man. All the crimes mentioned above, which each person violently commits against himself, do not stain the whole body; an individual sins, and consequently he alone becomes guilty. In fornication, however, the whole body is polluted, because the consent to contamination involves both man and woman. For this reason fornication is a grave offense. A person sins most wickedly when he seeks a partner in his crime for destruction.

If someone who lives well will receive a reward even for the person he has won, and an evil person becomes guilty not only for himself but also for the one whom he wished to have share his condemnation, how much more does the fornicator, who is known to contaminate himself twice over by one offense, sin grievously? For if he sins against the flesh that comes from himself, he certainly commits adultery against himself twice.

If anyone thinks that he can transform this question and apply the saying either to the Church or to the body of Christ, the interpretation will not stand. It would be an improper usage, and he would resemble Novatian, who, to establish the cause of his fury, declares that the fornicator does not sin against his own body but against Christ’s, because Christians are members and the body of Christ. Thus fornication would be made equivalent to sacrilege, and such a person would be said to sin against Christ in the same way as one who denies Christ.

This argument is weak and fragile, because in whatever direction it clings, it falls into a snare and does not escape. For if the fornicator sins against the body of Christ, other sins will not have been committed against Christ: if a Christian kills a brother, sacrifices to idols, or commits another kind of sin, then every sin is outside the body except fornication. But if every sin is not outside the body, and whatever the sin may be is committed against Christ, then the thief, the perjurer, the liar, the one who strikes his brother, and anyone who commits anything of the sort would be said to sin against Christ or against the Holy Spirit. This is entirely absurd.

Yet the Apostle calls the members of the Church the body of Christ.

[Note: [Col. 2405] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “calls the Church the members and body of Christ.”]

Thus we are members of one another. How, then, does the fornicator sin against his own body and not rather against Christ’s? For according to the mystery of the Church we are said not to be our own body but Christ’s. This is far removed from the issue, because the fornicator sins against his own body precisely because the whole Adam is contaminated.

## LI

[Note: [Col. 2405] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

Why did the Apostle Paul say that he became all things to all people (1 Cor. 9:22), when this appears to be the conduct of a flatterer and hypocrite?

A flatterer is one who gives his consent for the sake of not offending someone whom he wishes to have favorably disposed toward him. Whoever does something because of scandal—something not dangerous but unnecessary—seeks the salvation of the person whom he does not wish to suffer scandal.

When the Apostle Paul circumcised Timothy because of the Jews and entered the temple after purification, he acted in this way so that those who were zealous for their ancestral tradition might not take offense and either kill him or regard our religion as hostile to them. He therefore chose to do something lesser in order to gain something greater. He could have sinned gravely if he had not made himself as a Jew and gone into the temple to pray; therefore he subjected himself in order to benefit them.

With those who were under the Law, that is, with the Samaritans, he consented for this reason: they rightly confessed that the books of Moses were from God, and that circumcision and the Sabbaths had been given by God. From these things he showed them that the Christ whom they expected was the one whom he preached. Thus you have the Samaritan woman saying to the Lord: “I know that the Messiah is coming; when he comes, he will announce everything to us” (John 4:25). In accordance with this understanding, he followed the words of the books of Moses, who said: “For the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet [Col. 2406] from among your brothers” (Deut. 18:15).

With those who were without the Law, he consented in this respect: they say that the world and the human race were made by God. For he says: “As some of your own poets have said, ‘For we are indeed his offspring’” (Acts 17:28). Thus he became all things to all people, so that he might benefit their salvation.

## LII

[Note: [Col. 2406] Found above among the first published questions, near Question 99.]

What does the Apostle mean when he says, “Let no temptation seize you except a human one,” as though he wished such a thing to occur? And what is this human temptation? For by this he shows that there is also a divine temptation. He therefore indicates that the two must be distinguished.

Every question, if it is to be clarified, must be brought back to its origin. When the Apostle was complaining about the Jews’ faithlessness, etc.

## LIII

[Note: [Col. 2406] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

What does the Apostle mean when he says, “No one can say, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Cor. 12:3)? Can Photinus, then, who denies that Christ is God, confess our Lord Jesus Christ in the Holy Spirit? And can Marcion and Manichaeus, who deny that Christ came in the flesh, say in the Holy Spirit that Jesus Christ is Lord? Or can prostitutes and the impure do so, when the Holy Spirit does not dwell in a body subject to sins, and wisdom does not enter a malevolent soul (Wis. 1:4)?

Truth is neither proved nor disproved by a person’s status. Whatever is said well and truthfully is undoubtedly said in the Holy Spirit. Therefore, if someone is guilty in other matters, that must not be used against him here when he speaks the truth. Yet the objection is not really directed against him; it is directed against Christ the Lord. For whoever denies that this person speaks the truth does injury to Christ.

If the truth is spoken, but it is denied that what is true can be spoken in the Holy Spirit—something Christ himself accepts, since no good person condemns someone who speaks truth about himself, and what is learned through tradition is not learned through revelation—then no one who speaks the truth can be disapproved.

## LIV

[Note: [Col. 2406] Absent from the same manuscripts.]

The Apostle says that Christ died for all. For he says: “Therefore all have died, and he died for all” (2 Cor. 5:14–15). But the Lord himself says: “The Son of Man came to give his life as a ransom for many” (Matt. 20:28). This appears contradictory.

The words are different, but the meaning is one. Conversely, the same words can have different meanings, as in: “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14:23), and “The Law,” he says, “is not from faith” (Gal. 3:12), and yet the Law is not sin.

Those whom the Savior called “many,” the Apostle indicated by “all.” They are many because the greater part of every people and nation will believe in the Savior. The Apostle called these believers “all.” Thus, among other things, he says: “He died for all”—namely, for those who have believed and who will believe.

He also died for those who do not wish to believe. But since they do not receive the benefit, they do not wish Christ to have died for them; consequently, he does not appear to have died for those whom his death benefited nothing, but rather harmed. He is properly said to have died for those for whom victory has been won, who, understanding the mystery, give thanks to God through Christ our Lord.

## LV

[Note: [Col. 2406] Absent from the same manuscripts.]

Why did the Apostle Paul rebuke his fellow apostle Peter because, fearing those of the circumcision, he withdrew from the Gentiles (Gal. 2:11, 14), when Paul himself, fearing those of the circumcision, took Timothy and circumcised him, although he prohibited this from being done (Acts 16:3)? Should he, then, also be rebuked?

It is incredible that so great an apostle would rebuke another for something in which he knew himself to have failed. It is not right to believe that this was done by so great a man, for such conduct belongs to those who live carnally. Paul’s action therefore is free from reproach.

When he was preaching [Col. 2407] that people should not be circumcised, but wished to take Timothy with him—and Timothy had been born of a Jewish mother but a Greek father, and it would have been a scandal to the Jews for him to take a man born of a Jewish woman while uncircumcised—Paul submitted himself to subjection for the moment and circumcised him. He therefore did something unnecessary, with the permission of the one who suffered it.

Because Timothy was born of a Jewish mother and had been educated from childhood in the synagogue in the sacred writings—that is, in the books of the Hebrews—he permitted himself to be circumcised in order to remove the Jews’ offense, since they were zealous for their lineage. Finally, Paul says: “But when Titus was a Greek, he was not compelled to be circumcised” (Gal. 2:3). Timothy, however, because he was, as I have said, from a Jewish mother, was not permitted by the Jews to be accepted among the teachers while uncircumcised.

The Apostle took him for the purpose of ordaining him bishop, as he did. Since Timothy had been educated in the prophetic Scriptures, he was found to be a suitable teacher for defending Christ.

The Apostle Peter would not have been rebuked if he had separated himself from the Gentiles according to Jewish custom,

[Note: [Col. 2407] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “out of fear of the Jews.”]

so as not to be a scandal to them. But what was rebuked in the Apostle Peter was that, although he had previously lived as a Gentile among Greek believers, when Jews came from James he submitted through fear and taught the Gentile believers that they ought to judaize. Hence he hears: “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile, how can you compel the Gentiles to judaize?”

He had caused uncertainty concerning evangelical discipline; and this is a crime, since he was destroying what he had built. Therefore the Apostle Paul calls this hypocrisy. It is evident that if Paul had circumcised Timothy, he would not have concealed that he was doing something unnecessary because of their offense, and that he was yielding because Timothy had a Jewish mother. The Jews would not have persisted unless they had found an occasion in his Jewish mother, because they could not readily object to Gentiles or take offense at those who were not of Israelite descent.

He did not therefore do this hypocritically, but under compulsion. The previously mentioned situation involved considerable hypocrisy. For many were rebuked in this matter, so much so that some of the Jews and Barnabas also consented to this hypocrisy.

[Note: [Col. 2407] Morel maintains that the reading should be: “whom it is certain that he thus circumcised Timothy.” See *Elementa Critica*, pp. 264–265. M.]

## LVI

[Note: [Col. 2407] Found above among the first published questions, near Question 81.]

The Apostle says, “We are Jews by nature.” He therefore shows that Jews are born from Jews. Indeed, those who were born in the wilderness were Jews, although they were not circumcised. Circumcision, then, does not make a Jew; rather, it is birth produced under devotion to God the Creator.

If Jews are born from Jews and pagans from pagans, then Christians too are born from Christians.

Not everything that is born is identical with that from which it is born. For gold too is born from the earth, etc.

## LVII

[Note: [Col. 2407] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

Why was it necessary for the Apostle, while rebuking the Galatians, to insert this? To the Galatians, who after the Gospel were fleeing back to the Law, he says, among other things: “Now a mediator is not of one, but God is one” (Gal. 3:20), as though the Galatians were denying one God. They had been led into the Law precisely so that they might believe in one, singular God; but they believed that Christ had come merely as a minister, by predestination, to administer the gift of God’s grace.

It is clear that the Galatians had been led into the Law in such a way that they also professed Christ, but not as was proper. They did so in the manner of Photinus: since the Law preaches one God, they thought it contrary to the Law to say that Christ is God.

This is the Jews’ contrivance. Overcome by the greatness of Christ’s works, they believed after his crucifixion, yet continued to observe the Law while professing Christ, as though all hope ought not to be placed in Christ. These are the people whom the Apostle calls “false brothers” (Gal. 2:4; 2 Cor. 11:26).

After the Apostles’ tradition, these people had corrupted the Galatians’ understanding, making them Jews under the name of the Savior. Hence the Apostle says that Christ came as arbiter between circumcision and uncircumcision, just as he [Col. 2408] says to the Ephesians: “Making peace in one new man” (Eph. 2:15).

If Christ came as arbiter, an arbiter makes peace between two parties by establishing a new rule: removing both parties’ professions, he reconciles them, so that, following his judgment, they abandon their former disagreement. When the Jew claims circumcision and the Gentile uncircumcision, there is disagreement. When both are taken away, there is peace.

If this is so, how, he says, do you Galatians, having become Jews, corrupt Christ’s arbitration? Therefore he said to them: “You have been severed from Christ.” Despising the right of reconciliation that he had established between them, they returned to the Jews’ former understanding, accusing both themselves and the reconciler. For everything that displeases is accused.

Since this matter had compelled the Galatians to return to the Law, so that they might confess one God without the mystery—as though it were hostile to the Law to call Christ God—he says: “An arbiter, that is, a mediator, is not of one, but certainly of two; yet you, having returned to the Law, have rejected the arbiter. Nevertheless, God is one.”

By this statement he does not testify that he preaches Christ as God in such a way as to make another god or profess two gods. Rather, he says that God is one, just as it is also said in the Law. When Christ is proclaimed as God from God, this does not produce another God, because what is from God does not allow itself to be called another God. Whether one says “God” or “what is from God,” God is one. There is no difference between God and what is from God.

There is, however, another—another in respect of the person by which he is called Son, but the very same in respect of unity of substance. So that it may not seem objectionable that I have used the word “person”—for some people customarily reject this terminology—let us follow the Apostle, who says: “What I have forgiven, if I have forgiven anything, was for your sake in the person of Christ” (2 Cor. 2:10).

## LVIII

[Note: [Col. 2408] Found above among the first published questions, near Question 83.]

If salvation and true, perfect knowledge come through Christ, why did he not come earlier, so that our predecessors, who lived in ignorance, might learn the truth? Indeed, after Christ’s coming many more were saved than before; therefore, if he had come earlier, many more would have been saved. If this is so, it appears blameworthy.

If help is given beforehand to someone upon whom necessity is pressing, he will indeed be grateful, but he will not be able to understand very well what has been done for him, etc.

## LIX

[Note: [Col. 2408] The same; Question 82.]

No one doubts that pagans are under the elements. What, then, did the Apostle mean when he said, “We too were under the elements of this world, serving them”? If the Jews too were under the elements, how do they differ from pagans?

Pagans do not serve under the elements, but serve the elements themselves. For they worship the stars, etc.

## LX

[Note: [Col. 2408] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

When the Apostle says to the Galatians—whom he rebukes and reproves throughout the whole Epistle—“Become as I am, because I also am as you are” (Gal. 4:12), if he made himself like they were, it was superfluous to say, “Become as I am.” Or had he perhaps begun to imitate them in certain matters and wished them to become like him in others?

What could the Apostle imitate in them?

[Note: [Col. 2408] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “Who among them could imitate the Apostle?”]

Or what did the teacher of the nations lack? Rather, he urges them to be imitators of him. And since this is not impossible, he reproves them when he says, “Because I am what you are”: you are human beings, just as I am; therefore do what I do.

This may also refer to the statement that he became all things to all people by consenting in matters where they did not depart from the truth, especially in the case of Gentiles (1 Cor. 9:22). For he did not share anything of theirs that ought no longer to be practiced, although it had once been rightly practiced—such as circumcision, observance of Sabbaths, new moons, and foods. But if he approved anything belonging to the nations, he showed that it ought not already to have ceased.

They say that the world was made by God, and that human beings were made by God; this remains valid always. If, therefore, by agreeing with them in these matters he became like them, he urges them [Col. 2409] likewise to become like him by agreeing with his teaching.

## LXI

[Note: [Col. 2409] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

How are we free in judgment and will when the Apostle says, “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh, so that you do not do what you wish” (Gal. 5:17)? And if the flesh desires against the spirit, it is evil, since the spirit suggests what is good.

In this passage you should understand by “flesh” not the substance of the flesh, but evil acts and faithlessness signified by the flesh. Since all error arises from visible and worldly things, and the flesh is related to them—for it consists of the elements—he calls every error “flesh.” He calls not only adultery, fornication, and luxury works of the flesh, but also idolatry, sorcery, blasphemies, and similar things.

Does the flesh compel blasphemy or idolatry?

[Note: [Col. 2409] According to Lov.: “Does the flesh compel blasphemy or idolatry?” M.]

Are these not vices of the soul, when it consents to error? Yet he rightly says of those who act well that they are not in the flesh but in the spirit.

And certainly they are in the body for this purpose.

[Note: [Col. 2409] Morel maintains that the reading should be: “And certainly they are still in the body.” See *Elementa Critica*, p. 168. M.]

Whoever therefore walks well and does not lose confidence in the hope of believers is said, although placed in the flesh, not to be in the flesh. But one who lives wickedly and blasphemes is said to be in the flesh and to be flesh. For just as those who act well are spiritual while still in the flesh, so those who live wickedly are carnal even with respect to the soul. A person is called what his conduct reveals.

This error, then, which he calls “flesh,” desires against the spirit; that is, it suggests evils against the same spirit, which is the law of God. He introduces two laws: the law of God and the law of the devil. He calls the one “spirit” because the law of God is spiritual and struggles against the flesh—that is, against vices—in order to preserve the person for God.

The law of the devil, which is error, resists through the allurements of luxury and worldly sweetness. Between these opposing forces stands the human being. When he consents to the spirit, the flesh does not want it; but when he gives his hand to the flesh, he despises the spirit—that is, he disregards the law of God.

The spirit recalls the person who consents to the flesh, so that he may not do what he wishes. The flesh, however, solicits the person who assents to the spirit, so that he may not do what he thinks useful. The spirit rightly and prudently opposes and recalls him, in order to rescue him from Satan’s counsels. The flesh, which is the opposing law, therefore solicits and resists the spirit of the law, so that it may deceive through falsehood.

The Apostle therefore proclaims these things to show that human judgment determines to what it will entrust its will. He does not empty free judgment of its freedom; rather, he teaches judgment to what it should attach itself.

If there were no freedom of will, neither the law of the devil, which is the flesh, nor the law of God, which is the spirit, would solicit the person through their mutual opposition. Whoever solicits persuades; whoever persuades does not use force but deceives; and when a person is deceived, his will is changed by certain falsehoods. If there were no free judgment, a person would be dragged unwillingly toward things he does not want.

## LXII

[Note: [Col. 2409] Absent from the same manuscripts.]

If “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ” (Col. 2:3), how can the same Savior say that he does not know the day and hour of the coming judgment (Mark 13:32)? If he knows it but says that he does not, he appears to be lying.

This statement contains a twofold meaning. He says that all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in Christ in such a way that whoever possesses Christ regards him as surpassing all wisdom and knowledge.

[Note: [Col. 2409] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “believes him to be everything.”]

To know Christ is to know everything and to have comprehended all wisdom, as is said to the Colossians: “Let no one deceive you through philosophy and empty deceit, according to the elements of this world and not according to Christ, because in Christ the whole fullness of divinity dwells bodily” (Col. 2:8–9). [Col. 2410] That is, the person who believes in Christ lacks nothing necessary for salvation; rather, all such things abound in him, because the fullness of divinity is in his faith.

Again, in the same Epistle, among other things, he says: “Let no one deceive you through self-abasement and the worship of angels, taking his stand on things he has seen, vainly puffed up by the mind of his flesh, and not holding fast to the head, from whom the whole body, supplied and knit together, grows with the increase of God” (Col. 2:18–19).

If believers in Christ venerate him as the head of every principality and power, they lack nothing but possess everything necessary for salvation. It will not harm them to be ignorant of lower matters that contribute nothing to salvation, since they know what is necessary. Those who know what benefits them for salvation should therefore be said to know everything.

There is also this consideration: all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden in the Savior. He knows all the Father’s mysteries; he measures every creature; and “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5:22). “No one knows what is in God except the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2:11), and this Spirit also belongs to Christ.

How, then, can Christ be said not to know the day and hour of the coming judgment, when his Spirit knows what is in God, and he said of that Spirit that it would receive from him (John 16:14–15)? If the one who receives from him knows what is to come, how can Christ not know, since he sent the Holy Spirit? Can a judge be ignorant of the day of the coming judgment, when he has given all the signs indicating when it should be expected?

Perhaps those are also truly said to be unknown to him to whom he says: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25:12). Nor will he be said to know the foolish and careless virgins, since, when they say, “Lord, Lord, open to us,” he also says to them: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.”

The reason, therefore, is that he says he does not know what he does know. Thus he says: “Keep watch, because you do not know at what hour your Lord will come” (Matt. 24:42). To make us anxious and watchful, when asked he said that he did not know the day and hour of the coming judgment. But in order to benefit us, he denied that he knew what he did know.

Although we do not know what is beneficial for us, we desire to know everything; yet if we knew it, it would harm us. Christ, the guardian of our salvation, therefore said that he did not know, so that we would not hear what would be against us.

If someone in pain asks for a sword with which to kill himself, and the person who possesses it replies that he does not have one, although he knows that denying it would be contrary to the truth, should he be accused of lying?

## LXIII

[Note: [Col. 2410] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

Why, although the Apostles healed all the illnesses brought before them, did they not provide healing for their own sick? For Epaphroditus surely would not have been sick to the point of death (Phil. 2:27) if the Apostle’s intercession had been heard. Who could doubt that the Apostle often prayed for this, yet did not obtain it? If he had been heard, would not the illness have been removed immediately?

The Apostles performed signs and wonders so that unbelief would be compelled toward faith: seeing things accomplished that are impossible for human beings, people would recognize that the preaching came from God and would prove by the power of the deeds that there is reason in faith. Since words are always contradicted, power was set forth as a witness; when words yield to it, this signifies that faith contains a reason that cannot be expressed in words.

Among believers, therefore, signs and wonders are no longer necessary, but firm hope is. Once people learn that the promises are true, the mind arms itself for this purpose: by despising present things, it may prove worthy of future things, storing up merit for itself through labor. Solomon testifies to this when he says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in justice and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclus. 2:1).

Because a person progresses through temptations, these warnings were given. Hence the Apostle says: “Through tribulations we must enter the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:21). These temptations of tribulation occur in various ways, so that a steadfast mind may be crowned in the faith it has received.

A person is tested not only [Col. 2411] in faith, but also in illness, loss, persecution, and the death of loved ones. If, amid these sufferings, he is not led away to seek the aid of demons, he purchases martyrdom without the price of blood.

The Apostle therefore did not fail to obtain what he requested for Epaphroditus to his loss, but for his advancement. For in his own case, when he had asked, he heard: “My grace is sufficient for you, for power is made perfect in weakness” (2 Cor. 12:9).

## LXIV

[Note: [Col. 2411] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

The Apostle Peter says, “Christ died for you” (1 Pet. 2:21). But the Apostle Paul asserts that he also died for himself: “He became obedient,” he says, “unto death; therefore God bestowed on him the name that is above every name” (Phil. 2:8–9). If this is so, he will appear to have been imperfect, since through his works he produced an increase.

No believer doubts that the Son of God was born perfect from God. In being born from God the Father, he received all the Father’s divinity.

[Col. 2412]

Therefore he then received the name that is above every name—that is, so that he might be called what the Father is: God. Nothing is said to be future for him, for he possesses everything before himself. He was therefore born for the creation and restoration of all things.

The order and reason of the matter certainly require every knee to bow to the Father’s name. The Father bestowed this upon the Son because of what he was going to do; he bestowed it when he begot him. For he begot him in such a way that he was in the same honor in which the Father himself is.

## LXV

[Note: [Col. 2412] Found above among the first published questions, near Question 72.]

What is the meaning of what was said to John, as it is written in the Apocalypse: “Go and take the book and devour it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey”? What is this book, or how does it make the stomach bitter when it is sweet?

Frequently, the person who seeks a shortcut is accustomed to go astray. Why is it that you do not present everything that was said in relation to the matter, etc.

# SECOND PART OF THE QUESTIONS MIXED FROM BOTH SOURCES

[Col. 2411]

## FIRST QUESTION

[Note: [Col. 2411] Identical with the question found above among the first published questions, Question 21.]

What does it mean that God made the human being in his image and likeness, and is woman the image of God?

To have been made in the image of God means that one made one, etc.

## II

[Note: [Col. 2411] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class.]

The Gospel testifies that no one has seen God (John 1:18; 6:46; 1 Tim. 6:16). Yet Jacob, Moses, and Isaiah assert that they saw God (Gen. 32:30; Isa. 6:1). Someone may say, “No one has seen the Father.” What does that have to do with the matter? If the Son was seen, the Father too was seen, since the Father and the Son are one God both in substance and in image: the two have one image. As he himself says, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John 14:9).

How, then, has no one seen God the Father, when the Son says that the Father is seen when he himself is seen? Because there is not another God. If he is not another, then he himself, since he is one, was seen as God.

As far as the Evangelist is concerned, he said this about God the Father: “No one has ever seen God, except the only-begotten Son who is in the bosom of the Father; he has made him known.” Let us believe the Son; he himself has made it known that no one except him has seen God.

He said this in order to teach that he himself had always appeared to the patriarchs and prophets. This therefore does not refer to the one God in general, but to the person of the Father, of whom no other expression can be used than “God the Father.”

The Son, however, says that he was seen in such a way that he nevertheless remains invisible in the very thing in which he is thought to be seen. “Seen” here means understood; for he was not seen with the eyes, but understood by the mind. To have seen him meant to have understood that God was present in what appeared there.

When the Savior says, “Whoever sees me sees the Father also,” he certainly does not refer this to the sight of the eyes but to that of the mind, so that no difference between the Father and the Son would be supposed. Neither of them, therefore, was seen according to substance. Among the appearances, however, only the Son was seen by the mind, not by bodily eyes, because he is invisible just as the Father is.

## III

[Note: [Col. 2411] Absent from the same manuscripts.]

The Old Law records that God swore. For it says: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord” (Gen. 22:16). But the Savior prohibited swearing (Matt. 5:34). How, then, did he not destroy the ancient commandments?

Before knowledge of God existed on earth, it was not appropriate to summon people to an unheard-of hope in any other way than by making the promise an oath sworn to them by one whom they did not know as they ought. But once he began to be known, it was no longer appropriate for him to swear, since it would be unlawful to suppose that he could lie.

[Col. 2412] Therefore the Lord no longer commanded even servants to swear, but instructed them to make themselves such that their words would be believed. The solemnity of an oath was demanded either by faithlessness or by the deceitfulness of an inconsistent person: because people are accustomed to deceive, they may perhaps be restrained by fear and reverence for God; or at least it suffices that the person who is deceived thereby has grounds for offense.

## IV

[Note: [Col. 2412] Found above among the first published questions, near Question 67.]

What is the meaning of the Savior’s saying while hanging on the cross, “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing”? If they do not know, what is there to forgive, especially when Abimelech says to God, “Will you destroy those who are ignorant?”

Not everyone who is ignorant is free from punishment. For the person who could have learned but did not make the effort, etc.

V [Note: [Col. 2412] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class].—If no one is justified before God by the Law, why is it written, “Cursed is everyone who does not continue in all the things written in the book of the Law, so as to do them” (Deut. 27:26)? If people are justified by faith and not by the Law (Gal. 2:16), why is the one who has not fulfilled the Law accursed, since it does not advance him toward righteousness?

The Law given through Moses did indeed possess righteousness, but an earthly one: those who kept the Law were righteous for the present, so that they would not become liable to punishment. For the one who harms no one is righteous according to the Law. Hence the Apostle says, “The Law is not of faith; rather, the one who does these things will live by them” (Gal. 3:12). That is: the one who does the Law will not die, but lives for the present. The righteousness that comes from faith, however, justifies people before God, so that they may be rewarded in the age to come. They added the righteousness of faith to temporal righteousness. For it is righteous that we know from whom and through whom we exist, so that the true confession of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit may lead us to the heavenly kingdoms.

For even the ancients who not only kept the precepts of the Law but also loved God, having hope in the promise, were justified before God. He says that the Law alone does not justify people before God, just as faith alone, apart from good works, does not commend them before God; rather, the preservation of both earthly and divine righteousness makes them perfect. Hence the Lord says: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20).

VI [Note: [Col. 2413] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class].—What does David mean when he says, “Let those who say to me, ‘Well done, well done,’ be confounded and put to shame” (Ps. 69:4), while the Lord says, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matt. 25:21, 23), and so forth? What David took as evil, does the Savior show to be worthy of good merits?

This does not differ greatly from the preceding question. For one word has different meanings, as I mentioned above (in the second part of the *Questions from the New Testament*, question 54). David’s detractors, while favoring his ruin, congratulated themselves on his misfortunes. While he was suffering pressures and distress from Saul and from his son Absalom, they said that things were rightly and properly happening to him. It is as though someone were to say of a person suffering insults, “This is good for him,” rejoicing in his misfortunes—that is, “It serves him right; this is what he deserves.”

In the same way, the Savior, rejoicing in good works, declares a person’s merit by saying, “Well done, good and faithful servant.” He exults because the servant has made himself more worthy, saying, “Well”—that is, “You have acted rightly, so that you might attain a greater merit” [Note: [Col. 2413] So reads the Germanensis manuscript. The printed editions have *utinam* (“would that”)]. One word, therefore, is applied to two contrary circumstances.

For we commonly say of someone, “He has been adjudged.” But whether this is said for good or for evil is shown by the circumstance that follows or precedes. Sometimes it is said with reference to good, sometimes to evil. So too desire (*concupiscentia*) is sometimes applied to good and sometimes to evil.

VII [Note: [Col. 2413] Absent from the same manuscripts].—What does the Psalm mean when it says, “You will save humans and beasts” (Ps. 36:7), and when God says to the prophet Jonah, “Shall I not spare the city in which there are one hundred and thirty thousand human beings and many animals” (Jonah 4:11)? On the other hand, the Apostle says, “Is it oxen that God is concerned about?” (1 Cor. 9:9).

As far as the words are concerned, there appears to be a contradiction; but if the reason concerning human beings and animals is examined, it will become clear that there is no difference. God cares for all things, as the maker of all; but he does not preserve animals for their own sake. He preserves animals for the sake of human beings, not human beings for the sake of animals. Thus, because he cares for human beings, he protects animals, so that his concern is not for oxen but for human beings. For what hope is there in animals?

VIII [Note: [Col. 2413] Absent from the same manuscripts].—In Tobit it says, “It is honorable to reveal and confess the works of God” (Tob. 12:7). But the Savior, performing the work of God, says, “Tell no one” (Mark 8:26).

The Savior did not say that the work of God ought to be concealed. For elsewhere he says, “Go and tell how much God has done for you” (Mark 5:19). Rather, on one occasion he rejected their testimony and restrained their boasting, lest he himself appear—as would be absurd to the prudent—to bear witness to himself like a deceiver.

IX [Note: [Col. 2413] Absent from the same manuscripts].—On the eternity of the Son.

Since there are some who, not yet having dispelled the darkness of error or cleansed and wiped away the decay of an aged life, judge according to earthly understanding and doubt either about the Son of God or about whether the two are one—for the perfidious and obstinate nation of the Jews, to whom the fountain of the Law and the treasures of the sacraments were opened [Note: [Col. 2413] So reads the Germanensis manuscript. The printed editions have: “the treasures could show this.”], does not merely doubt but denies it with wicked words—I shall explain the matter briefly, as the shorter scope permits.

For those who are ignorant, hope remains intact if they are willing to learn; but eternal punishment is reserved for those who dissemble. Since almighty God is superior in greatness and goodness, he ought to have brought forth and displayed from himself something great and supremely good. But if he had brought forth something contrary to the measure of his excellence, he would either appear not to have been able to bring forth anything greater—which cannot be attributed to the Almighty—or not to have wished to do so—which is incompatible with the most benevolent. Certainly, it would not have been a great thing for the supreme God to make something placed beneath himself that did not possess the force of complete supremacy.

There was therefore nothing above him, for nothing overcomes God; and there was little beneath him, because what is less than the greatest was not fitting. Thus, creating his Son as his very likeness, he brought forth from himself, as it were, another self. In this way that supreme and greatest good which comes to us from God has overflowed to us through his propagation.

This principle must also be understood at the same time: the God who created this world—and who, among the other wonders of its beauty and order, granted it the nature of creating, so that it might produce offspring sufficient for every kind—must himself first have possessed what he gave. For no one gives what he himself does not have.

He who therefore possessed a Son corresponding to himself in every aspect of likeness—that is, one corresponding to one, upright to upright, good to kind, blessed to blessed, greatest to greatest, everlasting to everlasting—certainly possessed, before the world, the primacy of created offspring. From this he imparted a pattern to things that were to arise, so that the offspring of those who beget might be compelled to correspond to their own seeds.

Nor did the legitimate order permit otherwise than that the one who was to be the father of future things should first have been a father in his own right—that is, the father of his own offspring.

But when we have said that the Son was brought forth, this must not be understood as though his origin were like ours, or that he was born in the manner in which we see mortals born, when, as the offspring bursts forth, things come into existence that previously did not exist. Those beings, conceived from seeds implanted elsewhere, coalesce through the gathering of underlying elements into the form of their own kind [Note: [Col. 2414] The Germanensis manuscript reads: “through the separation of the elements they coalesce into a gathering in the form of their own kind”]. But this being, by divine action and without the admixture of any external assistance, brought forth and produced from itself that which it had always possessed in itself and with itself.

For if we say that light is born from the sun because it proceeds and flows from it, we do not mean that the sun could ever be or have been without light, or that at some time it generated light as something later than itself [Note: [Col. 2414] The Germanensis manuscript reads, “as something prior to itself”]. Rather, what it has always possessed with itself—namely, light, begotten from itself without any distinction of beginning—continually shines forth from it, as though it were always renewing the light it has given, so that it may always shine.

Thus the Son of God, wholly joined to the Father from eternity, also possessed this likeness to him, so that he has neither beginning nor end. As God is eternal without origin, so also is the Son eternal. And as God is one, simple, and the same, so he is mingled with the Father in such a way that, although they are distinct in names and affections, they are the same: one in both, and each continuing in the other in inseparable majesty.

God therefore does not contain the Son as something drawn from discordant materials, but as something brought forth from the simple and singular stock and seedbed of his nature, always possessed within himself and never at any time dismissed from himself by separation. He contains and embraces him with himself in such a way that nothing in the two is changed concerning that unity.

X [Note: [Col. 2414] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class].—What does the Apostle say to the Galatians: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring from him who called you into grace to another gospel, which is not another” (Gal. 1:6–7)? If it is certainly another, it is not the same; if it is not the same, how is it not another?

He calls it another gospel to which they had been called because it was not the one that the Galatians had subsequently begun to follow. Having been led away from the Gospel of Christ, they had been drawn into Judaism under the name of Christ, as though this were what they ought to follow, and they affirmed something other than what the Apostle preached. Hence one reads by implication: “As they persuade you.”

For the false apostles, when they were deceiving Gentile believers, said that what they themselves taught had been handed down by the Savior, as is contained in the Acts of the Apostles: “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved” (Acts 15:1).

Moved by grief at their overthrow, the Apostle therefore writes to them, saying: “I am astonished that you are so quickly transferring from him who called you into grace to another gospel, which is not another.” He is astonished because, after something light and less burdensome, they were turning to harshness and a burden. That is, after the simplicity of faith, they were allowing themselves to be circumcised for the sake of the elements, observing new moons and the Sabbath; they were subjected to and provoked by the elements—that is, by grace, not by the works of the Law [Note: [Col. 2415] The words “they were subjected to and provoked by the elements, that is, by grace, not by the works of the Law” are absent from the Germanensis manuscript].

And lest he seem to have given the false apostles an opportunity to say that what the Galatians had received was something other than what the tradition of truth contains, he immediately added, “which is not another,” except that there are some who trouble you and wish to turn the Gospel of Christ into something else.

The gospel, therefore, to which they had been called by the Apostle was other than that which they had begun to follow at the urging of the false apostles. Yet it was not other than what Christ had handed down, so that they might recognize by this very fact that they had been led into error and might follow faith alone, confessing Christ as God and affirming that he alone is sufficient to bestow salvation. Through him they had obtained the forgiveness of sins, not through the Law, because without the Law the grace of God grants pardon for offenses.

XI [Note: [Col. 2415] Absent from the manuscripts of the first class].—The Apostle Paul indicates that one should not grieve over the dead (1 Thess. 4:12). For grieving belongs to those without hope. Yet concerning Epaphroditus he himself says: “He was ill, close to death, but God had mercy on him—and not only on him but also on me, so that I might not have sorrow upon sorrow” (Phil. 2:27). How does he forbid grieving when he himself declares that he would have grieved if Epaphroditus had died?

He indicated that he would have grieved over Epaphroditus’s death, if it had occurred, for one reason, and forbids grieving for another. In this case he said that he would have grieved because he would have been deprived of the comfort of his assistance, which he used in the Gospel. But he forbids us to grieve in such a way that we mourn the dead as though they were extinguished and lost, despairing of the resurrection.

It is one thing to seek the comfort of someone absent, and another to grieve an end beyond which he will no longer exist. In the former case consolation ceases; in the latter despair is excluded.

XII [Note: [Col. 2416] The same as question 62 among the first published questions].—Why is Rachel said to mourn her sons when the sons of Leah, who belong to the tribe of Judah, were killed?

As far as the historical meaning is concerned, Rachel’s sons were formerly destroyed and erased from the other tribes on account of their wicked, Sodomite deed and the outrage they committed against the concubine of the Levite, and so forth.

# EXPOSITION OF THE APOCALYPSE OF JOHN

[Col. 2415]

## NOTICE CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING EXPOSITION OF THE APOCALYPSE

When you examine the commentaries of the ancients on the Apocalypse, a large part of the exposition that follows will meet you, compiled especially from the words of Victorinus the martyr—if, indeed, the commentary circulated under his name belongs to him—and from those of Primasius and Bede.

Some wished to accept this entirely as the work of Tichonius. Yet certainly it does not contain here the material that the Donatist had introduced into his work, namely, “many things,” as Primasius writes, “contrary to sound doctrine, so that, concerning the controversy between Catholics and Donatists, he sought places where he could inflict harm according to the perversity of his heart, and thought that the Catholic Church should be mockingly attacked by a harmful exposition.”

Indeed, many statements are deliberately expounded against the heresy of the Donatists, and the repetition of Baptism, which was practiced by those schismatics, is repeatedly rejected, as in Homily 6 on the Apocalypse, chapter 8, verse 11: “This,” says the author, “can plainly be understood of those who are rebaptized.” For this reason, certain interpretations reported by Bede under the name of Tichonius are also absent.

Moreover, when Tichonius sought in the Apocalypse to determine how the angels of the seven churches were to be understood, to whom John is commanded to write, “he reasons in many ways,” Augustine says in book 3 of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 30, “and arrives at the point that we understand the angels themselves as the churches,” using, certainly, “a most extensive argument.” But in this matter the writer of the work that follows is much shorter and more concise. He was evidently content to extract bare interpretations from the books of others, and perhaps from Tichonius himself, from whom Primasius and Bede likewise borrowed certain notable passages.

Therefore the Louvain theologians rightly judged that this work is nothing more than annotations collected through someone’s scholarly effort and later reduced to the form of homilies.

Furthermore, in the most ancient manuscript of the Abbey of Saint Peter at Chartres, Homily 16 is divided into two by the addition of certain words. In addition, Homily 1 does not have the same beginning there as in the printed editions, but a somewhat different one, under these words:

> “The things contained in the Apocalypse of Saint John, dearest brothers, have seemed to some of the ancient Fathers to signify either the whole or certainly the greater part of the day of judgment or the coming of Antichrist, as appears from the reading itself. But those who have treated the matter more carefully have understood that the things contained in this revelation began immediately after the Passion of our Lord and Savior and are to be brought to completion in this way up to the day of judgment, so that only a small portion seems to remain for the time of Antichrist. Therefore, whatever you hear being read in this passage—whether the Son of Man, the stars, the angels, the lampstands, the four living creatures, or the eagle flying in mid-heaven—and everything else, understand it as occurring in Christ and in the Church, or recognize that it was foretold as a type of them.
>
> “In the seven churches to which Saint John the evangelist wrote in Asia, the one Catholic Church is understood, on account of the sevenfold Spirit of grace. When he says, ‘the faithful witness,’ it is Christ, who bore witness under Pontius Pilate. ‘He made us,’ he says, ‘a kingdom and priests for God’: by ‘priests for God’ he means the whole Church, as Saint Peter says: ‘You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood’ (1 Pet. 2:9). And ‘I saw,’ he says, ‘seven golden lampstands’: the Church is in the seven lampstands. And ‘in the midst of the lampstands one like the Son of Man’ (Rev. 1:5–6, 12–13), that is, Christ. Whether the Son of Man or the seven lampstands—”

[Col. 2417]

# EXPOSITION OF THE APOCALYPSE OF BLESSED JOHN (C, G, S)*

## HOMILY I [Note: [Col. 2417] The title “Homily 1” is not found in the old Petrensis manuscript].

### [APOCALYPSE, CHAPTER 1]

In the reading of the revelation of the blessed Apostle John, dearest brothers, we have observed—and, with the Lord’s help, we shall strive to explain according to the spiritual sense—that the revelation of Jesus Christ is opened to our ears so that heavenly mysteries may be made manifest to our hearts.

“ The Apocalypse of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to make known to his servants”—that is, to reveal—“the things that must soon take place,” indicating this, that is, showing it. “To his servant John.” John is interpreted as “by the grace of God.”

“Writing to the seven churches that are in Asia.” Asia is interpreted as “Elevation” (*Elatio*), through which the human race is represented. These seven churches and seven lampstands must be carefully understood, because they signify the sevenfold grace given by God through Jesus Christ our Lord to us, the human race that has believed. For he himself also promised to send us from heaven the Paraclete Spirit, whom he sent to the Apostles who appeared to be in Asia—that is, in the elevated world—where he also granted us, through his servant John, the sevenfold grace in the seven churches.

“Grace to you and peace be multiplied from God the Father and from the Son of Man”—that is, from Christ. Whether the Son of Man, the seven lampstands, or the seven stars is mentioned, the Church with Christ her head is understood.

But when he says, “Girded across the breasts with a golden sash,” the one who was girded signifies Christ the Lord. Understand the two breasts as the two Testaments, which receive from the Lord Savior’s breast, as from an everlasting fountain, what nourishes the Christian people for eternal life.

The golden sash is the chorus, or multitude, of the saints. For just as the breast is tightened by a belt, so the multitude of the saints clings to Christ and, as it were, embraces the two breasts—the two Testaments—so that from them, as from holy breasts, they may be nourished.

“His head and his hair,” he says, “were like white wool and snow.” By the white hair he means the multitude of those made white—that is, neophytes emerging from Baptism [Note: [Col. 2417] The Petrensis manuscript reads “proceeding”]. He said “wool” because they are Christ’s sheep. He said “snow” because, just as snow descends freely from heaven, so the grace of Baptism comes without preceding merits.

Those who are baptized are Jerusalem, which daily descends from heaven in the likeness of snow. Jerusalem—that is, the Church—is said to descend from heaven because grace is from heaven; through it she is freed from sins and joined to Christ, the eternal head and heavenly bridegroom.

By contrast, the beast is said to ascend from the abyss—that is, the evil people who arise from an evil people. For just as Jerusalem is exalted by humbly descending, so the beast, that is, the proud people, is cast down by ascending arrogantly.

“His eyes were like a flame of fire.” In the eyes he signifies the commandments of God, as it is written: “Your word is a lamp to my feet, O Lord,” and, “Your utterance is tested by fire” (Ps. 119:105, 140).

“And his feet were like Libanian orichalcum” [Note: [Col. 2417] The printed editions have *clibani* (“of a furnace”); but *Libani* (“of Lebanon”) is clearly the reading, from Primasius and Autpertus], “refined as though in a furnace of fire.” In the fiery feet the Church is understood. As the day of judgment approaches, she must be tested by the excess of her tribulations and examined by fire.

And because the foot is the last part of the body, and he said that the feet were fiery, the Church of the final age is understood in the feet, to be tested by many tribulations like gold in a furnace. Whoever considers this carefully sees that it is already now being brought about by the multitude of iniquities.

For this reason he signified it by orichalcum, which is brought to the color of gold from bronze and much fire, together with a process of treatment [Col. 2418]: just as the Church is made purer through tribulations and sufferings.

The golden sash girded around the breast may also signify the spiritual knowledge and pure understanding given to the Church.

But the two-edged sword proceeding from his mouth signifies that it is Christ himself, who has now brought the good things of the Gospel to the whole world and previously brought knowledge of the Law through Moses. David likewise says of him, “God has spoken once; these two things I have heard” (Ps. 62:12). These, then, are the two Testaments, which according to the capacity of the time are called either new or old—the two-edged sword.

“His voice was like the voice of many waters.” The many waters are understood to be the peoples; in the voice, the preaching of the Apostles.

When he said above, “His feet were like orichalcum, as though molten in a furnace,” the Apostles may also be understood, since after the Passion they preached his word [Note: [Col. 2418] The Belgicus manuscript reads “through”]. For those through whom preaching walks are rightly called feet, as the prophet also said, “How beautiful are the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things” (Isa. 52:7), and, “We will worship in the place where his feet have stood” (Ps. 132:7).

When he said, “He held seven stars in his right hand,” he wished the Church to be understood. For in Christ’s right hand is the spiritual Church, to which, placed at the right hand, he says: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matt. 25:34).

The seven stars, therefore, are the Church. For we have said that the sevenfold Spirit of power was given to her by the Father, as Peter says to the Jews concerning Christ: “Therefore, exalted by the right hand of God, and having received the Spirit from the Father, he poured him out” (Acts 2:33).

He calls the seven churches by their own names, not because they alone are churches, but because what he says to one he says to all. Finally, whether in Asia or throughout the whole world, the seven churches signify all churches and are one Catholic Church, as he says to Timothy: “How you ought to conduct yourself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God” (1 Tim. 3:15).

And in Isaiah, he understands the seven women who “seized one man” (Isa. 4:1) to signify the seven churches, which are also one. By the man we understand Christ; by the women’s bread, the Holy Spirit, who nourishes them for eternal life.

And so that what has been said may be impressed more firmly upon you, we wish to make a brief recapitulation from it.
