The seven churches to which Saint John writes signify one Catholic Church, on account of the sevenfold grace. When he says, “the faithful witness,” it is Christ. The seven lampstands are the Catholic Church. “One like the Son of Man in the midst of the lampstands”: Christ is in the midst of the Church.

When he says, “girded above the breasts,” the breasts signify the two Testaments, which receive spiritual milk from Christ’s breast in order to nourish the Christian people for eternal life. The golden sash is the chorus, or multitude, of the saints, who, by continually devoting themselves to reading and prayer, are shown to cling to Christ.

Let these things suffice for your love. Meditate together among yourselves, in holy conversation, on what you have heard, until, with the Lord’s gift, you may hear what remains. May he himself deign to grant this, and so forth.

## HOMILY II [Note: [Col. 2418] The Petrensis manuscript has: “Here begins the continuation of the exposition of the Apocalypse”; and nearly the same appears in the others].

## [On Chapters II and IV]

Dearest brothers, in the lampstand about which you heard when the Apocalypse was read, the people are understood. But when he says, “I will move your lampstand,” this means: “I will disperse the people because of their sins.” “And I will fight against them with the sword of my mouth” [Col. 2419]—that is, “I will set forth my commandments, by which their sins or crimes will be reproved.”

But when he said, “His face was like the sun shining in its strength” (Rev. 1:16), this may be understood both of the coming or presence of Christ—for each person is manifested and recognized by his face—and of the Church, to which Christ promised this radiance, concerning which he says, “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13:43).

“The morning star”: he means the first resurrection, which takes place through the grace of Baptism. The morning star drives away the night and announces the light—that is, it removes sin and grants grace—provided that good works follow the grace received. For just as it is useless for a great tree to become green and yield no fruit [Note: [Col. 2419] The manuscripts read: “For it is not a great thing for a tree to live and not yield fruit. Thus it is useless.”], so it is useless to be called a Christian and not to have Christian works.

And therefore he says, “I counsel you to buy from me” [Note: [Col. 2419] The manuscripts read: “Counsel yourself; buy from me.”] “gold refined by fire” (Rev. 3:18)—that is, strive to suffer something for the name of Christ. “And anoint your eyes with salve,” so that what you gladly learn through the Scriptures you may fulfill in action.

John, the preacher of the New Testament, saw that a door stood open in heaven. [With what eyes did he see it? Insofar as the vision was figuratively displayed, not with the eyes of the flesh, but of the mind. But insofar as it concerned the truth of the thing itself, which had already been manifested when the Lord appeared in the flesh, he saw it not only with the eyes of the flesh, but also handled it with his hands. What, then, is signified by the door in this passage, if not Christ Jesus, the mediator between God and human beings, as the Lord himself says, “I am the door” (John 10:9), and so forth? Rightly, therefore, does he behold it not closed but open, because our same mediator became known to all the faithful by being born and dying, since he himself was the redeemer of the world.

What is signified by heaven, if not the Church? As he himself says, “Heaven is my throne” (Isa. 66:1); or the soul of the righteous, as Solomon testifies, is the seat of wisdom. Paul likewise declares that Christ is “the power of God and the wisdom of God” (1 Cor. 1:24). There is no doubt that heaven is the Church of the elect, in which the open door is seen, because in it our Redeemer is preached and believed to have been born, suffered, risen again, and ascended into heaven.

But what he heard while situated in this vision he makes clear by saying, “And the first voice that I heard was like a trumpet speaking with me, saying” [Note: [Col. 2419] The passages enclosed here in brackets, as well as the whole exposition of verse 3 below, which we have likewise distinguished by the same sign, are absent from the Petrensis and Belgicus manuscripts; they were added from Book 3 of Ambrosius Autpertus’s work On the Apocalypse.],] “Come up here.” When it is shown to be open, it is made clear that it had previously been closed to human beings.]

“The throne set in place” is the seat of the one judging, and upon it he saw a likeness resembling jasper and sardius. Jasper has the color of water, and sardius that of fire. In these two stones two judgments are understood: one, which has already taken place through water in the Flood; the other, which will take place through fire at the consummation of the age.

In this passage the life of God’s servants may also be understood, because, like water and fire, all the saints sometimes have prosperity in this life and sometimes suffer adversity.

[“And a rainbow was around the throne, like the appearance of an emerald.” The rainbow—*iris* in both Greek and Latin—is called an “arc” (*arcus*), which seems to appear on a rainy day. And what else is signified by it but the reconciliation of the world, which is known to have been accomplished through the dispensation of the incarnate Word?

If this is examined carefully, the effect of the rainbow itself seems to indicate this. The arc appears when a rain-bearing cloud has been illuminated by the sun’s rays. When the sun therefore illuminates the cloud, the rainbow, that is, the arc, appears; for the Word of the Father, who is the brightness of eternal light and the sun of righteousness, illuminated human nature by assuming it. This very assumption of his humanity—which is indeed called a cloud by the prophet (Isa. 19:1)—became the reconciliation of the world.

It is rightly called rain-bearing, because it is full of the utterances of preaching. Accordingly, in the New Testament the arc is figuratively described as having appeared for the reconciliation of the human race. In the Old Testament, too, it is understood to have been placed by the Lord in the clouds for this reason: so that, after the inundation of the Flood, peace might be recognized as restored to the earth through it; namely, so that almighty God, remembering his covenant by its appearance, would not thereafter allow the earth to be destroyed by the immensity of the waters.

If one letter is added to this name at the end, so that it is called *irini*, its interpretation seems to express the same meaning; for in the Greek word εἰρήνη (*eirēnē*) peace is called by that name. And in the Old Testament the Lord says to Noah, “Behold, I will establish my covenant with you” (Gen. 9:9).

The coherence of the figures should also be noted. Since in what follows flashes of lightning, voices, and thunder are related to proceed from the throne as from a cloud, it is fittingly said here that the same throne produced the likeness of an arc as the sun shone upon it. This arc, although of various colors and shining chiefly with two—namely, those of water and fire—is designated through the Flood [Note: [Col. 2420] More correctly, in Ambrosius Autpertus: “It is designated by it either as the Baptism of water and the Holy Spirit, or as the preceding judgment through the Flood,” and so forth.], and the subsequent judgment through fire. Here, however, it is not improperly compared to the appearance of an emerald, so that through it, as we have said, the divinity may be shown after the world has been reconciled.

The emerald is a stone of the deepest green. As I have already said in the preceding verse, this color is not inappropriately applied to the nature of divinity.]

“The glassy sea” is the gift of Baptism. It is said to be before the throne because it is given before the coming of judgment.

But when he says after this, “I have the keys of death and Hades,” he says this because whoever believes and is baptized is freed from death and from the underworld; and because the Church itself, just as it has the keys of life, also has those of the underworld. For it was said to her, “Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven him; and whose you retain, they are retained” (John 20:23).

Wherever in the Apocalypse he places an angel of a human being, he signifies that human being himself. Likewise, the Churches and their angels mentioned there should be understood only as either bishops or leaders of the Churches. He wished the catholic Churches to be understood under the name of angels to such an extent that he commands the angels to do penance. For the angels who are in heaven do not need penance, but human beings, who cannot be without sin, do.

Since “angel” is also interpreted as “messenger,” whoever—a bishop, priest, or even layperson—frequently speaks about God and announces how one may attain eternal life is rightly called an angel of God. Yet because no one can be without sin, it is said to him—that is, to the human being—that he should do penance. For whoever considers the matter carefully recognizes that not only laypeople but even priests ought not to spend a single day without penance. For just as there is no day on which a human being can be without sin, so there ought to be no day without the remedy of satisfaction.

The seven lampstands, and the one lampstand [Note: [Col. 2420] The Belgicus manuscript reads: “one toward the lampstand.”], may be understood as the sevenfold Church. Therefore, whatever appears to be spoken to the seven Churches is spoken to the one Church spread throughout the whole world, because all fullness is contained in the number seven.

Thus he calls the Churches angels, and in them he shows two parts, namely, the good and the evil. Therefore he not only praises but also rebukes, so that the praise may be directed to the good and the rebuke to the evil. In the Gospel, likewise, the Lord called the whole body of leaders one servant, both blessed and wicked, whom the Lord himself will divide when he comes.

How can one servant be divided, when a divided person cannot live? He calls the entire Christian people one servant. If that people were wholly good, it would not be divided. But because it contains not only the good but also the evil, it must be divided. The good will hear, “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom”; but the rapacious and adulterous, who have shown no mercy, will hear, “Depart from me, accursed ones, into eternal fire.”

What is said in the Apocalypse to the individual Churches, dearest brothers, applies to the individual human beings established in the one Church.

“These things says the one who holds the seven stars in his hand”: that is, the one who holds you in his hand, namely, in his power, and governs you.

“Who walks in the midst of the golden lampstands”: that is, in your midst, because those lampstands signify the Christian people.

But when he says, “I will move your lampstand from its place, unless you do penance,” observe that he did not say, “I will take it away,” but “I will move it,” because the lampstand signifies one Christian people. He says that the lampstand itself is to be moved, not taken away. This signifies that within one and the same Church the evil are moved while the good are strengthened; and that, by the hidden yet just judgment of God, what is taken away from the evil is increased for the good, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “To the one who has, more will be given; but from the one who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away” (Matt. 25:14–41).

But when he says, “To the one who conquers I will give to eat from the tree of life,” this means: from the fruit of the cross. “Which,” he says, “is in the paradise of my God”: he calls the Church paradise, for everything was made as a figure of it.

For when he says, “I know your works, your tribulation, and your poverty—but you are rich,” he speaks to the whole Church, which is poor in spirit and possesses all things.

But when he says, “You will have tribulation for ten days,” he assigns the whole span of time to the ten days, because the number ten is perfect. Within it, as the Apostle says, the Christian people enter the kingdom of heaven through many tribulations (Acts 14:21).

For when he says to the angel of the Church at Pergamum, “I know where you dwell, where Satan’s entrance is” (Rev. 2:13), he speaks to the whole Church under the name of one Church, because Satan dwells everywhere through his body. The body of Satan consists of proud and evil human beings, just as the body of Christ consists of the humble and good.

“To the one who conquers I will give to eat of the hidden manna”: that is, of the bread that descended from heaven. The manna in the wilderness was its figure; as the Lord himself said, many who ate it died (John 6:41). But even now, whoever eats unworthily eats judgment upon himself (1 Cor. 11:29).

That same bread is also the tree of life. By the manna we may likewise understand immortality.

“And I will give him a white stone”: that is, a body made white through Baptism. “And upon the stone a new name written”: that is, knowledge of the Son of Man. “Which no one knows except the one who receives it”—namely, through revelation. Therefore it is said concerning the Jews, “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2:8).

But when he says to the angel of the Church at Thyatira, “I have this against you, because you allowed the woman Jezebel,” he speaks to the leaders of the Churches who do not impose the strictness of ecclesiastical discipline upon the luxurious, the fornicators, and those committing any other evil.

This may also be understood of heretics: “who calls herself a prophetess,” that is, a Christian. For many heresies now flatter themselves with this name.

“And you did not know the depths of Satan”: that is, you did not reject [Note: [Col. 2421] The manuscripts read: “you look upon.”] his teaching, as the heresies do.

“I will not lay upon you any other burden”: that is, beyond what you are able to bear.

“But what you have, hold fast until I come. And the one who conquers and keeps my works until the end, to him I will give authority over the nations; and he will shepherd them with an iron rod, and they will be broken like a potter’s vessel, just as I too received from my Father.”

The Church has this power in Christ, as the Apostle says, “With him he has given us all things” (Rom. 8:32). He speaks of an iron rod because of the rigor of justice; by that same rod the good are corrected and the evil are broken.

## HOMILY III

### [On Chapters III and IV]

Now, dearest brothers, we have heard blessed John terrifyingly rebuke the sinful human being. Therefore, let us reflect with great fear and tremble at what was said: “I know your works, that you have a name that you are alive, but you are dead.”

No one dies except one who has committed a mortal crime, according to what was said: “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18:20). What is worse, many are known to carry dead souls within living bodies.

“Be watchful, and strengthen the rest that were about to die.”

“These things says the holy and true one who holds the keys of David”: that is, royal authority.

“He who opens, and no one shuts; who shuts, and no one opens”: it is clear that Christ opens the door of life to those who knock, but closes it to hypocrites, that is, to those whose life is feigned.

“Behold, I have set before you an open door”: this was said so that no one might say that the door which God opens to the Church throughout the whole world [Note: [Col. 2422] The Petrensis manuscript reads: “throughout the entire world.”] could be closed by anyone, even in part.

“Because you have little strength”: it is God’s praise that he opens the door to a Church of little faith.

“And I will write upon it the name of my God”: namely, the name by which we Christians are marked.

“And the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which descends from heaven”: he calls the heavenly new Jerusalem the Church, which is born from the Lord. He called it new because of the newness of the Christian name and because we are made new from old people.

“You are neither cold nor hot”: that is, you are useless. This may also be applied to the person of sterile rich people, who possess resources but do not use them to show mercy. Those who possess resources are not poor; those who do not act from their wealth are not rich.

“I advise you to buy gold for yourself”: that is, by giving alms and devoting yourself to good deeds, become gold yourself—that is, receive understanding from God and, through a good way of life, become worthy to suffer martyrdom.

“And behold,” he says, “a door was opened in heaven.” He calls Christ the open door, because he is the gate. He calls the Church heaven, where heavenly things are carried out, as the Apostle says, “To restore all things that are in heaven and that are on earth” (Eph. 1:10). Heaven is understood as the primitive Church from the Jews, while earth is understood as the Church from the Gentiles.

“Come up here, and I will show you”: this applies not only to John, but to the Church or to all believers. For whoever sees the door opened in heaven—that is, believes that Christ was born, suffered, and rose again—ascends to the heights and sees what is to come.

[By what steps, if not those of faith and belief? It is as though it were plainly said to any of the elect: “To come to know the mysteries of Christ and the Church, climb by faith and reach them through belief.” Rightly is John invited by the first voice to climb to the door of heaven and to heaven itself, because each of the elect, in order to reach through the Gospel the mysteries of true faith with an unwavering step of belief, is strengthened by the teaching of the Old Testament, which precedes the New. [Note: [Col. 2422] The Petrensis and Belgicus manuscripts lack these seven lines, which were copied from Book 3 of Ambrosius Autpertus’s work On the Apocalypse, as were the words set off in brackets somewhat later.]]

“And behold, a throne was set in heaven”: that is, in the Church. “And the one seated was like the appearance of a jasper stone or sardius”: these comparisons apply to the Church. Jasper has the color of water, and sardius that of fire. Through these, as has already been said, he wishes two judgments to be understood: one through water, which has already taken place through the Flood; the other, which will take place through fire.

[What is signified by jasper if not the divinity of our Mediator?]

“Around the throne I saw twenty-four seats, and upon the seats twenty-four elders seated.” He calls the elders the whole Church, as Isaiah says, “When he is glorified in the midst of his elders” (Isa. 24:23).

The twenty-four elders are the leaders and the people. In the twelve, understand the Apostles and the leaders; in the other twelve, understand the rest of the Church.

“And from the throne proceeded flashes of lightning and voices”: for heretics proceed from the Church, because “they went out from us.” There is also another interpretation: the flashes of lightning and voices may be understood as the preaching of the Church. In the voices, words are recognized; in the flashes of lightning, miracles.

“In the sight of the throne was a glassy sea”: the glassy sea is the font of Baptism. He said “before the throne,” that is, before judgment.

But at times also understand the holy soul as the throne, as it is written, “The soul of the righteous is the seat of wisdom” (Wis. 7); at times, the Church in which God has his seat.

“And in the midst of the throne were four living creatures”: that is, in the midst of the Church, the Evangelists [Note: [Col. 2422] The manuscripts read: “the Gospels.”].

“Full of eyes in front and behind”: that is, within and without. The eyes are God’s commandments. “In front and behind” means seeing what is past and what is to come.

“In the first living creature, one like a lion”: the strength of the Church is shown. In the calf, the passion of Christ. In the third living creature, which is like a human being, the humility of the Church is signified, because it does not flatter itself so as to think proudly, although it possesses adoption as children.

[Col. 2423] The fourth living creature, he said, was “like an eagle”: that is, flying and free, and lifted above the earth by two wings, as though raised by the guiding principles of the two Testaments or the two commandments.

For when the Evangelist John had examined these living creatures and recognized that the fourfold mystery had been fulfilled in Christ, and had seen a human being being born, a calf suffering, and a lion reigning, then he also saw an eagle returning to heavenly things.

“And each of them had six wings around it.” In the living creatures the twenty-four elders are shown, for the six wings of the four living creatures amount to twenty-four wings. Indeed, he saw the living creatures around the throne, where he had said that he saw the elders.

For how can a living creature with six wings be like an eagle, which has two wings, unless the four living creatures are one, possessing twenty-four wings, in which we understand the twenty-four elders who are in the Church that he compared to an eagle?

There is another interpretation: the six wings are the testimonies of the Old Testament. For just as a living creature cannot fly unless it has feathers, so the preaching of the New Testament has no credibility unless it possesses the testimonies foretold in the Old Testament, by which it is lifted from the earth and flies.

Whenever something previously announced as future is later found to have happened, it establishes indisputable credibility. For unless what the Prophets had foretold had been fulfilled in Christ, their preaching would be empty.

The catholic Church holds what was foretold beforehand and later fulfilled. Rightly, therefore, one living creature flies and is lifted from the earth into heaven [Note: [Col. 2423] In Victorinus: “the living creature.”].

“And those living creatures had no rest”: it is the Church, which does not rest but always praises God.

The twenty-four elders may also be understood as the books of the Old Testament, together with the Patriarchs and the Apostles. The flashes of lightning and thunder said to proceed from the throne are the preachings and promises of the New Testament.

“Casting their crowns before the throne”: this is because whatever dignity the saints possess, they attribute entirely to God. Likewise, in the Gospel they spread palms and flowers beneath his feet (Matt. 21:8), attributing to him everything they had conquered [Note: [Col. 2423] The Belgicus manuscript reads: “everything.”].

“For you created all things, and by your will they existed and were created”: they existed according to God, by whom all things were possessed before they came into being; they were created so that they might also be seen by us. As Moses says to the Church, “Is he not your Father, who made you, possessed you, and created you?” (Deut. 32:6). He possessed them in foreknowledge, made them in Adam, and created them from Adam.

## HOMILY IV

### [On Chapter V]

“And I saw upon the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and on the outside”: understand both Testaments—the Old on the outside, and the New within, which lay hidden inside the Old.

“Sealed,” he says, “with seven seals”: that is, obscured by the fullness of all the mysteries, which remained sealed until the passion and resurrection of Christ.

For just as what people make when they are dying is called a testament, and it is sealed until the death of the testator and opened after his death, so all the mysteries are revealed after Christ’s death.

“And I saw a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice: Who is worthy to open the book and to break its seals?”

There is a definite reason why the seals are broken first and the book then opened. Christ opened the book when, having undertaken the work of the Father’s will, he was conceived and born. He broke its seals when he was killed for the human race.

“And no one was able, neither in heaven nor on earth nor under the earth”: that is, neither an angel, nor anyone living on earth, nor anyone who had died.

“To open the book or to look upon it”: that is, to contemplate the splendor of the grace of the New Testament.

“And I wept greatly, because no one was found worthy to open the book and to look upon it”: the Church was weeping. John represented the Church, burdened and weighed down by sins, imploring her redemption.

“And behold, one of the elders”: understand one of the elders as the entire body of the Prophets. For the Prophets consoled the Church by announcing Christ from the tribe of Judah, the root of David.

He conquers every sin in us, and if anyone possesses anything good, he possesses it from him.

“And I saw, and behold, in the midst of the throne and of the four living creatures, and in the midst of the elders, a Lamb standing as though slain”: the throne, the living creatures, the elders, and the Lamb as though slain are the Church with her head, which dies for Christ in order to live with Christ.

The martyrs in the Church may also be understood as the Lamb who was slain.

“Having,” he says, “seven horns and seven eyes, which are the spirits of God sent into all the earth”: from this it is clearly known that no one can possess the Spirit of God apart from the Church.

“And he came and took the book from the right hand of the one seated upon the throne”: by the one seated upon the throne we understand both the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. The Lamb therefore took the book from the right hand of God; that is, he received from the Son the work of bringing the book to completion, as he himself says, “As the Father sent me, so I send you” (John 20:21), because he himself accomplishes in them what he gives.

“Each holding a harp”: that is, strings of praise.

“And golden bowls”: these are vessels in the house of the Lord, in which incense was customarily offered; therefore we rightly understand the prayers of the saints to be in them.

“And they sang a new song”: that is, the New Testament; singing a new song means publicly proclaiming their confession.

And it is truly new that the Son of God became human, died, rose again, ascended into heaven, and gave human beings the forgiveness of sins.

For the harp—that is, the string stretched upon wood—signifies the flesh of Christ joined to his passion; but the bowl signifies confession and the propagation of the new priesthood.

The unsealing of the seals is the opening of the Old Testament.

“And I saw and heard the voice of many angels”: he calls human beings angels, who are also called sons of God.

“Worthy is the Lamb who was slain to receive power and riches and wisdom,” and so forth.

He does not say this of God, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom (Col. 2:3), as though he were to receive them; rather, he speaks of the assumed human being and of his body, which is the Church, or of his martyrs who were killed for his name. For the Church receives everything in her head, as it is written, “With him he has given us all things” (Rom. 8:32).

The Lamb himself receives them, who says in the Gospel, “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28:18). He received them according to his humanity, not according to his divinity.

“All,” he says, “I heard saying to the one seated upon the throne,” that is, to the Father and the Son, “and to the Lamb,” that is, to the Church with her head:

“Blessing and honor and glory forever”—to him be honor, glory, and dominion forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY V

### [On Chapter VI]

As you heard just now while the divine reading was being read, blessed John says: “And behold, a white horse, and the one seated upon it had a bow; and a crown was given to him, and he went out conquering.”

The white horse is the Church; its rider is Christ. Through Zechariah this horse of the Lord, with its warlike bow, was previously promised in the following manner:

“The Lord God will visit his flock, the house of Israel, and will arrange it like a splendid horse in battle. From it he will look forth, from it he will arrange it, and from it the bow in wrath, and from it will go forth every pursuer” (Zech. 10:3–4).

We therefore understand the white horse as the Prophets and the Apostles. In the crowned rider who has a bow we recognize not only Christ but also the Holy Spirit. After the Lord ascended into heaven and opened all the mysteries, he sent the Holy Spirit, whose words, through the preachers, would reach the hearts of human beings like arrows and conquer unbelief.

The crown upon his head is to be understood as the promises given through the Holy Spirit.

“And when he had opened the second seal, I heard the second living creature saying, ‘Come and see.’ And a red horse went out. And to the one seated upon it was given power to take peace from the earth, so that they should kill one another; and a great sword was given to him.”

Against the victorious and conquering Church went out a red horse, that is, a sinister and evil people, bloodstained from its rider, the devil. Although we read in Zechariah of the red horse of the Lord, that horse was red with his own blood, whereas this one is red with the blood of others.

He was given a great sword [Col. 2425] so that he might take peace from the earth—namely, his own peace, that is, worldly peace. For the Church possesses the eternal peace that Christ left to her.

As was said above, therefore, he calls the white horse the Church, and its rider Christ or the Holy Spirit. The bow that he held in his hand is his commandments, which, like sharp arrows of the mighty one, are directed throughout the whole world to kill sins and to stir up [Note: [Col. 2425] The manuscripts read: “to exercise.”] the hearts of the faithful.

The crown upon his head is the promise of eternal life.

The red horse is the evil people; its rider is the devil, whom he called red because he was crimson with the blood of many.

But the fact that a sharp sword was given to him, and that he was to take peace from the earth, means that, at the devil’s persuasion, evil people continually stir up quarrels and discord among themselves, even to the point of death.

And in the black horse the sinister people who consent to the devil are understood.

But when he says, “He had a balance in his hand,” this is because, while the evil pretend to hold the scales of justice, they often deceive people in this way.

When he said, “Do not harm the wine and the oil,” the blood of Christ is understood in the wine, and the anointing of chrism in the oil.

In the wheat or barley, the whole Church is understood, whether in the great or in the small, or certainly in the leaders and the peoples.

And in the pale horse evil human beings are understood, who do not cease to stir up persecutions.

These three horses are one; they went out after and against the white horse. They have the devil as their rider, who is death.

The three horses therefore signify famine, wars, and pestilence—things that the Lord also foretold in his Gospel, which are already taking place and will occur still more as the day of judgment approaches.

But when he says that he saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been killed, the martyrs are understood.

When he says, “A great earthquake,” this is the final persecution.

When he says that the sun became black, the moon became blood-red, and the stars fell from heaven, the sun, moon, and stars are the Church spread throughout the whole world.

But when he says that they fell, the whole Church did not fall; rather, the whole is understood from a part. For in every persecution the good persevere, while the evil fall from heaven—that is, from the Church.

Finally, it follows: “As a fig tree casts its unripe figs when it is shaken by the wind,” so the evil fall from the Church when they are disturbed by some tribulation.

But when he says, “The sky receded like a scroll,” this is the Church, which is separated from the evil and, like a rolled-up scroll, contains within herself the divine mysteries known to her.

But when he says, “The kings of the earth fled and hid themselves in the caves of the earth,” this signifies that the whole world will have refuge among the good and holy in the Church, so that, established under her protection, it may reach eternal life, with the help of our Lord Jesus Christ, who lives and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

## HOMILY VI
[In the same place, chapters VI–VIII.] And I saw another angel ascending from the rising of the sun. By “another angel” he understands the same catholic Church, crying out from the rising of the sun—that is, from the Lord’s passion and resurrection—to the four angels of the earth. And he cried out in a loud voice, saying to the four angels who had been given power to harm the earth and the sea: “Do not harm the earth or the sea.” He receives the sword generally, whether against those whom he kills in this life, or against those whom he persuades to quarrel with one another over temporal matters even unto death.

Concerning the third seal he says that a black horse went out, and the one sitting upon it held a balance in his hand: “A balance,” he says, “he held in his hand,” that is, the examination of equity; for, while he pretends to uphold justice, he harms through hypocrisy. But when it is said, in the midst of the living creatures—that is, in the midst of the Church—“Do not harm,” it is shown that spiritual wickednesses have no power over the servants of God unless they have received it from God.

“Do not harm the wine and the oil”: by the wine and oil he means the anointing of chrism and the blood of the Lord; by the wheat and barley, however, he means the Church, whether in great or small Christians, or in rulers and peoples.

Concerning the fourth seal: “A pale horse. And the one sitting upon it was named Death, and hell followed him; and power was given to him over the fourth part of the earth, to kill with the sword, with famine, with death, and with the beasts of the earth.” These three horses are one: they went out after and against the white horse, and they have one rider, the devil, who is death. For that the rider is the devil and his companions he makes clear in the sixth sign, when he says that the horses will engage in the final battle.

The three horses, therefore, signify famine, wars, and plagues, as the Lord foretells in the Gospel. The white horse is the word of preaching throughout the world. In the red horse and its rider are signified the wars that are to come—or rather, that are already occurring—when nation rises against nation. By the pale horse and its rider, a great plague and mortality are signified. “And hell followed him”: that is, it awaits the devouring of many.

And when he had opened the fifth seal, I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain. He calls the Church the altar of God, beneath whose sight the martyrs were made. And although the souls of the saints are in paradise, nevertheless, because the blood of the saints is poured out upon the earth, they are said to cry out beneath the altar, as it says: “The blood of your brother cries out to me from the earth” (Gen. 4:10).

And when he had opened the sixth seal, a great earthquake occurred: that is, the final persecution. And the sun became black like a sackcloth garment, and the whole moon became like blood, and the stars fell to the earth. Whatever the sun and moon are, so also are the stars, namely, the Church; but the part is understood from the whole. For the whole Church does not fall, but those who are evil in the Church themselves fall from heaven. He said “the whole” because the final persecution will occur throughout the entire world.

And then those who are righteous will remain in the Church as in heaven; but the greedy, unjust, and adulterous will consent to sacrifice to the devil. And then those who had said in words alone that they were Christians will fall from heaven, which is the Church, like stars.

“As a fig tree, shaken by a great wind, casts its unripe figs.” He compared the shaken tree to the Church, the great wind to persecution, and the unripe figs to evil people, who are to be shaken off and depart from the Church.

And heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up. Here also he calls the Church heaven: it withdraws from the evil and contains within itself mysteries known only to itself, like a rolled-up book, which the wicked neither wish nor are able to understand at all.

And every mountain and island was moved from its places. What heaven signifies, the mountains and islands signify as well: namely, that when the final persecution occurs, the Church withdraws entirely from its place, whether the good by fleeing persecution or the evil by yielding in faith.

But this can apply in either direction, because the good part too is moved from its place by fleeing—that is, by losing what it possesses—as in the saying: “I will move your lampstand from its place” (Apoc. 2:5).

And the kings of the earth and the magistrates: by kings we understand powerful people. For people from every rank and condition will be converted to Christ. But those who will then be kings, apart from the one persecutor, hid themselves in caves and rocks of the mountains. In the present age all flee for refuge to the faith of the Church and are concealed within the hidden mystery of the Scriptures.

And they say, “Fall upon us”: that is, cover us. “And hide us”: that is, so that the old man may be hidden from the eyes of God.

And otherwise: Whoever considers the coming judgment turns to the mountains, that is, to the Church, so that his sins may be hidden through repentance in the present time and he may not be punished in the future.

“Until we seal the servants of our God upon their foreheads”: he announces the Church and says to the evil people—that is, to the left-hand side that causes harm—“Do not harm.” This is the voice that, in the midst of the four living creatures, says to the one causing harm, “Do not harm the wine and the oil.” By the wine and oil all who are righteous are understood, whom neither the devil nor evil people will be able to harm, except whenever God permits it for their testing.

“Do not harm the wine and the oil,” he says. The Lord commands that none of his spiritual earth be harmed until all have been sealed.

And I heard the number of those who had been sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel. The one hundred and forty-four thousand is the entire Church, absolutely.

Afterward I saw, and behold, a great multitude that no one could number, from every nation and peoples and languages. He did not say, “After this I saw another people,” but “I saw the people,” that is, the same people whom he had seen in the mystery of the one hundred and forty-four thousand; he saw this same people as innumerable, from every tribe, language, and nation, because all nations have been grafted into the root by believing.

In the Gospel the Lord demonstrates the whole Church, both from the Jews and from the Gentiles, in the twelve tribes of Israel, saying: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matt. 19:28).

Clothed in white robes: by the white robes he understands the gift of the Holy Spirit.

And all the angels stood around the throne: by the angels he means the Church, because he was describing nothing other than it.

And one of the elders answered me, saying: “These who are clothed in white robes—who are they?” The one of the elders who answered indicates the office of priests, because they teach the Church—that is, the people within the Church—what reward awaits the labor of the saints.

He said: “These are they who came out of the great tribulation and washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb.” They are not, as some think, martyrs alone, but the whole people in the Church, because he did not say that they washed their robes in their own blood, but in the blood of the Lamb, that is, in the grace of God through Jesus Christ our Lord, as it is written: “And his Son’s blood cleansed us” (1 John 1:7).

And the one who sits upon the throne will dwell over them: for they themselves are the throne over whom God dwells forever, that is, in the Church.

Neither will the sun fall upon them, nor the heat, as Isaiah says concerning the Church: “It will be in the shade from the heat” (Isa. 25:4).

And he will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life. All these things also happen spiritually to the Church in the present life: when, our sins having been forgiven, we rise again; when, stripped of the mournful former life and of the old man, we put on Christ in Baptism and are filled with the joy of the Holy Spirit.

And when he had opened the seventh seal, there was silence in heaven: that is, in the Church. “For about half an hour”: by the half-hour he indicates the beginning of eternal rest.

And I saw seven angels who stand in the presence of God. By the seven angels he meant the Church, “who received seven trumpets,” that is, perfect preaching, as it is written: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isa. 58:1).

And another angel came and stood before the altar. The other angel whom he mentions did not come after those seven, because he is the Lord Jesus Christ himself.

Having a golden censer: this is the holy body. For the Lord himself became the censer from which God received the fragrance of sweetness, and he was made favorable toward the world because he offered himself as a fragrance of sweetness (Eph. 5:2).

And the angel took the censer and filled it from the fire of the altar. Jesus took the body—that is, the Church—and, to accomplish the Father’s will, filled it with the fire of the Holy Spirit.

And there were voices and thunderings and flashes of lightning and an earthquake. All these are the spiritual preachings and powers of the Church.

And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound the trumpets: that is, the Church prepared itself to preach.

And the first angel sounded the trumpet, and hail and fire mixed with blood came to be. The wrath of God came to be, carrying within itself the death of many.

And it was cast upon the earth, and a third of the earth was burned, and a third of the trees, and all the green grass was burned. Whatever the earth is, so also are the trees and the grass, that is, human beings. By green grass understand flesh full of blood and lust, according to the saying: “All flesh is grass” (Isa. 40:6).

And the second angel sounded the trumpet, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea, and a third of the sea became blood. The burning mountain is the devil. And what is said of the third of the earth or trees is said also of the third of the sea.

And he said that there were people who had souls [Note: [Col. 2427] Manuscripts: “he said that there were trees having souls.”], in order to show that they were alive in the flesh but spiritually dead.

And they corrupted a third of the ships: by their teaching the heretics corrupted those who assented to them.

And the third angel sounded the trumpet, and a great star, burning like a torch, fell from heaven. He says that proud and impious people fell from the Church. He called it a great star because he means persons of high rank, and those possessing power [Col. 2428] or riches.

And the name of the star is called Wormwood, and a third of the waters became wormwood. A third of the people became like the star that fell upon them.

And many people died from the waters, because the waters had been made bitter. People died from the waters. This can plainly be understood of those who are rebaptized.

And the fourth angel sounded the trumpet, and a third of the sun, a third of the moon, and a third of the stars were struck. The sun, moon, and stars are the Church, a third part of which was struck; by the third part all the evil are understood. It was struck—that is, handed over to its evils and pleasures—so that, as sins multiplied and grew rank, it might be revealed in its own time.

And I saw and heard the voice of one eagle flying in the midst of heaven, saying: “Woe! Woe! Woe to those who dwell upon the earth!” By the eagle he understands the Church flying in the midst of heaven—that is, moving about in its midst—and proclaiming in a loud voice the plagues of the final time. For when a priest announces the day of judgment, the eagle flies in the midst of heaven.

As was said above, therefore, the other angel whom he said had ascended from the rising of the sun is the Church, ascending from the rising of the sun, that is, from the Lord’s passion or resurrection.

When he says, “Do not harm the earth or the sea,” the Church cries this out daily by preaching to evil people. When he says, “Do not harm the wine and the oil,” by the wine and oil all who are righteous in the Church are understood, whom no one can harm unless God permits it for their testing.

When he says that one hundred and forty-four thousand had been sealed, the whole Church is understood. Thus, also, in those of whom he said that he saw a great multitude whom no one could number, the same Church is signified.

When he said that they were clothed in white robes, the gift of the Holy Spirit is understood in the robes. By the angels standing around the throne he meant the Church, because he was describing nothing other than it.

The elder who answered and said, “Who are these, and from where have they come?” indicates the office of priests, who teach the people in the Church.

When he said, “They washed their robes,” he spoke of the whole Church, not of martyrs alone. Finally, he does not say “in their own blood,” but “in the blood of the Lamb,” which is fulfilled, of course, through the sacrament of Baptism.

And the one who sits upon the throne dwells over them: for they themselves are the throne over whom God dwells.

Neither will the sun fall upon them, nor any heat; and he will lead them to the fountains of the waters of life. All these things also happen spiritually to the Church in the present age and in these days, while it is so defended by the grace of God that it is tested by the persecutions of this world rather than conquered by them.

When he says that silence occurred in heaven for half an hour, he speaks of the Church and signifies the beginning of eternal rest.

And when the seven angels sound their trumpets: in the angels the Church is understood, and in the trumpets the preaching of the Church.

The other angel whom he said stood before the altar is Christ the Lord. Having a golden censer: namely, the holy body, through which God the Father received the incense of the passion as a fragrance of sweetness.

When he says, “There were voices, flashes of lightning, and thunderings,” these are the spiritual preachings of the Church.

The seven angels who prepared themselves to sound the trumpets are the Church, in which spiritual preaching is carried out throughout the whole world against every sin and crime.

When the first angel sounded and a third of the earth was burned, this signifies proud people devoted to pleasures, whom God in his just judgment permits to be consumed by the fire of lust or greed.

When the second angel sounded and the burning mountain fell into the sea, that mountain is the devil, and the sea is this world. The third of the sea, as was already said above, signifies wicked and impious people.

When the third angel sounded and the great star fell from heaven, great people are understood who fall from the Church as from heaven because of evil morals and wicked deeds.

When he says, “Many people died from the waters, because the waters had been made bitter,” this can be understood of those who are rebaptized.

When the fourth angel sounded and a third of the sun, moon, and stars was struck, the Church is understood in these things, in which those who are evil or hypocritical are daily struck in the soul by the wounds of sins at the devil’s persuasion [Col. 2429].

When he says, “The eagle flying in the midst of heaven and crying, ‘Woe! Woe! Woe!’” he wished the Church to be understood, flying in the midst of heaven—that is, in its own midst—and announcing, through the constancy of its preaching, the plagues of the final time.

For when a priest announces the day of judgment in the Church of God, the eagle flies in the midst of heaven.

May divine mercy grant that, while the priests strive continually to preach and the peoples faithfully fulfill what is preached, they may together deserve to reach eternal things [Note: [Col. 2429] Manuscripts: “eternal blessedness”], through the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, who lives, and so forth.

## HOMILY VII

[In the same place, chapters IX and X.] Just now, dearest brothers, when the Apocalypse was being read, we heard that, when the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, a star fell from heaven upon the earth. One star is the body of many people falling through sins.

And the key of the pit of the abyss was given to it. The star, the abyss, and the pit are human beings. Therefore the star fell from heaven: that is, the sinful people from the Church.

And it received the key of the pit of the abyss: that is, the power of its own heart, so that it might open its heart, in which the devil, once bound, is not restrained from doing his will.

And it opened the pit of the abyss: that is, it revealed its heart without any fear or shame of sinning.

And smoke rose from the pit: that is, from the people there rose what covers and darkens the Church, so that it is said: “The sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit.” He said that the sun was darkened, not that it had set [Note: [Col. 2429] Manuscripts: “had died.”]. For the sins of evil and proud people, which are committed everywhere throughout the world, darken the sun—that is, the Church—and at times cause darkness for the holy and righteous, because the number of the evil is so great that the good can scarcely sometimes be seen among them.

“As the smoke of a great furnace.” And from the smoke of the pit locusts came out upon the earth, and power was given them, as the scorpions of the earth have power: that is, to harm with poison.

And they were commanded not to harm the grass of the earth or any tree, but only human beings. And it was given to them not to kill them.

And because there are two parts in the Church, namely, the good and the evil, one part is struck so that it may be corrected, while the other is left to its pleasures. The part of the good is handed over to humiliation [Note: [Col. 2429] Manuscripts: “humiliation.”] for the recognition of God’s justice and the remembrance of repentance, as it is written: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I might learn your justifications” (Ps. 118:17).

It was given to them not to kill, but to torment. And their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person. This happens when the devil offers poisons through vices or sins.

And people will seek death. By death he meant rest. Therefore they will seek death from evils—that is, tribulations—so that they themselves may rest while the evils die.

“Upon their heads,” he says, “something like crowns resembling gold.” The Church was described above in the twenty-four elders, who have golden crowns; these, however, resembling gold, are heresies, which imitate the Church.

And they had hair like women’s hair. By women’s hair he wished to indicate not only an effeminate sex, but both sexes.

And they had tails like scorpions, and there were stings in their tails. By the tails of the heretics he means their leaders, as it is written: “The prophet who teaches falsehood, he is the tail” (Isa. 9:15). These are the false prophets, and they carry out the cruel commands of kings.

They have over them as king the angel of the abyss: that is, the devil or the king of the world. The abyss is the people.

His name in Hebrew is Abaddon, in Greek ἀπολλύων (*apollyōn*), and in Latin *Perdens* (“Destroyer”).

The first woe has passed; behold, two woes are coming after these.

And the sixth angel sounded the trumpet. Here the final preaching begins.

And I heard one of the four horns of the golden altar that is before God saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet: “Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.”

The altar that is before God [Col. 2430] is to be understood as the Church, which, at the time of the final persecution, dares to despise the words or commands of the most cruel king and to depart from those who obey him.

“Release the four angels at the river Euphrates.” By the river Euphrates he meant the sinful people, in whom Satan and their own will are bound. Euphrates is the river of Babylon, just as Jeremiah casts the book into the Euphrates in the midst of Babylon (Jer. 51:63).

And the four angels were released: that is, persecution began.

They were prepared for the hour, day, month, and year, to kill a third of humanity. These are the four periods of the three years, and a part of the time.

And he says: “The number of the armies was twice ten thousand times ten thousand. I heard their number.” But he did not say how many times ten thousand [Note: [Col. 2430] Thus Tichonius throughout, as Primasius bears witness.].

To kill a third of humanity: this is the third part of the proud, from which the Church descends.

And I saw horses in the vision, and those sitting upon them had breastplates of fire, hyacinth, and sulfur. By the horses he means human beings, and by the riders, evil spirits armed with fire, smoke, and sulfur.

And the heads of the horses were like lions: for raging in persecution.

From their mouths came smoke, fire, and sulfur: that is, blasphemies against God proceed from their mouths.

Their tails were like serpents. We have said that the tails are the leaders, and the heads the princes of the world. In these the devil causes harm, and without them he cannot cause harm: either sacrilegious kings harm by issuing wicked commands, or sacrilegious priests by teaching wickedly.

And I saw, he says, another strong angel descending from heaven, clothed with a cloud, and a rainbow—that is, an arc—was upon his head, and his face was like the sun. Clothed with a cloud: the Lord is understood, clothed with the Church. For we read that the saints are clouds, as Isaiah says: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isa. 60:8). Understand Christ, therefore, as clothed with a spiritual cloud, that is, with a holy body.

And a rainbow was over his head: that is, either the judgment that is taking place and is to come, or the enduring promise.

He describes the Church in the Lord, saying: “And his face was like the sun,” that is, because of the resurrection. For he appeared like the sun when he rose from the dead.

And his feet were like pillars of fire. By the feet he means the Apostles, through whom his teaching travels throughout the whole world. Or, since the foot is the last part of the body, he means the glory of the saints that the Church will have after the fire of the final persecution.

And he placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth: that is, to preach across the sea and throughout the whole world.

And he cried out in a loud voice, as a lion roars: that is, he preached boldly.

And when he cried out, the seven thunders uttered their voices, which are also the seven trumpets.

And I heard a voice from heaven saying: “Seal up the things that the seven thunders have spoken, and do not write them,” so that they might be withheld, lest the words of God be openly disclosed to all the impious.

Finally, in another place, for the sake of his servants he says: “Do not seal up the words of this prophecy.” And he showed for whom he commanded them to be sealed and for whom not: “Let the one who persists in doing harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is in filth remain filthy still” (Apoc. 22:10–11).

This means: “For this reason I speak to them in parables, so that the one who is righteous may do more righteous things, and likewise the one who is holy may do holier things.” That is: “Blessed are your eyes, because they see, and your ears, because they hear.” For the words of the book are not sealed for these people, but they are sealed for the evil.

And that angel swore that there would no longer be time, but that in the days of the seventh angel, when he begins to sound the trumpet, the seventh trumpet is the end of persecution and the coming of the Lord. Therefore the Apostle said that the resurrection would occur at the last trumpet (1 Cor. 15:52).

When, as was said above, he again said that, when the fifth angel sounded the trumpet, a star had fallen from heaven, this star too is the body of many stars falling from heaven—that is, from the Church—and it signifies a proud and impious people.

When the key of the abyss was given to it, it was released into the power of its own heart, so that it might open its heart to the devil and practice every evil without any reverence.

When smoke rose from the pit, that is, from the evil people, and darkened the sun and moon, he said that the sun was darkened, not that it had set. This is because the sins of evil and proud people seem to darken the sun, while through many tribulations they sometimes cause darkness for the holy and righteous. But they cannot extinguish their light, because the righteous do not consent to join them in evil.

When he says that locusts came out of the smoke of the pit and received power to harm, and that it was given to them not to kill them, this is because there are two parts in the Church, namely, the good and the evil. One part is struck so that it may be corrected; the other is left to its pleasures.

When he said, “Their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it strikes a person,” this happens when the devil offers poisons, in the manner of a scorpion, to lustful people through vices and sins.

And upon their heads were things like crowns resembling gold. The twenty-four elders, in whom the Church was described, had golden crowns; these, however, resembling gold, are the heresies that imitate the Church.

When they had women’s hair, by the hair he wished to indicate not only an effeminate sex but both sexes.

In their tails, which were like scorpions, the leaders or princes of the heretics are understood, as it is written: “The prophet who teaches falsehood, he is the tail.”

They had over them the king of the abyss: that is, the devil. In the abyss the evil people are understood, over whom the devil rules.

The altar that he said was before God is to be understood as the Church, which, like purified gold, dares at the time of the final persecution to despise the commands of the most cruel king and to depart from those who obey him.

When he says that the four angels were bound in the river Euphrates, the river Euphrates signifies the sinful people, in whom Satan and their own will are bound. Euphrates is the river of Babylon, which is interpreted as “Confusion.” Therefore all who carry out actions deserving confusion pertain to that river.

When he says that he saw horses, and those sitting upon them had breastplates of fire, hyacinth, and sulfur, by the horses he means proud people, and by their rider the devil and his angels.

When he says that the heads of the horses were like lions, this was said because of the violent persecution of evil people.

And from their mouths came fire, smoke, and sulfur: that is, blasphemies against God proceed from their mouths.

In the tails, which were like serpents, as was already said above, are the princes and rulers of the heretics, through whom the devil is accustomed to cause harm. Either sacrilegious kings harm by issuing wicked commands, or sacrilegious priests by teaching wickedly [Note: [Col. 2431] Manuscripts: “by preaching.”].

The angel whom he said was clothed with a cloud is the Lord and our Savior, clothed with a cloud—that is, the Church—because it is written concerning the saints: “Who are these who fly like clouds?”

When he said that his face was like the sun, he said this because of the Lord’s resurrection: for he appeared like the sun when he rose from the dead.

In his feet, which were like pillars of fire, the Apostles are represented, through whom his teaching travels throughout the whole world.

When he placed his right foot upon the sea, this signified that his preaching would go across the sea and throughout the whole world.

When he cried out like a roaring lion, this was because he preached boldly by his authority.

When he said, “Seal up the things that the seven thunders have spoken,” this was said concerning those who must be restrained, of whom the Gospel says: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7:6), that is, so that the word of God may not be openly disclosed to all the impious.

Finally, in another place, for the sake of his servants he says: “Do not seal up the words of this prophecy.” And he showed for whom he commanded them to be sealed and for whom not: “Let the one who persists in doing harm continue to do harm, and let the one who is in filth remain filthy still.”

Behold for whom the word of God is sealed. “For this reason I speak to them in parables, so that the one who is righteous may do more righteous things, and likewise the one who is holy may do holier things.” Behold for whom it is not sealed.

May we pray that the Lord in his mercy may also deign to fulfill this in us [Col. 2432], he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit. Amen.

## HOMILY VIII

[In the same place, chapters X and XI.] The voice from heaven is the command of God, who touches the heart of the Church and commands it to understand, because the Church, with the book opened, proclaimed the future peace [Note: [Col. 2432] Manuscripts: “of the Church.”].

And I went to the angel, so that he might give me the book. This is spoken by the Church in the person of John, desiring to be fully instructed.

And then he said to me: “Take it and eat it”: that is, unfold it within your inward parts and set it forth in the breadth of your heart.

“And it will make your belly bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet like honey”: that is, when you have received it, you will delight in the sweetness of divine speech, but you will feel bitterness when you begin to preach and practice what you have understood, as it is written: “Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways” (Ps. 16:4).

And alternatively: “It will be,” he says, “sweet like honey in your mouth, and bitterness in your belly.” In the mouth the good and spiritual Christians are understood; in the belly, the carnal and lustful. Thus, when the word of God is preached, it is sweet to the spiritual; but to the carnal, whose god, according to the Apostle, is their belly (Phil. 3:19), it appears bitter and harsh.

And a reed like a rod was given to me, saying: “Rise and measure the temple of God and the altar, and those who worship in it.” “Rise” is the awakening of the Church. For here John was not listening while seated [Note: [Col. 2432] The printed editions lack *sedibundus* (“seated”). It is found in the Petrine manuscript and in Bede.].

“Measure the temple and the altar and those who worship in it”: he commands that the Church be numbered and prepared for the end, together with those who worship in it.

But because not all who appear to worship do so, he therefore said: “Cast out the court that is outside the temple, and do not measure it.” They are the court who appear to be in the Church but are outside it, whether heretics or Catholics who live wickedly.

“For it has been given to the nations, and they will trample the holy city for forty-two months.” Both those who will be excluded and those to whom it will be given will trample it.

“And I will give to my two witnesses”: that is, to the two Testaments. “And they will prophesy for one thousand two hundred and sixty days.” He spoke of the period of the final persecution, of the future peace, and of the whole time from the Lord’s passion, because each of these periods has the same number of days, as will be said in its proper place.

“Clothed in sackcloth,” that is, in haircloth. He said that they were established in ἐξομολόγησις (*exomologēsis*), that is, in confession, because he said that they were clothed in sackcloth as an expression of humility.

Then he shows who these two witnesses are, saying: “These are the two olive trees and the two lampstands standing before the Lord of the earth.” These are the ones who stand, not those who will stand.

The two lampstands are the Church, but he said “two” on account of the number of the Testaments. Just as he called the four angels the Church, although there are seven according to the number of the angels of the earth, so, from the seven lampstands, if he names one or more according to their locations, the whole Church is meant.

For Zechariah saw one seven-branched lampstand and these two olive trees (Zech. 4:2–3), that is, the Testaments pouring oil into the lampstand, that is, into the Church.

Likewise there are there seven eyes, the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, which are in the Church, looking upon the whole earth.

And if anyone wishes to harm or kill them, fire will come out of their mouths and devour their enemies: that is, if anyone either harms or wishes to harm the Church, he will be consumed by the divine fire of the prayers of its mouth, either in the present age for correction or in the future age for condemnation.

They have power to shut heaven, so that it may not rain during the days of their prophecy. He says, “They have,” not “They will have.” He says this because he signified the time that is now in progress.

But heaven is also shut spiritually, so that it does not rain—that is, so that the blessing of the Church may not descend, by the hidden but nevertheless just judgment of God, upon the barren earth.

And when they have finished their testimony, the beast that rises from the abyss will make war against them. He openly shows that all these things will take place before the final persecution when he says, “when they have finished their testimony”: namely, the testimony that they offer [Note: [Col. 2432] Primasius: “bear”] until the revelation of Christ.

And he will conquer them and kill them. He will conquer them in those who succumb; he will kill them in those who confess God.

And their body will be cast into the streets of the great city. He speaks of the two as one body, sometimes as bodies, both to preserve the number of the Testaments and to show the one body of the Church [Note: [Col. 2433] Here the manuscripts add: “which is that: ‘You have cast my words behind you.’”].

“In the streets of the great city”: that is, in the midst of the Church.

And people from the nations, tribes, and languages will see their body for three and a half days: that is, for three years and six months. He mixes the times, now the present and now the future, just as the Lord says: “The hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16:2). It is both now and to come.

And they do not allow their bodies to be placed in a tomb. He expressed their determination to attack them, not that they could actually prevent the Church from being held in memory, just as in the saying: “You neither enter yourselves nor permit those who wish to enter to do so” (Matt. 23:13), although many have entered even while those people opposed them.

Thus they do not allow them to be placed in a tomb.

And those who dwell upon the earth rejoice over them, celebrate, and send gifts to one another. This has always happened, and now they send gifts to one another, and in the end they will rejoice and celebrate. For whenever the righteous are afflicted, the unjust exult and celebrate.

Because these two prophets tormented them: through the plagues by which the human race is afflicted for despising the Testaments of God. Finally, even the sight of the righteous burdens the unjust, as they themselves say: “He is burdensome to us even to look at” (Wis. 2:15).

They will rejoice wherever they are, as though they now had nothing left to endure unwillingly, once the righteous have been disturbed and killed and their inheritance possessed.

And after three and a half days, the spirit of life from God entered them. The matter of the days has already been explained. Up to this point the angel narrated what is future, and he introduces as accomplished what he hears will happen.

And they stood upon their feet, and great fear fell upon those who saw them.

And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying: “Come up here.” And they ascended into heaven in a cloud. This is what the Apostle said: “We will be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ” (1 Thess. 4:16).

But it is written that this cannot happen before the Lord’s coming: “Christ the beginning, then those who are Christ’s at his coming” (1 Cor. 15:23). Thus every suspicion is excluded concerning certain people who think that these two witnesses are two men who ascended into heaven in clouds before Christ’s coming.

How could those dwelling upon the earth rejoice over the death of the two, when they died in one city, and send gifts to one another if the period is three days, when, before they could rejoice over the death, they would be saddened by the resurrection?

Or what kind of feasts or pleasure could there be in the streets of those celebrating, when human corpses would make their feasts sickening through a three-day stench?

From this may the Lord deign to deliver us. Amen.

## HOMILY IX
[On Chapters XI and XII.] What we heard, brothers, in the reading that was recited—that in that hour there was a great earthquake—must be understood as the persecution which the devil customarily inflicts through wicked men. “And the tenth part of the city fell,” he says, “and seven thousand names of men were killed in the earthquake.” Ten and seven together form a complete number; if this were not intended, the whole would have to be understood from a part. For there are two buildings in the Church: one upon the rock, the other upon the sand. The one upon the sand is said to have fallen.

“And the rest were afraid and gave glory to God.” Those gave glory who had been built upon the rock and could not fall along with those who were upon the sand. He said “were afraid” because, when the righteous sees the destruction of the sinner, he is inflamed more strongly in observing the commandments, as it is said: “And he shall wash his hands in the blood of the sinner” (Ps. LVII, 11).

“And the temple of God in heaven was opened,” he says—that is, the mysteries of Christ’s incarnation were revealed in the Church; hence it is shown that the Church is heaven. “And the ark of his covenant was seen in his temple”—that is, it was understood that the Church is the ark of the covenant. “And there were flashes of lightning [Col. 2434] and thunderings and an earthquake”: all these are the powers of the Church’s preaching, radiance, and battles.

“And a great sign was seen in heaven: a woman clothed with the sun, and the moon under her feet.” He calls the Church “a woman,” and says that she has under her feet her own part—that is, hypocritical people and bad Christians. “And upon her head a crown of twelve stars.” These twelve stars may be understood as the twelve Apostles. Being clothed with the sun signifies the hope of the resurrection, because it is written: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII, 43).

“A great red dragon”: this is the devil, seeking to devour the child of the Church. “Having,” he says, “ten horns and seven heads”: the heads are kings, while the horns are kingdoms. In the seven heads he speaks of all kings, and in the ten horns of all the kingdoms of the world.

“And his tail dragged down a third of the stars of heaven, and cast them to the earth.” The tail signifies wicked prophets—that is, heretics—who, through repeated baptism, cast down to earth the stars of heaven that adhere to them; these are under the woman’s feet. Many think that these are the human beings whom the devil made his companions by bringing them into agreement with himself; many think they are angels who were hurled down with him when he fell.

“She is in labor and suffers in order to give birth.” Throughout all time, the Church gives birth each day, in prosperity and adversity. “And the dragon stood before the woman who was about to give birth, so that when she had given birth he might devour her child.” For the Church always gives birth amid sufferings, to Christ through his members; and the dragon always seeks to devour the one being born.

“And the woman gave birth to a male child”—that is, to Christ. Then his body, that is, the Church, continually gives birth to Christ’s members. He called him “male” because he is victorious against the devil.

“And the woman fled into the wilderness.” We appropriately understand this present world as the wilderness, where Christ governs and nourishes the Church until the end. In it, through Christ’s assistance, the Church tramples and crushes proud and impious people as though they were scorpions and vipers, and overcomes every power of Satan.

“And there was war in heaven”—that is, in the Church. “Michael and his angels fought with the dragon.” Understand Michael as Christ, and his angels as holy people. “And the dragon fought, and his angels”—that is, the devil and the people who obey his will. For far be it from us to believe that the devil dared to fight with his angels in heaven, since upon earth he did not dare to tempt even one Job unless he first asked the Lord that he might afflict him.

“And they did not prevail, nor was their place found any longer in heaven”—that is, among holy people. Once they have believed and expelled the devil and his satellites, they do not receive them again, just as Zachariah said: once idols have been exterminated, they are not again given a place.

“And the great dragon was cast out, that ancient serpent who is called the devil and Satan, and his angels with him.” The devil and all the unclean spirits, with their prince, were cast out from the hearts of the saints into the earth—that is, into people who think earthly thoughts and place all their hope in the earth.

“And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying: Now salvation and power and the kingdom of our God have come”—that is, of the Church. He shows in which heaven these things take place. With God there have always been the power, kingdom, and authority of his Son; but in the Church he said that, through Christ’s victory, salvation had come. Those who saw it—those of whom the Lord said, “Many righteous men and prophets desired to see what you see” (Matt. XIII, 17)—said: “Now the salvation of our Lord has come.”

“For the accuser of our brothers has been cast out,” and so forth. But if, as some think, this is the voice of angels in the higher heaven and not of the saints in the Church, they would not say “the accuser of our brothers,” but “our accuser”; nor would they say “he accuses,” but “he accused.” And if the angels called the righteous placed upon earth their brothers, there would be no joy that the devil had been sent down to earth, since the saints, with him placed among them on earth, would experience him as more troublesome than if, as is said, he were still in heaven.

Thus they curse the earth, saying: “Woe to you, earth and sea!”—that is, to those who are not heaven. “For the devil has come down to you, having great wrath, knowing that he has only a short time.” He says that he came down in order to preserve the allegory. Otherwise, all are in heaven—that is, in the Church, which is rightly called heaven. Hence the devil, cast down by the saints, descended into his own people, who, because of their love of earthly things, are earth.

But he did not speak of being cast down from heaven in such a way that this happened among people who had already become heaven, but among those who are—not among those who were to become heaven [Note: [Col. 2435] The Petrensis manuscript reads, “but among those who are, not among those who had been.”]. For the saints cannot become heaven unless the devil has been expelled. Therefore he did not call them heaven by the first designation, but by the second: those in whom the devil no longer found a place. From this danger may the Lord deign to free us under his protection, he who lives, and so forth.

## HOMILY X

[On Chapters XII and XIII.] Now, most beloved brothers, we heard that when the dragon saw that he had been expelled from the saints into the earth—that is, from heaven into sinners—he persecuted the woman who had given birth to the male child. For the more the devil is cast out from the saints, the more fiercely he persecutes them.

“And two wings of a great eagle were given to the woman,” that is, to the Church, “so that she might fly into the wilderness, to her place, where she is nourished for a time and times and half a time, away from the face of the serpent.” A “time” is understood as a year, and a hundred years. The two great wings are the two Testaments of the Church, which she received in order to escape the serpent into the wilderness.

He said “to her place,” that is, into this world, where serpents and scorpions dwell, because it was said to her, as the Lord says: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. X, 16); and Ezekiel says: “Son of man, you dwell among scorpions” (Ezek. II, 6).

“And the serpent cast from its mouth after the woman water like a river”—that is, the violence of persecutors. “And the earth helped the woman, and opened its mouth and swallowed the river which the dragon cast from its mouth.” He calls the earth holy—that is, the saints. Whenever persecutions are inflicted upon the Church, through the prayers of the holy earth—that is, through the prayers of all the saints—they are either removed or moderated. For our Lord Jesus Christ, who intercedes for us and removes these persecutions, does so while the earth itself sits at the right hand of Power.

Alternatively, by the woman flying into the wilderness he understands the Catholic Church itself, in which, at the end of time, the Synagogue will believe under Elijah. By the two wings of the great eagle he wishes two prophets to be understood: namely, Elijah and the one who will come with him. The water sent forth from the dragon’s mouth signifies the army of those persecuting her; the water being swallowed signifies vengeance inflicted upon the persecutors.

“And the dragon was angry with the woman, and went away to make war with the rest of her offspring”—that is, when he saw that the persecutions which he had been accustomed to inflict through the pagans could not continue, because they were removed by the mouth of the holy earth—that is, by holy prayers—he stirred up heresies.

“And he stood upon the sand of the sea”—that is, upon the multitude of heretics. “And I saw a beast rising from the sea”—that is, from the wicked people.
