He said “rising,” meaning being born, just as a flower rises from the root of Jesse in the favorable sense. By the beast rising from the sea he means the impious, who are the body of the devil.

“And the beast which I saw was like a leopard, and its feet were like those of a bear, and its mouth was like the mouth of a lion.” He compared it to a leopard because of the variety of nations; to a bear because of its wickedness and madness; and to a lion because of the strength of its body and the pride of its tongue. And because, in the times of Antichrist, his kingdom will be mixed with a variety of nations and peoples: its feet are like those of a bear, its leaders; its mouth is his command.

“And the dragon gave it his power.” As we now see heretics powerful in this world, possessing the devil’s power. Just as the pagans once ravaged the Church, so now they ravage it.

“And I saw one of its heads as though slain unto death, and its mortal wound was healed.” By saying “as though slain,” he means heretics, who pretend to confess Christ; and while they do not believe as the Catholic faith holds, they blaspheme, even though they proclaim him slain and risen again. For Satan himself transforms himself into an angel of light (II Cor. XI, 14).

Alternatively, heresies are slain by Catholics when they are crushed by testimonies from the Scriptures; but nevertheless, as though they were Satan’s wound revived, they carry out Satan’s works, do not cease blaspheming, and draw to their doctrine as many as they can [Col. 2436].

“And the whole earth marveled and followed the beast, and they worshiped the dragon who gave authority to the beast.” Heretics certainly possess authority, but especially the Arians. “And they worshiped the beast, saying: Who is like the beast? Or who can fight against it?” This is because heretics flatter themselves that no one believes better than they do, and that no one can conquer their people, who are designated by the name “beast.” Authority was given to it by the devil himself and permitted by God, so that it might speak great things and blasphemies; as the Apostle says: “There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may be made manifest among you” (I Cor. XI, 19).

“And power was given to it to act for forty-two months.” We understand the time of the final persecution in these forty-two months.

“Then it opened its mouth in blasphemy against God.” Here it is clear that those are signified who have withdrawn from the Catholic Church: those who previously seemed secretly, within the Church, to hold the true faith, but who during persecution bring forth blasphemy against God with open mouth.

“And against his tabernacle, and against those who dwell in heaven”—that is, against the saints who are contained within the Church, which is called heaven, because they themselves too are the tabernacle of God.

“And it was given power to make war with the saints and to conquer them.” We understand a part from the whole: the part that can be conquered. For it is not good Christians who are conquered, but those who are wicked.

“And authority was given to it over every tribe and language, and all who dwell on the earth will worship it.” He said “all,” but meant those dwelling on earth, not in heaven.

“Those whose name has not been written in the book of life of the Lamb.” He spoke of the devil or his people: his name has not been written in the book of life.

“Sealed from the foundation of the world.” Because, in God’s presence, the Church was foreordained and marked out beforehand.

May he himself grant this, and so forth.

## HOMILY XI

[On Chapters XIII and XIV.] In the reading that has just been recited, most beloved brothers, we heard blessed John saying: “And I saw another beast rising from the earth.” What is the sea but the earth? “And it had two horns like a lamb”—that is, the two Testaments, in the likeness of the Lamb, which is the Church.

“And it spoke like a dragon.” This is the one which, under the Christian name, presents a lamb in order secretly to pour in the dragon’s venom; this is the heretical Church. It would not imitate the likeness of the Lamb if it spoke openly; now it pretends to be Christian in order to deceive the unwary more securely. Therefore the Lord says: “Beware of false prophets,” and so forth (Matt. VII, 15).

“And it makes the earth and those who dwell in it worship the first beast, whose mortal wound was healed. And it will perform great signs, so that it even makes fire come down from heaven to earth.” Since the Church is heaven, what is it for fire to descend from heaven except for heresies to fall from the Church? As it is written: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (I John II, 19). Fire descends from heaven when heretics, who depart from the Church like fire, persecute the Church itself.

Thus the beast with two horns causes the people to worship the image of the beast—that is, the devil’s invention. “So that it gives them a mark upon their right hand or upon their forehead.” For he is discussing the mystery of the crime. The saints who are in the Church receive Christ in hand and forehead; hypocrites, however, receive the beast under Christ’s name.

“And if anyone did not worship the beast or its image, nor receive the inscription [Note: [Col. 2436] The Petrensis manuscript reads, “nor its image nor the inscription.”] upon his forehead or upon his hand, they would be killed.” It is not contrary to the faith to understand the beast itself as the impious city—that is, the assembly or conspiracy of all the impious and proud—which is called Babylon and interpreted as “Confusion.” Whoever wishes to engage in deeds deserving confusion belongs to it. It is the people of unbelievers, opposed to the faithful people and to the city of God.

Its image, however, is a pretense, namely in those people who profess something resembling the Catholic faith but live in unbelief. For they pretend to be what they are not, and are called Christians not by a true likeness but by a deceptive image. Of such people the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of godliness, but denying its power” (II Tim. III, 5). A considerable portion of these is contained within the Catholic Church.

The righteous, however, do not worship the beast—that is, they do not consent or submit—nor do they receive the inscription, the mark of crime: on the forehead because of profession, and on the hand because of action.

Thus they will make it so “that no one can buy or sell except one who has the name or mark of the beast, or the number of its name. Here is wisdom. Let the one who has understanding calculate the number of the beast, for it is the number of a man.” That is, of the Son of Man, Christ, whose name the beast has appropriated among the heretics.

Let us therefore calculate the number he mentioned, so that, having obtained the number, we may find the name and the mark. “Its number,” he says, “is six hundred and sixteen” [Note: [Col. 2437] So in the manuscripts. The printed editions read, “six hundred and sixty-six.”]. Let us form it according to the Greeks, especially since he is writing to Asia: “I am,” he says, “the alpha and the omega.” Six hundred and sixteen is formed in Greek letters as χιστ`. When these marks are separated, they constitute a number; when brought together into a monogram, they produce both a mark and a number and a name.

This sign is understood to be Christ’s, and it displays the likeness of him whom the Church worships in truth. The opposition of the heretics makes itself resemble him: although they persecute Christ spiritually, they nevertheless seem to glory in the sign of Christ’s cross. This is because it was said: “The number of the beast is the number of a man.”

“And I saw, and behold, the Lamb standing on Mount Zion, and with him one hundred and forty-four thousand, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads.” He revealed what imitation of the mark on the foreheads means, when he says that both God and Christ are written on the foreheads of the Church.

“And I heard a voice from heaven like the sound of many waters”—that is, of the one hundred and forty-four thousand. “And like the sound of great thunder; and the voice which I heard was like that of harpists playing their harps.”

When he said, “These are they who have not defiled themselves with women,” and so forth, let us understand “virgins” in this passage as not only those who are chaste in body, but especially the whole Church, which holds a pure faith, as the Apostle says: “For I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI, 2). Let us understand her as unpolluted by any adulterous mingling with heretics, and not bound, through an unhappy perseverance without the remedy of repentance, to the falsely flattering and deadly pleasures of this world until the end of her life.

After this he adds, saying: “And in their mouth no lie was found.” He did not say, “There was no lie”; rather, “No lie was found.” For when the Lord calls someone away from here, he judges him as he finds him. Through either baptism or repentance we can become virgins in the inner person and become free from falsehood.

Now he recapitulates again. “And I saw,” he says, “another angel flying in the midst of heaven”—that is, preaching moving throughout the midst of the Church—“having an eternal Gospel, to evangelize those dwelling on the earth, saying: Fear the Lord,” and so forth.

Some wish to understand the angel flying in the midst of heaven as Elijah, and the other angel who follows him as Elijah’s companion, who will preach at that time.

“And another angel followed”—that is, the preaching of the future peace—“saying: Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.” He calls Babylon the impious city, as was already said above: the congregation of the devil, that is, the people consenting to him, together with every desire and corruption which he seeks to bring about for the destruction of himself and of the human race.

For just as the Church is the city of God and the whole of heavenly conduct, so, conversely, Babylon is the city of the devil throughout the whole world, as the Lord says: “Behold, I will place Jerusalem as a stone to be trampled by all the nations” (Zech. XII, 3).

The Church therefore says: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great.” He speaks as though it had already been accomplished, although it was still future, just as in the words: “They divided my garments among themselves” (Ps. XXI, 19).

“She made all the nations drink from the wine of the wrath of her fornication.” “All the nations” means the city of the world—that is, all the proud and impious, whether placed outside the Church or within the Church.

“And I saw, and behold, a white cloud, and upon the cloud one seated like the Son of Man,” that is, Christ. He describes the Church in her glory, especially after she has been whitened by the flames of persecution [Col. 2438].

“Having upon his head a golden crown”: these are the elders with golden crowns. “And in his hand a sharp sickle.” This sickle separates Catholics from heretics and saints from sinners, as the Lord says concerning the reapers.

But if it must be thought that Christ himself was specifically seen as the reaper in the white cloud, who is the vintager except the same Christ, but in his body, which is the Church? Perhaps it is not wrong to understand these three angels who went out as the threefold interpretation of Scripture, according to the historical, moral, and spiritual senses; and the sickle as separation.

“And he cast it into the great winepress of the wrath of God”—not into a great winepress, but he cast the proud man himself into the winepress. “And the winepress was trodden outside the city”—that is, outside the Church. When division has occurred, every sinner goes outside. The treading of the winepress is the repayment of sins.

“And blood came out of the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles.” Vengeance will come as far as the rulers of the peoples. Indeed, vengeance for the blood that was shed will extend even to the devil and his angels in the final contest.

“For one thousand six hundred stadia”—that is, throughout all four regions of the world. For the quaternity is arranged in fourfold form, as in the four faces of the fourfold creatures and in their entirety. Four times four hundred makes one thousand six hundred [Note: [Col. 2438] In the Petrensis manuscript: “from whose protection may the Lord deign to free us.”].

## HOMILY XII

[On Chapters XV and XVI.] In the reading that was recited, most beloved brothers, Saint John said that he saw another great and wondrous sign in heaven: seven angels—that is, the Church.

“Having the seven last plagues, because in them the wrath of God is completed.” He called them “last” because the wrath of God continually strikes the rebellious people with seven plagues—that is, perfectly—as God himself frequently repeats in Leviticus: “I will strike you sevenfold because of your sins” (Lev. XXVI, 24).

“And I saw something like a glassy sea”—that is, the clear font of baptism—“mixed with fire”: that is, with the Spirit or with temptation. “And those who conquered the beast upon the glassy sea”—that is, in baptism—“having the harps of God”: that is, hearts dedicated to God in praise.

“And singing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”—that is, both Testaments. “Great and wondrous are your works.” These things are in both Testaments, which the aforementioned people sing.

He repeats what he had begun, saying: “After these things I saw, and behold, the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened.” We have already said that the temple is to be understood as the Church. The angel who went out from the temple and commanded the one seated upon the cloud signifies the Lord’s command. For going out is the result of a command, as the Evangelist says: “A decree went out from Caesar Augustus” (Luke II, 1).

“Clothed in pure and shining linen, and girded about their breasts with golden belts.” He plainly shows that the Church is signified by the seven angels. For this is how he described the beginning concerning Christ: “Having,” he says, “a golden belt around his breasts.”

“And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls, full of the wrath of God” (Rev. I, 13). These are the bowls which the elders and the living creatures, who are the Church, carry with fragrance; and these are also the seven angels. What the fragrances are, so too is the wrath of God, and so too is the word of God. Yet all these things give life to the good and bring death upon the wicked, as it is said: “To some we are an aroma of life unto life, to others an aroma of death unto death” (II Cor. II, 16).

For the prayers of the saints—which are the fire going out from the mouth of the witnesses—are wrath against the world and against the impious. This is because it is not enough for the proud and impious that they neither love nor imitate those who are holy; wherever they can, they also persecute them.

All these plagues are spiritual and take place in the soul. At that time, the whole impious people will be unharmed by every bodily plague, because it does not deserve to be scourged in the present world, as though it had received the full power to rage. But spiritually—that is, through voluntary and deadly sins, which are wounds in their souls—all the impious and proud suffer.

“The second poured out his bowl into the sea,” and so forth. The sea, the rivers, the springs of waters, the sun, the throne of the beast, the river Euphrates [Col. 2439], and the air—over these the angels poured out the bowls—signify the earth and human beings, because all the angels were commanded to pour them out upon the earth.

All these plagues, however, must be understood in the contrary sense. A plague is incurable wrath: to receive the power to sin, especially against the saints, without correction. A still greater wrath of God is to have the fuel of errors supplied to injustice. This is the plague of God’s wrath, these are the wounds: for each person to be pierced by sins and yet rejoice and take pleasure in them. Thus the prosperity of the wicked is the wounds of their souls, while the adversity of the righteous is the price of eternal joys [Note: [Col. 2439] The manuscripts read “rewards.”].

In the case of the third angel and the changing of the waters into blood, understand all the angels of the peoples—that is, weaker [Note: [Col. 2439] The manuscripts read “inner.”] people, bloodied in spirit.

The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and the people were scorched with great burning. This will still take place in the fire of Gehenna. For at present, when the devil kills his lovers in soul, he not only does not burn them in body, but, insofar as he is permitted, he makes them bright. The Holy Spirit has defined this brightness and joy as plagues and pains.

“And they blasphemed the name of God, who has power over these plagues, and they did not repent.” Because they are struck by these plagues not in body but in soul by God, they do not remember the Lord but advance toward what is worse; and therefore they blaspheme, persecuting his saints.

The fifth angel poured out his bowl upon the throne of the beast, and its kingdom became dark. The throne of the beast is its church—that is, the congregation of the proud—which is blinded by such plagues.

“They gnawed their tongues because of their pains”—that is, they harmed themselves by blaspheming in consequence of God’s wrath, because, though pierced, they considered them joys. “And they did not repent”: certainly, they were hardened by their joy.

“And the sixth angel poured out his bowl upon that great river, the Euphrates”—that is, upon the people. “And its water was dried up.” As he said above, the harvest of the earth withered—that is, it was prepared for burning.

“So that the way of those from the rising of the sun might be prepared”—that is, for Christ. For when these things have been perfected, the righteous set out to meet Christ.

## HOMILY XIII

[On Chapters XVI and XVII.] Saint John, most beloved brothers, while speaking about the bowls or plagues of the seven angels, following his customary manner and passing over the seventh angel, briefly recapitulates from the beginning, saying:

“And I saw from the mouth of the dragon, and from the mouth of the beast, and from the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs.”

He saw one spirit, but spoke according to the number and portion [Note: [Col. 2439] One manuscript reads “one spirit, participation.” Another reads “partition.”] of one body. The dragon—that is, the devil—the beast—that is, the body of the devil—and the false prophet—that is, the leaders of the devil’s body—are one spirit, like frogs.

“For they are spirits of demons performing signs.” Frogs, besides their natural repulsiveness, are also unclean in their dwelling place [Note: [Col. 2439] The manuscripts read: “They are not only naturally unclean, but also unclean in their dwelling place.”]. Although they appear to be inhabitants and natives of the waters, they are not only fugitives from water and unable to endure dryness; they also wallow in the waters themselves, in the filth and mud of the water.

Thus hypocrites do not dwell in water, as they are thought to do, but in the filth which believers lay aside in the water. People are also like frogs when they are not ashamed to wallow in the sins or crimes which others lay aside through repentance or baptism.

For when someone turns to God and repents of having been proud, adulterous, drunk, or greedy, another person who imitates the sins that he has left behind through confession thinks to himself and says: “I do what I want, and afterward, just as he does penance, so will I.” But suddenly, when the final day overtakes him, confession perishes and condemnation remains. Such a person, while wishing to imitate others not for good but for evil, is enveloped and wallows like a frog in the mud from which another has been freed.

The frogs therefore signify the spirits of demons performing signs. “They go out to the kings of the whole world to gather them for the battle of the great day of the Lord” [Col. 2440]. He calls the whole time from the Lord’s Passion “the great day.” But “day” must be understood according to the circumstances: sometimes he calls it the day of judgment, sometimes the final persecution that will occur under Antichrist, and sometimes the whole period, as through the prophet Amos: “Woe,” he says, “to those who desire the day of the Lord! And why do you desire the day of the Lord?” (Amos V, 18), followed by the rest of the passage.

All these things occur in this life, during the days whose darkness belongs to the Lord. Those who desire the day of the Lord are those who delight in this age, to whom it is pleasant, who serve pleasure and luxury in it and gain profits, who think that religion is a source of gain, to whom it is said: “Woe to you who are filled” (Luke VI, 25), not to those of whom it is said: “Blessed are those who mourn” (Matt. V, 5).

He recapitulates again from the same persecution, saying: “And there were flashes of lightning and thunderings, and a great earthquake occurred, such as had not occurred since human beings were made; and that great city was divided into three parts.” This great city is understood as the entire people under heaven, who will be divided into three parts when the Church has been separated: the Gentiles will be one part, heretics and false Catholics another, and the Catholic Church a third.

He continues and shows what the three parts are, saying: “The cities of the Gentiles fell, and Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of his wrath; and every island fled, and the mountains were not found.” The cities of the Gentiles are the nations; Babylon is the abomination of desolation; the mountains and islands are the Church. In the cities of the Gentiles he says that every defense and hope of the nations fell. For they do not have cities separate from Christians; rather, good and evil cities are depicted in human beings.

Thus Babylon fell or drank the wrath of God when it received power against Jerusalem, which is the Church. “The islands were not found”—that is, they were not overcome.

“And great hail, like a talent, came down from heaven upon human beings.” He calls hail the wrath of God. He says that all these plagues are figures of spiritual plagues. “And human beings blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, because its plague is exceedingly great.”

He recapitulates again, saying: “And one of the seven angels came and said to me: Come, I will show you the condemnation of the great prostitute who sits upon many waters, with whom the kings of the earth have committed fornication”—that is, all earthborn people.

“And he carried me in spirit into the wilderness, and I saw a woman sitting upon the beast.” In the beast, every wicked people is understood; in the woman, corruption is displayed. He says that the woman sits in the wilderness because she sits among the impious, who are dead in soul and abandoned by God. He said “in spirit” because such abandonment can be seen only in spirit.

He said that she was richly adorned because of the ornaments of luxury. For the beast upon which she sat, as has already been said, he calls the people; and these are the many waters, as he himself explains: “The waters which you saw, where the woman sits, are peoples and crowds, nations and languages.”

He says that corruption sits upon peoples in the wilderness. The prostitute, the beast, and the wilderness are one. The beast, as has already been said, is the body opposed to the Lamb. In that body, sometimes the devil is meant, sometimes the head appearing as though slain, which signifies heretics who seem to glory in Christ’s death. The beast is not to be understood as only the people of the proud; all of this is Babylon.

In the three spirits that proceeded from the mouth of the dragon like frogs, one means the devil; another, the false prophets or leaders of the heretics; and the third, the body of the devil—that is, all false, proud, or impious Christians, whose number is greatest within the Church.

Finally, those who are such, like frogs, wallow in every kind of filth and the squalor of luxury. People are also like frogs when they are not ashamed to wallow in the sins or crimes which others lay aside through repentance or baptism, saying to themselves: “For now I will fulfill my desires; afterward, just as these people were converted, so will I be converted to God.” Suddenly, when death arrives, confession perishes and condemnation remains.

When he says that people are to be gathered for the great day, he calls the whole period from the Lord’s Passion to the end of the world “the great day.” For those to whom it is pleasant, and who seek profits while serving pleasure and luxury in it, are changed into great misery, because the prophetic saying must be fulfilled in them: “Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord!” Through false and transitory sweetness they prepare eternal bitterness for themselves.

In this passage the great day may be understood as that desolation when Jerusalem was besieged by Titus and Vespasian. Apart from those who were led into captivity, fifteen hundred thousand are reported to have died [Note: [Col. 2441] The manuscripts read “eleven hundred thousand.”].

When he says, “He gathered them in the place called Hermagedon” [Note: [Col. 2441] The manuscripts read “Magedon.”], he wished all the enemies of the Church to be understood. For he continues and says: “They surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved holy city” (Rev. XX, 8)—that is, the Church.

As for the thunderings and the great earthquake, and the great city’s being divided into three parts: the great city is understood as the entire people, in which one part is pagans, another heretics, and the third Christians, among whom there are also hypocrites. When the good have been separated from this third part, then those who are false within the Church are joined to the other two parts and receive the judgment of God. This too is already being fulfilled in part at the present time. Babylon falls when the wicked receive power to persecute the good who belong to the Church.

As for the great hail descending from heaven like a talent, the wrath of God is understood in the hail. Even before the day of judgment comes, it is spiritually sent inwardly into the souls of the impious and proud.

The woman, the prostitute, whom he saw in spirit sitting upon the beast in the wilderness, is said to be in the wilderness because she sits among the impious—that is, among those who are dead in soul and abandoned by God. He says “in spirit” because such abandonment, which takes place inwardly in the soul, can be seen only spiritually.

The prostitute, the beast, and the wilderness are one; all of it is understood as Babylon. The beast, as has already been said, is the body of the impious opposed to the Lamb. In that body, sometimes the devil is meant, sometimes the head appearing as though slain, signifying the unbelief of the heretics, who seem to glory in Christ’s death while continually persecuting Christ’s Church.

And because not only heretics or pagans, but also bad Catholics—that is, the proud and impious—persecute those whom they see to be meek and humble within the Church, let us earnestly entreat God’s mercy, so that by his goodness he may correct them from such evil deeds to the good, and grant us happy perseverance in good works, he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

## HOMILY XIV
## [On chapter XVII]

Now, when the divine reading was being read, dearly beloved brothers, we heard blessed John say that he had seen a woman seated upon a scarlet beast—that is, a sinful, bloodstained woman. She was full of blasphemous names: he shows that there are many names in the beast, that is, among the ungodly people, as we have already said. She had seven heads and ten horns—that is, the kings and kingdom of this world, with whom the devil was seen in heaven.

And the woman—that is, the entire multitude of the proud—was surrounded with purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stone: that is, with every enticement of counterfeit truth. Finally, he explains what lies within this beauty, saying: “And she had in her hand a golden cup, full of abominations and the uncleannesses of her fornication.” The gold of uncleannesses is hypocrisy: outwardly they appear righteous to human beings, but inwardly they are full of every uncleanness (Matthew 23:28).

“And upon her forehead a name was written: Mystery, Babylon the great, mother of fornications and of the abominations of the earth.” No superstition marks the forehead except hypocrisy. The Spirit, however, reported what was written on the forehead.

> **Note:** [Column 2441] The printed editions read *non retulit* (“did not report”). The manuscripts lack *non*.

For who would openly assign such a title? He said that it was a mystery, and explained it by saying: “And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints and with the blood of the martyrs of Jesus.” There is one body that opposes the Church inwardly and outwardly: within the Church, false Christians; outside the Church, heretics or pagans. Although this body appears separated by place, during the persecution of the Church it nevertheless acts through the unity of one spirit.

“For it is impossible for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem, which kills the prophets” (Luke 13:33–34); that is, it cannot happen that good Christians suffer any persecution without bad Christians being involved. Thus the grandchildren are accused, by the agreement of their great-grandfathers, of having stoned Zachariah, although they themselves did not do it.

> **Note:** [Column 2442] The manuscripts read *pronepotes* (“great-grandchildren”) instead of *nepotes* (“grandchildren”).

“And the beast was, and is not, and is to come, and is to rise from the abyss, and it will go into the destruction of God’s wrath”—that is, it will arise from the people, so that one may say, “beast from beast, abyss from abyss.” For what is “beast from beast” and “abyss from abyss” except an evil people born from an evil people? This happens when evil children imitate their utterly wicked parents. The beast rises and survives, and goes into destruction, as did its fathers, from whom it arose. And they exist even now, because when some die, others succeed them. Thus there are never lacking—whether few or many, whether secretly or almost openly—those who continually lie in wait for the Church from the beginning.

By saying that he saw a woman seated upon a scarlet beast, he wished the sinful and bloodstained people to be understood. By saying that she was surrounded with purple and scarlet and adorned with gold and precious stone, he showed that the people of proud and ungodly human beings are filled with every enticement of counterfeit truth. By saying that she had in her hand a golden cup full of the abominations and uncleannesses of her fornication, he indicated hypocrites and false Christians, who outwardly appear righteous but inwardly are full of every uncleanness.

By saying that “Babylon, the mother of fornications,” was written upon her forehead, he indicated that no superstition marks the forehead except hypocrisy: that is, they pretend to be good while they are evil. By saying that the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints and the martyrs of Jesus, he wished the one body of the wicked to be understood, which always opposes the Church inwardly and outwardly, since there are false Christians within the Church and heretics or pagans outside it. And although they are sometimes separated in body, they are joined in one purpose in persecuting the Church.

By saying, “The beast was, and is not, and is to come, and is to rise from the abyss,” he indicated that an evil people is born from an evil people, so that one may say, “beast from beast, abyss from abyss.” What is “beast from beast” except an evil people born from an evil people? This happens when evil children imitate their utterly wicked parents. Thus, while some die and others succeed them, there are never lacking—whether few or many, secretly or openly—those who continually lie in wait for the Church from the beginning.

Since in this world we cannot be separated from their company bodily, let us pray for God’s mercy, so that we may be separated from them in conduct and not perish with them in eternal punishment. Rather, when they hear, “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire,” may we deserve to hear, “Come, you blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (Matthew 25:41, 34), through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

# HOMILY XV

## [On chapters XVII and XVIII]

In the reading that has been recited, dearly beloved brothers, the kings whom he said persecute Jerusalem are the evil people who persecute the Church of God. They are called kings, as it were, because they reign as though in a dream. Every evil person who persecutes the good does this as though in a dream, because the persecution of all evil people will not endure but will vanish like a dream, as Isaiah says: “They will be like one dreaming in sleep, the riches of all the nations” (Isaiah 29:7).

“These have one purpose”—that is, with one mind they persecute the good. He therefore says, “they have,” and not “they will have,” because the persecution of the wicked will exist not only when the day of judgment arrives, but does not cease even in the present.

“And they will give their power and authority to the devil.” He says this because ungodly people appear to give the devil power: instigated by him, they do evil. “These will fight with the Lamb”—that is, they oppose the Church until the end, until the saints receive the whole kingdom. “And the Lamb will conquer them”—that is, certainly, because God does not permit them to be tempted beyond what they can bear.

Therefore he says, “And the Lamb will conquer them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those who are with him are called, chosen, and faithful”: that is, the Church. He said “called and chosen” because not all who are called are chosen, as the Lord says: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20:16).

And the angel said to me: “The waters where the woman is seated are peoples, and crowds, and nations, and languages. And the ten horns that you saw hate the prostitute”—that is, that woman. The prostitute is a luxurious way of life, conducted through plunder and pleasures. He therefore said that they hate the prostitute because luxurious, proud, covetous, and arrogant people not only persecute the saints but also hate themselves.

They hate themselves in another sense as well, in whom what is written is fulfilled: “Whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10:6).

“And they will make her desolate and naked.” Through God’s anger and just judgment, by which they are abandoned by him, they make the world desolate while they are devoted to it and use it unjustly. “And they will eat her flesh.” This is because, according to the Apostle, they bite and devour one another (Galatians 5:15).

For this reason he added the explanation, saying: “For God put it into their hearts to carry out his judgment”—that is, he stirred up the scourges that he had justly and deservedly determined to inflict upon the world. “And they will give their kingdom to the beast until the words of God are fulfilled”—that is, evil people obey the devil until the Scriptures are fulfilled and the day of judgment arrives.

After this follows: “The woman whom you saw is the great city that has dominion over the kings of the earth”—that is, all the evil and ungodly. So also it was said concerning the Church: “Come, I will show you the woman of the Lamb”; and he showed me a city descending from heaven (Revelation 21:9–10).

After this I saw another angel descending from heaven, possessing great authority, and the earth was illuminated by his glory. And he cried out with a mighty voice, saying: “Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, and it has become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean and polluted bird.”

Can the fall of one city contain all unclean spirits or every unclean bird? Or, at the time when that city itself falls, will the whole world be abandoned to unclean spirits and birds, and will they dwell in the fall of one city? There is no city that can contain every unclean soul except the city of the devil, in which every uncleanness dwells among evil people throughout the whole world.

The kings whom he said persecute Jerusalem are evil people who persecute the Church of God, who lives and reigns, and so forth.

# HOMILY XVI

## [On chapters XVIII–XX]

Whenever you hear Babylon named, do not understand a city made of stones, for *Babylonia* is interpreted as “Confusion.” Understand instead that its name signifies proud, rapacious, luxurious, and ungodly people who persist in their evils. Conversely, whenever you hear the name Jerusalem, which is called “Vision of Peace,” understand holy people who belong to God.

Because Babylon represents the image of evil people, he therefore says of them in what follows: “For all the nations have drunk from the wine of the wrath of her fornication, and the kings of the earth who fornicated with her”—that is, with one another. For all the kings cannot fornicate with one prostitute; rather, while the luxurious—who are members of the prostitute—corrupt one another, they are said to fornicate with the prostitute, that is, with a luxurious way of life.

After this he says: “And all the merchants of the earth have become rich through the power of her luxury.” Here he calls them rich in sins, for excessive luxury makes people poor rather than rich.

“And I heard,” he says, “another voice from heaven saying: Come out of her, my people, so that you may not share in her sins, and so that you may not be harmed by her plagues.”

Here he shows that Babylon is divided into two parts. When, with God’s inspiration, evil people are converted to goodness, Babylon is divided; and the part that departs from it becomes Jerusalem. Every day some are transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem, and some are led astray from Jerusalem to Babylon, as evil people are converted to goodness and those who seemed good in hypocrisy are publicly revealed to be evil.

Finally, Scripture also says to the good through Isaiah: “Come out from their midst and do not touch what is unclean; come out from their midst and separate yourselves, you who bear the vessels of the Lord” (Isaiah 52:11).

The Apostle mentions this separation, saying: “The firm foundation of God stands, and the Lord knows those who are his; and let everyone who names the name of the Lord depart from iniquity” (2 Timothy 2:19).

“Do not share in her sins,” he says, “and do not be harmed by her plagues.” Since it is written, “Whoever is overtaken by death, if he is righteous, will be at rest” (Wisdom 4:7), how can the righteous become a participant in sin, when the city’s fall has carried him away along with the wicked?

Unless perhaps, when the good come out from the city of the devil—that is, from a luxurious and ungodly way of life—one of them should wish to remain and take pleasure in Babylon’s delights. If he does this, he will undoubtedly share in her plagues.

When he so often says, “Come out,” understand this not bodily but spiritually. One comes out from the midst of Babylon when one abandons an evil way of life. For Babylonians and inhabitants of Jerusalem may be together in one house, one Church, and one city; nevertheless, so long as the good do not consent to the evil and the evil are not converted to the good, Babylon is recognized in the evil and Jerusalem in the good.

They dwell together bodily, but are far divided in heart. The way of life of the wicked is always upon the earth, because they love the earth and establish all their hope and the whole direction of their mind upon earthly things. But, according to the Apostle, the mind of the good is always in heaven, because they seek the things above (Colossians 3:2).

“Come out of her, my people”—that is, out of Babylon—“so that you may not share in her sins and so that you may not be harmed by her plagues. For her sins have reached up to heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. Repay her as she herself repaid you, and repay double according to her works; in the cup in which she mixed, mix a double measure for her. As much as she glorified herself and indulged herself, so much give her torment and mourning in her cup.”

> **Note:** [Column 2444] Thus in the manuscript of Petrensis. The printed editions read *populo suo* (“for her people”) instead of *poculo suo* (“in her cup”).

God says all these things to the good Christians, that is, to the Church. For visible and invisible plagues go out from the Church into the world.

“For in her heart Babylon”—that is, the people of all the wicked and proud—“says: I sit as queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall see no mourning.” Therefore, in one day her plagues will come: death, mourning, and famine; and she will be burned with fire.

If she dies and is burned in one day, who will mourn the dead person in such a case? Or how great can one day’s famine be? By “day,” however, he meant the short period of the present life, during which they are afflicted both spiritually and bodily. For greater plagues come upon all the proud and those devoted to pleasures in the soul than in the body.

They are struck by a greater plague when, exalting themselves because of their iniquities, they are permitted by God’s just judgment to do evil in such a way that they are not deemed worthy to be chastised among the children of God. In them what is written is fulfilled: “They are not in the labors of human beings, nor are they scourged with human beings; therefore pride has held them fast” (Psalm 72:5–6).

“For the Lord God is strong, who will judge her.”

> **Note:** [Column 2444] The manuscript of Petrensis reads *judicavit eam* (“who judged her”).

“And the kings of the earth who fornicated with her will weep and mourn over her.” Which kings will mourn her overthrow, if the kings themselves will overthrow her? But what the city is, so also are the kings who will mourn her.

They do not mourn the evil of luxury because they sinned with her and are doing penance; rather, they mourn because they recognize that the prosperity of the world through which they served their pleasures has perished—or because the things that previously pleased them through luxury begin to cease among them.

The luxurious will consume one another, like smoke from the approaching Gehenna, standing far away because of fear of its punishment—not standing far away bodily, but in spirit, since each person fears for himself what he sees another suffering through accusations and the power of the proud.

They say: “Woe, woe, the great city Babylon, the strong city, because in one hour your condemnation has come!”

The Spirit speaks of the city’s name; but they mourn the world, which was cut off in a very brief time by punishment, and all its industry, weakened, has come to an end.

“And the merchants of horses, chariots, and pigs who were enriched by her will stand far away, weeping and saying: Woe, woe, the great city!”

> **Note:** [Column 2445] The manuscript of Petrensis reads *pardorum* (“leopards”) instead of *porcorum* (“pigs”).

Whenever the Spirit says that people were enriched by her, he signifies the riches of sins.

“She was clothed in fine linen, purple, and scarlet, and adorned with gold, precious stone, and pearls.” Is a city clothed in fine linen or purple, and not human beings? They therefore mourn themselves while they are stripped of the things mentioned above.

“And every helmsman, everyone who sails by ship, the sailors, and all who work upon the sea stood far away and cried out when they saw the smoke of the fire.” Could every helmsman and all the sailors who work upon the sea have been present to see the burning of one city? Rather, he says that all lovers of the world and workers of iniquity fear for themselves when they see the ruin of their hope.

After this he says: “And I saw the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies.” In the beast he signifies the devil; in the kings of the earth and in the army, his entire people. “Gathered to make war with the one seated upon the horse”—that is, with Christ and his Church.

> **Note:** [Column 2445] The manuscript of Petrensis adds *album* (“white”).

“And I saw another angel descending from heaven”: he calls the Lord Christ at his first coming. “Having the key of the abyss”—that is, authority over the people; for he wishes the abyss to be understood as the evil people. “And a great chain in his hand”: this means that God gave authority into his hand.

“And he seized the dragon, the ancient serpent, who is the devil and Satan, and bound him for a thousand years.”

> **Note:** [Column 2445] Thus reads the old manuscript of Petrensis. The printed editions, having removed sixteen verses, conflate the following homily with this one.

This refers, of course, to his first coming, as he himself says: “Who can enter the house of the strong man and plunder his goods unless he first binds the strong man?” (Matthew 12:29). For when he excludes the devil from the believing people, he sends him into the abyss, that is, into the evil people. He also showed this invisibly when, casting demons out of human beings into pigs that were destined to plunge into the abyss, he permitted them to enter them. This is fulfilled especially among heretics.

# HOMILY XVII

## [On chapters XVIII–XX]

Receive attentively, according to your custom, what your Charity has now heard from the reading of the Apocalypse. For blessed John the evangelist said that he saw heaven opened:

“And behold, a white horse, and its rider is called Faithful and True; his eyes are like a flame of fire, and upon his head were many diadems.” In him there is a multitude of crowned ones.

“He had a name written that no one knows except himself”: himself, certainly, and the whole Church that is in him.

“And he was clothed in a garment sprinkled with blood.” The garment of Christ is the Church, which he put on; it is variegated with the blood of sufferings.

“And his name is called the Word of God.” The armies that are in heaven followed him on white horses—that is, the Church, in bodies made white, imitates him, as it was said above: “These are the ones who follow the Lamb wherever he goes” (Revelation 14:4). They are clothed in clean white fine linen, which he defined as the righteous deeds of the saints.

“And from his mouth proceeds a sharp two-edged sword.” He is the one by whom the righteous are defended and the unrighteous punished.

“So that with it he may strike the nations, and he himself will rule them with an iron rod.” He treads the winepress of the indignation of the wrath of almighty God. He treads it even now, when he permits the wicked to do evil and leaves them to their pleasures. Later, outside the city—that is, outside the Church—he will tread it when he hands over to the fires of Gehenna those who have not done penance.

“Upon his garment and upon his thigh he has a name written: King of kings and Lord of lords.” This is the name that none of the proud recognizes, because the Church, by serving, reigns in Christ and rules over those who rule—that is, it conquers vices and sins.

The thigh signifies posterity, as in: “A ruler shall not fail from the thighs of Judah.” And Abraham, lest his posterity be mingled with foreigners, uses the thigh as a certain testimony between himself and his servant (Genesis 49:10; 24:2–4).

“And I saw,” he says, “an angel standing in the sun”—that is, a preacher in the Church.

> **Note:** [Column 2446] The manuscripts read *praedicationem* (“preaching”) instead of *praedicatorem* (“preacher”).

“And he cried out with a loud voice, saying to all the birds that fly in the midst of heaven.” We understand birds or beasts as good or evil according to the context, as in: “The beasts of the field will bless me” (Isaiah 43:20), and “the Lion from the tribe of Judah” (Revelation 5:5).

Here, therefore, by the birds flying in the midst of heaven he means the Churches, which he had said were gathered into one body when he spoke of the eagle flying in the midst of heaven.

“Come, gather for the great supper of God, so that you may eat the flesh of kings, the flesh of tribunes and the mighty, the flesh of horses and of those seated upon them, and the flesh of all free people and slaves, both small and great.”

For all nations, when they believe in Christ and are incorporated into the Church, are spiritually eaten by the Church.

After this he speaks of the devil: “And he shut him up and sealed him, so that he might not deceive the nations until the thousand years were completed.” These are understood as the thousand years that have unfolded since the coming of our Lord.

During these years the Lord forbade the devil to deceive the nations that were destined for life, whom he had previously deceived so that they would not be reconciled to God.

“After this he must be released for a short time”—that is, during the time of Antichrist, when the man of sin is revealed and receives the full power of persecution, such as he did not receive from the beginning.

He said “a thousand years,” using a part for the whole. Here he wished the remainder of the thousand years of the sixth day—during which the Lord was born and suffered—to be understood.

After this he says: “Woe, woe, that great city in which all those who had ships upon the sea were enriched, for in one hour she has been made desolate! Rejoice over her, heaven, and you saints, apostles, and prophets.”

Was Babylon alone, in the whole world, persecuting or having persecuted God’s servants, so that when it was destroyed all might be avenged? Babylon exists throughout the world in evil people, and throughout the world it persecutes the good.

“And an angel took up a stone like a great millstone and threw it into the sea, saying: Thus will that great city Babylon be thrown down with force.”

He calls Babylon a great millstone thrown down because the revolution of the ages crushes all lovers of the world like a millstone and casts them around in a circle. Concerning them it is written: “The wicked walk about in a circle” (Psalm 11:9). Their unhappy activity is always beginning anew, as it were.

“And it will no longer be found; and the voice of harpists, musicians, flute players, and pipe players will no longer be heard in her.” He says that the delight of the wicked passes away and will no longer be found.

He added the reason, saying: “For your merchants were the greatest of the earth”—that is, because during your life you received good things.

“For by your sorcery all the nations went astray, and in you was found the blood of prophets and saints, and of all who had been slain upon the earth by you.”

Did the same city kill the apostles, the prophets, and all the other martyrs? No. This is the city of all the proud, which Cain founded with the blood of his brother and called its name by the name of his son Enoch (Genesis 4:17), that is, “posterity.” For all evil people, in whom Babylon exists, succeed one another and persecute the Church of God until the end of the world.

In Cain’s city, therefore, all righteous blood is poured out—from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zachariah, that is, of the people and the priest—“between the temple and the altar” (Matthew 23:35), that is, between the people and the priests.

This was said because not only the people but also the priests conspired in Zachariah’s death. “Between the temple,” he says, “and the altar”: the priests are understood in the altar, and the people are signified in the temple.

> **Note:** [Column 2447] There was no other reason for naming the place.

This is the city that kills the prophets and stones those sent to it. This is the city built with blood, as it is written: “Woe to him who builds a city with blood and establishes a city upon iniquity” (Habakkuk 2:12).

Understand the Church in the white horse mentioned above; recognize Christ the Lord in its rider. By saying that he had a name written that no one knows except himself, he means himself and the whole Church that is in him.

In the garment sprinkled with blood, understand the martyrs who are in the Church. By saying that the army in heaven followed him on white horses, he means the Church in bodies made white.

In the two-edged sword, the power of Christ is understood, by which the righteous are defended and the unrighteous punished. In the iron rod, his justice is recognized: by it the humble are instructed, while the proud are broken like potter’s vessels.

By saying, “He himself treads the winepress of the wrath of almighty God,” he means that he treads it even now, when he permits the wicked to persecute the good and leaves them to their pleasures. Later he will repay them, when he sends those who have not done penance into Gehenna.

Understand the angel standing in the sun as preaching in the Church. The Church is compared to the sun because it is written concerning it: “Then the righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matthew 13:43).

By saying that he cried out to all the birds flying in the midst of heaven, understand those birds as the Church.

By saying, “Gather for the great supper, so that you may eat the flesh of kings and the flesh of tribunes,” we recognize that this truly takes place in the Church. For when all nations are incorporated into the Church, they are spiritually eaten; and those who had been devoured by the devil and were the devil’s body, when received by the Church, become members of Christ.

Concerning the devil, by saying, “He shut him up and sealed him, so that he might not deceive the nations until the thousand years were completed,” he means that these thousand years have unfolded since the Lord’s passion. During them the devil is not permitted to do as much as he wishes, because God does not permit his servants to be tempted beyond what they can endure (1 Corinthians 10:13).

When he says that the devil will later be released for a short time, the time of Antichrist is signified, during which the devil will receive greater power to rage.

When it says, “Woe, woe, the great city,” Babylon is understood. Nevertheless, it must be recognized that it is not only the city of Babylon that persecutes the saints, so that when it is destroyed all may be avenged. Babylon exists throughout the world in evil people, and throughout the world it persecutes the good.

When the angel threw a great stone like a millstone into the sea, saying, “Thus Babylon will be thrown down,” he called Babylon a millstone because the revolution of the ages crushes lovers of the world like a millstone and casts them around in a circle.

> **Note:** [Column 2447] The manuscripts read *mergetur* (“will be submerged”) instead of *mittetur* (“will be thrown”).

When he said, “By your sorcery all the nations went astray, and in you was found the blood of prophets and of all those whom you killed upon the earth,” he did not mean that the apostles, prophets, and other martyrs were killed in one city. Rather, this is the city of the proud, which persecutes the saints throughout the world.

It is the city that Cain founded with the blood of his brother and named after his son Enoch, that is, “posterity,” because all the evil people in whom Babylon exists, succeeding one another until the end of the world, persecute the Church of God.

May the Lord, in his mercy, deign to deliver us from their persecution—he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and so forth.

# HOMILY XVIII

> **Note:** [Column 2447] Also numbered XVII.

[Books XIX–XXII.] In the reading that has just been recited, dearest brothers, blessed John the Evangelist says:

“I heard a loud voice of a great multitude in heaven saying: ‘Alleluia! Salvation, and glory, and power belong to our God, for his judgments are true and just; for he has judged that great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her fornication, and he has avenged the blood of his servants at her hand.’” And again they said, “Alleluia.” This is the voice of the Church when the separation has taken place and all the wicked, who are to be consumed by eternal fire, have gone out from her. “And their smoke goes up for ever and ever.”

Listen, brothers, and be afraid, and know for certain that Babylon and the prostitute, whose smoke goes up for ever and ever, mean nothing other than greedy, adulterous, and proud people. Therefore, if you wish to escape these evils, do not commit such grave sins. “And their smoke,” he says, “goes up.” Does the smoke of a visible city that has been burned go up for ever and ever, and not that of people who persist in pride? It goes up—not “it will go up”—for even in the present age it is continually going toward destruction.

Babylon, however, is burned in part, just as Jerusalem, in those holy people who depart from this world, passes into paradise, as the Lord makes clear in the account of the poor man and the rich man (Luke 16:19–22).

“And I heard what seemed to be the voice of a great multitude, and what seemed to be the voice of many waters, and what seemed to be the voice of mighty thunderclaps, saying: ‘Alleluia! For the Lord our God the Almighty has begun to reign. Let us rejoice and exult and glorify his name, for the marriage of the Lamb has come, and his woman has prepared herself.’” The woman of the Lamb is the Church. “And it was granted her to clothe herself in shining, clean linen.” For the linen is the righteous deeds of the saints; that is, it was granted her to be clothed in her deeds, as it is written: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Psalm 131:9).

“These,” he says, “all lived and reigned with Christ for a thousand years”—that is, in the present age. And rightly he said, “All”: both the survivors and the souls of the righteous [Note: [Col. 2448] The Petrensis manuscript reads “of the saints.”]—that is, both those who still live in this world and those who have already departed from this life reign with Christ.

He certainly said “they reigned,” just as: “They divided my garments among themselves” (Psalm 21:19). For he was going to say, “They will reign.” To show, however, that these thousand years belong to this life, he says: “This is the first resurrection.” For this is the resurrection by which we rise through Baptism, as the Apostle says: “If you have risen with Christ, seek the things that are above” (Colossians 3:2); and again: “As living from the dead” (Romans 6:13).

For sin is death, as the Apostle said: “When you were dead in your trespasses and sins” (Ephesians 2:1). And just as the first death occurs in this life through sin, so also the first resurrection occurs in this life through the forgiveness of sins.

“Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection”—that is, the one who has preserved what he received when he was reborn in Baptism. “Over such the second death has no power”—that is, he will not experience eternal torments.

“But they will be priests of God and of Christ, and they will reign with him for a thousand years.” When he wrote these things, the Spirit referred to the Church reigning for a thousand years in this age, until the end of the world. It is clear that there should be no doubt about the perpetual kingdom, since even in the present age the saints reign. Those who, with God’s help, govern both themselves and others well even amid the very pressures of the world are rightly said to reign.

“And when the thousand years are completed, Satan will be released from his prison.” He said “completed,” meaning a part by the whole. For he will be released in such a way that three years and six months will remain for the final contest, in the time of Antichrist.

“And he will go out to deceive the nations that are at the four corners of the earth.” Here again he speaks of the whole by a part, for not all can be deceived. Only the proud and ungodly are deceived, because true and humble Christians are not deceived. For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matthew 20:16).

“And the devil and his people went up upon the height of the earth”—that is, into the exaltation of pride. “And they surrounded the camp of the saints and the beloved city”—that is, the Church. This is what he said above: that they had been gathered at Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).

For they could not be gathered from the four corners of the earth into one city; rather, in those four corners each nation will be gathered for the siege of the holy city—that is, for the persecution of the Church.

“And fire came down from heaven from God”—that is, from the Church—“and consumed them.” The fire is understood in this passage in two ways. Either, through the fire of the Holy Spirit, they believe in Christ and are spiritually consumed by the Church—that is, incorporated into the Church—or they are consumed by the fire of their sins and perish.

“And the devil who deceived them was thrown into the lake of fire and sulfur, where the beast and the false prophets also are.” The false prophets are understood either as heretics or as counterfeit Christians. From the time the Lord suffered, the beast and the false prophets die and are cast into the fire, until the thousand years from the Lord’s coming are completed.

“And they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever.”

“And I saw the dead, great and small, standing before the throne; and the books were opened, and another book was opened, which is the book of each person’s life.” By the opened books he means God’s Testaments, for the Church will be judged according to both Testaments. By the book of each person’s life he means the remembrance of our deeds—not that the one who knows hidden things has a commemorative book.

“And the dead were judged from what was written in the books, according to their works”—that is, they were judged from the Testaments according to whether they had or had not carried out God’s commandments.

“And the sea gave up the dead who were in it”: those whom the day of judgment will find alive are themselves the dead of the sea, because this age is the sea.

“Death and Hades gave up their dead”—that is, those who will be found in the tombs on the day of judgment.

“Death and Hades were thrown into the lake”: by death and Hades he means the devil and his people.

“And if anyone was not found written in the book of life”—the one who, having been abandoned to his pleasures, did not deserve to be judged by God while he lived, through the temporary testing in this age—“was thrown into the lake of fire.”

“And I saw a new heaven and a new earth.” For the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and the sea is no more.

“And I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God, prepared like a bride and adorned for her husband.”

“And I heard a loud voice from heaven saying: ‘Behold, the tabernacle of God is with human beings, and he will dwell with them; and they will be his people, and God himself will be with them as their God. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes; and death will be no more, and mourning will be no more.’”

He said all this about the glory of the Church, which it will possess after the resurrection.

“And he said: ‘Write, for these words are faithful and true.’ And he said to me: ‘I am α and ω, the beginning and the end. I will give to the thirsty from the spring of the water of life freely’”—that is, to the one who desires the forgiveness of sins through the font of Baptism.

“The one who conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son.”

“But for the cowardly and unbelieving, the detestable, murderers, sorcerers, idolaters, and all liars, their portion will be in the lake burning with fire and sulfur, which is the second death.”

What was said above—“He judged that great prostitute who corrupted the earth with her fornication, and he avenged the blood of his servants at her hand”—is the voice of the Church when all the wicked have gone out from her on the day of judgment, to be consumed by eternal fire.

“And their smoke goes up for ever and ever.” For it is not the smoke of a visible city that goes up for ever and ever, but that of people who persist in pride.

When he says, “For the marriage of the Lamb has come,” this is understood of Christ and the Church. When he says that she was covered in linen, the righteous works of the saints are understood in the linen, with which the righteous are clothed, according to what was said: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness.”

When he says that they reigned for a thousand years, the present time is understood, in which the saints are said to reign righteously because they govern themselves with God’s help in such a way that they cannot be conquered by sins.

And to demonstrate this clearly, he continues: “This is the first resurrection.” The first resurrection, by which souls rise from the death of sin to the life of righteousness, is now taking place throughout the whole of the present age; but the second, by which they return from the dust of the earth to bodily life, is awaited in the future [Note: [Col. 2449] The Belgian manuscript does not contain these words: “The first resurrection, by which souls rise from the death of sin to the life of righteousness, is now taking place throughout the whole of the present age; but the second, by which they return from the dust of the earth to bodily life, is awaited in the future.”].

For this is the resurrection by which we rise through Baptism. Just as the first death is in this life through sin, so also the first resurrection is through the forgiveness of sins.

“Blessed and holy is the one who has a share in the first resurrection”—that is, the one who has preserved what he received when reborn in Baptism.

When he says that the Church will reign for a thousand years, this is understood as occurring in the present age until the end of the world. Hence it is clear that there should be no doubt about the perpetual kingdom, since even in the present age the saints reign. For those who, with God’s help, govern both themselves and others well even amid the very pressures of the world are rightly said to reign.

When he says of the devil that he deceives the nations at the four corners of the earth, this is understood as the whole by a part. For only the wicked are deceived, according to the saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

When he says that the devil and his angels surrounded the camp of the saints and the city of the beloved, they could not have gathered from the four corners of the earth into one city. Rather, in those four corners each nation is gathered for the persecution of the Church.

When he says, “Fire fell from heaven and consumed them,” this is understood in two ways. Either they are spiritually consumed by the fire of the Holy Spirit when they are incorporated into the Church, or, if they refuse to turn to God, they are consumed by the fire of their sins and perish.

When he says that the books were opened, he wished the Testaments of God to be understood. For the Church will be judged according to both Testaments. By the book of each person’s life he means the remembrance of our deeds, because on the day of judgment nothing will remain hidden, and no one will be able to conceal his sins or crimes.

When he says that the sea gave up its dead, he means those whom the coming of Christ will find alive in this world. They are the dead of the sea because this age is the sea.

When he says, “Death and Hades gave up their dead,” those are understood who will be found in the tombs on the day of judgment.

“And death and Hades were thrown into the lake of fire.” In this passage he wished death and Hades to be understood as the devil and his people, who, having been abandoned to their pleasures, did not deserve to be judged through the temporary testing.

After explaining these matters, he adds the glory of the Church and says: “I will give the thirsty from the spring of the water of life freely”—that is, to the one who desires the forgiveness of sins through the font of Baptism.

“The one who conquers will possess these things, and I will be his God, and he will be my son”—may he himself grant this, who, with God the Father, and so forth.

HOMILY XIX [Note: [Col. 2450] Elsewhere 18.]

[Books XXI and XXII.] As we have just heard, dearest brothers, the angel of the Lord spoke to blessed John, saying: “Come, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb.”

“And he carried me away in the Spirit upon a great and high mountain.” By the mountain he means Christ.

“And he showed me the holy city Jerusalem, descending from heaven from God.” This is the Church, the city established on a mountain, the bride of the Lamb. For that city was then established on a mountain when, like a sheep, it was recalled to its own fold upon the shepherd’s shoulders (Luke 15:5).

If the Church is one thing and the city descending from heaven another, there will be two brides, which absolutely cannot be. For he also called this city the bride of the Lamb. Hence it is clear that it is the Church, which he describes in this way, saying:

“Having the glory of God. Its radiance was like a most precious stone.” The most precious stone is Christ.

“Having a great and high wall, having twelve gates, and twelve angels above the gates.” He shows that the twelve gates and twelve angels are the Apostles and Prophets [Note: [Col. 2450] Manuscripts read “Patriarchs”], since, as it is written, “we have been built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets” (Ephesians 2:20); and likewise the Lord said to Peter, “Upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16:18).

“Three gates on the east, three gates on the north, three gates on the south, and three gates on the west.” Because this city that is described is the Church spread throughout the whole world, three gates are said to exist on each of the city’s four sides, because throughout all four regions of the world the mystery of the Trinity is preached in the Church.

“And the wall of the city had twelve foundations, and on them twelve names of the Apostles of the Lamb.” What the gates are, so are the foundations; what the city is, so are the wall and its furnishings. [Col. 2451]

“And the one who spoke with me had a golden measuring reed.” In the golden reed he shows the people of the Church, established in fragile flesh but founded upon golden faith, as the Apostle says: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (2 Corinthians 4:7).

“And the furnishings of the wall and the city were pure gold, like pure glass.” For the Church is golden because its faith shines like gold, as represented by the seven lampstands, the golden altar, and the golden bowls; all this prefigured the Church.

He referred glass to the purity of faith, because what is seen outside is also within: nothing is feigned, but everything is transparent in the saints of the Church.

“The foundations of the wall of the city were adorned with every kind of precious stone. The first foundation was jasper, the second sapphire, the third chalcedony, the fourth emerald, the fifth sardonyx, the sixth sardius, the seventh chrysolite, the eighth beryl, the ninth topaz, the tenth chrysoprase, the eleventh hyacinth, and the twelfth amethyst.”

He wished to name the diversity of gems in the foundations in order to demonstrate the gifts of the diverse graces given to the Apostles, as it is said of the Holy Spirit: “Distributing to each one as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11).

“And twelve pearls, individually; and each gate was made of one pearl.” In these pearls, as has been said, he designated the Apostles, who are called gates because through their teaching they open the door of eternal life.

“And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass.” And I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb. This is because the Church is in God, and God is in the Church.

“The city has no need of sun or moon to shine upon it,” because the Church is not governed by light or by the elements of the world, but is led through the darkness of the world by Christ, the eternal sun.

“For the glory of God illuminated it, and its lamp is the Lamb,” as he himself says: “I am the light of the world” (John 8:12); and again: “I am the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1:9).

“The nations will walk by its light, until the end. And the kings of the earth will bring glory.” By the kings of the earth he means the children of God.

“And its gates will not be shut by day.” For there is no night there—throughout eternity.

“And they will bring the glory and honor of the nations,” namely, of those who believe in Christ.

“And nothing unclean will enter it, nor anyone who practices abomination and falsehood, except those written in the Lamb’s book of life.”

“And he showed me a river of water like crystal, flowing from the throne of God and of the Lamb, through the middle of its street.” He showed the font of Baptism in the midst of the Church, coming from God and Christ.

For what beauty could the city have if a river descended through the middle of its street as an obstacle to its inhabitants?

“And on both sides of the river was the tree of life, producing twelve fruits, yielding its fruit in each month.” He said this about the Lord’s cross. There is no tree that bears fruit at all times except the cross borne by the faithful, who are watered by the water of the ecclesiastical river and yield perpetual fruit at every time.

“And the throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it”—certainly from now and throughout eternity.

“And his servants will serve him, and they will see his face,” as he says: “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father” (John 14:9); and: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God” (Matthew 5:8).

“And his name will be on their foreheads. And night will be no more, and they will need no light from a lamp or from the sun, because the Lord God will illuminate them, and they will reign for ever and ever.” All these things began with the Lord’s Passion.

“And the angel said to me: ‘Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the one who is unjust continue to do injustice, and let the filthy continue to be filthy.’” These are the people for whom he had said: “Seal up the things that the seven thunders have spoken” (Revelation 10:4).

“And let the righteous continue to practice righteousness, and let the holy continue to be sanctified.” These are the people for whom he said: “Do not seal the words of the prophecy of this book.”

Thus the divine Scriptures are sealed to all the proud and to those who love the world more than God; but they are open to the humble and to those who fear God.

“Behold, I am coming soon, and my reward is with me, to repay each person according to his works. I am α and ω, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.

“Blessed are those who keep these commandments, so that they may have authority over the tree of life and may enter the city through the gates.” For those who do not keep the commandments do not enter through the gates, but by another way. In these matters the book is sealed, concerning whom it follows and says:

“Outside are dogs, sorcerers, fornicators, murderers, idolaters, and everyone who loves and practices falsehood.

“I, Jesus, sent my angel to testify these things to you in the churches. I am the root and offspring of David, the bright morning star.

“The Spirit and the bride say, ‘Come!’”—that is, the bridegroom and the bride, Christ and the Church.

“Let the one who thirsts come; let the one who wishes take the water of life freely”—that is, Baptism.

“I testify to everyone who hears the words of the prophecy of this book: If anyone adds to them, God will add to him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone removes from the words of this prophecy, God will remove his share from the tree of life and from the holy city, which are written in this book.”

He says this who testifies to these things because of falsifiers of the holy Scriptures, not because of those who simply say what they think.

“Indeed, I am coming soon.”

The high mountain on which holy John said he had ascended is understood as the Spirit [Note: [Col. 2452] The Petrensis manuscript reads “Christ.”]. In the city of Jerusalem that he said he saw there, the Church is signified. The Lord himself shows this in the Gospel when he says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew 5:14).

When he says that it had a light like a most precious stone, the glory of Christ is demonstrated in that stone.

In the twelve gates and the twelve angels, the Apostles and Patriarchs are understood, according to the statement: “Built upon the foundation of the Apostles and Prophets.” And because the city that is described is the Church spread throughout the whole world, three gates are said to exist on each of its four sides because of the mystery of the Trinity.

In the golden reed he shows the people of the Church, established in fragile flesh but founded upon golden faith, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.”

When he calls the city golden, and the altar golden, and the bowls golden, this is the Church because of right faith. In the glass, however, the purity of that faith is signified.

When he wished to name the various gems in the foundations, he demonstrated the gifts of the various graces given to the Apostles.

In those pearls he designated the Apostles, who are called gates because through their teaching they open the door of eternal life.

When he says that he saw no temple in it because the Lord Almighty is its temple, and the Lamb, this is because God is in the Church, and the Church is in God.

When he says that the city has no need of sun or moon, this is because the Church is not spiritually illuminated by the visible sun, but by the eternal light of Christ amid the darkness of this world, as he himself says: “I am the light of the world.”

He wished the kings of the earth to be understood as the children of God—that is, Christians.

In the river of water like crystal, he showed the font of Baptism in the midst of the Church, coming from God and Christ.

When he said that the tree beside the river gives fruit twelve times, in each month, the cross is understood. Throughout the whole world it offers fruit to God not only every month but every day, in those who are baptized.

When he says, “The Lord God will illuminate them, and they will reign for ever and ever,” all these things began with the Lord’s Passion.

When earlier in the book he said, “The signs that the seven thunders spoke,” he said this because of those about whom he says: “Let the filthy continue to be filthy, and let the one who is unjust continue to do injustice.”

But when he says, “Do not seal the words of the prophecy,” he wished this to be understood of the saints and the righteous.
