Thus the divine Scriptures are sealed to all the proud and to those who love the world more than God, but they are open to the humble and to those who fear God.

And because the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist concludes in this way, saying, “Behold, I am coming soon,” let us pray that, according to his promise, the Lord Jesus Christ may deign to come to us, free us by his mercy from the prison of this world, and in his goodness lead us to his blessedness: he who lives and reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit for ever and ever. Amen.

HOMILY XIX [Note: [Col. 2450] Elsewhere 18.]

### Book One

At the beginning, the whole work is divided so that the student of Scripture may be instructed both in investigating its meaning and in explaining it. After observing the distinction between the things about which instruction is to be given and the signs by which they are conveyed, the first book undertakes a discussion of things. Some things, moreover, are those in which one may enjoy participation, while others may only be used; and one must cleave in enjoyment to God alone. We are advanced toward him by the incarnation of the Word itself, by the things performed by him in time, and by the keys delivered to the Church. Among the things that are used, some are rightly objects of love, but only as referred to God. When these matters have been explained, it is taught that the fullness and end of all sacred Scripture is twofold love: love of God for his own sake and love of one’s neighbor for God’s sake. 19–20

### Book Two

Augustine now begins his discussion of the signs and words of sacred Scripture, and he shows that its genuine meaning is often not perceived because those signs are either unknown or ambiguous. Therefore, after first setting out the canon of the divine books, he proceeds to explain knowledge of which languages, and which disciplines and sciences, contribute most to removing ignorance of those signs. When the opportunity arises, he also discusses briefly but profoundly the rejection of superstitious arts and doctrines. At the beginning and end of the book he likewise explains what disposition of mind is required of one who is about to devote himself to the study of Scripture. 35–36

### Book Three

After dealing in the preceding book with removing ignorance of signs, the holy Doctor now turns to consideration of the ambiguity that occurs both in proper and in figurative signs. In proper signs, ambiguity arises from the punctuation and pronunciation of words and from their equivocal meaning. He shows that this kind of ambiguity can be resolved through the context of the discourse, comparison of interpreters, or examination of the language from which Scripture was translated. In translated signs, ambiguity occurs when an expression in Scripture is not used according to the literal sense of the words. On this subject he argues at greater length and gives rules by which one may determine whether an expression is figurative and, if it is figurative, how it ought to be explained. Finally, he examines one by one the seven rules of Tichonius. 65–66

### Book Four

Thus far the subject has been investigating the meaning of Scripture; now at last the subject is explaining it. Augustine does not wish the rules of the rhetorical art to belong to the purpose of this book; nevertheless, he pursues with the greatest care the duties of the Christian orator. He proposes the authors of sacred literature and the teachers of the Church as models to be imitated, since they are far superior in wisdom of speech, indeed even in eloquence, and he supplies examples of expression in various styles of speaking from their writings. Finally, he exhorts the ecclesiastical speaker above all to devote himself to prayer and to exhibit in his life and conduct precisely what he teaches others in words. 89–90

## Notice concerning the book *On True Religion*. 121–122

**The One Book of Saint Aurelius Augustine, Bishop of Hippo, *On True Religion*,** in which, after stating that true religion is not found among the pagans or in any sect except the Catholic Church, the history of the divine dispensation toward human salvation—which is indeed the head and foundation of the Christian religion—is explained in such a way that the errors of the Manichaeans, especially concerning the two natures and the origin and nature of evil, are refuted. The twofold way by which God provides for human beings is discussed: he calls believers to salvation through authority, and those who understand through reason. For the human being supported by reason is raised from lower things to God; indeed, he is admonished to pursue God by the very vices through which he is tested, and Augustine undertakes an extended discussion of their threefold kind. Finally, he concludes that the one true God—that is, the Trinity, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—must be worshiped through true religion. Ibid.

# PREFATORY NOTICE TO THE BOOKS ON THE HARMONY OF THE EVANGELISTS

Ibid.

**THE FOUR BOOKS OF SAINT AURELIUS AUGUSTINE, BISHOP OF HIPPO, ON THE HARMONY OF THE EVANGELISTS.** 1041–1042

# BOOK ONE

After briefly discussing the authority, number, order, and varied manner of writing of the Evangelists, Augustine, before treating their harmony, responds in this book to those who are troubled by the question why Christ himself wrote nothing, or who invent books on magic written by him; and also to those who assert against the evangelical teaching that Christ’s disciples not only attributed more to their master than was really the case by calling him God, but also, by forbidding the worship of other gods, taught something other than what they had learned from him. Against these people he vindicates the teaching of the Apostles from the utterances of the prophets, showing that the one God of Israel alone is to be worshiped. Although the Romans had previously refused to accept him because he forbade them to worship other gods with him, he ultimately subjected the Roman empire to his name and, among all peoples, as he had promised through his prophets would happen, shattered the idols through the preaching of the Gospel. Ibid.

**CHAPTER ONE.** The authority of the Gospels. Ibid.

**IX.** Some invent books on magic written by Christ. 1049

## BOOK THREE

The agreement of the Evangelists from the account of the supper to the end of the Gospel is demonstrated by bringing together and arranging in order the context of each account. 1157–1158

**CHAPTER I.** Concerning the Lord’s supper and the traitor who was explicitly identified: how the four agree with one another. Ibid.

**II.** Concerning Peter’s foretold denial: how it is shown that they do not conflict with one another. Ibid.

**XIV.** Concerning the two robbers crucified with him: how they all agree. 1189

**XV.** Concerning those who insulted the Lord: how Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree with one another. 1190

**XVI.** Concerning the insult of the robbers: how Matthew and Mark do not conflict with Luke, who said that one of them insulted him and the other believed. Ibid.

**XVII.** Concerning the drink of vinegar: how they all agree with one another. 1191

**XVIII.** Concerning the words uttered by the Lord immediately before his death: how Matthew and Mark do not conflict with Luke, nor those three with John. 1192

**XIX.** Concerning the tearing of the veil: how Matthew and Mark do not disagree with Luke regarding the order in which it happened. Ibid.

**XX.** Concerning the centurion’s amazement and that of those who were with him: how Matthew, Mark, and Luke agree with one another. 1193

**XXI.** Concerning the women who were standing there: how Matthew, Mark, and Luke, who said that they stood at a distance, do not conflict with John, who named one of them as standing near the cross. 1194

**XXII.** Concerning Joseph, who asked Pilate for the Lord’s body: how they all agree, and how John does not disagree with himself. 1195

**XXIII.** Concerning his burial: how the three do not disagree with John. Ibid.

**XXIV.** Concerning what happened around the time of the Lord’s resurrection: how they all do not disagree with one another. 1196

**XXV.** Concerning the fact that he afterward manifested himself to the disciples: how all the Evangelists do not conflict with one another, with the testimonies of the apostle Paul and of the Acts of the Apostles brought together. 1203

## BOOK FOUR

Concerning what is peculiar to Mark, Luke, and John. 1215–1216

**CHAPTER I.** In Mark’s Gospel, except for what he said together with Matthew, how no contradiction is demonstrated from the beginning up to the passage where he says, “And they enter Capernaum, and immediately on the sabbaths he was teaching them,” which he relates together with Luke. 1216–1217

**II.** Concerning the man from whom an unclean spirit was expelled while convulsing him: how Luke, who related this together with Mark, does not conflict with him. 1217

**III.** Concerning Peter’s name: how it is repeatedly emphasized that it does not conflict with John, who said when he received this name. Ibid.

**IV.** That he said, “The more he commanded them not to speak, the more they proclaimed it”: how this does not conflict with his foreknowledge, which is commended in the Gospel. 1218

**V.** Concerning the man whom John mentioned as casting out demons in his name although he was not associated with the disciples, and to whom he said, “Do not stop them; for whoever is not against you is for you”: how this does not conflict with the statement in which he says, “Whoever is not with me is against me.” 1219

**VI.** On the occasion of the man who was casting out demons in Christ’s name, although he did not follow with the disciples, Mark related that the Lord said more than Luke did. How it is shown that this belongs to the same matter: namely, that he forbade them to stop the man who was performing a mighty work in his name. 1220

**VII.** From this point up to the Lord’s supper, from which the consideration of all the material in all the Evangelists began, no question concerning Mark was treated. 1221

**VIII.** Concerning Luke’s Gospel: how its beginning agrees with the beginning of the book of Acts. Ibid.

**IX.** How it is shown that what Luke recalled concerning the catch of fish does not pertain to what John appears to have related in a similar way after the Lord’s resurrection; and from that point up to the Lord’s supper, from which all the material in all the Evangelists was considered through to the end, no question from Luke’s Gospel was treated either. 1222

**X.** Concerning John the Evangelist: how he differs from the other three. 1223
